div.p: Here is a genealogy ending with Abram, the friend of God.
It leads us toward Christ, the promised Seed, who would descend from Abram.
Only names and ages are recorded. The Holy Spirit seems to hurry through these generations to reach Abram's story.
How little we know about people who lived before us, even in the very places where we now live!
We know just as little about many people living far away from us today.
We have enough to do in attending faithfully to the responsibilities God has given us.
As the earth became more populated, human lifespans began to shorten. This was the wise ordering of God's providence.

div.title: Terah's family leaves Ur and settles in Haran (verses 27–32)
div.p: Here begins the story of Abram, whose name is celebrated in both Testaments.
Even the descendants of Eber had become worshippers of false gods.
Those who, through grace, are heirs of the promised land should remember the land from which they came: their corrupt and sinful natural condition.
Abram had two brothers.
One was Nahor, from whose family both Isaac and Jacob would later take wives.
The other was Haran, Lot's father, who died before his own father.
Children cannot assume that they will outlive their parents.
Haran died in Ur, before the family had the blessing of leaving that idolatrous country.
We should therefore hurry to leave our natural condition of sin before death overtakes us in it.
Abram left Ur of the Chaldeans with his father Terah, his nephew Lot, and the rest of his family, in obedience to God's call.
This chapter leaves them partway between Ur and Canaan.
They settled there until Terah died.
Many people come as far as Haran but never reach Canaan.
They are not far from God's kingdom, yet they never enter it.

row.cell: God calls Abram and blesses him with a promise of Christ.
He travels through Canaan and worships God there.
Famine drives Abram into Egypt, where he calls Sarai his sister.

div.title: God calls Abram and promises his blessing (verses 1–3)
div.p: God chose Abram out of the people around him, who worshipped idols.
His purpose was to preserve a people for himself, among whom the worship of the true God would continue until Christ came.
From this point on, Abram and his descendants become almost the only subject of the Bible's history.
God tested whether Abram loved him above everyone and everything else, and whether he would willingly leave all in order to follow him.
Abram's relatives and his father's household were a constant temptation. He could not stay among them without risking the spread of their idolatry into his own life.
Those who leave their sins and turn to God gain more than words can describe.
God's command to Abram resembles the gospel call. Natural affection must give way to divine grace when the two conflict.
We must forsake sin and everything that leads us into it, especially corrupting company.
God accompanied this command with great and precious promises. His commands come with promises for those who obey.
First, “I will make you a great nation.” God took Abram away from one people and promised to make him the head of another.
Second, “I will bless you.” Those who believe and obey are certain to inherit God's blessing.
Third, “I will make your name great.” God will certainly honor those who faithfully obey him.
Fourth, “You will be a blessing.” Godly people bring good to the nations and communities in which they live.
Fifth, “I will bless those who bless you, and curse the one who curses you.” God will not allow anyone who serves his people to lose by doing so.
Sixth, “In you all the families of the earth will be blessed.”
Jesus Christ is the world's greatest blessing—the greatest blessing it has ever received.
Every true blessing this world now enjoys or will ever enjoy comes through Abram and his descendants.
Through them we have received the Bible, the Savior, and the gospel.
They are the rootstock into which the Christian church has been grafted.

div.title: Abram leaves Haran (verses 4–5)
div.p: Abram believed that the blessing of the Almighty would more than compensate for everything he left behind.
God would supply all his needs and more than satisfy his deepest desires. Abram knew that disobedience could lead only to misery.
Believers who are justified by faith in Christ have peace with God.
They continue toward Canaan, neither discouraged by difficulties on the road nor drawn away by the pleasures they meet along it.
Those who begin the journey to heaven must persevere to the end.
Whatever we undertake in obedience to God's command and humble dependence on his providence will ultimately succeed and bring comfort.
Canaan was more than an outward possession, like other countries.
It was a picture of heaven. That is why the patriarchs valued it so deeply.

div.title: Abram worships God as he travels through Canaan (verses 6–9)
div.p: Abram found the land inhabited by Canaanites, who were troublesome neighbors.
He continued traveling from place to place.
Sometimes faithful people must live unsettled lives, moving repeatedly from one place to another.
Believers should remember that they are strangers and pilgrims in this world (Hebrews 11:8, 13–14).
Yet notice how much comfort Abram found in God.
He had little reason to enjoy fellowship with the Canaanites. But he found abundant delight in communion with the God who had brought him there and had not abandoned him.
We maintain fellowship with God through his word and prayer.
God makes himself and his favor known to his people gradually.
Earlier, he had promised to show Abram the land. Now he promised to give it to him.
As grace grows, comfort grows with it.
Abram seems to have understood the promise as a pledge of a better land, of which Canaan was a picture. He looked for a heavenly country (Hebrews 11:16).
As soon as Abram reached Canaan, though he was a stranger and traveler there, he established and maintained worship in his household.
He was concerned not only with the outward ceremonies of religion, such as offering sacrifices, but with sincerely seeking God and calling upon his name.
That is the spiritual sacrifice God delights to receive.
Abram also proclaimed the name of the Lord.
He taught his household and his neighbors to know the true God and his holy ways.
Family worship is not a recent invention. It is an ancient practice of God's people.
Abram was wealthy and responsible for a large household. He was unsettled and surrounded by enemies.
Yet wherever he pitched his tent, he built an altar.
Wherever we go, let us never leave our faith behind.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): Hebrews 13:14.
Verified editorial cross-reference: Heb.11.13; Heb.11.14.

div.title: Abram's failure in Egypt (verses 10–20)
div.p: No place on earth is free from trials, and no human character is free from flaws.
Even Canaan, the glory of all lands, suffered famine.
And even Abram, the father of the faithful, showed unbelief and all the troubles it brings.
Perfect happiness and perfect purity belong only to heaven.
When Abram had to leave Canaan for a time, he went to Egypt rather than returning to the country he had left. He intended to remain only as long as necessary.
But in Egypt he disguised his relationship with Sarai.
He used misleading words and taught his wife and servants to do the same.
He concealed the truth so thoroughly that he effectively denied it. In doing so, he exposed both Sarai and the Egyptians to sin.
Abram was especially known for his faith. Yet he fell into this failure because he did not trust God's providence—even though God had already appeared to him twice.
If strong faith can be shaken like this, what will become of weak faith?
How often God must rescue us from danger and distress we bring upon ourselves through our own sin and foolishness!
Without his deliverance, we would be ruined. He does not deal with us as we deserve.
God's corrections are blessings when they stop us on a sinful path and bring us back to duty.
That includes the duty to return whatever we have wrongfully taken or kept.
Pharaoh was right to rebuke Abram: “What have you done?”
What an unworthy action for someone wise and godly!
When professing Christians behave unfairly, deceive others, or speak in a way that borders on lying, they must expect to be corrected.
They should even thank those who have the courage to tell them the truth.
Pharaoh treated Abram kindly when he sent him away.
Far from planning to kill Abram, as Abram had feared, Pharaoh took special care to protect him.
We often torment ourselves with fears that have no foundation. We are afraid when there is nothing to fear.
Pharaoh also ordered his servants not to harm Abram.
Those in authority must do more than avoid harming others themselves. They must restrain their servants and everyone under their care from doing harm too.

row.cell: Abram returns from Egypt with great wealth.
Conflict between Abram's and Lot's herdsmen; Abram gives Lot the choice of land.
Lot chooses the region of Sodom.
God renews his promise to Abram, who moves to Hebron.

div.title: Abram returns to Bethel (verses 1–4)
div.p: Abram was exceedingly rich.
The Hebrew expression means that he was very heavy with wealth. Riches can indeed become a heavy burden.
Those who are determined to become rich load themselves down with what Scripture calls thick clay (Habakkuk 2:6).
Getting wealth brings the burden of anxiety; keeping it brings fear; using it brings temptation; misusing it brings guilt; losing it brings sorrow.
And at the end, we must give an account of what we have done with it.
Yet God's providence sometimes makes godly people wealthy.
God's blessing made Abram rich without bringing sorrow with it (Proverbs 10:22).
It is difficult for a rich person to enter heaven. But in some cases it is possible (Mark 10:23–24).
When outward prosperity is used wisely, it can adorn a godly life and give us more opportunities to do good.
Abram returned to Bethel.
His former altar was gone, so he could not offer sacrifices there. But he still called on the name of the Lord.
You are as likely to find a living person who never breathes as a true child of God who never prays.

div.title: Abram makes peace with Lot (verses 5–9)
div.p: Riches provide endless occasions for quarrels. They are among the things people fight about most often.
They also stir up the spirit of conflict itself by making people proud and greedy.
“Mine” and “yours” have caused countless disputes.
Poverty, work, deprivation, and wandering had not separated Abram from Lot. But wealth did.
Bad servants can cause tremendous trouble in families and among neighbors through pride, anger, lies, slander, and gossip.
The quarrel was especially damaging because the Canaanites and Perizzites lived in the land.
When those who profess faith quarrel, they bring disgrace on religion and give God's enemies an excuse to blaspheme.
It is best to preserve peace before it is broken.
But once a quarrel has begun, the next best thing is to put out the fire as quickly as possible.
Abram took the initiative, although he was the older man and held the greater position.
His calm spirit enabled him to control his anger and turn away wrath with a gentle answer.
Those who want peace must never answer insults with more insults.
Abram also showed humility. He was willing to plead for peace even with someone in a lower position than himself.
Whatever others may choose, God's people must be people of peace.
Abram gave a powerful reason for reconciliation: the people of the world may fight over trifles, but we who know better things and hope for a better country should not quarrel.
Christians should be especially careful to avoid disputes.
Many people claim to love peace but do nothing to make it happen. Abram was different.
If God himself stoops to plead with us to be reconciled to him, surely we can plead with one another.
Although God had promised the land to Abram's descendants, Abram offered Lot an equal or even better portion.
Lot did not have the same claim, but Abram would not use God's promise as an excuse to treat a relative harshly.
It is noble to give way for the sake of peace.

div.title: Lot chooses the land near Sodom (verses 10–13)
div.p: Abram gave Lot the choice, and Lot immediately accepted it.
Selfishness and strong desire often make people discourteous.
Lot looked at the land's fertility and assumed he would surely prosper in such a fruitful place.
But how did his choice turn out?
When people choose their relationships, work, homes, or places to settle mainly according to bodily desire, the attraction of what they see, or pride, they cannot expect God's presence and blessing.
They are often disappointed even in the thing they most wanted.
One principle should govern every choice: what is best for our souls is best for us.
Lot gave little thought to the character of the people who lived nearby.
Sodom's inhabitants were bold and unashamed in their sin.
The city's wickedness included pride, abundance of food, and an excess of idleness (Ezekiel 16:49).
God often allows great plenty to belong to great sinners.
It has frequently been the painful experience of godly people to live among wicked neighbors.
That pain is even greater when, as with Lot, they have brought the situation upon themselves through a poor choice.

div.title: God renews his promise to Abram (verses 14–18)
div.p: Those whose spirits are calm, rather than disturbed by angry passions, are best prepared to receive visits of God's grace.
God more than makes up for the outward advantages we give up to preserve peace with our neighbors by giving us spiritual peace.
Even when our relatives separate from us, God does not leave us.
Notice how God now comforted and enriched Abram through his promises.
He promised two things: a good land and many descendants to enjoy it.
What faith sees is richer and more beautiful than anything our eyes can see around us.
God told Abram to walk throughout the land.
He was not to imagine that he could settle there permanently. Rather, he would remain a pilgrim, moving toward a better Canaan.
Abram built an altar as a sign of his thankfulness.
When God meets us with gracious promises, he expects us to respond with humble praise.
When outward circumstances are difficult, believers find great benefit in meditating on the glorious inheritance the Lord has prepared for them at the end.

row.cell: The battle of the kings; Lot is taken prisoner.

div.title: The battle of the kings and Lot's captivity (verses 1–12)
div.p: Wars between nations often occupy a large place in historical accounts.
But this particular war would not have been recorded in Scripture if Abram and Lot had not been involved.
Lot had chosen to live in prosperous Sodom because he wanted its advantages, although the city was full of wickedness.
Among all the descendants of Canaan, its inhabitants were especially ready for God's vengeance.
The invaders came from Chaldea and Persia, which were then still small kingdoms.
They captured Lot along with the other inhabitants and took his possessions.
Lot was a righteous man and Abram's nephew. Yet he suffered alongside his wicked neighbors.
Neither our own godliness nor our relationship with those favored by God can guarantee that we will escape a time of public judgment.
Many upright people suffer because they live among wicked neighbors.
We should therefore wisely separate ourselves from such company, or at the very least show clearly that we do not share their sins (2 Corinthians 6:17).
As such a close relative of Abram, Lot ought to have been Abram's companion and disciple.
Having chosen to live in Sodom, he had only himself to blame when he shared in Sodom's losses.
When we leave the path of duty, we place ourselves outside the protection we might otherwise expect from God.
We cannot reasonably expect that a decision driven by sinful desires will end in comfort.
The invaders also took Lot's goods.
God is right to take away things we enjoy when we have allowed those very things to rob us of the enjoyment of him.

div.title: Abram rescues Lot (verses 13–16)
div.p: Abram seized this opportunity to prove that his friendship toward Lot was genuine.
We should be ready to help people in distress, especially relatives and friends.
Even when others have failed to do their duty toward us, we must not neglect our duty toward them.
Abram rescued the captives.
Whenever we have the opportunity, we should do good to everyone.

div.title: Melchizedek blesses Abram (verses 17–20)
div.p: Melchizedek is described as king of Salem, which is thought to have been the place later known as Jerusalem.
It is generally understood that he was an ordinary human being.
The apostle's words in Hebrews 7:3 mean only that Scripture says nothing about Melchizedek's ancestors.
That silence is intended to lift our thoughts toward Christ, whose generation cannot be fully declared.
Bread and wine were suitable refreshments for Abram's exhausted followers.
It is remarkable that Christ later appointed those same things as signs commemorating his body and blood—the true food and drink of the soul.
Melchizedek blessed Abram in God's name.
He also blessed God in Abram's name.
We should thank God for the blessings received by others as sincerely as we thank him for our own.
Jesus Christ, our great High Priest, is the Mediator of both our prayers and our praises.
He does not merely present ours to God; he also offers his own prayers and praises on our behalf.
Abram gave Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils (Hebrews 7:4).
When God shows us an extraordinary mercy, it is right to express our gratitude through a special act of godly charity.
Jesus Christ, our great Melchizedek, deserves our homage and humble acknowledgment as both King and Priest.
Not merely a tenth, but everything we have, should be given over to him.

div.title: Abram refuses the king of Sodom's offer (verses 21–24)
div.p: Notice the grateful offer made by the king of Sodom: “Give me the people, and take the goods.”
Gratitude teaches us to repay, as far as we can, those who have worked hard, faced danger, and spent their resources for our benefit.
But Abram generously refused the offer.
He explained why: he did not want the king to be able to say, “I made Abram rich.”
That would cast doubt on God's promise and covenant, as though God could not have enriched Abram without the spoils of Sodom.
For the sake of their testimony, God's people must avoid conduct that appears petty, mercenary, greedy, or selfish.
Abram could trust the Possessor of heaven and earth to provide for him.

row.cell: God's promise; Abraham is justified by faith.
God promises Abram the land of Canaan.
The promise is confirmed in a vision.
The promise is confirmed by a sign.

div.title: God assures Abram of his protection (verse 1)
div.p: God assured Abram that he would remain safe and happy.
“I am your shield,” he said.
In other words, God himself was near him, actively caring for him and protecting him.
God is a shield for his people—ready whenever they need him and surrounding them on every side.
If we truly understand that he is and will remain our shield, it should silence our distressing and tormenting fears.

div.title: The promised son and justification through faith (verses 2–6)
div.p: We must never complain about God, but we are allowed to bring our complaints to him and tell him all that troubles us.
It relieves a burdened heart to open its concerns to a faithful and compassionate friend.
Abram's grief was that he had no child and no reason to expect one.
The absence of a son distressed him so deeply that it overshadowed every other comfort.
If Abram was thinking only of earthly comforts, his complaint deserved correction.
But if his longing concerned the promised Seed, his desire was very good.
Until we know that we belong to Christ, we should not be satisfied.
What good will anything else do me if I remain without Christ?
If we persevere in prayer while humbly submitting to God's will, we will not seek him in vain.
God gave Abram an explicit promise of a son.
Christians can trust God for the ordinary concerns of life.
But the faith by which they are justified always looks to the person and work of Jesus Christ.
Abram believed God as the One who promised Christ.
We believe God as the One who has raised Christ from the dead (Romans 4:24).
Through faith in Christ's blood, we receive the forgiveness of sins.

div.title: God confirms the inheritance of Canaan (verses 7–11)
div.p: God assured Abram that the land of Canaan would belong to him as an inheritance.
Unlike human beings, who often promise more than they can deliver, God never promises anything beyond his power to accomplish.
Abram obeyed God's instructions.
He divided the animals, following the custom used for confirming covenants (Jeremiah 34:18–19).
After making the preparations God required, he waited for whatever sign the Lord might give.
We should also watch carefully over the spiritual sacrifices we bring to God.
When empty thoughts descend on our worship like birds upon the divided animals, we must drive them away.
Let us seek to give God our attention without distraction.

div.title: The vision of Israel's future (verses 12–16)
div.p: Abram fell into a deep sleep, and with it came a dreadful darkness.
What a sudden change!
Even God's children, who belong to the light, do not always walk in the light.
God then foretold several things.
First, Abram's descendants would suffer for a long time.
They would live as strangers. In a deeper sense, the heirs of heaven are strangers on earth.
They would become servants. But the Canaanites serve under a curse, while the Hebrews would serve under a blessing.
They would also suffer oppression. Those whom God loves and blesses are often cruelly treated by wicked people.
Second, God would judge their enemies.
He may allow persecutors and oppressors to trample upon his people for a long time, but in the end he will certainly call them to account.
Third, God would bring Abram's descendants out of Egypt.
Fourth, he would settle them happily in Canaan.
God's words also show that guilt grows until it reaches its appointed measure. Some people fill up that measure slowly.
Knowing the future would rarely make us happier.
Even the most favored families and the happiest lives contain so many afflictions that God shows mercy by hiding from us what will happen to us and those we love.

div.title: The smoking furnace and the burning lamp (verses 17–21)
div.p: The smoking furnace and the burning lamp probably represented Israel's severe trials and its joyful deliverance, along with God's gracious help in the meantime.
It is also likely that the furnace and lamp passing between the divided animals burned and consumed them.
If so, this completed the sacrifice and showed that God accepted it.
The sign therefore points to the truth that God's covenants with human beings are made through sacrifice (Psalm 50:5).
We too can know that God accepts our sacrifices when he kindles holy and devoted affections in our souls.
The boundaries of the promised land were stated.
God also named the nations and tribes that would be driven out so that Abram's descendants could live there.
Throughout this chapter, we see Abram's faith struggling against unbelief and finally overcoming it.
Believers, do not be surprised when you pass through seasons of distress and darkness.
God does not want you to remain crushed by fear.
Do not be afraid. All that he was to Abram, he will be to you.

row.cell: The Angel commands Hagar to return, promises her a son, and Ishmael is born.

div.title: Sarai gives Hagar to Abram (verses 1–3)
div.p: Sarai had stopped expecting to bear a child herself.
She suggested that Abram take another wife, whose children could be counted as hers.
Hagar was her enslaved servant, and under the custom of that time, Hagar's children would belong to Sarai.
But Sarai made this proposal without asking the Lord for counsel.
Unbelief was at work, and God's almighty power had been forgotten.
The result was a bad example and the beginning of many troubles.
Every relationship and situation in life brings some difficulty or burden that we must bear.
A large part of practicing faith is patiently accepting such trials, waiting for God's appointed time, and using only the means he has appointed to remove them.
Dangerous temptations can come disguised as reasonable and attractive plans.
Human wisdom, when governed by sinful desires, takes us away from God's way.
We could avoid much trouble if we sought God's counsel through his word and prayer before acting in doubtful matters.

div.title: The conflict between Sarai and Hagar (verses 4–6)
div.p: Abram's unhappy marriage to Hagar quickly brought serious trouble.
When we leave the path of duty, we have ourselves to blame for the guilt and grief that follow.
We see it plainly here.
People who are ruled by passion often quarrel with others about matters for which they themselves are responsible.
Sarai had given Hagar to Abram. Yet she cried out, “May the wrong done to me be upon you!”
Words prompted by pride and anger are never wise.
Those who loudly and confidently appeal to God are not always in the right.
Rash accusations and appeals to divine judgment often reveal guilt and a weak cause rather than innocence.
Hagar, for her part, forgot that she had first provoked the trouble by despising her mistress.
When people suffer because of their own faults, they ought to bear it patiently (1 Peter 2:20).

div.title: The Angel meets Hagar and sends her back (verses 7–16)
div.p: Hagar had left her proper place and abandoned her duty.
When the Angel found her, she was wandering farther and farther from the right path.
It is a great mercy when conscience or providence stops us from continuing along a sinful road.
“Where have you come from?”
The question urged Hagar to consider that she was fleeing her responsibilities and leaving behind the privileges she had enjoyed in Abram's household.
It is a blessing to live in a family where God is worshipped. Those who enjoy that blessing should remember its value.
“Where are you going?”
Hagar was heading toward sin and danger.
If she returned to Egypt, she would return to the worship of false gods. She would also face the dangers of the wilderness.
Thinking carefully about who we are often reminds us of what we ought to do.
Remembering where we came from shows us our sins and foolishness.
Thinking about where we are going reveals the danger and misery ahead.
Anyone who has left the place of duty should hurry back, however humbling that return may be.
The Angel spoke in God's own name and said, “I will.”
That declaration shows that this Angel was the eternal Word and Son of God.
Hagar could only marvel at the Lord's mercy.
How could someone as unworthy as she was have received such a gracious visit from him?
Her attitude changed.
She returned, and her changed conduct softened Sarai's heart, so that Sarai treated her more gently.
May we always live with this truth firmly in mind: “You are the God who sees me.”

row.cell: God renews his covenant with Abram.
Sarai receives a new name; Isaac is promised.
Abraham and his household are circumcised.

div.title: God renews the covenant with Abram (verses 1–6)
div.p: God's covenant would be fulfilled at the appointed time.
The promised Seed was Christ, and in him the promise extends to Christians.
All who live by faith share in the blessing given to faithful Abram. They receive the blessings of the same covenant.
As a sign of this covenant, God changed Abram's name.
Abram means “high father.”
Abraham means “father of a multitude.”
Everything the Christian world enjoys through the gospel is owed, under God, to Abraham and his promised Seed.

div.title: Circumcision is appointed as a sign of the covenant (verses 7–14)
div.p: The covenant of grace is everlasting.
It is everlasting in God's purposes, which preceded time, and everlasting in the consequences that flow from it.
Circumcision was the sign of that covenant.
Scripture even calls it the covenant that Abraham and his descendants were required to keep.
Those who want the Lord to be their God must resolve to be his people.
Circumcision was not required of Abraham and Isaac alone, or only of the descendants who would come through Isaac.
Ishmael and the servants in Abraham's household were also to receive it.
The sign sealed more than the promise of the land of Canaan to Isaac's descendants.
It also pointed to the promise of heaven through Christ for the whole church of God.
The outward sign belongs to the visible church.
But the inward seal of the Holy Spirit belongs only to those whom God himself knows to be believers. Only God can know them with certainty.
God required this ordinance to be observed and attached a very severe penalty to neglecting it.
It is dangerous to despise God's appointed ordinances or to live as though they do not matter.
The covenant carried great blessings that would reach the whole world through generations yet to come.
Even Abraham's own happiness and the rewards God gave him came for Christ's sake.
Abraham was justified not by his own righteousness but by faith in the promised Messiah.

div.title: Sarah's new name and the promise of Isaac (verses 15–22)
div.p: God promised Abraham that Sarah would give birth to a son, through whom the covenant promise would be fulfilled.
To confirm this, God changed Sarai's name to Sarah.
Sarai means “my princess,” as though her honor belonged to a single household.
Sarah simply means “princess,” suggesting a wider honor.
The more favors God gives us, the humbler we should become in our own eyes.
Abraham was filled with joy.
He laughed, but his laughter expressed delight rather than unbelief.
It was now that Abraham rejoiced to see the day of Christ. He saw it and was glad (John 8:56).
Abraham also feared that Ishmael might be abandoned or rejected by God. So he prayed for his son.
God allows us to bring particular requests to him in prayer.
Whatever troubles or frightens us should be laid openly before him.
Parents have a duty to pray for their children.
Above all, they should ask that their children may remain in covenant with God and receive the grace to walk uprightly before him.
God promised ordinary, earthly blessings to Ishmael.
For the sake of godly parents, he often gives outward good things even to children who do not share their parents' spiritual faith.
But the special covenant blessings were reserved for Isaac and assigned to him.

div.title: Abraham and his household obey (verses 23–27)
div.p: Abraham and everyone in his household received circumcision.
By accepting the sign of the covenant, they marked themselves off from families that had no part in it.
Abraham's obedience was complete.
He did exactly what God commanded without asking why or demanding an explanation. He obeyed simply because God had spoken.
His obedience was also immediate.
He acted that very day.
Sincere obedience does not delay.
Not only the teachings of God's revelation, but also the signs of his covenant, remind us that we are guilty and defiled sinners.
They show us our need for the blood of atonement.
They point to the promised Savior and call us to place our faith in him.
They teach us that without new birth, holiness through the Spirit, and the putting to death of our corrupt desires, we cannot truly belong to God's covenant people.
Remember, however, that the true circumcision is circumcision of the heart, performed by the Spirit (Romans 2:28–29).
Under both the old covenant and the new, many people have professed faith and received the outward sign without ever being sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise.

row.cell: God reveals Sodom's destruction to Abraham.

div.title: Abraham welcomes the visitors (verses 1–8)
div.p: Abraham was ready to welcome any tired traveler who came his way.
There were no inns like those we have today.
As Abraham sat there, he saw three men approaching.
They were three heavenly beings appearing in human bodies.
Some believe all three were created angels. Others believe one of them was the Son of God, the Angel of the covenant.
Washing guests' feet was a common act of hospitality in hot countries where people wore sandals.
We should not neglect to welcome strangers. In doing so, some have welcomed angels without knowing it (Hebrews 13:2).
More than that, we welcome the Lord of angels himself whenever we show kindness for his sake to the least of his brothers and sisters.
Cheerful and thoughtful kindness is one of the finest ornaments of a godly life.
Our gracious and humble Lord no longer visits us personally in the way he visited Abraham.
Yet through his Spirit he still stands at the door and knocks.
When we are willing to open, he graciously enters and provides a rich feast of comfort, which we share with him (Revelation 3:20).

div.title: Sarah's unbelief is corrected (verses 9–15)
div.p: The visitors asked where Sarah was.
Abraham replied, “In the tent.”
She was close by, in the right place, attending to her household duties.
There is nothing to gain from wandering around aimlessly.
Those who are faithfully carrying out their duties are most likely to receive comfort from God and his promises (Luke 2:8).
We are often slow to believe, and we need to hear the same truth repeatedly.
Other people may receive blessings through God's ordinary providence.
Believers receive those same blessings through his promises, which make them sweeter and more certain.
Abraham's spiritual descendants owe their life, joy, hope, and everything else to God's promise.
Sarah thought the news of a son too wonderful to be true.
She laughed because she could not yet bring herself to believe it.
At first we might not see any difference between Sarah's laughter and Abraham's laughter in Genesis 17:17.
But God, who searches the heart, saw that her laughter arose from unbelief, while his arose from faith.
Sarah then denied that she had laughed.
One sin often leads to another. When we question God's truth, we are less likely to speak the truth ourselves.
Yet the Lord rebukes, convicts, silences, and brings to repentance those whom he loves when they sin before him.

div.title: God tells Abraham about Sodom (verses 16–22)
div.p: Two of the visitors, understood to be created angels, went toward Sodom.
The third, called Jehovah throughout this account, remained with Abraham.
He chose not to hide from Abraham what he intended to do.
God sometimes shows great patience toward sinners.
They may wrongly conclude that he neither notices nor cares about what they do.
But when the day of his judgment comes, he will look toward them.
God told Abraham what he intended to do, giving him an opportunity to intercede and showing him the justice of his actions.
Abraham's character shines especially in the care he took over his family.
He not only prayed with them but taught and governed them conscientiously.
Those who expect the blessings of a godly family must also fulfill the duties of a godly family.
Abraham did not fill his household's minds with doubtful controversies.
He taught them to worship God sincerely and seriously, and to deal honestly with everyone.
How few households could receive such praise today!
How little care is often taken to teach those under our responsibility the foundations of true religion.
Do we watch, week after week, to see whether they are making progress or falling behind?

div.title: Abraham intercedes for Sodom (verses 23–33)
div.p: Here we find the first solemn prayer recorded in Scripture.
Abraham prayed that Sodom might be spared if only a few righteous people could be found there.
We should learn from him how deeply to care for sinners and how earnestly to pray for them.
The fervent prayer of a righteous person can accomplish much.
Abraham did not obtain what he requested for the whole city.
Yet Lot was delivered in a miraculous way.
Let this encourage us to pray earnestly for God's blessing upon our families, friends, and neighborhoods.
But we must do more than pray. We must also live as Abraham did.
Abraham knew that the Judge of all the earth would do what was right.
He did not argue that the wicked deserved to be spared on their own account.
Nor did he suggest that destroying them would be unjust or excessively severe.
He pleaded for the sake of the righteous people who might still be among them.
Only righteousness can serve as a plea before God.
How, then, did Christ intercede for transgressors?
Not by criticizing God's law or offering excuses that minimize human guilt.
He pleaded his own obedience, even to death.

row.cell: Sodom is destroyed and Lot is delivered.

div.title: Sodom's destruction and Lot's rescue (verses 1–29)
div.p: Lot was a godly man, but there was not another person of the same character in the city.
The people of Sodom had become thoroughly wicked.
God therefore took care to save Lot and his family.
Yet Lot hesitated and wasted time.
Many people are like him.
They become convinced that their spiritual condition is wrong and that they must change, but they delay the very change they know is necessary.
Even the most righteous people are saved through God's mercy, not through any merit of their own.

p.hi: We are saved by grace.

div.p: We must also recognize God's power in bringing people out of a sinful condition.
If God had not shown mercy to us, our hesitation would have destroyed us.
Lot had to flee for his life.
He must not keep longing for Sodom or looking back toward it.
Similar commands are given to everyone whom grace has delivered from sin.
Do not return to sin and Satan.
Do not settle down in yourself or in the world as though they could save you.
Reach toward Christ and heaven. That is what it means to flee to the mountain.
Do not stop before you reach them.
The destruction of Sodom reveals God's wrath against sin and against sinners in every age.
Let it teach us how evil and destructive sin truly is.
Sin leads to ruin.

div.title: Lot's sin and disgrace (verses 30–38)
div.p: Notice the danger of becoming too sure of ourselves.
In Sodom, Lot remained pure.
He grieved over the city's wickedness and testified against it.
Yet later, while alone in the mountains, believing himself safely beyond temptation, he fell into a shameful sin.
Whoever thinks he is standing high and securely must be careful not to fall.
Notice also the danger of drunkenness.
It is not only a serious sin in itself. It opens the door to other sins that leave deep and lasting wounds of shame.
People often do things while drunk that would horrify them to contemplate when sober.
There is also danger in temptations that come from relatives and friends.
These are people we love and respect, and from whom we expect kindness.
Yet we must fear a trap wherever we are and remain constantly on our guard.
Nothing can excuse the actions of Lot's daughters, or Lot's own conduct.
There is scarcely any explanation but the truth that the human heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked.
Who can understand it?
Scripture says nothing more about Lot from this point on.
That silence teaches us something about drunkenness: it not only makes people forget, but also causes them to be forgotten.

row.cell: Abraham stays at Gerar; Abimelech takes Sarah.

div.title: Abimelech is warned by God (verses 1–8)
div.p: Dishonest schemes do not prosper. They place both ourselves and others in danger.
God warned Abimelech that he was in danger of committing sin and of dying for it.
Every person who deliberately lives in sin is under a sentence of death.
But Abimelech pleaded that he had acted in ignorance.
When our conscience assures us that, although we may have been tricked into a dangerous situation, we have not deliberately sinned against God, that assurance brings comfort in a time of trouble.
Honest people can take comfort in knowing that God sees their honesty and will acknowledge it.
It is a great mercy to be prevented from committing sin, and God deserves all the glory for that protection.
Yet if we have done wrong without knowing it, our ignorance will not excuse us if we continue to do wrong after we learn the truth.
Everyone who does wrong—ruler or ordinary citizen—will certainly answer for that wrong unless they repent and, wherever possible, make restitution.

div.title: Abimelech rebukes Abraham (verses 9–13)
div.p: We find much to blame even in Abraham, the father of the faithful.
He failed to trust God.
He worried too much about his own life, intended to deceive others, and placed temptation in their path.
His actions brought suffering upon other people and exposed both himself and Sarah to justified rebuke.
Yet he still tried to excuse himself.
Scripture records these events to warn us, not to give us examples to imitate.
Even Abraham had no reason to boast before God.
He could never be justified by his works.
His justification depended entirely on the righteousness God gives to everyone who believes.
Yet we must not immediately condemn as hypocrites all who fall into sin, provided they do not continue in it.
Those who remain proud and refuse to repent must never use God's grace as an excuse for continuing to sin.
Abimelech received God's warning and took it seriously.
He truly feared both sin and its consequences.
So he rose early to carry out the instructions God had given him.

div.title: Sarah is restored and God brings deliverance (verses 14–18)
div.p: We often trouble ourselves because of suspicions that have no foundation.
Those fears can even draw us into temptation and sin.
Sometimes we discover reverence for God in the very people among whom we least expected to find it.
Agreements to deceive others usually end in shame and grief.
We should also thank God when he restrains us from sin, even if he does so through painful circumstances.
Though the Lord rebukes his people, he also forgives and delivers them.
He can give them favor in the eyes of those among whom they live.
When his people humble themselves over their failings, God can overrule those very weaknesses so that they become useful both to themselves and to others.

row.cell: Hagar and Ishmael are sent away and receive help from an angel.
Abimelech makes a covenant with Abraham.

div.title: Isaac's birth and Sarah's joy (verses 1–8)
div.p: Few people in Old Testament times were born with such great hopes resting upon them as Isaac.
In this he was a picture of Christ, the Seed whom the holy God had promised so long before and whom godly people had awaited for so many generations.
Isaac was born according to God's promise, at the very time God had appointed.
Whatever mercy God has promised will certainly come at the time he has chosen—and that time is best.
Isaac means “laughter.”
There was good reason for that name (Genesis 17:17; 18:13).
When the sun of comfort rises over our souls, it is good to remember how welcome the first light of dawn once was.
When Sarah first heard God's promise, she laughed with doubt and distrust.
When God gives us blessings we had almost given up hoping for, we ought to remember with sorrow and shame how we once doubted his power and his promise.
Now God's mercy filled Sarah with joy and wonder.
The blessings God gives his covenant people go far beyond what they or anyone else could have imagined.
Who could have expected him to do so much for those who deserve so little—and indeed deserve his judgment?
Who would have imagined that God would send his Son to die for us, and his Spirit to make us holy, and his angels to care for us?
Who could have imagined the pardon of such great sins, the acceptance of such insignificant service, and the admission of such unworthy creatures into his covenant?
Scripture gives a brief account of Isaac's infancy.
We should recognize God's special care and tenderness in the feeding and nursing of children and in their preservation through the dangers of early childhood (Psalm 22:9–10; Hosea 11:1–2).

div.title: Ishmael mocks Isaac (verses 9–13)
div.p: This family incident teaches us not to rely on outward privileges or on anything we have done ourselves.
Instead, let us seek the blessings of the new covenant through faith in its divine Guarantor.
Ishmael's mocking was persecution.
He showed wicked contempt for God's covenant and promise and acted with malice toward Isaac.
God notices what children say and do, even while they play.
He will hold them accountable when they do wrong, even if their parents overlook it.
Mockery is a serious sin that greatly offends God.
The children of the promise should therefore expect to be mocked.
Abraham was deeply troubled.
He grieved over Ishmael's misconduct and over Sarah's demand for such a severe punishment.
But God showed Abraham that Isaac must become the ancestor of the promised Seed.
Ishmael was therefore to be sent away, lest he corrupt Isaac's conduct or try to take away his rights.
Abraham's covenant descendants were to be a people set apart, not mixed with those outside the covenant.
Sarah did not understand the full meaning of what she was asking.
Yet God directed her words toward his own wise purpose.

div.title: Hagar and Ishmael receive help in the wilderness (verses 14–21)
div.p: If Hagar and Ishmael had behaved rightly in Abraham's household, they might have remained there.
But they had misused their privileges and were justly punished.
When we abuse privileges, we lose our claim to them.
People who do not appreciate their blessings while they have them may come to understand their value only when those blessings are taken away.
Hagar and Ishmael soon found themselves in distress in the wilderness.
Scripture does not say that all their supplies had run out, or that Abraham had sent them away without money.
But their water was gone.
They had lost their way, and in the heat Ishmael was quickly overcome with exhaustion and thirst.
Knowing that God is ready to help us in trouble must not make us less active in helping ourselves.
On the contrary, it should encourage us to do everything we can.
God repeated the promise concerning Ishmael to give Hagar a reason to rise and care for him.
We should work diligently for the good of children and young people, remembering that we cannot know what great work God may intend them to accomplish.
The angel showed Hagar where she could find water.
Many people have good reason to be comforted, yet continue mourning because they cannot see that reason.
There is a well of living water close at hand in the covenant of grace.
But they do not notice it until the same God who opened their eyes to see their wound opens them again to see the remedy.
Paran was a wild country, fitting for a wild man like Ishmael.
Those born merely according to the flesh are content with the wilderness of this world.
But the children of the promise long for the heavenly Canaan and cannot finally rest until they reach it.
Yet God was with Ishmael, and his outward prosperity came from that divine care.

div.title: Abraham and Abimelech make a covenant (verses 22–34)
div.p: Abimelech was convinced that God would keep his promises to Abraham.
It is wise to form good relationships with those whom God has blessed.
We also ought to repay kindness to those who have shown kindness to us.
Wells are scarce and precious in eastern countries.
Abraham made sure his right to the well was acknowledged, so that future quarrels could be avoided.
We cannot demand more of an honest person than a willingness to make things right as soon as a wrong is known.
Abraham now lived among good neighbors, so he remained there for a long time.
He not only practiced his religion privately but professed it openly.
He called upon the Lord as the everlasting God, probably in the grove he had planted as a place of prayer.
He maintained public worship, so that his neighbors could join him.
Godly people should do everything they can to help others become godly too.
Wherever we live as strangers, we must neither neglect nor be ashamed of worshipping the LORD.

row.cell: God commands Abraham to offer Isaac.
God provides another sacrifice instead of Isaac.
God renews the covenant with Abraham.

div.title: God tests Abraham (verses 1–2)
div.p: We are never beyond the reach of trials.
In Hebrew, the same word can express tempting, testing, or proving.
Every trial tests what is in the heart, showing whether its desires are holy or sinful.
But God tested Abraham without intending to draw him into sin, as Satan does when he tempts.
Strong faith is often tested by great difficulties and called to hard service.
The command to offer Isaac was expressed in words that made the trial more painful.
Every word was like a sword.

p.hi: First, consider whom he was to offer.

div.p: “Take your son”—not your cattle or your sheep. How willingly Abraham would have given them all to save Isaac!
“Your son”—not a servant.
“Your only son”—the only son born to Sarah.
“Isaac”—the very son Abraham loved.

p.hi: Second, consider where he was to offer him.

div.p: The place was a three-day journey away.
Abraham would have time to think about what he was doing and obey deliberately.

p.hi: Third, consider how he was to offer him.

div.p: He was to present Isaac as a burnt offering.
It was not merely a matter of killing his son, his beloved Isaac, but doing so as a sacrifice, with all the solemn ceremonies he normally used when offering a burnt offering.

div.title: Abraham obeys in faith (verses 3–10)
div.p: Never was gold tested in a hotter fire.
Who other than Abraham would not have argued with God?
A weaker heart would certainly have raised objections.
But Abraham knew the One with whom he had to deal: the Lord himself.
Faith had taught him to obey rather than argue.
He was certain that whatever God commanded was good and that whatever God promised could not fail.
Anyone who consults merely human feelings and reasoning in a matter of obedience to God will never give up their Isaac for him.
The godly patriarch rose early and began his painful journey.
Then he traveled for three whole days with Isaac still in his sight.
Suffering becomes harder when it continues for a long time.
Abraham told his servants, “We will come back to you.”
This shows that he expected Isaac to return with him, even if God had to raise him from the dead.
Then Isaac asked a deeply moving question.
“My father,” he said.
Those words alone must have touched Abraham's heart more deeply than his knife could have pierced Isaac.
Yet Abraham waited for his son's question.
Then, without intending to do so, Abraham spoke a prophecy: “My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering.”
Through his words, the Holy Spirit seems to point toward the Lamb of God, whom God would provide to take away the sin of the world.
Abraham arranged the wood as though preparing Isaac's funeral pyre.
Now he had to tell his son the astonishing truth: Isaac himself was the lamb appointed for the sacrifice.
No doubt he comforted Isaac with the same hopes of God's faithfulness that had strengthened his own heart.
Isaac had to be bound.
The great Sacrifice who would come in the fullness of time would also be bound.
When Isaac was bound, Abraham took the knife and reached out to strike the fatal blow.
This act of faith and obedience deserves to be witnessed by God, angels, and humanity.
Sometimes God's providence calls us to part with our own Isaac—whatever we love most.
When that happens, we must submit cheerfully to his holy will (1 Samuel 3:18).

div.title: God provides a sacrifice instead of Isaac (verses 11–14)
div.p: God had never intended Isaac actually to be sacrificed.
Yet in due time blood more precious than that of animals would be shed for sin: the blood of God's only Son.
Meanwhile, God would not permit human sacrifices to be offered.
Another sacrifice was provided.
We must see here a reference to the promised Messiah, the blessed Seed.
Christ was offered in our place, just as the ram was offered in Isaac's place.
Through Christ's death, our debt was discharged.
Notice also that the temple, where sacrifices were later offered, was built on this same Mount Moriah.
Calvary, where Christ was crucified, was nearby.
Abraham gave the place a new name to encourage believers in every age to trust and obey God with joy.
Jehovah-jireh: “The LORD will provide.”
The name probably alluded to Abraham's earlier words: “God will provide himself a lamb.”
The Lord always keeps his eye on his people in times of trouble and distress, ready to give them help when they need it.

div.title: God renews his promise to Abraham (verses 15–19)
div.p: In confirming his covenant, God declared his favor toward Abraham more gloriously than ever before.
Those willing to surrender anything for God will find that he makes up their loss with blessings beyond description.
The promise in verse 18 undoubtedly points to the Messiah and the grace of the gospel.
Here we see the loving-kindness of God our Savior toward sinful humanity.
He did not withhold his own Son—his only Son—from us.
And here we see Christ's love: he freely gave himself as the sacrifice for our sins.
Yet he lives!
He calls sinners to come to him and share in the salvation he purchased with his blood.
He calls those he has redeemed to rejoice in him and glorify him.
How can we repay him for all his benefits?
Let his love move us to live not for ourselves, but for the One who died for us and rose again.
Let us admire and worship his grace, giving everything to the service of the Savior who laid down his life for us.
Whatever we love most dearly on earth is our Isaac.
The only way to find true comfort in something earthly is to place it by faith into God's hands.
Yet remember: Abraham was not justified by his willingness to obey.
He was justified through the infinitely greater obedience of Jesus Christ.
Faith received that obedience, rested upon it, and rejoiced in it.
And that same faith prepared Abraham and enabled him to show such extraordinary self-denial and obedience.

div.title: Nahor's family (verses 20–24)
div.p: The chapter ends with a brief account of Nahor's family, who had settled in Haran.
This genealogy is included because of its connection with God's church.
Both Isaac and Jacob would later take wives from that family, so the list appears before those events are described.
Abraham enjoyed extraordinary privileges, had been brought into God's covenant, and had received the assurance of its promises.
Yet he did not look down upon his relatives.
He was glad to hear that their families were growing and doing well.

row.cell: Sarah dies; Abraham seeks a burial place.
Abraham purchases the place where Sarah will be buried.

div.title: Sarah's death and Abraham's request (verses 1–13)
div.p: Even the longest human life must come to an end before long.
Blessed be God that there is another world into which sin, death, vanity, and trouble can never enter!
Blessed be his name that not even death can separate believers from their union with Christ.
Those we love most deeply must soon die.
Even our own bodies, which we care for so tenderly, will become lifeless clay and be buried out of sight.
How lightly, then, we ought to hold earthly possessions and outward adornments!
Instead, let us seek to adorn our souls with the graces of heaven.
Abraham showed honor and respect to the leaders of the Hittites, though they belonged to the ungodly Canaanites.
The religion of the Bible requires us to show proper respect to people in authority.
But this does not mean flattering those who hold office or excusing their wrongdoing when their character is unworthy.
And the generous conduct of these Canaanites puts to shame the stinginess, selfishness, and bad temper of many who call themselves God's people.
Abraham did not refuse their gift out of pride or because he thought himself too important to owe Ephron anything.
He refused out of justice and wisdom.
Abraham could afford to pay for the field, so he would not take advantage of Ephron's generosity.
Both honesty and honor forbid us to exploit another person's kindness or impose upon those who freely offer us help.

div.title: Abraham purchases Sarah's burial place (verses 14–20)
div.p: Wisdom and justice alike teach us to deal fairly and openly with others.
A dishonest bargain cannot bear close examination.
Abraham paid the price without fraud or delay.
He paid the full amount at once, holding nothing back.
He weighed out the money in the currency accepted by merchants, without deceit.
Money has served trade since ancient times. We should pay honestly what we owe, when payment is due.
God had promised Abraham all the land of Canaan.
But the time when he would possess it had not yet arrived.
So Abraham bought and paid for the land he needed.

p.hi: Earthly dominion does not come from grace.

div.p: A believer's title to an eternal inheritance does not give that person a right to the property of others in this world or excuse doing them wrong.
Ephron, for his part, made the transfer honestly and gave Abraham a secure title to the land.
Just as buyers must pay fairly for what they purchase, sellers must deliver and guarantee honestly what they sell.
We should conduct business carefully and punctually so that quarrels can be avoided.
Abraham buried Sarah in the cave or vault on the field he had bought.
This would help make the land dear to his descendants.
It is remarkable that the only piece of land Abraham ever owned in Canaan was a burial place.
Those who possess little of this world will still find a grave in it.
The tomb lay at the end of the field.
Whatever land we own, there is a burial place at the end of it.
The burial also showed Abraham's faith and hope in the resurrection.
He was content to live as a stranger and traveler on earth.
But he secured a place where his body could rest in hope after death.
In the end, our greatest concern must be this: with whom will we rise?

row.cell: Abraham takes care over Isaac's marriage.
Abraham's servant journeys to Mesopotamia and meets Rebekah.
Rebekah and her relatives agree to the marriage.
Isaac and Rebekah meet and marry.

div.title: Abraham's concern for Isaac's marriage (verses 1–9)
div.p: The effects of godly example, careful teaching, and worship in a household will usually be seen in the devotion, faithfulness, wisdom, and affection of its servants.
It is a blessing from God either to live in such a household or to have servants of that character. We should value these blessings and receive them with gratitude.
Yet few decisions in life matter more to ourselves, to other people, or to God's church than marriage.
Marriage should therefore be approached with great care and wisdom. Above all, we should seek God's will and pray for his guidance and blessing.
When good parents are neither consulted nor respected, we cannot reasonably expect God's blessing.
Parents, in helping to arrange their children's marriages, should consider carefully what will benefit their souls and help them toward heaven.
Notice Abraham's instructions to his servant. He entrusted the task to someone whose conduct, loyalty, and affection for the household had been proved over many years.
Abraham remembered how wonderfully God's grace had called him away from his homeland.
He therefore trusted God to prosper his efforts without taking his son back to the country God had called him to leave.
What we undertake sincerely for God's glory will eventually bring us comfort.

div.title: The servant meets Rebekah (verses 10–28)
div.p: Abraham's servant openly acknowledged God.
We are free to bring our particular concerns before divine providence and pray about their details.
The servant asked for a sign.
He did not mean that he would abandon his task unless God gave him exactly the sign he requested. Rather, he was asking God to provide a good wife for his young master.
That was a good prayer.
He wanted a woman who was modest, hardworking, humble, cheerful, helpful, and hospitable.

Whatever fashions may change, both sound judgment and godliness show the value of those qualities in a wife and mother—a companion for her husband, a manager of the household, and someone entrusted with forming the minds of children.
When the servant went to look for a wife for Isaac, he did not go to a place of sinful pleasure or empty amusement and pray to find someone there.
He went to a well, expecting to meet someone properly engaged in ordinary duties.
He asked God to make the right path plain.
The timing of events, no less than the events themselves, is in God's hands.
But we should not tell God too boldly what he must do. If events do not turn out as we demanded, our faith might be weakened rather than strengthened.
God answered his servant and made the way clear.
Rebekah possessed all the qualities the servant was seeking.
She came to the well, filled her jar, and began to return home.
She did not stand staring at the stranger and his camels. She attended to her work and let nothing interrupt it except an opportunity to do good.
She did not begin an immodest or overly familiar conversation. She answered the stranger respectfully.
When the servant realized God had answered his prayer, he gave Rebekah ornaments customary in eastern countries and asked about her family.
Once he discovered that she belonged to Abraham's relatives, he bowed in worship and blessed God.
His words were addressed to the Lord, but Rebekah could hear them and understand something about who he was and where he had come from.

div.title: Rebekah's family agrees to the marriage (verses 29–53)
div.p: Scripture tells us in unusual detail how Isaac's marriage to Rebekah was arranged.
We should recognize God's providence in the ordinary events of life and practice wisdom and other Christian virtues in the midst of them.
Laban went to invite Abraham's servant into the house—but only after seeing the jewelry on his sister's hands.
We learn about Laban's character from his later actions. It is reasonable to think he might not have been so welcoming if he had not hoped for a generous reward.
The servant remained focused on his task.
Though he had finished a long journey and arrived at a comfortable home, he would not eat until he had explained why he had come.
Doing the work entrusted to us, whether by God or by others, should matter more than our food.
Our Savior said that doing his Father's will was his food and drink (John 4:34).
The servant told them what Abraham had instructed him to do and why.
He described what had happened at the well to support his request, clearly showing how God had guided the matter.
Events that appear to result from our choices, our plans, or chance are appointed by God.
That does not discourage us from using appropriate means. Rather, it encourages their wise and faithful use.
Rebekah's family willingly and gladly accepted the proposal.
A matter that comes from the Lord is likely to bring comfort.
The servant thanked God for the success of his mission.
He was humble, and humble people are not ashamed to acknowledge their position in life, whatever it may be.
Even our ordinary earthly concerns become sweeter when godliness is woven into them.

div.title: Isaac and Rebekah meet and marry (verses 54–67)
div.p: Abraham's servant preferred his work to his own pleasure and was eager to return home.
A wise and godly person who takes duty seriously has no place for needless delay and idleness.
Children should not marry without their parents' consent.
Likewise, parents should not marry off their children without their own consent.
Rebekah agreed to go and was willing to leave immediately.
Her good character shows that her response was not wrong, even though it did not follow the marriage customs common in Henry's own society.
We may hope she understood something of the faith and godliness of the household she was about to join.
Perhaps that helped make her willing to leave her own people and her father's home.
Her relatives sent her with suitable companions and sincere good wishes.
They blessed Rebekah.
When people we love enter a new stage of life, we should commend them to God's grace and blessing through prayer.
Isaac was engaged in good work when he met Rebekah.
He had gone out in the quiet of the evening, to a solitary place, for meditation and prayer.
Through these holy practices we commune with God and examine our own hearts.
Godly people love times of quiet. It benefits us to be alone often, provided we use the time well.
Indeed, we are never less alone than when we are alone with God.
Notice what a loving son Isaac was.
About three years had passed since his mother died, and only now did he find comfort.
Notice also what a loving husband he became.
Those who are dutiful sons are likely to become loving husbands. People who faithfully honor their first calling in life are likely to do the same in the responsibilities that follow.

row.cell: Abraham's children by Keturah, his death and burial.
God blesses Isaac; the descendants of Ishmael.
The birth of Esau and Jacob.
The different characters of Esau and Jacob.
Esau despises and sells his birthright.

div.title: Abraham's last years and death (verses 1–10)
div.p: Even the greatest and most faithful believers do not experience remarkable events every day.
Some years pass quietly, leaving little to record. Abraham's later years were like this.
We are told about his children by Keturah and the arrangements he made for his property.
After these sons were born, he put his household affairs in order with wisdom and fairness.
He did it while he was still alive.
It is wise to carry out whatever responsibilities we can while we have the opportunity to do so.
Abraham lived 175 years.
A full century had passed since he entered Canaan, and throughout that time he lived as a stranger in a foreign land.
Whether our lives are long or short matters little, provided we leave our families a good example and a testimony to the Lord's faithfulness and goodness.
Isaac and Ishmael buried their father together.
It appears that Abraham had helped bring the two brothers together before he died.
Let us not finish the story of Abraham's life without blessing God for such a remarkable testimony of faith's triumph.

div.title: Isaac receives God's blessing; Ishmael's descendants (verses 11–18)
div.p: Ishmael had twelve sons, whose descendants formed distinct tribes.
They populated a large region between Egypt and Assyria, known as Arabia.
The size and strength of his family fulfilled God's promise to Hagar and Abraham concerning Ishmael.

div.title: The birth of Esau and Jacob (verses 19–26)
div.p: Isaac seems to have faced fewer trials than his father and to have spent much of his life in quiet circumstances.
Jacob and Esau were children received through prayer.
Their parents had remained childless for a long time, but God finally answered them.
God's promises will certainly be fulfilled, yet their fulfillment often seems slow.
Believers' faith is tested and their patience exercised during the waiting.
And blessings long awaited become even sweeter when they arrive.
Isaac and Rebekah remembered God's promise that all nations would be blessed through their descendants.
They therefore longed for children and watched closely for signs of what those children would become.
In all our uncertainties, we should seek the Lord through prayer.
In many struggles with sin and temptation, we may take Rebekah's words upon our own lips: “If this is so, why am I like this?”
If I am God's child, why am I so careless or driven by sinful desires?
And if I am not God's child, why do I fear sin so deeply and feel its burden so heavily?

div.title: The contrasting characters of Esau and Jacob (verses 27–28)
div.p: Esau became a skillful and successful hunter.
He pursued wild animals so effectively that he became a conqueror who ruled over his neighbors.
Jacob was a quiet and straightforward man.
He preferred the genuine pleasures of a private life to outward show and false delights.
In his heart he lived as a stranger and pilgrim, and he remained a shepherd all his days.
Isaac and Rebekah had only these two sons.
One became his father's favorite, the other his mother's.
Godly parents may naturally feel especially drawn toward a child who loves the Lord.
Yet they must never show unfair favoritism.
Let affection lead them to treat every child justly and equally. Otherwise, serious trouble will follow.

div.title: Esau sells his birthright (verses 29–34)
div.p: Here we read about the bargain made between Jacob and Esau.
The birthright belonged to Esau by birth, but to Jacob by God's promise.
It concerned spiritual privileges.
Jacob desired the birthright, but he tried to obtain it by dishonest means, inconsistent with his otherwise straightforward character.
He was right to desire the best gifts earnestly.
He was wrong to take advantage of his brother's need.
The question was not who would inherit their father's ordinary possessions. That inheritance was not what Jacob sought in this bargain.
The birthright included the future possession of Canaan by his descendants and the covenant made with Abraham concerning Christ, the promised Seed.
Jacob valued these promises because he believed.
Esau despised them because he did not believe.
We should agree with Jacob in valuing the birthright but carefully reject his dishonest way of obtaining it.
Even the greatest advantage must never be sought through deceit.
Jacob's stew attracted Esau's attention.
“Let me have some of that red food!” he said.
That is why he was called Edom, meaning “red.”
The desire to satisfy bodily appetites has ruined thousands of precious souls.
Those who let their hearts follow what their eyes desire (Job 31:7), or live to serve their stomachs, will eventually suffer for it.
If we practice denying ourselves, many temptations lose much of their power.
We should not imagine that Esau was actually dying of hunger in Isaac's household.
His words seem rather to mean, “I am going to die one day.”
He was saying, in effect: “I may never live to inherit Canaan or enjoy those supposed future blessings. What difference does it make who receives them after I die?”
These were the words of a godless man, as the apostle describes him (Hebrews 12:16).
That is why Scripture condemns his contempt for the birthright.
It is foolish beyond measure to give up our share in God, Christ, and heaven for the wealth, honors, and pleasures of the present world.
Such a bargain is as bad as selling a birthright for a bowl of stew.
Esau ate and drank, satisfied his appetite, then got up and went away without serious thought or regret.
In that way he despised his birthright.
By continuing to neglect it, despising it, and justifying what he had done, he made the bargain irreversible.
People are not ruined merely because they do wrong.
They are ruined because they do wrong and refuse to repent.

row.cell: Isaac denies that Rebekah is his wife and is rebuked by Abimelech.
Isaac becomes wealthy and the Philistines envy him.
Isaac digs wells and receives God's blessing.
Abimelech makes a covenant with Isaac.

div.title: Isaac remains faithful during famine (verses 1–5)
div.p: Isaac had been raised to trust God's promise that Canaan would belong to him and his descendants.
Now famine had come upon the land, yet Isaac continued to hold fast to the covenant.
Difficult circumstances cannot diminish the true worth of God's promises to a believer.
If God has promised to be with us and we are where he wants us to be, only our own unbelief and distrust can rob us of our comfort.
Abraham's obedience to God's command was evidence of the faith through which he, a sinner, had been justified before God.
It was also the fruit of the love through which genuine faith works.
God declared his approval of Abraham's obedience to encourage others, especially Isaac, to follow his example.

div.title: Isaac deceives Abimelech (verses 6–11)
div.p: There is nothing about Isaac's denial that Rebekah was his wife that deserves imitation—or even excuse.
Isaac faced the same temptation that had overcome his father, and on two occasions.
That made his conduct even more blameworthy.
The falls of those who lived before us are like rocks on which ships have run aground.
Scripture records them as warning buoys to keep later sailors from the same danger.
This Abimelech was not the ruler who lived in Abraham's time, though both rulers behaved rightly.
When professing believers fall into sin, they bring shame upon themselves before people who do not profess true faith.

div.title: Isaac becomes prosperous, and the Philistines envy him (verses 12–17)
div.p: God blessed Isaac with a great harvest.
This should encourage poor tenants who work another person's land honestly and diligently.
The Philistines envied Isaac.
Here we see the emptiness of worldly riches: the more people possess, the more they may be envied, criticized, and harmed.
We also see how corrupt human nature can be.
What a terrible attitude it is to be miserable because someone else has received something good!
The Philistines drove Isaac out of their land.
Heavenly wisdom teaches us to give up even what we have a right to, when doing so avoids quarrels.
If people wrongfully drive us from one place, the Lord can provide room for us somewhere else.

div.title: Isaac digs wells and worships at Beersheba (verses 18–25)
div.p: Isaac faced repeated opposition as he dug wells.
Two were named for conflict and hatred.
This reveals the nature of worldly possessions: they become causes of quarrels.
Even peaceful people who refuse to start disputes cannot always prevent others from disputing with them.
What a blessing it is to have plenty of water, especially when we can enjoy it without fighting for it!
The more common a blessing becomes, the more reason we have to notice it and give thanks.
At last Isaac dug a well that no one disputed.
Those who strive to live quietly often succeed in finding peace.
When other people prove false or unkind, God remains faithful and gracious.
Indeed, he often shows that faithfulness most clearly when we are disappointed by others.
On the very night Isaac arrived at Beersheba, tired and troubled, God brought comfort to his soul.
Those who know God is with them can move from one place to another with confidence.

div.title: Abimelech makes peace with Isaac (verses 26–33)
div.p: When people's ways please the Lord, he can make even their enemies live at peace with them (Proverbs 16:7).
The hearts of kings are in God's hands.
He can turn them toward his people whenever he chooses.
There is nothing wrong with being careful when dealing with those who have treated us unfairly.
But Isaac did not insist on rehearsing every wrong they had done him.
He willingly made peace and entered into friendship with them.
True religion teaches us to be good neighbors and, as far as we can, to live at peace with everyone.
God's providence favored Isaac and blessed his work.

div.title: Esau's marriages grieve his parents (verses 34–35)
div.p: Esau acted foolishly in taking two wives at the same time.
He acted even more foolishly by marrying Canaanite women.
They were strangers to Abraham's covenant blessing and belonged to the people under Noah's curse.
His marriages grieved his parents because he had neither asked for nor received their counsel and consent.
They also grieved them because he married outside the worship of the true God.
Children who deliberately bring such distress upon godly parents have little reason to expect God's blessing.

row.cell: Isaac sends Esau to hunt for food.
Rebekah teaches Jacob how to obtain the blessing.
Jacob pretends to be Esau and receives the blessing.
Isaac trembles; Esau pleads for a blessing.
Esau threatens Jacob; Rebekah sends Jacob away.

div.title: Isaac intends to bless Esau (verses 1–5)
div.p: The promises of the Messiah and the land of Canaan had passed down to Isaac.
Isaac was now about 135 years old, and his sons about 75.
Yet he did not give proper attention to God's word about his two sons: the older would serve the younger.
Instead, he decided to give Esau, his older son, all the honor and authority included in the promise.
We are often tempted to make decisions according to our own reasoning rather than God's revelation.
When we do, we frequently lose our way.

div.title: Rebekah persuades Jacob to deceive Isaac (verses 6–17)
div.p: Rebekah knew that God intended the blessing for Jacob, and she expected him to receive it.
But she sinned against Isaac by deceiving him.
She sinned against Jacob by tempting him to do wrong.
She also placed a stumbling block before Esau, giving him an excuse to hate both Jacob and the true religion.
Everyone involved deserved blame.
This was one of those dishonest methods people adopt when trying to bring about God's promises, as though a good outcome could justify sinful means.
Many have done wrong while imagining they were helping Christ's cause.
God's answer to such reasoning is the same as his command to Abraham: “I am God Almighty; walk before me and be blameless.”
Rebekah's words were especially reckless: “Let the curse fall on me, my son.”
Christ has borne the curse of the law for all who accept the yoke of the gospel's commands.
But it is far too daring for any mere creature to say, “Let the curse fall on me.”

div.title: Jacob receives the blessing through deception (verses 18–29)
div.p: Jacob succeeded in obtaining the blessing, though not without difficulty.
The blessing was expressed in broad and general terms.
It did not explicitly mention the special mercies promised in God's covenant with Abraham.
Perhaps that was because Isaac believed he was blessing Esau.
He surely knew that Esau had despised the best things of God.
And Isaac's affection for Esau, which led him to disregard God's will, must have weakened his own faith in those promises.
We should therefore not be surprised that his blessing lacked much of the spiritual richness it might otherwise have contained.
Its limited scope reflected his own state of mind.

div.title: Esau's grief and Isaac's renewed blessing (verses 30–40)
div.p: When Esau learned that Jacob had received the blessing, he cried out with deep and bitter grief.
A day is coming when those who now despise covenant blessings and sell their spiritual inheritance for something worthless will beg for those blessings in vain.
When Isaac realized he had been deceived, he trembled violently.
Those who follow their own affections rather than God's revealed will bring confusion and distress upon themselves.
But Isaac soon recovered his composure.
He confirmed the blessing he had given Jacob: “I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed.”
Those who give up wisdom and grace, faith and a good conscience, in exchange for worldly honor, wealth, or pleasure have already judged themselves unworthy of the greater blessing.
They may pretend to be deeply concerned about it, but their final judgment will reveal their true choice.
Esau received an ordinary, earthly blessing. It was the kind of blessing he had desired.
Many people are deceived into ruin by a vague wish to be happy, without choosing the right goal or following the right path to reach it.
Multitudes go to hell with their mouths full of good wishes.
The great difference is that Esau's blessing said nothing that pointed to Christ.
Without Christ, the richness of the earth and the spoils of war will bring little lasting benefit.
So Isaac, by faith, blessed both sons according to the futures appointed to them.

div.title: Esau threatens Jacob, who leaves home (verses 41–46)
div.p: Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing he had received.
In doing so, he followed the way of Cain.
Cain murdered his brother because Abel received the favor with God that Cain had made himself unworthy to receive.
