Esau intended to prevent Jacob and his descendants from receiving authority by killing him.
People may rage against God's purposes, but they cannot change them.
Rebekah warned Jacob of the danger and told him to leave for his own safety.
Even with the most promising children, we should not presume too much on their wisdom or self-control.
We must take care to keep them away from danger and opportunities for evil.
As we read this chapter, we should remember that even the best people are examples to follow only so far as their conduct agrees with God's law.
We must never do evil so that good may come.
God overruled the wrong actions recorded here to accomplish his own purposes.
Yet his judgment upon those actions can be seen in the painful consequences suffered by everyone involved.
Jacob's special privilege was to carry spiritual blessings to all nations.
Christ, the Savior of the world, would be born within one particular family.
God chose Jacob's family rather than Esau's, according to his own wise pleasure.
He knows best what is right and has the unquestionable right to give his favors as he chooses (Romans 9:12–15).

row.cell: Esau marries a daughter of Ishmael.

div.title: Isaac sends Jacob away with a blessing (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jacob had received promises of blessing for this life and for the world to come.
Yet he was now leaving home for a life of hard work and service.
That was part of the correction he received for deceiving his father.
He would indeed receive the promised blessing, but he would also suffer for the dishonest way he had tried to obtain it.
Isaac sent Jacob away with a solemn command: he must not marry one of the daughters of Canaan.
Those who profess true faith should not marry people who have no concern for religion.
Isaac also gave him a solemn blessing.
Earlier he had blessed Jacob without knowing whom he was blessing. Now he did it deliberately.
This blessing was fuller than the first.
It was a gospel blessing, reaching beyond the earth toward heaven itself.
Canaan was a picture of that better heavenly country for which Jacob and the other patriarchs were looking.

div.title: Esau takes another wife (verses 6–9)
div.p: Good examples can make an impression even on people who are ungodly and filled with bitterness.
Yet Esau thought he could make up for his other wrongs by pleasing his parents in one matter.
People whose hearts are controlled by worldly desires are quick to imagine that they are good enough merely because they have improved in one small respect.
They overlook the ways in which they continue doing wrong.

div.title: Jacob dreams of the ladder (verses 10–15)
div.p: Jacob's conduct up to this point had hardly shown simple fear of God and trust in him.
But now he was troubled and forced to flee.
He looked to God alone for safety.
He could lie down in the open air with a stone for his pillow and sleep in peace.
Every true believer would gladly accept Jacob's hard pillow if it came with Jacob's vision.
God often visits his people with comfort when every other comfort and every other comforter has been taken away.
Jacob saw a ladder reaching from earth to heaven.
Angels were ascending and descending, and God himself stood above it.
This vision represents two things.

p.hi: First, God's providence.

div.p: Through providence, fellowship and communication continue between heaven and earth.
Jacob could therefore know that he had both a faithful Guide and a strong Protector.

p.hi: Second, Christ's mediation.

div.p: Christ himself is the ladder.
Its foot rests on earth, representing his human nature, while its top reaches heaven, representing his divine nature.
Christ is the Way.
Every blessing God gives us comes through him, and every act of service we offer to God comes through him too (John 1:51).
Through Christ, sinners may approach God's throne of grace and be accepted.
Faith enables us to see this way. Prayer enables us to draw near along it.
And God answers our prayers by supplying all the blessings of providence and grace that we need.
There is no other way for us to reach heaven except through Christ.
When faith grasps this truth, every place can become pleasant and every future prospect full of joy.
God will never leave his people until he has fulfilled his final promise to bring them into everlasting happiness.
The Lord spoke comfortingly to Jacob from the top of the ladder.
All the good news we receive from heaven comes through Jesus Christ.
The Messiah would descend from Jacob.
Christ is the great blessing of the world.
Everyone who receives God's blessing receives it in Christ. No family is excluded from that blessing except through its own refusal.
Jacob feared danger from his brother Esau, but God promised to protect him.
He faced a long journey into an unfamiliar country, but God said, “I am with you,” and promised to bring him back.
He seemed to have lost all his friends, but God assured him, “I will not leave you.”
God never abandons those whom he loves.

div.title: Jacob sets up the stone at Bethel (verses 16–19)
div.p: God made himself and his favor known to Jacob while Jacob was asleep.
The Spirit, like the wind, blows wherever he chooses.
God's grace, like dew, does not wait for human beings.
Jacob tried to make good use of the visit he had received.
Wherever we are—in a city or desert, at home or in a field, at work or in the street—we can maintain communion with heaven, unless we ourselves neglect it.
And the more we see of God, the more reason we discover for holy reverence and trembling before him.

div.title: Jacob makes a vow (verses 20–22)
div.p: Jacob made a solemn vow.
Notice, first, his faith.
He trusted God to accompany and protect him. He depended on the Lord's promise.
Notice, second, his modest desires.
He did not ask for luxurious clothing or expensive food.
If God gives us much, we should be thankful and use it for his service.
If he gives us little, we should be content and gladly enjoy God amid our limited possessions.
Notice, third, his devotion.
Above all, he wanted God to remain with him and keep him safe.
We need nothing more than that to make us truly secure and happy.
Jacob resolved to remain faithful to the Lord as his covenant God.
When God gives us extraordinary mercies, our gratitude should grow accordingly.
Giving a tenth is a fitting way to devote our resources to God and his work.
Yet the amount may be more or less, according to how God has prospered us (1 Corinthians 16:2).
Let us remember our own Bethels—the times when we made solemn promises to the Lord.
We have pledged ourselves to take him as our God and devote everything we have and everything we are to his glory.

row.cell: Jacob reaches the well near Haran.
Jacob meets Rachel; Laban welcomes him.
Jacob agrees to serve for Rachel, but Laban deceives him.

div.title: Jacob reaches the well near Haran (verses 1–8)
div.p: After enjoying sweet communion with God at Bethel, Jacob continued his journey with a cheerful heart.
Providence brought him to the field where his uncle's flocks came to drink.
The shepherds' care for their sheep can remind us of the tender love of our Lord Jesus, the great Shepherd of the church.
He is the good Shepherd who knows his sheep and is known by them.
A stone covered the mouth of the well to protect it.
Water was scarce, and this well was not available for anyone to use whenever they wished.
But having separate interests should never stop us from helping one another.
When all the shepherds arrived with their flocks, they drew water together like loving neighbors.
Kind words have great power (Proverbs 31:26).
Jacob was courteous toward these strangers, and they responded courteously to him.

div.title: Jacob meets Rachel and is welcomed by Laban (verses 9–14)
div.p: Notice Rachel's humility and diligence.
No one should be ashamed of honest, useful work.
Nor should such work stand in the way of a person's future advancement.
When Jacob discovered that Rachel was his relative, he was eager to help her.
Laban, though not especially pleasant in temperament, welcomed Jacob.
He was satisfied with Jacob's account of himself.
We should avoid being foolishly ready to believe everything we hear.
But we must also avoid becoming suspicious of others without good reason.

div.title: Jacob serves for Rachel and is deceived by Laban (verses 15–30)
div.p: Jacob was not idle during the month he spent in Laban's household as a guest.
Wherever we find ourselves, we should try to engage in some useful work.
Laban wanted Jacob to remain with him.
But a younger or less influential relative must not be taken advantage of. Honest work deserves proper reward.
Jacob told Laban that he loved Rachel.
He had no worldly property with which to provide for a marriage, so he promised to work for seven years.
Love makes long and difficult service seem short and easy.
That is why Scripture speaks of the labor of love (Hebrews 6:10).
If we learn to value the happiness of heaven properly, the sufferings of this life will seem like very little.
Even a lifetime of labor will pass like a few days for those who love God and long for Christ's appearing.
Jacob had deceived his father. Now his father-in-law deceived him in much the same way.
Laban acted unrighteously, but the Lord remained righteous in allowing Jacob to experience this reversal (Judges 1:7).
Even godly people who take a dishonest step are sometimes repaid for it during their lives on earth.
Many people who do not face Jacob's particular disappointment in marriage later discover, to their grief, that they have misunderstood their spouse's character.
Marriage should therefore be approached with thoughtful counsel and careful consideration on both sides.
There is reason to believe that Laban's explanation for his deception was not truthful.
His way of putting matters right only made them worse.
Jacob became caught up in the troubles of having more than one wife.
He could not refuse Rachel, to whom he had already committed himself, and still less could he refuse Leah.
At that time there was not yet an explicit command against taking more than one wife.
Henry regards the patriarchs' polygamy as a sin committed in ignorance.

But it cannot be used to justify the same practice now, when God's will has been made clear through the law (Leviticus 18:18) and still more fully through our Savior: one man and one woman are to be joined in marriage (1 Corinthians 7:2).

div.title: Leah's sons (verses 31–35)
div.p: The names Leah gave her sons expressed her concern both for God and for her husband.
Reuben means “See, a son!” Leah hoped, “Now my husband will love me.”
Levi means “joined.” She hoped, “Now my husband will become attached to me.”
Mutual affection is both a duty and a comfort in marriage.
Husbands and wives should seek to make themselves worthy of one another's affection (1 Corinthians 7:33–34).
Leah gratefully acknowledged God's kindness in hearing her.
Whenever something supports or comforts us in hardship, or helps to deliver us from it, we must acknowledge God as its source.
Her fourth son was called Judah, meaning “praise.”
Leah said, “Now I will praise the LORD.”
From Judah came Christ according to his human ancestry.
Whatever causes us joy should also cause us to give thanks.
New blessings should stir us to thank God more deeply for earlier blessings.
“Now I will praise the LORD”—more and better than before.
All our praise must center on Christ.
He is both the One for whom we praise God and the Mediator through whom our praise is offered.
He descended in the flesh from the man whose name means “Praise,” and he himself is our praise.
Is Christ being formed within my heart?
Then let me say: “Now I will praise the LORD.”

row.cell: Jacob makes a new agreement with Laban to work for livestock.

div.title: Rivalry in Jacob's household (verses 1–13)
div.p: Rachel envied her sister.
Envy means grieving over the good another person enjoys.
Few sins are more offensive to God or more harmful to our neighbors and ourselves.
Rachel failed to recognize that God had made the difference between her and Leah, and that she herself had advantages in other respects.
Let us carefully guard our minds against every beginning and movement of envy.
We should never resent the blessings given to our fellow servants simply because our Master has chosen to be good to them.
Jacob loved Rachel. That is why he rebuked her when she spoke wrongly.
Faithful correction can be evidence of genuine affection.
God can take the place of anything created that we lose.
But it is sinful and foolish to put a created thing in God's place, giving it the trust that belongs to God alone.
At Rachel's insistence, Jacob took her servant Bilhah as another wife.
By the custom of the time, Bilhah's children could be regarded as Rachel's children.
If Rachel had not been driven by sinful passions, she would have recognized that her sister's children were closer to her and had a stronger claim upon her love.
But children whom she could claim authority over were more attractive to her than children whom she had greater reason to love.
One early expression of that authority was her pleasure in giving Bilhah's children names that expressed rivalry with Leah.
See how envy and competition become roots of bitterness and bring trouble even among close relatives!
At Leah's insistence, Jacob then took Leah's servant Zilpah as another wife.
Consider the power of jealousy and competition.
And admire the wisdom of God's original appointment, which joins one man and one woman in marriage.
God has called us to peace and purity.

div.title: Rachel bears Joseph (verses 14–24)
div.p: The sisters' desire to become mothers of the promised Seed was good in itself.
But that desire could become excessive and disordered.
They also wanted the honor of many children and feared the shame of childlessness.
These desires helped produce their unworthy rivalry.
It seems clear that both sisters were influenced by God's promises to Abraham.
His descendants had been promised extraordinary blessings, and the Messiah was to come through his family.

div.title: Jacob's new agreement with Laban (verses 25–43)
div.p: After fourteen years of service, Jacob was ready to leave with no provision except God's promise.
Yet Laban owed him a fair reward for years of valuable work, and God intended Jacob to receive provision from it.
Rather than agree to fixed wages with a man as selfish as Laban, Jacob entrusted his cause to God.
He appears to have acted honestly, keeping only those animals whose colors had been specified in the agreement.
Laban selfishly assumed that the flocks would produce very few animals with colors different from their parents'.
Jacob's actions after the agreement have often been described as clever management.
But Henry understands them as something done at God's prompting and as a sign of his power.
In one way or another, the Lord will defend the cause of people who are oppressed and honor those who place simple trust in his providence.
Laban had no just complaint against Jacob.
Jacob received nothing more than Laban had freely agreed to give him.
Indeed, far from being harmed, Laban had greatly benefited from Jacob's work.
May we receive every blessing with thanksgiving and prayer.
Since our blessings come from God's generosity, let them always lead us back to his praise.

div.title: Jacob leaves Laban's household (verses 1–21)
div.p: Scripture gives us a detailed account of the affairs of these families, while saying nothing about what people would call the great political events of that age.
The Bible is meant to teach ordinary people the duties of daily life: how to serve God, enjoy the blessings he gives, and do good wherever he has placed them.
Selfish people imagine that anything which passes them by has been taken from them.
Greed can become so powerful that it swallows up even natural family affection.
The mistake of placing too high a value on worldly wealth lies at the root of covetousness, envy, and every kind of evil.
People whose hearts are set on this world get in one another's way. Each seems to be taking something from everyone else.
That is how discontent, jealousy, and quarrels grow.
Yet there are other riches, more than enough for everyone. Happy are those who seek them first.
Whenever we move from one place to another, we must pay attention to God's command and trust his promise.
If he is with us, we need not be afraid.
We face so many dangers that nothing else can give our hearts lasting courage.
When difficulties come, remembering earlier times when we enjoyed God's special favor and fellowship is deeply refreshing.
We should also often remember the vows we have made to him, so that we do not fail to keep them.

div.title: Laban pursues Jacob, and Rachel's idols are exposed (verses 22–35)
div.p: God can put a bridle in the mouths of wicked people and restrain their malice without changing their hearts.
Even when they have no love for God's people, they may pretend otherwise and try to make a virtue of doing what they cannot avoid.
How foolish of Laban to call things his gods when someone could steal them!
Enemies can steal what belongs to us, but they cannot steal our God.
Laban accused Jacob of things Jacob knew nothing about.
Those who entrust their cause to God are still free to defend themselves, provided they do so with gentleness and reverence.
When we read how Rachel stole her father's household images, what a sad picture of wrongdoing appears!
Nahor's family had left the idolatrous Chaldeans. Had that very family now become idolatrous itself?
Yes, it had.
They seem to have been like people in later times who swore both by the Lord and by Malcham (Zephaniah 1:5).
They were also like people in our own day who want to serve both God and wealth.
Many acknowledge the true God with their lips, while their hearts and homes remain full of spiritual idols.
A person who gives himself over to covetousness, as Laban did, has already made the world his god.
He need only live among openly idolatrous people to become an idolater himself—or at least someone who approves of their practices.

div.title: Jacob answers Laban (verses 36–42)
div.p: Jacob willingly endured the burning heat of day and the freezing cold of night to become Laban's son-in-law.
What, then, should we refuse to endure in order to become children of God?
Jacob spoke of God as his father's God.
He considered himself unworthy of God's attention, yet he was loved for his father's sake.
He called him both the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac.
Abraham had died and entered the world where perfect love casts out fear.
Isaac, however, was still alive, honoring the Lord in his heart as the one to be feared and revered.

div.title: Jacob and Laban make a covenant at Galeed (verses 43–55)
div.p: Laban could neither justify his own conduct nor prove Jacob guilty. So he wanted to hear no more about their dispute.
He would not admit his fault, as he should have done.
Instead, he proposed a covenant of friendship, and Jacob readily agreed.
They raised a heap of stones to preserve the memory of the occasion.
Henry explains this custom by saying that writing was either unknown or little used at that time.
They offered a sacrifice of peace offerings.
Peace with God gives true comfort to the peace we enjoy with our friends.
The two men then ate together, sharing the meal connected with the sacrifice.
In ancient times, people often confirmed covenants of friendship by eating and drinking together.
God is the judge between people who are in dispute, and his judgment is always right.
Whoever does wrong does so at his own peril.
They gave the place a new name meaning “heap of witness.”
After their angry exchange, they parted as friends.
God is often kinder to us than our fears lead us to expect.
He can direct the hearts of others in our favor far beyond anything we anticipated.
Trusting him is never in vain.

row.cell: Jacob's vision at Mahanaim, His fear of Esau.
Jacob's earnest prayer for deliverance, He prepares a present for Esau.

div.title: God's angels meet Jacob, and he fears Esau (verses 1–8)
div.p: God's angels appeared to Jacob to encourage him and assure him of divine protection.
When God intends to lead his people through great trials, he often prepares them with great comforts.
Jacob, to whom the promise belonged, had spent years in difficult service, while Esau had become a prince.
Jacob sent a respectful message to his brother, showing that he was not insisting on the rights of the firstborn.
Giving way can calm even serious offenses (Ecclesiastes 10:4).
We should not refuse to speak respectfully even to people who are unjustly angry with us.
Then Jacob heard that Esau was approaching with men prepared for conflict, and he was deeply afraid.
A sharp awareness of danger, and the fear it awakens, can exist alongside humble confidence in God's power and his promises.

div.title: Jacob prays and prepares a gift (verses 9–23)
div.p: Times of fear should become times of prayer.
Whatever frightens us should drive us to our knees before God.
Jacob had recently seen the angels who guarded him. But in his trouble, he turned to God, not to the angels.
He knew that the angels were servants of God, just as he was (Revelation 22:9).
Jacob's prayer is an excellent model of true prayer.
He gratefully remembered the undeserved kindness God had shown him.
He humbly confessed that he was unworthy of those blessings.
He plainly told God about his fears and his distress.
He placed the entire matter in the Lord's hands and rested all his hopes on him.
The best words we can bring to God in prayer are the words God himself has spoken to us.
In this way, Jacob made the Lord's name his strong tower, where he could find safety.
Fear did not drive Jacob into despair.
Nor did his prayer make him so presumptuous that he neglected the practical means God had given him.
God sometimes answers prayer by showing us how to arrange our affairs wisely.
Jacob sent Esau a gift in the hope of calming his anger.
We must not give up hope of reconciliation, even with those who seem most angry with us.

div.title: Jacob wrestles with the Angel (verses 24–32)
div.p: Long before daybreak, Jacob was alone, laying his fears more fully before God in prayer.
As he prayed, someone who appeared to be a man wrestled with him.
When the Spirit helps us in our weakness, our deepest and most earnest desires may be more than words can express.
We mean more than we can say. Prayer then truly becomes wrestling with God.
However severely we are tested or discouraged, we may persevere and prevail.
When we prevail with God in prayer, we will also prevail over the enemies who struggle against us.
Wrestling demands strength and unrelenting effort. It is a fitting picture of true faith and prayer.
Jacob held his ground.
The struggle lasted a long time, but it neither shook his faith nor silenced his prayer.
He was determined to receive a blessing. He would rather have every bone put out of joint than leave without one.
Those who seek Christ's blessing must resolve not to give up.
Fervent prayer is effective prayer.
The Angel gave Jacob a lasting mark of honor by changing his name.
Jacob means “supplanter.” From then on, he would be remembered not for clever schemes or cunning, but for genuine courage.
He would be called Israel, “a prince with God”—a greater title than any borne by the powerful rulers of the earth.
A true prince is someone who has power with God.
The people most worthy of honor are those who are strong in prayer.
Having prevailed with God, Jacob would also prevail with people. He would win Esau's favor.
Jacob gave the place a new name: Peniel, meaning “the face of God.”
He called it that because he had seen God's appearance there and received God's favor.
When God honors us, our proper response is to marvel at his grace.
Matthew Henry identifies the Angel who wrestled with Jacob as the second Person of the Holy Trinity.
This is the One who would later be revealed as God in the flesh, dwelling among us in human nature and called Immanuel (Hosea 12:4–5).
Jacob left the encounter limping because of his injured thigh.
That continuing weakness may have kept him from becoming proud of the extraordinary revelations he had received.
The sun rose as Jacob went on his way.
And for every soul that has enjoyed fellowship with God, it is truly a sunrise.

row.cell: The friendly meeting of Jacob and Esau.
Jacob comes to Succoth and Shalem, He builds an altar.

div.title: Jacob and Esau are reconciled (verses 1–16)
div.p: Having committed his situation to God in prayer, Jacob continued on his way.
Whatever happens, nothing can truly harm the person whose heart is firmly fixed on trusting God.
Jacob bowed before Esau.
Humble, submissive behavior can do much to turn away anger.
Esau embraced his brother.
God holds every person's heart in his hands. He can turn it whenever and however he pleases.
It is never useless to trust God or to call upon him in trouble.
When someone's ways please the Lord, God can even make that person's enemies live at peace with him.
Esau received Jacob as his brother, and the two showed one another great tenderness.
Esau asked, “Who are these people with you?”
Jacob answered this ordinary question in a way that revealed his character: he was a man whose eyes were continually turned toward the Lord.
Even after his fear had passed, Jacob urged Esau to accept his gift, and Esau took it.
It is a good thing when faith makes people generous, warmhearted, and openhanded.
But Jacob declined Esau's offer to travel with him.
It is unwise to become too closely attached to powerful relatives who do not fear God.
They may expect us to join in their worldly pleasures, or at least quietly approve of them, even while they criticize or mock our faith.
Such relationships may become a trap for us, or those relatives may take offense at us.
If we truly know the value of our souls, we will risk losing everything rather than placing them in danger.
If we truly love Christ, we will risk losing everything rather than renouncing him.
Finally, notice Jacob's tender concern for his family and his flocks.
It reminds us of the good Shepherd of our souls, who gathers the lambs in his arms, carries them close to his heart, and gently leads those nursing their young (Isaiah 40:11).
As parents, teachers, and pastors, we should all follow his example.

div.title: Jacob worships God at his new home (verses 17–20)
div.p: Jacob did more than speak words of thanks for the favor God had shown him.
He gave thanks through what he did.
He also maintained faith and worship in his family.
Wherever we have a tent, God should have an altar.
Jacob dedicated his altar to El-Elohe-Israel—“God, the God of Israel.”
In doing so, he honored the one living and true God.
He also honored the God of Israel as the God who had entered into covenant with him.
Israel's God is Israel's glory.
Blessed be his name! He is still the mighty God, the God of Israel.
May we praise his name and rejoice in his love throughout our pilgrimage on earth, and forever in the heavenly Canaan.

row.cell: The Shechemites murdered by Simeon and Levi.

div.title: Dinah and Shechem (verses 1–19)
div.p: Young people, especially young women, are safest and best cared for under the protection of godly parents.
Their lack of experience exposes them to danger, as do the flattery and schemes of wicked people who deliberately set traps for them.
They place themselves at risk when they are eager to go out, especially alone, among people who do not share true faith.
Parents are seriously at fault when they fail to prevent their children from exposing themselves to needless danger.
Children who have been allowed to do whatever they please, as Henry describes Dinah, often bring grief and shame to their families.
Dinah's stated purpose was to visit the daughters of the land—to see how they dressed and danced, and what was fashionable among them.
But Henry argues that she wanted not only to see others, but also to be seen herself.
She sought the acquaintance of the Canaanites and wanted to learn their ways.
Consider what followed from Dinah's restless wandering.
The beginning of sin is like water breaking through a barrier.
How great a blaze can begin with a small flame!
We should therefore carefully avoid opportunities for sin and even the paths that lead toward it.

div.title: Simeon and Levi's revenge against the Shechemites (verses 20–31)
div.p: The men of Shechem submitted to a sacred religious rite only because it served their immediate interests.
They wished to please their ruler and enrich themselves.
God was therefore just in bringing punishment upon them.
Nothing offers greater security than genuine religion.
But few things leave people more exposed than a mere pretense of religion.
Yet Simeon and Levi acted with the greatest injustice.
Those who do wicked things under the appearance of serving God are among the worst enemies of the truth.
They harden the hearts of many people, with destructive consequences.
Other people's sins never excuse our own.
How sadly one sin leads to another, spreading devastation like a fire!
Sinful pleasure leads to seduction.
Seduction gives rise to anger; anger develops into a thirst for revenge.
Revenge turns to deceit; deceit ends in murder; and murder is followed by further acts of lawlessness.
Henry concludes that the history of unlawful sexual relationships shows how often such wrongdoing ends in bloodshed—more often, he argues, than other kinds of sin.

row.cell: God commands Jacob to go to Beth-el, He puts away idols from his family.
Jacob builds an altar, Death of Deborah, God blesses Jacob.
Reuben's crime, The death of Isaac.

div.title: Jacob returns to Bethel and removes the idols (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jacob had forgotten Bethel.
But God reminds those he loves of duties they have neglected. He does this in one way or another, through conscience or through his providence.
When we make a vow to God, we should not delay keeping it.
Yet it is better to fulfill it late than never.
Jacob told his household to prepare not only for the journey, but also for worship.
Those who lead households should use their authority to maintain the worship of God within their families (Joshua 24:15).
The family had to put away its foreign gods.
Even in homes that appear religious and have an altar to God, much may be wrong.
There may be more idols than anyone expects.
The people were told to make themselves clean and change their clothes.
These outward acts were signs of the cleansing and renewal that must take place within the heart.
What good are clean or new clothes if the heart itself is neither clean nor new?
If Jacob had demanded the removal of those idols earlier, his family would have given them up earlier.
Sometimes efforts at reform succeed far better than we thought possible.
Jacob buried the images.
We must separate ourselves completely from our sins, just as we are separated from those who have died and been buried out of sight.
Jacob then moved from Shechem to Bethel.
The Canaanites were deeply angry at Jacob's sons for their brutal treatment of the Shechemites.
But God's power restrained them, and they did not seize the opportunity to take revenge.
The path of duty is the path of safety.
When we are carrying out God's work, we are under his special protection.
God is with us while we are with him. And if he is for us, who can stand against us?
God governs the world through hidden fears in people's minds far more often than we realize.

div.title: God renews his covenant with Jacob (verses 6–15)
div.p: The comfort believers receive through holy worship does not come chiefly from Bethel, the house of God.
It comes from El-Bethel, the God of that house.
Religious ordinances are empty if we do not meet God through them.
At Bethel, Jacob buried Deborah, Rebekah's nurse.
Her death was deeply mourned.
Long-serving members of a household who have been faithful and helpful deserve respect.
God appeared to Jacob and renewed his covenant with him.
“I am God Almighty”: God is completely sufficient, able to fulfill his promise at the proper time and to support and provide for Jacob in the meantime.
God promised Jacob two things.
He would become the father of a great nation, and he would possess a good land.
Both promises also had a spiritual meaning.
Jacob understood something of that meaning, although not as clearly or fully as we now can.
Christ is the promised Seed, and heaven is the promised land.
The promised Seed is the foundation of all God's favors, and the heavenly inheritance is their crowning completion.

div.title: Rachel's death and Benjamin's birth (verses 16–20)
div.p: Rachel once cried out passionately, “Give me children, or I will die!”
Now, after bearing children, she died.
The death of the body is the soul's departure into the world of spirits.
When will we learn that God alone truly knows what is best for his people?
In all earthly concerns, the safest course for a Christian is to say sincerely, “It is the Lord; let him do what seems good to him.”
Our safety and comfort lie in submitting our wills to his.
As Rachel was dying, she named her newborn son Ben-Oni, “son of my sorrow.”
Many sons become a source of grief to the mothers who bore them.
Mothers already suffer enough sorrow on account of their children.
Those children should therefore grow up seeking to bring their mothers joy and, as far as possible, make up for some of that grief.
But Jacob did not want every mention of the boy's name to renew the sorrow of Rachel's death.
So he renamed him Benjamin, “son of my right hand.”
The name expressed how dear Benjamin was to him: he would be the support of Jacob's old age, like a staff held in his right hand.

div.title: Reuben's sin and Isaac's death (verses 21–29)
div.p: The depth of the suffering caused by Reuben's sin is made clear in the brief words, “And Israel heard of it.”
Nothing more is said, but nothing more needs to be said.
Reuben probably thought that his father would never find out.
Yet those who count on keeping their sins secret are usually disappointed.
Scripture records Isaac's age and death, even though he did not die until after Joseph had been sold into Egypt.
Isaac lived for about forty years after he had made arrangements in expectation of his death (Genesis 27:2).
Putting our hearts and households in order early will not make us die even an hour sooner.
But it will help us die much better.
The account specifically mentions that Esau and Jacob were together in harmony at their father's funeral.
This shows how wonderfully God had changed Esau's disposition.
How terrible it is to see relatives quarreling over a little worldly property beside the graves of those they loved!
They do this even though they themselves are not far from the grave.

div.title: Esau and his descendants
div.p: The family records in this chapter show that God was faithful to his promise to Abraham.
Esau is called Edom here. That name kept alive the memory of his selling his birthright for a single meal.
Esau continued to show the same disregard for sacred and heavenly things.
In outward prosperity and honor, people who belong to God's covenant often fall behind, while those outside the covenant get ahead.
Imagine what a test of faith it must have been for the Israelites, living as slaves in Egypt, to hear about the splendor and power of Edom's kings.
Yet those who expect great things from God must be willing to wait for them.
God's time is always the best time.
Mount Seir is described as the land the Edomites possessed.
Canaan, at that point, was still only the land God had promised to Abraham's descendants.
The Edomites already held Seir, while Israel awaited Canaan.
The children of this world possess all they expect to have now, with nothing left to hope for beyond it (Luke 16:25).
God's children, by contrast, have almost nothing of their full inheritance in hand, but everything to hope for.
When all things are considered, it is incomparably better to have Canaan as a promise than to possess Mount Seir already.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections

row.cell: Joseph is loved of Jacob, but hated by his brethren.
Jacob sends Joseph to visit his brethren, They conspire his death.
Jacob deceived, Joseph sold to Potiphar.

div.title: Joseph is loved by Jacob and hated by his brothers (verses 1–4)
div.p: Joseph's history points us to Christ, who was humbled before being exalted. It also reflects the Christian's path: we must pass through many troubles before entering the kingdom.
Few accounts show so clearly the good and evil movements of the human heart, or God's remarkable providence in using both to fulfill his purposes.
Although Joseph was his father's favorite, he was not raised to be idle. Parents do not truly love their children when they spare them every task, effort, and hardship.
There is good reason why excessive pampering is called spoiling a child. Those who grow up doing nothing may end up good for nothing.
Yet Jacob made his preference obvious by dressing Joseph more finely than the rest. Parents should not favor one child over another without serious reason arising from their different conduct.
Children soon notice unequal treatment, and quarrels follow. Away from Jacob's supervision, his older sons behaved in ways they would never have dared at home.
Joseph reported their misconduct so that their father could restrain them. He was not spreading gossip to stir up discord; he acted as a faithful brother.

div.title: Joseph's dreams (verses 5–11)
div.p: God gave Joseph an early glimpse of his future promotion, to support and comfort him through the long and painful troubles that lay ahead.
Joseph dreamed of advancement, but not of imprisonment.
Many young people beginning life are much the same: they imagine only success and pleasure, never the suffering they may encounter.
Joseph's brothers understood the dreams correctly, but hated their meaning. They committed crimes to prevent the prediction from coming true, yet became the very instruments of its fulfillment.

Something similar happened with Christ. The Jews understood what he said about his kingdom. Determined that he should not reign over them, they plotted his death. By crucifying him, they opened the way to the very exaltation they wanted to prevent.

div.title: Joseph obeys his father; his brothers plot to kill him (verses 12–22)
div.p: How readily Joseph obeyed his father's instructions! Children who receive particular affection from their parents should be particularly ready to obey them.
See how deliberately his brothers plotted against him. They intended to kill him with calculated malice, in cold blood.
“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).
The sons of Jacob hated Joseph because their father loved him. New events, including his dreams, fed the resentment already festering in their hearts until they resolved to kill him.
God holds every heart in his hand. Reuben, the firstborn, had more reason than any of the others to be jealous of Joseph, yet he proved Joseph's best friend.
God overruled their actions to accomplish his own purpose: Joseph would save many people from death.
Joseph was also a picture of Christ, the beloved Son of his Father, hated by a wicked world. The Father sent him from his presence to visit us in great humility and love.
Christ came from heaven to earth to seek and save us. People plotted maliciously against him; his own people did not receive him, but crucified him.
He submitted to it willingly as part of his purpose to redeem and save us.

div.title: Joseph is sold (verses 23–30)
div.p: Joseph's brothers threw him into a pit to die of hunger and cold. How cruel were the supposed mercies of those who should have loved him!
They dismissed his distress and were not grieved by Joseph's suffering (Amos 6:6). While he languished in the pit, they sat down to eat.
They felt no remorse. Yet human wrath will praise God, and he will restrain whatever remains of it (Psalm 76:10).
Remarkably, the brothers were restrained from murdering Joseph. Just as remarkably, their decision to sell him was turned toward God's praise.

div.title: Jacob is deceived; Joseph is sold to Potiphar (verses 31–36)
div.p: Once Satan has taught people to commit one sin, he teaches them to hide it with another: theft and murder are covered with lies and false oaths.
But whoever conceals sin will not prosper for long. Joseph's brothers kept their dreadful secret for a time, but their wickedness eventually came to light and has now been made known to the world.
They sent their father Joseph's richly colored coat to cause him grief. Seeing it covered in blood, Jacob quickly assumed that a wild animal had torn Joseph apart.
Anyone who knows a parent's heart can imagine his agony.
His sons pretended to comfort him. What miserable, hypocritical comforters! If they had truly wanted to help, they could have told him the truth at once.
Sin has a strange power to harden the heart. Jacob refused to be comforted.
The more strongly we attach ourselves to any created thing, the more deeply we may suffer if it is taken away or becomes bitter to us. Excessive love often leads to excessive sorrow.
Wise parents do not raise their children in excessive luxury and ease. They cannot know what hardships their children may face before death.
The whole chapter leaves us marveling at God's providence.

The malicious brothers seem to have achieved their purpose. The merchants, interested only in profit and indifferent to what they trade, seem to have achieved theirs. Potiphar has acquired a fine young slave and has also obtained what he wanted.

Yet through all of this, God's plan is moving forward. Joseph's sale leads to Israel's descent into Egypt, then to Israel's deliverance through Moses, then to the establishment of true religion in the world, and ultimately to its spread among all nations through the gospel.
Thus human wrath will praise the Lord, and he will restrain the remainder.

p.hi: The profligate conduct of Judah and his family.

div.title: Judah and his family (whole-chapter exposition)
div.p: This chapter tells the story of Judah and his family. It is such a troubling account that we may wonder why our Lord should descend from Judah, of all Jacob's sons (Hebrews 7:14).
But God shows us that his choice rests on grace, not personal merit. Christ came into the world to save sinners, even the worst of them.
We also learn that Christ's worthiness comes from himself, not from the people among his ancestors.
How little reason the Jews, whose name came from Judah, had for the boasting described in John 8:41!
What fearful examples God gives, through his judgments, of his complete hatred of sin.
Let us seek his grace to avoid even the appearance of sin.

And let the humility of Jesus make him still dearer to us. When he came to put away sin by sacrificing himself, he submitted to being born from a family line that included people such as those described here.

row.cell: Joseph is falsely accused by his mistress.
He is cast into prison, God is with him there.

div.title: God is with Joseph in Potiphar's house (verses 1–6)
div.p: Our enemies may take away our outward signs of honor, but they cannot take away wisdom or grace.
They can separate us from friends, family, and country, but they cannot take away the Lord's presence.
They can deprive us of earthly blessings, rob us of freedom, and lock us in prison, but they cannot shut us out from fellowship with God, from the throne of grace, or from the blessings of salvation.
Joseph was blessed—wonderfully blessed—even in the house where he served as a slave.
When God is present with us, he makes what we do prosper.
Godly people are a blessing wherever they live. Faithful servants can be a blessing even if their position is low and they are little respected.
Sometimes the prosperity of wicked people comes, in one way or another, for the sake of the godly among them.
Here a wicked household was blessed because one good servant lived in it.

div.title: Joseph resists temptation (verses 7–12)
div.p: Physical beauty, in men or women, often becomes a trap both to the person who possesses it and to others.
We should therefore never become proud of beauty, and we must always watch carefully against the temptations that come with it.
We greatly need to make a covenant with our eyes, so that what we look at does not corrupt our hearts.
When lust gains control, people sacrifice decency, reputation, and conscience.
Potiphar's wife showed that her heart was entirely set on doing evil.
Satan had failed to overcome Joseph through the world's troubles and disapproval. Through them all, Joseph held firmly to his principles.
So Satan attacked him with pleasures—a temptation that has ruined more people than suffering has.
But God's grace enabled Joseph to resist and overcome. His escape was as striking a demonstration of divine power as the rescue of the three young men from the fiery furnace.
This particular sin could easily have entangled him.
The woman tempting him was his master's wife. Her favor might help him advance, while refusing her could turn her into a dangerous enemy.
The place and the time suited the temptation. And she urged him constantly and repeatedly.
Yet the almighty grace of God enabled Joseph to withstand this assault.
He remembered what he owed both to God and to his master.
Honor, justice, and gratitude all require us not to betray those who trust us, even if the betrayal could remain hidden.
Above all, Joseph would not offend his God.
He considered three things.
First, who was being tempted? He was a man in covenant with God, someone who openly professed faith and belonged to him.
Second, what was he being tempted to do? Others might call the sin a small matter, but Joseph refused to think of it that way.
Call sin by its proper name; never make it seem less serious than it is. Sins of this kind are great wickedness, exceedingly sinful.
Third, against whom would the sin be committed? Against God—against his nature, his rule, his love, and his purposes.
Those who love God therefore hate sin.
By God's grace, Joseph overcame the temptation by getting away from it. He did not remain to negotiate with it; he fled as though escaping for his life.
If we truly intend not to do evil, we must flee like a bird escaping a trap or a deer escaping a hunter.

div.title: Joseph is falsely accused (verses 13–18)
div.p: Joseph's mistress failed to make him guilty, so she sought revenge instead.
Those who have broken the restraints of decency may also disregard the restraints of truth.
It is nothing new for the best of people to be falsely accused of the worst crimes by people who are themselves deeply guilty.
How good it is to know that a day of disclosure is coming, when everyone will appear as they truly are.

div.title: God is with Joseph in prison (verses 19–23)
div.p: Joseph's master believed the accusation.
Henry considers it likely that Potiphar chose this prison because it was the worst available. But God intended it as the path toward Joseph's future honor.
God acknowledged Joseph and vindicated him.
Far from friends and relatives, he had no one to help or comfort him. Yet the Lord was with him and showed him mercy.
A person who has a clear conscience in prison has a good God there as well.
God caused the keeper of the prison to look favorably on Joseph and entrust him with responsibility for its affairs.
A good person will do good wherever he is, becoming a blessing even in imprisonment or exile.
But as we look at Joseph, let us not forget Jesus.
He suffered temptation without sin. He was slandered, persecuted, and imprisoned without cause; yet through the cross he ascended to the throne.
May God enable us to follow him in submission and suffering, and finally to the same place of glory.

row.cell: The chief butler and baker of Pharaoh in prison, Their dreams interpreted by Joseph.
The ingratitude of the chief butler.

div.title: The cupbearer's and baker's dreams (verses 1–19)
div.p: The chief cupbearer and the chief baker were troubled less by their imprisonment than by their dreams.
God has more than one way of bringing sorrow to a person's spirit.
Joseph showed compassion for them. We should care when we see sadness in the faces of our brothers and sisters.
Those who are in distress often find relief simply in being noticed.
We should also examine the causes of our own sorrow.
Is there a good reason for it? Is there no comfort sufficient to outweigh it, whatever the cause may be?
“Why are you cast down, O my soul?”
Joseph was careful to give all the glory to God.
The cupbearer's dream foretold his restoration to his position. The baker's dream foretold his death.
It was not Joseph's fault that he could bring the baker no happier news.
Ministers of God's word are likewise interpreters. They cannot change the message they have been given.
When they faithfully declare it, they are not to blame if people dislike what they hear.
Joseph did not bring up his brothers' cruelty in selling him. Nor did he dwell on the wrong done to him by his master's wife and his master.
He simply stated his own innocence.
When we must defend ourselves, we should avoid speaking badly of others as far as we can.
Let us be content to establish our innocence without reproaching others for their guilt.

div.title: The cupbearer forgets Joseph (verses 20–23)
div.p: Joseph's interpretation of both dreams came true on the exact day he had announced.
It was Pharaoh's birthday. His servants gathered before him, and the two prisoners' cases were considered.
We can all benefit from taking note of our own birthdays.
They give us an opportunity to thank God for the mercy of our birth, to grieve over the sins of our lives, and to look toward the day of our death as better than the day of our birth.
Yet it is strange that worldly people, so attached to life here, celebrate the passing of another year in their short time on earth.
Christians have reason to rejoice both that they were born and that they are drawing nearer to the end of sin and sorrow, and to everlasting happiness.
But the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph. He forgot him, even though Joseph had done him good.
We should not be surprised if love is repaid with hatred or kindness with neglect.
How quickly people at ease forget those who are still suffering!
Through this disappointment, Joseph learned to trust in God alone.
We cannot expect too little from people or too much from God.
Let us not forget our Redeemer's sufferings, promises, and love.
We blame the cupbearer for his ingratitude toward Joseph, but we are far more ungrateful toward the Lord Jesus.
Joseph only foretold the cupbearer's release. Christ actually accomplished ours, pleading for us before the King of kings.
Yet we forget him, despite frequent reminders and despite our own promises never to do so.
How poorly we repay him—like a foolish, unwise people.

row.cell: Joseph's counsel, He is highly advanced.
Joseph's children, The beginning of the famine.

div.title: Pharaoh's dreams (verses 1–8)
div.p: Pharaoh's dreams became the means by which Joseph was released from prison.

Henry says that, since God no longer speaks to us in this way, we need not pay much attention to our dreams or be eager to tell them. Recounting foolish dreams can produce little more than foolish conversation.
But these particular dreams were clearly sent by God: Pharaoh awoke deeply troubled.

div.title: Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams (verses 9–32)
div.p: God's time to deliver his people is always the most suitable time.
If the chief cupbearer had arranged Joseph's release earlier, Joseph would probably have returned to the land of the Hebrews.
Then he would not have received such blessing himself, or become such a blessing to his family.
When Joseph was brought before Pharaoh, he gave God the honor.
Pharaoh had dreamed that he was standing beside the Nile and saw both fat and thin cows emerging from it.
Henry observes that Egypt's plenty depends on the Nile's overflow rather than on rainfall.
See how many different ways Providence distributes its gifts! Yet our dependence remains on the same First Cause, who makes every creature—rain or river—what it is to us.
See how changeable the comforts of this life are. We cannot be certain that tomorrow will resemble today, or next year this one.
We must learn both how to live with little and how to live with abundance.
Notice God's goodness in sending seven years of plenty before seven years of famine, so that provisions could be stored.
The earth produces more in some seasons and less in others. Yet when all is considered together, those who gather much have nothing left over, and those who gather little lack nothing (Exodus 16:18).
Notice, too, how quickly worldly pleasures and possessions pass away.
The enormous harvests of the good years were swallowed up by the famine years. What seemed so plentiful was barely sufficient to keep the people alive.
But there is bread that lasts to eternal life. That is the bread worth working for.
Those who make earthly things their highest good will find little satisfaction in remembering that they once enjoyed them.

div.title: Joseph advises Pharaoh and is raised to power (verses 33–45)
div.p: Joseph gave Pharaoh wise counsel. A clear warning should be followed by good advice.
God has warned us in his word of a coming day of trial, when we will need all the grace we can receive.
We should therefore make provision now.
Pharaoh spoke honorably of Joseph, recognizing him as a man in whom God's Spirit was present. Such people deserve to be valued.
Pharaoh gave Joseph the marks of high rank and a name expressing the value he placed on him: Zaphnath-paaneah, which Henry explains as “revealer of secrets.”
Some have interpreted the name instead as “savior of the world.” Henry presents that as another proposed translation, not as the only possible meaning.
Joseph's advancement encourages everyone to trust God.
But all the brightest glory, even the glory of heaven, belongs to Christ.
God has entrusted the highest office to his hands and given him all authority in heaven and on earth.

div.title: Joseph prepares for the famine (verses 46–57)
div.p: In naming his sons Manasseh and Ephraim, Joseph acknowledged God's providence.
First, God made him forget his suffering. Second, God made him fruitful in the land where he had been afflicted.
The seven years of plenty came—and then they ended.
We should remember that both our times of prosperity and our opportunities to do good will come to an end.
We must not become complacent when life goes well or lazy about using our opportunities.
The good years will end. Whatever your hand finds to do, do it. Gather while there is time to gather.
Then the shortage came, and famine spread beyond Egypt into other lands.
Joseph had been diligent in storing food during the years of plenty. When famine arrived, he was prudent and careful in distributing it.
He was occupied with important and useful work.
Yet while he was doing all this, his father Jacob was saying, “Joseph is no more!”
How much trouble would vanish if only we knew the whole truth.
These events should turn our thoughts to Jesus.
Throughout the world there is a famine of the bread of life.
Go to Jesus and do whatever he tells you. Listen to his voice and come to him.
He will open his treasures and satisfy hungry souls in every age and nation, without money and without price.
But those who reject this provision must starve; his enemies will be destroyed.

row.cell: Jacob sends ten sons to buy corn.
Jacob refuses to send Benjamin to Egypt.

div.title: Jacob sends his sons to Egypt (verses 1–6)
div.p: Jacob saw that his neighbors had bought grain in Egypt and brought it home. Seeing others receive what they need can spur us to act.
Will other people find food for their souls while we starve, even though that food is available?
Once we know where help can be found, we should seek it promptly, without shrinking from the effort or resenting the expense.
This is especially true when our immortal souls are at stake.
Christ has made provision for us, but we must come to him and seek it from him.

div.title: Joseph deals sternly with his brothers (verses 7–20)
div.p: Joseph treated his brothers harshly, not to take revenge but to lead them to repentance.
When he did not see Benjamin with them, he suspected they might have disposed of him as they had disposed of Joseph.
He therefore gave them opportunities to speak about their father and brother.
In his providence, God sometimes seems harsh toward those he loves and speaks sternly to people for whom he has great mercy in store.
Joseph finally decided that one of the brothers would remain behind while the others returned home to bring Benjamin.
His statement, “I fear God,” should have encouraged them.
It was as though he said, “You can trust me not to wrong you. I dare not do so, because I know that someone greater than I am stands over me.”
We can expect fair treatment from those who truly fear God.

div.title: The brothers remember their guilt (verses 21–24)
div.p: One task of conscience is to bring back to mind things said and done long ago.
When Joseph's brothers first committed their crime, they treated it lightly and sat down to eat.
But now, many years later, their consciences accused them.
This shows one benefit of suffering: it can awaken conscience and bring forgotten sins back to our attention.
It also shows the burden of guilt for wrongs done to others.
When we think someone has wronged us, we ought to remember how we ourselves have wronged other people.
Reuben alone could look back with some comfort. He had done what he could to prevent the crime.
When others suffer, it is a great comfort to know that we did not join in their wrongdoing but spoke against it as best we could.
Joseph withdrew and wept.
His judgment told him to continue treating his brothers as strangers because they were not yet humbled enough.
But his natural love for them still moved him deeply.

div.title: The brothers return with grain and money (verses 25–28)
div.p: The brothers came seeking grain, and grain they received.
More than that, each found that his money had been returned.
Christ, like Joseph, provides what we need without money and without price. Even the poorest are invited to come and receive.
But a guilty conscience often interprets God's kindness as a threat.
People burdened by guilt may read evil meanings into events that are actually working for their good.

div.title: Jacob refuses to send Benjamin (verses 29–38)
div.p: Jacob was deeply troubled by the report his sons brought home.
Even the money Joseph had kindly returned frightened him.
He blamed his sons, fearing that they had provoked the Egyptians and had wrongfully taken back the money.
Jacob plainly distrusted them. He remembered that he had never seen Joseph again after Joseph went away with them.
A family is in a sad state when children behave so badly that their parents no longer know whether they can trust them.
Jacob regarded Joseph as lost and Simeon and Benjamin as endangered.
“All these things are against me,” he concluded.
But it turned out that all of them were working for his good and the good of his family.
We often think that something is against us when it is actually working in our favor.
We suffer in our health, possessions, reputation, and relationships and suppose that everything is against us.
Yet those very troubles can be working for us an eternal weight of glory.
So the Lord Jesus sometimes hides himself and his favor, correcting people for whom he has loving purposes.
Through painful correction and humbling conviction, he breaks the stubbornness and pride of the heart and brings people to true repentance.
Even before sinners fully know him or experience his grace, he seeks their good and sustains them as they wait for him.
May we do the same: refuse discouragement, look for no other refuge, and humble ourselves more and more under his mighty hand.
At the right time, he will answer our prayers and do more for us than we expect.

row.cell: Jacob is persuaded to send Benjamin into Egypt.
Joseph's reception of his brethren, their fears.
Joseph makes a feast for his brethren.

div.title: Jacob agrees to send Benjamin (verses 1–14)
div.p: Jacob urged his sons to go and buy a little more food. In a time of shortage, even a little must be enough.
Judah insisted that Benjamin must go with them.
Children do not dishonor their parents or neglect their duty when they humbly offer advice and, when necessary, reason with them.
Jacob saw that there was no alternative and agreed.
His prudence and fairness appeared in three decisions.
First, he sent back the money found in their sacks.
Honesty requires us to return not only what we obtained through our own fault but also what reached us through someone else's mistake.
Even when something comes to us by an oversight, keeping it after discovering the error is dishonest.
Second, Jacob sent twice as much money as before. Grain prices might have risen, or they might have to pay a ransom for Simeon.
Third, he sent a gift of products available in Canaan but scarce in Egypt, including balm and honey.
Providence does not distribute the same gifts everywhere.
Yet honey and spices cannot replace grain for bread.
Canaan was suffering from severe famine, but it still had balm, myrrh, and similar goods.
We can live adequately on plain food without delicacies, but we cannot live on delicacies without ordinary food.
Let us thank God that what we most need and find most useful is generally the most common and affordable.
People prize gold, silver, and the luxury products of each country.
But in a famine they readily exchange them for bread.
How little use will earthly treasures be on the day of wrath!
How readily we should count them all as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Jesus Christ.
If we wish to prevail with people, we should first prevail with God in earnest prayer.
Yet every request for the blessings of this life, and every request to be spared its sufferings, should end with “Your will be done.”

div.title: Joseph receives his brothers; they are afraid (verses 15–25)
div.p: Jacob's sons returned to Egypt for a second time to buy grain.
If we ever experience a famine of God's word, we should not complain about having to travel as far for spiritual food as these men did for physical food.
Joseph had instructed his steward to bring them into his house.
Even this frightened them. Those who are burdened by guilt tend to interpret everything in the worst possible light.
But the steward reassured them.
His words suggest that Joseph, a good master, had introduced him to the knowledge of the true God, the God of the Hebrews.
Faithful servants should take suitable opportunities to speak seriously and reverently about God and his providence.

div.title: Joseph prepares a feast for his brothers (verses 26–34)
div.p: Notice the deep respect Joseph's brothers showed him. In this way his dreams were increasingly fulfilled.
Joseph treated them with great kindness and generosity.
But notice also how early the distinction between Jews and Gentiles appears in this account.
In a famine, receiving enough food would have been a great blessing. Instead, they were given a feast.
Their worries and fears were now gone. They ate joyfully, believing that they were at peace with the ruler of the land.
If God accepts our work and what we bring before him, we have reason to rejoice.
Joseph showed special favor to Benjamin, testing whether his brothers would envy him.
We should be content with what we have and not resent what others possess.
Likewise, Jesus increasingly shows those he loves how much they need him.
He teaches them that he is their only refuge from destruction, overcomes their reluctance, and brings them to himself.
Then, when he sees fit, he lets them taste his love and welcomes them to the provision of his house as a foretaste of the greater blessings he intends for them.

row.cell: Joseph's policy to stay his brethren, and try their affection for Benjamin.

div.title: Joseph tests his brothers' love for Benjamin (verses 1–17)
div.p: Joseph wanted to discover how his brothers now felt about Benjamin.
If they still envied and hated Rachel's other son as they had hated Joseph, or if they still showed the same lack of concern for their father Jacob, their behavior would now reveal it.
When the cup was found in Benjamin's sack, they had an excuse to leave him behind as a slave.
But we cannot judge what people are now only by what they used to be, or predict what they will do simply by what they have done.
Joseph's steward accused them of ingratitude: they were repaying kindness with wrongdoing.
He also accused them of foolishness. Why steal a cup used every day, which would quickly be missed and carefully sought?
Henry explains that the steward's accusation can be understood in two ways.
Joseph might have had a particular attachment to the cup, so that he would search thoroughly for it if it disappeared.
Or Joseph might have left it at their table deliberately to see whether they were honest.
The brothers placed themselves at Joseph's mercy and acknowledged that God's judgment was righteous.
Perhaps they were thinking of their old wrong against Joseph and believed that God was now calling them to account for it.
Even when people wrong us and we suffer unjustly at their hands, we must still acknowledge that God is righteous and that he brings our sins to light.

div.title: Judah pleads for Benjamin (verses 18–34)
div.p: Even if Joseph had been a complete stranger to the family, as Judah supposed, Judah's powerful appeal could hardly have failed to move him.
But neither Jacob nor Benjamin needed an intercessor to persuade Joseph to love them. He already loved them.
Judah now remained faithfully at Benjamin's side in his distress.
Much later, that loyalty was repaid when the tribe of Benjamin remained with the tribe of Judah after the other tribes had abandoned it.
When the apostle discusses Christ's mediation, he notes that our Lord descended from Judah (Hebrews 7:14).
Christ not only interceded for transgressors; he became their Surety, showing tender concern for both his Father and his brothers and sisters.
Jesus, the great fulfillment of what Joseph foreshadows, humbles and tests his people even after they have enjoyed some of his kindness.
He brings their sins back to mind so that they may truly repent, show their repentance, and recognize how much they owe to his mercy.

row.cell: Joseph comforts his brethren, and sends for his father.
Pharaoh confirms Joseph's invitation, Joseph's gifts to his brethren.
Jacob receives the news of Joseph's being alive.

div.title: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers (verses 1–15)
div.p: Joseph allowed Judah to finish his appeal and listened to everything he had to say.
He saw that his brothers had been humbled for their sins. They had not forgotten Joseph, whom Judah had mentioned twice.
They showed respect for their father and deep tenderness toward Benjamin.
Now they were ready to receive the comfort Joseph intended to give them by revealing himself.
Joseph sent all his attendants out of the room.
In a similar way, Christ reveals himself and his loving kindness to his people beyond the sight and hearing of the world.
Joseph wept with tender and powerful affection. His tears swept away the sternness he had shown his brothers until then.
This reflects God's compassion toward sinners who return to him in repentance.
“I am Joseph, your brother.”
Those words must have humbled them still more because they had sold him. Yet the words also encouraged them to hope for kindness from him.
When Christ confronted Paul, he said, “I am Jesus.” When he comforted his disciples, he said, “It is I. Do not be afraid.”
When Christ reveals himself to his people, he invites them to draw near with sincere hearts.
Joseph likewise drew his brothers near, explaining that God had brought good out of the evil they had intended against him.
Sinners must still grieve over their sin and be angry with themselves, even when God brings good from their wrongdoing. They deserve no credit for the good he produces.
The likeness between Joseph's reconciliation and Christ's revelation of himself to a sinner's soul is remarkable.
When Christ makes himself known, the sinner does not begin to think that sin is a smaller evil, but a greater one.
Yet knowing what God has done protects the sinner from despair.
The believer can rejoice in God's saving work even while trembling at the danger and ruin from which he has escaped.
Joseph promised to provide for his father and the entire family.
Children must support and provide for their parents, as fully as they are able, whenever their parents need it. This is how they show godliness at home (1 Timothy 5:4).
Joseph embraced Benjamin, then embraced all his brothers. Afterward they spoke freely with him about their father's household.
Likewise, the signs of true reconciliation with the Lord Jesus are followed by the sweetness of communion with him.

div.title: Pharaoh welcomes Joseph's family (verses 16–24)
div.p: Pharaoh showed kindness to Joseph and, for Joseph's sake, to his relatives.
What they lost by moving would be made up to them in Egypt.
In the same way, those for whom Christ has prepared heavenly glory should not cling to worldly possessions.
Even the finest earthly treasures are only baggage. We cannot be sure we will keep them here, much less carry them away when we die.
We must not fasten our eyes or hearts on the world.
Better things await us in the blessed land where Christ, our true Joseph, has gone to prepare a place.
As Joseph sent his brothers away, he gave them a timely warning: “Do not quarrel on the way.”
He knew their tendency to argue. Having forgiven them all, he now forbade them to accuse one another.
Our Lord Jesus likewise commands us to love one another and not to quarrel, whatever has happened or may happen.
We are brothers and sisters, and we have one Father.
We have all been guilty. Rather than turning against one another, we have reason to be displeased with ourselves.
We have offended God, and we either have received or hope to receive his forgiveness. We should therefore be ready to forgive one another.
We, too, are on the way.
We are passing through a land like Egypt, where many eyes watch us and some seek an opportunity to accuse us.
But our road leads to the heavenly Canaan, where we hope to live forever in perfect peace.

div.title: Jacob learns that Joseph is alive (verses 25–28)
div.p: The news that Joseph was alive seemed too good to be true. Jacob was overwhelmed because he could not believe it.
We, too, grow weak when we fail to believe.
At last he was convinced.
Jacob was old and did not expect to live much longer. He wanted to see Joseph once more before his eyes closed forever.
Then he would need nothing else in this world to make him happy.
Consider Jesus revealing himself as a Brother and Friend to those who had once despised him and been his enemies.
He assures them of his love and of the riches of his grace.
He commands them to cast aside envy, anger, malice, and strife and to live in peace with each other.
He teaches them to abandon the world for him and for all his fullness.
He supplies everything needed to bring them home to himself, so that they may be where he is.
When he finally calls his people to himself, they may still feel doubts and fears for a time.
But the thought of seeing his glory and being with him will enable them to say, “It is enough. I am willing to die, because I am going to see and be with the One my soul loves.”

row.cell: Jacob and his family go to Egypt.
Joseph meets his father and his brethren.

div.title: God encourages Jacob (verses 1–4)
div.p: Even when an undertaking looks especially joyful, we should seek the Lord's counsel, help, and blessing.
As we take part in the worship he has appointed and receive assurances of his covenant love, we look for his presence and the peace that comes with it.
Every move from one home to another should remind us that one day we must leave this world.
Only Christ's presence can enable us to pass through the valley of the shadow of death without fear.

div.title: Jacob's family travels to Egypt (verses 5–27)
div.p: We are given a detailed account of Jacob's family.
God's promises are certain to come true, yet their fulfillment is often slow.
Henry notes that 215 years had passed since God promised Abraham that he would become a great nation (Genesis 12:2).
Yet the branch of Abraham's descendants in which the promise would surely be fulfilled had grown to only seventy people.
This careful record was kept to show God's power in making those seventy grow into an enormous multitude.

div.title: Joseph welcomes his family (verses 28–34)
div.p: It was only right that Pharaoh should know that a family had come to settle in his territory.
When others trust us, we must never repay that trust by deceiving them.
How would Joseph arrange things for his brothers?
Once they had plotted to get rid of him. Now he was planning how to settle them where they would prosper.
This is what it means to repay evil with good.
Joseph wanted them to live together in Goshen, near Canaan.
The Egyptians despised shepherds. Yet Joseph did not want his brothers to be ashamed to tell Pharaoh that shepherding was their occupation.
He could perhaps have obtained positions for them at court or in the army.
But such advancement might have aroused Egyptian jealousy and tempted them to forget Canaan and God's promise to their fathers.
There is nothing disgraceful about honest work.
We should be ashamed of being idle or having no useful occupation, not of doing humble work.
Usually it is best to remain in the occupation we know and have been trained to do.
Whatever work or position God has given us through his providence, we should adapt to it, be content with it, and not set our hearts on high status.
It is better to bring honor to a humble post than disgrace to an exalted one.
If we wanted to ruin our own souls or those of our children, we might chase great things for ourselves and for them.
But if we do not want that, we should be content when we have food and clothing.

row.cell: Joseph presents his brethren to Pharaoh.
Joseph's dealings with the Egyptians during the famine.
Jacob's age. His desire to be buried in Canaan.

div.title: Joseph presents his brothers to Pharaoh (verses 1–6)
div.p: Joseph had become a powerful man, especially in Egypt, but he was not ashamed to acknowledge his brothers.
The rich and influential should never overlook or despise their poorer relatives.
Our Lord Jesus is not ashamed to call us his brothers and sisters.
Pharaoh asked the brothers what work they did.
They answered that they were shepherds and had come to stay only for a time, while the famine continued in Canaan.
Pharaoh offered to employ them as shepherds if they were capable and hardworking.
Whatever our occupation, we should aim to do it well and show ourselves skillful and diligent.

div.title: Jacob blesses Pharaoh (verses 7–12)
div.p: Jacob prayed that the Lord would bless Pharaoh.
He did so with the dignity of old age, the devotion of a true believer, and the authority of a patriarch and prophet.
He was not ashamed of his faith. He also wanted to show gratitude to the ruler who had helped him and his family.
Jacob then gave a remarkable answer to an ordinary question.
He called his life a pilgrimage: the journey of a stranger living in a foreign land on the way to his true home.
Earth was not his permanent home. His dwelling, inheritance, and treasure were in heaven.
He counted his life in days.
Even measured that way, life is quickly numbered, and none of us can be sure of having even one more day.
Let us therefore learn to number our days.
Jacob said his days had been few. Although he was 130 years old, that was very little compared with eternity.
He said his days had also been difficult.
Human life is short and full of trouble. Since our days are marked by evil, it is well that they are few.
Jacob had lived through much suffering and had aged more quickly than some of his ancestors.
Young people should not be proud of their strength or beauty.
Neither should older people be proud of their age or gray hair, though others rightly show them respect.
Even those thought very old today do not reach the ages of the patriarchs.
Gray hair is a crown of glory only when it is found along the path of righteousness.
Jacob's answer must have reminded Pharaoh that earthly success and happiness cannot last or finally satisfy us.
After a life of emptiness and distress, everyone enters the grave, whether from a throne or a cottage.
Only the prospect of a lasting home in heaven can give us true happiness after our brief and weary journey on earth.

div.title: Joseph provides for the Egyptians during the famine (verses 13–26)
div.p: Once Jacob and his family had been provided for—the particular mercy that God intended in raising Joseph to power—the account turns to the preservation of Egypt itself.
There was no bread, and the people were close to death.
See how completely we depend on God's providence.
All our wealth could not save us from starvation if rain failed for two or three years.
We are utterly dependent on God's mercy. Let us remain in his love.
See also how much suffering is caused by our own lack of care.
If the Egyptians had stored grain during the seven years of plenty, they would not have been so desperate.
But they ignored the warning.
Silver and gold could not feed them; they needed grain.
People will give everything they possess to preserve their lives.
Henry cautions that Joseph's actions here should not be judged by the standards of his own later age. He notes that the Egyptians regarded Joseph as a public benefactor.
In Henry's assessment, Joseph acted consistently with his character, dealing between Pharaoh and the people in the fear of God.
The Egyptians themselves said to Joseph, “You have saved our lives.”
How many people will gratefully say to Jesus on the last day, “You saved our souls from the most dreadful destruction, when our need was greatest!”
The Egyptians surrendered their property, and even their freedom, to stay alive.
Should we then think it too much to count everything as loss and surrender all at Christ's command?
For his sake we can do so, because he saves our souls and promises to give us a hundredfold, even in this present world.
If Christ has saved us, we will gladly become his servants.

div.title: Jacob prepares to die (verses 27–31)
div.p: At last the time approached when Israel would die.
He had been a prince with God, had wrestled with the Angel, and prevailed. Yet he still had to die.
Joseph's provision of bread had saved him from death by famine, but could not protect him from death through old age or illness.
Jacob died by degrees, like a candle slowly burning down to its socket. He could see death approaching.
It is a mercy to recognize death's approach before feeling its full force, so that we are moved to do with all our strength whatever work remains.
But death is never very far from any of us.
As Jacob approached it, his concern was where he would be buried—not how grand his funeral would be.
He wanted to be buried in Canaan because it was the promised land.
Canaan pointed toward heaven, the better country he was waiting for (Hebrews 11:14).
Nothing eases a dying believer's heart more than the sure prospect of rest in the heavenly Canaan.
