When this request was settled, Jacob bowed at the head of his bed and worshiped God, as explained in Hebrews 11:21.
He thanked God for all his kindnesses, supported himself despite his weakness, and showed that he was willing to leave this world.
Even those who lived on Joseph's food—and even Jacob, whom Joseph loved so dearly—had to die.
But Jesus Christ offers the true bread, which we may eat and live forever.
Let us come to him and surrender ourselves to him.
As death draws near, the One who sustained us in life will meet us and assure us of everlasting salvation.

div.title: Joseph visits Jacob on his deathbed (verses 1–7)
div.p: The deathbeds of believers, together with their final prayers and counsel, can make a lasting impression on young people, those who live lightly, and those enjoying prosperity.
When it is appropriate, it is good to bring children to witness such moments.
If the Lord allows, it is a precious thing to bear witness at the end of life to his truth, his faithfulness, and the goodness of his ways.
We should aim to live in such a way that our dying words carry weight.
All true believers are blessed in death, though not everyone dies with the same abundance of spiritual comfort.
Jacob adopted Joseph's two sons.
He did not want them chiefly to inherit their father's wealth and influence in Egypt, but to share in the promised inheritance given to Abraham.
Through this act, the dying patriarch taught the young men to choose their place among God's people.
He appointed each to become the head of a tribe.
Those who, by God's grace, resist the temptations of worldly riches and advancement in order to embrace true faith—even in poverty or disgrace—are worthy of special honor.
Jacob wanted Ephraim and Manasseh to understand that it is better to occupy a humble place within God's people than a high place outside them.

div.title: Jacob blesses Ephraim and Manasseh (verses 8–22)
div.p: These two godly men recognized God's hand in their blessings.
Joseph said, “These are my sons, whom God has given me.”
Jacob said, “God has allowed me to see your children.”
Our blessings become doubly sweet when we recognize that they come from God's hand.
He does more than prevent what we fear; he exceeds what we hope for.
Jacob spoke of the care God had shown him all his life.
He had endured many hardships, but God had protected him from the evil in them.
As he approached death, Jacob looked forward to being redeemed forever from sin and sorrow.
Christ, the Angel of the covenant, redeems his people from every evil.
In Scripture, deliverance from misery and danger by God's power, coming through the ransom of Christ's blood, is often called redemption.
When Jacob blessed Joseph's sons, he deliberately crossed his hands.
Joseph wanted his firstborn to receive the leading blessing and would have rearranged his father's hands.
But Jacob was not confused, nor did he simply prefer one boy out of personal affection.
He acted by the Spirit of prophecy and according to God's direction.
God distributes blessings differently among his people.
He gives some more gifts, graces, comforts, and earthly blessings than others.
Often those we least expect to receive the most are the very ones God chooses.
He chooses the weak things of this world and lifts the poor out of the dust.
Grace does not follow the natural order, and God does not always give preference to the people we think most deserving.
He acts according to his own good pleasure.
How poor are people whose only riches belong to this world!
And how terrible it is to approach death with no solid hope of good—only fearful expectations of unending evil.

row.cell: Jacob calls his sons to bless them.
Jacob's charge respecting his burial, His death.

div.title: Jacob gathers his sons (verses 1–2)
div.p: All Jacob's sons were still alive.
By calling them together, he instructed them to remain united in love and not blend into the Egyptian people.
He also foretold that they would not be separated from one another, as the sons of Abraham and of Isaac had been. Instead, they would form one people.
We should not read Jacob's words merely as an expression of personal affection, resentment, or favoritism.
Henry understands them as the words of the Holy Spirit, declaring God's purposes for the character, circumstances, and future situation of the tribes descended from Jacob's sons.
Their later history shows how those purposes unfolded.

div.title: Reuben, Simeon, and Levi (verses 3–7)
div.p: Reuben was the firstborn, but through a serious sin he forfeited his birthright.
Jacob described him as unstable as water.
People often fail to prosper because they never settle firmly on a course.
Reuben's sin brought lasting disgrace on his family.
If we avoid doing evil, we need not fear having our deeds brought to light.
Simeon and Levi were hot-tempered and revengeful.
Their murder of the Shechemites revealed their character, and Jacob condemned that barbaric act.
Our souls are our honor. Their powers distinguish us from the animals that perish and raise us above them.
We should sincerely detest people who delight in bloodshed and harm.
“Cursed be their anger.”
Jacob cursed not their persons, but their sinful passions.
“I will divide them.”
For Levi, that judgment was later turned into a blessing.
The Levites served God acceptably when they acted with zeal against those worshiping the golden calf (Exodus 32).
God set them apart for the priesthood, and in that role they were scattered among the people of Israel.

div.title: Judah and the promised Messiah (verses 8–12)
div.p: The name Judah means “praise.”
God was praised when Judah was born (Genesis 29:35), praised by him, and praised in him.
It was fitting that his brothers should praise him.
Judah would become a strong and courageous tribe.
He was pictured not as a lion roaming furiously and causing distress, but as one resting peacefully in the satisfaction of his power and success.
That is a picture of true greatness.
Judah would become the royal tribe, the line from which the Messiah, the Prince, would come.
Shiloh, the promised Seed through whom the earth would be blessed, would come from Judah.
Henry gives the name the sense of “the peaceful and prosperous One” or “Savior.”
From far away in history, the dying Jacob saw the day of Christ.
That hope comforted and sustained him on his deathbed.
Judah retained authority until Christ's coming.

After Christ's crucifixion, according to Henry, that authority was diminished. As Jesus had foretold, Jerusalem was destroyed, and the remaining Jewish people, scattered and afflicted, were mingled together.
Much of the blessing pronounced over Judah applies to our Lord Jesus.
Christ has an abundance of everything that nourishes and refreshes the soul, sustains spiritual life, and fills it with joy.
He is the true Vine.
Wine is the appointed symbol of his blood: blood shed for sinners, received through faith, and truly life-giving.
All the blessings of the gospel are offered like wine and milk, without money or payment.
Every thirsty soul is welcome (Isaiah 55:1).

div.title: Zebulun, Issachar, and Dan (verses 13–18)
div.p: If prophecy declares that Zebulun will become a haven for ships, we may be certain that Providence will place his people there.
God determines the boundaries of the places where we live.
It is our wisdom and duty to accept our circumstances and make good use of them.
If Zebulun lives near the sea, let him make that shore a haven for ships.
Issachar saw that the land was pleasant.
It offered both beautiful views and fruitful harvests to reward his labor.
With the eyes of faith, let us see how good the rest of heaven is and how delightful that promised land will be.
That hope makes our present duties easier.
Dan would gain advantage over his enemies through skill, strategy, and surprise, like a serpent striking a traveler's heel.
Jacob was almost spent and near fainting.
He refreshed himself with the words, “I have waited for your salvation, O Lord!”
The salvation he awaited was Christ, the promised Seed.
As Jacob prepared to be gathered to his people, he longed for the One to whom the people would be gathered.
He openly confessed that he sought heaven, the better country (Hebrews 11:13–14).
Now he was about to enjoy that salvation, and it comforted him to know that he had waited for it.
We must wait upon Christ as our way to heaven, and wait for heaven as our rest in Christ.
For a dying believer, it is a deep comfort to have waited for the Lord's salvation, because at last he will receive what he has been waiting for.

div.title: Gad, Asher, and Naphtali (verses 19–21)
div.p: In speaking of Gad, Jacob alluded to his name, which means “troop,” and foretold the character of his tribe.
God's cause and God's people may for a time seem beaten down and defeated, but they will finally be victorious.
This is also a picture of the Christian's struggle.
The grace at work in the soul may seem to lose its battles when bands of sinful desires overcome it.
But the cause belongs to God.
In the end, grace will prevail, making the believer more than a conqueror (Romans 8:37).
Asher would become a prosperous tribe.
His inheritance bordered on Carmel, a place proverbial for its fruitfulness.
Naphtali is described as a deer set free.
Henry takes this as a description of the tribe's character.
Unlike the hard-working ox or donkey, it would prize freedom and ease.
It would be lively and quick to act, though less distinguished by steady, persistent labor.
It would also resemble a petitioner who uses gracious words to ask for mercy.
People with different temperaments and gifts should not criticize or envy one another.

div.title: Joseph and Benjamin (verses 22–27)
div.p: Jacob's blessing upon Joseph was especially rich.
What he said was both a history of Joseph's past and a prophecy of what would come.
Jacob recalled the many hardships and fiery arrows of temptation Joseph had endured.
Through those trials, Joseph's faith had not failed.
He carried his burdens steadily and did nothing unworthy of his calling.
All the strength we have to resist temptation and bear suffering comes from God.
His grace is enough.
Joseph became the shepherd of Israel, caring for his father and family.
He was also the stone of Israel, the foundation and strong support on which they depended.
In these ways Joseph foreshadowed the Good Shepherd and the tested Cornerstone of God's whole church.
The blessings promised to Joseph's descendants pointed toward the vast and everlasting blessings given to Christ's spiritual offspring.
Jacob blessed all his sons, but Joseph especially, calling him the one “separated from his brothers.”
That separation meant more than his years in Egypt.
He had also been raised to exceptional honor and had shown unusual devotion to God.
Of Benjamin Jacob said, “He shall devour like a wolf.”
The words came through the Spirit of prophecy, not through Jacob's natural preferences.
Otherwise he would have spoken more tenderly of Benjamin, whom he loved so dearly.
Instead, he foretold that Benjamin's descendants would become a warlike people—strong, bold, active, and enriched by the spoils of their enemies.
The apostle Paul belonged to this tribe (Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5).
Early in life he attacked like a wolf, devouring prey as a persecutor.
Later he distributed the spoils as a preacher of the gospel.
In doing so, he shared in the victory of the Lion of Judah and helped to advance his triumphs.

div.title: Jacob gives his final instructions and dies (verses 28–33)
div.p: Jacob blessed each son according to the blessings God intended eventually to give his descendants.
He instructed them about his burial place because he believed God's promise that Canaan would one day belong to his offspring.
When he had finished speaking his blessings and instructions, his testimony was complete.
He then prepared for the work of dying.
He drew his feet up into the bed.
This was not only a sign of patient submission to death, but also of someone gladly settling down to rest after a long and weary life.
He freely entrusted his spirit to God, the Father of spirits.
If God's people are our people, death will gather us to them.
Under the care of Israel's Shepherd, we will lack nothing necessary for body or soul.
We will remain here until our work is finished.
Then, breathing our souls into the hands of the One whose salvation we have awaited, we will depart in peace and leave a blessing to our children.

row.cell: Joseph's brethren crave his pardon, He comforts them.
Joseph's direction concerning his bones, His death.

div.title: Joseph mourns his father (verses 1–6)
div.p: When godly relatives or friends die, we may grieve our loss even if they lived to a good old age and we are confident they have gone to glory.
It is right to honor their memory by mourning them.
Grace does not destroy natural affection.
Instead, it purifies, moderates, and directs it.
We can no longer show tokens of affection to the departed soul.
Yet it is fitting to honor the body, from which we hope for a glorious and joyful resurrection, whatever may happen to its remains in this world.
Joseph showed both faith in God and love for his father.
He ordered Jacob's body to be embalmed, or preserved by wrapping it with spices.
Notice how frail and lowly our bodies become once the soul has departed.
Without preservation, they quickly decay and become offensive.

div.title: Jacob is buried (verses 7–14)
div.p: Jacob's body was accompanied not only by his family, but also by the leading people of Egypt.
As the Egyptians came to know the Hebrews better, they began to respect them.
Those who profess faith should seek, through wisdom and love, to overcome other people's prejudices against them.
Onlookers recognized how deeply everyone mourned.
The death of godly people is a loss to any place, and it deserves sincere lament.

div.title: Joseph forgives and reassures his brothers (verses 15–21)
div.p: Many reasons may have led Jacob's sons to remain in Egypt, despite Abraham's prophetic vision that his descendants would one day suffer bondage there.
Judging Joseph by the usual tendencies of human nature, they feared that he would now avenge himself on those who had hated and injured him without reason.
They could neither resist him nor run away.
So they sought to soften his heart by humbling themselves.
They pleaded as servants of the God whom Jacob had worshiped.
Joseph was deeply moved to see his dreams so completely fulfilled.
He told them not to fear him, but to fear God—to humble themselves before the Lord and seek his forgiveness.
He assured them that he himself would continue to treat them kindly.
What an excellent spirit Joseph showed!
Let us learn from him to repay evil with good.
He comforted his brothers and spoke tenderly to them, removing their fears.
People whose spirits have been broken need to be supported and encouraged.
If we love and forgive people, we must not only do good to them. We should speak kindly to them as well.

div.title: Joseph gives instructions about his bones and dies (verses 22–26)
div.p: Joseph had honored his father, and his days were long in the land God had given him for the time being.
When he knew his own death was approaching, he comforted his brothers with God's promise that their people would return to Canaan in due time.
We should comfort others with the comfort God has given us and encourage them to depend on the promises that sustain us.
To declare his own faith and strengthen theirs, Joseph instructed them not to bury his remains permanently until the great day when his people would settle in the promised land.
By faith in the resurrection and in God's promise of Canaan, Joseph gave instructions concerning his bones.
Those instructions would help keep alive the expectation of their departure from Egypt.
They would constantly turn the people's thoughts toward Canaan and keep Joseph's descendants closely bound to their brothers.
Joseph's death, like his life, showed the excellence of his faith.
Both encourage us to persevere in serving God.
How blessed it is to begin the race toward heaven early, continue steadfastly, and finish the course with joy.
Joseph did so, and by God's grace we may do the same.
Even when death's pains come, if we have trusted the One in whom the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles trusted, we need not fear to say:
“My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.”

div.title: Exodus — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: The book of Exodus tells how the children of Israel became a church and a nation.
Until now, we have seen true religion expressed mainly in family life.
Here we begin to see how it shapes the affairs of kingdoms and nations.
The name Exodus means “departure.”
The central event in the book is Israel's departure from Egypt and the bondage it suffered there.
That deliverance shows the fulfillment of several promises and prophecies God had given Abraham concerning his descendants.
It also foreshadows the church's journey through the wilderness of this world toward the heavenly Canaan, where it will find eternal rest.

div.title: Original chapter outline — corrected verse references

row.cell: The children of Israel increase in Egypt after the death of Joseph.
They are oppressed, but multiply exceedingly.

div.title: The children of Israel multiply (verses 1–7)
div.p: For more than two hundred years, while Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived in freedom, the Hebrew people increased only slowly.
Only about seventy people went down to Egypt.
Yet in roughly the same length of time, even under cruel slavery, they became a great nation.
This remarkable growth fulfilled the promise God had made long before to their fathers.
God may sometimes take a long time to fulfill his promises, but their fulfillment is always certain.

div.title: Israel is oppressed in Egypt (verses 8–14)
div.p: Egypt became a place of slavery for Israel.
A place where we once found happiness may soon become the place where we suffer.
What we once welcomed with the words “This same shall comfort us” may become our heaviest burden.
We must not put our trust in people or say of any place short of heaven, “Here I will rest.”
Everyone who knew Joseph loved him and treated his brothers kindly for his sake.
But even the best and most useful service someone renders to others is quickly forgotten after that person dies.
Our chief concern must be to serve and please God.
Unlike human beings, he is not unjust. He will never forget our work or our labor of love.
Israel's supposed offense was its prosperity.
Nothing is more hateful to a wicked person than to see the righteous flourish.
The Egyptians feared that the Israelites would join Egypt's enemies and escape from the land.
Wickedness is cowardly as well as unjust. It fears where there is nothing to fear and flees when no one is pursuing.
Human wisdom is often foolish and deeply sinful.
Taskmasters were placed over God's people not merely to make them work hard, but deliberately to make them suffer under their burdens.
Their labor served Pharaoh's interests, yet it also made their lives bitter.
Still, Israel continued to grow remarkably.
Christianity has often spread most when it was persecuted: the blood of the martyrs became the seed of the church.
Those who plot against the Lord and his people achieve nothing lasting. Their plans are vain, and they only increase their own distress.

div.title: Pharaoh orders the killing of Hebrew sons (verses 15–22)
div.p: The Egyptians tried to destroy Israel by murdering its children.
The hostility of the serpent's offspring toward the woman's Seed can make people abandon every feeling of compassion.
It was clear that the Hebrew people were under an extraordinary blessing.
We also see how acts of service toward God's Israel are often rewarded in kind.
Pharaoh ordered that all the Hebrew baby boys be drowned.
The same enemy who used Pharaoh to try to destroy the church in its infancy is still busy trying to suppress the first serious thoughts of repentance in the human heart.
Those who want to escape this enemy must fear committing sin and cry out immediately and earnestly to the Lord for help.

row.cell: Moses is born, and exposed on the river.
He is found, and brought up by Pharaoh's daughter.
Moses slays an Egyptian, and flees to Midian.
Moses marries the daughter of Jethro.

div.title: The infant Moses is placed by the river (verses 1–4)
div.p: Notice how God's providence works.
Just when Pharaoh's cruelty reached its height, with the order to drown Hebrew infants, the deliverer was born.
While people plotted the destruction of the church, God was preparing its salvation.
Moses' parents saw that he was a beautiful child.
Living faith can take encouragement from even the smallest indication of God's favor.
Hebrews 11:23 tells us they hid Moses by faith.
They trusted God's promise that Israel would be preserved.
Faith in God's promises moves us to use lawful means to seek his mercy.
Our responsibility is to do our duty; the outcome belongs to God.
Faith lifts us above the fear of human beings.
After three months, when they could hide the child no longer, they placed him in a basket made of reeds near the river and sent his sister to watch him.
If a mother's frail love took such care, what must the love and compassion of God be like, when they are as limitless as he is?
Moses was never more securely protected—not even later, when Israel surrounded his tent in the wilderness—than when he lay helpless and alone beside the water.
Neither river nor Egyptian could harm him.
When we seem most abandoned and helpless, God may be especially near.

div.title: Pharaoh's daughter rescues Moses (verses 5–10)
div.p: Look at the place where the great Moses lay as an infant: a little basket among the reeds at the water's edge.
If he had remained there long, he would have died.
But Providence led Pharaoh's daughter to that very place and moved her to pity the helpless child.
She dared to show compassion when others did not.
We should often remember and praise God's care for us in our earliest years.
Pharaoh was cruelly trying to destroy Israel.
Yet Pharaoh's own daughter took pity on a Hebrew baby.
Without knowing what she was doing, she preserved the man who would deliver Israel.
She even provided him with a good nurse: his own mother.
Through Moses' sister, the mother was brought back to care for him.
Moses was raised as the son of Pharaoh's daughter.
Many people born in poverty and obscurity are raised to prominence through surprising acts of Providence, so that the world may see that God reigns.

div.title: Moses defends his people and flees (verses 11–15)
div.p: Moses boldly identified himself with God's people.
Hebrews 11 shows that he acted in faith, fully prepared to leave the honors, wealth, and pleasures of his high rank among the Egyptians.
By God's grace he shared in faith in Christ, the faith that overcomes the world.
He was willing not only to risk everything but to suffer for Christ's sake, because he was convinced Israel was God's people.
Henry understands Moses' killing of the Egyptian as an act carried out by special authorization from heaven, and he explicitly says that this must not become a rule for other cases.
Moses rescued an oppressed Israelite.
He also tried to settle a dispute between two Hebrews.
The rebuke he gave still has value.
May it not also be addressed to people whose fierce disputes divide and weaken the Christian church?
They forget that they are brothers and sisters.
The person in the wrong quarreled with Moses.
Anger at correction is often a sign of guilt.
People do not realize how much they harm themselves when they reject faithful rebukes and despise those who give them.
Moses might have been tempted to say, “If this is how the Hebrews behave, I will return to court and be Pharaoh's daughter's son again.”
But we must not allow the foolishness or bad temper of some professing believers to turn us against God's ways and God's people.
Moses had to flee to Midian.
God directed even this flight toward wise and holy purposes.

div.title: Moses helps Reuel's daughters and marries (verses 16–22)
div.p: Moses found refuge in Midian.
Although he had been educated at court, he readily helped Reuel's daughters water their flocks.
He loved to act justly and to defend those he saw being wronged.
Everyone should do the same, as far as he is able.
Moses also loved doing good.
Wherever God's providence places us, we should want to be useful and look for ways to help.
When we cannot do all the good we would like, we should still do whatever good we can.
Moses gained the favor of the leader of Midian, who gave him one of his daughters in marriage.
They had a son named Gershom, meaning “a stranger there,” to keep alive the memory of the country where Moses had lived as a stranger.

div.title: God hears Israel's cries (verses 23–25)
div.p: Israel's enslavement continued, even though the killing of Hebrew infants had stopped.
Sometimes God allows wicked people to lay a heavy burden on the righteous for a very long time.
At last the Israelites began to turn their thoughts toward God in their suffering.
When God inclines and enables us to cry out to him for deliverance, that is often a sign that he is drawing near to rescue us.
He heard their groaning and showed that he had noticed their distress.
God remembered his covenant, which he never forgets.
He acted because of his promise, not because they had earned deliverance.
He looked upon the Israelites.
Moses had looked upon them with pity, but now God looked upon them and acted to help.
His attention was fixed on Israel, and he was about to reveal his favor.
God is always a very present help in trouble.
Take courage, then, all who know their own guilt and bondage and are looking to him for deliverance.
God in Christ Jesus looks upon you as well.
He joins his loving invitation to the Redeemer's promise: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

row.cell: God appears to Moses in a burning bush.
God sends Moses to deliver Israel.
The deliverance of the Israelites promised.

div.title: God appears in the burning bush (verses 1–6)
div.p: Moses' life may be divided into three periods of forty years.
He spent the first forty as a prince in Pharaoh's court, the second as a shepherd in Midian, and the third as a king in Jeshurun.
How changeable human life is!
When God first appeared to Moses, he found him tending sheep.
For someone with Moses' abilities and education, that might seem a humble occupation.
But Moses was content with it.
In this way, he learned meekness and contentment, qualities for which Scripture remembers him more than for all his learning.
Satan likes to find us idle. God is pleased when he finds us faithfully at work.
Solitude can also be a good companion to communion with God.
To Moses' astonishment, he saw a bush burning, though nothing had set it alight.
It burned without being consumed.
This was a picture of the church enslaved in Egypt.
It also reminds us of the church through every age: even under the fiercest persecution, God's presence preserves it from destruction.
In Scripture, fire can picture God's holiness and justice.
It can also represent the sufferings and trials through which God tests and purifies his people.
It even pictures the baptism of the Holy Spirit, through which sinful desires are consumed and the soul is transformed into God's likeness.
God called Moses graciously, and Moses answered promptly.
Those who seek fellowship with God must meet him in the worship he has appointed, wherever he chooses to reveal his glory—even in a bush.
Removing his shoes was Moses' sign of reverence and submission.
We should draw near to God with serious preparation and deep respect, avoiding everything careless, irreverent, or unsuitable for his service.
God did not say, “I was the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,” but “I am.”
The patriarchs are still alive, though their bodies have been in the grave for many years.
No passage of time can separate the souls of the righteous from their Maker.
God was teaching Moses about the life to come and strengthening his confidence in the future state.
Jesus himself explained the words in this way, using them to prove the resurrection of the dead (Luke 20:37).
Moses hid his face, ashamed and afraid to look upon God.
The more we see of God's grace and covenant love, the more reason we have to worship with reverence and godly fear.

div.title: God sends Moses to deliver Israel (verses 7–10)
div.p: God sees his people's suffering.
He knows even their hidden sorrows.
He hears the cries of those who are oppressed.
He sees their oppressors, however powerful; none is above him.
God promises a speedy deliverance, using means beyond the ordinary course of Providence.
And those whom God rescues by his grace from spiritual Egypt he will bring into the heavenly Canaan.

div.title: God reveals his name (verses 11–15)
div.p: Years earlier, Moses had believed himself able to deliver Israel and had rushed into the work before the right time.
Now, when he was the most suitable person on earth for the task, he was deeply aware of his weakness.
He knew God and himself better than before.
Earlier, self-confidence had been mixed with strong faith and zeal.
Now, even sinful distrust of God was slipping in under the appearance of humility.
Such weaknesses can mar even the finest graces and best actions of the most remarkable believers.
But God answered every objection with one promise: “I will certainly be with you.”
That was enough.
God now made himself known by two names.
The first declares who he is in himself: “I AM THAT I AM.”
This explains the name Jehovah.
It declares, first, that God is self-existent. His being comes from himself.
Second, he is eternal and unchangeable—the same yesterday, today, and forever.
Third, he is beyond complete human understanding.
We cannot discover all that he is by searching, and this name restrains our bold and prying questions about him.
Fourth, he is faithful and true to all his promises.
His word is as unchanging as his nature.
Israel was to know that “I AM” had sent Moses.
God alone exists by himself. Everything else receives its existence from him and depends completely on him.
The second name declares who he is to his people: “The Lord, the God of your fathers, has sent me to you.”
Moses had to revive among Israel the faith of its ancestors, which had almost disappeared.
Then the people could expect the promises made to their fathers to be fulfilled soon.

div.title: God promises to free Israel (verses 16–22)
div.p: Moses would succeed in speaking to Israel's elders.
God himself moves human hearts and opens their ears.
He could tell Moses beforehand, “They will listen to you,” because he would make them willing when his power was shown.
Pharaoh, however, would refuse to yield to requests, persuasion, and humble appeals.
Nor would he submit merely because of a mighty hand stretched out in signs and wonders.
Yet those who will not bow before the power of God's word will surely be broken by the power of his hand.
At their departure, Pharaoh's people would supply Israel with riches.
Pharaoh's tyranny and Israel's slavery picture the miserable condition of sinners.
They continue laboring under a painful yoke until God sends redemption.
God accompanies the gospel's invitations with the teaching of his Spirit.
Through that work, people become willing to seek and strive for deliverance.
Satan loses his power to keep them in bondage.
They come out with all they are and all they possess and devote everything to God's glory and the service of his church.

row.cell: God gives Moses power to work miracles.
Moses is loth to be sent, Aaron is to assist him.
Moses leaves Midian, God's message to Pharaoh.
God's displeasure against Moses, Aaron meets him, The people believe them.

div.title: God gives Moses miraculous signs (verses 1–9)
div.p: Moses feared that the people would not believe him unless he showed them a sign.
God therefore gave him power to perform miracles.
But those now called to deliver God's messages to others do not need miraculous powers to prove their mission.
Their character and teaching must be tested by the word of God to which they appeal.
These signs also pointed especially toward the miracles of Jesus Christ.
Only Christ could drive the devil's power out of the soul and heal the soul from the leprosy of sin.
It was therefore fitting that he should first cast the devil out of a person's body and heal bodily leprosy.

div.title: Moses hesitates, and Aaron is appointed to help (verses 10–17)
div.p: Moses continued to shrink from the work God had appointed for him.
His reluctance included cowardice, laziness, and unbelief.
But we should never judge people's worth by how easily they speak.
A slow tongue may accompany great wisdom and genuine goodness.
God sometimes chooses people with few natural advantages or speaking skills to deliver his message.
Then the glory of his grace becomes more visible.
Christ's disciples were not gifted public speakers until the Holy Spirit enabled them.
God graciously answered Moses' excuse.
Yet a lack of confidence in ourselves can be very displeasing to God when it keeps us from doing our duty or hinders us while doing it.
As we criticize Moses for drawing back from such dangerous service, let us ask whether we are neglecting duties that are much easier and less risky.
Aaron's speaking ability, joined with Moses' understanding and devotion, would make them fully equipped for the task.
God promised, “I will be with your mouth and with his mouth.”
Even Aaron, who spoke well, could say nothing truly effective unless God continually taught and helped him.
Without the ongoing help of divine grace, even our finest natural gifts will fail.

div.title: Moses leaves Midian; God warns Pharaoh (verses 18–23)
div.p: After appearing to Moses at the burning bush, God often spoke to him.
Pharaoh had already hardened his own heart against the cries and groans of the oppressed Israelites.
Now God, in righteous judgment, would harden Pharaoh's heart against the evidence of miracles and the terror of the plagues.
But whether Pharaoh listened or refused, Moses had to declare, “This is what the Lord says.”
He had to demand Israel's release.
“Let my son go.”
Israel was not merely God's servant—whom Pharaoh had no right to hold captive—but God's son.
This was God's son who served him and must therefore be released and protected.
If Pharaoh refused, the Lord would strike down Pharaoh's own son, even his firstborn.
People should expect to be treated as they treat God's people.

div.title: Moses obeys, and Israel receives the message (verses 24–31)
div.p: God met Moses in anger.
The Lord threatened him with death—or sent illness upon him—as punishment for failing to circumcise his son.
Whenever God shows us something wrong in our lives, we should be diligent to correct it without delay.
Every painful correction carries this call: return to the One who disciplines you.
God sent Aaron to meet Moses.
The more clearly they recognized God's hand in bringing them together, the happier their meeting became.
Israel's elders met them with faith and were ready to obey.
Work done according to God's will and for his glory often turns out to have fewer difficulties than we feared.
Let us rise and begin the work God has given us.
The Lord will be with us and will make our efforts prosper.
If the Israelites welcomed the good news of their deliverance and worshiped the Lord, how much more should we welcome the joyful news of redemption, receive it by faith, and adore our Redeemer!

row.cell: Pharaoh's displeasure, He increases the tasks of the Israelites.
The sufferings of the Israelites, Moses' complaint to God.

div.title: Pharaoh increases Israel's burdens (verses 1–9)
div.p: God will acknowledge his people, though they may be poor and despised, and he will find the right time to defend their cause.
Pharaoh treated everything he heard with contempt.
He did not know Jehovah, fear him, or love him. So he refused to obey him.
His pride, ambition, greed, and political shrewdness made his heart hard and led him toward destruction.
Moses and Aaron had made a reasonable request.
They asked only to travel three days into the wilderness for a good purpose: “We will offer sacrifices to the Lord our God.”
Pharaoh's answer was deeply unreasonable.
He accused the people of idleness, as though this were why they wanted to worship.
He twisted the truth to create an excuse for adding to their burdens.

Even now, people sometimes criticize their neighbors for spending a few hours away from ordinary work in the service of God, while making no objection to others spending twice as long in sinful pleasures.
Pharaoh's order was cruel.
Moses and Aaron themselves were to be made to carry burdens.
Persecutors often take pleasure in humiliating ministers and making their lives hard.
The Israelites had to produce the usual number of bricks without being given the usual straw to mix with the clay.
If they met the quota, the work would crush them. If they failed, they would be punished.

div.title: The Israelites suffer, and Moses appeals to God (verses 10–23)
div.p: The Egyptian taskmasters were extremely harsh.
How much we need to pray that God will deliver us from wicked people!
The Israelite foremen were right to complain to Pharaoh, but he only mocked them.
Satan's malice has often tried to make the worship and service of God appear suitable only for people who have nothing else to do, as though faith were merely the business of the idle.
But worship is a duty even for those who have the busiest lives.
People who faithfully serve God may be condemned as idle by others, yet they will escape God's judgment on the truly lazy servant.
The Israelites should have humbled themselves before God and acknowledged the shame of their own sin.
Instead, they quarreled with the very men whom God had sent to deliver them.
Moses returned to the Lord.
He knew that his words and actions had followed God's instructions, so he brought the matter before God.
Whenever our obedience to God leads us into confusion or difficulty, we should go to him and open our situation to him in earnest prayer.
Disappointments in God's work must not drive us away from God.
Instead, we should consider carefully why he has allowed them.

row.cell: Moses and Aaron again sent to Pharaoh.
The parentage of Moses and Aaron.

div.title: God renews his promise (verses 1–9)
div.p: Our efforts to glorify God and serve other people are most likely to succeed when we have learned from experience that we can do nothing by ourselves.
We must depend wholly on God and expect everything from him.
Moses had been waiting to see what God would do.
Now he would see what God was about to do.
God would make himself known by the name Jehovah—the God who fulfills his promises and completes the work he has begun.
He intended his people's happiness:
“I will take you as my own people, and I will be your God.”
We can ask for nothing greater and receive nothing better to make us happy.
God also intended to display his own glory:
“You will know that I am the Lord.”
These gracious and comforting words should have revived the discouraged Israelites and helped them forget their misery.
But they were so overwhelmed by their troubles that they paid no attention to God's promises.
When we indulge dissatisfaction and agitation, we deprive ourselves of the comfort God's word and providence could give us.
We remain without comfort because we refuse to receive it.

div.title: God sends Moses and Aaron back to Pharaoh (verses 10–13)
div.p: Moses' faith was so weak that he could scarcely be kept at his task.
Prompt obedience usually grows with the strength of our faith.
Our weaknesses should make us humble, but they should not discourage us from doing our best in the work God has given us.
When Moses repeated objections that had already failed, God did not continue arguing with him.
Instead, he gave Moses and Aaron a direct command, addressed both to the Israelites and to Pharaoh.
God's authority is enough to answer every objection.
It binds us to obey without complaining or arguing (Philippians 2:14).

div.title: Moses and Aaron's family and calling (verses 14–30)
div.p: Moses and Aaron were themselves Israelites, raised up from among their brothers.
Christ would also come from among Israel as its Prophet and Priest, Redeemer and Lawgiver.
Moses returned to his account and repeated both the command God had given him to address Pharaoh and the objection he had made against it.
Those who have spoken rashly should look back on their words with regret, as Moses seems to do here.
Scripture sometimes uses the word uncircumcised to describe something unfit to fulfill its proper purpose.
In the same way, the fleshly heart and corrupted nature of fallen humanity are entirely unfit for God's service and glory.
It is good for us to have no confidence in ourselves.
Our entire ability must come from the Lord.
We can never distrust ourselves too much or trust God too much.
As the apostle says, “I can do nothing by myself, but I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.”

row.cell: The rods turned into serpents, Pharaoh's heart is hardened.
The river is turned into blood, The distress of the Egyptians.

div.title: Moses and Aaron receive courage (verses 1–7)
div.p: God glorifies himself by making people know that he is Jehovah.
Israel would learn this through the fulfillment of his promises.
The Egyptians would learn it when his judgments were poured out upon them.
Moses came as Jehovah's ambassador, speaking in God's name.
He gave Pharaoh commands, announced judgments against him, and called those judgments down upon him.
Pharaoh, however proud and powerful he was, could not resist.
Moses no longer stood trembling before Pharaoh. Instead, Pharaoh trembled before him.
This seems to be what God meant when he said Moses would be “a god to Pharaoh.”
At last Moses was freed from his fears.
He raised no more objections but, strengthened in faith, began his task courageously and continued it faithfully.

div.title: The signs and Pharaoh's hardened heart (verses 8–13)
div.p: When people dislike something because it stands against their pride and sinful desires, they refuse to be convinced by it.
Yet they are easily persuaded to believe whatever they want to be true.
God always sends his word with sufficient evidence of its divine authority.
But when people are determined to disobey and eager to find objections, he may allow them to be caught by a trap they have chosen.
Henry describes Pharaoh's magicians as deceivers.
They attempted to imitate Moses' real miracles by hidden tricks and sleight of hand.
For a time they succeeded enough to mislead the people watching.
But eventually they had to admit that they could no longer reproduce what God's power was doing.
Few people contribute more to the ruin of sinners than those who resist the truth by entertaining others with a counterfeit imitation of it.
Satan is most dangerous when he disguises himself as an angel of light.

div.title: The waters of Egypt turn to blood (verses 14–25)
div.p: The first of the ten plagues turned water into blood.
What a dreadful judgment it was!
The sight of vast flowing streams of blood must have filled people with horror.
Nothing is more ordinary than water.
God has wisely and kindly arranged that something so necessary and useful for human life should usually be inexpensive and widely available.
But now the Egyptians had to drink blood or die of thirst.
Egypt had been a pleasant land.
The dead fish and blood made it a miserable place.
This plague was justly sent upon the Egyptians.
The Nile was treated as their god.
When we idolize some created thing, God may rightly take it away from us or make it bitter to us.
The Egyptians had stained the river with the blood of Hebrew infants.
Now God made that same river blood.
Those who thirst for blood will sooner or later receive more of it than they desire.
The plague also carried a warning.
Egypt depended heavily on its river (Zechariah 14:18).
By striking the Nile, God warned that the produce of the whole land could be destroyed.
Christ's love turns his disciples' ordinary blessings into spiritual benefits.
But God's anger turns the things his enemies most prize into misery and a curse.
Aaron was to bring the plague by striking the river with his staff.
He did so in front of Pharaoh and his attendants.
God's genuine miracles were not performed like Satan's lying wonders. Truth has no need to hide in corners.
Consider God's almighty power.
Every created thing becomes for us what he makes it—water or blood.
And see how quickly the conditions of worldly life may change.
What is always fleeting may soon become painful as well.
Notice the harm sin does.
If what once comforted us becomes a burden, we must often recognize our own responsibility.
Sin turns our water into blood.
The plague lasted seven days.
Yet throughout that time Pharaoh's proud heart would not allow him to ask Moses to pray for its removal.
In this way hypocritical hearts store up more and more judgment.
It is no wonder that God's anger had not passed away, but his hand was still raised against Egypt.

div.title: The plague of frogs (verses 1–15)
div.p: Pharaoh was struck by a plague of frogs.
Their overwhelming numbers made them a severe affliction to the Egyptians.
God could have sent lions, bears, wolves, or birds of prey against the land.
Instead, he chose creatures that people usually despise.
Whenever God pleases, he can turn even the smallest parts of creation against us.
In this way he humbled Pharaoh.
The Egyptians could neither eat, drink, nor sleep in peace.
Wherever they went, the frogs disturbed them.
God's curse pursues a person everywhere and weighs heavily on everything he does.
Under this plague, Pharaoh finally gave way and promised to let the people go.
Those who defy God and despise prayer will sooner or later be forced to recognize their need of both.
But when Pharaoh saw that he had relief, he hardened his heart once more.
Until God's grace renews the heart, the impressions made by suffering do not last.
Conviction fades, and promises are forgotten.
Until the climate changes, what thaws in the sunshine will freeze again in the shade.

div.title: The plague of gnats (verses 16–19)
div.p: The insects came from the dust of the ground.
God can take any part of creation and make it an instrument of judgment against rebels.
Even the dust obeys him.
These insects were both painful and humiliating for the Egyptians.
Their priests took extraordinary care to keep themselves free from vermin.
The plagues against Egypt were connected with the nation's sins, or were made especially severe by its customs.
Pharaoh's magicians tried to reproduce this sign but failed.
They were forced to admit, “This is the finger of God!”
The power that checks and restrains human beings must come from God.
Sooner or later even God's enemies will have to acknowledge his power.
Yet Pharaoh only became more stubborn.

div.title: The plague of flies (verses 20–32)
div.p: Pharaoh rose early to continue his false religious devotion to the river.
Should we, then, choose more sleep and idleness when there is work to do for the Lord?
The plague of flies would distinguish the Egyptians from the Hebrews.
The Lord knows those who belong to him.
He will make clear that he has set them apart for himself—perhaps in this world, and certainly in the next.
Pharaoh unwillingly began negotiating with Moses and Aaron.
He agreed to allow sacrifices to Israel's God, provided they took place inside Egypt.
But it would be offensive to God for Israel to offer the Egyptians' sacrifices.
And it would be offensive to the Egyptians if Israel offered to God the calves or oxen that were objects of Egyptian worship.
Those who wish to offer God acceptable worship must separate themselves from the wicked and profane.
They also need to withdraw from the distractions and temptations of the world.
Israel could not keep the Lord's feast among the brick kilns or beside Egypt's pots of meat.
The people had to sacrifice as God commanded—not according to some different arrangement.
Although they were enslaved to Pharaoh, they still had to obey God.
Pharaoh then agreed to let them go into the wilderness, but only if they stayed close enough for him to bring them back.
That is how some sinners behave.
For a moment, frightened by conviction, they part with their sins.
But they do not want those sins to go too far away.
When their fear fades, they return to them.
Moses promised that the plague would be removed and warned Pharaoh not to act deceitfully again.
God is not mocked.
If we think we can trick him with pretend repentance and an insincere surrender, we only deceive ourselves—and with disastrous results.
Pharaoh returned to his stubbornness.
Deeply rooted sinful desires break even strong restraints and lead people to break their promises.
Many seem genuinely serious about repentance, but keep something in reserve: a secret, beloved sin.
They refuse to recognize the danger of eternal misery.
They may turn from other sins, do many good works, give generously, and even submit to painful self-denial.
They may leave a cherished sin alone for a while, allowing it to go only a short distance.
But they will not decide to part with everything sinful and follow Christ, bearing the cross.
Instead, they risk everything to keep their sin.
They are sorrowful but turn away from Christ, determined to keep the world for now.
They hope that some later opportunity will allow them to receive salvation without so costly a surrender.
But at last the poor sinner may be swept away in wickedness, left without hope and forced to lament his folly.

row.cell: The plague of boils and blains.

div.title: Disease strikes the livestock (verses 1–7)
div.p: God demanded Israel's release, but Pharaoh resisted.
The contest would show whose word would stand.
The Lord's hand struck the Egyptian livestock, and many animals of every kind died from a deadly disease.
Their owners suffered a heavy loss.
They had made Israel poor. Now God would make them poor.
Even the illness and death of animals are within God's providence.
Not even a sparrow falls without our heavenly Father's knowledge.
None of Israel's livestock was to die.
The Lord would make a distinction between his people and the Egyptians.
The Egyptians worshiped their cattle.
When we turn something into an idol, God is just to take it away.
Pharaoh was a proud tyrant and cruel oppressor, and the righteous Judge of all the earth was just in making him an example.
No one who receives a punishment he deserves has a just reason to complain.
Hardness of heart is a condition in which neither threats nor promises, neither judgments nor mercies, leave any lasting impression.
Conscience becomes numb, while pride and presumption fill the heart.
Such people persist in unbelief and disobedience.
This is what Scripture also calls a heart of stone.
How different it is from a heart of flesh—a broken and repentant heart!
Sinners have only themselves to blame for the pride and ungodliness with which they misuse God's generosity and patience.
However God hardens a human heart, Henry says, he does so as a punishment for earlier sins.

div.title: The plague of boils (verses 8–12)
div.p: When the death of the livestock had no effect, God sent a plague that struck the Egyptians' own bodies.
If smaller judgments do not move people, greater ones may follow.
Sometimes God makes the punishment itself expose the sin.
The Egyptians had oppressed Israel in furnaces.
Now ashes from those furnaces became a source of terror to them.
The boils were a painful and severe affliction.
Even the magicians were struck.
Their power had already been restrained, but they had continued opposing Moses and strengthening Pharaoh in unbelief until they were forced to retreat.
Still Pharaoh remained obstinate.
He had hardened his own heart.
Now, as a righteous judgment, God gave him over to his own sinful desires, allowing Satan to blind and harden him further.
If people deliberately close their eyes against the light, it is just for God to close them.
Short of hell itself, this is the most dreadful judgment a person can suffer.

div.title: God warns Egypt about the hail (verses 13–21)
div.p: God commanded Moses to bring Pharaoh a fearful warning.
In his providence, God had placed before Moses a man as fiercely stubborn as Pharaoh.
Every circumstance would make the result an especially striking display of God's ability to humble his proudest enemies.
When divine justice threatens destruction, divine mercy also shows a way of escape.
God distinguished not only between Israel and Egypt, but also between Egyptians who listened and those who refused.
If Pharaoh would not yield and prevent the judgment, people who accepted the warning could at least seek shelter.
Some believed God's words, feared him, and brought their servants and livestock under cover.
They acted wisely.
Even among Pharaoh's servants, some trembled at God's word.
Should not Israel tremble at it too?
Others refused to believe and left their animals outside.
Stubborn unbelief ignores even the clearest warnings and wisest advice.
Those who perish after such warnings bear responsibility for their own destruction.

div.title: The hail falls (verses 22–35)
div.p: The hail caused terrible devastation.
It killed both people and livestock.
Crops already growing above the ground were destroyed, while those that had not yet emerged were spared.
Goshen was protected.
God can send rain or hail on one city and not another, either in mercy or in judgment.
Pharaoh humbled himself before Moses.
No one could have spoken better than he did.
He admitted that he was wrong and acknowledged that the Lord was righteous.
God must be acknowledged as just when he speaks, even when his voice comes in thunder and lightning.
Yet Pharaoh's heart remained hard.
Moses pleaded with God for him.
He had good reason to think Pharaoh would soon turn back from his apparent repentance, and he told Pharaoh so.
Still, Moses promised to intercede for him.
Moses left the city even though the hail and lightning kept Pharaoh and his servants indoors.
Peace with God makes a person unafraid even of thunder.
Pharaoh was terrified by the judgment.
But when it ended, he forgot his fine promises.
People who are changed by neither God's judgments nor his mercies usually become worse.

row.cell: The plague of locusts threatened, Pharaoh, moved by his servants, inclines to let the Israelites go.

div.title: Pharaoh is warned of locusts (verses 1–11)
div.p: Egypt's plagues show how sinful sin really is.
They warn everyone not to fight against their Maker.
Pharaoh had pretended to humble himself.
But God did not accept that display, because it was not sincere.
Moses warned him that a plague of locusts was coming, worse than any Egypt had ever known.
Pharaoh's servants urged him to reach an agreement.
He then offered to let the men go, falsely claiming that the men were all Moses had asked to take.
He refused to allow their children to leave.
Satan works hard to prevent people who worship God from bringing their children to worship him too.
He is a determined enemy of faith developed early in life.
Whatever seeks to keep us from bringing our children into God's service should make us suspicious of Satan's influence.
Young people themselves should remember that the Lord calls them to remember their Creator in the days of their youth.
Satan, by contrast, wants them to remain slaves to sin and the world.
Our great enemy tries to hold us through the ties of family affection.
Pharaoh meant to keep the women and children as hostages so that the men would return.
Satan is willing to share our worship and obedience with the Savior.
But the Savior will not accept such divided service.

div.title: The locusts devour Egypt (verses 12–20)
div.p: At God's command, Moses stretched out his hand, and locusts came.
An army might have been easier to resist than this enormous swarm of insects.
Who can stand before the great God?
The locusts covered the land and ate its crops.
Plants grow to serve human needs.
Yet God can allow insects to strip them away and take the bread from our mouths.
Let us labor not merely for homes and food that can be lost in this way, but for what endures to eternal life.
Pharaoh asked Moses and Aaron to pray for him.
Some people in trouble seek the prayers of others while having no desire to pray themselves.
This shows that they do not truly love God or delight in fellowship with him.
Pharaoh wanted the deadly plague removed, but not the sin of his hardened heart.
He wanted the locusts to go, but not the much more dangerous plague within him.
An east wind brought the locusts, and a west wind carried them away.
Whichever direction the wind blows, it fulfills God's word and follows his counsel.
From our viewpoint the wind blows wherever it wishes, but it is never independent of God.
Its change should have encouraged the Egyptians to repent.
God was showing that he was ready to forgive and quick to show mercy.
If he answered even outward signs of humility in this way, how much more would he do for those who were sincere!
If only God's kindness would lead us to repentance!
But Pharaoh returned again to his refusal to release Israel.
Those who repeatedly suppress their convictions may justly be left to their heart's sinful desires.

div.title: The plague of darkness (verses 21–29)
div.p: The darkness that covered Egypt was terrifying.
It was so thick that it could almost be felt.
People were amazed and frightened.
It lasted three days—like six nights in a row.
Even the brightest palaces became prisons of darkness.
Pharaoh now had time to think, if only he had used it well.
Spiritual darkness is a form of spiritual slavery.
Satan blinds people's eyes so that they cannot see.
He also binds their hands and feet, so that they do not serve God or move toward heaven.
They remain seated in darkness.
It was right for God to judge Egypt in this way.
The darkness of the air mirrored the blindness of their minds.
No mind was more blinded than Pharaoh's; no sky was darker than Egypt's.
Let us fear where sin leads.
If three days of darkness were so dreadful, what will everlasting darkness be?
Meanwhile, Israel's children had light in their homes.
We should not take ordinary blessings for granted, as though we owed God no thanks for them.
The difference also showed God's special favor toward his people.
Wherever a true Israelite is found in this dark world, there is light: a child of light.
Who would not prefer the poor cottage of an Israelite with its light to an Egyptian palace in darkness?
There is a genuine difference between the home of the wicked, under a curse, and the blessed dwelling of the righteous.
Pharaoh again negotiated with Moses and Aaron.
Now he agreed that the children could go, but demanded that the livestock remain behind.
Sinners often try to bargain with the Almighty.
They think they can mock him, but they only deceive themselves.
God's terms for reconciliation cannot be altered, however long people argue about them.
We must submit to his will; we cannot expect him to accept the compromises our sinful desires propose.
We must devote our own lives, our children, and all our possessions to God's service.
We do not know what use he may have for anything we own.
Pharaoh abruptly ended the discussion and refused to see Moses again.
Had he forgotten how often he had sent for Moses to seek relief from the plagues?
What empty hatred it was to threaten with death a man whom God had armed with such power!
See what hardness of heart and contempt for God's word can lead people to do.
After that, Moses did not return until Pharaoh sent for him.
When people drive God's word away from them, he may justly leave them to their own delusions.

row.cell: God's last instructions to Moses respecting Pharaoh and the Egyptians.
The death of the first-born threatened.

div.title: God's final instructions (verses 1–3)
div.p: While Moses was still standing before Pharaoh, God secretly revealed what was about to happen.
This enabled Moses to warn Pharaoh of the last and most terrible judgment before leaving him.
Israel's slavery was almost over.
The Egyptians who had abused the Israelites in their labor would have preferred to send them away with nothing.
But God made sure the workers would not lose the wages of their toil.
He commanded them to request payment when they departed, and it was given to them.
God will vindicate those who have suffered injustice and have quietly entrusted their cause to him.
Those who endure patiently will not finally lose by doing so.
The Lord gave Israel favor in the Egyptians' eyes by showing how greatly he himself favored them.
He changed the Egyptians' feelings toward the people they had oppressed, moving them to show compassion.
God honors those who honor him.

div.title: God announces the death of Egypt's firstborn (verses 4–10)
div.p: All the firstborn in Egypt would die at once.
This had been the first plague threatened, but it would be the last to take place.
See how slow God is to become angry!
The judgment was announced, and its time was fixed.
Every firstborn would fall into the sleep of death, not quietly, but amid the cries that would wake whole families at midnight.
The prince was not too powerful to be touched, nor was the slave working at the mill too lowly to be noticed.
While angels struck the Egyptians, not even a dog would bark against Israel's children.
This anticipated the difference that will appear on the great day between God's people and his enemies.
If people understood the difference God makes—and will make for all eternity—between those who serve him and those who do not, they would not treat religion as something unimportant.
They would not approach it so carelessly.
After delivering God's message, Moses left Pharaoh in great anger at his stubbornness, even though Moses was the meekest man on earth.
Scripture has foretold that many who hear the gospel will refuse to believe, so that their unbelief need not surprise or discourage us (Romans 10:16).
Let us never think less of Christ's gospel because others despise it.
Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, but he was forced to retreat from his arrogant demands until Israel was completely freed.
Likewise, God's people will find growing freedom from the enemy of their souls as they resist him in Jesus Christ's strength.
Every struggle against him through the blood of the Lamb, and every desire to become more like the Lamb and to love him more deeply, will be rewarded by greater release from his power.

row.cell: The beginning of the year changed, The passover instituted.
The people instructed how to observe the passover.
The death of the first-born of the Egyptians, The Israelites urged to leave the land of Egypt.
The Israelites' first journey to Succoth.

div.title: The Passover is instituted (verses 1–20)
div.p: The Lord makes everything new for people whom he releases from Satan's slavery and brings into his family.
The time of their deliverance becomes the beginning of a new life.
God instructed every Israelite household to kill a lamb on the night they would leave Egypt.
Where a family was small, two or three families could share one lamb.
They were to eat it in the manner God prescribed and put some of its blood on their doorposts.
This would distinguish their homes from Egyptian homes.
When the Lord's angel killed the firstborn of Egypt, he would pass over every house marked with the lamb's blood.
This is where the name of the holy feast comes from.
Israel was to celebrate the Passover every year, remembering its preservation and deliverance from Egypt and recognizing in it a striking picture of Christ.
The people's safety was not a reward for their righteousness.
It was a gift of mercy.
Through this ordinance they learned that God's blessings came to them through the shedding and application of blood.

p.hi: First, the Passover lamb pointed to Christ.

div.p: Christ is our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).
He is the Lamb of God (John 1:29), and the book of Revelation often calls him the Lamb.
The animal was to be in the prime of life.
Christ gave himself in the midst of his days, not as an infant at Bethlehem.
The lamb had to be without blemish.
Jesus likewise had no fault; even the judge who condemned him declared him innocent.
The lamb was chosen four days beforehand.
This pictured the appointment of Christ as Savior, both in God's purpose and in his promise.
The lamb was killed and roasted over fire.
This pictured Christ's painful suffering and death, even death on the cross.
God's wrath is like fire, and Christ became a curse for us.
Not one of the lamb's bones was to be broken.
This was fulfilled in Christ (John 19:33) and pointed to his unbroken strength.

p.hi: Second, the sprinkled blood pointed to the application of Christ's death.

div.p: The lamb's blood had to be put on the doors.
This pictured the personal application of the benefits of Christ's death.
We must receive the atonement (Romans 5:11).
Faith is like the bunch of hyssop with which the blood is applied.
Through faith we receive for ourselves God's promises and the benefits of Christ's blood contained in them.
The blood was placed openly on the doorposts.
This pointed to our public profession of faith in Christ.
It was not placed on the threshold.
This warns us never to trample underfoot the blood of the covenant.
It is precious blood, and it must be precious to us.
The blood on the doors protected Israel from the destroying angel, who had no authority in the houses where it was found.
In the same way, Christ's blood protects believers from God's wrath, the curse of the law, and eternal condemnation (Romans 8:1).

p.hi: Third, eating the lamb pictured our duty to receive Christ by faith.

div.p: The lamb was not merely to be looked at.
It had to be eaten.
So we must receive Christ as our own by faith and draw spiritual strength and nourishment from him, as we draw nourishment from food (John 6:53, 55).
The whole lamb had to be eaten.
Those who feed on Christ by faith must receive the whole Christ.
They must accept not only his crown but also his yoke and his cross.
The lamb had to be eaten that night, not saved until morning.
Christ is offered to us today, and we must receive him while it is still called today, before the sleep of death overtakes us.
Bitter herbs accompanied the meal, recalling the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.
We must receive Christ with grief and brokenness of heart as we remember our sin.
Christ will be sweet to us when sin has become bitter.
The Israelites ate standing, with their staffs in hand, ready to depart.
When we feed on Christ through faith, we must leave sin's rule behind and loosen our attachment to the world and everything in it.
We must give up everything for him, knowing that this is no loss (Hebrews 13:13–14).

p.hi: Fourth, the feast of unleavened bread pictured the Christian life (1 Corinthians 5:7–8).

div.p: Once we have received Jesus Christ as Lord, we should continue finding our joy in him.
No work was to interrupt the feast.
In the spiritual application, we should allow no worldly anxiety that is incompatible with this holy joy or diminishes it.
The Jews took great care that no leaven remained in their houses.
Our celebration must likewise be free of malice and full of love, free of hypocrisy and full of sincerity.
The feast was established as a lasting ordinance.
Throughout our lives, we must keep feeding on Christ, rejoicing in him, and gratefully remembering the great things he has done for us.

div.title: Israel is instructed to observe the Passover (verses 21–28)
div.p: On the night Egypt's firstborn were to die, no Israelite was to leave the house until the time came to depart from Egypt.
Their safety rested in the blood that had been applied.
To move outside its protection would put them in danger.
They were to remain inside and wait for the Lord's salvation.
That is a good thing for us to do as well.
In later generations, parents were to teach their children carefully what this ceremony meant.
It is good for children to ask questions about God.
Those who ask about the right way will find it.
The annual celebration looked in two directions.
First, backward, so that the people would remember what God had done for them and their ancestors.
Past mercies shown to us or to earlier generations must never be forgotten.
Remembering them brings praise to God and strengthens faith.
Second, forward, as a pledge of the great sacrifice the Lamb of God would make when the time was fulfilled.
Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us.
His death is our life.

div.title: Egypt's firstborn die, and Israel is released (verses 29–36)
div.p: For three days and nights the Egyptians had lived in terror because of the darkness.
Now their rest was broken by a much more dreadful disaster.
The firstborn—the joy and hope of their families—were struck down.
The Egyptians had killed Hebrew children.
Now God struck their children.
The judgment reached from Pharaoh's throne to the dungeon.
Princes and ordinary laborers are equal before God's judgments.
The destroying angel entered every dwelling not marked with blood.
Not one such house escaped death.
Imagine the great cry that filled Egypt, the long, agonizing wailing from family after family.
Something similar will happen when the Son of Man comes to judge sinners for the last time.
God's sons, his firstborn people, were now set free.
People would do well to accept God's terms from the beginning, because he will never submit to theirs.
Pharaoh's pride was brought low, and he yielded.
God's word will stand.
Argument and delay accomplish nothing against it.
In their terror the Egyptians were willing to give generously to secure Israel's favor and make the people leave quickly.
In this way God ensured that Israel was paid for its hard labor and provided with what it needed for the journey.

div.title: Israel sets out for Succoth (verses 37–42)
div.p: The Israelites departed without delay.
A mixed multitude went with them.
Some may have wanted to escape a country devastated by plagues.
Others may have followed from curiosity, and perhaps a few because they loved Israel and its faith.
But among the Israelites there had always been some who were not truly Israelites.
There are still hypocrites in the church.
Henry dates this great event to 430 years after the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:17).
For all that time, the promised settlement had not yet come.
God's promises may not be fulfilled quickly, but they will be fulfilled at the proper time.
That night belonged to the Lord.
Its remarkable events were to be commemorated through every generation.
The great things God does for his people are not meant to be talked about for a few days and then forgotten.
They should be remembered through the ages—especially Christ's work of redemption.
Israel's first Passover night was indeed a night to remember.
But the last Passover night, when Christ was betrayed and the original Passover along with the other Jewish ceremonies came to an end, is still more worthy of remembrance.
Then a yoke heavier than Egypt's was broken from our necks.
A land better than Canaan was placed before us.
That redemption will be celebrated in heaven forever.

div.title: Who may share in the Passover (verses 43–51)
div.p: In later times, all the congregation of Israel was required to keep the Passover.
Everyone who shares in God's mercies should join in giving thanks and praise.
The New Testament Passover, the Lord's Supper, should not be neglected.
Foreigners who received circumcision could take part in Israel's Passover.
This was an early indication of God's favor toward the Gentiles.
It taught Israel that membership among a people favored by God, not simply physical descent from Abraham, gave someone access to the people's privileges.
Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).
His blood is the only ransom for our souls.
Without the shedding of his blood, there is no forgiveness of sins.
Without its application to us, there is no salvation.
Have we, through faith in Christ, placed ourselves under the protection of his atoning blood and found shelter from the judgment we deserve?
Do we remain near him, continually depending on him?
Do we profess our faith in the Redeemer and our debt to him so openly that everyone who sees us can tell to whom we belong?
Are we ready to serve him, walk in his ways, and separate ourselves from his enemies?
These questions matter enormously for our souls.
May the Lord guide our consciences to answer them truthfully.

row.cell: The first-born sanctified to God, The remembrance of the passover commanded.
The firstlings of beasts set apart.
Joseph's bones carried with the Israelites, They come to Etham.
God guideth the Israelites by a pillar of cloud fire.

div.title: The firstborn are dedicated to God; the deliverance is remembered (verses 1–10)
div.p: God commanded Israel to dedicate its firstborn sons to him. This memorial joined two great events: the deaths of Egypt's firstborn, both human and animal, and Israel's deliverance from slavery.
The people were to remember that their lives had been spared through a ransom. That ransom pointed ahead to the atonement that would be made for sin at the appointed time.
Lives rescued from death are to be devoted to God's service.
Parents were not to think of their firstborn as belonging to them without first presenting them solemnly to God and acknowledging his claim upon them.
Whatever God spares for us through special mercy should be used for his honor. At the very least, we should acknowledge his goodness through grateful acts of devotion and charity.
Israel was to remember its departure from Egypt every year.
We should also remember the day of Christ's resurrection. In him we were raised from death's house of slavery.
Scripture does not expressly tell us the day of the year on which Christ rose, but it does tell us the day of the week. Henry therefore urges us to commemorate this greater deliverance weekly.
Israel observed the feast of unleavened bread. Under the gospel, we must do more than remember Christ in thought: we must also observe his holy Supper, as he commanded, in remembrance of him.
Parents must teach their children to know God. This is an ancient command to instruct them in the faith.
It is especially valuable to acquaint children with Bible history while they are young.
People who have God's law in their hearts should also have it on their lips. Speaking about it often strengthens their own hearts and teaches others.

div.title: The firstborn animals and the ransom (verses 11–16)
div.p: Firstborn animals that could not be offered as sacrifices had to be exchanged for animals that could, or else be destroyed.
Our own souls have been forfeited under God's justice. Unless Christ's sacrifice ransoms them, they will certainly perish.
These ordinances constantly reminded Israel of its duty to love and serve the Lord.

In a similar way, baptism and the Lord's Supper remind Christians of their profession and their duties—when these ordinances are explained and observed properly. They also give us opportunities to remind one another.

div.title: Israel takes the longer road (verses 17–20)
div.p: There were two possible routes from Egypt to Canaan.
One would take only a few days. The other, through the wilderness, was much longer.
God chose the longer route for his people.
The Egyptians would be drowned in the Red Sea, while the Israelites would be humbled and tested in the wilderness.
God's way is the right way, even when it seems a roundabout way.
If he does not lead us along the shortest path, we can be sure he leads us along the best one. We will see that clearly when we reach our journey's end.
The Philistines were formidable enemies. The Israelites needed to be prepared for the wars of Canaan through the hardships of the wilderness.
God measures his people's trials according to their strength (1 Corinthians 10:13).
The people departed in orderly formation. Henry records differing explanations of the formation: five abreast or divided into five companies.
They also carried Joseph's bones. This testified to their faith and hope that God would bring them to Canaan.

div.title: The Lord guides his people by cloud and fire (verses 21–22)
div.p: The Lord went ahead of Israel in a pillar—a visible sign of the divine presence.
Christ was with his church in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:9).
When God leads his people into a wilderness, he does not abandon or lose them there. He cares for them and leads them through it.
For Moses and the faithful Israelites, being sure of divine guidance was a great comfort.
We too may be sure that the Lord goes before us when we make his glory our goal, his word our rule, his Spirit the guide of our desires, and his providence the guide of our circumstances.
We cannot see him with our eyes. Now we must live by faith.
As Israel moved, the pillar went ahead and indicated the place where divine wisdom intended them to camp.
It sheltered them from the heat by day and gave them light at night.
God's word is likewise a lamp for our feet and a light for our path. Our Savior's love has provided it for us, and it testifies about Christ.
The Bible is to us what the pillar was to Israel.
Listen to the One who says that he is the light of the world: whoever follows him will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life (John 8:12).
Jesus Christ alone is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6).
He is made known to us in Scripture, and the Holy Spirit directs our souls to him in answer to prayer.

row.cell: God directs the Israelites to Pihahiroth, Pharaoh pursues after them.
The Israelites murmur, Moses comforts them.
God instructs Moses, The cloud between the Israelites and the Egyptians.
The Israelites pass through the Red sea, which drowns the Egyptians.

div.title: Pharaoh pursues Israel (verses 1–9)
div.p: Pharaoh expected the Israelites to become trapped in the wilderness, where they would be easy prey.
But God declared that he would gain honor through what happened to Pharaoh.
Everyone was made to honor the Creator. Those who refuse to honor him by willing obedience will nevertheless become occasions for the display of his justice and power.
What appears to threaten the church with destruction is often overruled by God to bring ruin upon the church's enemies.
Pharaoh pursued his malice and revenge, but in doing so he advanced the very purpose God had declared for him.
Although he had every reason to release Israel, he now regretted having done so.
God can turn the envy and rage people direct against his people into torment for those very enemies.
Those who turn toward heaven and seek to live godly lives in Christ Jesus must expect Satan to attack them with temptation and fear.
He does not willingly let anyone leave his service.

div.title: Israel fears; Moses calls the people to trust (verses 10–14)
div.p: No way was open for Israel except upward—to God. Their deliverance came from him.
We may be walking in obedience, following God toward heaven, and still find ourselves surrounded by trouble.
Some Israelites cried out to the Lord. Fear drove them to pray, and that was good.
God sometimes brings us into a desperate situation so that we will fall on our knees.
