Others shouted against Moses. Their fear led them to complain, as though God could no longer perform miracles.
They blamed Moses for bringing them out of Egypt. In effect, they were angry at God for the greatest kindness he had ever shown them.
Unbelief can be utterly unreasonable.
Moses told them not to fear.
When we cannot immediately escape trouble, it is still our duty and in our interest to rise above fear.
Let trouble strengthen our prayers and our efforts, not silence our faith and hope.
“Stand still” did not mean they should save themselves by fighting or fleeing. They were to wait for God's instructions and obey them.
They could quiet their minds through confidence in him and consider calmly the great salvation he was about to accomplish.
If God brings his people into a place where they can see no way out, he can still make a way for them.

div.title: The cloud protects Israel (verses 15–20)
div.p: Moses' silent prayers of faith accomplished more before God than Israel's loud cries of fear.
The pillar of cloud and fire moved behind the Israelites, where they needed protection, and became a wall between them and their enemies.
God's word and providence have a dark and threatening side toward sin and sinners, but a bright and gracious side toward his own people.
The God who first separated light from darkness (Genesis 1:4) now assigned darkness to Egypt and light to Israel.
There will be a still greater separation between the inheritance of God's people in light and the complete darkness reserved forever for hypocrites.

div.title: Israel crosses the sea; Egypt's army is destroyed (verses 21–31)
div.p: The division of the Red Sea terrified the Canaanites (Joshua 2:9).
For Israel it became a source of praise and triumph (Psalms 114:3; 106:9; 136:13).
It also foreshadowed baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2).
Israel's passage through the water pictured the conversion of souls (Isaiah 11:15), while the drowning of the Egyptians pictured the final destruction of all unrepentant sinners.
God displayed his almighty power by opening a path through waters extending for miles.
He can lead his people through the greatest difficulties and create a way where none exists.
Israel walked across on dry ground in the middle of the sea.
God did this to encourage his people in every age to trust him in their greatest distress.
What could be impossible for the One who accomplished this?
What will he not do for those who fear and love him, since he did so much even for these complaining, unbelieving Israelites?
Then God's just anger fell upon his enemies and the enemies of his people.
The sinners' own presumption brought them to ruin.
They could have left Israel alone but would not. When they finally wished to flee, they could not.
People often refuse to believe that attacking God's people harms themselves until it is too late.
Moses stretched out his hand at God's command, and the waters returned.
Pharaoh and his servants, who had encouraged one another to harden their hearts, fell together. None of the pursuing force escaped.
The Israelites saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore, and the sight deeply affected them.
When people see God's works and experience his goodness, they fear and trust him.
How much better it would be if we always lived with the same faith we sometimes show!
Consider the end toward which a Christian may look.
Our spiritual enemies may rage with great strength. Yet while we hold fast to God, we will pass safely through the waves under the protection of the same Savior whose power will defeat those enemies.
The enemies of our souls whom we see today, we will never see again.

row.cell: The song of Moses for the deliverance of Israel.
The bitter waters at Marah, The Israelites come to Elim.

div.title: Moses sings of Israel's deliverance (verses 1–21)
div.p: This is the oldest song known to us, Henry says.
It is a holy song entirely directed toward honoring God, lifting up his name and celebrating his praise.
It does not seek to magnify a human being in the least.
Every part of it declares holiness to the Lord.
The song can also be understood as a picture and prophecy of the final destruction of the church's enemies.
Happy are the people whose God is the Lord!
They have work to do, temptations to resist and troubles to bear. Left to themselves, they are weak; but God's grace is their strength.
They often experience sorrow, yet find comfort in him. He is their song.
Sin, death and hell threaten them, but God is and will remain their salvation.
The Lord is almighty. Woe to those who fight against their Maker!
He is perfect beyond comparison—glorious in holiness. His holiness is his glory.
That holiness appears in his hatred of sin and his wrath against stubborn sinners.
It appears also in Israel's deliverance and his faithfulness to his promises.
He is fearful in praise: the very works that cause his servants to praise him are terrifying to his enemies.
He performs wonders beyond the ordinary course of nature.
His people marvel because they have received such undeserved favor—far more than they had any reason to expect.
These are wonders of power and wonders of grace.
In both, God deserves to be worshiped with humility.

div.title: Bitter water at Marah; refreshment at Elim (verses 22–27)
div.p: In the wilderness of Shur, the Israelites had no water.
When they reached Marah, they found water, but it was too bitter to drink.
God can make the very things in which we expect the most comfort become bitter to us.
He often does so during our journey through the wilderness of this world, so that our needs and disappointments in created things may drive us to the Creator.
Only in his favor can we find lasting comfort.
In their distress the people became irritated and quarreled with Moses.
Hypocrites may show strong religious emotions and seem eager for worship, yet fall away when temptation comes.
Even true believers may be tempted to irritation, distrust and complaint when trials become severe.
In every trial, we should cast our cares upon the Lord and pour out our hearts before him.
A submissive will, a peaceful conscience and the Holy Spirit's comfort can make even the bitterest suffering bearable—indeed, sometimes pleasant.
Moses did what the people had neglected to do: he cried out to the Lord.
God graciously provided what they needed.
He directed Moses to a tree, which Moses threw into the water. Immediately the water became sweet.
Some interpreters, Henry explains, understand the tree as a picture of Christ's cross.
On that reading, the cross sweetens the bitter waters of suffering for believers and enables them to rejoice even in tribulation.
But a rebellious Israelite will fare no better than a rebellious Egyptian.
The warning of punishment is implicit; the promise is stated plainly.
God is the great Physician.
When we remain healthy, it is he who preserves us. When we recover from illness, it is he who restores us.
He is our life and the length of our days.
We must not forget that he rescues us from destruction and delivers us from our enemies so that we may serve him.
At Elim the Israelites found good water, and plenty of it.
God may allow his people to camp for a time beside the bitter waters of Marah, but that will not always be their condition.
Let us not lose heart in trouble.

row.cell: The Israelites come to the wilderness of Sin. They murmur for food, God promises bread from heaven.
An omer of manna to be preserved.

div.title: Israel complains; God promises bread from heaven (verses 1–12)
div.p: By the middle of the second month, the provisions Israel had brought from Egypt were gone. The people began to complain.
It is nothing new for people to describe the greatest kindness they have received as though it were the greatest injury.
They valued their deliverance so little that they wished they had died in Egypt—by the Lord's hand, meaning by the plagues that killed the Egyptians.
We cannot suppose that they had lived in plenty in Egypt. Nor did they need to fear starvation in the wilderness while they still possessed flocks and herds.
No one reasons more absurdly than people who are determined to complain.
When we begin to fret, we should remember that God hears every complaint we make.
Yet the Lord promised them a prompt and continuing supply of food.
He tested whether they would trust him, content to receive enough bread for each day as it came.
He was also testing whether they would serve him, and their ingratitude became plain.
When God struck Egypt with plagues, he showed that he was its Lord.
When he provided food for Israel, he showed that he was their God.

div.title: Quail and manna are provided (verses 13–21)
div.p: Quail came in the evening. The people were able to catch as many as they needed without difficulty.
Manna came down with the dew.
The Israelites called it manna, or manhu: “What is this?”
They could say of it, “This is the portion God has assigned us. We will receive it thankfully.”
It was pleasant and wholesome food.
It came from heaven. After the dew evaporated, the people saw small round pieces, like frost, resembling coriander seed and having the color of pearls.
Manna fell on six days of the week, with a double amount on the sixth.
If it was kept beyond one day, it developed worms and became foul—except when kept for the Sabbath.
The Israelites had never seen anything like it before.
They could grind it in a mill, crush it in a mortar, make it into cakes and bake it.
It continued for all forty years of their wilderness journey and wherever they camped, ceasing when they reached Canaan.
These features show that manna was different from anything familiar in their own day or ours.
They had to gather it every morning.

p.hi: First, this teaches diligence and prudence.

div.p: We should provide food for ourselves and our families through honest, peaceful work, not through idleness or deceit.
God's generosity does not remove our responsibility to act.
Even when bread literally rained from heaven, the people had to gather it before they could eat it.

p.hi: Second, this teaches contentment.

div.p: We should be satisfied with enough.
Those with the most possessions still need only food and clothing for themselves. Those with fewer possessions can generally enjoy these as well.
Thus, in actual enjoyment of life's necessities, the difference between rich and poor is not as great as the difference between what they possess.
The person who gathers much has nothing left over, and the one who gathers little does not lack what is needed.

p.hi: Third, this teaches dependence on Providence.

div.p: They could go to sleep peacefully even with no bread anywhere in the camp.
They could trust God to provide their daily bread the next morning.
Their food was safer and more certain in God's storehouse than in their own tents—and would arrive fresher and sweeter.
See the folly of hoarding out of distrust.
People who thought themselves wiser than their neighbors saved manna for the next day in case God failed to provide it.
But their stored manna bred worms and became useless.
What is selfishly and fearfully hoarded may become the very thing most thoroughly wasted.
Such riches become corrupted (James 5:2–3).
The same wisdom, power and goodness that supplied food from heaven each day to Israel continues to bring food from the ground each year through the ordinary course of nature.
He gives us richly everything we need to enjoy.

div.title: Manna and Sabbath rest (verses 22–31)
div.p: Here Scripture speaks of a Sabbath on the seventh day.
Henry emphasizes that this day was known before the law was given at Sinai, before Israel left Egypt—indeed, from the beginning (Genesis 2:3).
Setting apart one day in seven for holy activity, together with holy rest so that the activity may be enjoyed, is, in his account, one of God's most ancient laws for humanity.
God told Israel to rest on the seventh day and ensured that this obedience would not leave them worse off.
No one ultimately loses by serving God.
They were to gather and prepare enough manna on the sixth day for two days.
This teaches us to organize our family responsibilities so that they interfere as little as possible with Sabbath worship.
Necessary tasks can still be done that day.
Nevertheless, we should seek to minimize such tasks, so that we may give ourselves more fully to preparing for the life to come.
When the Israelites kept manna against God's command, it spoiled.
When they kept it according to his command, it remained good and sweet.
Everything is made holy by God's word and prayer.
God sent no manna on the seventh day.
They were not to expect it or go out gathering it. This showed that its daily appearance was a miracle.

div.title: A portion of manna is kept as a memorial (verses 32–36)
div.p: God had fed his people with manna throughout their journey. He commanded them to preserve the memory of that mercy.
Bread already eaten should not be forgotten.
God's extraordinary works and ordinary kindnesses deserve to be remembered.
God's word is the manna by which our souls are nourished (Matthew 4:4).
The Spirit's comforts are hidden manna (Revelation 2:17).
Like the manna in the wilderness, these gifts come from heaven and sustain the spiritual life of believers on their journey through this world.
Christ, as made known in the word, must be received and applied to the soul.
The means of grace must actually be used.
Every one of us must gather for ourselves.
We should begin gathering early in life and early whenever opportunities are offered.
If we let those opportunities pass, it may become too late.
Manna was meant to be eaten, not hoarded.
Those who have received Christ must live upon him through faith rather than receive his grace without benefit.
There was enough manna for everyone, but no one had too much.
Likewise, in Christ there is enough for us all, but not more than we need.
Those who ate the manna became hungry again. They eventually died, and God was displeased with many of them.
But those who feed on Christ by faith will never hunger and will die no more.
God will be pleased with them forever.
Let us earnestly seek the Holy Spirit's grace to turn everything we know about Christ crucified into genuine spiritual nourishment through faith and love.

row.cell: The Israelites murmur for water at Rephidim, God sendeth it out of the rock.
Amalek overcome, The prayers of Moses.

div.title: Water from the rock at Rephidim (verses 1–7)
div.p: The children of Israel traveled according to the Lord's command, guided by the pillar of cloud and fire.
Yet they arrived at a place where they had no water to drink.
We may be following our duty and still meet trouble. God's providence brings us into difficulties to test our faith and to glorify himself when he delivers us.
The people began to ask whether God was truly with them.
Scripture calls this testing God.
They distrusted him despite the remarkable proofs they had already received of his power and goodness.
Moses answered them gently.
It is foolish to respond to anger with more anger. That only makes a bad situation worse.
God graciously came to their help.
How wonderful is his patience with sinners who repeatedly provoke him!
To reveal his power as well as his compassion, and to make the provision an unmistakable miracle of mercy, he brought water out of a rock.
God can open springs for us where we would never expect them.
Those who keep to his path through the wilderness may trust him to provide what they need.
The miracle also directs us to Christ's grace.
The apostle says that the Rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). It was a picture of him.
God's curse could justly have fallen upon our guilty souls, but the Son of God was struck for us.
Let us ask and receive.
The water from the rock flowed in a constant, abundant supply.
However numerous the believers may be, Christ's Spirit has enough for them all.
Streams from the rock refreshed the desert and accompanied Israel on the way to Canaan.
Likewise, the grace flowing from Christ through his appointed ordinances refreshes our souls in the barren wilderness of this world until we reach glory.
The place received a new name.
But the name did not commemorate God's mercy in providing water. It remembered the people's sin in complaining.
Massah means testing, because they tested God.
Meribah means quarreling, because they argued with Moses.
Sin leaves a stain on a person's name.

div.title: Amalek attacks Israel; Moses prays (verses 8–16)
div.p: Israel fought Amalek in necessary self-defense.
God equips his people and calls them to different kinds of service for the good of his church.
Joshua fought while Moses prayed.
Both served Israel.
Moses raised his staff as a banner to encourage the soldiers and as an appeal to God for help.
Eventually his arms grew tired.
Even the strongest arm will fail when held up for a long time.
Only God's hand can remain stretched out without tiring.
We do not read that Joshua's hands became heavy during the battle, but Moses' hands became heavy during prayer.
The more spiritual an act of service is, the more likely we are to become weary and lose heart in it.
God wanted Israel to learn that Moses—the very man they had been quarreling with—was doing more for their safety through his lifted hands than they were doing through their swords.
The outcome shifted as Moses raised or lowered his hands.
The church's cause likewise prospers according to the strength of its friends' faith and the fervor of their prayers.
Even Moses, God's servant, welcomed help.
We should neither be embarrassed to ask for assistance nor reluctant to offer it.
With others supporting his arms, Moses kept them steady until sunset.
The people could take courage from the sight of Joshua before them in battle and Moses above them on the hill.
Christ fulfills both roles for us.
He is our Joshua, the Captain of our salvation who fights our battles, and our Moses, who lives forever to intercede for us so that our faith may not fail.
Weapons formed against God's Israel cannot prosper for long. They will finally be broken.
God instructed Moses to write down what had happened.
The record was to preserve the memory of Amalek's bitter hatred and cruel attacks.
But it must also preserve the memory of God's deliverance.
It foretold that Amalek would eventually be utterly defeated and destroyed.
Henry sees that destruction as a picture of the final destruction of the enemies of Christ and his kingdom.

row.cell: Jethro brings to Moses his wife and two sons.

div.title: Jethro brings Moses' family (verses 1–6)
div.p: Jethro came to rejoice with Moses over Israel's deliverance.
He also brought Moses' wife and two sons back to him.
Moses needed his family with him.
While governing God's people, he was to set a good example in caring for and leading his own household (1 Timothy 3:5).

div.title: Moses welcomes Jethro and praises God (verses 7–12)
div.p: Talking together about God's wonderful deeds is good for us and builds us up.
Jethro rejoiced not only because his son-in-law had received honor but because God had been so good to all Israel.
Those watching from outside were sometimes more deeply moved by Israel's blessings than those who had received them.
Jethro gave glory to Israel's God.
Whatever gives us joy should also move us to praise the Lord.
They offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving together.
Shared worship sanctifies friendship.
It is especially good for family members and friends to unite in the spiritual sacrifice of prayer and praise as people who meet in Christ.
The meal was modest. They ate bread—manna.
Jethro could see and taste the bread from heaven.
Though he was a Gentile, he was welcome at their table.
In the same way, Gentiles are welcomed to Christ, the Bread of Life.

div.title: Jethro advises Moses about judging the people (verses 13–27)
div.p: Moses worked tirelessly and zealously as Israel's judge.
He had already been used to redeem Israel from slavery.
Now he also foreshadowed Christ by giving laws and settling disputes among the people.
If the Israelites quarreled with one another as often as they quarreled with God, Moses must have heard many disputes.
Yet this was the work God had given him, and he carried it out with care and kindness.
Even the humblest Israelite could bring a case to him.
Moses worked from morning until evening.
Jethro saw that doing everything alone was too heavy a burden.
It also made justice painfully slow for the people who needed it.
We can try to do too much even when we are doing good.
Wisdom shows us how to avoid doing less than our duty while also avoiding responsibilities beyond our strength.
Jethro proposed a better arrangement.
People in important positions should not merely try to be useful themselves. They should also plan ways for others to become useful.
Those chosen to carry responsibility must be carefully selected.
They should understand people and affairs, show sound judgment, and not be intimidated by angry looks or loud complaints.
They must utterly reject bribes.
Above all, they should fear God.
True reverence for him keeps people from doing wrong even when they could conceal it and escape human punishment.
The fear of God is the strongest protection against the temptation to act unjustly.
Moses did not despise Jethro's advice.
People who think themselves too wise to receive counsel are not wise at all.

row.cell: The people come to Sinai, God's message to them, and their answer.
The people directed to prepare to hear the law.
The presence of God on Sinai.

div.title: God proposes his covenant at Sinai (verses 1–8)
div.p: Moses was called up the mountain to serve as the messenger of the covenant.
But the One who originated it and brought it into being was God himself.
He granted this blessed covenant entirely through his own free grace.
The covenant established at Sinai was a national covenant.
Through it, Israel became a people living under Jehovah's government.
It was a picture of the new covenant God would make with true believers in Jesus Christ.
But like other pictures and shadows, it was not the full reality of the good things to come.
Israel, as a nation, broke its covenant.
The Lord therefore promised a new covenant in which he would write his law not on stone tablets but on the people's hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:7–10).
The covenant that these passages describe as passing away was the national covenant that Israel forfeited through sin.
Unless we understand this distinction, we are likely to misunderstand the Old Testament.
We must not imagine that the Jewish nation was under a covenant of works.
Such a covenant knows nothing of repentance, faith in a Mediator, forgiveness of sins or grace.
But neither should we imagine that every Israelite possessed the character and privileges of a true believer, actually sharing in the covenant of grace.
All the people lived under a gracious administration and received outward privileges that could assist them toward salvation.
Yet most of them—like many who publicly profess Christianity—settled for the outward privileges and went no further.
Israel agreed to the covenant's terms.
With one voice the people declared that they would do everything the Lord had said.
How good it would have been if their hearts had truly matched their words!
Moses, serving as a mediator, reported their response to God.
Christ is the greater Mediator.
As our Prophet, he reveals God's will to us through his commands and promises.
Then, as our Priest, he brings our spiritual sacrifices before God.
These are not merely prayers and praises.
They also include sincere love for God and holy resolutions, all produced within us by Christ's own Spirit.

div.title: Israel prepares to hear God's law (verses 9–15)
div.p: God delivered the law in a solemn and awe-inspiring way so that Israel would recognize the majesty of the One who spoke.
The manner of its giving also exposed the people's guilt and taught them that their own obedience could never make them stand righteous before God's judgment.
Through the law, sinners learn three things: what they ought to be, what they actually are, and what they lack.
They discover the nature, necessity and glory of redemption—and of being made holy.
When the law has taught a sinner to flee to Christ and love him, that same law becomes the rule by which the believer lives in obedience and faith.

div.title: The Lord descends upon Sinai (verses 16–25)
div.p: No sermon like this had ever been preached before, nor has there been one like it since: God spoke to his church in the wilderness.
We might expect such fearsome signs to suppress human arrogance and curiosity.
Yet the hard heart of an unawakened sinner can treat even the most terrible warnings and judgments lightly.
As we draw near to God, we must remember his holiness and greatness.
We must also remember our own smallness and defilement.
We cannot stand before his judgment on the basis of perfect obedience to his righteous law.
When sinners become convinced of their guilt, they ask what they must do to be saved.
The answer is to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ and be saved.
The Holy Spirit first uses the law to convince us of sin.
Then he takes the things of Christ and makes them known to our souls.
The gospel tells us that Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us.
Through his blood we receive redemption, including the forgiveness of sins.
Through him we are justified from everything from which the law of Moses could not justify us.
Yet God's law remains binding as a rule of life.
The Son of God came down from heaven and endured poverty, shame, agony and death.
He did this not only to redeem us from the law's curse.
He also did it to bind us more closely to obey its commands.

row.cell: The preface to the ten commandments.
The commandments of the first table.

div.title: The preface to the Ten Commandments (verses 1–2)
div.p: God speaks to human beings in many ways: through conscience, through the events of his providence, and through his word.
We should listen carefully to them all.
But he never spoke in quite the same way as when he gave the Ten Commandments.
This law had already been given to humanity, written upon the human heart.
Sin had so thoroughly obscured it that God needed to renew people's knowledge of it.
The law is spiritual. It judges not only outward behavior but also the heart's hidden thoughts, desires and inclinations.
Its great demand is love. Without love, outward obedience is merely hypocrisy.
The law requires obedience that is perfect, unfailing and constant.
No legitimate law grants permission to disobey it.
Whoever keeps the whole law but breaks it at one point is guilty of all (James 2:10).
Whether in heart or action, in thought, word or deed, any departure from God's law is sin.
And the wages of sin is death.

div.title: The first four commandments: our duty toward God (verses 3–11)
div.p: The first table of the law, consisting of its first four commandments, describes our duties toward God.
It is right that these come first.
Before a person had a neighbor to love, that person already had a Maker to love.
How can someone be faithful to a brother or sister while being unfaithful to God?
The first commandment concerns the One whom we worship: Jehovah, and Jehovah alone.
It forbids worshiping created things.
Any failure in perfect love, gratitude, reverence or worship breaks this command.
Whatever we do should be done for God's glory.
The second commandment concerns the way we worship the Lord.
It forbids making an image or picture of the Deity in any form or for any purpose, or worshiping any creature or representation.
But its spiritual meaning reaches further.
It forbids every kind of superstition and every attempt to replace God's appointed worship with inventions of our own.
The third commandment concerns the reverence and seriousness with which we worship.
It forbids false oaths, careless appeals to God's name, profane cursing, and all irreverent use of sacred things.
There is no worthwhile advantage, honor or pleasure in doing such things.
The Lord will not hold guiltless the one who misuses his name.
The fourth commandment begins with the word Remember.
Henry takes this to mean that the Sabbath was not instituted here for the first time: it was already known.
One day in seven must be kept holy.
Six days are given for ordinary work, though not in a way that excuses neglecting God or our souls.
We should finish our ordinary work during those days rather than leaving it for the Sabbath.
Christ allowed works of necessity, mercy and piety.
The Sabbath was made for human beings, not human beings for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).
But works devoted to luxury, vanity or self-indulgence are forbidden.

Henry specifically includes trading, paying wages, settling accounts, writing business letters, secular study, idle social visits, unnecessary travel and frivolous conversation among activities that do not keep the day holy.
Laziness is a merely fleshly kind of rest, not holy rest.
The Lord's Sabbath should be rest from ordinary work and rest expressed through serving God.
Even its benefits for human health and happiness, alongside the opportunity it gives us to care for our souls, display the excellence of this command.
God has blessed the day and blesses people through it.
Henry notes that the command's blessing and call to holiness refer to the Sabbath day, rather than being restricted by their wording to the seventh day alone.

div.title: The final six commandments: our duty toward one another (verses 12–17)
div.p: The second table of the law concerns the duties we owe ourselves and other people.
These six commandments explain the call to love our neighbor as ourselves (Luke 10:27).
Godliness and honesty belong together.
The fifth commandment concerns our duties toward family members, particularly our parents.
Honoring father and mother includes respecting them in our conduct and willingly obeying their lawful commands.
Children should come when called, go when sent, do what they are told, avoid what is forbidden, and do all this cheerfully out of love.
It includes receiving parental advice and correction.
Children should seek their parents' comfort, make their old age easier and support them if they need help.
Jesus expressly includes this duty of material support (Matthew 15:4–6).
Henry observes that obedient children have often enjoyed particular earthly blessings, while disobedience has brought the opposite.
The sixth commandment requires us to value the life and safety of other people as highly as our own.
Magistrates and their officers may enforce lawful judgments; truthful witnesses do not break this command.
Self-defense is lawful.
But much that human law does not classify as murder still counts as murder before God.
Violent anger and drunkenness do not excuse the taking of life.
Duels are especially guilty expressions of pride and revenge.
Henry also condemns fighting for pay, fame, anger or hatred.
Leading people into vices or crimes that shorten life may violate this command.
So may cruel behavior that breaks the hearts or shortens the lives of parents, spouses or other relatives.
It forbids envy, malice, hatred, anger, provoking words and insults.
It also forbids destroying one's own life.
Positively, it calls us to kindness, patience and forgiveness.
The seventh commandment concerns purity.
We should fear what defiles the body as seriously as what destroys it.
Whatever feeds impure imagination or stirs lust falls under this command—including indecent pictures, books and conversation.
The eighth commandment applies love to other people's possessions.
What we gain honestly is the portion of this world's goods God has allotted us.
We should receive it thankfully, be content with it and trust Providence for tomorrow while using lawful means of support.
Taking advantage of people's ignorance, willingness to trust or desperate need violates this law, even where society hardly condemns it.
Those who plunder whole nations are not exempt merely because they escape human courts.

Defrauding the public, taking on debts with no realistic prospect of repayment, evading legitimate debts, extravagance, living on charity without need and squeezing the poor through unjust wages are also violations.
The command calls for diligence, thrift and contentment.
In matters of property, we should treat others as we would want them to treat us.
The ninth commandment protects our own reputation and that of our neighbors.
It forbids lying, deliberate ambiguity, deceit and any scheme to mislead.
It forbids unjust attacks on another person's reputation.
This includes false testimony, slander, gossip, backbiting and making someone's wrongdoing appear worse than it was.
It also forbids trying to improve our own standing by damaging another person's good name.
How often people of every social rank break this command!
The tenth commandment reaches the root of sinful desire: You shall not covet.
Other commands forbid desires that would lead us to harm our neighbor.
This one also forbids wrong desires to possess something merely to gratify ourselves.

div.title: Israel trembles before God's law (verses 18–21)
div.p: The law is so wide-reaching that we cannot measure all its demands, so spiritual that we cannot evade its judgment, and so reasonable that we cannot justly accuse it.
It governs our present conduct and will be the standard of God's future judgment.
Measured by it, we discover how thoroughly our lives have been marked by sin.
With such a holy law and such a solemn judgment before us, how could we despise Christ's gospel?
Knowing the law shows us our need to repent.
In every true believer, sin has been dethroned and crucified.
God writes his law on the heart and renews his own image there.
The Holy Spirit enables believers to hate sin and flee from it, and to love and obey God's law sincerely.
Nor do they ever cease repenting.

div.title: The Lord gives further instructions about worship (verses 22–26)
div.p: Moses entered the thick darkness and heard God speak the commands that follow through the end of chapter 23.
Most of these instructions explain and apply the Ten Commandments.
The laws immediately given here concern God's worship.
God assured Israel that he would graciously receive its offerings.
Under the gospel, people are encouraged to pray everywhere.
Wherever God's people gather in his name to worship him, he is present among them.
He will come to them and bless them.

div.title: Laws concerning servants (verses 1–11)
div.p: The laws in this chapter help explain the fifth and sixth commandments.
They reflect a society and customs very different from ours, and Henry says they are not binding on us as civil laws.
Nevertheless, they explain the enduring moral law and the basic principles of justice.
A person held in servitude pictured humanity's bondage to sin, Satan and the condemnation of the law.
People fell into this bondage when they robbed God of his glory by breaking his commands.
In the servant's release, we see a picture of the freedom Christ gives his people.
Christ, the Son of God, sets them free from slavery so that they become truly free.
That liberty is given freely, without money or payment, entirely through grace.

div.title: Laws protecting life and restraining violence (verses 12–21)
div.p: God gives and sustains life through his providence.
Through his law he also protects it.
A deliberate murderer was to be taken even from God's altar for judgment.
But God provided cities of refuge for people who caused another person's death without intending any harm.
They had not committed deliberate murder, but had caused an accidental death while doing something lawful.
Children should hear the solemn judgment God's word pronounces upon ingratitude and disobedience toward parents.
If they have cursed a parent—even secretly in their hearts—or struck a parent, they should remember that God will hold them accountable unless they repent and flee to the Savior for refuge.
Parents, meanwhile, should raise their children carefully.
They should give them a good example, particularly in controlling their own tempers and praying for them.
They must take care not to provoke their children to anger.
In times of poverty, Israelites sometimes sold their own labor or that of their children.
Magistrates could sell some offenders as punishment, and creditors were sometimes allowed to sell people who could not pay what they owed.
But kidnapping people for the purpose of enslaving them is classed in the New Testament among the gravest crimes.
These laws also required compensation when someone was injured, even if the injury did not lead to death.
The gospel instructs masters to restrain their threats (Ephesians 6:9).
They should remember Job's question: What will I do when God rises to judge me? (Job 31:13–14).

div.title: Further principles of justice (verses 22–36)
div.p: The cases in this passage give rules of justice for the society of Israel.
Their principles still help us judge similar situations.
They teach us to take great care not to wrong another person, whether directly or indirectly.
When we have caused a loss, we should be ready to make it good.
Indeed, we should desire that no one suffer loss because of what we have done.

p.hi: Judicial laws.

div.title: The spirit of these laws
div.p: God's people should always be ready to show gentleness and mercy, according to the spirit of the laws given here.
We must answer to God not only for the wrong we do deliberately, out of malice, but also for harm caused by our carelessness.
Therefore, whenever we have harmed our neighbor, we should make restitution, even when no human law forces us to do so.
Let these Scriptures remind us what God's grace does in those to whom it has truly appeared.
Grace teaches us and, by its holy power, enables us to turn away from ungodliness and worldly desires.
It teaches us to live with self-control, righteousness and devotion to God in this present world (Titus 2:12).
God's grace also teaches us that the Lord himself is our portion.
In him there is more than enough to satisfy every desire of our souls.

row.cell: The year of rest, The sabbath, The three festivals.
God promises to conduct the Israelites to Canaan.

div.title: Laws against falsehood and injustice (verses 1–9)
div.p: The law of Moses bears clear marks of sound moral judgment and wise government.
All its provisions serve its stated purposes: Israel was to worship the one true God and remain distinct from the pagan nations around it.
We must never allow partisan loyalties, friends, witnesses or popular opinions to distort our judgments.
They must not lead us to minimize serious wrongs or exaggerate minor ones.
They must not cause us to excuse guilty people, accuse innocent people or misrepresent the facts in any way.

div.title: The seventh-year rest, Sabbath, and festivals (verses 10–19)
div.p: Every seventh year, Israel's land was to rest.
The people were not to plow or sow it.
They could eat what grew on its own, but were not to collect it for storage.
Henry understands this law as teaching dependence on God's providence.
It also taught Israel to trust God's faithfulness in providing greater harvests while they followed his appointed seasons.
The rest of the land pictured the heavenly rest.
In that rest, the labors, worries and concerns of this world will end forever.
Israel was strictly forbidden to honor the gods of the surrounding nations.
The people were particularly inclined toward idolatry, so they were to erase even the remembrance of those false gods.
God also required his people to gather solemnly in worship at the place he would choose.
They were to come together before the Lord.
What a good Master we serve!
He has made rejoicing before him one of our duties.
We should gladly devote to his service the portion of time he requires.
His Sabbaths and appointed acts of worship should be feasts to our souls.
The Israelites were not to come before God empty-handed.
Likewise, we should never approach his worship empty-hearted.
Our hearts should be filled with holy longing for him and renewed dedication to his service.
God takes pleasure in spiritual sacrifices of this kind.

div.title: God promises to guide Israel to Canaan (verses 20–33)
div.p: God promised to guide and protect Israel throughout the wilderness journey and bring the people into the promised land.
He said that he would send his angel before them.
With this promise came a command: they must obey the angel God would send.
Christ is the Angel of Jehovah, Henry says, as the apostle teaches in 1 Corinthians 10:9.
God also promised Israel a secure and pleasant settlement in Canaan.
The condition was entirely reasonable.
They were to serve only the true God, not the gods of the nations—gods that were no gods at all.
Consider how generous God's promises were.
He promised good food, continuing health, growing possessions and long life.
In this way, godliness has a promise for the present life as well.
He also promised victory over their enemies.
God sent swarms of hornets ahead of Israel's armies.
He can use even such small creatures to judge the enemies of his people.
In kindness toward the church, God often defeats its enemies little by little.
That keeps us watchful and continually dependent on him.
In the same way, sinful habits and desires are driven from believers' hearts gradually, not all at once.
Alongside the promises came another command: Israel must not make alliances of friendship with idolaters.
Anyone who wants to avoid evil practices must also avoid company that draws them into evil.
Living among people devoted to wrongdoing can be dangerous.
Other people's sins may become traps for us.
Our greatest danger comes from people who lead us to sin against God.

row.cell: Moses is called up into the mountain, The people promise obedience.
The glory of the Lord appears.
Moses goes up into the mountain.

div.title: The covenant is confirmed with blood (verses 1–8)
div.p: God and Israel entered into a solemn covenant.
Its solemnity pointed toward the covenant of grace between God and believers through Jesus Christ.
As soon as God set Israel apart as his own people, he gave them his written word to govern their life.
He has continued to govern his people through his word ever since.
God's covenants and commands are just in themselves and intended for our good.
The more thoughtfully we consider them and the more fully and clearly they are explained, the more reason we see to accept them and obey.
Blood from the sacrifice was sprinkled on the altar, the book and the people.
Neither the people themselves, their moral obedience nor their religious services could be accepted by a holy God without the shedding and application of blood.
Every blessing God gave them was an act of mercy.
He intended to treat them kindly.
In the same way, a sinner who trusts in Christ's blood can offer obedience that is willing and acceptable to God.

div.title: The elders behold God's glory (verses 9–11)
div.p: Israel's elders saw the God of Israel.
They received a glimpse of his glory.
Whatever they saw could not be represented in an image or picture.
Yet they saw enough to know that God truly was with them.
Scripture describes only what was beneath his feet.
Sapphires formed the pavement under them.
May we also keep all the wealth of this world beneath our feet, rather than setting it in our hearts.
Believers now see the glorious justice and holiness of God much more clearly in the face of Jesus Christ than they saw them even through terrifying conviction of sin.
Through the Savior they can enjoy communion with the holy God.

div.title: Moses ascends into the cloud (verses 12–18)
div.p: A cloud covered the mountain for six days.
It was a sign of God's special presence there.
Moses trusted that the One who had called him upward would also keep him safe.
The very attributes of God that terrify the wicked are a cause of joy to believers who approach him with humble reverence.
Through faith in the atoning Sacrifice, we hope to receive an honor greater than anything Moses experienced on earth.
Now we see only dimly, as though through a mirror.
But when God appears, we will see him face to face.
That vision will not last for a few days.
It will continue throughout eternity, with joy that remains bright and may grow brighter still.

row.cell: What the Israelites were to offer for making the tabernacle.

div.title: Offerings for God's dwelling among Israel (verses 1–9)
div.p: God had chosen Israel as his own special people, above all other nations.
He himself would be their King.
He therefore commanded that a royal dwelling be prepared for him among them.
This dwelling was called the sanctuary, the holy place, or the habitation.
There God would show his presence among his people.
Because Israel lived in tents during its journey through the wilderness, God's royal dwelling was to be a tabernacle—a tent that could travel with them.
The people were to supply the materials Moses needed, each person giving freely and willingly.
The best use we can make of earthly possessions is to honor God through acts of devotion and charity.
We should ask not only, “What must we do?” but also, “What can we do for God?”
Whatever we give him, we should give cheerfully, not resentfully.
God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
We should consider money spent in his service well spent.
Yet everything done in God's service must also be done according to his directions.

div.title: The ark and the mercy seat (verses 10–22)
div.p: The ark was a chest covered in gold.
It was made to hold the two tablets of God's law.
Those tablets are called the testimony, because through them God testified to his will.
The law was a testimony for Israel, guiding the people in their duty.
If they disobeyed, it would also be a testimony against them.
The ark stood in the Most Holy Place.
The high priest sprinkled sacrificial blood and burned incense before it.
Above it appeared the visible glory that represented God's presence.
Henry sees the ark as a picture of Christ.
His human nature was without sin and did not undergo corruption.
It was personally united with his divine nature, and through his death he made atonement for our violations of God's law.
The golden cherubim faced each other, both looking down toward the ark.
They represented the angels' attendance upon the Redeemer, their readiness to carry out his will, their presence when the saints gather, and their desire to understand the mysteries of the gospel.
The ark was covered by a golden lid called the mercy seat.
God was said to dwell—or sit enthroned—between the cherubim above that mercy seat.
There, like a king seated on his throne, he gave his law and listened to those who came to him in prayer.

div.title: The table of the bread of the Presence (verses 23–30)
div.p: A wooden table covered with gold stood in the outer room of the tabernacle.
The bread of the Presence was always to be placed on it.
The table, its furnishings and their use seem to picture the fellowship the Lord enjoys with his redeemed people through his appointed means of worship.
They point to the provisions and feasts of his household.
They also picture the food believers find for their souls whenever they hunger for it.
Finally, they point to the delight God takes in his people's lives and service, which are presented before him in Christ.

div.title: The golden lampstand (verses 31–40)
div.p: The lampstand represented the light of God's word and Spirit, given through Jesus Christ to believers in this dark world.
That light guides their worship and obedience and brings them comfort.
Compared with the glory it will enjoy in heaven, the church is still in darkness, just as the tabernacle was.
Yet God's word shines like a lamp in a dark place (2 Peter 1:19).
How dark the world would be without it!
Verse 40 gives Moses an explicit warning.
Nothing was to be left to Moses' personal preference, to the workmen's creativity or to the people's wishes.
God's will had to be followed in every detail.
Christ likewise commanded his disciples to observe everything he had instructed them (Matthew 28:20).
Let us remember that believers themselves are temples of the Holy Spirit.
God's law is written on our hearts.
We should live in fellowship with him, enjoy the feast of his appointed ordinances, and be the light of the world—if we are truly following Christ.
May the Lord help us examine ourselves in the light of this description of faith and live accordingly.

row.cell: The vail of the holy of holies, and for the entrance.

div.title: The richly woven curtains (verses 1–6)
div.p: God made his presence known to Israel through a tabernacle, or tent, because that suited the people's life in the wilderness.
He adapts the signs of his favor and the gifts of his grace to the circumstances and needs of his people.
The inner curtains were to be richly made.
They were embroidered with cherubim.
Henry understands these figures as a reminder that God's angels camp around his church (Psalm 34:7).

div.title: The goats' hair curtains and coverings (verses 7–14)
div.p: The outer curtains were made of less valuable materials.
They were longer and wider than the inner ones, so that they covered them completely.
Other coverings of animal skins protected the whole structure.
Henry sees in these layers a picture of Christ's person and teaching, the church of true Christians, and heavenly realities.
Outwardly, these things may appear humble and unimpressive.
Inwardly, however, and in God's sight, they are glorious and precious.

div.title: The boards, bases and crossbars (verses 15–30)
div.p: Each silver base weighed about 115 pounds, according to Henry's reckoning.
The bases stood in rows upon the ground.
Strong boards of acacia wood, covered in gold, were fitted into pairs of bases by their joints.
Together they formed the walls along the two sides and the western end.
Bars passing through golden rings bound the walls together.
Curtains were then spread over the structure.
The tabernacle could be moved, yet it was solid and stable.
Its materials were also extremely costly.
In all this, Henry sees a picture of God's church.
It is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ himself as the chief cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20–21).

div.title: The veil of the Most Holy Place (verses 31–37)
div.p: A veil hung from pillars and divided the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.
It prevented people from looking into the innermost sanctuary.
The apostle explains its meaning in Hebrews 9:8.
The ceremonial law could not make worshipers perfect.
Simply observing its ordinances could not bring anyone into heaven.
The way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been fully revealed while the first tabernacle still stood.
Life and immortality remained hidden until the gospel brought them to light.
The tearing of the veil when Christ died pointed to that new revelation (Matthew 27:51).
Through Jesus' blood we now have freedom to enter the Most Holy Place in our worship.
But that access never removes our duty to approach God with holy reverence.
Another curtain hung at the outer entrance of the tabernacle.
That curtain was the only outward protection the sanctuary had.
God himself takes care of his church on earth.
If he chooses, a curtain can defend his house as effectively as bronze gates and iron bars.
With these pictures of Christ and his church before us, what judgment do we make of them?
Do we see glory in Christ's person?
Do we recognize excellence in his character, something precious in his salvation, and wisdom in the teaching of the cross?
Can our religion stand examination?
Are we more concerned to have hearts approved by God than reputations admired by other people?

div.title: The altar for burnt offerings (verses 1–8)
div.p: The altar stood in the court in front of the tabernacle.
The people brought their sacrifices there, and the priests offered them to God.
It was made of wood covered in bronze.
A bronze grate was fitted inside the hollow altar, near its middle.
The fire burned upon this grate, and the sacrifices were consumed there.
The grate was an open network, like a sieve, so that ashes could fall through it.
The bronze altar was a picture of Christ, who died to atone for our sins.
The wood would have been consumed by the fire from heaven if the bronze had not protected it.
In the same way, Henry says, Christ's human nature could not have endured God's wrath unless divine power had sustained it.

div.title: The court around the tabernacle (verses 9–19)
div.p: A court enclosed the tabernacle.
Henry describes it as about sixty yards long and thirty yards wide.
Curtains hung upon bronze pillars fixed in bronze bases formed its boundary.
Inside this enclosure, priests and Levites offered the sacrifices.
Other Israelites were also admitted into the court.
Henry understands these distinctions as pointing to the difference between the visible church of those who merely profess religion and the true spiritual church.
Only the latter truly has access to God and enjoys communion with him.

div.title: Oil and light for the lamps (verses 20–21)
div.p: The pure oil represented the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit.
Believers receive these from Christ, the good Olive Tree.
Without them, our light cannot shine before other people.
The priests were charged with lighting the lamps and tending them.
Likewise, ministers are charged with enlightening God's church on earth through preaching and explaining the Scriptures.
God's word is a lamp.
Blessed be God: this light is no longer confined to the Jewish tabernacle.
It has become a light for the Gentiles and a message of salvation to the ends of the earth.

row.cell: Aaron and his sons set apart for the priest's office, Their garments.
The breastplate, The Urim and Thummim.
The robe of the ephod, The plate of the mitre.

div.title: Aaron and his sons are appointed as priests (verses 1–5)
div.p: Until this time, the heads of households had served as priests and offered sacrifices.
Now the office was restricted to Aaron's family, and that arrangement continued until the coming of the gospel.
The priests' special clothing distinguished them from the people.
But it also represented the holy conduct that should be the glory and beauty of everyone who ministers in God's name.
Without such a life, both the minister and the ministry will be despised.
These garments also pointed to the glory of divine majesty and the beauty of perfect holiness.
Those qualities make Jesus Christ our great High Priest.
Under the gospel, our own adornment should not consist chiefly of gold and costly clothing.
It should be the garments of salvation and the robe of righteousness.

div.title: The ephod (verses 6–14)
div.p: The high priest wore a richly made ephod as his outer garment.
Other priests wore plain linen ephods.
The high priest's ephod was a short sleeveless garment, fastened closely around the body with a belt.
Its shoulder pieces joined together by precious stones set in gold.
One stone was placed on each shoulder, engraved with the names of Israel's children.
This pictured Christ, our High Priest, who carries his people before the Lord as a continual memorial.
Henry compares the ephod with Christ's seamless coat, woven in one piece from the top.
He also speaks of the golden bells associated with this garment: their value and pleasant sound represent the good profession believers make.
The pomegranates represent the good fruit they bear.

div.title: The breastplate; the Urim and Thummim (verses 15–30)
div.p: The high priest's finest ornament was his breastplate, a beautifully worked piece of cloth.
Each tribe's name was engraved upon a precious stone set into it.
These stones showed how precious and honorable God's people are in his sight.
Even the smallest and poorest tribe was represented by a jewel on the high priest's breast.
Likewise, every believer is dear to Christ, no matter how little other people value that believer.
The priest carried the tribes' names on both his shoulders and his breast.
This reminds us of the strength and love with which Jesus intercedes for his own.
He carries them with almighty power and holds them close with tender affection.
What comfort this gives us whenever we approach God!
The Urim and Thummim were placed in the breastplate.
Through them, God's will was made known in difficult or doubtful matters.
Their names mean light and integrity, Henry explains.
Many different ideas have been proposed about what they actually were.
He considers it most likely that they were the twelve precious stones in the breastplate.
But Christ is now our divine Oracle.
In these last days, God reveals himself and his will to us through his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2; John 1:18).
Christ is the true Light, the faithful Witness and the Truth itself.
From him we receive the Spirit of Truth, who guides us into all truth.

div.title: The robe and the golden plate (verses 31–39)
div.p: The robe worn beneath the ephod reached to the knees and had no sleeves.
Aaron had to minister in the garments God appointed.
We must serve the Lord with holy fear, remembering that in ourselves we deserve death.
A golden plate was fastened to Aaron's forehead.
On it were engraved the words “Holiness to the Lord.”
This reminded him that God is holy and that priests must be holy and wholly dedicated to him.
The declaration appeared openly on Aaron's forehead.
In the same way, our belonging to God should be openly professed.
The letters were engraved like those on a seal.
They were meant to be deep and lasting—not merely painted on, to be washed away.
Our holiness to the Lord must be just as durable and real.
Christ is our High Priest.
Through him our sins are forgiven and no longer counted against us.
Only because of Christ are our persons and actions pleasing to God.

div.title: Clothing for Aaron's sons (verses 40–43)
div.p: The priests' garments pointed to the righteousness of Christ.
Without that righteousness, we will appear before God bearing our own guilt and will die.
Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments (Revelation 16:15).
And blessed be God that he has given us a High Priest of his own choosing.
Christ has been appointed and set apart for his work.
The glory of his divine majesty and the beauty of his perfect holiness equip him fully for his great office.
Happy are we if the spiritual meaning of the law teaches us how perfectly suited he is to our need.
We cannot approach a holy God or find acceptance except through him.
We receive no light, wisdom or perfection apart from Christ.
We possess no true beauty or glory except through becoming like him.
Let us take courage from our High Priest's power, love and compassion.
We may come boldly to the throne of grace, where we will receive mercy and find grace for the help we need.

row.cell: The sacrifice and ceremony for the consecration of the priests.
The continual burnt-offerings, God's promise to dwell among Israel.

div.title: Aaron and his sons are consecrated (verses 1–37)
div.p: Aaron and his sons were to be set apart for the priestly office through solemn ceremonies.
Our Lord Jesus is the great High Priest whom we profess.
God appointed him to this work.
He was anointed with the Spirit, and so bears the title Messiah, or Christ.
He is clothed with glory and beauty.
He was sanctified through his own blood and made perfect—or fully consecrated to his mission—through sufferings (Hebrews 2:10).
All believers are also spiritual priests.
They offer spiritual sacrifices to God (1 Peter 2:5).
Washed in Christ's blood, they have been made priests to God (Revelation 1:5–6).
They too are clothed with the beauty of holiness and have received an anointing (1 John 2:27).
The Spirit of God is called the finger of God.
Compare Luke 11:20 with Matthew 12:28.
Through that Spirit, the merit of Christ is applied to our souls.
The priests' consecration therefore represents the admission of a sinner into the spiritual priesthood.
That person may now offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

div.title: The continual sacrifices and God's presence (verses 38–46)
div.p: One lamb was to be offered on the altar each morning, and another each evening.
These sacrifices pointed to Christ's continual intercession for his church.
He offered himself once for all.
Yet the benefits of that one sacrifice continue, as he lives forever to intercede.
The morning and evening lambs also teach us to present our own daily spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise to God.
Morning and evening worship are among the most necessary duties of each day.
They are also among the greatest comforts available to us.
We should observe prayer times as faithfully as meal times.
Those who do not keep coming to God's throne of grace starve their own souls.
Steadiness in serving God brings the comfort of fellowship with him.

row.cell: The holy anointing oil, The perfume.

div.title: The altar of incense (verses 1–10)
div.p: The incense altar represented the Son of God in his human nature.
The incense burning upon it pictured his pleading on behalf of his people.
Its daily offering, morning and evening, represented Christ's continual intercession.
Once each year, the blood of atonement was applied to the altar.
This taught that Christ's intercession draws all its power from the suffering he endured on earth.
We need no sacrifice or intercessor apart from Christ himself.

div.title: The ransom payment (verses 11–16)
div.p: The required contribution was half a shekel.
Henry compares this with about fifteen pence in the money of his own time.
The rich must not give more, and the poor must not give less.
The souls of rich and poor are equally precious.
God shows no favoritism (Acts 10:34; Job 34:19).
In other offerings, people gave in proportion to their financial means.
But this contribution represented the ransom of the soul and therefore had to be the same for everyone.
Every soul is of equal value.
All face the same danger, and all need a ransom.
The money collected supported the service of the tabernacle.
Those who benefit from public worship should not resent the expense of maintaining it.
Money cannot atone for anyone's soul.
But it can be used to honor the One who has made atonement and to support the proclamation of the gospel through which its benefits are applied.

div.title: The bronze basin for washing (verses 17–21)
div.p: A large bronze basin filled with water stood near the tabernacle entrance.
Aaron and his sons were required to wash their hands and feet there each time they entered to minister.
This taught them to serve God in purity and to dread the defilement of sin.
They were not merely to be washed once, when they first became priests.
They also had to wash repeatedly and remain clean whenever they came to serve.
We likewise need to come to God every day.
We must continually renew our repentance and look to Christ's blood for forgiveness.
We offend against God in many ways each day.

div.title: The holy oil and incense (verses 22–38)
div.p: God gave exact instructions for preparing the oil for anointing and the incense used in the tabernacle.
The fragrant oil, pleasing to the eye and to the sense of smell, pictured the excellence of holiness.
Christ's name is like perfume poured out (Song of Songs 1:3).
And the good name of a Christian is like precious ointment (Ecclesiastes 7:1).
The incense offered on the golden altar was made from sweet spices.
Before use it had to be crushed very fine.
Henry sees this as a picture of the Redeemer's bruising in sacrifice, an offering with a sweet fragrance to God.
The same oil and incense must not be manufactured for ordinary private use.
God thereby taught the people to revere the worship appointed for him.
We must not treat as common or misuse anything through which God reveals himself.
It is a great insult to God to make jokes about sacred things or amuse ourselves at the expense of his word and ordinances.
It is especially dangerous—and may prove fatal—to use an outward profession of Christ's gospel as a means of advancing worldly interests.

row.cell: Bezaleel and Aholiab are appointed and qualified for the work of the tabernacle.
Moses receives the tables of the law.

div.title: Bezalel and Oholiab receive gifts for the work (verses 1–11)
div.p: The Israelites had worked as builders and brickmakers in Egypt.
They had not learned the skill needed to produce the intricate workmanship required for the tabernacle.
But the same Holy Spirit who later enabled the apostles to speak in many languages miraculously gave Bezalel and Oholiab the abilities they lacked.
Honor received from God always comes with work to do.
To be employed in his service is itself a great honor.
When God calls people to a task, he either finds them fitted for it or makes them fit for it.
The Lord gives different gifts to different people.
We should each give diligent attention to the particular work entrusted to us.
And whatever skill or wisdom we possess, we must remember that God has put it into our hearts so that we may obey his commands.

div.title: The Sabbath must still be observed (verses 12–17)
div.p: God had ordered a tabernacle to be built for his worship.
But the people were not to imagine that the sacredness of the work, or their need to finish it quickly, gave them permission to build on the Sabbath.
The Hebrew word shabbath means rest or ceasing from work.
The Sabbath points toward the rest in glory that remains for God's people.
For this reason, Henry argues, the Sabbath's moral obligation continues until time itself gives way to eternity.

div.title: Moses receives the stone tablets (verse 18)
div.p: God wrote his law on tablets of stone.
Their material showed how enduring the law is.
But it also illustrated the hardness of the human heart.
It would be easier to carve words into stone than to write anything truly good upon our naturally corrupt hearts.
The tablets were written by the finger of God—by his will and power.
Only God can write his law on the human heart.
He gives us hearts of flesh.
Then, through his Spirit, who is called the finger of God, he writes his will within us (2 Corinthians 3:3).

row.cell: The people cause Aaron to make a golden calf.
God's displeasure, The intercession of Moses.
Moses breaks the tables of the law, He destroys the golden calf.

div.title: Israel makes the golden calf (verses 1–6)
div.p: While Moses was on the mountain receiving God's law, the people gathered noisily around Aaron.
They had grown tired of waiting for Moses to return.
Impatience leaves people exposed to many temptations.
We must wait for the Lord until he comes, even when he seems to delay.
The people readily gave up their earrings to make an idol.
Their willingness should shame our reluctance to give generously in the service of the true God.
They did not complain about the cost of idolatry.
Why, then, should we begrudge what true religion requires?
Aaron made an image of an ox or calf, shaping it with an engraving tool.
Then the people offered sacrifices to it.
They had put an image before themselves and exchanged God's truth for a lie.
Their sacrifices therefore became detestable.
Only a few days earlier, in that very place, they had heard God command them not to make a carved image.
They had also solemnly promised to obey everything he had said (Exodus 24:7).
Yet they broke his explicit command and defied his clear warning before even leaving the place where they had made the covenant.
This shows that the law has no more power to make us holy than to justify us.
Through it we learn what sin is, but we do not receive sin's cure.
God had appointed Aaron to the priesthood.
Yet a man who had disgraced himself by making an altar for a golden calf could never claim to deserve the honor of serving at God's altar.
He had to acknowledge that he owed it entirely to free grace.
This leaves no room for pride or boasting.

div.title: God's anger and Moses' intercession (verses 7–14)
div.p: God told Moses that the Israelites had corrupted themselves.
Sin corrupts the sinner, and people corrupt themselves by yielding to their own sinful desires.
They had left the right path.
That is what sin does: it turns us away from duty into a wrong way.
They had quickly forgotten God's mighty works.
God sees what human beings cannot detect.
No evil in the world is hidden from him.
We could not bear to witness even a thousandth part of the wickedness God sees every day.
God revealed the greatness of his just displeasure in a way that human beings could understand.
Moses prayed for the people's deliverance from ruin.
In this, he pictured Christ, through whose mediation alone God reconciles the world to himself.
Moses appealed to God's glory.
Just as honoring God's name ought to be our first request—as it is in the Lord's Prayer—it should also be our principal argument when we pray.
God's promises should likewise be the basis of our prayers.
He is fully able to do everything he has promised.
See how powerful prayer can be!
In response to Moses, God showed his purpose to spare the people, although earlier he had appeared determined to destroy them.
Scripture calls this change in the outward disclosure of God's purpose his relenting from the threatened judgment.

div.title: Moses destroys the idol (verses 15–20)
div.p: What a sharp contrast Moses experienced!
He came down from a mountain where he had enjoyed fellowship with God and entered a world full of wickedness.
In God's presence he had seen only purity and what is pleasing to him.
Among the people he now found sin and conduct that provoked the Lord.
To show that the idol was nothing at all, Moses ground the golden calf into dust.
He mixed the powder with the people's drink.
This pictured the truth that those who turn away in heart will be made to taste the bitter consequences of their own ways.

div.title: Aaron's excuse and the judgment on idolaters (verses 21–29)
div.p: No wise person ever offered a more foolish and worthless excuse than Aaron did.
We should never allow other people's words or actions to draw us into sin.
Others can tempt us, but they cannot force us to sin.
When Moses approached, the people's dancing turned to trembling.
Their sin had exposed them to shame.
Moses did not try to remove that disgrace by concealing what had happened or offering a misleading explanation.
He dealt with it by punishing the wrongdoing.
The Levites were commanded to kill the leaders of this rebellion.
Henry says that those executed were the people who openly persisted in standing against God.
Those who persist in sin are heading toward destruction.
In the morning some of these people had been shouting and dancing.
Before night they were dead.
How quickly God's judgments can overturn the careless pleasure of people secure in their sins.

div.title: Moses prays again for the people (verses 30–35)
div.p: Moses called Israel's wrongdoing a great sin.
One task of ministers is to show people the seriousness of their sins.
The dreadful evil of sin is seen in the great price required for pardon.
Moses pleaded with God for mercy.
He did not come to invent excuses for the people; he came to seek atonement.
We should not understand Moses to mean that he would willingly suffer eternal destruction in the people's place.
We must love our neighbors as ourselves, not more than ourselves.
But with the mind of Christ, Moses was willing to lay down his earthly life, however painfully, if it could preserve his people.
Even Moses could not completely turn aside God's anger.
That showed that the law given through Moses could not reconcile sinners to God or give them perfect peace with him.
Only in Christ does God forgive sin so completely that he remembers it no more.
This history also shows that a proud and worldly heart cannot long endure God's holy commands, humbling truths and spiritual worship.
But a god, a priest, a form of worship, a doctrine and a sacrifice adapted to worldly desires will always find plenty of followers.
Even the gospel itself can be distorted to suit worldly tastes.
How good it is for us that the Prophet greater than Moses, incomparably stronger and more merciful, has made atonement for our souls and continues to intercede for us.
Let us rejoice in his grace!

row.cell: The Lord refuses to go with Israel.
The tabernacle of Moses removed without the camp.
Moses desires to see the glory of God.

div.title: God withdraws the assurance of his presence (verses 1–6)
div.p: Even when God forgives his people, he must teach them what their sin deserved.
His command to go forward as they were expressed his displeasure powerfully.
He promised to keep his covenant with Abraham by giving the people Canaan.
Yet he withheld the signs of his presence with which he had previously blessed them.
The Israelites mourned over their sin.
Of all sin's painful results, the one true penitents fear and grieve most is the departure of God's presence.
Canaan itself would not be a pleasant land without the Lord.
Those who had gladly surrendered their ornaments to support idolatry could surely lay aside ornaments as a sign of grief and shame for it.

div.title: Moses pitches the tent outside the camp (verses 7–11)
div.p: Moses took the tabernacle and pitched it outside the camp.
This appears to have been a temporary building used for worship and for hearing disputes among the people.
The Israelites watched Moses as he went to it.
They longed to be restored to peace with God and were deeply concerned about what would happen next.
The pillar of cloud had withdrawn from the camp when the people defiled it through idolatry.
Now it returned.
If our hearts go out to meet God, he will graciously come to meet us.

div.title: Moses asks for God's presence and glory (verses 12–23)
div.p: Moses pleaded earnestly with the Lord.
Through Christ's intercession we receive more than rescue from destruction.
We also receive the promise of everlasting happiness.
Notice how Moses pleaded.
We find grace in God's sight when we have received grace in our hearts that directs and strengthens us to do our duty.
Moses spoke as someone who dreaded the thought of going forward without God's presence.
God's gracious promises and past kindness should not merely strengthen our trust.
They should also make us more earnest in prayer.
And notice how Moses prevailed.
His intercession foreshadowed Christ's, which continues forever on behalf of all who come to God through him.
Christ's intercession does not depend on any merit in those for whom he prays.
Moses also asked to see God's glory, and even that request was heard.
A complete revelation of that glory would have overwhelmed Moses himself.
Human beings are too lowly and unworthy, too weak to bear it, and too guilty not to fear it.
Only God's merciful revelation of himself through Jesus Christ can be endured by us.
Yet the Lord granted Moses enough to satisfy him abundantly.
God's goodness is his glory.
He would have us know him more by the glory of his mercy than by the glory of his majesty.
The rock gave Moses a suitable place from which to see God's goodness and glory.
The rock at Horeb pointed to Christ, the Rock of refuge, salvation and strength.
Happy are those who stand upon this Rock!
The cleft in it may also picture Christ as struck, crucified, wounded and slain.
The account then reminds us that even our knowledge of God through Christ is incomplete in this life.
Compared with the sight of him that awaits us in heaven, it is like seeing only the back of someone who has passed by.
The clearest revelation of God's glory, grace and goodness in Christ is reserved for the life to come.

row.cell: The tables of the law renewed.
The name of the Lord proclaimed, The entreaty of Moses.

div.title: God renews the stone tablets (verses 1–4)
div.p: When God created humanity in his own image, he wrote the moral law directly upon the human heart through his own power.
No outward instrument was needed.
But humanity broke the covenant.
Since then, the Lord has used human servants to write the law in Scripture and has also worked through them as he writes it anew upon people's hearts.
When he was reconciled to Israel, he ordered the stone tablets to be replaced and wrote his law on them.
Even under the gospel of peace through Christ, the moral law remains binding upon believers.
Christ has redeemed us from the law's curse, but not from its commands.
The earliest and surest sign that sin has been forgiven and peace made with God is that his law has been written upon the heart.

div.title: God proclaims his name and character (verses 5–9)
div.p: The Lord descended in a cloud, openly showing his presence and a glimpse of his glory.
He proclaimed his name—the divine qualities and character signified by Jehovah.
The Lord is merciful. He is ready to forgive sinners and help those in need.
He is gracious. He is kind and freely gives benefits that no one deserves.
He is patient. He is slow to anger, allowing time for repentance and punishing only when punishment is necessary.

p.hi: He abounds in goodness and truth.

div.p: Even sinners receive his generous gifts, though they often misuse them.
Everything he reveals is unfailing truth, and everything he promises he faithfully performs.

p.hi: He keeps mercy for thousands.

div.p: He continually shows kindness to sinners.
His store of mercy will never be exhausted, even to the end of time.

p.hi: He forgives iniquity, transgression and sin.

div.p: His goodness includes the full and free forgiveness of wrongdoing.

p.hi: Yet he will never treat the guilty as innocent.

div.p: God's holiness and justice are part of his goodness and love toward all his creatures.
In Christ's suffering, divine holiness and justice are displayed fully, and the true evil of sin is revealed.
God's forgiving mercy is always joined to grace that changes us and makes us holy.
None are pardoned without repentance and turning away from the deliberate practice of sin.
Those who abuse, neglect or despise this great salvation will not escape judgment.
Moses bowed before God and worshiped reverently.
Every aspect of God's revealed character gives believers reason to plead for forgiveness, holiness of heart and the growth of the Redeemer's kingdom.

div.title: Israel is warned against idolatry (verses 10–17)
div.p: The Israelites were ordered to destroy every object and monument connected with idolatry, however beautiful or expensive.
They were to refuse alliances, friendships and marriages that would draw them into the worship of false gods.
They were also to avoid idolatrous feasts.
God reminded them not to repeat their sin of making a metal image for worship.
Human jealousy is described as a fierce passion (Proverbs 6:34).
But God's jealousy is holy and righteous displeasure.
No one can worship God rightly without worshiping him alone.

div.title: The festivals and renewed covenant (verses 18–27)
div.p: Israel must rest one day every week.
Even plowing and harvesting had to stop.
Ordinary work must give way to holy rest, even when the harvest was ready.
Henry argues that observing the Sabbath during harvest would leave their work better blessed.
They were to show that they valued fellowship with God and their duty to him above the labor and joy of gathering crops.
Three times each year the people were to appear before the Lord God of Israel.
Canaan was a desirable land, and neighboring nations wanted its riches.
Yet God promised that those nations would not desire to seize Israel's land while the people gathered to worship.
