Let us restrain sinful desires in our own hearts—especially anything that opposes God's glory.
Then let us trust him to restrain the evil desires of others against us.
The way of duty is the way of safety.
Those who risk things for God's sake never finally lose through serving him.
Three feasts are named.
First, Passover remembered the deliverance from Egypt.
Second, the Feast of Weeks, or Pentecost, included the offering of firstfruits.
Third, the Feast of Ingathering, or Tabernacles, marked the gathering of the harvest.
Moses was commanded to write God's words so the people would know and understand them better.
We can never be thankful enough for the written word of God.
The Lord made his covenant with Israel through Moses as mediator.
In the same way, the covenant of grace is made with believers through Christ.

div.title: Moses' shining face and the veil (verses 28–35)
div.p: Deep spiritual fellowship with God strengthens and beautifies a renewed, holy character.
Sincere godliness can give a person's face a brightness that wins respect and love.
The veil Moses wore showed how much less clearly God's revelation was understood under the old covenant than it would be under the gospel.
It also pictured the natural veil over human hearts that prevents people from understanding spiritual realities.
Henry further applies the image to Israel's continuing difficulty in recognizing Christ.
He says this veil can be removed only through the Lord's Spirit, who reveals Christ as the goal of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
Fear and unbelief can also place a veil before us, hindering our free approach to the mercy seat above.
We should tell our heavenly Father about all our needs, both earthly and spiritual.
Let us speak openly of our obstacles, struggles, trials and temptations.
Let us confess our sins.

row.cell: The free gifts for the tabernacle.
The readiness of the people in general.
Bezaleel and Aholiab called to the work.

div.title: The Sabbath is to be kept (verses 1–3)
div.p: Christ's yoke is gentle and easy.
Because of him, our Sabbath duties are more joyful and its restrictions less burdensome than they were for the Jews under the old covenant.
But that only makes us more guilty if we neglect them.
God wisely gave us a Sabbath for merciful purposes.
It is sinful to treat this gift with contempt.
How can we despise a blessed day that the generous Lord has given us to grow in grace with the church on earth and prepare for happiness with the church in heaven?

div.title: Freely given materials and skilled work (verses 4–19)
div.p: The tabernacle would be dedicated to God's honor and used in his service.
Therefore, every contribution toward it was an offering to the Lord.
The rule was simple: whoever had a willing heart should bring a gift.
Everyone with the necessary skill was to do the work.
God distributes different gifts among his people.
Each person should use the gift received in service to others (1 Peter 4:10).
Those with wealth were to provide materials.
Those with skill were to use their abilities for the sanctuary.
The two groups needed each other, and the tabernacle needed them both (1 Corinthians 12:7–21).

div.title: The people give willingly (verses 20–29)
div.p: Without willing hearts, even very expensive offerings would be hateful to God.
But with genuine willingness, even the smallest gift is accepted.
We show that our hearts are willing when we gladly help the work of God advance.
People who work diligently and contentedly in humble occupations are just as acceptable to God as those who perform impressive public service.
The women who spun goats' hair were called wise-hearted, because they did the work wholeheartedly for the Lord.
Likewise, a laborer, craftsperson or servant who carries out ordinary work in faith and reverence for God may show as much wisdom in that calling as a highly useful minister.
Both are accepted by the same Lord.
Our wisdom and duty lie in giving God the glory for our abilities and using them for his purposes, whether we have many talents or few.

div.title: Bezalel and Oholiab lead and teach the work (verses 30–35)
div.p: God himself appointed the master craftsmen.
This prevented disputes over who should lead the work.
It also ensured that everyone who took part knew whose instructions to follow and to whom they were accountable.
God filled those whom he called by name with his Spirit.
Skill—even skill used in ordinary trades—is God's gift from above.
Yet some people are very good at assigning tasks to others.
They can explain exactly what everyone else should do, but refuse to lift a finger themselves.
Such people behave like lazy servants.
Bezalel and Oholiab were to do more than invent plans.
They had to carry out the work themselves and teach others to do it.
Those who lead should teach.
And anyone to whom God has given knowledge should gladly share it for the benefit of other people.

p.hi: The making of the tabernacle, The liberality of the people restrained.

div.title: The builders' faithfulness and the tabernacle's meaning
div.p: The builders began their work with eagerness and zeal.
They followed their instructions exactly.
And they were faithful enough to object when people brought more contributions than were needed.
Their example deserves to be followed.
We should serve God with that same readiness, care and honesty.
We should also serve those in authority over us faithfully in everything that is lawful.
Everyone entrusted with public responsibilities should hate dishonest gain and avoid every opportunity or temptation to become greedy.
Where do we see God's love toward us pictured so clearly—the love by which we live in him and he lives in us?
We see it in Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23).
This is the heart of the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).
It was also the purpose of the tabernacle of testimony.
The sanctuary visibly declared God's love for the human race, despite the fall from humanity's original condition.
That love was displayed fully when Christ came to live on earth.
The Word became flesh (John 1:14).
As the original expression suggests, he pitched his tabernacle among us.

p.hi: The making of the ark, and the furniture of the tabernacle.

div.title: The furnishings as pictures of worship and redemption
div.p: The furniture of the tabernacle pointed toward the spiritual worship that God accepts.
The incense represented the prayers of the saints.
The sacrifice offered on the altar pointed to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
The golden jar of manna, the bread from heaven, pointed to the flesh of Jesus Christ, which he gave for the life of the world.
The lampstand, with its burning lights, represented the teaching and illumination of the Holy Spirit.
The bread of the Presence pictured the abundant provision God gives to people who hunger and thirst for righteousness.
That provision is supplied through the gospel, the appointed means of grace and the sacraments celebrated in God's house of prayer.
The craftsmen took great care to follow the rule God gave them.
We should imitate that obedience.
Let us seek the Holy Spirit's influence, so that we may rejoice in God and glorify him during our earthly lives.
And in the end, may we dwell with him forever.

div.title: The bronze altar and basin (verses 1–8)
div.p: In every age of the church, some people have been especially devoted to God.
They attend faithfully to his appointed worship and are more willing than others to surrender even things they have a perfect right to keep for his sake.
Some women of Israel were deeply committed to the Lord and zealous for worship in the tabernacle.
They showed that zeal by giving up their mirrors.
These were polished bronze plates, which served the purpose of looking glasses before glass mirrors had been invented.
The women chose to give up something valuable and useful so that it could serve the Lord.

div.title: The court and its curtains (verses 9–20)
div.p: The walls around the tabernacle's court were only curtains.
Henry understands this as a reminder that the Jewish church's outward form was temporary and could change.
In time, that arrangement would be taken down and folded away.
The space occupied by the tent would then be enlarged, and its ropes extended, so that the Gentile world could be welcomed in.

div.title: The offerings and the meaning of the sanctuary (verses 21–31)
div.p: The foundation was made from heavy pieces of silver.
They pointed to the strength and purity of the truth upon which the church is founded.
As we read about the tabernacle's furnishings, let us keep our eyes on the Lord Jesus Christ.
When we look at the altar for burnt offerings, let us see Jesus.
In his righteousness and salvation there is a full and sufficient offering for sin.
Let our souls be washed in the basin of regeneration by his Holy Spirit, so that we may be clean.
And just as the Israelites gave willingly, may our own hearts be made willing.
Let us be ready to surrender anything for Christ and count everything else as loss in order to gain him.

div.title: The priestly garments are completed (verses 1–31)
div.p: The priests' clothing was rich and beautiful.
In the early life of the church, these visible symbols taught people about greater blessings that would come later.
But the reality to which they pointed is Christ and the grace of his gospel.
Christ is our great High Priest.
When he undertook to redeem us, he clothed himself for service.
He received and displayed the gifts and graces of the Spirit.
He fastened himself to his purpose, resolved to complete the task.
He took responsibility for all God's spiritual Israel.
He kept his people close to his heart, engraved them on the palms of his hands and presented them before his Father.
He crowned himself with holiness to the Lord, dedicating all his saving work to the honor of his Father's holiness.
True believers are also spiritual priests.
The pure linen of their clothing for service represents the righteousness of the saints (Revelation 19:8).

div.title: The tabernacle is completed (verses 32–43)
div.p: The tabernacle was a picture of Jesus Christ.
The Most High was visibly present in the sanctuary above the ark.
In the same way, God dwelt in the human nature of his beloved Son.
In Christ, all the fullness of deity lives bodily (Colossians 2:9).
The tabernacle also pictured every genuine Christian.
God the Father dwells in the soul of each true follower of the Savior.
He is the One that person worships and the source of every blessing enjoyed.
The tabernacle also represented the Redeemer's church.
The poorest and the most powerful are equally dear to the Father's love, freely given through faith in Christ.
Finally, the tabernacle was a picture of the heavenly temple (Revelation 21:3).
How magnificent will God's glory appear when the cloud is removed and his faithful worshipers see him as he truly is!

row.cell: The tabernacle is to be set up, Aaron and his sons to be sanctified.
The glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle.

div.title: The tabernacle is to be raised and the priests consecrated (verses 1–15)
div.p: Whenever a new year begins, we should seek to serve God better than we did in the previous year.
The tabernacle was completed in only half a year.
When many people are deeply committed to a good cause, much can be accomplished in a short time.
And when God's commands are continually followed as the rule for the work, everything will be done well.
The high priesthood remained within Aaron's family until Christ came.
In him—the reality to which all these earlier shadows pointed—the priesthood continues forever.

div.title: Moses carries out everything God commanded (verses 16–33)
div.p: When the tabernacle and its furnishings were ready, Israel did not postpone erecting it until the people reached Canaan.
They obeyed God's will and set it up in the middle of their camp.
People whose lives are unsettled must never use their circumstances as an excuse to neglect worship and faith.
We cannot say that it is enough to begin serving God after our lives have become stable.
No.
We need a tabernacle for God even in the wilderness.
Indeed, we may enter the next world before we ever find a settled home in this one.
We must also be careful not to deceive ourselves with an outward appearance of godliness.
The fact that so few of those who left Egypt eventually entered Canaan should warn young people in particular against putting off the care of their souls.

div.title: God's glory fills and guides the tabernacle (verses 34–38)
div.p: A cloud covered the tabernacle even on the clearest days.
It was not an ordinary cloud that sunlight could scatter.
All Israel could see it day and night as a sign of God's presence.
They should never again need to ask whether the Lord was truly among them.
The cloud guided the entire camp through the wilderness.
When it rested over the sanctuary, the people stayed where they were.
When it moved, they followed.
The Lord's glory filled the tabernacle.
In light and fire, the Shekinah—the visible sign of God's presence—made itself known.
God is light.
Our God is also a consuming fire.
The light was so dazzling and the fire so fearsome that Moses could not enter the tent of meeting until its splendor diminished.
But what Moses could not do, our Lord Jesus has accomplished.
God caused him to draw near.
And Jesus now invites us to come boldly even to the mercy seat.
The Holy Spirit teaches us to follow Christ's example as well as depend upon him.
If we attend to his appointed worship and obey his commands, we will not lose our way.
He will guide us along right paths until we reach heaven, where his holiness dwells.

p.hi: Blessed be God for Jesus Christ!

div.title: Leviticus — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: God established different kinds of offerings and sacrifices to assure his people that their offenses would be forgiven when they brought those offerings with true faith and obedience.
He also appointed the priests and Levites, giving instructions about their clothing, responsibilities, conduct and provision for their needs.
He specified the festivals they must celebrate and when they were to observe them.
Through all these sacrifices and ceremonies, God showed that the wages of sin is death.
He also taught that there can be no forgiveness of sins apart from the blood of Christ, the innocent Lamb of God.

row.cell: From the flocks, and of fowls.

div.title: The purpose of the offerings (verses 1–2)
div.p: From the fall of humanity until Christ came, offering sacrifices was part of true worship.
Until Israel lived in the wilderness, however, no very detailed regulations seem to have been given for those offerings.
The overall purpose of these laws is clear.
The sacrifices pointed forward to Christ.
They also portrayed the duties, character, privileges and fellowship with God of those who believe in him.
Hardly anything Scripture says about the Lord Jesus is without some connection to his people.
Leviticus begins with the laws of sacrifice.
The oldest form of sacrifice was the burnt offering.
God now gave Moses instructions about it.
These laws took for granted that the people would be willing to bring offerings to the Lord.
Even natural human understanding tells us that people owe honor to their Maker as their Lord.
Sacrifices had been instituted immediately after the fall.

div.title: Burnt offerings from the herd (verses 3–9)
div.p: When properly understood, the Levitical ordinances used visible things from the natural world to picture spiritual mysteries and events that were yet to come.
Without that understanding, the ceremonies would appear meaningless.
They pointed to the sufferings of the Son of God, who would become a sacrifice for the sins of the world.
A burning animal was only a faint image of the everlasting misery we have deserved.
Our blessed Lord bore the burden of our guilt in both body and soul when he died.
Consider the details.

p.hi: First, the animal had to be without blemish.

div.p: This pointed to the purity and strength of Christ and to the holy lives his people should lead.

p.hi: Second, its owner had to offer it freely.

div.p: Service that pleases God must flow from love.
Christ willingly offered himself for us.

p.hi: Third, it was offered at the tabernacle entrance.

div.p: There stood the bronze altar that sanctified the gift.
The offerer came to the entrance as someone unworthy to go farther in.
In doing so, the sinner acknowledged that communion with God is impossible apart from sacrifice.

p.hi: Fourth, the offerer laid a hand upon the animal's head.

div.p: That action expressed the desire and hope that God would accept the offering as atonement.

p.hi: Fifth, the animal was killed before the Lord.

div.p: The act was to be done reverently, in an orderly way that honored God.
It also signified that Christians must put to death the flesh with its corrupt desires and passions.

p.hi: Sixth, the priests sprinkled blood upon the altar.

div.p: Since life is in the blood, blood made atonement.
This pointed to our consciences being pacified and cleansed when we receive, through faith, the blood of Jesus Christ sprinkled upon them.

p.hi: Seventh, the animal was cut into pieces and burned upon the altar.

div.p: The burning pictured Christ's severe sufferings.
It also pictured the burning love and devotion with which Christians should offer their entire selves—spirit, soul and body—to God.

p.hi: Eighth, the offering was called a sweet-smelling sacrifice.

div.p: God received it with pleasure because it obeyed his command and pointed to Christ.
In the same way, believers' spiritual sacrifices become acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Peter 2:5).

div.title: Burnt offerings from sheep, goats or birds (verses 10–17)
div.p: People who could not afford to offer a bull could bring a sheep or a goat.
Those too poor to bring even those animals could offer a turtledove or a pigeon, and God would receive it.
The animals chosen were gentle, mild and harmless.
They pointed to Christ's innocence and meekness, qualities that should also appear in Christians.
A poor person's offering pictured Christ's atonement just as fully as an expensive sacrifice.
It also expressed repentance, faith and devotion to God no less completely.
We have no excuse for refusing the reasonable and joyful service God now requires.
Yet even a broken heart, praise or thanksgiving cannot be offered to God unless he first gives us what we need to offer it.
An Israelite could not bring a bull or goat without first receiving it from God.
The more we do in the Lord's service, the more we owe him for the desire, ability and opportunity to do it.
In many matters, God allows us to decide how much time or wealth we will devote to his service.
But where he has placed much within someone's power, a miserly offering does not express a willing heart and is not acceptable.
Let us devote both body and soul to serving him, whatever he may call us to give, risk, do or endure for his sake.

div.title: The grain offering (verses 1–11)
div.p: The offerings of flour, called meat offerings in Henry's English, may picture Christ as presented to God for us and as the Bread of Life for our souls.
But Henry thinks they more directly represent our debt of gratitude for God's providential gifts and the good works that please him.
In older English, meat could mean food of any kind.
Most of this offering was meant to be eaten, not burned.
These grain offerings appear after the burnt offerings.
That order matters.
Without a share in Christ's sacrifice and a heart devoted to God, even our good religious works cannot be accepted.
Leaven represents pride, malice and hypocrisy.
These are the opposites of the humility, love and sincerity that God delights in.
Honey represents sensual pleasure.
Attachment to such pleasure can draw people away from prayer and good works.
Christ's character and sacrifice were entirely free from everything pictured by leaven.
His life of suffering and his agonizing death were the very opposite of worldly self-indulgence.
His people are called to follow him and become like him.

div.title: The offering of firstfruits (verses 12–16)
div.p: Salt was required with every offering.
By this God taught Israel that even the sacrifices they brought were, in themselves, lacking what made them pleasing.
Every act of religious service must be seasoned with grace.
Christianity is the salt of the earth.
Instructions were also given for presenting firstfruits at harvest.
Someone grateful for God's goodness in providing an abundant crop could bring the first ripe, full heads of grain to him.
Whatever we offer God should be the best of its kind, even if all we have to give is a handful of green ears of grain.
Oil and frankincense were added to the firstfruits.
Wisdom and humility make young believers' hearts and service gentler and sweeter.
Then the first, still-green fruits of their lives become acceptable to the Lord.
God delights in early expressions of faith and devotion, the first ripe fruit of the Spirit.
Holy love toward God is the fire by which all our offerings are made.
The frankincense pictures Christ's mediation and intercession, through which our service becomes acceptable.
Blessed be God that we possess the reality of which all these observances were only shadows.
There is an excellence in Christ himself and in his work as Mediator that no picture or ceremony can fully show.
We must depend on him so completely that we never lose sight of him in anything we do, if we want our service to be accepted by God.

div.title: The fellowship offering from the herd (verses 1–5)
div.p: Peace offerings acknowledged God as the giver of everything good.
The offering was divided between the altar, the priest and the person who brought it.
It was called a peace offering because God and his people seemed to share a feast together, as a sign of friendship.
These offerings could be presented as requests for mercy.
When someone was asking God for a blessing, that person might add a peace offering to the prayer.
Christ is our Peace and our Peace Offering.
Only through him can we receive a peaceful answer to our prayers.
But peace offerings could also be given as thanksgiving for mercy already received.
We should continually offer God sacrifices of praise through Christ, our Peace.
Such praise pleases the Lord more than the sacrifice of an ox or bull.

div.title: The fellowship offering from the flock (verses 6–17)
div.p: The people were forbidden to eat either the fat or the blood of these sacrifices.
The fat meant the fat of the internal organs.
Like the blood, it belonged to God as his portion of each sacrifice.
God would not allow the blood that made atonement to be treated as an ordinary thing (Hebrews 10:29).
Nor will he allow us, even while enjoying the benefits of the atonement, to claim any share of the honor for having accomplished it.
The command taught Israel to distinguish between ordinary things and holy things.
It also kept the people separate from idol worshipers.
The blood poured out and the fat burned in solemn sacrifice were meant to impress upon them the sense that some great spiritual mystery was being shown.
Christ, the Prince of Peace, made peace through the blood of his cross.
Through him, believers are reconciled to God.
Having God's peace in their hearts, they also become eager to pursue peace with all people.
May the Lord multiply grace, mercy and peace to everyone who desires to bear the name of Christian.

row.cell: The sin-offering of ignorance for the priest.

div.title: The high priest's sin offering (verses 1–12)
div.p: Burnt offerings, grain offerings and peace offerings were known before the law was given at Sinai.
Through them, the patriarchs already sought atonement for sin.
Now Israel received more detailed instructions for bringing sacrifices to make atonement.
These offerings were shadows of greater blessings yet to come.
Their reality is Christ and the single offering of himself through which he put away sin.
The sins addressed by these offerings were understood to be outward acts.
They were things done that ought not to have been done.
Failure to do our duty is also sin and will come under God's judgment.
Yet something neglected earlier may sometimes still be done later, whereas a wrong act already committed cannot be undone.
These offerings particularly addressed sins committed through ignorance.
The instructions begin with the anointed priest.
This showed that God never established an infallible priest in his earthly church.
Even the high priest could commit sins through ignorance.
Henry therefore condemns claims to act without error as a mark of Antichrist.
The animal was taken outside the camp and burned completely to ashes.
This pictured repentance: putting away sin as something hateful that our souls reject.
The offering was itself called sin.
What was done to the animal is what we must do to our sins.
The body of sin must be destroyed (Romans 6:6).
The apostle also applies the sacrifice's removal outside the camp to Christ (Hebrews 13:11–13).

div.title: The whole congregation's sin offering (verses 13–21)
div.p: The people's leaders could make mistakes that led the whole community into wrongdoing.
In that case, an offering had to be brought, so that divine anger would not fall upon the congregation.
People on whose behalf a sacrifice was offered laid their hands upon the animal and confessed their sins.
When the sacrifice was for the whole community, the elders performed this action.
The guilt of the people was pictured as a burden placed upon an innocent animal.
Once the offering had been completed, the Lord declared that atonement had been made and the sin would be forgiven.
Whenever churches and nations are saved from destruction, they owe that deliverance to the satisfaction and mediation of Christ.

div.title: The ruler's sin offering (verses 22–26)
div.p: People who possess authority to call others to account must remember that they themselves are accountable to the Ruler of all rulers.
Even a ruler can sin through ignorance.
That sin must be brought to the ruler's attention, either by conscience or by the correction of friends.
Even the best and greatest people should receive such correction thankfully rather than resentfully.
Each day we should pray, “Teach me what I do not see,” and “Show me where I have gone wrong.”
Then, if ignorance leads us into sin, ignorance will not keep us living in it.

div.title: The ordinary person's sin offering (verses 27–35)
div.p: The law also provided an offering for anyone among the people.
A person accused of sin may say, “I acted without knowing,” or “Temptation took me by surprise.”
But that plea alone cannot secure acquittal.
The only sufficient plea is that Christ has died.
Even the ordinary person's sins of ignorance required sacrifice.
No one is too important to be under God's justice.
No one is so humble as to be overlooked by it.
Rich and poor meet here as equals.
Both are sinners, and both are welcome to come to Christ.
These laws teach us to hate sin, keep watch against it and greatly value Christ—the true and complete Sin Offering.
His blood cleanses from all sin.
The blood of bulls and goats could never actually take away sin.
When we have the Bible in our hands, our remaining mistakes and ignorance often result from pride, laziness and carelessness.
We therefore need to examine ourselves frequently.
We should study Scripture seriously and pray earnestly for the Holy Spirit's convicting work.
Then we may discover sins we did not recognize, repent of them and obtain forgiveness through Christ's blood.

div.title: Different kinds of wrongdoing (verses 1–13)
div.p: Several offenses are addressed here.

First, a witness sins by concealing the truth when under oath to tell it fully. A person may be afraid of offending a friend or an enemy and therefore say nothing or reveal only part of the facts. But that person bears guilt. Unless something is done to remove it, guilt is a burden that leads to destruction.
Anyone summoned to give evidence should remember this law, speak openly and without deception, and treat an oath before the Lord as sacred.

Second, a person might touch something ceremonially unclean. The contact itself caused ceremonial defilement; but refusing to wash in accordance with God's law showed carelessness or contempt, and brought moral guilt.
When God's Spirit makes us aware of a sin or duty, we should respond promptly, without being ashamed to admit we were mistaken.
Third, a rash oath could bind a person to do something unlawful or impossible. Thoughtfulness and caution before speaking would prevent many such difficulties.
In these cases the sinner was required to confess the particular offense and bring the appointed sacrifice.
The sacrifice was not acceptable without confession and humble prayer for forgiveness.
It is not enough to admit vaguely that we are sinners. Everyone can say that, while remaining reluctant to confess any specific sin. Such vague language can conceal deceit.
Honest, detailed confession is the path toward assurance of pardon and greater watchfulness against future sins.
Even the very poor could bring flour for their sin offering. The cost was deliberately kept low so that poverty would never prevent anyone from seeking forgiveness.
When two birds were offered, one was a sin offering and the other a burnt offering. We must first be reconciled to God before expecting him to accept our services for his glory.
Unlike other grain offerings, the flour offered for sin received neither oil nor frankincense. Its lack of pleasant taste or fragrance was intended to show how hateful sin is.

These sacrifices assured repentant sinners that forgiveness was available, so they need not despair under guilt. They also warned against further sin: atonement was costly and required serious effort.

div.title: Wrongdoing involving what belongs to the Lord (verses 14–19)
div.p: This section concerns trespasses connected with obligations toward God, including the unintentional misuse of something dedicated to him.
When we suspect that we have wronged God or someone else, we should be ready both to ask forgiveness and to make restitution, even before every detail of our fault is clear to us.

God's law extends very far. Opportunities to sin are numerous, and we are naturally inclined toward wrong. We should therefore stay watchful, consider our steps and pray continually to be kept from sin.
A true Christian acknowledges guilt before God each day and seeks pardon through the blood of Christ.
The gospel offers salvation freely enough for the poorest to receive it, and fully enough for even a heavily burdened conscience to find relief.
Yet the seriousness of sin is also exposed through that salvation. Everyone who has received pardon should learn to hate and fear sin.

div.title: Trespasses against one's neighbor (verses 1–7)
div.p: Every offense described here harms another person, but Scripture also calls it a trespass against the Lord.
The person injured may be poor or despised. Even so, wrongdoing against that person dishonors the God who commands us to love our neighbors as ourselves.
Human law may assign different penalties to different offenses. But every dishonest way of harming another person breaks God's law.
Even keeping something we have found is wrong if we are able to identify its owner.
Fraud is commonly accompanied by lies and sometimes by false oaths.
Anyone seeking to escape God's judgment must make full restitution, so far as it is possible, and seek forgiveness through faith in the one Offering that takes away the world's sin.
The offenses named in this law also violate the law of Christ. He insists upon justice and truth no less than the law of nature or the law of Moses.

div.title: Keeping the altar fire burning (verses 8–13)
div.p: This instruction particularly concerns the daily lamb offered in sacrifice.
The priests were to keep the fire on the altar burning continuously.
The first fire had come from heaven (Leviticus 9:24).
By preserving that same fire, the priests showed that every sacrifice was consumed by a flame originally sent from heaven, a sign of God's acceptance.
Our faith and love, and our habits of prayer and praise, should likewise remain alive continually.

div.title: The grain offering for the priests (verses 14–23)
div.p: The burnt offering required demanding service from the priests, yet they received no portion of its meat; only the hide belonged to them.
By contrast, most of a grain offering was for the priests' use.
God intends that those who serve him in ministry should receive the support they need.

div.title: The sin offering (verses 24–30)
div.p: The priests had to wash any garment on which the blood of a sin offering was splashed.
This pointed to the special reverence due to Christ's blood, which must never be treated as something ordinary.
If the meat was cooked in a clay vessel, that vessel had to be broken. A bronze vessel could instead be washed carefully.
These rules showed that the ceremonial sacrifice did not remove every impurity in itself.
But Christ's blood truly cleanses us from all sin.
The instructions also displayed sin's polluting power and pictured guilt passing from the sinner to the sacrifice.
Consider the love of Christ, who willingly became the sin offering for us so that our repeated sins and failures could be forgiven.
He knew no sin, yet was made sin for us—that is, a sin offering (2 Corinthians 5:21).
Through him we receive not only forgiveness, but also power over sin (Romans 8:3).

div.title: The guilt offering (verses 1–10)
div.p: In the sin offering and guilt offering, the sacrifice was divided between the altar and the priest.
The person bringing it received no portion, unlike the person who brought a fellowship offering.
The sin and guilt offerings expressed repentance and sorrow for wrongdoing. Fasting therefore suited them better than feasting.
Fellowship offerings, on the other hand, expressed communion with God through Christ after reconciliation, the joy and thankfulness of a forgiven sinner, and the privileges of a true believer.

div.title: The fellowship offering (verses 11–27)
div.p: God allowed more freedom in expressing gratitude for mercy than in acknowledging guilt.
Fellowship offerings could therefore be freely given, making the offerer's willing gift especially pleasing.
Yet God required sacrifices of atonement.
That requirement taught the necessity of the great sacrifice that would reconcile sinners to him.
The chief reason blood was prohibited as food was that God had appointed it for atonement.
This symbolic purpose reached its fulfillment in Christ, who offered himself and shed his blood, bringing the earlier sacrifices to an end.

p.hi: For that reason, Henry says this prohibition is no longer binding upon believers.

div.title: The lifted and waved portions (verses 28–34)
div.p: The officiating priest received the breast and the right shoulder.
After the animal was killed, the person making the offering was to present God's portion personally.
Doing so expressed a willing surrender to him.
The offerer raised it with both hands to acknowledge God as Lord of heaven.
Then it was waved from side to side to acknowledge him as Lord of all the earth.
Let us be encouraged to receive and enjoy Christ, our fellowship offering.
This blessed gift is not only for priests or exceptionally mature believers; it is also for ordinary people.
Do not delay in turning to Christ.
Some people plan to repent only when they are dying. But they should receive this fellowship offering now, before the time of God's patience has ended.
The provision that a fellowship offering could not be eaten on the third day underlines the urgency.
It will be too late to seek Christ after death and judgment.

div.title: The conclusion of the sacrificial regulations (verses 35–38)
div.p: Public acts of worship are not optional matters that we may accept or ignore according to personal preference.
Neglecting them puts us in danger.
Obedience to the laws of Christ cannot be any less necessary than obedience to the laws Moses delivered.

row.cell: The consecration of Aaron and his sons.

div.title: Aaron and his sons are consecrated (verses 1–13)
div.p: Aaron's consecration and that of his sons took place only after the tabernacle had been prepared and the rules for sacrifice had been given.
They were washed with water. This signified that they must turn away from every sinful desire and keep themselves pure afterward.
Christ washes in his own blood those whom he makes kings and priests to God (Revelation 1:5–6).
Those who approach God must also be washed with pure water (Hebrews 10:22).
Aaron's anointing foreshadowed Christ's anointing with the Holy Spirit, who was given to him without measure.
Every believer also receives an anointing.

div.title: The sacrifices accompanying consecration (verses 14–36)
div.p: These ceremonies picture our great High Priest, Jesus Christ.
By his own blood and the power of his Holy Spirit, he was appointed, anointed and set apart for his sacred office.
He sanctifies religious worship so that it benefits his people and honors God the Father.
For Christ's sake the Father accepts our worship, even though sin still mars it.
We can rejoice that Jesus is a merciful and faithful High Priest, full of compassion toward weak and troubled souls.
All true Christians are likewise consecrated as spiritual priests.
We should examine our daily lives carefully. Do we seek to live according to this calling?
Do we offer abundant spiritual sacrifices that are pleasing to God through Christ?
Even when the answer is yes, we have no reason to boast.
We should never despise other sinners. Remembering our own sins and the way God saved us, we should pray and work for their salvation too.

row.cell: The first offerings of Aaron for himself and the people.
Moses and Aaron bless the people, Fire cometh upon the altar from the Lord.

div.title: Aaron makes his first offerings (verses 1–21)
div.p: All these many sacrifices were brought to an end through the death of Christ.
They teach us that even our best services need to be washed in his blood.
Even our most careful acts of worship carry guilt that can be removed only through an offering purer and greater than ours.
Let us thank God that we have such a High Priest!
The priests were never excused from service for an entire day.
God's spiritual priests likewise have work to do continually, according to each day's responsibilities.
If we want to complete our service joyfully and give a good account of our lives, we must make good use of our time.
The glory of the Lord appeared openly before the people, showing his approval of their work.
We should not now expect this kind of visible manifestation.
Yet God still draws near to those who draw near to him.
He accepts the offerings made in faith.
Because Christian sacrifices are spiritual, the signs of their acceptance are spiritual as well.
When Aaron finished the sacrificial work, he raised his hands and blessed the people.
Aaron could ask God to bless them; God alone could command the blessing.

div.title: Fire from the Lord consumes the sacrifice (verses 22–24)
div.p: After the service had ended and the blessing had been pronounced, God openly declared his acceptance.
Fire came out from before the Lord and consumed the offering.
The same fire could justly have consumed the guilty people.
Instead it consumed their sacrifice, showing that God accepted the offering as atonement for the sinner.
This pointed toward greater blessings to come.
The Holy Spirit later descended upon the apostles in the form of fire.
The Spirit's holy fire also comes into our hearts, kindling love, reverence and zeal for God, while consuming fleshly desires.
That inward work is a sign of God's gracious acceptance of both our persons and our service.
We cannot offer God anything that did not first come from him.
His grace must provide the holy fire that makes our worship acceptable (Hebrews 12:28).
The people responded with the greatest joy and deepest reverence.
They rejoiced that God had come near, yet bowed humbly before his majesty.
Fear of God is wrong when it drives us away from him. Gracious reverence causes us to bow before him.

row.cell: The sin and death of Nadab and Abihu.
Aaron and his sons forbidden to mourn for Nadab and Abihu.
Wine forbidden to the priests when in the service of the tabernacle.

div.title: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire (verses 1–2)
div.p: After Moses and Aaron, few men in Israel seemed more likely to receive honor than Nadab and Abihu.
Henry considers it probable that they had become proud and had drunk wine.
While the people bowed down before the Lord in worship, the two men rushed into the tabernacle to burn incense.
They did so at the wrong time, both together rather than one at a time, and used fire that had not come from the altar.
If the offense had been committed unintentionally, they could have brought a sin offering.
But they acted presumptuously, showing contempt for God's majesty and justice.
Such deliberate defiance was to be punished by death.
They died while committing their sin.
This judgment exposed the incompleteness of the Aaronic priesthood from its very beginning.
It could not protect anyone from the fire of God's wrath, except insofar as it foreshadowed the priesthood of Christ.

div.title: Aaron responds to the death of his sons (verses 3–7)
div.p: The most comforting thoughts in suffering come from God's word.
Aaron had good reason to feel overwhelmed with grief and alarm.
Yet by remaining silent in submission, he showed reverence for God's righteous judgment.
When God corrects us or our families for sin, we should receive his correction and confess that he is the Lord and may do what seems good to him.
Whenever believers worship, they come near to God as spiritual priests.
We should therefore approach every act of worship seriously, remembering the holiness of the One before whom we stand.
God judges people who treat his sacred name carelessly or make light of his worship.

div.title: Priests must not drink while ministering (verses 8–11)
div.p: Aaron and his sons were forbidden to drink wine or strong drink while they served in the tabernacle.
Ministers of the gospel likewise must not be given to wine (1 Timothy 3:3).
A person may die suddenly, even while drunk.
Since death can overtake us at any time, we should practice sobriety.

div.title: Eating the holy offerings (verses 12–20)
div.p: Suffering should normally make us more diligent in carrying out our duties, not draw us away from them.
Nevertheless, God makes allowance when a person is genuinely unable to carry out a duty because of a natural, non-sinful weakness.
He desires mercy and not sacrifice.
Let this sad history warn us.
Some people approach worship with great zeal but little understanding, governed by fleshly feelings, superficial thoughts and human inventions.
Their worship may be outwardly impressive, but it is not the inward devotion of soul and spirit.
Their incense is then lit by a fire that did not descend from heaven—a fire the Holy Spirit never kindled in their hearts.

p.hi: What animals were clean and unclean.

div.title: Clean and unclean animals
div.p: Henry sees several purposes behind the laws distinguishing clean and unclean animals.
First, they tested Israel's obedience, just as Adam's refusal to eat from the tree of knowledge was a test.
They also taught self-denial and control over bodily appetite.
Second, they kept Israel distinct from other nations.
Many of the forbidden animals were objects of pagan superstition or idolatry.
Third, the laws taught the people to distinguish between the holy and the unholy when choosing companions and close relationships.
Fourth, the law prohibited not only eating unclean animals but also touching them.
Those who wish to avoid sin must also be careful to avoid its temptations and circumstances that draw them close to it.
The regulations contained very detailed exceptions.
Those details required continuous attentiveness and precise obedience, training the people to obey God's commands.
Christians are now free from these burdensome ceremonial rules.
Yet we must not misuse our freedom.
The Lord has redeemed and called his people to be holy as he is holy.
We must turn away from the sinful patterns of the world and avoid unnecessary close ties with those who remain spiritually dead.
We should be eager to do good, devoted to God and glad to keep company with his people.

p.hi: Ceremonial purification.

div.title: Purification after childbirth
div.p: After the laws concerning clean and unclean food come laws concerning people who were considered ceremonially clean or unclean.
Henry understands these regulations in light of the fallen condition inherited by every child.
Human beings pass their corrupt nature on to their descendants.

Apart from the atonement of Christ and the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit, even the original blessing to increase and multiply (Genesis 1:28) has become bound up with the transmission of sin and misery throughout the fallen human family.
Women who have received God's mercy in childbirth should respond with heartfelt gratitude for his goodness.
Such thanksgiving pleases him more than sacrifices.

row.cell: Directions to the priest to judge concerning leprosy.
How the leper must be disposed of.

div.title: The priest examines suspected skin disease (verses 1–17)
div.p: The affliction called leprosy was treated primarily as a condition of ceremonial uncleanness rather than an ordinary illness.
Henry notes that Christ is said to cleanse those afflicted, not simply to cure them.

The condition was widespread among the Hebrews during and after their time in Egypt. Henry considers it likely that their harsh lives and work in Egypt made them especially vulnerable to illness, and he sees no reason to think this particular affliction was familiar among them earlier.
Yet some cases were evidently direct judgments from God.
Miriam, Gehazi and King Uzziah were struck with leprosy in connection with particular sins. It was therefore important to distinguish this affliction from an ordinary illness.
The priests were appointed to examine suspected cases.
Leprosy pictured the moral pollution of the soul by sin, which defiles the conscience and from which only Christ can cleanse us.
A priest could declare someone unclean, just as the law reveals knowledge of sin.
But the priest could not remove that uncleanness. Christ can truly take sin away.
Determining our spiritual condition is very important, yet difficult.
We are all aware of faults and stains in ourselves. The question is whether our spiritual condition is clean or unclean.
Just as marks helped the priest identify the physical affliction, spiritual signs can reveal whether a person remains trapped in bitterness and corruption.
The priest was to take time before pronouncing judgment.
This teaches ministers and ordinary believers not to condemn people hastily or judge before the proper time.
Some people's sins become apparent before judgment, while the sins of others—and likewise their good works—become visible only later.
Even when the person proved to be clean, the clothes still had to be washed because there had been reason for suspicion.
We all need the blood of Christ to wash us from our stains, even when they are not the severe marks of leprosy. Who among us can claim to be entirely free from sin?

div.title: Further signs of the affliction (verses 18–44)
div.p: The priest received instructions for cases where suspected leprosy appeared in an old sore.
Henry compares this to the spiritual danger faced by people who escape the world's corruption but later become entangled in it again.
He also considers cases where the disease appears in a burn (verse 24).
He sees in this a warning that strife and angry disputes can expose and intensify the corruption of the heart.
Human life is surrounded by many afflictions.
We face countless diseases, all of which entered the world because of sin.
When we enjoy health, strength and bodily comfort, we should use our bodies to glorify God.
Special attention was required when leprosy appeared on the head.
If the leprosy of sin corrupts a person's judgment, leading that person to accept false principles that support wicked behavior, the danger is especially grave.
Few people recover easily from deeply corrupt convictions.
Soundness in the faith helps protect the mind from that spiritual disease.

div.title: The person declared unclean (verses 45–46)
div.p: When a priest declared a person unclean, ordinary work stopped.
The person was separated from friends and family and deprived of many worldly comforts.
Such a person was to humble himself beneath God's mighty hand rather than insisting on a cleanness the priest had denied.
The spiritual lesson is that we should acknowledge the shame of our own sin.
With sorrowful hearts we must confess that both our hearts and lives have been unclean: through the corruption inherited from Adam and through our own acts of disobedience.
Because of these sins, we deserve to be excluded forever from fellowship with God unless his infinite mercy intervenes.
The leper had to warn others not to approach too closely.
The person was also required to live outside the camp. Later, in Canaan, this meant outside the town or village, apart from everyone except others suffering the same affliction.
Henry sees this as a picture of the purity that ought to characterize the Christian church.

div.title: Suspected contamination in clothing (verses 47–59)
div.p: Clothing suspected of leprosy was not to be burned immediately.
First it had to be examined.
If a persistent affected patch was found, the whole garment—or at least the affected part—was to be destroyed.
If the garment proved free of the affliction, it could be washed and used.
This, too, showed the serious evil of sin.
Sin stains not only the conscience but also a person's possessions and activities.
Those who use their clothes to display pride or indulge lust may see them spiritually stained.
But the robes of righteousness never decay or become moth-eaten.

row.cell: Of declaring the leper to be clean.
The sacrifices to be offered by him.
Summary of the law concerning leprosy.

div.title: Declaring a person cleansed (verses 1–9)
div.p: The priests could not heal leprosy.
But after the Lord removed the affliction, they were responsible for following the appointed ceremonies so that the person could again join the worship and fellowship of God's people.
The ceremonies illustrated the duties of people who truly repent and the responsibilities of ministers toward them.
Applied to the spiritual leprosy of sin, they teach us that when we withdraw from people who live disorderly lives, we must not treat them as enemies but warn them as brothers and sisters.
When God brings such people to repentance, we should welcome them back with tenderness, gladness and genuine love.
We must neither encourage people to remain in sin nor discourage those who repent.
When the priest found that a person had been healed, he formally declared that person clean through the prescribed ceremonies.
One bird was killed. A second was dipped in the blood of the first and then released.
Henry suggests this may picture Christ shedding his blood for sinners, then rising and ascending into heaven.
After being declared free from the affliction, the restored person still had to remove every trace of it.
Likewise, those who have the comfort of forgiveness should carefully turn away from their sins.
Everyone who possesses this hope seeks to become pure.

div.title: Offerings for a restored person (verses 10–32)
div.p: The restored person was to appear before the Lord with the appointed offerings.
When God enables us to return to public worship after sickness, distance or other obstacles, we should show gratitude by using that opportunity diligently.
Both we and our offerings must be brought before God by the Priest who cleanses us—our Lord Jesus Christ.
Alongside the ordinary rites of the guilt offering, blood and oil were placed on the person being cleansed.
Where Christ's blood is applied to bring justification, the oil of the Holy Spirit is also applied for sanctification.
These two blessings cannot be separated.
The law made gracious provision for the poor.
Poor people were as welcome at God's altar as the rich.
They could bring less costly sacrifices, but the essential ceremony was the same for everyone.
Their souls were equally precious, and the same Christ and gospel were needed by both.
Even the poorest had to bring one lamb.
No sinner could have been saved without the Lamb who was slain and redeemed us to God through his blood.

div.title: Suspected leprosy in a house (verses 33–53)
div.p: Leprosy in a house, like leprosy in a garment, is difficult for us to understand.
But where sin rules a household, it becomes a plague there just as surely as it does in an individual heart.
Heads of households should watch for the first signs of sin in their families and remove it, whatever form it takes.
If an affected section of a house was discovered, it had to be removed.
If the affliction remained, the entire building was to be pulled down.
It was better to lose a home than to continue living in one that remained contaminated.
The leprosy of sin can ruin both families and churches.
Sin is so deeply woven into our mortal bodies that those bodies must finally be brought down by death.

div.title: Concluding instruction on the law of leprosy (verses 54–57)
div.p: God is rich in mercy.
Because of his great love, even while we were dead in sins, he made us alive by his grace (Ephesians 2:4–5).
When he does this, we show the change by repenting and abandoning our former sins.
Let us pursue holiness.
Let us also show compassion toward other poor sufferers, sincerely desiring, seeking and praying for their cleansing.

p.hi: Laws concerning ceremonial uncleanness.

div.title: Ceremonial uncleanness and the need for purity
div.p: We do not need to speculate in great detail about these laws.
Rather, we have reason to give thanks that Christians are no longer obliged to undergo burdensome ceremonial purifications.
What truly defiles us is sin.
These regulations remind us that God sees everything, even things people never notice.
They point to the great duties of the gospel: faith and repentance.
They also illustrate its great privileges: Christ's blood applied to our souls for justification and his grace given for our sanctification.

row.cell: The sacrifices on it, The scape-goat.

div.title: The yearly Day of Atonement (verses 1–14)
div.p: Without detailing every ceremony of the great Day of Atonement, we should remember that its observance was to remain binding while that former religious order continued.
As long as we continue sinning, we continue to need atonement.
The duty of humbling and grieving over our sins remains until we reach the place where every tear—even tears of repentance—will be wiped away.
The apostle notes that the sacrifices themselves could never take sin away or cleanse the conscience completely.
Their repetition every year brought the memory of sin back again (Hebrews 10:1, 3).
That repeated offering revealed the weakness of the old sacrifices to achieve final atonement.
Only the offering of Christ's body once for all could do that.
His sacrifice does not need to be repeated.

div.title: The sacrifices and the scapegoat (verses 15–34)
div.p: The ceremonies pointed toward two great privileges of the gospel: forgiveness of sin and access to God.
Both come through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Look first at the removal of guilt.
Christ is both the Priest who makes atonement and the Sacrifice by which atonement is made.
He is everything necessary for our reconciliation to God.
The two goats pictured these aspects of his saving work.
The goat killed in sacrifice pointed to Christ's death for our sins.
The goat sent away pictured Christ rising again for our justification.
The priest symbolically placed Israel's sins on the head of the living goat and sent it away into an uninhabited wilderness.
Its departure represented the complete and free removal of the people's sins.
It bore away all their iniquities.
Likewise, Christ the Lamb of God takes away the world's sin by bearing it himself (John 1:29).
Look also at access to God.
The high priest's entry into the Most Holy Place pointed to Christ opening the way into heaven for us (Hebrews 9:7).
Israel's high priest came out again.
Our Lord Jesus lives forever, interceding continually and appearing in God's presence for us.
Finally, the ceremonies illustrated two great duties of the gospel: faith and repentance.
By faith, we place our hands upon the head of our offering, relying on Christ as the Lord our Righteousness and pleading his sacrifice as the only ground of pardon.
By repentance, we humble ourselves over sin.
That includes more than temporary fasting from bodily pleasures. It means sincere inward sorrow and a life of self-denial.
God is faithful and righteous to forgive people who confess their sins and to cleanse them from all unrighteousness.
Through Christ's atonement we receive rest for our souls and all the glorious freedom belonging to God's children.
If Christ's blood has not been truly applied to our souls, we cannot approach God with comfort or assurance of acceptance.
Receive that blood by faith and discover how completely it reconciles us to him.

row.cell: All sacrifices to be offered at the tabernacle.
Eating of blood, or of animals which died a natural death, forbidden.

div.title: Sacrifices at the tabernacle (verses 1–9)
div.p: While the Israelites lived in the wilderness, every animal they killed from their herds was to be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle.
After being presented as an offering, its meat was returned to the owner to be eaten according to the regulations for fellowship offerings.
Once Israel entered Canaan, this requirement would apply only to animals offered in sacrifice.
Christians' spiritual sacrifices are no longer restricted to a particular location.
We have no earthly temple or altar that makes an offering acceptable.
The unity of the gospel is not founded on a single place, but on one heart and unity in the Spirit.
Christ is our Altar and the true Tabernacle.
God dwells among humanity in him.
Only through Christ can any offering be accepted by God.
To establish other mediators, altars or sacrifices supposed to make atonement would, in effect, be to establish other gods.
Yet God's willingness to accept the worship we offer in our homes is no excuse for neglecting the worship of his gathered people.

div.title: The prohibition concerning blood (verses 10–16)
div.p: The law forbidding Israel to eat blood is confirmed here.
But Henry explicitly says it was a ceremonial law and therefore no longer binds believers after Christ's coming.
The reality replaces its shadow.
Animal blood is no longer appointed as a ransom.
Only Christ's blood makes true and effective atonement.
The former reason for abstaining from blood has therefore ended, and it may now be used as ordinary nourishment.
But we must honor Christ's blood all the more.
It truly makes reconciliation with God.
We must never treat it as a common thing or regard it indifferently.

p.hi: Unlawful marriages and fleshly lusts.

div.title: Prohibitions against corrupt practices
div.p: This chapter forbids God's people to imitate the corrupt customs of the surrounding nations.
Its commands prohibit incest, degrading sexual acts and cruel idolatry.
The ruin of the Canaanites is given as a warning reinforcing these prohibitions.
God is giving moral commands here.
The most effective protection against gross sin is to keep closely and consistently to what God has appointed.
Only God's grace can preserve us from falling.
We should seek that grace through the means by which he has promised to give it.
God does not abandon people to their heart's sinful desires until they have first abandoned him and his service.

p.hi: laws.

div.title: Holy conduct toward God and neighbor
div.p: This chapter includes a few ceremonial regulations, but most of its commands still bind us.
They explain and apply the Ten Commandments.
God calls Israel to holiness because Israel's God is holy (verse 2).
His people must separate themselves from worldly and sinful conduct and devote themselves completely to him.
This remains the law of Christ.
May the Lord bring our every thought into obedience to him!
Honor your parents (verse 3).
Children must respect and obey their parents from the heart.
They should value them, treat them respectfully, try to please them and ease their burdens.
Worship God alone (verse 4).
False gods deceive their worshipers and lead them toward misery.
The true God makes his people holy and happy.
Do not even turn your eyes toward idols, much less your hearts.
Leave part of the harvest for the poor (verse 9).
Acts of devotion must always be joined with acts of charity, according to our means.
We should not grasp at everything we have the right to claim, demanding the full extent of our rights in every situation.
Be honest in every dealing (verse 11).
Make sure that what you possess was obtained justly.
Dishonest gain cannot make a person truly or lastingly rich.
Revere God's holy name (verse 12).
Treat it seriously and respectfully.
Do not keep what belongs to someone else (verse 13).
This especially includes wages due to workers.
Protect those who cannot defend themselves (verse 14).
Guard their safety and reputation.
Do not harm anyone simply because that person cannot—or will not—retaliate.
Avoid even making a weaker brother or sister stumble.
Fear of God should restrain us from wrongdoing even when it cannot provoke human punishment.
Judge impartially (verse 15).
All those entrusted with authority must administer justice without favoritism.
Spreading malicious stories and sowing discord among neighbors is among the worst things a person can do.
Correct your neighbor in love (verse 17).
It is better to rebuke someone gently than to harbor hatred because that person has wronged you.
If we fail to correct our neighbor when we should, we become guilty ourselves; such silence is a form of hatred rather than love.
A loving friend can say, “I will do this person the kindness of pointing out the fault.”
Love your neighbor as yourself (verse 18).
Put aside malice and practice brotherly love.
We often forgive ourselves for wrongs we have committed, without loving ourselves any less.
We should show a similar readiness to forgive those around us.
We must often give up something we want for the good of another person.
Reject occult practices (verse 31).
Christians insult God when they seek predictions of the future, use charms or spells, or practice similar things.
Asking whether these activities are harmless shows serious ignorance of their spiritual danger.
Respect older people (verse 32).
Faith teaches us good manners and the obligation to honor those who deserve respect.
Care for foreigners (verse 33).
Foreigners, widows and orphans are objects of God's special concern.
Wronging them is dangerous and sinful.
God's grace is open to foreigners, and we should do what we can to commend his ways to them.
Use honest weights and measures (verse 35).
We must not choose only the commands we like.
Our aim should be to carry out the whole will of God.
The nearer our lives and dispositions come to his law, the more happiness we will find and bring to people around us, and the better we will adorn the gospel.

row.cell: Law against sacrificing children to Moloch, Of children that curse their parents.

div.title: Child sacrifice and dishonoring parents (verses 1–9)
div.p: The cruelty of ancient idol worshipers who sacrificed their own children rightly shocks us.
But Henry warns that parents can also bring spiritual ruin on their children by teaching them evil, setting a wicked example and showing them habits of sin.
He regards this as an especially grievous wrong because it helps lead children toward eternal destruction.
What account will such parents give before God, and what will they say when they face their children at judgment?
Children, meanwhile, should remember the severe judgment pronounced on anyone who cursed a father or mother.
Christ confirmed the continuing moral force of this command.
These regulations repeat laws already given, this time with explicit penalties.
People ought to avoid evil because God's law declares it sinful.
But if they disregard that, they should at least fear the severe penalties for their own preservation.
Amid these solemn laws stands the command to consecrate ourselves and be holy.
The Lord himself makes his people holy and will accomplish his work, even when it is difficult.
His grace does not make our own effort unnecessary.
Rather, it powerfully encourages us to work out our salvation, because God is at work within us.

div.title: Repeated commands and the call to holiness (verses 10–27)
div.p: The laws in this passage repeat earlier instructions.
Such repetition was necessary: people need truth explained again and again.
How greatly we should praise God for showing us the evil of sin and the sure way to be delivered from it.
May his grace enable us to honor the teaching of God our Savior through everything we do.
May we refuse to participate in fruitless works of darkness and instead expose them.

p.hi: Laws concerning the priests.

div.title: Priestly holiness and the greater Priest
div.p: Israel's priests were appointed as pictures of Christ.
Ministers of the gospel should therefore imitate the Savior in their own lives, so that others may follow their example.
Christ was without blemish and separate from sinners.
He carried out his priestly work on earth in perfect holiness.
How serious, then, is the calling of anyone who ministers in his name!
Yet all Christians are spiritual priests.
Ministers are especially responsible for setting a good example, but the whole people of God should follow Christ.
Bodily weakness or disability, thank God, can no longer exclude anyone from serving him, enjoying his privileges or inheriting heavenly glory.
A healthy, beautiful soul may live within a physically weak or visibly impaired body.
And someone who is not suited to a particular form of ministry can still serve God joyfully through other responsibilities within the church.

p.hi: Laws concerning the priests and sacrifices.

div.title: Reverence, sincerity and trust in Christ's atonement
div.p: This chapter contains several laws about priests and sacrifices. Together they guard the honor of God's sanctuary.
We should remember gratefully that nothing can prevent our great High Priest, Christ, from performing his office.
The Lord requires us to revere his name, his truth, his appointed acts of worship and his commands.
We must beware of hypocrisy.
Let us examine ourselves for the sinful stains in our hearts and lives, seeking cleansing through Christ's blood and the sanctifying work of his Spirit.
A person who tries to atone for personal sin or approaches God proudly, relying on personal righteousness, dishonors Christ.
Such a person offends him just as seriously as someone who comes to the Lord's Table while deliberately indulging sinful desires.
A minister who loves people's souls must not allow them to remain deceived in this dangerous way.
The minister should urge them to repent of their sins and abandon them.
But repentance alone is not the whole message.
People must place their full trust in Christ's sacrifice, receiving forgiveness and acceptance with God through faith in his name.
Only in that way will the Lord make them holy as his own people.

row.cell: The feasts of the Lord, The Sabbath.
The Passover, The offering of first-fruits.
The feast of Trumpets, The day of atonement.

div.title: The Sabbath and appointed times (verses 1–3)
div.p: This chapter establishes holy times, including many already mentioned elsewhere.
The annual festivals brought the whole nation together at the sanctuary.
Yet even these great gatherings were no reason to give them more importance than the Sabbath.
On the Sabbath, the people were to cease from ordinary worldly work.
The rest pictured freedom from sin and the rest believers find in God.
The Lord's Sabbaths were to be observed faithfully not only in public worship but also at home, by individual families and by families gathered together.
Keeping God's Sabbath in the home would make it beautiful, strong and secure. It would help sanctify, strengthen and dignify family life.

div.title: Passover and the firstfruits (verses 4–14)
div.p: The Passover feast lasted seven days.
These were not meant to be idle days filled with games, as Henry says many people who call themselves Christians spend their religious holidays.
Offerings were made to God, and the people were to use the time for prayer, praise and godly reflection.
The sheaf of firstfruits pointed to our Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
Henry notes that Jesus rose on the very day when this offering of firstfruits was made.
The law also teaches us to honor the Lord with our possessions and the firstfruits of all our increase (Proverbs 3:9).
Israel could not eat the new grain before first offering God's portion.
We should likewise begin with God: at the beginning of every day, every meal, every undertaking and every business.
Seek God's kingdom first.

div.title: Pentecost and generosity toward the poor (verses 15–22)
div.p: The Feast of Weeks recalled the giving of the law fifty days after Israel departed from Egypt.
It also pointed ahead to the coming of the Holy Spirit fifty days after Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us.
On that day, the apostles presented to God the firstfruits of the Christian church.
The command concerning Pentecost was joined to a repeated instruction to leave gleanings in the fields for the poor.
People who truly recognize God's mercy to them will show mercy to the poor without resentment.

div.title: Trumpets and the Day of Atonement (verses 23–32)
div.p: The trumpet blasts pictured gospel preaching, summoning people to turn from sin and receive Christ's salvation.
That salvation was pictured by the Day of Atonement.
The trumpet also called the people to rejoice in God and to live as strangers and pilgrims in the world, a lesson pictured by the Feast of Tabernacles later in the same month.
At the beginning of the year, this sound urged the people to wake from spiritual laziness, examine their lives and change their ways.
The Day of Atonement followed nine days afterward.
They were given time to prepare through sincere and serious repentance so that the day might truly bring them atonement.
Humbling ourselves over sin and making peace with God require the fullest attention of both heart and mind.
On that day the Lord spoke peace to his people.
Therefore they were to set aside ordinary work so that they could hear his voice of comfort and joy more clearly.

div.title: The Feast of Tabernacles (verses 33–44)
div.p: During this feast, the people remembered their life in temporary shelters during the wilderness journey.
They also remembered how their ancestors had lived in tents in Canaan.
These memories reminded them of their origins and their deliverance.
The festival may also have pictured Christ dwelling on earth in human nature.
It certainly pictured the believer's life here: living as a stranger and pilgrim, with home and heart above, where the Savior is.
After seven days in temporary shelters, people would value the comfort of their own houses more deeply.
Those who live in ease and plenty benefit from occasionally learning what hardship feels like.
Harvest joy should make us rejoice still more in God.
Everything on earth belongs to him.
Whatever benefits we enjoy should therefore bring him glory, especially when his mercy has brought a task or season to completion.
These festivals were appointed in addition to the ordinary Sabbaths and voluntary offerings.
Extraordinary acts of service never excuse us from our regular duties.

row.cell: Oil for the lamps, The shew-bread.
The law of blasphemy, blasphemer is stoned.

div.title: Oil for the lamps and the bread of the Presence (verses 1–9)
div.p: The loaves of bread in God's sanctuary represented Christ, the Bread of Life, who nourishes his people's souls.
He is also the Light of the church and of the whole world.
His light shines through his word.
By that light, we recognize the spiritual food prepared for us.
We should feed upon it in our hearts each day, and especially from Sabbath to Sabbath, with thanksgiving.
The loaves remained before the Lord in his sanctuary.
Likewise, we should remain in God's presence until he sends us on our way.

div.title: The judgment of blasphemy (verses 10–23)
div.p: The person who offended had an Egyptian father and an Israelite mother.
Henry understands the mention of both parents as illustrating the harm that can come from religiously mixed marriages.
This event led to a permanent law prescribing the stoning of blasphemers.
Scripture places serious weight on the command.
It applied to foreign residents as well as native-born Israelites.
Foreign residents were to receive the protection of the law against injustice.
They were also subject to its penalties if they broke it.
People who dishonor God's name may escape human punishment, but they cannot escape God's righteous judgment.
What hostility to God must be in the human heart when people speak blasphemies against him!
If those who rejected Moses' law died without mercy, Henry asks how much greater the judgment must be for those who scorn and misuse the gospel of God's Son.
We should guard against anger, avoid wrongdoing, refuse harmful associations with wicked people and revere the holy name that sinners dishonor.

row.cell: The sabbath of rest for the land in the seventh year.
The jubilee of the fiftieth year, Oppression forbidden.
Redemption of the land and houses.

div.title: The seventh-year rest for the land (verses 1–7)
div.p: Just as ordinary work stopped on the seventh day, the ordinary cultivation of the land was to cease during the seventh year.
These regulations warned Israel against greed.
A person's life does not consist in owning many possessions.
We should willingly depend on God's providence for our support.
We are his tenants and stewards; our possessions should be used as he directs.
The year of rest pictured the spiritual rest all believers enter through Christ.
He lifts the burden of worldly anxiety and weariness.
Our ordinary work and concerns become more bearable and more useful when they are sanctified by him.
Through Christ we are enabled and encouraged to live by faith.

div.title: The Jubilee and the prohibition of oppression (verses 8–22)
div.p: The word jubilee refers to an especially joyful sound of silver trumpets.
That sound was heard on the evening of the great Day of Atonement.
The connection showed that the proclamation of freedom and salvation through the gospel flows from the Redeemer's sacrifice.
Israelite land could not be permanently sold away from the family to which it belonged.
A sale was more like a lease lasting until the next Jubilee, when the land returned to its family.
This protected the separate identity of tribes and families until the Messiah's coming.
Likewise, anyone who had lost personal liberty could regain it at the Jubilee.
The arrangement pictured Christ's redemption from slavery to sin and Satan, and the renewed freedom of God's children.
The principle governing every sale was that no one should oppress or exploit another.
We must not take advantage of a neighbor's ignorance or desperate need.
Fear of God should restrain injustice in speech and action.
The people were promised that observing the appointed years of rest would not leave them poorer.
If we are faithful to our duty, we can entrust our needs and comfort to God.
His provision for Israel during the fallow year was a miracle intended to encourage his people in every age to trust him.
We lose nothing by faith and self-denial when we obey.
Some Israelites asked what they would eat during the seventh year.
Christians also worry about future difficulties and hesitate to follow duty because they anticipate suffering.
But we should not torment ourselves with imagined future troubles.
Our obedience may appear foolish to people concerned only with this world's interests.
Even so, the path of duty remains the path of safety.

div.title: Redemption of land and houses (verses 23–34)
div.p: If land had not been redeemed before the Jubilee, it then returned to the original seller or that person's family.
This was a picture of God's free grace in Christ.
Through that grace—not through a payment or merit of our own—we are restored to God's favor.
Houses inside walled cities were more directly the result of human labor than farmland, which was a gift of God's generosity.
A person who sold a house within such a city therefore had only one year to buy it back.
These provisions also encouraged foreigners and converts to settle among Israel.

div.title: Caring for people who have become poor (verses 35–38)
div.p: Poverty and financial decline are common sources of deep suffering.
The poor will always be among us.
We should help them by sympathy, showing genuine compassion; by service, doing practical work for them; and by material help, giving according to their needs and our ability.
We must not exploit poor people who owe us money.
The law gives two reasons to restrain oppressive lending: fear God, and help the poor remain able to live among you.
Those who struggle financially can still contribute to the community.
Rich and poor need one another.
People who have received mercy should show mercy.

div.title: Laws for debt servants (verses 39–55)
div.p: An Israelite sold into service because of debt or wrongdoing was, in the situation Henry describes, to serve six years and be released in the seventh.
Someone who sold his own labor because of poverty had to be treated in a way appropriate to a descendant of Abraham.
Masters are required to treat their servants fairly and justly (Colossians 4:1).
At the Jubilee, the servant and the servant's children were to go free and return to the family.
This pictured our redemption from slavery to sin and Satan through God's grace in Christ.
His truth makes us free (John 8:32).
We cannot buy the freedom of another sinner's soul.
But we can point people to Christ.
Through his grace, our lives can honor his gospel, express love, show thankfulness and glorify his holy name.

row.cell: God promises to remember those that repent.

div.title: Promises given for obedience (verses 1–13)
div.p: This chapter reinforces the laws given through Moses.
God promises rewards for obedience and warns of punishment for disobedience.
As long as Israel honored God's worship, Sabbath and sanctuary as a nation, and did not turn toward idols, the Lord promised continuing earthly benefits and religious privileges.
These promises particularly concerned life in the present world.
Yet they also pictured the spiritual blessings secured to believers through Christ in the covenant of grace.
Henry identifies seven blessings.
First, abundance. The land would produce plentiful fruit. Every good and perfect gift comes from the Father of lights.
Second, peace. God would protect his people. Those who dwell in him are safe.
