Third, victory. God could save them in war whether their army was large or small.
Fourth, increase in population. In the spiritual picture, the church of the gospel would become fruitful.
Fifth, God's favor. This is the source of every real good.
Sixth, signs of God's presence through appointed worship. If we want his ordinances to remain among us, we must hold fast to them.
Seventh, the grace of the covenant. All the blessings are brought together in God's promise to be their God and make them his people.
Every covenant blessing rests upon redemption.
God had purchased Israel as his own people.
He would not cast them off until they first rejected him.

div.title: Warnings about disobedience (verses 14–39)
div.p: After the blessings God placed curses before his people.
These were warnings about what would make them miserable if they refused to obey.
Henry identifies two leading paths to ruin.
The first is despising God's commands.
People who first reject his rules may eventually reject his covenant altogether.
The second is despising God's correction.
If suffering does not teach them obedience, God himself will stand against them, which is the deepest cause of their misery.
All creation will become hostile toward them as God's judgments are sent upon them.
The warnings are detailed prophecies.
The Lord knew Israel's later rebellions and what would follow from them.
The judgments include earthly consequences.
People who refuse to part from sin when God commands them will be separated from it through his judgments.
Those who cling to their sinful desires will suffer enough from them.
The judgments also include spiritual consequences affecting the mind and conscience.
The people will find no acceptance with God and will continually be terrified by guilt.
It is just for God to leave arrogant sinners, who deliberately presume upon his mercy, without any sense of pardon.
Only free grace prevents us from wasting away under the sins into which we were born and which we have continued to commit.

div.title: God remembers those who repent (verses 40–46)
div.p: Among individuals in Israel, prosperity and suffering did not always correspond directly to a person's obedience or wrongdoing.
But the people had a unique national covenant.
Under it, national obedience was linked to national prosperity, and national disobedience brought national judgment.
Wickedness can ruin any nation, especially where God's word and the light of the gospel are available.
Sooner or later, sin brings both shame and destruction to a people.
May we humble ourselves for our sins now and turn away the approaching storm before it breaks.
May God grant that, while time remains, we attend to the things that bring lasting peace with him.

row.cell: The law concerning vows, Of persons and animals.
Devoted things not to be redeemed.

div.title: Vows concerning persons and animals (verses 1–13)
div.p: Zeal for God's service sometimes led Israelites to dedicate themselves or their children to lifelong work in the Lord's house.
Some people could actually serve as assistants there.
In general, however, those dedicated were to be redeemed by paying a stated value.
It is good to be eager and generous in serving God.
Yet we should carefully consider the obligations we take on.
Wise judgment must guide our decisions.
Rash promises followed by reluctance to fulfill them dishonor God and disturb our own peace of mind.

div.title: Vows concerning houses and land (verses 14–25)
div.p: Our homes, land, animals and all our possessions should be used to bring glory to God.
He welcomes gifts that support his worship and advance his cause.
But the Lord does not approve of reckless generosity that leaves a person's family ruined.
Our zeal must be guided by care for those entrusted to us.

div.title: What has been fully devoted to the Lord (verses 26–33)
div.p: The law distinguishes things that were devoted to God from those that were merely consecrated.
Fully devoted things were most holy and could not be taken back or used for another purpose.
Israel was also commanded to honor God with a tenth of the produce from which it benefited, wherever that produce could be given.
In doing this, the people acknowledged him as the owner of their land and the giver of its fruit.
They confessed that they were his tenants, depending on him for everything.
They expressed gratitude for abundance already received and asked for his continuing favor.
We too are taught to honor the Lord through our possessions.

div.title: The closing word of Leviticus (verse 34)
div.p: The final verse appears to refer to the entire book.
Many of these instructions are moral laws that remain binding.
Others are ceremonial regulations given specifically to Israel.
Yet even those ceremonies have a spiritual meaning from which Christians can learn.
Through them, the gospel was proclaimed to Israel and, in this sense, to us as well (Hebrews 4:2).
The teaching that sinners are reconciled to God through a Mediator is not made clearer by the smoke of burning sacrifices.
It is made clear through knowing Jesus Christ and him crucified.
We now live under the joyful and gentle ordinances of the gospel.
True worshipers approach the Father in spirit and truth, through Christ alone and in his name.
Nevertheless, freedom from ceremonial offerings does not mean that honoring God calls for only a little thought, time or expense.
Because Jesus' blood gives us boldness to enter the Most Holy Place, let us draw near with sincere hearts and the full assurance of faith.
May we worship with greater joy and humble confidence, continually saying:

p.hi: Blessed be God for Jesus Christ!

div.title: Numbers — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: This book is called Numbers because it records several censuses of the people of Israel.
Its account extends from the giving of the law at Sinai until Israel reached the plains beside the Jordan River.
It tells how the people complained and refused to believe, and how they were therefore sentenced to wander in the wilderness for nearly forty years.
The book also contains laws, some moral and others ceremonial.
The people's trials helped reveal the difference between wicked people and hypocrites, on the one hand, and God's true and faithful servants, who worshiped him sincerely, on the other.

row.cell: The Levites not numbered with the rest.

div.title: Israel's tribes are counted (verses 1–43)
div.p: God commanded a census of Israel.
The count showed his faithfulness in causing Jacob's descendants to increase so greatly.
It also helped organize the people for the coming wars and conquest of Canaan and established their family divisions for the future distribution of land.
The census counted, from each tribe, those able to serve in war.
Israel had not yet encountered these enemies, but battles awaited them.
Christians should likewise prepare to withstand the enemies of their souls, even when everything appears peaceful.

div.title: The total number of Israelites (verses 44–46)
div.p: The census gave a large total.
Consider how much food was needed to maintain such a crowd in the wilderness!
God supplied everyone's needs day by day.
When we recognize his faithfulness in fulfilling promises that once seemed impossible, we can take courage concerning the promises still awaiting fulfillment for his church.

div.title: The Levites are counted separately (verses 47–54)
div.p: The tribe of Levi was set apart.
Its members had distinguished themselves during the crisis of the golden calf.
Those who perform extraordinary service for God may receive extraordinary honors from him.
The Levites were entrusted with the tabernacle and its sacred treasures, both when Israel was camped and when it moved.
It honored the holy things that only those called by God could see or handle them.
None of us is naturally fit or worthy to enjoy fellowship with God.
We must first be called by grace into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
As the spiritual offspring of our great High Priest, Christians are made priests to God.
We should be especially careful to prevent sin, because preventing sin is also preventing the judgment it brings.
As a holy tribe, the Levites were not numbered with the other Israelites.
Those who minister in holy things should not allow worldly concerns to entangle them or become entangled themselves in worldly affairs.
Every believer should seek to do what the Lord has commanded.

p.hi: The order of the tribes in their tents.

div.title: The arrangement of Israel's camp
div.p: The tribes camped around the tabernacle, which stood in the middle of Israel's camp.
The tabernacle showed God's gracious presence among his people.
Yet the people had to place their tents at a respectful distance from the sanctuary.
The Israelites took their assigned positions without complaining or arguing.
Their orderly camp was both safer and more beautiful because of this obedience.
It is both our duty and our advantage to be satisfied with the position God has given us.
We should carry out our responsibilities well without envy, resentment, ambition or greed.
The church of the gospel should likewise be well joined together according to Scripture's pattern.
Each member should know and keep the appropriate place within the body.
When this happens, everyone who loves the church can rejoice at its good order (Colossians 2:5).

row.cell: The sons of Aaron, The Levites taken instead of the first-born.
The Levites numbered by their families, Their duties.

div.title: The Levites replace Israel's firstborn (verses 1–13)
div.p: Aaron and his two sons had a great deal of priestly work to carry out.
God appointed the Levites to help them.
Whenever he provides work for his servants, he can also provide the help they need.
The Levites were taken in place of Israel's firstborn.
When God saves us—as he saved Israel's firstborn—we receive an additional obligation to serve him faithfully.
The right God has over us through redemption confirms the right he already possesses as our Creator.

div.title: The families and duties of Levi (verses 14–39)
div.p: The Levites were grouped according to Levi's three sons: Gershon, Kohath and Merari.
Each group was further divided into families.
Moses' descendants received no special rank or privilege above the other Levites.
This showed that Moses was not using his position to advance his own household or obtain special honors for his family.
Levi was by far the smallest of Israel's tribes.
God's chosen people are likewise a small flock compared with the world.

div.title: The number of the firstborn and their ransom (verses 40–51)
div.p: The number of Israel's firstborn came close to the number of Levites.
God knows all his works before they happen.
The numbers were arranged in an exact relationship, which became clear when they were compared.
The small number of firstborn who exceeded the number of Levites were to be redeemed by a payment given to Aaron.
The church is called the church of the firstborn.
But it is not redeemed with silver or gold.
Because our sins have placed us under God's just judgment, only the precious blood of his Son can ransom us.
Every human being belongs to the Lord by creation.
Every true Christian belongs to him also by redemption.
We should each know our own responsibility.
No service required by such a Master should be dismissed as beneath us or too difficult.

row.cell: The duties of the Gershonites and Merarites.
The numbers of the serviceable Levites.

div.title: Levites in their prime serve the sanctuary (verses 1–3)
div.p: Levites aged thirty to fifty were appointed for the main service of the tabernacle.
Serving God deserves the best of our strength and the finest part of our lives.
Our time cannot be better spent than honoring him who is first and best.
We should take up God's work while we are most energetic and capable.
Those who postpone repentance until old age have failed to understand this.
They leave the most important work to the least favorable time.

div.title: The duties of Kohath's descendants (verses 4–20)
div.p: The Kohathites carried the tabernacle's most holy furnishings.
The sacred objects had to be covered, both to protect them and to treat them with reverence.
They were also kept from ordinary sight.
The covering pictured the mystery surrounding the spiritual truths represented by the sanctuary, and the limited light given under that earlier religious order.
Through Christ, our situation has changed.
We are now encouraged to approach the throne of grace boldly.

div.title: The duties of Gershon and Merari (verses 21–33)
div.p: The other two Levite families were assigned work that seemed less honorable than Kohath's responsibilities.
Yet their duties were just as necessary and had to be carried out carefully.
Each object was assigned to their care by name.
This illustrated God's concern for his church and for every individual member.
Scripture compares the death of believers to dismantling a tent (2 Corinthians 5:1) or taking it off (2 Peter 1:14).
But our bodies will be raised on the great day.
They will be transformed to resemble Christ's glorious body, and we will remain with him forever.

div.title: The number of Levites fit for service (verses 34–49)
div.p: God arranged the numbers in a surprising way.
Although the Merarites were the smallest family group, they had the greatest number of men capable of service.
God equips people for whatever work he assigns them.
He supplies strength suited to the task and sufficient grace to perform it.
Even the least numerous of Israel's other tribes had more able men than the Levites.
Similarly, more people devote themselves to the business of this world than to God's service.
May our souls be wholly given to serving him.

row.cell: The unclean to be removed out of the camp, Restitution to be made for trespasses.

div.title: Cleansing the camp and making restitution (verses 1–10)
div.p: Israel's camp had to be kept clean.
The church's purity deserves just as much attention as its peace and order.
Those who were ceremonially defiled had to be separated from the camp.
Wisdom from above is pure first, and then peaceable.
The more openly a home or family professes faith, the more carefully it should put away wickedness.
When one person cheats or exploits another, the offense is also committed against the Lord, who commands us to act justly.
What should someone do when an awakened conscience recalls dishonesty committed many years earlier?
The person must confess the sin both to God and to the neighbor who was harmed.
This can be humiliating, especially if it requires admitting a past lie. But it remains necessary.
Both the wrong against God and the financial loss suffered by the neighbor must be addressed.
Restitution alone is not enough without genuine faith and repentance.
And as long as someone knowingly keeps what was obtained through injustice, the guilt remains.
Neither religious sacrifices, prayers nor tears can erase an offense that the sinner is deliberately continuing to commit.
This principle is taught both by sound reasoning and by God's word.
It exposes hypocrisy, while guiding a tender conscience toward faithful action and the inward peace that comes through faith in Christ.

div.title: The trial of jealousy (verses 11–31)
div.p: This law encouraged Israelite wives to avoid conduct that gave reasonable grounds for suspicion.
It also restrained husbands from acting cruelly because of suspicion alone.
The guilty were not to escape judgment, and innocent wives were not to be condemned unjustly.
When there was no evidence sufficient to decide the case, the woman was called to appeal solemnly to the God who knows every heart.
If she was guilty, she could not sincerely accept the oath and drink the prescribed water unless she refused to believe God or defiantly disregarded his justice.
The water was called bitter because it brought a curse upon the guilty.
Sin, too, is bitter.
Anyone who pursues forbidden pleasures should remember the misery that follows them.
Henry draws three lessons.
First, God knows every secret sin.
He sometimes exposes hidden wrongdoing even during this life.
A final day is coming when God will judge human secrets through Jesus Christ (Romans 2:16).
Second, God will judge sexual immorality and adultery.
We no longer have this ordeal involving bitter water, but we have God's word, which should warn us no less seriously.
Sinful lust ends in bitterness.
Third, God will make the innocence of the innocent known.
The same act of providence can help some people while harming others, according to God's righteous purposes.

row.cell: The form of blessing the people.

div.title: The Nazirite vow (verses 1–21)
div.p: The word Nazirite means someone set apart.
Some people, including Samson and John the Baptist, were appointed by God before their birth for lifelong consecration.
Ordinarily, however, a Nazirite vow was taken voluntarily for a limited period.
It involved separation from ordinary worldly pleasures and special dedication to God's service.
Scripture already mentions Nazirites as a known class, but this chapter gives definite rules for their obligations.
God supplied those rules so that superstition would not endlessly add further restrictions.
Nazirites were forbidden wine, strong drink and even grapes.
Those who dedicate themselves to God must not let physical appetite rule them.
Christians should practice moderation in alcoholic drinks; once someone becomes ruled by them, Satan finds that person easier to trap.
Nazirites were to avoid everything produced by the vine.
This teaches us to keep away not only from sin itself but also from things near it that draw us into temptation.
They were forbidden to cut their hair or shave during the vow.
This marked their willingness to forgo bodily ease and outward adornment.
It was also the outward sign of Samson's lifelong separation.
They must not touch ritually unclean things.
Likewise, people devoted to God should keep their consciences pure from dead works.
Through every day of the vow they were to be holy to the Lord.
Without inward holiness, all their outward abstinence was worthless.
For deliberate, defiant violation of the vow, Henry notes that no specific penalty or sacrifice was appointed: the guilty would have to answer to God.
But the law made provision for those whose vows were disrupted without willful sin.
Henry contrasts these vows with the religious orders of the Roman Catholic Church as he understood them.
He argues that the rules are fundamentally different, not that Nazirites directly authorize those later orders.
Unlike those orders, Nazirites were not forbidden marriage, nor were they subject to a general ban on permitted foods.
They abstained completely from wine, whereas the orders Henry criticizes did not.
Ordinary Nazirites chose a temporary period rather than making a lifelong vow, and in certain circumstances a parent or husband had authority concerning the vow.
This is Henry's historical and confessional criticism; it should not be treated as an editorial claim independently established for the modern world.
Christ is not only our Surety, but also our example.

For his sake we should renounce sinful pleasures, resist fleshly desires, separate ourselves from sin, openly confess our faith, moderate our natural affections, cultivate spiritual thinking and devote ourselves to God's service.
Our lives should encourage others to follow him.

div.title: The priestly blessing (verses 22–27)
div.p: The priests were appointed to bless the people solemnly in the Lord's name.
What makes up this blessing?
God's almighty protection as our Savior.
His favor, like the smile of a loving Father or the warmth of sunlight.
His forgiveness of sins, provision for our needs, comfort in sorrow and grace preparing us for eternal glory.
Together these are the greatest blessings anyone can receive.
Compared with them, worldly pleasures scarcely deserve mention.
This blessing was also a form of prayer.
The name Jehovah appears three times.
Henry notes that Jewish interpreters saw a mystery in the repetition.
He believes the New Testament explains it: we are to look for grace from the Lord Jesus Christ, love from God the Father and fellowship from the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:14).
Each Person is Jehovah, yet there are not three Lords but one Lord.

row.cell: The offerings of the princes at the dedication of the tabernacle.
The offerings of the princes at the dedication of the altar.

div.title: The leaders' offerings for the tabernacle (verses 1–9)
div.p: The tribal leaders brought their offerings for the tabernacle's service after the sanctuary had been fully erected.
Required acts of worship must take priority over voluntary gifts.
The more authority and resources God grants someone, the greater the opportunity to serve him and the surrounding community.
No sooner had the tabernacle been established than the people made provision for moving it.
Even when life seems newly settled, we should prepare for future changes and especially for death—the greatest change.

div.title: The leaders' offerings for the altar (verses 10–89)
div.p: The leaders and prominent men were among the first to take part in honoring God.
People in authority should use their position, influence and wealth to promote faith and God's service wherever they live.
This was a joyful festival of dedication.
Yet a sin offering appeared among the sacrifices.
Even when we serve God at our best, we remain aware of sin and need repentance.
In every act of worship, faith must look toward Christ as our Sin Offering.
Each leader brought an offering on a different day.
God's work should not be carried out in a confused rush.
Taking time may not make us finish faster, but it will help us do it better.
A task extending across twelve days should not be treated as a tedious burden.
The offerings were identical.
This showed that every tribe had an equal share in the altar and an equal right to the blessings signified by its sacrifices.
The One who spoke to Moses from between the cherubim—the Shekinah, or visible divine majesty—was, Henry says, the eternal Word, the second Person of the Trinity.
All God's fellowship with human beings comes through his Son.
Through that Son he created the world and rules the church.
He is the same yesterday, today and forever.

row.cell: Consecration of the Levites, and their service.

div.title: Lighting the sanctuary's lamps (verses 1–4)
div.p: Aaron himself lit the sanctuary lamps.
In this he pictured his divine Master, Jesus Christ.
Scripture shines like a light in a dark place (2 Peter 1:19).
Without that light, even the church would remain in darkness—just as the tabernacle, which had no windows, would have been dark without its lamps.
Ministers serve by lighting these lamps spiritually, explaining and applying God's word.
Jesus Christ is the only Light of our dark and sinful world.
Through his atoning work, his word and the Holy Spirit, he spreads his light.

div.title: The Levites are cleansed and appointed (verses 5–26)
div.p: These verses provide directions for solemnly setting apart the Levites.
All Israel needed to know that the Levites had not claimed this honor for themselves.
They were called to it by God.
But merely being set apart from others was not enough.
Those appointed for God's work must devote themselves to him and to the responsibilities he has assigned them.
Christians are to be baptized, and ministers are to be ordained.
Before offering God our work, we must offer him ourselves.
The Levites were to be cleansed.
Those who carry the Lord's vessels must be clean.
Moses sprinkled the appointed purifying water over them.
This pictured Christ's blood being applied to our souls through faith, making us fit to serve the living God.
God declared his acceptance of the Levites.
Anyone who expects to enjoy the privileges of God's sanctuary should also be willing to perform its service.
On one hand, God does not need any of his creatures to serve him.
On the other, he never appoints anyone merely to carry a title while doing nothing.
Everyone he acknowledges as a servant receives work to do.
Even angels serve him.

div.title: The Passover and those unable to attend (verses 1–14)
div.p: God gave special instructions for observing this Passover.
So far as the record shows, Israel did not celebrate another Passover until arriving in Canaan (Joshua 5:10).
Henry sees this as early evidence that the ceremonial arrangements were not meant to last forever: some were allowed to fall into disuse for many years soon after they were established.
The Lord's Supper, by contrast, was not set aside during the church's earliest years, even though Christians then faced greater persecution and trouble than Israel had experienced in the wilderness.
Indeed, Henry says it was celebrated more frequently during the times of persecution than afterward.
Israel could hardly forget the Exodus while still living in the wilderness.
There was greater risk of forgetting it after settling in Canaan.
These verses also explain what should happen when people were ceremonially unclean at Passover.
Those whose hearts and consciences are polluted by sin cannot truly enjoy communion with God or the Christian Passover until they are cleansed through repentance and faith.
Notice how troubled the Israelites were when they were prevented from taking part in the Lord's offering.
We, too, should feel real sorrow when circumstances keep us from Sabbath worship or the Lord's Supper.
Moses did not decide the difficult case according to his own preference or feelings.
He waited for God's instruction.
Ministers must take their guidance from God's word.
When a case remains difficult, believers should take time to bring it before God in humble, trusting prayer, seeking the Spirit's direction.
God then gave a rule for this case and similar ones.
People who are unwillingly prevented from joining in God's ordinances may still expect his grace and favor amid their difficulties.
But people who deliberately refuse to participate should not presume upon his kindness.
God will not be mocked.

div.title: Israel moves when the cloud moves (verses 15–23)
div.p: The cloud was the visible sign of God's presence among Israel.
It taught the people that he remained near them day and night.
As long as the cloud rested above the tabernacle, they stayed in the same place.
Waiting for God's appointed time is never wasted time.
When the cloud rose, they traveled, even if the camp had been comfortable.
We do not know when we will leave the earthly tent of our bodies.
We should therefore remain prepared to move whenever the Lord calls us.
It is safe and good to go where God leads us and rest where he commands us to rest.
The cloud pictured the Holy Spirit's guidance.
We should not now expect the same visible signs of divine presence.
Yet God promises to direct his spiritual Israel by his counsel (Psalm 73:24), to guide them even to death (Psalm 48:14), and to lead all his children by his Spirit (Romans 8:14).
He makes straight the paths of people who acknowledge him in all their ways (Proverbs 3:6).
At every change of circumstance we should be willing to move or remain according to his command.
Our prayer should be, “Father, your will be done. Direct me and everything entrusted to me as you please. Only let me remain yours and follow my duty.”
Applying general biblical instructions to specific situations requires wise counsel and earnest prayer.
We must not confuse our own desires with divine guidance.
When something is obviously wrong—or even doubtful, and yet we strongly desire to do it—what someone calls “the cloud moving” may really be a temptation permitted by Satan.
People can imagine they are following God while actually following stubborn impulses.
The record of God's mercy and the truth of his word lead us reliably through Christ toward eternal peace.
Follow the pillar of cloud and fire: take the Bible to heart and humbly receive the word that can save your soul.

row.cell: The Israelites remove from Sinai to Paran.
Hobab entreated by Moses to continue.

div.title: The silver trumpets (verses 1–10)
div.p: These verses establish the trumpet signals used to communicate publicly with the camp.
Israel was to receive its laws from God in every detail, so even these signals were given to Moses by divine command.
The trumpets pictured the preaching of the gospel.
It sounds an alarm to sinners, calling them to repent.
It announces freedom to people enslaved to Satan and gathers God's worshipers.
It directs and strengthens them on the journey to heaven.
It calls them to fight against the world and sin, and gives them confidence of victory.
It points them to Christ's sacrifice and reminds them of the Lord's presence protecting his people.
The gospel trumpet must make a clear and distinct sound.
Its message must suit both the people addressed and the purpose for speaking: conviction, humbling, comfort, encouragement, correction or instruction.
God has appointed the public proclamation of the gospel, and everyone to whom it comes is called to listen.

div.title: Israel travels from Sinai to Paran (verses 11–28)
div.p: The Israelites had spent nearly a year at Mount Sinai.
Now that their worship had been organized, they set out toward Canaan.
True religion begins with knowing God's holy law and humbling ourselves over sin.
But we must keep growing in the knowledge of Christ and his gospel, and in the powerful reasons, encouragements and help he gives us for holiness.
The people traveled when God commanded them (Deuteronomy 1:6–8) and when the cloud led them.
Those who submit to God's word and Spirit can follow a steady course even when the route seems confusing.
If we are sure that we have not lost our God and Guide, we need not fear becoming lost ourselves.
They left the wilderness of Sinai and camped in the wilderness of Paran.
So many of our changes in this world simply move us from one wilderness to another.
Moves that we expect to improve our circumstances do not always do so.
We will not find perfect rest or a permanent home until we reach heaven.
But everything will be well there.

div.title: Moses invites Hobab to accompany Israel (verses 29–32)
div.p: Moses invited his relative Hobab to come with the people to Canaan.
Those traveling toward the heavenly Canaan should invite and encourage friends to come too.
Other people sharing the joys of heaven will not reduce our own happiness in the least.
It is good to enjoy fellowship with people who enjoy fellowship with God.
Yet the visible attractions of this world can powerfully distract people from the unseen blessings of eternity.
Moses explained that Hobab could be useful to Israel.
He did not need Hobab to decide where to travel or camp—the cloud provided that guidance.
But Hobab could help identify practical features of the places they passed through or stayed in.
Depending on God's providence is entirely consistent with accepting wise help from our friends.

div.title: Moses prays when Israel moves and rests (verses 33–36)
div.p: Israel's departures and arrivals teach us to begin and end our daily journeys and work with prayer.
When the ark moved, Moses prayed for God to rise and scatter his enemies.
There are people who openly or secretly oppose God, his truth, laws, worship and people.
But God's rising to act is sufficient to defeat them.
When the ark rested, Moses prayed for the Lord to return and dwell with his people.
Israel's well-being and happiness depended on God's continuing presence.
Its safety did not come from its numbers but from his favor and his willingness to remain among the people.
God would go ahead and provide suitable places to rest during their travels.
He promised never to abandon or forsake them.

row.cell: The people lust for flesh, and loathe the manna.
Elders appointed to divide the charge. Flesh meat promised.
The Spirit rests on the elders.

div.title: Fire breaks out at Taberah (verses 1–3)
div.p: The people complained.
This shows how sin can twist even something good into a reason for rebelling against God.
The law exposes sin but cannot conquer it.
Discontented people will always find something to complain about, however favorable their circumstances may be.
The Lord heard the murmuring, even when Moses did not.
He knows every secret resentment and complaint hidden in the heart.
God was displeased, and he sent a fire of judgment against the people.
They had allowed their anger against him to burn within them.
Now his just anger burned against their bodies.
Yet his judgment came gradually, leaving time for warning and repentance.
God does not delight in punishment.
Even after judgment begins, he is willing to stop when his people turn to him.

div.title: The people crave meat and reject manna (verses 4–9)
div.p: Human beings have lost their true place of rest and may remain dissatisfied even in prosperity.
Israel became tired of manna, though it was wholesome and nourishing food.
It cost nothing.
Gathering it took little labor.
Yet the people remembered the fish and other foods they had eaten in Egypt as though those meals had been free.
They forgot the crushing slavery through which they had paid for them.
While they ate manna, they were almost spared the burden of earning bread by the sweat of their faces.
Still they complained about God's provision.
A complaining spirit finds fault even with good gifts.
People who could be happy make themselves miserable through discontent.
They insisted they would not be satisfied unless they had meat.
A desire for bodily pleasure has become dangerous when it rules a person's choices.
We should not encourage any desire that we cannot sincerely turn into prayer.
Something lawful in itself may become sinful when God has not given it to us and we demand it out of uncontrolled appetite.

div.title: Moses complains under the burden of leadership (verses 10–15)
div.p: The people had provoked Moses terribly.
But his own response was not as fitting as it ought to have been.
He undervalued the honor God had given him.
He exaggerated the burden of his own work, even though divine wisdom guided him and almighty power could reward or correct the people.
His words showed distrust of God's grace.
If the work had been lighter, Moses could not have fulfilled it by his own strength.
If it had been heavier, he could still have done it through God's help.
Let us ask the Lord not to lead us into temptation.

div.title: Seventy elders are appointed; meat is promised (verses 16–23)
div.p: Moses was to choose people already recognized as wise and experienced elders.
God would equip them for the work.
If they were not already capable, he would make them capable.
God also promised meat to the discontented people, removing every excuse for further complaint.
Henry draws two lessons.
First, bodily pleasures are empty. They can overwhelm us through excess but cannot truly satisfy us.
Only spiritual pleasures satisfy and endure.
The world and its desires pass away.
Second, gluttony and drunkenness are degrading sins. They turn food and drink, which should nourish and strengthen the body, into causes of harm.
Moses questioned how God could provide such enormous quantities of meat.
Even great and genuine believers may find it difficult to trust God when visible circumstances seem hopeless.
God reminded Moses that the Lord is almighty.
He would soon see whether God's word came true.
When God speaks, he can accomplish what he promises.

div.title: The Spirit rests upon the elders (verses 24–30)
div.p: God fulfilled his promise to help Moses govern Israel.
He put his Spirit upon the seventy elders.
They spoke to the people about the things of God in a way that made his presence recognizable.
Two elders, Eldad and Medad, had not gone to the tabernacle.
Henry understands this as a sign that they felt unworthy and inadequate.
Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit met them in the camp, where they exercised gifts of prayer, preaching and praise.
The Spirit of God is not restricted to the tabernacle.
He moves where he wills, like the wind.
God exalts those who humble themselves.
People most capable of leadership are often those who are least ambitious for it.
Joshua wanted Eldad and Medad restrained.
He was not asking for punishment but feared their ministry might divide the people or rival Moses.
He acted out of concern for the unity of the community.
Moses, however, did not fear such consequences from the Spirit's genuine work.
We should not silence people whom Christ has acknowledged or prevent them from doing good simply because they disagree with us on some matters.
Moses longed for all God's people to become prophets and receive his Spirit.
Those seeking power should remember Moses' testimony: leadership is a burden.
It brings anxiety and responsibility to people who take their duty seriously.
For those who neglect it, the final accounting will be heavier still.
Leaders should welcome useful counsel and assistance rather than despising it.
If all God's people were enabled by Christ's Spirit to minister, there would still be enough work for everyone in calling sinners to repentance and faith, even if outward disagreements remained.

div.title: Quail are given and judgment follows (verses 31–35)
div.p: God gave Israel meat, as promised.
People are often much quicker to gather perishable food than to seek the food that lasts to eternal life.
We devote enormous energy to temporary advantages while neglecting our souls.
People ruled by fleshly desires may get exactly what they demand—even when fulfilling those desires ruins them.
Israel's feast proved costly.
God sometimes grants sinners' requests in judgment while denying his own people's desires in love.
What we crave improperly may become a source of grief and suffering if we obtain it.
Many people shorten their lives through excess.
Let us seek joys that truly satisfy, never sicken us through indulgence, and remain forever.

row.cell: God rebukes the murmuring of Aaron and Miriam.
Miriam struck with leprosy, and healed at the prayer of Moses.

div.title: Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses (verses 1–9)
div.p: Moses' patience was tested by his own family as well as by the people he led.
Miriam and Aaron objected to his marriage to a foreign woman.
But Henry considers it probable that they were really motivated by wounded pride and envy of his greater authority.
Opposition from relatives and from friends who share our faith can hurt especially deeply.
We should expect such difficulties and seek to keep Moses' gentle and humble spirit.
These trials helped prepare Moses for his calling.
God not only defended Moses but praised him.
Moses was entrusted with prophetic revelation in a way that placed him above the other prophets.
Yet the least person in the kingdom of heaven enjoys a greater privilege, and Jesus Christ is infinitely greater than Moses (Hebrews 3:1).
Miriam and Aaron should have considered whom they were insulting.
We should be cautious about speaking against God's servants.
It is presumptuous to speak contemptuously about those in positions of dignity (2 Peter 2:10).
Nothing shows God's displeasure more sadly than his presence being withdrawn.
Woe to us if he leaves!
He does not withdraw until our sins and foolishness have driven him away.

div.title: Miriam is afflicted; Moses intercedes (verses 10–16)
div.p: The cloud departed, and Miriam was struck with leprosy.
When God's presence goes, distress follows.
Bishop Hall, whom Henry quotes, observed that her offensive tongue was punished by an afflicted appearance.
Aaron, as a priest, had to judge the condition.
He could not pronounce Miriam unclean without trembling, since he knew he was equally guilty.
If speaking against Moses was so serious, what will happen to those who sin against Christ?
Aaron, who had just criticized Moses with Miriam, now had to plead with him on behalf of both.
He was forced to speak respectfully of the very person he had blamed.
People who despise God's servants may one day need their help.
Correction has a good effect when it leads to confession and repentance.
Even offenders who are disciplined and publicly humbled may be forgiven.
Moses showed that he had forgiven the personal wrong done to him.
We should imitate his mercy and the Savior's prayer, “Father, forgive them.”
Miriam had to remain outside the camp for seven days, accepting the disgrace that followed her sin.
Whenever God corrects us, we should humbly acknowledge our wrongdoing.
Israel's journey was delayed by this event.
Many things can slow our progress, but nothing hinders our journey toward heaven more seriously than sin.

row.cell: Twelve men sent to search the land of Canaan, Their instructions.

div.title: Twelve spies are sent to Canaan (verses 1–20)
div.p: This chapter begins the sad account, continued in the next chapter, of Israel turning back at the borders of Canaan.
Because of unbelief and complaining, that generation would be sentenced to wander and die in the wilderness.
According to Deuteronomy 1:22, the proposal to send scouts came from the people.
They trusted their own strategy more than God's wisdom.
This is how we harm ourselves when we trust what our senses report rather than what God has revealed.
We walk by sight rather than by faith.
Moses told the twelve men to be courageous.
Their task was difficult and required good judgment and determination.
But it was also a great responsibility requiring faithfulness.
True courage in such circumstances grows from strong faith.
Only Caleb and Joshua possessed that faith.

div.title: The spies explore the land (verses 21–25)
div.p: The scouts brought back a large cluster of grapes and other fruit.
These gave evidence of the land's goodness.
They were a sample and a promise of the harvest Israel could later enjoy in Canaan.
Likewise, the comfort we now receive through fellowship with God gives us a foretaste of the complete joy awaiting us in the heavenly Canaan.
From those present blessings, we gain some idea of what heaven will be like.

div.title: The spies give their report (verses 26–33)
div.p: It is astonishing that Israel waited forty days for the scouts' return when the people were already at the border, prepared to enter the land.
They had received every assurance that God's power and promise would bring success.
His earlier miracles should have confirmed that assurance.
Yet they distrusted both him and his word.
How much harm we bring upon ourselves through unbelief!
When the scouts returned, most of them discouraged the people.
Israel had depended upon human judgments when God's own promise was sufficient.
It was therefore just that the people's misplaced confidence brought this severe temptation upon them.
The land was as good as God had said.
But the scouts refused to believe that possessing it was as certain as he had promised.
They looked at military difficulties and despaired of receiving what the God of truth had guaranteed.
Caleb, supported only by Joshua, urged Israel to go forward.
He did not say, “Let us go conquer it,” but “Let us go possess it.”
Faith took hold of God's promise instead of relying on human power.
The difficulties in salvation become small when we exercise living, active faith in God's strength and promises.
Whatever God has truly promised is possible for those who believe.
We cannot trust merely worldly reasoning or people who profess faith while depending on sight.
Unbelief forgets God's power, magnifies dangers and fills the heart with fear.
May the Lord help us believe him and discover that his promise is certain.

row.cell: The people murmur at the account of the spies.
Joshua and Caleb labour to still the people.
The Divine threatenings, The intercession of Moses.
The murmurers forbidden to enter the promised land.
Defeat of the people, who now would invade the land.

div.title: The people refuse to trust God's promise (verses 1–4)
div.p: People who refuse to trust God continually trouble themselves.
The grief produced by worldly unbelief brings death.
Israel complained against Moses and Aaron, but in criticizing them the people were really rebuking the Lord.
They looked back at Egypt with unreasonable discontent.
Uncontrolled fear and anger can make people foolishly throw away even what they ought to treasure most: life itself.
They said they would rather die as guilty people under God's judgment than live as victorious people enjoying his favor.
Finally, they decided to return to Egypt rather than enter Canaan.
People who abandon God's counsel are choosing their own ruin.
Could Israel expect the cloud to guide them back or manna to accompany them?
Even if entering Canaan were as difficult as they feared, returning to Egypt would have been harder.
We often complain about our circumstances and wish to change them.
But there is no place or condition on earth where a determinedly dissatisfied person cannot find something to resent.
The better way to improve our situation is to cultivate a better spirit.
Turning from God leads inevitably toward disaster.

div.title: Joshua and Caleb urge the people to trust (verses 5–10)
div.p: Moses and Aaron were astonished that Israel could throw away its greatest blessings.
Joshua and Caleb assured the people that Canaan was good and worth entering.
They did not treat its conquest as an impossible problem.
If people understood how desirable the blessings of faith are, they would not shrink from the duties that come with it.
The Canaanites lived in strongly fortified towns, but their protection had departed from them.
The other scouts noticed the Canaanites' military power.
Joshua and Caleb recognized the Canaanites' wickedness and the judgment awaiting them.
No people can remain safe after provoking God to abandon them.
Though Israel lived in tents, God's presence was its defense.
With him, the most powerful enemy need not terrify us.
Sinners bring ruin on themselves through rebellion.
But people who, like Caleb and Joshua, stand faithfully for God may trust his special protection.
He will shelter them from human hostility either during this life or in heaven.

div.title: Moses intercedes after God's warning (verses 11–19)
div.p: Moses humbly prayed for Israel.
In this he pictured Jesus Christ, who prayed for those who treated him cruelly.
The pardon Moses sought was the removal of the nation's threatened punishment.
He pleaded earnestly that God's abundant mercy was consistent with forgiving them.

div.title: The unbelieving generation is excluded (verses 20–35)
div.p: The Lord answered Moses' prayer by not destroying the entire congregation immediately.
Yet refusal to believe God's promise excluded that generation from enjoying its fulfillment.
Those who despised the pleasant land would not enter it.
God would keep his promise to their children.
The people had said they would rather die in the wilderness.
Their sin became their ruin: God allowed their own words to be fulfilled, and their bodies fell in the desert.
They suffered under the heavy burden of their own wrongdoing.
The expression about God's broken promise indicated both the cause and the consequence of their loss.
The cause was their unbelief: God does not abandon people until they have first turned from him.
The consequence was their destruction.
But the children younger than twenty—whom their parents had feared would be captured—would be brought safely into Canaan.
In this way God distinguished between guilty adults and their children, judging the former without destroying the latter.
He did not utterly remove his covenant kindness.

div.title: The faithless spies die (verses 36–39)
div.p: The ten spies who had brought an evil report about Canaan died suddenly.
They had slandered the land God promised.
People provoke God severely when they misrepresent true religion or make others dislike it.
The complainers now became mourners.
Had they grieved over their sin while they were being warned, the sentence might have been prevented.
But their sorrow was chiefly over the punishment, so it did not help them.
There is a similar grief in hell, where tears cannot end the fire or relieve the suffering.

div.title: Israel attacks without God's blessing (verses 40–45)
div.p: Some Israelites now became eager to march into Canaan.
But the right time had passed.
How much better it would be if people sought heaven earnestly while the time for receiving God's grace remains, instead of waiting until it is too late!
An action that was our duty at the proper time may become sinful when done in defiance of God's later command.
People who abandon their duty cannot claim God's protection.
Israel refused to move when the Lord commanded it, then insisted on moving when he forbade it.
This is the hostility of a sinful mind against God.
Earlier the people distrusted God's power.
Now they presumed upon their own strength without him.
Their expedition therefore failed.
The judgment that their bodies would fall in the wilderness had begun.
Nothing founded upon sin can end well.
To enjoy peace with friends and success against enemies, we need the Lord's friendship and must remain in his love.
Let Israel's history warn us against dying through the same unbelief.
Let us go forward trusting God's mercy, power, promise and truth, confident that he will bring our souls to everlasting rest.

row.cell: The law of the meat-offering and the drink-offering, The stranger under the same law.
The sacrifice for the sin of ignorance.
The punishment of presumption, The sabbath-breaker stoned.
The law for fringes on garment.

div.title: Grain and drink offerings; one law for foreigners (verses 1–21)
div.p: God gave detailed instructions about the grain and drink offerings accompanying sacrifices.
The opening words were encouraging: when Israel came into the land that the Lord would give them.
This assured the people that the promised land would still be given to their descendants.
Because the offerings were considered the food of God's table, bread, oil and wine were to accompany the sacrifices of animals.
These rules fixed the appropriate proportions for each kind of offering.
They applied equally to native Israelites and foreigners living among them.
That equality anticipated the calling of the Gentiles and their acceptance into God's church.
If the Mosaic law made so little distinction between Jew and Gentile in these matters, the gospel breaks down the dividing wall even more completely and reconciles both to God.

div.title: Offerings for sins committed unknowingly (verses 22–29)
div.p: Ignorance may lessen a person's guilt in some respects, but it cannot justify people who could have learned God's will and failed to do so.
David prayed to be cleansed from his hidden faults, including sins he had not recognized.
Sins committed through ignorance can be forgiven through Christ, the great Sacrifice.
When he offered himself once for all on the cross, he prayed, “Father, forgive them; they do not know what they are doing.”
That prayer revealed part of the saving purpose of his offering.
It is also a gracious sign of God's favor toward Gentiles that the law explicitly included foreigners among those who could receive atonement for unintended sins.

div.title: Deliberate sin and the Sabbath-breaker (verses 30–36)
div.p: People sin presumptuously when they deliberately act against God's known will and glory.
Such sins are especially evil.
The deliberate offender insults the Lord and despises his word.
Presumptuous sinners behave as though they are too important, too good or too wise to accept its rule.
The account of the Sabbath-breaker is a particular example.
He gathered wood on the Sabbath to make a fire, though the people had been instructed to prepare their baking and cooking the previous day (Exodus 16:23).
His action was therefore a deliberate affront to both God's law and the One who gave it.
God is jealous for the honor of his Sabbath.
He will not overlook its contemptuous profanation, whatever people may do.
Henry sees the severe penalty under Israel's law as a warning that God's judgments are consistent with perfect justice and love.
God has a right to a day devoted to himself.
People deny that right when they listen to their pride and unbelief rather than to the Spirit of truth.
Henry then challenges Christians who turn their backs on the blessings of Sabbath worship in order to accumulate wealth or pursue sinful pleasures.
They may gain money or excitement, but they will also receive the dreadful consequences of their disobedience.
Sinful pursuits finally lead to ruin.

div.title: Tassels as reminders of God's commands (verses 37–41)
div.p: The Lord instructed Israel to put fringes or tassels on the borders of their clothes.
Their dress, like their diet, would distinguish them from surrounding nations.
They were taught not to conform to the pagan ways of those nations in other matters.
Wherever they went, they visibly acknowledged that they belonged to God and were not ashamed of his law.
The fringes were not intended mainly as decoration.
Their purpose was to stir memory and attention (2 Peter 3:1).
When temptation came, seeing them should remind an Israelite not to break God's commandments.
We should likewise use every good means to keep Scripture's truth and commands in our thoughts.
Such reminders strengthen obedience and prepare the mind to resist temptation.
We are to be holy to our God: cleansed from sin and sincerely devoted to his service.
The repeated reason for every command remains the same: he is the Lord our God.

row.cell: The rebellion of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram Korah contends for the priesthood.
The glory of the Lord appears, The intercession of Moses and Aaron.
The earth swallows up Dathan and Abiram.
The people murmur A plague sent.

div.title: Korah's rebellion against the priesthood (verses 1–11)
div.p: Pride and ambition cause much harm both within churches and in nations.
Korah's company challenged God's appointment of Aaron and his family to the priesthood.
They claimed that the whole congregation was holy and favored by God.
But Israel had repeatedly defiled itself through sin and was still living under signs of God's displeasure.
The rebels falsely accused Moses and Aaron of claiming special honor for themselves, when in fact God had called them to their offices.
Henry identifies their attitude as the spirit of people who refuse to accept the authority God has established over them.
He also reflects on the harsh treatment that faithful servants may receive after serving others.
Moses did not immediately retaliate.
He sought guidance from God, as wise people should do when considering how to answer difficult accusations.
He reminded the rebels of the privileges they already enjoyed as Levites.
They were despising gifts from God because they wanted the office he had given someone else.
One way to resist envy of those above us is to consider how many people have fewer opportunities than we do.

div.title: Dathan and Abiram refuse to obey (verses 12–15)
div.p: Moses summoned Dathan and Abiram to hear their complaints.
They refused to come.
They made thoroughly false accusations against him.
The people most deserving of honor are sometimes condemned most bitterly.
Moses was a remarkably gentle man, but he became deeply angry when God's honor was attacked through him.
He could not bear to see the people driving themselves toward ruin.
He appealed to God to bear witness to his integrity.
The rebels were ordered to appear with Aaron the following morning, when the morning incense would be offered.
Korah agreed.
Proud and ambitious people often arrange their own humiliation while imagining they are securing advancement.

div.title: God's glory appears; Moses and Aaron plead for the people (verses 16–22)
div.p: The same divine glory that had appeared when Aaron was first installed in his office (Leviticus 9:23) now appeared to confirm his calling and defeat his opponents.
Few things are more terrifying to a guilty conscience than the visible glory of God.
It is dangerous to associate closely with people engaged in serious rebellion and to join in their wrongdoing.
Although the Israelites had betrayed Moses and Aaron, the two men continued acting as faithful shepherds of the nation.
Someone else's failure to do right by us never cancels our obligation to seek that person's good.
Their earnest prayer was heard.

div.title: The earth opens beneath the rebels (verses 23–34)
div.p: The seventy elders accompanied Moses.
We should do what is right to support lawful authority when it is under unjust attack.
Anyone who wants to avoid sharing a sinner's destruction must separate from that person's evil conduct.
In response to Moses' prayer, God moved the congregation to withdraw from the rebels for safety.
The grace that leads people to separate from evil accompanies salvation.
God left the rebels to their own stubbornness and hard hearts.
Under divine instruction, Moses declared that if these men died ordinarily, he would accept being judged a fraud.
Immediately after he spoke, God opened the ground and swallowed up the rebels.
Their children also perished.
Henry admits that we cannot know all that might justify God's judgment of them, or all the mercy God might otherwise show them; but he maintains that infinite justice cannot do wrong.
The event was wholly miraculous.
God can appoint extraordinary judgments for people who persist in evil.
The earth is still burdened with human wrongdoing; Henry marvels that it does not sink beneath the weight.
The destruction of others should warn us.
If we could hear by faith the cries of those lost under judgment, we would be more diligent about escaping the same condemnation.

div.title: Fire consumes those offering unauthorized incense (verses 35–40)
div.p: Fire came from the Lord and consumed the 250 men who were offering incense.
Aaron remained alive among them.
God guards the honor of the worship he has appointed.
He will not allow people to seize offices and religious privileges he has not given them.
The sacrifice of the wicked is offensive to him.
The censers used by the rebels were set apart and then turned into a covering for the altar, so that even those objects would serve God's glory.
The covering reminded future Israelites of this judgment, warning them not to rebel in the same presumptuous way.
The rebels had brought destruction on themselves.
Likewise, those who break God's law and neglect his gospel choose the path of death.

div.title: A new complaint and Aaron's intercession (verses 41–50)
div.p: The earth had scarcely closed over the rebels when the people began complaining again.
They had ignored all the warnings.
They even called the condemned rebels God's people and accused divine justice of wrongdoing.
Their stubbornness, after both Sinai's awe-inspiring law and severe judgments, showed how necessary God's grace is to change human hearts.
Love can accomplish what fear alone cannot.
Moses and Aaron again pleaded for mercy.
They understood the seriousness of the people's rebellion.
Aaron hurried with incense and stood between the living and the dead.
He did not burn incense to purify the air.
He was pleading that God's offended justice would be satisfied and the plague stopped.
Because he cared about every Israelite's life, he went as quickly as possible.
We are called to repay evil with good.
Aaron here pictured Christ.
The world suffers from the deadly infection of sin.
Only Jesus Christ's cross and intercession can remove it.
He entered the defiled and dying camp of humanity.
He stood between the Judge and those condemned by sin.
Through his blood we receive redemption and forgiveness.
If we admire Aaron's willingness, how much more should we praise the Savior's love in taking our place and purchasing us with his life!
God showed his love while we were still sinners: Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).

row.cell: Twelve rods laid up before the Lord.
Aaron's rod buds, and is kept for a memorial.

div.title: The twelve staffs are placed before the Lord (verses 1–7)
div.p: God had already performed several miracles to punish Israel's sin.
Now, in his grace, he performed another miracle to prevent further sin.
Twelve staffs were brought before the Lord.
Henry considers it likely that these were old, dry staffs carried by the tribal leaders as signs of their authority.
The wood had no living sap left.
The people were told that the staff belonging to the leader whom God had chosen for the priesthood would sprout and blossom.
Moses did not say that the matter had been settled sufficiently already.
Nor did he try to decide the outcome himself.
He left the decision before the Lord.

div.title: Aaron's staff blossoms (verses 8–13)
div.p: The other staffs remained unchanged.
Aaron's dry staff became like a living branch.
It showed buds, blossoms and fruit at the same time.
This was unmistakably miraculous.
God thus confirmed that Aaron had received his special blessing and appointment.
Fruitfulness is among the best signs of a divine calling.
What God plants will flourish.
The staff was then preserved to stop the people's complaining before they brought death upon themselves.
God's work in providence and the reminders of what he has done are meant to turn us away from sin.
Christ himself came to take away sin.
Scripture describes him as a shoot growing from the root of Jesse.
By ordinary human expectations, there seemed little reason to think he would flourish.
But like the dead staff that came to life, he rose to confound his enemies.
The Israelites cried out in fear that they were all about to die.
Yet they were still resisting God's judgments rather than accepting responsibility for their own pride and stubbornness.
It is wicked to complain against God during suffering in a way that brings still more sin.
If we perish through our rebellion, the guilt is ours.
God's judgment will prevail.
Even the most stubborn opponents will eventually be forced to recognize their folly.
How great are the mercies offered to us through a clearer and better covenant, founded on better promises!

row.cell: The charge of the priests and Levites.

div.title: The responsibilities of priests and Levites (verses 1–7)
div.p: The Israelites complained that approaching God was difficult and dangerous.
God therefore reminded them that the priests were appointed to come near to him on their behalf.
Aaron had no reason to be proud of his promotion.
His office carried heavy responsibilities and serious risks.
People entrusted with great authority or important work should remain humble and reverent toward God.
The greater the trust placed in us, the more danger there is that we might betray it.
This is one reason not to envy another person's honors or seek a high position merely for status.

div.title: God's provision for the priests (verses 8–19)
div.p: All believers are spiritual priests, and God has promised to care for them.
Faithfulness to him carries promises for this life as well as the next.
From the provision made for Israel's priests, the apostle teaches that Christian congregations should support their ministers.
Poor or inadequate support can contribute to ministers' falling into disgraceful behavior.
Priests were to devote themselves fully to their sacred work.
They were not to be constantly distracted or disturbed by worries about earning a living through ordinary business.
Their lives should also demonstrate faith in God's providence and in the worship he had appointed.
The finest portions of firstfruits were to be offered to the Lord.
Those who try to save for themselves by giving God only unwanted leftovers deceive themselves.
God is not mocked.

div.title: God's provision for the Levites (verses 20–32)
div.p: Just as Israel was distinct from other nations, the Levites were distinct from the other tribes.
People who have God himself as their permanent inheritance and portion should regard the world's possessions with a holy freedom from attachment.
The Levites also had to give God his due from their tithes, just as the other Israelites gave from their harvests.
Henry draws two lessons from verse 31 about enjoying earthly possessions without guilt.
First, what we own must have been obtained honestly and through rightful work.
Food is best enjoyed when earned through labor.
Anyone unwilling to work should not expect to eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10).
Second, God must receive the portion due to him.
We can enjoy our possessions properly when we have honored the Lord through them.
Giving the best to him prevents our possessions from becoming occasions of sin.
We should also give generously to those in need, so that what remains is enjoyed gratefully and with a clear conscience.

div.title: The ashes of the red heifer (verses 1–10)
div.p: The heifer was to be burned completely.
Henry sees this as a picture of Jesus Christ enduring great suffering in body and soul when he offered himself as a sacrifice.
By bearing God's just anger against human sin, Christ made atonement.
The ashes were preserved for ceremonial purification.
They could not themselves wash away moral guilt.
But they pointed toward the true cleansing of sin accomplished by our Lord's death.
The benefits of Christ's blood are set before us through God's word and the sacraments.
They are like a continuing fountain of saving merit to which believers may come by faith, again and again, for the cleansing of their consciences.

div.title: Cleansing people made unclean through death (verses 11–22)
div.p: Why did touching a dead body produce ceremonial uncleanness?
Because death is the wages of sin.
Sin brought death into the world, and death continues to reign through sin's power.
The Mosaic law could not conquer death or abolish it.
But the gospel reveals life and immortality and opens the way to a better hope.
The ashes of the heifer represented Christ's saving merit.
The flowing water represented the power and grace of the Holy Spirit, whom Scripture compares to rivers of living water.
The Spirit applies Christ's righteousness to us, bringing genuine cleansing.
People who expect to benefit from Christ's righteousness while refusing the Spirit's sanctifying influence are deceiving themselves.
The ashes did not accomplish their purpose without water.
Likewise, Christ's saving work is not to be separated from the Spirit's transforming work.
Without their connection to Christ's sacrifice, these regulations would be difficult to understand.
Reading them alongside the New Testament makes their spiritual meaning clear.
They reveal the fallen human condition and the defiling power of sin.
They also warn us to keep away from evil influences and corrupting companionship.

row.cell: The people come to Zin, They murmur for water, Moses directed to smite the rock, The infirmity of Moses and Aaron.
The Israelites are refused a passage through Edom.
Aaron reigns the priest's office to Eleazar, and dies in mount Hor.

div.title: Israel complains again; Moses and Aaron fail (verses 1–13)
div.p: After thirty-eight weary years in the wilderness, Israel began moving toward Canaan once more.
There was no water for the congregation.
We live in a world full of needs.
Wherever we go, we should expect something to disturb our comfort.
Having abundant water is a great mercy. If we lacked it, we would value it more.
The people complained against Moses and Aaron.
They spoke the same unreasonable and bitter words their parents had spoken.
Their conduct was especially blameworthy because their families had suffered for years as a result of the earlier generation's complaining and unbelief.
Yet they repeated the very same sins.
God directed Moses to bring water from a rock again.
The Lord was no less able to supply his people than before.
But Moses and Aaron sinned in the way they handled the miracle.
They spoke as though the power belonged partly to themselves.
“Must we bring you water?”
That took some of the glory that belonged to God alone.
They were commanded to speak to the rock.
Instead, Moses struck it.
In this way they failed to honor the Lord as holy and failed to give him the complete glory he deserved.
Provoked by the people, Moses also spoke rashly.
Henry sees in this the continuing sinful desire of people to take over the work of the one appointed Mediator.
We try to become our own wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption.
But the gospel condemns every attempt to live independently of the Savior.

div.title: Edom refuses Israel passage (verses 14–21)
div.p: The shortest route to Canaan passed through Edom.
Moses sent messengers asking permission to travel through the country.
The Edomites refused.
They feared that Israel's large army might cause them harm.
Such fears might have been understandable if Israel were not under the discipline of the righteous God himself.
But Edom's hostility also continued the hatred that Esau had shown Jacob because of the blessing.
Now the old resentment reappeared as Jacob's descendants approached their inheritance.
We should not be surprised when unreasonable people reject fair requests or when people favored by God are treated with contempt.

div.title: Aaron dies and Eleazar becomes priest (verses 22–29)
div.p: God told Aaron to prepare for death.
The command expressed both displeasure and mercy.
There was displeasure because Aaron could not enter Canaan after his failure at the waters of Meribah.
But there was mercy because he was allowed to die peacefully, with honor, as someone received into the care of divine grace.
His exclusion from Canaan also had spiritual meaning.
It showed that the Levitical priesthood could not make anything perfect.
A better hope had to be introduced.
Aaron submitted to the appointed manner and time of his death.
As far as the record shows, he did so as peacefully as someone preparing to sleep.
He could see his beloved son Eleazar succeed him.
The priesthood would continue.
Even more importantly, that succession pointed toward the eternal priesthood of Christ.
A good person should want to remain useful for as long as God wills.
Why should we desire to stay in this world beyond the time when we can serve the Lord and our generation?

row.cell: The people murmuring, are plagued with fiery serpents, They repenting, are healed through the brazen serpent.
Sihon and Og overcome, Their land possessed.

div.title: Israel defeats the people of Arad (verses 1–3)
div.p: Before Israel began traveling around Edom, the Canaanite king of Arad attacked the Israelites in the wilderness and captured some of them.
The incident was meant to lead the people to trust the Lord more completely.

div.title: The bronze serpent and the healing of Israel (verses 4–9)
div.p: Israel became exhausted by the long journey around Edom.
The people complained bitterly about what God had already done and distrusted what he might do next.
If manna could not satisfy them, what would?
We must not let other people's contempt for God's word make us value it less.
That word is the real Bread of Life.
It nourishes to eternal life everyone who receives it by faith, no matter who dismisses it as worthless.
God justly judged the people for their complaints by sending venomous serpents into the camp.
Many were bitten and died.
They might never have admitted their sin without first suffering from its consequences.
But suffering led them toward repentance.
God then provided a remarkable cure.
Henry observes that Jewish interpreters themselves explain that merely seeing the bronze serpent did not heal people.
Rather, by looking up at it, the sufferers were looking toward God, the One who healed them.
The act was filled with gospel meaning.
Jesus himself said that just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that those who believe in him will not perish (John 3:14–15).
Our sickness is like theirs: sin bites and poisons the soul.
Their cure pictured ours.
They looked and lived.
We believe in Jesus and do not perish.
Faith turns our eyes toward him (Hebrews 12:2).
Anyone who looked was healed, however severe the bite, weak the eyesight or distant the sufferer.
God can save us through means that human reasoning would never invent.
How different people would live if they felt the poison of the ancient serpent's temptation as clearly as Israel felt those bites!
If we truly recognized the eternal danger of sin, we would not close our eyes to Christ or turn away from his gospel.
We would count everything else as loss compared with a crucified Savior.
We would call on him without delay.
Nor would we abuse the generosity of Christ's salvation once we understood the price he paid to provide it.

div.title: Israel's journeys and the well of water (verses 10–20)
div.p: These verses describe Israel's movements until the people reached the plains of Moab, from which they would later cross the Jordan into Canaan.
The end of their journey was near.
It would be good for us, as we draw nearer to heaven, to grow more active and fruitful in the Lord's work.
The record also recalls God's extraordinary victories for Israel, including events around the River Arnon, Waheb in Suphah and neighboring places.
At every stage—and indeed every step—of life, we should remember what God has done for us.
We should recall distinctly the help he gave at particular times and places.
The Lord provided water, and Israel received it with joy and thanksgiving.
Their gratitude made the gift sweeter.
When we reach heaven, we will come to the fountain of living water.
Even now we should draw joy from the wells of salvation (Isaiah 12:3).
The bronze serpent pictured Christ lifted up to heal us.
The well pictured the Holy Spirit poured out to comfort us, from whom flow rivers of living water (John 7:38–39).
If that water is flowing within our souls, we should enjoy its comfort and give God all the praise.
God promised water, but the Israelites still had to open the ground to receive it.
We should expect his gifts while using the lawful means he has placed within our reach, remembering that all real power belongs to him.

div.title: Sihon and Og are defeated (verses 21–35)
div.p: Sihon led his forces outside his own borders against Israel without provocation.
In doing so, he brought about his own defeat.
Enemies of God's church often destroy themselves through the plans they consider most clever.
Og, king of Bashan, could have learned from Sihon's defeat and sought peace.
Instead he made war and suffered the same destruction.
Wicked people make enormous efforts to protect themselves and their possessions from God's judgment.
But when judgment comes, their precautions cannot save them.
God gave Israel victories while Moses was still alive.
Moses could witness the beginning of the great conquest even though he would not live to see it completed.
These early victories were small compared with what lay ahead, but they promised greater things.
Christians must prepare for new struggles and new enemies.
We should make no compromise with the powers of darkness, expecting no permanent ceasefire with them.
Trusting God and obeying his commands, we will overcome every spiritual enemy.

row.cell: Balak's fear of Israel, He sends for Balaam.
The opposition to Balaam by the way.

div.title: Balak asks Balaam to curse Israel (verses 1–14)
div.p: The king of Moab formed a plan to have Israel cursed.
He wanted God, who had been fighting for Israel, to turn against the people.
He mistakenly imagined that a prophet's curse against Israel—and a blessing upon his own army—would enable him to defeat them.
Balaam had a remarkable reputation, so Balak sent far away to hire him.
Henry says we do not know whether God had spoken to Balaam or through him before these events.
It seems possible, but afterward God certainly did speak through him.
Yet Scripture gives convincing evidence that Balaam lived and died as a wicked person and an enemy of God and his people.
A curse uttered against someone cannot harm that person without just cause.
Balak's messengers brought payment meant to tempt Balaam into wrongdoing.
But God restrained Balaam and forbade him to curse Israel.
Balaam was not ignorant of Israel's situation.
He should have answered immediately that he could never curse a people whom God had blessed.
Instead he delayed overnight to consider the proposal.
When we bargain with temptation, we place ourselves in danger.
Balaam did not faithfully communicate the full force of God's command to the messengers.
People who soften divine prohibitions are particularly vulnerable to temptation, treating disobedience as though it merely required additional permission.
The messengers also misrepresented Balaam's reply when reporting it to Balak.
Flattering advisers can keep rulers and other people from recognizing their own folly.

div.title: A second delegation persuades Balaam (verses 15–21)
div.p: Balak sent a second group of messengers.
How good it would be if we persevered so firmly in doing right even after disappointments!
Balak appealed both to Balaam's greed and to his pride and ambition.
We should pray continually for God to mortify such desires within us.
Sinners spare neither time, cost nor humiliation when pursuing luxury or malice.
Should believers be less willing to do what is good?
Balaam knew that he was obligated to obey God.
His public words sounded excellent.
But speaking religiously proves nothing about the actual condition of the heart.
Many call God their Lord without truly belonging to him.
Balaam seemed to reject the offer, but he never expressed genuine hatred for the proposed sin.
He wanted the reward and hoped to receive God's permission to do what was already forbidden.
A heart is ruled by corruption when it asks God for permission to sin.
God left Balaam to pursue his own desires.
Just as God sometimes denies his children's requests in love, he may grant sinful desires in judgment.

div.title: The angel opposes Balaam on the road (verses 22–35)
div.p: God sometimes permits people to proceed in sin.
We must never interpret that permission as approval.
Holy angels oppose wrongdoing and may prevent more of it than we realize.
The angel was Balaam's adversary only because Balaam was pursuing the wrong road.
People who block our progress toward sin are often our truest friends.
God exposed his displeasure to Balaam through the donkey.
A person determined to do evil may force a way forward despite every warning placed in the path by Providence.
The Lord made the animal speak.
This was a real miracle of God's power.
The One who made humans able to speak could give a donkey a human voice whenever he chose.
The donkey protested Balaam's cruelty.
God's righteousness protects even the weakest creatures from abuse; he can provide them with a voice or defend them himself.
At last Balaam's eyes were opened.
God has many ways of humbling a stubborn heart.
When our spiritual eyes are opened, we recognize how dangerous our sinful choices are and how much mercy there was in being stopped.
Balaam said, “I have sinned.”
Yet he did not seem to understand or admit the corruption of his own heart.
He was prepared to turn back only because he could not continue.
Some people abandon their sins only because their sins can no longer be carried out.
The angel made clear that Balaam would not merely fail to curse Israel: he would be compelled to bless the people.
That would bring God greater honor, and Balaam greater shame, than if he had returned home.

div.title: Balaam meets Balak (verses 36–41)
div.p: Balak complained that Balaam had not come sooner.
Balaam warned the king that he could not say whatever he wanted.
He sounded annoyed.
