Yet he remained just as eager to please Balak as he had previously claimed to be eager to please God.
We desperately need to pray, “Our Father in heaven, do not lead us into temptation.”
We should watch over our own hearts.
Balaam shows how much knowledge a person may possess about God while still remaining without the saving grace of God.

row.cell: Balak's sacrifice, Balaam pronounces a blessing instead of a curse.
Balak's disappointment, and second sacrifice, Balaam again blesses Israel.

div.title: Balaam blesses instead of cursing (verses 1–10)
div.p: With the camp of Israel clearly visible, Balaam ordered seven altars to be built, with a bull and a ram offered upon each.
What foolish superstition it is to imagine that human beings can command God to do what they want!
Through God's controlling power and love for Israel, the curse Balaam intended was turned into a blessing.
God intended to accomplish his own glory through Balaam, and therefore met him.
If the Lord could place words in the mouth of a man who was hostile to both God and Israel, he can certainly provide words for people who sincerely want to glorify him and build up his people.
The God who made Balaam's donkey speak now made the wicked prophet say what his own heart did not want to say.
The miracle was as great in one instance as in the other.
Balaam declared that Israel was safe.
He admitted that he could do only what God allowed.
He declared Israel blessed for being distinct from the nations, numerous enough to have dignity and strength, and secure in its future.
He also wished to enjoy the end of a righteous person's life.
Death comes to everyone, including the righteous.
We do well to consider our own deaths.
The righteous are blessed not only while living but also when dying.
Their death can therefore be more desirable than life itself.
But many people want the death of a righteous person without being willing to live a righteous life.
They want to be saints in heaven but not on earth.
Balaam expressed a wish, not a prayer rooted in genuine commitment.
He wanted the good end without caring about the way to reach it.
Others likewise quiet their consciences with promises of future change or false hopes, while neglecting the one path by which sinners can be justified before God.

div.title: Balaam blesses Israel again (verses 11–30)
div.p: Balak became angry with Balaam.
A wicked prophet was forced to acknowledge God's governing power, frustrating a wicked king.
For a second time, an intended curse became a blessing—this time even stronger and more extensive than before.
Human beings change their minds and break their promises.
God does not change his mind or withdraw his promises.
When Scripture speaks of God repenting, Henry explains that this means a change in the way he deals with people, not a change within God's own mind.
There was sin among Jacob's descendants, and the Lord saw it.
Yet it was not the kind of settled rebellion for which he was now abandoning them to destruction.
When people trust God's mercy, accept his salvation, refuse to indulge cherished sinful desires, and seek to honor him, they may be assured of acceptance in Christ and the forgiveness of their sins.
Think of the wonders of Providence and grace: redeeming love, forgiving mercy and the Spirit making people new!
Balak could no longer expect to destroy Israel.
Balaam now warned that Balak had more reason to fear destruction by Israel.
Because Balaam would not pronounce the curse Balak wanted, the king told him to say nothing.
Yet God's purposes prevail over every human scheme.
Balak and Balaam resolved to make another attempt, despite possessing no divine promise of success.
We, by contrast, have God's sure promises.
Let us persevere earnestly in prayer (Luke 18:1).

row.cell: Balaam, leaving divinations, prophesies the happiness of Israel.

div.title: Balaam foretells Israel's happiness (verses 1–9)
div.p: Balaam was no longer expressing his own wishes.
He spoke words given by the Spirit who came upon him.
It is possible for someone's eyes to be opened while the heart remains closed.
People may receive spiritual knowledge without becoming holy.
Knowledge that only increases pride can serve to illuminate a person's road toward destruction.
The blessing resembled the earlier ones.
Balaam admired the beauty of Israel, whose righteous people were more excellent than their neighbors.
He spoke of Israel's fruitfulness and growth, dignity and advancement, power and victories.
He recalled the mighty things God had already done for the people.
He spoke of their courage and security.
The righteous can be as bold as lions without being aggressive toward others, because they rest safely in God's protection.
He also declared that the way other people treated Israel would matter to God himself.
The Lord regarded good or evil done to his people as good or evil done to him.

div.title: Balak sends Balaam away in anger (verses 10–14)
div.p: Balak's plan to bring a curse upon Israel had failed.
He became enraged at Balaam and expressed his frustration openly.
Balaam could answer that God had prevented him from speaking the curses he wanted to speak, and had compelled him to give blessings he did not want to give.

div.title: Balaam's final prophecies (verses 15–25)
div.p: Under the Spirit's prophetic power, Balaam announced Israel's future prosperity and far-reaching rule.
He boasted of having open eyes.
The prophets of earlier times were sometimes called seers.
Balaam had heard God's words.
But a person can hear the words of God without truly listening to God.
He claimed knowledge of the Most High.
Yet someone may possess extensive theological knowledge while remaining entirely without divine grace.
Balaam called God the Most High and the Almighty.
He seemed outwardly reverent, but lacked true love, fear and faith.
A person can advance very far in religious profession while never entering salvation.
Balaam's vision pointed to the great King who would be Israel's glory.
David partly fulfilled the pattern.
But the prophecy chiefly pointed to Jesus Christ, the promised Messiah.
Balaam would see Christ, but not in the way Job had seen his own Redeemer by faith.
He would see him from far away, without receiving him as his own.
When Christ returns in the clouds, everyone will see him.
Yet many will see him from a distance, as the rich man in torment saw Abraham.
The promised ruler would arise from Jacob and Israel as a Star and a Scepter.
The star spoke of his splendor and glory.
The scepter spoke of his power and royal authority.
Christ would reign not only over Israel but over the whole world.
Everyone will either willingly submit to his gracious royal rule or fall under his judgment.
Balaam also foretold what would happen to the Amalekites and Kenites, whose lands were nearby.
A nest high among the rocks cannot give permanent protection against God's purposes.
Henry understands the later prophecies to reach as far as the Greeks and Romans, showing that the rise and fall of kingdoms belongs to the Lord.
These upheavals would bring widespread destruction, leaving some survivors only as people snatched from a fire.
May God prepare us for the worst times!
Henry goes further in his confessional interpretation.

He understands Balaam as cursing Amalek as an early enemy of the church and Rome as its last enemy, and applies the latter not only to pagan Rome but also to papal Rome, which he associates with Antichrist and antichristian powers.
This is Henry's historical Protestant polemic and is preserved as his interpretation, not adopted as an independent modern editorial judgment.
What do we have that Balaam lacked?
Skill in public speaking, eloquent preaching or prayer, religious knowledge and even remarkable gifts cannot save anyone by themselves.
Balaam possessed such gifts, yet loved the rewards of wrongdoing and died an enemy of God.
Simple trust in the Redeemer's atoning blood and sanctifying grace, willing submission to God's will, and steady efforts to honor God and help his people may appear less impressive.
But those qualities truly accompany salvation.
No proud hypocrite possesses them, while even the weakest believer has something of them and prays daily for more.

row.cell: The Israelites enticed by the daughters of Moab and Midian.
Phinehas puts Zimri and Cozbi to death.

div.title: Israel is drawn into sin (verses 1–5)
div.p: The friendship of wicked people can be more dangerous than their open hostility.
Israel could not be overcome by enemies unless the people first yielded to the sinful desires within their own hearts.
No magical curse could defeat them in the way that worldly ambition, pleasure and temptation could.
The women of Moab and Midian enticed Israel into wrongdoing.
Those who draw others into sin may be our worst enemies, because nothing can harm us more seriously.
Israel's own sin accomplished what all Balaam's attempted curses had failed to do.
It brought God's judgment against the people.
Henry understands the outbreak of disease as a righteous consequence of serious prevailing sins.
Those who lead other people into such wrongdoing were to be publicly held accountable.

div.title: Phinehas acts against Zimri and Cozbi (verses 6–15)
div.p: Phinehas acted with courage, zeal and faith when he put Zimri and Cozbi to death in this historical judgment.
But Henry adds a decisive limitation.

p.hi: This action must never be treated as a precedent for private revenge, religious persecution or unauthorized public punishment.

div.p: The exceptional action recorded in Israel's history gives no license to carry out violence against others today.

div.title: The judgment against Midian (verses 16–18)
div.p: The account does not say that any Midianites died from the plague that struck Israel.
God instead judged them through the sword of an enemy, not through the corrective rod used against his own children.
We must oppose whatever draws us toward sin (Matthew 5:29–30).
Anything that tempts us to wrongdoing should become painful and unwelcome to us, like a thorn in the flesh.
Those who follow Satan's pattern by cleverly enticing others into sin will face especially serious judgment.

row.cell: Numbering of Israel in the plains of Moab.
None remaining of the first numbering.

div.title: The new census in Moab (verses 1–51)
div.p: Moses did not number Israel whenever he wished.
He did so only when the Lord commanded him.
This record lists not only Israel's tribes but also the families within them.
The total number of people was almost the same as at the earlier census at Mount Sinai.
Scripture specifically mentions the sons of Korah, who did not die as the children of Dathan and Abiram did.
They seem not to have joined even their own father in rebellion.
If we refuse to participate in other people's sins, we will not share the judgment brought upon them.

div.title: The division of Canaan (verses 52–56)
div.p: The inheritance was to be divided justly.
Larger tribes were to receive larger portions; smaller tribes, smaller portions.
Although the ruler's judgment played a part, the final outcome would be settled through God's providence.
The people should therefore accept his decision.

div.title: The Levites are counted separately (verses 57–62)
div.p: Levi was the tribe set apart for God.
It was therefore counted separately from the others.
The Levites were not included in the judgment that prevented the earlier generation from entering Canaan, with the exceptions of Caleb and Joshua.

div.title: The earlier generation has passed away (verses 63–65)
div.p: The judgment pronounced on the complaining generation had now been fulfilled (Numbers 14:29).
Not one of the people counted in the first census remained in the new census—except Caleb and Joshua.
This showed God's righteousness and the certainty of his warnings.
It also demonstrated his faithfulness in keeping the particular promises he had made to those two men.
Death brings enormous changes to families and nations.
Yet God's perfect wisdom, justice and truth govern every such change.
These truths should make us think seriously about the evil of sin, which brought death and so much destruction into the world.
Let us renew our repentance, seek forgiveness and value Christ's salvation.
Let us remember how frail we are, prepare for death and use the days given to us in serving our generation according to God's will.

row.cell: The daughters of Zelophehad apply for an inheritance, The law of inheritances.

div.title: The daughters of Zelophehad seek an inheritance (verses 1–11)
div.p: Zelophehad's five daughters were concerned about their inheritance.
Their father had died, and they had no brothers to inherit land on behalf of the family.
They trusted that God would keep his promise to give Canaan to Israel.
They wanted their own family to share in that promised inheritance.
They made their request modestly and honestly, without hidden resentment or complaining.
Henry sees three praiseworthy qualities in their conduct.
First, faith: they firmly believed God's power and promise concerning Canaan.
Second, earnest desire: they wanted both a place and a family name in the promised country, which pictured heaven.
Third, respect for their father: they treasured his memory after his death.
Their father had not been guilty of the particular rebellion that would exclude his children from a claim.
It comforts dying parents when, although they may have suffered because of their own sins, they do not know of any wrongdoing that will bring judgment upon their children.
God himself decided the matter.
His care extends beyond nations to individual households.
He governs their circumstances according to his wisdom.
The daughters' request was granted.
Those who seek an inheritance in the land of promise will obtain what they seek, with other blessings added.

div.title: Moses is warned that he will die (verses 12–14)
div.p: Moses had to die.
But God granted him the comfort of seeing the land he had promised Israel.
That sight of Canaan pointed toward Moses' believing expectation of a better, heavenly country.
Death would not finally cut him off.
It would bring him into the rest already enjoyed by the faithful patriarchs.
If we have lived as they lived and hope to reach the same peaceful end, we need not fear the passage through the valley of death.

div.title: Joshua is appointed Moses' successor (verses 15–23)
div.p: Envious people dislike those who succeed them.
Moses was not like that.
We should pray and work for the next generation, so that faith may continue and flourish even after we are buried.
God appointed Joshua to succeed Moses.
Joshua had shown courage in the battle against Amalek, humility while assisting Moses, and faith and honesty when he opposed the unbelieving report of the spies.
God chose a man in whom his Spirit dwelt.
Joshua had the grace of the Spirit.
He feared God, hated greed and acted from principle.
He possessed the judgment and courage needed to lead.
He also had the Spirit's prophetic gift.
No one is fully qualified for service in Christ's church by human abilities alone.
The grace and gifts of the Holy Spirit are indispensable.
Joshua's succession also reminds us that the law was given through Moses.
Because of sin, the law cannot bring us into the heavenly inheritance.
Grace and truth come through Jesus Christ, who brings salvation to everyone who believes.

row.cell: The offering on the sabbath and new moons.
Offerings at the passover, and on the day of first-fruits.

div.title: The daily offerings (verses 1–8)
div.p: God renewed the instructions concerning sacrifices.
Israel was entering a new generation, and the people would need to remain at peace with him while fighting their enemies.
The daily offering was called a continual burnt offering.
Christians are told to pray continually.
At the very least, we should offer solemn prayer and praise every morning and evening.
A particular instruction here is that the drink offering should use strong wine.
Henry understands this as a reminder to give God the best we possess.
The wine was also a figure of Christ's blood, remembered in the church through the wine of the Lord's Supper.
It also pictured the blood of martyrs, whose lives were poured out like a drink offering in the service of others' faith (Philippians 2:17).

div.title: The Sabbath and new moon offerings (verses 9–15)
div.p: Two additional lambs were to be offered each Sabbath, beyond the two offered daily.
Henry applies this to Christians by urging greater devotion on the Sabbath.
The purpose of Sabbath rest is to leave us freer for the holy work that should fill that day.
The monthly offerings showed gratitude for the renewal of God's earthly blessings.
Whenever Providence gives us a reason for joy, we should remember Christ's great sacrifice as the true foundation of all our spiritual happiness.
The New Moon celebrations also foreshadowed gospel worship (Isaiah 66:23).
Just as the moon receives light from the sun and is renewed through its influence, so the church receives light from Jesus Christ, the Sun of Righteousness.
Through him the church is continually renewed, especially under the gospel.

div.title: Passover and firstfruits offerings (verses 16–31)
div.p: These repeated offerings remind us of the lasting effectiveness of Christ's sacrifice and of our continuing need to rely upon it.
Busy responsibilities, threatening circumstances or times of prosperity should never make us neglect prayer and worship.
They should give us even greater reason to seek the Lord's help and return thanks.
Our religious duties must be accompanied by repentance, faith in Jesus Christ and love toward him.
They should result in genuine holiness in our conduct toward others.
Otherwise God rejects even impressive public worship and lengthy devotion.
Christ is able to meet every need of every day, week, month and year, in every act of worship and every circumstance.

row.cell: The offering at the feats of trumpets, and on the day of atonement.
Offerings at the feast of tabernacles.

div.title: Offerings for the trumpet feast and the Day of Atonement (verses 1–11)
div.p: More sacred celebrations were held in Israel's seventh month than in any other month. The harvest was over, and the time to sow new seed had not yet come.
Whenever our urgent earthly duties become less demanding, we should devote more time to serving God directly.
The blowing of trumpets had been commanded previously. This chapter gives the sacrifices that were to accompany it.
Those who want to understand God's mind through Scripture should compare its different passages carefully.
Later revelations of divine truth explain matters that were obscure in earlier passages and supply what had not yet been disclosed.
In this way God's servants are equipped and brought toward maturity.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): Leviticus 22:24.
Corrected printed citation (original preserved in source audit): Lev.23.24.

div.title: Offerings during the Feast of Tabernacles (verses 12–40)
div.p: The Feast of Tabernacles came soon after the Day of Atonement.
On the Day of Atonement, the people were to humble themselves over sin; during the following festival, they were to rejoice before the Lord.
Their joyful days were also days of sacrifice and worship.
Cheerfulness is a blessing when it encourages rather than distracts us from serving God.
The people offered sacrifices throughout their stay in temporary shelters.
We, too, live for a time in the temporary shelter of earthly life. Maintaining communion with God continually is both our duty and our benefit.
Different sacrifices were appointed for each of the seven days.
But every day included a sin offering, as in the other feasts.
Our offerings of praise cannot be accepted unless we depend upon Christ's great sacrifice, in which he became the Sin Offering for us.
Nor should special seasons of worship replace ordinary, regular devotion.
All these ceremonies remind us how continually we need forgiveness.
Our earthly lives must be lived by faith in the Son of God until we go to be with him, see his glory and praise his mercy.
He loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood.
To him be honor and glory forever. Amen.

row.cell: The cases wherein vows might be released.

div.title: The obligation to fulfill a lawful vow (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: No human being can become obligated by a personal promise to do something that God's command already forbids.
A vow cannot make wrongdoing lawful.
In other matters, the rule is straightforward: we must not break our word.
We may change our minds later, but that does not release us from a valid promise.

div.title: Cases in which a vow could be canceled (verses 3–16)
div.p: The law describes two circumstances in which another member of the household could confirm or cancel a vow.
The first concerns a daughter living in her father's home. When the father learns of her vow, he may allow it to stand or cancel it.
The second concerns a wife.
If the husband approves the vow, even merely by remaining silent, the vow stands.
If he objects, the marriage obligation takes precedence under the household order established by this law, and the vow is canceled.

Henry understands this provision in terms of the authority of husbands and fathers within the family. In his explanation, a wife is to be subject to her husband as to the Lord, and a man is to govern his household.
Rather than allowing a religious vow to break the family bonds and authority he believes God appointed, Henry argues that divine law releases the person from that vow.
He concludes that God's ordinances are intended to preserve the welfare of families and societies, so that the families of the earth may enjoy blessing.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections
The war with Midian (verses 1–6)
div.p: People who carry out private revenge without a commission from God must one day answer to him.
The same is true of those who make war and devastate kingdoms because of ambition, greed or personal resentment.
But Henry distinguishes such unjust violence from an extraordinary judgment expressly authorized by God.
Instead of an earthquake, epidemic or famine, God may appoint people to carry out a sentence against a nation.
Henry maintains that ancient Israel could demonstrate such a divine commission in this case, whereas no one today can claim one like it.
Israel's wars of judgment were commanded directly by God and were accompanied by miraculous victories.
Henry understands these judgments as punishment of nations whose sin had reached its full measure. He argues that objections arise from underestimating the evil of sin, which God hates.
This is his explanation of the historical account—not permission for private vengeance or contemporary religious warfare.

div.title: Balaam dies with Midian (verses 7–12)
div.p: Israel killed Midian's kings and Balaam.
God's providence had brought Balaam to the place where the judgment fell upon him.
If he had sincerely believed the words he had spoken about Israel's happiness, he would not have continued to associate with its enemies.
The wicked schemes by which Midian tempted Israel were Balaam's own projects.
It was just, Henry says, that he perish with those who had carried them out (Hosea 4:5).
The Israelites took women and children captive, burned the towns and strongholds, and returned to camp.

div.title: Those held responsible for leading Israel into sin (verses 13–18)
div.p: The ordinary sword of war should spare women and children.

But Henry distinguishes this from what he considers the execution of a divine judicial sentence, which must distinguish between the guilty and the innocent rather than merely between adults and children.
He says that in this particular judgment the Midianite women who had led Israel into sin bore the greatest guilt.
The female children were spared and would be raised among the Israelites, where they would not lead them into idolatry.
The account illustrates the hateful nature of sin and the grave responsibility involved in drawing others into it.
Henry applies it to the Christian's struggle: we should avoid opportunities for evil and refuse to spare our own sinful desires.

He also distinguishes the ancient custom of keeping war captives as slaves from the intention to use them for sexual immorality. This reflects his description of a historical practice, not a new endorsement of slavery.
He observes that in national disasters brought by war, disease or famine, children can suffer as a result of their parents' wrongdoing.
Yet he adds that children who die before committing actual sin are provided for by God's mercy in Christ with respect to their eternal happiness.

div.title: Purification after battle (verses 19–24)
div.p: Even though the war had been commanded by God and the fighters had committed no moral fault in obeying that command, they were required to undergo ceremonial purification.
They remained outside the camp for seven days.
This kept a strong sense of revulsion toward bloodshed alive in their minds.
The captured goods were also purified because they had previously been used by the Midianites.

div.title: The distribution of the spoils (verses 25–47)
div.p: Whatever we possess, the Lord has a rightful claim upon a portion of it.
The people's share was assessed at one part in fifty, while the soldiers' share was assessed at one part in five hundred.
Henry draws a practical lesson from that difference.
People with fewer opportunities to honor God through direct personal service should be especially ready to give from their possessions.

div.title: The officers' thanksgiving offerings (verses 48–54)
div.p: Israel's victory was remarkable: a small force overcame a much larger people.
Still more remarkable, no Israelite soldier was killed or missing.
The officers brought the gold captured in battle as an offering to the Lord.
In doing so, they acknowledged that even while serving God, they had no claim to a reward based on personal merit.
They needed forgiveness for anything sinful that had occurred.
They also wanted to express gratitude that their lives had been preserved, although they might justly have been taken away.

row.cell: The tribes of Reuben and Gad request an inheritance on the east of Jordan.
Moses reproves the Reubenites and Gadites.
They explain their views, Moses consents.
They take possession of the land to the east of Jordan.

div.title: Reuben and Gad ask for land east of the Jordan (verses 1–5)
div.p: The tribes of Reuben and Gad wanted the land Israel had recently conquered to become their own inheritance.
Two ordinary human temptations may have influenced them: the lust of the eyes and the pride of life.
They valued their own convenience more highly than the good of the whole community.
Many people still do something similar.
They pursue what benefits them personally rather than what advances the cause of Jesus Christ.
They allow worldly advantage to satisfy them, instead of seeking the heavenly Canaan toward which God's people are traveling.

div.title: Moses rebukes their request (verses 6–15)
div.p: The proposal suggested that they had little regard for Canaan, distrusted God's promise and wished to avoid the dangers of conquering the land.
Moses was rightly angry.
God's people should never remain comfortable and unconcerned while their brothers and sisters face difficult or dangerous work.
That duty applies both to the needs of the whole community and to those of individuals.
Moses reminded Reuben and Gad of the fatal consequences of Israel's earlier unbelief, when their fathers had also been close to entering Canaan.
If people seriously considered how sin ends, they would be far more afraid to begin it.

div.title: The tribes promise to assist their brothers (verses 16–27)
div.p: Moses' plain rebuke achieved a good result.
When their sin and its danger were shown to them, the tribes responded to their duty without resentment or pointless argument.
Everyone should care about the well-being of others as well as personal interests.
The law of love requires us, when needed, to work, take risks and suffer for one another.
The men of war promised to go fully armed before Israel into Canaan and not return until the conquest was finished.
Moses accepted their proposal.
But he warned them that breaking their promise would be a sin against the Lord, not merely a wrong against the other tribes.
God would call them to account.
“Be sure your sin will find you out.”
Sooner or later wrongdoing catches up with the person who committed it.
Our concern should be to find out our sins now—to recognize, repent of and abandon them—before they come to find us in judgment.

div.title: The tribes settle east of the river (verses 28–42)
div.p: The tribes built up their cities—that is, they repaired what was already there.
They also changed their names.
Henry thinks the old names may have been connected with idolatry and therefore deserved to be forgotten.
Selfishness, the desire to seek our own interests instead of those of Christ, is a common and dangerous attitude.

Someone who truly believes the gospel, recognizes God's goodness, is constrained by Christ's love and is made holy through the Holy Spirit cannot remain indifferent to the spread of faith or the spiritual welfare of others merely from love of comfort or fear of hardship.
Let your light shine before other people, so that they see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.

div.title: The stages of Israel's journey (verses 1–49)
div.p: This chapter looks back over Israel's travels through the wilderness.
It is a history worth remembering.
As the people moved toward Canaan, they were constantly being asked to break camp and move again.
That is also the condition of our lives in this world.
We have no lasting city here.
Most of the changes we make are little more than moving from one part of a desert to another.
Israel sometimes went forward and sometimes seemed to go backward.
Yet all the while, the pillar of cloud and fire directed the journey.
God did not lead them along the shortest route, but he led them along the right one.
The path by which he brings his people to himself is always the best path, though it does not always look the nearest.
Remembering earlier journeys should also remind us of God's care for us, our families and our country.
He has led us, fed us and preserved us throughout our lives.
Very few periods of life can be remembered without recalling both God's goodness and our own ingratitude or disobedience.
His kindness leaves us without excuse for our sins.
We would not want to live through the same years again unless God's grace enabled us to avoid the sins we committed and make better use of the opportunities we missed.
Our wanderings will soon end, and our eternal condition will then be fixed.
How important the present moment is!
Happy are those whom the Lord guides with his counsel now and will finally receive into his glory.
The gospel calls us to that happiness.
Now is the acceptable time. Now is the day of salvation.
Sinners should take hold of the opportunity and flee for refuge to the hope set before them.
Let us use our time to glorify God and serve the people of our generation.
He will lead us safely through the remaining journey into his eternal kingdom.

div.title: Israel is warned about the Canaanites (verses 50–56)
div.p: As Israel prepared to cross the Jordan, the people faced a renewed temptation to adopt the idols of Canaan.
God warned that sparing those idols or the idolaters would lead to judgment.
By doing so, they would be raising vipers close to their own hearts.
If they made peace with the Canaanites, even temporarily, those who remained would become like irritants in their eyes and thorns in their sides.
We should expect trouble from every sin we willingly indulge.
Whatever we allow to tempt us will eventually torment us.
The Canaanites were to be driven from the land.
But if the Israelites adopted their wicked practices, the Israelites would also be driven out.
Listen and fear.
If we do not drive out sin, sin will drive us out.
If we do not put our sinful desires to death, those desires will destroy our souls.

row.cell: The bounds of the promised land.
Those appointed to divide the land.

div.title: The boundaries of Canaan (verses 1–15)
div.p: Canaan was a relatively small country.
Henry reckons it at about 160 miles long and 50 miles wide within the boundaries described here.
Yet this was the land promised to Abraham, the father of the faithful, and to Israel's descendants.
For many centuries, this small region was the place where God alone was truly known.
It was the Lord's vineyard, a garden enclosed.
Just as small gardens and vineyards can be extraordinarily productive, Canaan's limited area was compensated for by the fruitfulness of its soil.
The whole earth belongs to the Lord, with everything in it.
Still, relatively few people know him and serve him.
Those few are blessed, because they bear fruit for God.
Notice how little of the world he gives even to his chosen people.
People who have their inheritance in heaven have good reason to be content with a small share of this earth.
The little that a righteous person possesses, received with God's love and blessing, is better and brings more comfort than the riches of many wicked people.

div.title: The people appointed to divide the land (verses 16–29)
div.p: God named the men who would distribute the inheritance among the tribes.
The certainty of Israel's coming victory was so great, since God would fight for the people, that he identified in advance the very men who would be entrusted with dividing the conquered land.

row.cell: The cities of refuge, The laws about murder.

div.title: Cities for the Levites (verses 1–8)
div.p: The cities assigned to the priests and Levites served two purposes.
They gave them places to live, and they placed teachers of God's law throughout Israel.
The ceremonial sacrifices of the tabernacle and later the temple were offered in one place.
But teaching God's word, praying and praising him were not confined to one location.
Each tribe gave cities from its own inheritance.
In doing so, each expressed gratitude toward God.
Every tribe also benefited from having Levites nearby, ready to teach the knowledge of the Lord.
No part of the country needed to remain in spiritual darkness.
Under the gospel, those who receive instruction from God's word should share their material blessings with those who teach them (Galatians 6:6).
Congregations should free ministers from distractions that prevent them from attending to the responsibilities of their calling.
Then ministers can give themselves fully to their work.
They should also use opportunities to show kindness, win people's trust and encourage them to listen to God's truth.

div.title: The cities of refuge and the law concerning killing (verses 9–34)
div.p: The law expressed God's strong hatred of murder and provided a way for murderers to be punished.
In the society described here, a close relative of someone killed could act as the avenger of blood, pursuing a known murderer.
But the law made a crucial distinction.
It did not distinguish a killing committed in sudden rage from one carefully planned in advance: both could be murder.
The distinction was between deliberately striking someone with an instrument likely to kill and causing death without intending it.
Only in the second case did the city of refuge offer protection.
Murder, whatever disguise it wears, defiles a country.
Henry condemns killings that were tolerated or left unpunished under names such as dueling and prizefighting.
There were six cities of refuge.
From any part of Israel, a person could reach one of them in less than a day's journey, Henry says.
A person who caused an accidental death could flee there and remain safe until a fair trial.
If cleared of murder, that person was protected from the avenger of blood.
Yet the person still had to remain inside the city's boundaries until the death of the high priest.
That restriction points us to Christ.
Only the death of the great High Priest brings forgiveness of sins and the sinner's complete freedom.
Henry understands the cities of refuge as clear pictures of the salvation Christ provides.
The Old and New Testaments allude to this provision (Zechariah 9:12; Hebrews 6:18).
He identifies six ways the cities point to the gospel.
First, their high towers offered protection. Christ has been lifted up on the cross and exalted to the Father's right hand as Prince and Savior, bringing repentance and forgiveness.
Second, their roads were made smooth and clear. The path to the Redeemer is open; its true obstacle is the unbelief of the sinful heart.
Third, signs pointed travelers toward the city. Ministers of the gospel are appointed to direct sinners toward Christ.
Fourth, their gates stood open day and night. Christ promises never to turn away anyone who comes to him.
Fifth, each city sustained those who entered it. Believers can live by faith on Christ, whose flesh is true food and whose blood is true drink.
Sixth, the cities offered refuge to everyone who qualified to flee there. The gospel likewise shows no partiality.
No person can claim to be so righteous that God's anger is undeserved.
Nor is any soul excluded from hoping for eternal life through simple faith in God's Son.
The riches of Christ's salvation demand our earnest attention and grateful response.

row.cell: The inheritance of the daughters of Zelophehad.
The daughters of Zelophehad are to marry in their own tribe.

div.title: The inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters (verses 1–4)
div.p: The leaders of Manasseh pointed out a difficulty.
If Zelophehad's daughters married into another tribe, the land granted to them might eventually leave their ancestral tribe.
The leaders wanted to preserve God's arrangement for the inheritances and prevent future disagreements and disputes.
People who possess property should take similar care.
They ought to settle their affairs and arrange their inheritances so as to prevent quarrels among those who come after them.

div.title: Marriage within the tribe (verses 5–12)
div.p: God answered their concern.
Those who consult his word because they want to secure their heavenly inheritance will receive not only guidance about what to do, but also his gracious acceptance of their honest search.
God would not allow one tribe to become richer at another's expense.
Each tribe was to keep its own inheritance.
Zelophehad's daughters submitted to that command.
How could they fail to marry well when God himself was directing them?
Henry draws a Christian application.
Those who belong to God's people should be especially careful about the people with whom they enter life's closest and most lasting relationships.
A true believer in Jesus ought to marry someone who also belongs to the Lord.
Our intentions and affections should submit to God's revealed will, particularly in marriage.
God's word allows genuine affection and personal preference.
But it does not approve of uncontrolled passion or an idolatrous attachment that refuses to consider the future.
A person who defies proper authority simply to satisfy desire acts against wisdom, the good of society, happiness in marriage and—most seriously—the religion of Christ.

div.title: The closing words of Numbers (verse 13)
div.p: These are the commands God gave Israel on the plains of Moab.
Most concerned the people's settlement in Canaan, which they were now about to enter.
Whenever God's providence brings us into a new situation, we should ask him to show us the duties it carries and to enable us to perform them.
We should do today's work today, and fulfill the responsibilities of each place while we are there.

div.title: Deuteronomy — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: Deuteronomy repeats much of the history and many of the laws found in the preceding three books.
Moses delivered this teaching to Israel shortly before his death.
He spoke it aloud so that it would deeply affect the people, and he wrote it down so that it would remain with them.
The generation to whom the law was first given had died.
A new generation had taken its place, and God wanted Moses himself to repeat the law as they prepared to possess Canaan.
The book shows God's extraordinary love for his church.
For his own mercy's sake, he continually preserved his people and intended that his name should still be invoked among them.
The whole book also displays Moses' love for Israel and makes him a remarkable picture of the Lord Jesus Christ.
May we apply its appeals and encouragements to our own consciences, so that we are moved to grateful, believing obedience to God's commands.

row.cell: The words Moses spake to Israel in the plains of Moab, The promise of Canaan.
Of the sending the spies—God's anger for their unbelief and disobedience.

div.title: Moses reminds Israel of the command to enter Canaan (verses 1–8)
div.p: Moses told the people everything the Lord had commanded him to say.
Horeb was only eleven days' journey from Kadesh-barnea.
Remembering that distance would help Israel understand how much suffering their own disobedience had brought upon them.
They had wandered for years because they had refused to believe God.
This memory should encourage them to recognize the benefits of obedience.
Now the Lord commanded them to move forward.
Although he brings his people through hardship and testing, he also knows when they have suffered long enough.
When he commands us to advance in the Christian life, he places the heavenly Canaan before us to encourage us.

div.title: The appointment of judges (verses 9–18)
div.p: Moses reminded Israel of its well-ordered system of government.
If the people used it properly, the system could make life peaceful and secure.
He acknowledged that God had fulfilled the promise to multiply Abraham's descendants.
He also prayed that the Lord would continue fulfilling it.
God's goodness and power are not limited. Why should our faith and hope be limited?
The Lord had given Israel good laws and provided good people to administer them.
This showed both his care for Israel and the care Moses had taken for the people.

div.title: The spies and Israel's unbelief (verses 19–46)
div.p: Moses recalled the difficult journey from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea through the great and terrifying wilderness.
By then the people were very close to Canaan.
The final ruin of hypocrites will be made more terrible by the realization that they had once been not far from God's kingdom.
Israel had every assurance that its God would go ahead.
But the people still wanted to send men ahead to investigate the land.
Everyone who saw Canaan had to admit that it was good.
What reason, then, did Israel have to distrust the Lord who promised to give it to them?
Unbelief lay beneath their whole rebellion.
Every refusal to obey God's law and every suspicion of his power and goodness ultimately springs from disbelief of his word.
True obedience, by contrast, flows from faith.
We would benefit from dividing our past lives into distinct periods.
For each period, we should thank God for the mercies we received, confess the sins we remember and seek forgiveness.
In this way we can renew our acceptance of God's salvation and our dedication to his service.
Our independent plans rarely lead us to the best outcome.
But courage born of faith and expressed through duty enables believers to follow the Lord fully, stand firm against obstacles, triumph over opposition and take hold of the blessings he promises.

row.cell: The Moabites and Ammonites to be spared.

div.title: Israel must not attack Edom (verses 1–7)
div.p: Moses gives only a brief account of Israel's many years in the wilderness.
God had corrected the people for complaining and unbelief.
But he was also preparing them for Canaan—humbling them over sin, teaching them to fight against sinful desires, follow him and find comfort in him.
God's people may wait a long time for deliverance and for their circumstances to improve.
Yet the promised time will eventually come.
Before God brought Israel into conflict with its enemies in Canaan, he taught the people to forgive their enemies in Edom.
They were not to use God's covenant or his guidance as an excuse to seize everything they could obtain.

p.hi: Property rights are not founded simply on possessing God's grace.

div.p: Israel would have a suitable place to live, but that did not mean the people could claim the whole earth for themselves.

p.hi: Religion must never become a disguise for injustice.

div.p: Israel did not need to depend upon Edom's generosity; the people had the all-sufficient God to trust.
They were to use what they already possessed wisely and gratefully.
Since God had supplied their needs through Providence, they were never to use crooked methods to obtain more.
These principles also apply to individual believers.

div.title: Israel must spare Moab and Ammon (verses 8–23)
div.p: The history explains the origins of Moab, Edom and Ammon.
It also reaches back to an even older population movement: the Caphtorites displaced the Avvim from their land.
Such changes show how uncertain earthly property and social position are.
Families lose their estates while other families increase.
Earthly possessions have never remained fixed forever.
These histories were meant to encourage Israel.
If God had given lands to Moab and Ammon through his providence, how much more surely would he fulfill his own promise to Israel!
But the Lord commanded Israel not to fight Moab or Ammon.
We must not wrong others merely because they are wicked.
God gives earthly benefits even to people who do not serve him.
These are not his best blessings.
He has far better gifts in store for his own children.

div.title: God gives Israel the Amorites' land (verses 24–37)
div.p: God tested Israel by forbidding it to seize the wealthy lands of Moab and Ammon.
Then he gave the people the land of the Amorites.
When we refrain from what God forbids, obedience will not ultimately harm us.
The earth and everything in it belong to the Lord, who distributes its possessions as he wills.
But unless someone receives a clear divine command, that person cannot claim God's authority as an excuse for taking another person's land.
Although God promised the Amorites' territory to Israel, the people still had to fight to take possession of it.
We must exert ourselves to obtain what the Lord gives.
What a different world Israel entered as it approached Canaan!
Still greater will be the change experienced by holy souls when they leave this world's wilderness for the better, heavenly country—the city that has firm foundations.
As we remember Israel's history, let us also remember the years we wasted through our sins.
Happy are those whom Jesus has delivered from the coming judgment and who have received his Spirit as the pledge of their inheritance.
That heavenly inheritance cannot be altered by the rise and fall of kingdoms or by changes in earthly possessions.

row.cell: The conquest of Og king of Bashan.
The land of Gilead and Bashan.

div.title: Og, king of Bashan, is defeated (verses 1–11)
div.p: Og was extremely powerful.
Yet he learned nothing from the destruction of Sihon.
He could have sought peace, but he continued trusting in his own strength.
His stubbornness led toward his destruction.
Those whom God's judgments against other sinners fail to awaken become more prepared to receive the same judgments themselves.

div.title: The tribes settle east of the Jordan (verses 12–20)
div.p: The lands of Gilead and Bashan were assigned to Reuben, Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 32).
Moses repeated the condition these tribes had accepted: they must help their brothers complete the conquest before settling down themselves.
When we have received peace, we should desire peace for others too.
We ought to do what we can to help other people obtain it.
We were not born only for ourselves.
We are members of one another.

div.title: Moses encourages Joshua and accepts God's answer (verses 21–29)
div.p: Moses strengthened Joshua, who would succeed him.
Older and more experienced believers should do everything they can to encourage younger people beginning to serve God.
Remember what God has done and what he has promised.
If God is for us, who can overcome us?
We dishonor our Leader when we follow him trembling with fear.
Moses prayed that, if it were the Lord's will, he might cross the Jordan and enter Canaan with Israel.
We should not cherish any desire that we cannot honestly present to God in prayer.
The answer Moses received combined mercy and judgment.
God sometimes chooses to deny us what we want.
A prayer can be accepted even though the exact request is not granted.
If God's providence does not give us our desire, but his grace makes us content without it, we have still received a great blessing.
Let it be enough to have God as our Father and heaven as our inheritance, even if we cannot possess everything we would like in this world.
God promised Moses a view of Canaan from the summit of Pisgah.
He would not possess it, but he would see it.
Even great believers now see heaven from a distance.
God also provided a successor for Moses.
Friends of Christ's church can be encouraged that the Lord's work will continue through others after they themselves have died.
If we have the pledge of heaven and can already see its prospect, let us be content with that.
We should submit to the Lord's will and stop insisting on what he has wisely refused.

row.cell: Earnest exhortations to obedience, and dissuasives from idolatry.
Warnings against disobedience, and promises of mercy.

div.title: Moses urges obedience and warns against idolatry (verses 1–23)
div.p: God's power and love toward Israel gave Moses many reasons to warn the people solemnly against sin.
The warnings particularly concerned Israel's national covenant, but they can also be applied to people who live under the gospel.
What purpose does a law serve if not to be obeyed?
Our obedience cannot earn eternal salvation.
But it is the only evidence that we have received God's gift of eternal life through Jesus Christ.
We are surrounded by many temptations, and corrupt desires remain within our hearts.
We therefore need to guard our hearts carefully.
People cannot walk on the right path if they walk carelessly.
Moses warned particularly against idolatry.
Anyone who thinks clearly should see how weak the temptation is.
The supposed gods—the sun, moon and stars—are creatures God has generously given to all nations.
How absurd it is to worship what he created to serve us!
We must take care not to forget the Lord's covenant.
We need vigilance, thoughtfulness and watchfulness to prevent the forgetfulness that would lead us away from faith.

div.title: Warnings, mercy and the greatness of God (verses 24–40)
div.p: Moses appealed to God's greatness, glory and goodness.
If we truly considered the One to whom we answer, we would take our duty seriously and not dare to sin against him.
Why turn away from a merciful God who will never abandon those who remain faithful to him?
Where else could we go?
May his love and mercy bind us to him.
Moses reminded Israel that God was its sovereign and that the people owed him obedience.
Keeping his commands was also wise for their own sake.
Fear of the Lord is wisdom.
People privileged to receive divine truth and law ought to live honorably and wisely, so that God is glorified.
God hears those who call on him in faith.
He is near enough to answer their prayers with peace.
His laws are just and righteous beyond the laws of other nations.
What Israel saw at Sinai gave a foretaste of the final day of judgment, when the Lord Jesus will be revealed in flaming fire.
The people must also remember what they heard there.
God reveals himself through the works of creation without human language, yet their testimony reaches everywhere (Psalm 19:1, 3).
At Sinai he spoke in words the people could hear, graciously adapting himself to their weakness.
Israel's origin was unlike that of every other nation.
God's free grace explains the distinction.
We are not loved because of some merit in ourselves, but for Christ's sake.
Moses also pointed out the benefits of obedience.
At the beginning of his speech (verse 1), he had said that obedience would enable them to live and enter the land.
At its end (verse 40), he promised that obedience would lead to good for them and their children.
Israel's national prosperity was bound to its faithfulness.
Apostasy would ruin the nation.
Moses foresaw that Israel would turn from the Lord to idols.
Only people who seek God with their whole heart will find him to their lasting comfort.
Afflictions often stir us to seek him, and through God's grace they bring many people back to sound judgment.
When such troubles come, return to the Lord: they show what follows from abandoning him.
Consider all these reasons together, and you will see that faith is entirely reasonable.
People abandon God's rule only after abandoning sound human understanding.

div.title: The cities of refuge and the next address (verses 41–49)
div.p: This passage introduces another address Moses would give to Israel in the following chapters.
He placed God's law before them.
It was to be the guide for their actions and the way they lived.
It was also to be a mirror in which they recognized their own natural condition.
Looking into this perfect law of liberty, they were to continue in obedience.
The instructions first given after Israel came out of Egypt were now repeated.
Moses gave them while the people were camped opposite Beth-peor, a Moabite center of idolatry.
Israel's recent victories offered another strong reason to obey God.
We should similarly understand our own condition as sinners and the gracious covenant to which we are invited.
That covenant reveals greater things than Israel witnessed at Sinai and provides mercies beyond what the people enjoyed in the wilderness or Canaan.
The One who speaks to us is infinitely greater than Moses.
He bore our sins on the cross and appeals to us through his dying love.

row.cell: The request of the people that the law might be delivered through Moses.

div.title: Israel is called to hear and obey (verses 1–5)
div.p: Moses urged Israel to pay attention.
When we hear God's word, we must learn it.
Once we have learned it, we must put it into practice.
That is the purpose of listening and learning.
We are not meant merely to fill our heads with religious information or our mouths with talk.
God's word should direct our affections and conduct.

div.title: The Ten Commandments are repeated (verses 6–22)
div.p: This account of the commandments differs in some wording from Exodus 20.
Henry compares that difference with the variations between the Lord's Prayer recorded in Matthew 6 and Luke 11.
We must care more about faithfully receiving the truths and commands than about insisting that every repeated account use identical words.
The original reason for observing the Sabbath—the Lord's rest after creating the world on the seventh day—is not mentioned here.
That reason remains valid, but it is not the only one.
Here Moses appeals to Israel's deliverance from Egypt.
That deliverance pointed to our redemption through Jesus Christ.
Henry connects it with the Christian Sabbath, which remembers that redemption.
Through Christ's resurrection we were brought into the glorious freedom of God's children, by his strong hand and outstretched arm.
How gentle and life-giving the gospel sounds to a soul burdened by the terrors of a broken law!

div.title: The people ask Moses to speak for them (verses 23–33)
div.p: Moses recalled how terrified the people had been when God gave the law.
Ever since humanity's fall, divine appearances have been frightening to guilty people.
But Christ has removed sin, and through him we are invited to approach the throne of grace boldly.
The people seemed sincere while they were deeply convicted by the word they had heard.
Yet conscience can be alarmed by the law without becoming clean.
Strong feelings may force people to make excellent promises without creating new and lasting principles within them.
God commended the words Israel spoke.
He truly desires the good and salvation of sinners.
He has supplied abundant evidence.
He gives people time and opportunity to repent.
He sent his Son to redeem us, promised the Spirit to those who ask, and declared that he takes no pleasure in sinners' destruction.
How good it would be if people always had the hearts they sometimes seem to have under conviction, painful providence or the approach of death.
The only way to be truly happy is to become holy.
It will go well with the righteous.
Believers should increasingly delight in learning and doing everything the Lord has commanded.

row.cell: General precepts, Instructions to be given to their children.

div.title: Obedience and the fear of God (verses 1–3)
div.p: In this passage, commandments appear to refer chiefly to the moral law, statutes to ceremonial regulations, and judgments to the law used by judges.
Moses taught the people everything God commanded him to teach—and nothing beyond it.
Ministers of Jesus Christ must likewise teach churches everything he commanded, neither more nor less (Matthew 28:20).
Reverence for God within the heart is the strongest motive for obedience.
We should earnestly desire that our children and grandchildren fear the Lord as we do.
Faith and righteousness strengthen the well-being of every community.

div.title: The Lord is one; love him with everything (verses 4 and 5)
div.p: This short confession summarizes the first principles of faith and obedience.
Jehovah our God is the only living and true God.
He alone is God, and he is one God.
We should desire no other.
Henry sees the threefold mention of divine names and the plural form of the word for God as hints of three divine Persons even within this proclamation of divine unity.
This is his Trinitarian interpretation of the text, not a change to its original words.
Happy are those who have this one Lord as their God!
One inexhaustible fountain is better than a thousand empty reservoirs.
One all-sufficient God is better than a thousand insufficient friends.
The first and great commandment is to love God and let love motivate every duty we perform toward him.
“Give me your heart,” says the Lord.
We must love him with all our heart, soul and strength.
Henry identifies five qualities of this love.
First, it is sincere. We love God inwardly and truly, not merely with our words.
Second, it is strong. We give him our whole affection, because the One who is everything to us deserves everything from us.
Third, it is supreme. We love God above every creature and love other things in relation to him.
Fourth, it is intelligent. We recognize good reasons to love him with both heart and understanding.
Fifth, it is undivided. Because he is one, our hearts should be united in loving him.
May God's love be poured out into our hearts!

div.title: Keeping God's word within the family (verses 6–16)
div.p: Four practices help preserve living faith in our hearts and homes.
First, meditate. Store God's words within your heart, so that they shape your thoughts every day.
Second, teach children. Repeat the words faithfully and carefully, teaching children and others under your responsibility.
Third, speak about God reverently. Discuss his truth with children, servants, friends and companions.
Focus on the plain teaching of Scripture and the truths that lead to peace, not endless arguments about doubtful questions.
Fourth, read Scripture frequently. God instructed Israelites to write words from the law on their walls and on parchment scrolls worn near their wrists.
Henry regards that literal command as binding upon Israel, while its purpose remains binding upon Christians.
We should use every good means to become familiar with God's word, ready to call it to mind when temptation comes or duty requires guidance.
We should never be ashamed to confess our faith or accept its authority over us.
We must be especially careful not to forget the Lord during times of comfort and prosperity.
When people receive gifts easily, they often forget the Giver.
A comfortable and secure life can tempt us to seek happiness in the world instead of in God, our only true rest.
Be watchful while life seems pleasant.
We must not test the Lord—either by despairing of his goodness while walking in obedience, or by presuming upon his help while deliberately departing from duty.

div.title: Faithful obedience and the instruction of children (verses 17–25)
div.p: Moses commanded the people to keep God's laws diligently.
Neglect leads toward ruin.
But without care and diligence, we will not enjoy salvation.
Faith is both our duty and our benefit: it is our life.
Godliness promises blessings in the present life insofar as those blessings serve God's glory.
It is also our righteousness—but only through the Mediator can we be righteous before God.
Knowing the spiritual reach and excellence of God's law reveals the sinner's need for a Savior.
It prepares the heart to welcome salvation as a free gift.
The gospel honors the law not only because the Son of God obeyed it perfectly.
It also brings rebels and enemies back to God through repentance, faith, forgiveness and renewing grace, so that they may begin to love him above everything even now.
In heaven, they will love him perfectly, as the angels do.

div.title: Israel must reject idolatry (verses 1–11)
div.p: Moses warned Israel strictly against friendship and fellowship with idols and those devoted to them.
Those who live in fellowship with God must not share in the fruitless works of darkness.
The commands to destroy these nations were restricted to the nations specifically named.
Henry explicitly says this restriction shows that later generations must not use these commands as a precedent.
An adequate understanding of sin's evil and of the mystery of the crucified Savior helps us recognize God's justice in both present and eternal judgments.
The Christian's own warfare, however, is with the sinful desires that attack the soul.
We should deal with those desires decisively, putting them to death instead of treating them gently.
Many people have been ruined by marriages that draw them away from God.
Henry warns that in a religiously unequal marriage it is more likely that the faithful person will be led astray than that the unfaithful person will be converted.
Those who choose a life partner outside shared faith cannot assume that partner will help them live for the Lord.

div.title: God's promises and the gradual defeat of sin (verses 12–26)
div.p: We risk sharing in the works of darkness when we take delight in the company of those who practice them.
Anything that becomes a trap to us exposes us to judgment.
If we remain constant in our duties, we may trust God's constant mercy.
Diseases, Henry says, are under God's providence: they go where he sends them and fulfill his purposes.
Putting our souls' sins to death is therefore good even for our bodily welfare.
Sin will never be completely destroyed within us during this life.
Indeed, it would exercise far less power over us if we were more alert and diligent.
God acts according to his own hidden purpose.
But that secret purpose gives no excuse whatsoever for laziness or neglect.
We should not imagine that because the church's deliverance or the defeat of our sinful desires does not happen immediately, it will never happen.
God carries out his own work in the way and at the time he chooses.
His method and timing are always best.
Corruption is gradually driven from believers' hearts.
Sanctification advances little by little and will finally end in complete victory.
But pride, carelessness and other sins encouraged by prosperity can be more dangerous than wild animals.
They are especially liable to increase in people who think themselves secure.

row.cell: Exhortations and cautions, enforced by the Lord's former dealings with Israel, and his promises.

div.title: Remembering God's care in the wilderness (verses 1–9)
div.p: Obedience should have three qualities.
First, it must be careful: we should pay attention and actually carry out God's commands.
Second, it must be complete: we should obey all his commands, not merely the ones we find convenient.
Third, it must arise from a right motive: we should regard God as our Lord and worship him with holy reverence.
Moses asked Israel to look back over the journey.
We should also remember the ways God's providence and grace have led us through life's wilderness.
Such remembrance encourages us to serve him cheerfully and trust him.
Israel's hardships humbled its pride and exposed its stubbornness.
They showed the people—and others—what was truly in their hearts.
They also showed that God had not chosen them because they possessed any merit that earned his favor.
The Lord provided food and clothing miraculously.
His children therefore need not distrust their Father or resort to sin to obtain necessities.
Through honest diligence and obedience, they may rely on him to provide.
The lesson also has a spiritual meaning.
God's word nourishes the soul.
Jesus Christ is the Word of God, and we live through him.
Israel had been corrected severely, and not without cause.
The proper use of suffering is to turn us toward faithful duty.
Moses also directed the people to look forward to Canaan.
Looking backward at God's care and forward toward his promise both encourage obedience.
Canaan pointed to a better land.
The gospel church is the New Testament Canaan, watered by the Spirit's gifts and graces, filled with trees of righteousness and bearing the fruits of righteousness.
Heaven is the true good land, where nothing necessary is lacking and joy is complete.

div.title: Warnings against pride when prosperous (verses 10–20)
div.p: Moses reminded Israel of its duty in prosperous times.
The people must remember their Benefactor and give thanks for everything they receive.
Prosperity brings strong temptations.
People who acquire wealth or engage in successful business may be tempted toward pride, forgetfulness of God and worldly-mindedness.
They may become anxious about many things.
In some ways, poor believers possess an advantage.
They often recognize God's provision more readily as an answer to trusting prayer.
Although they have less, they may find it easier to rely on him for each day's bread and may enjoy a particular sweetness in doing so.
They are also spared many temptations that come with wealth.
Remember God's former dealings with you.
His infinite wisdom and goodness lie behind the changes and trials he allows.
Israel's hard experiences were intended, in the end, to do the people good.
Human pride is deeply rooted.
Even people who had endured slavery in Egypt still needed the wilderness to humble them.
Hardly a week passes without our giving evidence of weakness, folly and sinful corruption.
Only a broken heart truly recognizes how precious the Savior is.
Even the most suitable outward trials cannot produce that response unless God's Spirit makes them effective within us.
God's gifts and our efforts are not competing explanations.
What we receive comes through his promises.
Those who follow other people into sin must expect to share their destruction.
If we behave as sinners do, we should not be surprised to suffer as sinners suffer.

row.cell: The Israelites not to think their success came by their own worthiness.
Moses reminds the Israelites of their rebellions.

div.title: Victory comes from God, not Israel's merit (verses 1–6)
div.p: Moses described the strength of the nations Israel was about to confront.
This was meant to drive the people toward God and teach them to place their hope in him.
He assured them of victory because the Lord would be with them.
But they must never imagine that their own righteousness had earned God's favor.
In Jesus Christ we receive both righteousness and strength.
We must boast in him alone, never in ourselves or in any ability of our own.
The nations of Canaan were driven out because of their own wickedness.
All those whom God rejects are rejected because of their wrongdoing.
But none whom he accepts is accepted because of personal righteousness.
In this way all human boasting is excluded (Ephesians 2:9, 11–12).
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): 2 Corinthians 11:12.
Verified editorial cross-reference: Eph.2.11; Eph.2.12.

div.title: The wilderness rebellions show Israel's need of mercy (verses 7–29)
div.p: Moses recalled the people's repeated rebellions.
If they believed their righteousness had brought them to Canaan, they should remember what a miracle of mercy it was that they had survived the wilderness at all.
We should often recall our former sins with sorrow and shame.
Doing so helps us understand our debt to free grace.
It reminds us that we have never deserved anything from God except righteous judgment.
Human pride is persistent.
It finds many different ways to return.
We readily imagine that our own goodness has gained us God's special favor, though our wickedness is often more obvious than our weakness.
On the day of judgment, when the hidden history of every human life is revealed, the whole world will stand guilty before God.
Yet we have an Advocate before the mercy seat.
He did not merely fast for us.

p.hi: He died upon the cross for our sins.

div.p: Through him, even sinners who condemn themselves may approach God and ask for undeserved mercy and eternal life as his free gift.
Let every victory, all glory and every expression of praise belong to him who alone brings salvation.

row.cell: God's mercies to Israel after their rebellion.

div.title: God's renewed kindness after Israel's rebellion (verses 1–11)
div.p: Moses reminded the Israelites how merciful God had been to them even after they had repeatedly provoked him.
He identified four signs that the Lord had reconciled himself to the people.

p.hi: First, God gave them his law.

div.p: The Lord has likewise entrusted us with Scripture, Sabbaths and sacraments as signs of his presence and favor.

p.hi: Second, he led them onward toward Canaan.

div.p: Their earlier rebellion had not brought his covenant promises to an end.
Third, he established a continuing ministry to care for holy things among the people.
Under the gospel, the Holy Spirit is poured out more abundantly and powerfully.
The Spirit continues to raise up ministers in every age, preparing their hearts and making them willing to serve.

p.hi: Fourth, God accepted Moses as an intercessor.

div.p: He also appointed Moses to remain Israel's leader.
In this, Moses pictured Christ, who lives forever to intercede for us and possesses all authority in heaven and on earth.

div.title: Our obligations to God, neighbor and ourselves (verses 12–22)
div.p: Moses explained our responsibilities in both conviction and conduct.
Toward God, we must fear the Lord, love him, delight in fellowship with him, walk in his appointed ways, and serve him sincerely with all our hearts and souls.
Our service should be willing and cheerful.
We must keep his commands.
Obedience offers true honor and joy.
We should also honor God and cling to him as the One whom we love, trust and delight in, and from whom we expect every good thing.
Toward our neighbors, God's generosity to humanity obligates us to honor all people.
Those who once suffered and have received God's mercy should be especially ready to show kindness to others in similar distress.
Toward ourselves, we are commanded to circumcise our hearts.
We must put aside the corrupt desires and affections that keep us from loving and fearing God.
By nature, human beings do not love him.
This is original sin, the source of our wrongdoing.
The sinful mind is hostile to God.
It neither submits to his law nor has the power to do so.
Those who live under the flesh's rule cannot please God (Romans 8:5–9).
Let us therefore come without delay or reservation to God, who has reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ.
In fellowship with him, we can love, serve and obey him acceptably.
Through the Spirit, we can be transformed into Christ's likeness, from one degree of glory to another.
God's greatness, glory, goodness and grace all encourage us to perform our duty.
Blessed Spirit, give us your cleansing, persevering and renewing power!
May we no longer remain strangers as our ancestors once were, but be counted among God's children and receive our inheritance with his saints.

row.cell: The great work God wrought for Israel.
Careful study of God's word requisite.
The blessings and the curse set forth.

div.title: Love for God expressed through obedience (verses 1–7)
div.p: Moses joined two duties that must always belong together: love the Lord and keep his commands.
Love leads to obedience.
Only obedience flowing from love is truly acceptable to God (1 John 5:3).
Moses recalled the great and fearful works of God that Israel had witnessed.
What we see with our own eyes, especially during our earliest years, should continue to influence us and improve our lives long afterward.

div.title: Blessings and warnings for Israel (verses 8–17)
div.p: Moses placed life and death, blessings and curses, before the people.
Their future depended on how they responded to the Lord's commands.
Sin tends to shorten human lives and to shorten a nation's prosperity.
If the people loved and served God, the Lord promised them abundant good gifts.
Godliness includes promises for the present life.
But the favor of God brings more true joy to the heart than an increase in grain, wine or oil.
Turning from the Lord to idols would lead to Israel's ruin.
Take care not to let your heart deceive you.
Everyone who abandons God to set the heart on a created thing will eventually discover that it was a terrible mistake.
Such people have contributed to their own destruction.
Their guilt is greater because they neglected the warnings they had been given.

div.title: Keeping God's word in heart, sight and speech (verses 18–25)
div.p: Henry identifies three rules for living under God's word.

p.hi: First, fill the heart with God's word.

div.p: Good conduct cannot continue without good thoughts, desires and convictions within us.

p.hi: Second, keep the eyes fixed on God's word.

div.p: Treat it as the guide for your path and the rule governing your work (Psalm 119:30).

p.hi: Third, employ the tongue in speaking about God's word.

div.p: Thoughtful teaching and conversation help God's truth remain alive among the people.
Nothing contributes more to a nation's prosperity and the preservation of true faith than the faithful religious education of children.

div.title: The blessing and curse announced (verses 26–32)
div.p: Moses summarized every reason to obey in two expressions: the blessing and the curse.
The people had to choose which they would receive.
He appointed a public and solemn proclamation of both, on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
We have broken God's law and fallen under its curse.
We cannot remedy that condition through our own power.
But in mercy, the gospel places a blessing and a curse before us again.
There is blessing for those who answer its call to repent, believe in Christ and receive new hearts and transformed lives through him.
There is terrible judgment for those who neglect such great salvation.
Let us welcome this good news with thanksgiving and joy.
Do not harden your hearts.
Hear God's voice while it is still called today, while he invites us to approach his throne of mercy.
Be diligent to make your calling and election sure.

row.cell: Monuments of idolatry to be destroyed.
The place of God's service to be kept.

div.title: Israel must reject pagan worship practices (verses 1–4)
div.p: Moses began explaining the laws Israel had to observe in Canaan with instructions about worshiping God.
The Israelites were not to introduce the customs and rituals of idolaters into their worship of the true God, even under the pretext of improving it.
We cannot serve both God and wealth.
We cannot worship both the living God and idols.
Nor can we claim to trust in Jesus Christ while also resting our hope on superstition or self-righteousness.

div.title: The place chosen by God and the worship he accepts (verses 5–32)
div.p: The command to bring sacrifices to the entrance of the tabernacle was now explained in view of Israel's settlement in Canaan.
Moral duties of worship were different.
People could pray and worship God wherever they lived, as they later did in synagogues.
The place God would choose for sacrifices was described as the place where he would put his name.
It would be his dwelling, where he, the King of Israel, could be approached reverently by his people.
Under the gospel there is no temple or altar that makes offerings acceptable except Christ himself.
The prophets foretold that spiritual incense would be offered to God everywhere (Malachi 1:11).
Jesus declared that true worshipers are accepted when they worship God in spirit and truth, not because they come to one mountain or to Jerusalem (John 4:21).
Even an Israelite who could not bring a sacrifice to the altar could honor God, maintain fellowship with him and receive his mercy.
The work of God should be done with holy joy and cheerfulness.
Children and servants were to rejoice before him as well.
Worship should be a pleasure and delight, not a dreary task.
People should be kind to ministers who instruct them faithfully and set them a good example.
We will continue needing their ministry until we reach a world where religious ordinances are no longer necessary.
Whether we eat or drink, or do anything else, everything should be done for God's glory.
Whatever we do should be done in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, thanking the Father through him.
Israel was not even to investigate the methods used in idol worship.
What spiritual advantage could come from exploring such depths of Satan?
We will find increasing contentment as we grow in love and good works springing from faith and the indwelling Spirit of Christ.

row.cell: Enticers to idolatry to be put to death.
Relations who entice to idolatry not to be spared.
Idolatrous cities not to be spared.

div.title: Resisting false religious teaching (verses 1–5)
div.p: Moses had already warned about the danger posed by the Canaanites. Now he warned against idolatry arising within Israel itself.
We must become familiar with the truths and commands of Scripture, because temptation often comes disguised as something good and error may appear to be truth.
Only the clear and explicit testimony of God's word can reliably expose such deception.
Sincere love for God is shown by refusing to abandon him and serve false gods, even when the temptation is presented attractively.

div.title: Resisting temptation from loved ones (verses 6–11)
div.p: Satan often seeks to lead us into evil through people we love.
We are least likely to suspect them of intending harm, are eager to please them and find it natural to follow their example.
The person tempting us might be a brother, child, wife or close friend—someone bound to us by family or affection.
Even so, we must put God and faithfulness to him before our dearest earthly relationships.
We must not break God's law merely to please those we love.
