We should refuse the invitation, even if the reason for considering it is curiosity, companionship or a desire to gain the person's affection.
“If sinners entice you, do not consent” (Proverbs 1:10).
Henry also reminds his readers that people must not obstruct God's justice.

div.title: The case of an idolatrous Israelite city (verses 12–18)
div.p: The law describes an Israelite city turning away from its God to worship idols.
Henry observes that even when ancient Israel was commanded to preserve its faith through force, it was not permitted to compel outsiders into that faith through fire and sword.
He distinguishes those ancient civil judgments from the gospel era.
Under the Christian dispensation, the spiritual judgments at stake are more dreadful than the execution of criminals.
Christians still have every reason to fear God's anger against sin.
We should especially beware the spiritual idolatry of greed and devotion to worldly pleasure.
Parents must not encourage such idolatry by their example or in the way they raise their children.
May the Lord write his law and truth upon our hearts, reign there and pour his love into us!

row.cell: The Israelites to distinguish themselves from other nations.

div.title: The privileges and holiness of God's people (verses 1–21)
div.p: Moses described three privileges God had given Israel to distinguish the people from other nations.
They were honors in themselves and pictures of the spiritual blessings believers receive in Christ.
First, election. “The Lord has chosen you.”
God did not choose Israel because the people had already made themselves superior to other nations.
He chose them through grace so they would become his own.
Believers are chosen in the same way (Ephesians 1:4).
Second, adoption. “You are children of the Lord your God.”
God did not need children, but the people needed a Father.
Every true spiritual Israelite is a child of God and shares in his favor and in the character he forms within his people.
Third, sanctification. “You are a holy people.”
God's people are called to holiness, yet any genuine holiness they possess comes from his grace.
Those whom he chooses as his children, he also forms into a people devoted to good works.
They should avoid whatever could bring disgrace upon their confession of faith in the eyes of those watching for their failures.
Our heavenly Father forbids nothing except for our benefit.
Do not destroy your health, reputation, family happiness or peace of mind.
Above all, do not ruin your soul.
Do not become a slave to bodily appetites or passions, making both yourself and others miserable.
Seek what is best and most useful.
The ceremonial rules regarding unclean animal flesh helped keep Israel separate from idolatrous neighbors.
The gospel makes clear that Christians are no longer bound by those food laws.
But we should ask whether we are truly God's children, separated from worldly ungodliness and dedicated to his glory through Christ's blood.
Does the Holy Spirit work within us?
Lord, teach us through these laws how pure and holy your people ought to live!

div.title: Tithes, generosity and care for the poor (verses 22–29)
div.p: A second portion of the land's produce was required.
The arrangement opposed human greed, mistrust and selfishness.
It encouraged friendliness, generosity and cheerfulness.
It also established provision for people who were poor.
Israel learned that earthly possessions are enjoyed most comfortably when shared with brothers and sisters in need.
God promised to bless the work of those who served him and did good with what they had.
His blessing is essential to earthly prosperity.
Without it, our efforts can achieve nothing lasting.
Yet that blessing rests upon working hands.
We should not expect God to bless idleness and the love of ease.
It rests also upon giving hands.
People who distribute their possessions generously may find their resources increased.
Free and generous support of religion and other good work is a safe and fruitful way of using wealth.

div.title: The year of release and generosity to the poor (verses 1–11)
div.p: The year of release pictured the grace of the gospel.
Through it, the Lord proclaims the acceptable year of salvation, in which our debts—our sins—are forgiven.
God's law is spiritual.
It restrains even the thoughts of our hearts.
We are mistaken if we think our thoughts are outside his knowledge or authority.
The law's command to forgive debts exposed the evil in some hearts.
Instead of being generous, certain people refused to lend or give because the year of release was approaching.
They used a law of generosity as an excuse for selfishness.
To avoid committing sin, we must reject sinful thoughts before they produce actions.
It is dreadful to make poor people cry out against us with good reason.
Do not resent helping a neighbor, and do not distrust God's provision.
Give freely and cheerfully, because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).

div.title: The release of servants (verses 12–18)
div.p: The law concerning Hebrew servants was repeated.
It included a requirement that masters provide some resources when servants were released, so that people who had worked without wages could begin to support themselves.
When members of a household take their duties toward one another seriously, they can expect God to bless their family life.
We should remember that we owe divine justice a debt we cannot pay.
We are like poor, dying slaves.
But the Lord Jesus Christ became poor and shed his blood so that our debt could be paid, our souls ransomed and all our needs supplied.
When the gospel is preached clearly, the Lord's year of release is announced.
It proclaims forgiveness of sin, freedom for the soul and rest in Christ.
As faith in Christ and love for him grow, they overcome selfishness and the world's unkindness.
They remove the excuses that unbelief, mistrust and greed continually invent.

div.title: The firstborn animals (verses 19–23)
div.p: This law prescribed what Israelites were to do with the firstborn animals of their flocks and herds.
Christians are not bound by that distinction.
We no longer make a difference between the first calf or lamb and the animals that follow.
Instead, we should apply the gospel lesson.
Dedicate yourself—and the first and best of your time and strength—to God.
Use every comfort and possession for his praise and according to his law, remembering that everything we enjoy came from his hand.

row.cell: Of judges, Groves and images forbidden.

div.title: The three annual feasts (verses 1–17)
div.p: Moses repeated the instructions for the three yearly festivals: Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles.
He also repeated the general requirement that Israel's people gather before God.
Believers must never forget the depth of guilt and suffering from which they have been rescued, or the great price their Redeemer paid.
Remembering that price allows gratitude and joy to live alongside sorrow for sin and patience through the hardships on the road to heaven.
The Israelites were to rejoice in what they received from God and in the worship and offerings they returned to him.
Our duty should be our delight.
Those who lived under the law were commanded to rejoice before God.
How much more should those living under the grace of the gospel rejoice!
Our duty is to rejoice continually and to rejoice in the Lord always.
When we rejoice in him, we should help others rejoice as well, comforting people who grieve and providing for those in need.
Everyone whose joy rests in God can rejoice in hope, because the One who made the promises is faithful.

div.title: Just judges and the rejection of idols (verses 18–22)
div.p: Moses gave instructions for the proper administration of justice.
Personal favoritism must be set aside.
Everyone should receive what is right, and no one should be wronged.
The people were also warned not to adopt the idolatrous practices of the surrounding nations.

Nothing misrepresents God more seriously—or damages human minds more deeply—than trying to portray the almighty and eternal Spirit, present everywhere, through a physical image and then worshiping that image.
Sadly, even under the gospel, with its better promises, human hearts still tend to create idols in one form or another.

row.cell: All sacrifices to be perfect, Idolaters must be slain.
The choice of a king, His duties.

div.title: Proper offerings and judgment on idolatry (verses 1–7)
div.p: No animal with a defect was to be brought to God as a sacrifice.
This reminds us of Jesus Christ, whose sacrifice was perfect, pure and without blemish.
It also reminds us to give God the best of our abilities, time and possessions.
If we deliberately withhold our best, our claimed obedience becomes hateful to him.
The Mosaic law ordered an Israelite idol worshiper to be put to death by stoning.
Henry treats this ancient, severe judicial sentence as a warning about how seriously God judges idolatry.
He urges people in his own day who have set up idols in their hearts to consider the judgment ancient Israel faced.
This is a description of Israel's historical law and Henry's spiritual application, not an instruction for private punishment today.

div.title: Difficult cases and the courts (verses 8–13)
div.p: Courts of judgment were to be established in Israel's towns.
The decisions of those courts did not have the direct authority of a divine oracle.
Nevertheless, they were to be made by wise, prudent and experienced judges.
They also benefited from God's promise concerning the administration of justice.

div.title: Choosing and instructing a king (verses 14–20)
div.p: The Lord himself was Israel's King in a special way.
If the people placed a human king over themselves, that person had to be the one God chose.
Later, when Israel asked for a king, the people approached Samuel, a prophet of the Lord.
Whenever God's choice can be known, it should guide and overrule our own preference.
Moses gave instructions for Israel's future king.
He must avoid everything that would turn him away from God and faithful worship.
Three major obstacles to devotion are wealth, honor and pleasure.
These correspond to the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life.
They are especially dangerous to people who hold positions of authority.
The king was therefore required to study God's law and make it the standard for his rule.
He was to write his own copy of Scripture and read it every day throughout his life.
Merely owning a Bible is not enough.
We must use it, and use it daily for as long as we live.
Christ's disciples never outgrow Scripture.
They will continue needing it until they reach the place where love and knowledge are made perfect.
And the king's copying and reading were worthless if he did not practice what he wrote and read.
Those who fear God and keep his commandments will benefit even in this present life.

row.cell: The abominations of the Canaanites to be avoided.

div.title: Provision for the priests and Levites (verses 1–8)
div.p: God took care that the priests would not become entangled in ordinary worldly business or seek to enrich themselves with the world's wealth.
They had more important work to do.
But the Lord also made provision so that they would not lack the ordinary comforts and necessities of life.
The people were responsible for supporting them.
Those who benefit from gathered worship ought to contribute to the adequate support of the ministers who serve and teach them.

div.title: Israel must avoid occult practices (verses 9–14)
div.p: Israel had received extraordinary blessings from God.
Yet the people remained at risk of turning to false teachers among the nations God had placed under judgment.
Moses therefore repeated the warning not to imitate the abominations of the Canaanites.
Henry explicitly condemns belief in lucky or unlucky days, charms for curing illness, amulets or spells intended to prevent harm, and fortune-telling.
These practices contributed to the judgment that fell upon Canaan.
Henry expresses astonishment that people still claimed occult powers in an age with such broad access to divine truth.
He regards them as impostors who deceive and exploit their followers.

div.title: Jesus Christ, the promised great Prophet (verses 15–22)
div.p: God promised to raise up a Prophet greater than all the prophets who came before.
Through him, God would reveal himself and his will to humanity more fully and clearly than ever before.
Henry identifies this Prophet as Jesus Christ.
He is the Light of the world (John 8:12).
He is the Word through whom God speaks to us (John 1:1; Hebrews 1:2).
Through his birth, he belonged to Israel.
In his resurrection, he rose in Jerusalem, and his teaching went out from there to the whole world.
God raised up his Son Jesus to bless us.
Christ is like Moses, but infinitely greater.
The promised Prophet has already come.
We are not to look for another.
His revelation of God is meant not to crush us with terror but to give us encouragement.
He speaks with both a father's tenderness and God's own authority.
Anyone who refuses to listen to Christ does so at great risk.
The One appointed as Prophet will also be Judge (John 12:48).
Those who reject his voice, salvation and rule face judgment.
But people who trust and obey him are blessed.
He guides them along safe and peaceful paths until he brings them into the land of perfect light, purity and joy.
Moses also warned against false prophets.
We urgently need a reliable test for every message we hear, so that we can distinguish what God has spoken from what he has not.
Anything contradicting the clear meaning of the written word, or encouraging people to sin, cannot be a message from the Lord.

row.cell: The cities of refuge, The man-slayer, The murderer.

div.title: Cities of refuge and the distinction between murder and accident (verses 1–13)
div.p: The law distinguished between the blood of an innocent person who had been murdered and the guilt of the murderer.
It also provided cities of refuge so that a person would not die as a criminal for causing a death that was not intentional.
Jesus Christ, the Lord our Righteousness, is a refuge for sinners who flee to him through faith.
But there is no shelter in Christ for people who presume upon mercy while deliberately continuing in sin.
Those who flee from their sins to Christ are safe with him.
Those who expect him to protect them while they remain in their sins are deceiving themselves.

div.title: Boundary markers must not be moved (verse 14)
div.p: The Lord commanded Israel to preserve boundary markers in Canaan.
He wants everyone to know what belongs to them, and safeguards to be maintained so that no one wrongs another person or is wronged.
This is a moral command that continues to apply.
Each person should be content with their own portion and act justly toward neighbors in every matter.

div.title: False witnesses and public justice (verses 15–21)
div.p: A person must not be condemned on the word of only one witness.
Someone who deliberately gives false testimony should be subject to the penalty that the witness had attempted to inflict upon the accused.
Henry regards this as a just provision.
Christians should therefore be careful not only when giving evidence before a court but also in private conversation.
They must not join in slander.
And anyone whose conscience accuses them of sin should flee immediately to the refuge offered in Jesus Christ.

row.cell: Exhortation and proclamation respecting those who went to war.
Peace to be offered, What cities were to be devoted.

div.title: Israel's soldiers must trust God (verses 1–9)
div.p: In wars fought according to God's command, Israel could rely on his help.
The Lord, not the people's weapons or numbers, was to be their confidence.
In this respect their battles pictured the Christian's spiritual warfare.
Men unwilling to fight were to be released from the military campaign.
Sometimes their reluctance arose from family or other personal circumstances.
God did not want his service performed by people dragged into it against their will.
“Your people will offer themselves willingly” (Psalm 110:3).
Those who run the Christian race and fight the good fight of faith must set aside everything that makes them reluctant to do their duty.
People who were weak or afraid could also return home.
One reason was to prevent their fear from spreading to their fellow soldiers.
We must not adopt the fears of people who are afraid (Isaiah 8:12).

div.title: Peace offered and the limits of ancient warfare (verses 10–20)
div.p: Israel received laws about warfare against other nations.
Henry finds in the offer of peace a picture of God's gracious way of dealing with sinners.
He proclaims peace and urges them to be reconciled to him.
This also teaches us how to treat other people.
Even if others want war, we should want peace.
The ancient law included a different provision concerning towns within the territory promised to Israel, where idol worshipers were not to remain and lead the people astray.
Henry emphasizes an essential distinction: these regulations do not govern Christians' conduct today.
Christ's law of love, not Israel's ancient rules for conquest, is our rule.
The horrors of war bring anguish to a compassionate heart whenever we remember them.
They demonstrate humanity's wickedness, Satan's power and God's just judgment on a sinful world.
More dreadful still is the condition of those fighting against their own Maker, refusing even the fitting service of praise and worship.
Their destruction is certain.
Christians need not fear the number or power of their spiritual enemies, or their own weakness.
The Lord saves his people.
But anyone whose heart still clings to this world or fears Christ's cross and the conflict should not imagine the spiritual battle can be fought halfheartedly.
Even during a siege, Israel was forbidden to destroy fruit trees unnecessarily.
God cares for human welfare better than we care for it ourselves.
His commands protect our necessities and comforts, while uncontrolled appetite and passion destroy them.
Jewish interpreters understand this law to forbid deliberate waste of any kind.
Every creature of God is good.
We should not refuse his gifts, but we should never abuse them.
The things we carelessly destroy today may be exactly what we need tomorrow.

row.cell: Respecting a captive taken to wife.
The first-born not to be disinherited for private affection.
A stubborn son to be stoned.
Malefactors not to be left hanging all night.

div.title: A murder whose perpetrator is unknown (verses 1–9)
div.p: When a murderer could not be identified, Israel was commanded to carry out a solemn ceremony acknowledging and removing the guilt from the land.
This demonstrated the deep horror with which God regarded murder.
His providence has often brought such hidden works of darkness to light.
The guilty person's sin has sometimes been revealed in unexpected ways.
Everyone should recognize the seriousness of murder and help prevent, investigate and punish it lawfully.
The elders solemnly declared that they had neither committed the murder nor helped it take place.
The priests prayed for the country and its people, asking God to show mercy.
Our prayers should seek to counter the evil with which others are filling the world.
We should learn to prevent, detect and oppose murder diligently.
We must also avoid becoming involved in other people's sins.
If we refuse to speak against fruitless works of darkness, we risk sharing in them.

div.title: A soldier and a captive woman (verses 10–14)
div.p: The law permitted an Israelite soldier, in certain circumstances, to marry a captive woman if he wished.
Henry emphasizes that allowing such a marriage did not mean approving of it.
The rule also revealed how strongly justice and honor should govern marriage, which is a sacred commitment.

div.title: The rights of the firstborn (verses 15–17)
div.p: A father was forbidden to disinherit his eldest son without just cause merely because he preferred another child.
This principle concerning children remains binding on parents.
They must give each child the rights that belong to them, without favoritism.

div.title: The stubborn and rebellious son (verses 18–21)
div.p: Notice how the offender is described.
He is stubborn and rebellious.
A child was not to be punished for limited understanding, slow learning or lack of intelligence.
The problem was deliberate refusal to obey.
Nothing draws people toward sin and makes them more obstinate than drunkenness.
People ruled by drinking forget their duty to honor their parents.
Both the father and mother were required to bring the complaint before the city's elders.
Children who deliberately reject their responsibilities should not blame their parents if affection eventually grows strained.
Under Israel's ancient law, the offender was to be publicly stoned.
Henry sees the punishment as showing the seriousness of persistent contempt for parental authority.
Though this offense does not receive that civil punishment in his own day, it remains offensive to God.
When young people become enslaved early to bodily appetite, the heart hardens and conscience loses its sensitivity.
Such a course leads toward rebellion and ruin.

div.title: The body of someone executed must be removed (verses 22 and 23)
div.p: Under the law of Moses, contact with a dead body made a person ceremonially unclean.
An executed person's body therefore could not be left hanging overnight, defiling the land.
This rule has a special connection with Christ.
Someone left hanging in such disgrace was described as cursed by God.
Henry explains that this language expressed the deepest humiliation: the person appeared rejected by both heaven and earth.
Moses used those words under the Spirit's guidance so that they could later be applied to Christ.
Through his death on the cross, Jesus endured the law's curse for us.
That reveals his love and invites us to trust him.

div.title: Neighborly kindness (verses 1–4)
div.p: If we consistently followed the rule of treating others as we would want them to treat us, many more detailed commandments would become unnecessary.
Finding an object that belongs to someone else never makes it our own property.
True religion teaches us to be good neighbors.
We should willingly do good and offer practical assistance to everyone.
We cannot know how soon we may need someone else's help.

div.title: Instructions for everyday conduct (verses 5–12)
div.p: God's providence extends to even the smallest details of life, and his commands teach us to honor him in those details.
We live under his care and watchful eye.
Some instructions may seem minor.
But because they belong to God's law, they concern matters of real importance.
If we want to show that we are his people, we must value his will and glory above the meaningless fashions of the world.
Even when choosing clothing, just as when eating or drinking, we should take care to preserve the purity of our own hearts and actions and avoid harming others.
Our purpose should be clear, our hearts sincere, and our conduct consistent in every part of life.

div.title: Laws concerning sexual purity (verses 13–30)
div.p: These and related regulations may have been necessary for Israel's historical circumstances.
But Henry says there is no need for Christians to investigate every difficult detail with undue curiosity.
Their continuing moral meaning is connected with the seventh commandment.
They restrain bodily lusts, which fight against the soul.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections

row.cell: Who are shut out from the congregation.
Of fugitive servants, Usury, and other precepts.

div.title: Those excluded from Israel's assembly (verses 1–8)
div.p: We should value the privileges of belonging to God's people, for ourselves and for our children, above every other advantage.
Under the gospel, no bodily defect, ancestor's offense or difference in nationality bars someone from the church's spiritual blessings.
But a corrupt heart can keep us from enjoying those blessings.
And the bad example of parents—or marriages that draw a family away from faith—can keep children from seeking them.

div.title: Cleanliness in Israel's camp (verses 9–14)
div.p: Nothing offensive or unclean was to be tolerated in the Lord's camp.
If Israel had to pay careful attention to the cleanliness of the body, how much more should we preserve purity of heart and mind!

div.title: The runaway servant, lending, vows and everyday generosity (verses 15–25)
div.p: It is honorable to shelter and protect someone vulnerable, provided the person is not deliberately engaged in wrongdoing.
People who convert to the truth should be treated with particular tenderness, so that they are not drawn back to worldly life.
We cannot honor God with our possessions unless we acquired them honestly.
What matters is not only what we give, but how we obtained it.
Where someone borrows money to engage in an activity that brings or may bring profit, Henry considers it just for the lender to share in that gain.
But people who borrow simply to obtain necessary food should be treated with compassion.
A solemn promise deliberately spoken must be fulfilled completely.
Israelites were allowed to pick and eat grapes or grain along their journey, but they were forbidden to carry any away.
This arrangement showed the abundant food Canaan would provide and made provision for poor travelers.
We should be similarly generous and hospitable, willing to give without treating every gift as a loss.
Yet we must not exploit the generosity of others or use permitted privileges as a way to take more than is right.
Faithfulness in our commitments and respect for other people's property should characterize God's people.

row.cell: Of new-married persons, Of man-stealers, Of pledges.

div.title: Divorce and the responsibility to bear hardship (verses 1–4)
div.p: Sometimes God's providence, or a person's own unwise choice in marriage, brings a Christian into a painful relationship rather than the companionship hoped for.
Such a person should sincerely prefer to bear the cross rather than seek a form of relief that leads toward sin, disorder and suffering.
God's grace can make that burden holy, sustain the person under it and teach conduct that gradually makes the situation more bearable.

div.title: Marriage, kidnapping and consideration for debtors (verses 5–13)
div.p: It is of great importance that love between a husband and wife be preserved.
Both should carefully avoid whatever might cause them to become distant or estranged from each other.
Kidnapping people and enslaving them was a capital crime, not an ordinary theft whose wrong could be settled merely by restitution.
The laws concerning leprosy also had to be followed carefully.
When we recognize guilt and fear God's judgment, we should not conceal the truth or try to shake off our convictions.
Instead, through repentance, prayer and humble confession, we should seek the path of forgiveness and peace.
God also gave regulations about the possessions a lender could hold as security for a loan.
We should consider another person's necessities and comfort as seriously as our own financial advantage.
Let a poor debtor keep the garment needed for sleeping and thank God for your kindness.
Debtors should recognize the generosity of creditors who refuse to take every legal advantage available to them.
Such restraint should not be regarded as weakness.

div.title: Justice and generosity toward those in need (verses 14–22)
div.p: Purity, reverence for God, justice, mercy, fair dealing, kindness to poor and vulnerable people, consideration for their needs and generosity of spirit are plainly pleasing to God.
These virtues are appropriate for everyone he has redeemed.
The difficulty lies not in proving their value, but in putting them consistently into practice in our everyday conduct.

row.cell: The ox that treadeth the corn.

div.title: Punishment must respect human dignity (verses 1–3)
div.p: Every punishment was to be carried out solemnly.
Those who saw it should be impressed by its seriousness and warned against similar wrongdoing.
The guilty might be shamed and made to suffer, but care had to be taken not to treat them as completely vile or without human dignity.
Happy are those whom the Lord disciplines in this life to humble them, so that they may not share in the world's final condemnation.

div.title: An ox working in the grain (verse 4)
div.p: Farmers were commanded to care for the animals working on their behalf.
But the command also teaches a wider duty.
We should be not only fair but kind toward everyone whose work benefits our souls (1 Corinthians 9:9).

div.title: Marriage to a brother's widow (verses 5–12)
div.p: The custom regulated here seems to have been established under Jewish law to keep family inheritances distinct.
Henry states that the same practice is not lawful now.

div.title: The use of honest weights (verses 13–16)
div.p: Dishonestly obtained wealth brings a curse upon a person's possessions, family and soul.
Happy are those who examine their own lives, repent of wrongdoing, turn away from sin and remove evil from their conduct before God brings judgment upon them.

div.title: Remembering Amalek (verses 17–19)
div.p: Everyone who persecutes or wrongs God's people should take warning from Amalek's history.
The longer judgment is delayed, the more fearful it may become when it finally arrives.
Amalek can also picture the enemies of our own souls.

May God enable us to put to death every sinful desire and corrupt influence within us or around us, together with the powers of darkness and worldly opposition that hinder us from coming to our blessed Savior.

row.cell: The prayer after disposal of the third year's tithe.
The covenant between God and the people.

div.title: Offering the firstfruits with grateful remembrance (verses 1–11)
div.p: When God fulfills his promises to us, he expects us to acknowledge the fulfillment and give him the honor for his faithfulness.
The comforts we receive through created things become doubly pleasant when we recognize that they flow from his promises.
A person bringing firstfruits was to remember the humble beginnings of the nation.
“My father was a Syrian who was about to perish.”
Moses describes Jacob as a Syrian.
Israel's ancestors had gone to live in Egypt as foreigners.
There they became enslaved.
They were once poor, despised and oppressed.
Even after becoming wealthy and powerful, the people had no reason for pride, self-confidence or forgetfulness of God.
Their offering should express heartfelt gratitude for the Lord's goodness to Israel.
The comfort we enjoy privately should make us grateful for public peace and abundant provision too.
Present blessings should call to mind mercies received long ago and those still promised for the future.
The worshiper brought the basket of firstfruits before God.
Whatever good gift we receive, he wants us to enjoy it gratefully, recognizing him as the source of every comfort.

div.title: Prayer after the third-year tithe (verses 12–15)
div.p: Even if the land produces an abundant harvest, it will give little true satisfaction unless God also adds his blessing.
This ceremony pictured the relationship between God, reconciled to his people, and each genuine believer.
It displayed the privileges and duties that belong to this relationship.
Under the covenant of grace in Jesus Christ, we should watch carefully over our lives.
We ought to show by our conduct that the Lord is our God and we are his people, while waiting in the way he appointed for the complete fulfillment of his generous promises.

div.title: The covenant and wholehearted obedience (verses 16–19)
div.p: Moses urged Israel to obey God's commands for the very purpose for which they were given.
They are the Lord's laws: do them.
Do not merely argue about them or turn away after hearing them.
Do not carry them out carelessly or hypocritically.
Obey with your whole heart and soul.
If we have professed to take the Lord as our God but refuse to follow his commandments, we have broken a sacred commitment.
We were chosen for obedience (1 Peter 1:2).
We were chosen to be holy (Ephesians 1:4).
We have been purified to become God's special people, eager not only to do good works but to devote ourselves zealously to them (Titus 2:14).
Holiness is true honor.
It is also the only path to everlasting honor.

row.cell: The law to be written on stones in the promised land.
The curses to be pronounced on mount Ebal.

div.title: God's law and the altar of uncut stone (verses 1–10)
div.p: As soon as Israel entered Canaan, the people were to erect a monument on which God's law would be written.
They were also to build an altar.

p.hi: God's word and prayer belong together.

div.p: Israelites were not free to set up other altars wherever they pleased.
But God could command one for a particular occasion.
The altar was to be built from rough, uncut stones found in the field.
Christ, our Altar, is the Stone cut from the mountain without human hands.
He was rejected by the builders as lacking outward beauty, yet God the Father accepted him and made him the chief cornerstone.
The Old Testament's written law carries a curse against transgression.
That curse would terrify us if the New Testament did not also reveal an altar—Christ—to console and save us.
Printed copies of Scripture now spare us from the need to write its words publicly in the particular manner Israel was commanded.
The purpose of gospel ministry should be to make God's word as clear as possible.
Yet even the clearest preaching cannot make us wise for salvation unless the Holy Spirit gives it saving power.
We should therefore pray continually and earnestly for the Spirit's work.

div.title: The curses announced on Mount Ebal (verses 11–26)
div.p: The six tribes assigned to pronounce blessings descended from the free women.
Henry relates this to the promise belonging to the free woman in Galatians 4:31.
Levi was included among the tribes.
Ministers should apply God's warnings and promises first to their own consciences.
They should agree with faith-filled Amen to what they announce to others.
They must encourage people through promised blessings and also warn them through the threatened curse.
Every curse was met with an Amen from the people.
That meant they accepted that God truly judges the ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings.
They also acknowledged that those who commit such wrongs deserve his judgment.
The final curse reached beyond the particular offenses named.
It included everyone who fails to carry out the whole law.
Not only committing the evil the law forbids but also neglecting the good the law commands brings guilt.
Without Christ's atoning blood, sinners cannot enjoy fellowship with a holy God or offer him anything truly acceptable.
God's righteous law condemns whoever breaks it, however briefly or in whatever way.
We remain under its curse until Christ's redemption is applied to our hearts.
Saving grace also teaches believers to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live with self-control, righteousness and reverence for God in the present world.
Such people assent to God's law and delight in it inwardly.
The truly holy life is the place where solid joy and genuine peace are found.

div.title: The blessings promised for obedience (verses 1–14)
div.p: This long chapter develops two words: blessing and curse.
Both refer to real conditions with real consequences.
The blessings are described first.
God is slow to become angry and quick to show mercy.
He delights to bless.
It is better to be attracted to goodness by the hope of God's favor, as children who trust their Father, than to be driven to obedience merely through the fear of slaves.
The promised blessing depended upon Israel's careful attention to God's voice.
If the people maintained both the outward form and inward reality of religion within their families and nation, God's providence would prosper their earthly affairs.

div.title: The curses associated with disobedience (verses 15–44)
div.p: Those who refuse God's commands not only lose the promised blessing but also place themselves under the curse.
The blessing includes true happiness; the curse brings misery.
Notice that the curse is just.
It does not come without reason or for a trivial offense.
Notice also its range and power.
Wherever the sinner travels, God's judgment follows.
Every possession and comfort becomes affected by the curse.
Earthly pleasures can turn bitter when God's anger is joined with them.
No genuine comfort remains.
Moses described many judgments that would come upon the Jewish people because of apostasy and disobedience.
Henry interprets them in light of what he believed had already happened to the Jewish people in his own day.
The final misery described includes loss of hope and comfort, leaving people close to despair.
People who live only by what they see, rather than by faith, risk losing even their sound judgment when the world around them becomes frightening.

div.title: Israel's ruin and the curse's final meaning (verses 45–68)
div.p: Consider how terrible the calamities can be when God brings judgment even in this life.
Yet these earthly sufferings are only the beginning of sorrows for those who remain under his curse.
What then will be the suffering of the place where the worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished?
Henry finds something astonishing in the history of Israel.
He describes a nation formerly favored by God as later rejected and scattered among other nations while retaining a distinct identity.
He cites the Babylonian exile, the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and later prohibitions on Jewish access to Jerusalem as fulfillments of the warnings.
These are Henry's historical and theological interpretations, retained as part of the commentary rather than new editorial judgments about Jewish people today.
He contrasts Israel's refusal to serve God joyfully with the prospect of being made to serve enemies.
Everyone will finally recognize God's greatness, willingly or under judgment.
Henry highlights the predicted loss of the land (verse 63), bodily rest (verse 65) and even peace of mind.
He observes repeated migrations, banishments and returns.
He considers the correspondence between these historical events and Mosaic prophecy evidence of Scripture's truth.
He also anticipates a future conversion of Jewish people to Christ.
He expects this to precede a wider spread of Christianity among the nations.
This, again, is Henry's reading of the prophecies, not an independent new historical claim.
Moses, speaking through God's Spirit, warned sinners before their ruin.
Such warning gives people an opportunity to repent in time, and leaves them without excuse if they refuse.
Let us be thankful that Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us.
He bore in his own person the judgment our sins deserve—judgment that otherwise would have remained upon us forever.
Let sinners flee to him for refuge.
Let believers rejoice and serve their reconciled God wholeheartedly, grateful for the abundance of his spiritual blessings.

row.cell: Moses calls Israel's mercies to remembrance.
The Divine wrath on those who flatter themselves in their wickedness.
The ruin of the Jewish nation.

div.title: Remembering past and present mercies (verses 1–9)
div.p: God's former kindnesses and his recent acts of mercy should both encourage us to obey him.
Hearing ears, seeing eyes and understanding hearts are gifts from the Lord.
Everyone who possesses them owes them to him.
God gives food, clothing, wealth and considerable possessions to many people whom he has not given saving grace.
Many enjoy the gifts without recognizing their Giver, or understanding their proper purpose.
Gratitude and wise self-interest, as well as faithful duty, therefore call us to keep the words of God's covenant.

div.title: The danger of self-confidence while sinning (verses 10–21)
div.p: The national covenant made with Israel pictured the covenant of grace with genuine believers.
It also represented the outward administration of religion under the gospel.

People who have consented to Christ's new covenant of mercy, and have dedicated themselves to be God's people, should take every opportunity to renew the public confession of their relationship to him.
Their lives should match that confession.
The sinner described here first turns away from God in the heart.
This is where the trouble begins.
Unbelief leads people to abandon the living God for lifeless idols.
The same temptation exists today.
People are drawn away by their own sinful desires and imagination.
Henry describes them as roots growing poisonous plants.
If not stopped, those weeds spread through an entire field.
Satan may disguise the bitterness of sin for a time.
But its true character will become clear, if not sooner, at the final judgment.
The presumptuous sinner hears God's warnings and still assumes there is no danger.
The threats in this passage are among the most serious in Scripture.
If only people who deliberately persist in wrongdoing would read them and tremble.
They are true declarations of God's anger against human ungodliness and injustice.

div.title: The danger of national idolatry (verses 22–28)
div.p: Moses warned that idolatry would destroy Israel as a nation.
God has sometimes brought ruin upon communities that claimed to be especially close to him.
He does not do so without just reason.
We should seek to recognize that reason, give glory to God for his justice and take warning ourselves.
The law of Moses leaves sinners under its curse and expelled from the Lord's land.
But through Christ's grace, sinners who repent and believe are planted again into his favor.
God's power then protects them from finally being torn away.

div.title: The revealed and hidden things of God (verse 29)
div.p: Moses ended his prophecy of Israel's rejection in a way comparable to Paul's conclusion on the same subject (Romans 11:33).
We are not meant to pry into God's secret purposes or claim certainty about what he has not revealed.
But we are commanded and encouraged to study diligently what he has revealed.
He has withheld nothing necessary or truly profitable for us.
Only what is good for us not to know remains hidden.
The aim of divine revelation is not to provide endless material for curious speculation or argument.
It is to enable us to obey God's law and receive his blessing.
Scripture plainly reveals what is needed for that purpose.
Going beyond it will not help us.
Through the light God has given, we may live and die in peace and finally be happy forever.

row.cell: Death and life set before them.

div.title: Mercy promised to people who return (verses 1–10)
div.p: Henry sees here a promise of mercy for Israel in the latter days.
He connects these verses with the warnings given in the previous two chapters and interprets their fulfillment through the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and Israel's long dispersion.
He also understands them as promising a future event that had not yet taken place in his time.
He expects Jewish people to be converted to faith in Christ.
Many interpreters, he notes, also expect a later return to the land of Canaan.
This is Henry's interpretation of prophecy, faithfully reported rather than newly asserted as an established prediction by the editor.
The language of this chapter is, in large part, unconditional promise rather than merely a conditional offer.
The Lord himself promises to circumcise the people's hearts.
When regenerating grace removes corruption and divine love replaces love of sin, people truly repent, turn to God and obey him.
The Lord then delights in doing good to them.
Their change is not merely outward or a change in opinions.
It reaches into their hearts.
It produces hatred of sin and wholehearted love for God, reconciled to them through Jesus Christ.
The people Henry wrote about were far from that condition.
But so were the people who helped kill Jesus before they were converted in one hour on the day of Pentecost.
In the day of God's power, a nation can be born in a day.
He will fulfill his purpose at his own time.
As a conditional promise, the passage also applies to individuals and peoples everywhere.
Even the worst sinners who repent and are converted will receive pardon and be restored to God's favor.

div.title: The command is near (verses 11–14)
div.p: God's command is not too high for ordinary people to understand.
Its meaning is not reserved for scholars.
It has been written plainly, so that even someone passing by can read it.
It is in people's mouths, in their ordinary language, available for reading and discussion with their children.
It has been made accessible even to those with little education.
This is especially true of the gospel of Christ, to which the apostle Paul applies these words.
God's word is close to us—and Christ is revealed in that word.
If we believe in our hearts that Jesus is the promised Messiah, and openly confess that faith with our mouths, we have Christ with us.

div.title: Life and death are set before the people (verses 15–20)
div.p: What appeal could be more moving or leave a deeper impression?
Everyone desires life, goodness and happiness, and hopes to escape death, evil and misery.
The Lord has shown great compassion by revealing through his word the path that leads to everlasting happiness.
If people refuse that path, the fault is theirs.
The matter can be stated simply.
Love and serve God, and you will find life and happiness.
Turn away from him, reject his service and follow false gods, and you will bring ruin on yourselves.
Since humanity's fall, there has never been more than one way to heaven.
The Old and New Testaments reveal the same way, although the New Testament makes it clearer.
Moses spoke of the same way of being accepted by God that Paul later explained more fully.
Paul spoke of the same obedience that Moses had expounded in greater detail.
Both Testaments bring the true and good way close to us and make it known.

row.cell: Moses encourages the people, and Joshua.
The law to be read every seventh year.
The Israelites' apostacy foretold, A song given to be witness against them.
The law delivered to the Levites.

div.title: Moses encourages Israel and Joshua (verses 1–8)
div.p: Moses assured Israel that God would continue to be present with the people.
The apostle applies this promise to God's spiritual Israel, giving every believer strong reason for faith and hope.
The gospel is preached to us as well: the Lord will never fail or abandon his people (Hebrews 13:5).
Moses presented Joshua as Israel's next leader.
The people already knew his wisdom, courage and affection.
God himself had appointed Joshua and would acknowledge and bless his leadership.
Joshua gladly received Moses' instruction to be strong and courageous.
Anyone who has God on their side should be bold.
Through him we can act bravely and overcome.
When we resist the devil, he will flee from us.

div.title: Reading the law aloud every seventh year (verses 9–13)
div.p: We should read God's word privately, but we must not think it unnecessary to hear it read publicly.
The law was to be read solemnly during the year of release.
That year pictured the grace of the gospel, the acceptable year of the Lord.
Forgiveness and freedom through Christ give us powerful reasons to obey his commands.
The law was to be read to all Israel: men, women, children and foreigners.
Everyone should become familiar with God's word, because its commands apply to everyone.
Those who remember how hard people once worked to obtain even fragments of Scripture should feel grateful that whole copies are so widely available today.
For many centuries, Israelites had lived under very different conditions.
Yet human hearts are naturally so careless that even abundant access to Scripture may not be enough to preserve the knowledge of God's truths, commands and worship.

div.title: Israel's future rebellion is foretold (verses 14–22)
div.p: Moses and Joshua stood before the divine Majesty at the entrance of the tabernacle.
The Lord reminded Moses that he would soon die.
Even people who are prepared and willing to die may benefit from being reminded of its approach.
God also foretold that Israel would break the covenant Moses had worked so hard to establish.
The people would abandon the Lord.
Then, in righteous judgment, he would abandon them.
Moses was instructed to give the people a song that would remain as a permanent witness.
It would testify for God, showing he had faithfully warned them, and against Israel, showing the people had neglected the warning.
God's word exposes the thoughts and intentions of the human heart.
Ministers who preach it cannot know all their listeners' thoughts.
But the God whose word they proclaim understands those thoughts perfectly.

div.title: The book of the law is entrusted to the Levites (verses 23–30)
div.p: Moses solemnly handed over the book of the law to the Levites.
It was to be placed in—or, more precisely, beside—the ark.
The song recorded in the next chapter was given to Moses and then to Israel.
He first wrote it as the Holy Spirit instructed him, then spoke it aloud before the people.
Moses warned that he knew they would become corrupt after his death.
That prospect must have caused him deep sorrow.
Yet he could take comfort in knowing that he had performed his duty.
God's glory would not fail, whether revealed through Israel's settlement in the promised land or through its dispersion.
The foundation of God's work remains secure.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections

row.cell: The character of God, The character of Israel.
The great things God had done for Israel.
The judgments which would come upon them for their sins.
The exhortation with which the song was delivered.
Moses to go up mount Nebo to die.

div.title: Moses' song begins (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Moses called heaven and earth to witness the truth and importance of what he was about to declare.
His teaching was the gospel: God's message about Jesus Christ, grace and mercy through him, and salvation and life received through him.

div.title: God's perfection and Israel's character (verses 3–6)
div.p: God is called a Rock here.
Henry notes that this is the first time Scripture uses that name for him.
The image expresses God's unchangeable power, faithfulness and love, revealed in Christ and the gospel.
We may build our hope upon that sure foundation and find shelter in him against enemies, burning heat and storms.
God's work is perfect.
This includes the saving work in which every divine perfection is displayed.
His dealings with creatures are directed by wisdom that cannot make mistakes and by flawless justice.
No one will suffer injustice at his hand.
The song also brings a serious charge against Israel.
Even God's children have faults and sinful stains while they remain in this imperfect life.
Anyone claiming complete freedom from sin is deceiving himself.
But Henry distinguishes the failings of God's children from a settled, notorious and unrepentant practice of sin, which he regards as a mark of the devil's children.
Israel acted foolishly in abandoning divine mercy for worthless idols.

div.title: God's extraordinary care for Israel (verses 7–14)
div.p: Moses recalled particular examples of the Lord's goodness toward Israel.
The eagle caring for her young was a beautiful picture of Christ's love.
Christ placed himself between God's justice and our guilty souls, bearing our sins in his body upon the tree.
Through gospel preaching and the Holy Spirit's power, he awakens sinners and draws them away from Satan's bondage.
The imagery in verses 13 and 14 also pictures believers overcoming their spiritual enemies—sin, Satan and the world—through Christ.
In him they are safe and victorious.
When their hearts are set above earthly affairs, they enjoy spiritual peace and joy.
Henry looks forward to such blessings for spiritual Israel in the latter days.

div.title: Israel abandons its Savior (verses 15–18)
div.p: Moses described two forms of Israel's wickedness, both involving apostasy.
The people were called Jeshurun.
Henry notes alternative explanations of the name: some interpret it as upright people, others as seeing people.
Israel soon lost the reputation for both righteousness and knowledge.
The people indulged bodily appetite as though their only task was to satisfy the flesh.
Proud and self-indulgent people effectively make gods of themselves and their appetites.
They turn away from the Lord and treat him as unimportant.
Henry insists that sinners have only one way of being accepted and sanctified before God.
False religion may commend other routes and call this openness, but that does not make those routes valid.
How foolish it is to forsake the Rock of salvation for the rock of ruin!

div.title: God's judgments against sin (verses 19–25)
div.p: The previous lines described Israel's rebellion.
These lines describe the judgments God's justice would bring.
We deceive ourselves if we think people may reject him while he remains indifferent.
Sin is hateful before the holy God.
We should see the harm it causes and reject the folly of laughing at it.

div.title: God withholds the vengeance Israel deserved (verses 26–38)
div.p: Israel's idolatry and rebellion deserved destruction.
Yet the Lord spared the nation.
Henry regards the preservation of the Jewish people as a continuing witness to Scripture's truth and as part of God's wise and holy purposes.
The prophecies, he says, give some idea of those purposes.
God will not allow his glorious throne to be dishonored.
It is wise to consider the end of one's life.
Such consideration often helps sinners return to him.
The passage speaks particularly about God's purpose for Israel in the latter days, but the warning applies more widely.
What happiness will sinners lose, and what misery will they encounter, if they continue rebelling against God?
“What will be the end of it?” (Jeremiah 5:31).
God will bring down his church's enemies at the time he chooses.
People who imagine themselves completely secure may suddenly be destroyed.
And the moment of greatest distress for God's people may be the moment when he appears to rescue them.
Anyone trusting in a refuge other than God will find that false refuge fail when it is needed most.
Henry understands the Jewish rejection of the Messiah as a continuation of Israel's earlier idolatry, apostasy and rebellion.
He anticipates a future humbling and repentance, followed by faith in the Mediator they have rejected and renewed deliverance and prosperity.
These are Henry's theological interpretations of the historical nation and prophecy, preserved as his words rather than asserted as new editorial judgments.

div.title: The Lord delivers his people (verses 39–43)
div.p: The end of the song contains three messages.
First, glory belongs to God. No one can escape his power.
Second, it brings terror to his enemies. God's judgment comes against those who hate him.
Third, it brings comfort to his own people. The song ends with joy.
Whatever judgments fall on sinners, those who belong to God will be cared for.

div.title: Moses urges Israel to remember the song (verses 44–47)
div.p: Moses delivered the song solemnly.
He charged Israel to remember all the good words God had spoken through him.
These matters are not trivial.
They concern life and death.
To heed them is to find everlasting life; to disregard them is to face ruin.
How good it would be if everyone were convinced that faith is the very life of the soul!

div.title: Moses is commanded to die on Nebo (verses 48–52)
div.p: Moses had completed his work.
Why should he desire to stay longer in this world?
God reminded him of the sin that had prevented him from entering Canaan.
Even the best believers should approach death with repentance for the sins and weaknesses they still remember.
But they may die peacefully whenever God calls them.
A sure hope of eternal life beyond death, founded on faith, allows them to do so even though they remember their faults.

row.cell: The blessings of the twelve tribes.

div.title: Moses blesses the tribes and describes God's majesty (verses 1–5)
div.p: Moses added a solemn blessing to all his previous instructions, warnings and prophecies.
He began by recalling the Lord's glorious appearance when he gave the law.
God's law works like fire.
When accepted, it softens hard hearts, warms and purifies them, burning away corrupt desires.
When rejected, it hardens, burns and destroys.
The Holy Spirit descended upon the church in divided tongues like fire.
The gospel is also a fiery law.
When God's law is written on a person's heart, it is evidence that divine love has been poured into that heart.
We should regard God's law as one of the gifts of his grace.

div.title: Moses blesses the tribes (verses 6–23)
div.p: The tribes were not blessed in the usual order.
The blessing pronounced on Judah may refer to the tribe as a whole or to David, who foreshadowed Christ.
Moses gave a particularly full blessing to Levi.
In our religious service, the greatest goal should be acceptance with God, whether other people approve of us or not (2 Corinthians 5:9).
Henry understands this blessing as a prophecy that the Lord will continue supplying ministers to his church until the end of time.
Benjamin's inheritance was close to Mount Zion.
Living near the appointed means of worship was a precious gift that should not be exchanged for any worldly benefit or pleasure.
We should gratefully receive the earthly gifts God sends through the seasons.
But his spiritual gifts are immeasurably greater.
They come from the Father of lights, through Christ the Sun of Righteousness, and through the Holy Spirit's influence like the rain that makes the earth fruitful.
These are the signs of God's special love: the Spirit's gifts, grace and comfort.
When Moses prayed for the favor of the One who dwelt in the burning bush, he recalled the covenant, which is the foundation of every hope we have of God's favor.
God assigns people their places to live and wisely directs them toward different occupations for the common good.
Whatever our situation or work, it is both wise and right to apply ourselves to it and be content.
We should not merely invite other people into God's service.
We should also abound in it ourselves.
The blessing on Naphtali leads Henry to a final observation: God's favor alone can satisfy the soul.
Those who have it are truly happy, and they recognize that in possessing it they need nothing more.

div.title: Strength for each day (verses 24 and 25)
div.p: For true believers, all their circumstances can be made holy.
When they travel along a difficult road, God equips them with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace.
“As your days, so shall your strength be.”
In Scripture, a day can mean the events and troubles that take place during it.
The promise is that God will continually and graciously sustain his people through whatever burdens or trials he appoints.
It belongs to all Abraham's spiritual descendants.
If they have work to do, they will be given strength for it.
If burdens are laid upon them, God will provide what they need to carry them.
He will never allow them to be tested beyond the strength he supplies.

div.title: The incomparable blessing of belonging to God (verses 26–29)
div.p: No people had a God like Israel's God.
The blessings proclaimed over Israel can also be applied to the spiritual church.
No people have a better dwelling place. Those who make God their home receive the comfort and protection of his presence (Psalm 91:1).
No people receive firmer support. God's everlasting arms hold up his people when they are brought very low.
His grace prevents their spirits from collapsing and their faith from failing (2 Corinthians 12:9).
No people are better governed. Through the Christ who loves them, believers become more than conquerors over their spiritual enemies.
No people enjoy better security. Israel can dwell safely, and those who remain close to God are protected by him.
No people receive a better inheritance. Every true Israelite looks by faith toward the heavenly Canaan, which contains better things than grain and wine.
No people have better help. In every danger or need, the eternal God is available to them.
Those whom he helps cannot finally be destroyed.
No people are better armed. Those who possess holiness in their hearts are defended by the complete armor of God (Ephesians 6).
No people have a surer promise of victory. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under believers' feet (Romans 16:20).
May the Lord help us set our hearts on things above, turning away from earthly possessions that will soon perish.
May we not share the hopelessness of Israel's enemies, but enter the realm of everlasting love and joy with God's true Israel.

row.cell: Moses views the promised land from mount Nebo.
The death and burial of Moses, The mourning of the people.
Joshua succeeds Moses, The praise of Moses.

div.title: Moses views Canaan from Mount Nebo (verses 1–4)
div.p: Moses had shown no desire to abandon his work before it was completed.
But once his work was finished, he showed no unwillingness to die.
God had made clear that Moses would not enter Canaan.
Yet the Lord also promised that he could see the land.
He gave him a view of the whole good country.
Believers sometimes receive a similar glimpse, through grace, of the happiness and glory prepared for them.
God may reserve the brightest discoveries of his kindness for his people near the end of life, to strengthen them as they die.
Those who die believing in Christ and hoping for heaven can leave this world joyfully.

div.title: Moses dies and Israel mourns (verses 5–8)
div.p: Moses obeyed God's command to die as willingly as the other commands he had received, though it might seem harder than any of them.
In this he resembled our Lord Jesus.
Yet there was a profound contrast.
Moses died peacefully, with honor, and without severe physical suffering.
Jesus died on a shameful and agonizing cross.
Moses died at the mouth of the Lord, according to God's command.
God's servants, when all their other work is done, must finally die.
They should be prepared to return home whenever their Master calls (Acts 21:13).
No one knew the place where Moses was buried.
If the soul is at rest with God, the place where the body lies matters comparatively little.
Moses' bodily strength had not failed.
His mind remained clear and active, and his memory was as strong as ever.
Henry regards this as a reward for his service and remarkable meekness.
Israel mourned solemnly for him.
But even after great losses, we must not allow grief to consume us.
If we hope to go joyfully to heaven, why should we approach the grave with nothing but sorrow?

div.title: Joshua succeeds Moses; Christ is greater than both (verses 9–12)
div.p: Moses brought Israel to the borders of Canaan and then died.
This pictured a deeper truth: the law makes nothing perfect (Hebrews 7:19).
It brings sinners into the wilderness of conviction but cannot bring them into the settled rest and peace of the heavenly Canaan.
That work belongs to Joshua, whose name is the same as the name of our Lord Jesus.
Joshua was a picture of him.
What the law could not accomplish, Jesus accomplished (Romans 8:3).
Through him we receive peace of conscience now and everlasting rest in heaven.
Moses was greater than every other Old Testament prophet.
Yet Jesus was greater than Moses by far more than Moses surpassed the prophets who came before or after him.
Notice the likeness between Israel's redeemer and the Redeemer of humanity.
Moses was sent by God to free Israel from cruel bondage.
He led the people out and overcame their enemies.
He became their deliverer, lawgiver and judge, bringing them to the very edge of the promised land.
Jesus came to rescue us from slavery to the devil and restore us to freedom and happiness.
He confirmed every moral command God had first given.
But he also writes the law, not upon stone tablets, but upon the living tablets of our hearts.
He will judge humanity.
God has appointed a day when Christ will expose the secrets of every person and reward or punish each one with perfect justice.
Because he is so much greater than Moses, we who follow Christ should obey him faithfully and live consistently with the holy faith we profess.
May God graciously enable us all to do so!

div.title: Joshua — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: The book of Joshua tells how Israel entered Canaan, conquered the land and divided it among the tribes under Joshua's leadership.
It also records the people's history until Joshua's death.
The book wonderfully reveals God's power and faithfulness in fulfilling his promises to Israel.
It also describes his carrying out the judgments he had justly threatened against the Canaanites.
These events should teach us to take seriously the fearful warnings God's word gives to sinners who refuse to repent.
They should also encourage us to seek refuge in Jesus Christ.

row.cell: The Lord appoints Joshua to succeed Moses.
The people promise to obey Joshua.

div.title: The Lord appoints Joshua (verses 1–4)
div.p: Joshua had served Moses faithfully for years.
The person now called to honor had first spent a long time working and learning.
Our Lord Jesus took the form of a servant.
Joshua had learned to obey before receiving authority.
Those who have learned to obey are best fitted to lead.
When useful servants of God are taken away, those who remain should become more diligent in doing good.
God ordered Joshua to rise and cross the Jordan.
At that time the river had overflowed its banks.
Joshua had no boats or bridge.
Yet, because God commanded the crossing, he had to trust that God would open the way.

div.title: The promise of God's presence (verses 5–9)
div.p: Joshua was to make God's law his rule.
He was commanded to meditate on it day and night so that he would understand it.
No amount of worldly business should cause us to neglect the one thing that is truly necessary.
Everything Joshua commanded the people and every judgment he gave had to agree with God's law.
He remained under that law himself.
No position of power or honor places anyone above God's commands.
Joshua was to draw courage from the promise of God's presence.
His personal weaknesses were no reason to despair.
The all-sufficient God had called, appointed and commissioned him and would uphold him in his duty.
When we are acting according to God's command, we have good reason to be strong and courageous.
Jesus Christ, whom Joshua pictured, was also strengthened through his suffering by his dedication to his Father's will and command.

div.title: Israel prepares to cross (verses 10–15)
div.p: Joshua told Israel that the people would cross the Jordan and possess Canaan because God had promised it.
We honor God's truth when we do not waver in unbelief concerning his promises.
The two and a half tribes who had settled east of the Jordan had to cross with their brothers.
When God gives us rest, we should consider how we can help others still struggling to obtain it.

div.title: The people promise obedience (verses 16–18)
div.p: Israel promised Joshua willing obedience.
The people would follow his commands without grumbling or arguing and go wherever he sent them.
The best thing we can ask God to give our civil leaders is his own presence.
That will make them a blessing to the people they serve.
When we pray for them in this way, we also seek our own good.
May we willingly follow the Captain of our salvation, obey his commands and fight the good fight of faith alongside everyone who trusts and loves his name.
Christ's authority will finally prevail.

row.cell: Rahab receives and hides two Israelites.

div.title: Rahab protects the spies (verses 1–7)
div.p: Faith in God's promises does not make careful action unnecessary.
Instead, faith encourages us to use the appropriate means.
God's providence guided Israel's spies to Rahab's home.
God knew there was someone there who would be faithful to them, although they could not have known it.
Rahab appears to have been an innkeeper.
Henry thinks her former reputation for immoral living is uncertain; if it was true, she had left those practices behind.
Events that appear accidental to us often serve great purposes under God's providence.
Rahab welcomed the spies despite her king and nation's hostility to Israel.
Her action was an expression of faith (James 2:25).
True faith gave her courage to rise above fear of other people and cast in her lot with God's people.
She helped them because she respected Israel and its God, not because she expected profit or intended wrongdoing.
But Henry refuses to excuse the falsehood she told.
Even if excuses can be suggested, we should not explain away her guilt.
Her knowledge of God's law was limited.
A similar lie told by someone possessing the fuller light of revelation would deserve serious correction.

div.title: Rahab and the spies agree on her protection (verses 8–21)
div.p: Rahab had heard of God's miracles for Israel.
She trusted that his promises and warnings would certainly come true.
She recognized that safety lay only in submitting to him and joining his people.
This revealed the genuine principle of divine faith within her.
Notice the spies' promises.
God's goodness is described through kindness and truth (Psalm 117:2).
We should imitate him in both qualities.
People who intend to keep promises conscientiously will make them carefully.
The spies included necessary conditions in their agreement.
The scarlet cord recalls the Passover blood placed upon Israelite doorposts.
It pictured the sinner's safety under Christ's atoning blood and the need to seek refuge there from God's righteous judgment.
The cord Rahab used to help save the spies would also be used for her own safety.
What we employ in honoring and serving God may become an instrument of his blessing toward us.

div.title: The spies report to Joshua (verses 22–24)
div.p: The spies returned with encouraging news.
The people of Canaan were losing courage because of Israel.
They had neither the wisdom to surrender nor the courage to resist.
A troubled conscience and fear of God's anger may terrify ungodly people without leading them to repentance.
That fear can be a warning that judgment is near.
But even the greatest sinners may still receive abundant grace.
Let them flee without delay to Christ, and all will be well.

row.cell: The Lord encourages joshua—Joshua encourages the people.
The Israelites pass through Jordan on dry land.

div.title: Israel approaches the Jordan (verses 1–6)
div.p: The Israelites approached the Jordan in faith.
They had been told they would cross and therefore came as far as they could.
When we know our duty, we should proceed as far as possible and trust the Lord to open the way.
Joshua rose early.
Scripture makes special mention of his early rising here and on other occasions.
He valued doing God's work more than personal ease.
People who accomplish important things must not be ruled by a love of sleep.
Anyone occupying public office should attend faithfully to the duties of that position.
The people were to follow the ark.
Likewise, we must follow God's word and the Holy Spirit's guidance in everything.
We should follow ministers only as far as they follow Christ.
The way across the Jordan was unlike anything Israel had encountered before.
Our lives also bring roads we have never walked and challenges we have never faced.
Yet in the path of duty we can go forward with courage and joy.
Poverty, suffering, exhausting work, persecution, public shame and even death may lie along that road.
But Christ, the Author and Perfecter of our faith, has already traveled it.
By faith we can see his footsteps along every dangerous stretch of the journey.
He invites us to follow him toward the glory where he now is.
Israel had to consecrate itself.
If we wish to experience God's love and power, we must put away sin and avoid grieving the Holy Spirit.

div.title: The Lord strengthens Joshua and Israel (verses 7–13)
div.p: God announced that the Jordan's waters would be cut off.
This would repeat the wonder of the Red Sea, though in different circumstances.
The Lord has just as much power to finish the salvation of his people as he has to begin it.
God's word was with Joshua as truly as it had been with Moses.
His acts of favor toward his people should strengthen our faith and hope.
The Lord's work is perfect.
He will preserve those who belong to him.
The Jordan's overflowing water could not keep Israel out of Canaan.
And the power of Canaan's inhabitants could not drive Israel out again while God stood with the people.

div.title: Israel crosses the river on dry ground (verses 14–17)
div.p: The Jordan had overflowed all its banks.
This made the miracle of crossing even more remarkable and displayed God's kindness.
However strong the opposition to God's saving work may become, he can overcome it.
After the long and weary wilderness journey, entering Canaan through the Jordan pictured a believer's passage through death into heaven.
Jesus, pictured by the ark, has gone before his people.
He crossed the river when it was overflowing.
Let us treasure our experiences of his faithful, tender care.
Their memory will strengthen our faith and hope in our final struggle.

row.cell: The twelve stones placed in Gilgal.

div.title: Memorial stones taken from the river (verses 1–9)
div.p: The Lord's works are so worthy of remembrance, and human hearts so prone to forget them, that we need frequent reminders.
Such reminders honor God.
They benefit us and our children.
God therefore commanded Israel to prepare a memorial of the Jordan crossing.

div.title: The crossing is completed (verses 10–19)
div.p: The priests carrying the ark did not move until the Lord directed them.
No one should grow weary of waiting while the signs of God's presence remain with them, even in the depths of hardship.
God also honored Joshua.
People are respected in the best way and for the best reason when others recognize that the Lord is with them and that they live before him.

div.title: The memorial at Gilgal (verses 20–24)
div.p: Parents should teach their children about God's words and works from an early age, training them to follow his ways.
In everything we teach children, we should lead them to fear and honor the Lord.
Sincere faith is the best education.
We are just as obligated as Israel to praise our God's kindness.
Should we not establish memorials of gratitude toward the Lord, who has brought us through danger and distress in so many remarkable ways?
He has helped us just as truly as he helped the faithful people of earlier generations.
How ungrateful and unthinking we are when we fail to recognize his hand in our repeated deliverances!

row.cell: The Canaanites are afraid, Circumcision renewed.
The passover at Gilgal, The manna ceases.
The Captain of the Lord's host appears to Joshua.

div.title: Circumcision is renewed at Gilgal (verses 1–9)
div.p: How dreadful is the condition of people who see God's righteous judgment approaching but cannot turn it away or escape it!
That will be the final condition of the wicked.
The anguish and fear cannot adequately be described.
If only sinners would heed the warning now, before it is too late, and flee to the refuge offered in the gospel!
God brought such fear upon the Canaanites, breaking their courage.
This gave Israel a brief period of rest.
Circumcision was renewed and the disgrace associated with Egypt was rolled away.
The people were publicly acknowledged as God's freeborn children, bearing the seal of his covenant.
When God completes his people's salvation, he silences their enemies and turns their reproaches back upon them.

div.title: Passover is observed and manna ceases (verses 10–12)
div.p: Israel celebrated the Passover at its appointed time on the plains near Jericho, despite the hostile Canaanites nearby.
The Lord fulfilled his promise that, when the people gathered for the appointed feasts, their land would remain under his special protection (Exodus 34:24).
Manna ceased as soon as the Israelites ate the old grain of Canaan.
God had provided it when they needed it.
He kept providing it for precisely as long as it was necessary.
We should not expect miraculous provision when the same needs can be met through ordinary means.
God's word and appointed acts of worship are like spiritual manna, feeding his people through the wilderness of this world.
Although we repeatedly forfeit these gifts through our sin, he graciously continues giving them while we remain here.
When we enter heavenly Canaan, we will no longer need them in the same way.

div.title: Joshua meets the Captain of the Lord's army (verses 13–15)
div.p: This is the first recorded appearance of God's glory to Joshua.
Someone appeared before him in the form of a man.
Henry identifies him as the Son of God, the eternal Word.
Joshua gave the visitor divine honor.
He received that honor, which a merely created angel would refuse.
He is also called Jehovah in Joshua 6:2.
Christ appeared to Abraham as a traveler and to Joshua as a warrior.
He meets his people in the way their faith and circumstances require.
The Captain held a drawn sword.
This encouraged Joshua to prosecute the war courageously.
It showed that Christ was ready to defend and rescue his people.
Joshua needed to know whether this person was a friend or enemy.
In the conflict between Christ and Satan, no one can remain neutral as they might in ordinary disputes.
Joshua's question showed his genuine desire to know and obey the Lord's will.
Every true Christian must fight under Christ's banner.
Through his presence and help, they will overcome.

row.cell: Jericho is taken, Rahab and her family are saved.

div.title: The siege of Jericho (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jericho was determined not to submit to Israel. The city was strongly fortified, both by its position and by human defenses, and its gates were shut.
But the people were foolishly strengthening themselves against the Almighty. Their hardened hearts would bring about their destruction.
God had determined that Israel would take Jericho, and quickly. The people were not commanded to prepare an ordinary military siege.
By this unusual method, the Lord honored the ark as the visible sign of his presence. He taught Israel that every victory would come from him.
The people's faith and patience were tested and strengthened.

div.title: Israel marches around the city (verses 6–16)
div.p: Wherever the ark went, the people followed.
Likewise, ministers should sound the trumpet of the everlasting gospel, proclaiming freedom and victory and encouraging Christians in their spiritual conflict.
God's promised deliverances must be sought in his way and awaited at his time.
At last, when the command came, the people shouted, and Jericho's walls fell.
This was a shout of faith: they believed God's promise that the walls would fall.
It was also a shout of prayer: they cried to heaven for help, and help came.

div.title: Jericho falls, and Rahab's family is spared (verses 17–27)
div.p: Jericho became a solemn and dreadful offering to God's justice against a people who had filled up the measure of their sins.
