The One who had given the inhabitants life as their Creator now carried out the sentence their sins had deserved.
Rahab was not destroyed with those who did not believe (Hebrews 11:31).
Her relatives were spared with her. In this Henry sees a picture of the salvation that comes to a household through faith in Christ (Acts 16:31).
They were rescued like burning pieces of wood snatched from the fire.
The choice before us is equally serious: will we belong to Rahab's company or to the people of Jericho?
Our portion depends on whether we receive or reject the sign of salvation—faith in Christ working through love.
Let us remember the weight of that choice and act accordingly.
Where God's curse rests, no one can escape its consequences. It brings ruin beyond remedy.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections

row.cell: God instructs Joshua what to do.
Achan is detected, He is destroyed.

div.title: Israel is defeated at Ai (verses 1–5)
div.p: Achan secretly took some of Jericho's possessions that God had forbidden Israel to keep.
Love for the world is a deeply rooted bitterness, difficult to remove from the heart.
We must guard against sin, lest others be troubled or defiled through us (Hebrews 12:15).
We should also guard against joining others in wrongdoing, lest we share their guilt.
Our responsibility to care for one another includes helping prevent sin, because one person's wrongdoing may injure many others.
Israel's easy victory at Jericho led the people to despise their next enemy and to expect God to win every battle without their using proper means.
People can similarly twist the doctrine of divine grace and God's promises into excuses for laziness and self-indulgence.
We must work out our salvation, even though God himself is at work within us.
Israel's defeat became a costly victory for the Canaanites.
Through it, Israel was awakened, corrected and reconciled to God, while its enemies became more hardened in the path leading toward their own ruin.

div.title: Joshua humbles himself and prays (verses 6–9)
div.p: Joshua was more concerned for the honor of God's name than even for Israel's fate.
That concern was an expression of the Spirit of adoption.
He feared that Israel's defeat would cast doubt upon God's wisdom, power, goodness and faithfulness.
He pleaded with the Lord.
We can present no better argument in prayer than: “Lord, what will you do for your great name?”
If God is glorified in everything, we may welcome whatever he chooses.

div.title: God reveals the hidden sin (verses 10–15)
div.p: God told Joshua what needed to be removed from the camp before Israel could prosper again.
Danger and distress should call us to reform our lives.
We must look into our hearts, households and habits for anything God condemns: a hidden desire, unjust gain or an improper withholding of something owed to God or others.
We cannot expect to prosper spiritually while we preserve what the Lord commands us to abandon.
When sin is exposed, we must acknowledge God's righteous judgment.
He distinguishes with perfect knowledge between the innocent and the guilty.
Even when righteous people belong to the same tribe, family or household as the wicked, God will not finally judge them as though they were the same.

div.title: Achan's crime is discovered and judged (verses 16–26)
div.p: How foolish it is for sinners to imagine that their wrongdoing can remain secret.
God has many ways of bringing hidden deeds to light.
When suffering comes, we should humbly ask him, as Job did, to show us why he is contending with us.
Achan's sin began with what he saw, just as Eve saw the forbidden fruit.
He allowed his heart to follow his eyes.
Those who want to avoid sinful actions must resist sinful desires, especially the craving for wealth.
With the eyes of faith, Achan would have recognized that the possessions were under God's ban and feared to take them.
Looking only with bodily eyes, he saw attractive objects and coveted them.
After taking them, he hid them.
They became a burden he could not openly use.
Temptations look very different from a distance than they do after we have yielded to them.
What seems delightful while we commit a sin becomes bitter when we remember it afterward.
Sin deceives.
People who rob God rob themselves of peace.
And their wrongdoing harms others around them.
Achan did not die alone. His sons and daughters died with him.
Henry considers it probable, not certain, that they knew of the hidden possessions and had helped conceal them.
The consequences of one person's sin may be fatal even to family members.
One sinner destroys much good.
What, then, will the final judgment be like?
Let us flee to Jesus Christ, the sinner's Friend, for refuge.
Achan's confession reveals the progress of sin from desire, to action, to concealment—a pattern present in many offenses against God's law and against the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.

row.cell: The destruction of Ai and its king.
The law read on Ebal and Gerizim.

div.title: God encourages Joshua again (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Only after Israel had faithfully removed the forbidden thing that separated it from God did the Lord speak fresh words of comfort and guidance.
When God shows us how to continue our work and spiritual warfare, we have good reason to believe he has restored us to fellowship with him.
Joshua was commanded to attack Ai again.
This time the possessions of the city were not forbidden, as they had been at Jericho. There was therefore no temptation to repeat Achan's particular trespass.
Achan had grasped at possessions God forbade him to take.
He lost both the goods and his life.
Israelites who refused the forbidden things soon received permitted possessions instead.
The way to enjoy what God allows us is to refrain from what he forbids us.
No one finally loses through self-denial.

div.title: Ai is captured (verses 3–22)
div.p: Notice Joshua's care, skill and good judgment.
Anyone seeking to persevere in spiritual conflict must not become devoted to ease.
Henry considers it probable that Joshua went alone into the valley to pray for God's blessing.
He did not seek it in vain.
Joshua did not withdraw before the work was finished.
Those who have raised their hands against spiritual enemies must not lower them prematurely.

div.title: Ai and its king are destroyed (verses 23–29)
div.p: God, the righteous Judge, had pronounced sentence upon the Canaanites because of their wickedness.
Israel carried out that ancient judgment.

p.hi: Nothing in Israel's conduct here should be treated as a precedent for other people.

div.p: Henry considers it likely that the king of Ai had committed exceptionally serious offenses—perhaps even blasphemy against Israel's God.
He offers this as a conjecture, not a verified fact.

div.title: The covenant is renewed at Ebal and Gerizim (verses 30–35)
div.p: Joshua reached the mountains Ebal and Gerizim.
He did not put off renewing the covenant merely because Israel had not yet fully settled in the land and enemies still threatened it.
He followed God's instructions (Deuteronomy 11; 27).
We must not postpone covenanting with God until our worldly circumstances are settled.
No ordinary responsibility should cause us to neglect the one thing that is necessary.
The path to real prosperity begins with seeking God first (Matthew 6:33).
Joshua built an altar, and the people offered sacrifices.
Through those offerings, Israel dedicated itself to God as a living sacrifice through a Mediator.
Through Christ's sacrifice of himself, we have peace with God.
It is a great mercy when a people possesses God's law in writing.
That written law should be available in a language people know, so that everyone can see and read it.

row.cell: They obtain peace, but are soon detected.
The Gibeonites are to be bondmen.

div.title: Canaan's kings unite against Israel (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Until this point, the Canaanites had mainly fought to defend themselves. Now their rulers planned to attack Israel together.
Although those nations had often been enemies of one another, they put aside their quarrels to oppose God's people.
How much better it would be if God's people learned to put the good of the whole community above private interests.
They should settle their disputes and unite in resisting the enemies of God's kingdom.

div.title: The Gibeonites seek peace (verses 3–13)
div.p: Most neighboring nations heard of God's works and responded by making war.
The Gibeonites heard the same news and sought peace.
The gospel likewise has different effects on different people.
For some it is the fragrance of life; for others, the fragrance of death (2 Corinthians 2:16).
The same sun softens wax and hardens clay.
The Gibeonites' deception was not justified.
We must never do evil in the hope that good will come from it.
Had they truly presented themselves as people submitting to Israel's God, Henry thinks Joshua might have been directed by God to spare them.
But after telling their first lie about coming from a far country, they needed more lies to support it.
One falsehood leads to another, and then another. The road of deceit runs steadily downhill.
Yet their faith and prudence in seeking mercy deserve praise.
By submitting to Israel, they submitted to the God of Israel and were turning away from their old idolatry.
We can do no better than throw ourselves upon the mercy of the perfectly good God.
Repentance is the way to meet and escape judgment.
Let us follow the Gibeonites by seeking peace with God, humbled over sin.
Let us become servants of Jesus, our blessed Joshua, and live.

div.title: Joshua and the leaders keep their oath (verses 14–21)
div.p: The Israelites examined the Gibeonites' provisions and quickly decided their story must be true.
They did not ask God for direction through his word and prayer.
When we hurry without consulting him, our haste often leads to trouble.
The lie was soon discovered.
But there was an important distinction.
An oath requiring someone to commit sin is not binding, because no promise can make an evil act right.
Yet sparing Canaanites who sincerely submitted and abandoned idolatry was not unlawful.
Joshua's promise therefore remained binding, despite the fraud.
A citizen of Zion keeps a sworn promise even at personal cost (Psalm 15:4).
Joshua and the leaders did not try to escape their oath by asking Eleazar to release them from it or by claiming that promises to deceptive people did not matter.
Their example teaches us to keep promises conscientiously and honor the agreements we have made.

div.title: The Gibeonites become servants (verses 22–27)
div.p: The Gibeonites did not attempt to justify their lie.
They explained that they had been afraid of losing their lives.
Their fear was not simply of Israel's military strength; it was of God's power, which they knew was acting against them.
Joshua assigned them permanent service connected with God's house.
Even humble work becomes honorable when it is done in the Lord's service.
Let us likewise submit to Jesus, our true Joshua, saying: “We are in your hand. Do with us whatever is good and right, but save our souls.”
If he appoints us to carry a cross and serve him, the work will not be shameful or cause us lasting grief.
The humblest service in his house comes with the promise of dwelling with him.
We do not approach Christ with only a remote possibility of acceptance.
He invites sinners to come near and assures us that he will never turn away the one who comes to him.
Even the hard and humbling demands that test the sincerity of our faith will ultimately benefit us.

row.cell: Joshua succours Gibeon, The sun and moon stand still.
The kings are taken, their armies defeated, and they are put to death.
Seven other kings defeated and slain.

div.title: Five kings attack Gibeon (verses 1–6)
div.p: When sinners abandon Satan's service and friendship with the world and seek peace with God, their former friends may turn into enemies.
They should not be surprised when the world hates them.
Satan uses fear of opposition to discourage many people who are convinced of their danger and almost persuaded to become Christians, but who fear the cross.
Such experiences should encourage us to ask God for protection, help and deliverance.

div.title: Joshua rescues Gibeon; the sun and moon stand still (verses 7–14)
div.p: Those who have only recently begun trusting God have as much right to protection and care as people who have served him faithfully for many years.
We should defend those who suffer because of their connection with us or because of the gospel.
Joshua did not abandon the Gibeonites, who had only recently become his dependents.
How much less will Jesus, our true Joshua, abandon anyone trusting him!
Our trust may be weak, but its object never fails.
God's promises should encourage our efforts, not replace them.
Joshua acted with great faith, and God answered through a miraculous prolonging of the day.
Henry explains that Joshua acted upon an impulse from the Holy Spirit.
It was not necessary for Joshua or the account of this miracle to use modern astronomical terms.
To the Israelites, the sun appeared above Gibeon and the moon above the valley of Aijalon.
They appeared to remain there for an entire day.
“Is anything too hard for the Lord?” answers every objection to God's power.
The miracle announced to the nations around Israel that the Lord was near his people in a remarkable way.

div.title: The five kings are judged (verses 15–27)
div.p: No one dared speak against Israel during its victory, showing how thoroughly God protected the people.
The kings were called to account as enemies of God's Israel.
Their wickedness had reached its full measure.
The act of public justice against them warned Israel how seriously God hated the sins of the nations being driven out.
Henry also sees this as a picture of Christ's victory over the powers of darkness and of believers' victories through him.
In spiritual warfare, one important victory is not enough.
We must pursue the remaining sins that arise within our hearts and continue the struggle until it is complete.
The Lord will give light and help for that work.

div.title: Other kings and cities are defeated (verses 28–43)
div.p: Joshua acted quickly.
How much can be accomplished in a short time when we are diligent and make good use of our opportunities!
The judgments displayed God's hatred of idolatry and the other serious sins in which Canaan had become involved.
Henry understands the destruction of those nations as a warning of the final judgment upon people who reject Jesus and despise the riches of his grace.
The Lord fought for Israel.
The people could not have won without his undertaking the battle on their behalf.
We overcome because God fights for us.
If he is for us, who can stand against us?

row.cell: Divers kings overcome at the waters of Merom.
All that country subdued, The Anakims cut off.

div.title: The kings are defeated at the waters of Merom (verses 1–9)
div.p: God's miracles for Israel were intended to encourage the people to act energetically themselves.
In the same way, preaching the gospel against Satan's kingdom was initially accompanied and helped by miracles.
Now that the gospel has been clearly demonstrated to be from God, we depend on his grace in its ordinary operation and use the sword of the Spirit.
God encouraged Joshua.
Fresh dangers and difficulties call for fresh support from the word of God, which is always near us and available in every time of need.
God measures our trials according to our strength and supplies strength according to our trials.
Joshua obeyed God's command to destroy the enemy's horses and chariots. His obedience showed self-denial.
Possessing things on which the worldly heart is tempted to rely can harm faith and fellowship with God.
It is better to lose worldly advantages than endanger our souls through dependence on them.

div.title: Hazor is captured and burned (verses 10–14)
div.p: The Canaanites had filled the measure of their sins.
As a judgment, God left them to their pride, stubbornness, hostility and Satan's power.
The restraints that might have checked them were removed.
God's providential dealings exposed them to despair.
Through their rebellion, they brought upon themselves the punishment they deserved.
The Israelites carried out the judgment God had commanded through Moses.

div.title: The territory is subdued and the Anakim defeated (verses 15–23)
div.p: Let God's Israel never fear the descendants of Anak: their fall will come at the appointed time.
The land had rest from war.
That was not a peaceful alliance with the Canaanites, which God had forbidden.
It meant that the Canaanites were no longer at war with Israel.
A better rest remains for God's people. They will enter it after their spiritual warfare is complete.
What happened here fulfilled what God had said to Moses.
When God's word and his works are considered together, each helps explain the other.
If we obey our duty conscientiously, we may trust that God will fulfill his promise.
But believers must never lay aside their armor or expect permanent peace in this life.
As their strength and usefulness grow, they may face more difficult trials.
Yet God will not allow any enemy to attack them before he has prepared them for the struggle.
Jesus Christ lives forever to intercede for his people.
Their faith will not finally fail, however severely Satan may attack.
Even when spiritual conflict is long, sharp and difficult, we can endure patiently through joyful hope.
Before long, the believer will rest from both sin and sorrow in the heavenly Canaan.

row.cell: The two kings conquered by Moses.

div.title: The two kings conquered under Moses (verses 1–6)
div.p: New blessings should not make us forget the mercies God gave us earlier.
Nor should the new work he gives us cause us to forget the good work others accomplished before us.
Moses gave part of the land promised to Israel to the two and a half tribes on the east side of the Jordan.
It was rich, fertile land.
But Joshua was to give the rest to Israel's tribes.
In this Henry sees a picture of Christ, the true Joshua, giving the inheritance of heavenly Canaan to all God's spiritual Israel.

div.title: The kings conquered under Joshua (verses 7–24)
div.p: The record names thirty-one kings defeated by Joshua.
Henry describes Canaan as exceptionally fruitful and pleasant at the time Israel entered it, so that many petty rulers could live there in relative prosperity.
He contrasts that description with the land's condition in his own day.
He interprets its loss of fruitfulness as connected to the Jewish rejection of Christ and appeals to Deuteronomy 29:23.
This is Henry's historical and theological assessment, not an independently verified modern claim about the land or its people.
God's judgments are righteous.
We should also remember that he fulfills his promises.
Let the record of former deliverances teach us gratitude for our own mercies.
Let it also lead us to trust God for the blessings still promised to his church.

row.cell: Bounds of the land not yet conquered.

div.title: The territory that remains to be taken (verses 1–6)
div.p: Joshua had grown old.
Henry considers him to have been around one hundred years old, but that is an estimate rather than a date stated in this passage.
It is a reminder that even the most useful servants of God must eventually be set aside from active work.
We are all moving toward the end of our earthly lives.
Whatever our hands find to do, we should do it with our strength (Ecclesiastes 9:10).
It is good when people who are advanced in age can look back on fruitful labor and encourage others to continue what remains unfinished.
Joshua still had work to arrange, even though he could not personally conquer all the remaining territory.
God's promises never fail merely because one human worker's strength is ending.
The Lord had promised to drive out the remaining Canaanites and would fulfill that promise at the proper time.
His people nevertheless had to exert themselves and act upon what he promised.

div.title: The distribution of land east of the Jordan (verses 7–33)
div.p: The territories were assigned to Israel's tribes according to God's direction, not seized merely by whoever was most powerful.
The Lord gives different people their rightful places.
We should accept our own portion with gratitude instead of grasping at what belongs to others.
Under the gospel, Joshua pictures Jesus Christ, who obtains the heavenly inheritance for his people and gives them their share in it.
Moses had already granted Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh land east of the Jordan.
Their possessions were to remain within their appointed boundaries.
They had no right to claim additional land merely because God had shown them favor.
The Levites, unlike the other tribes, did not receive an ordinary territorial inheritance.
The Lord himself was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20).
Those serving in sacred ministry should not be driven by desire for riches or entangled in worldly concerns.
The community ought to provide for their legitimate needs, allowing them to devote themselves to the work entrusted to them.
We should all seek a better inheritance than earthly wealth.
God himself is a more precious portion than all the possessions we could gain.

row.cell: The nine tribes and a half to have their inheritance.

div.title: The inheritance of the nine and a half tribes (verses 1–5)
div.p: The Israelites had to settle the land they had conquered. Conquering Canaan would have served little purpose if they did not go on to live there.
Yet each person was not free to choose any place that appealed to him. God would choose their inheritance.
Let us consider both the mercies God has already given us and the inheritance he has promised us—the eternal home in heaven.
Does God show favoritism? Is it not better to have our earthly happiness and suffering assigned by the infinite wisdom of our heavenly Father than by our own ignorance?

Christ has revealed the great mystery of godliness, and Jesus Christ has purchased our redemption. Those who have received such grace should gladly entrust their earthly affairs to the Father's wise arrangement.

div.title: Caleb receives Hebron (verses 6–15)
div.p: Caleb asked Joshua, “Give me this mountain”—that is, Hebron. God had promised it to him before, and Caleb wanted Israel to see how highly he valued that promise.
Those who live by faith prize what God has expressly promised more than what they receive merely through his providential care.
The Anakim still possessed Hebron. By asking for it, Caleb showed that he was not afraid of those enemies. He also intended to encourage Israel to continue its conquests.
Caleb lived up to his name, which Henry explains as meaning “all heart.” Hebron was granted to Caleb and his descendants because he had followed the Lord God of Israel wholeheartedly.
Happy are we if we follow the Lord in the same way. Exceptional faithfulness will be crowned with exceptional favor.

row.cell: The borders of the lot of Judah.

div.title: Judah's boundaries (verses 1–12)
div.p: Before Israel left Gilgal, Joshua assigned the inheritances of Judah, Ephraim and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
Later the people moved to Shiloh, where another survey was made and the other tribes received their portions.
In due time, all God's people will be settled in the inheritance prepared for them.

div.title: Caleb and his daughter Achsah (verses 13–19)
div.p: Achsah received land as a free gift from her father Caleb.
But it was land in the south, dry and easily parched.
She asked for more, and Caleb gave her both the upper and the lower springs.
Some understand the description as referring to a single field watered by rain from heaven and by springs rising from the ground.
This interpretation supports a familiar spiritual application.
When we pray, we may seek blessings for our souls and for heaven—the upper springs—and also blessings for our bodies and present lives—the lower springs.
Both kinds of blessing belong to God's children.
Through their relationship to Christ, they receive them freely from their Father as part of their inheritance.

div.title: The cities of Judah (verses 20–63)
div.p: This passage lists Judah's cities.
But Bethlehem is not named, though it later became David's city and was honored as the birthplace of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Even at its greatest, Bethlehem was a little place among Judah's towns (Micah 5:2).
At this time it was apparently so small that it was not included among the cities listed.

p.hi: The sons of Joseph.

div.title: Ephraim's inheritance
div.p: This chapter and the next should be read together. They describe the inheritances of Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's sons.
Next to Judah, these tribes were to receive a place of honor. They therefore received the first and best portions in northern Canaan, just as Judah received its portion in the south.
God's people continue, as in earlier times, to allow his enemies to remain.
Blessed Lord, when will all our enemies finally be subdued? The last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26). Drive them all out; you alone can do it.
The boundaries of these inheritances remind us that our circumstances and provision during this life, as well as our inheritance to come, are appointed by the only wise and righteous God.
We should therefore be content with our portion. He knows what is best for us, and everything we have is more than we deserve.

row.cell: The boundaries of Manasseh, The Canaanites not driven out.

div.title: Manasseh's inheritance (verses 1–6)
div.p: Manasseh was one of Joseph's two tribes, yet its inheritance was divided into two parts.
Zelophehad's daughters now received the benefit of their godly zeal and prudent foresight.
Those who take care, while traveling through this world's wilderness, to secure a place among the saints in light will enjoy the comfort of that inheritance in the next world.
But those who neglect it now will lose that blessing forever.
Lord, teach us to believe and obey here, and grant us an inheritance among your saints in eternal glory.

div.title: Manasseh's boundaries and the remaining Canaanites (verses 7–13)
div.p: The lands of Manasseh and Ephraim were closely connected.
Although each tribe had its own inheritance, their people could live among one another and show each other kindness.
They belonged to different tribes but were still one Israel, bound to love one another as brothers.
Yet they allowed the Canaanites to remain among them.
They did this against God's command, because it suited their own interests.

div.title: Joseph's descendants request more land (verses 14–18)
div.p: Joshua held public office and did not favor his own tribe over any other.
He governed without partiality or favoritism. Everyone entrusted with public responsibilities should follow his example.
Joshua told Joseph's descendants that their allotted land would be sufficient if they were willing to work and fight for it.
People invent many excuses to avoid hard work.
One especially convenient excuse is to rely on influential or wealthy relatives who might provide what we want.
We may then press those relatives to use positions of trust unfairly on our behalf.
But it is far kinder to point out opportunities that are already within someone's reach and encourage that person to use them than to encourage laziness and extravagance.
True religion never excuses such behavior.
The rule remains that those unwilling to work should not eat.
Many of the things we claim we “cannot” do are really things our laziness has made us reluctant to attempt.
This happens particularly in our spiritual work and warfare.
Apart from Christ we can do nothing.
But instead of trusting him and acting, we may simply sit still and attempt nothing.
If we truly belong to Christ, he will stir us to make our best efforts and cry to him for help.
Then our territory will be enlarged (1 Chronicles 4:9–10), and our complaints will cease—or better, become joyful thanksgiving.

row.cell: The tabernacle set up at Shiloh.
The remainder of the land described and divided.

div.title: The tabernacle is established at Shiloh (verse 1)
div.p: Shiloh lay within the territory of Ephraim, Joshua's own tribe. It was fitting for the tabernacle to be near the chief governor's home.
The city's name was the same as the name used in Jacob's prophecy about the Messiah (Genesis 49:10).

Some have suggested that the city received this name when it was chosen as the resting place of the ark. The ark pictured our great Peacemaker and the way he opens for us to approach a God reconciled to us.

div.title: The remaining land is surveyed (verses 2–10)
div.p: After a year or more, Joshua rebuked the people's delay and told them how to proceed.
Through his grace, God has given us a claim to a good land—the heavenly Canaan. Yet we are often slow to take possession of what he offers.
We fail to enter fully into the rest that we might already enjoy through faith, hope and holy joy.
How long will we continue hindering our own happiness and exchanging God's mercies for empty, deceitful things?
Joshua urged the Israelites to take possession of the lands assigned to them. He was prepared to do his part if they would do theirs.

div.title: Benjamin's boundaries (verses 11–28)
div.p: Each tribe's portion had its boundaries drawn clearly and its inheritance settled.
God's wise appointment prevented arguments and selfish demands.
He distributed the hills and valleys, fields of grain and pasture, streams and rivers, towns and cities.
If a servant of Christ receives a portion of affliction and sorrow, it comes under the Lord's authority. Let the Lord do what seems good to him.
If we receive prosperity and peace, they also come from above.
We should be humbled when we compare our gifts with how little we deserve them.
Never forget the One who gives good things, and always be willing to surrender them when he commands.

row.cell: The lot of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan.

div.title: Simeon's inheritance (verses 1–9)
div.p: Judah's people did not object when towns within their assigned territory were given to Simeon, once they understood that they had received more than was right.
If a true believer has gained an advantage improperly, even without intending it, that believer will give it up without complaining.
Love does not insist on its own interests or behave shamefully.
Where love dwells richly, it leads us to share what belongs to us with brothers and sisters who lack what they need.

div.title: Zebulun's inheritance (verses 10–16)
div.p: The division of land among Israel's tribes fulfilled the prophetic blessings spoken by Jacob.
Whether the people chose their portions or received them by lot, their inheritance was assigned in the places Jacob had foreseen.
How trustworthy the prophetic word is! It teaches us what to believe and confirms the truths God has revealed.

div.title: The other tribes and Joshua's own inheritance (verses 17–51)
div.p: Joshua waited until every other tribe had settled before asking for any land for himself.
He was content to have no settled place until the people were provided for.
This is a model for everyone serving in public office: place the common good before personal advantage.
Those who work hardest to benefit others should seek an inheritance in the heavenly Canaan.
It will be soon enough to enter that inheritance when they have completed all the service they can offer their brothers and sisters.
Nothing gives them greater assurance of their own inheritance than seeking to help others desire, seek and receive it.
Our Lord Jesus came to live on earth in poverty rather than splendor.
He provided rest for humanity while having no place to lay his own head.
Christ did not seek to please himself.
Nor did he enter his own inheritance until, through obedience even to death, he had secured the eternal inheritance for all his people.
He will not count his own glory complete until every person he has redeemed has entered heavenly rest.

row.cell: The law concerning the cities of refuge.

div.title: Israel appoints the cities of refuge (verses 1–6)
div.p: Once the Israelites had settled in the inheritance promised them, God reminded them to set apart cities of refuge.
The purpose and symbolic meaning of those cities had already been explained in Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19.
God's spiritual Israel has, and will continue to have, not only rest in Christ and heaven, but also a refuge where people can find safety.
These cities pictured the relief the gospel provides for repentant sinners.
In our Lord Jesus Christ, those who flee to him find protection from the law's curse and God's wrath (Hebrews 6:18).

div.title: The six refuge cities (verses 7–9)
div.p: The cities on both sides of the Jordan were positioned so that, from any part of the country, a person could reach one within half a day's journey.
God is always a refuge near at hand.
All six were Levite cities.

This arrangement was a kindness to fugitives. Someone who could not go up to the Lord's house would nevertheless have God's servants nearby to teach, pray and help make up for the lack of regular public worship.
Some interpreters also find spiritual meaning in each city's name:
Kedesh means holy: our Refuge is the holy Jesus.
Shechem means shoulder: the government rests on his shoulder.
Hebron means fellowship: believers are brought into fellowship with Jesus Christ our Lord.
Bezer means fortification: he is a stronghold for everyone who trusts in him.
Ramoth means high or exalted: God has exalted Christ at his right hand.
Golan means joy or exultation: in him all the saints are justified and will rejoice in his glory.

row.cell: The cities allotted to the Levites.
God gave the land and rest to the Israelites, according to his promise.

div.title: The Levites ask for their appointed cities (verses 1–8)
div.p: The Levites waited until the other tribes had received their portions before bringing their request to Joshua.
They based the request not on their own excellence or service but on God's command.
Support for ministers is not something a congregation may leave entirely to personal whim, as though it were free to let its ministers starve.
Those who preach the gospel should live from the gospel and should be able to live adequately.

div.title: The Levites live among the tribes (verses 9–42)
div.p: The Levites were distributed among Israel's other tribes.
They knew that the whole nation was watching them.
They therefore needed to live carefully so that no one could justly criticize their ministry.
Every tribe received some cities for the Levites.
This was God's gracious way of preserving true religion and making knowledge of his word available throughout the land.
Blessed be God that, under the gospel, his word has been spread more widely among us.

div.title: The Lord fulfills his promises (verses 43–45)
div.p: God had promised Abraham's descendants the land of Canaan.
Now they occupied it and settled there.
The promise of the heavenly Canaan is just as certain for all God's spiritual Israel, because it comes from the One who cannot lie.
No enemy could stand against them.
The Canaanites' later successes resulted from Israel's failure to act diligently and from its sinful willingness to tolerate the surrounding people's idolatry and wickedness.
Not one good thing God had promised Israel failed to come true.
At the proper time, all his promises will be fulfilled.
Then his people will acknowledge that the Lord has exceeded their greatest hopes, made them more than conquerors and brought them into the rest they desired.

row.cell: Reuben and Gad, with the half tribe of Manasseh, dismissed to their homes.
They build an altar of testimony, The congregation offended thereat.

div.title: The eastern tribes return home (verses 1–9)
div.p: Joshua dismissed these tribes with sound counsel.
Receiving a command is useless unless we obey it. We cannot obey rightly without paying careful attention.
Above all, we must love the Lord our God as the best of all beings and the best of friends.
As far as love governs the heart, we will continually seek to follow his ways, even when those ways are narrow and difficult, and to keep every one of his commands.
In every circumstance, we must purpose from the heart to cling to the Lord and serve him and his kingdom among people, with all our heart and soul.
This good counsel applies to everyone. May God give us grace to accept it!

div.title: The eastern tribes build an altar and cause concern (verses 10–20)
div.p: The tribes living east of the Jordan wanted to remain connected to Israel's worship.
At first their new altar seemed like an attempt to establish a rival to the altar at Shiloh.
God is jealous for the worship he has appointed, and we should be concerned about anything that resembles or leads to idolatry.
Corruption in religion is best confronted at its beginning.
But the Israelites' prudence in investigating their concern was no less commendable than their zeal to protect worship.
Many bitter disputes could be prevented or quickly resolved if people would first inquire into the alleged offense.
Remembering great sins committed earlier should make us watchful against sin's beginnings: the path of sin slopes downward.
We must warn a neighbor who does wrong, rather than allow that person to continue uncorrected (Leviticus 19:17).
The western tribes even offered to welcome their brothers to settle in the land where the Lord's tabernacle stood.
That generous offer expressed the true spirit of Israel.

div.title: The eastern tribes explain the altar (verses 21–29)
div.p: The eastern tribes received their brothers' criticism patiently.
They gave their explanation with humility and solemnity, doing everything possible to satisfy the others.
They spoke God's name with reverence.
Their brief confession of faith removed the suspicion that they intended to worship other gods.
We should always speak of God seriously and pause with reverence when mentioning his name.
A careless expression such as “God knows” may misuse his name.
But God truly does know everything, including our deepest thoughts and intentions.
In every religious act, it matters above all that we are sincere before him.
Yet we should also let other people recognize that sincerity by its fruits, especially when those who misunderstand us are genuinely concerned for God's glory.
The tribes rejected the evil purpose they were accused of and clearly explained the altar's true intention.
People who have received the benefits of God's appointed worship naturally want to preserve those blessings for their children.
They should take every appropriate step to ensure that their descendants are recognized as part of God's people.
Christ is the great Altar who makes every gift acceptable.
The clearest evidence that we belong to him is the work of his Spirit in our hearts.

div.title: Israel accepts the explanation and peace is restored (verses 30–34)
div.p: It was good that both sides wanted peace as well as faithfulness to God.
Religious disagreements can become especially fierce and difficult to resolve when wisdom and love are lacking.
Proud, irritable people may refuse to withdraw an accusation even when clear evidence shows they were wrong.
Israel did not act in that spirit.
The western tribes recognized their brothers' innocence as a sign of God's presence.
We should be glad when fears about another Christian's faithfulness prove unfounded and we discover that the person genuinely loves God and seeks holiness.
The altar was named Ed, meaning witness.
It testified to the tribes' determination to preserve pure worship, and it would stand as a warning to their descendants if they later abandoned the Lord.
How happy it would be if all professing Christians learned from Israel's example!
We need zeal and steadiness for God's truth together with fairness, gentleness, willingness to understand, readiness to explain and readiness to accept a brother's explanation.
May the Lord increase the number who preserve the Spirit's unity through the bond of peace.
May grace and comfort increase among everyone who sincerely loves Jesus Christ.

row.cell: Joshua warns the people of idolatry.

div.title: Joshua urges faithfulness before his death (verses 1–10)
div.p: Joshua was old and near death. The people therefore had special reason to listen carefully to his words.
He reminded them of the great things God had done during his leadership.
He urged them to be very courageous.
They must take care to keep what Scripture says, diligently do it and sincerely respect it.
They must also work cautiously to remove every reminder of pagan idolatry, so that its worship would never return.
Henry laments how casually people who call themselves Christians use the names of pagan gods, making them familiar in everyday conversation.
Joshua called Israel to perseverance.
There may have been many faults among the people, but they had not altogether abandoned the Lord their God.
One way to help people become better is first to recognize whatever good is already present in them.

div.title: Joshua warns Israel against idolatry (verses 11–16)
div.p: If we want to remain close to the Lord, we must stay watchful. Many souls are lost through sheer carelessness.
Love God, and you will not want to leave him.
He has remained faithful to you; do not be unfaithful to him.
The One who promised is faithful (Hebrews 10:23).
Every Christian's experience confirms this truth.
Struggles may be long and difficult, and trials may be numerous and severe.
Yet in the end the believer will acknowledge that goodness and mercy followed throughout life.
Joshua explained exactly how apostasy would progress.
First, the people would become friends with idolaters.
Next, they would intermarry with them.
Finally, they would worship their gods.
Sin's path runs downhill. People who deliberately share fellowship with sinners cannot avoid becoming involved in sin.
Joshua warned that such a course would destroy them.
The excellence of the heavenly Canaan, and God's freely given and unfailing promise of it, will only deepen the misery of people who remain excluded from it forever.
Their awareness of how happy they might have been will make them see more clearly how miserable they have become.
Let us watch and pray against temptation.
Let us trust God's faithfulness, love and power, appeal to his promises and cling to his commands.
Then we will be blessed in life, in death and forever.

row.cell: Joshua renews the covenant between the people and God.
Joshua's death, Joseph's bones buried, The state of Israel.

div.title: Joshua recalls God's goodness (verses 1–14)
div.p: We should never consider our work for God finished until our lives are finished.
If God gives us more years than we expected, as he gave Joshua, it is because we still have work to do.
Anyone seeking to have the mind of Jesus Christ should be glad to give a final testimony to the Savior's goodness.
We should tell everyone around us how deeply God's undeserved kindness obligates us to him.
Israel gathered in solemn worship.
Joshua addressed the people in God's name and as his messenger.
His address had two parts: teaching and application.
In the first, Joshua recalled the great things God had done for Israel and for the generations before them.
Then he applied that history of mercy by urging the people to fear and serve the Lord out of gratitude, so that his favor might continue among them.

div.title: Joshua calls Israel to choose and renew the covenant (verses 15–28)
div.p: God's people must serve him with willing minds.
Love is the only genuine principle from which acceptable service to God can spring.
The Father seeks worshipers who worship in spirit and truth.
Our natural, fleshly minds are hostile to God and cannot perform such spiritual worship.
We therefore must be born again.
Many people are content with outward religious forms, which they regard as imposed duties rather than a delight.
Joshua told the people to choose whom they would serve.
He did not mean that serving God was an optional matter of indifference.
He set the issue clearly before them and declared his own decision, whatever others might do.
Those traveling toward heaven must be willing to go against the current.
They must not simply follow the majority, but follow the example of the best.
No one can live faithfully in any position without serious attention to religious duties in family life.
Israel responded, “We also will serve the Lord.”
Joshua's example had a powerful influence because he had been such a blessing to the people.
People with great influence can do much good when they are zealous for true faith.
Joshua led them to express a sincere determination to cling to God.
But they needed to abandon every confidence in their own strength.
Without God's help, their resolutions would fail.
After they had deliberately chosen to serve God, Joshua bound them to that decision through a solemn covenant.
He erected a memorial.
In this moving way, he took his final leave of them.
If they later perished through rebellion, they would bear responsibility for their own blood.
The house of God, the Lord's table and even the walls and trees before which we have made solemn promises could testify against us if we turn away from him.
Yet we may trust God to put his reverence within our hearts so that we will not abandon him.
Only God can grant saving grace.
Nevertheless, he blesses our efforts to encourage others to serve him.

div.title: Joshua dies; Joseph's bones are buried (verses 29–33)
div.p: Joseph died in Egypt but commanded that his bones should not finally remain there.
He wanted them brought to the promised land once Israel had entered its rest.
Joshua also died and was buried, as was Eleazar the high priest.
Even the most useful servants of God eventually die, having served their generation according to his will.
One after another, they fall asleep and their bodies decay.
But Jesus, who completed his earthly life with a saving work far greater than that of Joshua or Joseph, rose from the dead and did not undergo corruption.
Those whom the Lord has redeemed will inherit the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.
In amazement at Jesus' grace, they will declare:

p.hi: To him who loved us and washed us from our sins by his own blood, and made us kings and priests to God his Father—to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

div.title: Judges — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: The book of Judges tells Israel's history during the time of the judges.
These were deliverers whom God raised up at particular times to rescue Israel from oppressors, reform the nation's religious life and administer justice to the people.
In this book, God's people appear less prosperous and less devoted to him than we might have expected.
Nevertheless, many believers remained among them, and the worship of the tabernacle continued.
This history demonstrates the repeated warnings and predictions Moses had given.
We should pay close attention to it, for it is full of important instruction.

row.cell: Proceedings of the tribes of Judah and Simeon.

div.title: Judah and Simeon begin the conquest (verses 1–8)
div.p: The Israelites knew that the war against the Canaanites had to continue after Joshua's death. What they did not know was how best to proceed.
They therefore inquired of the Lord.
God assigns work according to the strength he has given. Those who are most able should be prepared to do the most.
Judah held the first place in dignity and therefore should also stand first in duty.
Judah's effort would achieve nothing without God's blessing. Yet God would not give success while Judah refused to act.
Judah was the largest and most important tribe, while Simeon was the smallest.
Even so, Judah asked for Simeon's friendship and help.
Israelites should help one another against the Canaanites. Likewise, Christians from different groups should support and strengthen one another.
People who help each other in love have reason to hope that God will graciously assist them both.
Adoni-bezek was captured.
He had been a cruel tyrant.
The Israelites, Henry believes, acted under God's direction in making him suffer the kind of cruelty he had inflicted on others.
His own conscience acknowledged the justice of what happened to him.
God's righteousness is sometimes displayed when a sinner's punishment corresponds to the sin committed.

div.title: Hebron and other cities are taken (verses 9–20)
div.p: The Canaanites had chariots made with iron, but Israel had the Lord on its side.
His chariots are thousands of angels (Psalm 68:17).
Nevertheless, the Israelites allowed fear to overcome faith.
Caleb's actions have already been described in Joshua 15:16–19.
The Kenites also settled in the land.
Israel allowed them to live where they wished because they were a peaceful and contented people.
They troubled no one, and no one troubled them.
Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.

div.title: Other tribes leave enemies unconquered (verses 21–36)
div.p: Israel grew careless in both duty and its own long-term interests.
Out of laziness and fear, the people refused to finish conquering the land.
Greed contributed as well: they hoped to profit from allowing Canaanites to remain among them.
They did not hate or fear idolatry as they should have done.
The same unbelief that had kept their ancestors wandering for forty years now prevented them from possessing Canaan fully.
Distrusting God's power and promises deprived them of blessings and brought new troubles.
The same can happen to believers who begin their Christian lives well.
Their spiritual graces become weak, sinful desires revive, Satan attacks them through temptations suited to their character, and the world regains its influence.
Their consciences become burdened with guilt, their hearts with sorrow, their reputations with disgrace, and the gospel itself suffers dishonor.
A believer may be corrected severely and eventually restored without being lost.
Even so, the person may mourn those foolish decisions throughout life and, when approaching death, regret opportunities lost to glorify God and serve the church.
Fellowship with God's enemies, whether around us or in our own hearts, can only harm us.
Our wisdom is to continue the struggle against them without making peace with sin.

row.cell: The angel of the Lord rebukes the people.
The wickedness of the new generation after Joshua.

div.title: The angel of the Lord rebukes Israel (verses 1–5)
div.p: The One speaking to Israel was the great Angel of the covenant—the Word, the Son of God.
He spoke with divine authority as Jehovah and called the people to account for their disobedience.
The Lord reminded them both of what he had done and what he had promised.
People who turn away from fellowship with God to share in fruitless works of darkness do not understand what they are doing.
Soon they will have no excuse when called to account.
Their folly has consequences.
Those who expect to benefit from friendship with God's enemies deceive themselves.
God often allows people to experience their sin as its own punishment.
Thorns and snares lie on the path of those who stubbornly oppose him.
The people wept, recognizing their folly and ingratitude.
They trembled at God's word, and with good reason.
It is remarkable that sinners can read Scripture without tears.
If Israel had remained close to the Lord and kept its duty, the sound of its assemblies would have been joyful singing.
But through sin the people had brought themselves to tears.
Worship is naturally a matter for joy, praise and gratitude.
Our sins make weeping necessary.
It is good to weep over sin, but tears, prayers and even corrected behavior cannot atone for wrongdoing.

div.title: A new generation forgets the Lord (verses 6–23)
div.p: This passage summarizes the pattern of Israel's history during the judges.
Abandoning God made the nation weak and miserable.
Faithfulness would have made it strong and happy.
The punishment corresponded to the sin.
The Israelites worshiped the gods of surrounding nations, even the lowest of them, and God allowed the rulers of those nations to dominate them.
Anyone who has seen God keep his promises can be equally certain that he will keep his warnings.
He could have abandoned the Israelites justly.
Yet his compassion led him to raise up judges.
The Lord was with these judges, and so they became deliverers.
Even when the church experiences terrible distress, God will find or equip people to help it.
Israel, however, was not thoroughly reformed.
The people remained devoted to idols and obstinately returned to sin.
Those who abandon a way of life they once knew and professed can become increasingly bold in wrongdoing and hardened in heart.
God allowed Canaanites to remain, and Israel suffered from the very people it had chosen to tolerate.
Likewise, people cherish their corrupt desires.
God may justly leave them to the power of those desires until they become the cause of their ruin.
Scripture tells us that our hearts are deceptive and deeply wicked.
Yet we seldom believe that warning until we have recklessly approached temptation and discovered it through bitter experience.
Let us examine ourselves, pray without ceasing, be rooted in love and have Christ dwelling in our hearts through faith.
Let us declare war against every sin and pursue holiness throughout our lives.

row.cell: The nations left to prove Israel.

div.title: Nations left to test Israel (verses 1–7)
div.p: Israel was a picture of God's church on earth.
The people were not meant to live carelessly or lazily.
The Lord allowed some of the Canaanite nations to remain so that Israel's faith would be tested.
Temptations and trials expose the wickedness in sinners' hearts.
They also strengthen the graces of believers as they struggle each day against Satan, sin and this evil world.
Christians must live within the world, but they do not belong to it and must not adopt its sinful patterns.
This distinguishes Christ's followers from people who merely profess faith.
Friendship with the world is more deadly than the world's hostility.
Hostility can kill the body, but worldly friendship has destroyed many precious souls.

div.title: Othniel delivers Israel (verses 8–11)
div.p: Othniel was the first judge.
He had already become known during Joshua's lifetime.
Soon after Israel settled in Canaan, the nation's purity was corrupted and its peace disturbed.
Suffering can make people cry out to God when they had scarcely spoken to him before.
The Lord returned to them in mercy and raised up a deliverer.
The Spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel.
The Spirit gave him wisdom and courage to fit him for the task, and power to move him to perform it.
Othniel first governed Israel, rebuked its sins and worked for its reform.
Only then did he go to war.
Let us first conquer the sin within us, the worst enemy of all.
Then it will be easier to face outward enemies.
Let Christ be our Judge and Lawgiver, and he will save us.

div.title: Ehud delivers Israel from Eglon (verses 12–30)
div.p: Israel sinned again, and God raised up another oppressor.
The Israelites did wrong, and the Moabites did even worse.
Yet because God corrects his own people in this life, Israel grew weaker and Moab stronger against it.
If small troubles do not bring repentance, God may send greater ones.
When Israel prayed again, the Lord raised up Ehud.
As a judge carrying out divine justice, Ehud killed Eglon, king of Moab.
Henry understands this act as the execution of God's judgment against an enemy of the Lord and his people.
But he immediately makes an essential distinction.

p.hi: Our rule today is to obey rulers and authorities in everything that is lawful. No such special commissions are given now. Claiming one would be blasphemy against God.

div.p: Ehud's words to Eglon remind us that a proud rebel can expect a message of judgment from God.
Scripture contains such a warning.
Ministers must declare it boldly, neither fearing the anger of sinners nor showing favoritism.
But blessed be God, his ministers also bring a message of mercy and free salvation.
The warning of judgment is for people who reject God's gracious offer.
After Ehud's victory, the land had peace for eighty years.
That was a long rest, but it cannot compare with the everlasting rest of the saints in the heavenly Canaan.

div.title: Shamgar delivers Israel (verse 31)
div.p: The Philistines threatened the southwestern region.
The Lord raised up Shamgar to deliver it.
Without a sword or spear, Shamgar took the nearest available tool—an oxgoad.
God can use people for his glory and the good of his church even when their birth, education or occupation seem humble and obscure.
The weapon itself is not what matters if God directs and strengthens the person using it.
He often works through unlikely means so that everyone can see the excellence of his power.

row.cell: Israel again revolts, and is oppressed by Jabin.
Deborah concerts their deliverance with Barak.
Sisera put to death by Jael.

div.title: Israel falls under Jabin's oppression (verses 1–3)
div.p: The land had enjoyed peace for eighty years.
That long period should have strengthened Israel's faith.
Instead, prosperity made the people feel secure and indulge their sinful desires.
In that way, the prosperity of fools becomes their destruction.
Jabin and his general, Sisera, oppressed Israel severely.
This enemy was nearer than the former oppressors.
Distress finally made the Israelites cry out to the Lord, because they could see no other possibility of relief.
People who ignore God while prosperous may find themselves compelled to seek him when trouble comes.

div.title: Deborah calls Barak to deliver Israel (verses 4–9)
div.p: Deborah was a prophetess.
The Holy Spirit had instructed her in divine knowledge.
She judged Israel as God's messenger, correcting abuses and setting right the people's grievances.
At the Lord's direction, she told Barak to gather an army and confront Jabin's forces.
Barak insisted that Deborah accompany him.
She agreed.
She would not send him into danger while refusing to go there herself.
Those who call others to do their duty in God's name should be prepared to assist them.
Barak cared more about assurance of mind and success in his calling than about receiving personal honor.

div.title: Barak defeats Sisera (verses 10–16)
div.p: Sisera placed his confidence chiefly in his chariots.
But if we have reason to believe that God goes before us, we can proceed cheerfully and courageously.
Do not be dismayed by difficulties in resisting Satan, serving God or suffering for him.
Has the Lord not gone ahead of you?
Then follow him faithfully.
Barak went down from the mountain to the plain, although Sisera's iron chariots would have an advantage there.
Barak left the favorable ground because he was trusting in God's power.
Salvation belongs to the Lord alone (Jeremiah 3:23).
His trust was not disappointed.
When God goes before us in spiritual conflict, we must still exert ourselves.
And when he graciously grants success over the enemies of our souls, we should use that victory as encouragement to remain watchful and resolute.

div.title: Sisera is killed by Jael (verses 17–24)
div.p: Sisera's chariots had been his pride and confidence.
Such confidence in created things is doomed to disappointment.
What we lean upon may prove like a broken reed that not only gives way but wounds us.
An idol can soon become a burden (Isaiah 46:1).
God can make us weary of what we once desperately wanted.
Henry thinks Jael probably intended to show kindness to Sisera at first.
He believes that afterward a special divine impulse led her to recognize Sisera as a determined enemy of the Lord and his people and to kill him.
This is Henry's interpretation of the exceptional historical event, not a model for private violence.
We must break off associations with God's enemies if we want the Lord to be our God and his people our people.
Sisera intended to destroy Israel with many iron chariots.
Yet he himself was killed with a single iron tent peg.
Thus God uses weak things to confound the strong.
Israel would have avoided much harm if the people had earlier removed the Canaanites as God had commanded and enabled them.
Yet it is better to become wise late, through painful experience, than never to learn wisdom at all.

row.cell: Praise and glory ascribed to God.
The distress and deliverance of Israel.

div.title: Deborah and Barak praise the Lord (verses 1–5)
div.p: We should waste no time thanking the Lord for his mercies.
Praise is most acceptable to him and most helpful to us when it rises from a full heart.
Thanksgiving strengthens and deepens believers' love and gratitude.
It also makes God's wonderful acts more widely known and remembered for longer.
Whatever Deborah, Barak or the army had accomplished, the Lord must receive all the praise.
The will to act, the power to perform and the success achieved all came from him.

div.title: Israel's suffering and deliverance (verses 6–11)
div.p: Deborah described Israel's misery under Jabin so that its deliverance would appear all the more gracious.
She identified the cause of the suffering: idolatry.
Israel had chosen new gods with new names.
But behind those images, Henry says, the people were in fact serving Satan.
Deborah had been a mother to Israel by diligently seeking the people's spiritual welfare.
She called everyone who benefited from their great deliverance to thank the Lord.
Those who regained their freedom and position should praise God for that restoration.
The Lord himself accomplished it.
In judging his enemies, he also displayed his righteousness.
During persecution, attending the worship God has appointed may place a believer's life in danger.
Satan always tries to keep believers from approaching the throne of grace, the fountain of life's water.
Notice also God's tenderness toward frightened people.
His glory includes protecting those most exposed to danger and helping the weakest.
Let us value public peace, especially the safety enjoyed by those living in villages, and thank God for it.

div.title: Courage commended; indifference condemned (verses 12–23)
div.p: Deborah called upon her own soul to awaken and praise God.
Anyone who hopes to kindle love for Christ in others must first be burning with that love.
Praise is a task to which we should awaken both ourselves and our affections.
She described three groups: those who fought against Israel, those who fought for Israel, and those who kept away.
The enemies were stubborn and dangerous opponents of God's people.
The tribes that fought for Israel deserved honor.
God must receive the highest praise, but the people who serve him well should also be acknowledged, so others will be encouraged.
Indeed, the whole creation is against those who have made God their enemy.
The River Kishon fought against Sisera's forces.
Usually it was shallow, but Henry considers it likely that heavy rain had made it deep and powerful, drowning those who attempted to cross.
Deborah herself was earnestly engaged in the struggle.
When our souls become deeply involved in worship and holy duties, God's grace helps us overcome spiritual enemies.
Other tribes failed to help when their aid was needed.
Many people are held back from duty by fear of trouble, love of ease, and excessive concern for business or wealth.
Selfish people scarcely care what happens to the church so long as they can earn, keep and save money.
All seek their own interests (Philippians 2:21).
Those reluctant to serve can always find excuses for staying at home when an undertaking is dangerous or difficult.
But we cannot remain neutral in the conflict between the Lord and his enemies.
Even though God needs no human help, he accepts the service of those who employ their gifts in his cause, and he calls everyone to do so.

div.title: Jael is praised; Sisera's mother waits in vain (verses 24–31)
div.p: Jael received a special blessing.
People whose lives are spent in a small or humble setting will not lose their reward if they faithfully serve God with the gifts and opportunities they have.
Sisera's mother waited confidently for her son's return.
She had no thought that his campaign could have failed.
Her anxious hopes concerned worldly triumph and the display of greatness.
We should beware of setting our hearts on temporal advantages, especially those that feed pride and empty glory.
What a picture her wishes give of a heart ruled by worldly appetite!
The old mother's hopes and the attendants' speculations were foolish and shameful.
God can bring ruin upon his enemies precisely when they feel most confident and proud.
Deborah ended by praying for the defeat of all God's enemies and the well-being of everyone who loves him.
Those who sincerely love the Lord will finally shine like the sun in all its brightness.

div.title: Israel suffers under Midian (verses 1–6)
div.p: Israel renewed its sins, and the same pattern of suffering returned.
Everyone who persists in sin should expect painful consequences.
The Israelites hid in caves and rocky shelters.
Their guilty consciences had made them fearful.
Sin robs people of courage.
The invaders left them no food except what they managed to hide away in the caves.
The people had devoted to Baal what ought to have been used to serve God.
The Lord therefore justly allowed an enemy to take their produce away at harvest time.

div.title: A prophet calls Israel to repentance (verses 7–10)
div.p: The Israelites cried out to God for a deliverer.
First he sent a prophet to teach them.
When God provides a country with faithful ministers, it is a sign that he has mercy in store for that country.
The prophet accused Israel of rebellion.
God intended to bring the people to repentance.
Repentance is genuine when we grieve chiefly because our sin was disobedience against God, not merely because of the trouble that followed it.

div.title: Gideon is called to deliver Israel (verses 11–24)
div.p: Gideon had courage and an active character, but these gifts remained obscure because of Israel's distress.
God now stirred him to a great task.
The Lord was truly with Gideon because the Angel of the Lord was with him.
Yet Gideon's faith was weak.
He struggled to reconcile God's promised presence with the suffering Israel had endured.
The Angel answered his objections and told him to act as Israel's deliverer.
Gideon needed no further qualification than the divine call and assurance.
Bishop Hall observed that when God called Gideon valiant, he also made him valiant.
The Lord delights in raising up humble people.
Gideon asked for his faith to be confirmed.
But under the Spirit's ministry today, we should not expect the same visible signs Gideon received.
Instead, we should pray for God to show us the inward evidence of his grace through the powerful work of the Holy Spirit in our hearts.
The Angel turned Gideon's food into an offering consumed by fire.
This showed that he was not an ordinary human being who needed food, but the Son of God, worthy of sacrificial worship and destined to offer himself as the sacrifice in the fullness of time.
The sign assured Gideon that God favored him.
Since human sin brought guilt and the divine curse, a heavenly message often terrifies sinful people.
The invisible spiritual world is unfamiliar and awe-inspiring to us.
Gideon grew afraid, but God spoke peace to him.

div.title: Gideon destroys the altar of Baal (verses 25–32)
div.p: God's grace showed its power by raising up a reformer, and its kindness by choosing a deliverer from the household of a leader in idolatry.
Gideon could not be content merely to avoid worshiping at Baal's altar.
He had to remove that altar and offer sacrifice in another place.
He needed to make peace with God before making war on Midian.
Until sin has been forgiven through the great Sacrifice, we can expect no real good.
The Lord governs every heart.
He moved Joash, Gideon's father, to defend him from the supporters of Baal—even though Joash had formerly worshiped Baal himself.
Let us do our duty and entrust our safety to God.
Joash challenged Baal to show whether he could do good or harm.
The challenge exposed how foolish it was to pray for help to a god who could not even defend his own altar.

div.title: Gideon receives the signs of the fleece (verses 33–40)
div.p: The signs God gave were genuinely miraculous and full of meaning.
Gideon was preparing to lead a small Israelite force against the larger Midianite army.
Could God distinguish between Israel's small fleece and Midian's broad threshing floor?
The miracle showed that he could.
Gideon wanted the dew of God's grace to fall on him personally.
The fleece became wet with dew, reassuring him that God could do so.
He also wanted God to be like refreshing dew to all Israel.
Then the entire ground became wet.
We Gentile believers have every reason to bless the Lord.
The heavenly gifts that once seemed restricted to Israel have now been spread among the peoples of the earth.
Nevertheless, the means of grace are still received in different measures according to God's purposes.
Even within one congregation, one person's soul may resemble the dew-covered fleece while another remains like dry ground.

row.cell: The Ephraimites take Oreb and Zeeb.

div.title: God reduces Gideon's army (verses 1–8)
div.p: God arranged matters so that all the praise for the coming victory would belong to him alone.
He chose to use just three hundred men.
Trusting God does not excuse us from active service and careful judgment in our lawful undertakings.
But when the Lord sees people tempted to forget him, to shrink from danger through unbelief or to boast proudly of their abilities, he may set them aside and accomplish his work through others.
Many people find excuses for abandoning God's cause or avoiding the cost of discipleship.
A company of believers may become smaller when such people depart, yet grow purer and receive greater blessing from the Lord.
He chooses servants who are not merely favorable toward his work but eager and zealous for it.
Those who stayed did not resent the liberty granted to those sent home.
When doing what God requires of us, we should not be governed by how willing or unwilling other people seem, or by what they choose to do.
The question is what God has asked us to do.
It is rare to accept without resentment that others may have greater gifts, blessings or freedom.
Only special grace enables us to heed God's command rather than keep comparing our responsibilities with those of others.

div.title: God encourages Gideon's faith (verses 9–15)
div.p: The dream Gideon overheard seemed almost meaningless by itself.
But its interpretation showed plainly that God had arranged it.
Gideon's name had already filled the Midianites with fear.
He took the dream as a firm promise of success.
Without delay, he worshiped and praised God, then returned to his three hundred men with confidence.
We can speak to and worship God wherever we are.
When something strengthens our faith, he should receive the praise.
We should also recognize his providence in small events that seem accidental.

div.title: The Midianites defeat themselves (verses 16–22)
div.p: The unusual defeat of Midian can picture the destruction of Satan's kingdom through the preaching of the everlasting gospel.
The trumpet is sounded and the light is displayed from fragile clay vessels—like gospel ministers (2 Corinthians 4:6–7).
God chooses what seems foolish in the world's eyes to humble the wise.
A simple barley loaf could overturn the tents of Midian, so that all would see that the surpassing power belonged to God.
The gospel is a sword not held in a hand but proclaimed from a mouth.
It is the sword of the Lord and Gideon, of God and Jesus Christ—of the One on the throne and the Lamb.
God often allows wicked people to turn against and destroy one another, driven by delusion and uncontrolled passion.
It is a shame when people who belong to the church behave in that same way.

div.title: Ephraim captures Oreb and Zeeb (verses 23–25)
div.p: The people of Ephraim captured and killed two leading Midianite commanders.
Their cooperation teaches a valuable lesson.
When work remains to be done, we should be ready to help others finish it.
When another person begins something good and useful, we should welcome the chance to work together to complete it instead of hindering one another.

row.cell: Succoth and Penuel refuse to relieve Gideon.
Gideon declines the government, but given occasion for idolatry.

div.title: Gideon calms the Ephraimites (verses 1–3)
div.p: People unwilling to risk anything in God's cause may be the first to criticize those who serve with greater zeal and courage.
Those most reluctant to undertake difficult work can also be the most offended when they do not receive credit for it.
Gideon gave a remarkable example of self-denial.
He showed that humility is the best answer to envy.
The Ephraimites expressed their anger in excessive and improper words.
Their bitter language showed how weak their complaint really was: when scolding grows louder, reasoning often grows weaker.

div.title: Gideon's exhausted men continue the pursuit (verses 4–12)
div.p: Gideon's men were exhausted but still pursuing.
They were weary from what they had done, yet eager to continue the campaign.
This is often the experience of a true Christian.
A believer may feel faint and yet keep striving.
The world understands little of the long struggle faithful believers maintain against the sin in their own hearts.
The strength that enabled them to begin came from God.
They must continue trusting that same divine strength, because only through him can the conflict end in victory.

div.title: Succoth and Penuel are punished (verses 13–17)
div.p: Active servants of the Lord can meet more dangerous opposition from people who merely profess faith than from open enemies.
They must not let the conduct of Israelites in name but Midianites in heart discourage them.
Even when ready to faint from inward struggles and outward hardship, they should pursue the enemies of their souls and of God's work.
The Lord will give them strength to persevere.
The less help people offer—and the more they try to hinder—the more God's assistance may become evident.
The towns had disregarded Gideon's warning.
The resulting punishment was just.
Many people learn through the thorns of affliction because they would not learn in any gentler way.

div.title: Gideon confronts the kings of Midian (verses 18–21)
div.p: The kings of Midian had to answer for the killing of Gideon's brothers.
They acknowledged that they had committed murder.
Gideon acted as the avenger of blood, being the nearest relative of those who were killed.
The kings had not expected to be confronted about these crimes so long afterward.
Yet murder seldom goes entirely unpunished, even in this life.
Sins people have forgotten must still be accounted for before God.
What poor comfort it is to hope that death may involve less pain or disgrace than someone else's death!
Many people worry more about those things than about the coming judgment and what follows it.

div.title: Gideon refuses kingship but makes an ephod (verses 22–28)
div.p: Gideon refused the position of ruler offered by the people.
No good person should be pleased by receiving honor that belongs to God alone.
Gideon wanted the great victory to be remembered.
He therefore made an ephod from the finest spoils.
Henry thinks it probable that this ephod was associated with a teraphim and that Gideon intended it to be consulted as an oracle.
A single wrong decision by a good person can lead many others into false practices.
The ephod became a trap even to Gideon himself and eventually helped bring ruin upon his family.
How quickly possessions and ornaments that flatter desire, stir pride and encourage bodily indulgence can bring shame upon those attached to them!

div.title: Gideon dies, and Israel forgets him (verses 29–35)
div.p: While Gideon lived, he restrained the people from abandoning the worship of Israel's God.
After he died, they felt free to follow the Baals.
They also showed no kindness to Gideon's family.
It is hardly surprising that those who forget God should also forget their friends.
We know our own failures of gratitude toward the Lord and see ingratitude all around us.
We should therefore learn to bear unkind treatment patiently, even when it follows good service.
Following God's example, let us resolve not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good.

row.cell: Abimelech murders his brethren, and is made king.

div.title: Abimelech murders his brothers and becomes king (verses 1–6)
div.p: The people of Shechem chose Abimelech as king without consulting God.
They did not ask whether Israel should have a king at all, much less whom God would appoint.
If parents could foresee everything their children would do and suffer, their present joy would often turn to sorrow.
We should be thankful that the future is hidden from us.
Above all, we should watch carefully against sin.
Our wrongdoing may damage our families long after we ourselves are dead and buried.

div.title: Jotham rebukes Shechem through a parable (verses 7–21)
div.p: The trees had no need to choose a king.
They were already all trees planted by the Lord.
Likewise, Israel had no need to appoint a king, because the Lord himself was the nation's King.
Trees that bear fruit and contribute to the good of others deserve more honor from wise people than trees that merely look impressive.
The fruitful trees gave much the same reason for refusing promotion.
Ruling brings a great deal of labor and anxiety.
Those entrusted with public power must give up private advantages and interests for the good of others.
A position of honor can also threaten a person's fruitfulness.
That is why people whose main desire is to do good may be reluctant to become too important.
Jotham compared Abimelech to a bramble or thornbush—a worthless plant destined to be burned.
That is what Abimelech proved to be.

div.title: Shechem conspires against Abimelech (verses 22–29)
div.p: Abimelech occupied the throne Gideon had declined.
But how long did his glory last?
After only three years, the bramble was withering and beginning to burn.
The prosperity of the wicked is brief and uncertain.
The Shechemites suffered from Abimelech himself.
They had wrongly placed him on the throne, and they were the first to feel the weight of his rule.

div.title: Abimelech destroys Shechem (verses 30–49)
div.p: Abimelech meant to punish the Shechemites because they no longer respected him.
But God was punishing them for having helped Abimelech murder Gideon's sons.
When God uses human beings as instruments of his judgment, he may intend something very different from what those people themselves intend.
What the Shechemites expected would bring them safety became a trap.
Anyone who seeks shelter in idols will discover that they are a false refuge.

div.title: Abimelech's death (verses 50–57)
div.p: The people of Shechem were destroyed by Abimelech.
Now he, who had led them into wickedness, was called to account.
Evil pursues sinners and can overtake them even when they feel secure and triumphant.
Wickedness may prosper temporarily, but it will not prosper forever.
Much of human history, if told truthfully, would resemble this chapter.
