Many events celebrated as great achievements are actually struggles for power.
Such scenes reveal the Bible's teaching about the deceitful wickedness of the human heart, the force of sinful desires and Satan's influence.
Lord, you have given us your word of truth and righteousness.
Pour upon us your Spirit of purity, peace and love, and write your holy law upon our hearts.

row.cell: The Philistines and Ammonites oppress Israel.

div.title: Tola and Jair govern Israel (verses 1–5)
div.p: Peaceful periods of government give historians less to write about, even though they are often the best times in which to live.
Such were the days of Tola and Jair.
They were humble, energetic and useful men, appointed by God to govern.

div.title: Philistines and Ammonites oppress Israel (verses 6–9)
div.p: God's warning now came true: Israel would be unable to stand against its enemies (Leviticus 26:17, 37).
Through their own sinful ways and actions, the people had brought this misery upon themselves.

div.title: Israel turns toward God (verses 10–18)
div.p: God can multiply punishments to correspond with the number of people's sins and idols.
But hope remains when sinners cry to the Lord for help and grieve over both their open wrongdoing and their deeper ungodliness.
True repentance requires recognizing that whatever we have placed alongside God as an object of trust cannot save us.
Israel acknowledged what the people deserved but begged God not to treat them according to that desert.
We must submit to God's justice while hoping in his mercy.

p.hi: Repentance means not merely being sorry for sin, but turning away from it.

div.p: Just as a loving father is grieved by the disobedience and suffering of a child, God is grieved by the wrongdoing of his people.
No one seeks his mercy in vain.
The trembling sinner and the believer who has nearly despaired after falling away should stop debating God's hidden purposes.
Nor should they demand encouragement from their earlier religious experiences before daring to hope.
Instead, let them throw themselves upon the mercy of God our Savior.
Let them humble themselves before him, seek freedom from the powers of darkness, separate from sin and its temptations, diligently use the means of grace and wait for the Lord's appointed time.
Then they will surely rejoice in his mercy.

row.cell: Jephthah's vow. He vanquishes the Ammonites.

div.title: Jephthah and the elders of Gilead (verses 1–11)
div.p: People should not be blamed for their parentage when their own conduct and character remove any disgrace associated with their birth.
God had forgiven Israel, and Jephthah was therefore willing to forgive the people who had rejected him.
Jephthah did not presume that victory was certain.
He knew God could justly allow the Ammonites to succeed as a further punishment for Israel's sins.
Nor did Jephthah place confidence in himself.
If he succeeded, the Lord would have given the enemy into his hands.
In saying so, he reminded the people to look to God as the Giver of victory.
Henry applies the conversation to those who desire salvation through Christ.
If Christ saves you, will you accept him as your Ruler?
There is no salvation on terms that exclude his authority.
If he makes you happy, will you also let him make you holy?
If he becomes your Helper, will you acknowledge him as your Head?
Jephthah was willing to risk his life for a little earthly honor.
How could Christians turn away from spiritual conflict merely because it is difficult, when Christ promises the crown of life to the one who overcomes?

div.title: Jephthah seeks peace with Ammon (verses 12–28)
div.p: One way to honor God is to use our possessions rightly.
We should receive them from him, use them for him and surrender them when he calls for them.
Jephthah's message shows that he knew the books of Moses well.
His argument was clear, and his demand was reasonable.
People whose faith gives them the greatest courage are often also the most willing to pursue peace and make the first efforts to secure it.
But greed and ambition may disguise their purposes under claims of justice, making sincere attempts at peace ineffective.

div.title: Jephthah's victory and difficult vow (verses 29–40)
div.p: Henry draws five lessons from Jephthah's vow.
First, traces of distrust and uncertainty may remain even in the hearts of genuine and remarkable believers.
Second, our vows should express gratitude to God, not attempt to purchase the favor we desire.
Third, we must consider vows carefully before making them, lest they trap us.
Fourth, what we have solemnly promised to God should be done when it is possible and lawful, even if fulfilling it is painful or difficult.
Fifth, children should submit willingly and cheerfully to their parents in the Lord.
What exactly happened when Jephthah fulfilled his vow is difficult to determine.
Henry says it is thought that Jephthah did not offer his daughter as a burnt offering, because such a sacrifice would have been abhorrent to the Lord.
The proposed alternative is that she remained unmarried and lived apart from her family.
But he does not present this explanation as certain.
Learned interpreters disagree over this and several other difficult passages.
We do not need to be overwhelmed by questions whose answers are uncertain.
Thanks be to God, what is necessary for our salvation is plain.
Those who remember Christ's promise about the teaching of the Holy Spirit and submit to that heavenly Teacher will receive the truth they need to understand.

row.cell: Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon judge Israel.

div.title: Ephraim quarrels with Jephthah (verses 1–7)
div.p: The people of Ephraim picked the same quarrel with Jephthah that they had previously picked with Gideon.
Pride lay at the bottom of it.
Pride is what so often produces strife.
It is wrong to attach insulting names to people or to entire countries, especially to those already facing outward disadvantages.
Such language can provoke quarrels with terrible consequences, as it did here.
Few disputes are more bitter than quarrels among brothers or between people competing for honor.
How carefully we need to watch and pray against sinful tempers!
May the Lord lead all his people to pursue everything that makes for peace.

div.title: Ibzan, Elon and Abdon govern Israel (verses 8–15)
div.p: This passage briefly records three more judges of Israel.
The happiest lives and the happiest condition of a community are often those that produce the fewest dramatic events for historians.
What should a wise person truly desire?
To live honorably and quietly.
To be peacefully useful to those around us.
To enjoy a clear conscience.
But above all, without which nothing else is sufficient, to enjoy fellowship with God our Savior throughout life and die at peace with both God and other people.

div.title: The birth of Samson is announced (verses 1–7)
div.p: Israel did evil again, and God gave the people into the hands of the Philistines.
During this period of suffering, Samson was born.
His parents had long been childless.
Many remarkable servants of God were born to mothers who had waited a long time for children.
Mercies awaited patiently often become extraordinary blessings.
They also encourage others not to give up hope in God's kindness.
The angel showed that he knew Manoah's wife's affliction.
God often sends comfort at exactly the right time, when his people feel their troubles most deeply.
Samson, the coming deliverer, was to be set apart for the Lord.
Manoah's wife was convinced that the messenger came from God.
She gave her husband a detailed account of both the promise she had received and the instructions given.
Husbands and wives should share how God has met them and what they have learned about him.
In that way they can help one another grow in holy living.

div.title: The angel gives further instruction (verses 8–14)
div.p: Blessed are those who believe without seeing, as Manoah did.
Good people care more about knowing what duty God requires of them than about knowing exactly what the future holds.
Our duty belongs to us; events belong to God.
He will direct those who sincerely ask him to teach them what they ought to do.
Godly parents, in particular, should ask for his help.
The angel repeated the earlier instructions.
We need great care in ordering both our own lives and our children's lives properly, remaining distinct from the world's sins and offering ourselves as living sacrifices to the Lord.

div.title: Manoah offers sacrifice (verses 15–23)
div.p: When Manoah asked for guidance in his duty, he received an answer.
When he asked merely to satisfy curiosity, the answer was withheld.
Scripture gives us sufficient direction about our responsibilities.
But God has never promised to satisfy all our questions.
Secret matters remain beyond our knowledge, and we must accept not understanding them during this life.
The Lord's name is wonderful and mysterious.
Yet through his wonderful acts he reveals everything we truly need to know of him.
Prayer is the soul rising toward God.
Without Christ dwelling in the heart by faith, our services are only offensive smoke.
In him, they rise like an acceptable flame.
Henry sees in the angel ascending through the sacrificial flame a picture of Christ offering himself.
Through his own blood he entered the Most Holy Place once for all (Hebrews 9:12).
Manoah responded with terror, fearing they would die.
His wife showed greater faith.
As his suitable helper, she encouraged him.
Believers may have experienced fellowship with God through his word and prayer, recognized his gracious presence and received signs that he has accepted their service.
Those memories should encourage them when later days become dark and difficult.
God would not have begun his gracious work in their souls merely to abandon them to destruction.
His work is perfect.
We should reason as Manoah's wife did: if the Lord intended to destroy us in wrath, he would not first have granted the signs of favor he has given.

div.title: Samson is born and begins to show God's gifts (verses 24 and 25)
div.p: The Spirit of the Lord began to move Samson while he was still young.
This showed that God had blessed him.
Where the Lord gives a special calling, he also gives his Spirit to prepare people for it.
Blessed indeed are those in whom God's Spirit begins the work of grace during childhood.
Samson drank no wine or strong drink.
Yet he was strong and courageous because the Spirit of God moved him.
Therefore, do not be drunk with wine; instead, be filled with the Spirit.

row.cell: Samson desires a wife of the Philistines.

div.title: Samson wants to marry a Philistine woman (verses 1–4)
div.p: As an ordinary marriage decision, Samson's desire was weak and foolish.
He was not merely an Israelite; he was also a Nazirite set apart for the Lord.
Why should he seek marriage with a worshiper of Dagon?
The account gives no reason to think the woman was wise, virtuous or likely to make a good companion.
Samson simply saw something attractive in her.
Anyone who chooses a spouse solely by what the eyes see and by personal fancy has only himself to blame if the marriage proves spiritually harmful.
Still, Samson did well to speak with his parents before going further.
Henry says children ought not to marry or even begin pursuing marriage without parental counsel and consent.
Samson's parents were right to warn him against being unequally joined to someone who did not share his faith.
It seems that God allowed Samson to follow his own strong desire while intending to bring good from what happened.
His parents eventually consented because he remained determined.

p.hi: But this account is not given to us as an example to imitate.

div.title: Samson kills a lion (verses 5–9)
div.p: By empowering Samson to kill the lion, God showed him what he could do through the strength given by the Lord's Spirit.
This should have encouraged him not to fear even the greatest difficulties.
Samson was alone in the vineyards after wandering away.
Young people often fail to recognize the danger they face when wandering away from wise, godly parents.
The devil is like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour.
People also fail to notice how many dangerous lions lurk in vineyards—especially where red wine and its temptations are found.
Our Lord Jesus has conquered Satan, the roaring lion.
Believers, like Samson, can therefore find honey in the defeated lion: strength and spiritual satisfaction enough for themselves and for their friends.

div.title: Samson's riddle and the betrayal of his trust (verses 10–20)
div.p: Literally, Samson's riddle simply meant that he had obtained honey for food and pleasure from the body of a fierce lion.
But Henry sees it as pointing toward Christ's victory over Satan.
Through Christ's humiliation, suffering and death came victory and exaltation, glory for the Father and great spiritual blessings for his people.
Even death itself, that devouring enemy, has been stripped of its sting and terror.
Instead of preventing blessedness, it now helps believers pass into eternal joy.
Thus food comes from the eater and sweetness from the strong.
Samson's companions forced his wife to obtain the answer to the riddle.
A spouse or friend who is controlled by worldly loyalties can become an enemy within the camp, always ready to betray the believer.
A close relationship cannot remain secure or happy when confidential matters cannot be shared without danger of betrayal.
Satan could not do so much harm through temptation unless he could use the corruption of our own hearts.
His greatest advantage comes from his cooperation with our deceitful desires.
This experience helped separate Samson from his new relationships.
It would be good if every disappointment and act of unkindness we experienced from the world led us, through faith and prayer, to return to our heavenly Father's house and find rest there.
Human friendship can be unreliable.
However warmly someone may profess friendship, a person devoted to the world may quickly grow tired of a faithful believer.

row.cell: Samson is denied his wife, He smites the Philistines.
Samson kills a thousand of the Philistines with a jaw-bone.

div.title: Samson is denied his wife and fights the Philistines (verses 1–8)
div.p: When relatives disagree, the wisest and best are those most willing to forgive, forget offenses, and yield for the sake of peace.
In considering Samson's unusual methods, we should recognize God's power in making them successful.
Through them God humbled the Philistines' pride and punished their wickedness.
The Philistines had threatened to burn Samson's wife and her father's household.
Trying to save herself and please her countrymen, she betrayed her husband.
But the very disaster she feared and tried to avoid through wrongdoing came upon her.
Her own countrymen burned her and her father's household.
Often, by using unlawful means to escape trouble, we bring that very trouble upon ourselves.

div.title: Samson kills a thousand Philistines with a jawbone (verses 9–17)
div.p: Sin destroys courage and blinds people to what would bring them peace.
The Israelites blamed Samson for acting against their enemies, as though his efforts to defend them were a terrible offense.
In a similar way, the Lord Jesus performed many good works, yet people were ready to stone him for them.
When the Spirit of the Lord came upon Samson, the cords binding him came loose.
Where the Lord's Spirit is, there is freedom.
People whom the Spirit frees are truly free.
Christ likewise triumphed over the powers of darkness when they believed they had him helplessly in their control.
Samson defeated many Philistines using nothing more impressive than a donkey's jawbone.
God chose a foolish-looking instrument to show that the excellent power was his, not human.
The victory came neither from the weapon nor from Samson's arm, but from the Spirit of God moving the weapon through his arm.
We can do everything through the One who strengthens us.
When a poor Christian resists temptation with the help of advice that seems weak or unimpressive, we see another Philistine overcome by an unlikely jawbone.

div.title: Samson prays for water (verses 18–20)
div.p: The people of Judah showed so little concern for their deliverer that he was nearly left to die for lack of drinking water.
Those who perform the greatest service may receive the greatest ingratitude.
Samson prayed to God in his distress.
People who forget to praise the Lord may find themselves compelled to pray when trouble comes.
Remembering God's power and kindness in the past gives us good reasons to ask him for fresh mercy.
Samson pleaded that his suffering would expose him to God's enemies.
Our strongest grounds for prayer are those concerned with God's glory.
The Lord provided relief at just the right time.
The place was called Lehi, after the jawbone.
There God caused a spring of water to appear near Samson.
We would be more grateful for ordinary water if we considered how quickly life would fail without it.
The people of Israel now submitted to the man they had earlier betrayed.
God was with him, and he began to lead them as their judge.

row.cell: Samson enticed to declare his strength lay.
The Philistines take Samson, and put out his eyes.
He destroys many of the Philistines.

div.title: Samson escapes from Gaza (verses 1–3)
div.p: Samson's character has appeared remarkable, even glorious in some respects.
But here he behaves so wickedly that some people question whether he was truly godly.
The apostle settles that question by including him among those commended for faith (Hebrews 11:32).
We can learn from this account by attending to Scripture's teaching about Satan's tricks, the heart's deceitfulness and God's ways of dealing with his people.
Some circumstances in Samson's time were exceptional.
Conduct connected with his calling would be gravely criminal in our time without a specific command from heaven.
Samson may also have shown genuine piety on occasions that Scripture does not record.
Yet his danger is plain.
People who indulge in drunkenness or sexual sin should recognize how they expose themselves to spiritual enemies seeking their ruin.
The more securely they sleep in their sins, the more dangerous their position becomes.
We may hope that when Samson awoke and saw his danger he resolved not to return to his wrongdoing.
It was bad to lie down without such fear of sin, but would have been worse to remain there without repentance.

div.title: Delilah leads Samson into a trap (verses 4–17)
div.p: Samson had repeatedly suffered trouble through improper relationships with women.
Yet he ignored the warnings and fell into the same trap again.
This third occasion brought disaster.
Sexual immorality is one of the sins that steals the heart.
Many people fall into this deep pit.
Few escape, except through an extraordinary mercy that often costs nearly everything: reputation, usefulness and outward well-being, even where the soul is saved.
The pain that follows such sin may be ten thousand times greater than the brief pleasure it provided.

div.title: Samson is blinded and imprisoned (verses 18–21)
div.p: False security has deadly consequences.
Satan flatters people into believing they are safe.
They stop watching and fearing.
Then he takes away their strength and honor and leads them captive.
While we sleep spiritually, our enemies remain awake.
Samson's eyes had first drawn him into sin.
Now his punishment fell upon those eyes: the Philistines blinded him.
With his physical sight gone, he had time to remember how earlier sinful desires had already blinded his judgment.
The surest way to preserve our eyes is to turn them away from worthless sights.
Let Samson's fall warn us to watch diligently against sinful physical desires.
When our consecration to God is profaned, our spiritual protection departs.

div.title: Samson's strength begins to return (verses 22–24)
div.p: Samson's suffering became the occasion for deep repentance.
Losing physical sight opened the eyes of his understanding.
After losing bodily strength, he received renewed spiritual strength from the Lord.
God sometimes permits people to wander far into sin, yet finally brings them back.
Through severe earthly consequences, he shows his displeasure at sin while keeping them from eternal ruin.
Hypocrites may misuse such stories as excuses to sin.
Unbelievers may mock them.
But faithful Christians should become more humble, cautious, watchful and dependent upon God.
They should pray more earnestly for grace to avoid falling and thank God for preserving them.
If they do fall, they should not despair of his mercy.

div.title: Samson's final prayer and death (verses 25–31)
div.p: Few actions increase a person's guilt more quickly than mocking and mistreating God's servants, even when those servants have brought disgrace upon themselves through their own folly.
Henry understands Samson as a publicly appointed judge acting under God's direction to vindicate the Lord's cause, Israel's cause and his own.
The strength Samson lost through sin was restored through prayer.
Henry argues that his action arose from holy zeal rather than merely private revenge because God accepted and answered the prayer.
The building collapsed through God's almighty power, not Samson's natural strength alone.
In this exceptional historical situation, Henry does not regard Samson as guilty of taking his own life.
He sought Israel's deliverance and the defeat of its enemies, rather than his own death.
Samson died in captivity among the Philistines—a severe correction for his sins.
Yet he died repentant.
Henry sees his death as a picture of Christ, who willingly laid down his life among transgressors, overthrew Satan's kingdom and secured deliverance for his people.
Samson's sin was great, and he deserved the judgments he brought upon himself.
Nevertheless, he found mercy at the end.
Everyone who repents and flees to Jesus Christ—the Savior whose blood cleanses from every sin—may also obtain mercy.

p.hi: But nothing in Samson's story gives anyone permission to continue sinning on the assumption that repentance and salvation can be postponed until the end.

row.cell: The beginning of idolatry in Israel, Micah and his mother.
Micah hires a Levite to be his priest.

div.title: Micah and his mother turn to idols (verses 1–6)
div.p: The events described here and in the remaining chapters of Judges took place soon after Joshua died (see Judges 20:28).
The history shows how unhappy Israel could become without a judge, in contrast with the comparative peace experienced under the judges.
Love of money made Micah dishonor his mother by stealing from her.
That same love of money made his mother curse her own son.
Losses drive godly people toward prayer but can drive ungodly people toward cursing.
This woman's silver was already her god before it was shaped into a carved or cast image.
Micah and his mother agreed to turn their wealth into an idol and establish false worship in their home.
What caused this corruption?
Everyone did whatever appeared right in his own eyes.
Soon they began doing what was evil in the Lord's sight.

div.title: Micah hires a Levite as priest (verses 7–13)
div.p: Micah saw the arrival of a Levite at his house as evidence that God favored him and his idols.
This is how people can deceive themselves.
When they are already pleased with their own false beliefs, they may treat any unexpected circumstance that helps them continue in wrongdoing as proof that God approves of it.
But an apparent success in Providence is no evidence that a sinful course has become right.

p.hi: The Danites seek to enlarge their inheritance, and rob Micah.

div.title: The stolen idols of Micah
div.p: The Danites decided to take Micah's gods with them.
How foolish they were!
How could they expect those gods to protect them when the gods could not even protect themselves from being stolen?
Taking the images for their own worship was a double crime.
It showed that they neither feared God nor respected other people.
They had lost both true religion and ordinary honesty.
Micah was equally foolish.
He called objects his gods, although he himself had made them.
The only One worthy of our worship as God is the One who made us.
Whatever we value as though our whole life depended upon it has taken God's place in our hearts.
If people devoted to idols are willing to live for those false gods, how much more should we love and serve the only true God!

p.hi: The wickedness of the men of Gibeah.

div.title: The wrongdoing at Gibeah
div.p: The final three chapters of Judges tell a deeply distressing story about the wickedness of the people of Gibeah, in the tribe of Benjamin.
The righteous Lord sometimes permits sinners to carry out his just judgments against one another.
If the history described here is horrifying, how much more dreadful will be the things revealed on the day of judgment!
Every one of us should therefore consider how to escape the coming wrath.
We should put to death the sins in our own hearts, resist Satan's temptations and keep away from the pollution of the world.

p.hi: The tribe of Benjamin nearly extirpated.

div.title: The near destruction of Benjamin
div.p: Israel was right to hate the terrible crime committed at Gibeah and to resolve that those guilty of it should be punished.
But the Israelites acted too quickly and with too much confidence in themselves when they made their plans.
The destruction of most of Benjamin was dreadful.
Yet the eternal destruction of human souls is more fearful still.

p.hi: The Israelites lament for the Benjamites.

div.title: Israel's rash oath and the cost of misguided zeal
div.p: The Israelites mourned for the tribe of Benjamin.
They were troubled by the oath they had made not to allow their daughters to marry Benjamite men.
People often care more about defending their own authority and decisions than about respecting God's authority.
They would have acted better if they had repented of their rash oath, brought the prescribed sin offerings and sought forgiveness in the way God appointed.
Instead, they tried to avoid being guilty of breaking their oath by doing things just as wrong as breaking it.
The fact that people may advise treachery or violence while believing they are fulfilling a moral duty shows how blind the human mind can become when left to itself.
It also reveals the disastrous consequences of a conscience misled by ignorance and error.

div.title: Ruth — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: This book gives excellent examples of faith, devotion to God, patience, humility, diligence and loving-kindness in the ordinary events of life.
It also shows how carefully God's providence attends to even our smallest concerns.
That should encourage us to place our full trust in him.
We may read Ruth as a beautiful and natural picture of human life, as a detailed record of important events, and as part of God's plan of redemption.

row.cell: Elimelech and his sons die in the land of Moab.
Orpah stays behind, but Ruth goes with Naomi.

div.title: Elimelech's family in Moab (verses 1–5)
div.p: Elimelech was not wrong to care about providing for his family.
But Henry says his decision to move to Moab cannot be justified.
The move ended with the loss of his family.
It is foolish to imagine we can escape a hardship that God has placed in our path and calls us to bear.
Moving somewhere else seldom improves our spiritual situation.
We do not know what may happen when we bring young people into harmful company and remove them from public worship.
We may think their religious foundations are strong and that they are well prepared to resist temptation.
Yet we cannot see the outcome.
The text does not say that the Moabite women whom Elimelech's sons married had converted to Israel's faith.
All earthly trials and pleasures last only a short time.
Death continually removes people of every age and condition, undoing our worldly comforts.
We should therefore value most highly the good things that endure forever.

div.title: Naomi decides to return (verses 6–14)
div.p: After the deaths of her sons, Naomi began planning to return home.
When death enters a family, the survivors should consider what needs changing in their lives.
God sometimes allows earthly life to become bitter so that heaven becomes more precious to us.
Naomi appears to have been a woman of faith and devotion.
She said goodbye to her daughters-in-law with prayer.
Friends should part in love and prayer.
Was Naomi right to discourage them from accompanying her, when going with her might help them escape Moab's idolatry and worship Israel's God?
Henry says Naomi certainly wanted that good outcome, but she did not want them to adopt Israel's religion only to please her.
People who profess faith merely to satisfy friends or enjoy their company make unreliable converts.
If they accompanied Naomi, they should make a considered, personal decision, understanding its cost.
Anyone professing faith should count the cost first.
Many people prefer the earthly rest of marriage, financial security or comfortable circumstances to the rest Christ offers their souls.
When their loyalty is tested, they may leave Christ, perhaps with real sorrow.

div.title: Orpah stays; Ruth follows Naomi (verses 15–18)
div.p: Consider Ruth's determination and genuine love for Naomi.
Orpah was distressed at parting, but she did not love Naomi enough to leave Moab for her sake.
Similarly, many people value Christ and feel affection toward him, yet fail to receive his salvation because they will not give up other things for him.
They love him in a sense, but leave him because they love something else more.
Ruth is an example of God's grace moving a soul to choose the better portion.
Naomi could ask for nothing more than Ruth's solemn declaration.
A firm resolution is powerful against temptation.
When someone follows a religious path without a settled decision, that person is like a half-open door inviting a thief.
A determined heart closes and bolts the door, resists the devil and causes him to flee.

div.title: Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem (verses 19–22)
div.p: They came to Bethlehem.
Suffering can change a person's situation very quickly and dramatically.
May God's grace prepare us for every such change, especially the greatest change of all.
Naomi means pleasant or lovable.
Mara means bitter or bitterness.
Naomi felt that sorrow described her life.
She returned home empty: poor, widowed and without children.
But believers possess a fullness no hardship can empty, a good portion that cannot be taken away.
Suffering is a bitter cup.
Naomi acknowledged that hers had come under God's providence.
When the Lord humbles us through our circumstances, we should humble our hearts before him.
Suffering is not beneficial merely because it hurts; it does us good when we respond to it rightly.

row.cell: Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz.
The kindness of Boaz to Ruth.

div.title: Ruth goes to glean in Boaz's field (verses 1–3)
div.p: Notice Ruth's humility.
When Providence made her poor, she accepted her circumstances cheerfully.
Proud people might rather starve than take a humble position.
Ruth was different.
She herself proposed gathering leftover grain.
She asked permission with modesty.
We should not demand another person's kindness as though it were owed to us, but ask for it and accept it gratefully, even in small matters.
Ruth was also diligent.
She had no desire to eat the food of idleness.
Her example is especially valuable for young people.
Diligence promises good both for this life and for the next.
We must not be ashamed of any honest work.
No lawful occupation is beneath us.
Sin should be beneath us; nothing else is shameful when Providence calls us to it.
Ruth also cared for her mother-in-law and trusted in God.
The Lord wisely orders even events that seem unimportant or uncertain, directing them to his glory and the good of his people.

div.title: Boaz treats Ruth kindly (verses 4–16)
div.p: The godly, kindly words exchanged between Boaz and his workers show that there were faithful people in Israel.
How different this was from the immoral and corrupt speech heard too often in workplaces!
A stranger who heard them would gain a very different impression of Israel from what someone might gather from the careless speech common elsewhere.
Genuine faith teaches people to behave rightly whatever their social position.
It produces kind employers, faithful workers and harmony within households.
It fosters love and kindness between people of different ranks.
Boaz prayed for his workers when he arrived.
They replied with respect rather than speaking bitterly about him as soon as he was gone.
Relationships work well where employers and workers share such goodwill.
They expressed kindness by praying for one another.
Boaz noticed the unfamiliar woman and ordered that she be treated well.
Employers must ensure not only that they themselves do no wrong but also that people under their authority do not mistreat others.
Ruth humbly acknowledged that she had no right to expect these favors, having been born and raised among pagans.
We should all think humbly of ourselves, regarding others as worthy of honor.
Boaz's kindness toward poor Ruth also points to the Lord Jesus Christ's kindness toward needy sinners.

div.title: Ruth returns with the grain she gathered (verses 17–23)
div.p: Even humble work like gleaning produces something useful.
This should encourage diligence.
Ruth valued what her hard work had obtained and took care to preserve it.
We should likewise guard against losing the spiritual good we have worked for (2 John 1:8).
Parents should ask children about their daily activities as Naomi did.
They should not question them so harshly that they dread being home or feel tempted to lie.
Instead, they should praise what is good and gently correct or caution them when needed.
Each evening we should ask ourselves: Where have I gleaned today?
Have I grown in knowledge and grace?
What have I done that will bear lasting good fruit?
When the Lord deals generously with us, let us not search for happiness or satisfaction in another field.
We lose divine favors when we treat them lightly.
Ruth carefully followed Naomi's instructions.
When the harvest ended, she stayed home to keep her elderly mother-in-law company.
Dinah once went out merely to visit the daughters of the land, and her vanity ended in shame (Genesis 34).
Ruth went out only to obtain food and help provide for Naomi.
Her humility and hard work finally led to honor.

row.cell: The directions given to Ruth by Naomi.
Boaz acknowledges the duty of a kinsman.

div.title: Naomi advises Ruth about marriage (verses 1–5)
div.p: Marriage ought to provide as much lasting rest and security as anything can provide in this world.
It should establish a lifelong relationship and settle a person's affections.
That is why marriage should be entered into seriously, with earnest prayers for God's guidance and blessing and with careful attention to his commands.
Parents should advise their children thoughtfully on this important matter, seeking their spiritual good.
Always remember: what is best for us is what is best for our souls.
Naomi's advice may seem strange to modern readers, but it reflected the laws and customs of Israel.
Henry argues that Naomi would not have recommended it if the action had carried the appearance of wrongdoing.
Ruth had now joined the true faith.
The laws and customs of Israel gave her a legal claim involving Boaz as a possible family redeemer.
Widows customarily asserted such claims (Deuteronomy 25:5–10).
But this conduct is not recorded for imitation in other times, nor should it be judged as though the ancient custom were the same as today's.
Had the proposal been wrong, Henry believes Ruth's virtue and good judgment would have led her to refuse it.

div.title: Boaz responds to Ruth's request (verses 6–13)
div.p: Something improper in one country or period is not necessarily improper in another.
Boaz, as a judge of Israel, could explain what Ruth should do.
He could also determine whether he possessed the right of redemption and what steps and ceremonies were necessary for marriage to him or to another relative.
His conduct deserves the greatest praise.
He did not exploit Ruth or treat her with contempt because she was a poor foreign widow.
Nor did he suspect her of evil intentions.
He spoke respectfully of her as a virtuous woman and made her a promise.
As soon as morning came, he sent her away with a gift for Naomi.
Boaz's promise was conditional: a nearer relative had the first right of redemption.

div.title: Ruth returns home to Naomi (verses 14–18)
div.p: Ruth had done everything appropriate for her to do.
Now she needed to wait patiently for the result.
Boaz had accepted responsibility and would deal with the matter carefully.
Believers have even stronger reason to entrust their worries to God, because he has promised to care for them.
Our strength may sometimes be to remain quiet and wait (Isaiah 30:7).
This history encourages us to come by faith to the feet of Jesus Christ.
He is our close Relative, having taken our human nature.
He possesses the right to redeem us.
We should seek his guidance and ask, “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts 9:6).
Christ will never condemn us for asking him such a question.
Let us also desire and seek this same spiritual rest for our children and friends, so that all may be well with them.

row.cell: The kinsman refuses to redeem Ruth's inheritance.

div.title: The nearer relative declines redemption (verses 1–8)
div.p: The matter was governed by the laws Moses had given about family inheritances.
Henry assumes it was settled openly and according to the required legal procedures.
When the nearer relative heard all the conditions, he refused to redeem the property.
Many people respond similarly when presented with the great redemption offered by God.
They have heard good things about faith.
They have no particular criticism of it.
They may even speak respectfully of it.
But they remain unwilling to commit themselves, because they fear that doing so will reduce their worldly wealth or opportunities.
The nearer relative therefore surrendered his right to Boaz.
Everyone who desires to be a genuine Israelite, without deceit, must act with honesty and fairness in contracts and trade.
In the end, honest dealings prove the wisest policy.

div.title: Boaz takes Ruth as his wife (verses 9–12)
div.p: People are quick to seize chances to enlarge their estates.
Yet few recognize how precious true devotion to God is.
The world calls some people wise whom the Lord calls foolish.
They neglect their souls and reject Christ's salvation because they fear losing earthly advantage.
God, however, honored Boaz by making him part of the Messiah's family line.
The other relative, who worried about reducing his property and position, is forgotten.
His name, family and inheritance have disappeared from the record.

div.title: Ruth gives birth to Obed (verses 13–22)
div.p: Ruth bore a son, through whose descendants thousands upon thousands would belong to God.
As a direct ancestor of Jesus Christ, she played a part in bringing blessing to everyone who would be saved through him.
That included Gentiles as well as Jews.
Ruth's story was a witness to the Gentile world that God had not abandoned its peoples forever.
In due time they would become one with his chosen people and share in his salvation.
Prayer accompanied the marriage, and praise accompanied the birth of the child.
How sad that such expressions of faith are uncommon among Christians—or become empty formalities!
This passage also traces David's descent from Ruth.
The time eventually came when Bethlehem in Judah witnessed wonders far greater than those recorded in her story.
There, another child was born in humble circumstances.
His birth affected the decrees of the Roman ruler of the world.
It brought princes and wise men from the east to his feet, carrying gold, frankincense and myrrh.
His name will endure forever.
All nations will call him blessed.
In that promised Offspring, all the nations of the earth will receive blessing.

div.title: 1 Samuel — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: This book tells us about Eli and the wickedness of his sons, and about Samuel's character and actions.
It then describes Saul's rise to become king of Israel and his misconduct, ending with his death and preparing the way for David's succession.
David was an outstanding picture of Jesus Christ.
His patience, humility, perseverance, and suffering under persecution from both open enemies and false friends provide an example to the church and to every one of its members.
Many events in this book encourage suffering believers to remain faithful, hopeful and patient.
The book also contains useful cautions and solemn warnings.

row.cell: Samuel, Hannah presents him to the Lord.

div.title: Elkanah's household (verses 1–8)
div.p: Elkanah continued to worship at the Lord's altar even though his household was divided by unhappy conflict.
When family worship does not bring an end to disagreements, the disagreements must not bring an end to family worship.
It is unkind to reduce our rightful affection for a relative because of some weakness that person cannot overcome and already suffers from.
Doing so would turn God's providence into an excuse for breaking his command to love and would add suffering to someone already afflicted.
It is an ugly disposition to enjoy grieving a person whose spirit is sorrowful or upsetting someone easily distressed.
We should carry one another's burdens, not increase them.
Hannah found the provocation difficult to bear.
People who are easily upset and take injuries too much to heart harm themselves, depriving themselves of many comforts in life and faith.
We should notice the comforts God gives us so that we do not become absorbed in our troubles.
Remember what is for us, not only what is against us.

div.title: Hannah prays in distress (verses 9–18)
div.p: Hannah prayed with tears.
She trusted that the merciful God knew the grief of her soul.
The Lord permits us not only to ask generally for good things, but to name the particular blessing that we most desire and need.
Hannah prayed quietly; no one heard her words.
This showed that she believed God knows the heart and its desires.
Eli was the high priest and also a judge in Israel.
He misjudged Hannah.
We should not be quick to accuse others of serious wrongdoing when the matter is still uncertain and unproved.
Hannah did not respond by reminding Eli of his own sons' wicked conduct.
When someone judges us unfairly, we should be doubly careful about our words and not answer accusation with accusation.
Hannah simply explained herself.
We should be willing to do the same.
Eli, in turn, was ready to admit his error.
Hannah left with peace of mind.
She had committed her trouble to the Lord in prayer, and Eli had prayed on her behalf.
Prayer brings relief to a heart that trusts God.
It should even soften the face and visible expression of sorrow.
Those who rightly use the privilege of approaching the mercy seat of God, reconciled to us through Jesus Christ, will not remain forever without comfort.

div.title: Hannah presents Samuel to the Lord (verses 19–28)
div.p: Elkanah's family had a journey to make, with children to bring along.
Even so, they would not set out until they had worshiped God together.

p.hi: Prayer and provision do not delay a journey.

div.p: People who hurry into travel or business without taking time to worship may go forward without God's presence and blessing.
Although Hannah loved worshiping at God's house, she asked to remain at home for a time.
God desires mercy rather than sacrifice.
Those prevented from attending public worship because they must nurse or care for young children may take comfort from her example.
If they perform that work in a faithful spirit, God will graciously receive it as service to him.
When Hannah presented Samuel to the Lord, she gratefully acknowledged that he had answered her prayer.
Everything we give God was first something we asked for and received from him.
Our gifts to him begin as his gifts to us.
Even as a child, Samuel showed genuine devotion.
Young children should be taught to worship God.
Parents should teach them, bring them to worship and encourage them to participate as well as they can.
God will graciously accept their young efforts and teach them to serve him better.

row.cell: The wickedness of Eli's sons, Samuel's ministry.

div.title: Hannah praises the Lord (verses 1–10)
div.p: Hannah's heart rejoiced not chiefly in her son Samuel, but in the Lord.
She looked beyond the gift and praised the One who had given it.
She rejoiced in God's salvation and looked ahead to the coming of the One who is the complete salvation of his people.
God can weaken the strong and strengthen the weak whenever he chooses.
If we are poor, the Lord has allowed our poverty; this should encourage contentment with our circumstances.
If we are rich, he has provided our wealth; this should encourage gratitude, cheerful service and generosity toward others.
God is not impressed by worldly wisdom or the qualities people boast about.
He chooses those whom the world considers foolish, teaches them their guilt and helps them recognize the priceless value of his freely given salvation.
Hannah's prophecy looks forward to the kingdom of Christ.
After describing the Lord's rule over his providential world, she speaks of his kingdom of grace.
Here Henry identifies the first appearance of the title “Messiah,” or “Anointed.”
Those who belong to Christ's kingdom will be kept safe.
Its enemies will be ruined.
The Anointed One, the Lord Jesus Christ, has power both to save and to judge.

div.title: Eli's sons act wickedly; Samuel serves faithfully (verses 11–26)
div.p: Samuel had been set apart for God's service in a special way.
From childhood he performed the sanctuary duties appropriate to his ability.
Because his heart was devoted to God, Scripture describes even those simple tasks as ministering to the Lord.
The Lord blessed him.
Young people who serve God as faithfully as they can will be helped to improve and serve him still better.
Eli, however, avoided inconvenience and exertion.
He indulged his children instead of using parental authority to restrain and correct them while they were young.
He overlooked abuses at the sanctuary until they became established habits and led to serious wrongdoing.
His sons should have been teaching worshipers what was good.
Instead, they encouraged them toward evil.
Their wrongdoing happened even in the setting of sacrifices for sin, which pictured the Savior's atonement.
To sin against the very provision for atonement is especially dangerous.
It amounts to trampling the blood of the covenant underfoot.
Eli's rebuke was much too weak and gentle.
Children brought up in godly households may become especially corrupt if they break through every restraint.

div.title: A prophecy announces judgment on Eli's household (verses 27–36)
div.p: Parents who knowingly allow children to continue in wrongdoing and make no proper effort to restrain them are effectively honoring their children more than God.
Eli's example should move parents to oppose the first signs of wickedness and raise children in the Lord's teaching and correction.
Yet amid the judgment pronounced on Eli's house, God promised mercy to Israel.
His work will not fail because there are no servants available to carry it out.
Jesus Christ is the merciful and faithful High Priest whom God raised up when the Levitical priesthood gave way.
He perfectly performed his Father's will.
God will build him a lasting house, founded securely on a rock, against which hell itself cannot prevail.

row.cell: The word of the Lord first revealed to Samuel.
God tells Samuel the destruction of Eli's house.
Samuel established to be a prophet.

div.title: God calls the young Samuel (verses 1–10)
div.p: When divine grace intends that a call should be effective, the Lord will repeat the call until the person responds.
Eli realized that Samuel was hearing the Lord's voice and taught him how to answer.
It was a humbling matter for Eli that God addressed Samuel rather than him.
Nevertheless, he helped the younger boy understand what to do.
Older believers should do everything they can to support and improve the abilities of younger people who are coming after them.
We should not withhold help even from people who may soon be given a higher position than our own (John 1:30).
Children should learn good words and responses while they are young, so that they become prepared to learn spiritual truth and take it seriously.

div.title: Samuel hears judgment against Eli's house (verses 11–18)
div.p: How much guilt and corruption remains in us!
We are often aware of sins that our own hearts know well.
People who have the responsibility and power to restrain others from wrongdoing, yet refuse to act, share in that guilt.
They will be accountable as participants in the wrong.
Eli's response to the fearful sentence showed that he recognized God's right to act as he saw fit.
He trusted the Lord would do nothing unjust.
The gentleness, patience and humility of Eli's words show genuine repentance.
He accepted the consequences of his own failure.

div.title: Samuel grows as God's prophet (verses 19–21)
div.p: Every increase in wisdom and grace comes from God being with us.
The Lord graciously continues his visits to those who receive them rightly.
Early faith is a young person's greatest honor.
Those who honor God will be honored by him.
Young people should consider Samuel's example and remember their Creator during their youth.
Even small children are capable of genuine faith.
Samuel shows that their worship and trust can please the Lord.
His gentle and beautiful qualities of character are the brightest adornment of youth and a sure source of true happiness.

row.cell: The Israelites overcome by the Philistines.

div.title: Israel is defeated by the Philistines (verses 1–9)
div.p: Israel was defeated because sin—the accursed thing—remained in its camp, giving its enemies every advantage they needed.
The people recognized that God had allowed their trouble.
But instead of submitting, they complained angrily, as though they had done nothing to provoke him.
A person's own foolishness spoils the way, and then the heart becomes angry with the Lord (Proverbs 19:3), finding fault with him.
Israel supposed that bringing the ark into camp would force God to appear and fight for them.
People who have declined spiritually can sometimes become extremely attached to outward religious observances, imagining that these will save them.
The ark represented God's throne.
But bringing that throne into a military camp could not bring anyone to heaven while the world and the flesh ruled the heart.

div.title: The ark is captured (verses 10 and 11)
div.p: The Philistines took the ark.
This was a terrible judgment on Israel and a sure sign of God's displeasure.
Let no one imagine that an outward profession of religion can shelter a person from God's wrath.

div.title: Eli dies (verses 12–18)
div.p: The army's defeat grieved Eli deeply as a judge of Israel.
As a father, he also suffered when he learned that his two sons had died—the very sons he had treated with such indulgence, and who, he had reason to fear, died without repentance.
But the greatest blow came when the messenger announced that the ark of God had been taken.
That news struck Eli to the heart, and he died at once.
A person can die in terrible circumstances without necessarily being lost eternally.
Someone may experience an untimely and distressing death yet have peace with God in the end.

div.title: Ichabod is born (verses 19–22)
div.p: The wife of Phinehas appears to have been a godly woman.
As she was dying, she grieved most over the ark being captured and God's glory departing from Israel.
What value could earthly happiness have for someone who was facing death?
At that moment, only joy that is spiritual and divine can truly comfort.

And how can people enjoy the comforts of creation when they have lost God's word and appointed worship—especially when they no longer enjoy the blessing of his gracious presence and the light of his face?
If God departs, the glory departs, and with it all that is truly good.
Woe to us if he leaves!
Yet even when God's glory is withdrawn from one sinful nation, town or village after another, it never disappears from the earth altogether.
When his light is hidden in one place, he causes it to shine somewhere else.

row.cell: Dagon is broken before the ark.

div.title: Dagon falls before the ark (verses 1–5)
div.p: See how the ark of God triumphed over Dagon.
In the same way, Satan's kingdom will surely fall before Christ's kingdom.
Error will give way to truth, irreverence to godliness, and sinful corruption to grace within believers' hearts.
Even when true religion seems close to defeat, we can remain confident that its victory will come.
When Christ, the true Ark of the covenant, enters a fallen human heart, he enters what had been Satan's temple.
Then the idols fall.
Every attempt to restore them is vain.
Sin is abandoned, unjust gain restored and the Lord takes his rightful place upon the throne.
Yet pride, self-love and worldly desires, although overthrown and crucified, still remain within us like Dagon's broken stump.
We must watch and pray that they do not regain power.
Let us seek the more complete destruction of every lingering sin.

div.title: God's judgment falls on the Philistines (verses 6–12)
div.p: The Lord's hand was heavy upon the Philistines.
He not only demonstrated the folly of their idol worship but severely corrected their insolence.
Still they would not abandon Dagon.
Rather than seek God's mercy, they tried to remove his ark.
People whose hearts are ruled by worldly desires may suffer under God's judgments and still prefer to push him away instead of entering fellowship with him and seeking his friendship.
But every plan they made to escape God's judgment only increased their suffering.
Anyone who insists on fighting against God will soon discover the cost.

row.cell: The Philistines consult how to send back the ark.
The people smitten for looking into the ark.

div.title: The Philistines prepare to return the ark (verses 1–9)
div.p: The Philistines endured punishment for seven months while the ark remained among them.
They prolonged their own misery because they refused to send it away sooner.
Sinners often do the same when they will not part with their sins.
The Israelites themselves made no effort to recover the ark.
How rarely concern for true religion outweighs other concerns!
In a time of public disaster, people fear for themselves, their families and their nation.
But who is concerned for God's ark?
We have been granted the gospel, yet it is often neglected or despised.
We should not be surprised if that privilege is removed.
For many people, even the loss of the gospel—one of the gravest possible judgments—would bring no sadness.
They would be as satisfied with almost any religious profession as with Christianity.
But other people prize God's house, word and ministry more highly than their greatest possessions.
They dread losing these blessings even more than death.
Ungodly people are eager to avoid the conviction of their own consciences.
When trouble comes, they insist it is merely chance rather than acknowledging a warning from God.

div.title: The ark comes to Beth-shemesh (verses 10–18)
div.p: The two cows recognized their great Owner—the Lord—whom Hophni and Phinehas had failed to recognize rightly.
God's providence attends even to animals and makes use of them for his purposes.
When the harvesters saw the ark return, they rejoiced.
Their joy over the ark was greater than their joy over the harvest.
When public worship and God's appointed ordinances return after persecution or trouble, there is good reason for great rejoicing.

div.title: Judgment follows irreverent curiosity (verses 19–21)
div.p: People seriously offend God when they pry into secret matters that do not belong to them (Deuteronomy 29:29; Colossians 2:18).
Humanity's ruin began with the desire for forbidden knowledge.
The Lord will not allow his ark to be treated irreverently.
God cannot be mocked.
Those who refuse to revere his goodness or receive his gracious gifts with respect may be made to experience his justice.
Henry notes that the number of people killed is expressed unusually in the original text, and he considers 1,170 a probable interpretation.
This is his textual estimate—not a change to the biblical text or a claim about the exact numbering of any modern Bible edition.
The people now wanted the ark removed.
What foolishness, to run from one extreme to another!
Instead of demanding that the ark leave, they should have asked, “How may we be reconciled to God and recover his favor?” (Micah 6:6–7).
Similarly, when God's word awakens terror in a sinner's conscience, some refuse to accept their own guilt.
They quarrel with Scripture and push it away.
Many suppress their convictions and thereby reject the salvation offered to them.

row.cell: They are subdued, Samuel judges Israel.

div.title: The ark is brought to Kiriath-jearim (verses 1–4)
div.p: God will provide a resting place for his ark.
If some people push it away, he will incline others to receive it.
There is nothing unusual about the ark being kept in a private home.
Christ and his apostles taught from house to house when public places were unavailable.
Twenty years passed before Israel deeply felt the lack of God's ark.
During that time Samuel worked to revive true religion.
The Bible uses very few words to describe it, but they speak powerfully.
It was one of Israel's most effective seasons of spiritual renewal.

div.title: Israel confesses its sin (verses 5 and 6)
div.p: The people drew water and poured it out before the Lord.
This expressed humility and sorrow for wrongdoing.
They poured out their hearts before him in repentance.
Their confession was frank and complete.
They firmly resolved to abandon their sinful practices.
Publicly they acknowledged, “We have sinned against the Lord.”
In doing so, they gave God the glory and accepted the shame of their own guilt.
If we confess our sins in this way, we may trust that God is faithful and righteous to forgive us.

div.title: God defeats the Philistines (verses 7–12)
div.p: The Philistines invaded Israel.
When sinners begin to repent and change their conduct, they should expect Satan to bring his whole force against them and work through every available instrument to discourage them.
The Israelites urgently asked Samuel to pray for them.
What comfort it is that our great Intercessor in heaven never stops praying for us!
Jesus Christ continually appears in God's presence on our behalf.
Samuel's sacrifice without prayer would have been an empty picture without the reality to which it pointed.
The Lord answered graciously.
Samuel set up a memorial to honor God and encourage Israel.
Across the generations, the church has had many reasons to erect its own Ebenezers, monuments to fresh deliverances.
Neither outward persecution nor inward sin has prevailed against the Lord's church, for “Thus far the Lord has helped us.”
He will continue helping his people until the end of the world.

div.title: Samuel continues to lead Israel (verses 13–17)
div.p: During this great revival of true religion, the ark was not returned to Shiloh.
Nor was it placed with the tabernacle anywhere else.
Henry sees this lack of emphasis on the old ceremonial arrangement as evidence that its principal purpose lay in what it pictured.
When the spiritual meaning was neglected, the ceremonies became empty activity.
They could not compare with repentance, faith and love toward God and other people.

row.cell: The evil government of Samuel's sons.
The Israelites ask for a king.

div.title: Samuel's sons govern corruptly (verses 1–3)
div.p: Samuel's sons do not seem to have been as openly profane and immoral as Eli's sons.
Yet they were corrupt judges.
They pursued dishonest gain and accepted bribes.
Samuel himself had not done so.
His sons, however, allowed bribes to distort their judgments.
The people's suffering was worsened by the threat of invasion from Nahash, king of the Ammonites.

div.title: Israel asks Samuel for a king (verses 4–9)
div.p: Samuel was displeased by the demand for a king.
He could patiently bear criticism directed at himself or his family.
But the people's words, “Give us a king to judge us,” reflected upon God, and that greatly troubled him.
Samuel brought his distress before the Lord in prayer.
When something upsets us, it is both our duty and our benefit to tell God about it.
The Lord instructed Samuel to grant the people's request.
That did not mean God approved of it.
Sometimes God opposes our desires out of love.
At other times, he gives us what we demand as an act of judgment.
That is what happened here.
He knows how to bring glory to himself and accomplish his wise plans even through human foolishness.

div.title: Samuel warns Israel what a king may demand (verses 10–22)
div.p: If the Israelites wanted a king who ruled like the rulers of surrounding eastern nations, they would discover how heavy that form of government could become.
Those who place themselves under the rule of the world and sinful desires also need to know how severe those masters can be.
Sin is a tyrant.
God's law and ordinary human conduct differ greatly.

p.hi: God's law should govern how we treat others.

div.p: But what people usually do may teach us what disappointments to expect from them.
Israel would complain under the new system, but God would not immediately answer those complaints.
When we create suffering for ourselves through sinful wishes and schemes, we may forfeit the comfort of prayer and the benefit of God's help.
The people were stubborn and insistent.
Rash wishes and sudden decisions may create problems requiring long, painful repentance.
It is wise to be thankful for the advantages of whatever government we live under and patient with its disadvantages.
We should pray continually for our rulers, asking that they govern with reverence for God and that we may live peaceful, godly and honest lives.
It is a hopeful sign when our desires for worldly things can tolerate delay and when we are willing to entrust both the timing and manner of their fulfillment to God's providence.

div.title: Saul searches for his father's donkeys (verses 1–10)
div.p: Saul readily went to look for his father's lost donkeys.
His willingness to obey his father was worthy of praise.
His servant suggested that, since they were near Ramah, they should consult Samuel.
Wherever we go, we should make good use of opportunities to learn from wise and godly people.
Many would seek advice from a servant of God if one happened to be nearby, but would never go out of their way to obtain spiritual wisdom.
People feel losses of money or property keenly and make great efforts to recover them.
Yet how little effort they devote to the salvation of their souls—and how quickly they grow weary of that search!
If ministers could guarantee people a profitable business or wealth, their advice would be sought more eagerly than it is now.
They teach people how to escape eternal misery and receive eternal life, yet many prefer to learn their fortune rather than their duty.
Samuel did not need the visitors' payment.
He would not have refused advice merely because they brought no gift.
The offering expressed respect for his office and followed the custom of presenting gifts to people in authority.

div.title: God reveals Saul's arrival to Samuel (verses 11–17)
div.p: Even the young female servants of the town could tell Saul's party where to find the prophet.
They knew about the coming sacrifice and that Samuel would have to attend it.
There is real benefit in living among people who value God and his worship.
We should always be ready to help those seeking one of God's messengers.
Although the Lord had granted Israel's request for a king out of displeasure, he nevertheless chose a man who could lead them and deliver them from the Philistines.
God acted graciously in hearing his people's cry.

div.title: Samuel receives Saul (verses 18–27)
div.p: Samuel was not jealous of Saul or hostile toward him.
Instead, he was the first to honor him.
Samuel spoke with Saul on the flat rooftop that evening and again early the next morning.
Henry believes Samuel likely convinced Saul that God had selected him to govern Israel and made clear his own willingness to step aside.
How different God's purposes for us may be from our own plans!
Saul may be the only person who literally went looking for donkeys and found a kingdom.
But many others have traveled or moved house seeking wealth or pleasure and unexpectedly encountered people through whom God led them toward salvation.
Someone seemed to know the secrets of their lives and hearts, and they began to pay serious attention to the Lord's word.
If this has happened to us, we should not grieve that our original earthly plans failed.
God has given us—or is preparing to give us—something far better.

div.title: Samuel anoints Saul (verses 1–8)
div.p: The sacred anointing used for Israel's king pointed forward to the Messiah, the Anointed One.
Jesus Christ is King of the church and the great High Priest we confess.
He received the Holy Spirit without measure, far above Israel's former priests and rulers.
Samuel gave Saul signs that would happen that same day to confirm his calling.
The first place Samuel directed him to was an ancestor's tomb.
Saul needed to remember his mortality.
Even with a crown waiting for him, he must remember the grave where every earthly honor becomes dust.
From Samuel's time onward, there seem to have been schools or meeting places where godly young people learned spiritual truth.
Saul would feel strongly moved to join them.
He would be changed into another man.
The Spirit of God has power to transform people wonderfully.
Yet Henry distinguishes a temporary change in Saul's conduct from the new birth.
By praising God among his people, Saul became another man.

p.hi: Whether he became a genuinely new man in the saving sense remains doubtful.

div.title: The signs are fulfilled; Saul prophesies (verses 9–16)
div.p: Every sign Samuel gave came true exactly.
God granted Saul another heart, a different attitude for his new task.
Yet outward devotion and an immediate change of manner must not be trusted too readily.
Saul among the prophets was still Saul.
His anointing was kept private.
He allowed God to carry forward the work through Samuel and waited to see how the matter developed.

div.title: Saul is publicly chosen as king (verses 17–27)
div.p: Samuel told Israel that it had rejected God that day.
At first Saul was reluctant to accept a position of power.
Later, once he possessed it, he would be unwilling even to consider surrendering it.
He hid himself when the people sought him.
It is good to recognize our unworthiness and weakness before accepting an important duty.
But we should not go to the opposite extreme and refuse the work that God and his church have entrusted to us.
Most of the people responded with indifference.
Saul returned quietly to his own house.
A group of men accompanied him because God had moved their hearts to support his authority.
Whenever a human heart inclines toward what is right, it is because God has touched it.
One touch is enough when it comes from him.
Others despised Saul.
This division pictures different responses to our exalted Redeemer.
Some submit to Jesus Christ and follow him wherever he leads, because the Lord has changed their hearts and made them willing.
Others despise Christ and ask, “How can this man save us?”
They are offended by him and will face judgment if they persist.

div.title: Saul rescues Jabesh-gilead (verses 1–11)
div.p: Saul's first great act as king was to rescue Jabesh-gilead from the Ammonites.
People may be willing to surrender their freedom, or even lose their eyes, to save their earthly lives.
Would it not be wiser to surrender a cherished sin, however dear to us—like our right eye—rather than be cast into the fire of judgment?
Notice Saul's faith and confidence.
From that faith came his courage and determination.
Notice also how actively he carried out the work.
When the Lord's Spirit comes upon people, he can make them skillful even when they lack experience.
When zeal for God's glory and love for brothers and sisters move us to energetic service, and the Lord is pleased to help, great results can follow very quickly.

div.title: Saul's kingship is confirmed (verses 12–15)
div.p: The people who had despised Saul now honored him.
Turning an enemy into a friend benefits us more than killing that enemy.
One day everyone will acknowledge the Savior they once despised as the Lord's Anointed King.
For now, Christ receives repentant rebels at his mercy seat.
He even intercedes for them.
But the day is approaching when he will sit upon the throne of righteous judgment and condemn those who persist in opposing him.

div.title: Samuel bears witness to his integrity (verses 1–5)
div.p: Samuel not only cleared his own character; he also gave Saul an example and reminded the people how ungrateful they had been both to God and to Samuel.
Everyone owes a proper duty to a good reputation, particularly those serving in public offices.
They should protect it from unjust accusations and suspicions, so that they may complete their work with honor as well as joy.
When we know we have acted honestly in our responsibilities, that knowledge can comfort us even if others treat us with contempt or ingratitude.

div.title: Samuel reminds Israel of God's justice (verses 6–15)
div.p: Ministers must reason with those they teach.
It is not enough simply to exhort people or give instructions.
They should seek to persuade, convince the mind and thus win both the will and the affections.
Samuel reminded Israel of the righteous works God had done for the people.
The Lord will enable those who continue to follow him faithfully to go on following him.
But disobedience would bring certain ruin upon Israel.
We are deeply mistaken if we suppose we can escape God's justice merely by refusing his authority.
Even if we declare that he will not rule us, he will still judge us.

div.title: God sends thunder during the wheat harvest (verses 16–25)
div.p: At Samuel's word the Lord sent thunder and rain during the wheat harvest, a season when such weather was highly unusual in that country.
The storm occurred on a clear day.
Samuel also announced it in advance.
The unusual timing and prophecy together convinced Israel of the wrong it had done in demanding a king.
The people had expected more from human strength than from God's power or Samuel's prayers.
Could their new king command a storm as the prophet could through prayer?
They were deeply shaken.
Some sinners will not recognize their guilt until God confronts them through the storm and thunder of severe providence.
Israel begged Samuel to pray for the people.
Now they recognized their need of the man they had recently disregarded.
Likewise, people who refuse Christ's rule over their lives may still wish to have him intercede for them to turn away God's wrath.
Samuel's goal was to strengthen Israel's faith.
Anything we make into a god will eventually disappoint us.
Created things are good in their proper place, but they become empty substitutes when we put them in God's place.
It is sinful to abandon prayer, and especially to stop praying for God's church.
The people asked Samuel to pray, but he promised something more: he would also teach them.
He gave two reasons for faithful service.
Gratitude, because God had already done such great things for them.
And their own welfare, because they must consider what would happen if they continued in wrongdoing.
As a faithful watchman, Samuel warned them and thereby fulfilled his own responsibility before God.
When we remember God's great acts—above all the work of redemption—we need never lack reasons, encouragement or help for serving him.

row.cell: Saul sacrifices, He is reproved by Samuel.

div.title: The Philistines invade Israel (verses 1–7)
div.p: Saul reigned for a year without any remarkable events.
In his second year, the events in this chapter occurred.
For more than a year, he had allowed the Philistines time to prepare for war and weaken and disarm the Israelites.
When people grow proud and trust their own sufficiency, they often make foolish decisions.
The enemies of God's people gain many of their best opportunities through the misconduct of those who claim to be the people's friends.
When Saul finally sounded the alarm, the Israelites were dissatisfied with his leadership or terrified by the enemy's strength.
Many failed to come to his aid, and others soon deserted him.

div.title: Saul offers an unlawful sacrifice (verses 8–14)
div.p: Saul broke the specific instruction Samuel had given about what to do in an emergency (1 Samuel 10:8).
He offered the sacrifice himself without Samuel.
But Saul was neither a priest nor a prophet.
When challenged about his disobedience, he defended himself and showed no repentance.
He wanted to present a rebellious act as prudent leadership and genuine religious devotion.
People who lack inward godliness often place great importance on outward acts of worship.
Samuel told Saul that he had harmed himself.
Those who disobey God's commands act foolishly against their own good.
Sin is folly, and people deeply committed to it are deeply foolish.
Our response to seemingly small matters often reveals whether our hearts truly desire to obey God.
Human observers might consider Saul's act a minor offense.
But the Lord saw the unbelief and distrust, contempt for divine authority and justice, and rebellion against conscience that lay behind it.
Blessed Savior, may we never bring you our poor offerings or imagined peace offerings without trusting in your precious, entirely sufficient sacrifice.
You alone have made peace for us through the blood of your cross.

div.title: The Philistines keep Israel without weapons (verses 15–23)
div.p: The Philistines acted cleverly when they gained the advantage.
They not only prevented the Israelites from making weapons.
They forced them to depend upon their enemies even for the tools needed to cultivate the land.
Saul had acted foolishly by failing to correct this danger when his reign began.
Lack of true judgment accompanies lack of grace.
Sins that seem small to us may have very dangerous consequences.
How miserable a guilty, defenseless nation is!
Yet even more miserable are those who lack the whole armor of God.

row.cell: Saul forbids the people to eat till evening.

div.title: Jonathan attacks the Philistines (verses 1–15)
div.p: Saul seemed confused and unable to help himself.
No one who believes himself outside God's protection can truly feel secure.
Saul therefore called for a priest and the ark, hoping to put matters right with the Almighty through a partial religious reform.
Many people do this while their hearts remain proud and unchanged.
They prefer ministers who tell them only pleasant things.
Jonathan, however, felt an impression from God calling him to this daring undertaking.
The Lord will guide those who acknowledge him in all their ways, sincerely seek his direction and fully intend to follow what he shows.
Sometimes the greatest comfort comes from events we did not plan or arrange, when we recognize the unexpected ways God's providence has guided us.
The Philistine camp was seized with trembling.
It was described as a trembling from God.
The panic was not only severe and impossible to resist; it came from God's hand.
The One who made the human heart knows how to make it tremble.

div.title: The Philistines are defeated (verses 16–23)
div.p: God's power turned the Philistines against one another.
The more clearly it became evident that God had achieved the victory, the more carefully Saul ought to have asked whether God wanted him to do anything further.
But he hurried to attack an enemy already falling apart.
He would not even finish his religious inquiry or wait for God's answer.
Those who believe God will not hurry in this way, as though any business were so urgent that there was no time to seek the Lord's guidance.

div.title: Saul forbids food during the battle (verses 24–35)
div.p: Saul's severe order was foolish.
It may have saved some time, but it cost the soldiers the strength they needed to keep pursuing the enemy.
God made our bodies so that we cannot carry out the work of each day without the food of each day.
Our Father graciously provides our daily bread.
Saul was turning away from God.
Yet he became especially zealous for the outward form of religion just when he was denying its inward power, beginning to build altars.

div.title: Saul seeks an offender among the people (verses 36–46)
div.p: If God seems unwilling to answer our prayers, we have reason to search for any cherished sin within our hearts and put it away.
We should examine ourselves first.
But an unrepentant person looks suspiciously at everyone else, searching everywhere except the heart for the cause of trouble.
Jonathan was identified as the one who had broken Saul's order.
People most indulgent toward their own sins may be the harshest judges of others.
Those who least respect God's commands are often most offended when people fail to obey their commands.
Careless curses can place both the speaker and the family in danger.
Saul's behavior on this occasion displayed rashness, pride, malice and irreverence.
It illustrates the corrupt dispositions of human nature when people are left to themselves.

div.title: Saul's family and reign (verses 47–52)
div.p: The chapter gives a general account of Saul's household and military establishment.
He had little reason to boast of his royal dignity.
Nor did his neighbors have much reason to envy his position.
After gaining the throne, he enjoyed little lasting happiness.
Sometimes earthly glory shines most brightly immediately before a dark period of shame and sorrow.

row.cell: Agag put to death, Samuel and Saul part.

div.title: Saul receives judgment against Amalek (verses 1–9)
div.p: God had announced judgment on the Amalekites long before (Exodus 17:14; Deuteronomy 25:19).
That judgment was delayed until their sins had reached their full measure.
Henry insists that the righteous Lord does no injustice.
The Kenites' ancestors had shown kindness to Israel.
God remembered that kindness and spared their descendants, even while judging Amalek for its ancestors' cruelty.
Henry sees this contrast as evidence of divine justice in this exceptional historical judgment.
It is dangerous to remain in the company of people under God's judgment.
We should separate from their wrongdoing rather than share in their sins and plagues (Revelation 18:4).
God's command to Saul was explicit and tested his obedience.
Saul's failure revealed a proud and rebellious heart.
He destroyed only the animals and goods that were least valuable.
He kept the better things for himself.
The things destroyed were understood in the narrative as given over to divine judgment.
