The ancient command is described here as a historical act of judgment, not a license for private violence or a modern religious campaign.

div.title: Samuel confronts Saul's self-justification (verses 10–23)
div.p: When Scripture speaks of God repenting, Henry explains that this does not mean God changes his mind as people do.
It means a change in the way God deals with people.
The change was in Saul: he had turned away from following the Lord.
Through his rebellion, he made God his enemy.
Samuel prayed for Saul through an entire night.
The rejection of sinners grieves believers.
God does not delight in their death, and neither should we.
Saul boasted that he had obeyed.
Sinners often try to escape God's judgment by defending themselves.
But the sound of the animals Saul had spared spoke against him, like rust testifying against a hoarder (James 5:3).
People often claim to obey God while their indulgence of sinful desires, love of the world, angry and unkind attitudes, and neglect of holy responsibilities testify otherwise.
Consider how much harm arises from greed!
The deepest evil of sin is disobedience to God.
Saul's hearts—and ours when ruled by fleshly desires—try to excuse disobedience by presenting it as something pleasing or useful.
It is difficult to persuade the disobedient that they are wrong.
But God values humble, sincere, conscientious obedience more than any burnt offering or sacrifice.
Obedience honors God and requires us to deny ourselves more than a visible ceremony does.
It is much easier to bring an animal to the altar than to bring every proud thought and our whole will into submission to God.
People unwilling to submit to God's rule are unworthy to rule other human beings.

div.title: Saul's confession is insincere (verses 24–31)
div.p: Henry identifies three signs of hypocrisy in Saul's repentance.
First, Saul sought Samuel's approval and forgiveness, appearing more anxious about Samuel's opinion and favor than God's.
Second, he continued making excuses even while admitting wrongdoing.
That is not the response of genuine repentance.
Third, he cared chiefly about preserving his reputation and influence among the people.
Human beings are changeable and weak.
They alter their plans, fail to accomplish what they intend, and meet events they could not foresee.
But God is not like that.
The Strength of Israel does not lie or fail.

div.title: Samuel judges Agag and mourns Saul (verses 32–35)
div.p: Many people imagine that their greatest danger is past when it is actually near.
They put the thought of death and judgment far away.
Samuel called Agag to account for his own evil acts.
Agag had followed the cruelty of his ancestors, and Henry understands the judgment upon him as reckoning with that history of bloodshed.
Saul seemed unconcerned that God had rejected him.
But Samuel grieved for Saul continually.
In a similar way, Jerusalem remained comfortably careless while Christ wept over it.
Do we truly desire to do all God's will?
Let us turn to him, not merely with outward forms and appearances, but sincerely.

row.cell: Samuel sent to Bethlehem to Jesse.
Saul troubled with an evil spirit, is quieted by David.

div.title: Samuel is sent to Bethlehem (verses 1–5)
div.p: Saul had become very wicked. If he could even contemplate killing Samuel, what evil might he not commit?
The elders of Bethlehem trembled when Samuel arrived. We should stand in awe of God's messengers and tremble at his word.
Samuel answered that he had come in peace, to offer a sacrifice.

When the Lord Jesus came into the world, people might have feared that he had come to condemn it. Instead, he assured them that his mission was peace: he came to sacrifice, bringing the offering himself. God had prepared a body for him.
Let us therefore consecrate ourselves to the Lord and rely upon Christ's sacrifice.

div.title: David is anointed (verses 6–13)
div.p: Samuel had been disappointed by Saul, whose impressive appearance and height had recommended him. Yet Samuel almost made the same mistake again.
We see how people look. God sees what they truly are.
He examines the heart, valuing the faith, reverence and love planted there—qualities beyond ordinary human sight.
We often judge other people's characters wrongly.
Nor does God distribute his favor to our children according to our partial preferences. He frequently blesses those whom others esteem least.
At last David was chosen. He was Jesse's youngest son, apparently the least regarded. His name means “beloved,” and Henry sees him as a picture of God's beloved Son.
The Lord's Spirit came upon David from that day onward.
His anointing was not an empty ceremony. Divine power accompanied the appointed sign.
Although David's outward situation did not immediately change, he received growing wisdom, courage and the qualities needed for kingship. This confirmed that God had chosen him.
In the same way, the best evidence of being appointed to the kingdom of glory is the Spirit of promise sealing us, and the work of grace experienced within our hearts.

div.title: David's music relieves Saul (verses 14–23)
div.p: Saul had become a terror to himself. The Spirit of the Lord departed from him.
If we do not let God and his grace rule us, sin and Satan will take possession.
With God's permission, the devil troubled Saul through his disordered bodily condition and the passions of his mind. He became irritable, dissatisfied and at times frenzied.

Music can improve a person's state of mind. It is therefore regrettable when it is misused to support vanity, luxury or distraction from God and serious thought. Such misuse drives away the good Spirit, not the evil spirit.
Music, recreation, company and business may temporarily quiet an injured conscience.
But only Christ's blood, received by faith, and the sanctifying Spirit, assuring the soul of pardon through holy comfort, can accomplish genuine healing.
Every other attempt to silence spiritual conviction without dealing with sin will eventually deepen the distress, whether in this life or the next.

div.title: Goliath challenges Israel (verses 1–11)
div.p: Human beings depend entirely on God in everything.
When he withdraws his help, even the bravest and most determined people find themselves without courage or strength. Everyday experience confirms this truth.

div.title: David arrives at the camp (verses 12–30)
div.p: Jesse had no idea what would happen when he sent his son to the army at such a critical moment.
But God wisely orders human activities and circumstances to accomplish his own purposes.
When most people have grown formal and lukewarm in religion, anyone willing to go farther or risk more for God's cause is likely to be accused of pride and ambition.
Such criticism may come especially from close relatives, like Eliab, or careless superiors.
This tested David's gentleness, patience and perseverance.
Although reason and justice were on his side, he did not repay insult with insult. A gentle reply turned away his brother's anger.

p.hi: Conquering his own temper was a greater honor than defeating Goliath.

div.p: People who undertake important public service should expect to be misunderstood or opposed, even by those whose encouragement and assistance they had anticipated.
They must humbly keep working despite enemies' threats and friends' suspicions.

div.title: David offers to fight Goliath (verses 31–39)
div.p: David had come straight from caring for sheep that very morning.
Yet this young shepherd had more courage than Israel's mighty warriors.
God often sends useful counsel and accomplishes great things through people whom the world considers weak or foolish.
Just as David answered his brother's anger with gentleness, he answered Saul's fear with faith.
When he tended sheep, David had been careful and tender toward them.
This reminds us of Christ, the good Shepherd, who not only endangered himself for the sheep but gave his life for them.
Past deliverances should encourage us to trust God now and act boldly in our duty. The One who delivered before is still able and willing to deliver.
Saul gave David permission to fight.
But David was not comfortable wearing Saul's armor, which he had never used.
God arranged even this, so that David's victory would be seen clearly as the fruit of faith, not impressive equipment.
A tool is not valuable to us merely because it is excellent in itself. It must be suitable for the person and the work.
Saul's fine coat and strong armor could not help David when they did not fit him.
But faith, prayer, truth, righteousness, the whole armor of God and the mind of Christ are needed by every servant of God, whatever that servant's calling.

div.title: David goes out to meet Goliath (verses 40–47)
div.p: Foolish self-confidence and presumption lead to destruction.
David's answer displayed extraordinary humility, faith and devotion.
He expected God to give him victory.
He was content to appear poorly armed and outwardly insignificant, so that everyone would know the victory belonged to the Lord alone.

div.title: David defeats Goliath (verses 48–58)
div.p: Human life is frail and uncertain, even when someone believes himself fully protected.
How quickly death can come through a very small thing!
Let the strong never boast of their strength, nor the armed of their weapons.
God resists the proud and brings shame upon those who defy him and his people.
No one who stubbornly sets himself against God will ultimately prosper.
The account encourages us to serve God's cause with courage and unwavering trust in him.
Every follower of the Lamb must enter a conflict against an enemy more formidable than Goliath.
The devil still challenges God's people.
But resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Go forward with David's faith, and the powers of darkness will not stand against you.
How often, however, Christians suffer defeat through the unbelief still found in their own hearts!

div.title: Jonathan and David become friends (verses 1–5)
div.p: The friendship between David and Jonathan was a work of divine grace.
Grace brings genuine believers into fellowship, giving them one heart and one soul and causing them to love one another.
This union comes from sharing the Spirit of Christ.
When God has united hearts, worldly differences are too weak to tear them apart.
Those who love Jesus Christ as they love their own souls will gladly enter an everlasting covenant with him.
It was a remarkable sign of God's grace in David that he received so much praise and honor without becoming proud or imagining himself greater than he was.

div.title: Saul tries to kill David (verses 6–11)
div.p: David's troubles followed immediately after his triumph.
Indeed, they arose because of that triumph.
This shows how empty even the greatest worldly success can be.
A person who has become irritable, envious, suspicious and malicious like Saul displays signs that God's Spirit no longer governs the heart.
Compare David holding a harp, seeking to serve Saul, with Saul holding a spear, seeking to kill David.
Notice both the gentleness and usefulness of God's persecuted servant and the cruelty of the persecutor.
David's safety, however, belonged to God's providence.

div.title: Saul fears David and seeks his destruction (verses 12–30)
div.p: David lived for a long time under the constant threat of being killed by Saul.
Yet he continued behaving with gentleness, respect, wisdom and restraint toward the very person persecuting him.
How rare such sound judgment and self-control are amid insult and provocation!
We should ask whether we follow David's example.
Do we behave wisely in every part of our lives?
Are there avoidable failures of duty, rash words or sinful reactions in us?
Other people's stubbornness or unfair treatment never justifies sinful anger in ourselves.
It should instead make us more careful to fulfill the responsibilities belonging to our own position.
Consider Christ, who endured sinners' hostility against himself, so that you do not become weary and lose heart (Hebrews 12:3).
David considered it an honor to become the king's son-in-law.
How much more should we value the privilege of being children of the King of kings!

row.cell: Jonathan reconciles his father to David, Saul again tries to slay him.

div.title: Jonathan pleads for David, but Saul attacks him again (verses 1–10)
div.p: How powerful a truthful and well-reasoned appeal can be!
For a time, Jonathan convinced Saul that his hatred toward David was unreasonable.
Yet Saul soon returned to his murderous hostility.
This shows how deeply rooted the serpent's hatred is against the woman's offspring, and how deceptive and desperately corrupt the human heart remains without God's grace (Jeremiah 17:9).
A temporary conviction of wrongdoing is not the same as a lasting change of heart.

div.title: David escapes and seeks counsel from Samuel (verses 11–24)
div.p: Michal's plan to gain time for David to escape was permissible, Henry says.
But the falsehood she told could not even be excused as necessary.
Her conduct showed that she did not possess the same spirit of godliness that had shaped Jonathan's words to Saul.
David fled to Samuel because he made God his refuge.
As a prophet, Samuel could offer the most reliable advice in a time of distress.
David had found little rest or satisfaction at Saul's court.
He now sought rest among the worshipers gathered around Samuel.
Those who enjoy fellowship with God may have few pleasures in this world, yet those pleasures are precious.
David returned to that fellowship in trouble.
Saul was so determined to kill David that repeated providential defeats of his plans did not convince him David was under God's special protection.
When God chose to protect David by an extraordinary means, Saul himself prophesied.
Many people possess remarkable spiritual gifts but lack saving grace.
They may even prophesy in Christ's name and still be rejected by him.
Let us therefore ask daily for renewing grace, which will become a spring of water welling up into eternal life.
Let us remain firmly devoted to truth and holiness.
In every danger and difficulty, seek God's protection, comfort and guidance through the means of worship and instruction he has appointed.

row.cell: Saul, missing David, seeks to kill Jonathan.

div.title: David seeks Jonathan's help (verses 1–10)
div.p: The troubles David suffered were preparing him for future honor.
God often deals this way with those he is preparing for glory.
He does not immediately place them in possession of his kingdom.
Instead, he leads them through many afflictions and uses those afflictions to prepare them to receive it.
They should not complain about his gracious plan or distrust his care.
They should look forward joyfully to the crown reserved for them.
At times we feel that only a single step separates us from death.
In reality, this is always possible, so we should be prepared.
Yet no danger can end our lives until God's purpose concerning us has been accomplished.
If we are believers, we will not die until we have served our generation according to his will.
Jonathan generously offered David his help.
That is genuine friendship.
Christ similarly assures his people of his love: ask, and it will be done for you.
We should demonstrate our own love for him by keeping his commandments.

div.title: Jonathan renews his covenant with David (verses 11–23)
div.p: Jonathan faithfully promised to tell David how his father felt about him.
We do well to become friends with people whom God favors and to make his friends our friends.
Such a relationship benefits not only us but our families.
True friendship rests on a firm foundation.
It can overcome ambition, selfishness and excessive concern for what others think.
But who can fully understand the love of Jesus?
He offered himself as a sacrifice for rebellious and polluted sinners.
How powerfully should his love move us to love him, support his cause and care for his people!

div.title: Saul turns his anger against Jonathan (verses 24–34)
div.p: David was exceptionally faithful in attending God's appointed worship.
He would not have missed it except because staying away was necessary for his safety.
When great danger threatens, an opportunity for public worship may reasonably be passed by.
But unless there is real necessity, it harms us to neglect regular opportunities to worship God.
Jonathan acted wisely for himself and his family by remaining faithful to David, though Saul attacked him for it.
It is always good to make God's people our people.
That decision will finally benefit us, even when the world considers it contrary to our interests.
Saul's rage was savage.
How anger turns people into beasts—or makes them behave even worse than beasts!

div.title: David and Jonathan part (verses 35–42)
div.p: The separation grieved both faithful friends.
David's position was even more painful because he was leaving behind all his comforts, including the blessings of God's sanctuary.
Yet Christians need not mourn like people without hope.
United with Christ, they are also united with one another.
Before long they will meet again in his presence, never to part.
There God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.

row.cell: David at Gath feigns himself mad.

div.title: David visits Ahimelech (verses 1–9)
div.p: In distress, David fled to God's tabernacle.
It is a great comfort in trouble to have a God to whom we can go, explain our circumstances and ask confidently for guidance.
But David told Ahimelech a serious lie.
How should we regard this?
Scripture does not conceal it, and we must not defend it.
David did wrong, and the consequences were dreadful: his lie contributed to the killing of the Lord's priests.
Later, he remembered the deed with regret.
David had shown strong faith and courage before, but both failed him here.
Fear and weak trust led him into disgraceful wrongdoing.
Had he relied properly on God, he would not have resorted to such a sinful method to preserve himself.
The record is given as a warning, not permission to imitate him—even under the greatest pressure.
David asked Ahimelech for food and a sword.
The priest considered it lawful for David and his companions to eat the bread of the Presence.
Christ, the Son of David, later used this incident to teach that mercy takes precedence over sacrifice, and ceremonial restrictions must yield to moral duty.
Doeg entered the sanctuary just as David did.
We cannot tell merely by someone's attendance at public worship what is in that person's heart.
Some come sincerely to serve God.
Others pretend to worship while observing teachers and gathering accusations against them.
Only God, and later events, can distinguish David from Doeg when both are present in the tabernacle.

div.title: David pretends to be insane at Gath (verses 10–15)
div.p: Persecuted believers have sometimes been treated more kindly by Philistines than by Israelites.
David had reason to trust Achish.
Yet fear overcame him.
His behavior was humiliating and revealed that his courage and faith were wavering.
The more simply we trust and obey God, the more safely and peacefully we can make our way through this troubled world.

row.cell: David at Adullam, Many resort to him.
Saul destroys the priests of Nob.

div.title: David at Adullam (verses 1–5)
div.p: Consider how God can use people who seem weak and unsuitable to carry out his purposes.
The Son of David is ready to receive suffering people who willingly submit to his leadership.
He welcomes everyone who comes to him, however sinful and miserable they may be.
He transforms them into a holy people and employs them in his service.
Those who desire to reign with Christ must be willing first to suffer with him and for him.
Notice how tenderly David cared for his elderly parents.
His first concern was to find them a quiet, safe place to live, whatever might happen to himself.
Children should learn to honor their parents by caring for their comfort and well-being.
Even if they rise to positions of honor or become occupied with demanding work, they must not forget their aging parents.
The Lord directs the steps of a righteous person.
He will preserve his people for the work he has appointed, however hated and exposed they may be.

div.title: Saul orders the slaughter at Nob (verses 6–19)
div.p: Saul's conduct shows the cruelty of jealous malice and the miserable tricks it employs.
He considered everyone around him an enemy simply because they did not agree with everything he said.
Ahimelech answered Saul with the clear conscience of an innocent man.
But the evil spirit ruling Saul drove him to increasingly terrible wrongdoing.
He made accusations that were completely false and unproved.
Cruel rulers seldom lack instruments willing to carry out their cruelty.
After Doeg killed the priests, he went to Nob and killed the other inhabitants.
People whom God abandons to their own sinful desires can commit the vilest deeds.
Yet this judgment fulfilled the Lord's earlier warning concerning the house of Eli.
Saul acted wickedly, but God was righteous in permitting these events.
Not a single word of God's will and warning will fail.

div.title: Abiathar escapes and finds David (verses 20–23)
div.p: David mourned the calamity deeply.
It pains a good person to discover that something he did contributed to other people's suffering.
David must have felt particularly distressed because his earlier lie had helped bring about this terrible event.
He assured Abiathar that he would protect him and spoke confidently of his own preservation.
All who belong to the Son of David may be certain of finding refuge with him (Psalm 91:1).
Despite the disorder, danger and constant urgency of his circumstances, David still made time for fellowship with God and drew strength and comfort from it.

row.cell: God warns him to escape from Keilah.
He is rescued from Saul by an invasion of the Philistines.

div.title: David rescues Keilah (verses 1–6)
div.p: When rulers persecute God's people, they should expect trouble from other directions as well.
A country is most likely to enjoy peace when it allows God's church to live in peace.
While Saul pursued David, the Philistines attacked Saul's country.
But David still regarded himself as a protector of the land.
Jesus Christ, our Savior, likewise acted for the good of those who mistreated him and left us an example.
Those who refuse to do good merely because their past service has not been rewarded are not following David.

div.title: God warns David to leave Keilah (verses 7–13)
div.p: David could rightly complain that his enemies repaid good with evil and love with hostility.
Christ was treated in the same shameful way.
David sought guidance from his great Protector.
As soon as the ephod was brought, he made use of it.
We possess the Scriptures.
Whenever we face a difficult choice, we should consult them: bring the Bible here.
David's prayer was both reverent and extremely specific.
God permits us to pray this way, explaining exactly which matter troubles us and asking for direction.
He knows not only what will happen, but also what would happen under circumstances that never take place.
Thus he knows how to deliver godly people from temptation and how to judge everyone according to their deeds.

div.title: Jonathan encourages David (verses 14–18)
div.p: David made no attempt to harm Saul.
He continued along God's path, waited for God's appointed time and was content to remain hidden in forests and wildernesses.
The world's cruelty toward some of its best people should lessen our love for it and increase our longing for the kingdom in which goodness and holiness will receive everlasting honor.
Jonathan came to comfort David.
As a godly friend, he directed David's attention to God, the foundation of all comfort.
As a self-denying friend, he rejoiced in David's approaching rise to the throne.
As a faithful friend, he renewed their covenant of friendship.
We should regularly renew our own covenant commitment to God and sustain our fellowship with him.
If a single conversation with a true friend can strengthen and comfort us, how much more can we expect from the continual support and powerful love of Jesus Christ—the covenant Friend of believers?

div.title: Saul is forced to abandon the pursuit (verses 19–29)
div.p: Even during his worst wrongdoing, Saul liked to speak as though he were deeply religious.
Such language, without corresponding actions, can deceive both the people hearing it and the people speaking it.
The mountain that separated Saul's forces from David became a picture of divine Providence standing between David and his destroyer.
Do not despair at the thought of problems yet to come.
Trust the Lord, whose counsel is wonderful and whose work is excellent.
Before he allows his promise to fail, he will use even an invasion by Philistines to bring about our escape—at the very moment when the danger appears greatest.
God requires complete dependence upon himself.
“If you do not believe, you will not be established” (Isaiah 7:9).

div.title: David refuses to kill Saul (verses 1–7)
div.p: God placed Saul within David's reach.
But this was an opportunity for David to demonstrate faith and patience.
God had promised David the kingdom.
He had not commanded David to kill the king.
David argued strongly against harming Saul, speaking both to himself and to the men accompanying him.
Sin is something that should alarm us.
We must resist every temptation toward it.
David was not satisfied merely with refusing to do wrong himself.
He also restrained the people around him from doing it.
By doing so, he repaid good for evil to the man who had repaid his good with evil.
All who call themselves Christians should follow this pattern: never be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

div.title: David explains his innocence (verses 8–15)
div.p: David had been falsely accused of seeking Saul's life.
He showed that God had given him the opportunity to harm Saul, but he refused to do so on principle.
He declared that he would never take private vengeance.
When people wrong us, we can trust the Lord to put matters right.
Even if justice does not come in this life, it will come at the judgment of the last day.

div.title: Saul is moved but remains unchanged (verses 16–22)
div.p: Saul seemed overwhelmed by David's kindness.
But many people grieve over their sins without truly repenting.
They weep bitterly yet remain attached to the very sins they mourn.
God fulfilled the promise David had trusted: he would bring David's righteousness into the light (Psalm 37:6).
People who carefully preserve a good conscience can entrust their reputation to God.
Sooner or later, he will make even hardened opponents recognize the people he loves.
Saul and David parted peacefully.
Yet Saul was convinced, not converted.
He was ashamed of his envy but still carried bitterness in his heart.
He was frustrated because, after finally finding David, he could not bring himself to kill him as planned.
Malice may appear dead while merely sleeping, and may later awaken with doubled strength.
Whether God protects us by restraining an enemy's hands or by changing that person's heart so that the enemy will not harm us, the deliverance comes from him.
It is evidence of his love and a pledge of his salvation, for which we should be grateful.

row.cell: Abigail takes a present to David.

div.title: Samuel dies (verse 1)
div.p: All Israel mourned Samuel, and with good reason.
He had prayed for the people every day.
People have hard hearts when they can bury faithful ministers without sorrow and fail to feel the loss of those who prayed for them and taught them the Lord's way.

div.title: Nabal refuses David's request (verses 2–11)
div.p: We might never have heard of Nabal if nothing had happened between him and David.
His name means “fool.”
Wealth makes people appear impressive in the world's eyes, but to someone who judges rightly, Nabal was a very small man.
He had no honor or honesty. He was rude, quarrelsome, ill-tempered, oppressive and willing to use fraud or violence to gain and preserve possessions.
What reason have we to admire worldly wealth when such a man can be rich while a good man such as David lacks necessities?
David pointed to the protection and kindness he had given Nabal's shepherds.
David's followers were themselves distressed, indebted and discontented, while supplies were scarce.
His careful leadership had kept them from taking what belonged to others.
But Nabal responded angrily to a request for help.
Greedy people often try to cover one sin with another, abusing the poor as a way of excusing their refusal to help them.
God is not deceived by that behavior.
We should learn to endure insults and false portrayals cheerfully and patiently, as many excellent believers have had to do.
Nabal insisted that the food on his table belonged to him.
But we are mistaken if we imagine that owning something gives us unlimited moral authority to use it however we please.
We are only stewards of possessions entrusted to us by their true Owner.

div.title: David plans revenge (verses 12–17)
div.p: God is kind even to the wicked and ungrateful. Why should we not act similarly?
David, however, decided to kill Nabal and everyone belonging to his household.
Could this really be David, who had spent so long suffering and should have learned patience?
Usually calm and thoughtful, he now became so enraged by a few offensive words that he was ready to destroy a whole family.
Even the best believers may show terrible corruption when God allows them to discover what is in their own hearts.
How urgently we need to pray: Lord, do not lead us into temptation.

div.title: Abigail brings a gift and speaks wisely (verses 18–31)
div.p: Abigail's gift made up for Nabal's refusal.
She approached David with great humility, speaking as someone asking for pardon.
A humble, yielding response can calm even a serious offense.
She could not defend her husband's conduct.
Rather than trusting the cleverness of her own arguments, she depended on God's grace to soften David's anger.
She reminded David that taking revenge on a weak and contemptible opponent like Nabal was beneath him.
Nabal would not do him good, but neither could he truly harm him.
God would preserve David and bring him through his present troubles to a glorious future.
It would therefore be wrong for David to take away anyone's life unjustly or unnecessarily, especially the lives of God's own people.
Abigail's strongest argument came last.

p.hi: Refusing revenge would protect David's peace and conscience.

div.p: Many people have acted in fury and later regretted the decision a thousand times.
The sweetness of vengeance quickly becomes bitter.
Whenever we feel tempted to sin, we should ask how the action will appear to us afterward.

div.title: David is restrained; Nabal dies (verses 32–39)
div.p: David thanked God for sending someone to stop him before he committed a grievous sin.
Whenever we receive helpful counsel, encouragement, warning or timely correction, we should recognize God's kindness in sending it.
We should be thankful for providential events that prevent us from sinning.
Most people consider it enough to endure criticism patiently.
Few are grateful for correction or praise the person who gives it as a friend.
Yet the closer we have come to doing wrong, the greater the mercy of being stopped.
Sinners are often most confident of their safety when their danger is greatest.
Nabal, meanwhile, was drunk and felt completely secure.
He could not enjoy abundance with moderation or be pleasant with his companions without becoming beastlike through excess.
Nothing more surely reveals how little wisdom a person has—or destroys what wisdom remains—than habitual drunkenness.
The next morning his joy gave way to terror.
His heart, lively with wine the previous evening, became heavy as stone.
Such is the deception of fleshly pleasures: laughter quickly gives way to grief.
Those who drink to excess are saddened when they reflect on their own foolishness.
About ten days later, the Lord struck Nabal and he died.
David thanked God that he himself had been prevented from killing him.
Worldly disappointment, injured pride or a terrified conscience can end the pleasure of someone who lives for appetite and wealth.
But whatever instrument is used, death comes when God appoints it.
div.note: Editorially restored separate Concise exposition; absent from the pinned MHCC 0.1.1 compiled K body. See source provenance ledger.
div.title: David marries Abigail (verses 39–44)
div.p: Abigail believed that David would become Israel's king.
She highly valued his godly and excellent character.
Although he was now in distress, she regarded his marriage proposal as an honor and a benefit.
She agreed humbly, in a way consistent with the customs of the time, and was willing to share his trials.
Those who unite themselves to Christ must similarly be willing to suffer with him now, trusting that afterward they will reign with him.

row.cell: Saul goes after David, who again spares Saul's life.

div.title: David spares Saul again (verses 1–12)
div.p: How quickly an ungodly heart loses the good impressions once made by conviction!
Saul and all his men were completely helpless.
They might as well have been disarmed and chained, yet their only limitation was that God had put them into a deep sleep.
How easily the Lord can weaken the strongest, confuse the wisest and frustrate the most watchful!
David remained determined to wait until God himself thought it right to avenge him.
He would never seize the promised kingdom through sinful methods.
The temptation to kill Saul was powerful.
But David knew that giving in would be a sin against God.
He therefore refused it and entrusted the outcome to the Lord.

div.title: David speaks with Saul (verses 13–20)
div.p: David reasoned earnestly and affectionately with the king.
People who prevent us from attending God's appointed worship are doing everything they can to estrange us from God and make us live as heathens.
Anything that exposes us to sin should be counted among the greatest wrongs another person can do us.
David suggested that if the Lord had stirred Saul against him as a judgment on either of them, they should both seek reconciliation.
If an evil spirit permitted by God was troubling Saul, the answer was still to seek peace with God.
David therefore urged a sacrifice and reconciliation.

div.title: Saul acknowledges wrong but does not repent (verses 21–25)
div.p: Saul again spoke pleasant words and expressed good wishes.
Yet he gave no evidence of genuine repentance toward God.
David and Saul parted for the last time.
No peace between human beings is secure unless it rests upon peace with God through Jesus Christ.
People who sin against God are acting foolishly and making serious mistakes.
Many glimpse this truth for a moment, then deliberately close their eyes to it.
Fair promises do not make someone trustworthy after a long pattern of knowingly disobeying God's light.
Nevertheless, the admission of wrongdoing by a stubborn sinner can assure believers that they are acting rightly and encourage them to keep going.
Their true reward must be expected from the Lord alone.

div.title: David seeks refuge in Gath (verses 1–7)
div.p: Even good people easily fall into unbelief when they face outward conflict and inward fear.
It is difficult to overcome both.

p.hi: Lord, increase our faith!

div.p: We should be ashamed that a Philistine's word proved more reliable for David than an Israelite's word.
The city of Gath became a refuge for him because Israel's cities refused to provide a safe home.
David secured a comfortable place to live.
It was some distance from Gath, yet near enough to Israel that he could remain in contact with his own people.

div.title: David deceives Achish (verses 8–12)
div.p: While living in Philistine territory, David attacked surviving peoples of nations that had been marked for ancient judgment.
Henry understands those enemies as having long been condemned.
It can be wise to avoid public notice, but we should never become idle.
In every situation, we should seek an appropriate opportunity to serve God's cause.
David concealed his expeditions from Achish.
But an ambiguous statement intended to mislead is no better in its moral purpose than an outright lie.

p.hi: Deceptive evasion is especially dangerous because it can appear respectable while carrying the same intention as falsehood.

div.p: Even genuine believers often show serious imperfections.
But they cannot ultimately be persuaded to abandon God's service, unite their interests with his enemies or become permanent slaves of sin and Satan.
How many evils grow out of unbelief!
When we forget God's former mercies and his promises, anxiety and fear may overwhelm us.
Then we may adopt disgraceful means to escape our difficulties.
Nothing gives firmer steadiness in holy conduct or offers greater protection against needless distress than unwavering trust in God's promises in Jesus Christ.

row.cell: Achish puts confidence in David, Saul's fear.
Saul consults a witch at Endor.

div.title: Achish trusts David; Saul becomes afraid (verses 1–6)
div.p: David faced a very difficult situation.
Refusing Achish's demand for military assistance would expose him to danger.
But if he promised help and then remained neutral—or turned against the Philistines—he would act ungratefully and betray their trust.
If he fought against Israel, he would sin gravely.
He seemed unable to escape without compromising his conscience.
Yet his ambiguous answer, intended to gain time, was not worthy of a true Israelite.
Trouble becomes terrifying to those who live in disobedience.
In his distress Saul inquired of the Lord.
But he did not approach in faith.
His divided heart made him unstable.
Saul had enforced the law against people who consulted familiar spirits (Exodus 22:18).
Some people appear zealous against wrongdoing only when they personally suffer from it.
They care little for God's honor and do not really hate sin because it is sin.
They condemn in others what they willingly practice themselves.
Saul tried to drive the devil from his kingdom while harboring envy and malice in his own heart.
How foolish to seek help from the very people he had tried to remove in obedience to God's law!

div.title: Saul consults the medium at Endor (verses 7–19)
div.p: Once we depart from the plain path of duty, nearly every choice leads us farther astray and increases confusion and temptation.
Saul asked the woman to summon someone from the dead.
God had expressly forbidden such practices (Deuteronomy 18:11).

Whether it is genuine occult activity or merely a pretended one, the attempt to obtain help or knowledge through a creature that cannot be obtained from God in the path of duty is either malicious or deeply ignorant.
While Samuel lived, Scripture never describes Saul consulting him in difficult decisions.
He should have sought that counsel then.
Now Samuel was dead, Saul asked for him to be brought back.
Some people despise and persecute godly ministers while they live and wish to have them back only after their deaths.
Henry concludes that this episode cannot be explained as a mere human trick or deception.
The woman had no power to summon Samuel by her own will.
But God may have permitted Samuel's appearance in response to Saul's inquiry.
The woman's surprise and terror show that what happened was unusual and unexpected.
Saul had rejected Samuel's solemn warnings during Samuel's lifetime.
Now he hoped, in defiance of God's command, to receive encouragement or advice from him.
God may instead have allowed the departed prophet to appear in order to confirm his earlier judgment and announce Saul's approaching death.
The words “You and your sons shall be with me” establish only that they would be in the world of the dead.
They do not establish the spiritual or eternal state of Saul or his sons.
The event solemnly shows God permitting a departed prophet to confirm from beyond the grave what he had already declared on earth.

div.title: Saul falls into despair (verses 20–25)
div.p: Anyone seeking help or comfort outside God's appointed ways will be disappointed as Saul was.
His terror led almost to despair, but not to humility.
He did not confess his sin.
He offered no sacrifices or prayers for pardon.
Nor does he appear to have considered the fate of his children and people or tried to escape the danger.
Instead, in stubborn despair, he moved toward destruction.
God has placed a few such examples in Scripture as warnings.
They teach us never to suppress conviction or despise the divine word.
But any sinner who still has even one thought of genuine repentance must not suppose himself beyond hope.
Let that person humble himself, seek the Lord's mercy and determine to continue seeking it throughout life.
Such a person will not seek God in vain.

row.cell: David objected to by the Philistines.

div.title: The Philistine commanders object to David (verses 1–5)
div.p: David waited with a secret hope that the Lord would rescue him from his difficult position.
Yet his agreement to accompany Achish seems to have been influenced too strongly by fear of human beings.
It is hard to come right to the edge of sin without falling into it.
God inclined the Philistine commanders to object to David's taking part in the battle.
Their hostility became a blessing to him.
It gave him a kind of help that even his closest friends could not have provided.

div.title: Achish sends David away (verses 6–11)
div.p: David had rarely received a greater deliverance than being released from such a dangerous and morally compromising obligation.
God's people should behave in ways that, as far as possible, earn the respect of everyone with whom they deal.
And when others have acted honorably, it is right to speak well of them.

row.cell: He recovers what had been lost.

div.title: Ziklag is plundered (verses 1–6)
div.p: When we travel in the path of duty, we may confidently hope God will care for our families during our absence.
But we cannot claim that assurance when we deliberately abandon duty.
If we return from a journey and find our home peaceful rather than devastated, as David found his, we should thank the Lord.
David's men complained bitterly about him.
People who possess great faith must expect severe trials.
But notice that David was brought to this very low position immediately before being raised to the throne.
When circumstances appear worst for God's church and people, improvement may already be near.

p.hi: David strengthened himself in the Lord his God.

div.p: His men's sorrow turned into anger and impatience, adding to their suffering.
David had more cause than any of them to grieve, yet he handled the calamity better.
They gave their passions free rein.
He put his spiritual graces to work.
While they discouraged one another, he kept his spirit calm by seeking encouragement in God.
Those who have chosen the Lord as their God can find strength in him even in the darkest circumstances.

div.title: David pursues the Amalekites (verses 7–15)
div.p: We should acknowledge God in all our ways, even when—as here—the justice of what we are doing appears beyond doubt.
Then we may trust him to direct our steps, as David did.
David showed tenderness toward his exhausted men.
He refused to make them continue beyond their strength.
The Son of David likewise considers the condition of his followers.
They do not all possess equal energy or strength in spiritual effort and conflict.
Where we are weak, Christ is kind.
More than that, his strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9–10).
A young Egyptian servant, abandoned and almost dead, became the means by which David found the raiders.
God used this cruelly treated servant in the defeat of the Amalekites.
He hears the cry of the oppressed.
Those who withhold compassion from people in distress do not deserve the name of true Israelites.
We should neither harm nor refuse kindness to anyone.
One day, even the most insignificant person may have the power to repay a kindness—or an injury.

div.title: The stolen goods are recovered (verses 16–20)
div.p: Sinners are often closest to ruin when they feel most secure and proclaim peace and safety.
They put the thought of the coming day of judgment far from themselves.
Indulgence in bodily pleasures gives our spiritual enemies a special advantage.
Eating, drinking and dancing have provided a pleasant-looking path by which many have gone down to death.
David recovered everything that had been stolen.
Nothing remained lost, and much more was gained.

div.title: David shares the spoils fairly (verses 21–31)
div.p: Whatever God gives us should be used to do good.
David distributed the recovered goods with both justice and generosity.
People who take pleasure in imposing hardships on their brothers and sisters, caring nothing if others go hungry as long as they themselves have plenty, are truly wicked.
David treated his friends generously and kindly.
Everyone who recognizes the Lord as the Giver of abundance should distribute what has been received with fairness and liberality.

row.cell: Saul's body rescued by the men of Jabesh-gilead.

div.title: Saul is defeated and dies (verses 1–7)
div.p: We cannot determine anyone's spiritual or eternal state merely from the way that person dies.
Death comes to the righteous and the wicked.
Saul was badly wounded and could neither resist nor flee.
Yet he showed no concern for his immortal soul.
His only stated concern was that the Philistines might insult him or cause him pain.
He then took his own life.
Henry condemns that final action as sinful.
He also warns that the devil tempts people in great distress to believe such a desperate act is an answer to suffering.
We should guard against that temptation by understanding its moral seriousness before God and the grievous consequences it can bring to others.
But our real security does not come from our own strength.
It comes from the Lord who keeps Israel.
Let us watch and pray, and put on the whole armor of God, so that we may stand firm in the evil day and remain standing after the conflict.

div.title: The men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve Saul's body (verses 8–13)
div.p: Scripture records what became of the bodies of Saul and his sons.
It does not say what became of their souls after death.
Hidden things do not belong to us.
The way we die, or what happens afterward to our physical remains, matters far less than our eternal relation to God.
If our souls are saved, our bodies will be raised incorruptible and glorious.
But refusing to fear the One who can destroy both body and soul in hell is extreme folly.
The honor people give the dead cannot help those suffering under God's judgment.
Impressive funerals, magnificent monuments and generous praise may preserve a person's public reputation.
Yet those things cannot change the soul's condition.
We should therefore seek the honor that comes from God alone.

div.title: 2 Samuel — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: This book records the reign of King David.
It describes his victories, Israel's increasing prosperity and his efforts to reform the nation's religious life.
It also records the serious sins David committed and the troubles that came upon his family and his nation as punishment.
Many events in this history deserve to be imitated, while others were written to warn us.
Scripture gives a truthful account of David's reign rather than concealing his failures.
Anyone who weighs his many virtues and excellent qualities fairly alongside his faults will recognize him as a great and godly man.

row.cell: Tidings brought to David of the death of Saul.
The Amalekite is put to death.
David's lamentation for Saul and Jonathan.

div.title: David receives news of Saul's death (verses 1–10)
div.p: The event that opened David's way to the throne happened at about the same time he was suffering severe distress.
People who have entrusted their concerns to the Lord can wait quietly for his will to be done.
David's response showed that he had not desired Saul's death and had not grown impatient to receive the kingdom.

div.title: The Amalekite is put to death (verses 11–16)
div.p: David genuinely mourned Saul.
All those with him humbled themselves beneath God's hand, which had fallen heavily upon Israel in its defeat.
David ordered the man who brought the news to be executed because the man had confessed to murdering the king.
Henry argues that David did not act unjustly in this case.
If the Amalekite's account was true, the man had committed treason and deserved death under the law of that time.
But if he had lied to David, the lie had brought about his own death.
So lies will sooner or later turn against the people who tell them.
David showed zeal for public justice without allowing his own personal advantage to influence the matter.

div.title: David laments Saul and Jonathan (verses 17–27)
div.p: Henry thinks Kasheth, meaning “the bow,” was probably the title of David's funeral song.
David did not praise Saul for virtues he had not possessed.
In particular, he said nothing about Saul's religious devotion or personal goodness.
Yet Jonathan had been a dutiful son and Saul an affectionate father, and they loved one another.
David had good reason to say that Jonathan's love for him had been extraordinary.
Next to the love shared between Christ and his people, the affection that flows from such love produces the strongest friendships.
The suffering of God's people and the victories of his enemies always grieve true believers, even when those events may bring the believers personal advantage.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections

row.cell: Abner makes Ishbosheth king Battle between Abner's men and those of Joab.

div.title: David is made king at Hebron (verses 1–7)
div.p: After Saul died, many people gathered around David at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:22).
But David trusted the Lord, who had promised him the kingdom, to give it in the proper time and way.
Confidence in God's promise does not discourage diligent effort.
It encourages it.
Someone chosen for the crown of life should not say, “Then I need do nothing.”
Rather, that person should say, “Then I will do everything God directs me to do.”
David made this use of his calling, and all whom God chooses should do likewise.
When we travel or move to a new home, it is a great comfort to know the Lord goes before us.
We may have that confidence when faith and prayer set him before us.
God directed David's steps as promised.
David's rise was gradual.
In the same way, the kingdom of the Messiah, the Son of David, advances by stages.
Christ already is Lord of all, though we do not yet see everything subjected to him.

div.title: Abner supports Ish-bosheth; civil war begins (verses 8–17)
div.p: Most of Israel refused to recognize David.
The Lord used that rejection to train his servant for later responsibility and usefulness.
David's conduct under repeated difficulties displayed the strength of genuine godliness.
He was a picture of Christ, whom Israel would not receive even though the Father had anointed him as Prince and Savior.
Abner suggested that the young soldiers should “play” before the leaders.
But he was proposing a deadly contest.
Fools make a game out of sin.
Anyone who treats human bloodshed as entertainment is unworthy of being called human.

div.title: Asahel pursues Abner and dies (verses 18–24)
div.p: Death often approaches by a path we do not expect.
The very abilities we take the greatest pride in can become our undoing.
Asahel's speed, which he trusted so confidently, did not save him.
Instead, it hastened his death.

div.title: The rival armies withdraw (verses 25–32)
div.p: Abner appealed to Joab to consider the terrible consequences of civil war.
Those who make light of such unnatural conflict will eventually find it bitter for everyone involved.
People easily appeal to reason when it benefits them, though they refused to listen to reason when it worked against their interests.
Notice how quickly a change in circumstances can change a person's opinion.
What seemed enjoyable in the morning can appear dreadful by night.
Those most eager to enter a dispute often regret it before it ends.
They would have done better to avoid the quarrel at the start, as Solomon counsels.
The same is true of every sin.
Would that people considered early enough how bitter its outcome will be!
The account mentions Asahel's burial.
People distinguish the graves and remains of important individuals from those of others.
But at the resurrection only one distinction will endure forever: godly or ungodly.

row.cell: Joab kills Abner David mourns for him.

div.title: David grows stronger (verses 1–6)
div.p: The long conflict tested David's faith and patience.
When he finally established his kingdom, the blessing was all the more welcome because he had waited for it.
This struggle pictures the war between grace and corruption in the hearts of believers.
It is a long conflict.
The flesh desires what opposes the Spirit, and the Spirit opposes the flesh.
As God's work of holiness progresses, corruption gradually grows weaker—like the household of Saul—while grace grows stronger, like the household of David.

div.title: Abner leaves Ish-bosheth for David (verses 7–21)
div.p: Many people commit disgraceful offenses but are too proud to bear correction or even the suspicion that they may be guilty.
Those who continue in sin while pretending not to care often know within themselves that they are fighting against God.
Some pursue only their own advantage.
They will betray the people who trust them when they see something to gain.
Even through people driven by revenge, ambition or sinful desire, the Lord can carry out his own purposes.
But because such people do not intend to honor him, they may ultimately be cast aside with contempt.
David's willingness to receive Michal showed generosity both toward her and toward the memory of Saul.
He probably recalled that he had once owed his life to her love.
He also knew her separation from him had occurred partly through her father's authority.
No one should set his heart upon someone or something to which he has no rightful claim.
If disagreement has separated husband and wife, those who desire God's blessing should seek reconciliation and live together in love.

div.title: Joab murders Abner; David mourns (verses 22–39)
div.p: Abner had acted scornfully, and judgment awaited him.
Yet Joab's killing of him was wicked.
David was deeply distressed by the murder and publicly demonstrated his hatred of the crime.
The guilt of murder can bring a curse upon families.
If human courts fail to hold murderers accountable, God will.
People act foolishly when they shorten their own days or make no preparation for the world to come.
How desirable is human authority, really?
A ruler can hold the title and bear responsibility, yet find his ability to do right severely limited.
David should have performed his duty and then trusted God with the outcome.
But worldly calculation led him to spare Joab.
The Son of David may delay judgment for a long time.
He will never fail to judge unrepentant sinners.
The One who now reigns on David's throne possesses a much greater kingdom.
Everything he does is observed with joy by those who willingly belong to him.

row.cell: David puts to death the murderers.

div.title: Ish-bosheth is murdered (verses 1–7)
div.p: Consider how Ish-bosheth was killed!
When difficulties arise, they should encourage us to act wisely and vigorously.
If instead they drain away our courage and effort, we may lose both our earthly lives and the heavenly crowns toward which we should be striving.
Do not love sleep so much that it leads to poverty and ruin.
A soul made idle is an easy target for the destroyer.
None of us knows where or when death will come.
Whenever we lie down to sleep, we cannot be certain we will wake again.
Nor can we know from whose hand death may reach us.

div.title: David judges the murderers (verses 8–12)
div.p: We may be glad to receive something to which we have a rightful claim while sincerely grieving over the unlawful means by which it came into our hands.
We may mourn the death of a person even if that death appears to benefit us.
The men who killed Ish-bosheth shed innocent blood for wicked, self-interested reasons.
David was right, in Henry's judgment, to carry out the historical punishment against them.
He refused to accept help toward the throne when it came through wrongdoing.
The Lord had already brought David through many difficulties and dangers.
David trusted him to complete the work he had begun, without the help of criminal schemes.
David spoke of being delivered from every adversity as though it were already accomplished.
He knew that the God who had delivered him in the past would continue to deliver him, though many storms still lay ahead.

row.cell: He takes the strong-hold of Zion.

div.title: David becomes king over all Israel (verses 1–5)
div.p: David was now anointed king for the third time.
His rise had been gradual so that his faith could be tested and he could gain experience.
In this way his rule pictured the kingdom of the Messiah, which also grows toward its full glory by stages.
Jesus became our Brother.
He took our human nature and lived within it so that he could become our Prince and Savior.
A humbled sinner can take courage from this close and loving relationship.
Such a person seeks his salvation, submits to his authority and asks for his protection.

div.title: David takes Zion (verses 6–10)
div.p: God's enemies often feel most confident in their strength shortly before their fall.
The pride and insults of the Jebusites stirred David to action, and the Lord God of hosts was with him.
Similarly, on the day of God's power, Satan's stronghold—the human heart—can become God's dwelling through the Spirit.
It becomes the throne on which the Son of David rules and brings every thought into obedience to himself.
May Christ enter our hearts, claim them, cleanse them, overthrow every idol and reign forever!

div.title: God establishes David's kingdom (verses 11–16)
div.p: David's house was not made less holy or less fit to be dedicated to God because foreign builders helped construct it.
The gospel church is described in similar language:
The sons of foreigners will rebuild its walls, and their kings will serve it (Isaiah 60:10).
David's kingdom became firmly established.
Likewise, the Son of David reigns securely, as do those who through him are made kings and priests to God.
Israel had never appeared so great as it did at this time.
Many people enjoy God's favor and love without recognizing it and therefore miss the comfort they might have had.
To receive his favor and know that we have it is great happiness.
David recognized that God had raised him to power for the good of his people, so he could bless them and they could live happily under his leadership.

div.title: David defeats the Philistines (verses 17–25)
div.p: The Philistines overlooked the fact that David enjoyed God's presence, which Saul had lost.
In the same way, as soon as the Messiah's kingdom was established in the world, it came under attack from powers of darkness.
Nations raged and rulers stood against it, but in vain (Psalm 2:1).
The eventual defeat would fall upon Satan's own kingdom.
David confessed his dependence upon God for victory.
He asked whether the Lord would fight for him and submitted to God's decision.
The promise of victory over our spiritual enemies should give us courage in spiritual conflict.
David waited until God moved.
Then he acted—but not before.
He was being trained in dependence on God and his providence.
The Lord performed what he had promised, and David made good use of every opportunity provided.
Likewise, before the apostles began their work against Satan's kingdom, they had to wait for the promised Spirit.
He came upon them with a sound from heaven like a rushing, powerful wind (Acts 2:2).

row.cell: Uzzah smitten for touching the ark, Obed-edom blessed.
David brings the ark to Zion.

div.title: The ark leaves Kiriath-jearim (verses 1–5)
div.p: God remains present with the souls of his people even when they lack outward signs of that presence.
But now that David was established as king, the ark began to receive proper honor again.
Let us learn to speak and think reverently about the Lord and about the means of worship he has appointed.
Those means are signs of his presence among us, just as the ark was for Israel (Matthew 28:20).

p.hi: Christ is our Ark.

div.p: Through him God shows his favor and accepts our prayers and praise.
The ark especially pictured Christ's mediation, in which the Lord's name and glory are displayed.
The priests should have carried the ark on their shoulders.
The Philistines had moved it in a cart without being punished.
But when Israelites, who had received a specific instruction, used a cart, they did so at their peril.
God's appointed way of worship matters.

div.title: Uzzah is judged; Obed-edom receives a blessing (verses 6–11)
div.p: Uzzah died after touching the ark.
God saw presumptuous irreverence in his heart.
Familiarity with holy things can lead people to treat them casually and with contempt.
How serious it is to claim the privileges of God's covenant without receiving them on the terms he has appointed!
Obed-edom welcomed the ark into his house without fear.
He knew that the ark brought judgment only upon those who treated it wrongly.
The same divine hand that judged Uzzah's arrogance rewarded Obed-edom's reverent confidence.
We should not despise the gospel because some people who reject it come under judgment.
Consider instead the blessings it brings to those who welcome it.
Heads of households should be encouraged to maintain genuine religion in their families.
A home that welcomes the ark is blessed, and everyone living there benefits.

div.title: David brings the ark to Zion (verses 12–19)
div.p: People could see that those living near the ark were blessed.
Christ is a stumbling stone and a cause of offense to those who disobey.
But to believers he is a chosen, precious cornerstone (1 Peter 2:6–8).
Let us welcome the blessing of fellowship with him.
We do not need to deprive others of such blessing to receive it ourselves.
When David resumed the procession, he first offered sacrifices.
Our undertakings are more likely to go well when we begin with God and seek peace with him.
We are unworthy and our worship is imperfect.
Therefore even our greatest religious joy must remain joined to repentance and faith in Christ's atoning blood.
David celebrated with deep and wholehearted delight.
We should serve God with every power and ability of body and soul.
David put aside his royal clothing and wore plain linen garments.
He prayed with and for the people, and as a prophet he formally pronounced the Lord's blessing over them.

div.title: Michal despises David's worship (verses 20–23)
div.p: After the celebration, David returned home to bless his family.
He intended to pray with them and for them and lead them in thanksgiving for this national mercy.
Even angels worship God.
Surely such service cannot degrade even the greatest person.
Yet the houses of kings are not free from family troubles.
Acts of sincere devotion often look foolish or undignified to people who have little religious life themselves.
If we can approve our conduct before God, acting sincerely in his presence, we need not fear their criticism.
Faithfulness to God deserves public acknowledgment.
We should not be careless in our service, or afraid or ashamed to profess it.
David was content to defend his conduct.
He did not continue rebuking Michal for her contempt.
But God judged her.
Those who honor the Lord will be honored, while those who despise him and his servants will be brought low.

div.title: David desires to build a house for God (verses 1–3)
div.p: Now that David enjoyed peace in his palace, he began considering how best to use his free time and prosperity in God's service.
He planned to build a temple for the ark.
Nathan encouraged him.
In this conversation, however, Nathan was not speaking as a prophet with a divine message.
He was expressing his private judgment as a godly man.
We should make every effort to encourage other people's good purposes and help them undertake worthwhile work whenever we have an opportunity.

div.title: The Lord makes a covenant promise to David (verses 4–17)
div.p: God promised blessings to David's family and descendants.
These promises concerned Solomon, David's immediate successor, and the continuing royal line of Judah.
But they also reached beyond those kings to Jesus Christ, who is often called David or the Son of David.
God gave Christ all authority in heaven and on earth, including power to judge.
Christ would build the gospel temple, a house honoring God's name: the spiritual temple of true believers, where God dwells through the Holy Spirit.
The promise that David's house, throne and kingdom would be established forever finds its complete fulfillment only in Christ and his kingdom.
David's earthly royal dynasty eventually came to an end.
The statement about a son committing wrongdoing, however, cannot apply to the sinless Messiah himself.
It applies to his spiritual descendants, true believers who still possess weaknesses and faults.
They may expect divine correction, but not final rejection.

div.title: David prays and gives thanks (verses 18–29)
div.p: David's prayer breathes deep love and devotion toward God.
He thought humbly of his own merits.
Everything we possess must be regarded as a divine gift.
David spoke with great reverence and gratitude about the Lord's favor.
Considering what human beings are, and their fallen condition, it is astonishing that God should deal so graciously with them.

p.hi: The promise of Christ contains every blessing.

div.p: If the Lord God belongs to us, what more could we ask or imagine (Ephesians 3:20)?
God knows us better than we know ourselves.
Let us therefore be satisfied with his dealings.
What could we add to our prayers that he has not already anticipated through his promises?
David ascribed everything to God's free grace—both what the Lord had done for him and what he had made known to him.
All was for his word's sake, which Henry understands as for Christ's sake, the eternal Word.
Many people begin praying while their hearts are wandering.
David had found his heart: gathered it away from distraction, fixed it upon God and devoted it to prayer.
Words from the tongue alone do not please God.
Prayer must rise from the heart, which is lifted up and poured out before him.
David's confidence rested upon the certainty of divine promise.
He asked God to fulfill what he had said.
Unlike human beings, God's speaking and God's doing cannot be separated.
He will act as he promised.
His promises are not addressed to each of us by name as they were to David.
Yet they belong to everyone who believes in Jesus Christ and appeals to them in his name.

row.cell: David subdues the Philistines, the Moabites, and the Syrians.

div.title: David defeats surrounding nations (verses 1–8)
div.p: David subdued the Philistines, who had troubled Israel for many years.
In the same way, after the saints have fought long and often against the powers of darkness, the Son of David will place those enemies beneath their feet and make them more than conquerors.
David also defeated the Moabites and made them pay tribute.
Two portions were destroyed, and a third was spared.
Henry urges that the line of mercy should be stretched as far as possible.
David also defeated the Syrians.
The Lord preserved him through these wars, and in his psalms David repeatedly gave God the glory for his victories.

div.title: The captured treasures are dedicated to God (verses 9–14)
div.p: David set apart the precious things he obtained for the future construction of the temple.
He had destroyed the golden idols of the Philistines (2 Samuel 5:21), but dedicated the golden vessels to God's service.
The grace of the Son of David acts in a similar way when it wins a soul.
Everything that stands opposed to God must be destroyed.
Every sinful desire must be put to death and crucified.
But whatever can honor God should be dedicated to him.
In this way its purpose and rightful ownership are changed.
God employs his servants differently.
Some, like David, fight battles.
Others, like Solomon, build.
One servant prepares work that another completes, and God receives the glory for both.

div.title: David governs with justice (verses 15–18)
div.p: David neither committed injustice nor withheld or delayed justice from anyone.
He worked diligently and was ready to receive requests and appeals.
He judged without favoritism.
In these qualities he pictured Jesus Christ.
Let us submit to Christ, seek his friendship and regard his service as our joy.
Let us diligently perform the duties he has given each of us.
David appointed his sons to important positions of authority.
But believers, who are Christ's spiritual descendants, receive still greater honor.
Through him they are made kings and priests to God (Revelation 1:6).

div.title: David remembers Jonathan's family (verses 1–8)
div.p: Amid many responsibilities, we easily forget the gratitude we owe and the promises we have made—not only to our friends, but to God himself.
Yet people whose faith is genuine cannot remain content until they fulfill these duties.
The people who most deserve practical kindness and charity do not always come to our attention without some effort to find them.
Jonathan had been David's friend, bound by solemn promise.
David therefore sought out Jonathan's son Mephibosheth to show him kindness.
God remains faithful to us.
We must not act unfaithfully toward one another.
If Providence lifts us into a better position while our friends or their families suffer poverty or disgrace, we should regard this change as an especially good opportunity to help them.

div.title: David provides for Mephibosheth (verses 9–13)
div.p: David pictured Jesus Christ, who is both David's Lord and Son—his Root and Offspring.
David's kindness to Mephibosheth therefore reminds us of God's astonishing love toward fallen humanity.
David owed something to Jonathan because of their covenant.

p.hi: God, however, was under no such obligation to save sinners.

div.p: The Son of God came looking for a lost and ruined human race.
Human beings were not seeking him.
He came to seek and to save them.

div.title: Hanun humiliates David's messengers (verses 1–5)
div.p: Nahash had been an enemy of Israel, yet he had treated David kindly.
David therefore decided to repay that kindness with gratitude.
Even if a Pharisee gives charity for prideful motives, so that God will not reward the giver, the person receiving that help should still be thankful.
People who bear hostility toward their neighbors often refuse to believe that those neighbors could wish them well.
Even the best-intentioned action may be twisted into an insult by someone who loves nobody but himself.
Faithful people should not be surprised to have their motives misrepresented in this way.
Love does not suspect evil without reason.
According to the customs of the time and place, Hanun treated David's ambassadors with extreme contempt.
David showed real concern for his humiliated servants.
We should not allow unjust accusations or insults to crush our spirits.
Such reproaches will eventually fade and reflect shame upon their authors.
An unfairly damaged reputation can recover, just as the ambassadors' beards would grow again.
God will bring the righteousness of his servants into the light.
We should wait for him patiently (Psalm 37:6–7).

div.title: The Ammonites are defeated (verses 6–14)
div.p: Those who oppose the Son of David both provoke and initiate conflict with him.
God has forces at his disposal to answer those who defy his judgment (Isaiah 5:19).
They will discover that no one can harden his heart against God and prosper.
Those who fight under Christ's leadership should strengthen one another in spiritual warfare.
We should omit nothing that belongs to our duty, regardless of the result.
When we have acted conscientiously, we may leave the outcome with God in peace, trusting that he will save in his own way and time.

div.title: The Syrians are defeated (verses 15–19)
div.p: After being defeated once, the Syrians made a new attempt.
A beaten cause may revive while any strength remains within it.
The enemies of the Son of David behave in the same way.
But this victory fulfilled God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:18) and repeated to Joshua (Joshua 1:4) that Israel's boundaries would reach the Euphrates.
This teaches us the danger of helping people who have deliberately set themselves against God.
When they fall under his judgment, their allies will fall with them.

row.cell: He tries to conceal his crime.

div.title: David commits adultery (verses 1–5)
div.p: Consider what led David into this serious sin.
First, he neglected his responsibilities. He remained in Jerusalem when his duty called him elsewhere.
When we leave the path of our duty, we place ourselves in the path of temptation.
Second, he chose an easy, idle life. Laziness gives the tempter an advantage.
Third, he allowed his eyes to wander. He had not made a covenant with his eyes as Job had—or had forgotten that promise.
Consider also the steps by which one sin led to another.
Sin is a downhill path.
Once people begin doing wrong, they often find it very difficult to stop.
Consider how much worse David's sin became because of the responsibilities and privileges he possessed.
How could he rebuke or punish others for conduct that he himself knowingly practiced?

div.title: David tries to conceal his wrongdoing (verses 6–13)
div.p: Giving way to sin hardens the heart and provokes the Holy Spirit to withdraw.
Taking away someone's ability to reason rightly is worse than taking away that person's money.
And enticing someone to sin is worse than bringing that person into any ordinary worldly trouble.

div.title: David arranges Uriah's death (verses 14–27)
div.p: Adultery often leads to murder.
One wicked act may be used to conceal another.
We should dread even the beginning of sin because no one knows where it may end.
Can someone who truly believes act this way?
Can a person committing such crimes really be God's child?
Henry teaches that even if God's saving grace is not finally lost in such a terrible fall, the assurance and comfort of grace must be suspended.
David's spiritual vigor and joy in religion were, for the time, destroyed.
No person living in such deliberate wrongdoing can reasonably claim to possess evidence that he or she is a genuine believer.
The greater a person's confidence while sunk in sin, the more that confidence is presumption and hypocrisy.
Someone resembling David only in his transgressions must not use David's story to reassure himself that he is merely a temporarily fallen believer.
He must first follow David in humiliation, repentance and the other exceptional graces of his character.
Opponents of Christianity should not say, “These are the fruits of faith.”
No.
David's crimes were the fruit of corrupt human nature.
We should all watch against the earliest movements of self-indulgence and keep far away from evil.
Yet with the Lord there is mercy and abundant redemption.
He will not reject a humble, repentant believer or allow Satan to snatch his sheep from his hand.
God restores his people in a way that makes his hatred of their sins clear.
In this way, no one who takes his word seriously will be encouraged to abuse the comfort of divine forgiveness.

div.title: Nathan confronts David (verses 1–14)
div.p: God will not allow his own people to remain undisturbed in sin.
Through a parable, Nathan led David to pronounce judgment upon himself.
Those who correct others need wisdom and care in choosing how to speak.
But once Nathan applied his story, he was completely faithful.
He told David plainly: “You are the man.”
God's response demonstrates how much he hates sin, even when it occurs among his own people.
He will not simply ignore it wherever it is found.
David made no excuses and did not minimize his wrongdoing.
He confessed it freely.
When David said that he had sinned, Nathan recognized genuine repentance and assured him that his sin had been forgiven.
“You shall not die” meant, according to Henry, that David would not suffer eternal death or be separated from God forever.
But David would continue to suffer the Lord's discipline during his earthly life.
He would not be condemned with the world.
One especially dreadful consequence of public sin by people who profess faith is that it gives God's enemies material for mockery and blasphemy.
David's case shows that even when sin is forgiven, God may still correct his children severely.
A fleeting gratification of shameful desire brought David many years of painful distress.

div.title: David's child dies; Solomon is born (verses 15–25)
div.p: Henry connects Psalm 51 with this period of David's life.
Although David had been told he was forgiven, he prayed earnestly for pardon, lamented his wrongdoing and remained willing to bear its shame.
He was prepared to remember it repeatedly and receive reproof for it.
God permits us to pray earnestly for particular blessings on the basis of his general mercy and power, even when no specific promise assures that those requests will be granted.
David submitted patiently when his child died.
Later God compensated that loss through the birth of another child.
The best way to retain earthly comforts or have a loss made up in some other way is to surrender them willingly to the Lord.
God showed special favor to Solomon and directed that he be called Jedidiah, meaning “Beloved of the Lord.”
Henry expresses confidence that prayers for one's children are graciously answered both when children die in infancy—being well cared for by God—and when others live and are loved by the Lord.

div.title: David treats the Ammonites harshly (verses 26–31)
div.p: David subjected the people of Ammon to severe slavery.
Henry regards this harshness as evidence that David's heart had not yet been softened by repentance when these events occurred.
The more deeply we recognize our own need for the Lord's forgiveness and experience its sweetness, the more compassionate, kind and forgiving we should become toward others.

row.cell: David's grief, Absalom flees to Geshur.

div.title: Amnon assaults his sister (verses 1–20)
div.p: From this point onward, David faced one trouble after another.
Adultery and murder had been his own sins.
Now similar sins among his children began the punishment God had announced.
David had been too indulgent toward his children.
He could trace their wrongdoing back to failures in his own conduct.
That recognition must have made the pain of their sins still more difficult to bear.
No one should expect kindness from someone willing to attempt sexual seduction or abuse.

p.hi: It is better to suffer the greatest wrong than to commit even the smallest sin.

div.title: Absalom murders Amnon (verses 21–29)
div.p: Several things made Absalom's offense especially serious.
He arranged for Amnon to be killed when Amnon was least prepared to die.
He also led his servants into sharing the guilt of murder.
Servants have been taught badly when they obey a wicked master against God's commands.
