Children whom parents indulge without correction often become a heavy sorrow to their godly parents.
Such parents neglect their duty to God because of misguided affection for their children.

div.title: David mourns; Absalom escapes (verses 30–39)
div.p: Jonadab was guilty in connection with both Amnon's sin and his death.
People who advise us to do wrong turn out to be false friends.
After a while David longed to see Absalom again.
Instead of recoiling from him as a murderer, he began desiring his return.
This was a weakness in David.
Henry adds an important qualification.
God must have seen something in David's heart that distinguished him from Eli.
Otherwise we might conclude that David too had honored his sons above God.

row.cell: He is admitted to his father's presence.

div.title: Joab arranges an appeal for Absalom (verses 1–20)
div.p: Notice how the woman presenting her case to David appeals to God's mercy and to his kindness toward guilty sinners.
The state of sinners is one of banishment from God.
Yet God never forgives in a way that dishonors his own law or justice.
Nor does he pardon people who remain unrepentant, encourage further wrongdoing or authorize harm to other people.

div.title: David permits Absalom to return (verses 21–24)
div.p: David was inclined to show kindness to his son.
But to preserve the honor of his position as judge, he waited for another person to appeal on Absalom's behalf.
Henry sees in this a picture of God's gracious dealings.
God has compassion toward miserable sinners and does not delight in their destruction.
Yet sinners can be reconciled to him only through a Mediator who pleads on their behalf.
God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.
Christ came into the land of our banishment in order to bring us back to God.

div.title: Absalom's outward beauty (verses 25–27)
div.p: Nothing is said about Absalom's wisdom or devotion to God.
The passage praises only his physical appearance.
What poor praise for someone who possesses no greater virtue!
A morally polluted soul can live in a handsome body.
Absalom had an impressive head of hair.
It was so heavy as to become burdensome, yet he preferred to bear its weight rather than cut it.
People rarely complain about something that feeds their pride, even when it causes discomfort.
May the Lord give us the beauty of holiness and the adornment of a gentle, quiet spirit!
Only those who revere him are truly happy.

div.title: Absalom gains admission to David's presence (verses 28–33)
div.p: Absalom behaved insolently toward Joab until Joab agreed to intercede for him.
His bold and insolent demand then secured what he wanted from the king.
When parents and rulers encourage such a person by yielding to his behavior, they may soon suffer serious consequences.
But if a human father's compassion could lead him to receive an unrepentant son, why should truly repentant sinners doubt the mercy of the Father of mercies?

div.title: Absalom's ambition (verses 1–6)
div.p: David allowed Absalom to display his wealth and rank.
Parents who encourage pride in their children do not understand the harm they may be causing.
Many young people are ruined by pride.
And people most eager to obtain authority often understand its duties least.

div.title: Absalom conspires against David (verses 7–12)
div.p: Loving parents naturally want to believe the best about their children.
How wicked it is for children to exploit that trust and deceive them through an appearance of religion!
Some prominent men of Jerusalem attended Absalom's celebration connected with a sacrifice.
Godly people are pleased to see others displaying devotion.
That very willingness to encourage religion can make them vulnerable to deception.
The schemes of wicked people and the cunning of Satan can draw good people into supporting evil plans.

div.title: David leaves Jerusalem (verses 13–23)
div.p: David decided to leave Jerusalem.
He accepted the flight as a penitent submitting to God's discipline.
Before an unrighteous opponent like Absalom, David could have defended himself and stood his ground.
But before the righteous God, he had to condemn his own sin and submit to the judgment following it.
He therefore accepted its consequence.
Godly people also worry about other people's suffering when trouble comes upon themselves.
David did not force anyone to go with him.
Those who preferred Absalom could join him, and they would share in his fate.
In the same way, Christ does not force people to become his followers.
David especially wanted to protect Ittai, a foreign exile and recent convert, from hardship.
He thought Ittai should receive encouragement and kindness, not danger.
But Ittai valued David's wisdom and goodness so highly that he refused to leave him.
A true friend loves at all times and remains loyal through adversity.
Let us cling wholeheartedly to the Son of David.
Neither life nor death can separate us from his love.

div.title: David sends the ark back (verses 24–30)
div.p: David cared deeply about the ark's safety.
It is right to care more about the prosperity of Christ's church than our own comfort.
We should prefer the success of the gospel over our wealth, reputation, ease and even safety.
Notice how willingly David placed his circumstances into God's hands.
Accepting the Lord's will is both our duty and our best interest.
Recognize his hand in every event.
Then, because you know that every event rests under his authority, you need not be afraid of the future.
David's sin was always before him (Psalm 51:3).
Yet it had never seemed as evil to him as during this humiliation.
He had never wept like this when Saul pursued him.
A wounded conscience makes suffering heavier (Psalm 38:4).

div.title: David prays about Ahithophel's counsel (verses 31–37)
div.p: David prayed against Ahithophel's counsel, not against the man himself.
He trusted that God controls the hearts and words of human beings.
Yet he also worked to oppose that counsel.
Prayer must be joined with lawful effort.
Otherwise we would be testing God.
No ordinary human being combines wisdom and simplicity so perfectly that nothing remains needing forgiveness.
But when the Son of David experienced every possible form of betrayal and cruelty, his wisdom, gentleness, honesty and patience remained perfect.
Let us follow him, hold to him and serve him in life and in death.

div.title: Ziba falsely accuses Mephibosheth (verses 1–4)
div.p: Ziba slandered Mephibosheth.
People in positions of great authority should always be cautious about flatterers.
Before making a judgment, they should take care to hear both sides.

div.title: Shimei curses David (verses 5–14)
div.p: David endured Shimei's curses better than he had endured Ziba's flattery.
Flattery had led him into making an unjust judgment about someone else.
The curses led him to judge himself rightly.
For this reason, the world's smiles can be more dangerous than its frowns.
David had spared Saul's life more than once while Saul tried to kill him.
Yet he was now accused of bloodguilt.
Innocence does not always protect us from malice and lies.
We should not be surprised to be accused of the very wrongdoing we have been especially careful to avoid.
It is a comfort that human beings are not our final judges.
Our Judge is the Lord, who judges according to truth.
Notice how patiently David bore this insult.
His conduct reminds us of Christ, who prayed for those who mocked and crucified him.
A humble person can turn insults into useful rebukes and learn from them rather than responding in anger.
David recognized God's hand in what had happened and trusted that the Lord would bring good out of his suffering.
We may depend upon him to reward not only our good service but also the suffering we endure in faithfulness.

div.title: Absalom follows wicked counsel (verses 15–23)
div.p: Ahithophel and Hushai were regarded as the wisest advisers of their day.
Absalom imagined that having both meant his success was certain.
He relied upon their counsel instead of seeking God, even though the ark was with him.
But neither could truly guide him to good.
Hushai had no intention of giving Absalom wise advice.
Ahithophel intentionally advised him to do something wicked.
That was just as harmful, because anyone who advises sin is advising a person toward destruction.
In the end, honesty is the best policy.
Ahithophel's counsel was designed to make reconciliation between David and Absalom impossible.
Such a scheme came from the devil.
How desperately wicked the human heart can be!

row.cell: He hangs himself, Absalom pursues David.

div.title: God defeats Ahithophel's counsel (verses 1–21)
div.p: What an astonishing effect of divine Providence!
God blinded Absalom's judgment and influenced his heart so that he would not accept Ahithophel's advice immediately, but would also seek Hushai's counsel.
No one can successfully resist the God who can turn a person's own actions against that person and destroy a scheme through its author's mistakes and uncontrolled desires.
Ahithophel's earlier counsel had been followed because God intended to discipline David.
But his later counsel was rejected because God had no intention of allowing David to be destroyed.
The Lord can overrule every human plan.
Whatever wisdom or assistance people provide, success comes from God alone.
He will not allow his people to perish finally.

div.title: Ahithophel dies; friends help David (verses 22–29)
div.p: When Ahithophel realized his counsel had been rejected, his frustrated pride became unbearable.
What breaks a proud person's heart may not even disturb a humble person's sleep.
Ahithophel recognized that Absalom's cause would probably fail.
He also feared that he himself would be punished publicly.
In despair, he ended his own life.
Henry describes this as a self-inflicted judgment driven by injured pride and fear, not as an example for others to follow.
Thus a mind filled with plans to do harm came to a wretched end.
Absalom pursued David.
But notice how God sometimes provides comfort and practical help through strangers when our own relatives have disappointed or betrayed us.
Our great King does not need our help.

Nevertheless, Christ promises to accept and reward acts of kindness toward the least of his brothers and sisters—those who are sick, poor or lacking basic necessities—as though they had been done to him personally.

div.title: David's forces defeat Absalom (verses 1–8)
div.p: David repaid evil with good.
Absalom had wanted only David to be killed.
David wanted Absalom alone to be spared.
This contrast partly resembles the difference between humanity's rebellion against God and God's mercy toward humanity.
Which is more astonishing: human wickedness or divine kindness?
Israel now learned what happens to those who conspire against the Lord and his anointed king.

div.title: Absalom dies (verses 9–18)
div.p: Young people should remember Absalom's terrible end.
He hung helplessly from a tree, condemned and abandoned.
His death displayed God's displeasure against rebellion toward parents.
Nothing can finally protect people from misery and contempt except heavenly wisdom and the grace of God.

div.title: David grieves too intensely (verses 19–33)
div.p: Ahimaaz prepared David to hear of his son's death by first encouraging him to thank God for the victory.
The more our hearts are fixed upon sincere gratitude for God's mercies, the better prepared we are to bear suffering that accompanies them.
Some interpreters believe David's wish to die in Absalom's place arose from concern about his son's eternal condition.
Henry thinks it more likely that David spoke without adequate reflection.
He criticizes David's excessive affection for a son who had lived without godliness.
He also reproaches him for disputing God's justice and for resisting the judgment that David, as king, was responsible for administering.
The rightful claims of public justice should have been placed above his private natural affection.
Even the best believers are not always in a healthy spiritual state.
We often grieve too much for what we have loved too much.
Let us learn from David's example to avoid indulging or neglecting our children sinfully.
But even in David's love and sorrow, may we see a faint picture of the Savior's greater love.
Jesus wept over, prayed for and died for sinful, rebellious human beings who had set themselves against him.

row.cell: Joab causes David to cease mourning.

div.title: Joab challenges David's grief (verses 1–8)
div.p: It was very unwise and unworthy for David to continue mourning so intensely for such a wicked son as Absalom.
Joab criticized him.
But Joab did not speak to his king with the proper respect and deference.
A clear case can be presented fairly to those in authority.
They can even be corrected for their wrongdoing.
But correction must not be delivered with rudeness or insolence.
David accepted the reproof and the advice with prudence and gentleness.
Yielding promptly when we have taken a mistaken course usually prevents much of its harmful effect.

div.title: David is invited back to Jerusalem (verses 9–15)
div.p: Through the appeals of the priests and the influence of Amasa, God brought the people to invite David back as king.
David did not act until that invitation came.
Likewise, the Lord Jesus rules in the hearts of those who invite him to take his throne there.
Before they invite him, he first moves their hearts and makes them willing on the day of his power.
Then he rules in the midst of his enemies (Psalm 110:2–3).

div.title: David forgives Shimei (verses 16–23)
div.p: People who now insult and reject the Son of David may wish desperately to be reconciled to him when he comes in glory.
But then it will be too late.
Shimei did not delay in seeking David's pardon.
Because the insults had been directed against him personally, David found them easier to forgive.
This is the fitting response of godly people to personal wrongdoing.

div.title: Mephibosheth is vindicated (verses 24–30)
div.p: David reversed the forfeiture of Mephibosheth's property.
Mephibosheth rejoiced at David's return.
A good person can endure personal losses contentedly while the people of Israel enjoy peace and the Son of David is exalted.

div.title: David parts with Barzillai (verses 31–39)
div.p: Barzillai considered it an honor merely to have been able to help David.
In the same way, when Christ's people enter their inheritance, they will be amazed that their reward is so much greater than the little service they offered (Matthew 25:37).
A godly person does not wish to become a burden to other people.
If such a person must depend on someone, he would rather be a burden to his own household than to strangers.
Everyone should think seriously about dying.
That is especially appropriate for those who are growing old.
The grave is ready for me.
I should prepare to enter it.

div.title: Israel and Judah quarrel (verses 40–43)
div.p: The people of Israel believed they had been slighted.
The people of Judah responded with increasingly angry words.
The quarrel led to very harmful consequences.
Much evil could be prevented if we watched against pride and remembered that a gentle answer turns away anger.
Even when we have justice and reason on our side, God is displeased if we defend our position fiercely and without kindness.

div.title: Sheba rebels against David (verses 1–3)
div.p: One trial follows another for God's people, for their good, until they reach the place where sin and sorrow are forever removed.
Angry people arguing with one another often misunderstand or twist each other's words.
Proud people insist that everything go their way or else refuse to give any assistance.
The favor of the crowd is not dependable.
Consider how quickly the cries of “Hosanna to the Son of David” changed into “Crucify him! Crucify him!”

div.title: Joab murders Amasa (verses 4–13)
div.p: Joab murdered Amasa brutally.
The more deliberate planning involved in a sin, the worse it is.
Joab readily sacrificed the interests of both the king and the kingdom to satisfy his own desire for revenge.
How could someone guilty of murder bring himself to pursue a traitor?
How could he enter danger so boldly when his conscience was weighed down with such guilt?
His conscience had become hardened and unfeeling.

div.title: Sheba finds refuge in Abel (verses 14–22)
div.p: A city that knowingly shelters a traitor exposes itself to judgment.
The human heart fares no better when it protects rebellious sinful desires that will not allow Christ to reign.
A wise woman acted prudently.
She satisfied Joab's demand and saved the city from destruction.
Wisdom is not restricted by social position or sex.
Nor does it consist merely in knowing many complicated things.
It consists in understanding how to act when a problem arises, how to prevent harm and how to secure a good outcome.
Many disasters could be prevented if the parties involved made an effort to understand one another and clear up mistaken assumptions.
The condition for peace here was to surrender the traitor.
Henry sees a picture of how God deals with the soul when it is troubled by conviction.

p.hi: Sin is the traitor.

div.p: A cherished sinful desire is the rebel.
If we part with that desire and cast away the wrongdoing, we can find peace.
There is no peace with God while we insist on protecting rebellion against him.

div.title: David's officers (verses 23–26)
div.p: This passage describes David's court after he regained his throne.
It is good when competent people are appointed to carry out public duties.
Let everyone who receives responsibility seek to carry it out faithfully, as a servant of the Son of David.

row.cell: Rizpah's care for the bodies of Saul's descendants.

div.title: The Gibeonites' wrong is answered (verses 1–9)
div.p: All suffering arises from the entrance of sin into the world and should lead us to humility and repentance.
Some disasters especially call earlier sins to remembrance.
God's judgments may concern wrongdoing committed a long time before.
We should not object as though we understood all the reasons behind his governance.
The people's suffering for Saul's wrongdoing may have reflected their participation in it.
Likewise, a later generation may suffer consequences arising from an earlier generation's sins.
The passage does not disclose every reason, and God has not promised to explain every aspect of his providence.
Delay does not remove guilt.
Nor can sinners assume that because judgment has been postponed, they will escape it.
A financial payment could not satisfy the demand for justice after bloodshed.
Henry understands Saul's descendants as possibly having followed his violent example, since the family is described as a house of bloodshed.
He argues that the Gibeonites' demand was not driven by personal vengeance but by concern for public justice.
The sentence was carried out at the beginning of harvest.
Henry views it as an extraordinary judicial action under Israel's covenant order, intended to remove the judgment that had withheld productive harvests for years.
He argues that public penalties directed toward the common welfare should not automatically be condemned as cruelty.
This is his interpretation of an ancient historical judgment, not a contemporary authorization for collective punishment or private violence.

div.title: Rizpah honors the dead (verses 10–14)
div.p: When a guilty land has enjoyed many years of prosperity, its people should be thankful.
When abundance is misused, it is not surprising if scarcity follows.
Yet people often spend far more effort identifying physical causes of hardship than asking whether sin has contributed to their troubles.
The Lord defends the cause of those who cannot or will not avenge themselves.
The prayers of poor people are powerful.
When God sent rain upon the earth, the bodies were buried.
The rain showed that the Lord had heard prayer and granted mercy to the land.
Henry sees in these events a picture of Christ.
He was hung upon a tree and became a curse for us, removing our guilt though he himself was innocent.
Through him, God is reconciled to us.

div.title: David fights the Philistines (verses 15–22)
div.p: These events appear to have occurred near the end of David's reign.
David grew exhausted but did not flee.
The Lord provided help when he needed it.
Even strong believers sometimes grow weary in spiritual conflict.
Satan may attack them most fiercely at such moments.
But those who stand firm, resist him and trust the Lord will receive help.
At last they will become more than conquerors.
Death, the Christian's last enemy, is like a mighty descendant of Anak.
But through the One who has already triumphed on our behalf, believers will finally overcome even death itself.

p.hi: David's psalm of thanksgiving.

div.title: Praise for deliverance
div.p: This chapter is a psalm of praise.
Almost the same song appears later as Psalm 18.
Those who trust the Lord while walking in the path of duty will find him ready to help them in their greatest dangers.
David experienced this personally.
When God preserves us in a remarkable way, we should remember those particular mercies and mention them specifically when praising him.
We will not be completely delivered from every enemy until we reach heaven.
But God will preserve all his people until then (2 Timothy 4:18).
People who have received great mercy from God should give the glory to him.
David sang this song on the very day when the Lord delivered him.
While the mercy is still fresh and we are deeply moved by it, we should bring our offering of thanks.
The warmth of our gratitude can kindle the offering.
David's hopes and joys finally centered upon the great Redeemer.
All our own hopes should end in him as well.

div.title: David's final words (verses 1–7)
div.p: David's final testimony deserves serious attention.
Those who have spent many years enjoying God's goodness and finding wisdom in his ways should bear witness to the truth of his promises as their earthly lives draw to a close.
David declared that God had inspired his words.
The Holy Spirit spoke through him.
Like other holy men, he spoke and wrote as the Spirit moved him.
David had many failures to confess.
He had neglected duties and sometimes acted wrongly.
Yet he found comfort in the Lord's everlasting covenant with him.
Above all, David meant the covenant of mercy and peace.
He received it as a sinner who believed in the promised Savior, accepted God's promised blessing and surrendered himself to serve the Lord as someone redeemed by grace.
Believers will enjoy these covenant blessings forever.
God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit will receive eternal glory through their salvation.
Forgiveness, righteousness, grace and everlasting life are secured as God's gifts through Jesus Christ.
Christ possesses limitless riches of grace and every blessing for people who seek salvation through him.
David knew enough of the holy law to understand the greatness of his own sin.
He therefore knew how deeply he needed Christ's salvation.
The covenant was all his salvation and therefore all his desire.
Compared with this hope, every earthly thing became less attractive.
David was ready to surrender earthly things or leave them behind at death so that he could enjoy perfect happiness with God (Psalm 73:24–28).
Yet he grieved that sinful desires remained powerful within him and that his own faith, hope and love were often weak.
He would readily have admitted that his carelessness and lack of watchfulness had contributed to these weaknesses.
Nevertheless, the hope of being made perfect in heavenly glory encouraged him as he approached death.

div.title: David's mighty men (verses 8–39)
div.p: David once longed for water from the well at Bethlehem.
His desire seems to have been a moment of weakness.
Thirsty and remembering the water he had drunk there when he was young, he spoke without sufficient thought.
His mighty men were eager to risk their lives at even a slight suggestion from their king.
How much more eagerly should we seek to please the Lord Jesus, obeying his will as revealed through Scripture, the Holy Spirit and his providence!
But David refused to drink that water.
He poured it out to the Lord as a drink offering.
In this way he opposed his own foolish desire, disciplined himself for indulging it and showed that sober reflection could correct his rashness.
He understood the need for self-denial.
David treated that water as especially precious because his men had risked their blood to obtain it.
How much more highly should we value the blessings purchased for us through the blood of the Savior!
Let us not neglect so great a salvation.

div.title: David orders a census (verses 1–9)
div.p: Because Israel had sinned, God allowed David to act wrongly.
The people then shared in the punishment that followed.
This teaches something important about God's government of the world.
The sin was the pride in David's heart.
By counting the nation, he hoped to appear more powerful and intimidating.
He trusted human strength more than he should have done, although he had written so often about trusting God alone.
The Lord does not judge sins as we do.
An act that appears to us harmless, or at worst a small mistake, may be deeply sinful before him.
God searches the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
Sometimes even ungodly people recognize wrong attitudes or behavior in believers when those believers remain unaware of them.
Yet God rarely allows those he loves to enjoy for long the things they selfishly covet.

div.title: David chooses the plague (verses 10–15)
div.p: It is good for us when, after sinning, our consciences convict us.
When we confess our sins, we may pray with faith for forgiveness and for God's mercy to remove the guilt we abandon through sincere repentance.
It is just for God to take away what we boast about, or turn it into something bitter, so that our pride becomes a source of correction.
The punishment involved the people as well as David.
Although David's sin opened the way for judgment, the people's own sins also contributed.
David chose a judgment that would come directly from God.
He knew God's mercies were very great.
He preferred this to falling into the hands of enemies who would rejoice at Israel's suffering and become further hardened in their idolatry.
The plague would place David and his family in as much danger as the poorest Israelite.
It would also last for a shorter time than the other offered judgments, however severe its effects.
The rapid destruction showed how easily God can bring down the proud and how much we owe each day to his patience.

div.title: God stops the destroying angel (verses 16 and 17)
div.p: Henry suggests that Jerusalem may have been especially guilty of sin and pride, leading the destroying angel to stretch out his hand toward that city.
But God relented.
As elsewhere, Henry explains that this means a change in God's manner of dealing with people, not a change in his eternal mind.
At the place where Abraham had been prevented from killing his son, the destroying angel was likewise stopped from destroying Jerusalem.
It is because of the great Sacrifice, Jesus Christ, that lives otherwise forfeited are protected from final destruction.
David showed a true shepherd's heart by offering to bear the judgment himself in order to save his subjects.

div.title: David offers sacrifices; the plague ends (verses 18–25)
div.p: God's encouragement to offer him spiritual sacrifices is a sign that he is bringing us into fellowship with himself.
David purchased the ground on which he would build an altar.
God hates offerings acquired by injustice.
People who care chiefly about making their religion easy and inexpensive, involving little effort or money, do not understand true devotion.
What else are our possessions for, if not to honor God?
How could they be put to better use?
David offered burnt offerings, expressing honor for God's justice, and fellowship offerings, expressing honor for his mercy.
Christ is both our Altar and our Sacrifice.
Only through him can we expect to escape God's righteous judgment and receive his favor.
Death is destroying people all around us through many different causes, often suddenly.
It is foolish not to expect our own death and prepare to meet God.

div.title: 1 Kings — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: The history in this book describes the kingdoms of Judah and Israel.
But its special concern is the way God's kingdom was present among the people.
It is therefore sacred history.
The events it records occurred in an earlier period than the events described in ordinary histories.
This account also teaches us far more and is of greater interest than ordinary historical works.

row.cell: Solomon is anointed king, and Adonijah's usurpation stopped.

div.title: David grows old (verses 1–4)
div.p: David had become weak in his old age.
He was experiencing the correction of his recent sins and the lasting effects of his earlier labors and hardships.

div.title: Adonijah tries to take the throne (verses 5–10)
div.p: Parents who indulge their children instead of correcting them often suffer afterward through those children's disobedience and impatience to possess the family inheritance.
Neither worldly wisdom, long experience nor an outwardly holy reputation can guarantee that someone ruled by selfishness will remain on a good path.
We may especially wonder how Joab and Abiathar allowed themselves to be drawn into Adonijah's rebellion.

div.title: David confirms Solomon as king (verses 11–31)
div.p: Consider Nathan's words to Bathsheba.
He offered her advice intended to save both her life and her son's.
Ministers of Christ give us similar counsel in his name.
They urge us to be diligent so that no one takes our crown (Revelation 3:11) and so that our own souls are saved.
David made a solemn declaration that he would keep his earlier decision to appoint Solomon as his successor.
As the weakness of old age increased and death approached, David remembered the many troubles from which the Lord had rescued him.
These memories increased his comfort, strengthened his hope and encouraged him to perform his remaining duty.

div.title: Solomon is anointed; Adonijah's plan collapses (verses 32–53)
div.p: The people rejoiced greatly when Solomon became king.
Every true Israelite likewise rejoices at the exaltation of the Son of David.
Conspiracies founded upon evil principles collapse quickly when personal interests shift.
How can people who do evil expect joyful news?
Adonijah had despised Solomon, but he soon feared him.
This scene helps us understand the exaltation of Jesus Christ, Son of David and Son of God, to his glorious throne despite all opposition.
His kingdom is much greater than David's, and all God's people rejoice sincerely in its advancement.
But the prosperity of Christ's kingdom brings grief and fear to its enemies.
Clinging to an altar's horns, observing outward religious forms, or claiming to be devout will not help people who refuse his authority and salvation.
If their submission is merely hypocritical, they face destruction without remedy.

row.cell: David's charge as to Joab and others.
Solomon reigns, Adonijah aspiring to the throne is put to death.
Abiathar banished, Joab put to death.

div.title: David's final instruction to Solomon (verses 1–4)
div.p: David told Solomon to keep the Lord's command.
A dying father's authority deserves serious respect, but it is far below that of the living God.
The Lord had promised that the Messiah would come from David's descendants, and that promise was unconditional.
But the promise that David's family would never lack someone on Israel's throne was conditional.
The descendants must walk before God sincerely, with zeal and determination.
To do this, Solomon would need to watch over his own conduct carefully.

div.title: David's instructions about Joab and others (verses 5–11)
div.p: David's dying counsel concerning Joab and Shimei did not arise from private anger.
It was intended to preserve Solomon's throne and prevent future wrongdoing.
Joab had already committed murders, and David believed he would repeat them if doing so furthered his plans.
Although punishment had been delayed, Joab would finally be called to account.
The passage of time does not erase guilt, especially the guilt of murder.
David warned Solomon not to regard Shimei as innocent or a genuine supporter.
He believed the same malice still remained in Shimei's heart.
David's final words are recorded as spoken under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit (2 Samuel 23:1–7).
In them the Lord revealed to David the offices and salvation of the coming Messiah.
All David's hope and comfort rested upon that Savior.
The passage gives convincing evidence that David died with genuine faith and hope, under the Spirit's influence.

div.title: Adonijah's request leads to his death (verses 12–25)
div.p: Solomon treated his mother Bathsheba with all the honor due to her.
But we should never ask a person to do something that person has no right to grant.
A godly person should neither make an improper request nor support an unjust cause.
In the royal customs of the time, Adonijah's request to marry Abishag clearly expressed another attempt to seize the throne.
Solomon could not be secure while Adonijah continued that ambition.
Restless, ambitious people often prepare their own destruction.
Many have lost their lives trying to seize a crown.

div.title: Abiathar loses office; Joab is executed (verses 26–34)
div.p: Solomon's words to Abiathar, and Abiathar's silence, suggest that recent conspiracies had been taking place.
Kindness shown toward God's people will be remembered favorably.
Solomon spared Abiathar's life because of his earlier service, but removed him from his offices.
The altar provided refuge in matters where the appointed sacrifice could atone.
But Joab's murders did not fall within that category.
Solomon looked to God as the Author of peace and toward eternity for peace's perfect fulfillment.
The Lord of peace himself will give us everlasting peace.

div.title: Shimei is punished (verses 35–46)
div.p: Old hostility remains within a heart that has not been changed.
We should be cautious about people who have demonstrated enmity but shown no evidence of repentance.
Worldly people can become so determined to pursue their own plans that neither solemn commitments nor danger will restrain them.
They continue even when doing so forfeits their lives and souls.
God will not bend his judgment to suit our preferences.
He sees everything we do.
We should live as though continually in his presence, because we are.

Every act, word and thought should be governed by the knowledge that a time is approaching when the smallest details of our lives will be revealed and our eternal condition will be fixed by an entirely righteous Judge.
Solomon's throne was established in peace.
It pictured the Redeemer's kingdom of peace and righteousness.
Although Christ's enemies rage, they plot in vain.
His throne stands firm, and no one can overthrow it.

row.cell: His vision, His prayer for wisdom.

div.title: Solomon loves the Lord (verses 1–4)
div.p: Someone who loves the Lord should, for his sake, seek a spouse among the Lord's own people.
Solomon was wise, wealthy and powerful.
Yet his brightest commendation was one shared by every genuine believer, even the poorest: he loved the Lord.
Where God gives much, he rightly expects much in return.
Those who genuinely love him and his worship will not resent the cost of serving him.
We should never regard what we spend in God's service as wasted.

div.title: Solomon asks for wisdom (verses 5–15)
div.p: Solomon's dream was no ordinary dream.
Although his bodily powers were asleep, God strengthened his mind and soul so that he could receive a divine vision and make a fitting choice.
The Lord likewise puts us on the way toward true happiness by assuring us that he will provide what we genuinely need and ask for.
Solomon's decision, made while his ordinary reasoning faculties were least active, showed that the choice arose from God's grace.
He felt humbly how little wisdom and strength he possessed.
He pleaded that he was like a small child.
The wiser and more thoughtful people become, the more clearly they recognize their weakness and the more cautious they become about trusting their own judgment.
Solomon asked God for wisdom.
We must do the same (James 1:5), so that we can fulfill our own calling and respond well to the many circumstances we face.
The Lord accepts people who prize spiritual blessings above earthly advantages.
Solomon's prayer was effective—and God gave him more than he asked.
He received wisdom greater than that of any other ruler, together with wealth and honor.
If we secure wisdom and grace, they may bring outward benefits, or they will sweeten the lack of those benefits.
To receive spiritual blessings, we must seek them earnestly in prayer.
Concerning earthly benefits, we must entrust ourselves to God's decision.

p.hi: Solomon received wisdom because he asked for it, and wealth because he did not ask for it.

div.title: Solomon identifies the true mother (verses 16–28)
div.p: This judgment demonstrates Solomon's God-given wisdom.
The situation was difficult.
To discover which woman was the child's mother, he could not test which woman the child loved most.
He therefore tested which woman loved the child most.
When a child appeared to be in danger, the true mother's love became clear.
Parents should show love to their children chiefly by caring for their souls, seeking to rescue them like brands from a fire.
Solomon's wisdom in this and other judgments made him greatly respected throughout Israel.
Such wisdom did him more good than weapons of war.
Through it he became both feared and loved.

div.title: Solomon appoints his officials (verses 1–19)
div.p: Solomon's wisdom surely showed itself in his choice of leading officials.
Several of them had also served during David's reign.
Solomon arranged the kingdom's contributions so that no single district was exhausted by the responsibility of supplying the royal household.
Every region gave its proper share.

div.title: Solomon's kingdom enjoys peace (verses 20–28)
div.p: Israel's royal crown never shone more brightly than it did when Solomon wore it.
Peace surrounded his kingdom.
In this it pictured the kingdom of the Messiah, who would receive the nations as his inheritance and to whom princes would come in worship.
The spiritual peace, joy and holy security enjoyed by all faithful subjects of the Lord Jesus were pictured by Israel's earthly happiness.
But God's kingdom is not food and drink.
It consists of something infinitely better: righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
The enormous amount of food prepared for Solomon's household shows the crowds who served and visited him.
Christ is greater than Solomon.
He feeds all his people, not with perishable bread, but with the food that endures to eternal life.

div.title: Solomon's God-given wisdom (verses 29–34)
div.p: Solomon's wisdom brought him more honor than his wealth.
He possessed what Scripture calls largeness of heart, meaning extraordinary mental capacity.
He received both wisdom and the ability to communicate it effectively.
Those with great gifts should have equally generous hearts, using their abilities for the benefit of others.
How much wisdom and knowledge is wasted when people do not share what they possess!
Yet the holy Scriptures contain every kind of knowledge necessary for salvation.
People came from faraway places because they valued knowledge more highly than their neighbors.
Solomon pictured Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
Those riches are hidden for us: Christ has been made our wisdom by God.
His fame will spread throughout the earth.
People of every nation will come to him, learn from him, take his gentle yoke upon themselves and find rest for their souls.

div.title: Solomon makes an agreement with Hiram (verses 1–9)
div.p: Solomon intended to build the Lord's temple.
At this time Israel had no enemy, no Satan—that is how Henry explains the word.
There was no instrument of Satan hindering Solomon's plans or drawing him away from his purpose.
Satan constantly tries to obstruct work done for God's house.
When no active obstacle stands before us, we should be especially ready to do what is good.
God's promises should strengthen and quicken our efforts.
Every worldly talent, advantage and practical skill should be used in the interests of Christ's kingdom.
Tyre supplied Israel with craftsmen, while Israel supplied Tyre with grain (Ezekiel 27:17).
In the wisdom of divine Providence, one nation needs and benefits another.
This mutual dependence gives people opportunities to glorify God.

div.title: Workers prepare the temple materials (verses 10–18)
div.p: The temple was largely built through the wealth and labor of Gentiles.
This pictured the future calling of the Gentile peoples into God's church.
Solomon commanded that expensive stones be prepared for the foundation.
Jesus Christ is the chosen and precious Foundation Stone.
We should make sure the foundation of our faith is secure.
The part of our religious lives that people cannot see deserves our greatest care and effort.
Blessed are those who become living stones, joined together into a spiritual house in which God dwells through his Spirit.
Who among us will help build the Lord's house?

div.title: Solomon builds the temple (verses 1–10)
div.p: The building was called the house of the Lord because God himself directed its form and construction.
It was to be devoted to his service.
This made it beautiful with the beauty of holiness, a beauty greater than every outward ornament.
It was a temple for the God of peace.
Therefore no iron tool was to be heard during its construction.
Quietness and silence are fitting for religious devotion and help us carry it out.
God's work should be performed carefully, but with little noise.
Shouting, disorder and violence tend to obstruct rather than advance his work.
So too God's kingdom grows silently within the human heart.
Henry attaches the reference Mark 5:27 to this image.

div.title: God's promise and warning to Solomon (verses 11–14)
div.p: Whenever people work for God, his eye is upon them.
But God warned Solomon plainly that the great responsibility and expense of building the temple could not excuse disobedience to divine law.
Nor would building such a house protect him from judgment if he turned away from the Lord's commands.

div.title: The spiritual meanings of the temple (verses 15–38)
div.p: Henry identifies four realities pictured by this temple.

p.hi: First, Christ himself is the true Temple.

div.p: In him all the fullness of deity dwells.
All God's spiritual Israel meet in him.
Through him we approach God with confidence.

p.hi: Second, each believer is a living temple.

div.p: The Spirit of God dwells within the believer (1 Corinthians 3:16).
This living sanctuary is built upon Christ as its foundation and will become perfect at the appointed time.

p.hi: Third, the gospel church is God's spiritual Temple.

div.p: It grows into a holy temple in the Lord, enriched and beautified by the Spirit's gifts and graces.
It stands firmly upon the Rock.

p.hi: Fourth, heaven is the eternal Temple.

div.p: There God's people will remain forever.
Everyone who will become part of that heavenly building must be prepared and fitted for it during the present life.
Let sinners come to Jesus, the living Foundation, so that they may be built upon him, made part of his spiritual house and devoted in body and soul to God's glory.

div.title: Solomon builds his other houses (verses 1–12)
div.p: All Solomon's buildings were beautiful, but they were also intended for practical use.
Solomon began with the temple.
He built for God before building his other houses.
The surest foundations of lasting prosperity are laid in early devotion to the Lord.
Solomon spent thirteen years building his palace but a little more than seven years building the temple.
That did not mean he cared less about the quality of his own house.
He simply gave greater urgency and effort to the Lord's work than to his own comfort.
We should likewise value God's honor above our ease and satisfaction.

div.title: Furnishings for the temple (verses 13–47)
div.p: The two bronze pillars at the temple entrance may, Henry says, have taught worshipers to depend on God alone for stability and strength in every act of worship.
Jachin can be understood as, “God will establish this wandering heart.”
It is good for the heart to be established by grace.
Boaz points to strength found in God, who works within us both to will and to act.
Spiritual strength and stability are received at the door of God's temple as we wait upon his appointed means of grace.
Spiritual priests and spiritual sacrifices must be washed in the cleansing basin of Christ's blood and regeneration.
We must wash frequently because we become defiled by sin every day.
The Lord has provided everything necessary for cleansing.
If we finally remain among the unclean, we have only ourselves to blame for rejecting what he provided.
Let us praise God for the fountain opened by Christ's sacrifice for sin and impurity.

div.title: The vessels of gold (verses 48–51)
div.p: Christ is now both the Temple and its Builder.
He is the Altar and the Sacrifice.
He is the Light of our souls and the Bread of Life.
He can meet every need of those who have come or will come to him.
No outward image can adequately represent his worth.
Words cannot express it, and the human mind cannot fully imagine his love.
Come to him.
Let his blood wash away your sins, and seek the cleansing grace of his Spirit.
Through his intercession, remain in fellowship with the Father.
Give yourself and everything you possess to his service.
Strengthened by him, you will become accepted, useful and happy.

div.title: The ark is placed in the temple (verses 1–11)
div.p: Bringing the ark into the temple completed the work.
The people did so with great solemnity.
The ark was placed inside the Most Holy Place, where Israel expected God to speak from his mercy seat.
The poles were drawn out so that they pointed toward the mercy seat and guided the high priest when he entered once a year to sprinkle blood.
They were still useful, even though they were no longer needed for carrying the ark.
God's glory appeared in a cloud.
Henry sees two images in this darkness.
First, the earlier religious order was comparatively dark when set beside the light of the gospel, through which believers behold the Lord's glory more openly.
Second, our present lives are comparatively dark when set beside heaven, where God's glory will be fully revealed and seeing him will make his people happy.

div.title: Solomon encourages the priests (verses 12–21)
div.p: The priests were astonished by the dark cloud.
Solomon encouraged them.
When God's providence seems dark, we should hurry toward the hope given in the gospel.
The best comfort comes from remembering God's word and considering his works in its light.
Whenever we accomplish something good, we should see it as God fulfilling his promise to us, not merely us fulfilling promises we made to him.

div.title: Solomon prays to God (verses 22–53)
div.p: Solomon's prayer is a model for ours.
He gave glory to God before seeking further blessings.
New experiences of God's faithfulness should lead to fuller praise.
We should appeal to his promises, depending upon them in our requests.
People who desire new mercies should remain thankful for those already received.
God's promises should guide what we desire and form the ground of what we hope for in prayer.
The sacrifices, incense and ministry of the temple pictured Christ's priestly office, offering and intercession.
That is why people were to keep the temple in mind.
One word expresses all Solomon sought for Israel: “forgive.”
Every misery ultimately springs from sin.
Forgiveness therefore opens the way for the removal of evil and reception of good.
Without pardon, even an outward deliverance cannot become a true blessing.
Solomon also asked God to teach the people through his word and through his discipline, making their suffering spiritually useful.
Each person must recognize the plague of his own heart.
This includes the painful burden of guilt and the sinful desires still living within us.
Every true believer should learn to recognize these spiritual diseases, watch against their return and put them to death.
Awareness of inward sin drives us to prayer.
Solomon ultimately asked the Lord to hear his praying people.
Under the gospel, no special building or physical direction adds anything to a prayer.

p.hi: Christ is the reality to which the temple pointed.

div.p: Whatever we ask in his name according to God's promise may be granted.
Through Christ, God's people are established and sanctified, the wanderer restored, the foreigner welcomed, mourners comforted and God's name glorified.
Sin causes our troubles; repentance and forgiveness lead toward human happiness.

div.title: Solomon blesses and exhorts Israel (verses 54–61)
div.p: Solomon's farewell words were especially likely to remain with the people.
The blessings he requested are now obtained through Christ's intercession, of which his prayer was a type.
We receive sufficient, suitable and timely grace whenever we truly need it.
No human heart is naturally willing to obey the gospel call to repentance, faith and a renewed life.
Yet Solomon called the people to walk wholeheartedly in God's commands.
That is the way Scripture teaches us.
We must obey the law and the gospel's summons.
Because we know how sinful and weak we are, we pray for divine help, through which Christ enables us to serve God.

div.title: Solomon celebrates with offerings (verses 62–66)
div.p: Solomon made many sacrifices.
He apparently observed the Feast of Tabernacles after the temple dedication.
Let us likewise return home rejoicing after worship, thankful for the Lord's goodness.

row.cell: The presents of Solomon and Hiram.

div.title: God answers Solomon's prayer (verses 1–9)
div.p: After Solomon completed and dedicated the temple, the Lord warned him against pride and called him to reverent fear.
Even after all the service we can offer, our standing before God remains the same.
Nothing we do can purchase permission to sin.
A genuine believer would never desire such permission.
The believer would rather be corrected by God than continue comfortably and prosperously in wrongdoing.

div.title: Solomon and Hiram exchange gifts (verses 10–14)
div.p: Solomon gave twenty cities to Hiram.
Hiram was displeased with them.
If Solomon wanted to please him, it would be better to cooperate with him in trade, as the two kings eventually did.
See how God's providence suits different parts of the earth to people's varied needs and dispositions.
He also suits people to the lands where they live.
Through this arrangement, human beings depend upon one another and work together for their common benefit.

div.title: Solomon's prosperity and trade (verses 15–28)
div.p: This passage further describes Solomon's greatness.
He began in the right order.
He built God's house first, and only after finishing it did he undertake his own palace.
Then the Lord blessed his other building projects with success.
Let devotion come first, profit afterward, and pleasure last.
When we make real sacrifices for God's glory and for other people's good, the work may also bring benefit to us.
Canaan, the holy land and glory of all lands, had no gold of its own.
This reminds us that the most valuable production is often what sustains human life—our own lives and our neighbors'—rather than what brings luxury.
Canaan produced those necessary goods.
Solomon gained much wealth through commerce.
Yet he recommended a better trade, one available even to the poorest people.
Wisdom is better than silver, and its profit is greater than fine gold (Proverbs 3:14).

row.cell: The queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon.

div.title: The queen of Sheba visits Solomon (verses 1–13)
div.p: The queen of Sheba came to hear Solomon's wisdom so that she might increase her own understanding.
Our Savior refers to her search for knowledge of God through Solomon in order to rebuke those who fail to seek God through Jesus Christ himself.

We, too, can find our way through difficulties by waiting upon God in prayer, diligently searching the Scriptures, seeking advice from wise and experienced Christians, and putting what we learn into practice.
Solomon's wisdom impressed the queen more deeply than his riches, power and magnificence.
The excellence of heavenly things, and of Christians whose conduct agrees with their faith, is greater than any report about them can adequately express.
In the queen's experience the truth exceeded the reports.
All who, by grace, enjoy fellowship with God will likewise discover that not even half the pleasure and benefit of walking in wisdom was told them beforehand.
How much more will the glorified saints say, when they enter heaven, that not even a thousandth part of its happiness had been described to them (1 Corinthians 2:9)!
The queen called those who continually attended Solomon happy.
We have still greater reason to call the servants of Christ blessed: those who dwell in his house will continue praising him.
She brought Solomon a generous gift.
Christ does not need anything we give him, but he calls us to give as an expression of gratitude.

A believer who has enjoyed fellowship with Jesus will return to ordinary responsibilities ready to fulfill them with better motives, while looking forward to the day when being absent from the body will mean being present with the Lord.

div.title: Solomon's riches (verses 14–29)
div.p: Solomon's wealth increased until silver was scarcely valued.
This is the nature of worldly riches: when they become plentiful, people tend to value them less.
How much more should the enjoyment of spiritual wealth diminish our attachment to earthly possessions!
If abundant gold makes silver seem insignificant, should not wisdom, grace and foretastes of heaven—which are worth far more than gold—make gold itself seem small to us?
Solomon's greatness fulfilled God's promise.
Let that encourage us to seek first God's kingdom and his righteousness.

Yet Solomon was also the man who, after experiencing every kind of earthly pleasure, wrote a book declaring that worldly things are vanity, accompanied by vexation of spirit, and that setting our hearts on them is foolish.
He recommended sincere godliness as bringing far greater happiness than all the riches and power he possessed.
Through God's grace, that true happiness is available to us.

row.cell: Solomon's wives and concubines, His idolatry.

div.title: Solomon turns to idolatry (verses 1–8)
div.p: Few passages in Scripture give a more sorrowful or astonishing example of human corruption than this one.
Solomon became a public worshiper of detestable idols.
He probably yielded little by little to pride and luxury and lost his taste for true wisdom.
Nothing in ourselves can make us safe from the deceitfulness and corruption of the human heart.
Nor does old age remove our sinful inclinations.
Unless sinful desires are crucified and put to death through God's grace, they will never simply disappear. They can remain even when the opportunity to satisfy them is gone.
Anyone who thinks he stands securely must be careful not to fall.
Without divine grace we are weak.
Let us therefore depend continually upon that grace, stay alert and keep sober judgment.
We are fighting a dangerous battle in enemy territory, while our worst enemies are the traitors within our own hearts.

div.title: God announces judgment on Solomon (verses 9–13)
div.p: The Lord told Solomon, probably through a prophet, what his apostasy would bring upon him.
We have reason to hope Solomon repented and found mercy.

p.hi: But the Holy Spirit did not expressly record his repentance.

div.p: Scripture leaves the matter uncertain, as a warning against deliberate sin.
Guilt may be forgiven while its disgrace remains.
We cannot determine before the day of judgment whether Solomon was finally left under God's everlasting displeasure.

div.title: God raises opponents against Solomon (verses 14–25)
div.p: As long as Solomon walked closely with God and kept his duty, enemies did not disturb him.
Now two adversaries rose against him.
If God is for us, even powerful opponents cannot prevail.
But if he is against us, even a small trouble can frighten us; a mere grasshopper may become a burden.
These adversaries acted from ambition or revenge.
Nevertheless, God used their actions to correct Solomon.

div.title: Jeroboam is promised the kingdom (verses 26–40)
div.p: When Ahijah explained why the kingdom would be torn from Solomon's house, he warned Jeroboam not to lose his own advancement through sin.
Yet David's house would continue, because the Messiah was to come from it.
Solomon tried to kill the man who would succeed him.
Had he not taught other people that however many plans human beings make, the Lord's counsel will stand?
Yet now Solomon himself imagined he could defeat that counsel.
Jeroboam took refuge in Egypt.
He was content for a time to live in obscurity and exile because he had the promise of a kingdom.
Should we not be equally content, when we have an even better kingdom promised to us?

div.title: Solomon dies (verses 41–43)
div.p: Solomon's reign lasted as long as his father's, but his life was shorter.
His sin shortened his days.
If earthly possessions and opportunities could satisfy the soul and bring true joy, Solomon would have found it.
Instead, they disappointed him.
He left the record of his experience to warn us: vanity and vexation of spirit.
The New Testament announces that one greater than Solomon has come to rule over us and inherit the throne of his father David.
Solomon's greatness faintly represents something of Christ's far greater excellence.

row.cell: Rehoboam's accession, The people's petition, His rough answer.

div.title: Rehoboam answers the people harshly (verses 1–15)
div.p: Israel's tribes complained to Rehoboam about their burdens.
They did not complain about Solomon's idolatry or his turning away from God.
Their greatest grievance should have been his religious rebellion, but they hardly cared about that as long as they could live comfortably and avoid taxes.
People inclined to division can always find something to complain about.
Considering Scripture's account of the peace, wealth and prosperity Israel enjoyed under Solomon, Henry judges their accusations to have been false or greatly exaggerated.
Rehoboam followed the advice of the younger men.
Few rulers have been more blinded by pride and the desire for arbitrary power—nothing is more destructive.
Through his foolish reply, God's prior judgment was fulfilled.
God left Rehoboam to his folly and withheld the discernment that would have led to peace, so that the kingdom would be divided.
The Lord accomplishes his wise and righteous purposes even through human errors and sins.
People who lose the kingdom of heaven likewise throw it away through stubbornness and folly, as Rehoboam threw away his kingdom.

div.title: The ten tribes rebel (verses 16–24)
div.p: The people spoke disrespectfully about David.
How quickly a good person's service to the public is forgotten!
Remembering that God governs even the losses and hardships that come to us, and that other people may be only the instruments involved, should keep us from plotting revenge.
Rehoboam and his people finally listened to the Lord's word.
When we know what God commands, we must submit even when it directly contradicts what we wanted.
If we possess God's favor, the whole universe cannot truly harm us.

div.title: Jeroboam establishes false worship (verses 25–33)
div.p: Jeroboam distrusted God's providence.
He devised his own way to protect himself and his kingship, even when doing so required sin.
Practical disbelief in God's complete sufficiency lies beneath our departures from him.
He probably intended the new worship to honor Jehovah, the God of Israel.
Yet representing God in this way violated divine law and dishonored his majesty.
People might accept worship of the God of Israel through an image more readily than openly worshiping Baal.
But that compromise paved the way for later idolatry.
Blessed Lord, give us grace to honor your temple, appointed worship, house of prayer and Sabbaths.
Never let us imitate Jeroboam by installing a detestable idol in our hearts.
Be everything precious to us.
Rule in our hearts as our hope of glory.

row.cell: The disobedient prophet is slain, Jeroboam's obstinacy.

div.title: Jeroboam's altar is condemned (verses 1–10)
div.p: By threatening the altar, God's prophet also pronounced judgment upon its founder and worshipers.
False worship would not continue, but the Lord's word would remain forever.
The prophecy plainly announced that David's family would continue and support true religion, while the ten tribes would be powerless to stop what God had decreed.
When the Lord judicially hardens a sinner's heart, the person may become unable to draw back through repentance the hand that was stretched out in wrongdoing.
Such spiritual judgment, represented by Jeroboam's injured hand, is far more dreadful than a physical disability.
When Jeroboam needed help, he turned not to the golden calves, but to God's power and favor.
A time may come when people who hate faithful preaching will gladly ask faithful ministers to pray for them.
Yet Jeroboam asked only for his hand to be healed.
He did not seek pardon for his sin or a changed heart.
He was briefly impressed by both judgment and mercy, but the impression faded.
God forbade his messenger to eat or drink at Bethel to express his abhorrence of the people's idolatry and apostasy and to teach us not to share in works of darkness.
We have not learned genuine self-denial if we cannot refuse even one forbidden meal.

div.title: The prophet is deceived (verses 11–22)
div.p: The old prophet's behavior showed that he was not truly godly.
When Jeroboam changed the nation's worship, this man had preferred his comfort and interests to faithfulness.
He employed a wicked way of persuading God's messenger to return.
His story was entirely a lie.
Believers may be particularly vulnerable to temptation when disobedience comes disguised under plausible claims of holiness.
Why was the lying prophet apparently left unpunished while the faithful messenger, who was deceived, received immediate and severe judgment?
God's judgments are deeper than we can understand.
There will also be a judgment to come.
No excuse can justify deliberate disobedience.
The story illustrates the danger of listening to the great deceiver.
Those who give in to the devil when he tempts them will find him terrifying when he becomes their tormentor.
He flatters people to draw them into sin and afterward works to drive them into despair.

div.title: The disobedient prophet dies; Jeroboam does not repent (verses 23–34)
div.p: God is displeased by the sins of his own people.
Neither religious office, closeness to God nor past faithful service protects someone who willfully disobeys him.
God calls those he employs to observe his instructions strictly.
We cannot determine a person's spiritual state merely from suffering, nor measure a sin's guilt by the punishment immediately received.
For some, bodily suffering may lead to the salvation of the spirit.
For others, the body may enjoy prosperity while the soul becomes ready for judgment.
Jeroboam refused to turn from his evil way.
He believed the golden calves would secure his family's crown.
In reality, they contributed to the destruction of that crown and his house.
People who try to preserve their position through sin betray their own interests.
Let us fear success in sinful ways rather than treat it as a blessing.
Pray to be guarded against falsehood and temptation, and strengthened to follow God's commands with self-denying perseverance.

row.cell: Abijah being sick, his mother consults Ahijah.

div.title: Jeroboam sends his wife to Ahijah (verses 1–6)
div.p: When Jeroboam was doing evil, his child became sick.
When sickness enters a family, we should examine whether we have been cherishing a particular sin from which God means to turn us through this hardship.
Jeroboam would have acted more faithfully by asking why God was contending with him, requesting the prophet's prayers and throwing away his idols.
But many people would rather learn their future fortunes than hear about their faults and duties.
Jeroboam sent to Ahijah because that prophet had foretold his rise to the throne.
People who make themselves unfit to receive comfort through their sins may still expect good ministers to speak only peace to them.
In doing so they wrong both themselves and the ministers.
Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise so the prophet would answer only her question about their son.
Some people similarly try to limit their ministers to pleasant messages.
They fear hearing the full counsel of God because it might warn of judgment rather than promise comfort.
But Jeroboam's wife would learn from the prophet's first words what she must expect.
The news of a hypocrite's final portion will be dreadful.
God judges people by what they truly are, not how they appear.

div.title: Judgment is announced against Jeroboam's family (verses 7–20)
div.p: Whether or not we remember God's former mercies, he remembers them.
If we respond with ingratitude, he can bring those gifts back before us as evidence against us.
Ahijah foretold the child's approaching death.
Henry interprets this as a mercy to the child.
Of all Jeroboam's family, the boy alone showed affection for the true worship of God and disliked the worship of the calves.
God's sovereign grace can save someone from the worst household, wherever there is a genuine inclination toward the Lord God of Israel.
The righteous may be taken away from coming evil in this world and brought to the good awaiting them in a better world.
When the best member of a family dies first, it can be a warning to the others; yet death does not deprive that righteous person of any eternal blessing.
The death of the boy should have instructed both the household and the nation.
The prophet also announced judgment on Israel because its people had adopted Jeroboam's false worship.
After the ten tribes left David's house, their kingship rarely remained long in a single family.
One ruling house displaced and destroyed another.
Families and kingdoms are ruined by sin.
When influential people act wickedly, they draw others into both their guilt and its consequences.
Their condemnation is especially severe because they must answer not only for their own wrongdoing but also for the sins they encouraged others to commit and continue.

div.title: Rehoboam's evil reign (verses 21–31)
div.p: Scripture says nothing good about Rehoboam here and much that condemns the behavior of his subjects.
Jerusalem was the city God had chosen for his temple and worship.
Yet its people practiced some of the most shameful sins of the pagan nations.
This shows that nothing can transform fallen human hearts except the sanctifying grace of the Holy Spirit.
We should depend upon that grace and pray daily for it, for ourselves and everyone around us.
The splendor of the temple, the ceremonies of the priesthood and every outward advantage of the nation's religion could not keep the people faithful to God.
Only an outpouring of the Spirit can do that.
Sin exposes a people to danger, makes it poor and weakens it.
Shishak, king of Egypt, came and took away Jerusalem's treasures.
Sin tarnishes gold, makes what was precious grow dim and replaces it with inferior brass.

row.cell: Wicked reign of Abijam, king of Judah.
Good reign of Asa, king of Judah.
The evil reigns of Nadab and Baasha in Israel.

div.title: The reign of Abijam (verses 1–8)
div.p: Abijam's heart was not wholly devoted to the Lord his God. He lacked sincerity. He began well but then fell away, walking in the sins of his father and imitating his bad example even though he had seen its harmful results.
Nevertheless, David's family remained a lamp in Jerusalem. It preserved true worship there when divine truth seemed to have been extinguished everywhere else.
The Lord continues to preserve his own cause, even when people who should have served it faithfully live and die in their sins.
The Son of David will remain a light to his church, establishing it in truth and righteousness until the end of time.
Henry distinguishes two ways of fulfilling God's law.
The first is legal fulfillment: carrying out everything the law requires through one's own obedience. Only Christ—and Adam before his fall—fulfilled it in this way.
The second is gospel fulfillment: believing in Christ, who fulfilled the law on our behalf, and sincerely endeavoring with our whole being to obey every command of God.
God accepts this obedience from everyone who is in Christ. In that sense Scripture says that David and other believers fulfilled the law.

div.title: Asa brings reform to Judah (verses 9–24)
div.p: Asa did what was right in the Lord's eyes. What God judges to be right is right indeed.
His reign was a period of reform.
Reformation begins by removing evil, and Asa found a great deal of evil to remove.
When idolatry was present within his own royal household, he removed it there too.

p.hi: Reformation must begin at home.

div.p: He respected and loved his mother, but loved God more.
People who possess authority are blessed when they have hearts willing to use it well.
Yet we must not merely stop doing evil; we must also learn to do good.
We should not only throw away our sinful idols but dedicate ourselves and all we possess to God's glory.
Asa was sincerely committed to serving God. His sins did not come from a presumptuous desire to rebel.
But his alliance with Ben-hadad arose from unbelief.
Even genuine believers find it hard to trust the Lord wholeheartedly in urgent danger.
Unbelief makes room for worldly schemes, and one sin can lead to another.
Christians have sometimes sought help from the Lord's enemies in their disputes with their own brothers and sisters.
In this way, people who once shone brightly may find their final years clouded over.

div.title: Nadab and Baasha rule Israel (verses 25–34)
div.p: During Asa's single reign in Judah, Israel's government passed into six or seven different hands.
Notice the destruction of Jeroboam's family.
Not one word of God will fall to the ground.
His warnings of judgment are not spoken merely to frighten people without consequence.
Wicked people sometimes carry out God's righteous judgments against one another.
Yet amid dreadful sins and apparent confusion, the Lord continues fulfilling his own plan.
When that plan is finally complete, his glorious justice, wisdom, truth and mercy will be admired and worshiped forever.

row.cell: The reigns of Baasha and Elah in Israel.
Reigns of Zimri and Omri in Israel.

div.title: Baasha and Elah (verses 1–14)
div.p: This chapter concerns only the northern kingdom of Israel and the repeated upheavals in its government.
God still called the Israelites his people, though they had become terribly corrupt.
Through Jehu, God announced that Baasha's family would suffer the same destruction that Baasha had been used to bring upon Jeroboam's family.
Those who imitate another person's sins may expect to share the consequences, particularly when they condemn wrongdoing in others while tolerating it in themselves.
Baasha himself died peacefully and received an honorable burial.
That fact reminds us that the judgments we should fear most may come after death.
Elah's end warns people who drink excessively.
Death can surprise them while they are drunk.
Beyond the diseases caused by overdrinking, intoxicated people are easy prey for enemies and vulnerable to accidents.
It is dreadful to be overtaken by death while committing sin and unprepared for prayer or any act of devotion.
The Lord's word came true, and the sins of Baasha and Elah were brought to account.
Their idols are called vanities, because idols cannot help or save anyone.
How miserable are those who depend on empty gods!

div.title: Zimri and Omri (verses 15–28)
div.p: People who forsake God may be left to destroy one another.
Ambitious, proud people bring each other to ruin.
Omri fought Tibni for several years.
We do not always understand the principles by which God governs individuals and nations in his providence.
Nevertheless, this history offers clear warnings.
When tyrants follow one another, and massacres, conspiracies and civil wars multiply, the people have every reason to recognize God's displeasure against sin.
They are urgently called to repentance and reform.
Omri became notorious for his wickedness.
Many evil people have also been powerful and famous.
They have built cities and had their names preserved in history, yet possess no name in the book of life.

div.title: Ahab's sin and the rebuilding of Jericho (verses 29–34)
div.p: Ahab did more evil than the kings who ruled before him.
He showed particular hostility toward both Jehovah and Israel.
He was not content with breaking the second commandment by worshiping images.
He broke the first commandment by worshiping other gods.
Treating smaller sins lightly opens the way to greater sins.
Marriage to people who are bold in wrongdoing also encourages sin and may hurry someone toward terrible extremes.
One of Ahab's subjects, Hiel, followed that example of presumption when he began rebuilding Jericho.
Like Achan, he took for his own purposes what had been placed under God's judgment.
He defied the curse that was well known in Israel.
No one who hardens his heart against the Lord can ultimately prosper.
Let the chapter make us consider the dreadful end of all who persist in evil.
Across every rank and circumstance of human life, the record of ungodly people provides similar sorrowful warnings.

row.cell: Elijah raises the widow's son to life.

div.title: Ravens feed Elijah (verses 1–7)
div.p: God wonderfully equips people for the work he has prepared for them.
The times called for an Elijah, and Elijah was suited to those times.
The Holy Spirit knows how to equip servants for their particular circumstances.
Elijah announced to Ahab that God was displeased with Israel's idolatry.
The Lord would discipline the people by withholding rain, something the gods they worshiped could never provide.
God told Elijah to hide himself.
When providence calls us to quietness and solitude, we should accept it.
If we cannot perform useful work, we should be patient.
When we cannot work actively for God, we should sit quietly and wait for him.
The Lord appointed ravens to bring Elijah meat, and they did so.
Anyone who lives from one day's provision to the next can learn to trust God's care for each day's bread on the day it is needed.
God could have sent angels instead.
He chose ravens to show that even the humblest creatures can accomplish his will as effectively as the mightiest.
Elijah seems to have lived this way for more than a year.
The brook's natural supply of water, which came through ordinary providence, failed.
But the miraculous food that God had expressly promised never failed.
When the heavens fail to give rain, the earth's resources fail as well.
Created comforts may disappear precisely when we most need them, like streams drying up in summer.
But the river that makes glad the city of God never runs dry.
There is a spring of water that wells up to eternal life.
Lord, give us that living water!

div.title: Elijah is sent to Zarephath (verses 8–16)
div.p: Many widows lived in Israel during Elijah's lifetime.
Some might gladly have received him into their homes.
Yet the Lord sent him instead to a city in Sidon, among the Gentiles.
In that sense, he became the first prophet sent to the Gentiles.
Jezebel was Elijah's greatest enemy.
To show how powerless her hatred was, God found a place of refuge for Elijah in her own country.
God chose no rich or powerful host.
He chose a poor, lonely widow who herself lacked food.
He made her both willing and able to sustain his servant.
It is his way and his glory to use and honor those considered weak and foolish.
The widow demonstrated extraordinary faith.
She trusted the prophet's promise that giving to him first would not leave her without food.
People who rely on God's promises are prepared to give themselves and what they possess in his service.
The growth of this woman's faith was as remarkable a miracle in the kingdom of grace as the continuing increase of her flour and oil was in the kingdom of providence.
Blessed are those who believe and obey hopefully even when circumstances offer no hope.
The widow shared the food she had for a single meal.
Through God's provision, she and her son then ate for more than two years during famine.
Food supplied by God's special favor, and enjoyed in Elijah's company, was doubly sweet.
Those who trust the Lord have his promise that in evil times they need not be ashamed and that in famine he can satisfy them.

div.title: Elijah raises the widow's son (verses 17–24)
div.p: Neither genuine faith nor faithful obedience keeps suffering and death out of our lives.
When the widow's child died, she spoke to Elijah mainly to express her grief, not because she expected him to revive the boy.
When God takes away our comforts, we may remember sins committed long before, perhaps in our youth.
His purpose may be to teach us to remember those sins against ourselves and repent.
Elijah's prayer was undoubtedly directed by the Holy Spirit.
The child came back to life.
See the power of prayer, and the power of the One who hears prayer.

row.cell: Elijah sends Ahab notice of his coming.
Elijah's trial of the false prophets.

div.title: Elijah prepares to meet Ahab (verses 1–16)
div.p: Even the severest judgments cannot, by themselves, humble or change a sinner's heart.
Only the blood of Jesus Christ can atone for sin's guilt, and only the sanctifying Spirit of God can cleanse its corruption.
The priests and Levites had gone to Judah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 11:13–14).
In their place God raised up teachers who read and explained his word.
These prophets probably came from the schools established earlier by Samuel.
They did not possess Elijah's special prophetic gift, but they taught the people to remain faithful to the God of Israel.
Jezebel tried to destroy these teachers.
The few who escaped death were forced to hide.
God preserves faithful people among every social rank, both high and low.
He accepts the faith, reverence and love produced by his Spirit through the Redeemer.
Observe how wonderfully he raises up friends for his servants, giving shelter in difficult times.
Bread and water were scarce.
Yet Obadiah found enough to keep the hidden prophets alive.
Ahab worked hard to save his livestock, but did nothing to save his own soul.
He searched for grass instead of seeking God's favor.
He tried to protect himself from the consequences of judgment without asking how to remove its cause.
It is a hopeful sign for a people when God calls his ministers to appear openly again.
Then even the bread of affliction is easier to bear because they can see and hear their teachers.

div.title: Elijah confronts Ahab (verses 17–20)
