div.p: We can often tell how people feel about God from how they treat his people and ministers.
Even the best and most useful servants, including Elijah, have been accused of disturbing a nation.
But those who bring God's judgment upon themselves through wrongdoing cause the trouble, not those who announce the warning and call people to repentance.

div.title: Elijah and the prophets of Baal (verses 21–40)
div.p: Many Israelites wavered in their convictions and changed their conduct.
Elijah called them to decide whether Jehovah or Baal was the true, self-existent, supreme God, the Creator, Governor and Judge of the world—and then to follow him alone.
It is dangerous to waver between serving God and serving sin, between Christ's rule and the control of our sinful desires.
If Jesus is the only Savior, we should trust him alone for everything.
If the Bible is God's word, we should reverence and receive all of it, submitting our understanding to the divine teaching it contains.
Elijah proposed a test.
Baal had every outward advantage, but God's servants learned they need never fear people's opposition when defending the truth.
Let the God who answers by fire be acknowledged as God.
Sacrifice and atonement came before the removal of judgment in mercy.
The God who can pardon sin and signify his acceptance by consuming the sin offering is the One able to bring relief from the nation's calamity.
God has never required his worshipers to honor him through the practices of Baal's followers.
Serving the devil may sometimes flatter bodily pleasure, but it is ultimately cruel, as envy, drunkenness and false religion show.
The Lord calls us to put sinful desires to death, but he takes no pleasure in bodily penances and needless harsh treatment.
Who commanded those practices?
A few words prayed with confident faith, earnest love for God's glory and concern for souls can accomplish far more than bodily torment.
Such prayer may arise from longing for God's likeness and his favor.
The earnest prayer of a righteous person is powerful.
Elijah was seeking God's glory and Israel's good, not personal recognition.
When fire fell, the people agreed: Jehovah is God.
Some, we hope, were genuinely changed in heart.

p.hi: Most may have been convinced without being converted.

div.p: Blessed are those who have not seen such a miracle and yet believe and respond to God more deeply than some who witnessed it.

div.title: Elijah prays until rain comes (verses 41–46)
div.p: Israel had gone some distance toward reform by acknowledging the Lord as God and agreeing to the judgment of Baal's prophets.
God therefore allowed blessing to return to the land.
Elijah continued praying.
Even when an answer to earnest prayer is delayed, we should keep praying with faith rather than becoming weary or giving up.
At last a little cloud appeared.
It soon spread across the sky and watered the land.
Great blessings often begin almost invisibly.
Heavy rain can come from a cloud the size of a hand.
We should not despise the day of small beginnings.
The same is true of God's gracious work within the soul.
The Spirit's first movements may be barely perceptible, but eventually grow to the astonishment of people and the praise of angels.
Elijah sent Ahab home and accompanied him.
God will strengthen his people for every service to which his commands and providence call them.
God's justice and holiness can frighten sinners, produce confessions and secure outward obedience for a time.
But they must also learn his mercy, love and truth in Jesus Christ before they are drawn to genuine humility, trust and love.
The Holy Spirit uses both in converting sinners.
When people are impressed by divine truth, we should urge them to practice the duties Christ commands.

div.title: Elijah flees into the wilderness (verses 1–8)
div.p: Jezebel sent Elijah a threatening message.
What should have convinced and humbled her instead made her sinful heart harder and angrier against God.
Even great faith does not remain equally strong at all times.
Elijah might still have served Israel usefully, and he had every reason to trust God's protection while doing God's work.
Yet he fled.
His desire to die was not the calm longing of grace expressed by Paul when he wished to depart and be with Christ.
God allowed Elijah to experience his own weakness.
This taught him that whenever he had acted bravely and powerfully, his strength had come from the Lord, not from himself.
By nature he was no better than his ancestors.
God knows what services and trials he intends for us, even when we do not.
He will ensure that his grace is sufficient for what he calls us to face.

div.title: God appears to Elijah (verses 9–13)
div.p: God asked, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”
This was a rebuke.
We should regularly ask ourselves whether we are where duty calls us.
Am I in the place where God wants me, where my work lies and where I can be useful?
Elijah complained about Israel's stubbornness in sin.
He believed he was the only faithful person left.
Despairing of success has prevented many good undertakings.
Yet if Elijah had come to seek God, he would discover that God intended to meet him.
The strong wind, earthquake and fire did not move Elijah to cover his face.
The quiet voice did.
Hearts touched by grace are often more deeply moved by God's tender mercies than by terrifying displays of power.
The gentle voice of the One who speaks from the cross and mercy seat is especially powerful in taking hold of the heart.

div.title: God answers Elijah's complaint (verses 14–18)
div.p: The Lord repeated his question.
Elijah once more expressed his discouragement.
Where should God's prophets take their complaints except to their Master?
The Lord answered.
He announced judgment on Ahab's wicked house and on Israel's sins.
He also showed that Elijah was not alone, contrary to what he had believed.
A helper would be raised up for him.
In this way God addressed every part of Elijah's complaint.
God's faithful people are often hidden ones (Psalm 83:3).
At times the visible church almost disappears.
It is like wheat buried in chaff or gold mixed with dross, until the day when everything will be sifted, refined and separated.
The Lord knows those who belong to him, even when we do not see them.
In heaven, we may not meet some people we expected to find there.
But we will meet others whom we never imagined would be there.
God's love is often far broader than human generosity and charity.

div.title: Elisha is called (verses 19–21)
div.p: Elijah found Elisha as God had directed.
He found him not in a school of prophets, or occupied with reading, praying or sacrifices, but plowing a field.
Idleness honors no one, and farming is no disgrace to anyone.
An honest earthly occupation does not prevent a person from receiving a heavenly calling.
The Holy Spirit moved Elisha's heart, and he became willing to leave everything to follow Elijah.
When Christ exercises his saving power, his people become willing.
No one would come to him unless drawn in this way.
It was a discouraging time for anyone to begin serving as a prophet.
Someone consulting only human advantage would hardly have wanted Elijah's mantle.
Yet Elisha left everything cheerfully to accompany him.
Likewise, when Jesus called people to follow him, they willingly left close friends and profitable work and took up difficult duties out of love for his name.
May the power of his grace work deeply in us.
May we submit to him without reservation and make our calling and election sure.

div.title: Ben-hadad besieges Samaria (verses 1–11)
div.p: Ben-hadad sent Ahab an arrogant demand.
Ahab answered with a disgracefully submissive reply.
Sin brings people into such difficulties because it leaves them without God's protection.
If the Lord does not rule us, our enemies will.
Guilt saps people's confidence and makes them cowardly.
Ahab became desperate.
People will surrender even the things they love most in order to preserve their earthly lives.
Yet many would rather lose their souls than give up a single sinful pleasure or interest in order to save them.
Amid this folly, Ahab spoke one of his wisest sayings.
No one should boast before an approaching battle, since none of us knows what tomorrow will bring.
We should apply this to spiritual conflicts.
Peter fell because he was overconfident.
Blessed is the person who never neglects to keep watch.

div.title: Ben-hadad is defeated (verses 12–21)
div.p: The proud Syrian army was defeated, and the despised Israelites won.
The drunken king's orders confused his troops and prevented them from attacking effectively.
People who feel most secure are often the least courageous when danger comes.
Ahab inflicted a severe defeat.
God sometimes makes one wicked person an instrument of judgment against another.

div.title: The Syrians are defeated again (verses 22–30)
div.p: Ben-hadad's advisers suggested changing the battlefield.
They assumed that Israel's gods, rather than Israel itself, had won the earlier battle.
But their view of Jehovah was deeply mistaken.
They imagined that Israel worshiped several gods whose powers were limited to particular kinds of land.
They showed the emptiness of pagan ideas about God.
Great practical cleverness in worldly affairs can coexist with astonishing folly in understanding divine things.

div.title: Ahab makes peace with Ben-hadad (verses 31–43)
div.p: Sinners have strong reason to repent and humble themselves before God.
Have we not heard that the God of Israel is merciful?
Have we not experienced his mercy?
Gospel repentance arises from recognizing God's mercy in Jesus Christ, through whom forgiveness is available.
Ben-hadad's conduct showed how quickly a person can change from arrogance in prosperity to humiliation in adversity.
An evil disposition may shape behavior in both conditions.
Ahab was one of those people whom prosperity failed to improve.
He did not know how to use success in serving God, helping his generation or even protecting his own true interests.
A wicked person may receive favor and still fail to learn righteousness.
A prophet confronted Ahab through a parable.
An obedient prophet was called upon to strike another by divine command.
Refusing that command brought punishment.
How much more blameworthy was Ahab for sparing God's enemy and his own enemy when the Lord had required judgment?
Ahab returned home resentful and displeased.
He did not truly repent or seek to put right what he had done.
His victory had not made him happy.
Many hear the good news of Christ and yet remain so occupied and distracted that the day of salvation passes them by.

div.title: Ahab covets Naboth's vineyard (verses 1–4)
div.p: Naboth may once have been pleased to own a vineyard close to the royal palace.
But that location proved fatal to him.
Possessions often become traps, and living near powerful people can be dangerous.
Discontent is a sin that punishes itself, making people miserable through their own restless desires.
It also produces itself.
Discontent does not arise simply from outward circumstances, but from the mind.

p.hi: Paul was content in prison; Ahab was discontent in a palace.

div.p: Ahab enjoyed every pleasure of Canaan, a beautiful and fruitful country.
He possessed the wealth of a kingdom, the luxuries of a royal court and the honor and authority of a throne.
Yet none of those things satisfied him without Naboth's vineyard.
Sinful desires continually expose us to distress.
People determined to complain can always find some cause for dissatisfaction, however comfortable their lives may be.

div.title: Jezebel has Naboth murdered (verses 5–16)
div.p: A wife ought to be a suitable helper to her husband.
But a cunning, unscrupulous and beloved spouse who acts as Satan's agent can bring terrible consequences.
Few rulers have ever given more wicked orders than those Jezebel sent to the leaders of Jezreel.
Naboth was to be murdered under the appearance of religion.
People have sometimes used religious language to cover even the most horrible wrongs.
The murder would also be made to appear lawful through the formal procedures of justice.
The episode reveals the cruelty of the wicked and Satan's influence among those who disobey God.
We should entrust our lives and earthly comforts to the Lord, because innocence does not always protect people from harm in this world.
Yet we may rejoice that all wrongs will finally be put right at the day of judgment.

div.title: Elijah announces judgment on Ahab (verses 17–29)
div.p: The apostle Paul lamented being sold under sin (Romans 7:14), like a helpless captive opposed to his own bondage.
Ahab was different.
He willingly sold himself to sin, choosing its dominion and loving it.
Jezebel encouraged him to continue in wrongdoing.
Elijah confronted Ahab and exposed his sin.
A person has reached a miserable condition when he regards God's word as his enemy.
It is even more desperate when he considers ministers his enemies simply because they tell him the truth.
Ahab adopted the outward clothing and behavior of a repentant person.
But his heart remained proud and unchanged.
He showed only what others could see.
His repentance was external, not genuine.
Nevertheless, his outward humiliation brought a delay in the announced judgment.
Let this encourage everyone who truly repents and sincerely believes the gospel.
If God granted a reprieve to a merely outward and partial penitent, surely a sincere believer may hope to go home justified, not merely reprieved.

row.cell: Jehoshaphat makes a league with Ahab.
Micaiah predicts the death of Ahab.

div.title: Jehoshaphat makes an alliance with Ahab (verses 1–14)
div.p: Some genuinely godly people are naturally agreeable and accommodating.
That disposition can tempt them into friendship with open enemies of true religion.
It is especially dangerous because they may begin tolerating speech and behavior they ought to oppose.
A godly person should take faith along wherever he goes and should not be ashamed to acknowledge it among people who disregard it.
Jehoshaphat had not left his respect for God's word behind in Jerusalem.
He openly requested it even at Ahab's court.
Ahab's prophets used the name of Jehovah to please Jehoshaphat.
But their message of guaranteed success was designed to please Ahab.
False prophets may imitate true prophets' speech, but those with mature spiritual discernment can recognize the deception.

p.hi: One faithful prophet of the Lord was worth all of them.

div.p: Worldly people have always been unreasonable about religion.
They expect preachers to adjust their doctrine to current fashions and the audience's taste, while still claiming divine authority for words people want to hear.
They treat someone who refuses such manipulation as foolish or uncivil, as though deceiving others were merely a sensible way of protecting one's interests.

div.title: Micaiah foretells Ahab's death (verses 15–28)
div.p: One of the greatest acts of kindness we can do for a person on a dangerous path is to warn that person clearly.
Micaiah described his vision to leave Ahab without excuse and teach everyone listening.
The scene is represented in language suited to human understanding.
We must not imagine that God needs to form new plans, consult angels or other creatures about what to do, or change his mind after receiving advice.

p.hi: Nor should we imagine that God is the author of sin or the cause of a person telling or believing a lie.

div.p: Micaiah did not strike Zedekiah back when the false prophet struck him.
Zedekiah loudly claimed the Spirit's authority, as people ignorant of the Holy Spirit's true work often do.
Micaiah left him to discover his error when the prophecy was fulfilled.
People unwilling to let God's word correct their mistakes in time will eventually be undeceived by divine judgment, when it is too late.
We might be ashamed of calling our own difficulties severe if we considered what faithful servants of God have endured.
Yet a life without trouble may prove even more dangerous.
We can be drawn toward unfaithfulness and worldly conformity more easily through flattery and rewards than by threats.

div.title: Ahab dies in battle (verses 29–40)
div.p: Ahab intended to expose Jehoshaphat to danger while protecting himself.
See the reward of joining oneself to wicked people!
How could Ahab be trustworthy toward a friend when he had been unfaithful to God?
Jehoshaphat had told Ahab, “I am as you are.”
Now, because of the way they went into battle, he was mistaken for Ahab.
People who associate with evildoers risk sharing the harm that comes upon them.
God rescued Jehoshaphat, showing that though he was displeased with the alliance, he had not abandoned his servant.
The Lord is a friend who never fails when other friends do.
No one can hide from divine judgment.
God directed the arrow that struck Ahab.
Those whom God has appointed to die cannot escape that sentence by their own planning.
Ahab survived long enough to see part of Micaiah's prophecy come true.
He had time to feel himself dying and to remember the evil he had done.
What terror those memories must have brought!

div.title: Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah (verses 41–50)
div.p: Jehoshaphat's reign was among the best for both true devotion and prosperity.
He pleased God, and God blessed him.

div.title: Ahaziah's reign over Israel (verses 51–53)
div.p: Ahaziah's reign was very brief—less than two full years.
God brings some sinners to judgment quickly.
Scripture gives Ahaziah a terrible character.
He would not receive instruction or learn from the warnings he saw.
He imitated his wicked father and followed the counsel of his still-living mother, Jezebel, who was even more corrupt.
Children are deeply miserable when their parents not only pass on a sinful nature but actively teach them to increase their wickedness.
Parents who encourage their children toward destruction bring dreadful consequences upon their own households.
Hardened sinners can rush forward without fear along the same paths that have already brought others to eternal ruin.

row.cell: The revolt of Moab—Sickness of Ahaziah, king of Israel.
Fire called from heaven by Elijah—Death of Ahaziah.

div.title: Moab rebels; Ahaziah becomes ill (verses 1–8)
div.p: When Ahaziah rebelled against the Lord, Moab rebelled against him.
Sin weakens us and brings us into poverty and distress.
A person's rebellion against God is often punished by the rebellion of those who owe that person obedience.
Ahaziah fell through a lattice or railing.
Wherever we are, there is only a step between us and death.
People call their homes their castles, yet no house can protect its occupants from divine judgment.
The whole creation groans under the weight of human sin.
Ultimately it, too, will give way under that burden, like the lattice through which Ahaziah fell.
No one is safe while making God an enemy.
Those who refuse to consult God's word to find comfort will eventually hear it as a warning of judgment, whether they wish to hear it or not.

div.title: Elijah calls down fire; Ahaziah dies (verses 9–18)
div.p: Elijah prayed for fire from heaven to consume the arrogant and defiant men sent against him.
He did not do so merely to preserve his own safety.
His purpose was to confirm his prophetic mission and reveal God's anger against ungodliness and injustice.
Henry explains that Elijah acted by an exceptional divine prompting.
But when Jesus' disciples wanted to do something similar, the Savior refused to permit it (Luke 9:54).
The gospel's dispensation of the Spirit and grace does not allow his disciples to act in that way.
Elijah was moved by concern for God's glory, whereas the disciples were defending their own reputation.
The Lord judges deeds according to the motives behind them, and his judgment is true.
The third captain humbled himself and appealed to the mercy of God and Elijah.
Nothing good can be gained by fighting against God.
Those who learn submission from the dreadful consequences of others' stubbornness act wisely.
The courage of faith has often frightened even the proudest sinners.
Ahaziah was so terrified by Elijah's message that neither he nor anyone around him attempted to harm the prophet.
Who can hurt someone under God's protection?
Like Ahaziah, many people expecting to prosper through sin are suddenly taken from this life.
Everything in this chapter warns us to seek the Lord while he may be found.

row.cell: Elijah is taken up into heaven.
Elisha is manifested to be Elijah's successor.
Elisha heals the waters of Jericho, Those that mocked Elisha destroyed.

div.title: Elijah parts the Jordan (verses 1–8)
div.p: The Lord had made it known to Elijah that his departure was near.
He therefore visited the different schools of the prophets to give his last encouragements and blessing.
Elijah's departure pictured Christ's ascension and the opening of heaven's kingdom to all believers.
Elisha had followed Elijah for years.
He was unwilling to leave him now, when he hoped to receive a final blessing.
Let those who follow Christ beware of growing tired and giving up just before the end.
Long before, the Jordan had parted for the ark.
Now it parted before Elijah's mantle as a sign of God's presence.
For God's faithful people, death is like the Jordan they must cross to reach heaven.
Christ's death has opened a path through those waters for the redeemed.
O death, where are your sting, injury and terror?

div.title: Elijah is taken to heaven (verses 9–12)
div.p: The source of divine fullness from which prophets and apostles received their gifts still exists.
We are encouraged to ask God freely for abundant grace.
By faithfully attending Elijah, especially in his final hours, Elisha put himself in the position most suited to receive a greater share of his spirit.
What departing believers say about their experience of God can strengthen our resolve and brighten our own hope.
Elijah was carried to heaven in a fiery chariot.
Many questions about the event cannot be answered.
It is enough to notice what his Master found him doing when the hour arrived.
He was having a serious conversation with Elisha, encouraging and instructing him about God's kingdom among people.
We are wrong to imagine that preparing for heaven consists only of contemplation and acts of worship.
The chariot and horses appeared like fire, not burning but radiant and glorious.
Through the way Elijah and Enoch left the world, God gave a glimpse of the eternal life revealed in the gospel and the glory awaiting the bodies of believers.
It also represented Christ's ascension.
Yet even though Elijah entered heaven triumphantly, Israel could hardly spare him.
People who feel no sorrow when faithful and useful servants of God die have hard hearts.
Elijah's counsel, rebukes and prayers had protected the nation more effectively than its greatest military force.
Christ left the gospel with his disciples as Elijah left his mantle.
It is a sign of divine power working to overthrow Satan's rule and establish God's kingdom.
That same gospel remains with us, although the miraculous powers have been withdrawn.
It still has divine power to bring sinners to conversion and salvation.

div.title: Elisha receives Elijah's mantle (verses 13–18)
div.p: Elijah left his mantle to Elisha.
It represented the Spirit's gift and was worth far more than a fortune of gold or silver.
Elisha did not treat it as a sacred relic to worship.
He took it as a meaningful garment for use.
Elisha's question after Elijah's departure sought two things.
First, he sought God, the One to whom we may always turn when the human comforts we love are removed.
Second, he sought the God whom Elijah had served, honored and trusted.
The Lord God of the holy prophets remains the same yesterday, today and forever.
What use are the mantles, positions or books left by faithful people if we do not share their Spirit and their God?
Elisha parted the Jordan.
God's people need not fear the final crossing of death, because the Lord opens the way.
The sons of the prophets insisted on searching for Elijah, although the search was unnecessary.
Wise people may sometimes consent to a harmless but pointless request for the sake of peace and goodwill.
Yet searching hills and valleys will never bring us to Elijah.
Following his faithful and zealous example may, in God's appointed time, bring us to where he has gone.

div.title: Jericho's water healed; mockers judged (verses 19–25)
div.p: Elisha healed the water of Jericho.
Those who serve as prophets should make the places they visit better through their ministry, softening bitter hearts and making fruitless souls productive through God's word.
That word is like the salt Elisha put into the water.
The miracle pictured God's grace changing a sinful human heart.
Through the gospel, entire families, towns and cities have been transformed from wrongdoing to fruitful works of righteousness, to God's glory through Christ.
The young people of Bethel mocked Elisha as the Lord's prophet.
Their curse was not without cause.
They mocked him by saying “Go up,” referring contemptuously to Elijah's ascent to heaven.
Henry describes Elisha's curse as acting under an exceptional divine prompting.
He reasons that the ensuing judgment would not have followed unless the Holy Spirit directed that solemn action.
God is righteous, hates sin and will call it to account.
Young people should beware of wicked words.
God notices what they say.
They must not mock anyone's physical or intellectual limitations.
Mocking another person for doing good is especially dangerous.
Parents who desire true comfort from their children should teach them well from their earliest years and work to restrain the foolishness growing within them.
How terrible it will be for parents to discover at judgment that their bad example, carelessness or corrupt instruction contributed to their children's destruction!

row.cell: War with Moab, The intercession of Elisha.

div.title: Jehoram rules Israel (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jehoram learned something from God's judgments and removed the image of Baal.
Yet he continued to support worship of the golden calves.
Those who abandon only the sins that have brought them obvious loss, while clinging to sins they expect to profit from, have not truly repented or reformed.

div.title: War with Moab; Elisha's intercession (verses 6–19)
div.p: Israel's king lamented the army's desperate lack of water and the danger it faced.
Yet he had summoned the other kings into the war.
Now he blamed Providence for the trouble.
Human foolishness corrupts our path, and then the heart becomes angry with the Lord (Proverbs 19:3).
Jehoshaphat did well to ask for the Lord's guidance, but he should have done it before entering the war.
Even good people sometimes neglect their duties until hardship drives them to perform them.
Wicked people often benefit from companionship with faithful believers.
Elisha told the kings to dig the valley full of trenches to receive water.
This tested their faith and obedience.
People expecting God's blessings should prepare to receive them—digging pools for promised rain, as in the Valley of Baca, making it a place of springs (Psalm 84:6).
There is no need to speculate where the water came from.
God is not restricted to ordinary natural causes.
People who sincerely seek the dew of his grace will receive it and become more than conquerors through it.

div.title: Water comes; Moab is defeated (verses 20–27)
div.p: It is a great blessing to live among people who are able to approach God through effective prayer.
A kingdom may survive and prosper because of the earnest prayers of those who are precious in God's sight.
We should esteem most highly the people whom he values most.
When sinners assure themselves that all is peaceful and safe, destruction may suddenly overtake them.
Despair then follows their reckless confidence.
Under Satan's influence, human beings have committed horrible acts that naturally make the heart recoil.
The king of Moab sacrificed his son in such a desperate and dreadful act.
It is wise not to drive even very wicked people to desperation when that can be avoided.
Rather, we should leave them to God's judgment.

row.cell: The Shunammite's son restored to life.
The miracle of healing the pottage, and of feeding the sons of the prophets.

div.title: Elisha multiplies the widow's oil (verses 1–7)
div.p: Elisha's miracles were works of real charity.
So were the miracles of Christ.
They were not merely extraordinary displays of power but acts of great kindness to the people who received them.
God shows both his greatness and his goodness.
Elisha listened willingly to a poor widow's trouble.
People who leave their families burdened with debt often have little idea how much suffering they cause.
Everyone who professes faith in the Lord should trust him for daily provision without testing him through carelessness or wastefulness.
We should avoid running into debt.
Few practices bring more disgrace upon the gospel or leave more hardship for surviving family members.
Elisha helped the widow find a way to pay what she owed and support herself and her children.
The provision was miraculous.
But it also illustrated a wise ordinary way of helping distressed people: assist them in using what little they possess through their own diligent work.
The oil continued flowing while empty containers remained.
There is no shortage in God or in the riches of his grace.
The limitations are in ourselves: our faith fails, not his promise.
He gives more than we ask.
If more containers had been provided, there was sufficient oil to fill them.
God has enough for all and enough for each.
The Redeemer is sufficient to provide salvation for every sinner who comes to him, and his saving resources will not be exhausted.
The widow was to pay her debt first, before using the remainder to provide for the children.
Though her creditors had been harsh, the debt remained due.
One of the chief duties of Christian living is to pay every just debt and give each person what rightly belongs to them, even if doing so leaves little for ourselves.
We should act from conscience, not merely compulsion.
Honest people cannot comfortably enjoy their daily bread unless it is truly theirs.
Then the widow and her family could live on what remained, using the proceeds from the oil to support an honest livelihood.
We should not expect miracles of this kind today.
But we can expect God's mercy as we seek him and wait upon him.
Widows in particular may trust the Lord who rules human hearts and can provide just as effectively without an outward miracle.

div.title: The Shunammite woman is given a son (verses 8–17)
div.p: Elisha had earned the king's regard through his past service.
Yet a good person can find just as much happiness in serving others as in gaining influence or raising personal status.
The Shunammite woman did not require a favor from the king.
She was content to live among her own people, who loved and respected her and whom she could help.
Many people would be happier if they could recognize when their situation is already good.
God sees even a secret desire that we have held back in submission to his will.
He may hear the prayers of his servants on behalf of those who have helped them and send blessings that were neither requested nor expected.
The promises made by God's true servants must not be treated as mere attempts to flatter or deceive, like worldly promises.

div.title: The Shunammite's son is restored to life (verses 18–37)
div.p: The child died suddenly.
All a mother's tenderness could not preserve the life of a child who had come through promise and prayer and been received as a gift of love.
Yet the mother's restraint under this terrible suffering was remarkable.
She did not utter a bitter or irritable word.
She trusted God's goodness so deeply that she was ready to hope he would restore what he had taken away.
What great faith!
The One who gave that faith would not disappoint it.
She asked her husband for permission to go immediately to the prophet.
Although she was a woman of rank, she did not rely solely on occasional visits from Elisha to her home.
She also participated in public worship.
God's ministers should ask sincerely about the welfare of their friends and families.
The woman's answer was, “It is well.”
How could everything be well when her child was dead at home?
Everything God does is well ordered.
All is well for those who have died if they have gone to heaven, and all may be well for those who remain if suffering helps them continue toward heaven.
Whenever an earthly comfort is removed, it is well if by grace we can say that our hearts had not made an idol of it.
If we had loved it too much, we have reason to fear it may have been given and removed as discipline.
Elisha prayed to God in faith.
The child was brought back to life and returned to his mother.
People who seek to bring spiritual life to those dead in sin must feel deep concern for them and pray with earnest effort.
No minister can give another person divine life.
Nevertheless, ministers should use every means and work as diligently as though they could.

div.title: Harmful food purified and a small meal multiplied (verses 38–44)
div.p: There was a famine of bread, but not a famine of hearing God's word.
The sons of the prophets were gathered around Elisha, listening to his teaching.
Elisha made dangerous food wholesome.
If our meal consists of nothing more than a pot of stew, remember that even this great prophet and his guests had no more.
The table can become a trap.
Food that should nourish us may instead bring danger, which is reason to eat with a healthy awareness of our dependence on God.
As we receive life's provisions and comforts, we must remember death's approach and the danger of sin.
We should thank the Lord for making our food healthy and nourishing.
He is the Lord who heals us.
Elisha also made a little food sufficient for many.
What he had freely received, he freely gave.
God has promised his church that he will bless her provisions abundantly and satisfy her poor with bread (Psalm 132:15).
When he provides, his gift is enough.
What he blesses can accomplish a great deal.
Christ's later miracle of feeding the crowds was greater still.
Yet both teach that those who wait upon God while following their duties may trust his providential care.

div.title: Naaman seeks healing (verses 1–8)
div.p: Although the Syrians were idol worshipers who oppressed God's people, Scripture attributes the deliverance Naaman had achieved to the Lord.
This is the right way to speak about history.
People who write about ordinary affairs often seem not to think of God at all.
No amount of human greatness or honor can keep severe suffering away.
Beneath fine clothing, many important people suffer in sick and broken bodies.
Every person has some “but”—a weakness that qualifies outward success, diminishes glory or interrupts pleasure.
Naaman's servant, a young Israelite girl, knew about the famous prophet among her people.
Children should be told about God's wonderful works while they are young, so they can speak of him wherever life takes them.
Though she was a captive and served against her will, she desired her master's recovery.
How much more should people serving others by choice seek their employers' welfare!
Those working in households can become a great blessing by speaking faithfully of God's glory and his servants.
Naaman did not reject the girl's counsel because of her low social position.
How good it would be if people felt the weight of sin as keenly as they feel bodily illness!
When we seek the blessings God grants in answer to prayer, we must come as beggars receiving a free gift, not as lords demanding or purchasing one.

div.title: Naaman is cleansed (verses 9–14)
div.p: Elisha knew Naaman was proud.
He wanted him to learn that all people stand on the same level before the great God.
Every command of God tests the human heart, especially those telling sinners how to seek salvation.
Naaman's reaction showed pride's foolishness.
He was unwilling to accept a cure unless it came with the ceremony and spectacle he expected.
He wanted to be healed on his own terms.
Likewise, the way sinners receive forgiveness and holiness—through Christ's blood and Spirit, by faith in his name alone—does not flatter human pride or provide a role for self-salvation.
Human wisdom prefers to invent supposedly better methods.
People in authority should listen to reason.
We should refuse evil advice even from prominent and respected people.
But we should be ready to receive good counsel even from those under our authority.
Naaman's attendants asked whether he would not do something difficult to be healed.
When spiritually sick people are willing to do anything, submit to anything and give up anything to receive healing, they have begun to hope rightly.
The remedy for sin is plain.
No one may claim it was hidden or needlessly complicated.

p.hi: Believe and be saved. Repent and be pardoned. Wash and be clean.

div.p: Believers follow the Savior's instructions without neglecting them, changing them or adding to them.
Thus they are cleansed of guilt.
Those who reject his way remain in the leprosy of sin.

div.title: Elisha refuses Naaman's gifts (verses 15–19)
div.p: Naaman was more deeply affected by the mercy of his cure than by the mere miracle.
People who experience divine grace themselves are best equipped to speak about its power.
Naaman expressed gratitude to Elisha.
The prophet refused payment.
He did not do so because receiving gifts was always unlawful; he had accepted them on other occasions.
Instead, he wanted this new convert to understand that the servants of Israel's God regarded worldly wealth as unimportant.
The entire work came from God.
The prophet would not give directions beyond what the Lord had authorized him to say.
We should not always oppose every smaller mistake immediately when someone first comes under conviction of divine truth.
People cannot be moved forward faster than the Lord prepares them to receive instruction.
Nevertheless, anyone entering a covenant relationship with God while knowingly reserving a favorite sin breaks that covenant.
People who truly hate evil will make an effort to avoid even its appearance.

div.title: Gehazi's greed and lies (verses 20–27)
div.p: Naaman was a Syrian court official and soldier, with many servants.
Those servants acted wisely and kindly.
Elisha, a holy prophet, had only one servant, and he turned out to be a dishonest liar.
Love of money, the root of every kind of evil, lay beneath Gehazi's wrongdoing.
He imagined he could deceive Elisha.
But he discovered that the Spirit of prophecy could not be deceived.
Lying in this situation was an attempt to lie to the Holy Spirit.
It is foolish to commit a sin with the hope that nobody will discover it.
When we stray into a hidden path, our conscience still accompanies us.
God's eye follows us too.
Those who cover wrongdoing will not prosper.
A lie lasts only briefly.
All the schemes of people devoted to the world lie open before God.
There are times when seeking more wealth is altogether wrong—particularly when it would dishonor God or religion or injure other people.
Gehazi was punished.
If he insisted on receiving Naaman's money, he would receive Naaman's disease along with it.
What had Gehazi gained by receiving two talents, if he lost his health, reputation, peace and service—and, unless he repented, his soul forever?
Let us beware of hypocrisy and greed and fear the lasting spiritual leprosy of sin.

row.cell: The sons of the prophets enlarge their habitations, Iron made to swim.
Elisha discloses the counsels of the Syrians.
Samaria besieged, A famine, The king sends to slay Elisha.

div.title: The prophets build more living space; the iron ax head floats (verses 1–7)
div.p: Fellowship with God's servants has a sweetness that can make people forget the tiredness and pain of physical labor.
But even the sons of the prophets needed to work.
No one should think that honest employment is shameful or a burden beneath them.
Work done with the mind can be as difficult as work done with the hands—and often more demanding.
We ought to be as careful with borrowed possessions as with our own, doing to others what we would want them to do to us.
The man who lost the borrowed ax head cared about this obligation.
For a person with an honest conscience, the hardest part of poverty may not be hunger or damaged reputation, but the inability to pay just debts.
The Lord attends to even the smallest concerns of his people.
His grace can also raise up a heart as heavy and hard as iron, sunk into the mud of earthly concerns, and lift affections that naturally cling to the ground.

div.title: Elisha reveals Syria's plans (verses 8–12)
div.p: Israel's king paid attention to Elisha's warnings of danger from the Syrians.
Yet he ignored the prophet's warnings concerning the danger of his sins.
Most people behave similarly.
They are eager to save their lives from death but show little concern about saving their souls from judgment.
Nothing anyone does, says or thinks—at any time or place—is hidden from God's knowledge.

div.title: Elisha and the Syrian army (verses 13–23)
div.p: Elisha's words to his servant also comfort all God's faithful servants when there are conflicts outside and fears within.
Do not fear with the kind of fear that brings torment and confusion.

p.hi: Those who are with us to protect us are more numerous than those seeking to destroy us.

div.p: Elisha's servant's physical eyes were open, and they could see the danger.
Lord, open the eyes of our faith to see your protecting hand!
The more clearly we recognize heaven's authority and power, the less we fear earthly troubles.
Satan, the god of this world, blinds people's eyes and thereby leads them toward ruin.
But when God opens their eyes, they recognize that they are surrounded by enemies, enslaved to Satan and exposed to judgment—even if they once believed themselves secure.
When Elisha had the Syrian soldiers in his power, he demonstrated divine goodness as well as divine power.
Let us not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
The Syrians realized it was useless to continue attacking such a godly and good man.

div.title: Samaria is besieged and suffers famine (verses 24–33)
div.p: Hardship should make us value ordinary abundance and give thanks for it.
In famine, money becomes almost worthless when people will surrender it gladly for anything edible.
King Jehoram's words to the woman may have expressed despair.
The events fulfilled God's earlier warnings about the consequences of Israel's sin.
Among those warnings was the horrific possibility that people would eat their own children (Deuteronomy 28:53–57).
The episode showed both the truth and the dreadful justice of God's word.
What terrible misery human sin has brought upon the world!
Yet a person's foolishness ruins the path, and the heart then turns in anger against God.
The king threatened to kill Elisha.
Wicked people blame almost anyone for their troubles rather than admit their own wrongdoing or give it up.
Tearing clothing is no substitute for a broken and repentant heart.
Wearing sackcloth is useless without being renewed inwardly.
If external signs were sufficient, sinners would not remain stubbornly opposed to the Lord.
May the whole word of God grow in us a reverent fear and a holy hope.
May we remain firm and immovable, always abounding in God's work, knowing that labor done for the Lord is never wasted.

row.cell: The flight of the Syrian army.

div.title: Elisha promises abundant food (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Human desperation gives God an opportunity to display his glory through saving power.
He often comes to his people's aid when their own strength is exhausted.
Unbelief greatly dishonors and displeases God.
It also deprives people of the blessings he intended for them.
Those who refuse to believe the promise of eternal life may see its fulfillment at a distance, but never enjoy it.
Yet even temporal deliverance and mercies will do sinners no lasting good unless the Lord's kindness leads them to repentance.

div.title: The Syrian army flees (verses 3–11)
div.p: God can make the strongest heart tremble whenever he chooses.
If people refuse to fear him, he can make them afraid even at the shaking of a leaf.
Through Providence, the men with leprosy arrived after the Syrians had fled.
Their consciences warned them that it would be wrong to keep the discovery to themselves.
Ordinary human sympathy and fear of punishment restrain selfishness even in those without saving faith.
Such feelings help preserve order and kindness in society.
But those who have discovered the unsearchable riches of Jesus Christ possess a still greater reason to share good news promptly with others.
They do so from love for Christ, not merely from fear or self-interest.
That same love should move them to share earthly provisions generously with brothers and sisters in need.

div.title: Samaria receives food (verses 12–20)
div.p: God supplied Israel in a way no one expected.
This encourages us to trust his power and goodness in our deepest difficulties.
We can rely upon God's promises, because not one of his words will fail.
The nobleman who had doubted Elisha saw the restored abundance.
That sight exposed the foolishness of his unbelief and silenced his doubts.
But he did not eat the food he saw.
People who expect God's promises to fail may rightly discover that the promises of the world disappoint them instead.
Let this chapter teach us how seriously the Lord regards distrust of his power, providence and word.
Earthly life and enjoyment are uncertain.
God's warnings of judgment are certain and will come upon those who remain guilty.
May the Lord help us discover whether we are exposed to his warnings or have an interest in his promises.

row.cell: A famine in Israel, The Shunammite obtains her land.
Elisha consulted by Hazael, Death of Benhadad.

div.title: The Shunammite receives her land back (verses 1–6)
div.p: God rewarded the kindness the Shunammite woman had shown Elisha by caring for her during famine.
It is wise to recognize coming danger and, when we can do so lawfully, seek a place of safety.
After the famine she returned from the Philistines' territory.
That was not an appropriate place for an Israelite to remain longer than necessity required.
She had once been so securely established among her own people that she needed no one to speak for her to the king.
But life is uncertain.
People and things we depend on may fail, while unexpected people become our helpers.
Sometimes seemingly small events have large consequences.
The king had just been listening to Gehazi recount Elisha's works.
The woman's appearance confirmed what he had heard and helped persuade him to grant her request.
God thereby provided for someone whose life had already benefited from his miraculous care.

div.title: Elisha speaks with Hazael; Ben-hadad dies (verses 7–15)
div.p: Affliction often changes people's feelings about God's ministers.
Those who once hated or despised them may come to value their advice and prayers.
Elisha did not learn Hazael's future crimes by studying his face.
God revealed them to him, bringing tears to his eyes.
Knowing more about what lies ahead can increase sorrow.
A person may honestly recoil from an evil act while natural conscience still restrains him, then later become reconciled to that very act.
People occupying low positions seldom understand how strong the temptations of power and prosperity can become.
If they later gain authority, they may discover that their own hearts are far more deceitful and wicked than they imagined.
Satan ruins people by assuring them they will recover and prosper, lulling them into false security.
Hazael's false report harmed the king, depriving him of the warning he needed to prepare for death.
It also injured Elisha's reputation, because it made the prophet appear dishonest.

p.hi: Henry does not claim certainty that Hazael murdered Ben-hadad.

div.p: He says it is possible Hazael caused his death without deliberately intending to do so.
Hazael certainly behaved deceptively and later persecuted Israel.

div.title: Jehoram's wicked reign in Judah (verses 16–24)
div.p: Scripture gives an overall account of Jehoram's wickedness.
His father had undoubtedly taught him true knowledge of the Lord.
But his father acted unwisely in arranging his marriage into Ahab's family.
No spiritual good could come from union with a household so devoted to idolatry.

div.title: Ahaziah's wicked reign in Judah (verses 25–29)
div.p: Names do not determine a person's character.
Still, it was a bad sign for Jehoshaphat's family to borrow names from the house of Ahab.
Ahaziah's connection to that family helped bring about both his wrongdoing and his destruction.
Anyone choosing a spouse should remember that they may also be choosing the future parent of their children.
God's providence arranged for Ahaziah to be destroyed with Ahab's house when the measure of their sin was full.
People who willingly share in another's wrongdoing should expect to share the consequences.
May the changes, trouble and wickedness we witness in the world make us increasingly eager to receive salvation through Jesus Christ.

row.cell: Joram and Ahaziah slain by Jehu.

div.title: Elisha sends a messenger to anoint Jehu (verses 1–10)
div.p: In this and similar events, we should acknowledge the hidden work of God, who moves people to accomplish his purposes concerning them.
God specially chose Jehu to be Israel's king.
Even then the Lord had a remnant of faithful people, and he intended to preserve his worship among them.
Jehu was reminded of this when he received his commission.
He was commanded to destroy Ahab's house.
To the extent that he acted in obedience to God and from right motives, he need not be discouraged by criticism or opposition.
The killing of God's prophets received special attention in the judgment announced.
Jezebel persisted in idolatry and hatred toward Jehovah and his servants until her wrongdoing reached its full measure.

div.title: Jehu and the officers (verses 11–15)
div.p: People who faithfully bring God's message to sinners have often been dismissed as mad.
Their judgment, language and conduct differ from those of other people.
They are willing to suffer for aims and purposes that worldly people cannot understand.
The accusation is especially often made by the ungodly, who are themselves truly irrational.
By contrast, faithful servants of God demonstrate that their beliefs and actions are wise and reasonable.
Some confidence in God's word seems to have strengthened Jehu for the undertaking before him.

div.title: Jehu kills Joram and Ahaziah (verses 16–29)
div.p: Jehu possessed an intensely energetic temperament.
God's wisdom is seen in the different characters of the people he employs.
Yet being known for fury is no honor to anyone.
A person who rules his own spirit is greater than a mighty warrior.
Joram met Jehu on the land belonging to Naboth.
God sometimes arranges circumstances so that a punishment corresponds strikingly to the crime, as one face reflects another in a mirror.
The path of sin can never become a path of peace (Isaiah 57:21).
What real peace can sinners have with God while they persist in sin?
But when sins are repented of and abandoned, peace is possible.
Joram died under the sentence of divine law.
Ahaziah had bound himself to Ahab's family and become one of them through wrongdoing.
Association with evildoers is dangerous because it entangles us in their guilt and suffering.

div.title: Jezebel dies (verses 30–37)
div.p: Jezebel did not hide or show fear of God's judgment.
Instead, she continued defiantly to mock the very danger facing her.
A heart hardened against God may resist him boldly to the very end.
Nothing more surely predicts destruction than a heart still proud and unrepentant under circumstances meant to humble it.
Anyone who tempts other people into wickedness or leads them away from truth and righteousness should consider Jezebel's behavior and death.
Jehu called for assistance, and her attendants handed her over.
Thus her life ended.
The destruction of pride and cruelty calls us to acknowledge the Lord's righteousness.
When we indulge bodily desires, remember how perishable the body is.
Soon it will decay, whether beneath the ground or exposed to animals above it.
May we all flee from the divine wrath revealed against human ungodliness and unrighteousness.

row.cell: Ahab's sons and Ahaziah's brethren put to death.
Jehu destroys the worshippers of Baal.

div.title: Ahab's descendants are killed (verses 1–14)
div.p: Even in the most terrible events, including those marked by human crimes, we must acknowledge God's truth and justice.
The Lord never commands anything unjust or unreasonable.
Jehu destroyed the surviving members of Ahab's household who had shared in that family's wickedness.

When we think about the immense amount of human suffering and death, and when we consider the resurrection and final judgment, we may be overwhelmed by the multitude of unrepentant sinners awaiting judgment.
We may ask what ultimately caused all this death and misery.
The answer is sin.
Why then should we welcome sin into our hearts and look for happiness in what has caused so much suffering?

div.title: Jehu destroys Baal worship (verses 15–28)

p.hi: “Is your heart right?”

div.p: This is a question we should often ask ourselves.
We may make an impressive profession of faith and gain a good reputation.
But are our hearts truly right before God?
Are we sincere with him?
Jehonadab supported Jehu in both the acts of judgment and religious reform he undertook.
An upright heart is satisfied with God's approval and seeks nothing more.
If our purpose is to win people's applause, our foundation is wrong.
We cannot be sure whether Jehu himself aimed higher than human recognition.
Under the civil law of ancient Israel, idolatry was subject to death.
For the time being, that worship was removed from Israel.
May we desire equally that idolatry be uprooted from our own hearts.
The recorded civil penalty is part of this ancient history, not a command for present-day religious persecution.

div.title: Jehu continues in Jeroboam's sin (verses 29–36)
div.p: It is right to question whether Jehu acted from a godly principle and whether he made wrong choices even while doing the work of reform.
Nevertheless, God does not leave genuine service rendered to him unrewarded.
True conversion requires turning not only from grossly wicked acts, but from every sin.
It requires abandoning not only false gods, but also false ways of worshiping the true God.
It demands leaving behind not only sins that damage our earthly interests, but also those from which we profit and through which we protect our wealth and standing.
Abandoning profitable sins especially tests our ability to deny ourselves and trust God.
Jehu displayed great zeal for removing false religion.
But he neglected faithful service in true religion.
He did not take care to please God or fulfill his duty.
Where such care is absent, we have reason to fear that saving grace is absent as well.
The people were equally careless.
It is therefore unsurprising that the Lord began to reduce Israel's territory, wealth and strength.
The people had fallen short in their duty toward him, and he caused their nation to fall short in power and prosperity.

row.cell: Athaliah usurps the government of Judah, Jehoash made king.
The worship of the Lord restored.

div.title: Athaliah seizes power; Jehoash becomes king (verses 1–12)
div.p: Athaliah tried to destroy everyone she knew to have a claim to the throne.
But one of the king's sons, Jehoash, was hidden.
God's promise to David now seemed to depend upon a single life, yet it did not fail.
Similarly, according to his promise, the Lord preserves a spiritual family for the Son of David.
His people may sometimes be hidden and unseen, but they are safe under God's protection.
Athaliah ruled tyrannically for six years before the rightful king was brought before the people.
He was only a child, but he had a good guardian—and, better still, the good God to whom he could turn.
We should welcome the reign of Christ within our own hearts with such joy and satisfaction.
Let Satan the usurper be cast out and the true King established upon his throne.
May Jesus live and reign forever in my soul and throughout the world.

div.title: Athaliah is put to death (verses 13–16)
div.p: Athaliah hurried toward her own ruin.
She was herself the greatest traitor, yet she was the first and loudest to cry out, “Treason! Treason!”
Those most deeply guilty are often the quickest to accuse others.

div.title: The worship of the Lord is restored (verses 17–21)
div.p: The king and people would be most faithfully united to one another when both were united to the Lord.
It is good for a nation when political changes help revive and strengthen true religion.
Solemn covenants remind us of duties that already bind us and strengthen our commitment to fulfill them.
The people immediately put an end to idolatry.
In accordance with their covenant, they also expressed their willingness to help one another.
The people rejoiced, and Jerusalem was peaceful.
The path to lasting joy and peace is wholehearted service to God.
Joy and thanksgiving are heard in the homes of the righteous, but there is no peace for the wicked.

row.cell: Jehoash orders the repair of the temple.
He is slain by his servants.

div.title: Jehoash repairs the temple (verses 1–16)
div.p: It is a great kindness to young people, especially to those born into positions of influence, to have advisers who teach them to do what is right in the Lord's sight.
Those who are willing to receive good counsel act wisely.
The temple needed repairs, and Jehoash ordered them to be made.
The king showed zeal for the work.
God expects people with authority to use it in support of true worship, in correcting wrongs and repairing what has fallen into decay.
Jehoash first placed the priests in charge, expecting them to care deeply about the temple.
Yet little effective work was accomplished until the twenty-third year of his reign.
A different arrangement was then adopted.
When public funds are distributed faithfully, people become willing to contribute them generously.
Even while collecting what was needed to repair the temple, the people did not take away the priests' regular support.

p.hi: Those serving in the temple must not be left hungry under the pretext of repairing its walls.

div.p: The people entrusted with the money handled their responsibilities carefully and honestly.
They did not buy ornaments until the necessary repairs were finished.
This teaches us to give priority to essential needs in our spending and to handle public money as carefully as our own.

div.title: Jehoash is killed by his servants (verses 17–21)
div.p: Consider Jehoash's character and the lessons his life offers.
His beginning was so promising, but the conclusion was deeply sorrowful.
It should prompt us to examine any decline in our own spiritual lives.
If we know Christ as the foundation of faith and hope, let us desire above all to know Christ.
May the work of the blessed Spirit be evident in our souls.
May we see and feel our need of Jesus and seek him earnestly in all the fullness and grace suited to us.
In this way our souls will turn away from dead works to serve the living and true God.

row.cell: Jehoash, king of Israel, Elisha dying.
Elisha's death, The victories of Jehoash.

div.title: Jehoahaz rules Israel (verses 1–9)
div.p: In earlier times Israel had been honored as a people devoted to prayer.
In his distress, Jehoahaz appealed to the Lord for help.
He did not seek the help of the golden calves—what help could they offer?
He sought the living God.
Notice how quickly God shows mercy, how ready he is to hear prayer, and how willing to find a reason to act graciously.
Otherwise, he would not have appealed to the ancient covenant that Israel had broken and forfeited so many times.
This should draw us to him and encourage even those who have turned away to repent and return.
With the Lord there is forgiveness, so that he may be feared.
If he answers even a distressed person's request for temporary relief, how much more will he regard a prayer of faith for spiritual blessings!

div.title: Jehoash visits the dying Elisha (verses 10–19)
div.p: King Jehoash came to receive Elisha's last counsel and blessing.
There can be great spiritual benefit in visiting faithful believers during illness or near death.
The comfort they find in God as they die can strengthen our own faith.
Elisha promised the king success.
Yet Jehoash still had to seek God's direction and strength rather than rely entirely on his own hands.
The dying prophet's weak hands, signifying God's power, gave the arrow greater meaning and strength than the king's vigorous hands alone.
By treating the sign lightly, the king lost part of what it represented.
This grieved the dying prophet.
Good people are distressed when others reject blessings they could have received and lose opportunities for victory over spiritual enemies.

div.title: Elisha dies; Jehoash defeats Syria (verses 20–25)
div.p: God has many ways of correcting a people who have offended him.
Trouble may arrive from the direction least expected.
The invasion mentioned after Elisha's death suggests that losing faithful prophets can be a warning of coming judgment.
Elisha's dead body became the means by which another dead man was restored to life.
This miracle confirmed the truth of his prophecies.
It may also point toward Christ, through whose death and burial the grave has become a safe passage to life for every believer.
Jehoash defeated the Syrians as many times as he had struck the ground with the arrows.
Then his victories stopped.
Many people later regret the smallness of their faith and desires when it is too late to regain the blessings they neglected.

row.cell: Amaziah provokes Jehoash king of Israel, and is overcome.

div.title: Amaziah begins well (verses 1–7)
div.p: Amaziah began his reign well but did not continue as he began.
It is not enough merely to repeat the good actions of faithful ancestors because those actions have become customary.
We must act from the same inward faith and devotion, with the same sincerity and determination that led them to do what was right.

div.title: Amaziah challenges Jehoash and loses (verses 8–14)
div.p: Soon after the kingdoms divided, Judah suffered greatly from Israel's hostility.
After Asa's time, Judah suffered still more from friendship and alliances with Israel.
Now hostility returned.
A humble person might almost smile to hear two proud and contemptuous rulers compete in belittling each other.
Unholy success produces pride.
Pride leads to conflict.
And proud people find the pride of others unbearable.
These tendencies cause trouble and sin in private life.
When they govern rulers, however, entire nations suffer.
Jehoash warned Amaziah about the folly of his challenge: “Your heart has made you proud.”
The root of every sin is in the heart.
Outward events, the circumstances Providence brings, or the opportunities we meet do not themselves make people proud, self-confident or discontented.
Such reactions come from the heart.

div.title: Amaziah is killed (verses 15–22)
div.p: Amaziah outlived the king who had defeated him by fifteen years.
He was later killed by his own subjects.
Azariah, also called Uzziah, appears to have been very young when his father died.
Henry understands his regnal years as counted from that event, although he thinks Azariah was not fully established as king until eleven years later.
This is Henry's chronological explanation, not an alteration of the biblical dates.

div.title: Jeroboam II's wicked reign (verses 23–29)
div.p: God raised up the prophet Jonah and through him announced merciful purposes toward Israel.
The continued presence of faithful ministers is a sign that God has not completely abandoned his people.
Henry gives two reasons why God granted Israel victories.
First, the people's suffering was so severe that they became objects of his compassion.
Second, the decree for their destruction had not yet been issued.
Israel had known many prophets.
But, according to Henry, none had left written prophetic books until this period.
Hosea began prophesying during Jeroboam's reign.
Amos was active around the same time; Micah came soon afterward, followed by Isaiah in the days of Ahaz and Hezekiah.
Even during the church's darkest and most corrupt periods, God raises up people who shine brightly.
Through their preaching and example they guide their own generation.
And through the writings of some of them, they continue to give light to later generations.

row.cell: Reign of Azariah, or Uzziah, king of Judah.

div.title: Azariah, also called Uzziah (verses 1–7)
div.p: Uzziah generally did what was right.
It was a blessing for Judah that a good reign lasted a long time.

div.title: Israel's later kings (verses 8–31)
div.p: This history shows how confused and troubled the kingdom of Israel had become.
Judah also suffered difficulties.
Yet compared with Israel, Judah's situation was a happy one.
The weaknesses that remain in genuine believers are very different from the deliberately permitted wickedness of people who do not fear God.
Such is our fallen human nature.
If our hearts were left entirely to themselves, they would prove deceitful above everything else and desperately wicked.
We have good reason to thank the Lord for restraints that have held us back from wrongdoing and for being kept away from temptation.
We should continually ask him to renew a right spirit within us.

div.title: Jotham rules Judah (verses 32–38)
div.p: Jotham showed great respect for the temple.
Rulers may not be able to accomplish everything they wish in restraining vice and irreverence.
When that happens, they should work all the more diligently to support and encourage godliness and moral virtue.

row.cell: Ahaz, king of Judah, His wicked reign.
Ahaz takes a pattern from an idol's altar.

div.title: Ahaz's wicked reign (verses 1–9)
div.p: Ahaz's days were few and filled with evil.
Those whose own consciences condemn them will turn almost anywhere for help in trouble rather than turn to God.
His sin became its own punishment.
It is common for people to try to escape the difficulties created by one sin through committing another.

div.title: Ahaz copies a foreign altar (verses 10–16)
div.p: Until this time God's altar had remained in its appointed place and had been used for worship.
Ahaz replaced it with another.
Human beings have a natural inclination toward some form of religion, and that inclination is not easily extinguished.
But unless it is governed by God's word and Spirit, it can produce foolish superstition or detestable idolatry.
At best, it may quiet a guilty conscience through meaningless ceremonies.
People who reject true faith have often been especially willing to believe ridiculous falsehoods.

div.title: Ahaz damages the temple (verses 17–20)
div.p: Ahaz treated the Sabbath with contempt, opening the way for many other sins.
He did this to please the king of Assyria.
People who once had ready access to the Lord's house but turn away from it to please their neighbors are rapidly moving toward ruin.

row.cell: Reign of Hoshea in Israel, The israelites carried captives by the Assyrians.
The nations placed in the land of Israel.

div.title: Hoshea and Israel's exile (verses 1–6)
div.p: When sin reaches its full measure, the Lord no longer delays judgment.
Samaria's inhabitants must have suffered terribly.
Some poor Israelites remained in the land.
Most of those carried into distant exile were absorbed among the other nations.

div.title: Why Israel was taken captive (verses 7–23)
div.p: The destruction of Israel's northern kingdom is reported briefly, but these verses explain its causes in detail.
The ruin came from the Almighty.
Assyria was only the rod of his anger (Isaiah 10:5).
Those who bring sin into a country or household bring disaster with it and must answer for the suffering that follows.
The world's outward acts of wrongdoing are enormous.
Yet even greater are the hidden sins of the human heart—evil thoughts, desires and intentions.
Some public sins carry obvious disgrace.
But ingratitude toward God, neglect of him, hostility to him, idolatry and the ungodliness arising from them are even more deeply malignant.
No one possesses genuine godliness without turning from every evil path and keeping God's commands.
But such obedience must grow out of faith in God's testimony concerning his anger against all unrighteousness and his mercy in Jesus Christ.

div.title: The peoples settled in Israel (verses 24–41)
div.p: The terror of divine judgment can produce forced or feigned submission in people whose hearts remain unconverted.
This happened among the foreigners brought to settle in Israel.
Such people hold unworthy views of God.
They expect outward religious forms to satisfy him.
They also attempt the impossible task of combining his service with love of the world and indulgence of sinful desires.
May the fear of the Lord, which begins true wisdom, take hold of our hearts and direct our conduct.
Then we will be prepared for whatever change life brings.
Earthly homes and settlements are uncertain.
We do not know where we may be driven before death, and in any case we must soon leave this world.
But the righteous have chosen the good portion that will never be taken away.

row.cell: Good reign of Hezekiah in Judah, Idolatry.

div.title: Hezekiah's good reign and removal of idolatry (verses 1–8)
div.p: Hezekiah was a true son of David.
Other kings had done what was right, but had not followed David's example as closely.
We must not assume that when times and people become bad, matters must inevitably grow worse.
After many evil kings, God raised up someone who resembled David himself.
The bronze serpent had been carefully preserved as a memorial of God's kindness to Israel in the wilderness.
Yet burning incense to it was foolish and wicked.
Attempts to help worship by means not authorized in Scripture interrupt the exercise of faith and lead toward superstition and other serious evils.
Fallen human nature corrupts such practices.
True faith has no need of these artificial aids.
God's word, considered daily and accompanied by prayer, provides all the outward assistance needed.

div.title: Sennacherib attacks Judah (verses 9–16)
div.p: Sennacherib's invasion brought great suffering upon Judah.
Through it, God tested Hezekiah's faith and corrected the people.
Hidden unbelief, hypocrisy and spiritual lukewarmness among many required correction.
For sincere believers, such trials purify faith and hope and lead to simple dependence upon God.

div.title: Rabshakeh speaks against the Lord (verses 17–37)
div.p: Rabshakeh tried to persuade Judah that resistance was pointless.
He asked, “What is this confidence you are trusting?”
How good it would be if sinners applied a similar question to themselves and sought peace with God!
It is wise to submit to the Lord because resistance against him cannot succeed.
What basis for confidence do people have when they stubbornly oppose him?
Rabshakeh's speech was clever and carefully constructed.
Yet it was full of pride, malice, falsehood and blasphemy.
Hezekiah's officers remained silent.
There is a time to remain silent as well as a time to speak.
Some people are so determined to mock what is holy or reject reason that presenting religious truths to them is like throwing pearls before pigs.
Their silence made Rabshakeh even prouder and more confident.
Sometimes the wisest response is to let people continue their insults rather than argue.
A firm expression of abhorrence can be sufficient witness against such behavior.
We must leave the whole matter with the Lord, who holds every heart in his hands, entrusting ourselves to him with humility, hope and earnest prayer.

row.cell: Hezekiah receives an answer of peace.
The Assyrian army destroyed, Sennacherib slain.

div.title: Hezekiah hears a message of reassurance (verses 1–7)
div.p: Hezekiah was deeply troubled by the dishonor Rabshakeh's blasphemy brought upon God.
When we receive God's word through his messengers, we should especially desire that they pray to God for us.
The great Prophet is also our great Intercessor.
People who lift their hearts to the Lord in prayer may expect his help.
Human desperation provides a special occasion for God to show his power.
While the Lord's servants must announce warnings to the irreverent, proud and hypocritical, they also bring words of comfort to discouraged believers.

div.title: Sennacherib's letter and Hezekiah's prayer (verses 8–19)
div.p: Prayer is an unfailing refuge for Christians facing temptation, whether the struggle comes from outward troubles or inward enemies.
At the mercy seat of our all-powerful Friend, we may open our hearts and lay our problems before him, as Hezekiah spread out the letter.
We may appeal confidently to his mercy.
When we recognize that God's glory is involved in our cause, faith receives fresh strength and rejoices that it will not be shaken.
Our strongest reasons for asking God's help are those drawn from his own honor.

div.title: God foretells Sennacherib's defeat (verses 20–34)
div.p: Every movement of Sennacherib was known to God.
The Lord himself promised to defend the city.
Any person or place he has undertaken to protect is secure.
The Assyrian invasion probably prevented Judah's fields from being sown that year.
Henry supposes that the following year was a Sabbath year.
Yet God promised enough food from the land to sustain the people through those two years.
This provision would follow the destruction of Sennacherib's army.
The future harvest therefore served as a sign to strengthen Hezekiah's present faith, assuring him that the promised deliverance would come and that the Lord would continue caring for Judah.
God promised these things not because the people deserved them but for his own glory.
May our hearts be good soil in which his word takes root and bears fruit through our lives.

div.title: The Assyrian army is destroyed (verses 35–37)
div.p: That very night, after God's message reached Hezekiah, the greater part of the Assyrian army was killed.
See how weak even the strongest people are before Almighty God!
Who has hardened himself against the Lord and prospered?
Sennacherib's own sons later murdered him.
Parents who suffer from disobedient children should ask whether they themselves have disobeyed their Father in heaven.
This history powerfully confirms the value of steadfast trust in God.
He may afflict his people, but he will not abandon them.
It is good when troubles drive us to prayer.
Yet our dependence on emergencies may also expose our unbelief.
How reluctant we are to rest entirely on God's promises!
How eagerly we want to know how he will save us!
How impatient we become when relief is delayed!
We must wait for his word to be fulfilled.
Lord, help our unbelief!

row.cell: Hezekiah's sickness, His recovery in answer to prayer.
Hezekiah shows his treasures to the ambassadors from Babylon, His death.

div.title: Hezekiah becomes ill and recovers (verses 1–11)
div.p: Hezekiah became gravely ill, close to death, in the same year that the king of Assyria besieged Jerusalem.
Isaiah brought him a warning to prepare for death.
Prayer is one of the best ways to prepare for death.
Through prayer we receive grace and strength from God to finish life well.
Hezekiah wept bitterly.
Some understand this as an unwillingness to die, and it is natural for human beings to dread the separation of body and soul.
But Hezekiah's circumstances were special.
He was in the midst of useful service.
His prayer, recorded also in Isaiah 38, helps us understand his tears.
Nothing in it suggests that he was tormented by the enslaving fear of death.
His devotion to God made his sickbed easier to bear.
He prayed, “Lord, remember me.”
He did not imply that God needed reminding, or that he could demand a reward as something owed to him.
Only Christ's righteousness has purchased mercy and grace.
Hezekiah did not simply pray, “Spare my life.”
He prayed that God would remember him.
Whether he lived or died, he wanted to belong to the Lord.
God always hears the prayers of the brokenhearted.
He grants health, longer life and earthly deliverance for as long as those gifts are truly good for his people.
Hezekiah was instructed to use means of recovery.
Yet his disease was so advanced, and the change so sudden, that his healing was miraculous.
When ill, we should use appropriate treatments that support the body's natural healing.
Refusing such help does not display faith in God; it tests him.
To confirm Hezekiah's faith, God caused the sun's shadow to move backward, miraculously lengthening the period of light.
The sign showed the Lord's power in heaven as well as on earth, his attention to prayer and his kindness toward those he has chosen.

div.title: Hezekiah displays his wealth (verses 12–21)
div.p: At that time the king of Babylon was independent of Assyria, though he would soon be conquered by it.
Hezekiah proudly showed the visitors his treasures, weapons and other evidence of wealth and power.
This revealed pride, love of display and a departure from simple trust in God.
It also seems he missed an opportunity to tell the Babylonian visitors about the Lord who had performed the miracles that interested them and to explain why idolatry was foolish and wrong.
Showing visitors our homes and possessions is not wrong in itself.
But when we display them because we want praise for ourselves while withholding glory from God, it becomes sin, as it did for Hezekiah.
We may expect trouble from anything in which we take excessive pride.
Isaiah had often comforted Hezekiah.
Now he came to correct him.
The blessed Spirit is likewise both Comforter and Reprover (John 16:7–8).
Ministers must fulfill both roles when needed.
Hezekiah acknowledged the justice of God's sentence and his goodness in delaying it.
Yet the announcement of what would happen to his family and nation must have been painful.
Hezekiah had truly been humbled for his pride.
Blessed are those who die in the Lord: they rest from their work, and their deeds follow them.

row.cell: Wicked reign and death of Amon.

div.title: Manasseh's evil reign (verses 1–9)
div.p: Young people often long to be independent and to possess wealth and power before they have acquired good judgment.
But early independence can destroy their future comfort and harm others.
It is often far better for young people to remain under the care of parents or guardians until growing experience and wisdom prepare them to make decisions.
Even if they receive fewer immediate indulgences, they may later be thankful for the protection.
Manasseh committed enormous wickedness before the Lord, almost as though he wanted to provoke divine anger.
He became more wicked than the nations the Lord had previously driven out.
He progressed from evil to worse until he was carried captive to Babylon.
The people readily complied with Manasseh's desires.
Some wanted his favor; others found his commands suited their own corrupt inclinations.
When a great community undergoes reform, many people are merely following the advantage of the moment.
Such people fall away quickly under temptation.
