div.title: God's judgment is announced against Judah (verses 10–18)
div.p: This passage announces what will happen to Judah and Jerusalem.
The image describes the city being emptied and left desolate, yet not finally destroyed.
It would be cleaned out and preserved for the Jews to inhabit again later.
Judah would be abandoned for a time, but not forever.
Its outward privileges would be lost, yet individual believers would be preserved even during judgment.
The Lord may reject a community that professes his name while dishonoring him through wrongdoing.
He will never abandon his cause on earth.
The book of Chronicles records Manasseh's repentance and God's acceptance of him.
That should keep us from despairing even over the recovery of very great sinners.
But no one should continue deliberately in sin, assuming repentance and reform can be postponed until a convenient time.
Scripture gives some striking examples of the conversion of notorious sinners so no one will despair.
Yet they are few so no one will presume.

div.title: Amon's evil reign and death (verses 19–26)
div.p: Amon polluted God's house with idols.
God then permitted his own house to be stained with his blood.
Those who killed him acted wickedly, yet God was righteous in allowing it.
Judah now experienced a remarkable change: from one of its worst kings to one of its best.
Once more the nation was given an opportunity for reform.
Whether the Lord patiently delays judgment on stubborn sinners or ends their lives quickly, all who continue refusing his ways face destruction.

row.cell: Josiah's good reign, His care for repairing the temple, The book of the law found.

div.title: Josiah repairs the temple; the book of the law is found (verses 1–10)
div.p: Josiah became king at a young age, as Manasseh had done, yet their lives developed very differently.
This must be attributed to the distinguishing grace of God.
Those who raised Josiah probably also helped shape that difference.
His character was excellent.
If the people had joined his reforms as sincerely as he continued them, wonderful blessings could have followed.
But the people had become deeply corrupt and foolish through idolatry.
To understand Judah's true spiritual condition, we should read not only its historical records but also the writings of prophets who lived at the time.
While the temple was being repaired, the book of the law was discovered and taken to the king.
It appears to have been missing for a long time.
Perhaps it had been carelessly set aside, as some people leave their Bibles neglected in corners.
Or perhaps some idolaters had deliberately concealed it.
God's providential care of Scripture shows how precious it is to him.
Whether or not this was the only surviving copy, the truths it contained seemed new to both king and high priest.
No collection of summaries, extracts or lessons can preserve knowledge of God and his will as reliably as Scripture itself.
We should not be surprised that the people became so corrupt when the law had become scarce.
Those who led them astray probably tried to keep the book away from them.
Possessing many Bibles makes the sin of neglecting Scripture even more serious.
What greater contempt can we show for God than refusing to read his word—or reading it without believing and obeying it?
The holy law teaches us to recognize sin.
The blessed gospel reveals salvation.
When sinners discover the strictness and excellence of God's commands, they begin to ask, “What must I do to be saved?”
The ministers of the gospel point them to Jesus Christ, the fulfillment and goal of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

div.title: Josiah consults the prophetess Huldah (verses 11–20)
div.p: The law was read before the king.
Those who honor their Bibles most deeply are the people who study them, feed on them daily and let their light direct their steps.
Awareness of sin and divine judgment should lead us to ask how we may be saved, what to expect and how to prepare.
People who truly recognize the seriousness of God's anger cannot remain indifferent to the question of salvation.
Huldah told Josiah what judgments were coming upon Judah and Jerusalem.
Most of the people remained hardened and unrepentant.
But Josiah's heart was tender.
He humbled himself before the Lord.
Those who fear God's judgment most sincerely are less likely to experience its final condemnation.
Although Josiah would be mortally wounded in battle, Henry says he died at peace with God and entered glory.
Whatever suffering faithful people must endure or witness, they will be gathered to the grave in peace and enter the rest God has prepared for his people.

row.cell: Josiah reads the law, and renews the covenant.
The reformation extended to Israel, A passover kept.
Wicked reigns of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim.

div.title: Josiah reads the law and renews the covenant (verses 1–3)
div.p: God had told Josiah that Jerusalem's destruction could not now be prevented and that he would escape the coming disaster personally.
Nevertheless, Josiah carried out his duty and left the results with the Lord.
He solemnly called the people to abandon idolatry and serve God with genuine righteousness and holiness.
Most probably followed only outward forms or acted hypocritically.
Yet the reform would still prevent much public wickedness.
Each person remained accountable before God for personal conduct.

div.title: Josiah destroys idols (verses 4–14)
div.p: What extraordinary wickedness was found in Judah and Jerusalem!
It scarcely seems possible that such practices could flourish where God was known and where his name was honored—in Salem and Zion, where his dwelling place stood.
Josiah had already reigned eighteen years.
He had personally set an excellent example and upheld religion according to God's law.
Yet when he investigated idolatry, he discovered that it reached very deeply and widely.
Both ordinary history and Scripture teach that all genuine godliness and goodness found on earth come through the recreating Spirit of Jesus Christ.

div.title: Reform reaches Israel; the Passover is celebrated (verses 15–24)
div.p: Josiah extended his reform to the cities of Israel he could reach.
He preserved the grave of the man of God from Judah who had foretold the destruction of Jeroboam's altar.
After the land had been cleansed of the old leaven of idolatry, the people returned to celebrating the feast.
No Passover like this had been held during the previous reigns.
The revival of a neglected ordinance brought holy joy.
God rewarded their zeal in removing idolatry with unusual signs of his presence and favor.
We have reason to think true religion flourished through the rest of Josiah's reign.

div.title: Josiah is killed by Pharaoh Neco (verses 25–30)
div.p: Reading these events, we must confess that although God's righteousness is as clear and solid as great mountains, his judgments are deep and beyond our understanding.
The reforming king died while he was still useful.
This was a mercy to Josiah because it spared him from seeing the approaching disaster.
But it was a judgment on his people, since his death opened the way for the nation's devastation.

div.title: Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim rule wickedly (verses 31–37)
div.p: After Josiah's burial, one disaster followed another.
Within twenty-two years, Jerusalem was destroyed.
Many wicked people perished.
The remaining people were purified.
Josiah's reform had helped raise up others who joined the small number of faithful people, preserving the precious seed of the future church and nation.
Sometimes a short period and people with limited abilities are enough to undo the good for which faithful servants labored over many years.
But, blessed be God, the good work he begins through his regenerating Spirit cannot be undone.
That work withstands every change and temptation.

div.title: Jehoiakim comes under Nebuchadnezzar's rule (verses 1–7)
div.p: If Jehoiakim had served the Lord, he would not have had to serve Nebuchadnezzar in this way.
Had he accepted his position as a subject and kept his word, his situation need not have become worse.
But he rebelled against Babylon and brought still more suffering upon himself.
Consider how important it is for nations to mourn and turn from the sins of earlier generations, lest they suffer the consequences.
The Lord's warnings will be fulfilled just as surely as his promises unless sinners turn from their wrongdoing through repentance.

div.title: Jehoiachin is taken captive (verses 8–20)
div.p: Jehoiachin reigned only three months.
Yet this was enough time to show that he walked in the sins of his predecessors and brought upon himself the consequences of their wrongdoing.
His uncle was appointed to govern.
Zedekiah was the final king of Judah.
The judgments that had fallen on the previous three kings should have warned him.
Instead he continued doing evil as they had done.
When people entrusted with the decisions of a nation act foolishly and against the nation's real interests, we should recognize in that conduct the warning of God's displeasure.
Because of a people's sins, the Lord may hide from them the things that would bring public peace.
To fulfill the hidden purposes of his justice, he need only leave people to the blindness of their minds or the desires of their own hearts.
The gradual approach of God's judgments offers sinners time to repent.
It also gives believers time to prepare for coming trouble.
At the same time, it exposes the stubbornness of those who refuse to abandon their sins.

row.cell: The temple burnt, The people carried into captivity.
The rest of the Jews flee into Egypt, Evil-merodach relieves the captivity of Jehoiachin.

div.title: Jerusalem falls and Zedekiah is captured (verses 1–7)
div.p: Jerusalem was so strongly defended that its attackers could not capture it until famine weakened the people inside and made resistance impossible.
Jeremiah's prophecy and Lamentations describe these events more fully.
Here it is enough to note how terrible the people's wickedness and suffering had become.
Eventually the city was stormed.
The king, his household and leading officials escaped at night through secret passages.
But those who think they can escape God's judgments deceive themselves just as surely as those who imagine they can resist them.
Zedekiah's fate fulfilled two prophecies that initially appeared contradictory.
Jeremiah said he would be taken to Babylon (Jeremiah 32:5; 34:3).
Ezekiel said he would not see Babylon (Ezekiel 12:13).
Both statements came true.
Zedekiah was taken to Babylon, but his eyes had been put out, so he never saw it.

div.title: The temple is burned and the people exiled (verses 8–21)
div.p: Jerusalem and its temple were burned.
Henry considers it probable that the ark was destroyed in the fire.
This showed how little God values the outward splendor of worship when its living power and reality are neglected.
Jerusalem's walls were demolished.
Its people were carried into captivity in Babylon, and the temple's vessels were taken away.
When the people had rejected the realities the sacred symbols represented, why should the symbols remain?
It was just for God to remove the blessings of true worship from people who had preferred false forms of worship.
Those who had insisted on having many altars would now have none.
God did not spare angels who sinned.
He has appointed death for fallen humanity and judgment for those who refuse to believe.
Nor did he spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all.
Therefore we should not be astonished that he brings serious judgments upon guilty nations, churches or individuals.

div.title: Gedaliah is killed; Jehoiachin receives relief (verses 22–30)
div.p: The king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah as governor and protector of the Jews who remained in the country.
But the people did not recognize the opportunity for peace given to them.
Ishmael treacherously killed Gedaliah and his associates.
The surviving Jews then went to Egypt against Jeremiah's counsel.
Through their folly and disobedience they brought further ruin upon themselves (Jeremiah 40–45).
After thirty-seven years in prison, Jehoiachin was released.
No one should say that good can never return merely because suffering has continued for a long time.
Even people in extreme distress cannot know what change God's providence may yet bring to their circumstances, or what comfort may await them after years of affliction.
Even in this life, the Savior gives freedom from bondage to the distressed sinner who seeks him, granting a foretaste of the pleasures at his right hand forever.

p.hi: Sin alone can truly harm us; Jesus alone can truly do good to sinners.

div.title: 1 Chronicles — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: The two books of Chronicles repeat much of the history found in Samuel and Kings.
Yet they also contain excellent and useful details that are recorded nowhere else.
The first book traces the Jewish people from Adam and then recounts the reign of David.
The second book continues the history of Judah's kingdom through its progress and decline, and also records the return of the Jews from Babylonian captivity.
Jerome said that people who think they understand the Scriptures without knowing Chronicles deceive themselves.
These books preserve events passed over in other accounts, genealogical names and connections between passages.
They also help explain many questions concerning the gospel.

div.title: Genealogies from Adam to Abraham (verses 1–27)
div.p: This chapter and many that follow bring together genealogies—lists of parents and descendants—already found elsewhere in Scripture, while adding other details.
When we compare these lists with other passages, we may notice differences.
But those differences should not cause us to lose confidence in God's word.
We should instead thank him that the truths necessary for salvation are sufficiently clear.
This record traces the Jewish nation's ancestry to the first man created by God.
That makes it different from the obscure, legendary or absurd claims about national origins that have circulated elsewhere.
People of different nations have since become so mixed with one another that no present-day nation—or even most of its population—can be said to descend exclusively from a single ancient line.
One thing remains certain: God made all nations from one blood.
We are all descended from one Adam and one Noah.
Do we not all have one Father?
Has not one God created us? (Malachi 2:10)

div.title: Abraham's descendants (verses 28–54)
div.p: From this point onward, the genealogy concentrates on Abraham's descendants.
As we read so many names, we should think about the multitudes who have lived on earth, played their part in its history and then departed.
One generation passes, including generations of sinful people, and another comes after it (Ecclesiastes 1:4; Numbers 32:14).
This succession will continue as long as the earth remains.
Our own passage through time into eternity is very short.
May we be distinguished as people who truly belong to the Lord.

p.hi: Genealogies.

div.title: The families of Israel
div.p: We now come to the register of the children of Israel, the people set apart from the nations, who were to dwell as a distinct people and not be counted among other nations.
But in Jesus Christ, everyone who comes to him is welcome to his salvation.
All have equal privileges through faith in him, love for him and wholehearted devotion to him.
Everything truly valuable lies in God's favor, peace and likeness, and in a life dedicated to his glory by seeking the well-being of other people.

p.hi: Genealogies.

div.title: David's descendants
div.p: Among all Israel's families, none was more distinguished than David's family.
This chapter gives a full account of that line.
Jesus Christ, as to his human ancestry, came from David's family.
Attentive readers will also notice how many advantages the children of the righteous enjoy.

p.hi: Genealogies.

div.title: Judah, Simeon, and the prayer of Jabez
div.p: This chapter gives additional family records for Judah, the largest and most famous of Israel's tribes, and also for Simeon.
The most remarkable person mentioned is Jabez.
Scripture does not tell us why he was more honorable than his brothers.
But it does show that he was a man of prayer.
True greatness comes through desiring to do God's will and praying earnestly.
Jabez prayed to the living and true God, the only One who can hear and answer.
In approaching God he recognized the Lord as the One who had made a covenant with his people.
Jabez did not state a promise of his own.
He left his commitment understood, unwilling to make assurances in his own strength, while sincerely desiring to dedicate himself entirely to God.
The attitude of his prayer can be expressed like this:

p.hi: Lord, if you bless and preserve me, you may do whatever you will with me. I will remain at your command and disposal forever.

div.p: His prayer expressed a deep and affectionate longing for God's blessing.
It contained four requests.
First, that God would truly bless him. Spiritual blessings are best, because God's blessings are real and bring real results.
Second, that God would enlarge his territory. We should desire that the Lord enlarge our hearts, and thus increase our share in him and in the heavenly Canaan.
Third, that God's hand would be with him. God's hand guiding, protecting, strengthening and working in us and for us is entirely sufficient for all our needs.

Fourth, that God would protect him from evil. This includes the evil of sin, painful troubles and the harmful plans of enemies, so that such things would not injure him or make him truly a Jabez—a man of sorrow.
God granted what Jabez asked.
The Lord remains ready to hear prayer.
His ear is not too heavy to hear us now.

p.hi: Genealogies.

div.title: The tribes east of the Jordan
div.p: This chapter gives an account of the two and a half tribes that settled on the east side of the Jordan.
They were later taken captive by the king of Assyria because they had abandoned the Lord.
Only two events are highlighted in Henry's summary of their history.

p.hi: First, they shared a victory.

div.p: Happy are people who live in harmony and help one another resist the common enemies of their souls, trusting the Lord and calling on him together.

p.hi: Second, they shared captivity.

div.p: They had sought the best land, without considering that its position made it especially exposed to enemy attack.
Strong desires for earthly possessions can draw us away from God's appointed means of worship and prepare us for destruction.

p.hi: Genealogies.

div.title: Levi's descendants
div.p: This chapter records the descendants of Levi.
More than any other Israelites, the priests and Levites needed to preserve and be able to prove their ancestry clearly.
The honors and privileges of their priestly service depended on that descent.
Under the gospel, however, the Spirit of God calls ministers to service without limiting them to any particular family.
At the same time, both then and now, ministers and believers may be very useful to the church, but only our great High Priest, Jesus Christ, can make atonement for sin.
No one can be accepted by God except through Christ's atoning sacrifice.

p.hi: Genealogies.

div.title: The missing records of Zebulun and Dan
div.p: This chapter contains no genealogical account of either Zebulun or Dan.
We cannot explain why only these tribes were omitted.
Yet it is a disgrace connected with Dan that idolatry began among its settlers in Laish, the city they renamed Dan (Judges 18).
Later, Jeroboam established one of his golden calves there.
Henry also notes that Dan is omitted from the tribal list in Revelation 7.
People become detestable when they abandon the worship of the true God in order to worship some created thing.

p.hi: Genealogies.

div.title: Benjamin's family record
div.p: This chapter gives a longer genealogical account of the tribe of Benjamin.
Many details that now seem difficult, sudden or confusing probably made good sense to the original readers and fully served the purpose for which these records were written.
At that time, many great and powerful nations existed and many distinguished people were famous.
Their names have now been completely forgotten.
Yet the names of many ordinary people who belonged to the Israel of God remain permanently recorded here.

p.hi: The memory of the righteous is blessed.
Genealogies.

div.title: The people who returned from Babylon
div.p: One purpose of preserving these genealogies was to guide the Jews returning from captivity.
The records helped them identify which people to join and where to live.
The chapter also describes the good order restored to the work of worship after the return from Babylon.
Everyone knew the duty entrusted to them.
Work is more likely to be done well when people know the responsibilities of their own position and take them seriously.

p.hi: God is a God of order.

div.p: The earthly temple thus pictured the heavenly sanctuary, where worshipers never cease praising God day or night (Revelation 4:8).
Blessed be his name!
In heaven believers will praise him not in rotating shifts, but all together and without interruption, day and night.
May the Lord make each of us fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light.

p.hi: The death of Saul.

div.title: Saul's death and the way opened for David
div.p: A major purpose of Chronicles appears to be preserving the history of David's family.
That is why the writer does not repeat Saul's whole reign.
He records only Saul's death, which opened the way for David to become king.
Henry draws three lessons from Saul's downfall.
First, sinners' wrongdoing will eventually catch up with them, whether sooner or later.
Saul died because of his transgression.
Second, no one's importance or social rank can exempt that person from God's judgments.
Third, disobedience brings death.
Saul died because he did not keep the Lord's word.
May we be delivered from unbelief, impatience and despair.
By waiting for the Lord, we will obtain a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

row.cell: A list of David's mighty men.

div.title: David becomes king over Israel (verses 1–9)
div.p: David came to occupy Israel's throne after reigning for seven years in Hebron over Judah alone.
God's purposes will be fulfilled at last, whatever obstacles stand in the way.
True greatness consists in being genuinely useful and dedicating all our abilities to the Lord.

div.title: David's mighty men (verses 10–47)
div.p: This passage records the distinguished men who served David.
Yet David attributed his success not to the mighty men with him but to the mighty God, whose presence matters more than anything else.
By strengthening David, these men also strengthened themselves and advanced their own interests, because his advancement benefited them.
We likewise gain by doing what we can, in the places God gives us, to support the kingdom of the Son of David.
Those faithful to Christ will find their names recorded with far greater honor than these men's names in the records of earthly fame.

row.cell: Those who came to David at Ziklag.

div.title: Those who joined David at Ziklag (verses 1–22)
div.p: This is an account of people who openly befriended and supported David while he was being persecuted.
Neither difficulty nor danger should keep a sinner from coming to the Savior or drive a believer away from the path of duty.
Those who press through such obstacles and overcome them will receive an abundant reward.
Amasai's words teach us how to express our love and loyalty to the Lord Jesus: we must belong entirely to him and be ready to stand and act on his side.
When the Spirit rules our hearts, we want to belong among Christ's people and declare ourselves on their side.
When faith and love move us to embrace Christ's cause, he receives us, employs us and advances us.

div.title: Those who joined David at Hebron (verses 23–40)
div.p: When Christ's throne is established in a person's soul, there is—or ought to be—great joy.
There is also provision for that soul, not merely for the few days described here but for all of life and throughout eternity.
Happy are those who wisely recognize that submitting to Jesus Christ, the Son of David, is both their duty and their best interest.
They abandon whatever is incompatible with allegiance to him.
Their efforts to do good are guided by the wisdom God gives through his word, experience and observation.
If any of us lacks that wisdom, let us ask God. He gives generously to everyone without reproach, and the wisdom will be given.

div.title: David consults about the ark (verses 1–5)
div.p: David did not ask what magnificent or pleasurable thing he should now do. He asked what godly thing he should do, so that he might enjoy the comfort and benefit of God's sacred oracle.
He wanted the ark brought among the people to be a blessing to them.
Those who honor God also do what truly benefits themselves.
People beginning their lives in the world act wisely when they bring God's ark with them.
Those who begin with reverence for God are well placed to continue enjoying his favor.

div.title: The removal of the ark and Uzza's death (verses 6–14)
div.p: Uzza's sin warns us to avoid presumption, rashness and irreverence when approaching holy things.

p.hi: A good intention never makes a wrong action right.

div.p: His punishment teaches us not to treat God lightly when we approach him.
Yet through Jesus Christ we may come boldly to the throne of grace.
The ark brought death to Uzza; similarly, for some the gospel is an aroma leading from death to death.
But when we welcome the gospel with love for its truth, it becomes an aroma leading from life to life.

p.hi: David's victories.

div.title: David's victories
div.p: This chapter records three things: David's kingdom being established, his family being built up, and his enemies being defeated.
The account repeats events recorded in 2 Samuel 5.
David's reputation and fame point toward the far greater exalted honor of the Son of David, Jesus Christ.

row.cell: Preparations for the removal of the ark.

div.title: Preparing to bring the ark (verses 1–24)
div.p: Even wise and godly people can make mistakes. When they become aware of them, they should correct them.
David did not try to justify what had been done wrongly or blame others.
He acknowledged that he, together with others, had failed to seek God in the proper order.

div.title: The ark is brought to Jerusalem (verses 25–29)
div.p: We should recognize God's providential help even in activities that are naturally within our abilities.
Without his assistance, we could not take a single step.
Whenever we fulfill a religious duty rightly, even to a small degree, we must acknowledge that God helped us. Left to ourselves, we would have made serious errors.
Everything we undertake must be done in dependence on God's mercy through the Redeemer's sacrifice.

row.cell: The solemnity with which the ark was fixed.
Setting in order the worship of God.

div.title: The ark is established (verses 1–6)
div.p: God's word and appointed ordinances may seem clouded or eclipsed for a time, but they will shine again after that obscurity.
The ark was housed only in a tent, a humble dwelling. Yet David spoke of that tabernacle with deep affection throughout his psalms.
God had been gracious to David, and David now showed generosity toward his people.
Those whose hearts have expanded with holy joy should show that joy through openhanded generosity.

div.title: David's psalm of praise (verses 7–36)
div.p: Let our praise bring glory to God, while also teaching and encouraging other people, so that even strangers to him may learn to worship him.
Let us rejoice in the Lord and trust him. People who give glory to God's name may rightly rejoice in that name.
God's everlasting covenant should be the great source of our joy. We should remember it with thanksgiving, as his people did in earlier times.
Day by day, announce his salvation—the salvation promised through Jesus Christ.
We have reason to celebrate it every day because we receive its benefits daily, and the subject can never be exhausted.
Even in the midst of praise, do not forget to pray for God's servants who are suffering.

div.title: Worship is organized (verses 37–43)
div.p: Worshiping God should be part of every day. David established an orderly pattern.
At Jerusalem, where the ark stood, Asaph and his companions ministered continually with songs of praise.
No sacrifices or incense were offered there because the altars were elsewhere.
Yet David's prayers rose like incense, and his raised hands were like the evening sacrifice. Spiritual worship was already taking the place of ceremonial worship in this respect.
Still, God had instituted the ceremonial ordinances, so they must not be neglected.
At Gibeon, where the altars stood, the priests continued offering sacrifices and incense morning and evening, in accordance with Moses' law.
Those ceremonies pictured the mediation of Christ, making their appointed observance important.
The faithful presence of ministers whom God appoints is right in itself and encourages the people.

p.hi: David's purposes; God's gracious promises.

div.title: God's promise to David
div.p: This chapter repeats the account in 2 Samuel 7. The comments on that chapter also apply here.
There is, however, a notable difference in wording: what Samuel calls “for your word's sake” is described here as “for your servant's sake” (verse 19).
Jesus Christ is both the Word of God (Revelation 19:13) and the Servant of God (Isaiah 42:1).
God fulfills his promises to all believers for Christ's sake and because of his mediation. In him, every promise is Yes and Amen.
For his sake the promises are fulfilled and made known. We owe all this greatness to him and look to him for the great things still to come.
These are the unsearchable riches of Christ.
If through faith we recognize their worth, both in themselves and in the Lord Jesus, we cannot help praising them as the only true greatness and speaking honorably of them.
May we seek this blessedness through life's trials, when we feel death approaching, and for the children who come after us.

p.hi: David's victories.

div.title: David's victories
div.p: This chapter repeats the events recorded in 2 Samuel 8.
Our good fight of faith, under the Captain of our salvation, will end in everlasting triumph and peace.
The happiness of Israel through David's victories and his just government was only a faint picture of the happiness awaiting God's redeemed people in heaven.

p.hi: David's wars.

div.title: David's wars
div.p: This chapter repeats the history recorded in 2 Samuel 10.
A sinner's only safety is to submit to the Lord, seek peace with him and become his servant.
We should help one another in a good cause.
But let us be careful: we may be used as instruments of good for others and yet, through unbelief and sin, fail to receive salvation ourselves.

p.hi: David's wars.

div.title: David's wars
div.p: The Lord may severely correct the sins of his believing people, but he will not abandon them to their enemies.
His help will overcome every advantage in numbers and strength held by those who oppose his Israel.
Everyone who trusts in Christ will become more than a conqueror through the One who loves them.

p.hi: David's numbering the people.

div.title: David's census and the place of the temple
div.p: Chronicles does not recount David's sin concerning Uriah or the troubles that followed it; those events were not necessary to the particular subjects being addressed here.
But this book does recount David's sin in numbering the people.
The atonement made for that sin revealed the place where the temple would be built.
God's command that David build an altar was a blessed sign of reconciliation.
The Lord also showed that he accepted David's offerings on that altar.
This points to Christ, who was made sin and a curse for us.
The Lord was pleased to crush him so that through him God might be, not a consuming fire against us, but a God reconciled to us.
It is good to continue attending the ordinances in which we have already experienced signs of God's presence and discovered that he truly is with us.
We can say, “God graciously met me here; therefore I will continue to expect to meet him here.”

div.title: David prepares to build the temple (verses 1–5)
div.p: After the terrible judgment upon Israel for David's sin, God showed him where the temple should be built.
David was therefore moved to make preparations for this great work.
Although David was not to build it himself, he would do everything he could.
Before his death, he made abundant preparations.
Whatever our hands can do for God, our souls and the people around us, let us do with all our strength while life remains. After death there is no more work or planning.
When the Lord does not employ us in the role we hoped for, we should not become discouraged or idle.
We should do all we can, even in a humbler sphere.

div.title: David instructs Solomon (verses 6–16)
div.p: David gave Solomon three reasons for building the temple.
First, God had appointed Solomon. Nothing more strongly encourages service than knowing the Lord has assigned it to us.
Second, Solomon would have the peace and opportunity to complete it. When God gives rest, he expects us to use it for work.
Third, God had promised to establish Solomon's kingdom. God's gracious promises should strengthen and encourage our service.
David explained how much he had already prepared.
He was not boasting; he wanted Solomon to enter the work cheerfully.
Solomon should never imagine that constructing a temple would give him permission to sin.
On the contrary, the work would not be acceptable if he failed to obey God's commands.
In both spiritual service and spiritual conflict, we need courage and determination.

div.title: Others are instructed to help (verses 17–19)
div.p: Anything done to make God's word more widely known and obeyed is like contributing a stone or a bar of gold to the temple's construction.
That should encourage people distressed by seeing so little fruit from their efforts.
Much good may appear after our death that we never expected.
Let us not grow weary of doing good.
The work belongs to the Prince of Peace.
He begins and completes it, and graciously employs us as his instruments.
Therefore, let us rise and work, encouraging and helping one another.
Let us follow his rule and example, depend upon his grace and remain assured that our work in the Lord will not be wasted.

div.title: Solomon's succession and temple service (verses 1–23)
div.p: After giving instructions about the temple's construction, David organized its service and appointed the officers responsible.
When members of the same family work together in God's service, it should encourage them to love and assist one another.

div.title: The Levites' work (verses 24–32)
div.p: The population of Israel had grown, and more workers were needed in the temple.
Every Israelite arriving with an offering should find a Levite ready to help.
When there is more work to do, it is fitting to have more workers.
The great difference between a true Christian and other people is a new heart and a spiritual mind.
A person with such a heart takes great delight in God's commandments and finds refreshment in his appointed worship.
For a spiritual person, every form of service brings satisfaction.
Such a person wants to abound continually in the Lord's work and is happiest serving so good a Master in so pleasant a task.
It does not matter whether the person is called to lead or to serve under someone else's leadership.
May we seek the Lord and serve him sincerely, trusting his word and leaving everything else to his wise disposal.

p.hi: The divisions of the priests and Levites.

div.title: The priests and Levites receive their duties
div.p: When everyone has a place, understands the work assigned to it and carries out that work faithfully, having more people involved is a blessing.
In Christ's mystical body, every member contributes something useful to the good of the whole.
Christ is the High Priest over God's house.
All believers have been made priests, yet they are to submit to him.
In Christ there is no difference in spiritual acceptance between bond and free, or between older and younger.
Younger brothers and sisters, if sincere and faithful, are no less acceptable to Christ than their elders.
May we all be children of the Lord, prepared to sing his praises forever in the heavenly temple.

p.hi: The singers and musicians.

div.title: The musicians appointed to worship
div.p: David organized those appointed to sing and play music in the temple.
Here, to prophesy means to praise God with great earnestness and devout affection under the influence of the Holy Spirit.
Poetry and music were used to awaken these affections.
But unless the Spirit of God brings life and fervor into our worship, even the most carefully ordered services remain lifeless and worthless forms.

p.hi: The offices of the Levites.

div.title: The Levites' duties and the temple treasury
div.p: The temple's gatekeepers and treasurers needed strength and courage. They had to prevent unauthorized entry into the sanctuary and protect its sacred treasures.
Each day the altar consumed considerable supplies: flour, wine, oil, salt and fuel. The lamps also needed provisions.
Stores of these items were kept ready, together with the sacred clothing and utensils.
These were the treasures of God's house.
They pictured the abundance available in our heavenly Father's house, where there is more than enough for all.
From the unsearchable riches of Christ, pictured by those treasuries, our needs are supplied.
Having received from his fullness, we should give him all the glory and use our abilities and possessions according to his will.
The chapter also records officials and judges.
Civil government, like the ministry of God's word, is an ordinance of God for the good of his church and must not be neglected.
The Levites who served directly in the sanctuary, the singers and the gatekeepers were not also assigned this outward administrative work. Each responsibility already required their full attention.
Whatever our position, we need wisdom, courage, strong faith, holy affections and steadfastness in doing our duty.

div.title: David's military organization (verses 1–15)
div.p: In earthly kingdoms, being prepared for war helps preserve peace.
In the same way, nothing encourages Satan's attacks more than spiritual carelessness.
As long as we stand equipped with the whole armor of God, exercising faith and keeping our hearts ready for the struggle, we will certainly be secure and probably also enjoy peace within.

div.title: The rulers and officers (verses 16–34)
div.p: David's officers were responsible for managing the fields, vineyards, herds and flocks that formed the wealth of kings in that part of the world.
The wisdom of rulers is often shown by their choice of ministers and officials.
Ordinary people show wisdom in choosing advisers as well.
Yet with all these counselors around him, David preferred God's word above them all.
“Your testimonies are my delight and my counselors.”

row.cell: David exhorts the people to the fear of the Lord.
He gives instructions for the temple.

div.title: David calls Israel and Solomon to know and serve God (verses 1–10)
div.p: During David's last illness, many of the leading priests and Levites were in Jerusalem.
When he found himself able to speak, David recalled his desire to build the temple, God's refusal of that plan, and the gracious purpose God had for Solomon.
He called them to remain steadfast in their duty and faithfulness to the Lord.
We cannot do our work properly without resolution and strength received from God's grace.
True religion has two distinct parts: knowing God and worshiping God.
David called Solomon to know the God of his father and serve him with a whole heart and willing mind.
God makes himself known through his works and his word.
Only divine revelation fully reveals his character: his providence, holy law, judgment on sinners, blessed gospel and the Spirit's work in all genuine believers.
A person governed only by natural human thinking cannot receive this knowledge.
But through God's revelation, we understand the worth of the Savior's atonement and the Spirit's sanctifying work, which move us to obey his commandments.

The sinner then takes the proper place at the foot of the cross, acknowledging guilt, helplessness and deserved judgment while expecting all necessary gifts from the free mercy and grace of God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Having been forgiven much, the repentant sinner learns to love much.

div.title: David gives Solomon the temple plan (verses 11–21)
div.p: The temple was sacred and pointed toward Christ.
Its form had to be directed by God.
Christ is the true temple, the church is the gospel temple, and heaven is the everlasting temple.
All are established according to God's wise and eternal purpose for his glory and our good.
David gave Solomon the design so that he would follow God's rule.
He also prepared costly materials and utensils.
Then David encouraged Solomon to look to God first for help.
Do not be discouraged: the Lord will help you.
The God who cared for our fathers and enabled them to complete the service entrusted to their generation will not leave us while he still has work to accomplish in us or through us.
Good work prospers when everyone involved sincerely supports it.
Let us hope in God's mercy: if we seek him, he will be found by us.

row.cell: David induces the princes and people to offer willingly.

div.title: David and the people give willingly (verses 1–9)
div.p: Works of devotion and charity should be carried out willingly, not under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
David led by his example.
He gave not because he had to or because he wanted to impress people.
He gave because his heart was devoted to God's house, and he believed he could never do too much to advance the good work.
Those who want to encourage others toward good must take the lead themselves.

div.title: David's prayer of thanksgiving (verses 10–19)
div.p: We can scarcely imagine the grandeur of the temple and its surrounding buildings, made with so much gold and silver.
Yet Christ's unsearchable riches surpass the temple's splendor infinitely more than the temple itself surpassed the humblest cottage.
Instead of boasting about their generous gifts, David gave solemn thanks to the Lord.
Everything they offered for God's temple already belonged to him.
Had they tried to keep it all, death would soon have taken it from them.
The only way to use it for their true advantage was to dedicate it to the service of the One who had given it.

div.title: Solomon is enthroned (verses 20–25)
div.p: The entire assembly joined David in worshiping God.
Whoever leads the congregation in prayer, only those who join sincerely benefit.
It is not primarily a matter of bowing the head but lifting up the soul.
Solomon sat upon the Lord's throne.
His kingdom was a type of the kingdom of the Messiah, whose throne is truly the Lord's.

div.title: David's reign and death (verses 26–30)
div.p: After reading 2 Samuel, we might hardly have expected David to appear so honorable at the end of his life.
Yet his repentance had been as remarkable as his sin.
His patient conduct through suffering and during his final years seems to have had a good effect on the people around him.
Blessed be God: even the greatest sinners may hope for a glorious departure when they repent and flee to the atoning blood of the Savior.
Notice the difference between David, the man after God's own heart, as he lived and died, and false professors who imitate only his sins and use his failures as excuses for their own crimes.
Let us watch and pray, lest temptation overcome us and sin dishonor God and wound our consciences.
When we recognize that we have offended him, may we imitate David's repentance and patience, looking forward to a glorious resurrection through our Lord Jesus Christ.

p.hi: Solomon's choice of wisdom, His strength and wealth.

div.title: Solomon seeks wisdom
div.p: Solomon began his reign by visiting God's altar publicly and reverently.
People who eagerly pursue present and earthly things are likely to be disappointed.
Those who entrust their circumstances to God's providence may not possess the most, but they enjoy the greatest comfort in what they have.
Those who make this world their ultimate goal fail to obtain the next world, and are disappointed with this one as well.
Those who aim instead for the world to come will receive it, with complete satisfaction; meanwhile they will also receive as much of this world's goods as is truly good for them along the way.
Let us therefore be content without the impressive things that people usually covet, since those things often become deadly traps for the soul.

p.hi: Solomon's message to Huram respecting the temple, His treaty with Huram.

div.title: Solomon sends to Huram concerning the temple
div.p: Solomon told Huram about the particular services that would be performed in God's temple.
Unlike the mysteries of pagan superstition, the truths and mysteries of genuine faith do not need to be concealed.
Solomon wanted Huram to form great and exalted thoughts of the God of Israel.
We likewise should not be fearful or ashamed of any opportunity to speak about God and impress others with the importance of his favor and service.
While Israel remained faithful to God's law and worship, neighboring nations were willing to learn true religion from the Israelites.
Earlier, when Israel had turned from the Lord, the people had willingly absorbed the superstition and idolatry of neighboring nations.
A wise and godly king is evidence of God's special love for his people.
How much greater was that love when God gave his only Son to believing people as their Prince and Savior!

p.hi: The building of the temple.

div.title: The temple is constructed
div.p: The building of the temple is described more fully in 1 Kings 6.
It had to be built on the ground David had prepared: not merely land he purchased, but the place he selected by God's direction.
Clear instructions allow us to begin work with confidence and continue it with peace.
Blessed be God, the Scriptures thoroughly equip his people for every good work.
Let us search the Bible daily, praying that the Lord will enable us to understand, believe and obey his word.
Then our path and work will become clear, and everything can be begun, continued and completed in him.
As we contemplate God through Jesus Christ, his true Temple, far more glorious than Solomon's, may we ourselves be formed into a spiritual house, a dwelling place of God through the Spirit.

p.hi: The furniture of the temple.

div.title: The temple's furnishings
div.p: This chapter further describes the furnishings of God's house.
Both outside and inside, the objects pictured gospel grace and pointed toward good things still to come, whose substance is Jesus Christ.
The bronze altar appears here, though the account of its construction was not included in Kings.
Every sacrifice was offered upon it, and it sanctified the gift.
People worshiping in the courts could see the sacrifices burning.
That sight might lead them to consider the great Sacrifice who would come in the fullness of time to take away sin and end death—something the blood of bulls and goats could never accomplish.
As the smoke rose, they could direct their own hearts to heaven in holy longing for God and his favor.
In all our worship, the eye of faith should remain fixed on Christ.
The temple contained more furnishings than the tabernacle had done.
This pictured the future enlargement of God's church and multiplication of worshipers.
Blessed be God, there is enough in Christ for every one of them.

row.cell: The ark placed in the temple.

div.title: The ark is placed in the temple (verses 1–10)
div.p: The ark was a picture of Christ and therefore a sign of God's presence.
Jesus has promised to be with his followers always, even to the end of the world.
When we claim that promise through faith and prayer, its effect is as though the ark itself were brought into our worship gatherings.
We should seek that presence earnestly.
When Christ is formed within a person, God's law is written upon the heart.
The ark of the covenant has, in that sense, been established there.
The soul becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit, and finds genuine satisfaction.

div.title: God's glory fills the temple (verses 11–14)
div.p: God took possession of the building by filling it with a cloud.
This showed that he accepted the temple as he had accepted Moses' tabernacle and assured his people that he would continue to be the same gracious God to them.
If we want God to dwell in our hearts, we must make room for him: everything else must yield.
The Word became flesh.
When he comes to his temple like a refiner's fire, who can endure the day of his coming?
May he prepare us for that day.

p.hi: Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple.

div.title: Solomon prays at the dedication
div.p: Notice the order of Solomon's prayer.
First, and most importantly, he asks for repentance and forgiveness. This is the greatest blessing and the only secure foundation for other acts of mercy.
Only afterward does he pray for temporal benefits.
In this way Solomon teaches us what we should value and seek most earnestly in our prayers.
Jesus Christ teaches the same thing in his perfect pattern of prayer: only one request concerns outward needs, while the others concern spiritual blessings.
The temple pictured the human nature of Christ, in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily.
The ark pictured his obedience and suffering, through which repentant sinners receive access to God reconciled to them and enjoy fellowship with him.
In the person of Emmanuel, Jehovah has made our human nature his permanent dwelling place. Through him he dwells among his church of redeemed sinners and delights in them.
May our hearts become his dwelling place.
May Christ live in them by faith, making them temples dedicated to him and pouring his love into them.
May the Father look upon us through his Anointed One, remember us and bless us according to his mercy toward sinners through Jesus Christ.

p.hi: God's answer to Solomon's prayer.

div.title: God answers Solomon
div.p: God graciously answered Solomon's prayer.
His mercy toward sinners was shown in a way that impressed all who received it with his majesty and holiness.
The people worshiped and praised him.
When God reveals himself as a consuming fire to sinners, his people can rejoice in him as their light.
Indeed, they had good reason to say he was good in doing this.
It is because of God's mercy that we ourselves are not consumed. Instead, a sacrifice was offered on our behalf, for which we should be deeply thankful.
Anyone who truly looks in faith upon the Savior suffering and dying for human sin will experience deeper godly sorrow, greater hatred of sin, closer watchfulness and a holier life.
Solomon successfully completed his plans for beautifying God's house and his own.
People who begin by serving God are likely to prosper in their other responsibilities.
It was to Solomon's credit that he completed what he undertook, though it was God's grace that made his success possible.
Let us reverence God and not sin.
Let us fear his displeasure, hope in his mercy and walk according to his commands.

p.hi: Solomon's buildings and trade.

div.title: Solomon's works, worship and trade
div.p: Governing a family in the fear of God sometimes requires more wisdom and determination than governing a kingdom with honor.
That task becomes harder when one's spouse is a hindrance rather than a fitting helper.
Solomon maintained the appointed sacrifices according to Moses' law.
Building the altar and seeing fire descend from heaven would have been useless if sacrifices were not then continually brought.
We, too, are required to bring spiritual sacrifices every day and every week.
A settled pattern of devotion is good.
When temple service had been properly organized, the house of the Lord was said to be complete.
The work of worship, not merely the building, was the essential matter.
The temple was not truly finished until those duties were established.
Canaan was a rich land, yet its people needed to obtain gold from Ophir.
Israel was a wise nation, yet relied on the king of Tyre's sailors for expertise at sea.
Grace is better wealth than gold, and knowledge of God and his law is better than worldly expertise.
Let the children of this world struggle over its toys.
As God's children, let us store treasure in heaven, because our hearts will follow what we treasure.

div.title: The queen of Sheba (verses 1–12)
div.p: This story has already been considered in 1 Kings 10.
Yet our Savior used the queen of Sheba as an example of someone who earnestly sought him (Matthew 12:42).
We should not pass over the lesson.
People who know the value of genuine wisdom will begrudge no expense or difficulty involved in obtaining it.
The queen traveled far and spent much to hear Solomon's wisdom.
She learned from him to serve God and fulfill her duty, and believed that knowledge more than repaid her effort.
Heavenly wisdom is the pearl of great price.
Even if we surrender everything to receive it, we make a good bargain.

div.title: Solomon's wealth and death (verses 13–31)
div.p: The imported objects listed here suggest that prosperity had led Solomon and his people to value things that were rare and interesting but not useful in themselves.
True wisdom and happiness always belong together.
There is no similar necessary connection between wealth and enjoyment of this life.
Let us draw near to the Savior to find rest for our souls.
Solomon ruled with unprecedented wealth, power, ease and abundance.
He reigned in profound peace for forty years, unlike the great kings chiefly remembered for warfare.
God fulfilled his promise to give him riches and honor beyond those of other kings.
His splendor was a faint image of the spiritual glory of Messiah's kingdom, whose throne stands above every throne.
Yet Solomon died and left all his wealth and power to a successor whom he knew would act foolishly (Ecclesiastes 2:18–19).
That was vanity and vexation of spirit.
Neither power, riches nor wisdom can prevent death or prepare the soul for it.
But thanks be to God: through Jesus Christ our Lord, he gives the true believer victory even over that dreaded enemy.

p.hi: The ten tribes revolt from Rehoboam.

div.title: The division of the kingdom
div.p: Moderate and reasonable counsel is usually the wisest and best.
Gentleness can accomplish what force and harshness cannot.
Most people respond better to words spoken kindly.
Good words cost us only a little self-denial, yet they may accomplish a great deal.
To ruin people, it is often enough merely to leave them under the rule of their own pride and anger.
Yet whatever human beings plan, God continues accomplishing his purposes through everything and fulfilling the word he has spoken.
No one can pass on wisdom or prosperity as an inheritance to children by simply choosing to do so.
Nevertheless, our conduct—whether good or bad—usually affects those who come after us.
Therefore, let us pursue the good things that will belong to us forever.
Let us seek God's blessing for our children and their descendants rather than wealth or worldly promotion.

row.cell: Rehoboam forbidden to war against Israel.
The priests and Levites find refuge in Judah.

div.title: Rehoboam is forbidden to fight Israel (verses 1–12)
div.p: A few kind words might have prevented Rehoboam's subjects from rebelling, but all the military power of his kingdom could not bring them back.
When God has made his purpose known to us, it is useless to fight against it.
Even people without genuine faith may sometimes show enough regard for God's word to be restrained from wrong actions they would otherwise be inclined to commit.

div.title: Priests and Levites find refuge in Judah (verses 13–23)
div.p: When the priests and Levites came to Jerusalem, faithful Israelites followed them.
People whose hearts were set upon seeking the Lord God of Israel left their ancestral land and moved to Jerusalem.
They wanted free access to God's altar and freedom from the temptation to worship the golden calves.

p.hi: What is best for our souls is best for us.

div.p: In every decision, we should give spiritual advantages a higher priority than outward convenience.
God's faithful people should seek fellowship with his faithful ministers.
When we demonstrate willingness to give up worldly interests as far as Christ and his gospel require, we have evidence that we truly are his disciples.
It also benefits a nation to protect true religion and people devoted to it.

p.hi: Rehoboam, forsaking the Lord, is punished.

div.title: Rehoboam is punished for abandoning God
div.p: Once Rehoboam became powerful enough to believe he had nothing to fear from Jeroboam, he abandoned even his outward profession of godliness.
It is common, and deeply regrettable, for people who appear eager to seek and serve God during danger, illness or fear of death to abandon religion after receiving merciful deliverance.
God soon brought trouble upon Judah to awaken the people to repentance before their hearts became hardened.
When Providence corrects us, we should acknowledge God's justice and our own guilt.
If humiliating circumstances produce a genuinely humble heart, the suffering has accomplished its purpose.
It may then be removed or changed in its character.
The more we compare God's service with other kinds of service, the more reasonable and easy it appears.
Do laws requiring self-control seem difficult?
The consequences of excess are far harder.

p.hi: Serving God is perfect freedom. Serving sinful desires is complete slavery.

div.p: Rehoboam never possessed a stable inward faith.
He did not entirely reject God, but he also never set his heart on seeking him.
He failed to serve the Lord because he failed to seek the Lord.
He did not pray as Solomon had for wisdom and grace, consult God's word as his guide or follow its directions.
Religion mattered little to him because he never truly committed his heart to it.
He did wrong because he was never firmly resolved to do good.

p.hi: Abijah overcomes Jeroboam.

div.title: Abijah defeats Jeroboam
div.p: Jeroboam and his people had deserved severe punishment for their idolatry and apostasy.
Henry understands the victory God permitted Abijah to win as an act of judgment against them.
Yet Abijah himself was not genuinely devoted to God, as his character in 1 Kings 15:3 shows.
He drew confidence from his people's faith, not from a faithful life of his own.
People who deny the power of godliness often boast in its outward form.
Many who have very little genuine faith themselves still value it in others.
Nevertheless, Judah did include many sincere worshipers, and its cause was more righteous.
Surrounded by danger, where could they look for rescue but upward?
What an extraordinary comfort it is that the way to God remains open.
They cried out to the Lord.
Earnest prayer is truly a cry for help.
They added a shout of faith to their prayer, and became more than conquerors.
Jeroboam escaped Abijah's sword, but God struck him.
No one escapes God's judgment.

p.hi: Asa's piety, He strengthens his kingdom.

div.title: Asa seeks God and strengthens Judah
div.p: Asa wanted to please God and sought his approval.
Happy are those who live by that rule—not doing what seems right merely in their own eyes or in the eyes of the world, but what is right before God.
Experience teaches us that seeking the Lord is good.
It brings rest, whereas chasing the world brings only distress and frustration.
Asa discussed with his people how to use the peace God had given them well.
Together they decided that peace was no excuse for laziness or careless self-confidence.
A formidable army of Ethiopians invaded his kingdom.
God permitted the trial so that Asa's faith would be tested.
His prayer was short, but expressed genuine faith and confidence in God.
When we go forward in God's name, we have reason to trust that he will work everything for the good of those whom he favors.

p.hi: The people make a solemn covenant with God.

div.title: Asa and the people renew their covenant
div.p: Full religious reform appeared so difficult that Asa had not dared undertake it until he received assurance of God's help and acceptance.
He and the people offered sacrifices of thanksgiving for past blessings and prayer for further mercy.
Under the gospel, our spiritual sacrifices are prayer and praise.
The people voluntarily entered a covenant to seek the Lord, with each person doing so earnestly.
What is true religion if not seeking God—inquiring after him and turning to him in every circumstance?
Religion is worth nothing to us unless it engages our hearts.
God requires the whole heart, or none of it.
Our devotion to God our Savior should be acknowledged and demonstrated solemnly and openly.
Anything done in hypocrisy is merely burdensome, empty labor.

p.hi: Asa seeks the aid of the Syrians, His death.

div.title: Asa's misplaced trust and death
div.p: A prophet of the Lord faithfully rebuked Asa for making an alliance with Syria.
God is displeased when people distrust him and rely more heavily upon human strength than on his power and goodness.
It is foolish to lean on a broken reed when we have the Rock of Ages to support us.
To show Asa his folly, the prophet reminded him that he, of all people, had good reason to trust God, who had already proved such a powerful Helper.
Our many experiences of God's goodness make later distrust more blameworthy.
Yet see how deceitful our hearts can be!
When we have no other source of help and necessity drives us to God, we trust him.
But when other supports appear, we readily depend on them too much.
Asa became angry at the prophet's correction.
What can human beings become when God leaves them to themselves?
Asa abused his authority to persecute God's prophet and was then left to misuse it further by oppressing his own subjects.
Two years before his death, Asa developed a disease in his feet.
Using physicians was his duty.
His sin and folly lay instead in trusting those physicians as though they could give what only God could give.
During every conflict and suffering, we must especially examine our hearts, seeking wholeness toward God through faith, patience and obedience.

p.hi: Jehoshaphat promotes religion in Judah, His prosperity.

div.title: Jehoshaphat teaches the law in Judah
div.p: Jehoshaphat found widespread ignorance among his people and worked to ensure they were well taught.
In every age, the public teaching of God's word is the principal means of promoting true godliness.
Through it, people are taught to understand, while their consciences are awakened and directed.
This chapter also describes Jehoshaphat's prosperity.
His large army was not what stopped neighboring nations from attacking Judah.
They were restrained by the fear of God, which came upon them as Jehoshaphat reformed the land and established a teaching ministry.
God's appointed ordinances are a kingdom's greater strength and security than soldiers and weapons.
Scripture continually calls us to notice God's hand in every event, yet few people take that call seriously.
Let everyone make use of the abilities they possess, being faithful even in small matters.
Establish the worship of God in your homes.
Caring for a family is an important responsibility.
Why should we not teach our families from the book of the Lord's law, as Jehoshaphat taught his people?
But live consistently.
Do not recommend one thing while practicing another.
Begin with yourselves.
Seek the Lord God of Israel, and then invite children and servants to follow your example.

p.hi: Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab.

div.title: Jehoshaphat's alliance and rescue
div.p: This history has already been recorded in 1 Kings 22.
Great wealth and honor offer many opportunities to do good, but they also carry many traps and temptations.
Those who eagerly seek riches in the belief that wealth will enable them to accomplish good often fail to understand Satan's schemes and the deceitfulness of their own hearts.
Who can harm those whom God protects?
Who can shelter those whom God has decided to judge?
Jehoshaphat remained safe in his royal robes, while Ahab was killed despite his armor.
The race does not belong automatically to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.
We should beware of becoming entangled in the worldly projects of wicked people, and be even more careful never to join their sinful undertakings.
Nevertheless, God can deliver his faithful people even from dangers they brought upon themselves through sinful choices, when they cry to him.
All hearts are in his hand, and he can rescue them easily.
Blessed is the person who trusts in the Lord.

p.hi: Jehoshaphat visits his kingdom.

div.title: Jehoshaphat receives correction and reforms Judah
div.p: Whenever we return home safely, we should recognize that Providence preserved our coming and going.
After escaping unusual danger, we have special reason to give thanks.
Exceptional mercies create exceptional obligations.
A prophet plainly told Jehoshaphat that joining Ahab had been very wrong.
Jehoshaphat received the rebuke well.
Notice how it affected his conduct: he searched his kingdom carefully to identify what remained to be corrected.
The prophet's words also showed him that his earlier reforms had pleased God.
That encouraged him to complete what was unfinished.
It is good when commendation spurs us on toward greater faithfulness.
Different gifts and kinds of service come from the same Spirit and are given for the common good.
Everyone who has received a gift should use it to serve others.
We should thank God for judges and ministers, scholars and officials, people who work with books and people who work in practical affairs.
Jehoshaphat charged them to do everything in reverence for God, with sincere and upright hearts.
They were to work constantly to prevent sin, knowing that it offends God and can bring judgment upon the people.

row.cell: The danger and distress of Judah.

div.title: Judah faces danger and prays (verses 1–13)
div.p: In every danger, whether public or personal, our first response should be to seek God's help.
This is one benefit of days set aside for national fasting and prayer.
Throughout our approach to God, we must humble ourselves over our sins and rely upon his mercy and power alone.
Jehoshaphat acknowledged God's sovereign rule over all events and asked him to exercise it on Judah's behalf.
Whom else should they seek or trust for relief but the God they had chosen and served?
Those who use their possessions for God may hope confidently in his protection.
Every true believer is a child of Abraham and a friend of God, included in his eternal covenant and entitled to its promises.
God's love is assured to us because he has dwelt in human nature in the person of the Savior.
Jehoshaphat appealed to the temple as a sign of God's gracious presence.
He also described the injustice of his enemies.
We may appeal to God when people repay good with evil.
Though Jehoshaphat commanded a large army, he acknowledged, “We have no strength without you; we depend entirely on you.”

div.title: Jahaziel announces victory (verses 14–19)
div.p: The Spirit of prophecy came upon a Levite while the people were gathered together.
Like the wind, the Spirit acts where and upon whom he wills.
The message encouraged them to trust the Lord.
When a Christian soldier goes out against spiritual enemies, the God of peace will make that believer more than a conqueror.
Our trials can become our gain.
We receive the benefit, but all the glory belongs to God.

div.title: Judah celebrates deliverance (verses 20–30)
div.p: Jehoshaphat encouraged the troops to maintain firm faith in God.
Faith gives genuine courage.
Nothing more firmly establishes a heart during unstable and frightening times than confidence in God's power, mercy and promise.
In every act of trust and praise, we should especially remember his everlasting mercy toward sinners through Jesus Christ.
The invading forces destroyed one another in an extraordinary defeat.
God often allows wicked people to destroy one another.
Few victories have ever been celebrated with thanksgiving as solemn as Judah's was.

div.title: Jehoshaphat joins Ahaziah (verses 31–37)
div.p: Jehoshaphat remained devoted to God's appointed worship and worked to keep his people faithful.
But after God had granted him such remarkable gifts—not only victory, but wealth—his alliance with a wicked king was deeply ungrateful.
He should have expected the Lord's displeasure.
It appears, however, that he accepted the later warning.
When Ahaziah again pressed him to join in a project, Jehoshaphat refused (1 Kings 22:49).
The alliance ended, and God's rebuke produced a change, at least for a time.
Let us be thankful for losses that may have prevented the far greater loss of our immortal souls.
Praise the Lord, who sought us and did not leave us to perish in our sins.

div.title: Jehoram's wicked reign (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jehoram hated his brothers and killed them for the same reason Cain hated and killed Abel: their godliness condemned his ungodliness.
In the mysterious workings of Providence, such wicked people sometimes prosper for a time.
Yet God has righteous reasons for permitting those events.
We can understand some of those purposes now; the rest will become clear in the future.

div.title: Jehoram's miserable death (verses 12–20)
div.p: God sent Jehoram a warning.
The Spirit of prophecy may have directed Elijah to write it in advance, foreseeing Jehoram's crimes.
Jehoram was told plainly that his sins would bring ruin.

It is no surprise that sinners ignore warnings of punishment in the world to come, when even the certainty of suffering in this life—losing possessions or health—does not make them abandon wicked practices.
Jehoram lost every comfort.
God made clear that he was confronting both the king and his household.
Jehoram had killed his brothers to make himself secure.
Now all but one of his sons were killed.
Yet David's family would not be destroyed entirely as many northern royal families were, because the promise of the Messiah belonged to David's line.
Good people may also suffer disease, but for them illness is fatherly correction.
God's comfort can keep the soul at rest even while the body is in pain.
To be ill and poor or ill and lonely is distressing.
But to be ill while living in sin, under God's judgment and without grace to endure it is far more terrible.
Wickedness and irreverence make people contemptible even to those with little religion themselves.

p.hi: The reign of Ahaziah, Athaliah destroys the royal family.

div.title: Ahaziah's reign and Athaliah's attempt to destroy David's line
div.p: The counsel of wicked people ruins many young people as they begin adult life.
Ahaziah allowed himself to be led by evil advisers.
People who encourage us to do wrong are advising us toward our destruction.
Though they pretend to be friends, they are our worst enemies.
Consider the harm caused by bad company.
Even when we escape being infected by its wickedness, we should still fear sharing its destruction (Revelation 18:4).
Here a wicked woman tried to destroy David's house, while a good woman preserved it.
Not one word of God's promise will fail.
At this point the prophecies that the Messiah would descend from David—and thus the salvation of the world—seemed to depend upon the fragile life of a single infant.
The ruling power wanted that child dead.
But God had made his purpose known, and the efforts of earth and hell could not defeat it.

p.hi: Joash crowned, and Athaliah slain.

div.title: Joash becomes king
div.p: Recognizing ourselves and one another as the Lord's people should make us earnest in carrying out our duties both toward God and toward other human beings.
In this way the change of government was accomplished successfully, and the people rejoiced.
When the Son of David is enthroned within a person's soul, peace and joy follow.
For the related account, see 2 Kings 11.

row.cell: Joash, of Judah, The temple repaired.
Joash falls into idolatry, He is slain by his servants.

div.title: Joash repairs the temple (verses 1–14)
div.p: Joash showed even greater zeal for repairing the temple than Jehoiada did.
Yet it is easier to build or repair a temple than to become a temple of God oneself.
Repairing places used for public worship is still a good work that everyone should help advance.
Many worthy projects remain unfinished simply because no energetic person takes responsibility for moving them forward.

div.title: Joash abandons God and is killed (verses 15–27)
div.p: The death of a faithful, zealous and useful servant of God can be a great judgment on a ruler or people.
This shows why our faith must spring from an inward principle, not depend entirely on the presence of another human being.
Otherwise, when a parent, minister or friend dies, we may lose our religion along with that person.
Rulers and ordinary people alike have often been flattered into ruin.
Only genuine grace enables a person to keep bearing spiritual fruit until the end.
Zechariah, Jehoiada's son, stood up in the Spirit of prophecy and exposed the people's sin.
That is the task of ministers: using God's word like a lamp, they reveal wrongdoing and explain the meaning of divine Providence.
The people stoned Zechariah to death in the temple court.
As he died, he called upon the Lord to see and require judgment for the crime.
Henry says this was not a cry of private revenge but a prophetic declaration.
God struck Joash with severe illness, whether in body, mind or both, before the Syrians left.
When judgment pursues sinners, the end of one trouble may simply introduce another.
Joash's own servants killed him.
The judgments were described as burdens because God's wrath is a load too heavy for any person to bear.
May God help us learn from the warning, remain upright in heart and persevere in his ways until the end.

row.cell: Amaziah worships the idols of Edom.

div.title: Amaziah's reign begins (verses 1–13)
div.p: Amaziah was not an enemy of true religion, but he was a lukewarm and indifferent friend.
Many people do what is right without doing it with their whole hearts.
Rash decisions create painful work for repentance.
Yet Amaziah deserved honor for obeying God's command when it required sacrifice.
A firm belief that God is fully able to uphold us in duty and make up for losses suffered in serving him makes his commands easier to bear.
When we must surrender something for God and his worship, we can be content knowing he can provide something much better.
Sinners who have been convinced intellectually but do not possess genuine faith often object when obedience requires self-denial.
Like Amaziah, they ask, “But what shall we do about the hundred talents?”
What if keeping the Sabbath means losing good customers?
What if obedience costs a profitable business opportunity or the world's friendship?
People often try to quiet their consciences by claiming that forbidden practices are necessary.
The answer remains the same: the Lord can give you far more than that.
Even in this life, he can make up for what is surrendered for his sake.

div.title: Amaziah worships Edom's idols (verses 14–16)
div.p: After defeating the Edomites, Amaziah worshiped the gods who had failed to protect the people he conquered.
What absurdity!
If people seriously considered how powerless the things they turn to are, they would not abandon the Lord and harm themselves.
The prophet's rebuke was so just that Amaziah could not answer it, except by ordering the prophet to stop speaking.
Sinners may feel relieved when they silence those correcting them.
But people who refuse to hear correction are becoming ready for destruction.

div.title: Amaziah challenges Israel and is humiliated (verses 17–28)
div.p: Few proud rulers have been more completely humbled than Amaziah by Jehoash, king of Israel.
Pride brings a person low (Proverbs 29:23).
It goes before destruction and rightly produces it.
Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.
Someone who rushes into a quarrel may find himself humiliated and at a loss when his opponent answers him (Proverbs 25:8).
What are we when we try to establish our own righteousness or justify ourselves before the Most High God?
We resemble contemptible thistles imagining themselves majestic cedars.
Temptations and sinful desires are like wild beasts that trample such proud pretensions into the dust.
A person's destruction can often be traced to the moment the person turned away from the Lord.

div.title: Uzziah's prosperous reign (verses 1–15)
div.p: As long as Uzziah sought the Lord and paid attention to true religion, God made him prosper.
Only those whom God makes prosperous truly prosper, because success comes from him.
Many people can testify that they prospered while they sought God and attended to their duties, but difficulties multiplied when they turned away.
God does not continually bless laziness or withhold his blessing from diligence.
No one who sincerely seeks him does so in vain.
Uzziah became famous throughout the neighboring countries.
Having a good reputation before God and godly people is true honor.
He did not delight in warfare or excessive amusement, but loved agriculture.

div.title: Uzziah tries to burn incense (verses 16–23)
div.p: Earlier kings had sinned by abandoning God's temple and burning incense at idolatrous altars.
Uzziah's sin was different: he entered God's sanctuary and tried to burn incense on God's own altar.
How difficult it is to avoid one extreme without falling into the opposite!
Pride lay at the root of his wrongdoing.
Instead of lifting up God's name in gratitude for everything he had received, Uzziah lifted up his own heart to his own harm.
The desire for forbidden knowledge and honors beyond one's proper place often comes from pride.
Our prayers, like incense, must be placed by faith into the hands of Jesus Christ our great High Priest, or we cannot expect God to accept them (Revelation 8:3).
Uzziah argued with the priests but could not prevail against his Creator.
He was afflicted with leprosy and lived apart from society until death.
His punishment corresponded to his sin.
Because he sought unlawful honor, God humbled and disgraced him.
Those who covet forbidden honors may lose the honors lawfully available to them.
Adam reached for knowledge from the forbidden tree and thereby lost access to the tree of life.
Let everyone who reads this acknowledge the Lord's righteousness.

If God sees fit to set aside even useful and prosperous people, like broken vessels, and raises up others to take their place, they should willingly lay aside worldly concerns and devote their remaining days to preparing for death.

p.hi: Jotham's reign in Judah.

div.title: Jotham's reign
div.p: The people continued acting corruptly.
Perhaps Jotham did not do all he could to reform the land.
Even a very good person may lack the courage and zeal to perform duties that are within reach.
The people's own conduct certainly deserved blame.
Jotham prospered and became powerful.
