The more steadfastly we follow God, the stronger we become—both in resisting evil and in doing good.
The Lord often removes wise and devout rulers and gives a people others whose folly and wickedness punish them for having failed to appreciate earlier blessings.

p.hi: The wicked reign of Ahaz in Judah.

div.title: Ahaz's wicked reign
div.p: Israel defeated Judah because the Lord was angry with Judah and used the northern kingdom as an instrument of his judgment.
Yet he also reminded Israel of its own sins.
Sinners have no right to act cruelly toward others.
How could they expect God's mercy if they refused mercy and justice to their brothers?
Remember that every human being is our neighbor and fellow human being, even when not a fellow Christian.
Henry makes an explicit statement here: anyone who knows God's word should be able to maintain confidently that slavery is contrary to the law of love and the gospel of grace.
How can someone hold a brother in bondage without breaking the rule to treat others as one would wish to be treated?
When sinners are abandoned to their own sinful desires, however, they grow more desperate in evil.
God commanded the Israelites to release the captives, and they obeyed.
The Lord brought Judah low.
People who refuse to humble themselves under God's word will rightly be humbled by his judgments.
Wicked people often have no real love for those who abandon true faith to join them, nor any desire to help them.
Ahaz became worse, not better, because of his suffering.
In distress he continued sinning more and set his heart even more firmly on wrongdoing.
When people misunderstand both the source of their troubles and the source of help, they turn their loyalties toward the wrong objects.
Wickedness and misery may grow rapidly together.
It is dreadful to consider a sinner dying and entering eternity while still hardened in sin.

div.title: Hezekiah begins reform (verses 1–19)
div.p: As soon as Hezekiah became king, he began to reform Judah's worship.
Those who begin their work with God begin at the right place, and he can bless their efforts.
Turning away from God's appointed worship is genuinely a way of turning away from God himself.
People still neglect true worship if Scripture is not read and explained, pictured by lighting the temple lamps, or if prayer and praise are not offered, pictured by burning incense.
Neglect of worship had caused the troubles Judah had endured.
Only the Lord can prepare a human heart for living faith.
When much good is accomplished quickly, all the glory belongs to him.
Those who love God and care about people's souls will rejoice.
Everyone who does good work should seek to do it well.

div.title: The offerings of atonement (verses 20–36)
div.p: When Hezekiah learned the temple was ready, he acted at once.
The sins of the preceding reign required atonement.
Mourning over sin and abandoning it were not enough; the people also brought a sin offering.
Likewise, our repentance and reform do not themselves earn pardon.
Forgiveness is available only through Jesus Christ, who became sin—that is, a sin offering—for us.
While the offerings burned, the Levites sang.
Grief over sin must never prevent us from praising God.
The king and congregation consented to the proceedings.
Merely being present where others worship is not enough.
We must worship God with our own hearts.
Our spiritual sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving should be accompanied by giving ourselves and everything we possess to God.
These sacrifices become acceptable to the Father only through the Redeemer.

div.title: Hezekiah invites all Israel to the Passover (verses 1–12)
div.p: Hezekiah made the Israelites from the northern kingdom as welcome to the Passover as his own subjects.
Let us give ourselves to the Lord.
Instead of insisting on doing what pleases us, resolve to do what pleases him.
Our fallen minds are naturally stubborn and unwilling to comply with God's ways.
We have inherited that disposition from our ancestors, and it must be overcome.
People whom grace has turned to God should do everything they can to bring others to him.
Many will mock the invitation.
Yet some will be humbled and blessed, perhaps where we least expect it.
God's rich mercy is the strongest reason for calling sinners to repentance.
Even the worst sinners who humble themselves before the Lord, seek his grace and devote themselves to his service can be saved.
How wonderful it would be if messengers went through every city, village and country with this good news!

div.title: The Passover is celebrated (verses 13–20)
div.p: The essential thing in attending God's solemn worship is a heart sincerely directed toward him.
Without this, everything else is worthless.
Even with a sincere, settled heart, worshipers may fall short of some sanctuary purification requirements.
Those defects need God's pardoning and healing grace.
Failing within a duty can be sinful, just as failing to perform the duty at all can be sinful.
If God judged even our best acts by the strict standard of his justice, we would be condemned.
Forgiveness must be sought through prayer, through the blood of Christ.
Every defect is cause for humility and repentance, not for despair.
But nothing can replace a heart prepared to seek the Lord.

div.title: The Feast of Unleavened Bread (verses 21–27)
div.p: Many prayers accompanied the fellowship offerings.
In these prayers the people recognized the Lord as the God of their fathers, their covenant God.
There was also much faithful preaching.
The Levites read and explained the Scriptures.
Faith comes through hearing, and true religion has often flourished when preaching was abundant.
The people sang psalms every day.
Praising God should occupy a large place in our gatherings.
After observing the feast for seven days, they found such joy in worship that they continued for another seven days.
They did so gladly.
Holy duties should be performed with holy joy.
When sinners humble themselves before the Lord, they can expect to rejoice in his appointed worship.
Those who taste that joy will not soon grow tired of it.
They will gladly prolong their time with God.

p.hi: Hezekiah destroys idolatry.

div.title: Hezekiah's reforms continue
div.p: After celebrating the Passover, the Israelites worked energetically to destroy the monuments of idolatry.
Public worship should encourage us to cleanse our hearts, homes and workplaces from the pollution of sin and the idolatry of greed.
It should also move us to encourage others to do the same.
How we respond after a solemn act of worship is extremely important for our personal faith, our families and public religion.
The people had tasted the sweetness of the recent Passover and therefore contributed willingly to support temple worship.
Those who genuinely enjoy the benefits of a steady and faithful ministry will not resent the expense of supporting it.
Hezekiah was wholehearted in his purpose and sincere in his dependence upon God in everything he did for the Lord.
God granted him success.
Whether we have many gifts or few, may we work to use and develop them and encourage others to do likewise.
Work undertaken sincerely for God's glory will finally bring us honor and comfort.

row.cell: The invasion of Sennacherib, His defeat.
Hezekiah's sickness, His prosperous reign, and death.

div.title: Sennacherib invades Judah (verses 1–23)
div.p: Those who trust God to keep them safe must still use appropriate means of protection; otherwise they are testing him.
God will provide, but we must also take responsible action.
Hezekiah gathered his people and spoke words of comfort to them.
Confidence in the Lord raises believers above the fear of human beings.
Let faithful subjects and soldiers of Jesus Christ rest upon his word and boldly declare, “If God is for us, who can be against us?”
Through God's favor, enemies are defeated and friends are gained.

div.title: Hezekiah's illness and death (verses 24–33)
div.p: God allowed Hezekiah to experience a trial without the usual supporting grace.
This exposed what remained in his heart and showed that he was not as mature in grace as he imagined.
It is good to discover our own weakness and sinfulness so that we do not become conceited or self-confident.
We must live in continual dependence on divine grace.
We do not know how corrupt our hearts may become or what we might do if God leaves us to ourselves.
Hezekiah's sin was that his heart became proud.
People who are great, godly or useful need especially to examine their weaknesses and remember how much they owe to freely given grace.
Let us ask God earnestly to keep us humble.
Hezekiah repaid the Lord poorly by turning the very gifts he had received into fuel for his pride.
We should avoid occasions of sin: company, amusements, books and even sights that feed our sinful desires.
Let us continually commit ourselves to the Lord's care and ask him never to abandon us.
Blessed be God, death will finally end the believer's conflict.
Then pride and every other sin will be abolished.
Never again will a believer be tempted to withhold the praise that belongs to the God of salvation.

div.title: Manasseh repents (verses 1–20)
div.p: We have already seen Manasseh's terrible wickedness.
Here Scripture records his repentance, a remarkable demonstration of God's rich forgiving mercy and renewing grace.
Manasseh lost his freedom, was separated from the advisers and companions who had encouraged evil, and faced the prospect of dying in a miserable prison.
He began to look back on his life and cry out for deliverance and mercy.
He confessed his sins, condemned himself, humbled himself before God and despised the dreadful wickedness he had committed.
Yet he still hoped to receive pardon through the Lord's abundant mercy.
Now Manasseh knew that Jehovah is God, able to save and deliver.
He learned to fear, trust, love and obey him.
From then on, his character changed and he began to walk in newness of life.

Who can tell how much pain of conscience he suffered while remembering his long years of apostasy, the many people he led into sin and destruction, and the blood of faithful people shed through his persecution?
Who can claim that the way to heaven has been closed against them when someone so wicked was admitted through repentance?
However much evil you recognize in your own heart, here is someone equally guilty who discovered the way to repent.

p.hi: Do not deny yourself what God has not denied you.

div.p: It is not sin alone, but unrepentance, that keeps a sinner outside heaven.

div.title: Amon's wicked reign (verses 21–25)
div.p: Amon's father did evil, but Amon did worse.
Whatever warnings or convictions he experienced, he never humbled himself before God.
His life was soon cut short while he remained in his sins.
He stands as a warning to everyone tempted to treat God's patience and mercy toward Manasseh as permission to continue sinning.
May God help us be truthful with ourselves and judge our own character correctly before death fixes our condition forever.

p.hi: Josiah's good reign in Judah.

div.title: Josiah seeks the Lord from his youth
div.p: Our earliest childhood years cannot usually be devoted to much useful service to others.
That makes it wise to dedicate our earliest youth to God, rather than waste the short life that remains.
Happy are those who seek the Lord and prepare to be useful while young, when others are chasing sinful pleasures, acquiring destructive habits and forming harmful relationships.
Who can calculate the sorrow prevented by early faith and the blessings it produces?
Careful self-examination and vigilance reveal the deceitfulness and wickedness of our hearts and the sins within our lives.
Josiah's example encourages us to humble ourselves before God and seek him.
Believers also learn not to fear death but to welcome it when it spares them from evils still to come.
Nothing hastens a nation's ruin more than rejecting earnest attempts at reform.
God will not be mocked.
Only he can turn the deepest flow of a person's affections, raising those who are dead in trespasses and sins.
His grace in the lives of those who seek the Savior while young has a special beauty.
Has Jesus, the Day-spring from on high, visited you?
Can you, like Josiah, remember first recognizing this light and life during your youth?
What extraordinary happiness comes from knowing Jesus from one's earliest years!

div.title: Josiah celebrates the Passover (verses 1–19)
div.p: The book of Kings describes more fully how Josiah destroyed idolatry.
Chronicles instead gives an account of his solemn celebration of the Passover.
The Lord's Supper resembles Passover more closely than any other Jewish festival.
Observing it rightly is a sign of growth in true godliness and devotion.
Only God can make our hearts holy and prepare us to worship him properly.
Nevertheless, there are duties that we must perform, through which we seek and receive his blessing.

div.title: Josiah dies in battle (verses 20–27)
div.p: Scripture does not directly condemn Josiah for confronting Pharaoh.
Yet Henry considers it possible that Josiah was wrong not to consult the Lord after receiving a warning.
His death might have corrected him for rashness.
At the same time, it was a judgment upon the hypocritical and wicked people of Judah.
For someone who has lived in repentance, faith and obedience, the unexpected or sudden manner of death cannot destroy the person's eternal hope.
The people mourned Josiah.
Yet many people grieve over disasters while refusing to abandon the sins that caused God to send them.
Only repentance can turn away divine judgment.
If we judge Josiah's conduct to have been wrong, let us also watch our own actions, lest we die in a way that dishonors our Christian confession.

div.title: Jerusalem is destroyed (verses 1–21)
div.p: The ruin of Judah and Jerusalem unfolded gradually.
God repeatedly tried to call the people back through his word, ministers, conscience and the events of Providence.
These were all signs of his compassion and his desire that sinners not perish.
Consider the dreadful destruction that sin brings!
If we value our earthly blessings and want them to last, we should keep sin—the worm that attacks their root—away from them.
The people had often plowed and sown the land during seventh years when it should have rested.
Now it remained unsown and uncultivated for seventy years, ten times seven.
In the end, human disobedience cannot deprive God of the glory due to him.
If the people would not let the land rest, God would make it rest.
O Lord, what place will your justice spare if Jerusalem itself has fallen?
If the city where you delighted could be destroyed for wickedness, let us not grow proud, but fear.

div.title: Cyrus announces the return (verses 22 and 23)
div.p: God promised the restoration of the exiles and the rebuilding of Jerusalem after seventy years.
At last the appointed time to favor Zion came.
God's church may be cast down, but it is not cast off.
His people may be corrected, but they are not abandoned.
They may be put into a furnace, but they will not be destroyed or left there longer than necessary for the worthless material to be refined away.
God may contend with his people for a long time, but he will not contend forever.
As the books of Chronicles close, we should reflect on the destruction that sin has brought into the whole world—and even into God's own church.
Let us tremble at these records while recognizing in a few faithful lives that God has never left himself without witnesses.

Having considered this truthful picture of fallen human nature, compare it with human nature renewed through God's almighty grace, through the justifying righteousness of our Savior Jesus Christ that adorns the soul.

div.title: Ezra — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: This book records the fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy concerning the return of the Jews from Babylon.
Its history especially teaches that every good work will meet opposition from enemies and may be damaged by the wrongdoing of friends.
Yet God will make his cause prevail, despite all obstacles and adversaries.
The restoration of the Jewish people was an event of extraordinary importance.
It helped preserve true religion in the world and prepared the way for the coming of the great Deliverer, Jesus Christ our Lord.

row.cell: The proclamation of Cyrus for the rebuilding of the temple.
The people provide for their return.

div.title: Cyrus announces the return (verses 1–4)
div.p: The Lord stirred the spirit of Cyrus.
The hearts of kings are in God's hands.
God governs the world by influencing human hearts, and whenever people do good, he is the One who moves them to do it.
During the Jewish people's captivity, God used them especially to draw the nations' attention toward himself.
Cyrus expected that those Jews who were able would willingly contribute offerings toward God's temple.
He also directed that they receive material support from his kingdom.
Those who say they wish the temple well should also act for its good.

div.title: The people prepare to return (verses 5–11)
div.p: The same God who moved Cyrus to proclaim freedom moved the captives to take advantage of that freedom.
Some were tempted to stay in Babylon.
Others had the courage to return, because the Lord stirred their hearts by his Spirit and grace.
Whatever good we do comes through God's grace.
By nature, our affections tend downward toward earthly things.
When they rise toward what is good, God is the One who raises them.
The gospel's invitations resemble Cyrus's proclamation.
Those enslaved by sin may be set free through Jesus Christ.
Anyone willing to return to God through repentance and faith finds that Christ has opened the way out of bondage into the glorious freedom of God's children.
Many who hear the good news still choose to stay in Babylon, loving their sins and refusing the risks of a holy life.
But others overcome obstacles and are willing to follow, because God has lifted their spirits above the world and sinful desires.
Thus the heavenly Canaan will be populated even though many perish in their Babylon.
The gospel's invitation will not be made in vain.
The return from exile therefore represents the redemption of sinners through Jesus Christ.

row.cell: The numbers of the priests and Levites.

div.title: Families returning from exile (verses 1–35)
div.p: A record was kept of the families who returned from captivity.
See how sin can bring down a nation that righteousness would have raised up!

div.title: Priests and Levites (verses 36–63)
div.p: Those who undervalue their relationship to the Lord during times of reproach, persecution or hardship will not enjoy its benefits when that relationship becomes honorable or advantageous.
People who possess no evidence of having become spiritual priests to God through Jesus Christ by the new birth have no right to claim the comfort and privileges belonging to Christians.

div.title: Gifts for the temple (verses 64–70)
div.p: No one should complain about the necessary cost of their religion.
Seek first God's kingdom, favor and glory; other things will then be supplied.
Their offerings were small compared with the gifts given by the leaders in David's time.
Yet because they were proportionate to the givers' abilities, they were just as acceptable to God.
The Lord will carry his people through work undertaken according to his will, directed toward his glory and dependent on his help.
Those who hear the gospel, turn away from sin and return to the Lord will be guided and protected through the dangers of the journey.
They will reach safely the homes prepared in God's holy city.

row.cell: The foundations of the temple laid.

div.title: The altar is restored (verses 1–7)
div.p: Israel's conduct on returning to Jerusalem teaches us to begin with God.
We should do what we can in God's worship even when we cannot do everything we wish.
They could not build a temple immediately, but they would not remain without an altar.
Fear of danger should move us toward duty, not away from it.
If enemies surround us, all the more reason to seek God's friendship and continue in fellowship with him.
Our fears should drive us to our knees.
For a poor community, the prescribed sacrifices were costly.
Nevertheless, many people gave additional voluntary offerings.
They also began preparing for the temple without delay.
Whatever God calls us to do, we may trust his Providence to supply the means required.

div.title: The temple foundation is laid (verses 8–13)
div.p: As the foundation was laid, the people experienced remarkably different emotions.
Those who had known only life without a temple shouted with joy.
To them, even the foundation appeared magnificent.
We should give thanks when mercy begins, even before its work is complete.
But people who remembered the glory of the former temple wept loudly because this new building seemed likely to be so much poorer.
They had reason to grieve, especially if they mourned the sins that brought about the loss of the first temple.
Yet it was wrong to cast gloom over everyone else's joy.
They were in danger of despising the day of small things and failing to thank God for the gifts now before them.
Do not let the memory of former troubles overwhelm your gratitude for present mercies.

row.cell: The building of the temple is hindered.

div.title: Opposition to the rebuilding (verses 1–5)
div.p: Every sincere attempt to revive true religion provokes the opposition of Satan and those under his influence.
These adversaries were the Samaritans, who had been settled in Israel's territory (2 Kings 17).
They clearly did not intend to join in worship of the Lord according to his word.
Those who discourage a good project or weaken its workers should consider whose example they are following.

div.title: The temple work is obstructed (verses 6–24)
div.p: It is an old slander to claim that the prosperity of God's church endangers kings and rulers.
Nothing could be further from the truth.
Genuine faith teaches people to respect and obey lawful authorities.
But when divine commands and human laws directly conflict, we must obey God rather than human beings, patiently accepting the consequences.
Everyone who loves the gospel should avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing, so as not to provide needless encouragement to the church's opponents.
The world is often ready to believe any accusation against God's people while refusing to listen to their defense.
The king was misled through fraudulent reports and falsehoods.
Rulers often see and hear through other people's eyes and ears and make decisions based on descriptions of events that are inaccurate or dishonest.
But God's judgment is entirely just.
He sees everything as it really is.

row.cell: The leaders forward the building of the temple.

div.title: The leaders renew the temple work (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Construction of the temple had been interrupted for about fifteen years.
Then God sent the people two faithful ministers to urge them to resume.
It is a sign that God intends mercy for a people when he raises up prophets to help them in the work and ways of the Lord—as guides, overseers and leaders.
The prophet Haggai shows us what mighty things God accomplishes through his word and through the Spirit working with that word.

div.title: The elders answer the opposition (verses 3–17)
div.p: When we are engaged in God's work, his eye rests upon us for good and we receive his special protection.
That should encourage us to continue even when difficulties seem overwhelming.
The Jewish elders explained to their opponents what they were doing and why.
We should learn to be ready, with gentleness and reverence, to explain the hope within us and to give truthful reasons for our acts of service.
We must first understand our own responsibilities, then state them clearly.
While living in this world, we must acknowledge that our sins provoke God's anger.
Our troubles spring from human wrongdoing, while all our comforts come from his undeserved mercy.
Even when the work seems obstructed, Jesus Christ is carrying it forward.
His people are being built together as a holy temple in the Lord, a dwelling place of God through the Spirit.

row.cell: The decree for completing the temple.

div.title: The decree allows the work to resume (verses 1–12)
div.p: When God's appointed time comes to fulfill his gracious purposes for the church, he can raise up unexpected people to assist.
Zechariah directs our attention beyond Jerusalem's temple to a greater spiritual building.
Jesus Christ continues laying stone upon stone.
Let us assist his great work.
Difficulties may delay the construction, but opposition must not discourage us.
At the appointed time the work will be completed to Christ's praise.
He will set its finishing stone in place amid shouts of “Grace! Grace to it!”

div.title: The temple is completed (verses 13–22)
div.p: The gospel church, God's spiritual temple, has been under construction for a long time.
Yet it will be finished when the whole mystical body is complete.
Every believer is also a living temple, growing in the most holy faith.
Satan and our own sinful desires oppose the work.
We may work carelessly and stop and start repeatedly.
But the One who began the good work will bring it to completion.
Then the spirits of righteous people will be made perfect.
The people of Israel were freed from the sting of their earlier suffering as their sins were taken away.
They worshiped joyfully.
Let us receive God's appointed worship gladly and serve the Lord with joy.

row.cell: Ezra blesses God for his favour.

div.title: Ezra travels to Jerusalem (verses 1–10)
div.p: Ezra went from Babylon to Jerusalem seeking the welfare of his people.
The king favored him and granted all his requests, supplying what he needed to serve his country.
Many people accompanied him.
He enjoyed the king's favor because of God's favor.
Every person and created thing can become to us only what God makes them.
We should recognize his hand in everything that happens and thank him.

div.title: The king commissions Ezra (verses 11–26)
div.p: The generosity of pagan kings in supporting God's worship put to shame the actions of many kings of Judah.
It also rebukes wealthy professing Christians who refuse to give toward God's cause.
But the weapons of Christian ministers are not physical or military weapons.
Their means of bringing people into obedience to Christ are faithful preaching, holy living, earnest prayer and patient suffering when called to it.

div.title: Ezra thanks God (verses 27 and 28)
div.p: Ezra blessed God for two things.
First, his commission. Whenever we find good in our hearts or in others', we must acknowledge that God put it there and praise him.
He is the One who works in us both to will and to do what is good.
Second, his encouragement. God had extended mercy toward Ezra.
Ezra acted bravely, yet attributed his courage to God's hand, not to his own strength.
When he supports us, we are bold and joyful.
When he withdraws his help, we become weak as water.
Whatever good we can accomplish for God or our neighbors, all the glory belongs to him.

div.title: Ezra gathers companions (verses 1–20)
div.p: Ezra assembled people scattered from Israel and Judah.
God moved the hearts of a small remnant to go with him.
How unfortunate it is when good people fail to do worthy work simply because no one invited or encouraged them!

div.title: Ezra prays for protection (verses 21–23)
div.p: Ezra recruited Levites to accompany him.
Yet what good would their help be if the Lord were not with him?
Those who sincerely seek God are safe under the shelter of his wings even in great danger.
Those who abandon him are always exposed.
When entering a new period of life, we should make sure we are not carrying unrepented sins from our former way of life into it.
Whenever danger arises, seek peace with God first.
Then nothing can truly harm us.
We should entrust our own welfare, our families and our possessions to God through prayer, leaving their care with him.
Sometimes we should decline even a lawful advantage if taking it could make other people stumble or dishonor God.
Ask him for the wisdom to know when to use and when to refuse a lawful opportunity.
We will not ultimately lose anything by taking risks, suffering or surrendering something for the Lord.
Their prayers were answered, as the outcome demonstrated.
No one who has sincerely sought God has done so in vain.
During trouble or danger, setting aside a time for private or shared prayer is among the best means available for finding relief.

div.title: Treasures are entrusted to the priests (verses 24–30)
div.p: If we expect God to preserve through his providence the possessions he has entrusted to us, let us also preserve the things that belong to him through his grace.
Let his honor and interests be our concern; then we may trust him for our lives and comforts.

div.title: Ezra reaches Jerusalem (verses 31–36)
div.p: Enemies waited to attack the travelers, but God protected them.
Even ordinary journeys should begin with prayer and end with thanksgiving.
How much greater will our gratitude be when the Lord guides us safely through the whole pilgrimage of life, through death's dark valley, beyond every enemy and into eternal joy!
Among the offerings, Israel brought a sin offering.
Atonement gives sweetness and security to every mercy received.
No mercy can bring lasting comfort unless sin is taken away and peace with God is made.
Then God's people could rest.
Their journey points toward sinners being brought out of spiritual slavery and led, under God and Savior's care, to the heavenly Jerusalem.

row.cell: Ezra mourns for the Jews' conduct.

div.title: Ezra grieves over Israel's wrongdoing (verses 1–4)
div.p: Even the most careful leaders may fail to see some of the corruption hidden among the people.
Some Israelites had disobeyed God's explicit command concerning marriage with the nations (Deuteronomy 7).
Their unwillingness to trust God's complete sufficiency lay behind the compromises they made to help themselves.
Through those relationships they exposed themselves and their children to the idolatry that had already ruined their church and nation.
People who merely profess religion may dismiss such concerns or explain away God's commands about separation.
Those who know Scripture well recognize their seriousness.
It should astonish and grieve faithful believers when people who profess Christ defend serious wrongdoing.
Everyone claiming to be God's people should support those who stand and act against sin and irreverence.

div.title: Ezra confesses the people's sins (verses 5–15)
div.p: The sacrifice, especially the evening sacrifice, pointed toward the Lamb of God, who in the latter time would take away sin through his own offering.
Ezra confessed his people's sins in a spirit of repentance.
There is comfort for true penitents: although sins reach to heaven, God's mercy also reaches to heaven.
Ezra spoke with shame.
Genuine repentance needs holy shame as well as sorrow.
He spoke with amazement.
The more we consider guilt, the worse sin appears.
Let us cry, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.”
Ezra also spoke with fear.
There is hardly a clearer sign of approaching ruin than returning to wrongdoing after severe judgments and great deliverances.
Everyone in God's church should be astonished that they have not exhausted the Lord's patience and brought destruction upon themselves.
What, then, of the openly ungodly?
The true penitent has nothing to plead in self-defense.
But our heavenly Advocate pleads powerfully on our behalf.

div.title: Ezra encourages reform (verses 1–5)
div.p: Shecaniah acknowledged the nation's guilt.
The situation was sad but not hopeless.
The sickness was threatening but not incurable.
As the people began to mourn, a spirit of repentance appeared to have been poured out.
There was hope that the Lord would forgive and show mercy.
The sin that troubles us in the right way will not destroy us.
Even in dark times, we should notice what gives us hope as well as what warns us.
Grace provides grounds for hope even when we recognize great guilt before God.
The matter was clear.
As far as possible, what had been done wrongly needed to be undone.
Genuine repentance requires putting sin away with the settled intention of never returning to it.
Goods unjustly obtained must be restored.

p.hi: Rise and act courageously.

div.p: In this situation, weeping was good, but reform was better.
Henry distinguishes the ancient law from the gospel era.
He teaches that believers should not enter marriages unequally yoked with unbelievers.
But he also expressly says that such marriages are not now nullified as they were under Israel's former separation laws, because the gospel has ended the separation between Jews and Gentiles.
The record must therefore not be taken as an instruction to dissolve existing marriages today.

div.title: Ezra assembles the people (verses 6–14)
div.p: There is hope when people recognize not merely that abandoning sin would be good but that it is necessary.
God's mercy is so rich and his redemption so abundant that even the worst sinner who hears the gospel and willingly accepts its freely offered salvation can hope.
When people mourn over wrongdoing and tremble at God's word, we may hope they will abandon their sins.
Anyone seeking to move others toward godly sorrow or love for God must first be moved personally.
Ezra and the people made careful plans for the reform.
Decisions made in haste seldom produce lasting results.

div.title: The reform is carried out (verses 15–44)
div.p: Even the best reformers can only make their best efforts.
When the Redeemer comes to Zion, he will effectively turn ungodliness away from Jacob.
When people truly repent and abandon sin, God forgives.
But Christ's blood, shed as our sin offering, is the only atonement that removes guilt.
An outward appearance of repentance or better behavior brings no lasting benefit if someone rejects Christ.
Self-reliance shows that the heart is still proud and unrepentant.
Every name written in the book of life belongs to a repentant sinner, not someone claiming self-righteousness and denying any need to repent.

div.title: Nehemiah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The Old Testament's historical narrative closes with the book of Nehemiah.
It records how Nehemiah's heart responded as he managed public affairs, along with many devout reflections.

p.hi: Nehemiah's distress for the misery of Jerusalem, His prayer.

div.title: Nehemiah's concern and prayer
div.p: Nehemiah served as cupbearer to the Persian king. When God has work to accomplish, he will always have suitable people to do it.
Nehemiah lived comfortably and held an honored position. Nevertheless, he remembered that he was an Israelite and that his fellow Israelites were suffering.

He was ready to help them in every way he could. To find out how best to help, he asked about their condition. We should take a special interest in the condition of God's church and the state of religion.
Every earthly Jerusalem has shortcomings that need the support and service of its friends. Only the heavenly Jerusalem is without defect.

Nehemiah went first to God in prayer so that he could approach the king with greater confidence. Our strongest arguments in prayer come from God's own promises—the word on which he has taught us to hope.
We must also use the practical means available to us, but the earnest and effective prayer of a righteous person accomplishes much. Fellowship with God best prepares us for dealing with other people.
After we have entrusted a concern to God, our minds are set free. We gain contentment and composure, and our difficulties no longer seem insurmountable.
We know that if what we seek would harm us, God can readily prevent it; and if it would be good for us, he can just as readily bring it about.

div.title: Nehemiah asks the king (verses 1–8)
div.p: Our prayers must be accompanied by serious efforts; otherwise we are making a mockery of prayer.
We are not restricted to fixed times when approaching the King of kings. We may turn to him at any moment. It is never the wrong time to approach his throne of grace.
Yet God's displeasure and the suffering of his people cause sorrow to his children—a sorrow that no earthly pleasure can remove.
The king encouraged Nehemiah to explain what troubled him. This gave Nehemiah courage to speak.
How much greater courage should we take from Christ's invitation to pray and his promise that our prayers will be heard! We can approach the throne of grace with confidence.
Nehemiah prayed to the God of heaven, who is infinitely greater than the powerful earthly king standing before him.
He raised his heart to the God who understands the language of hearts.
We should never undertake anything for which it would be wrong to seek and expect God's guidance, help and blessing.
His prayer received an immediate answer: the descendants of Jacob have never sought the God of Jacob in vain.

div.title: Nehemiah comes to Jerusalem (verses 9–18)
div.p: After studying the situation, Nehemiah told the Jews that God had put it into his heart to rebuild Jerusalem's wall.
He did not intend to accomplish this work without them.
When we encourage ourselves and one another toward what is good, we strengthen one another to do it.
We perform our duties weakly when we are indifferent or careless.

div.title: Opposition to the work (verses 19 and 20)
div.p: The hostility of the serpent's offspring toward Christ's cause is not limited to any particular age or country.
The lesson for us is clear. God's church needs our help. Is it not exposed to attacks and sometimes left desolate?
Does its low condition grieve us?
We must not become so absorbed by business, amusement or support for a particular group that Zion and its welfare no longer matter to us.

p.hi: The rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem.

div.title: Rebuilding Jerusalem's walls
div.p: The work was divided so that everyone knew the particular task assigned to them and could attend to it with a desire to do it well.
They competed only in doing as much good as possible for the community, not in pursuing conflicting interests or quarrelling with one another.
Every Israelite should lend a hand in building up Jerusalem.
People in high positions should never consider a task beneath their dignity when it will benefit their country. Even some women joined in the work.
Some worked on sections opposite their own houses, and one worked opposite his room.
When a great common task needs doing, everyone should begin with the part within their own reach.
If everyone swept the space outside their own door, the whole street would be clean. If everyone repaired one part, the entire wall would be repaired.
Some who had finished their own assignments helped their neighbors finish theirs.
The broken walls and piles of debris around Jerusalem picture the desperate condition of the world around us.
The number and malice of the people hindering the construction give us some small idea of the enemies Christians meet while doing God's work.
Everyone must begin at home. By advancing God's work in our own souls, we can contribute most effectively to the good of Christ's church.

May the Lord stir up his people's hearts to set aside petty disputes and consider worldly interests insignificant compared with rebuilding Jerusalem's walls and defending truth and godliness against open enemies.

div.title: Sanballat and others oppose the work (verses 1–6)
div.p: Proud and arrogant mockers have despised many a good work.
People who disagree about almost everything may nevertheless unite in persecution.
Nehemiah did not answer foolish insults in kind. He looked up to God in prayer.
God's people have often been despised, but the Lord hears every insult directed toward them. This knowledge comforts them.
Nehemiah had reason to believe these enemies had become desperately hardened in heart; otherwise he would not have prayed that their sins never be wiped away.
Good work progresses well when people have the heart to do it. Enemy insults should make us more diligent in duty, not drive us away from it.

div.title: The enemies plan to stop the building (verses 7–15)
div.p: Wicked people aim to obstruct good work and expect their plans to succeed. But work done for God is his work, and it will prosper.
God can expose and defeat the plans of his church's enemies in many ways.
If our enemies cannot frighten us away from duty or deceive us into sin, they cannot truly hurt us.
Nehemiah entrusted himself and his cause to God's protection, as we should.
He laid all his cares, sorrows and fears before God.

p.hi: He prayed before taking practical measures. Then, after praying, he appointed a guard.

div.p: If we expect prayer to protect us without vigilance, we are lazy and put God to the test.
If we depend on vigilance without prayer, we are proud and disregard God.
Either way, we abandon the path of his protection.
God's care for our safety should encourage us to perform our duties vigorously.
Once the danger has passed, let us return to work and trust him when new trouble comes.

div.title: Nehemiah's precautions (verses 16–23)
div.p: We must remain watchful against spiritual enemies and not imagine that the struggle ends before our work is finished.
The word of God is the sword of the Spirit.
It should always be within reach, so that we never have to search for it when we are working or fighting as Christians.
Every true Christian is both a worker and a soldier, building with one hand and fighting with the other.
Good work progresses when those doing it treat it seriously.
Satan fears the watchful Christian. If he does attack, the Lord fights for his servant.
We must continue until the end of life, never putting aside our armor until our work and warfare have finished.
Then we will be welcomed into our Lord's rest and joy.

div.title: The people's grievances (verses 1–5)
div.p: People exploit one another. Those who despise the poor insult their Creator.
This is disgraceful conduct for anyone, but especially hateful when practiced by people who profess to be Christians.
We should sympathize with oppressed people and grieve over the hardships under which so many suffer.
We ought to put ourselves in their place, remembering them both in prayer and through practical help.
People who show no mercy must expect judgment without mercy.

div.title: Nehemiah confronts the abuses (verses 6–13)
div.p: Nehemiah knew that however high, thick or strong he built Jerusalem's walls, the city would remain insecure while injustice continued inside.
The right way to reform people's conduct is to convince their consciences.
Those who truly fear God will not covet worldly wealth or treat brothers and sisters cruelly.
Nothing brings more disgrace upon religion than worldliness and hardheartedness in those who claim to practice it.
People who insist harshly on every one of their own rights can scarcely persuade others to give up theirs.
When reasoning with selfish people, it is helpful to contrast their conduct with the generosity of others.
But the greatest example is Christ, who was rich and became poor for us, so that through his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).
The people did what they had promised.
Good promises are valuable, but doing what was promised is better.

div.title: Nehemiah's restraint as governor (verses 14–19)
div.p: Those who truly fear God will not dare to act cruelly or unjustly.
Everyone holding public office should remember that its purpose is to do good, not to enrich the officeholder.
Nehemiah asked God in prayer to remember his service.
He was not claiming to have earned favor from God.
Instead, he trusted God to make up for what he had spent or sacrificed for God's honor.
He spoke and acted as a person conscious of his own sin.
He did not demand a reward as a debt owed to him.
He looked to the Lord who graciously rewards even a cup of cold water given to a disciple for Christ's sake.
Fear and love of God, together with true love for brothers and sisters, lead to every good work.
These works are proper evidence of justifying faith, not the price paid to obtain it.
Our reconciled God regards such people for good according to their service for his people.

row.cell: False prophets try to frighten Nehemiah.
The wall finished, Treachery of some among the Jews.

div.title: Sanballat plots to hinder Nehemiah (verses 1–9)
div.p: When worthless companions try to lure us into idle, amusing gatherings, we can answer: We have work to do, and we must not neglect it.
We must never allow repeated pressure to wear us down into doing something sinful or unwise. When the same temptation returns, we must resist with the same reasons and determination.
Malicious people often claim that everyone wants something when in reality only they want it.
Nehemiah understood their intention. He denied not only the charges against him but also the claim that such rumors were being circulated.
His reputation was too well established for the accusations to be credible.
We should never abandon a known duty for fear that others may misunderstand it. Instead, maintain a good conscience and entrust your reputation to God.
Even when God's people are widely insulted, their good name may be far stronger than their opponents suggest.
Nehemiah sent up a brief prayer to heaven.
Whenever Christians face a task or a spiritual conflict, they may pray: God, strengthen my hands for the work and the temptation before me.
Every attempt to distract us from our duty should make us more determined to perform it.

div.title: False prophets attempt to frighten Nehemiah (verses 10–14)
div.p: The worst harm enemies can do to us is to frighten us away from good work or persuade us to sin.

p.hi: Never abandon a good work; never do a bad one.

div.p: Test every piece of advice and reject whatever contradicts God's word.
All believers should pursue consistency with their calling.
Can I profess to be a Christian, a saint, God's child, a member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit, yet still be greedy, sensual, proud, envious, impatient, discontented or angry?
Can I give in to laziness, unbelief or lack of mercy?
What influence will such behavior have on other people?
Everything God has done for us, given us or accomplished through us ought to make us vigilant, self-denying and diligent.
After sin's inherent evil, we should dread the scandal our sin brings upon God's cause.

div.title: The wall is completed despite betrayal (verses 15–19)
div.p: The wall was completed in fifty-two days, even though the workers rested on the Sabbaths.
Much can be accomplished in little time when people undertake a task sincerely and keep at it.
The alliances created through marriages with foreigners became harmful here.
Once people became relatives of Tobiah, they soon bound themselves to his cause.
Sinful affection can lead to sinful alliances.
The enemy of souls uses many agents and many schemes to disgrace active servants of God or draw them away from their service.
But we should follow the One who gave his life for the sheep.
Those who remain simply and faithfully devoted to the Lord and his work will receive his support.

row.cell: Register of those that first returned.

div.title: Jerusalem is entrusted to Hananiah (verses 1–4)
div.p: After completing the wall, Nehemiah returned to the Persian court.
He later came back to Jerusalem under a new commission.
Public safety depends in part upon every person's care to guard themselves and their households against sin.

div.title: The list of those who first returned (verses 5–73)
div.p: Nehemiah knew that, under God, a city's safety depends more on the character of its inhabitants than on the strength of its walls.
Every good gift and good work comes from heaven.
God grants both knowledge and grace. Everything comes from him, so everything should be devoted to him.
When human foresight produces good results, we must acknowledge the direction of divine Providence.
How terrible for those who turn away from the Lord because they love the present world!
How happy those who dedicate themselves and their possessions to God's service and glory!

row.cell: The reading and expounding the law.
The people called upon to be joyful.
The feast of tabernacles, The joy of the people.

div.title: The law is read and explained (verses 1–8)
div.p: Sacrifices had to be offered at the entrance of the temple.
Prayer and preaching, however, could be carried out acceptably in many different places, both then and now.
Household leaders should bring their families to public worship.
Women and children have souls that need salvation. They therefore need to know God's word and attend the means of grace.
Young children should be taught religion as soon as they become capable of understanding it.
Ministers should take their Bibles into the pulpit, as Ezra did.
Scripture must be the source of their knowledge and the standard for everything they teach.
Reading Scripture aloud in a gathered congregation is an ordinance God has appointed to honor himself and build up his church.
Listeners need to understand what they hear. Otherwise it is only an empty sequence of words.
Teachers must therefore explain the text and make its meaning clear.
Reading is valuable and preaching is valuable. But explaining the meaning of Scripture helps people understand what is read and makes preaching more convincing.
In almost every age God has raised up preachers and also writers who explain biblical truth.
Some commentators have made matters darker through ignorant words, but the work of others has been extremely useful.
Nevertheless, every teaching must be tested by Scripture.
The people listened eagerly and paid attention to every word.
God's word deserves our close attention. If carelessness makes us miss much while listening, forgetfulness may cause us to lose everything afterward.

div.title: The people are told to rejoice (verses 9–12)
div.p: The people's tears when they heard God's law showed that their hearts had become tender.
They were told to send food to those who had nothing prepared.
Both a solemn feast and a solemn fast should move us to compassion for hungry people.
God's generosity should make us generous, not only to people who come asking but also to those we must actively seek out.

p.hi: Their strength lay in joy in the Lord.

div.p: The more deeply we understand God's word, the greater comfort we find in it.
Much of the darkness we experience in trouble comes from ignorance.

div.title: The Feast of Tabernacles (verses 13–18)
div.p: Through careful study, the people rediscovered the law concerning the Feast of Tabernacles.
People who diligently search Scripture often find instructions they had forgotten.
The feast pictured the believer's temporary dwelling in this world and the holy joy of the gospel church.
Zechariah's prophecy pictures the nations coming to faith in Christ through this feast (Zechariah 14:16).
True religion makes us recognize ourselves as strangers and pilgrims on earth.
We read and hear God's word rightly when we do what it commands, including renewing duties long neglected.
The people observed the reality signified by the ceremony. Without that, the outward rite would have been useless.
They obeyed while rejoicing in God and his goodness.
These are the appointed means through which the Holy Spirit brings sinners to reverence, repentance and humility before God.
But those who continually indulge sorrow—even sorrow for sin—and refuse the comfort offered through God's word and Spirit become enemies of their own growth in holiness.

div.title: The people fast and read God's word (verses 1–3)
div.p: Scripture directs and strengthens our prayers because the Spirit uses it to help us in our weakness.
Careful study of God's word increasingly shows us our sinfulness and the abundance of his salvation.
It calls us both to mourn our sin and to rejoice in him.
Every new discovery of divine truth should make us more diligent, not less diligent, in hearing God's word and taking part in his worship.

div.title: Prayer, history and confession (verses 4–38)
div.p: Scripture preserves a summary of the prayers offered on this occasion. Undoubtedly much more was said.
Whatever ability God gives us for our duties should be used as fully as possible for his glory.
When confessing sin, it is good to remember God's mercies. His generosity makes our ingratitude more evident and deepens our humility and shame.
The Lord's treatment of Israel displayed his goodness and patience alongside the stubbornness of the people's hearts.
The prophets' testimony was the Spirit's testimony through them—the Spirit of Christ speaking through the prophets.
They spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit, so their words must be received accordingly.
The account moved the people to wonder at God's mercy and to recognize that their sins had brought them into their present condition.
Only unearned love could deliver them.
Is their history not a picture of our common human nature?
Let us examine our nation's history and our own lives.
Recall the advantages we had from childhood and ask how we first responded to them.
Do this often so we may remain humble, grateful and alert.
Pride and stubborn resistance to God destroy the soul.
Yet sometimes it is just as difficult to persuade a brokenhearted sinner to hope as it once was to persuade that sinner to fear.
Are you in that condition?
Consider the wonderful promise that God is ready to forgive.
Do not stay away from him because you feel unworthy.
Come boldly to his throne of grace, where mercy and timely help can be found.

p.hi: He is ready to forgive.

row.cell: The covenant, Those who signed it.

div.title: The covenant is signed (verses 1–31)
div.p: Conversion means separating from the ways and habits of this world and devoting ourselves to the conduct commanded in God's word.
When we bind ourselves to obey God's commands, we undertake to obey all of them.
We also acknowledge that he is not only the Lord in a general sense, but our Lord.

div.title: The people undertake renewed worship (verses 32–39)
div.p: Having made a covenant against the sins they had committed, the people now undertook the duties they had neglected.
We must do more than stop doing evil: we must learn to do good.
No community should expect God's blessing while allowing public worship to fall into neglect.
Families are more likely to prosper when God's house and its work are properly supported.
When everyone contributes, even if each individual gift is small, the combined contribution can be substantial.
We must do what we can in acts of devotion and charity.
Whatever our circumstances, we should joyfully carry out our duty to God. This is the surest path to freedom and contentment.
God's appointed ordinances nourish and strengthen believers' souls, so they should not resent the expense of supporting them.
Yet many people let their souls go hungry.

p.hi: The distribution of the people.

div.title: The people settle in Jerusalem
div.p: In every age, people have often preferred their personal comfort and advantage to the common good.
Even those who profess faith frequently seek their own interests rather than the interests of Christ.
Few have loved holy things and places enough to give up their comforts for them.
Yet our souls should delight to live where faithful people and opportunities for spiritual growth are plentiful.
If we have no love for the city of our God, or for anything that helps us enjoy fellowship with the Savior, how will we gladly depart this life to be with the Lord?
To a worldly-minded person, the perfect holiness of the New Jerusalem would be even more difficult to bear than the holiness of God's church on earth.
Let us seek first God's favor and glory.
Let us learn patience, contentment and usefulness in whatever place he has assigned us, looking forward with cheerful hope to entering the holy city of God.

row.cell: The priests and Levites that returned.
The officers of the temple settled.

div.title: The priests and Levites who returned (verses 1–26)
div.p: We owe faithful ministers a debt of gratitude.
Remember the leaders who taught us God's word.
It is good to learn what our godly predecessors were like, so that we can learn what we ought to become.

div.title: The wall is dedicated (verses 27–43)
div.p: All our towns and houses should bear the mark “Holy to the Lord.”
A believer should undertake no task without dedicating it to him.
When our hands are to be used in God's work, we should cleanse those hands and purify our hearts.
Those called to help others become holy must first consecrate themselves to God.
For people sanctified to him, the good gifts and comforts of creation also become holy in their use.
The people rejoiced greatly.

p.hi: Everyone who benefits from a public blessing should share in public thanksgiving.

div.title: Temple officers are appointed (verses 44–47)
div.p: A day of thanksgiving truly benefits both ministers and people when it leaves them more careful and joyful in fulfilling their duties.
Whatever we do must be cleansed by the atoning blood and through the grace of the Holy Spirit.
Otherwise our work cannot be acceptable to God.

row.cell: Nehemiah turns out the mixed multitude.
Nehemiah's reform in the house of God.

div.title: Nehemiah removes unlawful influences (verses 1–9)
div.p: Israel was a people set apart and was not to mix indiscriminately with the surrounding nations.
Notice the benefit of the public reading of God's word.
When we listen properly, Scripture shows us sin and duty, right and wrong, and where we have wandered from the Lord.
We profit when it moves us to separate ourselves from evil.
Anyone seeking to drive sin out of the heart—the living temple of God—must also remove what supplies it with pleasure and strength.
Take away the food and fuel of sinful desire. This is what it means to put sin to death.
Once repentance has driven sin from the heart, Christ's blood must be applied by faith, and the heart should be furnished with the graces of the Holy Spirit for every good work.

div.title: Nehemiah corrects the support of worship (verses 10–14)
div.p: Sacred office does not excuse someone from correction or deserved discipline when that person sets an evil example.
The Levites had been wronged because their allotted support had not been paid.
They had gone elsewhere to earn a living for themselves and their families. Their service in the sanctuary could no longer sustain them.

p.hi: Inadequate support leads to an impoverished ministry.

div.p: The work was neglected because the workers had been neglected.
Nehemiah held the rulers accountable.
Ministers and people who abandon religious duties, as well as rulers who fail to uphold them according to their responsibility, must answer for their actions.
Nehemiah acted promptly to restore the Levites to their places and ensure that they were paid fairly.
He continually looked to God and entrusted all his concerns to him.
It pleased him to have been useful in restoring and supporting religion among his people.
He asked God to remember the work, not from pride, but as a humble appeal regarding the honesty of his intentions.
He prayed, “Remember me”, not “Give me what I have earned.”
He asked that his work not be forgotten, not that it be advertised for praise.
Yet God both rewarded him and preserved the record of what he had done.
God does more than we can ask.

div.title: Nehemiah stops Sabbath-breaking (verses 15–22)
div.p: People seeking to promote godliness must pay attention to keeping the Lord's day holy.
True religion cannot flourish while Sabbaths are treated with contempt.
No wonder Judah's faith and conduct had deteriorated when the people neglected worship and profaned the Sabbath.
Those who profane it often fail to recognize the harm they do.
We must answer for sins encouraged in others by our own example.
Nehemiah condemned their conduct as evil because it sprang from contempt for God and disregard for their souls.
He reminded them that violating the Sabbath was among the sins that had brought earlier judgments.
Repeating the same sins would expose them to further judgment.
His courage, zeal and prudent action provide an example. Henry considers it likely the reform endured.
Nehemiah nevertheless confessed himself a sinner who could demand nothing from God on the basis of justice.
He asked the Lord for mercy.

div.title: Nehemiah confronts unlawful marriages (verses 23–31)
div.p: If one parent is ungodly, human sinful nature may incline children to follow that parent's example.
This is a serious reason why Christians should not enter marriages that bind them unequally to unbelievers.
Parents must also give careful attention to how their children speak, so that they do not learn the corrupt and irreverent language associated here with Ashdod.
Nehemiah exposed the evil of these marriages.

Those who remained stubborn were punished. Henry explains the physical punishment as ordered through the lawful officers under the civil law then in effect (Deuteronomy 25:2–3), rather than describing a private beating.
He prayed that God would remember them—that the Lord would convince and convert them and remind them of their duty.
Even the best public service may be forgotten by its beneficiaries.
Nehemiah therefore entrusted his reward to God.
His final request also expresses what we most need:

p.hi: “Remember me, my God, for good.”

div.p: We may hope humbly that God will remember us and the service we have rendered, while still acknowledging our sins and seeking mercy after a whole life of useful work.
Like Nehemiah, we have reason to repent deeply and pray to be spared according to the abundance of God's mercy.

div.title: Esther — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The book of Esther shows God's care for the Jews who had been scattered among the peoples of a foreign empire.
He preserved them wonderfully when they faced destruction.
Although God's name does not appear in the book, his providential hand can be seen in the smallest events that contributed to the deliverance of his people.
The events belong historically between Ezra chapters 6 and 7.

row.cell: Vashti's refusal to appear, The king's decree.

div.title: Ahasuerus holds a royal feast (verses 1–9)
div.p: Pride rose in Ahasuerus's heart as his kingdom became magnificent, and he gave an extravagant feast.
This was an exhibition of empty self-glory.
A simple meal of vegetables enjoyed in peace is better than an enormous banquet of wine accompanied by noise and disorder.
Unless grace rules a person's heart, self-exaltation and self-indulgence will govern life in one form or another.
Yet the king did not require anyone to drink. Those who became drunk had only themselves to blame.
Even this precaution by a pagan ruler should shame many who call themselves Christians.
Some pressure their companions into drinking to excess under the pretense of celebrating one another's health.
In doing so they encourage sin and bring spiritual death alongside it.
God's warning against such people is serious (Habakkuk 2:15–16).
Let them read it and tremble.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): 2 Corinthians 2:16.
Verified editorial cross-reference: Hab.2.16.

div.title: Vashti refuses; the king makes a decree (verses 10–22)
div.p: Through his own folly Ahasuerus turned his festival into distress.
Special celebrations often end with trouble and annoyance.
People in authority should be careful not to give commands that others may reasonably refuse to obey.
When wine governs a person, sound judgment is lost.
Ahasuerus ruled 127 provinces but could not govern his own temper.
Whether the decree served his anger or his political interests, divine Providence used it to prepare the way for Esther to become queen.
God was already defeating Haman's wicked plot before Haman even imagined it or rose to power.
We should rejoice that the Lord reigns.
He can overrule human frenzy and foolishness to accomplish his own glory and secure his people's welfare and happiness.

row.cell: Mordecai discovers a plot against the king.

div.title: Esther becomes queen (verses 1–20)
div.p: Without divine revelation, people have often embraced unreasonable social practices.
The arrangement described here shows the need for the gospel of Jesus Christ, which cleanses people of sinful desires and calls them back to the original design of marriage.
Esther was chosen as queen.
Henry warns against accusing her of sin merely for entering this situation without understanding the customs of the time and region.
In Henry's account of those customs, any woman whom the king took became his wife, though she might hold a lower rank than the queen.
How far human nature has fallen when worldly status and bodily pleasure become people's highest goals!
Disappointment and trouble inevitably accompany such pursuits.
The person best placed to enjoy even this present life is the one who most carefully obeys God's commands.
Yet amid these human practices, we should recognize God's wise and merciful providence, carrying forward purposes both hidden and holy.
A change in social position never excuses us from our duties to our parents or to people who have fulfilled a parent's role in our lives.

div.title: Mordecai discovers a conspiracy (verses 21–23)
div.p: Good citizens must not conceal a plot they know about against the ruler or the public peace.
Mordecai received no immediate reward for exposing the conspiracy.
But a written record preserved his service.
Similarly, people who serve Christ may not receive their reward until the resurrection of the righteous.
Yet God keeps an account of every act of faithful work and loving service.
He does not unjustly forget any of it.
Those who serve God should faithfully discharge every trust and remain watchful for the interests of those who employ them.
Even if they appear to be overlooked now, their service will be remembered later.
Nothing we do is forgotten. Even hidden thoughts are recorded in enduring books (Revelation 20:12).

row.cell: Haman seeks to destroy the Jews.
He obtains a decree against the Jews.

div.title: Haman seeks to destroy the Jews (verses 1–6)
div.p: Mordecai refused to show Haman the reverence demanded of him.
The Jewish faith forbade giving any human being honors that resembled idolatrous worship, especially a wicked person like Haman.
Human beings naturally tend toward idolatry: self is our favorite idol, and we enjoy being treated as though everything belonged to us.
Faith does not abolish good manners. On the contrary, it teaches us to give appropriate honor to those who deserve it.
Yet someone belonging to Zion must regard a wicked person like Haman as contemptible, not only inwardly but in judgment and conduct (Psalm 15:4).
True believers cannot obey decrees or follow fashions that violate God's commands.
They must obey God rather than human beings, leaving the consequences in his hands.
Haman became furious.
His plot reflected the spirit of the murderer from the beginning, whose hatred toward Christ and the church rules those who follow him.

div.title: Haman obtains a decree (verses 7–15)
div.p: Anyone who knows the human heart and human history should understand how a ruler could agree to a proposal so cruel and contrary to his own interests.
We should be thankful for mild and just government.
Haman tried to discover, through his superstition, an auspicious day for the massacre he intended.
God's wisdom used that folly to accomplish his own purposes.
The lot Haman cast delayed the date of the planned killing and thereby helped bring about his defeat.
The episode displays God's particular Providence in human affairs and his care for the church.
Haman feared that the king might be troubled by what he had approved, so he encouraged him to continue drinking.
People often try to drown their convictions and harden their own hearts and others' hearts through intoxication.
Everything seemed to be moving toward Haman's goal.
Yet God can allow sinners to progress far in their plans before his unseen, almighty power turns them back.
Even the strongest attack against Jehovah is vain.
If Haman had destroyed the Jewish people, how could God's promises and prophecies about the world's Redeemer have been fulfilled?

p.hi: God's everlasting covenant would have had to fail first.

row.cell: Esther undertakes to plead for the Jews.

div.title: The Jews grieve over the decree (verses 1–4)
div.p: Mordecai openly acknowledged his connection with the Jewish people.
Trouble affecting God's church should weigh more heavily upon us than private misfortune.
It is especially painful to know that our own conduct has contributed to other people's suffering.
God will preserve those whose sensitive consciences expose them to danger.

div.title: Esther decides to intercede (verses 5–17)
div.p: We naturally shrink from tasks that may cost us dearly or endanger us.
But when Christ's cause and people need our service, we must take up our cross and follow him.
Christians should be corrected when they seek personal comfort or safety at the expense of the public good.
The Persian law against approaching the king uninvited was explicit and widely known.

p.hi: It is not like that at the court of the King of kings.

div.p: We may always come boldly to the throne of grace, expecting God's peaceful answer to faithful prayer.
Through Jesus' blood, we are welcome even into the holiest place.
God's Providence had arranged for the king's affection toward Esther to cool by this time, according to Henry's interpretation.
This made her faith and courage face a greater test and the king's eventual kindness more remarkable.
Haman, Henry supposes, had probably also tried to turn the king against her.
Mordecai believed that the Jewish people's cause would succeed one way or another.
Esther could therefore undertake her duty with confidence.
This was the language of strong faith, trusting God's promise even when hope seemed impossible.
Someone who tries to preserve life through sinful methods instead of trusting God while doing duty will lose it by sin.
Esther's royal position had been prepared through Providence for precisely such service.
Gratitude obliged her to act for God and his people.
Otherwise, she would fail to fulfill the purpose of her promotion.
God's wise counsel is at work in every event, directing it toward the church's ultimate good.
Each of us should consider why God has placed us where we are and seek to fulfill our calling before the opportunity passes.
Once we have committed ourselves and our cause to God, we may courageously undertake his service.
Every earthly danger is small compared with the danger of losing our souls.
Sinners who tremble before God can resemble Esther before the king: they fear entrusting themselves entirely to his mercy.
Let such a person approach with earnest prayer.
God will receive them even more graciously than Ahasuerus received Esther.
God's cause will prevail, and those united to it are safe.

div.title: The king receives Esther (verses 1–8)
div.p: Esther had prevailed with God, as Jacob did, and therefore found favor with a human ruler too.
Whoever is willing to lose life for God will save it, or receive a better life.
The king encouraged her.
Let that encourage us to pray continually and not give up.
Esther approached a proud, imperious man.
We approach the God of love and grace.
Esther was not invited, but we are invited: the Spirit and the bride say, “Come.”
She faced a law against her.
We have many promises in our favor: Ask, and it will be given.
She had no friend to accompany her or plead for her.
Indeed, the king's current favorite was her enemy.
But we have an Advocate before the Father, one in whom the Father delights.
Therefore, approach the throne of grace boldly.
God moved Esther to postpone her request for one more day.
She did not know what would happen that very night, but God did.

div.title: Haman plans Mordecai's execution (verses 9–14)
div.p: Haman's behavior illustrates Proverbs 21:24.
People who admire and flatter themselves are actually deceiving themselves.
The higher Haman rose, the less patiently he endured even a small sign of disrespect.
Mordecai's conduct ruined his pleasure in everything else.
A slight insult that a humble person might scarcely notice can torment a proud person almost to madness.
Those determined to be unhappy will always find something to make them unhappy.
Proud people can possess nearly everything they desire, yet if they lack one thing, all the rest becomes worthless in their eyes.
Many admire the wealthy and powerful who surround themselves with splendor.
But this is a mistaken view of happiness.
Many poor families in small cottages have far less anxiety than wealthy people living amid supposed advantages.
Whoever does not know Christ is poor, however much wealth that person possesses, because the only true riches are missing.

row.cell: Providence recommends Mordecai to the king's favour.
Haman's friends tell him of his danger.

div.title: Providence brings Mordecai to the king's attention (verses 1–3)
div.p: God's Providence governs even the smallest human concerns.
Not even a sparrow falls to the ground without him.
Consider the steps through which Providence brought Mordecai into a place of honor.
The king could not sleep because God had a purpose to accomplish through his wakefulness.
Nothing suggests an illness interrupted his sleep.
God simply withheld it, though sleep itself is a gift from him.
A man who could command 127 provinces could not command one hour of sleep.

div.title: Haman advises the king to honor Mordecai (verses 4–11)
div.p: See how pride deceives people.
Nothing reveals the deceitfulness of our hearts more clearly than our exaggerated opinion of ourselves and our achievements.
We must continually watch and pray against this tendency.
Haman assumed the king could not possibly honor anyone but him.
He was mistaken.
We should be cautious about assuming the admiration other people express is as great as it appears.
That caution protects us against self-importance and excessive dependence upon people's favor.
What a shock Haman received when the king ordered him to honor Mordecai the Jew, the very person Haman hated most and was planning to kill!

div.title: Haman returns humiliated (verses 12–14)
div.p: Mordecai did not become proud because of his new honor.
He returned to his place and his duty.
Honor is well given to those who do not believe themselves above ordinary work.
Haman, however, could not bear the humiliation.
What real harm had Mordecai's honor done him?
Yet something that scarcely interrupts a humble person's sleep can break a proud person's heart.
Haman's wife and friends now foretold his downfall.
They recognized plainly that the scattered Jewish people enjoyed God's special protection.
But they were miserable comforters.
They did not tell Haman to repent, only that destruction was unavoidable.
God's wisdom appears in the timing of his church's deliverance, which brings glory to his own name.

row.cell: Haman hanged on his own gallows.

div.title: Esther accuses Haman (verses 1–6)
div.p: If our love of life causes us to plead earnestly before people who can only kill the body, how much more fervently should we pray to God, who can judge both body and soul!
How earnestly should we pray for the salvation of family, friends and everyone around us!
When petitioning powerful people, we must sometimes hold back even just complaints for fear of offending them.
But when we approach the King of kings with reverence, we cannot ask or expect too much.
Although we deserve only God's judgment, he is both willing and able to do far more than we can ask or imagine.

div.title: Haman dies on the gallows he built (verses 7–10)
div.p: The king became angry.
People who act according to their own will sometimes later condemn themselves for their actions.
When anger rises, we should delay making decisions and thus show control over ourselves and obedience to sound reason.
People who are proudest and most overbearing when powerful often become the most servile and timid when their position collapses.
The day will come when those who hate and persecute God's chosen people will gladly seek help from them.
The king returned even angrier with Haman.
His attendants were ready to carry out his judgment.
How little confidence proud people can have in the influence they imagine they possess!
The enemies of God's church have often been trapped by their own schemes.
Such judgments display the Lord's righteousness.
The king's anger was finally satisfied.
Few would pity Haman for dying on the gallows he had constructed for another; Henry calls readers to recognize God's justice in the outcome.
Let those who commit evil tremble, turn to the Lord and seek forgiveness through Jesus' blood.

row.cell: Esther makes suit for the Jews.
Mordecai honoured, The joy of the Jews.

div.title: Mordecai receives Haman's former position (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Esther intended to use for good what Haman had meant to use for evil.
The responsibility and trust the king had given Haman now passed to Mordecai—a welcome change.
See the emptiness of accumulating treasure on earth.
The person who stores up wealth cannot know who will eventually enjoy it.
Had Haman known that his most hated enemy would take control of everything he worked to acquire, even looking at his possessions would have brought distress instead of pleasure.
We should therefore seek riches that cannot be left behind, but will accompany us into eternity.

div.title: Esther pleads for her people (verses 3–14)
div.p: With the church of God in danger, earnest action was necessary.
Though Esther herself was safe, she fell before the king and begged him to rescue her people.
No tears are recorded when she sought protection for her own life.
But when her people's safety was at stake, she wept.
Such compassion and tender concern most closely resemble Christ.
Persian government treated royal decrees as unchangeable and impossible to recall.
Far from proving the wisdom of its rulers, this displayed their pride and folly.
It resembled the arrogant desire to be like gods.
Only God has the right to declare what cannot be changed or withdrawn.
Nevertheless, a solution was found: a second decree permitted the Jews to defend themselves.
The decree was published in the languages of all the provinces.
If earthly rulers make their laws available in languages their subjects understand, how could Christians justify keeping God's words and commands in a language his servants cannot understand?

div.title: Mordecai is honored and the Jews rejoice (verses 15–17)
div.p: Mordecai now wore splendid royal clothing.
This mattered not for its own sake but as evidence of the king's approval and of God's favor toward the church.
A country is fortunate when positions of honor are filled by people of genuine devotion.
When God's church prospers, many will join it who would avoid identifying with it during persecution.
When believers experience peace and walk in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit, they grow in number.
Satan's attempts to destroy the church ultimately help bring more people into genuine Christian faith.

row.cell: The feast of Purim in remembrance of this.

div.title: The Jews are delivered (verses 1–19)
