div.p: The enemies of the Jews expected to defeat them under the earlier royal decree.
Had those enemies not tried to harm God's people, they would not themselves have suffered.
The Jews acted together and strengthened one another.
We should likewise remain firm in one spirit and with one mind, standing together against the spiritual enemies who seek to rob us of faith, a possession worth more than life.
The Jews refused to enrich themselves through plunder.
This honored their faith by showing that they sought only their own preservation.
In every circumstance God's people should be compassionate and free from selfish motives.
They may wisely decline advantages they could lawfully claim.
The Jews celebrated the day after their work ended.
Whenever God grants a great mercy, we should respond promptly with thanksgiving.

div.title: The Feast of Purim is established (verses 20–32)
div.p: The continued observance of Jewish festivals publicly testifies to the truth of the Old Testament Scriptures.
Henry argues from that truth that the promised Messiah has already come and that Jesus of Nazareth alone fulfills the promise.
Purim was established through public authority, yet under God's guidance by the Holy Spirit.
The name Purim comes from a Persian word meaning “lot.”
That name reminded the Jews how the Almighty used even pagan superstition to carry out his purposes.
When we remember God's mercies, we should also remember the fears and distress from which he delivered us.
We must not forget personal mercies and thereby lose their comfort or withhold the glory owed to God.
May he teach us to rejoice with a holy joy that anticipates and prepares us for heaven's happiness.
Every act of divine goodness toward us creates a fresh obligation to do good to others, especially to those in greatest need.
Above all, our redemption through Christ calls us to mercy and generosity (2 Corinthians 8:9).

p.hi: Greatness of Ahasuerus—Mordecai's advancement.

div.title: Mordecai's greatness and service
div.p: Many more stories of Ahasuerus's greatness could have been told.
They were recorded in Persian chronicles that have long since disappeared.
But Scripture will remain as long as time endures.
The Holy Spirit considers the concerns of the Lord's despised worshipers more important than the exploits of even the most impressive earthly ruler.
Mordecai was truly great, and his higher position gave him greater opportunities to do good.
He did not deny his people, the Jews, and undoubtedly continued in the true faith.
He sought not his own wealth but his people's welfare.
Few have the opportunity to do as much good as Mordecai.
Yet all have the ability to do harm, and everyone has some ability to do good.
We are not required to do what lies beyond our abilities or outside the responsibilities of our position.
But we are all called to live according to the spirit displayed by the faithful people whose examples Scripture records.
If we live by faith in Christ, we will actively use whatever opportunities and abilities he gives us to promote his glory and other people's highest good.

p.hi: Genuine faith works through love.

div.p: Wait upon God in faith and prayer.
The final outcome will be secure and glorious, because our salvation is certain through our Lord Jesus Christ.

div.title: Job — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The book takes its name from Job, whose prosperity, suffering and restoration it records.
Henry places Job's lifetime soon after Abraham, or possibly before him.
He regards it as most likely that Job himself wrote the book, and calls it the most ancient book in existence.
These are the commentator's historical judgments; the text does not establish them as independently verified conclusions.
The lessons drawn from Job's patience and trials remain as necessary now as ever.
We live under the same divine Providence and the care of the same heavenly Father, who corrects his children to lead them toward righteousness.
Job showed considerable courage and patience, but even these weakened under severe suffering.
His faith, however, remained directed toward his coming Redeemer. That faith gave him endurance while every other support was tested and consumed, particularly the pride of self-righteousness.
Another great teaching displayed throughout the book is divine Providence.
The narrative shows that the Lord watched over Job with the affection of a wise and loving father.

row.cell: The piety and prosperity of Job.
Satan obtains leave to try Job.
The loss of Job's property, and the death of his children.

div.title: Job's godliness and prosperity (verses 1–5)
div.p: Job was wealthy, yet he was also godly.
Although it is difficult and rare for a rich person to enter God's kingdom, it is not impossible.
By God's grace, people can overcome the temptations that accompany wealth.
The record of Job's faith and prosperity comes before the account of his great suffering.
This shows that neither wealth nor godliness keeps a person free from trouble.
Job rejoiced in his children's companionship and happiness, yet his understanding of the human heart made him concerned about their spiritual condition.
He called them to be consecrated, examine their conduct, confess sin and seek forgiveness.
He offered a burnt offering for each child, trusting in acceptance through the promised Savior.
This reveals his concern for their souls, his understanding of human sin and his full dependence upon divine mercy in the way God had appointed.

div.title: Satan receives permission to test Job (verses 6–12)
div.p: Job's trials began through Satan's hostility, under God's permission and for purposes that were wise and holy.
An evil spirit opposes God and all righteousness.
He continually tries to trouble, mislead and, if possible, destroy those who love God.
We do not know how far his influence extends, but Henry judges it probable that much instability and unhappiness among Christians can be attributed to his attacks.
While we remain in this world, we are within his reach.
We must therefore be sober and alert (1 Peter 5:8).
Satan slandered Job by suggesting something he had no reason to believe.
This is the ordinary way of people who defame others.
We should fear actually being hypocrites more than almost anything else.
But we need fear very little when people falsely call us hypocrites without evidence.
It is not wrong to be encouraged by the hope of eternal reward.
It is wrong, however, to practice religion merely to gain worldly advantages.
God specially protects his people and what belongs to them.
Even Satan recognized that the Lord's blessing had made Job prosper.
God permitted the testing of Job, just as he later allowed Peter to be sifted.
Our comfort is that God holds the devil on a chain (Revelation 20:1).
Satan cannot lead people into sin without their consenting to it.
Nor can he afflict them beyond what divine permission allows.
The conversation in this passage is described in human terms to teach us that the Lord rules all affairs of the world.

div.title: Job loses his possessions and children (verses 13–19)
div.p: Satan brought these disasters upon Job when his children were gathered for one of their feasts.
The troubles arrived in rapid succession.
Before one messenger had finished reporting a disaster, another came.
Then Job learned that his ten children had died.
They were his dearest possessions and would have been the greatest comfort to him amid the loss of everything else.
They were taken precisely when he most needed them.

p.hi: Only in God do we have help available at every moment.

div.title: Job responds in humble faith (verses 20–22)
div.p: Job humbled himself before the Lord.
He considered the condition shared by every human being.
We bring none of this world's possessions into life.
Everything we have is received from others, and we must leave it to others when we die.
Job had only been returned to the condition in which he entered the world—and to which he must eventually have come.
He had been stripped of his earthly burdens earlier than he expected.
Taking off clothing before bedtime may be inconvenient, but it is easier to bear when the hour of rest is already close.
The One who gave these gifts had also taken them away.
Job looked beyond the human agents and instruments of his suffering to the First Cause.
Suffering should drive us toward God, not away from him.
If we turn to him in every difficulty, he will sustain us.
The Lord is righteous.
Everything we possess is his gift. Through sin we have forfeited any claim upon it, so we cannot accuse God of injustice if he takes some of it away.
Discontent and impatience effectively accuse God of foolishness.
Job resisted that temptation, as we must.
God has acted both justly and wisely, even though we have often acted wickedly and foolishly.
May Satan's hostility make the Savior all the more precious to us.
Christ came to destroy the devil's works and, for our salvation, suffered far more from that enemy than Job did or we can imagine.

row.cell: Satan obtains leave to try Job.
His friends come to comfort him.

div.title: Satan is permitted another test (verses 1–6)
div.p: It is a great comfort that neither human beings nor evil spirits will be our final judges.
Our judgment comes from the Lord, who never makes a mistake.
Job continued holding firmly to his integrity as his defense.
God spoke with pleasure about the power of his own grace at work in Job.
People naturally desire to preserve their lives and protect their interests.
But Satan presented Job as though he were entirely selfish, concerned only for personal comfort and safety.
The devil and his agents frequently misrepresent God's servants in this way.
Satan was granted another opportunity to test Job, but only within a limit set by God.
If the Lord did not restrain this roaring lion, how quickly he would devour us!
In being falsely accused by Satan, Job was a figure of Christ, about whom the first promise declared that the serpent would wound his heel but be defeated.

div.title: Job's bodily suffering and his wife's words (verses 7–10)
div.p: The devil tempts his own followers, draws them into sin and torments them after their ruin.
With this child of God, he first inflicted suffering and then tempted Job to respond sinfully to the suffering.
He urged Job to curse God.
Job's disease was extremely painful.
When we suffer severe illness, we should not imagine God has treated us in a way wholly unknown to his most faithful servants.
Job humbled himself under God's mighty hand and sought to bring his thoughts into agreement with his circumstances.
His wife remained alive but became another source of pain and temptation to him.
Satan still attempts to draw people away from God, as he tempted the first parents, by persuading them to think harshly and falsely about the Lord.
Job resisted and overcame this temptation.
We receive countless blessings we have not earned from a just and holy God.
How could we refuse to accept suffering when our sins deserve more than we endure?
Let us reject murmuring as firmly as boasting.
So far Job had withstood the trial and shone most brightly in the furnace.
Some sinful impulses may have stirred in his heart, but grace prevailed over them.

div.title: Job's friends come to comfort him (verses 11–13)
div.p: Job's friends appear to have been people of high standing as well as wisdom and godliness.
Much of life's comfort comes from friendship with thoughtful and virtuous people.
They came to mourn with Job and showed genuine sorrow.
They came to comfort him and sat beside him.
Yet they apparently began to suspect that his unprecedented troubles were punishment for some hidden wrongdoing concealed under his profession of godliness.
Some people regard visiting a suffering friend as no more than a polite duty.
We should regard it as a genuine obligation of compassion.
If the example of Job's friends does not move us to pity the afflicted, let us seek the mind of Christ.

row.cell: Job complains that he was born.

div.title: Job laments his birth (verses 1–10)
div.p: Job's friends had sat beside him for seven days without offering comfort.
Meanwhile Satan attacked Job's mind, attempting to undermine his confidence and fill him with harsh thoughts about God.
The divine permission seems to have extended to such inward attacks as well as to physical pain.
Job was in a special way a figure of Christ.
Our Savior's inward suffering, in Gethsemane and upon the cross, was especially dreadful. Henry relates much of it to Satan's attacks in that hour of darkness.
These inward trials help explain why Job's response changed from complete submission to the impatience heard here and later in the book.

Believers who have tasted the bitterness of inward spiritual trials know they can be more dreadful than even severe outward trouble, especially in comparison with the sweetness of enjoying God's love and presence.
We should therefore not be astonished that Job shared ordinary human weaknesses.
Yet we should rejoice that Satan failed to prove him a hypocrite.
Job cursed the day of his birth, but he did not curse his God.
Henry believes Job afterward regretted these wishes, and supposes he would judge them even more clearly now in everlasting happiness.

div.title: Job asks why he did not die at birth (verses 11–19)
div.p: Job complained about the tender care he had received from those present at his birth.
No creature enters the world more helpless than a human baby.
God's power and Providence sustained our fragile lives.
His mercy and patience spared lives already forfeited through sin.
God himself placed natural affection for children in parents' hearts.
There is an important difference between desiring to depart and be with Christ, free from sin and desiring death simply as an escape from life's suffering.
The first desire can grow from grace; the second betrays remaining sin.
Wisdom and duty require us to make the best of our present condition, whether living or dying.
We should live for the Lord and die for the Lord, belonging to him in either case (Romans 14:8).
Job described the grave as a place where the wicked no longer trouble anyone and the weary rest.
When persecutors die, they can no longer persecute.
Those who are exhausted cease from their labors.
But an even better rest—free from sin, temptation, conflict, grief and labor—awaits believers in the enjoyment of God's presence.
There they rest in Jesus.
Even now, insofar as we trust and obey Christ, we find rest for our souls amid the troubles of this world.

div.title: Job finds life unbearable (verses 20–26)
div.p: Job felt like someone who had lost the way and could see no hope of escape or better days.
Yet this was a poor state of mind in which to approach death: he was unwilling to go on living.
Our constant concern should be to prepare for the life to come and leave to God the timing of our departure.
Grace teaches us to be willing to die even amid life's greatest comforts, and willing to live even amid its greatest sorrows.
Job's path was hidden from him. He did not understand why God was contending with him.
A suffering and tempted believer may know something of that heaviness.
When we have concentrated too much on things we can see, a heavenly Father's discipline may expose the misery of life apart from renewed assurance of his presence.
Only God can restore the joy of salvation.
Blessed be God: though the earth contains much human wickedness, it is also filled with his goodness.
We can live through hardship by attending to the duties he gives us.
Those willing to receive Christ as Savior may look ahead to everlasting mercy.

row.cell: And maintains that God's judgments are for the wicked.

div.title: Eliphaz rebukes Job (verses 1–6)
div.p: Satan was attempting to prove Job a hypocrite by making him suffer.
Job's friends reached a similar conclusion because Job was suffering and had shown impatience.
We must keep this distinction in mind if we are to understand their conversation.
Eliphaz spoke with some sympathy for Job, but accused him of being weak and fainthearted.
People often make very little allowance for someone who has taught others.
Even godly friends may call something a slight touch when the sufferer feels it as a deep wound.
We should help suffering people stop dwelling exclusively on their troubles and turn their thoughts to the merciful God present in them.
What better way to do that than to look at Jesus Christ, whose incomparable sorrows teach God's children to put their own sufferings in perspective?

div.title: Eliphaz argues that judgment falls upon the wicked (verses 7–11)
div.p: Eliphaz made two arguments.
First, he claimed that upright people were never ruined in this way.
But the same outward events happen to the righteous and the wicked in life and death (Ecclesiastes 9:2).
The great and lasting distinction appears after death.
Some of our worst mistakes arise from drawing false conclusions out of truths that are otherwise undeniable.
Second, Eliphaz said wicked people frequently experience sudden ruin.
He appealed to what he had observed.
We, too, can see many such cases.
The general observation, however, did not establish that Job was wicked.

div.title: Eliphaz recounts a vision (verses 12–21)
div.p: Eliphaz described a frightening vision.
Quiet reflection on our hearts can be a fitting occasion for the Holy Spirit to speak to us (Psalm 4:4).
Since humanity fell into sin, communication from heaven has often filled human beings with terror because of the guilt of their consciences.
How could sinful people claim to be more righteous or more pure than God, their Creator, Lord and Owner?
Human pride is dreadful, and God's patience is astonishing.
Look at the human condition.
We live in fragile houses of clay whose foundations are in dust.
Some people stand upon a larger pile of dust than others, but all of us stand upon earth that will soon receive our bodies.
Some lives end suddenly.
Others are consumed slowly by illness, like clothing eaten by a moth.
No one can resist death through personal power.
Beauty, strength, learning, wealth and influence cannot keep death away.
These advantages die with us or pass to others.
How can weak, sinful, dying creatures accuse God of injustice or claim to be purer than their Maker?
Instead of quarreling with their suffering, they should wonder that they are not already in hell.
Can people cleanse themselves of guilt without their Creator?
God can justify sinful humans only through the righteousness and gracious help of the promised Redeemer.
Even angels who once served before God's throne suffered deserved judgment when they sinned.
Though people who live without God may seem unpunished for a time, their judgment is as certain as that of fallen angels.
Yet careless sinners notice so little that they do not prepare for death or consider their final end.

row.cell: Eliphaz urges that the sin of sinners in their ruin.
God is to be regarded in affliction.
The happy end of God's correction.

div.title: Eliphaz argues that sinners bring ruin upon themselves (verses 1–5)
div.p: Eliphaz challenged Job to answer his arguments.
Had any of God's holy servants suffered the kinds of judgments Job was experiencing, or behaved as Job did under them?
The word saints means holy or, more precisely, consecrated people.
Henry sees it as a term used through the ages for God's people, whose reconciliation is established through the covenant sacrifice.
Eliphaz rightly held that sin leads sinners toward destruction.
People destroy themselves through their sinful desires.
He therefore assumed Job must have acted foolishly to bring about his current troubles.
Eliphaz's language alluded plainly to Job's earlier wealth.
But there was no evidence of Job's wickedness.
Applying these truths to Job was unfair and harsh.

div.title: Eliphaz teaches Job to look to God in suffering (verses 6–16)
div.p: Eliphaz reminded Job that troubles do not occur at random or arise ultimately from secondary causes.
Prosperity and suffering do not alternate with the regularity of day and night or summer and winter.
They come under God's wise direction.
We must not attribute our afflictions to blind fortune, for they are from God.
Nor should we attribute our sins to fate, since they arise from ourselves.
Human beings are born in sin and therefore born to trouble.
Sin and trouble are the only things in this world to which we are born with a natural claim.
Outward acts of sin are like sparks flying out from the furnace of our original corruption.
Our bodies are fragile and earthly comforts do not last.
Troubles rise from this condition like sparks rising from a fire: numerous and often coming one after another.
Eliphaz rebuked Job for arguing with God rather than seeking him.

p.hi: When afflicted, pray.

div.p: Prayer relieves the heart and brings healing to its wounds.
Eliphaz spoke about rain, something we often take for granted.
Yet if we reflect on how it is produced and what life it sustains, we recognize a wonderful work of divine power and kindness.
We fail to notice the Giver of ordinary comforts because they appear so regularly.
God's providential treatment of some people encourages others to hope even in the worst circumstances.
He brings help to the helpless and hope to the hopeless.
He can also confound people who persist boldly in wickedness and make them acknowledge the justice of his judgments.

div.title: Eliphaz describes the blessing of God's discipline (verses 17–27)
div.p: Eliphaz told Job not to despise the Almighty's correction.
Such discipline can come from a father's love for the child's good.
We should receive it as a message from heaven.
Eliphaz urged Job to submit and encouraged him with promises.
A good person can remain blessed amid suffering because fellowship with God and the hope of heaven are not lost.
Indeed, affliction can bring blessings.
It restrains sinful desires, loosens attachment to the world, draws the heart nearer to God, opens the Bible and brings us to our knees.
God may wound his people, yet he also sustains them during their trials and eventually delivers them.
Making a wound can be part of a cure.
Eliphaz promised much to Job if Job would humble himself.
Trouble cannot truly harm the godly when the Lord keeps them from sin.
Christ's servants may not always be delivered out of outward trouble, but they can be delivered by means of it.
Though they seem overcome by a particular trial, they remain conquerors in God's sight.
Slander cannot rob them of the blessings God intends.
He provides the wisdom and grace needed for their responsibilities.
The greatest blessing in our work and enjoyment is to be kept from sin.
God's people will finish their course with joy and honor.
A person has lived long enough when the assigned work is complete and the soul is prepared for the world to come.
Dying at the appointed time can be a mercy, like grain gathered when it has ripened, neither too early nor left standing too long.
Our times belong in God's hands.
Believers must not expect great riches, unusually long lives or freedom from trials.
But God will arrange everything for their ultimate good.
Job's experience teaches how difficult it is to maintain steady faith during severe trials.
When life goes well, faith may have little opportunity to exercise its strength.
But when God allows storm after storm, and even seems distant while we pray, trusting him when we cannot trace his ways becomes the patience of the saints.
Blessed Savior, how precious it is to look to you, the Author and Perfecter of faith, in those moments!

row.cell: Job reproves his friends as unkind.

div.title: Job defends his complaints (verses 1–7)
div.p: Job continued defending his expressions of distress.
In addition to his outward suffering, an inward sense of divine wrath destroyed his courage and resolve.
Feeling that God is angry with us is harder to bear than outward affliction.
How much more must the Savior have endured in the garden and upon the cross when he bore our sins and offered his soul to divine justice for us!
Whatever burden of suffering God is pleased to lay upon us, whether in health or circumstances, we can submit more readily while our judgment remains clear and our conscience is at peace.
But when either sound reasoning or peace of conscience is disturbed, the sufferer's condition calls for deep sympathy.
Job rebuked his friends' accusations.
Their words brought no relief, but seemed tasteless, repulsive and burdensome.

div.title: Job asks for death again (verses 8–13)
div.p: Job had wished for death to end his suffering.
Eliphaz rebuked that wish, but Job repeated it more forcefully.
It was rash to speak as though God should destroy him.
Who could endure even an hour of the Almighty's wrath if God unleashed its full force?
Let us rather pray with David that God would spare us a little longer.
Job took some comfort from his conscience, knowing he had in some measure served God's glory.
People who possess grace, know something of its presence and exercise it also have spiritual wisdom to help them in their darkest times.

div.title: Job rebukes his friends' lack of compassion (verses 14–30)
div.p: During prosperity, Job expected much from his friends.
Now he was disappointed.
He compared them to streams that dry up in summer.
Anyone who makes created things the foundation of hope will find them fail just when help is most needed.
But those who trust God find grace in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).
People who make gold their hope will eventually be ashamed of that confidence.
We are wise to stop relying ultimately upon human beings.
Trust the Rock of Ages, not broken reeds; the Fountain of Life, not broken cisterns.
Job's words carried a sharp accusation: “Now you are nothing.”
If only we could keep the same recognition of created things' frailty that we sometimes have at a sickbed, at death's approach or under the weight of guilt!
Job reproached his friends for treating him harshly.
He asked them for neither money nor rescue, but only a kind look and a kind word.
We often receive less than we expect from people, even when we expect little.
From God we receive more than we expect, even when we expect much.
Job was willing to admit error if his friends could demonstrate it.
Even if he had been wrong, they should not have treated him so severely.
He held firmly to his integrity.
He knew he had not committed the extraordinary wickedness they imagined.
Yet it is best to entrust our reputations to the Lord who preserves our souls.
On the final day, every upright believer will receive God's approval.

div.title: Job describes life's exhausting labor (verses 1–6)
div.p: Job tried to excuse a wish he could not truly justify: the desire for death.
Remember where human beings live: on earth, not yet in hell.
Our time here has an appointed limit, determined by the One who created us and sent us.
Life during that time is a struggle.
We are like day laborers assigned work to be finished before night, when we must give an account.
Job thought he had as much reason to long for death as a tired laborer has to long for evening and sleep.
Rest is sweet to someone exhausted by work.
Even a wealthy person may not find as much enjoyment in riches as a laborer finds in earned wages.
Job complained that his days had become useless and had remained so for a long time.
Yet when we are no longer able to work actively for God, quietly waiting for him can still be acceptable service.
His nights were restless.
When something painful has been appointed for us, it helps to believe that it has some holy purpose.
When we enjoy comfortable nights, we should recognize them as gifts and give thanks.
Job's body had become repulsive to him.
What fragile bodies we inhabit!
Life was moving rapidly toward its end.
Each day leaves a thread behind, like a weaver's shuttle.
Many weave only a spider's web, which cannot endure (Job 8:14).
But if we live for God in faithful service and loving work, we will eventually reap what we have sown and wear what we have woven.

div.title: Job reasons with God about mortality (verses 7–16)
div.p: Thinking personally about life's brevity, uncertainty and certain ending can make these truths useful to us.
We die only once.
Therefore we need to prepare well, because mistakes made at death cannot be corrected afterward.
Other clouds rise after one disappears, but the identical cloud never returns.
New generations arise, while earlier generations vanish from the earth.
Glorified believers never return to the grief and responsibilities of their old earthly homes.
Condemned sinners never return to their old entertainments and pleasures.
We should prepare for a better dwelling place when we die.
Job might have used these truths to reach a better conclusion than simply, “I will complain.”
With only a few breaths remaining, we ought to devote them to the holy breathings of faith and prayer, not words that express sinful rebellion.
We should ask the Keeper of Israel, who neither slumbers nor sleeps, to watch over us while we sleep.
Job wanted rest in the grave.
Henry judges that to have been weakness.
A godly person may choose death rather than sin, but should remain willing to live as long as God appoints, since earthly life gives opportunities to glorify him and prepare for heaven.

div.title: Job seeks forgiveness (verses 17–21)
div.p: Job challenged God's treatment of human beings.
Yet amid the questioning his thoughts seem to have risen toward God with some faith and hope.
Notice how seriously Job regarded his sins.
Even the best believers have sins to confess, and the holier they become, the more aware they are of that sin.
God preserves human life and saves everyone who believes.
In this passage Henry considers it probable Job meant the Observer of human beings, whose eyes see everyone's conduct and heart.
Nothing can be hidden from him.
Let us plead guilty before his throne of grace, so that we do not stand condemned before his judgment seat.
Job denied his friends' charge that he was a hypocrite or wicked man.
Yet he admitted to God that he was a sinner.
Even the best people must do that.
Job wanted to know how to find peace with God and prayed urgently for forgiveness.
His desire was greater than relief from outward pain.
He wanted God's favor to return.
When God removes sin's guilt, he also breaks sin's power.
Job appealed to his approaching death as a reason to seek forgiveness now.
If his sins remained unforgiven when he died, he would be lost.
How miserable it is to live in sin without knowing the Savior!

row.cell: Bildad applies God's just dealing to Job.

div.title: Bildad rebukes Job (verses 1–7)
div.p: Job had said much that deserved thoughtful consideration.
But Bildad, like an impatient and angry debater, dismissed it all by asking how long Job would continue talking this way.
People often misunderstand someone's meaning and then rebuke that person as though they had committed wrongdoing.
Even in discussions about religion, people too readily answer with harshness and treat others' arguments with contempt.
Bildad's speech shows that he already held a poor opinion of Job.
Job agreed that God never perverts justice.
But this did not mean his children were rejected by God or that they had died because of some extraordinary sin.

p.hi: Extraordinary suffering is not always the punishment of extraordinary wickedness.

div.p: At times it is instead the testing of extraordinary grace.
When we judge another person's case, we should lean toward the charitable interpretation.
Bildad offered Job hope that an upright person would eventually experience a good outcome.
God does enrich his people with growing grace and comfort.
What begins small can grow toward completeness, like early dawn brightening toward midday.

div.title: Bildad describes the fate of hypocrites (verses 8–19)
div.p: Bildad spoke truly about hypocrites and the eventual destruction of their hopes and pleasures.
He appealed to earlier generations and the testimony of ancient teachers.
Those who speak out of sincere hearts and personal experience of divine things can teach most effectively.
Consider a plant growing in marshy soil.
It appears vividly green, yet quickly withers when conditions dry up.
This is a picture of religious profession sustained only by prosperity.
A spider's web may be intricately woven, but it can be swept away at once.
So it is with the confidence of someone who claims religion while lacking God's grace in the heart.
A person who merely performs religious forms may flatter himself, assume he is safe, remain untroubled about salvation and deceive others with empty confidence.
A garden tree may flourish and fasten its roots around a rock, yet later be cut down and forgotten.
It pictures wicked people who seem firmly established before being suddenly removed.
Bildad's teaching about false confidence is true in general, but it cannot fairly be applied to Job if restricted to what happens in this life.

div.title: Bildad applies the argument to Job (verses 20–22)
div.p: Bildad insisted that people receive the outcome appropriate to their character.
He and Job's other friends therefore concluded that Job's present suffering proved his wickedness.
God will not finally reject an upright person.
Such a person may be brought low temporarily but will never be abandoned forever.
Sin does bring ruin upon people and their families.
But calling Job ungodly and wicked because he suffered was unfair and unloving.
The friends' mistake was failing to distinguish the present life of trial and discipline from the future state of final judgment.
May we seek the portion and confidence of the righteous, carry their cross and die their death.
Until then, let us avoid hurting others with hasty judgments and troubling ourselves needlessly over other people's opinions.

row.cell: He is not able to contend with God.
Men not to be judged by outward condition.

div.title: Job acknowledges God's righteousness (verses 1–13)
div.p: Job answered his friends by saying that his denial of hypocrisy did not mean he questioned God's justice.
How could any person claim to be righteous in a dispute with God?
Before him Job admitted countless sins.
If God called him to account for every thought, word and action in his life, he could not justify one in a thousand.
He therefore deserved more suffering than he had experienced.
When Job thought of God's wisdom and power, his complaints temporarily disappeared.
We are not qualified to judge all God's ways, because we do not know everything he is doing or intends.
God acts with power no creature can resist.
Those who believe themselves strong enough to rescue others cannot even rescue themselves when God confronts them.

div.title: Job cannot contend with God (verses 14–21)
div.p: Nevertheless, Job remained too righteous in his own eyes (Job 32:1).
Though he spoke of God's greatness, his words began to treat his dispute with Providence as a matter of power rather than right.
The evil fruits of pride and self-righteousness were emerging.
Job was beginning to condemn God in order to justify himself, for which he would later be corrected.
Even then, he understood enough about himself to know he could not endure a trial before God.
If we claim to have no sin, we deceive ourselves and offend God.
We contradict Scripture and sin by making the claim.
Yet Job's assertion that his troubles were entirely without cause failed to give due weight to God's goodness and justice.

div.title: Outward suffering does not prove wickedness (verses 22–24)
div.p: Here Job addressed the central disagreement.
His friends believed good people always prosper in this life and only wicked people experience severe suffering.
Job answered that wicked people may prosper while righteous people suffer greatly.
He was right about the facts.
Yet his words expressed too much anger, because God does not willingly afflict people.
When dispute or discontent heats our spirits, we need to guard our lips.

div.title: Job laments and longs for a mediator (verses 25–35)
div.p: How little we need empty entertainments, and how greatly we need to use time well, when it rushes so quickly toward eternity!
Earthly pleasures are vain and can vanish even while we remain alive.
The memory of fulfilling our duty can bring lasting satisfaction.
The memory of having accumulated wealth cannot, once all the wealth has disappeared.
Job spoke as though God would never be appeased or moved toward mercy.
That was the language of his remaining sinful nature.
But there is a Mediator, a Daysman, an Umpire between us and God.
He is God's beloved Son.
Through the blood of his cross he has purchased peace.
He saves completely everyone who comes to God through him.
When we trust his name, our sins are buried in the depths of the sea.
We are washed from our pollution, made whiter than snow and freed from condemnation.
We are clothed with righteousness and salvation, adorned with the Holy Spirit's graces and presented faultless before God's glory with great joy.
May we learn the difference between justifying ourselves and being justified by God.
Let every suffering, storm-tossed soul remember Job.
Others have passed through such a dreadful place.
Although they found it hard to believe that God would hear or deliver them, he calmed their storms and brought them to safety.
Resist the devil.
Do not indulge bitter thoughts about God or despairing conclusions about yourself.
Come to the One who invites the weary and burdened and promises never to turn them away.

row.cell: He pleads with God as his Maker.

div.title: Job complains of suffering (verses 1–7)
div.p: Job had grown weary of life and resolved to express his pain.
Yet he did not intend to accuse God of injustice.
He asked to be delivered from the sting of his afflictions—sin.
When God afflicts us, he may be contending with us.
There is a reason for his dealings, and it is useful to learn that reason so we can repent and leave behind whatever wrong he confronts.
But when we speak from bitterness, as Job did, we can add guilt and further distress to our situation.
We should not cherish harsh thoughts of God.
Later we will understand that they had no foundation.
Job knew that God does not investigate or judge things as humans do.
He therefore struggled to understand why God continued afflicting him, as though time were needed to discover his sin.

div.title: Job appeals to the God who made him (verses 8–13)
div.p: Job spoke as though God had formed and preserved him only to make him suffer.
God made us; we did not make ourselves.
How sad it is when bodies capable of becoming temples of the Holy Spirit are instead used as instruments of unrighteousness!
The soul, however, is the center of life and personhood, and it too is God's gift.
Remembering our Creator should move us to duty: God made me and keeps me alive.
The same fact gives us grounds to ask for mercy:

p.hi: You have made me. Remake me. I am yours; save me.

div.title: Job complains of God's severity (verses 14–22)
div.p: Job did not deny that, as a sinner, he deserved suffering.
But he felt that justice was being applied to him with exceptional harshness.
His gloom, unbelief and bitter thoughts about God came not only from outward trials and the sin still remaining within him.
They also arose from Satan's inward temptations and his anguish over what he felt as divine displeasure.
Our Creator has also become our Redeemer in Christ.
He will not destroy his own work in a humble believer.
He will renew that person in holiness and grant eternal life.
If earthly suffering can make the grave seem attractive, how dreadful is the state of those condemned to everlasting darkness!
May every sinner seek rescue from such a fate.
May every believer thank Jesus, who delivers us from the wrath to come.

row.cell: Zophar assures Job of blessings if he repented.

div.title: Zophar rebukes Job (verses 1–6)
div.p: Zophar attacked Job forcefully.
He portrayed him as someone who enjoyed hearing himself speak despite having nothing useful to say, and who defended lies.
Zophar wished God would show Job that his punishment was actually less than he deserved.
In our disputes, we are often too eager to call upon God to intervene.
We assume that if he spoke, he would certainly agree with our side.
We should submit every disagreement to the Lord's judgment, because his judgment accords with truth.
But those most eager to invoke divine judgment are not necessarily the ones who are right.

div.title: Zophar speaks about God's greatness (verses 7–12)
div.p: Zophar spoke well about God's greatness and glory and human folly and vanity.
We should recognize our own weakness and be humbled.
God sees the foolishness of human beings who want to become wise and be recognized as wise, though their hearts are like an untamed wild donkey's colt.
Human beings are empty and foolish, yet proud of themselves.
They desire the appearance of wisdom without submitting to wisdom's laws.
They reach for knowledge God has forbidden.
Like the first parents, they try to become wise beyond what has been written and lose the tree of life through seeking the tree of knowledge.
How can a creature in this condition claim to argue on equal terms with God?

div.title: Zophar promises good if Job repents (verses 13–20)
div.p: Zophar urged Job to repent and offered encouragement.
Yet even this counsel was mixed with harsh assumptions about Job.
Zophar believed prosperity in this life always belonged to the righteous.
He thought Job should be considered a hypocrite unless worldly prosperity returned.
Zophar said Job could lift his face without stain.
In Henry's spiritual application, people may approach the throne of grace confidently rather than with the fear Job described earlier (Job 9:34).
When God looks upon us through his Anointed One, our downcast faces can rise.
Though once polluted, we can be washed by Christ's blood and presented without stain.
We can draw near in full assurance of faith when our hearts have been cleansed from guilty consciences (Hebrews 10:22).

row.cell: Job speaks of the wisdom and power of God.

div.title: Job rebukes his friends (verses 1–5)
div.p: Job criticized his friends for thinking their wisdom was so much greater than his.
We often mistake correction for insult and imagine we are being mocked when someone offers advice or warning.
That is our own folly.
But here Job had some reason to object.
He suspected his friends treated him this way because poverty and suffering had lowered his social standing.
This is how the world often behaves.
Even upright people may be despised when troubles overshadow their lives.

div.title: Wicked people often prosper (verses 6–11)
div.p: Job appealed to observable facts.
Bold robbers, oppressive people and those who openly despise God often enjoy prosperity.
Yet this is not simply chance.
The Lord governs these things.
Worldly prosperity has little value in his sight.
He has better gifts for his children.
Job referred everything to God's complete ownership of every created thing.
He asked his friends to let him consider and assess their claims, appealing to any fair judgment.

div.title: Job celebrates God's wisdom and power (verses 12–25)
div.p: Here Job gave a noble account of God's wisdom, power and sovereignty.
The Lord governs all human affairs according to the counsel of his will.
No one can resist him.
Wise and godly people who disagree about lesser matters would do well to dwell chiefly on the great truths they share.
Doing so brings honor, comfort and benefit to themselves and to others.
Here Job offered neither accusations nor complaints.
He described numerous ways God rules human affairs, overruling every scheme and overcoming every opposition.
Possessing all wisdom and power, God knows how to use even foolish and wicked people.
If he did not govern the world, so much foolishness and dishonesty would have brought it to ruin long ago.
These truths should have made Job and his friends recognize that they were out of their depth when claiming to know why God had afflicted Job.
God's ways are beyond searching, and his judgments cannot be fully traced.
Scripture contains many wonderful examples of divine wisdom in sovereignty.
But the greatest and most important is the crucifixion of Jesus Christ—which Henry attributes to what he calls “the malice of the Jews.”
Only God could have known that this terrible act would become the salvation of the world.

row.cell: He professes his confidence in God.
Job entreats to know his sins.

div.title: Job challenges his friends' claims (verses 1–12)
div.p: Job spoke too highly of himself when he insisted that his friends had nothing to teach him.
Those who argue are tempted to magnify themselves and belittle others.
Whenever fear of judgment, spiritual temptation or suffering overwhelms us, we should turn to the Physician of our souls.
He rejects no one, never prescribes the wrong remedy and never leaves a case without a cure.
We may speak to him whenever we need.
For broken hearts and wounded consciences, every created comfort without Christ is an ineffective physician.
Job spoke to his friends in unmistakable anger.
His friends had expressed some truths that were relevant to Job, but an unhumble heart does not receive human correction gently.

div.title: Job expresses confidence in God (verses 13–22)
div.p: Job resolved to stand by his conscience's witness to his integrity.
He relied on God for justification and salvation, the two great blessings we hope for through Christ.
Job expected little in the way of earthly deliverance.
But he remained confident concerning his eternal salvation.
He believed God would not only save him and make him happy but also be his salvation, the One whose presence and enjoyment would be his happiness.
He knew he was not a hypocrite and concluded that God would not finally reject him.
We should be satisfied to have God as our Friend, even at times when his dealings seem those of an enemy.
We must trust that all things will work for our good, even when everything appears to be against us.
Cling to God even when he gives no immediate sense of comfort.
In the hour of death, seek living comfort from him.
This is what it means to trust him though he slays us.

div.title: Job asks God to reveal his sins (verses 23–28)
div.p: Job wanted his sins to be made known to him.
A genuinely repentant person is willing to know the worst about personal wrongdoing.
We should all desire to see our transgressions clearly so that we can confess them and avoid them in the future.
Job lamented how severely God seemed to deal with him.
Time does not erase the guilt of sin.
When God brings bitter things to our remembrance, he may intend us to recall neglected sins and turn from them.
Young people should beware of indulging sin.
Even in this life, moments of sinful pleasure can produce months of sorrow.
It is far wiser to remember the Creator in youth and gain an assured hope and a peaceful conscience that will comfort us in later years.
Job also complained that his present missteps seemed to be examined with excessive strictness.
But God does not treat us according to what our sins deserve.
Job's complaint arose from a gloomy view of his circumstances.
If God strictly examined our steps and paths in judgment, both body and soul would feel his righteous vengeance.
That will be the dreadful condition of unbelievers.
But salvation has been planned, provided and revealed in Christ.

row.cell: By sin man is subject to corruption.

div.title: Job reflects on human life (verses 1–6)
div.p: Job continued reflecting on the human condition while also addressing God.
Every descendant of fallen Adam has a short life.
Human beauty, happiness and splendor vanish before disease or death, like a flower cut down or a shadow fading away.
How can a person's conduct be entirely free from sin when the heart is unclean by nature?
Henry regards this as clear evidence that Job understood original sin.
Job seems to have raised this truth to ask God to treat him not according to his own works, but according to mercy and grace.
God has determined how long each of us will live.
Our times are in his hands, and natural processes operate under his rule.
In him we live and move.
Remembering how brief and uncertain life is, and how quickly earthly pleasures fade, can help us greatly.
But even more important is to understand the cause and the remedy of our condition.
Until the Holy Spirit gives us new birth, nothing spiritually good dwells in us or comes from us.
Even the little good performed by regenerated people remains mixed with sin.
We should therefore humble ourselves and depend entirely upon God's mercy through our divine Surety, Christ.
Seek the Holy Spirit's daily renewal and look toward heaven as the only place of perfect holiness and happiness.

div.title: Job considers death and resurrection (verses 7–15)
div.p: A tree that has been cut down may sprout again if water is available.
A human being who dies, however, is permanently removed from the former place in this world.
Human life resembles floodwaters that spread widely and then quickly dry up.
Henry understands Job's words as expressing belief in the resurrection.
Job's friends had proved such miserable comforters that he turned toward the hope of a future change.
If our sins have been forgiven and our hearts made holy, heaven will be our souls' rest.
Meanwhile our bodies will lie hidden in the grave, no longer harmed by enemies or troubled by the corruption and discipline of earthly life.

div.title: Job struggles with sin, suffering and mortality (verses 16–22)
div.p: At moments Job's faith and hope became stronger and the work of grace appeared renewed.
But soon his remaining sinful nature prevailed again.
He spoke as though God had pushed his judgment to the furthest extreme against him.
The Lord will prevail against everyone who tries to contend with him.
God may send disease and pain, remove the companionship of those we love and take away every earthly hope.
Yet he will receive the believer into eternal happiness.
What a different end awaits the prosperous unbeliever when summoned before God's judgment seat!
The Lord still sits upon a throne of mercy, ready to show grace.
May sinners consider their final end while there is still time.
The body that human beings hesitate to lay aside may suffer intensely near death.
The soul they hesitate to surrender may experience sorrow.
Dying can be difficult work and death's pain severe.
It is foolish to postpone repentance until a deathbed, when weakness may make the one most necessary task difficult to perform.

div.title: Eliphaz criticizes Job again (verses 1–16)
div.p: Eliphaz began his second attack upon Job.
Instead of becoming gentler after hearing Job's suffering, he became harsher.
He wrongly accused Job of abandoning reverence for God, neglecting prayer and losing all regard for the Lord.
Henry summarizes much of religion in two duties: fearing God as a vital inward principle, and praying to God as a vital practice.
Eliphaz also charged Job with conceit and with despising the advice and comfort his friends offered.
We often imagine our own words are of great importance when others, sometimes with good reason, find little value in them.
Eliphaz accused Job of resisting God himself.
Yet he should not have placed such harsh interpretations upon the words of someone long known for godliness and now enduring temptation.
These speakers clearly recognized original sin and the deep corruption of fallen human nature.
But that true doctrine did not make their harsh accusations against Job just.
Let us marvel at God's patience in enduring sinners.
Let us marvel even more at his love in redeeming us through his beloved Son, Jesus Christ.

div.title: Eliphaz describes the unrest of wicked people (verses 17–35)
div.p: Eliphaz correctly taught that wicked people are in a miserable condition.
But from that truth he drew a false conclusion: because Job was miserable, Job must be wicked.
The fact that some of God's people prosper in the world does not mean those who experience poverty or loss cannot also belong to him.
Eliphaz described the anxiety of wicked people, especially oppressors.
Such people often live in fear and die in misery.
If the prosperity of unrepentant sinners ends in ruin, we should regard other people's disasters as warnings.
God's correction does not feel pleasant while we undergo it.
Nevertheless, it can produce the peaceful fruit of righteousness in those who learn from it.
No hardship, however severe, can rob a true follower of the Lord of his favor.

p.hi: What can separate us from Christ's love?

row.cell: He represents his case as deplorable.

div.title: Job calls his friends miserable comforters (verses 1–5)
div.p: Eliphaz had claimed Job's words were useless and irrelevant.
Job now made the same charge against Eliphaz's words.
People who condemn others' speech should expect their own to be condemned in turn.
This is easy, and the exchange can continue indefinitely.
But what good does it accomplish?

p.hi: Angry replies excite passions. They do not convince minds or make truth clearer.

div.p: Job's judgment of his friends also reminds us of the limits of every created comfort compared with God.
Eventually we will all discover that without him, created things are poor comforters.
When sin weighs on the conscience, judgment terrifies or death approaches, the Holy Spirit alone can give truly effective comfort.
In times of suffering, all other comfort without his work accomplishes little.
We should sympathize deeply with the sorrows of our brothers and sisters, as if they were our own.
Soon enough, those troubles may become our own.

div.title: Job describes his misery (verses 6–16)
div.p: Job gave a painful account of his suffering.
How much reason do we have to thank God if we are not experiencing troubles like his!
Even good people find it hard, during great distress, to prevent bitter thoughts about God.
Eliphaz had accused Job of refusing humility.
Job replied that he understood humility all too well: dust was the right place for him.
In this he reminds us of Christ, the Man of Sorrows, who pronounced mourners blessed because they would receive comfort.

div.title: Job defends his innocence and seeks a witness (verses 17–22)
div.p: Job's position was terrible.
Yet his conscience testified that he had not willingly practiced any grave, deliberate sin.
He remained ready to acknowledge sins arising from human weakness.
Eliphaz had accused him of religious hypocrisy.
Job therefore pointed to prayer, a central act of true religion, and maintained that his prayers had been sincere, though not free from every imperfection.
He still had a God to whom he could turn, confident that the Lord fully knew his suffering.
People who pour out tears before God may have many faults and be unable to defend themselves.
Yet they have a Friend who pleads for them—the Son of Man.
Our hope of acceptance before God must rest upon him.
Death is a journey from which we do not return to earthly life.
Each of us must make that journey, certainly and soon.
Should the Savior not therefore be precious to us?
Should we not be prepared to obey and suffer for him?

If our consciences have been cleansed by his atoning blood and testify that we are not continuing deliberately in sin or hypocrisy, death will become release from prison and entrance into everlasting joy.

row.cell: Job appeals from man to God.
His hope is not in life, but in death.

div.title: Job appeals to God (verses 1–9)
div.p: Job reflected on his friends' harsh judgments and, considering himself near death, appealed to God.
Our time on earth is coming to an end.
We should use its remaining days wisely, preparing for eternity.
The righteous should learn from Job's troubles, whether they came from God, from enemies or from friends.
Instead of becoming discouraged from serving God because Job, his faithful servant, was treated so severely, believers should become more determined to persevere.
Those who keep heaven as their destination will keep their feet on the path of faith, whatever hardships or discouragements meet them along the way.

div.title: Job looks beyond earthly recovery (verses 10–16)
div.p: Job's friends tried to comfort him by predicting a return to worldly prosperity.
But it is unwise to offer comfort grounded entirely in the possibility that earthly circumstances may improve.
We should encourage ourselves and others through the promises of God, his love and grace, and a well-founded hope of eternal life—comforts that cannot fail.
Job learned to make peace with the thought of the grave.
Believers can be willing to die because, in one sense, death is like going to bed after a long day.
They are tired, and it is time to rest.
Why should they refuse when their Father calls them?
Our bodies are already linked to decay, worms and dust.
Let us seek the living hope that will be fulfilled when the wicked person's false hope has disappeared into darkness.
While our bodies rest in the grave, our souls may enjoy the rest God has reserved for his people.

div.title: Bildad rebukes Job again (verses 1–4)
div.p: Bildad had previously given Job some useful counsel and encouragement.
Now his speech contained only rebukes and predictions of destruction.
Because Job would not agree that he was wicked, Bildad wrongly concluded he was excluding God's Providence from human affairs.

div.title: The wicked fall into snares (verses 5–10)
div.p: Bildad described the misery of wicked people.
Much of his teaching is true when understood as a warning: sin is a dreadful condition, and without repentance it leads to destruction.
But Bildad thought he could easily apply those warnings to Job.
That conclusion was neither safe nor just.
Angry debaters frequently classify their opponents as enemies of God and draw false conclusions from important truths.
Bildad pictured the wicked person as an animal trapped in a snare or a criminal brought into custody.
From the beginning Satan has been both a murderer and a robber.
He sets traps for sinners wherever they go.
If he makes people sinful like himself, he also makes them miserable like himself.
He hunts for their precious lives.
A wicked person's own transgression becomes a trap, and God prepares judgment for that wrongdoing.
See how sinners run into traps they themselves have made possible.

div.title: Bildad warns of the wicked person's end (verses 11–21)
div.p: Bildad described judgment awaiting wicked people in the world to come, a judgment sometimes anticipated in this life.
Sin leads to fear and everlasting confusion.
The terrors of a guilty conscience can be foretastes of that end, as seen in Cain and Judas.
The death of an unrepentant sinner is miserable, even if the person once lived confidently.
At death, every earthly support fails.
How blessed are the saints, and how indebted to Jesus Christ!
Through him death's terror has been so transformed that death becomes a servant and even a friend to the believer.
Bildad described the destruction of wicked people's households and children.
Those who want their family's true welfare should fear destroying it through sin.
God's judgments may continue affecting a wicked person's reputation and family after death.
Henry sees this as evidence of a deeper eternal judgment.
The memory of the righteous brings blessing, while the wicked person's name decays (Proverbs 10:7).
May these warnings encourage sinners to flee from coming wrath, which human strength, cunning and wealth cannot escape.
But Jesus lives forever to deliver everyone who trusts him.
Take courage, suffering believers.
Your sorrow will last only a little while.
Your beloved Savior will see you again, your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.

row.cell: God was the Author of his afflictions.

div.title: Job grieves over his friends' harshness (verses 1–7)
div.p: Job's friends condemned him as wicked because of his suffering.
Job described how cruelly they treated him and how his words deserved more understanding than their criticism allowed.
Harsh words from friends add great weight to already painful troubles.
Yet we should be careful not to let those words produce resentment in our hearts.
Look instead to Jesus Christ, who endured hostile sinners speaking against him and was treated with far greater cruelty than Job or we have suffered.

div.title: Job describes his abandonment (verses 8–22)
div.p: How painful Job's complaints sound!
What makes hell dreadful is the wrath of God.
People whose consciences have become hardened may feel no fear of it now, but they will experience it later.
Those whose consciences have been enlightened fear that judgment now, yet through Christ they will not experience it in eternity.
We must not assume that people whom God afflicts are therefore being treated as his enemies.
Every created thing affects us as God's Providence permits it.
But that truth does not excuse the cruelty of Job's relatives and friends.
Human friendship is uncertain.
If God is our Friend, however, he will never fail us in the hour of need.
Our bodies remain vulnerable to diseases arising within them, however much care we take.
Job appealed to his friends for compassion and rightly criticized their harshness.
It is deeply distressing for someone who loves God to lose both earthly comforts and the inward feeling of God's consolation.
Yet even such suffering does not weaken the evidence that a true believer is a child of God and an heir of glory.

div.title: Job confesses faith in his living Redeemer (verses 23–29)
div.p: At this point the Spirit of God seems to have worked powerfully within Job.
He made a beautiful confession of faith and expressed sure hope.
His words are full of Christ and heaven.
They show that he sought a better homeland, a heavenly one.
God had taught Job to trust in a living Redeemer, to expect the resurrection of the dead and to look for the life of the world to come.
These hopes comforted him.
Job believed this Redeemer would free sinners from Satan's power and sin's condemnation.
He trusted that the Redeemer was his own Redeemer and expected salvation through him.
He believed the Redeemer was alive already, though he had not yet appeared in human flesh.
At the last day the Redeemer would appear as the world's Judge, raise the dead and complete his people's redemption.
How gladly Job spoke of this hope!
May the Holy Spirit engrave these truths deeply upon our hearts.
We all need to make sure that the root of true religion is in us.
It is a living, strengthening, governing work of grace in the heart—necessary to faith as the root is necessary to a tree's stability and fruitfulness.
Job and his friends disagreed about the ways of Providence.
But they agreed about this root principle: there is another world.

row.cell: Zophar speaks of the short joy of the wicked.

div.title: Zophar says sinful joy is brief (verses 1–9)
div.p: Zophar spoke about the certain misery awaiting the wicked.
The apparent triumph of evil people and the happiness of hypocrites do not last.
Sinful pleasures and gains bring suffering, regret and pain.
They ultimately end in remorse, distress and destruction.
Pretended religion adds hypocrisy to other wrongdoing, so its guilt and final judgment are greater.

div.title: Zophar describes the bitterness of sinful gain (verses 10–22)
div.p: Zophar described the dreadful condition of wicked people.
He spoke of sinful bodily desires as the sins of youth.
A sinner may hide cherished sinful pleasures, savoring them secretly as though keeping something sweet beneath the tongue.
But God knows what is in the heart.
He knows what is hidden beneath the tongue and will expose it.
Love of the world and its wealth is sinful when it governs the heart.
Violence and injustice bring divine judgment on individuals, families and nations.
The pleasure of sin becomes bitter poison to the person who embraced it.
The same is true of unlawful wealth.
Even in the midst of abundance, wicked people may experience distress because their minds are filled with anxiety.
It is a great mercy when God's sanctifying grace leads someone to return what was unjustly gained, as Zacchaeus did.
But when the horror of a despairing conscience forces restitution, as with Judas, the act brings no true comfort or spiritual benefit.

div.title: Zophar announces the wicked person's judgment (verses 23–29)
div.p: After describing the suffering produced by wicked conduct, Zophar described the ruin brought by God's judgment.
Only Christ protects against that storm, as the refuge promised in Isaiah 32:2.
Zophar concluded that this was the divinely appointed portion of a wicked person.
Henry's verdict is striking: never was a doctrine better explained or worse applied.
Zophar intended to prove Job a hypocrite, though he had no grounds for doing so.
We should receive the sound warning and apply it to ourselves, learning reverence and turning from sin.
One true sight of Jesus, opened and impressed upon us by the Holy Spirit, can quiet a thousand sinful questions about why believers suffer.

row.cell: The judgement of the wicked is in the world to come.

div.title: Job asks his friends to listen (verses 1–6)
div.p: Job came directly to the central issue.
Does outward prosperity prove that someone belongs to God's true people, so that the loss of prosperity proves hypocrisy?
His friends answered yes. Job answered no.
Anyone looking at Job could see enough suffering to deserve sympathy.
Instead of speaking with such certainty about God's mysterious purposes, his friends should have responded with reverent silence and wonder.

div.title: Wicked people may prosper (verses 7–16)
div.p: Job observed that notorious sinners sometimes experience extraordinary judgments, but not always.
Why does God allow some wicked people to prosper?
This is a time of divine patience.
God can use even the prosperity of ungodly people to carry out his plans, while their unrepentance moves them toward destruction.
Another reason is to show clearly that there is a world beyond this one.
Some wealthy sinners disregard God and religion, imagining that because they have everything they want in this world, they have no need to consider the next.
Yet true religion is not empty.
If it brings us no benefit, we may have only embraced its outward appearance without its living reality.
Job exposed the folly of such confidence.

div.title: Providence deals differently with different sinners (verses 17–26)
div.p: Job contrasted wicked people's prosperity with his friends' assertion that they must always be visibly ruined in this life.
This did not contradict God's holiness or justice.
Even when wicked people prosper, their condition remains spiritually empty.
Their power and splendor can disappear in a moment.
Why one evil person enjoys a longer period of prosperity while another suffers early belongs to God's wisdom.
He is the Judge of the whole earth, and he will act justly.
Time is so brief compared with eternity that earthly differences become small in view of final judgment.
If hell is the final lot of unrepentant sinners, it makes little difference whether one goes there singing and another sighing.
Whether one dies in a palace and another in a prison, the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched are the same for both.
We should therefore avoid becoming consumed with questions about why earthly fortunes differ.

div.title: Judgment awaits beyond the grave (verses 27–34)
div.p: Job rejected the idea that all wicked people must suffer a visible and dramatic fall in this life, and that only wicked people suffer such a fall.
This was the false assumption his friends used to condemn him.
The full punishment of unrepentant sinners belongs chiefly to the world to come, not necessarily to present life (Jude 1:14–15).
A wicked person may retain power until death and receive a magnificent funeral.
But what is there to boast about in that?
A splendid tomb and a beautiful burial place with water to keep its grass green were considered honorable in the ancient East.
They are still empty earthly distinctions.
Death brings worldly prosperity to an end.
The fact that others died before us is little comfort when we ourselves approach death.
True courage at that hour comes from remembering that Jesus Christ died and was buried not only before us but for us.
He went ahead of us, died for us and now lives for us.
That is genuine comfort in the hour of death.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): 1 Corinthians 1:15.
Verified editorial cross-reference: Jude.1.15.

row.cell: Eliphaz shows that a man's goodness profits not God.

div.title: Eliphaz says God gains nothing from human goodness (verses 1–4)
div.p: Eliphaz misunderstood Job's complaints as an accusation that God was unjust to afflict him.
Job had not actually meant that.
Eliphaz's teachings here were wrongly applied to Job, yet their main principle was true.
God is not indebted to us when he gives us good things.
Human godliness does not enrich him or provide something he lacks.
The benefit of religion to human beings is infinitely greater than any loss we sustain through obedience.
God is sovereign and does not have to justify his choices to created beings.
Nevertheless, his character is entirely wise, righteous, faithful, good and merciful.
He delights in holiness that reflects his own character and in the fruit of his Spirit.
He accepts the humble believer's grateful service but rejects the proud claims of people who think their goodness earns his favor.

div.title: Eliphaz accuses Job of oppressing others (verses 5–14)
div.p: Eliphaz leveled serious accusations against Job.
He had no real grounds for them except his belief that God must have punished Job as he always punishes wicked people.
Eliphaz therefore charged Job with using his former wealth and influence to harm and oppress others.
Henry presents these statements as baseless accusations, not as facts about Job.

div.title: Eliphaz invokes the people before the flood (verses 15–20)
div.p: Eliphaz asked Job to consider the ancient paths of wicked people and the destruction toward which they led.
That history is a warning we should study so we do not follow the same path.
But when others suffer and we are spared, we must not boast over them or congratulate ourselves, as Eliphaz did.
We ought instead to thank God for mercy and take the events as warnings to ourselves.

div.title: Eliphaz tells Job to repent (verses 21–30)
div.p: Eliphaz's counsel wrongly implied that Job had never truly known God and that conversion would necessarily restore his worldly prosperity.
Much of the counsel was good in itself.
But its application was based on the false supposition that Job was a stranger and enemy to God.
We must avoid slandering our brothers and sisters.
If we suffer unjust accusations, remember Job's treatment—and even more, how Jesus was insulted.
These examples can strengthen our patience.
We should still examine whether any part of the criticism has merit.
Let us live carefully and avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing.

row.cell: Job complains that God has withdrawn.

div.title: Job longs to bring his case before God (verses 1–7)
div.p: Job appealed from his friends to God's righteous judgment.
He wanted his case to be heard immediately.
Blessed be God: we know where we can find him.
He is in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, and sits upon a throne of mercy, ready to show grace.
There the sinner may come.
There the believer may present a case and plead on the basis of God's promises, his covenant and his glory.
Patiently waiting for death and judgment is wise and right, accompanied by holy reverence.
Passionately demanding that they come immediately is sinful and foolish.
Such impatience was unworthy of Job.

div.title: Job speaks of his upright conduct (verses 8–12)
div.p: Job knew the Lord was present everywhere.
But his distress confused his thinking so badly that he could not grasp God's merciful presence or find comfort in laying his troubles before him.
Everything seemed dark.
He felt that God stood far away and looked on him with displeasure.
Nevertheless, Job believed that God would test him and finally approve him, because he had sought to keep God's commands and delighted in his word.
Yet here he was justifying himself more than God, even against God (Job 32:2).
Job was right to reject the baseless charges of his friends.
But he was wrong to assert so confidently that God's affliction could not involve discipline for sin.
Henry also finds a second mistake: Job appeared to deny that Providence sometimes brings justice to injured people or punishes wickedness in this present world.

div.title: Job trembles before God's sovereignty (verses 13–17)
div.p: Job never doubted that his trials came under God's hand.
He did not believe in blind chance.
How then did he understand them?
He emphasized that the complete reward of God's servants lies in another life, since wicked people often escape their deserved consequences on earth.
Yet God's grace already gives believers a first taste of the Spirit and a promise that God will complete the good work he has begun.
A suffering believer should not conclude that prayer is useless or that despair is justified.
God may intend the affliction to awaken repentance and prayer.
May we obey and trust him amid suffering and remain willing to live or die according to his will.
We do not know what good purposes may be served by extending or shortening our earthly lives.

div.title: Wickedness may go unpunished for a time (verses 1–12)
div.p: Job continued discussing the prosperity of wicked people.
He had already shown in chapter 21 that people who disregard God can live comfortably.
Here he observed that some who openly defy justice succeed in their wicked actions without receiving visible punishment in this life.
He considered both those who act unjustly under the cover of law and authority and robbers who use force.
Job said that God did not immediately call them to account for their folly.
He did not mean God failed to see their deeds.
He meant that judgment did not come at once, exposing them publicly as foolish.
Yet the person who becomes rich through injustice will finally be exposed as a fool (Jeremiah 17:11).

div.title: Wicked people avoid the light (verses 13–17)
div.p: Consider the energy and effort sinners invest in carrying out harmful plans.
Their determination should shame our laziness about doing what is good.
They work hard to indulge sinful desires and then to conceal what will end in death and hell.
With less effort than they spend pursuing and hiding sin, they could instead put sinful desires to death and crucify the flesh—the path leading to life and heaven.
Shame entered the world through sin, and lasting shame awaits those who persist in it.
Sinners live with constant fear of being discovered.
How foolish!
They are afraid of human eyes, yet they do not fear the eye of God, which always sees them.
They are not frightened of committing deeds they are terrified others may discover.

div.title: Job reflects on the judgments of the wicked (verses 18–25)
div.p: Some wicked people decline gradually and die quietly.
They may be honored in life and forgotten after death, along with their violence and oppression.
Death gathers people as a harvest worker gathers ears of grain.
Some of Job's observations may appear to match what we see in Providence.
But Henry warns that Job's conclusions about God's purposes were distorted by partial knowledge.
The Lord governs human affairs with complete justice and wisdom.
We must remember this whenever he tests us.

p.hi: God cannot do wrong.

div.p: The unequaled suffering of God's Son would seem puzzling if viewed apart from this truth.
But when we see Christ as the sinner's Surety, bearing the curse we deserved, we understand how divine justice could be satisfied and his people saved through such suffering.

p.hi: Bildad shows that man cannot be justified before God.

div.title: Bildad considers human impurity before God
div.p: Bildad no longer discussed the question of why wicked people sometimes prosper.
Instead, he spoke of the immense distance between God's glory and human beings' weakness.
He reminded Job of truths Job had not considered sufficiently.
Even human righteousness and holiness at their best are nothing compared with God's holiness (Psalm 89:6).
How can guilty and polluted people stand before a God so glorious and great?
We must be born again by water and the Holy Spirit.
We must continually turn to the blood of Jesus Christ, the fountain opened to cleanse sin (Zechariah 13:1).
Let us humble ourselves as weak and sinful creatures and abandon every confidence in our own merit.
Yet awareness of our unworthiness makes Christ's condescension and love shine even more brightly.
Every sinner he redeems will eternally glorify the riches of his mercy and the power of his grace.

row.cell: Job acknowledges the power of God.

div.title: Job rebukes Bildad (verses 1–4)
div.p: Job mocked Bildad's answer.
His words combined irritability with too high an opinion of himself.
Bildad should have offered Job the Almighty's consolations instead of only warnings of terror.
Jesus Christ knows how to speak the right word to a weary person (Isaiah 50:4).
His ministers should not needlessly distress someone whom God has not intended to make sorrowful.
We are often disappointed by people from whom we expected help and consolation.
But the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, never makes a mistake or fails to accomplish his purpose.

div.title: Job describes divine power (verses 5–14)
div.p: Job gave striking examples of God's wisdom and power in creating and preserving the world.
Look around at earth and water and you see divine power.
Think of hell beneath, though it is hidden from our sight, and consider how God's power is made known even there.
Look up at heaven and you see further displays of his might.
Through his eternal Spirit, who moved over the waters, and through the breath of his word, God not only made the heavens but adorned them (Psalm 33:6).
Yet the work of redemption surpasses every other marvelous work of God.
Through it we can draw near to him, taste his grace, learn to love him and delight in his commands.
The central disagreement between Job and his friends was their belief that his afflictions proved he had committed exceptionally grave crimes.
They failed to give adequate consideration to the guilt of original sin and God's gracious purpose in purifying his people.
Job himself also spoke about things beyond his understanding.
Yet his view was clearer than theirs.
He does not appear to have claimed his personal righteousness as the ground of his hope before God.
However, by continually describing his sufferings as undeserved and excessively severe, he practically contradicted what he had acknowledged about human sin.
Those complaints showed why the Lord was further humbling him.

row.cell: The miserable end of the wicked.

div.title: Job maintains his sincerity (verses 1–6)
div.p: Job's friends finally let him speak without interruption.
He continued with gravity and useful instruction.
Job trusted in both the justice of his cause and the goodness of his God.
He willingly entrusted his case to him.
Yet Job did not show proper reverence when he said God had denied him justice and afflicted his soul.
Holding firmly to our integrity, while resolving not to give our conscience reason to accuse us, frustrates the evil one's designs.
