div.title: The hypocrite has no secure hope (verses 7–10)
div.p: Job considered the position of hypocrites and wicked people deeply miserable.
Even if an insincere profession of religion brought them advantages throughout life, and they held on to false confidence until death, what good would that do when God required their souls?
The more genuine comfort we find in religion, the more firmly we cling to it.
People who find no delight in God are readily drawn away by the pleasures of this life and overcome by its difficulties.

div.title: The final ruin of the wicked (verses 11–23)
div.p: Job's friends had described the worldly suffering of wicked people as always matching the severity of their sins.
Job considered that even if that does not happen, the outcome after death is dreadful.
He therefore presented a truer view of the matter.
For a godly person, death is like a favorable wind carrying a ship toward a heavenly homeland.
For an unrepentant sinner, it is like a storm driving the person toward destruction.
During life, such a sinner benefits from God's patient mercy.
But death ends that period of patience, and God pours out his wrath.
When the Lord brings someone down, no one can flee from or withstand his anger.
Those who refuse now to flee to the arms of divine grace, stretched out to receive them, will not escape the arms of divine wrath, stretched out to destroy them.
What good is it to gain the entire world and lose one's own soul?

row.cell: Wisdom is the gift of God.

div.title: Human beings search for earthly riches (verses 1–11)
div.p: Job argued that God's Providence is governed by perfect wisdom.
To illustrate this, he described the extraordinary knowledge and wealth people can gain.
People can discover hidden caverns and minerals beneath the earth, yet they cannot uncover God's hidden counsels in heaven.
Look at miners, those who grow lazy in religion, and learn from their courage and diligence.
They labor intensely for treasures that will perish.
Should their example not shame our indifference and discouragement in seeking true, eternal riches?
Wisdom is better than gold—and safer and easier to obtain in the way God provides.
Yet people pursue gold while neglecting grace.
Why should the uncertain hope of earthly treasure motivate such effort while the certain promise of heavenly riches fails to move us?

div.title: Wisdom is worth more than wealth (verses 12–19)
div.p: Job spoke of wisdom as knowing God and ourselves, and enjoying fellowship with him.
Its worth is infinitely greater than every earthly treasure.
It is the gift of the Holy Spirit and cannot be bought with money.
We should esteem most highly whatever God esteems most.
Job sought wisdom as someone who sincerely desired to find it, knowing that it was found in God alone, and by means of his revelation.

div.title: God gives true wisdom (verses 20–28)
div.p: There are two kinds of wisdom.
One is hidden within God and is his secret knowledge, which does not belong to us.
The other is revealed by him so that human beings may understand and obey.
Even the events of a single day and a single person's affairs are connected in ways that only God can see fully.
Only the One who sees all at once can judge each part rightly.
But knowledge of God's revealed will is available to us and will do us good.
Let everyone regard this as true wisdom:

p.hi: Fear the Lord and turn away from evil.

div.p: Someone who learns that has learned what matters most.
Where is such wisdom found?
Its treasures are hidden in Jesus Christ, revealed in Scripture, received through faith and communicated by the Holy Spirit.
It will not feed our pride, flatter vanity or satisfy empty curiosity.
Instead it teaches and encourages sinners toward reverence for God, repentance and faith.
It does this without requiring us to solve all the mysteries of this life's events.

row.cell: The honour paid to Job, His usefulness.

div.title: Job remembers former comfort (verses 1–6)
div.p: Job contrasted his earlier prosperity with his present misery, when he felt that God's comforting presence had been withdrawn.
A soul governed by grace rejoices more in God's favor than in the world's approval.
Job had once enjoyed four particular blessings.
First, confidence in God's protection.
Second, the enjoyment of God's favor.
Third, fellowship with God's word.
Fourth, assurance of God's presence.
God's presence can turn even a small cottage into a fortress and palace.
Job had also enjoyed happiness in his family.
But wealth and flourishing households can be extinguished as quickly as a candle.
When the Holy Spirit enlightens the mind and people live in the light of God's countenance, every outward comfort is doubled and every difficulty becomes easier to bear.
This light guides them cheerfully through life and through death.
Yet the conscious comfort of God's presence may be withdrawn for a time.
Often this follows spiritual neglect or grieving the Holy Spirit.
Sometimes it is instead a test of faith and grace.
We should examine ourselves, seek the cause through earnest prayer and become more watchful.

div.title: Job recalls his public usefulness (verses 7–17)
div.p: People of every social rank had honored Job, not merely because of his position but because of his wisdom, honesty, integrity and good management.
Those endowed with such abilities have great opportunities to honor God and serve others.
They must also guard carefully against pride.
A community blessed with good leaders has reason for gratitude.
Job's own measure of the value of his prosperous life was his usefulness.
He restrained violent and arrogant people and protected the vulnerable.
Good public officials should similarly hold back evildoers and defend innocent people, using courage and determination.
Such people are blessings to society.
They resemble the Savior, who rescues poor sinners from Satan.
How many who were about to perish now bless him!
Let us trust his mercy and imitate his truth, justice and love.

div.title: Job recalls his expectation of a peaceful old age (verses 18–25)
div.p: Because Job was respected and useful, he expected to die in peace and honor at an advanced age.
Such hope is good when it grows from active faith in God's promises and Providence.
But if it rests upon confidence in our own wisdom or in changeable earthly circumstances, the foundation is wrong and becomes sinful.
Not everyone who has wisdom is gifted for leadership.
Job had both wisdom and the ability to govern.
He also possessed a tender heart that could console other people.
Those memories were precious to him now that he was mourning.
Jesus Christ is the true King who hates wickedness and upon whom the blessing of a world ready to perish rests.
Let us listen to him.

row.cell: Job's honour is turned into contempt.

div.title: Job's honor becomes contempt (verses 1–14)
div.p: Job compared his present humiliation with the respect and authority he once enjoyed.
How little reason anyone has to become ambitious or proud of earthly honors when they can disappear so easily!
How foolish to place our ultimate confidence in them!
When wicked people despise, insult or hate us, we should not become overwhelmed.
Look instead to Jesus Christ, who endured the hostility of sinners against himself.

div.title: Job struggles under inward and outward suffering (verses 15–31)
div.p: Job complained bitterly.
At this point, his most persistent sin was cherishing harsh thoughts about God.
When inward temptations are added to outward calamities, the soul can become like a ship tossed in a storm, full of confusion and distress.
Yet how dreadful is the position of people who truly have God as an enemy!
Compared with the eternal ruin awaiting unrepentant sinners, what are even the most severe outward or inward sufferings of this present life?
Job found some comfort, though little.
He expected death to end his trials.
God's wrath might bring him to death, but his soul would be safe and happy in the world of spirits.
Even if no human being pities us, God both corrects and pities his children, as a father does.
Let us direct our thoughts more toward eternity.
There the believer's mourning will end and be replaced by joyful praise for redeeming love.

row.cell: Job not guilty of covetousness or idolatry.
Job not guilty of hypocrisy and violence.

div.title: Job declares his integrity (verses 1–8)
div.p: Job was not boasting.
He was answering accusations of hypocrisy.
He understood that God's commands reach beyond outward actions into the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
Normally our conduct should speak for itself.
But when serious false charges threaten both our reputation and God's cause, there are times when we ought solemnly to protest our innocence.
Two dangers have ruined countless people: sinful bodily desires and love of the world.
Job had watched carefully against both.
God examines us even more closely than we examine ourselves.
We should therefore live carefully.
Job avoided dishonest ways of gaining wealth.
He feared forbidden profit as much as forbidden pleasure.
We can use our possessions with comfort, or lose them without disgrace, when they were honestly gained.
Without strict honesty and faithfulness in business and relationships, we have no sound evidence of genuine godliness.
Yet many who profess faith cannot pass this test.

div.title: Job defends his conduct toward his household (verses 9–15)
div.p: The sins that pollute a life arise from a heart that has been deceived.
Lust is like a fire burning within.
When people indulge it, it consumes what is good in the soul and leaves the conscience ruined.
It kindles the fire of God's wrath, which will consume even to eternal destruction unless quenched by the blood of Christ.
It may also destroy the body and waste a person's possessions.

p.hi: Burning desires bring burning judgments.

div.p: Job had managed a large household.
He remembered that he too had a Master in heaven.
If God treated us with the strictness we deserve, we would be ruined.
Therefore we should treat everyone entrusted to our care with gentleness and fairness.

div.title: Job speaks about mercy toward the poor (verses 16–23)
div.p: Job's conscience bore witness to his charitable and just treatment of poor people.
He spoke particularly at length about this because his friends had accused him directly of oppressing them.
He had sought to be tender toward everyone and harmful to no one.
What restrained him from cruelty and lack of compassion?
He feared the Lord and knew that God would oppose him if he harmed the poor.
Concern for worldly reputation may restrain people from committing visible offenses.
But God's grace alone can make them truly hate, fear and avoid sinful thoughts and desires.

div.title: Job rejects greed, idolatry and malice (verses 24–32)
div.p: Job made four denials.
First, he had never set his heart upon worldly wealth.
How few prosperous people who profess religion can sincerely say they never rejoiced merely because their wealth increased!
The determination to become rich can ruin souls and pierce lives with sorrow.
Second, Job had not practiced idolatry.
Its source lies in the heart, and it corrupts people and brings judgment on communities.
Third, he had never wished harm upon an enemy or taken delight in an enemy's misfortune.
Another person's hatred does not justify our hatred.
Fourth, he had never been unkind to strangers.
Hospitality is a Christian duty (1 Peter 4:9).

div.title: Job rejects hypocrisy and injustice (verses 33–40)
div.p: Job denied the charge of hypocrisy.
Human beings are reluctant to confess wrong, eager to make excuses and inclined to blame others.
But people who cover their sins will not prosper (Proverbs 28:13).
Job cited his courage in doing right as evidence of sincerity.
People who acquire wealth unjustly may rightly lose every comfort they expected from it.
Their field may be sown with wheat, but the crop will be thistles.
What is not honestly obtained can never bring lasting good.
Here Job's speeches ended.
He concluded with a strong appeal to God concerning the accusations against his moral and religious character.
But despite Job's confidence, we will later see that he was mistaken in some of his claims (Job 40:4–5; 1 John 1:8).
Let us all examine ourselves.
Where we have sinned, seek pardon through the blood of Jesus Christ, which cleanses us from every sin.
May God have mercy on us and write his law upon our hearts.

row.cell: Elihu is displeased at the dispute between Job and his friends.

div.title: Elihu is distressed by the argument (verses 1–5)
div.p: Job's friends had stopped speaking, but they were not persuaded.
Other people had been listening.
Elihu was rightly displeased with Job for being more eager to clear his own reputation than to defend God's justice and goodness.
He was also displeased with Job's friends because they had not treated Job fairly.
Few quarrels begin—and even fewer continue—without some wrongdoing on both sides.
People who seek truth must not reject what is right in either party's arguments or defend what is wrong in either one.

div.title: Elihu corrects both parties (verses 6–14)
div.p: Elihu professed to speak under the Holy Spirit's inspiration and sought to correct both Job and his friends.
He recognized that older people with more experience should normally speak first.
Yet God distributes wisdom as he chooses.
This gave Elihu courage to express his view.
Through careful attention to God's word and dependence upon the Holy Spirit, young people may become wiser than older people.
But real wisdom makes them quick to listen, slow to speak and willing to hear others patiently.

div.title: Elihu speaks without flattery (verses 15–22)
div.p: Even if we are convinced the Holy Spirit has given us something valuable to say, we should wait for the proper opportunity.
God brings order, not confusion.
A faithful person finds refreshment in speaking for God's glory and helping others grow in faith.
The more we contemplate the majesty of God our Maker, and the more we fear his wrath and justice, the less we will fear or flatter people.
If we keep the Lord's mercy and the terrors of his wrath before us, we can remain steady in whatever duty he assigns us.

row.cell: Elihu offers to reason with Job.
Elihu blames Job for reflecting upon God.

div.title: Elihu offers to reason with Job (verses 1–7)
div.p: Job had wanted an impartial judge to hear his case.
In one sense Elihu was an answer to that request: he was another human being like Job.
To persuade people rightly, we must use reason rather than terror, fair arguments rather than force.

div.title: Elihu corrects Job's accusations against God (verses 8–13)
div.p: Elihu charged Job with speaking against God's justice and goodness.
When we hear statements that dishonor God, we should testify against them.
Job had described God as harshly recording his wrongs.
Elihu said he had spoken improperly and ought to humble himself and withdraw those accusations through repentance.
God is not accountable to human beings.
It is unreasonable for weak and sinful creatures to quarrel with the infinitely wise, powerful and good God.
He acts with perfect justice, wisdom and goodness, even when we cannot see the reasons.

div.title: God calls people to repentance (verses 14–18)
div.p: God speaks through conscience, Providence and ministers.
Elihu considered all three.
At that time, Henry says, no written divine revelation was known to be available; written Scripture is now our principal guide.
When God intends a person's good, he may use inward conviction to open the heart, as he opened Lydia's heart, and open the ears so that a warning is heard.
These messages aim to keep people from sin, especially pride.
Sinners who indulge sinful plans and pride are moving toward destruction.
Turning them away from sin saves them from hell.
An awakened conscience that restrains sin is a great mercy.

div.title: God uses affliction for the soul's good (verses 19–28)
div.p: Job concluded from his illness that God was angry with him.
His friends made the same assumption.
Elihu explained that God often afflicts the body for the good of the soul.
Understanding this can help us respond wisely to sickness as a means by which God speaks.
Pain entered the world through sin.
Yet through divine grace, bodily suffering can help the soul.
When an affliction has accomplished its purpose, it may be removed.
A ransom or atoning sacrifice has been found.
Henry identifies Jesus Christ as both the Messenger and the Ransom of which Elihu speaks, just as Job had called him his Redeemer.
Christ is both the One who purchases redemption and its price, the Priest and the Sacrifice.
A human soul is so valuable, and sin has brought such ruin, that nothing less than the blood of God's Son could provide redemption.
He gave his life as a ransom for many.
When recovery from illness follows forgiveness of sin, that recovery is especially precious.
Everyone who truly repents will find mercy with God.
The works of darkness bear no good fruit.
Sin's apparent gains are much less than the harm it brings.
We must confess sin to God with a broken and humble heart (1 John 1:9).
Confession has three parts.
First, acknowledge the fact of sin rather than making excuses.
Second, acknowledge its wrongness: I have distorted what is right.
Third, acknowledge its folly: I acted foolishly and without understanding.
We have every reason to confess this way.

div.title: Elihu asks Job to listen (verses 29–33)
div.p: Elihu taught that God's gracious purpose toward human beings is to rescue them from everlasting misery and bring them into lasting happiness.
Whatever he uses to turn us away from ruin deserves our thanksgiving, even when the experience itself is painful.
Those who finally perish are without excuse because they refused the healing offered to them.

row.cell: Elihu accuses Job of charging God with injustice.

div.title: Elihu calls for judgment on Job's words (verses 1–9)
div.p: Elihu invited the people present to consider Job's words with him and determine what was right.

An ordinary Christian whose mind has been enlightened, whose heart has been sanctified by God's Spirit, and who knows Scripture can often judge whether a belief, statement or action agrees with true religion better than someone depending only on personal understanding.
Job had spoken as though he intended to justify himself completely.
Someone who says, “I have kept my hands clean for nothing,” offends God's children and speaks in agreement with God's enemies rather than his friends (Psalm 73:13–15).

div.title: God cannot act unjustly (verses 10–15)
div.p: Elihu had already explained that God did not intend to harm Job through his suffering.
Rather, he intended Job's spiritual good.
Now Elihu argued that God did him no wrong in afflicting him.
If knowing God's good purpose did not satisfy Job, remembering God's justice should have silenced his complaints.
The Almighty never does evil or injustice.
Some faithful service remains unrewarded in this life, and some sins seem to go unpunished.
But the day of judgment is coming, when God will repay everyone according to their works.
A believer cannot be finally condemned, because the Savior has paid the ransom.
Even so, our sins deserve far worse than any outward suffering we experience, so no injustice is done when God tests us severely.

div.title: God's rule is righteous and complete (verses 16–30)
div.p: Elihu appealed directly to Job.
Could he seriously imagine that God resembles unjust earthly rulers who hate righteousness and become scourges to those they govern?
It is presumptuous to condemn God's ways because we dislike our circumstances.
Elihu reminded Job of God's greatness and sovereignty so that he would submit.
Job had often wanted to bring his case personally before God.
What could he accomplish by doing so?
Everything God does is right, and eventually it will be seen to be so.
A soul resting securely in God cannot be made truly miserable by worldly troubles.
But the approval of the whole world cannot comfort a person who remains under God's displeasure.

div.title: Elihu corrects Job's complaints (verses 31–37)
div.p: When we rebuke someone for doing wrong, we must also show the person what would be right.
Job's friends had demanded that he confess to being a wicked man.
Elihu instead urged Job to acknowledge that he had spoken rashly and unwisely.
We should not exaggerate another person's fault when correcting it.
Elihu taught Job to humble himself, accept God's discipline and pray to discover whatever sins needed to be addressed.
A godly person is willing to know even unpleasant truths about personal faults.
Especially in suffering, a believer wants to understand why God is contending with him.
It is not enough to regret sin: we must turn away from it.
Children who love their father are willing to speak honestly with him and open their minds to him.
We often want everything concerning us to happen exactly as we planned, but that expectation is unreasonable.
Job should ask whether his complaints revealed sin and folly.
The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works (Psalm 145:17).
A believer may therefore say: Let my Savior, my wise and loving Lord, choose everything for me. His choice will be the wisest, bringing the greatest glory to him and the most lasting good to me.

row.cell: Why those who cry out under afflictions are not regarded.

div.title: Our conduct cannot enrich God (verses 1–8)
div.p: Elihu reproved Job for caring more about his own justification than God's honor.
He directed Job's attention to the heavens.
They stand far above us, and God is infinitely greater still.
Neither human sins nor our faithful service can diminish or enrich him as though he depended on us.
We have no reason to complain when God does not give everything we hoped to receive.
Instead, we should be thankful that he has already given more good than we deserve.

div.title: Why some cries during suffering go unanswered (verses 9–13)
div.p: Job had wondered why God did not intervene when oppressed people cried out against their oppressors.
He found this difficult to reconcile with God's justice.
Elihu answered that people often ignore the mercies they receive during their suffering.
Instead of recognizing and thanking the Lord for these blessings, they focus entirely on their trouble.
God gives songs in the night.
When our circumstances are dark and sorrowful, his providence and promises offer enough comfort to strengthen us and even make us rejoice amid trials.
If we refuse the consolations God offers and attend only to what we have lost, we have no right to demand that he answer every prayer as we wish.
Events that kill the body cannot destroy the soul.
When God has not removed an affliction, it does not follow that his arm lacks power or his ear cannot hear.
Elihu taught that the sufferer may still need to be humbled.
This is Elihu's explanation in the present dispute, not a license to assume that every unanswered plea for relief proves a particular sin in another sufferer.

div.title: Elihu corrects Job's impatience (verses 14–16)
div.p: During prosperity we may imagine our mountain will never be moved.
During suffering we may imagine the valley will never be filled.
But expecting tomorrow to resemble today is as foolish as thinking that fair or stormy weather will last forever.
Job had no reason to despair when looking to God.
A day of final judgment is coming.
Then what appears wrong will be seen in the light of divine justice, and what is dark or difficult will be understood.
Henry says that if divine wrath is present in our troubles, it is because we quarrel with God, grow fretful and distrust his Providence.
He applies this diagnosis to Job.
Elihu was directed by God to humble Job, because Job had spoken rashly about matters beyond his knowledge.
When we suffer, we should not speak only of how great our pain is.
We should also consider and praise how great God's mercy is.

row.cell: The methods in which God deals with men.
The wonders in the works of creation.

div.title: Elihu asks Job to listen (verses 1–4)
div.p: Elihu maintained that Job's affliction had been sent to test him.
It continued because Job had not yet been humbled fully under it.
Elihu wanted to ascribe righteousness to his Maker and show that God is righteous in everything he does.
We cannot learn this truth fully from fallen nature alone.
It must be taught through God's word and Spirit.
Elihu's answer was relevant to Job's dispute with his friends.
He explained that the trials had been sent for Job's spiritual good.
This corrected the friends' false assumption that every such calamity was a punishment proving great wickedness.
God had treated Job with mercy, even amid severe suffering.

div.title: God's purposes in affliction (verses 5–14)
div.p: God rules righteously.
He is always ready to defend people who are treated unjustly.
When our eyes remain turned to God in faithful service, his eyes remain upon us in mercy, even when we have reached our lowest point.
The Lord can use hardship to remind us of past sins and make us willing to receive instruction.
Through grace working with the trial, an afflicted person may learn lessons previously rejected.
God also uses trouble to discourage future sin.
The lesson is not only to recognize wrongdoing but to have nothing more to do with it.
Those who serve God faithfully have a promise of the good things of the present life, as far as those things promote God's glory and their own true welfare.
Who would wisely wish for more?
They also enjoy inward pleasures and the deep peace of those who love God's law.
If affliction fails to do its work, a person should expect the furnace to be heated until it consumes them.
Those who die without knowledge and without grace are lost forever.
Hypocrisy is principally a condition of the heart.
It loves the world and bodily desires while outwardly appearing devoted to God and religion.
Whether sinners die young or live long enough to heap up wrath, their end is dreadful.
The souls of the wicked live beyond bodily death, but in everlasting misery.

div.title: Elihu warns Job against contending with God (verses 15–23)
div.p: Elihu believed Job was prolonging his own suffering through proud resistance.
He urged Job not to persist in stubbornness.
Even godly people need reminders to fear God's anger because the best and wisest still have sinful tendencies.
Job should not continue quarreling with divine Providence.
Nor should we ever approve of sin, cherish it or make room for it.
In Elihu's judgment, Job had preferred the gratification of pride and an irritable temper over mortifying those tendencies through humble submission and acceptance of discipline.
It is absurd for human beings to try to instruct the One who is himself the source of light, truth and all knowledge.
God teaches us through the Bible, the best book, and through his Son, the best Teacher.
He is righteous in all his dealings.

div.title: The marvels of creation (verses 24–33)
div.p: Elihu directed Job's thoughts to God's greatness, so that he might submit with renewed willingness.
Unlike animals, human beings can look at creation and recognize their Creator's hand.
They should therefore give him glory.
Evildoers should tremble before him.
Faithful children of God, however, should rejoice, even when their Father speaks in judgment against his enemies.
Even the clearest light may be hidden temporarily by a cloud.
The light of God's favor is the most blessed of all, yet sin can darken our experience of his love.
When sins come between us and his countenance, we may no longer perceive the sunshine of his kindness.

row.cell: Elihu observes the power of God.
Job required to explain the works of nature.
God is great, and is to be feared.

div.title: God's power displayed in weather (verses 1–13)
div.p: Changes in the weather occupy much of our thinking and conversation.
Yet how seldom do we speak about them as Elihu did—with reverence toward God, who directs them!
We should recognize his glory not only in frightening thunder and lightning, but also in ordinary, quieter changes such as snow and rain.
Animals instinctively seek refuge when a storm comes.
Should humans alone remain without a shelter?
God warns people in many ways to flee from the wrath to come.
He also invites them to receive his salvation and be happy.
People reveal how little they trust divine Providence by the way they complain about the weather.
The outcome of an entire year often shows how foolish those complaints were.
Believers should avoid this pattern.
No day is made evil by the Lord.
We make many days miserable through our own sin.

div.title: Job cannot fully explain God's works (verses 14–20)
div.p: Thinking carefully about God's works in nature can reconcile our hearts to the events of his Providence.
God sends both the freezing north wind and the warm, thawing south wind.
The Holy Spirit is compared with both because he convicts and comforts (Song of Songs 4:16).
Even the best human beings understand little about God's glorious character and government.
People who through grace know much about God still know almost nothing compared with everything that remains to be known.
How much greater will our knowledge be when what is perfect has come!

div.title: God's greatness and the clouds over human understanding (verses 21–24)
div.p: Elihu concluded with statements about God's majesty.
Sunlight continues shining even when clouds hide it.
In the same way, the light of God's favor continues toward his faithful servants even when they cannot perceive it.
Sin can come between our hearts and that comforting light.
Sorrow can also darken our minds.
But God has a wind that can scatter the clouds: the Holy Spirit.
As a wind sweeps clouds across the sky, God's Spirit removes the ignorance, unbelief, sin and harmful desires clouding the soul through regeneration.
The Spirit also removes the clouds that trouble a believer's conscience through consolation.
Now that the Lord was about to speak for himself, Elihu summed up his discourse.
With God is majestic and awe-inspiring power.
Sooner or later, every human being will fear him.

row.cell: God calls upon Job to answer.

div.title: The Lord calls Job to answer (verses 1–3)
div.p: Job had silenced his friends but had not persuaded them.
Elihu had silenced Job without bringing him to acknowledge his fault before God.
Now the Lord himself intervened.
God humbled Job and brought him to repent of the passionate words he had spoken about divine Providence.
The Lord did so by setting a series of contrasts before him:
God lives forever, while Job's life is brief.
God knows everything, while Job's knowledge is limited.
God possesses almighty strength, while Job is weak.
It seriously offends God when human folly obscures the counsel of his wisdom.
Humble faith and sincere obedience give us the clearest understanding of his will.

div.title: God questions Job about earth and sea (verses 4–11)
div.p: To humble Job, God showed that he knew so little even about the earth and the sea.
We are not qualified to find fault with God's work.
Nor need we fear that his work will fail.
The works of his Providence and creation are secure.
So is the work of redemption, whose foundation and cornerstone is Jesus Christ.
God's church rests on a foundation as firm as the earth.

div.title: Light, darkness and our ignorance (verses 12–24)
div.p: The Lord challenged Job to recognize the extent of what he did not know.
When we examine ourselves in this way, we discover how little our knowledge is compared with everything unknown to us.
Through God's tender mercy, the Dayspring from on high has visited us, bringing light to people sitting in darkness.
God enlightens hearts so they receive his truth like clay receiving the impress of a seal (2 Corinthians 4:6).
God's way in governing the world is described as being in the sea—hidden from us.
If we are assured that the gates of heaven will open to us after death, we need not fear the gates of death.
Someone unable to measure even the breadth of the earth should not presume to search the full depths of God's counsel.
At the brightest noon, do not assume it will always be day.
At the darkest midnight, do not despair of morning's return.
This applies to our inward spiritual condition as well as outward circumstances.
How foolish to fight against God, when our greatest interest lies in making peace with him and remaining in his love!

div.title: Other mighty works and divine compassion (verses 25–41)
div.p: Earlier, God's questions exposed Job's ignorance.
Now they also exposed his weakness.
Knowing so little, Job should not put God's plans on trial.
Being able to accomplish so little, he should not oppose Providence.
The Lord's care is enough to satisfy the needs of every living creature.
He even feeds young ravens.
Surely he will not neglect his own people.
That example of compassion is only one among countless gifts God provides every day without our awareness.
Every glimpse of divine perfection should remind us that God deserves our love, that sin against him is evil, and that we need his mercy and salvation.

p.hi: God inquires of Job concerning several animals.

div.title: God teaches Job through animals
div.p: The Lord continued to humble Job through questions about the living creatures he had made.
The nature and circumstances of each animal reveal something of the power, wisdom and variety of God's works.
Consider the wild donkey.
It is better to work diligently and accomplish something useful than to wander without purpose and be of no use.
If Job could not command even the colt of a wild donkey, how unfit was he to issue instructions to divine Providence!
Henry also describes the powerful creature called the unicorn in his biblical witness.
It possesses the strength to perform useful service but is unwilling to do so.
God challenged Job to compel it to work.
When the Lord gives someone the strength to serve, it is a special mercy if he also gives a willing heart.
We should pray for that willingness and reason ourselves into it, because unlike animals we can reflect on our duty.
The most impressive-looking qualities are not always the most valuable gifts.
Henry contrasts the nightingale's song with the peacock's beautiful tail.

He would rather possess the eagle's eyesight and soaring wings, and the stork's parental affection, than the ostrich's fine feathers, since the ostrich cannot soar and appears to lack natural care for its young.
The description of the warhorse pictures presumptuous sinners.
As a horse rushes into battle, so people fully committed to evil hurry along the way their desires and passions have chosen.
They may refuse to fear the wrath of God and the fatal consequences of sin, however recklessly their desires drive them.
Some sinners believe themselves secure in their sin, like an eagle nesting high among inaccessible rocks.
But the Lord declares that even from such a height he can bring the proud down (Jeremiah 49:16).
Every wonderful image of animal life and behavior should teach us to honor the Creator's wisdom, which sustains everything he has made.
Job's failure to recognize how completely divine wisdom is present in God's works led him to speak in unworthy ways about Providence.

row.cell: The Lord reasons with Job to show his righteousness, power, and wisdom.

div.title: Job humbles himself before God (verses 1–5)
div.p: Fellowship with the Lord truly convinces and humbles the believer, making that person willing to abandon even deeply cherished sins.
Before the Lord grants remarkable deliverances, his people often need to be thoroughly convinced of their faults and brought low before him.
God had shown Job how little he understood about the works of nature.
Job therefore could not claim the wisdom needed to judge all God's purposes or methods of Providence.
The Lord asked whether someone who contended with the Almighty had the knowledge to instruct him.
Now Job began to soften into genuine repentance.
His friends had not persuaded him.
But the Lord's voice possesses power.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he convinces the heart.
Job yielded to divine grace.
He acknowledged that he had done wrong and could say nothing to justify himself.
He understood his own sinfulness and called himself vile.
True repentance changes the way a person thinks about self.
Job now recognized himself as a weak, foolish and sinful creature who should never have spoken against God's wise conduct.
One glimpse of God's holiness would terrify the strongest rebel.
How then will the wicked endure his glory at judgment?
But when divine glory is revealed to us in Jesus Christ, we are humbled without being destroyed by terror.
We can lower ourselves before him while still loving him as children love their Father.

div.title: God shows Job who can humble the proud (verses 6–14)
div.p: People who learn from what God has said become ready to receive more instruction.
Even those genuinely convicted of sin often need to be convinced more thoroughly and humbled more deeply.
Only God has the power to bring the proud down.
He also has the wisdom to know when and how to do it.
We have no right to instruct him how to govern the world.
Our own hands cannot save us.
We cannot make ourselves acceptable through our achievements, much less protect ourselves from God's justice.
We must therefore commit ourselves into his hand.
A believer's continuing renewal follows the same path as the first conversion: conviction of sin, humility and watchfulness against what remains.
When we recognize several sins, we may still need God to expose many more.

div.title: Behemoth demonstrates God's power (verses 15–24)
div.p: God described a vast animal with astonishing strength.
Behemoth means beasts.
Henry says most readers of his time understood the creature as the river-horse, or hippopotamus, familiar from Egypt.
That identification is reported as his interpretation, not treated as a zoological certainty established by the original text.
God made this enormous creature, fearfully and wonderfully formed.
Its strength is itself a gift from the Creator.
If even this animal overwhelms human strength, how much more ought we to humble ourselves before the Lord!
The God who made the human soul knows every way to reach it.
He can bring the sword of his justice and wrath against it.
But godly people have spiritual weapons: the whole armor of God, by which they resist and overcome the tempter.
Thus their immortal souls may remain safe whatever happens to their fragile, mortal bodies.

p.hi: Concerning Leviathan.

div.title: God illustrates his power through Leviathan
div.p: The Lord continued showing Job his own weakness and God's unlimited power through a description of Leviathan.
Henry reports that readers debated whether the creature was a whale or a crocodile.
He does not settle the question.
God demonstrated that Job was unable to subdue this mighty animal, then displayed something of the divine power that had made it.
If the language used about Leviathan shows such frightening strength, what language could fully express the power of God's wrath?
Let us recognize our own sinfulness and weakness and honor the majesty of God.
Let us take up the place and responsibilities he has assigned to us, cease depending proudly on our own wisdom, and give every part of the glory to our gracious God and Savior.
Every good gift comes from him and has been entrusted to us for a purpose.
Remembering both the Giver and his purpose, may we walk humbly with the Lord.

div.title: Job submits humbly to God (verses 1–6)
div.p: Job now recognized his guilt.
He stopped making excuses and abhorred himself as a sinner in heart and conduct, especially for his complaints against God.
He was ashamed and repented.

When the Spirit of grace enlightens our understanding, the new knowledge we gain of God's character is as much greater than what we previously knew as seeing something for ourselves is greater than hearing reports about it.
God reveals his Son to us through other people's teaching.
But through the Spirit he reveals his Son within us (Galatians 1:16), changing us into his likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).
When we recognize our sins, we must humble ourselves deeply for them.
Henry says self-abhorrence accompanies true repentance.
God will bring those he loves to worship him humbly.
Saving grace moves us to confess sin without trying to justify ourselves.

div.title: Job prays for his friends (verses 7–9)
div.p: After Job was convinced of his faults and humbled in repentance, the Lord recognized him, comforted him and honored him.
Satan had tried to prove Job a hypocrite.
His three friends had condemned him as a wicked man.
But when God approves a servant, the accusations of others matter little.
The friends had misrepresented God.
They had made earthly prosperity a sign of the true church and suffering certain evidence of God's anger.
Job had recognized more clearly that judgment and reward belong chiefly to the coming world.
In that respect he had spoken more rightly about God than they had.
Job prayed and offered sacrifice on behalf of the very friends who had hurt him.
In this he was like Christ, who prayed for his persecutors and always lives to intercede for sinners.
Henry regards Job's friends as good men who genuinely belonged to God, despite their errors.
The Lord would not let them continue in their mistakes any more than he had allowed Job to continue in his.
He had humbled Job by speaking from the whirlwind.
He humbled the friends in another way.
They were no longer to argue.
They had to unite through a sacrifice and a prayer, so that reconciliation could be achieved.
Believers may differ over lesser matters of judgment, yet they belong together in Christ, the great Sacrifice.
Therefore they should love one another and bear with one another.
When God was displeased with Job's friends, he still showed them the way to peace.
The offense begins on our side, but reconciliation begins through God's mercy.
Peace with him comes only in his appointed way and on his terms.
Those who understand how precious that peace is will accept even humbling conditions with gratitude.
Job did not use his vindication to insult his friends.
Once God had received him graciously, he readily forgave them.
In all our prayers and service, we should seek God's approval, not people's admiration.

div.title: Job's prosperity is restored (verses 10–17)
div.p: At the beginning of the book, Job's patience during suffering provided an example.
The conclusion gives encouragement to follow that example by showing his joyful end.
His trials began through Satan's hostility, which God restrained.
His restoration began through God's mercy, which Satan could not oppose.
Notice the turning point.
Job's possessions were not restored while he continued arguing with his friends.
Restoration came when he prayed for them.
The Lord is pleased by warm devotion, not heated disputes.
He doubled Job's possessions.
We may lose much for the Lord, but we will never ultimately lose anything because of the Lord.
Whether he grants health or material advantages in this life or not, those who endure suffering patiently according to his will will be happy in the end.
Job's wealth increased.
The Lord's blessing gives people the ability to gain wealth and grants success to honest work.
Sometimes the last days of a godly life become its best days, the latest acts its best service and the final comforts its sweetest.
The believer's path resembles the light of morning, growing brighter and brighter until the perfect day.

div.title: Psalms — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: David wrote most of the Psalms, though some were plainly written by others and the authorship of some is uncertain.
All were written through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.
No part of the Old Testament is cited or referred to more often in the New Testament.
Every Psalm either points directly to Christ—his person, character and offices—or can lead believers to think about him.

The Psalms give words to the hearts of believers in every condition: mourning over sin, longing for God or rejoicing in him; bearing affliction, struggling with temptation or celebrating the hope or experience of deliverance; contemplating God's perfections, thanking him for his mercy, meditating on his truths or delighting in his service.
They provide a divinely appointed measure of spiritual experience by which believers can examine themselves.
As true religion grows stronger within the heart, the Psalms become increasingly valuable.
Through the psalmists' words, the Spirit helps us pray.
When we become familiar with them, we find help approaching the throne of grace to confess sin, ask for mercy or give thanks.
Whatever holy affection fills the heart—desire, hope, sorrow or joy—we can find worthy language for it in this book.
Through the generations, the church has offered its prayers and praises to God using these inspired words.

row.cell: The holiness and happiness of a godly man.
The sinfulness and misery of a wicked man, The ground and reason of both.

div.title: The godly person and God's word (verses 1–3)
div.p: To meditate on God's word means to speak with ourselves about the great truths it contains, applying our minds closely and thinking about them steadily.
God's word should guide our actions and provide our comfort.
We should keep it continually in our minds both day and night.
No time is unsuitable for meditating upon it.

div.title: The ungodly person and final judgment (verses 4–6)
div.p: The ungodly differ from the righteous both in character and in condition.
Instead of delighting in God's law, they accept wicked advice, walk in sinful ways and finally settle into the position of those who mock what is holy.
They produce no good fruit.
The righteous resemble useful, fruitful trees.
But the ungodly resemble chaff blown away by wind—the worthless material a farmer wants removed from the threshing floor.
They have no spiritual value before God, however highly they regard themselves.
Every new temptation can blow them in a different direction.
Chaff may remain mixed with wheat for a time, but the One who holds the winnowing fan will completely cleanse his threshing floor.
Those who have made themselves like chaff through sin and folly will be found to be so when God's judgment comes like a storm and fire.
The final outcome of the ungodly is fixed if they remain in their sin.
Yet someone who recognizes guilt and misery may enter the company of the righteous through Jesus Christ, the living way.
In him that sinner becomes a new creation.
Desires, pleasures, hopes, fears, sorrows, friendships, occupations, thoughts, words and deeds are all changed.
Through divine grace, the person takes on a new life and character, as the soul is increasingly transformed into the Redeemer's image.
How different the characters and final outcomes of the righteous and ungodly are!

row.cell: Threatenings against the enemies of Christ's kingdom.
Promise to Christ as the Head of this kingdom.
Counsel to all, to espouse its interests.

div.title: The enemies of Christ's kingdom (verses 1–6)
div.p: The Psalm describes those who oppose Christ.
The present world is under Satan's rule, and people without saving grace, of every social position, party and character, can be stirred by him against God's cause.
Earthly rulers have often been particularly active in this opposition.
Christian truth and the commands of Christ expose the ambitions and selfish desires of worldly power.
His opponents want to cast off the restraints of conscience and the commands of God, treating them as chains to be broken.
Yet they can give no good reason for rejecting a government so righteous and holy that, if everyone received it, it would make earthly life resemble heaven.
Their resistance cannot succeed against so powerful a kingdom.
Jesus Christ possesses all authority in heaven and on earth.
He is Head over everything for the church, whatever plans his enemies make.
His throne is established within his church, in the hearts of believers.

div.title: The Father's promise to the Son (verses 7–9)
div.p: The Messiah's kingdom rests upon the eternal decree of God the Father.
Jesus himself referred to that decree and conducted his mission accordingly.
God declared to him, “You are my Son.”
Each of us should answer, “You are my Lord and Sovereign.”
When the Son asks for the nations as his inheritance, he seeks their happiness in him.
He intercedes for them continually.
He lives forever to do this and can save completely everyone who comes to God through him.
Multitudes among the nations will become his willing and loyal subjects.
Christians belong to Jesus Christ.
They bring him honor and praise.
The Father gives them to the Son by working through the Spirit and grace so that they gladly submit to Jesus.

div.title: The call to trust and serve Christ (verses 10–12)
div.p: Whatever we enjoy in this world, we should rejoice with reverence, because every earthly possession and circumstance is uncertain.
Welcoming Jesus Christ and submitting to him is both our duty and our greatest good.
Let him become precious to us.
Love him sincerely and deeply, as the woman who had been forgiven much showed her love by kissing his feet (Luke 7:38).
Greet the Son with a kiss of loyalty.
Accept his rule, submit to his laws, entrust your circumstances to his Providence and give yourselves entirely to his cause.
Unbelief rejects the only remedy for sin.
It will bring destruction to those who persist in it.
They will perish in their sinful path, in their empty hopes and in the loss of the true way to happiness.
Christ is the way to God.
People may suppose they are walking the right path, but if they reject Christ they will lose it.
Blessed are those who have made Christ their Refuge through faith.
They will be safe even on the day of divine wrath.

row.cell: David complains to God of his enemies, and confides in God.
He triumphs over his fears, and gives God the glory, and takes to himself the comfort.

div.title: David trusts God while enemies surround him (verses 1–3)
div.p: The more an active believer is driven away from God by painful Providence or the accusations of enemies, the more firmly that person clings to him.
A child of God is alarmed even by the thought of despairing of divine help.
David knew that God provided his people with three blessings.
First, safety: the Lord was his shield, protecting him.
Second, honor: everyone whom God receives as his own possesses genuine dignity.
Third, joy and deliverance: even in the worst times, believers may lift their heads with gladness, knowing that everything will work for their good.
They recognize that God gives them both reasons to rejoice and hearts capable of rejoicing.

div.title: Prayer, rest and victory through God (verses 4–8)
div.p: Distress and sorrow bring good when they lead us to pray earnestly.
David had repeatedly found God ready to answer.
Nothing can sever the connection between God's favor toward us and the faith he produces within us.
David had lived safely under God's protection.
Even the ordinary mercy of sleeping each night deserves our thanks every morning.
Many people cannot sleep because of pain, anxiety or frightening events.
But David's words especially describe his inner calm amid danger.
Through grace and the comforts of the Holy Spirit, the Lord gave him peace.
A mind resting firmly upon God is a great mercy in trouble.
Consider the Son of David lying down to rest on the cross, that bed of sorrows, and entrusting his Spirit to the Father's hands with confidence in a joyful resurrection.
Christian, let faith teach you how to sleep and how to die.
Sleep is a brief kind of death, and death is a longer sleep.
The same God watches over you on your bed and in your grave.
David's faith became triumphant.
He began by describing his enemies' strength and cruelty.
He finished by rejoicing in God's power and grace, recognizing that more were on his side than against him.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
No danger exceeds his power to save.
Those who know the Lord as their God can be sure of salvation, for he is the God of salvation.

row.cell: The children of men proved, and the happiness of godly people.

div.title: Reverence, self-examination and trust (verses 1–5)
div.p: Our strongest plea in prayer is to ask God to hear us for his mercy's sake.
People who refuse to ask for forgiveness, the righteousness that justifies and eternal life will perish because they have rejected blessings they desperately need.
It is a dreadful choice.
The psalmist warns against sin.
Keep a holy reverence for God's greatness and glory.
There is much we ought to say to our own hearts.
Do not leave it unsaid.
Examine your heart through serious reflection.
Fix your thoughts on what is good and hold to it.
Before going to sleep, review the day's conduct and ask especially what you did wrong, so that you can repent.
When you wake at night, meditate on God and what leads to peace with him.
During illness, give particular attention to examining your ways.
Be still.
When you question your conscience, remain serious and quiet long enough to hear its answer.
Do not rush to excuse sin.
All confidence must rest in God alone.
Therefore, after speaking of sacrifices offered in righteousness, the psalmist commands us to trust in the Lord.

div.title: The happiness of God's favor (verses 6–8)
div.p: Worldly people ask for good things, but not usually the greatest good.
They want outward, immediate and partial benefits: good food and drink, a successful business, comfortable possessions and wealth.
But how much are these worth?
Most people will accept almost any benefit.
Someone whose heart is ruled by grace cannot be satisfied with these things alone.
Such a person prays: Lord, let us know your favor. Let us be sure of your loving kindness. That is enough.
Many people search for happiness.
David had found it.
When God gives grace to the heart, he also gives gladness to the heart.
Comforted in this way, David could pity prosperous sinners without envying or fearing them.
He committed his concerns to God and became willing to accept God's wise will.
But salvation is in Jesus Christ alone.
Those who reject him as Mediator and insult him through his disciples are in grave danger.
May they stand in awe, turn from sin and stop resisting the only remedy.

row.cell: God will certainly hear prayer: David gives to God the glory, and takes to himself the comfort.
He prayed for himself, that God would guide him, and for all the Lord's people, that God would give them joy, and keep them safe.

div.title: The God who hears prayer (verses 1–6)
div.p: God hears prayer.
He has always done so, and he remains as ready to receive prayer as ever.
One of our strongest reasons for confidence in prayer is that we approach him as our King and our God.
David prayed to the God who hates sin.
Sin is folly.
Those who persist in it are fools of their own making.
People who are determined to be wicked hate God and rightly face his judgment.
If they continue in that condition, their misery and destruction will be everlasting.
We should learn to value truthfulness and sincerity in every part of life.
Liars and murderers resemble the devil and show whose ways they follow.
The Lord abhors such wrongdoing.
David's enemies displayed these characteristics.
People who behave in the same way still oppose Christ and his church.

div.title: God guides, protects and brings joy (verses 7–12)
div.p: David regularly prayed on his own.
Yet he was also faithful in attending public worship.
God's mercy must always be the foundation of our hope and joy in everything involving him.
Our prayers should reach beyond ourselves to other believers.
Grace be with everyone who sincerely loves Jesus Christ.
Every blessing comes through Jesus Christ, the Righteous One, just as God's favor was previously shown to Israel through David, whom he protected and established upon the throne.
Christ is the righteous Savior, Israel's King and the source of blessing for every believer.
His favor is the defense and protection of his church.

row.cell: The psalmist deprecates God's wrath, and begs for the return of his favour.
He assures himself of an answer of peace.

div.title: A humbled heart seeks divine favor (verses 1–7)
div.p: These words express a truly humbled heart, a broken and contrite spirit enduring great suffering.
The affliction was allowed to awaken the psalmist's conscience and help put sinful desires to death.
Illness reminded him of his sins, and he feared that it showed God's displeasure.
Bodily suffering can be endured when the soul enjoys God's consolation.
In his own suffering, Christ's deepest complaint concerned the anguish of his soul and the apparent withdrawal of his Father's favor.
Every part of Scripture declares that salvation belongs to the Lord alone.
Human beings are sinners, whose condition can be remedied only by mercy.
That mercy shines especially brightly when God restores people who have wandered from him.
We may rightly pray that, if it is God's will and he has further work for us or our loved ones to do on earth, he will preserve our lives for continued service.
For the saints, departing to be with Christ is the greater happiness.
Yet remaining alive may be more useful for the church.

div.title: Confidence that God will answer (verses 8–10)
div.p: What a remarkable change in the psalmist's words!
After laying his request before God, he became confident that sorrow would turn into joy.
Through grace working within his heart, he knew his prayer had been accepted and trusted that an answer would come in due time.
Our prayers are acceptable because they rise to God through the hands of Christ our Mediator.
The words describe prayer to God as the righteous Judge and the God of the believer's righteousness, who will defend the right and put wrongs right.
Through Christ's blood and righteousness, a believer can approach a righteous God to ask for forgiveness and cleansing.
God is both just and faithful to grant these blessings.
The psalmist's words regarding his enemies may be either a prayer for their conversion or a prediction of their downfall.

row.cell: The psalmist prays to God to plead his cause, and judge for him.
He expresses confidence in God, and will give him the glory of his deliverance.

div.title: David appeals to the Judge of hearts (verses 1–9)
div.p: David fled to God for help and protection.
Yet Jesus Christ alone could call heaven to witness that he was completely upright in every respect.
All his works were righteous.
The prince of this world could find nothing in him that deserved accusation.
Nevertheless, for our sake Christ accepted being treated as guilty and suffered every evil.
He remained innocent and triumphed over them all.
David's appeal was directed to the righteous God who examines hearts and the deepest desires.
God knows the hidden sins of wicked people and how to bring their wrongdoing to an end.
He also knows the secret sincerity of those who live uprightly and can establish their cause.

Anyone who has first made peace with God concerning personal sins through the sacrifice of the Mediator, according to God's mercy and grace, may then appeal to divine justice when falsely accused by enemies.

div.title: The righteous God saves and warns (verses 10–17)
div.p: David trusted that God would be a powerful Savior.
The threatened destruction of a sinner may be avoided through repentance and conversion.
The warning is therefore an act of mercy.
God gives people time to repent and escape the judgment they otherwise face.
He is patient and slow to punish, not delighting in the destruction of sinners.
In verses 14–16, sinners are pictured exerting great effort in destroying their own souls.
If those same efforts were turned toward repentance and obedience, they could lead toward salvation.
In this sense, the description applies to everyone who continues in sin.
Throughout our trials we must look to the Savior.
Blessed Lord, grant that we may follow your spotless example as you go before your church in suffering.
When persecution and trouble mark our smaller path, may looking to Jesus strengthen our minds and comfort our hearts.

row.cell: God is to be glorified, for making known himself to us.
And for making even the heavenly bodies useful to man, thereby placing him but little lower than the angels.

div.title: God's name is glorious (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: The psalmist wanted to give God the glory his name deserves.
How brightly that glory shines even in our earthly world!
God is our Lord because he created us, protects us and cares for us specially.
The birth, earthly life, preaching, miracles, suffering, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ have become known throughout the world.
No other name is so widely recognized and no influence so generally felt as the Savior's.
But divine glory shines even more brilliantly in heaven.
Here on earth we hear God's excellent name and praise it.
The angels and blessed spirits see his glory and praise him for it.
Nevertheless, God is exalted beyond even their worship and thanksgiving.
Sometimes divine grace is seen wonderfully in little children.
At other times God accomplishes great things within his church through weak and unlikely people, so that everyone can recognize that the power came from him, not them.
Through such actions he silences his enemies.

div.title: Humanity's dignity under God and Christ (verses 3–9)
div.p: Considering the heavens should lead us to turn our desires toward heavenly things.
What are human beings—so small—that God should honor them?
What are human beings—so sinful—that he should show them favor?
Humanity has been given authority over lesser creatures, subject to God.
This passage also points specifically to Jesus Christ.
In Hebrews 2:6–8, the apostle uses these words to demonstrate Christ's supreme authority.
Jesus is the Man and Son of Man who has received dominion over the works of God's hands.
The greatest honor ever given to human nature, and the greatest mercy ever shown to our race, are displayed in Christ.
The psalmist therefore had every reason to finish as he began:

p.hi: Lord, how excellent is your name in all the earth!

div.p: The earth has been honored by the Redeemer's presence and continues to receive the light of his gospel and the governance of his wisdom and power.
How could our words be sufficient to praise the One who has every right to our obedience as Redeemer?

row.cell: David praises God for protecting his people.
And for cause to praise him.

div.title: David thanks God for protecting his people (verses 1–10)
div.p: For our praise to be acceptable to God, we must offer it sincerely with our whole hearts.
When thanking him for a particular mercy, remember the earlier mercies already received.
Our greatest joy must be in the Giver, not merely the gift.
The victories of the Redeemer should be celebrated as the victories of all the redeemed.
The strongest of God's enemies are powerless before his almighty strength.
We can be confident that the Lord's judgments are true and free of all injustice.
His people may flee to him through faith as their Refuge.
They can depend upon his power and promises for safety, so that no lasting harm comes upon them.
Those who recognize God as faithful and truthful will rejoice in his promises and rest upon them.
Those who know him as their everlasting Father will entrust their souls to him as their greatest concern.
They will trust him continually, persevering in faithful service throughout life.
Who would refuse to seek the One who has never abandoned those who seek him?

div.title: Reasons to call others to praise (verses 11–20)
div.p: People who truly believe God deserves praise do not want merely to praise him more faithfully themselves.
They also want others to join them.
The day is coming when God will show that he has not forgotten the cries of humble people—their prayers or the testimony of their blood.
No suffering can bring us so low, or so close to death, that God cannot raise us up.
If he has already rescued us from spiritual and eternal death, we can confidently look to him for help in every distress.
God's Providence often brings wicked people to ruin through the very plans they made to destroy others.
The drunkard destroys his health.
The spendthrift impoverishes himself.
The quarrelsome person brings trouble upon his own life.
These examples show how sin contains the seeds of its punishment.
The ultimate destruction of those who continue in sin comes through their own choices.
Sin originally entered human life through the wicked one.
Those who stubbornly remain under his dominion face his dreadful end.
The true condition of nations and individuals can be measured by a simple question:

p.hi: Do their actions show that they remember God, or that they have forgotten him?

div.p: David urged God's people to wait patiently for deliverance, even when it appears long delayed.
God will prove that he has never forgotten them.
How strange that human beings—creatures made of dust and destined for dust—often need severe suffering before they recognize who they are!

row.cell: The psalmist complains of the wickedness of the wicked.
He prays to God to appear for the relief of his people.

div.title: The psalmist laments the wicked (verses 1–11)
div.p: When God seems to withdraw his presence, his people find it deeply painful, especially in trouble.
Often it is our unbelief that keeps us distant from God, even as we complain that he is distant from us.
Angry words against wicked people often accomplish more harm than good.
If we must speak of their sins, bring the matter before God in prayer.
He can transform them.
The sinner proudly celebrates worldly strength and success.
Wicked people do not seek God or call upon him.
To live without prayer is to live without God.
They think about countless projects, schemes and possessions, yet give no thought to God in any of them.
They do not submit to his will or seek his glory.
The cause is pride.
They imagine genuine religion is beneath them.
People would not so readily disregard justice and kindness toward other humans unless they had first rejected reverence for God.

div.title: A prayer for the oppressed and tempted (verses 12–18)
div.p: The psalmist was amazed both at the bold wickedness of human beings and at God's patience in allowing it to continue.
God prepares hearts for prayer.
He awakens holy desires, strengthens faith, directs attention and raises affections toward himself.
Then he graciously accepts the prayer.
Preparing the heart is itself God's work, so we should ask him to prepare our hearts.
Poor, afflicted, persecuted or tempted believers should remember that Satan is the prince of this present world and the father of the ungodly.
We cannot expect justice or mercy from people of the same spirit as those who crucified the Lord of glory.
But Jesus, who once suffered, now rules as King over all the earth.
His reign will never end.
Entrust yourselves to him, humbly relying on his mercy.
He will rescue his followers from every temptation, break the power of oppressors and soon crush Satan beneath their feet.
In this present life believers already taste something of the promised deliverance.
But only in heaven will sin and temptation finally be excluded altogether.

p.hi: David's struggle with, and triumph over a strong temptation to distrust God, and betake himself to indirect means for his own safety, in a time of danger.

div.title: Trusting the Lord rather than worldly advice
div.p: Everyone who sincerely fears and serves God may trust him with confidence.
Before David described his temptation to distrust the Lord, he stated his decision to trust him in life and in death.
Believers may not be frightened by their enemies, yet they can still be tempted by the fears of their friends.
Well-meaning companions may persuade them to abandon their position or neglect their assigned work.
These friends see the danger but fail to recognize the believer's safety in God.
Their advice comes from worldly calculation rather than heavenly wisdom.
The truths of faith are the foundation of Christian confidence and hope.
We must hold firmly to them against every temptation to unbelief.
Without God to turn to, God to trust and the hope of eternal happiness, believers would be ruined.
The prosperity of wicked people and the hardship endured by godly people had tested David's faith.
Yet we do not need to climb to heaven to bring down a God we can trust.
His word is close to us, and God is present in his word.
His Spirit dwells within his saints, who are living temples.
The Lord is that Spirit.
God governs the world.
We may know only how people appear.
God knows what they truly are, as a refiner knows gold after testing it.
He examines hearts with eyes that cannot be deceived.
When the Lord afflicts righteous people, he tests them for their ultimate good.
Persecutors and oppressors may prosper temporarily, but if they remain unrepentant they will perish.
God is holy and therefore hates evil.
He is a righteous Judge and therefore will punish it.
At death, the wicked are carried away in a dreadful storm.
Every person receives an appointed portion.
Sinner, consider your danger: judgment is approaching, and without repentance death leads toward eternal wrath.

p.hi: Hurry to the cross of Christ.

div.p: Ask yourself: what is the relationship between God and my soul?
Is Christ my hope, my comfort and my protection?
Only through him can the soul safely pass through all its troubles and spiritual conflicts.

p.hi: The psalmist begs help of God, because there were none among men whom he durst trust.

div.title: Seeking God amid moral decline
div.p: This Psalm provides wise thoughts and prayers for difficult times.
What makes a time truly bad?
Ask worldly-minded people, and they will mention lack of money, declining trade or the destruction caused by war.
But Scripture points to deeper causes.
Perilous times arrive when sin becomes widespread (2 Timothy 3:1).
When godliness declines, the times are genuinely evil.
The One who made the human mouth will judge how it is used—whether for proud, profane, deceitful or even useless words.
When poor and needy people are oppressed, times are very bad.
God hears their sighs and sees their suffering.
When wickedness becomes widespread and those holding authority encourage it, the situation is especially grave.
Yet God provides three consolations for such times.
First, we can approach the Lord to ask him to put right every wrong.
Second, he will punish and restrain those who persist in pride and falsehood.
Third, he will deliver his oppressed people in the most suitable time.
Human beings may lie, but God remains faithful.
People may fail our trust, but God can be trusted.
His word is as precious and reliable as silver refined repeatedly to the highest purity.
Its truth and power have been demonstrated again and again.
However dark the age becomes, God will preserve his chosen remnant.
Until the end of the world, there will continue to be proud and wicked generations.
But God's people have been entrusted to Jesus Christ our Savior.
No one can snatch them from his hands.
They are built upon Christ the Rock, safe even against the fiercest persecution and temptation.

p.hi: The psalmist complains that God had long withdrawn. He earnestly prays for comfort. He assures himself of an answer of peace.

div.title: From long sorrow to confidence in mercy
div.p: At times God hides his face, and his children are left uncertain about their relationship with him.
They feel this more deeply than any outward hardship.
Yet believers often burden themselves with anxieties beyond what is necessary.
The bread of sorrow may become their daily food.
Our own Master, Jesus Christ, was a Man of Sorrows.
During long afflictions, a common temptation is to imagine that suffering will never end.
People who have been without joy for a long time may begin losing hope as well.
Let our complaints drive us to prayer, not away from it.
Nothing is more devastating to the soul than feeling deprived of God's favor.
Nothing is more reviving than the return of that favor.
The sudden, joyful changes recorded in the Psalms are remarkable.
In verse 4, everything seems full of gloomy despair.
But in verse 5, the psalmist rises above his fears and throws himself entirely upon the mercy and care of his divine Redeemer.
See the power of faith and the goodness of approaching God.
When we bring our troubles to the throne of grace and leave them there, we can depart as Hannah did, no longer looking sad (1 Samuel 1:18).
The psalmist's faith rested upon God's mercy, not upon any merit of his own.
Once he trusted that mercy, his heart rejoiced in salvation.
Joy and peace come through believing.
He became so confident of God's promised salvation that he spoke as though it were already accomplished.
Believers may pray in the same way, abandoning every hope except God's mercy through the Savior's blood.
Sometimes their burdens lift suddenly.
At other times relief comes slowly.
When comfort returns, they recognize that many earlier fears were unnecessary and confess that the Lord has dealt generously with them.

p.hi: A description of the depravity of human nature, and the deplorable corruption of a great part of mankind.

div.title: Sin, human corruption and salvation from Zion
div.p: The fool says within the heart, “There is no God.”
The sinner described rejects the existence of a Judge governing the world and a Providence ruling human affairs.
But the denial begins within the heart.
Such a person cannot truly establish that God does not exist.
Instead, the person wishes there were no God and takes pleasure in the mere possibility that no divine judgment will come.
This is foolishness.
The sinner's wicked and irreverent conduct is both evidence of that folly and a cause of it.
God's word reveals the thoughts and desires behind it.
No one willingly denies divine accountability in this way until sin has hardened the heart so deeply that having no Judge appears desirable.
The disease of sin has infected all humanity.
Everyone has turned aside.
No one does good as the holy law demands—not even one.
Whatever good exists in human beings or is done through them comes from God's work within them, not from their own independent goodness.
People have turned away from the path of obedience and happiness and entered paths leading to ruin.
We should grieve over human corruption and recognize how greatly we need God's grace.
It is therefore no surprise that Scripture insists we must be born again.
We should not rest in anything less than union with Christ and a new creation through his Holy Spirit, producing holiness.
The psalmist tried to warn sinners who imagined themselves wise, upright and secure.
Those who show no concern for God's poor and his people show that they do not truly love God.
People continue committing wrong because they do not seek God's grace through prayer.
How much good can we expect from a life without prayer?
People unwilling to fear God may nevertheless become terrified by something as small as a shaking leaf.
The knowledge of our common corruption should make salvation coming from Zion precious to us.
In heaven alone will all the redeemed rejoice completely and forever.
The world is deeply sinful—how we should long for the Messiah to come and transform it!
The victories of Zion's King will be the joy of Zion's children.
Christ's second coming will finally overthrow the rule of sin and Satan and complete salvation.
This hope should comfort God's people amid the sins committed by sinners and the suffering endured by saints.

p.hi: The way to heaven, if we would be happy, we must be holy. We are encouraged to walk in that way.

div.title: The character of a citizen of Zion
div.p: This Psalm asks who belongs among the citizens of Zion.
The glorified saints are happy because they dwell on God's holy mountain.
They are at home there and will remain there forever.
We should examine whether we have a place among them.
The Psalm gives a clear and practical answer.
Scripture faithfully directs anyone sincerely wanting to know the path of duty, and conscience helps apply that direction.
A citizen of Zion is sincere in faith.
Such a person is genuinely what they claim to be and seeks to obey all God's will.
They deal justly with God and other people, speaking the truth from the heart.
They reject deceit, fraud and dishonest gain.
No bargain obtained through lies can truly be a good or profitable one.
Anyone who cheats a neighbor will eventually discover that the greatest injury fell upon the cheater.
The faithful person is careful not to harm anyone.
Such people do not slander others or turn their faults into daily entertainment.
They interpret others' conduct charitably.
When a malicious story is told, they try to correct it.
If they cannot, they do not pass it on.
They evaluate people according to character and true godliness rather than wealth or public reputation.
They do not despise a person's faith because that person is poor or occupies a humble position.
They recognize that sincere godliness confers more honor than wealth or a famous name.
They seek fellowship with godly people, appreciate their prayers and gladly show them kindness and respect.
By these marks we can examine ourselves.
A good and wise person may make a promise that later proves costly.
But a promise must still be kept even if this requires personal or family sacrifice.
It is better to bear loss than to wrong a neighbor.
God's people refuse to gain wealth through extortion or bribery.
No hope of personal advantage should persuade them to injure a righteous cause.
Every genuinely living member of Christ's church, like the church as a whole, is built upon a Rock.
The person who lives this way will not ultimately be shaken.
God's grace will remain sufficient.
But such attitudes and conduct can arise together only through repentance from sin, faith in the Savior and love for him.
Let us examine and test ourselves accordingly.

p.hi: This psalm begins with expressions of devotion, which may be applied to Christ; but ends with such confidence of a resurrection, as must be applied to Christ, and to him only.

div.title: David's devotion and the hope of Christ's resurrection
div.p: David sought God's protection with joyful confidence.
Everyone who has acknowledged the Lord as their own Lord should remember that commitment often, draw comfort from it and live consistently with it.
David gave himself to honoring God by serving God's people.
We must become saints on earth if we hope to join the saints in heaven.
Those renewed by divine grace and devoted to God's glory are saints already.
God's people in this world are excellent, though some are so poor that they need practical kindness.
David resolved not to share in works of spiritual darkness.
He renewed his deliberate choice of God as his portion and happiness, took comfort from it and gave God the glory.
Most people choose this world as their greatest good.
But the faithful person says: However poor my circumstances may be, let me enjoy God's love and favor, be accepted by him and have the promised right to future life and happiness. That is enough.
Heaven is our true inheritance, home, rest and everlasting good.
We should consider the present world merely the country through which we travel toward our Father's house.
