Anyone who has God as the appointed portion possesses a beautiful inheritance.
Return to rest, my soul.
People ruled by grace continue desiring more of God, but not more than God.
They are satisfied with his loving kindness and do not envy others' merely physical pleasures.
Yet without his sustaining grace we are foolish enough to surrender real mercies for empty substitutes.
God had counseled David through his word and Spirit.
As he meditated during the night, his own thoughts reinforced the determination to live by faith for God.
The apostle Peter quoted verses 8–11 in his Pentecost sermon (Acts 2:25–31).
Peter declared that David spoke of Jesus Christ, especially his resurrection.
As Christ is the Head of his body, the church, these verses also encourage believers who are guided and strengthened by Christ's Spirit.
Always place the Lord before you.
Then your heart and tongue may rejoice in him.
Death destroys ordinary earthly hopes, but not the hope of a true Christian.
Christ's resurrection is the pledge of the believer's own resurrection.
Sorrow belongs to the present world.
In heaven there is fullness of joy, and where earthly pleasures quickly vanish, the pleasures at God's right hand endure forever.
Lord, through your beloved Son and our Savior, show us the path of life.
Justify our souls now, and raise our bodies on the last day, when earthly sorrow becomes heavenly joy and pain becomes everlasting happiness.

row.cell: The character of his enemies. His hope of happiness.

div.title: David prays with an upright heart (verses 1–7)
div.p: This Psalm is a prayer.
Prayers that only pretend to be sincere are useless.
But when our hearts lead our prayers, God receives them graciously.
David was accustomed to prayer.
He had not waited until suffering and danger to begin seeking God.
His faith therefore encouraged him to expect a hearing.
Steadfast determination and vigilance against sins of speech provide important evidence of integrity.
Knowing the natural human inclination toward evil and his own particular temptations, David had used God's word as protection against Satan's destructive paths.
It brings comfort in trouble to remember that grace has enabled us to avoid sinful ways.
Those following God's paths should pray continually that he will keep their feet steady on those paths.
David asked God to hold him up.
Everyone who wants to continue in divine service must obtain fresh daily strength and grace through faith and prayer.
He requested the Lord's wonderful loving kindness—not merely ordinary gifts but the special favor God shows to those who love his name.

div.title: Protection amid hostile enemies and eternal hope (verses 8–15)
div.p: David was surrounded by enemies and asked the Lord to keep him safe.
Henry understands the prayer as pointing prophetically toward Jesus Christ, preserved through every trial of humiliation until the glory and joy of exaltation.
It also teaches Christians to entrust their souls to God, believing he will preserve them for his heavenly kingdom.
Our worst enemies are those who threaten our souls.
Those who threaten our bodies act under divine Providence.
They are like God's sword, which cannot move without his permission and which he will put away when its work is finished.
They are like his hand, by which he disciplines his people.

p.hi: We cannot escape God's hand except by fleeing into it.

div.p: It brings comfort when human power seems terrifying to remember that every such power depends upon God's sovereignty.
Most people consider worldly possessions their highest good and make no provision for the coming life.
What this world calls treasures becomes worthless rubbish when compared with eternal blessings.
The poorest and most afflicted Christian need not envy someone who possesses the world but has no better portion.
Clothed in Christ's righteousness, with a heart and life renewed by grace, may we look upon God's face by faith and continually set him before us.
Each morning may his likeness, shown in Scripture and impressed upon us by renewing grace, satisfy our hearts.
True eternal happiness is prepared for those who are justified and sanctified.
They receive it when the soul awakens at death from its bodily life, and when the body rises at the resurrection from the grave.
No soul is fully satisfied except in God's favor and gracious work.
Even that satisfaction will not become complete until heaven.

row.cell: David rejoices in the deliverances God wrought for him.
He takes the comfort of his integrity, which God had cleared up.
He gives to God the glory of all his mighty deeds.

div.title: David praises the Lord for deliverance (verses 1–19)
div.p: The opening words, “I will love you, Lord, my strength,” express the main message of the Psalm.
Those who truly love God can rejoice in him as their Rock and Refuge and confidently call upon him.
When God grants deliverance, we should consider all the details that reveal his power and kindness.
David prayed, and God proved himself a God who hears prayer.
When we pray as David did, we may trust the same gracious God.
The description of God's majestic appearing, especially in verses 7–15, goes beyond what happened in the ordinary history of Jesse's son.
Henry sees someone greater than David in the extraordinary language of divine power.
God will not merely bring his people out of trouble at the proper time.
He will also support them under it while it lasts.
The eighteenth verse directs Henry's thoughts to Gethsemane and Calvary.
Christ faced his deepest distress when Judas betrayed him, his friends abandoned him, the crowd mocked him, the comfort of his Father's love was withheld and the powers of darkness assailed him.
Surrounded by the sorrows of death, he prayed in deep anguish (Hebrews 5:7).
At the Savior's death the earth trembled and rocks split.
The Father brought him from the grave through resurrection, showing his pleasure in the Son and the work he had undertaken.

div.title: David recalls his integrity and God's favor (verses 20–28)
div.p: Those who abandon God's ways turn away from God himself.
Even when we recognize many personal missteps, we must avoid a deliberate and settled departure from him.
David kept God's commands before his eyes.
Our careful resistance to the sin that most easily traps us provides evidence of an upright heart.
Even people who show mercy to others still need mercy from God.
Those faithful to him will discover that he fulfills his promises.
God's word is pure, reliable and sweet.
People who resist him and deliberately live contrary to him will find that he opposes them (Leviticus 26:21–24).
David described a gracious reward that, in general, belongs to those acting from sincere motives.
He spoke comfort to the humble and warning to the proud.
He also found courage in the promise that God would light his lamp.
The Lord would revive his sorrowful spirit, guide him around danger and give him opportunities and strength to work for God.
People walking through discouragement and darkness can take courage:
God himself will be their light.

div.title: All strength and victory belong to God (verses 29–50)
div.p: When we praise God for one mercy, we should also remember the countless others that have surrounded us throughout life.
Many things helped bring David to his present position.
He recognized God's hand in all of them, teaching us to do the same.
From verse 32 onward, Henry sees the gifts by which God equips the spiritual warrior for conflict, following the example of the victorious Leader.
We must seek deliverance through Christ, not through our own strength.
Prayer cannot be accepted apart from reconciliation with God through Jesus.
David, as a type, points to Jesus our Redeemer.
Christ endured enemies, overwhelming sorrow, violent ungodliness, death itself and God's wrath for our sake.
He called upon the Father with strong cries and tears.
He was delivered from the grave.
He continues overcoming his enemies until even death, the last enemy, is destroyed.
Therefore love the Lord, our strength and salvation.
Call upon him in every trouble and praise him for each deliverance.
Seek to walk with him in righteousness and holiness, resisting sin.
If we belong to Christ, he conquers and reigns for us.
We will conquer and reign through him and share the mercy promised to the Anointed King and all his descendants forever.
Amen.

row.cell: His holiness and grace as shown in his word.
Prayer for the benefit of them.

div.title: Creation declares God's glory (verses 1–6)
div.p: The heavens proclaim God's glory, wisdom, power and goodness so clearly that those who ignore him are without excuse.
Their very existence shows that they must have been made by a Creator who is eternal, infinitely wise, powerful and good.
The continuous alternation of day and night displays divine power.
It also reminds us that in Providence, as in nature, God makes light and creates darkness (Isaiah 45:7), placing them alongside each other.
The sun is a picture of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, the church's Bridegroom and the Light of the World.
Through his gospel he brings divine light and salvation to nations everywhere.
He delights to bless the church he has chosen as his bride.
His course is as tireless as the sun's until the earth is filled with his light and salvation.
We should pray for the day when every nation enjoys the life-giving light of the Savior.
The heavens have no ordinary words or language, yet their voice is heard.
People everywhere can understand this testimony in their own tongue.
Give God the glory for the comfort and benefit received from heavenly lights.
Yet always look beyond them to the Sun of Righteousness.

div.title: God's word reveals grace and holiness (verses 7–10)
div.p: The Holy Scriptures offer something far more important than day, night, the air we breathe or sunlight.
Fallen human beings need God's word to be restored.
The word translated “law” can also be understood as teaching, embracing everything by which God instructs us in true religion.
The whole is perfect.
It turns the soul away from sin and worldly dependence toward God and holiness.
It shows our sinfulness and misery when we depart from God and the necessity of returning to him.
God's testimony is certain and reliable.
People without education who believe what he says can become wise for salvation.
His word is a trustworthy guide for duty, a living source of comfort and the foundation of lasting hope.
The Lord's statutes are right and bring gladness to the heart.
His commands are pure, holy, just and good.
They reveal our need of the Savior and teach us how to honor his gospel.
The Holy Spirit uses the commandments to enlighten our eyes, showing us sin and misery and guiding us toward duty.
Fear of the Lord, that is, genuine godliness, cleanses our ways and lasts forever.
The ceremonial law has long since ended, but the obligation to fear God has not changed.
His judgments and commands are entirely true and righteous.
Gold serves bodily and temporary interests.
Grace serves the soul and eternity.
God's word received by faith is more precious than gold and sweeter to the soul than honey.
Physical pleasures soon become excessive but never truly satisfy.
The joys of true religion are substantial, lasting and satisfying, without danger of excess.

div.title: The word warns and leads us to pray (verses 11–14)
div.p: God's word warns the wicked not to continue in evil and warns the righteous not to abandon the good path.
There is a reward not only after keeping God's commands, but in keeping them.
True religion makes our ordinary comforts sweeter and our crosses easier to bear.
It makes life valuable and even death something a believer can welcome.
David wanted forgiveness and cleansing not only for sins he had already discovered and confessed, but also for sins he had forgotten or overlooked.
Everything Scripture teaches us about our guilt should drive us to the throne of grace.
There we should pray.
Our dependence is the same as that of believers who confess that in Jesus Christ alone they have righteousness and strength.
No prayer is acceptable apart from our Redeemer's strength and mediation.
He became our divine Kinsman by taking human nature, so that he could redeem us to God and restore the inheritance we had lost.
May the excellence of God's word deeply affect our hearts, along with the wickedness of sin and the danger sin brings.

p.hi: This psalm is a prayer for the kings of Israel, but with relation to Christ.

div.title: A prayer for the king in the light of Christ
div.p: Even the greatest human beings experience serious trouble.
Neither the crown on a king's head nor grace within the heart makes someone immune to suffering.
Even great people must therefore be people of prayer.
No one should expect to benefit from the prayers of the church or friends while neglecting personal prayer when capable of it.
The psalm asks God to protect the king and preserve his life.
It also asks that the king may continue working for the public good.
We may recognize that God accepts our spiritual sacrifices when his Spirit kindles a holy fire of devotion and love within our souls.
The psalm also asks the Lord to give success to the king's work.
In spiritual warfare, the first step toward victory is trusting only God's mercy and grace.
Those who depend upon themselves will fall.
Believers triumph in God and in the way he has revealed himself to them.
That distinguishes them from people who live as though God did not exist.
Those who praise God's name may also trust God's name.
This was shown when the power and pride of Jewish unbelief and pagan idolatry fell before the preaching and example of humble followers of Jesus.
It remains true in spiritual conflict today.
Believers engage their enemies in Christ's name, Spirit and strength.
It will also be seen at the last day, when the world and its evil prince are brought down.
Then believers will rise through the resurrection of the Lord, stand before him and sing his praise in heaven.
Let us rejoice in the salvation Christ gives.
Raise our banners in the name of the Lord our God.
Through the saving strength of his right hand, we may be confident of victory over every enemy.

div.title: Giving thanks for victory (verses 1–6)
div.p: Happy are the people whose ruler places confidence in God's strength and finds joy in God's salvation.
Such a king takes pleasure in the advance of God's kingdom and trusts the Lord to sustain every effort made in its service.
All our blessings are gifts of God's goodness, not wages earned by our own worthiness.
Sometimes those blessings arrive earlier than expected, are greater than we imagined, or come before we even asked.
Sometimes God gives precisely what we had feared we would not receive.
In these circumstances we can say that he went ahead of us with his blessings.
Nothing can come before Christ himself.
But for humanity, no blessing has ever more wonderfully come before our request than redemption through Christ.
The Father has made the Son a universal and everlasting blessing to the world.
Through him the families of the earth have been and will be blessed.
Christ finds joy in the Father's favor toward him and toward the work he has accomplished.
Henry sees the Spirit of prophecy moving here beyond what can be said of an earthly ruler into what belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
No merely human king is blessed forever, much less a blessing for the whole world forever.

div.title: Confidence in the Messiah's ultimate victory (verses 7–13)
div.p: The psalmist teaches us to look forward through faith, hope and prayer, considering what God will yet accomplish.
David's victories foreshadow the complete defeat of Christ's enemies.
Some people could have received Christ as the One who would rule and save them.
But they rejected him and fought against him.
If they continue in rebellion, the memory of that refusal will become a torment that does not end.
God works in sinners through his grace, making them willing to come, receiving them into his favor and rescuing them from coming judgment.
May he exalt himself in our hearts by almighty grace, destroying every stronghold of sin and Satan.
How great should our joy be when we see our Brother and Friend upon his throne and think of every blessing we may receive from him!
Yet Christ himself delights in his exaltation because he can now bestow happiness and glory upon sinners who have learned to love and trust him.

div.title: The suffering of Christ and the complaint of abandonment (verses 1–10)
div.p: The Spirit of Christ, who spoke through the prophets, testified in this Psalm about Christ's sufferings and the glory that would follow.
The Psalm begins with a sorrowful complaint about God's apparent withdrawal.
It may also give language to believers crushed by grief and fear.
For a child of God, the felt loss of God's presence is more painful than any other suffering.
Even the anguish of that loss can show that spiritual life remains active, because the soul still longs for God.
Complaining, Why am I sick? Why am I poor?, can reveal dissatisfaction with the world and its comforts.
But crying, “Why have you forsaken me?”, reveals a heart whose happiness depends upon God's favor.
These words belong especially to Christ.
He spoke them upon the cross as he poured out his soul before God (Matthew 27:46).
Being truly human, Jesus naturally recoiled from such dreadful sorrows.
Yet his zeal and love prevailed.
In his deepest suffering Christ still declared the holiness of his heavenly Father.
Indeed, his suffering itself demonstrated that holiness and became reason for his people to praise God more than for all their other deliverances.
No one who has truly hoped in God has ultimately been ashamed of that hope.
No one who sincerely sought him has done so in vain.
The Psalm also describes the contempt and scorn of human beings.
The Savior expressed the humble and despised condition into which he had been brought.
The history of Christ's birth and suffering helps explain the prophecy.

div.title: Christ suffers and prays for deliverance (verses 11–21)
div.p: Here we see Christ suffering and Christ praying.
His example prepares us for suffering and teaches us to seek God within it.
Henry sees even the manner of Christ's death foretold, though crucifixion was not practiced by the Jews in the psalmist's time.
His hands and feet were pierced and nailed to the cursed tree.
His body was suspended in extreme pain and torment.
His natural strength gave way under the suffering and the divine wrath he bore.
Who can stand before God's anger?
The life of sinners had been forfeited.
The life of the Sacrifice therefore had to become their ransom.
Jesus was stripped of his clothes upon the cross so that he might clothe us in his righteousness.
These things happened as Scripture foretold, confirming that Christ was the true Messiah.
They should also deepen our love for him as the best of friends, who endured all this for us.
During his agony Jesus prayed earnestly.
He asked that the cup of suffering might pass from him.
When we cannot rejoice in God as the object of our song, let us still rest upon him as our strength.
When the feeling of spiritual delight is absent, we can still receive the support of his grace.
Christ prayed to be delivered from the wrath of God.
The Lord has delivered, continues delivering and will deliver.
We should meditate upon Christ's suffering and resurrection until we experience in our souls the power of his resurrection and fellowship in his sufferings.

div.title: Praise for redemption and the risen Savior (verses 22–31)
div.p: Now the Savior speaks as risen from the dead.
Christ himself used the opening words of the Psalm's lament upon the cross.
The opening words of its triumphant praise are expressly applied to him in Hebrews 2:12.
All true praise must ultimately return to the work of redemption.
The suffering of our Redeemer was accepted by the Father as a full satisfaction for sin.
Although he offered himself on behalf of sinful people, the Father did not reject that offering.
This deserves our continual thanksgiving.
Humble hearts renewed by grace can find complete satisfaction and happiness in Christ.
Those hungering and thirsting for his righteousness will not waste their labor on what cannot satisfy.
People who pray much will also give thanks much.
Those who turn to God will devote themselves carefully to worshiping him.
Every tongue should confess Jesus Christ as Lord.
People of every social condition—high and low, rich and poor, enslaved and free—meet in him.
Since we cannot preserve our own lives, it is wise to entrust our souls through obedient faith to Christ, who can save and keep them alive forever.
A generation will continue serving the Lord.
God will maintain a church in the world until the end of time.
He will regard those future believers as his own, just as he cared for previous generations.
They will proclaim his righteousness, not their own, as the foundation of their hope and source of their joy.
Redemption by Jesus Christ is God's own work.

Here we see the free love and compassion of the Father and the Lord Jesus toward sinful people—the source of all grace and consolation, the pattern for Christian conduct and a guide through the treatment believers can expect in this world.
Every humbling and saving lesson can be found here.
Let those who attempt to establish their own righteousness ask why God's beloved Son would have needed to suffer so terribly if human deeds could atone for sin.
Let those who claim Christ's name while despising God's law ask whether Jesus suffered in order to give them permission to disobey it.
Let careless sinners flee the coming wrath.
Let trembling souls entrust themselves to this merciful Redeemer.
And let distressed and tempted believers confidently expect that the Lord will bring a happy end to every trial.

p.hi: Confidence in God's grace and care.

div.title: The Lord is my Shepherd
div.p: The words “The Lord is my shepherd” express a believer's confidence and satisfaction in the care of the great Shepherd of all, the Redeemer and Preserver of humanity.
It is a wonderful thing to have a shepherd—and to know that this shepherd is the Lord himself.
A peaceful flock of sheep in green fields, tended by a wise, watchful and loving shepherd, pictures believers brought back to the Shepherd of their souls.
The wealthiest person who lives only for sensual pleasure finds even abundant possessions a dry pasture.
A godly person with little money has green pasture when faith enables that person to recognize God's goodness in everything received.
God gives the heart quietness and contentment regardless of its circumstances.
When his appointed ordinances provide green pasture, we should not merely pass through them but remain and feed upon them.
The Holy Spirit's consolations are the still waters beside which God's saints are led. They flow from the Fountain of living water.
People who walk in the paths of righteousness enjoy this comfort. The path of duty is genuinely pleasant, because righteousness produces peace.
Yet no one can walk that path unless God leads them into it and continues leading them onward.
Discontent and distrust spring from unbelief and lead to unsteady conduct. Trust the Shepherd's care and listen to his voice.
The valley of the shadow of death may refer to the deepest suffering or the darkest work of Providence.
It also describes the death separating the flock still on earth from the flock already in heaven.
But the psalm's expression reduces our fear: it is only death's shadow. A serpent's shadow cannot sting; a sword's shadow cannot kill.
It is a deep, dark valley, but valleys may be fruitful, and even death can bring spiritual comfort to God's people.
We walk through the valley. Christ's sheep will not be lost there: they reach safety on the other side.
Death is a king of terrors, but not to those who belong to Christ.
As they die, God restrains their enemy, guides them with his rod and upholds them with his staff.
The gospel contains enough comfort for believers in death, and everlasting arms support them.
At the Lord's table, his people feed upon the provisions of his love.
Satan and wicked people cannot destroy their true comfort while they are anointed by the Holy Spirit and drink from the full cup of salvation.
Past experience teaches believers to expect divine goodness and mercy to follow them throughout life.
They resolve to seek happiness in serving God now and hope to enjoy his love forever in heaven.
The Lord can make any condition pleasant through his Spirit's anointing and the joy of his salvation.
But those who hope to enjoy the blessings of God's house must also remain attentive to its duties.

row.cell: Concerning the kingdom of Christ, and the subjects of that kingdom.
Concerning the King of that kingdom.

div.title: The kingdom and its people (verses 1–6)
div.p: We do not belong to ourselves. Our bodies and souls belong to God.
Even people who neither know him nor acknowledge their relationship to him still belong to him.
Anyone who understands that the soul will exist forever, after surveying all the earth and its possessions, will recognize that worldly things cannot satisfy it.
Such a person will begin to desire to approach God and ask: What must I do to live in the happy and holy place where God makes his people holy and happy?
Religion is worthless if it never becomes a matter of the heart.
Only Christ's blood can cleanse our sins, and only the Holy Spirit's washing can renew us in holiness.
Through this work we become God's people and receive blessing from the Lord and righteousness from the God of our salvation.
God will make those who truly belong to him happy, completely and forever.
When God grants righteousness, his intention is also salvation.
Those whom he prepares for heaven will reach heaven safely and find what their souls have been seeking.

div.title: The King of glory (verses 7–10)
div.p: The magnificent entrance described here first refers to the solemn arrival of the ark in the tent David prepared for it, or in Solomon's later temple.
Henry also applies it to Christ's ascension into heaven and the welcome he received there.
Our Redeemer found heaven's gates closed because of sin, but having made atonement by his own blood, he could demand entry with full authority.
The angels were commanded to worship him (Hebrews 1:6).
They ask in wonder who this King is, and the answer declares that he is mighty in battle, powerful to save his people and subdue his and their enemies.
The psalm may also be applied to Christ entering human hearts through his word and Spirit, making them his temples.
He stands at the door and knocks (Revelation 3:20).
The heart's gates should open to him as a property is delivered to its rightful owner.
The psalm can also point us toward his glorious second coming.
Lord, open the everlasting door of our souls by your grace. May we receive you now and belong wholly to you, and finally be numbered with your saints in glory.

div.title: Confidence in prayer (verses 1–7)
div.p: When we worship God, we should lift our souls toward him.
Anyone who waits upon God with faith and hopes in him with confidence will never have reason to be ashamed of that trust.
Even the most mature believer still needs and desires God's instruction.
If we sincerely want to know our duty and are determined to do it, we can trust the Lord to guide us.
David was especially eager for forgiveness.
When God pardons sin, Scripture says that he remembers it no more. This describes complete remission.
Our claim upon forgiveness and every needed good must rest on God's goodness, not ours; on his mercy, not our merit.
We should make that appeal while recognizing our unworthiness and trusting the riches of grace.
How vast is the mercy that can cover forever the sins and follies of a youth lived without God and without hope!
Blessed be the Lord: the blood of the great Sacrifice can cleanse every stain.

div.title: God guides and forgives sinners (verses 8–14)
div.p: We are all sinners, and Christ came into the world to save sinners, teach them and call them to repentance.
We judge the reliability of a promise by the character of the One making it. That is why we can depend on God's promises.
All the Lord's paths—his promises and providential dealings—are mercy and truth.
Through every circumstance, even severe affliction, his people may discover his mercy and the fulfillment of his word.
When they reach the end of their journey, they will understand more clearly that every path was merciful and true.
Humble people distrust themselves, want to be instructed and seek divine guidance.
God directs them by the written word, enabling them to find rest for their souls in the Savior.
Even when the body is sick and hurting, the soul may remain at peace in God.

div.title: Help during suffering (verses 15–22)
div.p: David ended as he began: looking to God and expressing his dependence and longing.
It is good to hope and wait quietly for the Lord's salvation.
If God turns toward us in favor, it matters little who turns away.
David appealed to the integrity of his dealings with his enemies.
He remained a sinner before God, but his conscience testified that he had not wronged those accusing him.
The Lord would finally give Israel rest from its enemies.
In heaven, God's people will be perfectly redeemed from every trouble.
Blessed Savior, you have graciously taught us that without you we can do nothing.
Teach us how to pray, how to approach you in your appointed way and how to lift our whole hearts and desires toward you, for you are the Lord our righteousness.

p.hi: David, in this psalm, appeals to God touching his integrity.

div.title: Integrity through grace
div.p: Under the Spirit of prophecy, David speaks of himself in a way that also makes him a type of Christ.
The claim of complete and spotless innocence is fully and uniquely true of Christ. It is through him that we are made complete.
Someone who walks sincerely while trusting wholly in God's grace is accepted according to the covenant mediated by Jesus, on the basis of Christ's perfect obedience even to death.
Such a believer asks God to examine and test the innermost soul.
Recognizing how deceitful the heart can be, the person seeks to discover and put to death every sin, to know whether faith is genuine and to obey God's holy commands.
Carefully avoiding evil company is both evidence of integrity and an important means of keeping it.
Hypocrites can attend God's appointed worship, so attendance alone cannot prove sincerity.
But coming in repentance, conscientious obedience and genuine devotion is a good sign of integrity.
David felt secure in God's grace. He delighted in blessing the Lord among congregations on earth and hoped soon to join the great assembly in heaven, praising God and the Lamb forever.

row.cell: His desire toward God, and expectation from him.

div.title: The Lord as light and strength (verses 1–6)
div.p: The Lord is the believer's light and the strength of that person's life.
We live and move not merely through him but in him.
His gracious presence, power, promises, readiness to hear prayer and the Spirit's witness within believers form the secret shelter of his tabernacle.
There his people find holy confidence and inward peace.
David longed for continual fellowship with God through his appointed ordinances.
All God's children desire to live in their Father's house.
They do not want merely to visit it like travelers spending one night, nor remain temporarily like servants who must eventually depart.
They want to dwell there all their days, as children belonging to their father.
If we expect praising God to fill our eternity, should it not also occupy our present lives?
However a Christian's earthly circumstances may differ, the favor and service of God remain the one necessary thing.
The believer seeks it, prays for it and rejoices in it.

div.title: Seeking God's face (verses 7–14)
div.p: Wherever a believer may be, there is a path through prayer to the throne of grace.
God calls us through his Spirit, his word and worship, and through particular events—both merciful and difficult.
When we foolishly pursue false and worthless things, he graciously calls us to seek our true happiness in him.
The invitation “Seek my face” goes out generally, but each of us must answer personally: “I will seek your face.”
The word is not useful to us until we receive its instruction.
Grace makes hearts willing to answer God's gracious call.
David asked for the Lord's favor, continuing presence, guidance and protection.
God's help often comes when every human helper has failed.
He is a more reliable Friend than even the most devoted earthly parents could ever be.
David believed he would see the goodness of the Lord.
The hope of everlasting life, together with foretastes of its glory and pleasures, is a powerful defense against fainting in trouble.
Meanwhile the Lord gives strength to bear present burdens.
Let us look to the suffering Savior, pray in faith and encourage one another to wait for the Lord with patience and earnest prayer.

div.title: Prayer in danger (verses 1–5)
div.p: David prayed earnestly in faith, trusting the Lord as the Rock on whom his hope rested.
Believers should continue praying until they receive some assurance that God has heard them.
David asked not to be numbered with wicked people.
He wanted deliverance from their traps and from the danger of being infected by their sins.
His request was that God would never allow him to adopt the deceitful and treacherous methods his enemies were using against him.
Even the best believers are conscious of how readily they may be drawn aside. We should therefore pray diligently for preserving grace.
Those careful not to share in wicked deeds have reason to hope they will escape the judgments pronounced upon them.
David spoke in verse 4 of God's righteous judgments against evildoers.
Henry is explicit that this was not the expression of revenge or uncontrolled passion.
It was a prophetic statement that God will judge everyone who persists in wrongdoing.
The Lord will call sinners to account not only for the harm they have done, but also for the evil they planned and attempted.
Disregarding God's works is a source of sin and ultimately of ruin.

div.title: Thanksgiving and intercession (verses 6–9)
div.p: When God answers prayer, we should bless him.
He is our strength, upholding us through every service and suffering.
A believing heart will eventually rejoice. We should expect joy and peace through faith, and give all the praise to God.
The saints rejoice not only in their own comfort but also in the blessings of others.
The more people share in sunlight—or in God's favorable presence—the less none of us receives.
David ended with a short but comprehensive prayer for God's people, who are his precious inheritance.
He asked God to save them, bless them with every good gift, and especially nourish their souls through his appointed ordinances.
He prayed that God would guide their conduct and direct events for their good, not merely for his present generation but for all who would follow.
Only in heaven will God's people be lifted up forever, never again to fall or be cast down.
Lord Jesus, save us from our sins. As the Son of Abraham, bless us with righteousness.
As the good Shepherd of the sheep, feed us, and as the Resurrection and the Life, lift us forever from the dust.

p.hi: Exhortation to give glory to God.

div.title: The glory and power of the Lord
div.p: The powerful and honored people of this world are especially obligated to worship God and give him glory.
Yet few approach him in the beauty of holiness.

When we come to God through the Redeemer of sinners in repentance, faith and love, he accepts our imperfect service, pardons the sin still mixed with it and approves the holiness the Holy Spirit has enabled us to exercise.
This is the nature of true worship: giving the Lord the glory due to his name.
Every act of worship should be holy, devoted to God, his will and his glory.
Holiness is beautiful and gives beauty to everything done in worship.
David also described the Lord's power in the natural world.
Thunder, lightning and storms testify to his glory. We should respond by thinking highly of God's greatness and worshiping him with reverence.
The brilliance of lightning matches the terror of thunder.
These displays remind us both of God's power and of human weakness.
They also warn of how defenseless unrepentant sinners will be at the final judgment.
Yet the work of God's word upon human souls through the Holy Spirit is more extraordinary than any thunderstorm.
The proudest are humbled, stubborn hearts tremble, hidden thoughts are revealed, sinners are converted, and people once cruel, sensual and corrupt become gentle and pure.
If we have heard God's voice and fled to the hope he offers, we need not fear our Father's voice even when he speaks in judgment against his enemies.
Those who remain without shelter may tremble, but people who have entered his appointed refuge can thank him for their security.
They may look toward judgment without terror, as Noah was secure in the ark.

div.title: Praise after deliverance (verses 1–5)
div.p: The great things the Lord has done for us through Providence and grace call us to grateful service.
We should do all we can to advance his kingdom, even though our greatest efforts are small.
The saints in heaven sing God's praises; why should not believers on earth sing to him too?
Of all God's attributes, none inspires more fear in the wicked or more comfort in godly people than his holiness.
It is a good sign that we share something of his holiness when we sincerely rejoice to remember it.
Our happiness rests upon God's favor.
If we possess that favor, we have enough, whatever else may be missing.
Yet while a believer feels God's displeasure, sorrow continues.

div.title: Learning from prosperity and trouble (verses 6–12)
div.p: When life goes well, we easily begin to imagine that it will always be so.
Recognizing our mistake should make us ashamed of carnal self-confidence.
If God hides his face, a faithful person may be distressed even without any other suffering.
But if God turns away for wise and just reasons, it would be foolish for us to turn away from him.
Instead, learn to pray in the dark.
A sanctified soul that returns to God will praise him forever.
The body that has become dust cannot perform the earthly service of God's house: the grave is a place of silence and no further earthly labor.
We rightly ask to remain alive when we want our lives to be devoted to God's praise.
In due time the Lord delivered David.
The tongue is our glory, and it is never better used than when blessing him.
David intended to continue praising God until he entered the place where praise would become his everlasting work.
Yet everyone must beware complacency during prosperity.
Neither external success nor inward comfort is permanently secure in this life.
God's favor grounds a believer's safety as firmly as a deep-rooted mountain, but temptations and trials still come.
If we become careless and sin, the Lord may hide his face; comfort fades and troubles return.
Let us therefore remain watchful, dependent upon his grace and constant in praise.

div.title: Confidence in God (verses 1–8)
div.p: Faith and prayer belong together. It is the prayer of faith that prevails.

David entrusted his soul to God in a particular way. Our Lord Jesus used the words of verse 5 when he gave up his last breath on the cross, offering himself willingly as a sacrifice for sin and laying down his life as a ransom.
David, however, spoke as a man in distress. His greatest concern was for his soul—his spirit and better part.

Some people think worldly business or multiplying worries excuse them from caring for their souls. In fact, troubles make such care even more urgent, so that the inner person need not suffer harm when the outward person wastes away.
The redemption of the soul is so precious that without Christ's undertaking, it would be lost forever.
Trusting divine mercy gives David reason to rejoice.
God observes whether suffering humbles us for sin and makes our souls better. His people will face dangers and rescues throughout life, until he finally delivers them from death, their last enemy.

div.title: Prayer amid distress (verses 9–18)
div.p: David's troubles made him a man of sorrows, picturing Christ, who was acquainted with grief.
There is an important difference: David recognized that his own sins deserved correction, while Christ suffered for our sins.
David's friends were too afraid to help him. We need not be surprised when human support fails, but we should make sure we have a Friend in heaven who never fails.
Those who place their spirits in God's hands can trust him to arrange everything for their ultimate good.
Our times are in God's hands: he may lengthen or shorten life and make its circumstances bitter or sweet according to his wise purposes.
Neither our own hands nor those of friends or enemies finally determine our course.
David therefore prayed to be saved for God's mercy, not because of personal merit.
He looked ahead to the day when those who slander and attack God's people will be silenced by divine judgment.
Meanwhile, let us seek to silence foolish accusations, if possible, by doing good.

div.title: Praise for God's goodness (verses 19–24)
div.p: Instead of giving way to despair or impatience, we should reflect upon how good God is to those who fear and trust him.
All mercy reaches sinners through the extraordinary gift of God's only Son as the atoning sacrifice.
Do not surrender to unbelief or assume that hardship means you have been cut off from God's sight and handed over to arrogant human enemies.
Lord, pardon our complaints and fears. Increase our faith, patience, love and gratitude. Teach us to rejoice in trouble and in hope.
Christ's deliverance and his victory over enemies should strengthen believers in every earthly affliction. Having suffered courageously with their Master, they will enter his joy and glory.

row.cell: The happiness of a pardoned sinner.
The misery that went before, and the comfort that followed the confession of sins.

div.title: Happiness through forgiveness (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Sin is the source of human misery. But the true believer's transgressions of God's law have been forgiven because they are covered by the atoning sacrifice.
Christ bore our sins; therefore God does not count them against us. Christ's righteousness is credited to us. God laid our sins upon him and made him a sin offering for us.
The decision not to count sin against someone belongs to God the Judge. It is God who justifies.
Yet the forgiven person is also sincere and seeks holiness through the Holy Spirit's power.
Such a person does not pretend to repent while intending to keep sinning because God is gracious. True believers do not misuse the doctrine of free grace as a license for sin.
God promises every kind of genuine blessing to those whose sins he forgives.

div.title: From the burden of sin to comfort (verses 3–7)
div.p: It is difficult to persuade sinners to receive free mercy humbly, confess their wrongdoing fully and condemn their own sin.
Yet confessing our sins before God is the only true path to peace of conscience.
Confession and repentance do not earn forgiveness, but are necessary to experience God's pardoning mercy.
How happy is the moment when a burdened soul is enabled to pour out its sorrow before God and embrace his covenant mercy in Christ Jesus!
We should seek the Lord when Providence calls us and his Spirit stirs us to turn toward him.
When guilt has softened the heart, every human refuge has failed and the troubled mind can find no rest, God applies the healing balm by his Spirit.

div.title: Instruction and encouragement (verses 8–11)
div.p: God teaches by his word and guides his people through his will.
The psalm warns sinners because the path of sin ends in sorrow.
It also comforts the saints: life in fellowship with God is truly the happiest and most satisfying life.
Lord Jesus, teach us to rejoice in you and in your salvation, so that our joy may be real.

row.cell: His people encouraged by his power.

div.title: God deserves our praise (verses 1–11)
div.p: Holy joy is at the heart of genuine praise. Thankful singing gives voice to that joy and is a fitting way to worship the Lord.
Every ability God has given us should be used with skill and earnestness in his service.
His promises are wise and good. His word is right, and we are right only insofar as we agree with it. Everything he does is done in truth.
Because the Lord is righteous, he loves righteousness.
How sad that an earth so full of signs of God's goodness should be so lacking in praise! Multitudes depend upon his generosity, yet so few live for his glory.
Whatever God does, he does effectively and permanently.
He overrules the plans of human beings and makes them serve his own purposes, even when the result surprises us. Nothing can prevent the fulfillment of his eternal counsel.

div.title: God's people trust his power (verses 12–22)
div.p: God knows every movement and intention of the human soul—even things hidden from all other people. He understands our hearts better than we do.
Our lives and hearts are in his hands; he formed the spirit of each person.
Every created power depends upon him. Without God it can accomplish nothing.
When we are secure in his favor, we need not fear what stands against us. Let us give him the glory for his particular grace.
Humanly devised methods to save our souls are useless. But the Lord's watchful eye rests on people who fear his name because they hope in his mercy.
He helps them in difficulty and preserves them from spiritual harm amid danger.
Whoever fears God and his judgment must also hope in his mercy. We cannot escape from him except by fleeing to him.
Lord, let your mercy be upon us. Give us its benefit and comfort—not according to what we deserve, but according to your promise and the faith your Spirit has created within us.

row.cell: David praises God, and encourages to trust him.

div.title: David praises God and invites others to trust (verses 1–10)
div.p: If we hope to spend eternity praising God, we should devote much of this life to praising him.
He has never told anyone to seek him without hope of an answer.
David's prayers helped overcome his fears. Many others have looked to God through faith and prayer and found renewed courage and comfort.
Looking to the world leaves us perplexed and uncertain. Looking to Christ is essential to our salvation and every blessing that belongs to it.
The poor person whom society neither respects nor notices can still approach the throne of grace. The Lord hears and delivers.
Holy angels minister to the saints and defend them against powers of darkness. Yet all glory belongs to the Lord of the angels, not to his servants.
Taste and sight allow us both to discover and to enjoy. Taste and see that the Lord is good: recognize his kindness and take comfort in it.
Whoever truly trusts him is blessed.
For the coming life, God's people receive grace sufficient to sustain them spiritually. For this life, they receive what is genuinely necessary from him.
Paul could say he possessed everything and abounded because he had learned contentment (Philippians 4:11–18).
Those who trust only their own strength and efforts will eventually find themselves lacking. Those who rely on the Lord and quietly carry out their responsibilities will be cared for.

div.title: Learn the fear of the Lord (verses 11–22)
div.p: Young people should begin life by learning to fear the Lord. Those who start early in his service enjoy a greater opportunity for comfort now and happiness forever.
Everyone wants to be happy. But human life is short and troubled, so genuine happiness must reach beyond this world.
The way of faith requires watchfulness over heart and tongue.
Not harming others is not enough: we must strive to be useful and do good.
We should seek peace and pursue it, willingly giving up some personal advantage for its sake.
When genuine believers suffer, they habitually call upon God and are comforted that he hears them.
The righteous are humble about their sins and do not think highly of themselves.
Nothing is more necessary for true godliness than a contrite heart free from self-confidence. Grace flourishes in such soil, and the free, rich gospel of Jesus Christ is its encouragement.
The Lord specially protects righteous people, yet they still experience many trials and hatred from others. Divine mercy itself may correct them, and the enemy of their souls also attacks them.
But their troubles cannot ultimately destroy their souls, because the Lord keeps them from falling into sin during suffering.
No one is truly desolate except the person whom God has abandoned.

row.cell: And calls upon God to support him.

div.title: David prays for protection (verses 1–10)
div.p: It is no surprise for righteous people or righteous causes to have enemies. The hostility of the serpent's offspring against the woman's Seed has been present since the beginning.
David in affliction, Christ in suffering, the persecuted church and the tempted Christian all look to Almighty God to defend their cause.
We often justify anxiety and anger over unjust treatment by saying we gave others no reason to mistreat us.
Yet our innocence should actually bring comfort: we may more confidently entrust the case to the Lord.
David asked God to make his presence known in the trial and to grant inward consolation amid outward distress.
If God's Spirit assures us inwardly that he is our salvation, we need nothing else to make us truly happy.
If God is our Friend, it does not matter who opposes us.
Henry understands David's words against his enemies as prophetic announcements of just divine judgment, anticipating the fate of Christ's enemies.

He adds an essential distinction: Christians must not desire or pray for the destruction of human opponents. The enemies whose ruin we should seek are our sinful desires and the evil spirits that seek our destruction.
A traveler caught at night on a slippery, dangerous road pictures the sinner moving through temptation.
Having entrusted his cause to the Lord, David expected deliverance and pledged to praise God with all his strength.
Such language is even more fitting when applied to heavenly rescue in Christ.

div.title: David describes the ingratitude of enemies (verses 11–16)
div.p: Few accusations are worse than that someone has repaid kindness with cruelty.
That was the character of David's enemies. In this experience he pictured Christ.
David had shown genuine tenderness while his enemies suffered.
We should grieve over the sins of people who do not grieve for themselves.
Doing good to the ungrateful is never ultimately wasted.
Let us learn patience and gentleness from David—and still more from Christ's example.

div.title: David asks God to rescue his soul (verses 17–28)
div.p: God's people seek peaceful lives, yet their enemies often devise false accusations and plots against them.
David prayed: My soul is in danger. Lord, rescue it. It belongs to you, the Father of spirits; claim and save what is yours. Do not stand far off as though I were a stranger.
The One who exalted the once-suffering Redeemer will also defend his people.
The roaring lion will not destroy their souls, any more than he could destroy Christ, their Surety.
Believers entrust their souls to God's hands. Through faith they are united with Christ, precious in God's sight and assured of deliverance from ultimate destruction.
Their rescue will lead them to give thanks in heaven.

row.cell: The bad state of the wicked.

div.title: The condition of wicked people (verses 1–4)
div.p: This psalm should deepen our hatred of sin and our desire for God's loving-kindness.
The root of wickedness is contempt for God and the refusal to show him proper reverence. Another root is self-deception.
We should ask God every day to protect us from flattering ourselves.
Sin does terrible harm to the person practicing it, and for that reason should be hated. Yet sinners too easily regard it as harmless.
If people deceive themselves, it is not surprising when they deceive others. A person false to their own soul can scarcely be trusted by anybody.
It is wrong to do evil; it is worse to plan evil deliberately, organizing it with care.
When we willingly drive holy thoughts from our minds during quiet hours, Satan is ready to replace them with sinful imaginings.
Hardened sinners become so stubborn that they defend their actions as though they could justify them before God himself.

div.title: The goodness of God (verses 5–12)
div.p: Human beings may refuse compassion, but God's mercy remains available. That is great comfort to believers.
God acts wisely and well. We do not now understand everything he does, but we will know enough at the proper time.
His loving-kindness is precious to those who trust him. They place themselves beneath his protection and find security and peace.
A gracious person always wants more of God, but never wants anything greater than God.
God's providential gifts allow believers to be content with what they possess.
His appointed ordinances are sweet and strengthen spiritual life, yet complete satisfaction is reserved for the world to come.
God prepares his people to desire those pleasures and fills them by his Spirit with joy and peace in believing.
He gives life to whom he wills. Whoever is willing may come and take freely from the water of life.
May we know, love and sincerely serve the Lord. Then no proud enemy on earth or power from hell can separate us from his love.
Faith looks ahead as though the promised things had already occurred. It shows us the Lord upon his throne of judgment and the dominion of sin overthrown forever.

p.hi: David persuades to patience and confidence in God, by the state of the godly and of the wicked.

div.title: Do not envy the wicked (verses 1–6)
div.p: The world contains many wicked people who prosper and live in comfort. That was true in David's day and should not surprise us now.
Their success tempts us to be resentful, to mistake them for the happiest people and eventually to imitate them.
But outward prosperity fades. Those who look forward with faith see no reason to envy wicked people, whose judgment is everlasting.
True religion is trust in the Lord expressed through diligent obedience. To claim trust while neglecting duty is to test God, not trust him.
Life does not consist in possessions. Enough food and provision for our needs is more than we deserve and sufficient for someone traveling toward heaven.
Delighting in God is both a duty and a privilege.
He has not promised to gratify every bodily appetite or whim, but to satisfy the desires of a soul renewed and made holy.
The true desire of a godly heart is to know, love and serve God.
To commit our way to the Lord is to roll its burden upon him: bring our concerns before him in prayer and avoid tormenting ourselves about future events.
We must do our duty and leave what happens afterward in his hands.

div.title: Wait patiently for the Lord (verses 7–20)
div.p: Trust that God will make everything work for our ultimate good. Do not become agitated by what you see in this world, because a discontented spirit invites many temptations.
The little given to a righteous person is better and more useful than abundant wealth acquired or used wickedly. It comes from the hand of special divine love.
God provides for his servants both when they work and when they wait.
They possess something better than worldly wealth: peace of conscience, peace with God and peace in God—peace the world cannot give.
God knows all the days of his people, and not one day's faithful work will go unrewarded.
Earthly days are quickly numbered, but heavenly happiness endures forever.
Those resting upon the Rock of Ages need not envy wicked people leaning upon broken reeds.

div.title: Righteousness, generosity and divine guidance (verses 21–33)
div.p: God requires us to act justly and give others what is owed.
It is a serious sin to refuse payment of a just debt when able to pay; it is a serious hardship to be unable to pay.
Truly merciful people continue showing mercy. We must abandon sin, learn to do good and persist in doing so.
God's blessing is the source, sweetness and security of every earthly comfort. Those assured of his favor will lack nothing truly good for them.
By grace and the Holy Spirit, he directs the thoughts, affections and plans of his people; by Providence he orders events to guide them.
He does not always show the whole road. He often leads one step at a time, as a parent guides a child.
A believer may fall into sin or trouble, and the sin may bring real pain. But God will keep such a person from ultimate ruin.
Few, if any, have seen a consistent believer and all that believer's children left in complete, friendless destitution.
God does not abandon his saints in affliction. Their permanent home, however, is heaven.
Even when Satan buffets a faithful person severely, God does not leave that person in the enemy's hands.

div.title: Trust the Lord for the outcome (verses 34–40)

p.hi: Duty belongs to us; outcomes belong to God.

div.p: Verses 35 and 36 picture the apparently flourishing enemy of God whose prosperity soon disappears.
The Lord brings proud plans to nothing, especially plans of persecutors.
No one is perfect in personal righteousness; believers are made complete in Christ Jesus.
Even if a believer's whole life seems dark and cloudy, the final days may be peaceful. And if death itself comes under a cloud, eternal peace still awaits.
Salvation belongs to the Lord. He helps his people fulfill their duties, bear their burdens, endure difficulties profitably and, in his time, escape them.
Let sinners therefore turn from evil and do good. Let them repent, abandon sin and trust God's mercy through Jesus Christ.
Let them take Christ's yoke and learn from him, so that they may dwell in heaven forever.
Consider the different endings of human lives, and always depend on God's mercy.

div.title: The burden of sin (verses 1–11)
div.p: Nothing troubles a godly heart as much as the feeling that God is angry.
We remain at peace by keeping ourselves in his love.
Yet the guilt of sin is too heavy for any person to bear. Without God's pardoning mercy, it leads to despair and destruction.

Henry sees human sickness and pain as effects of sin's entrance into creation: without sin there would be no suffering in the body. The whole creation groans beneath the burden of guilt and corruption.
That burden falls upon sinners either as sorrow drawing them to seek mercy or as final destruction if they remain unrepentant.
When we understand our condition, we will value and seek the Good Physician.
Many allow their spiritual wounds to worsen because they delay going to their merciful Friend.
During bodily illness, we should remember how our bodies have dishonored God and ask him to teach us repentance.
Even groanings too deep for words are known to the One who searches hearts and knows the Spirit's mind.
David's suffering also pictured Christ in his agony and upon his cross, suffering amid abandonment.

div.title: Suffering, patience and prayer (verses 12–22)
div.p: Wicked people may hate goodness even while benefiting from it.
In his descriptions of hostile enemies, David again points toward Christ.
Other people can do us lasting harm only if they persuade us to abandon God and neglect duty.
The true believer's distress can become useful through learning to wait upon God rather than looking only to the world or personal power for relief.
Often our minds will be quieter when we pay less attention to the insults and injuries others inflict.
David suffered correction for his own transgressions, but Christ suffered for our sins alone.
Why should sinners respond with anger or impatience when God mercifully corrects them?
David was aware of sinful impulses still working within him.
When good people continually look only at their suffering, they may lose their balance; when they keep God before them, they remain standing.
True repentance makes us patient during correction.
For a suffering believer, nothing is more painful than the fear of being abandoned by God.
Therefore the heartfelt prayer is: “Do not be far from me.”
The Lord will come to help those who trust him as their salvation.

row.cell: He applies for pardon and deliverance.

div.title: Guarding speech and remembering mortality (verses 1–6)
div.p: When an evil thought arises, we should suppress it.
Habitual watchfulness is the bridle on the horse's head; watchfulness in particular moments is the hand holding the bridle.
When we cannot avoid the company of wicked people, we should remember that they watch our words and may twist them to injure us.
Sometimes silence is necessary, even when what we could say is good. But generally we do wrong if we continually avoid opportunities for speech that would help others.
Impatience begins within us, often through brooding thoughts. Its outward consequence is a burning agitation of the soul.
Even in excellent health and prosperity, every person is fragile and passing away. No one can live long by earthly standards, and death may arrive very soon.
This is certain, yet we are reluctant to accept it.
Let us ask God to enlighten our minds by his Holy Spirit and fill our hearts with grace, so that we are prepared to die at any day or hour.

div.title: Pardon, deliverance and hope (verses 7–13)
div.p: Created things cannot provide lasting satisfaction.
We find it only in the Lord and fellowship with him; disappointments should bring us back to that truth.
If the world is empty and passing, may God prevent us from seeking our ultimate portion in it.
When confidence in created things fails, we still have God to whom we can turn and in whom we can trust.
Recognizing that a good God orders our affairs helps us accept his discipline without accusing him.
David sought forgiveness and asked to be protected from shame.
We must watch and pray against sin. When God corrects us, we should seek relief from him, not put our confidence elsewhere.
Our own conduct often brings trouble, as though we are struck by a rod we made ourselves.
Human beauty is a poor foundation for pride. It will certainly fade, perhaps very quickly.
The body is like a garment worn by the soul. Sin has introduced a moth into that garment, wearing away its beauty, then its strength, and finally its very substance.
Watching a slow disease or the progress of age makes this image painfully clear.
Suffering can stir us to prayer. If it does, we have reason to hope God will hear us.
Believers may expect weariness and poor treatment while traveling toward heaven, but their journey here is short.
Walking by faith, they can continue without abandoning their course or collapsing under hardships.
How blessed it is to hold earthly things loosely as we go home to our Father's house, using the world without misusing it.
Let us look toward the city whose Builder and Maker is God.

div.title: Deliverance after patient waiting (verses 1–5)
div.p: Fears and doubts about our eternal state can feel like a dreadful pit full of sticky mud, even to a dearly loved child of God.
Yet the Lord has enough power to help the weakest and enough grace to help the most unworthy person who trusts him.
The psalmist waited patiently, continuing to believe, hope and pray.
Henry sees these words as applying especially to Christ, whose agony in Gethsemane and on the cross resembled that dreadful pit.
Those who wait for God will never wait in vain.
Believers who have suffered spiritual despair and then found relief by God's grace recognize themselves in verse 2.
Christ is the Rock on which a struggling soul can stand securely.
Where God grants firm hope, he also expects a steady and orderly life.
David received not only peace through faith but also joy.
Multitudes have looked in faith to Christ's suffering and glory and learned both to fear God's justice and to trust his mercy.
God loads us daily with benefits through Providence and grace.

div.title: The work of redemption (verses 6–10)
div.p: Here David foretold the wonder of redemption through Jesus Christ.
The true substance had to appear. Animal sacrifices could never give God the glory or human beings the saving grace accomplished by Christ.
The psalm speaks of Jesus being set apart to serve as Mediator.
The scroll of the book spoke of him.
Henry also sees the covenant of redemption as recorded in God's eternal counsel, and points to the Old Testament's testimony about Christ (John 19:28).
Now that the price of salvation has been paid, its proclamation goes out, inviting people freely and openly to receive it.
Preaching Christ is not easy. People commissioned to proclaim the gospel may face pressure to hide its truth, but Christ sustains those he calls.
May we believe his testimony, trust his promises and submit to his authority.

div.title: Seeking mercy and grace (verses 11–17)
div.p: Even the best saints know they would be undone without God's continuing protection and grace.
See how seriously David regarded sin. This makes the discovery of a Redeemer especially welcome.
When he examined each part of his life, he found something wrong.
A clear view of our sins without an equally clear view of the Savior would overwhelm us.
Yet Christ has triumphed over our spiritual enemies, and through him we are more than conquerors.
Let everyone who seeks God and loves his salvation rejoice and praise him.
No poverty or sorrow can make a person who fears the Lord truly miserable. God himself, together with all he has done and promised, is the source of that person's joy.
The prayer of faith draws upon his inexhaustible fullness, sufficient for every need.
His promises are certain and their fulfillment approaches.
The One who first came in humility will return in glorious majesty.

div.title: God's care for those who care for the needy (verses 1–4)
div.p: God's people are not exempt from poverty, illness or outward suffering. But the Lord considers their condition and gives them what they need in due time.
Following their Master's example, believers learn to show concern for poor and suffering brothers and sisters. This kind of godliness often receives earthly blessings.
Yet nothing troubles a repentant believer more than the fear of God's displeasure or the discovery of sin still living in the heart.
Sin is the sickness of the soul. Pardoning mercy heals its guilt, and renewing grace heals its corruption.
We should therefore seek spiritual healing with greater earnestness than we seek bodily health.

div.title: David suffers betrayal and praises God (verses 5–13)
div.p: We rightly lament the scarcity of sincere friendship among human beings, but the past was no better.
Someone whom David deeply trusted joined his enemies.
We should not be surprised when people we considered friends treat us badly.
Yet we ourselves have broken promises made to God. We receive food from his hand every day and still raise our heel against him.
We must not delight in the downfall of our enemies. We can, however, rejoice when their harmful plans are defeated.
A mercy becomes doubly precious when we recognize God's favor behind it, whether the blessing concerns one person or the public good.
Without his constant sustaining grace, we could not remain standing.
While still on earth, let us join wholeheartedly in the praise that God's redeemed people offer to their God and Savior both here and in heaven.

p.hi: The conflict in the soul of a believer.

div.title: Longing for the living God (verses 1–5)
div.p: The psalmist regarded the Lord as his highest good, and directed his heart toward him.
By fixing his anchor there from the beginning, he was able to endure the storm.
A gracious soul cannot be content merely to attend worship if it does not encounter God himself.
Living souls cannot truly rest anywhere short of the living God.
The upright person longs to appear before him; the hypocrite dreads that meeting.
Few things trouble a believer more than attempts to shake confidence in the Lord.
David was not merely missing the pleasures of royal life. He grieved over the free access to God's house he formerly enjoyed and the happiness of worshiping there.
People who search their own hearts often discover thoughts that need correction.
Here is the remedy for sorrow: when the soul relies on itself, it sinks; when it holds fast to God's power and promise, it remains above the waves.
Present troubles are bearable when we know we will find consolation in God.
We have real reasons to mourn our sin, but despair and despondency often spring from unbelief and a rebellious will. We should therefore pray and struggle against them.

div.title: Remembering God's mercies (verses 6–11)
div.p: The way to forget our misery is to remember the God who has shown us mercy.
David recognized that his suffering had been permitted by God, and this sometimes discouraged him.
Yet if troubles arrive one after another and seem to combine against us, remember that they remain subject to the Lord's appointment and government.
David regarded divine favor as the source of everything good he hoped to receive.
Let us hope and pray in the Savior's name.
One word from the Lord can calm a storm, turn midnight into midday and change bitter complaints into joyful thanksgiving.
Our confident expectation of mercy should make us more earnest in asking for it.
At last faith overcame David's fears. He determined to rely on the Lord and added the personal words, “my God.”
That thought carried him above sorrow.
Never imagine that the God who gives us life and is the Rock of our salvation has forgotten us, if we have taken refuge in his mercy, truth and power.
The psalmist struggled with discouragement until faith and hope prevailed.
Let us challenge unbelieving doubts, receive God's promises personally and then plead those promises in prayer.

p.hi: David endeavours to still his spirit, with hope and confidence in God.

div.title: Hope in God's light and truth
div.p: When David considered his own sin before God, he prayed that the Lord would not enter into strict judgment with him, knowing he would be condemned.
But regarding the conflict his enemies had brought upon him, he could rightly ask God to judge his cause and act on his behalf.
Even when we cannot experience spiritual joy in God, we may still rely on him.
Spiritual support remains available when spiritual delight seems absent.
God has never finally cast away anyone who trusts him, however frightened that person may be about personal spiritual condition.
We need nothing more for true happiness than the good that comes from God's favor and is included in his promises.
Those whom God leads, he directs toward his holy hill.
People who claim to follow the Spirit while turning their backs on God's appointed worship deceive themselves.
We should pray for the Spirit of light and truth, who supplies what is lacking now that Christ is no longer bodily present with his church.
He guides us along the road to heaven.
Whatever brings us joy or triumph, the Lord himself must remain the joy within it.
David returned to God as his never-failing hope.
May the Lord send out the truth of his word and the light of his Spirit to guide us in holiness, peace and salvation.
Like the suffering prophet, a Christian longs to be saved from sin as well as from sorrow.
May the heavenly wisdom shining through Jesus Christ teach us righteousness and lead us by that light and truth into the New Jerusalem.

p.hi: A petition for succour and relief.

div.title: Remembering previous deliverances (verses 1–8)
div.p: Past experiences of God's power and goodness strengthen faith and provide compelling reasons for prayer during present distress.
Israel did not win its victories through human strength or merit. Success came from God's favor and free grace.
The less praise this permits us to claim, the more comfort it offers: the achievement rests on his goodness.
God fought for Israel; otherwise its people would have fought in vain.
The same applies to the establishment of the Christian church. It did not arise through human strategy or power.

p.hi: Christ, through his Spirit, went out conquering and to conquer.

div.p: The One who planted the church will sustain it by the same power and love.
God's people trust and triumph in him, so let anyone who boasts boast in the Lord.
If they find comfort in his name, they should also give him all its due glory.

div.title: The church suffers and fears abandonment (verses 9–16)
div.p: Believers experience times of temptation, suffering and discouragement. The church also passes through seasons of persecution.
In such circumstances God's people may fear he has cast them off and that his truth and name are being dishonored.
But they should look beyond the human instruments of their distress and recognize that even their worst enemies can do no more than God permits.

div.title: Faithfulness under persecution (verses 17–26)
div.p: Affliction must never drive us to obtain relief through sinful compromise.
We should continue reflecting upon the truth, purity and complete knowledge of God, who searches the heart.
Hidden sin and inward motives are known to him and will be brought into account. He understands the secret thoughts beneath words and deeds.
As long as suffering does not drive us away from duty to God, we should not permit it to drive us from comfort in God either.
Be careful that prosperity and ease do not make the heart complacent and spiritually lukewarm.
The true church cannot be forced by persecution to forget God, nor will the believer's heart finally turn from him.
Henry sees the Spirit's prophecy as pointing toward people who suffered to death for their testimony to Christ.
The appeal in verses 25–26 is not based upon personal merit or righteousness but upon the plea of a needy sinner.
No one belonging to Christ will finally be rejected. Every one of them will be saved forever.
God's mercy, purchased, promised and continually supplied to believers, overcomes the doubts arising from their sins.
Let us therefore pray in faith: Redeem us for your mercy's sake.

p.hi: This psalm is a prophecy of Messiah the Prince, and points to him as a Bridegroom espousing the church to himself, and as a King ruling in it, and for it.

div.title: The Messiah's beauty and victory (verses 1–5)
div.p: God's Spirit guided the psalmist's tongue as a skilled writer's hand guides a pen.
This psalm concerns King Jesus, his kingdom and government.
It is a shame we speak so little about him when there is more in Christ to engage our love than in any created thing.
This world's attractions continually draw our hearts away from him. We should therefore learn how far he exceeds everything else in worthiness.
Through his word, promises and gospel, God's goodwill becomes known and his gracious work begins and grows within us.
In verses 3–5, the psalmist joyfully foretells the Messiah's advancing kingdom.
The arrows of conviction trouble sinners until they are humbled and reconciled; the arrows of vengeance bring still more terrible judgment upon enemies who refuse to submit.
Those who have seen Christ's glory and tasted his grace rejoice when his word and Spirit bring former enemies and strangers under his rule.

div.title: The eternal King and his bride (verses 6–9)
div.p: The throne of this almighty King stands forever.
The Holy Spirit leads Christ's people to his cross, where they see both the evil of sin and the beauty of holiness.
None can rightly use Christ's work as encouragement to remain in sin.
The Mediator is God. Otherwise he would neither have been able to accomplish his work nor fit to wear the Mediator's crown.
The Father, as Christ's God with respect to his human nature and mediatorial office, gave him the Holy Spirit without measure.
Anointed as Prophet, Priest and King, Christ possesses the Spirit's gifts and graces in fullness and shares them with his human brothers and sisters.
The Spirit is called the oil of gladness because Christ rejoiced in accomplishing salvation.
The angels rejoice when sinners are saved; how much more does the Son himself!
As believers are conformed to Christ's holy image, they experience the Comforter's joyful influence.
The fragrance of Christ's garments pictures his excellences, the suitability of his offices and the sufficiency of his grace.
His church, composed of true believers, is compared to a queen, betrothed to Jesus by an everlasting covenant.
She is the Lamb's bride.
Her purity resembles fine linen and her costly honor resembles gold. Both her redemption and her beauty depend on the Son of God's precious blood.

div.title: The bride's holiness and the nations' hope (verses 10–17)
div.p: To share these blessings, we must listen to Christ's word and abandon sinful attachments and worldly pursuits.
He must be our Lord as well as our Savior.
Every idol must be cast away so that we can give him our whole heart.
This renunciation has a rich reward: Christ values the beauty of holiness in his church and every believer.
Grace is the Spirit's own workmanship, forming Christ's image in the soul and giving a share in divine holiness.
There is no sin in that work of grace itself; the old corrupt nature has no true glory.
The Father's gift of Christ's righteousness clothes his church.
No one comes to Christ unless brought by the Father.
The clothing and entrance of the bride picture conversion and the garments of salvation Christ gives his people.
Those who love him sincerely and remain close to him share the bride's grace, privileges and salvation.
They will all be brought to the King; not one will be forgotten.
The New Testament church, including Gentile believers, will succeed the Old Testament church in this prophetic picture.
As we look forward to eternal happiness, let us remember Christ as the only way and teach his name to generations still to come, so that his praise endures forever.

div.title: Confidence in God's presence (verses 1–5)
div.p: This psalm encourages hope and trust in God's power, Providence and gracious presence with his church, even during the most difficult times.
It also speaks to our conflicts with spiritual enemies and the promise that through Christ we will overcome them.
God is a help, a present help—someone we have already experienced as our helper.
He is always near and available. We cannot desire a better refuge or find an equal among created beings.
People whose confidence rests upon unstable foundations will panic when the waters rage.
But those led to the Rock can stand securely.
The psalm gives the church joy even amid sorrow.
Its river pictures the Holy Spirit's graces and consolations, flowing throughout the church through God's appointed ordinances and bringing joy to every believer.
God promises that his church will not finally be moved.
When he dwells in our hearts and his word lives richly within us, he will establish and help us.
Let us trust him and refuse to be afraid.

div.title: Behold God's works (verses 6–11)
div.p: Look at the consequences of devastating judgments and stand in reverence before God.
At the same time, recognize the church's ultimate safety and the promise of lasting peace.
Pray that those glorious days will arrive soon.
Worship and trust our almighty Sovereign with humble submission.
