Let all believers rejoice that the Lord of hosts, the God of Jacob, has been with us, is with us and will remain with us.
He is our refuge.
Take hold of this assurance and answer every fear with it:

p.hi: If God is for us, who can be against us?

div.p: Let that confidence sustain us both in life and in death.

p.hi: The people exhorted to praise God.

div.title: The Sovereign gathers the nations (verses 1–4)
div.p: The Lord with whom we have to do possesses awesome majesty.
The universal and absolute sovereignty of a holy God would be terrifying even to contemplate if it were not exercised through his Son from a throne of mercy.
Now it brings terror only to those who persist in wickedness.
God's people should encourage each other in joyful trust and obedience.
Sinners should submit to his authority and receive the salvation he offers.
Jesus Christ will bring Gentile nations under his rule, drawing them like sheep into the fold—not to kill them, but to preserve them.
He will transform their affections and make them willing subjects in the day of his power.
His kingdom also grants rest and security.
In its spiritual meaning the psalm teaches that the Lord himself becomes his people's inheritance.
This is the faith and submission of the saints:

p.hi: “The Lord will choose my inheritance for me; he knows what is best for me better than I do.”

div.title: Praise with understanding (verses 5–9)
div.p: We should praise God frequently and generously.
Yet one rule must always govern our worship: sing praises with understanding.
Know why you are praising God, what he has done and what the service means.
Worship is not acceptable when it is mindless and unreasonable.
We should never lose sight of the purpose of Messiah's exaltation.
The prophets continually return to the conversion of the nations through the gospel of Christ.
It is empty to imagine we belong to Christ if his Spirit does not reign in our hearts by faith.
Lord, you are exalted as Prince and Savior to grant repentance and forgiveness.
Establish your kingdom in us.
Bring every thought into obedience to Christ and turn all the powers and desires of redeemed souls toward holy love, reverence and joy in you.
May praise with understanding rise from every heart both now and forever.

p.hi: The glories of the church of Christ.

div.title: The beauty of God's city (verses 1–7)
div.p: Jerusalem is the city of God.
Henry teaches that those belonging to the spiritual Jerusalem are the ones who truly honor him on earth.
Happy is any kingdom, city, family or individual heart where God is great and God is everything.
There he is known.
The more clearly we understand his greatness, the more praise should arise from us.
Sin has disfigured the earth.
Therefore the place adorned with divine holiness could rightly be called the joy of the whole earth—a reason for all nations to rejoice that God truly dwells with humanity.
The earthly kings feared it.
The destruction of an entire fleet in a storm provides a fitting picture of paganism being overcome by the Spirit of the gospel.
Both require the Lord's mighty power.

div.title: The security and everlasting guide of the church (verses 8–14)
div.p: God's people should learn from every glorious act of his favor.
Let such deliverances strengthen faith in his word, encourage hope in the church's stability and fill our minds with worthy thoughts of him.
Every stream of mercy flowing toward us must be traced back to the fountain of his loving-kindness.
Give God the glory for everything great he has done.
Every member of the church should take comfort from what the Lord does for his people.
Consider the church's beauty, strength and safety.
It is founded upon Christ the Rock, fortified by divine power and guarded by the One who never slumbers or sleeps.
His appointed ordinances are like palaces, and his promises are like defensive walls.
Recognize these blessings, be encouraged to belong to his church and tell others about them.
The God who has done great things for us does not change in his love or care.
If he is our God, he will guide and preserve us to the end.
He will take us beyond death's reach, so that death cannot finally harm us, and bring us into a life where death no longer exists.

div.title: A warning for everyone (verses 1–5)
div.p: Few psalms begin more solemnly, because few truths are more important.
Everyone should listen and apply this teaching personally.
Poor people may be harmed by excessive longing for wealth, just as wealthy people may be harmed by excessive enjoyment of it.
The psalmist first applied the warning to himself, which is the right way to approach divine truth.
Before he described the foolishness of worldly self-confidence, he explained the security that comes through trusting God instead of possessions.
At judgment, the sins of our past lives will confront us.
Worldly sinners will rightly fear.
But why should someone fear death if God is with that person?

div.title: The folly of trusting wealth (verses 6–14)
div.p: A person may possess riches and still have a heart enlarged by love, gratitude and obedience, using wealth for good.
It is not merely having possessions that makes someone worldly, but treating them as the highest good.
Worldly people may think occasionally about God, yet their deepest, most lasting thoughts center on earthly things.
Even the richest person cannot buy back the life of a beloved friend.
The psalm points beyond that limit toward the eternal redemption accomplished by the Messiah.
Redeeming a soul costs more than any earthly fortune.
But once Christ has accomplished that redemption, it never needs to be repeated.
The Redeemer rose before seeing corruption and lives forever (Revelation 1:18).
How foolish to sell one's soul for possessions that can never purchase its salvation!
No wealth can protect its owner from death.
Yet one generation after another praises the wisdom of making money the goal of life.
Even professing Christians imitate the rich fool in Luke 12:16–21.
Death will confront the proud sinner with the question: Where are all your possessions and splendor now?
At resurrection, the upright will be raised to honor while unrepentant sinners face everlasting shame (Daniel 12:2).
We should assess riches and holiness now as they will appear then.
The beauty of holiness alone cannot be damaged by the grave.

div.title: Hope beyond death (verses 15–20)
div.p: Believers need not fear death.
The enormous inequalities of wealth and rank we see during life disappear at the grave.
But differences in people's spiritual condition become enormously significant at and after death.
God, who created human life, is also able to redeem it from eternal ruin.
Believers are tempted to envy worldly prosperity.
Other people praise someone who has built a large fortune and secured an influential family.
Yet what does human approval matter if God condemns us?
People rich in the Spirit's grace and comfort possess something death cannot take away. Indeed, death will bring them into a fuller enjoyment of it.
By contrast, worldly possessions must all be left behind.
We brought nothing into the world and can take nothing away.
Gaining the whole world is worthless if it means losing one's soul.
Without true heavenly wisdom, a person fails to live and die as a being made in God's image.
Yet some people still prefer the lot of the wealthy sinner to that of poor Lazarus, even when they consider the life to come.
How deeply we need the teaching of the Holy Spirit, since our supposed wisdom can still make us foolish about what matters most!

row.cell: Sacrifices to be changed for prayers.

div.title: God's glory and judgment (verses 1–6)
div.p: This psalm instructs us about Christ's coming and the final judgment, when God will call humanity to account.
The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of judgment.
Everyone needs to know how to worship the Lord in spirit and truth.
On the great day, those who refused to hear God's law will be made to hear his judgment.
Happy are people who enter the covenant of grace through faith in the Redeemer's atoning sacrifice and show genuine love through righteous conduct.
God rejects people who rest upon outward religious performances.
He graciously receives those who seek him sincerely.
Only through Christ, the great Sacrifice, can anyone be accepted by God. The sacrifices of the Mosaic law had value only through their relation to him.
God's judgments are righteous and true.
Even sinners' consciences will finally acknowledge his justice.

div.title: Prayer and thanksgiving beyond empty ritual (verses 7–15)
div.p: Obedience is better than sacrifice, and loving God and neighbor is worth more than every burnt offering.
We must never rest in the performance of ceremonies—or in any external form of religion.
God demands the heart.
How could invented religious forms please him when repentance, faith and holiness are neglected?
In distress, we should call upon the Lord through earnest prayer.
Even when suffering comes under his providential correction, it should drive us toward him, not away from him.
We should acknowledge him in all our ways, depend upon his wisdom, power and goodness, and entrust ourselves wholly to him.
Thus we maintain fellowship with God, meeting difficulty with prayer and deliverance with praise.
A believing worshiper receives not only a gracious answer but also grace to thank God for that answer.

div.title: God requires sincere obedience (verses 16–23)
div.p: Hypocrisy is wickedness, and God will judge it.
People who teach God's laws to others too often live in disobedience to those same commands.
They deceive themselves by abusing God's patience and misunderstanding his character and gospel.
At final judgment, sinners' wrongdoing will be exposed completely.
God will set their sins in order—from childhood and youth through adulthood and old age—to their lasting shame and terror.
Those who have forgotten him, persisted in wickedness or neglected salvation should recognize the urgency of their condition.
The Lord's patience is extraordinary, especially considering how badly people misuse it.
If they refuse to turn, they will recognize their mistake when it is too late.
People who forget God also forget who they themselves are.
Our highest purpose is to glorify him.
Whoever offers true praise gives him glory, and such spiritual sacrifices are accepted through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Priest and the altar to whom we entrust them.
Let us praise God fervently in spirit, receive his mercy with gratitude and seek to glorify him in both words and deeds.

row.cell: The psalmist prays for mercy, humbly confessing and lamenting his sins.
He pleads for pardon, that he may promote the glory of God and the conversion of sinners.
God is pleased with a contrite heart, A prayer for the prosperity of Zion.

div.title: Confession and plea for mercy (verses 1–6)
div.p: After becoming convinced of his sin, David poured out his heart to God in prayer for mercy and grace.
Where else can children who have wandered return but to the Lord who alone can heal them?
Under divine instruction, David described the movements of his repentant heart. Genuine penitents are not ashamed to acknowledge repentance. His words also teach others how to confess and pray.
Although David had done and suffered much in God's cause, he relied only upon God's infinite mercy for pardon and peace.
Christ's blood, applied to the conscience, removes transgression and reconciles us not only to God but also to ourselves.
A true believer wants every debt of sin forgiven and every stain cleansed.
A hypocrite secretly reserves some favored sin and wants it spared.
David's sense of guilt was so deep that it continually filled him with sorrow and shame.
His deliberate sin had been against God, whose truth sinners deny and whose trust they betray.
True repentance traces actual sins back to the fountain of original corruption.
David confessed the sinful inclination present from childhood—the attraction toward evil and reluctance toward good that burden renewed believers and ruins the unconverted.
Yet he hoped God would receive him with grace.
God desires truth in the inward parts.
Where sincerity is found, God gives wisdom.
Those who genuinely seek to obey will be taught their duties, while expecting all spiritual good from divine grace overcoming a corrupt nature.

div.title: Cleansing, new life and restored praise (verses 7–15)
div.p: David prayed to be purified with hyssop—an image of Christ's blood applied to the soul through living faith, just as water of purification was sprinkled by a bundle of hyssop.
Christ's blood is called the blood of sprinkling (Hebrews 12:24).
If that cleansing blood washes us, we are truly clean (Hebrews 10:2).
David did not ask to feel comfort before receiving cleansing.
First the bitter root of sorrow—sin—must be removed.
Then he could ask for lasting peace created by God, so that the bones broken by conviction might rejoice.
He asked God to hide his face from his sins, and blot them from his book, as sunlight disperses a cloud.
But the believer wants renewal in holiness as much as the joy of salvation.
David now recognized the uncleanness of his heart and knew he could not change it by personal power.
He therefore begged the Lord to create a clean heart within him.
He had grieved the Holy Spirit through sin and feared losing the Spirit's gracious presence more than anything else.
He asked that comfort might return.
Sin can make a person doubt participation in salvation, which undermines joy.
David therefore prayed to be upheld by the Spirit, lest he fall into further sin or despair.
The Spirit is free: he acts freely, and makes willing service possible.
The greater our joy in duty, the more steadily we perform it.
This is the freedom contrasted with slavery (Galatians 5:1), the Spirit of adoption speaking peace to the heart.
Because God is the God of salvation from sin, we may pray for deliverance not only from sin's guilt but also from its dominion.
When our lips are opened by mercy, they should sing of God's forgiving grace.

div.title: The sacrifice of a broken heart (verses 16–19)
div.p: Anyone truly aware of sin's danger would give much to be forgiven.
Yet human beings cannot make satisfaction for their sins through gifts or sacrifices.
God receives acts of devotion only as expressions of love and duty, not as the price of pardon.
The work of grace in a true penitent produces a broken spirit and a contrite heart, tender and responsive to God's word.
May we all possess such hearts!
God graciously accepts contrition rather than treating outward burnt offerings as sufficient.
Yet a broken heart is accepted only through Jesus Christ; there is no genuine repentance separated from faith in him.
People despise what is broken, but God will not reject a truly contrite heart.
That heart does not pay for sin; only grace receives it.
Those who have suffered spiritually learn to pity and pray for others in similar distress.
David also feared that his sin might bring judgment upon the city and kingdom.
Even personal trouble and a wounded conscience must not make a gracious soul indifferent to the church's welfare.
May all the redeemed continually rejoice that through Christ's blood they have forgiveness according to his abundant grace.

row.cell: The enemies of the truth and the church described, Their destruction.

div.title: Those who boast in wrongdoing (verses 1–5)
div.p: People who boast about sin are really boasting about their own shame.
Sinners abuse God's patience and restraint as an excuse to become hardened in wrongdoing.
But enemies of the church boast uselessly in their harmful plans, while believers may depend upon God's mercy.
A statement that contains some truth may still be a lie when its words are arranged to give an intentionally false impression.
The more cunning and careful the planning behind an evil deed, the more it reflects Satan's character.
When faithful people die, they are transplanted from earthly life into heaven, the Lord's garden, where they take root forever.
But wicked people who persist in sin are uprooted and perish.
Believers recognize that God will finally destroy people who refuse to make him their strength.

div.title: The righteous trust God's mercy (verses 6–9)
div.p: Those who think power and wealth can sustain them without God deceive themselves.
The wicked person trusts the abundance of riches and expects wicked schemes to preserve them.
Such a person may acquire and retain possessions by any means, destroying anyone who stands in the way.
That seems to promise strength, but its end is ruin.
People who dwell through faith and love in God's house are like green olive trees.
To flourish in this way, we must live in holy confidence in God and his grace.
Praising him frequently gives beauty to our profession of faith and helps every grace become fruitful.
We can never run out of reasons to praise.
His name alone is our refuge and strong tower.
It is good to wait upon his saving name.
Nothing calms a troubled spirit more or keeps us from crooked methods of escape than patiently hoping for the Lord's salvation.
No one has followed his guidance and reached a bad end.

p.hi: The corruption of man by nature.

div.title: Humanity's corruption and Christ's saving work
div.p: This psalm closely resembles Psalm 14.
Its purpose is to convince us of our sins.
Through David, God reveals the seriousness of human corruption and confirms it by his perfect knowledge.
He warns persecutors, among the worst sinners, and encourages his suffering people.
Why are human beings so wicked?
Because they do not fear God.
Bad behavior flows from corrupted convictions.
People may profess to know God while denying him through their thoughts and conduct.
Sin is foolishness.
Those who cherish such thoughts are fools in God's sight, and his judgment cannot be mistaken.
The results of sin show how far people can fall when their hearts are hardened by self-deception.
Yet the saints' faith offers hope of a cure.
A Savior is coming, bringing great salvation—the salvation of human beings from sin.
God will deliver his church from enemies and believers from their own sinful bondage, so they can never again be carried captive by sin.
That freedom will bring everlasting joy.
For this saving work the Redeemer received the name Jesus, because he would save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).

row.cell: David complains of the malice of his enemies.
Assurance of the Divine favour and protection.

div.title: David appeals to God's name (verses 1–3)
div.p: God is faithful even when human beings prove unreliable.
How good it is for us that his faithfulness does not depend on theirs!
David had no plea beyond God's name, and no strength to rely upon except God's strength.
He made these his refuge and confidence, assured that God could answer his prayer.
David was betrayed by people from Judah, and Jesus was betrayed by one of his own apostles.
Why should we expect anything but ingratitude, treachery or cruelty from people who refuse to set God before them?
If people abandon the fear of God, what human ties of friendship, family, gratitude or solemn agreement will restrain them?
Selah: pay attention to this.
Let us set God before us continually, because without that practice we are in danger of despair.

div.title: Assurance of God's help (verses 4–7)
div.p: God is my helper.
If we belong to him, he is for us. And if he is for us, we need not fear.
Every creature can do for us only what God appoints it to do.
He will save his people in due time.
Meanwhile he sustains them so that the spirits he created do not fail.
God's threats are true just as surely as his promises. Sinners who refuse repentance will discover that at their own cost.
David's present deliverance gave assurance of further rescue.
He spoke about the final completion as though it had already happened, because God's promise made it certain.
The Lord would ultimately deliver him from all his troubles.
May he enable us to carry our crosses without resentment and finally share Christ's victory and glory.
The voice of praise and thanksgiving should never fall silent in the church of the redeemed.

row.cell: Prayer to God to manifest his favour.
The great wickedness and treachery of his enemies.
He is sure that God would in due time appear for him.

div.title: David prays under fear and grief (verses 1–8)
div.p: These verses show David praying and weeping.
Prayer is healing medicine for every wound and a relief for spirits burdened by sorrow.
Tears can lighten grief, while sorrows never expressed may grow heavier.
David was deeply alarmed.
Henry regards it as likely that the revolt of Absalom, with many people deserting David, lay behind these words.
The memory of David's sin concerning Uriah may also have intensified his fear.
When conscience is guilty, we may mourn deeply; even strong believers can be temporarily overwhelmed by dread.
Yet no one suffered deeper anguish than the holy Jesus, when the Lord laid our sins upon him and made his soul an offering.
In his agony he prayed earnestly and was heard and delivered.
Trusting and following him, we too will be sustained through every trial.
David was weary of human ingratitude and betrayal, and of the cares and disappointments attached to his high position.
He longed to hide in a wilderness away from the changeable anger of his people.
He was seeking rest, not victory.
Even a barren wilderness seemed desirable if it offered quiet.
The wisest and best people often value peace most deeply, especially after constant noise and distress.
One reason death can become desirable to God's child is that it brings final escape from this world's storms into perfect and everlasting rest.

div.title: The pain of betrayal (verses 9–15)
div.p: Nothing grieves a believer more than discovering serious wickedness among people who profess to belong to God's church.
We should not be astonished by corruption within the earthly church, but should long for the New Jerusalem.
David described an especially active enemy.
God sometimes brings down hostile groups by dividing them; a cause divided against itself cannot stand.
Christians must expect suffering even from people who once claimed close friendship.
That is a painful trial, but looking to Jesus enables us to endure it.
Christ was betrayed by a companion, disciple and apostle, whose wrongdoing and end resembled those of Ahithophel.
Both were soon overtaken by divine judgment.
Henry understands the psalm's prayer against treachery as a prophecy of the final ruin of those who persist in opposing the Messiah.

div.title: Cast every burden on the Lord (verses 16–23)
div.p: In every trial, call upon the Lord.
He will hear us, and will not rebuke us for coming too often; the more often we pray, the more welcome we are.
David had imagined everyone was against him.
Now he recognized that many people were still on his side—more than he had thought.
He gave the credit to God, who raises up friends and makes them faithful.
There are more genuine believers, and God's people have more friends, than they sometimes imagine during their darkest hours.
His enemies would face judgment.
They could not relieve their fears through trust in God as David could.
No matter how powerful human beings appear, they are easily humbled before the eternal Lord.
People who refuse to be corrected through suffering face destruction.
Affliction is a heavy burden, especially when Satan's temptations accompany it.
There is also the burden of sin and corruption.
The only sure relief is to look to Christ, who carried that burden.
Whatever you desire God to grant, leave him to give it in his own time and way.
Worry makes the heart stoop.
To cast our burdens upon the Lord is to rest upon his providence and promises, letting him do what he knows to be best.
He will carry us in his mighty arms as a nurse carries a child, and strengthen our spirits through his Spirit.
He will never allow the righteous to be so shaken by trouble that they finally abandon duty or comfort in him.
He will not let them be utterly cast down.
The Savior who carried the burden of our sorrows invites us to give him the burden of our cares.

p.hi: Why should we refuse to trust Christ to govern the world he has redeemed?

row.cell: David seeks mercy from God, amidst the malice of his enemies.
He rests his faith on God's promises, and declares his obligation to praise him for mercies.

div.title: David seeks God's mercy (verses 1–7)

p.hi: “Be merciful to me, O God.”

div.p: This request includes every blessing we seek at the throne of grace. If God grants us mercy, nothing further is needed to make us truly happy.
It also expresses the best ground for our prayers: not our merit, but God's free and abundant mercy.
Surrounded by danger and difficulties, we may flee toward that mercy and trust it.
David's enemies were too strong for him unless God intervened.
He resolved to make God's promises the subject of praise. We have good reason to do the same.
We should not place our trust in human strength when it is on our side, nor become terrified by that strength when directed against us.
The sin of wicked people will never make them truly secure.
Who knows how powerful God's righteous judgment can be or how far it will reach?

div.title: God's care for every sorrow (verses 8–13)
div.p: The prolonged and severe trials endured by many faithful believers should teach us patience under our smaller difficulties.
Yet we easily complain and become discouraged over little sorrows.
David comforted himself with the knowledge that God saw every injury and every grief.
God has a bottle and a book for his people's tears—tears shed over sin as well as over suffering.
He notices them with tenderness.
Every genuine believer can say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what anyone can do to me.”
Human power is limited to what God allows.
David's vows were not an oppressive burden. They marked him as God's servant, restrained him from harmful actions and guided him in duty.
Promises of thanksgiving rightly accompany prayers for mercy.
When God saves us from committing sin or removes its guilt through pardon, he has delivered our souls from death, the wages of sin.
The good work God begins he will carry through to completion.
David hoped to be kept even from the appearance of evil.
We should seek rescue from sin and outward difficulty so that we may serve God more faithfully and without fear.
When his grace has saved us from spiritual death, he will bring us to heaven, where we will walk before him in light forever.

row.cell: David begins with prayer and complaint.
He concludes with joy and praise.

div.title: Prayer during danger (verses 1–6)
div.p: David depended entirely upon God.
Even the strongest believers need to repeat the tax collector's prayer: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
When we entrust our souls to the Lord, we can be certain even in great danger that our troubles will eventually pass.
Until they do, faith and prayer must make God our refuge.
Though God is exalted above everything, he stoops to arrange all things for the good of his people.
This encourages us to pray earnestly.
Wherever we look on earth, help may fail, but heaven remains open to prayer.

Those who have fled from coming judgment to Jesus Christ may trust that the Savior who has done everything needed to purchase salvation will also accomplish everything necessary for them and within them so that they may enjoy it.
David grieved that people hated him so much.
Yet their harmful designs eventually returned upon themselves.
Even at the lowest point of shame and suffering, David did not say, “Lord, exalt me,” but “Lord, exalt your own name.”
The glory of God offers the strongest encouragement in prayer.
We should care for it even more than for our own comfort when asking for mercy.

div.title: A heart established in praise (verses 7–11)
div.p: Through living faith, David's complaints and prayers turned immediately into songs of praise.
His heart was fixed upon God and therefore prepared to face whatever might happen.
When God's grace gives us such a calm and steady frame of mind, we have great reason for gratitude.
Nothing worthwhile is accomplished in religion unless it comes from the heart.
The heart must be prepared for worship and remain attentive during it.
Our tongue is our glory, and never more so than when praising God.
Dull, half-asleep religious exercises are not acceptable worship.
Let us rise early and begin our day with God.
When his mercies first approach us, let us meet them with thankful praise.
David desired other people to join him.
Through his psalms he continues to praise God among his people and sing among the nations.
May our hearts remain fixed upon his boundless mercy and unfailing faithfulness.
Let us glorify him with body, soul and spirit, which belong to him, and pray that the gospel's blessing reaches every land.

row.cell: A prayer that they may be disabled, and their ruin predicted.

div.title: Corrupt judgment and sinful human nature (verses 1–5)
div.p: When injustice is committed under the appearance of law, it is especially evil.
It is particularly grievous when people who claim to belong to God unite to attack his people.
We should thank the Lord for restraints that prevent the full expression of human wickedness.
We should earnestly seek renewing grace, watch our own conduct and show patience with the effects of fallen nature in others.
Corruption of human nature is the root of bitterness from which wrongdoing grows.
Even in childhood we can see the beginning of the world's wicked tendencies.
Children turn away from God and duty as soon as sinful desires begin to express themselves.
How early they learn to lie!
Parents therefore have a duty to teach children carefully and, above all, to pray that God's converting grace will make them new creatures.
Although the poison of sin is already present, much of its harmful influence can be restrained.
When the Savior's word is received, even a person once like a dangerous serpent can become harmless.
But those who finally refuse heavenly wisdom face dreadful destruction.

div.title: A prayer against the power of evil (verses 6–11)
div.p: David asked God to prevent enemies of his church and people from continuing to cause harm.
We may pray with faith against the harmful plans of those opposing God's people.
The psalm also foretells their ruin.
Who can measure God's righteous anger?
The victories of the Just One, Jesus Christ, both personally and through his servants, produce joy that springs not from a desire for revenge but from recognizing God's mercy, truth and justice.
Through Christ's victory we see the redemption of his chosen people, the punishment of persistent wickedness and the fulfillment of divine promises.
Anyone who thinks seriously about these things should seek the reward of righteousness and worship the Providence that orders everything rightly in heaven and on earth.

row.cell: David prays for deliverance from his enemies.

div.title: David prays for rescue (verses 1–7)
div.p: Here we hear David's voice while confined within his own house, surrounded by enemies.
We may also hear Christ amid merciless opponents, the church under the world's oppression, and individual Christians facing temptation, suffering and persecution.
That is how earnestly we should pray each day for protection from spiritual enemies—Satan's temptations and the corruption within our own hearts.
We should fear suffering as evildoers, but never be ashamed of hatred from those who do wrong.
People who persuade themselves that God pays no attention to what they say will often speak with no restraint or consideration.
Where reverence for God is absent, there is little to guarantee proper respect for other people.

div.title: God's mercy as our defense (verses 8–17)
div.p: During danger and difficulty, it is wise and right to wait upon the Lord.
He is our defense and the place where we are safe.
Prayer becomes especially comforting when we remember him as the God of our mercy: the Author of every good thing within us and the Giver of every good thing we receive.
Wicked people can never be satisfied.
That discontent is a terrible misery, even when they possess much.
A contented person may not have everything desired but does not continually quarrel with Providence or fill the heart with resentment.
It is not poverty itself, but discontent, that makes someone miserable.
David would praise God because he had repeatedly found him to be a refuge in times of trouble.
The One who does so much for us deserves our deepest love, praise and service.
God's people's trials will end in joy and thanksgiving.
When the night of affliction passes, they will sing of divine power and mercy in the morning.
Let believers begin now to praise him with assured faith and hope for the blessings they will enjoy and praise forever.

row.cell: David prays for the deliverance of Israel from their enemies.
He entreats God to carry on and complete their victories.

div.title: Prayer for Israel's restoration (verses 1–5)
div.p: David recognized God's displeasure as the source of the hardship he had suffered.
When the Lord begins turning his hand toward us in favor, we should remember our earlier troubles.
Since the people's trials had begun through divine displeasure, their restoration needed to begin through God's renewed favor.
Human folly and corruption create divisions and breaches in society.
Only God's wisdom and grace can truly heal them, by pouring out a spirit of love and peace.
Such reconciliation is essential to saving a nation from ruin.
Henry describes human misery, private and public, as the consequence of sin and God's righteous displeasure against it.
The proper response is to return to God through repentance, faith and prayer, asking him to return to us in mercy.
Christ, David's Son, is the banner given to those who fear the Lord.
In him God's people are gathered into one and receive courage.
Through Christ's name and strength they engage in the spiritual struggle against powers of darkness.

div.title: Confidence in the coming victories (verses 6–12)
div.p: If Christ belongs to us, everything will ultimately contribute to our eternal good.
Anyone made a new creation in Christ may rejoice in the precious promises God has spoken.
Present spiritual privileges and the Spirit's sanctifying influence are certain pledges of heavenly glory.
David rejoiced over victories against neighboring nations hostile to Israel.
God's spiritual Israel becomes more than conquerors through Christ.
At times believers may feel abandoned by the Lord, yet he will ultimately bring them into the strong city.
Faith in his promises assures us that the Father delights to give his people the kingdom.
But the victory is not complete yet.
No sincere believer will use these promises as an excuse for laziness or presumptuous self-confidence.
Hope in God gives genuine courage.
What do people need to fear if the Lord is on their side?
Every victory comes from him.
Those who submit willingly to our anointed King will share his glory, while every enemy will finally be put beneath his feet.

row.cell: David seeks God upon former experience.

div.title: Seeking shelter on the higher Rock (verses 1–4)
div.p: David began with tears and prayer, but ended with praise. A soul lifted toward God may recover peace and a sense of its true condition.
Wherever we find ourselves, there is a way open to the throne of grace. When earthly comforts are withdrawn, their absence should turn us toward God, the fountain of every comfort.
An overwhelmed heart may still be lifted up in prayer. Indeed, the act of crying to God can sustain and relieve it. Weeping should make us more earnest in prayer, not prevent prayer.
God's power and promises are a rock higher than we can reach by ourselves. That Rock is Christ.

David was like a shipwrecked sailor tossed by waves at the foot of a rock so high that he could not climb it without help. Though he wanted to rest upon divine mercy, he knew he could not place himself securely on the Rock of salvation.
We therefore need God to lead us to Christ and establish us in him. In him there is safety; in ourselves there is none.
David resolved to make service to God his constant occupation. Everyone who expects the Lord to be a shelter and strong tower must do the same. God's grace will then be a continual source of comfort.

div.title: Service grounded in everlasting promises (verses 5–8)
div.p: God has a people who fear his name, and a particular inheritance belongs to them. Even now they experience comfort in the soul, an advance pledge of happiness to come.
Those who fear God have enough in him and should not complain. We need desire no better inheritance than theirs.
Those who live before God, serve him and walk in reverent fear live to a good purpose in this world; they will dwell before him forever.
Henry also understands these words to refer especially to the Messiah, of whom the angel said that he would receive David's throne and reign without end (Luke 1:32).
The promises of God do not make prayer unnecessary. They encourage and strengthen prayer.
No protection is better than God's mercy and truth. Through the grace and truth that came by Jesus Christ, believers have reason to praise him whatever their outward circumstances.
A renewed experience of God's mercy and truth toward his people in Christ is therefore the chief reason for our joy and thanksgiving.

row.cell: No trust to be put in worldly things.

div.title: David waits quietly on God (verses 1–7)
div.p: We find both duty and comfort when our souls wait upon the Lord: cheerfully placing ourselves and all our concerns under his will and wisdom, accepting the ways of his Providence and patiently trusting his goodness for the outcome.
David had good reasons for such confidence. God's grace had sustained him, and divine Providence had delivered him.
God alone could be his Rock and salvation. Created beings have no strength independently of him, so David looked beyond them to the Lord himself.
Trust in God establishes the heart. When God is for us, we need not fear what other human beings may do.
Remembering former occasions when waiting upon the Lord proved good, we should continually encourage our souls to depend upon him. This produces greater inner quietness.
If God saves my soul, I may safely leave everything else to his judgment, knowing that he will direct it toward my salvation.
As David's faith became steadier, his joy rose toward holy triumph. Meditation and prayer are blessed means of strengthening both faith and hope.

div.title: Trust God, not people or wealth (verses 8–12)
div.p: Those who have discovered comfort in God's ways naturally invite others to join them. We lose nothing when others share these blessings.
Trust him at all times—not reserving for ourselves or any created thing the confidence that belongs to him alone.
Look to him for guidance in doubt, protection in danger, provision in need and strength for every good word and work.
Pouring out the heart means placing our needs and desires before God, then patiently submitting those desires to his will.
God is a refuge for all who come to take shelter in him.

Do not make people the foundation of your hope. An ordinary crowd is as changeable as the wind; great and wealthy people may promise much, but those depending upon their promises are often disappointed.
Weighed in Scripture's balance, all human ability to make us happy is lighter than vanity.
Even wealth gained honestly can become dangerous when our affections rest upon it. A pleasant and prosperous world can turn our hearts away from God.
A consistent believer receives possessions as a trust from God, managing them for his glory like a steward who will give an account.
God has declared that power belongs to him. He can judge and destroy. Mercy also belongs to him.
The fact that he rewards his people's imperfect service and forgives their transgressions for the Redeemer's sake displays his abundant mercy.
Let us therefore abound in his work and expect every blessing from his grace alone.

row.cell: His dependence upon God, and assurance of safety.

div.title: David thirsts for God (verses 1 and 2)

p.hi: “Early will I seek you.”

div.p: A true Christian devotes the morning to God. As the eyes of the body open, the eyes of understanding should awaken to righteousness.
Such a believer wakes with a thirst for comfort the world cannot provide, and immediately turns in prayer to the Fountain of the water of life.
The immortal soul cannot be satisfied by anything this sinful world offers. It seeks happiness in God as its portion.
The more actively faith and hope work, the more the world resembles a dry and weary desert.
Then the heart longs for the joys of heaven, of which believers receive some foretastes through God's appointed ordinances here on earth.

div.title: God's love is better than life (verses 3–6)
div.p: Even during affliction there are reasons to praise God.
A believer rightly values God's loving-kindness above earthly life. That kindness gives spiritual life, which is better than bodily existence.
Our praise should therefore arise from holy joy. Lips offering praise should be joyful lips.
David was continually in danger. Anxiety and fear kept him awake through exhausting nights.
Yet he found consolation in remembering God.
When the Lord's mercies come to mind during the night watches, they sustain the soul and make even the darkness cheerful.
How happy will be the final morning, when believers awaken satisfied with God's likeness and enjoy his fullness!
There will be no night, grief or sighing there, only joyful praise.

div.title: Following God because his hand upholds us (verses 7–11)
div.p: Christians may sometimes speak with the confidence David expresses here, though too often their souls cling to the dust.
Having entrusted ourselves to the Lord, we ought to rest in his care without surrendering to fear.
Those who earnestly follow God would soon fail if his right hand did not uphold them.
He is the One who strengthens and comforts.
The psalmist expected that, although he was sowing in tears, he would eventually reap in joy.
The Messiah, our Prince, rejoices in God. He has entered the joy set before him, and his glory will be complete at his second coming.
Blessed Lord, let our desire for you increase every hour. May our love remain fixed upon you, and may all our joy and satisfaction be found in you.
Be everything to us during our present wilderness journey and bring us home to enjoy you forever.

row.cell: The destruction of the wicked, encouragement to the righteous.

div.title: Prayer against dangerous speech and plots (verses 1–6)
div.p: The psalmist earnestly asked God to preserve him from paralyzing fear.
The tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things and can do terrible harm.
Upright people become targets of the wicked, who refuse to speak peacefully either about them or to them.
No human precaution can fully guard against a false tongue.
Doing wrong is evil, but encouraging oneself and others to do wrong is even worse.
A heart firmly committed to wrongdoing shows how deeply it has hardened.
At the root of all wickedness lies a practical denial of God's complete knowledge.
The greatest comfort of a good cause and a clear conscience often appears when no person can rescue us from our enemies and God alone remains our help.
He is always present to save.

div.title: The Lord judges evil and vindicates the innocent (verses 7–10)
div.p: When God turns upon wrongdoers the mischief they planned for others, their own schemes become a dreadful judgment against them.
Those who delight in cursing will find that curses return upon them.
Observers should recognize God's hand in these events; otherwise they fail to learn from the workings of Providence.
The righteous rejoice in the Lord, not because fellow human beings suffer or perish, but because God is glorified, his word fulfilled and innocence effectively defended.
They do not base their joy on people, their own cleverness, strength, riches, morality or any created pleasure.
They rejoice in Christ, in whom God's true people are justified and may glory, and in everything he has done and continues to be for them.

row.cell: God is to be praised in the kingdom of grace.

div.title: Praise in the kingdom of grace (verses 1–5)
div.p: All praise offered to God from earth comes from Zion, arising through the Spirit of Christ and becoming acceptable through him.
At times praise is silent because no words can express the greatness of God's goodness.
The Lord reveals himself at a mercy seat, ready to hear everyone who comes by faith in Jesus Christ.
Our sins prevail against us.
We cannot balance them with any personal righteousness.
Yet by God's free mercy, and through a righteousness he himself supplies, our transgressions will not bring us into condemnation.
Communion with God is a great blessing. It means enjoying fellowship with him as One we love and value, making devotion to him the ordinary business of our lives.
Such fellowship is possible only because God freely chooses to welcome us.
His house contains abundance enough to satisfy every soul—enough for everyone and enough for each, always ready and without money or price.
Wherever we live, faith and prayer allow us to maintain this fellowship and receive comfort.
But sinners receive these blessings only through Jesus Christ, who approaches the Father as our Advocate and Surety.

div.title: Praise in the kingdom of Providence (verses 6–13)
div.p: The almighty strength that establishes mountains also supports the believer.
The word that calms stormy seas can silence the enemies of God's people.
Morning and evening bring different blessings: the watchman longs for morning, while the laborer welcomes evening's shade.
Some understand the psalm's language as a reference to morning and evening sacrifices.
Whatever the interpretation, let daily worship—both private and with our families—be a necessary duty and a cherished comfort.
The fruitful earth depends upon gifts from above, and every good and perfect gift comes from God.
He generously enriches a world full of human sin. Surely he has both power and willingness to feed the souls of his people.
These earthly provisions picture greater spiritual blessings.
Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, rises upon sinners, and the Holy Spirit, the river of God full of living water, brings salvation and life.
By that work, barren hearts become fruitful in good deeds, and whole nations are transformed more wonderfully than the ground changes through sunshine and rain.
Where the preached gospel goes forward accompanied by the Spirit, God's paths overflow with abundance.
The gospel will reach the wilderness and the nations. People will hear, rejoice and bear fruits of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the Father's glory.
Lord, your works of creation and grace are many and marvelous. In loving-kindness you made them all.

row.cell: Praise for God's sovereign power in the creation.
For his favour to his church.
And the psalmist's praise for his experience of God's goodness.

div.title: Praise for God's sovereign power (verses 1–7)
div.p: The holy church throughout the world should raise its voice to praise the name above every name.
By both words and deeds, believers should make the praise of Jesus glorious, so that others will be moved to glorify him.
No one can praise God rightly unless his effective grace recreates the heart in holiness.
The redemption accomplished through Christ's death and the wonderful deliverances that flow from it are greater works than Israel's rescue from Egyptian slavery.
We should remember these mighty acts when inviting all the nations to worship God.

div.title: God's kindness toward his church (verses 8–12)
div.p: The Lord not only preserves our bodily lives; he sustains the spiritual life he has given believers.
Through suffering, his people are tested like silver in the furnace.
The trials of the church will certainly end well.
Through conflicts and troubles, people enslaved by Satan are delivered from his rule and brought to joy and peace in believing.
Believers must pass through many tribulations before entering God's kingdom.

div.title: A testimony to answered prayer (verses 13–20)
div.p: Tell others who fear God what he has done for your soul.
Describe how he heard and answered prayer, and invite them to join in thanksgiving. This encourages everyone and brings glory to the Lord.
But the comforts of fellowship with God cannot be enjoyed while we cherish the love of sin in the heart, even if we avoid openly committing it.
Deliberately protecting a cherished sin destroys the comfort and effectiveness of prayer. God finds the sacrifice of the wicked detestable.
There is, however, an important difference between welcoming sinful desires and grieving over their presence while firmly resisting them.
If we feel sin within but sincerely long to be freed from it and refuse its demands, that is evidence of genuine repentance and sincerity.
Prayers offered with simplicity and godly sincerity will be answered according to God's goodness.
Then our gratitude rises toward the One who has not turned away either our prayer or his mercy.

p.hi: Prayer did not obtain deliverance by its own power; God's mercy sent the deliverance.

div.p: That mercy is the foundation of hope, the fountain of comfort and the proper object of praise.

p.hi: A prayer for the enlargement of Christ's kingdom.

div.title: A prayer for the nations
div.p: Every part of our happiness depends upon God's mercy. Therefore the first request is that God show mercy to sinners like us and forgive our sins.
Forgiveness comes through his blessing and is secured in it.
If we walk with him through faith, we may hope for his face to shine upon us.
The psalmist then prayed for the conversion of the Gentiles.
This shows that the saints of the Old Testament desired the privileges they enjoyed to be shared with others.
Many biblical promises and prophecies appear in the form of prayers.
God's answers to the prayers of the church are as certain as the fulfillment of his promises.
The joy desired for the nations is holy joy.
Let them rejoice that the Lord governs kingdoms by Providence and will bring even the kingdoms of this world under the reign of Christ.
That prospect offers every blessing.
The spread of the gospel brings benefits even to earthly society: righteousness exalts a nation.
God's blessing makes our created comforts genuinely sweet and useful.
The psalm looks forward to the whole world worshiping the Lord.
Once the gospel begins to spread, it continues onward until it reaches the ends of the earth.
It is good to join those whom God blesses.
Without Scripture's promises about the conversion of nations, efforts to evangelize them might appear hopeless.
But God has spoken so confidently that we may undertake missionary work trusting he will fulfill his word.
How could we refuse to share the knowledge of God and the salvation in which we rejoice?
Those who have never heard cannot learn unless someone teaches them.
Let us therefore go forward in God's strength and seek the Holy Spirit's accompanying power upon the proclaimed word.
Then Satan's kingdom will be overthrown, and our Redeemer's kingdom established.

row.cell: A prayer—The greatness and goodness of God.
The wonderful works God wrought for his people.
The presence of God in his church.
The glory and grace of God.

div.title: God's greatness and tender compassion (verses 1–6)
div.p: No one has hardened the heart against God and found lasting prosperity.
The Lord is his people's joy. Let them rejoice when they come before him.
God receives his existence from no one; he is the source of every created being.
Yet he has freely committed himself through promise and covenant to bless his people.
We should praise him for mercy and compassion.
He continually cares for the afflicted and oppressed.
Repenting sinners are helpless and exposed, even more so than fatherless children. God receives them into his own family and makes them sharers in its blessings.

div.title: God's remarkable care for Israel (verses 7–14)
div.p: Fresh experiences of mercy should awaken memories of earlier mercies.
When God leads his people into a wilderness, he goes before them there and will also lead them out.
He sustained Israel in the wilderness and later in Canaan. The daily manna seems especially relevant to this passage.
These provisions also picture the nourishment of God's spiritual Israel.
The Spirit of grace and the gospel of grace are the generous rain that strengthens the Lord's inheritance and makes it fruitful.
Christ comes like showers watering the earth.
The record of Israel's victories looks forward to the exalted Redeemer's triumph over death and hell for all who belong to him.
Israel's suffering in Egypt's brick kilns seemed wretched.
Its later glory in Canaan under David and Solomon seemed wonderful by contrast.
So those once enslaved by Satan become honorable when justified and sanctified through Christ.
When they enter heaven, the last remnants of sin disappear.
They become like the wings of a dove covered in silver and its feathers shining gold.
Through complete salvation, those once filthy with guilt become white as snow.

div.title: The ascended Christ bestows gifts (verses 15–21)
div.p: Henry understands these verses as speaking especially of Christ's ascension, as Paul applies them in Ephesians 4:8.
Through the purchase of his death, Christ received the gifts necessary for sinners' conversion and believers' salvation.
He continually distributes these gifts, even among people formerly rebellious, so that the Lord may live among them as Friend and Father.
As Jesus said, the Father gave him authority over all people to give eternal life to those entrusted to him (John 17:2).
Christ came to a rebellious world not to condemn it, but that the world might be saved through him.
He is Savior and Benefactor to his willing people, but a consuming fire to those who persist in rebellion.
His gifts are so many and weighty that God can be said to load us with benefits.
He will not offer merely temporary comforts as our inheritance: he himself will be the God of our salvation.
Christ removes death's sting for believers when they die and grants complete victory over death when they rise again.
He will strike down the pride of the enemy and crush the serpent's head.

div.title: Christ's victories for his people (verses 22–28)
div.p: The victories God gave David over Israel's enemies pictured Christ's victories for himself and everyone trusting him.
Those who take him as their Savior can regard him as their God and King acting for their good, answering their prayers, especially through his word and appointed ordinances.
The Messiah's kingdom will gain the submission of rulers and learned people across the world.
Henry notes that verse 28 seems to address the king.
Yet its words may be applied to the Redeemer, his church and every sincere believer.
We pray: Lord Jesus, complete the undertaking you began for us by finishing your good work within us.

div.title: The nations invited into the church (verses 29–31)
div.p: The psalm gives an urgent invitation to those still outside God's church.
Some submit because fear and conscience compel them, as Providence exposes the foolishness of their opposition and draws them to make peace with the church.
Others submit willingly.
Henry associates both responses with the language of verses 29 and 31.
The beauty and goodness of serving God, and of the gospel that went out from Jerusalem, are sufficient reasons to invite sinners from every nation.

div.title: All power belongs to God (verses 32–35)
div.p: All who worship in God's holy places should admire and adore him with reverence and godly fear.
The God of Israel gives his people strength and power.
Only through Christ strengthening us can we do what he calls us to do.
We must therefore give him every part of the glory, thanking him humbly for enabling our work and for graciously accepting what his own hands accomplish within us.

row.cell: He declares the judgments of God.
He concludes with joy and praise.

div.title: The sufferings of David and Christ (verses 1–12)
div.p: We should regularly contemplate the Person who suffered in this psalm, and ask not merely what he suffered but why.
Meditation on Christ's suffering should humble us for our sins, awaken us to their danger and fill us with gratitude and love that move us to live for the One who died to save us.
When afflicted, entrust the soul to God. This keeps suffering from making us bitter or driving us toward despair.
David was wrongfully hated, but these words apply more fully to Jesus Christ.
Because injustice is common, we should not be surprised when people become our enemies without cause.
Our concern should be that we never do wrong ourselves. Then we can better bear wrong committed against us.
Through his blood Christ made satisfaction for our sins, restoring what he had not taken away and paying a debt that was ours.
Even when innocent of human accusations, we must acknowledge that before God our own sins deserve judgment.
Our sins spring from folly and are all committed in the Lord's sight.
David suffered rejection from friends and family.
Christ also faced unbelief from his brothers and desertion by his disciples.
He made satisfaction not only through the honors he rendered to God, but also by submitting to extraordinary public dishonor.
If zeal for God's truth, commandments or worship brings mockery, we should not lose courage.

div.title: Prayer when trouble overwhelms us (verses 13–21)
div.p: Whatever deep waters of affliction, temptation or oppression seem to engulf us, we should persevere in prayer for the Lord's salvation.
Even in severe outward trouble, signs of God's favor can keep the soul from sinking.
If we continue thinking rightly of God during hardships, we can trust him to deal wisely and kindly with us.
When we suffer reproach for Christ's name, it comforts us that he knows our shame.
A damaged reputation pains someone who values a good name.
Yet being considered worthy to suffer for Jesus should prevent that pain from overwhelming us.
The psalm foretold aspects of Christ's suffering so accurately that its fulfillment confirms Scripture's divine truth and Jesus as the true Messiah.
The vinegar and gall given to him were a faint image of the far more bitter cup he drank so that we could receive the cup of salvation.
We should expect little from human comforters and much from the God of all consolation.

div.title: Divine judgment and the offer of mercy (verses 22–29)
div.p: Henry understands these words as prophecies of judgment upon Christ's persecutors, not as an instruction for private revenge.
Verses 22 and 23 are applied by Paul to judgment on unbelieving Jews in Romans 11:9–10.
When bodily pleasures and ordinary supports of life become the food and fuel of sin, even the table becomes a snare.
Those people refused to see the light because they loved darkness.
Their punishment was that they could no longer see clearly: God left them to the desires and hardening of their own hearts.
Everyone who rejects the great salvation freely offered by God must take seriously the warning of divine judgment.
Yet even those who have greatly multiplied their sins may still find mercy through the Mediator's righteousness.
God excludes no one from that righteousness who does not, through unbelief, exclude themselves.
Those too proud or stubborn to accept it choose their own ruin.
A person poor and sorrowful with God's blessing is better off than someone rich and cheerful while under his judgment.
Henry also applies this contrast to Christ.
When he lived on earth, he was a Man of Sorrows with nowhere to rest his head. Yet God exalted him.
Let guilty and afflicted sinners call upon God: his salvation lifts them up.

div.title: Joy, praise and the future of Zion (verses 30–36)
div.p: The psalm began with sorrow and complaint but ends in holy praise.
Humble thanksgiving pleases God more than the most impressive and expensive outward sacrifice.
The humble will seek him and rejoice; those who seek him through Christ will live and receive consolation.
God will accomplish great things for his gospel church.
Let everyone who loves his people rejoice in that prospect.
Future generations will serve him on earth, and his servants will inherit his heavenly kingdom.
Those who love his name will dwell before him forever.
God did not spare his own Son but gave him for us all. With him he will freely give us everything needed for salvation.
Lord, great Restorer of ruined places, arise and turn ungodliness away from your people.

p.hi: The speedy destruction of the wicked, and the preservation of the godly.

div.title: Prayer in urgent trouble
div.p: This psalm repeats almost the same words as the last five verses of Psalm 40.
Here we see Jesus Christ portrayed in poverty and distress.
At the same time the words announce righteous and fearsome judgment on his enemies—Jewish, pagan and antichristian opponents in Henry's historical and theological language.
The psalm also appeals for the joy and happiness of Christ's friends, to the honor of his Father.
Let us apply its teaching to our own troubles, remembering them and their sinful causes with faith rather than carelessness or resentment.
Urgent trials should awaken earnest prayer.

row.cell: Prayers that God would deliver and save.

div.title: A prayer for protection throughout life (verses 1–13)
div.p: David asked God never to let him be ashamed for trusting him.
Every true believer can come boldly to the throne of grace with the same plea.
Remember the gracious care of divine Providence from our birth and throughout infancy.
The One who has been our Help from birth should also be our Hope from youth.
We should not expect lasting ease or comfort from the world.
Those who love the Lord are often hated, persecuted or regarded as strange because of their convictions and conduct.
Yet God has always been their strong refuge.
His faithful servants may trust that he will not reject them in old age or forsake them when their strength declines.

div.title: Praising Christ's righteousness through old age (verses 14–24)
div.p: David resolved to speak about Christ's righteousness and the great salvation obtained through it.
This would occupy his speech not only on Sabbaths but on every day of the week, every year and throughout his life.
He would proclaim it not merely during appointed seasons of worship but on every occasion, all day long.
Why return so often to this subject? Because its riches cannot be counted.
Christ's righteousness is beyond expression, and the salvation it provides is everlasting.
God does not abandon his grey-haired servants when they can no longer work as they once did.
Indeed, he often strengthens their inner lives while their bodily strength declines.
Older disciples of Christ owe a testimony to those who come after them.
They should speak earnestly about the benefits of true religion, the certainty of God's promises and, especially, the Redeemer's everlasting righteousness.
With confidence in God's final deliverance, let us spend whatever days remain praising the Holy One of Israel with all our abilities.
While we tell of his righteousness and sing his praise, faith can lift us above fear and frailty and grant us foretastes of heaven's joy.
Above all the Lord's works, redemption deserves our praise.
The Lamb who was slain and redeemed us to God is worthy of every blessing and all thanksgiving.

row.cell: David begins with a prayer for Solomon.
He passes into a prophecy of the glories of his reign, and of Christ's kingdom.

div.title: David prays for Solomon (verse 1)
div.p: Part of this psalm concerns Solomon, but it belongs more fully and clearly to Christ.
Solomon was both a king and a king's son.
His godly father asked that God would give him wisdom, so that Solomon's reign might become a memorial and picture of the Messiah's kingdom.
This is a father's prayer for his child and a final blessing near the end of life.
The best thing parents can ask God to give their children is wisdom and grace to understand and fulfill their duties.

div.title: The Messiah's enduring kingdom (verses 2–17)
div.p: The psalm foretells the kingdom of Christ, and many of its promises cannot be fulfilled by Solomon.
At the beginning of Solomon's rule there were righteousness and peace.
But before his reign ended, trouble and injustice appeared.
The kingdom described here lasts as long as the sun, whereas Solomon's kingdom soon came to an end.
Henry adds that even Jewish interpreters understood it as speaking of the Messiah.
The glorious promises find their complete fulfillment only through Christ's reign.
Where his kingdom is established, discord and conflict diminish in families, churches and nations.
Christ's law written upon the heart makes people honest and just, willing to give each person what is owed and to live in love.
This produces abundant peace.
Holiness and love endure in his kingdom.
The world and human lives change constantly, but Christ's kingdom remains.
He descends through the grace and comfort of his Spirit like rain on freshly cut grass—on the living grass remaining to grow again, not on the pieces already cut off.
His gospel has been preached, or will be preached, to every nation.
Christ does not need human gifts or services, yet he deserves our best.
People who possess worldly wealth should use it to serve him and do good.
Prayer is offered through him and for his sake. Whatever we ask the Father, we should ask in Christ's name.
He is also worthy of praise, because our obligations to him are beyond measure.
Christ alone will be reverenced throughout the generations.
His name will be praised to the end of time and throughout eternity, and all nations will call him blessed.

div.title: Praise for redeeming love (verses 18–20)
div.p: We are taught to bless God in Christ, praising him for everything accomplished for us through his Son.
David earnestly prayed that the promise about the Messiah's kingdom would be fulfilled.
It is sad to see how little glory God receives from the world, although he is so generous toward it.
May we, like David, submit to Christ's authority and share in his righteousness and peace.
Let us bless God for the wonders of redeeming love.
May our days be spent—and our lives end—in prayer for the spread of Christ's gospel.

row.cell: How he gained a victory over it.

div.title: The temptation to envy the wicked (verses 1–14)
div.p: The psalmist was strongly tempted to envy prosperous wicked people.
Many of God's faithful servants have faced the same testing.
He began, however, with an unshakable truth: God is good.
Remembering that goodness guards the mind against Satan's temptations.
Even strong believers can find their faith badly shaken. Some storms test the firmest anchors.
Foolish and wicked people sometimes enjoy great outward success and seem to escape many troubles.
They may live without fearing God and still become wealthy and influential.
Some remain relatively healthy until death and die without much pain, while godly people may spend their lives in illness and die with severe suffering.
Others experience no apparent terror when facing death.
But we cannot judge a person's state after death from the circumstances of that death.
These observations made God's people uncertain what to say, especially when their own suffering was bitter.
The psalmist spoke from real pain.
He felt tempted to believe that serving God had been pointless.
Yet genuine sanctification calls us to cleanse both soul and body from sin.
The heart is purified by Christ's blood received through faith and by the Holy Spirit beginning his work within.
That inward change appears outwardly in a heartfelt determination to pursue holiness and a blameless way of life.
Serving God and keeping his ordinances are never in vain.

div.title: The sanctuary reveals the end of the wicked (verses 15–20)
div.p: The psalmist restrained himself from speaking his harmful doubts to others.
He still respected God's people and did not want to injure their faith.
When we stop ourselves from giving voice to evil thoughts, that restraint may show genuine repentance for those thoughts.
Few things wound God's people more than hearing that serving the Lord is useless, because this contradicts their whole experience.
He prayed for understanding and came before God in the sanctuary.
There he considered the end toward which the wicked were moving.
They seemed secure at the height of prosperity, yet were preparing for ruin.
A suffering righteous person's troubles end in peace.
The wicked person's pleasures end in destruction.
Their prosperity is fleeting and precarious, like walking on slippery ground.
It is a show without substance, a shadow or a dream that appears pleasant during sleep but may itself disturb the sleeper.

div.title: Learning to draw nearer to God (verses 21–28)
div.p: God would not allow such a temptation if his grace were insufficient not merely to preserve his people, but also to make them spiritually richer through the trial.
Envy and discontent hurt the soul.
Looking back, the psalmist recognized his own folly and ignorance.
When good people fall into wrong thoughts, words or actions during intense temptation, they should afterward acknowledge them with sorrow and shame.
The credit for deliverance belongs not to our wisdom but to God's gracious presence and Christ's intercession.
Those committed to the Lord receive counsel from his word and Spirit, their best guides here.
Then he receives them into glory.
The hope of heaven can reconcile believers to dark and mysterious earthly Providence.
This experience drew the psalmist closer to God.
Even heaven would not make us happy without God's presence and love.
The world's beauty and splendor vanish.
Our bodies lose their strength through illness, age and death. When bodily strength fails, confidence and comfort often fail too.
But Jesus Christ offers to be everything needed by any poor sinner willing to renounce other final hopes.
Our sins have separated us from God.
A mere profession of Christ while we continue in deliberate sin only increases condemnation.
Let us therefore draw near and remain near through faith and prayer.
Those who sincerely trust the Lord always have reason to thank him.
Blessed Lord, since you have promised to be our portion in the coming world, keep us from choosing anything else as our portion here.

div.title: Lament over a devastated sanctuary (verses 1–11)
div.p: Henry understands this psalm as appearing to describe the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple by the Chaldeans.
The people of God laid their terrible situation before the Lord and left it in his hands.
They recalled what he had previously done for them.

If the deliverance from Egypt encouraged Israel to trust that God would not abandon his people, Christians have even stronger reason to believe he will not reject those redeemed through Christ's own blood.
Unbelievers and persecutors may silence faithful ministers, close places of worship and boast that they will destroy both God's people and their religion.
For a long time such schemes may appear successful.
The oppressed may see no possibility of escape.
Yet God preserves a remnant of believers, the seed of a future harvest.
The church that appears despised today has outlived many enemies who once celebrated victory over her.
When hostile power is most terrifying, take refuge in God's power through earnest prayer.

div.title: Remember the God of creation and covenant (verses 12–17)
div.p: The church turned from complaint to the memory of God's ancient works as her King.
What he had done before encouraged his people to trust him again.
These deliverances were his work, which no one else could have accomplished.
Remembering Providence strengthens faith and hope under present difficulties.
The God of Israel is also the God of nature.
He faithfully maintains the order of day and night.
He will likewise remain faithful to those he has chosen.
We have as much reason to expect affliction in this world as to expect night and winter.
But we have no more reason to despair of comfort's return than to despair that day and summer will return.
In the world to come these changes will finally disappear.

div.title: Prayer for the poor and oppressed (verses 18–23)
div.p: The psalmist asked God to defend his church against enemies.
The folly of those who despise his gospel and servants will become evident.
We should pray that he will enlighten nations living in darkness and rescue his people.
Then the poor and needy will have reason to praise his name.
Blessed Savior, you are the same yesterday, today and forever.
Make your people more than conquerors.
Be everything to them in every place and every circumstance, so that even your poor and afflicted servants will praise your name.

row.cell: The psalmist declares his resolution of executing judgment.
He rebukes the wicked, and concludes with resolutions to praise God.

div.title: Gratitude, justice and the rule of Christ (verses 1–5)
div.p: We often pray repeatedly when we are seeking mercy.
After receiving mercy, should we thank God only once or twice?
The Lord shows that he is near us through the blessings we seek from him.
Everyone entrusted with public responsibility must administer it with integrity and justice.
Henry understands these words as especially applicable to Christ and his government.
Human sin threatened the ruin of all creation, but Christ saved the world from complete destruction.
The One whom God has made our wisdom commands us to be wise.
He warns proud and defiant sinners not to boast of their power or persist in contempt for God.
Every hope humanity has for the present and every prospect of future happiness flows ultimately from the Son of God.

div.title: All judgment and promotion belong to God (verses 6–10)
div.p: No human cause, considered by itself, can bring people to positions of honor without the First Cause—God.
Advancement comes neither from the east, west nor south.
Henry notes the absence of the north: in the language of the source, the word for north can also refer to a hidden place, which leads him to relate promotion to the secret counsel of God.
From the Lord alone every person receives the final judgment appointed to them.
In the cup of affliction offered to God's people, mercy and grace are mixed with suffering.
For unrepentant wicked people, the same image points to a mixture of divine judgment.
God's people may experience the same public disasters as other people, but the dregs of the cup are reserved for those who remain in sin.
The exaltation of David's Son, Christ, will be the subject of everlasting praise among the saints.
Let sinners submit to the King of righteousness.
Let believers rejoice in him and obey his commands.

row.cell: The psalmist speaks of God's power.
All have to fear and to trust in him.

div.title: God is known among his people (verses 1–6)
div.p: Happy is a people whose land is filled with the knowledge of God.
Happy, too, are individuals whose hearts are filled with that knowledge.
It is the glory and happiness of a nation to have God present through his appointed ordinances.
The enemies of God's church may act with great pride. But the Lord will demonstrate that he is greater than those opposing him.
See how powerful even God's rebuke can be.
Christians may read these words joyfully in view of the benefits bestowed upon them through the Redeemer.

div.title: Holy fear and confidence in God's justice (verses 7–12)
div.p: God's people are described as the meek of the earth—quiet and peaceable people who endure wrong but refuse to do wrong themselves.
The righteous Lord may seem silent for a long time. Eventually, however, he will make his judgment heard.
We live in an angry, provoking world.
Human rage often hurts us, and the anticipation of further harm may make us even more afraid.
But God sets limits to human anger.
Whatever will not ultimately serve his glory, he will prevent from coming to pass.
He restrains human wrath as he restrains the roaring sea: it may come this far, but no farther.
Everyone should therefore submit to him.
Our proper offerings are prayers, praise and above all our hearts.
God's name is glorious; he alone deserves our highest reverence.
The Lord can humble the proudest rulers with astonishing ease.
Henry compares the removal of a prince's courage to picking a flower from its stem or a cluster of grapes from its vine.
God can take away the boldness of the most defiant people.
Since no one can successfully contend against him, our wisdom and duty are to submit, seek his favor as our portion, and entrust all our concerns to his care.

row.cell: He encourages himself by the remembrance of God's help of his people.

div.title: Distress, prayer and dangerous conclusions (verses 1–10)
div.p: Days of trouble should be days of prayer.
When God seems to withdraw his presence, we must continue seeking him.
The psalmist did not look for a distraction in work or amusement. He sought God himself, his favor and his grace.
People troubled in spirit should pray, not merely brood over their distress.
The psalmist concentrated so much on suffering that his usual means of consolation increased his sorrow.
When he remembered God, his thoughts turned only to divine justice and anger.
His spirit felt overwhelmed.
Yet we should not let grief over comforts lost make us ungrateful for comforts that remain.
He tried to recall the promises and past mercies that had sustained him during earlier difficulties.
The words express the condition of a grieving soul that feels deserted and walks in darkness—a condition even believers may experience (Isaiah 50:10).
Few things wound a godly soul more deeply than the thought that God is angry with it.
During dark periods, Christians may be tempted to draw false conclusions about their own spiritual state and the future of God's church.
We must resist these thoughts.
Let Scripture answer the questions unbelief raises.
A troubled fountain may eventually clear again.
Remembering former times of comfort can encourage fresh hope and bring relief.
Such fears arise from weakness in faith.
Despair and distrust are too often weaknesses of believers during affliction.
When unbelief stirs within us, we should recognize it sorrowfully and suppress it.

div.title: Remembering God's works (verses 11–20)
div.p: The remembrance of God's works is a powerful remedy against distrust of his goodness and promises.
He is God and does not change.
His way is in the sanctuary.
We can be certain that everything he does is holy.
Nevertheless, his purposes are often like deep waters that cannot be sounded, or the course of a ship that leaves no trace.
God brought Israel out of Egypt.
This deliverance pictured the greater redemption accomplished in the fullness of time through Christ—both by the price he paid and by the power he exercises.
If we have entertained doubts about God's kindness, turn promptly to meditate on the One who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all.
How can we doubt that with Christ he will graciously give everything necessary for our salvation?

row.cell: The mercies of God to Israel contrasted with their ingratitude.

div.title: Scripture and the duty to teach children (verses 1–8)
