div.p: The teachings in this psalm are called deep or dark sayings because they deserve careful examination.
God's law was given with an express command that parents should teach it diligently to their children, so that God's people would continue serving him through future generations.
The record of his providential dealings—both mercy and judgment—should help children recognize God's will and obey it.
Remembering his mighty works strengthens our resolve to keep his commandments.
Hypocrisy opens a broad road toward apostasy.
People whose hearts are not rightly devoted to God will not remain faithful.
Negligent or wicked parents may be responsible for the spiritual destruction of their children.
Young people must honor their parents and obey everything that is lawful.
But they must not obey commands requiring sin or imitate evil parental examples.

div.title: Israel's repeated unbelief (verses 9–39)
div.p: Sin drains courage and weakens the heart.
Forgetting God's works causes disobedience to his commands.
The history of Israel displays a long conflict between divine goodness and human wickedness.
God hears people's complaining and distrust and is greatly displeased with it.
Those who will not trust his merciful power may come to experience his righteous judgment.
We cannot claim to trust God for eternal salvation while consistently refusing to trust his Providence along the way.
He opens heaven's door to those who ask, seek and knock through faith and prayer.
Our distrust, therefore, aggravates our sins.
God sometimes punished Israel not by refusing their sinful cravings but by granting what they demanded.
Unrestrained desires never become satisfied.
Those who indulge a lust do not thereby escape it.
Hard indeed are hearts that neither divine kindness melts nor divine judgment breaks.
People who persist in sin should expect continuing trouble.
Our own lives are often joyless and unproductive because we do not live by faith.
Under correction, Israel sometimes professed repentance.
But their conduct soon showed their insincerity and lack of perseverance.
Israel's history reflects the condition of our own hearts and lives.
Its record also resembles the history of nations and churches, which often ignore both divine mercy and judgment until wrongdoing reaches its full measure.
Great spiritual privileges have not always kept even churches faithful to God's word.
True believers also acknowledge years in which they abused Providence's kindness.
When they enter heaven, they will marvel at God's patience and mercy in bringing them there.

div.title: Wilderness guidance and settlement (verses 40–55)
div.p: Receiving divine mercy should never make us feel free to sin.
That misuse of mercy may bring judgment closer.
But people corrected for sin should not become discouraged from repentance.
The Holy One of Israel acts for his own glory and for the ultimate good of his people.
When Israel forgot his previous favors, it began to limit God in its expectations for the future.
God led his people out like a flock of sheep and guided them through the wilderness with the tenderness and care of a shepherd.
So Jesus, the true Joshua, leads his church through the spiritual wilderness.
No earthly Canaan and no worldly advantage should make believers forget that the church remains in a wilderness during this life.
A far more glorious rest is still reserved for God's people.

div.title: God's mercy despite continued ingratitude (verses 56–72)
div.p: Once Israel settled in Canaan, the children repeated their parents' sins.
Though God gave them his testimony, they turned away.
Deliberate sin among people bearing God's name insults his holiness and exposes them to his justice.
Those whom the Lord abandons become easy prey to destructive enemies.
Yet sooner or later he also brings disgrace upon the enemies of his people.
He gave Israel good government through a king after his own heart.
Henry sees this final act of divine favor as the climax of the psalm.
David pictured Christ, the great and good Shepherd.
Christ was first humbled and afterward exalted.
He is filled with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, and his subjects may trust both the uprightness of his heart and the skill of his hands.
His government and peace will have no end.
Every test of human nature confirms the Bible's warning that the heart is deeply deceitful and corrupt.
Only being recreated by the Holy Spirit can cure human ungodliness.

row.cell: The deplorable condition of the people of God.

div.title: A devastated holy city (verses 1–5)
div.p: God's people brought their distress before him.
Where else could children go but to their Father, who is able and willing to help?
Sin had brought a dreadful change upon the holy city.
The people themselves defiled it through wrongdoing, and God permitted their enemies to defile it through violence and contempt.
They longed for reconciliation with him.
People who regard God's favor as better than life naturally dread his displeasure as worse than death.
Whenever we suffer, we should first beg the Lord to cleanse away the guilt of sin.
Then we can look for the comfort of his tender mercy.

div.title: A plea grounded in God's mercy (verses 6–13)
div.p: Those who continually ignore God and refuse to pray show that they do not know him rightly.
However unrighteous the invaders' actions were, the Lord was righteous in permitting those events within his Providence.
Deliverance from trouble becomes a genuine mercy when it rests upon forgiveness of sin.
We should therefore pray even more earnestly for sin to be removed than for suffering to end.
The people claimed no merit before God.
Their only hope was his mercy.
They appealed to the glory of his name: Help and pardon us for your name's sake.
Christians should remember that they too may be bound by chains of sin.
The world can resemble a prison, and every person lives under a sentence of death whose execution may come suddenly.
How earnestly should we pray that the sighing of prisoners reaches God, and that he preserves those appointed to die!
What a glorious day it will be when the church, victorious over sin and sorrow, sees every spiritual enemy finally disarmed!
Then, generation after generation, the redeemed will praise their great Shepherd, Bishop, King and God.

row.cell: The psalmist complains of the miseries of the church.
Its former prosperity and present desolation.

div.title: A cry to the Shepherd of Israel (verses 1–7)
div.p: The One who dwells upon the mercy seat is the good Shepherd of his people.
Yet we cannot enjoy the consolation of his love or expect the protection of his mighty arm unless we receive his converting grace.
When the Lord seems displeased even with his people's prayers, several explanations may apply.
Their aims in praying may be wrong.
They may be secretly indulging a cherished sin.
Or he may be testing their patience and perseverance in prayer.
When God is displeased, his people may weep while their enemies rejoice.
Every salvation comes from his favor; no true conversion takes place apart from his grace.

div.title: The vine planted and cared for by God (verses 8–16)
div.p: The church is pictured as a vine and a vineyard.
Christ is the root; believers are the branches.
A vine is weak and needs support, yet it can spread widely and produce abundant fruit.
But if it produces no fruit, hardly any tree is so useless.
Have we not been planted in a carefully tended garden with every opportunity to bear the fruits of righteousness?
Yet empty leaves of religious profession and barren branches of doctrinal talk and ceremonial form often far outnumber genuine godliness.
The vineyard had been ruined.
There was a righteous reason for the change in God's dealings with his people.
Our condition is good or bad according to whether his favor rests upon us.
When we observe even the most faithful part of the visible church, we should not be surprised if God sends severe correction.
The psalm calls upon God to protect and restore the vine.
Lord, you formed this vineyard for yourself, so we may humbly commit its care to you.

div.title: The Man at God's right hand (verses 17–19)
div.p: The Messiah, Protector and Savior of the church, is the Man at God's right hand, the Arm of the Lord, to whom all authority has been given.
Through him we receive the strength to persevere to the end.
The vine cannot finally be destroyed, and no genuinely fruitful branch will perish.
But barren branches will be cut off and thrown into the fire.
We were redeemed so that we might serve the One who redeemed us, not return to the sins from which he rescued us.

row.cell: God is praised for what he has done for his people.

div.title: Praising the God who delivers (verses 1–7)
div.p: All the worship we can give God falls short of his excellence and of what we owe him—especially for redeeming us from sin and judgment.
Israel was commanded to remember God's mighty deeds through appointed public festivals.
To appreciate the greatness of a deliverance, we should remember how dreadful the danger or bondage was from which we were rescued.
We must not forget the degrading and ruinous slavery into which Satan, our oppressor, once brought us.
When distress of conscience drives us to cry to the Lord, he answers and sets us free.
Conviction of sin and the trials of affliction may become signs of his faithful concern for us.
If Israel remembered deliverance from Egypt on its feasts, how much more should Christians remember the greater redemption accomplished through Jesus Christ when gathering on the Christian Sabbath!
He has rescued us from a bondage far worse than Israel's slavery.

div.title: God calls his people to listen and obey (verses 8–16)
div.p: We should expect little from created things and much from the Creator.
By faith and prayer, we may receive from God everything truly necessary.
The wickedness of the world arises from human willfulness.
People refuse true religion because they do not want to submit to it.
God is not the author of their sin.
He leaves stubborn sinners to the desires of their own hearts and to their own plans. If they fail to do good, they must bear responsibility.
The Lord does not desire that any should perish.
What terrible enemies sinners become to themselves!
Sin prolongs our troubles and delays our enjoyment of salvation.
The fertile hills and fields of Canaan pictured spiritual and eternal blessings held through faith and obedience.
Christ is the Bread of Life, the Rock of salvation, and his promises are as sweet as honey to a godly soul.
But those who reject him as Lord and Master cannot expect to enjoy him as Savior and reward.

div.title: Judges must govern for the public good (verses 1–5)
div.p: Magistrates have been entrusted with authority for the public good.
They serve God's Providence in maintaining order and peace, punishing wrongdoing and protecting people who act rightly.
God directs the decisions of rulers who desire justice and restrains those who intend evil.
We should acknowledge God's authority behind the offices and governors he permits to rule.
But when people responsible for justice twist it into wrongdoing, no good can be expected.
The wrong actions of public officials bring harm upon the public.

div.title: Every ruler will answer to God (verses 6–8)
div.p: Human beings find it difficult to receive honor and authority without becoming proud.
Yet all earthly rulers will die.
Every title and earthly dignity will be brought down into the dust.
God himself governs the world.
There is a righteous God to whom we may turn and on whom we may depend.
Henry also sees these words as pointing toward the Messiah's kingdom.
When we look at the world's disorder, we have good reason to pray that Jesus Christ will soon rule openly over every nation, bringing truth, righteousness and peace.

row.cell: The designs of the enemies of Israel.

div.title: The enemies of God's people make plans (verses 1–8)
div.p: At times God seems not to be responding to unjust treatment of his people.
Then we may call upon him as the psalmist did.
All wicked people oppose God in some sense, and persecutors especially show themselves to be his enemies.
The Lord's people are his hidden ones.
The world does not truly know them, but he takes them under his special care.
If the enemies of the church can agree in their effort to destroy it, should not its friends unite in defending it?
Wicked people often wish religion would disappear from human society.
They would welcome the removal of every restraint it places upon their conduct, and would silence those who preach, profess and practice it.
They would go further if they had the power.
There have always been many enemies of God's church.
Their number makes the Lord's power in preserving a people for himself still more wonderful.

div.title: Prayer for God's judgment and enemies' repentance (verses 9–18)
div.p: Everyone who persists in opposing Christ's kingdom should take seriously the judgment described here.
God remains the same toward his people and toward those who attack them.
The psalm asks God to make the enemies' purposes as unstable as a turning wheel, and to scatter them like stubble.
It also uses the image of stubble consumed by fire to speak of final judgment.
But Henry makes an essential pastoral distinction:
We should desire no humiliation for our enemies or persecutors except what may help lead them to repentance and conversion.
The judgment of God will overtake those who continue to resist him unless they turn and seek the pardoning mercy of the Lord they have offended.
God's victories demonstrate that Jehovah possesses all power and perfection in himself.
Let us fear his judgment, surrender willingly to him and seek his mercy.
Above all, let us seek deliverance through the destruction of our own sinful fleshly desires, which fight against the soul.

row.cell: The psalmist expresses his affection to the ordinances of God.
His desire towards the God of the ordinances.

div.title: Longing for the Lord's house (verses 1–7)
div.p: God's appointed ordinances comfort believers in this troubled world.
Through them they enjoy the living God's presence.
That explains their sorrow when they cannot join in public worship.
These ordinances are to their souls what a nest is to a bird.
Yet their blessings are only an advance taste of the happiness of heaven.
How can people sincerely desire heaven's holy dwelling while complaining that worship here is wearying and unpleasant?
Truly happy people continue in the practice of true religion through the strength supplied by Jesus Christ.
Every part of our ability comes from him.
Pilgrims traveling toward the heavenly city may cross many valleys of tears and dry deserts.
But God opens wells of salvation and sends consolation to support them.
Those who press forward in Christian duty receive grace added to grace.
As they grow in grace now, they will eventually be made perfect in glory.

div.title: Seeking the God of worship (verses 8–12)
div.p: Whenever we approach God, we should ask him to look favorably upon Christ, his Anointed One, and receive us for Christ's sake.
Without the Mediator, we would not dare present ourselves before the Father.
But looking toward Christ in faith, we may confidently pray that God will regard us through him.
The psalmist loved God's ordinances.
We should regard one day in God's courts as better than a thousand elsewhere, and prefer the humblest duty in his service to the highest worldly promotion.
We live in darkness, but God is our Sun, giving light, life, guidance and direction.
We face dangers, but he is our Shield, protecting us from the fiery darts that surround us.
God has not promised riches and honors.
He has promised grace and glory to those who seek him through his appointed way.
Grace is heaven begun on earth through knowing, loving and serving God.
Glory is the completion of that blessedness: becoming like him and enjoying him fully forever.
Let us seek to walk uprightly and trust the Lord to provide everything that is truly good for us.
Even when we cannot go to the Lord's house, we may approach the Lord of the house through faith.
In him we can find genuine happiness and peace whatever our outward circumstances.

row.cell: Prayers for the continuance of former mercies.

div.title: Remembering mercy and seeking pardon (verses 1–7)
div.p: Present trouble should not make us forget God's earlier acts of mercy.
His favor is the source of happiness for nations and individuals alike.
When God forgives sin, he covers it completely.
Forgiveness is not a partial hiding of the transgressions of his people.
Christ, our Intercessor, stood on their behalf.
Because of his mediation, the Lord turned away his anger and showed compassion.
Only when we have been reconciled to God can we expect to enjoy the comfort of being reconciled to him.
Salvation flows from mercy alone.
When believers sin, they may experience severe and prolonged correction.
Yet when they humbly repent and pray, God can restore their joy in him.

div.title: God speaks peace through Christ (verses 8–13)
div.p: Sooner or later the Lord speaks peace to his people.
He may not give outward peace, but his Spirit can speak inwardly to their hearts.
This peace is promised to those who turn away from sin.
Every sin is folly, and backsliding is especially foolish because it means returning to wrongdoing once rejected.
Whatever our difficulties, God's salvation remains near.
His glory is also involved, so that honor may dwell among his people.
The truthfulness of God's promises appears in his mercy in sending the Redeemer.
Divine justice has been satisfied through the great atonement.
Christ, the Way, the Truth and the Life, came from the earth when he took our human nature.
The Father looked upon him with satisfaction.
For Christ's sake God grants every good thing, and especially the Holy Spirit, to those who ask.
Through Christ, forgiven sinners become fruitful in good works.
By looking to and trusting the Savior's righteousness, they find their feet established on the path of duty.
Righteousness guides them both in approaching God and in following him.

row.cell: The psalmist pleads his earnestness, and the mercy of God, as reasons why his prayer should be heard.
He renews his requests for help and comfort.

div.title: Poverty, prayer, and divine mercy (verses 1–7)
div.p: When we recognize our poverty and misery, these needs become powerful reasons for approaching the throne of grace.
The safest way to preserve ourselves is to entrust ourselves to God's keeping.
The believer can appeal to the Lord as someone he has favored, set apart for himself, and made a participant in his sanctifying grace.
It is a great encouragement to prayer to know that God's converting grace has taught us to trust him and become his servants.
As we maintain fellowship with God, we may expect to receive comfort from him.
God's goodness is displayed in both giving and forgiving.
Whatever others may do, we should keep calling upon the Lord and commit our cause to him. We will not seek him in vain.

div.title: Asking to know God's way and receive his help (verses 8–17)
div.p: Our God alone possesses unlimited power and infinite love.
Christ is the Way and the Truth.
The believing soul wants to be taught God's truth and his ways, in order to walk in them, even more than it wants relief from earthly trouble.
Those who refuse to set the Lord before them pursue the souls of believers.
Yet the Lord's compassion, mercy and truth provide refuge and consolation.
People whose parents served the Lord may also mention that heritage when asking him to hear and help them.
As we consider David's experience and our own, we must not forget the One who was rich but became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich through his poverty.

row.cell: It is filled with the Divine blessing.

div.title: Christ, the church's foundation (verses 1–3)
div.p: Christ himself is the foundation that God has laid for his church.
Holiness gives the church strength and stability.
We should not be ashamed of Christ's church, even when its outward condition is humble, or of the people who belong to it.
God has spoken glorious things about it.
No one can lay another foundation than Jesus Christ.

The glorious promises about Zion, spoken by the Spirit, point toward Christ and his work, the different offices he fulfills, the gospel church and its privileges and members, and finally heaven with its perfect happiness and glory.

div.title: The blessing of belonging to Zion (verses 4–7)
div.p: Christ's church is more glorious and excellent than any earthly nation.
The records of heaven include even the humblest person who has been born again.
When God judges everyone according to their works, he will take account of those who enjoyed the privileges of his sanctuary.
Much is required of those to whom much has been given.
Those who belong to Zion should remember their privileges and live consistently with their profession of faith.
The songs of Zion will be sung with joy and triumph.
Worldly-minded people look for happiness in wealth and pleasure.
But a soul transformed by grace finds its springs of joy in God's word and prayer.
Every grace and comfort flows from Christ through his appointed ordinances to believers' souls.

row.cell: The psalmist pours out his soul to God in lamentation.
He wrestles by faith, in his prayer to God for comfort.

div.title: A believer's deeply troubled soul (verses 1–9)
div.p: The psalm's opening words are its only words of comfort and support.
Even godly people can suffer terribly. They may think very dark thoughts about their suffering and reach bleak conclusions about their future, because of melancholy and weakened faith.
The psalmist's greatest distress was his sense of God's displeasure.
Even those whom God loves may sometimes imagine themselves to be objects of his wrath.
No outward affliction is as painful as that fear.
The psalmist was probably describing his own troubles, but Henry also directs us to Christ.
We look to Jesus, wounded and bruised for our sins.
The divine wrath poured into his cup brought its greatest bitterness and weighed him down into darkness and the depths.

div.title: Continuing in prayer while comfort is delayed (verses 10–18)
div.p: Departed souls may declare God's faithfulness, justice and lovingkindness.
But dead bodies can neither enjoy his favors with comfort nor praise him in response.
The psalmist resolved to continue praying, especially because deliverance had not come quickly.
When our prayers are not answered soon, we must not abandon them.
The more severe our troubles, the more earnest and serious our prayers should be.
Nothing grieves God's child more than losing the sense of his presence; nothing is more frightening than the thought of being cast away from him.
When the sun is covered by clouds, the earth grows dark. If the sun left the earth entirely, it would become a dungeon.
Likewise, even people destined to experience God's favor may for a time feel his terrors.
The psalmist suffered that fear deeply.
When Providence or death separates us from friends, we rightly consider that loss an affliction.
This was the desperate condition of a godly person.
Yet Henry sees the psalm's appeals as particularly fitting to Jesus Christ.
We should not imagine that Jesus suffered for us only in Gethsemane and on Calvary.
His whole earthly life involved work and sorrow.
He endured unparalleled affliction from his youth onward and was prepared throughout life for the death he would eventually taste.
No other person could share the redemptive sufferings through which others would be saved.
When the hour came, everyone deserted him and fled.
Blessed Jesus, we often forsake you. Do not forsake us; do not take your Holy Spirit from us.

row.cell: God's mercy and truth, and his covenant.
The glory and perfection of God.
The happiness of those in communion with him.
God's covenant with David, as a type of Christ.
A calamitous state lamented, Prayer for redress.

div.title: God's unbreakable covenant (verses 1–4)
div.p: Our expectations may disappoint us, but God's promises remain established in heaven.
They belong to his eternal purposes and cannot be defeated by opponents on earth or in hell.
Trust in God's boundless mercy and everlasting truth can comfort us even through our deepest trials.

div.title: God's majesty, power and righteousness (verses 5–14)
div.p: The more we learn of God's works, the more reason we have to admire them.
True praise confesses that no one is like him.
Therefore our worship should be marked by reverence.
How little reverence is sometimes present in our congregations! We have reason to humble ourselves for that neglect.
The almighty power that struck Egypt will also defeat the church's enemies.
Those who trust God's mercy may rejoice in his name.
Mercy and truth direct all God's works. From his eternal counsel to the eternal results of his actions, everything rests upon justice and righteous judgment.

div.title: The joy of knowing God (verses 15–18)
div.p: Happy are those who truly know the joyful message of the gospel: they obey it, experience its power within their hearts and show its fruit in their lives.
Believers possess nothing in themselves, yet have everything in Christ Jesus, so they may rejoice in his name.
May the Lord enable us to do so.
Joy in the Lord strengthens his people.
Unbelief, by contrast, weakens our courage and discourages others. Though it can disguise itself as humility, it is actually a form of pride.
Christ is the Holy One of Israel. In him God's people are more blessed than through any other gift.

div.title: God's covenant with David points to Christ (verses 19–37)
div.p: The Lord anointed David with holy oil.
The anointing represented the grace and gifts David received, but it also pointed forward to Christ, the King, Priest and Prophet, who received the Holy Spirit without measure.
David was persecuted after being anointed, but his enemies were unable finally to overcome him.
Even this was only a faint picture of the Redeemer's suffering, rescue, glory and authority.
Only in Christ are the promises fully fulfilled.
He is the mighty God, the appointed Redeemer who alone can finish the work of our salvation.
We should seek assurance of our part in those blessings through the Holy Spirit's witness in our hearts.
David's descendants were corrected for their sins, and so are God's people.
But their correction is a rod, not a sword: it is intended to correct, not to destroy.
It rests in the hands of a wise and gracious Father who knows when discipline is necessary and what is best.
As the sun and moon remain in the heavens even when their appearance changes, God's covenant of grace in Christ remains secure despite changes in how his people experience it.

div.title: Lament, the cross, and continuing hope (verses 38–52)
div.p: At times God's providential dealings are difficult to reconcile with his promises.
Yet we know his works always fulfill his word.
When Christ himself hung upon the cross, it seemed as though God had rejected his Anointed One.
But the eternal covenant was not broken.
The honor of David's royal family faded. Crowns and thrones are easily brought into the dust.
Yet an unfading crown of glory awaits Christ's spiritual descendants.
Sin has brought devastation to many households, even distinguished families where true faith was once found.
Still, the Lord's unchanging truth and faithfulness reassure us that he will not finally reject the people he has chosen and brought into covenant with himself.
People mocked the faithful for serving God.
Likewise, the scoffers of the last days mock the Messiah's promised return (2 Peter 3:3–4).
God's dealings with David's household help us understand his dealings with believers and the church.
Their suffering may be terrible, but God will not finally abandon them.
Those who merely deceive themselves may misuse this promise, while other believers bring darkness and trouble upon themselves by careless living.
Yet true believers may rely on God's faithfulness as they perform their duties and bear the cross.
The psalm ends in praise despite its grief.
Those who thank God for his past actions may also thank him for what he will yet do.
The Lord will continue showing mercy to those who continue praising him.

row.cell: The eternity of God, the frailty of man.

div.title: The eternal God and our brief lives (verses 1–6)
div.p: Henry supposes this psalm concerns the judgment pronounced upon Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 14).
God's favor and protection are the only lasting refuge and comfort for our souls in this troubled world.
Christ Jesus is the dwelling place and refuge to whom we may always turn.
Our lives are passing away, and every earthly comfort is temporary.
But God lives forever, and believers discover his faithfulness.
When sickness or suffering brings us close to death, God calls us to turn back to him through repentance and a renewed life.
A thousand years count for nothing beside his eternity.
There is some relationship between one minute and a million years, but no comparable measure between time and eternity.
The events of a thousand years, whether past or future, are more fully present to the eternal mind of God than yesterday's events are to ours.
At the resurrection, body and soul will be reunited.
Time slips past almost unnoticed, as when people sleep.
Life resembles floodwater that passes quickly.
We flourish briefly like grass.
Old age may cause us to wither gradually, or illness and disaster may cut us down suddenly.

div.title: Receiving God's discipline with reverence (verses 7–11)
div.p: The trials of God's people often arise from his fatherly love.
But the judgments of sinners—and believers' chastisements for particular sins—must also be recognized as signs of his displeasure toward wrongdoing.
God knows every secret sin. No one succeeds in hiding transgression from him.
Our years cannot be recalled any more than words already spoken.
Life is marked by toil and trouble, and it may be cut short in the years we expected to enjoy.
We should therefore stand in awe before God.
Fallen angels know his anger.
Sinners undergoing final judgment know it.
Yet who among us can fully describe its power?
Few consider it seriously enough.
Those who mock sin or take Christ lightly do not understand divine judgment.
Who can endure that consuming fire?

div.title: Asking for wisdom and enduring mercy (verses 12–17)
div.p: To gain true wisdom, we must ask God to teach us through the Holy Spirit.
We need his instruction and the comfort and joy that accompany renewed assurance of his favor.
We appeal to mercy, not to any merit of our own.
God's favor is a fountain of lasting joy and can more than compensate for past suffering.
May grace within us produce good works, and may divine comfort bring gladness to our hearts and faces.
We ask God to establish the work of our hands—and, in order for that work to stand, to establish us in it.
Do not waste these brief precious days pursuing fantasies that leave us spiritually poor.
Seek instead forgiveness of sins and the heavenly inheritance.
Pray that the Holy Spirit will convert our hearts and that the beauty of holiness will be visible in our behavior.

row.cell: The safety of those who have God for their refuge.

div.title: God is the believer's refuge (verses 1–8)
div.p: Those who choose God as their protector through faith will find in him everything they need or can rightly desire.
People who have experienced that comfort want others to find refuge in him too.
God's grace preserves spiritual life from Satan's temptations, pictured as the traps of a birdcatcher, and from the contagion of sin, pictured as a deadly disease.
Great security is promised to believers even when they are surrounded by danger.
Wisdom prevents groundless fear; faith keeps us from being overwhelmed by justified fear.
Whatever happens, our heavenly Father's will is fulfilled. We need not be ruled by terror.
God's people will see both his promises fulfilled and his warnings carried out.
Therefore sinners should approach his mercy seat through the Redeemer's name and encourage others to trust him.

div.title: God's care in trouble and at life's end (verses 9–16)
div.p: No event can ultimately harm a believer.
Trouble and suffering may still come.
They can be painful rather than pleasant for the present, but God will make them work for the believer's good.
Those who truly know God will love him and continually call upon him in prayer.
His promise is to deliver the believer in his appointed time and, meanwhile, to be with that believer in trouble.
The Lord will govern their earthly concerns and preserve their lives as long as remaining here is truly good for them.
They look to Jesus for encouragement.
The believer will live long enough to complete the work assigned by God and become ready for heaven.
Why would anyone want an additional day after God had no further work to do in them or through them?
Someone may die young yet have a satisfying life.
A wicked person, by contrast, may live for many years without ever being satisfied.
At last the believer's struggle ends.
Then sin, suffering and temptation are gone forever.

row.cell: Praise is the business of the sabbath.
The wicked shall perish, but God's people shall be exalted.

div.title: Thanksgiving on the Sabbath and every day (verses 1–6)
div.p: It is a privilege to praise the Lord and hope that he will accept our worship morning and evening.
This is not only for the Sabbath, but for every day; not only in public gatherings, but also alone and with our families.
Each morning, thank him for the mercies of the night.
Each evening, thank him for the mercies of the day.
When going out or coming home, bless his name.
His work of Providence toward us, his work of grace within us, and above all his great work of redemption give us reason for joy.
Many people neither know nor care about his purposes.
Those who have learned to appreciate them through grace have even greater reason for gratitude.
If the ancient believers rejoiced in distant glimpses of the promised Deliverer, how much more should we love and praise him!

div.title: Brief prosperity and lasting fruitfulness (verses 7–15)
div.p: God sometimes allows wicked people to prosper as a judgment against them.
Their flourishing lasts only briefly.
Let us therefore seek the salvation and grace of the gospel, so that the Holy Spirit continually anoints us and we may see and share in the Redeemer's glory.
Christ's grace, communicated through his word and Spirit, supplies everything that keeps believers spiritually alive and fruitful.
Ordinary trees cease bearing fruit as they grow old.
But in God's trees, spiritual strength need not fade as bodily strength diminishes.
The final days of faithful people may be their best, and their last work their finest.
Perseverance is reliable evidence of sincerity.
May every Sabbath, as we contemplate God's faithfulness, find us resting more firmly upon the Lord our righteousness.

p.hi: The majesty, power, and holiness of Christ's kingdom.

div.title: The majesty and holiness of Christ's kingdom
div.p: God could have revealed only his justice, holiness and fearful power in dealing with fallen humanity.
Instead, he has chosen to reveal the riches of his mercy and the power of his renewing grace.
In this great work the Father has given all authority to his Son, the Lord from heaven, who has made atonement for our sins.
Christ is able not only to pardon, but also to deliver and protect everyone who trusts in him.
He has given his word, and all God's people may rely upon it.
Everything foretold about the Messiah's kingdom will be fulfilled at the appointed time.
His people ought to live in strict holiness.
The church is God's own house, set apart from sin and devoted to his service.
Where purity is found, peace will follow.
Let each person examine carefully whether this kingdom has been established within the heart.

row.cell: The danger and folly of persecutors.
Comfort and peace to the persecuted.

div.title: Entrusting injustice to the righteous Judge (verses 1–11)
div.p: We may appeal to God with confidence because he is the almighty Judge before whom everyone must answer.
Those treated unjustly can be encouraged to endure the wrong without seeking private retaliation, entrusting their cause to the One who judges righteously.
Henry understands these prayers as prophetic warnings to violent people.
A day of reckoning will come for all the arrogant and cruel words ungodly people have spoken against God, his truth, his ways and his servants.
It is astonishing how many rational people live, think, speak, hear and act freely while behaving as though the Lord will never call them to account for misusing his gifts.
Every form of knowledge comes from him, so he certainly knows every human thought.
The inclinations of fallen hearts are continually evil.
Even thoughts that are good in themselves may be wandering and unsettled; this too can be called vanity.
We must therefore watch our thoughts carefully.
God notices them all.

p.hi: Our thoughts are words before him.

div.title: The comfort of divine correction and care (verses 12–23)
div.p: Blessed is the person whom God disciplines and teaches his truth through Scripture and the Holy Spirit.
Such a person can recognize mercy even within suffering.
Rest remains for God's people after their days of trouble, which will not continue forever.
The same Lord who sends affliction will also send relief.
When the psalmist's earthly friends failed him, he found help only in God.
We depend not only upon God's power, but also upon his compassion, to keep us spiritually secure.
If he preserves us from falling into sin or abandoning duty, all glory belongs to him.
We should share that encouragement with others.
The psalmist had many anxious thoughts about his situation, what he should do and how things might end.
Indulging such anxious speculation and fear adds to our cares and weakens trust, making circumstances appear darker and more confused.
Even faithful believers can be troubled by distressing thoughts about God.
They should return to the great and precious promises of the gospel.
Worldly comforts offer little relief to a soul overwhelmed by melancholy.
But God's consolation gives a peace the world cannot provide or remove.
God is his people's refuge, where they may safely shelter.
He will also judge wickedness.
No one can be made more miserable than their own wrongdoing will make them when the Lord finally calls it to account.

row.cell: part. An exhortation to praise God.
A warning not to tempt Him.

div.title: Worshiping the Lord and our Shepherd (verses 1–7)
div.p: Whenever we come into God's presence, we should come with thanksgiving.
There is no shortage of reasons to praise him; the problem is often that our hearts are not ready to do so.
How great is the God to whom the whole earth and everything in it belong!
He directs and disposes of all creation.
The Lord Jesus is the great God whom we are called to praise.
Among his titles are the mighty God and God over all, blessed forever.
He has received authority in heaven and on earth.
He is our God, and we should praise him.
He is our Savior and the source of our true happiness.
The gospel church is his flock.
Christ is the great and good Shepherd who searched for his people when they were lost and brought them safely into his fold.
div.note: Editorially restored separate Concise exposition; absent from the pinned MHCC 0.1.1 compiled K body. See source provenance ledger.
div.title: Hearing Christ's voice today (verses 7–11)
div.p: Christ calls his people to listen to his voice.
If we call him Master and Lord, we ought to become willing and obedient servants.
Listen to his teaching, his commandments and the voice of his Spirit speaking through them.
Do not merely hear; pay attention and yield.
We must hear Christ's voice today.
Today's opportunity will not last forever.
We should use it while it remains.
To hear Christ truly is to believe in him.
Hardness of heart lies beneath all distrust of God.
Other people's sins should warn us not to repeat them.
Israel's murmuring in the wilderness was recorded for our instruction.
God is not subject to passions as we are, yet he is truly angry at sin and sinners.
What deserves such a punishment must certainly be evil.
His threats are as certain as his promises.
We must watch the evil tendencies of our hearts, which would draw us away from him.
There is a rest appointed for believers, an eternal refreshment that begins in this life and reaches its fullness in the life to come.
This is the rest God calls his own rest.

row.cell: A call to all people to praise God.

div.title: All the earth called to worship (verses 1–9)
div.p: When Christ completed his earthly work and was received into heavenly glory, the church began to sing a new song to him and bless his name.
His apostles and evangelists proclaimed his salvation among the nations and his marvelous works among all peoples.
The whole earth is summoned to worship the Lord.
We should worship him in the beauty of holiness, as the God who in Christ reconciles the world to himself.
The glorious truths spoken about Christ are both reasons for praising him and the very substance of our praise.

div.title: The coming reign and judgment of Christ (verses 10–13)
div.p: We should hope and pray for the time when Christ will reign in righteousness over every nation.
He will rule human hearts through the power of truth and the Spirit of righteousness.
His coming is drawing near.
The King and Judge stands at the door, but the appointed day has not yet arrived.
The Lord welcomes the praise of those who seek the advance of Christ's kingdom.
The sea can roar, but we do not know how trees show their rejoicing.
God searches hearts and knows the mind of the Spirit.
He understands even the halting words and broken language of the weakest.
Christ will come to judge the earth, justly punishing his enemies and fully accomplishing his greatest promises to his people.
What will that day mean for us?
Would we welcome his coming?
If we are not prepared, now is the time to get ready to meet God through forgiveness of our sins and renewal of our hearts in holiness.

row.cell: The Lord Jesus reigns in power that cannot be resisted.
His care of his people, and his provision for them.

div.title: The irresistible reign of Christ (verses 1–7)
div.p: Many have already found happiness in Christ, yet there is still room for others.
All have good reason to rejoice in his reign.
We cannot fully search the depth of his purposes, but righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne.
Christ's rule could be a cause of joy for everyone.
Yet for some it will become a cause of terror.
That is their own fault, because they reject him.
Even the most determined and fearless opposition will fail before the Lord.

p.hi: Jesus Christ will come and bring every form of idolatry to an end.

div.title: The Lord's care for those who love him (verses 8–12)
div.p: Faithful servants of God rightly rejoice when he is glorified.
Anything that honors him gives pleasure to his people.
God cares for their safety.
But the protection promised goes far beyond preserving their earthly lives.
The Lord will guard his people's souls from sin, apostasy and despair, even under their most severe trials.
He will rescue them from the power of the evil one and bring them safely into his heavenly kingdom.
Those who rejoice in Jesus Christ and his exaltation have sources of joy prepared for them.
People who sow in tears will reap with joy.
Joy is assured to those whose hearts are upright, while a hypocrite's joy lasts only briefly.
Sinners tremble at God's holiness, but his saints rejoice in it.
God hates sin, yet freely loves the repentant sinner who believes in Christ.
He will finally separate the person he loves from the sin he hates, sanctifying his people completely in body, soul and spirit.

div.title: Singing a new song for redemption (verses 1–3)
div.p: The song of redeeming love is new because it celebrates a mystery hidden from earlier ages and generations.
Those converted to Christ sing in a new way, very different from their former songs.
If God puts a new heart within us, he also gives us a new song.
We should sing it to his praise because of the marvelous works he has accomplished.
The Redeemer overcame every obstacle in the way of our salvation.
Neither the services nor the sufferings appointed for him discouraged him.
Praise the Lord for revealing his salvation and righteousness to the world, fulfilling the Old Testament prophecies and promises.
To accomplish this purpose, God sent his Son Jesus not only as a light to the nations, but also as the glory of Israel.
We should examine whether his holy arm has won the victory within our hearts, overcoming Satan, unbelief and sin.
If he has, we will exchange shallow songs of vanity for songs of gladness and thanksgiving.
Our lives will proclaim the Redeemer's praise.

div.title: The whole creation invited to rejoice (verses 4–9)
div.p: Everyone has reason to rejoice in the establishment of Christ's kingdom, because all may benefit from it.
The psalm seems to use figurative language to describe different orders of rational creatures throughout the universe rejoicing under the great Messiah's reign.
Christ's kingdom will bring blessing to the whole creation.
We await his second coming, when his glorious reign will be fully displayed.
Then heaven and earth will rejoice, and the joy of the redeemed will be complete.
But sin and its devastating consequences will not be entirely removed until the Lord comes to judge the world in righteousness.
Because we await these things, we should strive to be found by him at peace, spotless and blameless.

row.cell: The happy government God's people are under.

div.title: God's holy government (verses 1–5)
div.p: God governs the world through his providence and governs the church through his grace.
He governs both through his Son.
Earth's inhabitants have reason to tremble before him.
Yet the Redeemer still waits to show mercy.
Everyone who hears his warning should seek his grace.
The more we humble ourselves before the Lord, the more truly we exalt him.
We should worship with reverence because he is holy.

div.title: God's servants call upon him (verses 6–9)
div.p: Israel's happiness is illustrated by the leaders who served the people best.
They made God's word and law their standard in everything, knowing that without obedience they could not expect their prayers to be heard.
They repeatedly prevailed in prayer.
The Lord performed miracles in answer to their requests.
They interceded for the people and received gracious answers bringing peace.
But our Prophet and High Priest is of infinitely greater dignity than Moses, Aaron or Samuel.
He has received and declared the Father's will to us.
Therefore, do not exalt God with your lips alone.
Give him the throne in your heart.
As we worship before his mercy seat, remember always that he is holy.

p.hi: An exhortation to praise God, and rejoice in him.

div.title: The whole earth called to joyful worship
div.p: This psalm of praise can be read as a prophecy and also offered as a prayer for the day when people everywhere will know that the Lord is God.
They will become his worshipers and the sheep of his pasture.
We have strong encouragement to worship him cheerfully.
We had wandered like sheep.
If God has brought us back into his fold, we have abundant reason to bless his name.
The reasons and themes of our praise are of the highest importance.
Know God for who he is, and understand who he is to you.
Consider these truths and apply them to your life.
Doing so will make your worship more faithful and regular, more heartfelt and earnest.
The covenant of grace is revealed throughout the Scriptures of both Old and New Testaments.
Its rich promises strengthen the faith of even the weakest believer.
They provide a firm foundation for our praise and joy.
When we look at ourselves, our spirits may be heavy and full of sorrow.
But when we look toward God's goodness, mercy and the promises of his word, we find many reasons to give thanks and receive comfort.

p.hi: David's vow and profession of godliness.

div.title: A household and a kingdom governed under God
div.p: David declared how he intended to manage his household and his kingdom, resisting wrongdoing and encouraging godliness.
The psalm therefore applies to private families as well as rulers; it can be called the householder's psalm.
It teaches everyone who has authority, whether great or small, to use it so that evildoers are restrained and those who do right are encouraged.
David chose to sing of God's mercy and judgment.
The Lord's dealings with his people commonly include both.
He sets them beside each other, like rain and sunshine, for their good.
We should thank God appropriately for both his mercies and his judgments.
Family blessings and family afflictions alike should move us to maintain faithful worship at home.
Public responsibility never excuses neglect of one's household.
Indeed, those who hold public office have an even stronger duty to set a good example by governing their families well.
When someone has a home, that person should seek to have God dwelling there.
Those who walk faithfully, sincerely and uprightly may expect the Lord's presence.
David resolved first to refuse evil in his own conduct.
He also resolved not to surround himself with wicked servants or place ungodly people in positions of trust.
He did not want his household corrupted by their example.
A perverse and quarrelsome heart is destructive to fellowship, which is bound together by Christian love.
David would neither tolerate slanderers who delight in damaging their neighbors' reputations nor favor proud and deceitful people who lie or cheat without remorse.
Everyone should work diligently to reform their own heart and conduct, starting without delay.
Remember the coming day when the righteous King will remove evildoers from the heavenly Jerusalem.

row.cell: A sorrowful complaint of great afflictions.
Encouragement by expecting the performances of God's promises to his church.

div.title: Giving sorrow a voice in prayer (verses 1–11)
div.p: All of God's word helps guide our prayers.
But in passages like this, the Holy Spirit places words directly in our mouths.
This prayer has been provided for afflicted people; let them bring it before God.
Even faithful believers can be nearly overwhelmed by trouble.
It is both our duty and our good to pray.
A suffering soul finds relief in humbly telling the Lord about its pain.
Still, we must say, Blessed be the Lord's name, whether he gives or takes away.
The psalmist viewed himself as nearing death, his days passing like a shadow.

div.title: Trusting the Lord's promises for his church (verses 12–22)
div.p: We are dying creatures, but God lives forever and continues to protect his church.
We can be confident that he will not neglect it.
When we consider our sinfulness, spiritual darkness, lifelessness and the many failings of our prayers, we may fear they will not be received in heaven.
But the gospel assures us otherwise.
We have an Advocate with the Father, and we live under grace rather than law.
Redemption is the subject of the Christian church's praise.
Israel's earthly rescue and restoration pictured that far greater work.
Lord Jesus, look upon us and bring us into the glorious freedom of your children, so that we may bless and praise your name.

div.title: The unchanging God and our passing lives (verses 23–28)
div.p: Illness can quickly weaken our strength and cut short the years we expected to have.
We should prepare for that possibility.
We must acknowledge God's hand in this and recognize that even an early death can be consistent with his love.
People who have used their strength faithfully sometimes grow weak.
Others whom we believe the world can hardly spare have their lives shortened.
Amid every change and danger facing the church, it is comforting to remember that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever.
When our bodies die or friends are taken from us, we may remember that God is everlasting.
Do not miss the assurance of a happy end to the believer's trials.
Everything else changes, wears out and perishes, like clothing being folded away.
Jesus lives forever.
Because he lives, the future of his people is secure.
He has promised, Because I live, you also will live.

row.cell: An exhortation to bless God for his mercy.
And to the church and to all men.
For the constancy of his mercy.
For the government of the world.

div.title: Bless the Lord for forgiveness and healing (verses 1–5)
div.p: When God forgives sin, he removes the obstacle that kept good things from us and restores us to his favor.
Think how much our sins have provoked him—yet they are pardoned.
So many provocations, yet all forgiven!
As we continue to sin and repent, God continues to forgive.
Because of Adam's fall, our bodies experience weakness and disease, and our souls suffer their own infirmities.
Christ alone forgives all our sins and heals all our infirmities.
The person who has experienced healing from the disease of sin has good reason to be assured of forgiveness.
When God's Spirit renews his people's weakened faith, granting grace, comfort, fresh life and joy as a pledge of eternal life, their strength seems restored like the vigor of youth (Job 33:25).

div.title: The compassion of our heavenly Father (verses 6–14)
div.p: God is good to all, but he has shown particular favor to Israel through revealing himself and his grace.
His ways include the commandments he calls us to obey, along with his promises and purposes.
He has always been full of compassion.
How unlike God are those who seize every excuse to rebuke someone and never know when to stop!
What would become of us if God treated us that way?
Scripture speaks constantly of his mercy, and we have all experienced it.
A father has compassion on his children in many situations.
When they lack understanding, he teaches.
When they are stubborn, he bears patiently.
When they are sick, he comforts.
When they fall, he helps them rise.
When they do wrong and submit, he forgives.
When they are wronged, he sets things right.
This is how the Lord takes pity on those who fear him.
He remembers how frail our bodies are and how foolish our souls can be.
He knows how little we can accomplish and how little we can endure.
His compassion takes account of all these limitations.

div.title: God's faithful mercy outlasts life (verses 15–18)
div.p: Human life is brief and uncertain.
A garden flower may last longer because its wall and gardener shelter it.
But a flower growing in an open field is exposed not only to its own decay, but also to cold weather and animals that may cut or trample it.
That is our condition.
God knows our frailty and has compassion on us.
We should remember it ourselves.
His mercy is better than life, because it will last longer than life.
His righteousness and his faithful promises remain blessings to children and grandchildren who follow their faithful ancestors in godliness.

div.title: The Lord reigns over everything (verses 19–22)
div.p: The One who made everything also rules everything, accomplishing both through his powerful word.
He directs people and events toward his glory.
Holy angels continually praise him.
Let all his works praise him.
Unceasingly delighting in God would have been natural to us if humanity had not fallen.
Through new birth, such delight begins to return.
In heaven it will be perfect forever.
We cannot be completely happy until we find unwearied joy in perfectly obeying God's will.
Let every redeemed heart say, Bless the Lord, O my soul!

row.cell: God's majesty in the heavens, The creation of the sea, and the dry land.
The regular course of day and night, and God's sovereign power over all the creatures.
A resolution to continue praising God.

div.title: The glory of the Creator (verses 1–9)
div.p: Everything we see calls us to praise and bless the Lord, who is great.
His eternal power and divine nature are evident in what he has made.
God is light, and there is no darkness in him.
The Lord Jesus, the beloved Son, is the Light of the world.

div.title: God's provision for every creature (verses 10–18)
div.p: As we consider the provision made for every living creature, we should notice how their existence offers natural praise to God.
Yet human beings, so forgetful and ungrateful, enjoy the largest share of their Creator's kindness.
Do not overlook the spiritual blessings pictured by these provisions: the fruitfulness of the church through grace, the bread of eternal life, the cup of salvation, and the oil of gladness.
If God provides for creatures of lesser strength and understanding, surely he will remain a refuge to his people.

div.title: Day, night, work, resurrection and Providence (verses 19–30)
div.p: Praise God for the continuing pattern of day and night.
People who wait for darkness in order to commit wicked acts resemble wild animals that emerge at night, keeping company with the fruitless works of darkness.
God hears the needs expressed by creatures according to their nature, including ravenous beasts.
How much more will he graciously understand the language of his own people, even weak, broken groanings that cannot be put into words?
Each day's work should be performed during the time given for it.
We should take up our responsibilities each morning and continue until evening.
Rest will come when night arrives, when no one can work.
The psalmist marvels at God's creation.
Human art often reveals roughness when examined closely.
But God's natural works appear even more detailed and orderly the closer we look.
Everything is made in wisdom, answering the purpose for which it was created.
Each spring suggests the resurrection, when new life seems to rise out of the ruin of the old world.
But unlike the other creatures described, human beings alone live beyond bodily death.
When God takes away breath, the soul enters another condition, and the body will rise again either to glory or misery.
May the Lord send his Spirit to make our souls new in holiness.

div.title: Creation's fading glory and the greater work of redemption (verses 31–35)
div.p: Human glory fades, while God's glory endures forever.
Creatures change, but their Creator never changes.
If contemplating the beauty of creation brings such delight to the soul, how much more wonderful is the work of redemption to an enlightened mind!
Only through that work can a sinner find sound grounds for confidence and joy in God.
He sustains everything with pleasure, governs everything and rejoices in his works.
May our souls, transformed by grace, keep reflecting upon him and praising his name.

row.cell: A solemn call to praise and serve the Lord.
Their deliverance from Egypt, and their settlement in Canaan.

div.title: Seeking the Lord's strength and favor (verses 1–7)
div.p: This psalm calls us to stir ourselves up to praise God.
Seek his strength—meaning his grace, and the power of the Holy Spirit to accomplish in us the good we cannot do by ourselves.
That strength comes from him, and we must keep asking for it.
Seek his favor for eternity.
Continue seeking him throughout this life.
God will not only be found by those who seek him; he rewards those who diligently seek him.

div.title: God's covenant care and the story of Joseph (verses 8–23)
div.p: Remember the Redeemer's marvelous works, his wonders and the judgments he has spoken.
True believers may be few and live as strangers and pilgrims on earth.
Yet through God's covenant they have been promised an inheritance far greater than Canaan.
If the Holy Spirit has anointed them, nothing can ultimately harm them.
Even afflictions can be among their mercies.
They test faith and love, humble pride, loosen the hold of the world and make prayer more earnest.
Bread is called the staff of life because it supports the body.
When that support is taken away, the body weakens.
Likewise, God's word sustains the soul and is the bread of spiritual life.
Among the worst judgments is a famine of hearing the Lord's word.
Such a famine was severe in all lands when Christ appeared in the flesh.
Joseph's story pictures Christ's coming and its blessings.
At the appointed time, Christ was exalted as Mediator, holding all the treasures of grace and salvation.
Perishing sinners come to him and receive help.

div.title: Israel's deliverance as a picture of salvation (verses 24–45)
div.p: Believers often grow most in their souls when they carry the cross.
Likewise, the church may grow in true holiness and increase in number during persecution.
Yet God raises up instruments of deliverance, and persecutors may receive judgment.
See how he provided for Israel in the wilderness.
Every blessing given to Israel as a nation pictured spiritual blessings in Christ Jesus.
Christ has redeemed us by his blood, restored our souls toward holiness and freed us from Satan's bondage.
He guides and guards his people throughout their journey.
He feeds them with the bread of heaven and gives them the water of life from the Rock of salvation.
He will bring them safely to heaven.
He redeems them from iniquity and purifies them as his own people, eager to do good works.

div.title: The joy of God's people (verses 1–5)
div.p: Neither our sins nor our sufferings should keep us from giving God glory and praise.
The less deserving we are, the more astonishing his kindness becomes.
Those who trust in the Redeemer's righteousness should try to follow his example, praising him by both word and action.
God's people have good reason for joy.
They have no need to envy the pleasures or pride of people who live only for this world.

div.title: Israel's sins and God's faithfulness (verses 6–12)
div.p: The psalm now turns to confession.
We must acknowledge that the Lord has acted rightly, while we have acted wickedly.
Though correction may be fully deserved, there is still hope that God will not abandon his people completely.
Even when suffering, they admit their guilt before him.
We begin to distrust the Lord when we forget his earlier mercies.
If God did not save us for his own name's sake, demonstrating his power and grace, all of us would perish.

div.title: Repeated rebellion and the hunger of the soul (verses 13–33)
div.p: Those who refuse to wait for God's counsel may justly be left to follow their own desires and schemes.
Excessive desire can become sinful even when the thing desired is lawful.
God showed his displeasure by filling them with uneasiness of mind, terror of conscience and painful self-reproach.
Some people eat lavishly every day and possess strong, healthy bodies, yet their souls are wasting away.
They have no love for God, no thankfulness and no appetite for the Bread of life.
Feeding the body while starving the soul is dreadful folly.
Even faithful believers have abundant reason to say that only the Lord's mercy has kept them from destruction.
We have often set up idols within our hearts, clinging to forbidden things.
Had One greater than Moses not stood to turn away the Lord's anger, we would have been destroyed.
God dealt severely even with Moses for rash words.
What, then, do people deserve when they frequently speak proudly and wickedly?
The Lord may justly take away relatives and others whose relationships have blessed us when we are irritable toward them, provoke them and grieve them.

div.title: Israel's failures in Canaan and the final appeal (verses 34–48)
div.p: Israel's conduct in Canaan and the Lord's dealings with the people teach that the path of sin runs downhill.
Neglecting a commanded duty opens the door to committing further sins.
The Israelites failed to drive out the pagan peoples and then learned their practices.
One sin led to many others and brought divine judgment.
In part, their sin became its own punishment.
Those who led sinners into evil may later become instruments of their ruin.
Satan first tempts and then torments.
Yet eventually God showed pity to his people for the sake of his covenant.
His unchanging compassion and faithful love led him to replace judgment with mercy.
Henry explains that when Scripture speaks of God's repenting, it does not mean a change in his merciful nature, but a change in how he deals with the people.
The condition of the visible church should sober us.
If Christian nations persist in grave sin, we should not be surprised when God humbles them.
Without widespread and deep repentance, they can expect further trouble.
The psalm closes with a prayer that the Lord will complete his people's deliverance and praise for what he has already begun to do.
May the entire world soon answer Amen.

row.cell: God's providential care of the children of men in distresses, in banishment, and dispersion.
God's hand is to be seen by his own people.

div.title: God's help for travelers and exiles (verses 1–9)
div.p: These verses refer to Israel's deliverance from Egypt and perhaps also the return from Babylon, though the latter connection is uncertain.
They also describe the dangers experienced by travelers crossing the deserts of those lands.
It is difficult to imagine their suffering while wandering across featureless sand under the burning sun.
These travelers picture people whom the Lord has redeemed from Satan's bondage.
Believers pass through a world that can resemble a dangerous, desolate wilderness, sometimes fainting under trials, fears and temptations.
Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for God himself and for fellowship with him will be satisfied by the goodness of his house, now in grace and ultimately in glory.

div.title: God's mercy to prisoners (verses 10–16)
div.p: The prisoners described here are isolated and sorrowful.
Henry notes the severe treatment inflicted in eastern prisons.
Suffering should lead us toward humility.
If our hearts remain proud and unbroken through hardship, we lose an important benefit of the trial.
Earthly captivity pictures a sinner's rescue from a far worse imprisonment.
Once awakened to sin, a person recognizes guilt and misery.
After attempting in vain to secure freedom through personal effort, the sinner discovers that help can come only through God's mercy and grace.
The Lord forgives and breaks the power of sin and Satan, while the Holy Spirit brings sanctification and comfort.

div.title: Healing bodily and spiritual illness (verses 17–22)
div.p: Had humanity never sinned, sickness would not have entered the world.
Sinners behave foolishly when they damage their bodies through excess and endanger their lives by indulging uncontrolled appetites.
Such conduct is its own folly.
Illness weakens the body, but recovery comes through God's power and mercy.
We should thank him for every restoration of health.
Christ's miraculous healings also pictured his power to heal the diseases of the soul.
The Spirit of grace accomplishes such spiritual healing.
God sends his word to convict, convert and make people holy.
Even in ordinary bodily recovery, Providence operates at God's command.
Likewise, his word and Spirit restore the soul to spiritual health and holiness.

div.title: Deliverance from danger at sea (verses 23–32)
div.p: People who travel and work on the sea have special reason to reflect upon God's greatness.
Sailors witness terrible storms and extraordinary rescues that others can barely imagine.
How appropriate it is to pray during such danger!
Storms at sea also picture the terrors of a troubled conscience and the painful experiences some Christians endure.
When they cry to the Lord, he can turn their storm into calm and bring their trials to an end with joy.

div.title: Recognizing God's providence in changing fortunes (verses 33–43)
div.p: Human circumstances change in surprising ways.
The desolate condition of Judea and other lands offered illustrations to Henry's readers.
People may grow from humble beginnings to prosperity, yet fall from that success into nothing just as quickly.
Worldly riches are uncertain.
Those who possess them may suddenly lose them.
God has many ways of making people poor.
The righteous have reason to rejoice.
Such reversals will eventually silence those who deny divine Providence.
Sinners who see God justly taking away blessings they abused will have no valid defense.
We greatly benefit from recognizing God's goodness and allowing it to affect our hearts.
Wisdom calls us to perform our duty and leave our comfort to him.
A genuinely wise person will treasure this psalm and learn from it both human weakness and misery and God's power and lovingkindness—shown not because we deserve them but because he is merciful.

p.hi: No independent topical heading is supplied in the CCEL witness.

div.title: Praise, faith and confidence in God's help
div.p: We can help our worship by selecting passages from different psalms, as this psalm does from Psalms 57 and 60.
Such passages can strengthen devotion and awaken gratitude.
When the heart is steadfast in faith and love, the tongue brings honor to its owner by speaking and singing God's praise.
Every gift received from the Lord benefits and honors the person who receives it when it is used in God's service and for his glory.
Believers can pray with confident faith and hope for every blessing of salvation.
These blessings are guaranteed by God's faithful covenant and promise.
They may therefore expect God's help in every trouble and victory in every conflict.
Whatever we accomplish or obtain, God must receive all the glory.
Lord, visit all our souls with this salvation and with the favor you show your chosen people.

div.title: Turning to God when enemies accuse us (verses 1–5)
div.p: It is an inexpressible comfort to believers that God is for them, whatever enemies oppose them.
They may appeal to him with confidence because he willingly cares for their cause.
David's enemies ridiculed his devotion, but they could not make him abandon it.

div.title: A prophetic warning of judgment (verses 6–20)
div.p: Henry understands these denunciations as words that the Lord Jesus may speak in his role as Judge, announcing the sentence awaiting certain enemies in order to warn others.
When people reject Christ's salvation, even their prayers may become sinful.
What leads some people to shameful deaths and causes others' families and property to collapse?
What brings disgrace, poverty, misery and ruin upon their descendants, making them and their families despised and hateful to others?
Sin—that destructive and poisonous evil—is the source of such devastation.
Consider the effect of the final sentence “Go, you cursed” upon the bodies and souls of the unrepentant.
What fear, pain, horror, anguish and despair it brings!
Sinners, take these warnings seriously: tremble and repent.

div.title: Praying for mercy and trusting the risen Advocate (verses 21–31)
div.p: The psalmist appealed to God's comfort in great humility.
He was distressed in mind.
His body had grown thin and weak.
Yet it is better to have a weak body with a spiritually healthy soul than to feast the body while starving the soul.
He was mocked and insulted by his enemies.
But if God blesses us, we need not fear human curses.
People cannot place a curse upon those whom God has chosen to bless.
The psalmist pleaded for God's glory and the honor of his name.
Save me, Lord—not because I deserve it, for I claim no merit—but because of your mercy.
He ended with the joyful confidence of faith, convinced his present struggle would end in victory.
Everyone who suffers according to God's will should commit their souls to his care.
Jesus, unjustly put to death and now risen, is the Advocate and Intercessor of his people.
He is always ready to appear on their behalf against a corrupt world and the great accuser.

p.hi: Christ's kingdom.

div.title: The eternal King and Priest
div.p: This psalm speaks glorious truths concerning Jesus Christ.
He is not only greater than all the rulers of the earth.
He already existed in glory as the eternal Son of God.
Christ sits at God's right hand.
Sitting is a posture of rest after labor and suffering, and one from which the King exercises judgment and authority.
It also signifies permanence: he reigns forever.
All his enemies are already in chains, though they have not yet been made his footstool.
His kingdom has been established and will continue despite every power of darkness.
Christ's people are willing people.
The Holy Spirit's power makes them willing to serve him.
They worship him clothed with the beauty of holiness, which belongs to his house forever.
Many will dedicate themselves to him.
We should consecrate even the earliest days of our youth to the Lord Jesus, like fresh dew appearing at dawn.
Christ is not only King but also Priest.
He serves on God's behalf toward us and pleads our cause before the Father.
He is therefore the Mediator between God and humanity.
His priesthood follows the order of Melchizedek, earlier than Aaron's priesthood and superior to it in several ways.
It represents the priesthood of Christ more fully.
His place at God's right hand brings joy to his people and terror to his enemies.
Ultimately his victory will bring the final overthrow of those who oppose him.
The Redeemer saves and comforts his friends.
He was humbled, drinking from the stream along his path.
Henry understands this as a possible picture of the curse of the law and the wrath associated with our redemption, which Christ endured.
He drank the waters of suffering on the road toward his throne of glory.
He was humbled, but now he is exalted.
What about us?
Has Christ's gospel become God's saving power in our lives?
Does he reign in our hearts?
Are we willing subjects?
We once did not recognize our need for his salvation and resisted his rule.
Are we now willing to abandon every sin, turn away from an evil and deceptive world, and rest only upon his merit and mercy?
Do we welcome him as Prophet, Priest and King, and desire holiness?
Those transformed in this way receive the blessings of his sacrifice, intercession and grace.

p.hi: The Lord is to be praised for his works.

div.title: Praise for God's works and covenant faithfulness
div.p: The psalmist resolved to praise God himself.
Our personal example should agree with what we encourage other people to do.
God's works are the proper subject of praise, including his providence toward the world, his church and individual people.
Although the Lord's works are many, they can be spoken of as one work, because all the different events of Providence contribute to a single wise purpose.
When we examine his works humbly and diligently, we discover that they are just and holy.
Of all God's works, his forgiveness of sin is the most wonderful, and we should remember it for his glory.
God never forgets his covenant.
He has always remembered it and always will.
His works of Providence follow the truth of his promises and prophecies.
They are therefore true.
Because he has the right to govern the earth as he chooses, they are also righteous.
The same is true of his work of grace in human hearts.
Every divine command is sure.
All God's commandments were fulfilled by Christ, and they remain our standard of conduct in him.
The Lord redeemed his people from Egypt and delivered them repeatedly afterward.
These rescues pictured the greater redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ in the fullness of time.
In that redemption, everlasting righteousness shines together with boundless mercy.
No one is truly wise without the fear of the Lord.
That reverence leads to repentance, faith in Christ, vigilance and obedience.
Those who live this way possess real understanding, even if they are poor, lack formal learning or are despised by others.

p.hi: The blessedness of the righteous.

div.title: The blessing of trusting and fearing God
div.p: We should praise the Lord because there are people in the world who fear and serve him, and because they are happy through his grace alone.
Their fear is not the terror that love drives away.
It is the reverence that love produces: a desire not to offend the One they love.
This fear belongs together with trust.
When the Holy Spirit touches a heart, it turns quickly toward God, like a compass needle touched by a magnet.
It does so with loving reverence and awe.
God has stored up blessings for the faithful and their descendants.
He gives them genuine riches, together with as much earthly property as is truly beneficial to them.
Even during their darkest troubles, hope and peace can dawn within them, and timely help can turn grief into joy.
Their Lord teaches them to be compassionate, kind and fair in every relationship.
They use good judgment so that their generosity may do the greatest good.
Envy and slander may temporarily hide their true character, but they will be remembered with lasting honor.
They do not need to fear every alarming report.
Their hearts can become stable.
True believers seek to keep their thoughts fixed upon God, making their hearts calm.
He has promised both reasons for confidence and grace to exercise it.
Trusting him is the firmest foundation for the heart.
Human hearts cannot settle with complete satisfaction anywhere except in the truth of God.
Faith gives them a stable footing and patience to wait for the appointed outcome.
Compare this with the distress of the wicked.
They envy the happiness of God's people.
But their desires are entirely bound to worldly pleasure and the flesh.
When these perish, their joy perishes too.
The blessings of the gospel are spiritual and everlasting.
They belong to Christ's church through Christ its Head, who is the example of every righteous life and the giver of all grace.

p.hi: An exhortation to praise God.

div.title: Praise the God who raises the lowly
div.p: God receives praise from his own people.
They have special reason to praise him because they know him as his servants and experience so much of his kindness.
Speaking well of such a Master is a joyful and pleasant task.
His name ought to be praised everywhere, from east to west.
It should be praised throughout the world, though this is not yet the case.
One day all nations will come to worship him.
God is exalted above every blessing and praise we can offer.
We should ask with holy amazement: Who is like the Lord our God?
How astonishing that he stoops to observe the affairs of the earth!
How much more astonishing that the Son of God came from heaven to earth and took our human nature to seek and save the lost!
He loved guilty sinners so greatly that he became human to ransom their souls.
Sometimes the Lord displays his wisdom and power by choosing people whom nobody would have considered capable of important work—not even the people themselves.
He called fishermen to become fishers of people.
That is his customary way in the kingdom of grace.
He receives people who are naturally beggars and even traitors, makes them his friends and children, and gives them honor as kings and priests.
He counts them among the princes of his chosen people.
All our comforts come from him.
They can be especially welcome after a long delay, when we had given up expecting them.
Let us pray that countries still barren of gospel fruit will soon become fruitful and that many converts will join in praising the Lord.

p.hi: An exhortation to fear God.

div.title: God's presence in redemption and renewal
div.p: We should recognize God's power and goodness in delivering Israel.
