Those events point toward the far greater wonder of our redemption through Christ.
They should encourage us and others to trust God in the greatest difficulties.
When Christ comes to save his people, he releases them from sin and Satan's power.
He separates them from a godless world, forms them into his own people and becomes their King.
No sea or river Jordan is too wide or deep for the Lord.
When the appointed time comes, he can divide it and drive its waters back.
The same power established the Christian church in the world.
Satan and the powers of idolatry trembled before it.
But the most personal application concerns the Spirit's work within a heart.
What turns the current of a regenerated person's affections?
Why do sinful desires and corrupt habits retreat?
How are prejudices removed and an entire person made new?
It happens through the presence of God's Spirit.
At the Lord's presence even mountains and the whole earth may tremble, for creation has been placed under a curse through human sin.
God both protected and provided for Israel through miracles.
One was the stream of water flowing from a hard rock.
That rock pointed to Christ.
The Son of God, the Rock of Ages, gave himself in death to open a fountain that washes away sins and supplies believers with water of life and consolation.
No promised blessing is too great for them to expect from his love.
But sinners should fear their righteous and holy Judge.
Let us prepare now to meet God so we may stand before him with confidence when he comes.

row.cell: Glory to be ascribed to God.
by trusting in him and praising him.

div.title: Glory belongs to God alone (verses 1–8)
div.p: We must never appeal to our own merit in our prayers or praises.
Any good we accomplish comes from God's grace, and every good thing we possess is a gift of his free mercy.
He therefore deserves all the praise.
When we seek mercy and wrestle in prayer, we should look for encouragement in God alone.
Lord, act for us—not so that we may take the credit or comfort for ourselves, but so that your mercy and faithfulness will receive the glory.
The gods of the nations are lifeless things, made by human hands.
A painter, a sculptor or a craftsman cannot give life to an image and therefore cannot give it sensation or knowledge.
The psalm shows the folly of those who worship such idols.

div.title: Trust, praise and the living God (verses 9–18)
div.p: Trusting lifeless images is foolish.
Trusting the living God is wise, because he is help and shield to everyone who relies on him.
True reverence for God can be joined to cheerful confidence in him.
Those who respect his word may trust it.
He has always proved faithful.
The greatest people need his blessing.
He will not deny his blessing to the humblest person who fears him.
God's blessing brings growth, especially spiritual growth.
We should praise the Lord for his wide generosity in giving the earth to human beings for their use.
After their souls are released from the burdens of their mortal bodies, faithful believers continue praising him.
But a dead body cannot praise God.
Death ends our opportunity to glorify him through work and struggle in this present world.
Other people have died, bringing their earthly service to an end.
We should therefore strive to do more for God while we still live.
We should also encourage others to praise him, even after we ourselves are gone.
Lord, you alone deserve our faith and love.
Help us praise you while living and as we die.
May your name be first and last upon our lips, and may its sweetness refresh our souls forever.

row.cell: The psalmist declares his love to the Lord.

div.title: Loving the God who saves (verses 1–9)
div.p: We have many reasons to love the Lord, but his kindness affects us especially deeply when he rescues us from terrible trouble.
When sinners become aware of their true condition and fear that God's righteous judgment will destroy them, they experience great sorrow and distress.
Let them call upon the Lord to save their souls.
They will find him gracious and faithful to his promises.
Neither a person's former ignorance nor guilt will prevent salvation when that person trusts the Lord.
We should describe God according to our experience of him.
Have we ever found him anything other than just and good?
Only his mercy prevents us from being consumed.
Let those who labor and carry heavy burdens come to him and receive rest for their souls.
If they wander from that rest, let them return quickly, remembering how generous he has been.
We should live with a continual sense of being in his presence.
It is a great mercy to be kept from being swallowed up by overwhelming sorrow.
It is also a mercy when God upholds our right hand so that temptation does not overpower and overthrow us.
When we enter the heavenly rest, deliverance from sin and sorrow will be complete.
We will see the Lord's glory and walk in his presence with a joy we cannot yet imagine.

div.title: Gratitude expressed in service and devotion (verses 10–19)
div.p: During trouble, it is often best to be quiet because pain may lead us to speak rashly.
Genuine faith may coexist with struggles of unbelief, but faith will eventually prevail.
When we humble ourselves for distrusting God's promises, we can experience his faithfulness.
What can a forgiven sinner, or anyone rescued from danger, offer in return for the Lord's goodness?
We cannot benefit him in any way.
Even our very best offering is unworthy of his acceptance.
Yet we should dedicate ourselves and all we possess to him.
The psalmist resolves to take the cup of salvation.
This includes the drink offering appointed by the law as a thankful response to God.
It also includes receiving the cup of affliction: bitter suffering can be sanctified to God's people and become a means of spiritual healing.
And it includes the cup of consolation: accepting God's comforts as gifts from his hand and recognizing his love in blessings enjoyed now as well as in the coming inheritance.
The psalmist chooses to be God's servant regardless of whom others serve.
People may become servants in two ways.
First, through birth: the psalmist was born in the Lord's household as the son of one of his servants.
Having godly parents is a great mercy.
Second, through redemption: God broke his bonds and rescued him.
Those loosened bonds made him more firmly devoted to his Redeemer.
Doing good is a sacrifice that pleases God, and it must accompany thanksgiving.
Why would we offer the Lord something that costs us nothing?
The psalmist resolved to fulfill his vows immediately.
He would do so publicly, not to boast, but to show that he was not ashamed of God's service and to invite others to join in.
Such are God's genuine saints, whose lives and deaths will bring him glory.

p.hi: All people called upon to praise God.

div.title: All nations invited to praise the Lord
div.p: This psalm solemnly calls every nation to praise the Lord and gives them reasons to do so.
We soon grow tired of doing good if we do not keep devout and loving affection for God alive within us.
The spiritual sacrifice of praise needs to be kindled and kept burning.
This is a gospel psalm.
The apostle Paul quotes it in Romans 15:11, showing that the gospel was intended to be preached among the nations and would be welcomed by them.
For many centuries, God was known and praised especially within Judah.
The nations outside Israel were not yet receiving this call in the same way.
But Christ's gospel has been commanded to be preached to all nations.
Through him, people who were once far away have been brought near.
We ourselves are among the people to whom the Holy Spirit speaks through this psalm, inviting us to join God's ancient people in praise.
Grace has therefore abounded toward multitudes of sinners who were heading toward destruction.
Let us receive God's gracious invitation and pray for the day when every nation on earth will proclaim his praise.
Bless the Lord for the unsearchable riches of gospel grace.

row.cell: It is good to trust in the Lord.
The coming of Christ in his kingdom.

div.title: Trusting God's mercy in every trial (verses 1–18)
div.p: The psalmist's account of his suffering is especially applicable to Jesus Christ.
Many hated Christ without cause.
The Lord also subjected him to severe suffering, bruising and grieving him so that through his wounds we might be healed.
At times God strengthens his people when he is not yet their delight.
They may receive spiritual support without the immediate pleasure of spiritual comfort.
Believers can find abundant reasons for praise whether they look back to the Lord's everlasting kindness and mercy or forward to his promised blessings.
Every answer to prayer reminds us that the Lord is on our side.
Therefore we need not be ruled by fear of what other people can do.
We must faithfully perform our duties toward everyone and trust God alone to accept and bless our service.
Seek to live so that you can declare God's works and encourage others to serve and trust him.
This confidence also characterized the triumphs of the Son of David, who knew the Lord's purpose would prosper in his hands.

div.title: Christ, the rejected stone who became the cornerstone (verses 19–29)
div.p: Even ancient believers who saw Christ's coming from a great distance had reason to praise God in anticipation.
The prophecy about the stone rejected by the builders (verses 22 and 23) may refer in part to David's promotion, but it points principally toward Christ.
First, his humiliation: he is the stone the builders rejected.
They attempted to continue their work without him, and their rejection brought their own ruin.
Those who reject Christ are themselves rejected by God.
Second, his exaltation: Christ became the chief cornerstone of the foundation.
He is also the final topstone that completes the building and therefore deserves preeminence in everything.
His name is Wonderful, and the redemption he accomplished is the greatest of God's marvelous works.
We should rejoice in the Lord's day, not only because he has appointed it, but because it celebrates Christ becoming the Head.
Sabbaths ought to be joyful days, giving us a foretaste of heaven.
Let this Savior be my Savior and Ruler.
May my soul prosper and be in health through the peace and righteousness of his reign.
May he give me victory over desires that fight against my soul and, through grace, bring my heart under his rule.
The duties he commands come with true light.
Our response to the privilege of redemption must include sacrifices of gratitude.
These are not bodies killed upon an altar, but ourselves as living sacrifices, bound to the altar in grateful dedication to God.
They also include spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise in which our hearts sincerely participate.
The psalmist praises the Lord and invites everyone nearby to give thanks for the good news of great joy: there is a Redeemer, Christ the Lord.
In him the covenant of grace is secure and everlasting.

div.title: Original authorial introduction
div.p: The chief purpose of this psalm is to honor God's law and show its greatness.
Henry identifies ten terms used here for divine revelation, each teaching us something about what the Lord expects of us and what we may expect from him.

1. His law is enacted by God, our Sovereign. 2. His way describes the rule of his Providence. 3. His testimonies are solemnly declared to the world. 4. His commandments are given with divine authority. 5. His precepts are binding rather than optional. 6. His word or saying declares God's mind. 7. His judgments proceed from infinite wisdom. 8. His righteousness is the standard of what is right. 9. His statutes remain continually binding. 10. His truth or faithfulness endures forever.
The original secondary witness presents this introduction before the first exposition, without assigning it to an invented verse section.

div.title: Wholehearted obedience through grace (verses 1–8)
div.p: This psalm can be read as the spiritual experience of a believer.
Our attitudes, desires and affections come from the Holy Spirit only to the extent that they agree with what the psalm expresses.
God's forgiving mercy in Christ is the only source of lasting happiness for a sinner.
The happiest people are those preserved most carefully from sin's pollution, who believe the Lord's testimony and rely on his promises.
A heart divided between God and the world is in a dangerous condition.
The saints do not claim to have no remaining sin. They know there are many things within them that hinder obedience.
Yet they do not willingly embrace the wickedness that would draw them entirely away from the Lord's paths.
The tempter would persuade people that obeying God's word is merely a personal choice.
But a godly person's desires and prayers agree with God's will and commands.
We cannot expect obedience in one duty to purchase permission for disobedience in others.
Such hypocrisy will be exposed: if its shame is not faced in this life, everlasting shame will be its portion.
The psalmist wanted to learn God's law and give him glory.
Believers know that if God abandons them to themselves, the tempter will be too strong.

div.title: God's word treasured in the heart (verses 9–16)
div.p: To the corruption inherited from Adam, all people have added their own actual sins.
Young people may ruin themselves by living without any standard or by choosing a false one.
Let them use Scripture as their rule of life.
Distrusting our own wisdom and strength and depending upon God show a sincere desire for holiness.
God's word is a treasure worth storing.
Its safest resting place is within the heart.
We then answer sin's demands with God's precepts, its attractions with his promises, and its threats with his warnings.
Ask the Lord to teach his statutes, so that sharing in his holiness we may also share in his blessedness.
Those nourished by the bread of life ought to feed others through their words.
God's commands lead us toward the unsearchable riches of Christ.
But meditation is not truly useful unless good thoughts produce good actions.
We should not merely consider God's statutes, but practice them gladly.
Test the sincerity of obedience by examining what motivates it, and test love for God by whether his appointed duties are performed cheerfully.

div.title: Strangers on earth, sustained by God's counsel (verses 17–24)
div.p: If God judged us with complete strictness, every one of us would perish.
Our lives should therefore be spent in his service.
We find true life through keeping his word.
To see the wonders of God's law and gospel, we must ask for understanding through his Spirit's light.
Believers know they are strangers on earth.
They fear losing their way or forfeiting comfort through disobedience.
A sanctified soul hungers for God's word as for food without which life cannot continue.
Every deliberate sin contains an element of pride.
God can silence liars.
Reproach and contempt may humble us and do us good before they are removed.
If the cross seems too heavy for us, the One who carried it for us can give us strength to carry it.
He will not let those upheld by him finally sink.
It is especially painful when people who should protect the innocent betray them.
The psalmist nevertheless continued in duty and found comfort in Scripture.
When other consolations become bitter, the Lord's word may become even sweeter to the believer.
To delight in God's testimonies, we must accept their guidance.
May he direct our repentance and our faith in Christ.

div.title: Repentance and an enlarged heart (verses 25–32)
div.p: Worldly-minded people cling to the earth as their ultimate possession.
Believers, by contrast, grieve over the remaining earthly desires within their own hearts.
It comforts them deeply to know how tenderly God receives their complaints.
We can speak of the wonders of redeeming love when we understand God's way and walk in it.
Repentance melts the heart with sorrow for sin.
Even a patient believer may be overcome by affliction and should then pour out the soul before God.
The way of falsehood includes every deceptive path—whether we deceive others, ourselves, or are misled by Satan and his agents.
Those who know and love God's law want to know it better and love it more.
The way of sincere godliness is the way of truth and the only true road to happiness.
We must take it seriously at every step.
Those who hold to God's word may pray in faith for acceptance.
Lord, do not let me act in a way that brings shame upon me, and do not reject my service.
Those journeying toward heaven must continue pressing forward.
God's Spirit enlarges the heart as he gives wisdom and freedom from sin.

div.title: Understanding God's law through his Spirit (verses 33–40)
div.p: Teach me your statutes, Lord—not merely their words, but how they apply to my life.
The Holy Spirit gives right understanding.
Having revelation written in Scripture is not enough unless the Spirit gives wisdom in the heart.
God puts his Spirit within believers and moves them to obey his statutes.
The psalmist prays particularly against covetousness.
To have the love of God rooted in our hearts, we must uproot the love of the world.
Friendship with the world is hostility toward God.
Give me new life in your way, so that I redeem my time and perform my duties eagerly.
Staring at empty attractions slows us down.
A traveler cannot reach the destination while stopping to inspect every passing sight.
God's promises assure believers of his preserving care.
When Satan persuades one of God's children to compromise with the world, he later reproaches that believer for the very fall he caused.
Victory comes through Christ's cross.
The sweetness of God's commands makes us want to know them more.
Where the Lord has given the will to obey, he will also provide the strength to act.

div.title: Freedom through obedience (verses 41–48)
div.p: Lord, faith has shown me your mercies.
Let prayer bring me to enjoy what you promised.
When the salvation of the saints is complete, everyone will see that trust in God's word was never wasted.
Pray that we will never be ashamed or afraid to acknowledge God's truth before other people.
The psalmist resolved to continue obeying, without turning back.
Serving sin is slavery. Serving God is freedom.
Complete happiness and genuine liberty cannot be separated from following the Lord's law.
We must openly confess our faith without fear or shame.
The more we delight in God's service, the more closely we approach the holiness for which we were created.
We should do more than approve the law as good.
We should enjoy it as good for us and exert our strength to follow it.
Something of this attitude of Christ belongs to every true disciple.

div.title: Remembering God's promises in adversity (verses 49–56)
div.p: Those who have made God's promises their portion may humbly yet boldly appeal to them.
The Spirit who creates faith within us will also act for us.
God's word gives comfort during suffering.
If it makes us holy through grace, it can sustain our peace in any condition.
Be sure that what you believe is genuinely taught by divine Scripture.
Then do not allow mockers to frighten you away from it.
God's earlier judgments comfort us because he remains the same.
Sin becomes hateful to those whom the Lord sanctifies.
Soon believers will be absent from the body and present with him.
Meanwhile his statutes give us constant reasons for praise.
During affliction and in the quiet hours of night, the psalmist remembered the Lord's name and returned to his commandments.
Everyone who has made true religion a priority will recognize how richly it has benefited them.

div.title: The Lord is my portion (verses 57–64)
div.p: Faithful believers choose the Lord as their inheritance.
Nothing less can satisfy them.
The psalmist prayed with his whole heart because he valued the blessing he requested.
He desired the promised mercy and depended upon God's promise to receive it.
He abandoned wrong paths and returned to the Lord's testimonies without delay.
Sinners should hurry to escape destruction, and believers should be equally eager to glorify God.
Neither anxiety nor sorrow should erase Scripture from our minds or rob us of its comfort.
There is no earthly situation in which a believer lacks reasons for thanksgiving.
We should be ashamed if others are more willing to lose sleep for sinful pleasures than we are to rise and praise the Lord.
Let us pray earnestly for hearts filled with mercy, grace and peace.

div.title: Affliction that teaches God's statutes (verses 65–72)
div.p: However God has treated us, he has treated us better than we deserve, acting in love for our ultimate good.
Many people have knowledge but little judgment.
Those with both are better prepared against Satan's traps and for God's service.
We are often most inclined to wander from the Lord when life is comfortable.
Because we do not know everything that is good for us, we should entrust our concerns to him.
Lord, you are a generous Benefactor.
Direct our hearts toward faith and obedience.
The psalmist resolved to continue faithfully and steadfastly.
Proud people become so filled with worldly riches and pleasures that they grow spiritually dull and careless.
God sometimes afflicts his people so they will learn his statutes.
Not only his promises but also his commands, however difficult they seem to unbelievers, are desirable and beneficial.
They guide us toward eternal life with safety and joy.

div.title: The compassion that sustains the upright (verses 73–80)
div.p: God created us to serve and enjoy him.
But our own sin has made us unfit to do either.
We must continually ask him, through the Holy Spirit, to give us understanding.
When other believers experience comfort from God, it should make us rejoice with them.
It is easy to say God's judgments are right until those judgments affect us personally.
Every support we receive during suffering comes from his mercy and compassion.
His mercies are tender.
They resemble a father's care and a mother's compassion for her child.
They come toward us even when we are unable to go toward them.
Groundless reproach does not truly harm us and should not divert us from duty.
The psalmist found comfort in continuing faithfully.
He prized the goodwill of fellow believers and desired fellowship with them.
An upright heart means sincere dependence upon God and wholehearted devotion to him.

div.title: Hope that continues when strength fails (verses 81–88)
div.p: The psalmist asked to be delivered from sin, enemies and fear.
Waiting for salvation made him weary; his eyes had grown tired looking for relief.
Yet when our eyes fail, faith must not fail.
His suffering was severe.
He compared himself to a leather bottle hung in smoke, dried out and shriveled.
Even then, we should remember God's statutes.
The days of believers' mourning will end; beside eternity, those days are brief.
Their enemies use cunning as well as strength, despising God's law.
But his commands remain reliable guides toward peace and safety.
We can especially hope for God's help when, like our Master, we do good and suffer because of it.
Wicked people may nearly destroy the believer on earth, but the believer would rather abandon everything else than abandon the Lord's word.
For every good work we depend upon divine grace.
The surest sign that God favors us is his good work within us.

div.title: God's word stands forever (verses 89–96)
div.p: The permanence of God's word in heaven stands against the changes and revolutions of the earth.
His covenant is established more firmly than the earth itself.
All created things fulfill the purposes for which they were made.
Should humanity, uniquely endowed with reason, become the one unprofitable burden upon creation?
Scripture can be our pleasant companion at any hour.
Yet the written word will not give spiritual life without God's grace.
The best aid for imperfect memory is strong affection.
Even if we forget the exact words, remembering their true meaning is valuable.
I belong to you, Lord—not to myself or the world.
Save me from sin and ruin.
God gives peace to the person whose mind remains fixed on him.
The perfections of this world all have limits and eventually fade like grass.
But God's word is complete and sufficient for every age and every situation.
It leads us away from confidence in human wisdom, strength and righteousness, directing us to seek happiness and comfort in Christ alone.

div.title: Loving and meditating on Scripture (verses 97–104)
div.p: We naturally think often about what we love.
All true wisdom comes from God.
A faithful believer carries the Bible everywhere—not necessarily in the hand, but in mind and heart.
Meditating on Scripture can give us deeper understanding than respected teachers possess, particularly when we learn to understand our own hearts.
The written word is a more reliable guide to heaven than all the fathers, teachers and ancient authorities of the church.
We cannot confidently approach God in worship while knowingly clinging to guilt or walking along sinful paths.
Divine grace enabled the psalmist to receive the Lord's instruction.
The soul has tastes and appetites, just as the body does.
Our delight in God's word grows as our appetite for worldly and fleshly pleasures diminishes.
Every path of sin is wrong.
The better we understand God's commands, the more deeply we hate sin.
And the better we know Scripture, the better equipped we become to answer temptation.

div.title: A lamp for every step (verses 105–112)
div.p: God's word directs our work and our path.
Without it, this world would be terribly dark.
His commandments are like a lamp, kept burning by the oil of the Spirit.
They guide both our choice of direction and the steps we take along it.
This obedience belongs to a sinner living under mercy and a believer who shares in the covenant of grace.
Though frequently afflicted, the psalmist continued longing for holiness and praying daily for life-giving grace.
Nothing we offer to God is acceptable unless he first teaches us how to offer it.
Holding our life continually in our hands means living under constant danger.
Yet the psalmist did not forget God's promises or commandments.
Wicked people set countless traps.
Blessed is the servant whom those traps do not turn away from the Master's way.
Heavenly treasures are an everlasting inheritance.
Those who value them can be content with little wealth on earth.
Comfort is found in the way of duty faithfully performed.
Through grace, a godly person brings the heart fully into the work and performs it well.

div.title: Watching against the first movements of sin (verses 113–120)
div.p: The psalmist feared even the first beginnings of sinful desire.
The more we love God's law, the more carefully we guard against empty thoughts that would draw us away.
To progress in obedience, we must separate ourselves from the influence of evildoers.
Believers cannot live spiritually without grace.
But when God's hand supports them, their spiritual life is preserved.
Their security rests upon divine help.
Departing from the Lord's statutes is error that leads toward destruction.
Wicked people's clever schemes are ultimately deceitful.
A day is coming when the wicked will face everlasting fire, the fitting place for dross.
Considering sin's consequences, we should fear coming short of the promised heavenly rest (Hebrews 4:1).

div.title: Justice, grace and Christ our Surety (verses 121–128)
div.p: Happy are those who practice justice toward others from gospel principles.
Christ our Surety has paid the debt and ransom of his people and secured all the blessings of salvation for genuine believers.
The psalmist expected the fulfillment of God's righteous word.
He looked for no salvation beyond what God had promised.
That word cannot fail.
We deserve no favor from God.
Our hearts find most rest when we entrust ourselves entirely to his mercy.
Those resolved to obey as God's servants will be taught his testimonies.
We should do everything within our power to support true religion, then ask God to take the work into his own hands.
Claiming to love his commandments more than our earthly interests is hypocrisy if our conduct proves otherwise.
The path of sin is a false path because it contradicts God's righteous commands.
Those who truly value his law hate sin and refuse to make peace with it.

div.title: Tears over disobedience (verses 129–136)
div.p: The wonders of redeeming love should fill our hearts with reverent admiration.
Scripture shows us what we were, what we are, and what we shall become.
It reveals God's mercy and justice, heaven's joy and hell's suffering.
In a short time, even people without advanced education can learn from it truths that philosophers searched for over many centuries.
Believers tired by the cares of life and the struggle against sin long for the comfort God's word supplies.
Everyone may pray: Look upon me and show me mercy, as you do to those who love your name.
Ask the Holy Spirit to direct every step.
We should fear sin's domination and earnestly pray against it.
Human oppression may become more than we can endure in our own strength.
The God who knows our frame can remove that pressure in answer to prayer.
Henry argues that the ancient Israelites' confidence in approaching God's throne indicates they understood more of gospel blessings through sacrifices and worship than people often suppose.
We should approach the same gracious throne through the name and merit of Jesus. We will not, and cannot, plead there in vain.
Those whose hearts have been transformed by grace often express that grace in tears.
Lord, receive the tears our blessed Redeemer shed for us during his earthly life, and teach us also to grieve over our own sins and the suffering of others.

div.title: God's righteousness and Christ's obedience (verses 137–144)
div.p: God has never done and never can do anything unjust.
He fulfills every promise faithfully.
Zeal against sin should make us act against it, beginning with greater faithfulness in our own lives.
Love for Scripture demonstrates love for God because it aims to make us participants in his holiness.
Genuine excellence makes people humble in their own eyes.
When we are overlooked or despised, we especially need to remember God's commands for encouragement.
His law is truth, the standard of holiness and the rule of happiness.
Yet only Christ's obedience justifies the believer.
Even saints experience sorrow and many trials.
Sometimes they taste the sweetness of God's word most deeply when suffering and distress surround them.
Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (John 17:3).
May we live now by faith and grace, then enter the life of glory.

div.title: Seeking the Lord morning and night (verses 145–152)
div.p: Wholehearted prayer belongs to people who truly desire God's salvation and love his commandments.
Where should a child go but to the Father?
Lord, save me from my sins, corruptions, temptations and everything that hinders obedience.
Christians who have good health should not waste the early hours of morning.
Hope in God's promises encourages us to keep praying.
It is better to give up some sleep than to find no time for prayer.
We may approach God at every hour.
When our first thoughts in the morning turn to him, we are better prepared to live in his fear throughout the day.
Ask him to give life, joy and cheerfulness.
He knows our needs and what is good for us.
When we are engaged in his service, we need not fear those who place themselves as far as possible from the commands of his word.
When trouble comes near, God is also near.
All his commandments are true, and all his promises will be fulfilled.
Everyone who has trusted him has found him faithful.

div.title: The living word and the inexhaustible mercy of God (verses 153–160)
div.p: The more closely we hold God's word as both our rule and our support, the stronger our confidence in deliverance.
Christ is the Redeemer and Advocate of his people.
Those whom the Spirit once made alive when they were dead in sins still need fresh grace to revive them according to God's promises.
The wicked do not obey God's statutes; they do not even seek to know them.
They flatter themselves that they are traveling toward heaven.
But as long as they continue in sin, they move further from it.
God's tender mercies are a fountain that never runs dry.
The psalmist begged for renewed life-giving grace.
Someone steadily performing duty need not fear numerous enemies.
Those who truly hate sin hate it because it violates God's law and breaks his word, not merely because it is inconvenient.
Obedience is pleasing to God and joyful to us only when it springs from love.
In every age, everyone who receives Scripture with faith and love discovers that every word of it is faithful.

div.title: Great peace through love for God's law (verses 161–168)
div.p: Those who stand in awe of God's word will endure human anger rather than break his commandments.
Through Scripture we receive immeasurable benefit.
Everyone dislikes being lied to.
But we should hate telling lies even more, because that insults God directly.
The more we love truth's beauty, the more we recognize the ugliness of falsehood.
We should praise God even for trials, because his grace can use them for our good.
People who love this world experience great unrest because it disappoints them.
Those who love God's word find great peace, because it exceeds their expectations.
Genuine love for the Lord keeps us from unnecessary doubts and from constantly taking offense at other believers.
A sound hope of salvation motivates us to obey.
Our love for Scripture must also weaken sinful desires and uproot fleshly attachments.
It must engage the heart, or it accomplishes nothing.
We keep God's commands through obedience, and keep his promises through reliance upon them.
God sees us continually.
That should make us careful in all our conduct.

div.title: Seek me and give me life (verses 169–176)
div.p: The psalmist asked for the grace and strength needed to pray, and for God to receive his petitions.
He wanted to know more of God in Christ, to understand Scripture's teachings and carry out his duties.
He knew his unworthiness and approached with reverent concern.
He appealed to what God had promised, not to his own merit.
We have not truly learned from God unless we have learned to praise him.
His word must govern our speech.
We must avoid both sinful speaking and sinful silence.
Our hands are insufficient, and no creature can provide all the help we need.
We look to the One who made us for support.
The psalmist had deliberately chosen to follow God.
Every saint longs for eternal salvation and therefore prays for help along the way.
May all God's ordinances and providential dealings advance his glory in our lives.
The believer looks back with both shame and thankfulness on being lost.
Still needing tender care, we pray to the Shepherd who purchased his flock with his own blood and grants eternal life.
Seek me means find me.
God never seeks in vain.
Turn me, Lord, and I shall be turned.
Let this psalm examine our hearts and lives.
Do our hearts, washed in Christ's blood, truly make its prayers, promises and confessions our own?
Is the Lord's word the standard of what we believe and how we live?
Do we plead its promises before Christ for what we need?
Happy are those who find delight in living this way.

row.cell: The psalmist prays to God to deliver him from false and malicious tongues.

div.title: Rescued from deceitful accusations (verses 1–4)
div.p: The psalmist suffered greatly because of lying tongues.
May every godly person be rescued from malicious falsehoods.
His enemies had invented accusations against him.
When he was distressed, he turned to the Lord in earnest prayer.
God can restrain the tongues of slanderers.
The psalmist received a gracious answer.
Sinners would hardly dare to act as they do if they understood and seriously considered the end of their wrongdoing.
God's terrors are compared to arrows, and his wrath to burning juniper coals that give intense heat and retain it for a long time.
Such judgment awaits persistent liars.
All who love and practice falsehood will face the final judgment described as the everlasting lake of fire.

div.title: Grieved by hostile neighbors, seeking peace (verses 5–7)
div.p: Living among wicked people can be a heavy burden for someone who loves God and hopes eventually to be separated from their company forever.
Here we see a mark of a godly person: a desire to live peaceably with everyone.
David also pointed forward to Christ.
Let us follow that example.
When distressed, call upon the Lord, and he will hear.
Pursue peace and holiness, making every effort to overcome evil with good.

p.hi: The safety of the godly.

div.title: Our help comes from the Lord
div.p: We must not put ultimate trust in human beings, methods, tools or secondary causes.
Should I depend upon the strength of the hills, on rulers or on powerful people?
No. My confidence is in God alone.
Or perhaps we are being called to look beyond the hills to the God who gives all earthly things their place and value.
All our help comes from him.
We should expect it from him in his own way and time.
This psalm teaches us to find comfort in the Lord especially when danger and difficulty are greatest.
His almighty wisdom plans the safety of those who place themselves under his care, and his almighty power accomplishes it.
He is a watchful Keeper.
He never tires, sleeps or even grows drowsy.
We may rest under his shelter with joy and confidence.
He is always near his people to protect and refresh them.
Our right hand represents our working hand.
When we turn toward the duties he has given us, we may find him ready to grant us success.
He guards his people from being finally overthrown.
Neither open attacks nor secret plots can cause them ultimate harm.
The Lord may prevent the trouble they fear or sanctify, remove or lessen the suffering they experience.
Above all, he protects their souls from sin's pollution, from being crushed under trials and from eternal destruction.
He watches over believers during life and death.
He is with them when they go out to work in the morning of life and when they return to rest in life's evening.
The Holy Spirit, their Preserver and Comforter, stays with them forever.
Let us therefore remain faithful in our work, confident in the blessing promised here.

div.title: Rejoicing in the gathering of God's people (verses 1–5)
div.p: The pleasure and benefit we receive through God's means of grace should make us willing to endure inconvenience and tiredness in order to attend them.
We should encourage one another toward what is good.
When Christian friends undertake some worthwhile work, we should want them to invite us and include us in it.
How eagerly should we look forward to the heavenly Jerusalem!
How cheerfully should we bear our cross and face death when we hope to receive a crown of glory!
Jerusalem is called a beautiful city.
It pictured the gospel church, whose members are joined together through holy love and Christian fellowship, making one united community.
If all Christ's disciples shared one mind and maintained the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, their enemies would lose many of their greatest advantages.
But Satan has always tried to divide in order to conquer, and too few Christians recognize his schemes.

div.title: Praying for Jerusalem's peace (verses 6–9)
div.p: Even those who cannot do anything else for Jerusalem's peace can pray.
We should regard all who sincerely seek the Redeemer's glory as brothers and sisters and fellow travelers, without allowing differences that do not affect eternal salvation to divide us.
Blessed Spirit of peace and love, who dwelt in the soul of the holy Jesus, come upon his church and fill its people with your heavenly character.
Put an end to bitter disputes and make us united in heart.
Love for fellow believers and love for God should move us to imitate Jesus through fervent prayer and tireless work for human salvation and God's glory.

p.hi: Confidence in God under contempt.

div.title: Looking to our heavenly Master for mercy
div.p: Jesus taught us to approach God in prayer as our Father in heaven.
A godly person lifts the soul toward him in every prayer, especially when suffering.
We ask for mercy, trust he will grant it, and continue waiting until it comes.
Servants watch their master's hand for several reasons.
First, for direction: they expect him to assign their work.
Second, for provision: they look for the food they need at the right time.
Likewise, we look to God for daily bread and sufficient grace, receiving both with thanksgiving.
Third, for protection: if servants are mistreated while fulfilling their duties, their master should defend them.
Fourth, for correction: when we sin, we ought to turn humbly to the very One who has disciplined us, submitting under his mighty hand.
Finally, for reward: faithful servants look to their master's kindness.
Hypocrites look to the world's approval and receive the reward of worldly honor.
But genuine Christians regard God as both their Master and their Rewarder.
God's people may receive little mercy from other human beings.
Their comfort is that the Lord is full of mercy.
Mockery and contempt have always been, and will likely continue to be, part of the suffering of God's people.
It is difficult to endure.
Yet those who serve the Lord should not be surprised to receive treatment like that given to his beloved Son.
When suffering nearly overwhelms us, look to Jesus and entrust ourselves through faith and prayer to the mercy of God.

div.title: The Lord saves his people (verses 1–5)
div.p: Sometimes God allows his people's enemies to advance so far that his power is displayed more clearly when he rescues them.
Happy are those whose God is the Lord, the all-sufficient One.
We can apply this psalm to the deliverances he gave in ancient times or to rescues experienced in our own day.
But above all, let us remember the great redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ, through which believers were delivered from Satan's power.

div.title: All the glory belongs to God (verses 6–8)
div.p: God is the author of all our deliverances and deserves all the glory for them.
Enemies lay traps to draw his people into sin and trouble and then keep them there.
At times those plans appear to succeed.
Yet those who put their trust in the Lord will not ultimately be put to shame.
Believers credit their salvation entirely to God's power, mercy and faithfulness.
Looking back on his guidance, they respond with wonder and thanksgiving.
Let us rejoice that all our help for the future is in the One who made heaven and earth.

row.cell: Prayer for them, The ruin of the wicked.

div.title: A security stronger than mountains (verses 1–3)
div.p: Minds firmly resting upon God find true stability.
They are like Mount Zion, strong through Providence and even stronger through God's promise.
Those who trust him cannot finally be driven away from their confidence.
His grace within them is a pledge of their eternal life in glory.
Because they entrust themselves to God, they are safe from their enemies in the ultimate sense.
Even mountains eventually crumble and rocks are moved.
But God's covenant cannot be broken, and his care for his people cannot cease.
Their suffering will not exceed what the Lord enables them to bear.
Wicked people may strike believers and affect their bodies, property, freedoms, families and reputations.
But they cannot destroy the believer's soul.
Their oppression may reach the righteous person's earthly circumstances, but it will not remain there forever.
God will work all these things together for their good.
Wicked people become a rod of correction, not a sword of destruction.
Even that rod will eventually be removed, so that believers will not be left thinking God has abandoned them.

div.title: Prayer for the upright and warning to the crooked (verses 4 and 5)
div.p: God's promises should encourage our prayers.
The path of holiness is straight.
It does not twist and turn in dishonest compromises.
But the ways of sinners are crooked.
They change their purposes and use deceit to get what they want.
Disappointment and misery will eventually come upon them.
Those who remain on God's path may suffer along the way, but their final destination is peace.
Their Savior's intercession secures God's sustaining power and preserving grace for them.
Lord, count us among them now and for eternity.

row.cell: Those returned out of captivity are to be thankful.
Those yet in captivity are encouraged.

div.title: Thankfulness for deliverance (verses 1–3)
div.p: It is good to pay attention to God's deliverances of his church and to share in the joy those rescues bring.
How highly should we value the greater redemption that saves us from the coming judgment, the power of sin and Satan!

When a sinner becomes aware of guilt and danger, looks to the crucified Savior, receives peace of conscience and finds new strength to abandon sinful conduct, the change may be so wonderful that it hardly seems real.

div.title: Praying and sowing through tears (verses 4–6)
div.p: The beginnings of God's mercy encourage us to pray that he will complete what he has started.
As long as we remain in this world, there will always be something to pray for, even when we have abundant reasons for praise.
Suffering believers often cry.
They share the hardships of human life and commonly endure an even greater share than others.
Yet they sow while they weep.
They perform their duties even in a painful season.
Tears must not keep us from sowing.
We should seek spiritual benefit from times of suffering.
Those who sow to the Spirit, even amid tears of godly repentance, will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
What a joyful harvest that will be!
Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted forever.
When we grieve over sin or suffer for Christ, we are sowing in tears and will one day reap with joy.
Remember also that God cannot be mocked: we will reap what we sow (Galatians 6:7–9).
Disciple of Jesus, see here a picture of your present work and future reward.
The day is coming when your harvest will be abundant and your joy in the Lord will be great.

p.hi: The value of the Divine blessing.

div.title: The Lord builds, protects and provides
div.p: We must continually recognize God's Providence.
In every matter affecting a household, we depend upon his blessing.
Henry describes three areas.

p.hi: First, establishing a family.

div.p: If we do not recognize God, we have no reason to expect his help.
Even the most carefully made plans fail unless he grants success.

p.hi: Second, protecting a family or city.

div.p: Unless the Lord guards the city, watchmen keep watch in vain, even if they never sleep.
Danger may arise that no amount of early detection can prevent.

p.hi: Third, providing for a family's needs.

div.p: Some people pursue money so eagerly that their continual worry makes every comfort bitter and turns life into a burden.
They labor to acquire wealth, yet all their efforts are vain unless God prospers them.
Those who love the Lord, act diligently in lawful work and entrust their cares to him may receive what is needed without being consumed by anxiety.
We should seek to remain in God's love and be content whether we possess little or much.
But this never excuses laziness: we must use appropriate means diligently.
Children are gifts from God, a heritage and reward.
They should be counted as blessings rather than burdens.
We can trust that the One who gives children can also provide for their needs.
Children may become a source of strength and defense for the household.
When they are young, parents can direct them like arrows toward a target—God's glory and the good of their generation.
Once children have gone out into the world, they are arrows released from the hand; their earlier direction can no longer be changed in the same way.
Yet arrows in the hand can also become arrows in the heart, bringing pain to godly parents.
When children are raised according to God's word, however, they generally offer valuable support later in life.
They remember what their parents have done for them and care for them in old age.
All earthly comforts remain uncertain.
Yet the Lord will surely comfort and bless those who serve him.
And those who labor for the conversion of sinners will find that their spiritual children are their joy and crown at the day of Jesus Christ.

p.hi: The blessings of those who fear God.

div.title: The happiness of those who walk in God's ways
div.p: Only people who are truly devoted to God are truly happy.
We cannot reasonably claim to fear him if we do not strive conscientiously to walk in his ways.
Everyone who reverences the Lord can be blessed—whether powerful or obscure, rich or poor.
If we fear him and walk in obedience, life will be good under his care; death will bring something better, and eternity the greatest happiness.
With God's blessing, the faithful can earn an honest living.
Henry sees a twofold promise here.
They will have worthwhile work to do, because idleness is miserable and joyless.
They will also be given the ability, bodily strength and mental capacity needed for the work.
They need not live by exploiting the labor of others.
Quietly working and eating our own bread is both a duty and a mercy.
They and their families may enjoy the results of that labor.
Those who fear the Lord and follow his ways are blessed regardless of social position.
They will find abundant comfort in their family relationships and receive the good things God has promised and for which they pray.
Yet a good person gains little lasting consolation from seeing grandchildren if there is no peace for Israel.
Every genuine believer rejoices in the welfare and growth of God's church.
Beyond this life we will see far greater blessings: the everlasting peace and rest reserved for God's Israel.

row.cell: A believing prospect of the destruction of the enemies of Zion.

div.title: Remembering deliverance amid persecution (verses 1–4)
div.p: The enemies of God's people have often sought cruelly to wear down and destroy the saints of the Most High.
Yet the Lord has repeatedly delivered his church through grace.
Christ built his church upon a rock.
He has many ways of restraining evildoers and preventing them from accomplishing the harm they plan.
The Lord acts righteously when he refuses to allow his people to be completely destroyed, because he has promised to preserve a people for himself.

div.title: The fate of those opposing Zion (verses 5–8)
div.p: God's people can flourish like a fruit-bearing palm or green olive tree.
Their enemies, however, are like grass growing on rooftops.
In the lands described here, roofs were flat and the thin layer of soil allowed grass to grow briefly but never mature.
That is the future of schemes directed against God's people.
No wise person asks God to bless people engaged in such destructive work.
Remember that Jesus rose and now reigns.
Remember how his people have survived like the bush that burned but was not consumed.
Therefore, do not be overcome by fear.

div.title: Crying to the God who forgives (verses 1–4)
div.p: A soul entangled in sin can find true relief only by turning to God.
Many amusements distract us, and many supposed remedies offer help.
But the soul discovers that the Lord alone can heal it.
Until we recognize our guilt and abandon our self-reliance to come directly to him, we will look in vain for peace.
The Holy Spirit awakens people to a fresh understanding of their deep need and moves them to earnest prayer in faith.
For their souls' welfare and God's glory, they must not neglect this duty.
Why do some continue in uncertainty for so long?
Often it is because laziness or discouragement makes them settle for merely routine, customary prayers.
Let us take action and seek the Lord.
We can approach him safely.
We must humble ourselves as guilty before God.
We cannot justify ourselves or claim innocence.
But what an inexpressible comfort that forgiveness is available with him, exactly what we need!
Jesus Christ is the great Ransom and our continual Advocate.
Through him we hope to receive pardon.
There is forgiveness with God not so that we can treat sin lightly, but so that we will fear and reverence him.
The fear of God often describes the whole life of worshiping him.
For sinners, the great invitation and encouragement is simply this: the Lord offers forgiveness.

div.title: Waiting for abundant redemption (verses 5–8)
div.p: My soul waits for the Lord himself, for the gifts of his grace and the work of his power.
We should hope only for what God has promised in his word.
A watchman longs for the morning light before day breaks.
In the same way, a godly soul waits even more eagerly for signs of the Lord's favor and renewed grace.
Everyone devoted to the Lord should remain confident in him.
This redemption delivers us from all sin.
Jesus Christ saves his people from their sins, removing both sin's condemnation and sin's power to command.
His redemption is abundant.
The Redeemer possesses a fullness sufficient for everyone and for each believer individually.
There is enough for me, too.
Freedom from sin includes freedom from every other evil that would finally destroy us.
Through Jesus' atoning blood, his people will be fully redeemed from all their sins.
Everyone who waits upon God for mercy and grace can look forward to peace.

p.hi: The psalmist's humility. Believers encouraged to trust in God.

div.title: A quiet heart before the Lord
div.p: The psalmist did not aim at worldly greatness.
He wanted to be content in whatever circumstances God assigned him.
Humble believers think less highly of themselves than other people think of them.
When love for God rules the heart, it weakens selfish pride.
A proud heart often shows itself through a proud expression.
Knowing God and understanding our duties is already learning enough to occupy our lives well.
Wisdom keeps us from meddling with things that do not belong to us.
The psalmist was willing to accept any condition in which the Lord placed him.
He had become like a young child being weaned, content to remain entirely under God's direction just as a child depends upon a mother or nurse.
We must become like little children (Matthew 18:3).
Our hearts naturally cry out for worldly possessions and pleasures.
But as grace makes the soul holy, it gradually weans us from those desires.
A child being weaned may complain and grow restless.
Soon, however, the longing for milk fades, and the child can receive more substantial food.
In a similar way, a renewed soul learns to be quiet when deprived of favorite comforts or disappointed in cherished hopes.
When circumstances do not match our wishes, we should learn to bring our wishes into submission to our circumstances.
Then we find rest within ourselves and live more peaceably with others.
The psalmist used his experience to encourage all God's people to trust him.
It is good to hope in the Lord and quietly wait for his salvation throughout every trial.

div.title: David desires a dwelling place for the Lord (verses 1–10)
div.p: David committed himself to finding a place for the ark, the sign of God's presence.
When we have work to do for the Lord, it helps to set aside a time to do it.
Each morning we can plan the work of the day while submitting our plans to Providence, since we do not know what the day will bring.
Before anything else, let us seek without delay to have our hearts made God's dwelling place through the Holy Spirit.
David prayed that the Lord would inhabit the sanctuary prepared for him.
He also prayed that God would give the priests and other ministers grace to fulfill their duties.
David pleaded that he was the Lord's anointed, pointing forward to Christ, the great Anointed One.
We possess no merit of our own that would recommend us to God.
But Christ possesses an abundance of merit, and for his sake we ask to receive favor.
Every genuine believer is also anointed in Christ, receiving the grace of the Holy One.
Our prayer is that God will hear and answer for his Son's sake.

div.title: God's promise and the reign of Messiah (verses 11–18)
div.p: The Lord does not turn away those who plead his covenant through the Anointed Prophet, Priest and King.
What astonishing love God shows toward his church!
He desires to dwell with his people, while we desire so little to dwell with him.
He remained in Zion until Israel's sins led him to hand the city over to enemies.
Lord, although we too are sinful, do not abandon us.
God's people enjoy a special blessing even on life's ordinary comforts.
That blessing gives them an added sweetness.
Zion's poor may be content with little earthly wealth because far better treasures are prepared for them.
The Lord richly nourishes the new spiritual life, satisfying those poor in spirit with the bread of life.
He gives more than we ask.
When he gives salvation, he also grants abundant joy.
God would frustrate every attempt to destroy David's royal house until the King Messiah arose from it to sit upon his Father's throne.
All the promises are fulfilled in Christ.
Those who refuse to acknowledge his reign will finally face everlasting shame and confusion.

p.hi: The excellency of brotherly love.

div.title: The blessing of living together in peace
div.p: We cannot say too much to encourage people to live in peace with one another.
Such peace is good for our dignity and comfort, and it gives continued joy to those who enjoy genuine unity.
The beauty of this fellowship is compared with the sacred anointing oil.
Brotherly love is a fruit of the Holy Spirit, evidence of union with Christ, and an adornment to the gospel.
It is not only pleasant but beneficial.
Its blessings are as numerous as drops of dew.
As dew cools the air and refreshes dry ground, love cools the burning heat of human anger.
It softens the heart and prepares it to receive and bear fruit from the seed of God's word.
The excellence of this love is confirmed by God's promise: where brothers and sisters live together in unity, the Lord commands his blessing.
Human beings can only request a blessing.
God commands it.
Believers who live in love and peace have the God of love and peace with them now.
Soon they will be with him forever in a world of perfect and unending peace.
May everyone who loves the Lord bear with and forgive one another, as God has forgiven them for Christ's sake.

p.hi: An exhortation to bless the Lord.

div.title: Using every available moment for praise
div.p: We should encourage our souls to give glory to God and to hope for his mercy and grace.
It is an excellent practice to fill otherwise unused moments with prayer, praise and godly meditation.
Then spare time need not become a burden.
We will not waste our hours on empty conversation, idle entertainment or indulgence of sinful desires.
The Lord's blessing is enough to make us happy.
We should pray for spiritual blessings not only for ourselves, but also for others.
Let our prayer be more than Lord, bless me.
Let us also say to another person, May the Lord bless you.
In doing so we declare that God has enough mercy for others as well as for us.
We also demonstrate genuine love and goodwill toward them.

row.cell: God to be praised for his mercy.

div.title: Praising the Lord's gracious election (verses 1–4)
div.p: Our praise should center on the blessings of grace flowing from God's everlasting love.
We should love and honor his name because he is our covenant God and Father through Christ, blessing us with every spiritual blessing in him.
The Lord chose a people to belong to him, so that his name would be honored and praised through them.
If they fail to thank him for this special favor, they show extraordinary ingratitude and unworthiness.

div.title: God's power and faithfulness to his people (verses 5–14)
div.p: The Lord is, and will always be, the same gracious, faithful God who works wonders for his church.
And his church, in response, will remain a thankful people who praise him.
In this way his name endures through every generation.
He will return to his people with mercy and will delight in doing them good.

div.title: Rejecting idols and witnessing through a holy life (verses 15–21)
div.p: The psalm teaches believers to resist idolatry and false worship by showing what sort of gods the nations had been worshiping.
The more tragic their condition, the more thankful we should be that we have received a greater knowledge of God.
We ought to pity them, pray for them and seek their good, not treat them with contempt.
May we glorify God's name and commend his truth not merely through speech, but also through holy lives that imitate the goodness and faithfulness of Jesus Christ.

row.cell: God to be praised as the Creator of the world.

div.title: God's everlasting mercy in creation (verses 1–9)
div.p: We are so forgetful that we need to hear essential truths repeatedly. Here every refrain reminds us that God's mercy endures forever.

Mercy means more than a general disposition to kindness. It is the Lord's willingness to rescue people made miserable and vile through sin and includes everything he has provided to redeem sinners through Jesus Christ.
The purposes of that mercy are eternal. Its saving effects endure forever for those who receive it.
God remains as ready to show mercy to those who seek him as he ever was. This is the foundation of our comfort and hope.

div.title: God's saving mercy to Israel (verses 10–22)
div.p: The Lord's extraordinary works in bringing Israel out of Egypt were mercies whose benefits continued for generations.
The greater redemption accomplished by Christ, which those events pictured, endures forever.
We should examine the history of God's favors carefully, remembering in each event that his mercy lasts forever.
He brought Israel into a fruitful land. This too served as a picture of the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ.

div.title: Mercy in every gift and all our praise (verses 23–26)
div.p: God's everlasting mercy is praised here in the deliverance of his church, in all his glorious works and in all the gifts he provides.
Blessed be God, who has made known and provided salvation through his Son.
May we know and experience his redeeming power, so that we serve him in righteousness throughout our lives.
The Lord gives food to every living creature. Let us ask him to feed our souls with eternal life and stir up our affections through grace, so that we thank and praise his holy name.
Trace every blessing to its true source, and keep offering him praise, for his mercy endures forever.

div.title: Refusing to turn Zion's songs into a mockery (verses 1–4)
div.p: The Jews' enemies had carried them captive into a foreign land.
They then added insult to their grief by demanding laughter and songs.
That cruelty was also profanity, because their captors wanted to hear the songs of Zion.
We should not comply with the demands of those who mock what is holy.
The captives were not merely saying they were too sad to sing. Their objection was that these were the Lord's songs, which they dared not offer as entertainment among idolaters.

div.title: Remembering Jerusalem and entrusting vengeance to God (verses 5–9)
div.p: We naturally think about what we truly love.
Those who rejoice in God make Jerusalem their joy for his sake.
The Jewish exiles resolved never to lose that affection.
During suffering, we should recall with godly sorrow the mercies we forfeited and the sins through which they were lost.
Far from taking private revenge, we must leave vengeance to the Lord, who has declared that it belongs to him.
People who rejoice in others' suffering, especially the calamities of Jerusalem, will not escape judgment.
We cannot pray for the promised success of God's church without looking toward the ruin of her enemies, even if we do not voice a prayer for that ruin.
Above all, remember that our hope of reaching the heavenly Jerusalem rests entirely on God's grace and Christ's finished salvation.

row.cell: The psalmist praises God for answering prayer.
The Lord's dealing with the humble and the proud.

div.title: Wholehearted thanks for answered prayer (verses 1–5)
div.p: When we can praise the Lord with all our hearts, we should not hesitate to let the whole world see our gratitude and joy.
Those who depend on God's lovingkindness and truth through Jesus Christ will always find him faithful to his word.
If God did not spare his own Son, will he not also freely give us all things with him?
The Lord may strengthen our souls even while outward affliction remains.
He gives us grace to carry burdens, withstand temptation and fulfill our duties.
He strengthens us to hold firmly to him by faith and wait patiently for the outcome.
Such grace deserves our sincere thanksgiving.

div.title: His mercy to the humble and distance from the proud (verses 6–8)
div.p: Although the Lord is exalted, he regards every humble sinner.
The proud and unbelieving, however, will be excluded from his blessed presence.
God's consolations can revive us even in the middle of suffering.
He saves his people so that the Holy Spirit, the giver of life and holiness, can renew them.
When we give God glory for his mercy, we may receive the comfort of that mercy ourselves.
Confidence in his promises should increase our prayers, not make us stop praying.
Any good present in us is the Lord's work.
He works within his people both to will and to act.
He will complete the salvation of every genuine believer and will not abandon those whom he has made new in Christ Jesus for good works.

row.cell: The psalmist's hatred to sin, and desire to be led aright.

div.title: The Lord knows every thought (verses 1–6)
div.p: God possesses perfect knowledge of all we think and do.
It is better to meditate upon this truth and apply it to our own lives in prayer than merely to dispute about it out of curiosity.
Everyone readily acknowledges God's omniscience—his knowledge of all things—and omnipresence—his presence everywhere.
Yet few live as though they really believe them.
The Lord notices every step, whether right or wrong.
He knows what rule guides us, where we are heading and whose company we seek.
When we withdraw from everyone else, he knows our inward life.
Before we speak a good or empty word, he knows the thoughts and intentions from which it arises.
Wherever we are, we live beneath his eye and within reach of his hand.
We cannot explain fully how he knows us so thoroughly.
This truth should restrain us from sin.

div.title: No darkness hides us or separates us from his care (verses 7–16)
div.p: We cannot see God, but he sees us.
The psalmist did not really want to escape the Lord.
He asked where anyone could go to leave God's presence.
Neither the furthest parts of the world nor heaven nor hell lie beyond his reach.
No veil of darkness hides an action or person from him.
Even secret wrongdoing is as plain before him as evil committed in daylight.
But this is also a great encouragement.
No suffering or location can remove the believer from the supporting and comforting presence of the almighty Friend.
If a persecutor kills a believer's body, the soul will all the sooner enter heaven.
Even the grave cannot separate the body from the Savior's love.
He will raise the body in glory.
No outward circumstance can ultimately divide the believer from the Lord.
Those who continue doing their duty may find joy in faith, hope and prayer wherever they are.

div.title: God's precious thoughts and a prayer for a cleansed heart (verses 17–24)
div.p: God's plans for his people are too deep for us to search out.
We cannot count his many mercies.
What a help it would be in keeping us reverent toward the Lord throughout the day if our first thoughts each morning were of him!
And how much more will we praise him when we awaken in the world of glory!
Our bodies were wonderfully formed.
We should never use their members or senses as instruments of sin.
Our immortal, rational souls are even greater gifts.
Yet if God had not loved sinners, our reason and immortality would make our guilt and eternal loss all the more dreadful.
Let us therefore meditate with delight upon God's love to sinners in Jesus Christ, which surpasses calculation.
People who fear God hate sin, but grieve for sinners.
Even when they avoid their wrongdoing, they should pray for their conversion and salvation, because God can accomplish both.
The Lord knows us fully, while we know ourselves only imperfectly.
Ask him through his word and Spirit to search and test our hearts.
If any wicked way is within us, may he show it and remove it.
The old and good way of godliness is pleasing to God, beneficial to us and leads to everlasting life.
All saints want to remain on that path without wandering away or growing weary.

row.cell: He prays for, and prophesies the destruction of, his persecutors.

div.title: Praying for protection from open and hidden danger (verses 1–7)
div.p: The greater the danger, the more seriously we should turn to God in prayer.
Everyone sheltered by the Lord is safe.

p.hi: If God is for us, who can be against us?

div.p: We should especially watch and pray that the Lord will establish our steps in his ways and keep us from stumbling.
God is just as able to preserve his servants from hidden deceit as from open violence.
Our experience of his care in one danger should strengthen our confidence that he will help in other dangers too.

div.title: The Lord's judgment and the righteousness of Christ (verses 8–13)
div.p: Believers may rightly pray that God will not grant the desires of wicked people or help their evil schemes succeed.
Those who make false accusations bring their own trouble upon themselves, even the fiery coals of divine judgment.
The righteous will dwell before God and thank him forever.
Real thanksgiving must become thanks-living.
Every deliverance should move us to serve the Lord more faithfully and cheerfully.
Those who are slandered or mistreated by others can nevertheless be accepted as righteous before God.
That is possible only through the righteousness of Jesus Christ, imputed to them and received through faith.
Its effect in their lives is that they begin to live self-controlled, upright lives.
They give thanks to God for the righteousness by which they are counted righteous and for every gift of grace and mercy they receive.

row.cell: David prays for God's acceptance and assistance.
That God would appear for his rescue.

div.title: Prayer, self-control and protection from sin (verses 1–4)
div.p: The more we value God's gracious presence, the more earnestly we will seek him in prayer.
David asked God to come quickly.
Our prayers become acceptable to him through the sacrifice and intercession of Jesus Christ, just as the daily sacrifices and burning of incense were acceptable under the former covenant.
Prayer is a spiritual sacrifice in which we offer our souls and best affections to God.
Faithful people know the danger of sins committed with the tongue.
When enemies provoke us, we may speak rashly and do wrong.
Because we live in a fallen world and have sinful hearts, we need grace to keep us from being enticed or driven into evil.
Sinners imagine that sin offers them delicious food.
But its pleasures quickly turn bitter.
Those who understand this pray that the Lord will remove such enticements and turn their hearts against them.
God's people pray against the pleasures of sin.

div.title: Welcoming correction and seeking rescue (verses 5–10)
div.p: We should receive our heavenly Father's correction and welcome loving rebuke from fellow believers.
It will not break my head if it helps to break my hard heart.
We should respond to such correction gratefully.
Those who formerly ignored God's word may welcome it eagerly once suffering has opened their ears to instruction.
When the world tastes bitter, God's word tastes sweet.
We should pray for deliverance from Satan's traps and from the schemes of people devoted to wrongdoing.
Lord, let our inadequate prayers express the fact that you alone are our hope and confidence.
Prepare us for faithful prayer through your grace.
Clothe us in Christ's righteousness and plant the Holy Spirit's gifts within our hearts.

p.hi: David's comfort in prayer.

div.title: Bringing every trouble before God
div.p: No danger or sorrow is so severe that a believer cannot receive comfort by praying in faith.
We are often tempted to examine our troubles repeatedly in our own minds, only making them appear worse.
That accomplishes little.
How much better to lay those troubles before the Lord, casting our cares upon the One who cares for us!
We should never allow ourselves to complain inwardly or to other people in a way that we would be ashamed to bring before God.
When our spirits are overwhelmed and discouraged, when enemies have placed traps along the way we are trying to obey, we can remember that the Lord knows our path.
Those who sincerely receive the Lord as their God find him completely sufficient as their Refuge and their Portion.
Everything else is a refuge of lies and an inheritance of no value.
David therefore prayed earnestly.
The psalm also describes the spiritual condition of believers struggling with doubt and fear.
They should ask the Lord to set their souls free so that they can run eagerly in the way of his commandments.
God delivered David from enemies stronger than himself and treated him generously.
He likewise raised the crucified Redeemer to the throne of glory and made him Head over all things for the benefit of his church.
A sinner awakened to guilt cries for help and is eventually brought to praise God among the redeemed.
All genuine believers will finally be delivered from this evil world, sin and death, and will praise their Savior forever.

row.cell: David complains of his enemies and distresses.
He prays for comfort, guidance, and deliverance.

div.title: Pleading God's righteousness rather than our merit (verses 1–6)
div.p: We possess no righteousness of our own that would justify our prayers.
We must therefore appeal to God's righteousness and the promises he has freely given us.
David asked for the forgiveness of sin before asking to be relieved from suffering.
He relied on mercy alone for pardon.
He confessed the heaviness of his heart under trouble.
But he also looked back to remember God's earlier deliverances—those granted to Israel and those he had personally experienced.
He looked around at God's works in creation.
The more we consider God's power, the less we will fear the power or threats of other people.
He lifted his thoughts toward God and longed earnestly for his favor.
This is the best response when our spirits are overwhelmed.
The believer never forgets that even the best acts remain mixed with sin.
Meditation and prayer help restore our souls.
A sorrowing heart reaches toward God like an infant stretching out its hands to a tender mother, and longs for consolation like dry earth thirsting for rain.

div.title: Asking to know and do God's will (verses 7–12)
div.p: David prayed for God's favor and for the assurance that he enjoyed it.
He knew how miserable he would be if the Lord withdrew his consoling presence.
But the night of affliction will eventually end in a morning of comfort and praise.
He asked to understand God's will.
Henry calls this the first work of the Spirit.
The faithful person does not ask merely which road is easiest or most pleasant.
The right road matters more than the comfortable road.
Lord, do not only reveal your will to me; teach me how to carry it out.
Those who know the Lord as their God have the Holy Spirit as their Guide.
David also asked for renewed life and strength to obey.
Above all, we should ask for our sins to be destroyed, since they are our most dangerous enemies, so that we can serve the Lord faithfully.

row.cell: David acknowledges the great goodness of God, and prays for help.
He prays for the prosperity of his kingdom.

div.title: Remembering mercy and asking for more (verses 1–8)
div.p: When people become skilled and successful despite having few natural advantages, they should be especially aware that God has been their Teacher.
The greatest victory he gives is victory over one's own spirit, through self-control.
A prayer for further help should begin with thanksgiving for the mercy already received.
God exercised special power by moving Israel's people to submit to David.
That event pictured the way souls are brought into obedience to the Lord Jesus Christ.
Our earthly lives have little lasting substance.
It is strange that a soul destined to live forever devotes so many of its concerns to a body that will soon die.
Life passes like a moving shadow.
Even when believers enjoy great honor, they should remember their own unworthiness and sin, so that they are protected from pride and self-importance.
The Lord often comes to help his people when they are sinking and every other source of help has failed.

div.title: Praying for families, peace and the Lord's rule (verses 9–15)
div.p: New mercies call for new thanksgiving.
Praise God not only for what he has already granted, but also for the good he has promised and we still hope to receive.
Physical deliverance, whether from a sword or from wasting disease, would be of little ultimate value if a person remained under sin's dominion and the judgment to come.
David therefore prayed for his kingdom's prosperity.
Parents find joy in seeing their children likely to grow and do well.
May they be like healthy plants, not weeds or thorns.
May they grow rather than wither, bear fruit for God in their generation and become strong in the Spirit while young.
It is right to desire prosperity and full storehouses if these gifts make us more thankful toward God, generous to friends and charitable to poor people.
If our abundance produces none of these things, what profit is there in it?
We should also desire peace.
War causes countless harms, whether a people are attacking others or defending themselves.
A nation's real happiness declines as its people neglect God's worship and service.
Those who belong to the Savior, the Son of David, share the blessings of his kingdom and victories.
They are happy because the Lord is their God.

row.cell: David extols the power, goodness, and mercy of the Lord.
The glory of God's kingdom, and his care of those that love him.

div.title: Thanksgiving for the Redeemer's goodness (verses 1–9)
div.p: Those who pray earnestly through troubles and temptations will eventually have abundant reason to thank God.
Grateful praise is the true language of holy joy.
Above all, we should celebrate God's wonderful work of redemption as we speak of his greatness.
Neither Israel's rescues nor the punishment of sinners reveals God's justice as clearly to an enlightened mind as the cross of Jesus Christ.
Everything the Lord Jesus says and does is marked by goodness and grace.
He is full of compassion.
That is why he came into this world to save sinners.
During his earthly life, he showed mercy to both people's bodies and their souls.
He healed bodily sickness and taught them heavenly wisdom.
He is the merciful High Priest through whom God shows mercy to sinners.

div.title: The Lord's care and the glory of his kingdom (verses 10–21)
div.p: All God's works declare his praise.
He supplies the needs of every living creature.
