div.p: Failure to perform known duties, including performing duties carelessly, may harm the soul just as surely as committing active sins.

div.title: Verses 10 and 11 — God's strong tower versus wealth's illusion
div.p: The Lord's divine power, revealed through Jesus Christ, is a strong tower for those who trust him. Wealthy people who put ultimate confidence in earthly possessions imagine they live behind high and secure walls. Those defenses will fail when most needed, leaving them before the judgment of the One they rejected as Savior.

div.title: Verse 12 — Pride and humility
div.p: Pride raises the heart before a fall. Genuine honor follows humility.

div.title: Verse 13 — Listen before answering
div.p: Eagerness mixed with self-confidence exposes a person to shame when answering before understanding.

div.title: Verse 14 — When the spirit is wounded
div.p: Firmness of character can sustain people through many bodily pains. But a conscience tortured by remorse overwhelms even human courage. What, then, will hell be like?

div.title: Verse 15 — Knowledge must reach the heart
div.p: We should seek knowledge not merely to fill the mind but to change the heart.

div.title: Verse 16 — Welcome at the throne of grace
div.p: Bless the Lord, who welcomes us to his throne without money and without price. May the gifts he bestows make room for him within our souls.

div.title: Verse 17 — Hear what opponents say
div.p: Listening to criticism from our enemies can help us form a fairer judgment of ourselves.

div.title: Verse 18 — The seriousness of drawing lots
div.p: Matters were sometimes entrusted to God by casting lots with solemn prayer. But the lot has been profaned when used for entertainment or to seek another person's possessions; Henry raises this as an objection to such practices now.

div.title: Verse 19 — Avoid quarrels among relatives
div.p: Great care is needed to prevent conflict between relatives and others bound together by obligation. Wisdom and grace make forgiveness easier; sinful corruption makes it harder.

div.title: Verse 20 — What fills the heart determines satisfaction
div.p: The word belly here stands for the heart. Our inward peace and contentment depend upon what fills that heart.

div.title: Verse 21 — A tongue can destroy lives
div.p: Many people have caused their own death or the death of others through malicious or dishonest speech.

div.title: Verse 22 — A good marriage is God's gift
div.p: A good wife is a great blessing to her husband and a sign of the Lord's favor.

div.title: Verse 23 — Poverty and humble petitions
div.p: Poverty teaches that we cannot simply order others to serve our wishes. Before the throne of God's grace we all come as needy petitioners.

div.title: Verse 24 — Christ, the faithful Friend
div.p: Jesus Christ never abandons those who love and trust him. For his sake, may we show that kind of friendship to others. Having loved his own in the world, he loved them to the end; we are his friends if we obey his commands (John 15:14).

div.title: Verse 1 — The honor of poor believers
div.p: A poor person who fears God is more honorable and happier than someone lacking wisdom and grace, however rich or powerful.

div.title: Verse 2 — Think before moving
div.p: A soul without knowledge cannot live wisely. Rushing ahead without considering where our feet are going is sinful.

div.title: Verse 3 — Folly followed by resentment
div.p: People get themselves into trouble through foolishness, then become angry about God's providential arrangements.

div.title: Verse 4 — The power money holds
div.p: This verse exposes how strongly money can attract and govern human affection.

div.title: Verse 5 — Small lies grow
div.p: People who habitually lie in ordinary conversation are moving toward the still graver sin of false testimony.

div.title: Verse 6 — All gifts come from God
div.p: We have no excuse for withholding wholehearted love from God. His gifts are innumerable, and even other people's kindnesses are fruits of his generosity.

div.title: Verse 7 — Christ understands abandonment
div.p: Even Christ was deserted by his disciples, but the Father remained with him. The Savior's experience of poverty and rejection encourages our faith.

div.title: Verse 8 — Love your soul rightly
div.p: Only those who acquire true wisdom love their own souls as they ought.

div.title: Verse 9 — The danger of lying
div.p: Lying is a destructive sin that brings condemnation.

div.title: Verse 10 — True enjoyment requires grace
div.p: Without wisdom and grace, a person has no rightful claim to lasting joy. Those enslaved to sin should not oppress people whom God has made free.

div.title: Verse 11 — Overcome evil with good
div.p: The greatest honor belongs to those who most consistently seek to overcome evil through good.

div.title: Verse 12 — Christ the King
div.p: Christ's wrath against his enemies is terrifying like a roaring lion, while his favor toward his people is refreshing like dew.

div.title: Verse 13 — The uncertainties of comfort
div.p: The world's vanity appears when our greatest griefs arise from relationships or possessions in which we expected the greatest comfort.

div.title: Verse 14 — A virtuous spouse is precious
div.p: A prudent and godly wife is worth more than houses and wealth.

div.title: Verse 15 — Sloth brings want
div.p: A lazy disposition produces poverty and need. The warning applies to spiritual life as well as earthly affairs.

div.title: Verse 16 — Grace does not cancel obedience
div.p: Keeping God's word protects us from what is truly harmful. We abuse the doctrine of free grace if we claim it makes obedience unnecessary. Those who live carelessly will die; the warning should awaken even hardened sinners.

div.title: Verse 17 — God values care for the poor
div.p: God has chosen people who are poor in this world to be rich in faith and heirs of his kingdom.

div.title: Verse 18 — Correct children with wise affection
div.p: Parents must overcome misguided softness and correct their children; this is one way to help children grow into people who bring comfort and are happy themselves.

div.title: Verse 19 — Indulgence feeds violent anger
div.p: A child allowed every desire without correction is likely to become an adult with an uncontrolled temper.

div.title: Verse 20 — Learn while young
div.p: Those hoping to be wise at life's end must receive teaching and proper guidance while they are young.

div.title: Verse 21 — Let our plans agree with God's will
div.p: What better thing can we desire than that all our plans should agree with God's holy purposes?

div.title: Verse 22 — Good intentions without ability
div.p: It is better to have the heart to do good but lack the means, than to have ample means but no desire to help.

div.title: Verse 23 — Reverence brings true satisfaction
div.p: Those who live in the fear of God gain lasting security, contentment and happiness.

div.title: Verse 24 — Laziness can become helplessness
div.p: Habitual idleness grows until a person no longer has energy even for necessary self-care.

div.title: Verse 25 — Gentle correction is effective
div.p: A mild rebuke often does more to reach someone with understanding than harsh punishment.

div.title: Verse 26 — Honor parents and protect them
div.p: A young person who wastes a father's possessions or leaves an aged mother destitute behaves shamefully and will be disgraced.

div.title: Verse 27 — Avoid corrupting speech
div.p: Young people wisely refuse to listen to conversation that would implant sinful principles in the mind.

div.title: Verse 28 — Delighting in sin
div.p: The worst sinners actively welcome opportunities to do wrong.

div.title: Verse 29 — Christ's suffering guarantees judgment's reality
div.p: Human unbelief cannot cancel God's warnings. When Christ bore sins that were not his own, he was not spared: divine justice fell upon our blessed Surety. How could stubborn sinners expect impunity?

div.title: Verse 1 — The folly of drunkenness
div.p: Even highly capable people, as well as those lacking education, may make themselves foolish through the taste and excitement of strong drink.

div.title: Verse 2 — Fear the greater King
div.p: Earthly rulers may terrify those who provoke them. How much more foolish it is to provoke the King of kings!

div.title: Verse 3 — Choose peace over quarrels
div.p: Seeking disputes is great folly. For peace's sake, be willing to yield even a claim that is technically just.

div.title: Verse 4 — Work now for a future harvest
div.p: Those who labor patiently in preparing for eternity are also likely to be diligent in honest earthly responsibilities.

div.title: Verse 5 — Draw out wise counsel
div.p: People capable of giving valuable advice do not always volunteer it. Those who patiently draw it out will be well rewarded.

div.title: Verse 6 — Do good rather than boast
div.p: It is rare to find people who do more good than they talk about, or than they even care to hear praised.

div.title: Verse 7 — Integrity gives peace to the family
div.p: Honest people need not constantly devise schemes or fear their past deceit. Their households also benefit from their integrity.

div.title: Verse 8 — The responsibility of good rulers
div.p: People in high authority who are themselves good can accomplish much good and prevent much evil.

div.title: Verse 9 — Cleansing is the Holy Spirit's work
div.p: By grace, some can truthfully say they are purer than before. But this improvement is the work of the Holy Spirit.

div.title: Verse 10 — God rejects dishonest commerce
div.p: Love of money produces many kinds of deceit. The Lord will not bless wealth acquired through fraudulent practices.

div.title: Verse 11 — Watch children's behavior
div.p: Parents should carefully observe their children's conduct so they can guide and correct them appropriately.

div.title: Verse 12 — Use God's gifts for God
div.p: All our powers, senses and abilities come from God and should be used for his service.

div.title: Verse 13 — Work rather than indulge idleness
div.p: Those who surrender themselves to sleep and pleasure may lack even life's necessities, which honest labor could have supplied.

div.title: Verse 14 — Do not cheat in bargaining
div.p: People sometimes manipulate sellers or buyers in order to get a favorable price. They should be ashamed of fraud and lies, not proud of a bargain.

div.title: Verse 15 — Knowledge exceeds riches
div.p: Those who prefer true knowledge to wealth follow the path of godliness and happiness. If we believed this fully, God's word would be cherished and worldly wealth would lose its seductive attraction.

div.title: Verse 16 — Avoid reckless guarantees
div.p: Those who guarantee obligations recklessly or entangle themselves in immoral relationships put themselves in danger. Such arrangements do not deserve our confidence.

div.title: Verse 17 — Fraud's sweetness turns bitter
div.p: Dishonest gain may taste sweet to a sinful mind pleased by its own cleverness, but the memory of it will become bitter.

div.title: Verse 18 — Counsel for spiritual conflict
div.p: We especially need wise counsel in spiritual warfare. God's word and Spirit are the best advisers on every question.

div.title: Verse 19 — Do not purchase flattering praise
div.p: People who trust someone simply because that person speaks pleasantly may pay dearly for such admiration.

div.title: Verse 20 — The misery of disrespecting parents
div.p: Children who persist in dishonoring their parents will find neither genuine peace nor comfort.

div.title: Verse 21 — Sudden riches can vanish
div.p: A fortune gained too quickly may disappear just as quickly.

div.title: Verse 22 — Wait for the Lord
div.p: Trust the Lord's timing, obey his will, and rely upon him for protection rather than seeking revenge.

div.title: Verse 23 — Dishonesty makes a bad bargain
div.p: A deal achieved through fraud eventually proves to be a loss.

div.title: Verse 24 — Depend on God for every undertaking
div.p: We cannot wisely plan our lives or manage our affairs independently of the Lord.

div.title: Verse 25 — Watch conscience's evasions
div.p: The excuses people offer to quiet their own consciences show how deceitful the fallen heart can be.

div.title: Verse 26 — Justice distinguishes right from wrong
div.p: Just authority should restrain and punish evil, distinguishing wicked conduct from virtuous conduct.

div.title: Verse 27 — Conscience as a lamp
div.p: The rational soul and conscience are like a lamp within us. We should use that light to examine our motives and attitudes by God's revealed will.

div.title: Verse 28 — The glories of God's throne
div.p: Mercy and truth are the glories of God's kingship.

div.title: Verse 29 — Different ages, different strengths
div.p: Both young and old possess distinctive advantages. Neither should envy or despise the other.

div.title: Verse 30 — Correction may purify
div.p: Severe correction can sometimes accomplish real good. Fallen human nature makes us dislike rebuke, but if God uses painful trials to purify our hearts and prepare us for his work, we have reason to thank him.

div.title: Verse 1 — The Lord governs every heart
div.p: As a farmer directs water through the land, God directs human hearts as he chooses. Believers therefore ask him to turn their own hearts and others' hearts toward faith, reverence and love.

div.title: Verse 2 — Do not trust self-assessment
div.p: We are partial and biased when judging our own motives and actions.

div.title: Verse 3 — Outward worship cannot excuse injustice
div.p: Many deceive themselves by imagining that religious ceremonies make unjust behavior acceptable.

div.title: Verse 4 — Sin becomes the wicked person's life
div.p: Pride, ambition, honor, joy and daily occupation can all become expressions of a wicked person's devotion to sin.

div.title: Verse 5 — Diligence plans ahead
div.p: Truly diligent people combine steady work with thoughtful preparation.

div.title: Verse 6 — Unlawful wealth brings death
div.p: Those seeking riches through forbidden practices are actually pursuing their own ruin.

div.title: Verse 7 — Injustice returns upon its author
div.p: The injuries people inflict through injustice eventually rebound upon them, bringing destruction both here and hereafter.

div.title: Verse 8 — The crookedness of fallen nature
div.p: Without divine grace, humanity's ways are perverse and estranged from God.

div.title: Verse 9 — Seek relief from quarrels through prayer
div.p: It is wiser to avoid bitter conflict by pouring our hearts out before God. Through prudence, patience and constant prayer, God may remove the burden.

div.title: Verse 10 — Evil desires corrupt conduct
div.p: The wicked heart's desires lead to degrading behavior.

div.title: Verse 11 — Learn from warning and teaching
div.p: The inexperienced can learn wisdom from the punishment of evildoers and from instruction given to willing students.

div.title: Verse 12 — Do not envy evil prosperity
div.p: Good people recognize the curse hidden in the apparent success of wicked people and do not envy them.

div.title: Verse 13 — Listen to the poor
div.p: Those who oppress poor workers through low wages, refuse help when able, or neglect justice while in authority stop their ears to the needy. Charity still requires wise discernment, but not hardness of heart.

div.title: Verse 14 — Restrain passions by better motives
div.p: If money can calm human fury, surely reason, reverence for God and Christ's command should be strong enough to restrain it.

div.title: Verse 15 — The joy of true faith
div.p: Genuine joy is found in living according to true religion.

div.title: Verse 16 — Even straying sinners may return
div.p: Those who turn deliberately toward spiritual darkness are in special danger. Yet the all-sufficient Savior still offers hope: let them flee to him without delay.

div.title: Verse 17 — Worldly pleasure brings ruin
div.p: A life dedicated to sinful and worldly pleasures leads to destruction.

div.title: Verse 18 — God's providence delivers the righteous
div.p: The righteous may be delivered from trouble while the wicked fall into it instead, appearing almost as a ransom in their place.

div.title: Verse 19 — Unrestrained passions ruin relationships
div.p: Unchecked passions destroy peace and comfort within families and other close relationships.

div.title: Verse 20 — Prudence preserves provision
div.p: Abundance gained through wisdom, steady work and thrift is valuable. Foolish people waste what they possess on selfish desires.

div.title: Verse 21 — Faith produces a righteous life
div.p: True repentance and trust in God's mercy through Jesus Christ lead believers to pursue righteousness and mercy in their own conduct.

div.title: Verse 22 — Wisdom may overcome strength
div.p: Wise people can accomplish great things even against opponents confident in their superior physical power.

div.title: Verse 23 — Keep the soul from needless trouble
div.p: We should especially guard our souls against becoming trapped, agitated and disturbed.

div.title: Verse 24 — Pride becomes habitual anger
div.p: Proud and arrogant people often become so passionate that anger seems to be their regular occupation.

div.title: Verses 25 and 26 — The misery of laziness and greed
div.p: The lazy person's hands refuse honest work that could supply a living, while the heart never stops craving wealth, pleasure and honor. The righteous and industrious find their legitimate desires satisfied.

div.title: Verse 27 — Hypocritical worship is hateful
div.p: It is especially detestable to pretend holiness while secretly intending wickedness.

div.title: Verse 28 — False witnesses face judgment
div.p: Those who bear false testimony cannot escape its ultimate consequences.

div.title: Verse 29 — Ask what God requires
div.p: Wicked people defy both God's law and Providence's warnings. Good people ask instead, “What does God require of me?”

div.title: Verses 30 and 31 — Means are necessary, but salvation comes from God
div.p: We must make responsible use of available means, but our safety and salvation belong to the Lord alone. In spiritual warfare, put on the whole armor of God, relying for strength upon his mighty power.

div.title: Verse 1 — Value a good reputation
div.p: We should be more careful to acquire and preserve a good name than to increase our wealth.

div.title: Verse 2 — Rich and poor before God
div.p: Providence has ordered that some people are wealthy and others poor. Yet all are sinners before God, and the poor are as welcome as the rich at his throne of grace.

div.title: Verse 3 — Find refuge before the storm
div.p: Faith sees the judgment approaching sinners and turns to Jesus Christ as the sure refuge.

div.title: Verse 4 — Reverence produces humility
div.p: The fear of the Lord leads to humility, spiritual riches and ultimately eternal life.

div.title: Verse 5 — Two very different paths
div.p: The way of sin is dangerous and distressing, while the way of duty is safe and good.

div.title: Verse 6 — Train children toward the Savior
div.p: Raise children not along the path their fallen hearts naturally choose, but in the way they should follow. Lead each child to know the Savior as early as possible.

div.title: Verse 7 — Beware unnecessary debts
div.p: The danger of debt makes it important to avoid careless borrowing and obligations. Though rich and poor differ in this life, remember that the Lord governs the difference.

div.title: Verse 8 — Misused power fails
div.p: The strength and authority abused by wicked people will not last.

div.title: Verse 9 — Compassion receives blessing
div.p: Those who seek to relieve other people's needs and suffering receive God's blessing.

div.title: Verse 10 — Scoffing destroys peace
div.p: Profane mockers and slanderers disturb peaceful fellowship.

div.title: Verse 11 — Sincerity and divine friendship
div.p: God becomes the Friend of those whose hearts are without deceit. This honor belongs to all his faithful people.

div.title: Verse 12 — The defeat of treachery
div.p: God turns the clever plans of dishonest and treacherous people toward their own confusion.

div.title: Verse 13 — Laziness invents a lion
div.p: The lazy person imagines a lion waiting outdoors while ignoring the real danger of the devil—the roaring lion—and of idleness destroying the soul.

div.title: Verse 14 — Sexual impurity clouds judgment
div.p: Sexual wrongdoing can so darken the mind that recovery becomes exceedingly difficult.

div.title: Verse 15 — Foolishness in the human heart
div.p: Sinful folly belongs to human nature from childhood and clings to the soul. We all need correction from our heavenly Father.

div.title: Verse 16 — Responsible stewardship
div.p: We are stewards of what God entrusts to us and must use his gifts according to his will.

div.title: Verses 17–21 — Listen and trust God's word
div.p: Bend the ear to God's teaching and apply the heart to it through faith and love. The foundation of practical religion is delighting in God and depending upon him. The sure way to understand the truth of God's word is to live conscientiously according to it.

div.title: Verses 22 and 23 — Defend the poor
div.p: Those who exploit and oppress poor people do so at great danger to themselves. If others refuse to defend them, God himself will take up their cause.

div.title: Verses 24 and 25 — Avoid contagious anger
div.p: Our fallen hearts contain so much dry tinder that close association with people continually throwing sparks of anger is dangerous.

div.title: Verses 26 and 27 — Do not waste what families need
div.p: Everyone owes justice to themselves and their families. Carelessly guaranteeing debts or wasting needed possessions violates that duty.

div.title: Verse 28 — Respect property and work diligently
div.p: Do not infringe on another person's rightful property. True diligence is rare and valuable: it can lift people to higher responsibility. Most importantly, be diligent in God's work and in the duties of faith.

div.title: Verses 1–3 — Restrain appetite
div.p: God's limits upon our appetites are intended to protect us from injuring ourselves.

div.title: Verses 4 and 5 — Do not make wealth your goal
div.p: Do not become someone whose whole purpose is getting rich. Worldly possessions cannot satisfy the soul, and even what we grasp firmly cannot be held for long.

div.title: Verses 6–8 — Avoid insincere hospitality; welcome God's feast
div.p: Do not make yourself dependent upon people whose welcome is insincere. But when God invites us to his own feast, we can safely receive the Bread of Life and delight in his provision (Isaiah 25:6; 55:2).

div.title: Verse 9 — Know when silence is appropriate
div.p: We ought to speak about God's truth whenever there is a fitting opportunity, but when someone plainly refuses to listen, wisdom sometimes requires silence.

div.title: Verses 10 and 11 — God protects the fatherless
div.p: Fatherless children receive God's special care. He is their mighty Redeemer, fully able to defend them.

div.title: Verses 12–16 — Teach and lovingly correct children
div.p: A parent urges a child to give serious attention to Scripture, corrects wrongdoing with prayer while trusting God's blessing, and encourages obedience by showing what will bring genuine good. What joy parents have when children follow this faithful teaching!

div.title: Verses 17 and 18 — Do not envy temporary prosperity
div.p: The believer's hope will not be disappointed. Both present trials and the apparent prosperity of sinners are drawing toward their end.

div.title: Verses 19–28 — Give the whole heart to God
div.p: The gracious Savior purchased pardon and peace and calls us with a loving parent's affection to listen, become wise and follow his guidance. Young people should heed godly parents: when the heart is directed, the steps follow. Buy the truth and never sell it, not even for pleasure, honor or wealth. God requires the whole heart, not a portion divided between himself and the world. Follow Scripture, Providence and faithful examples. Guard particularly against drunkenness, which dulls the mind, and sexual immorality, which takes away the heart due to God and is difficult to escape once welcomed.

div.title: Verses 29–35 — The self-destruction of drunkenness
div.p: Avoid even the beginnings of alcohol's sinful allurements. Excess brings strife, impurity, insolence, uncontrolled speech and dulled conscience. A drunken person may face mortal danger yet feel secure, like someone sleeping atop a ship's mast. Even while judgment approaches, the person may insist, “I will seek it again.” What sensible person would sell themselves to a habit that risks dying senseless and waking under judgment? Henry understands Wisdom's words as Christ addressing sinners.

div.title: Verses 1 and 2 — Do not envy sinners
div.p: Never long to cast away God's restraints in order to live like those who reject him.

div.title: Verses 3–6 — Wisdom builds and strengthens
div.p: Godliness and prudence in outward affairs together form a wise person. Knowledge fills the soul with the Spirit's graces and comforts and strengthens us for spiritual service and warfare.

div.title: Verses 7–9 — Do not surrender to ignorance or devise harm
div.p: The foolish imagine wisdom is beyond them and refuse to seek it. Doing evil is wrong, but planning evil is worse. Even sinful thoughts as they first arise require repentance. People who try to make others hateful often become hateful themselves.

div.title: Verse 10 — Take heart in trouble
div.p: Trouble can tempt us to despair. Be courageous, and God will strengthen your heart.

div.title: Verses 11 and 12 — Rescue those in danger
div.p: If someone is threatened by an unjust action, we must do everything within our power to help. How much more should we seek to rescue immortal souls through our words and example?

div.title: Verses 13 and 14 — Taste the sweetness of wisdom
div.p: The pleasure and benefit of wisdom should move us to seek it. Most people readily enjoy sweet food, but too many have no taste for truth that is sweet to a renewed soul and makes us wise for salvation.

div.title: Verses 15 and 16 — The righteous rise after falling
div.p: Sincere believers may stumble like travelers over a stone, but they get up and proceed with greater care. Henry says this refers chiefly to falling into affliction rather than actual sin.

div.title: Verses 17 and 18 — Do not rejoice over an enemy's distress
div.p: We are forbidden to take sinful pleasure in the calamity of our enemies.

div.title: Verses 19 and 20 — Do not envy the prosperity of the wicked
div.p: Whatever outward success evildoers enjoy, it does not amount to true happiness.

div.title: Verses 21 and 22 — Faithfulness and social peace
div.p: Godly people promote peace in their communities. Better changes may sometimes be necessary, but avoid restless people who delight in upheaval.

div.title: Verses 23–26 — Be fair and give an honest answer
div.p: God's wisdom equips people for the duties of their positions. A fair and well-suited answer earns the lasting gratitude of those it benefits.

div.title: Verse 27 — Provide necessities before extras
div.p: Attend to necessary work and responsibilities before optional comforts. Do not go into debt carelessly.

div.title: Verses 28 and 29 — The duties of a truthful witness
div.p: Henry observes that these verses identify three faults of a witness. We should examine the warnings carefully and avoid giving false or retaliatory testimony.

div.title: Verses 30–34 — The neglected field and neglected soul
div.p: Farming is a blessing: without it the earth would be a wilderness. Even ordinary work is ruined by laziness and self-indulgence. Fields full of thorns and broken walls picture hearts left untended, where sinful desires grow as people fall asleep spiritually. Let that sight move us to greater diligence in every good work.

div.title: Verses 1–3 — God knows all; rulers must investigate
div.p: God never needs to investigate: nothing can be hidden from him. Rulers, however, are honored when they carefully search out matters and bring hidden wrongdoing into the light.

div.title: Verses 4 and 5 — Reforming government
div.p: A ruler best establishes a government by removing evil and correcting vice among the people.

div.title: Verses 6 and 7 — Choose humility before honor
div.p: True religion teaches humility and self-denial. Anyone who has seen God's glory in Jesus Christ recognizes personal unworthiness.

div.title: Verses 8–10 — Prevent unnecessary disputes
div.p: Rushing into conflict produces needless difficulty. Every war eventually ends; often it would be better not to have begun. The same is true of private quarrels: do everything possible to settle them.

div.title: Verses 11 and 12 — Words that suit their moment
div.p: Counsel and correction offered at the proper time are beautiful, like fine fruit enhanced by a vessel of silver.

div.title: Verse 13 — Be a faithful messenger
div.p: The aim of anyone entrusted with a task is to carry it out faithfully. We should especially welcome a faithful minister who serves as Christ's messenger.

div.title: Verse 14 — Do not claim gifts you have not given
div.p: Those who pretend to possess or have given gifts they never had are like clouds promising rain but leaving the fields dry.

div.title: Verse 15 — Persuasion needs patience
div.p: Bear a temporary injury patiently and speak without anger. Gentle persuasion is often more effective than force against a stubborn mind.

div.title: Verse 16 — Good things require moderation
div.p: God permits us to enjoy pleasant things, but warns against excess.

div.title: Verse 17 — Be a considerate neighbor
div.p: Even sincere neighbors need discretion to live peacefully together. God is a better Friend than any human friend: the more often we come to him, the more welcome we are.

div.title: Verse 18 — False testimony injures
div.p: A lying witness brings danger into every matter in which testimony is needed.

div.title: Verse 19 — An unreliable helper increases pain
div.p: Trusting an unfaithful person during hardship brings not merely disappointment but additional suffering.

div.title: Verse 20 — Do not trivialize sorrow
div.p: Trying to comfort grieving people by forcing merriment upon them is the wrong approach.

div.title: Verses 21 and 22 — Love even enemies
div.p: Loving enemies is already commanded in the Old Testament. Jesus Christ provided the supreme example, loving us while we were his enemies.

div.title: Verse 23 — Do not reward slander with attention
div.p: Slander would be spoken less readily if people did not eagerly listen to it. Sin loses courage when it meets firm resistance.

div.title: Verse 24 — Choose peace over miserable companionship
div.p: Solitude is better than sharing life with someone who continually destroys its peace.

div.title: Verse 25 — Good news from the far country
div.p: Heaven is a distant homeland. How refreshing is its news in the everlasting gospel, and in the Spirit's witness that we are God's children!

div.title: Verse 26 — When the righteous yield to sin
div.p: A righteous person led into wrongdoing harms others like a public spring whose waters have become poisoned.

div.title: Verse 27 — Resist excessive appetite and praise
div.p: By grace we must learn to deny not only bodily indulgence but also craving for other people's admiration.

div.title: Verse 28 — Ask the Spirit for self-control
div.p: A person unable to govern anger can easily lose peace. May we surrender ourselves to the Lord, ask him to put his Spirit within us, and follow his commands.

div.title: Verse 1 — Honor must be fitting
div.p: It is inappropriate to grant honor to people unfit or unworthy to receive it.

div.title: Verse 2 — A baseless curse cannot injure
div.p: A curse spoken without cause does no more lasting harm than a bird flying over someone's head.

div.title: Verse 3 — Correction suited to character
div.p: Every creature must be treated according to its nature. Careless and wicked people often refuse persuasion or reason. Human beings are naturally untamed, but God's grace changes some hearts.

div.title: Verses 4 and 5 — Answer fools with discernment
div.p: Choose how to respond according to the person and circumstances, addressing the conscience in whatever way may best end the dispute.

div.title: Verses 6–9 — Foolishness misuses wise sayings
div.p: Fools are unfit to carry important messages or receive great honors. Even wise proverbs lose their value when handled or applied foolishly.

div.title: Verse 10 — Two possible meanings of divine judgment
div.p: Henry allows two readings: the Creator will deal with sinners according to guilt, or powerful human rulers should disgrace and punish wicked conduct. Neither possibility should be silently replaced by the other.

div.title: Verse 11 — Returning to sin
div.p: A dog returning to its own filth is a revolting image of sinners who repeatedly return to their vices (2 Peter 2:22).

div.title: Verse 12 — The danger of self-conceit
div.p: Some people know very little yet are extraordinarily proud of it. They resemble those who think their spiritual condition is sound when it is desperately wrong.

div.title: Verse 13 — Imaginary dangers and real duties
div.p: The lazy person fears work and invents dangers. It is foolish to avoid a real duty through imagined difficulties, especially duties of faith.

div.title: Verse 14 — Movement without progress
div.p: Love of bodily ease produces spiritual sickness. Some religious people resemble a door turning on its hinges: they perform outward exercises but make no progress toward heaven because the world and flesh hold them fast.

div.title: Verse 15 — Laziness refuses even nourishment
div.p: The idle person may leave bed but still accomplish nothing. People neglecting duty often claim they cannot perform it. The spiritually lazy refuse to feed their souls on the Bread of Life or draw near in prayer for promised blessings.

div.title: Verse 16 — Labor in the Lord is not wasted
div.p: People who work diligently in spiritual service know they serve a good Master, and their labor will not be in vain.

div.title: Verse 17 — Avoid meddling in others' quarrels
div.p: Interfering without necessity in other people's disputes is a way of deliberately exposing ourselves to temptation.

div.title: Verses 18 and 19 — Do not excuse harm as a joke
div.p: People who sin as a joke must repent seriously or their wrongdoing will destroy them.

div.title: Verses 20–22 — Gossip sustains quarrels
div.p: Conflict can inflame families and communities. Whispering and malicious backbiting often kindle and feed the fire.

div.title: Verse 23 — The disguise of an evil heart
div.p: A wicked heart covered by attractive speech resembles a broken piece of pottery coated with the waste of silver.

div.title: Verses 24–26 — Beware flattering deceit
div.p: Be cautious of pleasing words unless the speaker's character is trustworthy. Satan spoke attractively to Eve; trusting his flattering temptations was ruinous.

div.title: Verse 27 — Schemes rebound upon their makers
div.p: Plotting evil is hard work, like digging a pit or rolling a heavy stone, but the plotter is often preparing the danger for himself.

div.title: Verse 28 — Two kinds of destructive lies
div.p: Henry distinguishes slandering lies, whose harm is plain, from flattering lies, which destroy secretly. A wise person may have more reason to fear a flatterer than a slanderer.

div.title: Verse 1 — Do not presume on tomorrow
div.p: We do not know what tomorrow may bring. This does not forbid sensible preparation; it forbids assuming tomorrow is guaranteed. Do not postpone the one necessary work of conversion.

div.title: Verse 2 — Avoid praising yourself
div.p: There may be times to defend your conduct, but self-praise is not fitting.

div.title: Verses 3 and 4 — Uncontrolled passion is a heavy burden
div.p: People unable to govern their emotions are often crushed by the weight of those passions.

div.title: Verses 5 and 6 — Faithful correction is love
div.p: A plain and sincere rebuke is better than hidden hatred or affection that praises a person while allowing sin to destroy the soul.

div.title: Verse 7 — Hunger makes the gospel sweet
div.p: Poor people often appreciate their modest comforts more and thank God for them more sincerely. Likewise the self-satisfied disdain the gospel, while those hungry for righteousness receive comfort even from a simple book or sermon about Christ.

div.title: Verse 8 — A proper place for duty
div.p: People have their own responsibilities and places in society where they can serve safely and contentedly.

div.title: Verses 9 and 10 — The nearer and better Friend
div.p: Do not assume relatives can help merely because of kinship. Seek trustworthy help from those able to respond. Above all there is a Friend closer than a brother; place complete confidence in him.

div.title: Verse 11 — Good conduct honors the gospel
div.p: Wise parents desire children whose prudent lives bring them joy. Likewise believers' consistent behavior offers the strongest answer to people who criticize the gospel.

div.title: Verse 12 — Do not walk toward temptation
div.p: People who knowingly expose themselves to temptation may fall into sin and reap painful consequences.

div.title: Verse 13 — Do not ruin yourself with rash debts
div.p: Someone may become poor while remaining honest. But it is not honest to bring ruin upon oneself through reckless financial undertakings.

div.title: Verse 14 — Beware craving praise
div.p: Loving admiration for its own sake is foolish and exposes us to the temptation of pride.

div.title: Verses 15 and 16 — Relentless quarreling
div.p: A neighbor's quarrel may be like a brief, sharp shower; perpetual disputes within marriage resemble continuous rain.

div.title: Verse 17 — Make one another wiser
div.p: Be thoughtful about whom you keep company with. Let the aim of conversation be to help one another grow wiser and better.

div.title: Verse 18 — Faithful service receives honor
div.p: Even a tiring or socially despised occupation can bring worthwhile results when performed faithfully. God honors those who serve him loyally.

div.title: Verse 19 — Examine the heart
div.p: Corrupt hearts resemble one another, as do hearts sanctified by God: the first bear the earthly image, the second the heavenly. Compare your own heart carefully with Scripture.

div.title: Verse 20 — Unsatisfied sin; satisfied faith
div.p: Death and sinful desire are never satisfied. The worldly heart always wants more profit or pleasure. Those looking toward the Lord, however, find their satisfaction in him forever.

div.title: Verse 21 — Praise tests character
div.p: As silver and gold are tested in the furnace, a person's character is tested by the way praise is received.

div.title: Verse 22 — Grace alone renews entrenched sin
div.p: Some people remain hardened even under severe correction. Only God's recreating grace can finally change a heart.

div.title: Verses 23–27 — Diligence, Providence and lasting treasure
div.p: Everyone should pursue useful work rather than idleness or interfering in matters they do not understand. Work diligently and wisely. Yet nothing earthly can be permanently secured, so choose a lasting inheritance. Trust God's blessing upon honest labor to provide as much temporal prosperity as is genuinely good for us.

div.title: Verse 1 — Sin makes cowards
div.p: Sinful people are often fearful. Those walking in their duty before God can remain courageous even amid real difficulties.

div.title: Verse 2 — Public wrongdoing disturbs a nation
div.p: A nation's sins undermine its public peace and stability.

div.title: Verse 3 — Oppression by the needy
div.p: When poor or needy people obtain power to exploit others, they may oppress more severely than the already wealthy.

div.title: Verse 4 — Sin encourages sin
div.p: Wicked people support and strengthen one another in their wrongdoing.

div.title: Verse 5 — Seek God to understand rightly
div.p: Seeking the Lord is evidence of some true understanding and one of the best means of gaining more.

div.title: Verse 6 — Godly poverty is better
div.p: An honest and reverent poor person is better than a wealthy but ungodly one, having greater inward comfort and bringing more good to the world.

div.title: Verse 7 — Bad company shames a family
div.p: Those who join the company of reckless people both grieve their parents and bring shame on them.

div.title: Verse 8 — Dishonest gain cannot endure
div.p: Wealth acquired through evil practices will not last, however large it grows. God may use its loss to help the poor and honor his justice.

div.title: Verse 9 — Do not reject God's commands while praying
div.p: The prayer that displeases God comes from someone who stubbornly refuses obedience to his known word.

div.title: Verse 10 — The misery of wicked success
div.p: The apparent success of ungodly people ultimately contributes to their own suffering.

div.title: Verse 11 — Wealth can blind judgment
div.p: Rich people are often flattered until they imagine themselves superior to everyone else.

div.title: Verse 12 — Freedom for the righteous benefits the land
div.p: A nation enjoys honor and well-being when faithful people have liberty.

div.title: Verse 13 — Confess sin to receive mercy
div.p: Excusing and concealing sin cannot bring real peace. Whoever confesses sin humbly with genuine repentance and faith finds mercy. The Son of God is our great atoning sacrifice; in our guilt and danger we may seek the mercy that reigns through righteousness to eternal life in Jesus Christ.

div.title: Verse 14 — Reverent fear without terror
div.p: There is a holy fear that brings happiness. Faith and love deliver believers from the fear of eternal condemnation, but we should always fear offending God and falling into sin.

div.title: Verse 15 — A wicked ruler is a predator
div.p: Whatever title society gives a cruel ruler, Scripture compares that ruler to a roaring lion and a roaming bear.

div.title: Verse 16 — Oppression is foolish
div.p: Oppressors lack understanding and damage even their own honor, ease and security.

div.title: Verse 17 — The burden of murder
div.p: People guilty of murder may be pursued by overwhelming terror. Henry speaks of their deserved punishment and the reluctance of others to protect them from it.

div.title: Verse 18 — Uprightness brings security
div.p: Integrity gives people holy confidence even in dangerous times, while dishonest and deceitful people can never feel truly secure.

div.title: Verse 19 — Honest labor provides
div.p: Diligent people choose the path toward a stable and comfortable livelihood.

div.title: Verse 20 — Holiness and honesty before quick wealth
div.p: The best route to happiness is a holy, honest life, not gaining a fortune rapidly without regard for right or wrong.

div.title: Verse 21 — Judgment must be impartial
div.p: Justice is corrupted whenever any consideration other than what is truly right governs a decision.

div.title: Verse 22 — Riches can vanish
div.p: People who rush to become wealthy seldom reflect on how quickly God may strip them of riches and leave them poor.

div.title: Verse 23 — Faithful rebuke is better than flattery
div.p: After reflection, most people value someone who corrected them honestly more than someone who merely soothed them with praise.

div.title: Verse 24 — Do not exploit parents
div.p: It is wicked to treat robbing one's parents as no sin, whether through manipulation, threats, squandering their goods or running up debts against them.

div.title: Verse 25 — Trusting grace brings peace
div.p: Those who continually depend upon God and his grace, living by faith, find inward rest.

div.title: Verse 26 — Do not trust the deceitful heart
div.p: A fool places confidence in personal strength, merit and righteousness, and in a heart that is deceitful and has already misled that person many times.

div.title: Verse 27 — Look for people in need
div.p: A selfish person not only fails to seek opportunities for compassion, but deliberately looks away when the need becomes visible.

div.title: Verse 28 — Wicked authority and Christ in Proverbs
div.p: When power belongs to the wicked, wise people may withdraw from public office. Henry concludes that even where Proverbs seem to speak least directly of Christ, careful reading will uncover truths that lead to him.

div.title: Verse 1 — Flee from the coming judgment
div.p: If God wounds, who can heal? His word warns everyone to flee from the wrath to come and take hold of the hope set before us in Jesus Christ.

div.title: Verse 2 — Righteousness in government
div.p: People have reason to rejoice when their rulers are righteous and to mourn when those rulers are wicked.

div.title: Verse 3 — Wisdom protects against lust
div.p: Divine wisdom is our strongest safeguard against the sinful desires that bring people to ruin.

div.title: Verse 4 — Christ rules with justice
div.p: The Lord Jesus is the King who will administer true justice among his people.

div.title: Verse 5 — Flattery disarms
div.p: Flatterers cause people to lower their guard, making it easier to draw them into foolish behavior.

div.title: Verse 6 — Sin entangles; righteousness frees
div.p: Transgression ends in distress, while righteous people walk in liberty and safety.

div.title: Verse 7 — Care for the poor
div.p: The righteous show compassion for people in poverty and distress. The wicked disregard their needs without feeling.

div.title: Verse 8 — Mockery and public peace
div.p: Scornful people laugh at holy and serious matters. Those who advance true religion and wisdom help turn away God's wrath.

div.title: Verse 9 — Argument with a conceited person
div.p: When a wise person disputes with a quarrelsome, conceited opponent, anger or ridicule often follows, and little good results.

div.title: Verse 10 — Love for those who hate us
div.p: Christ warned his disciples that people would hate them. Yet the righteous, even when hated by bloodthirsty people, willingly do what they can for those people's salvation.

div.title: Verse 11 — Keep counsel
div.p: A fool says everything that comes to mind or has been learned and cannot keep a confidence.

div.title: Verse 12 — Bad leadership spreads lies
div.p: A ruler who welcomes flatterers and listens to slander makes liars and false accusers of those who serve him.

div.title: Verse 13 — All live under God's gifts
div.p: Some people are poor, while others possess great wealth dishonestly acquired. They meet in daily business, and God supplies life's comforts to both. He also gives saving grace to some among both groups.

div.title: Verse 14 — Defend those without power
div.p: Rich people usually look after their own interests. A ruler should protect poor and needy people and plead their cause.

div.title: Verse 15 — Correct children wisely
div.p: Parents should consider both the good that comes from appropriate correction and the harm caused by excessive indulgence.

div.title: Verse 16 — Do not be shaken by growing evil
div.p: Believers should not allow the multiplication of wickedness and wicked people to overthrow their faith or hope. Wait patiently upon the Lord.

div.title: Verse 17 — Do not neglect necessary correction
div.p: When children act wrongly, parents must not simply leave them without correction.

div.title: Verse 18 — The precious open vision of Christ
div.p: A place without Bibles and faithful ministers is spiritually exposed and vulnerable to the enemy of souls. The gospel is an open vision revealing Christ: it humbles sinners, exalts the Savior and promotes holiness in everyday conduct. These precious truths sustain spiritual life and preserve souls from destruction.

div.title: Verse 19 — Serving only from fear
div.p: The servant described here is lazy, unprofitable and wicked. The service arises neither from love nor from conscience, but only from fear.

div.title: Verse 20 — Rash self-conceit
div.p: A self-important person who speaks rashly and constantly quarrels can be less open to correction than even ignorant or openly immoral people.

div.title: Verse 21 — Kindness is not indulgence
div.p: Good treatment of a servant does not mean indulgence that ultimately ruins the servant, just as it could ruin a child. The body serves the soul: pampering its every demand encourages it to forget that proper relationship.

div.title: Verse 22 — The fruit of an angry spirit
div.p: A passionate, angry disposition provokes other people and also offends God.

div.title: Verse 23 — Humility before honor
div.p: Only those who humble themselves will be exalted and firmly established.

div.title: Verse 24 — Receiving stolen goods
div.p: Someone knowingly receiving stolen property shares in the thief's wrongdoing.

div.title: Verse 25 — Do not be ashamed of Christ
div.p: Many people are ashamed to acknowledge Christ now. He will not acknowledge them at judgment. But trust in the Lord saves us from this snare.

div.title: Verse 26 — Seek the supreme Ruler's favor
div.p: The wisest course is to seek God's favor, for he is the Ruler of rulers. Every creature becomes to us what God makes that creature to be.

div.title: Verse 27 — Hate sin, not souls
div.p: The righteous hate the wicked person's sin and avoid corrupting company. Christ exposed human wickedness but prayed for his persecutors while they crucified him. A Christian must hate sin within oneself and others, while seeking sinners' salvation. Those who remain unholy, however, have a deep hostility to godliness.

div.title: Verses 1–6 — Agur's humility and God's sufficient word
div.p: Agur describes himself as lacking righteousness and having acted foolishly. We should likewise think humbly about ourselves.

He says he needs revelation to guide him into truth and wisdom. The more understanding people gain, the more clearly they see how much they do not know. They become eager to discover still more of God and the riches of his grace in Jesus Christ.
Henry understands verse 4 as a prophetic reference to the One who descended from heaven to become our Teacher and Savior, then ascended to heaven as our Advocate.
The Messiah is presented here, in Henry's reading, as a Person distinct from the Father, although his name remained hidden at that time.

Even the Redeemer's wonderful works of providence and grace cannot be completely searched out. Without Christ, Henry says, the foundations of the earth would have sunk beneath the curse brought upon creation through human sin.
Who is the mighty One accomplishing all this?
God's word lacks nothing necessary to fulfill its purpose. Adding to it opens the way for error and corruption.

div.title: Verses 7–9 — Neither poverty nor riches
div.p: Agur wisely asks to be kept in a middle condition, away from the temptations associated with both poverty and wealth.
He prays for daily bread appropriate to his circumstances, family and genuine welfare. His prayer strikingly resembles parts of the Lord's Prayer.
If God removes vanity and lies from us, grants us a share in Christ's pardoning love, becomes our portion and teaches us to walk with him, we have far more than everything we need spiritually.
People who possess abundance are tempted to abuse it. Poverty also brings distress and temptation.
That is why Agur's prayer is wise, although seldom offered sincerely.
What is appropriate provision for one person or family may not be appropriate for another. We can nevertheless trust our heavenly Father to provide whatever is genuinely good for us.
Why should we desire more than that?

div.title: Verse 10 — Do not slander a servant
div.p: Do not maliciously accuse a servant to an employer, even in relatively small matters, in order to cause trouble.

div.title: Verses 11–14 — Four kinds of deeply corrupt people
div.p: Every age contains people who repay their parents' care with monstrous ingratitude.
Others persuade themselves they are holy while secretly practicing wickedness and cherishing sinful hearts.
Still others display outrageous pride.
And in every age there have been people of exceptional cruelty.

div.title: Verses 15–17 — Greed, cruelty and contempt for parents
div.p: Cruelty and covetousness are like the two daughters of the leech, endlessly demanding, “Give, give!”
Such passions never give their owners peace. They resemble four things that can never be satisfied.
People who continually crave more wealth are never truly rich.
Many who came to a terrible end later acknowledged that their wicked course began when they despised their parents' authority.

div.title: Verses 18–20 — Wonders of nature and the hidden ways of sin
div.p: Four things lie beyond complete human understanding.
Nature itself is full of astonishing mysteries.
But Henry describes the fourth example as a mystery of iniquity: the tactics through which a corrupt seducer wins a woman's affection and those through which an immoral woman conceals her misconduct.
His comments here concern the hidden tactics of wrongdoing, not a claim that every relationship or woman resembles these examples.

div.title: Verses 21–23 — Four kinds of troublesome people
div.p: Henry describes four types of people whose behavior causes considerable disturbance.
The first is someone who rises from humble beginnings to authority but possesses a base and tyrannical spirit. The problem is not poverty or low birth, but the abuse of power.
The second is a foolish, violent person given over to excess.
The third is a woman with a contentious spirit and corrupt habits.
The fourth is a servant who gains improper influence and abuses it.
Those whom Providence raises from humble circumstances should particularly guard against temptations that could corrupt their new position.

div.title: Verses 24–28 — Wisdom learned from small creatures
div.p: Four small creatures deserve our admiration for their wisdom.
They remind us that people who are poor, obscure and considered of little importance in the present world may nevertheless be wise concerning their own souls and the life to come.

div.title: Verses 29–33 — Self-government and peace
div.p: We can learn appropriate conduct even from animals.
We should learn particularly to govern our temper when others provoke us.
An evil thought must not be allowed to become evil speech. Nor should we stir up anger in other people.
Let us act and speak without violence, showing gentleness and calmness.
How often we have acted foolishly in rebellion against the Lord our King!
Let us humble ourselves before him.
Having found peace with God, let us pursue peace with everyone.

row.cell: An exhortation to king Lemuel to take heed of sin, and to do duties.
The description of a virtuous woman.

div.title: Lemuel's mother's instructions (verses 1–9)
div.p: While children are under a mother's care, she has an important opportunity to shape their minds in the right way.
Even after growing up, people should often remember the faithful lessons they received during childhood.
Many young people who once appeared promising have been ruined through immoral relationships or love of wine. Their example warns us against these dangers.
Wine, Henry says, can properly be used in need or as medicine. Every creature of God is good, and wine has legitimate purposes, although people often abuse it.
The same principle applies figuratively to praise and consolation.
Encouragement is like a restorative medicine when offered to people who are downcast, struggling or tempted. It is not appropriate to flatter someone already self-satisfied and overconfident.
People in positions of authority should practice even greater temperance than others.
They should also defend people who cannot or dare not speak for themselves.
Our blessed Lord did not refuse even the most bitter suffering in the cup his Father appointed him.
Yet he places the cup of consolation in the hands of his people and brings joy to those experiencing the deepest grief.

div.title: The virtuous woman (verses 10–31)
div.p: This passage describes a virtuous woman living in its own historical setting. Henry says that its broad principles are appropriate for every age and nation.

She carefully seeks her husband's respect and affection, understands his wishes and willingly accepts his authority. This reflects Henry's original account of marital relationships, rather than a new editorial judgment about social expectations.
Henry then describes eight qualities.
1. Trustworthiness and devotion to her husband's good. Her husband can confidently entrust his household to her care. Her constant intention is to do him good and bring happiness to their home.
2. Industry and joy in duty. She works diligently and takes pleasure in her responsibilities. She makes good use of time, rises early, does her work energetically and refuses to waste her days.
3. Prudent household management. She makes wise use of what her work produces, does not spend beyond the family's means and provides thoughtfully for current and future needs.
4. Responsible leadership of the household. She watches over the affairs of her household so that everyone can fulfill duties toward God, one another and herself.
5. Cheerful generosity. She is as ready to give as to receive, helping others freely and gladly.

6. Wise and gracious speech. She acts with discretion, governs her words by wisdom and advises others carefully. The law of kindness and love is written upon her heart, and it is evident in the way she speaks.
Even while her hands are occupied with earthly responsibilities, her heart is filled with the world to come.

7. Reverence for the Lord. More important than every other quality is her fear of God. Beauty alone proves neither wisdom nor goodness and can mislead people who choose a spouse on that basis. But reverence for God is the beauty of the soul, a beauty that endures forever.

8. Strength to endure hardship. She can bear disappointments and trials with courage. When she grows old, she can look back with comfort upon a youth devoted to useful work, and she can rejoice in the hope of the coming life.
She is a great blessing to her family.
Good fruit deserves a good reputation, but she does not need to praise herself: her work speaks on her behalf.
Everyone should seek the honor that comes from God and evaluate others by that standard.
Henry urges women who wish to be respected, loved and useful to study this picture regularly.
He also invites a spiritual application to the church.
Scripture describes God's church as a virtuous bride.
Through grace, God gathers a church of true believers from among sinful human beings and forms in it the excellent qualities described here.

div.title: Ecclesiastes — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The title Ecclesiastes means “The Preacher.”
Here God's wisdom preaches to us through Solomon, whom Henry identifies as the author.
Henry presents the book as a record written by Solomon near the end of his life, when he had come to understand his own sin and foolishness.
Solomon described his experience for the benefit of others; Henry calls the book the record of his repentance.
His conclusion concerning earthly goods was that they are all vanity and vexation of spirit.
This book teaches the emptiness of the world and its inability to make us happy. It also exposes sin's evil and the misery toward which sin inevitably leads.
No created good can finally satisfy the soul.

p.hi: True happiness is found in God alone.

div.p: Through the teaching of the blessed Holy Spirit, this truth must lead the heart to Jesus Christ.

row.cell: Solomon shows that all human things are vain.
Man's toil and want of satisfaction.
The vexation in pursuit of knowledge.

div.title: Solomon declares the world's vanity (verses 1–3)
div.p: We can learn a great deal by comparing one part of Scripture with another.
Here we see Solomon returning from the world's broken and empty cisterns to the Fountain of living water.
He records the foolishness and shame of his former choices, the bitterness of disappointment and the lessons he learned.
People who have themselves been warned and have turned away from death should warn others not to continue toward destruction.
Solomon does not merely say that worldly things are vain. He says they are vanity itself.

p.hi: “Vanity of vanities! All is vanity!”

div.p: This is the central theme of the Preacher's message, and he never loses sight of it throughout this book.
If life in this fallen world were all we could look forward to, living for it would be futile.
Even the greatest abundance of wealth and pleasure cannot make a human being happy.
What do we gain from all our work?
We cannot use its profits to meet the soul's needs, satisfy its desires, atone for its sins or prevent its destruction.
What will worldly wealth profit the soul at death, in judgment or in eternity?

div.title: Human work never finally satisfies (verses 4–8)
div.p: Everything changes, and nothing remains at rest.
Despite all human effort, people are no nearer to finding true rest than the sun, the wind or the flowing river.
Our souls will find no lasting rest unless it comes from God.
Our bodily senses soon grow weary of what they experience, yet they still long for something new and untried.

div.title: Nothing is truly new (verses 9–11)
div.p: Human hearts are still marked by the same fallen corruption as in earlier generations.
Their desires, pursuits and complaints have not fundamentally changed.
Recognizing this should lead us to stop expecting happiness from created things and to seek eternal blessings instead.
How many people and accomplishments were celebrated as extraordinary in Solomon's time, yet no one remembers them now?

div.title: Even great knowledge leaves the soul unsatisfied (verses 12–18)
div.p: Solomon examined every kind of pursuit and found vanity.
Even his studies and investigations into knowledge wearied him, not only physically but mentally.
The more deeply he considered what happens under the sun, the more clearly he saw its emptiness, and the more troubled he became.
He could neither gain the satisfaction he hoped for nor accomplish as much good for others as he had imagined.
Pursuing wisdom and knowledge exposed human wickedness and misery.
The more Solomon learned, the more reason he saw for sorrow.
Let us therefore hate and fear sin, the cause of the world's emptiness and misery.
Let us value Christ and seek our rest in knowing, loving and serving the Savior.

row.cell: The vanity and vexation of mirth, sensual pleasure, riches, and pomp.
This world to be used according to the will of God.

div.title: Pleasure, wealth and magnificence cannot satisfy (verses 1–11)
div.p: Solomon soon discovered that laughter and pleasure were vanity.
Loud, glittering entertainment does little to make a person genuinely happy.
The many things people attempt in order to find satisfaction in the world—and the way they keep moving from one to another—resemble a feverish person's restless tossing.
When Solomon realized the folly of giving himself to wine, he turned to the expensive amusements and entertainments of rulers.
Poor people reading the description may be tempted to envy him or resent their own circumstances.
But the remedy is to listen to the wealthy man's own judgment on those pleasures.
They were all vanity and vexation of spirit.
The same experiences would bring us the same disappointing result.
Having food and clothing, let us learn to be content.
Solomon retained his great human knowledge and understanding throughout these experiments.
Yet worldly pleasure, when separated from spiritual blessings, leaves the mind still longing for more and never truly satisfied.
Happiness does not come from the social position or circumstances we occupy.
Final blessedness comes only through Jesus Christ.

div.title: Human wisdom cannot make a person finally happy (verses 12–17)
div.p: Solomon found that knowledge and prudence are better than ignorance and foolishness.
Nevertheless, human learning and wisdom cannot give eternal happiness.
The greatest scholar who dies without knowing Jesus Christ is lost just as surely as the person who never received an education.
What value will worldly praise have for the body in the grave or the soul in hell?
And those whose spirits have been made perfect in heaven have no need of it either.
If this world were all we had, these things might cause us to despair of earthly life as nothing but vanity and vexation of spirit.

div.title: Use this world's gifts according to God's will (verses 18–26)
div.p: Our hearts are often reluctant to give up their expectation of finding something truly great and lasting in the created world.
Solomon eventually learned to surrender that expectation.
Even wealthy people live in a valley of tears.
It is foolish to become a slave to worldly pursuits when they can provide nothing greater than support for the body.
At best we can enjoy a moderate and cheerful use of earthly things, suited to our circumstances and position.
But we should also take joy in honest work.
The things God gives us should help us fulfill our ordinary responsibilities diligently and cheerfully.
This contentment is God's gift.
Wealth can be either a blessing or a curse, depending on whether a person has a heart that uses it wisely.
God gives those he accepts joy and satisfaction in knowing and loving him.
But sinners who make the world their entire portion find labor, sorrow, emptiness and vexation—then ultimately leave the wealth they pursued to other people.
Let sinners reflect seriously upon their end.
Seeking a lasting inheritance in Christ's love and the blessings that follow from it is the only way to enjoy even present life in a truly satisfying way.

div.title: The changing seasons of human life (verses 1–10)
div.p: Anyone seeking lasting happiness in an ever-changing world will be disappointed.
It is our duty and wisdom to accept the circumstances God appoints and live faithfully in them.
His whole plan for governing the world will eventually prove wise, just and good.
We should therefore seize favorable opportunities for every good purpose and task.
The time when we must die is coming quickly.
Meanwhile human life is full of labor and sorrow.
Yet God allows us to experience this work so that we always have something useful to do.
No one was sent into the world merely to be idle.

div.title: God's purposes do not change (verses 11–15)
div.p: Things truly are as God has made them, not necessarily as they appear to us.
Worldly concerns so fill our hearts and minds that we often lack the time or desire to notice God's hand in events.
The world not only takes possession of our affections; it also leads us to form unfair thoughts about the beauty of God's works.
We are mistaken if we think we were born only for ourselves.

p.hi: Our task is to do good during a brief and uncertain life.

div.p: Because our time for such service is limited, we must use it carefully.
Being content with God's Providence means trusting that all things work together for good for those who love him.
God acts so that people will reverence him.
As the world has been, so it is now and so it will be.
Every change and temptation we meet belongs to the kinds of experiences shared by humanity.
We are not enduring some entirely unprecedented form of testing.

div.title: Worldly power cannot escape final judgment (verses 16–22)
div.p: Without reverence for the Lord, human authority is empty.
When judges cast aside fear of God, they misuse their power.
But another Judge stands at the door.
God has appointed a time to correct injustices, even if we do not yet see that correction.

Solomon appears to wish that people would recognize this: by choosing the present world as their ultimate portion, they bring their lives down toward the level of animals, while still enduring the anxieties of this life and awaiting an account of their conduct.
Both humans and animals return to the dust from which they were taken.
How little reason we have to boast about our bodies or physical accomplishments!
But the human rational soul and an animal's life are fundamentally different, even if few people think properly about the difference.
Henry explains that the human spirit goes upward to judgment, where its eternal state is fixed in unchanging happiness or misery.
The life of an animal, by contrast, perishes with the animal's death.
How pitiable are those whose greatest wish is simply to die as animals die!
Our crucial question is how eternal existence may become eternal happiness.
That is the great purpose of revelation.

p.hi: Jesus is revealed as the Son of God and the Hope of sinners.

div.title: The misery caused by oppression (verses 1–3)
div.p: Solomon grieved when he saw power overcoming justice.
Wherever we look, we see sorrowful evidence of human wickedness and misery.
People create suffering both for themselves and for one another.
Those treated cruelly may become so miserable that they wish they had never been born.
But a godly person, though suffering in this life, has no true reason to make that wish.
Such a person may be glorifying the Lord even in the fire and will ultimately enjoy everlasting happiness.
The ungodly have still greater reason to desire that their present lives continue, despite their troubles, because if they die unrepentant their future condition will be far worse.
If earthly and human things were the highest possible good, then given all the world's oppression, not existing would be preferable.
But they are not the highest good.

div.title: Envy and indolence both cause trouble (verses 4–6)
div.p: Those who work diligently and succeed often attract envy and opposition.
Other people, seeing the difficulties and hostility faced by hardworking neighbors, imagine they would find greater happiness in doing nothing.
But idleness is a sin that brings its own punishment.
Let us earn enough through honest work to obtain our necessities—the metaphorical one handful—rather than grasping for two overflowing handfuls and filling our lives with anxiety.
Moderate effort and moderate gain are best.

div.title: Selfish greed cannot be satisfied (verses 7 and 8)
div.p: Often the more people possess, the more they desire.
They become so absorbed in accumulating wealth that they cannot enjoy what they already own.
Selfishness lies at the heart of this folly.
Such people care for almost no one—not even enough for themselves to allow sufficient rest for themselves or their workers.
They may have everything necessary for their employment and family but still feel that their eyes have not seen enough.
Worldliness can rob people not only of God's favor and eternal life but also of this life's ordinary pleasures.
Relatives or strangers may inherit the fortune they accumulated, yet will feel no gratitude for the sacrifice.
Greed grows with practice and advancing age, sometimes becoming strongest when the grave is near.

How astonishing that people claiming to follow Christ, who became poor for our sake though he was rich, can still obsessively hoard money while excusing themselves through talk of prudent provision and the dangers of extravagance!

div.title: Mutual assistance and fellowship (verses 9–12)
div.p: Someone working hard to support loved ones gains more satisfaction than a miser laboring only to accumulate money.
Cooperation makes many things safer and more effective.
This is especially true of fellowship between Christians.
Believers strengthen one another through encouragement and friendly correction.
They warm one another's hearts by speaking of Christ's love and singing his praise together.
Let us use our opportunities for Christian friendship well.
Not everything in such fellowship is vanity, although its joys remain imperfect in this life.
When two people unite in holy love and fellowship, Christ by his Spirit joins them, forming a threefold cord.

div.title: Even royal favor changes (verses 13–16)
div.p: People are rarely satisfied for long.
They become eager for change and easily grow tired of their rulers.
That is nothing new.
Kings can find themselves rejected by people they made great efforts to help.
Such is the emptiness and frustration of worldly honor.
But the willing servants of our King, the Lord Jesus, rejoice in him alone, and their love for him will grow forever.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections
Worship, words and wandering thoughts (verses 1–3)
div.p: When approaching God in worship, take time to prepare your mind.
Guard your thoughts against wandering, and keep your affections from becoming absorbed in wrong things.
We should avoid meaningless repetition.
The passage does not condemn long or detailed prayers in themselves.
It condemns prayers made up of words that carry no sincere meaning.
Our thoughts wander so frequently that attendance at God's appointed worship can become little better than the sacrifice of fools.
Hasty and thoughtless words in prayer reveal a foolish heart, a low view of God and carelessness concerning our souls.

div.title: Vows, fear of people and injustice (verses 4–8)
div.p: When people make promises rashly, their own words lead them into sin.
Henry describes a person coming before the priest and trying to excuse a vow by claiming it was rash or wrong to fulfill.
Such mockery of God could bring his displeasure and destroy the gain the person hoped to retain improperly.
Do not be controlled by fear of other people.
Keep God before your eyes.
When you see the poor oppressed, do not use that wrongdoing to accuse divine Providence of injustice.
Nor should you despise the institution of civil government merely because people corrupt its purposes.
Likewise, do not reject religion because faithful people sometimes suffer mistreatment.
Even if oppressors seem secure for a long time, God will call everyone to account.

div.title: The vanity of great riches (verses 9–17)
div.p: The kindness of God's Providence is distributed more widely than a careless observer may imagine.
A king needs the same basic necessities of life as other people.
Poor people may enjoy simple food more than a king enjoys a luxurious feast.
Certain bodily needs cannot be satisfied by silver, and worldly abundance cannot satisfy the soul's spiritual desires.
More wealth requires a bigger household, more servants, more guests and more people depending upon it.
A laborer often sleeps well, not only because of physical tiredness, but because there are few anxious responsibilities to interrupt the night.
The believer who has worked diligently in God's service can also rest sweetly in him, even in the long sleep of death.
By contrast, people who possess almost everything may still be unable to obtain a good night's sleep.
Their abundance itself becomes the source of anxiety.
Riches can harm their owners, leading the heart away from God and duty.
Rich people may also use wealth to indulge their own sinful desires and oppress others.
At death they discover that their work was labor for the wind.
They cannot tell where the benefits have gone.
When worldly people lose what they coveted, they often respond not with godly repentance but by anger toward God's Providence and everyone around them, multiplying their misery.

div.title: Enjoy God's gifts with grateful obedience (verses 18–20)
div.p: Life is God's gift.
We should not regard our vocation as mere drudgery but seek appropriate joy in the work God has assigned us.
A cheerful spirit is a great gift.
It makes duties easier and suffering more bearable.
Those who have used wealth rightly may remember earlier days with thankfulness and comfort.
Solomon repeatedly describes God as the Giver of both life and its enjoyment.
We must therefore receive his gifts and use them according to his will and for his glory.
Let this passage lead us to Christ's gracious command:
Do not labor only for food that perishes, but for food enduring to eternal life.
Christ is the Bread of Life, the soul's only true food.
Everyone is invited to receive this heavenly provision.

row.cell: The vanity of riches. Also of long life and flourishing families.
The little advantage any one has in outward things.

div.title: Riches, children and long life cannot guarantee happiness (verses 1–6)
div.p: A person may possess everything needed for earthly comfort, yet the Lord may leave that person to greed or other sinful dispositions, so that these gifts are neither used wisely nor enjoyed peacefully.
Eventually those possessions pass into the hands of strangers.
Such a life is vanity and a grievous affliction.
Among the Hebrews, a large family was highly desired and honored.
Nearly everyone also wants a long life.
Yet even when a person enjoys both advantages, that person may still gain no happiness from wealth, family or length of days.
Someone in this condition seems to have passed through the world without accomplishing anything useful or good.
Solomon even says that a child who lives for only a moment and then dies has a better portion than someone who lives a very long life in nothing but continual suffering.

div.title: Outward advantages cannot satisfy the soul (verses 7–12)
div.p: Only a little is needed to support life in reasonable comfort.
Great abundance can do no more than provide for those basic needs.
Worldly wealth has nothing that can satisfy the soul's deepest desires.
The poor can enjoy comfort just as the wealthy do, and poverty does not necessarily put them at a true disadvantage.
We should never say that what the eyes can see is better than the soul's rest in God.
It is better to live by faith in future blessings than to be governed only by immediate sights and pleasures.
God has appointed our circumstances.
What he chooses to give should satisfy us.
Even the greatest possessions and honors cannot lift us above the ordinary changes and hardships of human life.
What then do we finally gain through all our worldly plans and pursuits, when those pursuits only multiply vanity?
Life upon earth is measured in days.
It is short and uncertain, and it contains little that can sustain our hopes permanently.
Let us return to God, trust his mercy through Jesus Christ and submit to his will.
Soon we will pass through this troubled world and enter the place where joy is full and pleasures last forever.

row.cell: The benefit of a good name; of death above life; of sorrow above vain mirth.
Experience of the evil of sin.

div.title: A good name, sober reflection and godly correction (verses 1–6)
div.p: A reputation for godliness and honesty is worth more than all this world's wealth and pleasure.
It can be more beneficial to visit a funeral than a feast.
Both can be lawful at the proper time.
Our Savior attended a wedding celebration at Cana and wept at the grave of a friend in Bethany.
But because we are easily led toward vanity and indulgence of sinful desires, visiting mourners may be particularly useful.
There we learn what becomes of every human life in this world.
Serious thought is better for us than noisy amusement when it teaches what truly matters.
What benefits the soul is best for us, even when it does not feel pleasant.
It is better for our sinful inclinations to be corrected by a wise person's rebuke than to have them flattered by the songs of foolish people.
The laughter of fools quickly vanishes, and its end is sorrow.

div.title: Be patient; do not idealize the past (verses 7–10)
div.p: The outcome of trials and difficulties is often better than we first imagined.
A patient spirit is far better than one proud, rash and impatient.
