Do not become angry quickly or respond immediately to every insult.
Nor should anger remain for a long time.
Even a wise person may feel anger, but it should pass through like a traveler, not take up permanent residence.
Anger makes its home only among fools.
It is foolish to complain continually about the wickedness of the present age when we have even more reason to lament the wrongdoing within our own hearts.
Even now we enjoy many mercies.
It is equally foolish to imagine that earlier generations were uniformly better.
They had their own reasons for complaint and trouble.
Nostalgia of this kind often springs from discontent and a readiness to quarrel even with God.

div.title: Wisdom, correction and the limits of self-righteousness (verses 11–22)
div.p: Wisdom is as valuable as an inheritance, indeed more valuable.
It protects the heart during life's storms and scorching heat.
Money cannot lengthen the natural life appointed to us.
But true wisdom brings spiritual life and strengthens people to serve God amid suffering.
We should regard our circumstances as governed by him; the end will show the justice and goodness of his decisions.
Even while pursuing righteousness, do not be carried away by passionate temper—not even by zeal for God.
Avoid being impressed by your own abilities, finding fault with everything or intruding needlessly into other people's affairs.
Some people who are unmoved by the fear of God or the dread of hell still avoid sins that might destroy their health or wealth, or expose them to public justice.
But those who truly fear God have one great purpose, so they act more consistently.
If we claim we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.
Every sincere believer should be ready to say, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
At the same time remember: personal obedience and a life renewed in holiness are the only genuine evidence that we have received by faith the Redeemer's righteousness.
Wisdom teaches us not to take offense quickly.
We need not go looking for what people say about us.
Praise can feed our pride, while criticism can excite anger.
Seek God's approval and a clear conscience, then give less attention to what others say.
It is easier to overlook twenty insults than to avenge just one.
When someone hurts us, ask whether we ourselves have hurt other people in a similar way.

div.title: Solomon discovers sin's corruption (verses 23–29)
div.p: Solomon had been deceived in his efforts to understand human affairs through personal inquiry.
Now he speaks with godly sorrow.
Someone who continually seeks to please God may hope to escape the worst temptations.
But a careless sinner may fall and never recover.
Solomon now recognized more clearly the evil of the sin he had committed by loving many foreign women (1 Kings 11:1).
He said he had not found a thoroughly faithful and godly woman among them.
How could he expect to find one among the women he had gathered under those circumstances?
Even anyone originally well disposed might have been badly influenced by that setting.
Henry says Solomon's warning was directed against his own sinful choices, not against the possibility of finding a virtuous wife.
Many godly husbands can gratefully acknowledge having found a prudent and faithful woman in marriage.
But someone who follows Solomon's path has little reason to expect the same blessing.
Solomon traced every stream of actual transgression back to its source.
Human nature is corrupted and has turned away from its original creation.
God made humanity upright, but human beings have invented countless ways of making themselves wicked and miserable.
Let us thank God for Jesus Christ and seek his grace, that we may belong to his redeemed people.

row.cell: To prepare for sudden evils and death.
It shall be well with the righteous, and ill with the wicked.

div.title: The excellence of wisdom (verses 1–5)
div.p: No person distinguished by wealth, power, honor or worldly skill is as excellent, useful or truly happy as the person who possesses wisdom.
Who but the wise can interpret God's words rightly and teach others from his truth and providential dealings?
How senseless it is for weak, dependent creatures to rebel against the Almighty!
Many people judge wrongly and thereby bring misery upon themselves, both in this life and the life to come.

div.title: Be ready for change and death (verses 6–8)
div.p: In his wisdom God has kept the future hidden from us so that we may always be ready for unexpected change.
We must all die.
No flight or hiding place will save us from death, and no weapon can ultimately defeat it.
Henry illustrates this with estimates of how many people die each day, minute and moment.
These figures express his own historical estimate; they are not updated demographic statistics.
How solemn the reality is!
May we become wise, understand our condition and consider our final end.
Only the person who believes in God is prepared to answer death's summons.
Wickedness sometimes enables people to escape human justice, but it can never exempt them from death.

div.title: God will finally distinguish the righteous and wicked (verses 9–13)
div.p: Solomon observed that people sometimes gain power over others and use it to injure them.
Prosperity may harden sinners in their wickedness.
Those who take long delays of punishment as evidence that judgment will never come deceive themselves.

p.hi: Divine vengeance may come slowly, but it will certainly come.

div.p: A godly person's days have substance and a good purpose.
The wicked person's days pass like a shadow, empty of lasting worth.
May we see eternal realities as close, certain and supremely important.

div.title: The mysteries of Providence (verses 14–17)
div.p: Only faith in God can steady the heart in a world where good people often suffer and wicked people sometimes prosper.
Solomon recommended a kind of joy arising from holy confidence in God.
In this world, people cannot do better than soberly and gratefully use the things of life according to their responsibilities and circumstances.
But faithful people have something infinitely better above the sun.
Solomon did not teach us to imagine we can explain all God's dealings.
Let us leave the unresolved problems of Providence for the Lord to clarify in his own time.
Meanwhile, we may gratefully enjoy what he provides and patiently endure our trials.
Through all outward changes, peace of conscience and joy in the Holy Spirit can remain ours.
They will continue even when bodily strength and earthly comfort fail.

row.cell: Good and bad men fare alike as to this world.
All men must die, Their portion as to this life.

div.title: Righteous and wicked people experience similar earthly events (verses 1–3)
div.p: We should not give up studying God's word and works merely because we cannot answer every question they raise.
Such study still teaches us many things useful to ourselves and others.
But human beings cannot always tell from outward circumstances whether someone is especially loved by God or lies under his wrath.
God will certainly distinguish the righteous from the wicked in the coming world.
In the present life, the difference between them lies especially in the inward help and comfort the righteous receive and in the spiritual benefit they gain from trials as well as mercies.
Human hearts, when left to themselves, are full of wrongdoing.
Prosperity can make sinners increasingly bold, even encouraging defiance of God.
On this side of death the righteous and the wicked often seem to receive the same treatment.
On the other side, their conditions will be utterly different.

div.title: Mortality and duties in the present life (verses 4–10)
div.p: Even the poorest and least respected living person's condition is better than that of an honored person who has died without repentance.
Solomon urges the wise and godly to enjoy cheerful confidence in the Lord, whatever their place in life.
The simplest food received in answer to prayer, as a gift from their Father's love, can be especially pleasant.
This does not mean setting our hearts on sensual enjoyment.
It means wisely and gratefully using the things God has given us.
The gladness described here springs from knowing God's favor.
This world is the place where we serve.
The next is the place where we receive our reward.
Whatever our circumstances, we have work to do.
Above all, sinners must seek the salvation of their souls.
Believers should demonstrate the reality of their faith, honor the gospel through their conduct, glorify God and serve the people of their generation.

div.title: Human expectations often disappoint (verses 11 and 12)
div.p: Success rarely comes exactly as we expect.
We must make proper use of available means without placing our final confidence in them.
If we succeed, give God praise.
If our efforts are frustrated, submit to his will.
People who postpone concern for their souls risk being caught in Satan's net.
He offers some attractive worldly object, for which they turn away from or neglect the gospel, and they continue in sin until destruction overtakes them suddenly.

div.title: Wisdom achieves what power cannot (verses 13–18)
div.p: A person may accomplish through wisdom what cannot be achieved through physical strength.

p.hi: If God is for us, who can stand against us?

div.p: Solomon recognizes the remarkable power of wisdom even when the wise person suffers social disadvantages.
How powerful words spoken appropriately can be!
Good and wise people may nevertheless have to find satisfaction simply in having done good or tried to do it.
They may be unable to accomplish everything they hoped or to receive the honor their work deserved.
One sinner can destroy enormous amounts of good.
People who ruin their own souls destroy much that is valuable.
They may also draw many others along the same destructive path.
This shows who truly benefits or harms a nation or household: one faithful servant may do much good, and one sinner may destroy much good.

row.cell: To preserve a character for wisdom.

div.title: Preserve a reputation for wisdom (verses 1–3)
div.p: People who profess true religion have special reason to avoid even the appearance of evil.
The wise person has important advantages over the fool, who is constantly uncertain when anything needs doing.
Wherever sinners go, sin brings them disgrace and exposes their folly.

div.title: Patience, government and mutual care (verses 4–10)
div.p: Solomon seems to warn against seeking redress for injury too hastily or allowing pride and revenge to govern our decisions.
Do not abandon the duties of your position simply because someone has offended you.
Wait, remain steady and be ready to yield where you can.
Gentleness can settle even serious offenses.
People are not always promoted according to their merit.
Those most eager to advise or interfere are sometimes the least aware of the difficulty and consequences of what they propose.
Henry applies the same lesson to the church, the body of Christ: all its members should show equal concern for one another.

div.title: The danger of foolish speech (verses 11–15)
div.p: Henry refers to an eastern practice of charming serpents through music.
The person who constantly talks foolishly or maliciously has a tongue that is unruly and full of deadly poison.
Direct contradiction may make such a person angrier and more violent.
We need wisdom to keep the peace.
Through rash, immoral or slanderous speech, people bring vengeance upon themselves, either openly or secretly.
If we remembered how little we know of what the future holds, we would stop saying many of the pointless things we now multiply.
Foolish people labor to no good purpose.
They may not even understand something as simple as the road into a great city.
By contrast, Henry speaks of the road to the heavenly city as a clearly marked highway on which even inexperienced travelers need not lose their way.
The CCEL witness attaches the reference “Is. 25:8” to that comparison; the cited verse requires primary-source and biblical-reference checking before any editorial correction.
Sinful folly can nevertheless cause people to miss the one way leading to true happiness.
div.note: Corrected printed citation (original preserved in source audit): Isa.35.8.

div.title: The duties of public leaders and citizens (verses 16–20)
div.p: A country's happiness depends in part upon the character of its leaders.
People suffer when their rulers behave immaturely and devote themselves chiefly to pleasure.
Laziness harms public as well as private responsibilities.
Money itself cannot feed or clothe anyone, but in ordinary economic life it can be exchanged for necessities and comforts.
The human soul, however, can neither be redeemed nor sustained through perishable things like silver and gold.
God knows what human beings do and hears what they say in secret.
Whenever he chooses, he can bring hidden things to light through surprising means.
If people can endanger themselves through secret insults against earthly rulers, how much more serious are words, acts and thoughts of rebellion against the King of kings and Lord of lords!
He sees what is hidden.
His ear is always open.
Sinner, do not curse this King even in your most private thought.
Your curse cannot injure him.
But his curse, coming down upon you, can sink you to the lowest hell.

row.cell: An admonition to prepare for death, and to young persons to be religious.

div.title: Give generously and continue doing good (verses 1–6)
div.p: Solomon calls people who possess wealth to do good to others.
Give generously, even when it seems that what you give has been thrown away or lost.
Help many people.
Do not use the good you have already done as an excuse for refusing further opportunities to help.
Such generosity is not wasted but wisely invested.
We should expect that difficult times will sometimes come, since human beings are born to trouble.
That is one reason to do good while we are prosperous.
Riches cannot truly benefit us if we refuse to use them for the good of others.
Every person should labor to become a blessing in the community where God's Providence has placed them.
Wherever we live, there is useful work for us if our hearts are willing.
But if we magnify every small obstacle, invent objections and imagine terrible hardships, we will never begin the work, much less finish it.
Winds and clouds of trouble are in God's hands.
He uses them to test us.
His work will fulfill his word, whether or not we can see how.
We may trust the Lord to provide for us without constant anxious and distressing worry.
Do not grow tired of doing good.
At the proper time, God's time, you will reap (Galatians 6:9).

div.title: Young people should prepare for death and eternity (verses 7–10)
div.p: Life is sweet to people who reject God because the present world is their only portion.
Life is also sweet to godly people because it allows them to prepare for something far better.
In that sense, life is sweet to all.
Yet even when life seems most pleasant, we should remember death is approaching.
Solomon speaks particularly to young people.
They long to pursue many pleasures.
He challenges them: follow those desires if you wish, but remember that God will bring you into judgment.
How many young people indulge every appetite and rush toward destructive pleasures!
God records their sinful thoughts and desires, their idle words and their wicked speech.
Those who want to escape remorse and terror, possess comfort and hope near death, and avoid lasting misery must recognize the vanity of sinful pleasures in youth.
Henry emphasizes that Solomon is condemning sinful pleasures, not legitimate joy.
His goal is to lead the young toward purer and lasting happiness.
Solomon does not speak out of envy because he is too old to share in youthful amusement.
He speaks, in Henry's account, as someone rescued through a remarkable act of divine mercy from a dangerous course that few people escape.
He wants young people not to repeat his experience.
If you desire genuine happiness now and lasting happiness afterward, remember your Creator during your youth.

row.cell: A description of the infirmities of age.
All is vanity: also a warning of the judgment to come.

div.title: Remember your Creator before old age (verses 1–7)
div.p: Remember the sins you have committed against your Creator.
Repent and seek his forgiveness.
Remember also the duties you owe him and begin fulfilling them, looking to him for grace and strength.
Do this early in life, when the body is strong and the mind active.
Someone who reaches old age with the painful memory of a wasted life may finally abandon sinful pleasure only because it has become impossible to enjoy.
When such a person says, “I no longer find pleasure in these things,” sincerity in renouncing sin can reasonably be questioned.
Solomon then gives a figurative description of old age and its infirmities.
Some details of the figures are difficult to interpret.
But their central meaning is clear: the ordinary disabilities of old age often bring great discomfort.
Henry reads verses 2–5 as images of weaknesses commonly accompanying advancing age, and verse 6 as an image of what happens at the hour of death.
If sin had not entered the world, these weaknesses would not have appeared.
People who are old therefore have special reason to reflect upon the evil of sin.

div.title: Vanity, true religion and final judgment (verses 8–14)
div.p: Solomon repeats the central statement of his preaching:

p.hi: “Vanity of vanities! All is vanity!”

div.p: He speaks as someone who has paid dearly to learn how empty the world is.
Earthly possessions and accomplishments cannot free people from the burden of sin.
Because Solomon understood the worth of souls, he considered carefully the words he spoke and wrote.
Truthful words will always be fitting and valuable.
God's truths resemble goads, urging on those who grow lazy and shrink back, and nails, holding steady those who wander or become unstable.
They give the heart firmness so that we neither neglect our responsibilities nor abandon them under pressure.
The Shepherd of Israel gives inspired wisdom.
Every genuine teacher and guide receives instruction from him.
Scripture also applies the title Shepherd to the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
The prophets searched diligently to understand the time and circumstances of the sufferings of Christ and the glory that would follow, as the Spirit of Christ testified through them.
Writing many books is tiring, and human life is short.
In Solomon's time producing and reading books required still greater effort than today.
But all our studies would end in vanity if they did not bring us to this conclusion:

p.hi: Fear God and keep his commandments: this is the whole duty of humanity.

div.p: The fear of God includes all the affections directed toward him through the Holy Spirit's work.
Terror may exist without love, and may even be accompanied by hatred.
But the gracious fear of God resembles the reverence of a loving child.
It can stand for the whole of true religion within the heart and for the obedience that flows from it.
Let us pursue the one necessary thing.
Come to Christ now as a merciful Savior, for he will soon appear as the almighty Judge, bringing to light everything hidden and exposing the intentions of every heart.
Why has God told us so plainly that all is vanity?
So that we will not deceive ourselves and destroy our souls.
God has made our duty our true good.
May his command be written within every heart:

p.hi: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this concerns every human being.

div.title: Song of Solomon — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Henry reads this book as a divine allegory of the love between Christ and his church of true believers.
Its images arise from the relationship and affection between a bridegroom and his promised bride.
Scripture often uses marriage as a picture of an especially close, firm and secure relationship.
Henry points readers to Psalm 45; Isaiah 54:5–6; 62:5; Jeremiah 2:2; 3:1; Ezekiel; Hosea; Matthew 9:15; 25:1; Revelation 21:2, 9; and Ephesians 5:27.

He believes every kind of believer and every circumstance that believers experience can be recognized somewhere in this song when the book is carefully compared with other Scriptures, with the Holy Spirit's help in response to prayer.
However, he warns that expositors and translators have often misunderstood its figurative language.
We must particularly consider the important differences between the customs of Europe and the ancient Near East.
The limited understanding of eastern customs possessed by many earlier translators and interpreters prevented them, in some cases, from rendering the expressions correctly.
Changes in European languages during the previous two or three centuries also affected how particular phrases were understood.
Expressions from other ages must not be judged uncritically according to modern assumptions.
Nevertheless, Henry concludes that the book's main themes, rightly understood, are consistent with the sincere Christian's affections and spiritual experience.

row.cell: The church beseeches Christ to lead her to the resting-place of his people.
Christ's commendation of the church, Her esteem for Him.

div.title: The title of the song (verse 1)
div.p: This is the Song of Songs, superior to every other song in Henry's reading.
It is wholly concerned with the glory of Jesus Christ and the love between him and the people he has redeemed.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): 2 Corinthians 3:1; 1 Corinthians 7:8.
Verified editorial cross-reference: Jer.3.1.
Section reference (editorially corrected): Song.1.7; Song.1.8.

div.title: The believer confesses sin while longing for Christ (verses 2–6)
div.p: The church, or more particularly the individual believer, speaks here as the bride of the Messiah, the King.
The kisses of his mouth represent assurances of pardon.
Those assurances fill believers with peace and joy in faith and cause them to overflow with hope through the Holy Spirit's power.
Gracious souls find their greatest pleasure in loving Christ and being loved by him.
His love is better and more desirable than any good the world can offer.
The name of Christ is no longer like perfume shut up in its container.
It is like perfume poured out: the gospel openly reveals the fullness and freeness of his grace.
Those whom Christ redeems and sanctifies are pictured as the young women who love and follow him wherever he goes (Revelation 14:4).
They ask him to draw them, giving spiritual life and strength through the Holy Spirit.
The more clearly we see Christ's glory, the more we recognize our inability to follow him as we should—and the more strongly we want to follow.
Notice how quickly this prayer receives an answer.
Those waiting at Wisdom's entrance are led into truth and comfort.
In the King's chamber, sorrows disappear.
Everything we enjoy spiritually comes from Christ, to whom we owe all gratitude.
We should remember his love with thanksgiving longer and more deeply than anything else.
Only sincere love is acceptable to him (Ephesians 6:24).
The daughters of Jerusalem may represent people who profess faith but are not yet established in it.
The bride is dark like the tents of nomadic Arabs, yet lovely as the splendid curtains in Solomon's palace.
Likewise, a believer is sinful and defiled by nature, yet made beautiful through divine grace and renewed in God's image.
Even after renewal, some sinful corruption remains.
Yet the believer is lovely because accepted in Christ.
Someone despised by the world may be precious in God's sight.
The bride's darkened appearance reflects the difficult treatment she endured.
Those belonging to the church as her mother—but not to God as Father—had acted harshly toward her.
Their demands caused hardships and made her neglect the care of her own soul.
Here is a picture of a poor and suffering woman chosen to marry a prince.
Christ's love similarly finds people burdened with sin, exhausted by labor and heavy with sorrow.
What a great change occurs when his love becomes known to them!

div.title: The believer asks Christ for guidance and rest (verses 7 and 8)
div.p: How affectionate is the title given to Christ: “You whom my soul loves.”
Those who truly love him may approach with boldness and humble confidence.
Are God's people under the noon-day heat of outward suffering or inward spiritual conflict?

p.hi: Christ has rest for them.

div.p: Believers want to share fully in the privileges of Christ's flock and fear straying away from him more than any other danger.
God is ready to answer their prayers.
Follow the good old way and the footsteps left by faithful believers.
Learn from their example and listen to the guidance of trustworthy ministers—the under-shepherds.
Bring those entrusted to your care; they too are welcome.
Christians should pray that God will direct their earthly work, circumstances and employment so that their Savior remains before them at all times.

div.title: Christ praises the church, and the church values him (verses 9–17)
div.p: The Bridegroom praises the bride.
In Christ's eyes his believers are excellent and valuable, fitted to serve as instruments of his glory.
The ornaments used in that culture picture the spiritual gifts and graces Christ grants every true believer (Song 1:10–11).
The graces are many and depend upon one another.
The One who began this good work will also finish it.
The grace believers receive from Christ's fullness produces faith, loving affections and gratitude.
Yet Christ himself, not merely his gifts, is their greatest treasure.
Henry explains the word translated “camphire” as meaning “atonement or propitiation”.
Christ is precious because he is the propitiation for our sins.
No rival may occupy his place in the soul.
Believers desire him to remain in their hearts through the whole night of earthly troubles.
Christ delights in the good that his grace has produced within their souls.
Those made holy should give thanks for the grace that made them beautiful when by nature they were corrupted.
The bride's modest, humble gaze suggests simplicity and godly sincerity.
Her eyes are illuminated and guided by the Holy Spirit, the blessed Dove.
In response, the church praises Christ:

p.hi: He is the perfect original; I am only a faint and imperfect copy.

div.p: Someone may be physically attractive but unpleasant in character.
Christ is both beautiful and delightful.
In verse 16, the believer praises the appointed means of grace through which faithful people enjoy fellowship with Christ.
Whether worshiping in God's courts, resting privately, doing daily work, lying sick in bed or even confined in prison, a sense of God's presence can turn any place into paradise.
Daily communion with the Father, Son and Holy Spirit gives the soul a living hope of an inheritance that cannot perish, be defiled or fade away.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): 1 Corinthians 10:11.
Section reference (editorially corrected): Song.1.10; Song.1.11.

row.cell: The mutual love of Christ and his church.
The hope and calling of the church.
Christ's care of the church, Her faith and hope.

div.title: Christ and his church love one another (verses 1–7)
div.p: Believers are lovely because they are clothed in Christ's righteousness and fragrant with the graces of his Spirit.
They flourish under the refreshing rays of the Sun of Righteousness.
The lily of the East may grow tall while possessing a fragile stem.
So the church is weak in itself but strong in Christ who supports it.
The wicked, who do not love Christ, are like thorns that injure and destroy.
Sinful corruption is itself like thorns in the flesh.
But the lily now surrounded by thorns will one day be transplanted into a paradise without any thorn or briar.
The world is a barren tree for the soul.
Christ is a fruit-bearing tree.
People dried out by conviction of sin, fear of the law or earthly troubles may find rest under his shade.
But merely passing by this shade is insufficient.
We must sit beneath it, receiving and enjoying his protection.
Believers have tasted the goodness of the Lord Jesus.
His fruit consists of the privileges of the new covenant, bought by his blood and given through his Spirit.
His promises are sweet, but so are his commands.
Forgiveness is sweet, as is peace of conscience.
When our taste for sinful pleasures has been lost, divine consolation becomes especially precious.
Christ leads souls to find comfort through his appointed ordinances, like a banqueting house where believers feast with him.
The banner over them is Christ's love, shown in his death and his word.
How much better to be overwhelmed by love for Christ than by love for the world!
Even when Christ seems absent, he remains a very present help.
His people are held in his hands with extraordinary tenderness.
The soul, recognizing Christ nearby, fears losing communion with him.
We can grieve the Spirit through sinful attitudes.
Let those who enjoy his consolation be careful not to sin away their comfort.

div.title: Christ calls the church out of winter (verses 8–13)
div.p: The church delights in the prospect of deeper fellowship with Christ.
He alone can speak directly to the heart.
The believer sees him approaching.
Henry says this image may refer to the Old Testament believers' expectation of Christ's coming in human flesh.
Christ comes gladly to fulfill his saving mission, and he comes quickly.
Even if he seems to leave his people, the absence is brief; he returns with enduring loving-kindness.
The saints of earlier times saw him through sacrifices and ceremonial ordinances.
We also see him imperfectly, as through a lattice.
Christ calls newly converted people to rise from idleness and discouragement and leave behind sin and worldly vanity in order to enjoy fellowship with him.
Winter may represent years of ignorance and unfruitfulness, or the storms of conviction concerning guilt and danger.
Even the earliest, unripe fruits of holy living are pleasing to the One whose grace produced them.
These tokens of divine kindness encourage the soul to follow Christ more wholeheartedly.
Rise and leave the world and the flesh for fellowship with Christ.
All this change comes from the Sun of Righteousness and his gracious influence.

div.title: Christ protects and guides his church (verses 14–17)
div.p: The church is Christ's dove, returning to him as to Noah.
Christ is the Rock where the dove finds refuge from birds of prey.
He invites her to come boldly before the throne of grace.
There she has a great High Priest to hear and present her requests.
Speak freely.
Do not fear contempt or rejection.
Prayer is sweet and acceptable to God.
Those whom he sanctifies possess their true beauty.
The little foxes picture the first beginnings of sinful thoughts and desires, frivolous distractions, wasted visits, small departures from the truth and the desire to conform to the world.
Believers must put such things away, mortifying passions that would destroy new spiritual growth.
Whatever prevents progress in what is good should be removed.
Christ feeds among the lilies: he is graciously present with his people.
Even when believers feel abandoned, they should remember his kindness and resist temptation.
The shadows of Jewish ceremonial worship disappeared as the gospel day dawned.
And after a night of spiritual absence, a new day of consolation will come.
Christ will cross the mountains of Bether, the mountains that divide, and ultimately cross every obstacle to bring his people home to himself.

row.cell: The trials of the church by the withdrawing of Christ.
The excellences of the church, The care of Christ for her.

div.title: Seeking Christ when his presence seems withdrawn (verses 1–5)
div.p: For the Old Testament church, discerning Christ through the ceremonial law was difficult. Its watchmen often gave little assistance to those seeking him.
Night can picture spiritual coldness, darkness, drowsiness and uncertainty.

When believers first become troubled by a loss of felt fellowship with Christ, they may make only weak attempts to recover that comfort. When these efforts fail, they are stirred to greater diligence.

The streets and squares suggest the appointed means of grace in which we should seek the Lord. The soul asks those responsible for watching over others, but still does not immediately find satisfaction.
We must not stop at the outward means. By faith, turn directly to Christ.
Taking hold of him and refusing to let go pictures persistent, humble prayer joined with active faith in his promises.
The Lord is not offended by earnest requests from believers who cling to him in faith. He welcomes such pleading.
A person who has found the Savior wants to help others know him too.
Wherever Christ is found, welcome him into our homes and especially our hearts.
Let us remind ourselves and one another not to grieve the Holy Spirit, our Comforter, or provoke the withdrawal of the Beloved's comforting presence.

div.title: Christ safely carries his people through the wilderness (verses 6–11)
div.p: The wilderness pictures the present world. Believers come out of it when they turn away from its sinful pleasures, goals and patterns and seek happiness in fellowship with the Savior.
Through the Comforter's guidance, even a poor and weary soul will rise like incense from the altar, with affections directed toward heaven.
The Holy Spirit makes the believer's devotion lively and fills the heart with heavenly graces.
Christ is the Peace of his people and the King of heavenly Zion. He has prepared a safe way to carry his redeemed through the wilderness.
The decorated bed or portable litter represents a place of rest and secure travel, made splendid in a manner befitting its owner.
The church is strongly guarded: more are with her than against her. Even when believers fear the dangers of night, they are safe when resting in Christ.
Henry understands the chariot as a picture of the covenant of redemption and the way of salvation, designed both for Christ's glory and for the comfort of his people, securely ordered in every part.
The purple covering represents the blood of the covenant, which shelters believers from divine wrath and the storms of this life.
At its center is Christ's love surpassing knowledge, on which believers rest.
The crown points to the honor, power and kingship belonging to Christ as he reveals himself through the gospel.

row.cell: Christ sets forth the graces of the church.
The church desires further influences of Divine grace.

div.title: Christ praises the graces of his church (verses 1–7)
div.p: Henry cautions readers against giving a confident spiritual meaning to every detail of every comparison in this poem. Many such explanations are uncertain, and fanciful guesses can lead to serious mistakes.
The mountain of myrrh appears to him to refer to Mount Moriah, where the temple stood, incense was offered and God's people worshiped.
Christ was present there until the shadows of Moses' law gave way to the dawn of the gospel and the rising of the Sun of Righteousness.
Though Christ, in his human nature, is absent from his earthly church until the heavenly day breaks, he remains spiritually present with his people through his appointed ordinances.
How beautiful believers become when they are justified through Christ's righteousness and adorned with spiritual graces!
Their thoughts, words and actions remain imperfect but are increasingly pure, showing hearts nourished by the gospel.

div.title: Christ's love and protection (verses 8–15)
div.p: Christ's call to his church has two aspects.
First, it is a command to turn away from the world. Its mountains may appear pleasant, but they conceal lions and leopards—dangers for the soul.
Second, it is a promise: people will be gathered into the church from many places, and the Lord will finally deliver his people from persecution. For now they may dwell among lions (Psalm 57:4).
Christ's heart is with his church, where he has placed his treasure. He delights in its love toward him, shown both in the heart and in action.
The bride's perfume pictures the gifts and graces of the Spirit. Love and obedience please Christ more than sacrifices or incense.
Christ has clothed his people with his righteousness and given them holy joy and consolation. He walks in his garden, though unseen.
He has placed a protective hedge around it that the powers of darkness cannot break.
Believers' souls are like enclosed gardens containing a well of living water, the work of the Holy Spirit (John 4:14; 7:38).
The world does not know this saving fountain, and its enemies cannot corrupt it.
The fruits and spices picture believers and the graces growing within them. They are planted, not self-generated; precious and lasting beyond the fading flowers of this life.
When grace reaches glory, it will endure forever.

p.hi: Christ is the source that makes every garden fruitful.

div.title: The church asks for the Spirit's renewing work (verse 16)
div.p: The church prays for the Holy Spirit to make the garden of the soul fruitful.
Its spices represent the precious graces worked within believers. The Spirit acts like wind: a north wind bringing conviction and a south wind bringing comfort.
He awakens holy desires and produces both the willing and the doing of what is good.
The church invites Christ to enjoy the garden. Everything growing there already belongs to him.
Let him receive the honor of its fruit; may we enjoy the comfort of knowing that he accepts it.
A believer cannot rightly rejoice in spiritual fruit unless it contributes to Christ's glory.
Let us therefore remain separate from the world's sinful patterns, like a garden enclosed, and refuse to conform to them.

row.cell: The disappointments of the church from her own folly.

div.title: Christ welcomes his people's invitation (verse 1)
div.p: See how readily Christ accepts his people's invitation!
Whatever small measure of goodness remains in us would disappear unless he preserved it.
He also invites those he loves to eat and drink abundantly: the acts of worship in which his people honor him are means through which he gives grace.

div.title: Carelessness interrupts fellowship with Christ (verses 2–8)
div.p: Churches and individual believers may, through carelessness and false security, provoke Christ to withdraw the comfort of his presence.
We should recognize our periods of spiritual slumber and unhealthy attitudes.
Christ knocks to awaken us through his word and Spirit, through difficulties and through conscience. Henry points to Revelation 3:20.
Even when we neglect Christ, he does not forget us. His love should move us to respond with love, including acts of self-denial; such surrender benefits us.
Careless souls make little of the Lord Jesus. We cannot send someone else to open the door for us.
We make excuses: we have no desire, no strength or no time. But these excuses amount to taking Christ lightly. Refusing to leave a warm bed or face a cold wind for him is a kind of contempt.
The image of the Bridegroom putting his hand to the door represents the powerful influence of God's grace and the Spirit working upon the heart.
The sweet-smelling myrrh on the door handles represents the believer rising above self-indulgence, seeking Christ in prayer and removing obstacles to fellowship.
Yet the Beloved has gone away. Through this loss of felt communion, Christ teaches believers to prize his gracious visits more highly.
Nevertheless, the soul still calls him her Beloved. The sense of desertion does not necessarily mean despair.
We may confess both faith and weakness: “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.”
Once God awakens us, memories of ignored conviction and rejected invitations become painfully bitter.
The believer searches diligently, not only praying but also seeking Christ in the places and ways where he is ordinarily found.
The watchmen wound her. Henry notes that some interpreters understand this as ministers applying God's word wrongly to people with awakened consciences.
Her appeal to the daughters of Jerusalem expresses the distressed believer's desire even for the prayers of the weakest Christian.
An awakened soul feels Christ's withdrawal more keenly than any outward distress.

div.title: The church praises Christ's excellence (verses 9–16)
div.p: Even people who know little of Christ may notice something beautiful in believers who bear his likeness.
When people begin to ask about his character and perfections, there is reason for hope.
Christians who know him should eagerly help others know him too.
To a heart enlightened to discern spiritual things, his divine glory makes him altogether lovely.
Henry interprets his white appearance as the innocence of Christ's spotless life, and his red appearance as the blood shed in his suffering and death.
The other images belong to the figurative language of their original time, depicting bodily beauty and gracious character. We may not immediately understand every allusion.
Christ will ultimately be glorified in his saints and admired by everyone who believes.
May his love constrain us to live for his glory.

row.cell: Inquiry where Christ must be sought.
The work of grace in the believer.

div.title: Those who hear of Christ seek him (verse 1)
div.p: People who learn something of Christ's excellence and of the comfort of belonging to him naturally want to know where they may find him.
Anyone wishing to find Christ must seek him early and diligently.

div.title: Christ among his people (verses 2 and 3)
div.p: Christ's church is like a sheltered garden, set apart from the world. He cares for it, visits it and delights in it.
Those wishing to find him should attend the means through which he makes himself known: his word, the sacraments and prayer.
When Christ comes among his people, he comes to welcome his friends and also to take believers to himself.
Henry pictures him gathering his lilies one by one. At the final day he will send angels to gather them all, so that he may be glorified in them.
The death of a believer is like a gardener picking a treasured flower. Christ preserves that flower from fading and causes it to flourish forever, with increasing beauty.
If our conscience can testify that we truly belong to Christ, we need not doubt his commitment to us: the covenant will not fail on his side.
The church takes comfort in knowing that Christ finds delight among the lilies—his own redeemed people.

div.title: Christ's praise of the church (verses 4–10)
div.p: Every genuine form of holiness on earth belongs to the life of Christ's church.
Christ continues conquering his enemies, while believers fight and gain victories over the world, sinful desires and the devil.
He shows tenderness toward the people he redeemed and delights in the work of his own grace within them.
Only true believers possess the beauty of holiness, and when their real character becomes evident, that beauty will be recognized.
At conversion, believers resemble the morning dawn: their light is still small but growing.
In sanctification, the church is fair as the moon, receiving every ray of holiness and grace from Christ.
In justification, believers are clear as the sun, clothed in the righteousness of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness.
Under his banner they persevere in the spiritual fight of faith.

div.title: The Spirit's work and the Shulammite (verses 11–13)
div.p: Christian character grows through private reflection and meditation, but not through lazy, self-indulgent withdrawal from responsibility.
When ordinary duties allow some quiet, the believer no longer finds the world's entertainments attractive.
Instead, the heart prays that the things belonging to God's Spirit may grow within it and around it.
The world may misunderstand this life and imagine such a person has abandoned true interests. In fact the believer is occupied with matters of lasting worth.
A humble Christian may prefer to avoid public notice, yet the Lord delights to honor that person.

Henry also sees a possible reference here to angels sent to receive a believer's soul at death. Their arrival may startle the departing Christian, but the Lord will be that soul's strength and eternal portion.

Henry understands the title Shulammite to signify perfection and peace. The church does not possess these in herself but in Christ—complete through his righteousness, reconciled by his blood and given peace by his Spirit.

row.cell: The delight of the church in Christ.

div.title: The beauty of holiness in the church (verses 1–9)
div.p: The images in this chapter differ from those used earlier. Henry explains that their original language evokes splendid and beautiful clothing.
The saints have such honor through being clothed with Christ. Their character should make the teaching of God their Savior attractive in every respect.
Believers who act consistently with their confession honor Christ, commend the gospel and may awaken sinners to its truth.
The church is compared to a tall, spreading palm tree. Her love for Christ and the obedience arising from that love bear precious fruit from the true Vine.
The King is pictured among the galleries. Christ delights in the assemblies and appointed worship of his people. He takes pleasure in the fruit of his own grace within them.
These images describe the beauty of holiness in the church and in each believer, who will ultimately be presented to the heavenly Bridegroom.

div.title: The church desires deeper fellowship with Christ (verses 10–13)
div.p: The church rejoices that she belongs to Christ and that Christ belongs to her.
She humbly asks him to walk with her, guiding, teaching and comforting her. She wants to speak freely with him about every need and grief, without interruption.
All who have been made holy sincerely desire this fellowship. Those who would walk with Christ must turn away from the world's sinful attractions.
We can enjoy communion with God wherever he places us. We should never go willingly somewhere we cannot ask him in faith to accompany us.
Begin seeking him early: early in life and early each day. Even a poor dwelling becomes pleasant through God's presence, while the loveliest countryside cannot satisfy a soul that lacks the Beloved.
Our souls are vineyards. They should produce useful fruit, and we should frequently ask whether our lives are bearing righteousness.

Christ's presence makes the vines flourish, as sunlight renews a garden. If we can sincerely say to him, “You know all things; you know that I love you,” and if his Spirit assures us that our souls are growing, we have reason for confidence.
Yet we must also ask him to search our hearts and show us our true condition.
Every gracious act and fruit of holiness pleases Jesus. Keep such fruits ready for him, so that by bearing much fruit we glorify him.

p.hi: All grace comes from Christ; therefore all its fruit should be offered to Christ.

div.title: Longing for closer fellowship with Christ (verses 1–4)
div.p: The church longs for the open affection and constant closeness that brothers and sisters share. By grace believers become participants in God's nature, and Christ has become their Brother.
Wherever we meet him, let us acknowledge our relationship to him and our love for him without fearing the contempt of others.
Do we truly desire to serve Christ more faithfully? What fruits of holiness have we prepared to express our love for him?
The church warns her children not to drive away Christ's gracious presence. When tempted, we should remind ourselves not to grieve the Holy Spirit.

div.title: Love that survives every trial (verses 5–7)
div.p: The Jewish church came out of the wilderness through God's power and favor. Christ's grace also raised his church from a desolate condition.
A sinful life is a wilderness without true comfort. We cannot escape by relying on our own reasoning or righteousness. We must lean upon Christ, the Lord our Righteousness, by faith.
The church asks to remain secure in Christ's heart and under his protection, like a seal impressed upon his heart.
Those who love him fear anything that would draw them away—especially their own actions, which might interrupt the comfort of fellowship.

No flood can drown Christ's love for his people. Neither threats nor attractions of the world should lessen our love for him. His love strengthens believers against both persecution and prosperity's temptations.

div.title: The church prays and works for others (verses 8–12)
div.p: Henry sees the church here interceding for the Gentiles, who had not yet received God's word and the ordinary means of grace.
People brought to Christ should seek ways to bring others to him. Stronger Christians should constantly pray for those who are young or weak in faith.
The images of a wall and door suggest a church founded securely on Christ, the precious Foundation and Cornerstone, and a lasting entrance through the removed barrier between peoples.
The Lord promises his care for those not yet called, and the church should likewise remain concerned for them.
Our hearts are vineyards to be guarded diligently. All their fruit belongs to Christ's praise. Serving him is no loss: those who labor for him ultimately receive a far greater gain.

div.title: The prayer for Christ's return (verses 13 and 14)
div.p: At the close of this dialogue, Christ addresses the church dwelling in the gardens—among his people and in their appointed worship.
He calls her to persevere in prayer and praise, which delight him. She responds by asking him to return quickly and bring her fully into his presence.
Until that day, Christ is in heaven, pictured as mountains of sweet spices. At the appointed time, every eye will see him in the glory of the world to come.
Believers look forward to that day and seek to be ready for it. They should faithfully fulfill their present duties, so that others may see their good works and glorify the Father.
Continuing in prayer and thanksgiving, we may grow in joy and strength and look toward death and judgment without fear.

p.hi: Even so, come, Lord Jesus.

div.title: Isaiah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Isaiah prophesied during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.

He has rightly been called the evangelical prophet, because he speaks frequently and at length about the Messiah—his coming and character, his ministry and preaching, his suffering and death, and the extent and lasting nature of his kingdom.
Behind the promised deliverance from Babylon, Isaiah also reveals a far greater deliverance to be accomplished by the Messiah.

He seldom speaks of the nearer rescue without also pointing toward the greater one. Sometimes he becomes so absorbed in the later deliverance that he seems to leave the nearer event behind, speaking at length about the Messiah's person, work, character and kingdom.

row.cell: The corruptions prevailing among the Jews.
The state of Judah is lamented; with gracious promises of the gospel times.

div.title: Judah's widespread corruption (verses 1–9)
div.p: Isaiah means the salvation of the Lord, a fitting name for a prophet who speaks so frequently about Jesus the Savior and his salvation.
God's professing people failed to recognize that every comfort and even life itself came from his fatherly kindness.
Many people are equally careless about their souls. Failing to consider truth we already know can harm us as much as not knowing truth we ought to learn.
Wickedness had spread throughout the land.
The prophet pictured the nation as a sick body whose disease threatened death. From foot to head—from the poorest worker to the most powerful ruler—there was no spiritual health.
Guilt and corruption were everywhere, the sorrowful effects of Adam's fall. Henry understands this picture as declaring the total depravity of fallen human nature.
When people refuse to repent, their spiritual wounds remain untreated, and ruin approaches.
Jerusalem stood exposed like the temporary huts built to watch over ripening fruit. Such shelters were familiar in the East.
Yet the Lord preserved a small faithful remnant in the city.
It is because of his mercy that we have not been destroyed.
The evil nature described here exists in each of us. Only Jesus Christ and his sanctifying Spirit can restore our souls to spiritual health.

div.title: Sacrifice without repentance is unacceptable (verses 10–15)
div.p: Judah's countryside lay desolate and cities had burned. Those judgments moved the people to offer sacrifices.
But they approached worship as though they might pay God to remove punishment while continuing in sin.
Many are willing to surrender expensive offerings who remain unwilling to surrender their sinful practices.
They regard religious forms as good deeds that entitle them to reward.
Yet even the costliest worship is unacceptable without a genuine change of heart and life.
God not only refused such sacrifices; he hated their hypocrisy.
Sin is deeply offensive to him.
If we continue secretly cherishing forbidden sins or reject Christ's salvation, even our prayers become offensive rather than acceptable.

div.title: Turn from evil and begin doing good (verses 16–20)
div.p: Repentance is not merely sorrow over past actions. Stop practicing evil and begin doing the good God commands.
We must not stand idle when there are duties to fulfill.
The sacrifices prescribed in Moses' law could not of themselves atone even for the nation's outward crimes.
But God has opened a fountain of cleansing, available to sinners of every age and social rank.
Our sins may be like scarlet and crimson, dyed deeply and repeatedly: first in the wool of original corruption, then through the many threads of our own deliberate transgressions.
Even after repeated backsliding, God's pardoning mercy can remove the stain (Psalm 51:7).
Life and death, good and evil, are set before us.

p.hi: Lord, incline us all to live for your glory.

div.title: Zion's corruption and promised redemption (verses 21–31)
div.p: Neither a holy city nor a royal capital fulfills its purpose if true religion no longer lives within it.
Impure metal may still resemble silver. Diluted wine may still look like wine. In the same way, outward appearances may conceal spiritual corruption.
People who oppress the vulnerable rather than help them bear grave responsibility.
Human rules and restraints can accomplish something outwardly. But only God can change hearts effectively through his Spirit acting in judgment and renewal.

p.hi: Sin is the worst form of captivity and slavery.

div.p: Henry regards these verses as fitting most fully the redemption of spiritual Zion through Christ's righteousness, death and powerful grace.
The unrepentant face complete ruin. They resemble a tree scorched by heat or a garden without water, quickly ruined in a dry land.
Those who put their trust in idols or human strength will perish.
Even a strong person will become like dry tinder, easily broken and readily set on fire.
When sinners make themselves like stubble and meet God as a consuming fire, nothing can prevent their destruction unless they receive his mercy.

row.cell: The conversion of the Gentiles, Description of the sinfulness of Israel.

div.title: The nations called to God's light (verses 1–9)
div.p: Isaiah foretells the calling of the Gentiles, the spread of the gospel and a still wider proclamation yet to come.
Christians should encourage and strengthen one another.
God teaches his people through his word and Spirit.
Christ advances peace as well as holiness. If every human being were a genuine Christian, war would no longer exist.
But the complete fulfillment of this vision has not yet appeared in the world.
Whatever others do, let us walk in the light of that peace.
When true faith flourishes, people delight in gathering for worship and urge others to join them.
We should be cautious about making those who do not know God our closest guides and companions; we easily imitate the habits of people with whom we spend time.
God does not condemn people simply for owning silver or gold, horses or chariots.
The wrong lies in depending upon possessions and military strength, as though they guaranteed safety, comfort and happiness or as though we could have none without them.
Sin disgraces people of every rank.
Countries that describe themselves as Christian may no longer be filled with literal idols. Yet they can be full of wealth treated as a god.
When people are consumed with their gains and pleasures, they forget or despise God's truth and commandments.

div.title: Human pride humbled before the Lord (verses 10–22)
div.p: Henry regards the Chaldean conquest of Jerusalem as the first historical judgment in view, during which Jewish idolatry was brought low.
Yet the passage also turns our attention toward the final destruction of Christ's enemies.
People who face God's judgment cannot hide or find safe shelter from it.
The shaking of the earth will terrify those who have attached their hearts to earthly things.
Human arrogance will be brought low, either through God's grace convincing people of pride's evil or through Providence removing the things in which they took pride.
The Lord's day of judgment comes against everything in which sinners place their trust.
Those unwilling to listen to warning and reason may eventually be forced to recognize their danger through terror.
People who make money their god will discover it has become a burden.
Henry also applies this passage to an awakened sinner willing to surrender everything to receive salvation.
The Jews had been inclined to depend on neighboring nations instead of the Lord.
We face the same temptation to depend upon mortal human beings.

p.hi: Let no person become your ultimate fear or your ultimate hope. Place your hope in the Lord your God.

row.cell: The calamities about to come upon the land.
The distress of the proud, luxurious women of Zion.

div.title: Judah is deprived of its supports (verses 1–9)
div.p: God was about to remove every support on which Judah depended.
Jerusalem and the land would become desolate because the people's words and deeds were rebellions against the Lord, even at his holy temple.
When people refuse to rely upon God, he may take away their other sources of security. Then they discover how weak they truly are.
Jesus Christ is the Bread of Life and the Water of Life. If he is our support, we possess a lasting portion that cannot be taken away (John 6:27).
Henry draws three lessons from the threatened judgment.
First, the condition of unrepentant sinners is deeply miserable.
Second, it is the soul that sin most seriously damages.
Third, people who continue in sin bring the evil they suffer upon themselves.

div.title: Righteousness and oppression (verses 10–15)
div.p: Whether the nation is prosperous or suffering, God's final principle remains unchanged:

p.hi: It will be well with the righteous and ill with the wicked.

div.p: The godly therefore have abundant reason to trust him, and sinners have every reason to repent and return.
The time had come for the Lord to demonstrate his power and call leaders to account for their use of the wealth and authority entrusted to them.
Neglecting the needs of poor people is sinful.
How much more hateful is the conduct of those who first reduce people to poverty and then exploit them!

div.title: The pride and luxury of Zion (verses 16–26)
div.p: Isaiah warned the women of Zion that suffering would follow their pride and extravagance.
God notices outward vanity, even in dress.
The threatened judgments corresponded to the sins being condemned.
Henry describes repulsive illness as one form such judgment could take.
The precise kind of ornaments worn is not the essential point. Fashions change, and what seems impressive in one age might look absurd in another.

p.hi: Human nature, however, remains the same.

div.p: Wasting time and money on self-display while neglecting faith, generosity and even justice displeases the Lord.

Even people who profess religion sometimes treat excessive luxury and ornamentation as morally harmless. But Henry asks why the Holy Spirit would have directed the prophet to expose it so carefully if it were not a serious evil.
Jerusalem would be conquered and reduced to ruins.
The prophet pictures it as a grieving woman sitting on the ground.
Henry notes a later Roman medal celebrating Jerusalem's destruction with a similar image of a seated, mourning woman.
Whenever sin is deliberately sheltered inside a city's walls, grief and mourning are likely to arrive at its gates.

div.title: The consequences of war (verse 1)
div.p: Henry observes that this opening verse continues the subject of chapter 3.
As disaster swept through the land, unmarried women—who faced social shame under the customs of the time—would depart from customary behavior and seek husbands for themselves.
This was one consequence of the war and devastation Isaiah foretold.

div.title: The Branch of the Lord and Zion's cleansing (verses 2–6)
div.p: Isaiah's promise concerns not only Christ's kingdom established in the apostolic age, but also its future enlargement as scattered Jews are gathered into the church.
Christ is called the Branch of the Lord because God's power plants him and causes him to flourish for divine praise.
The gospel is the Branch's fruit. All its blessings, spiritual graces and consolations spring from Christ.
It is called the fruit of the earth because its work appeared in this world and meets our needs in our present condition.
We show that we belong to true Israel when we see our greatest beauty in Christ and holiness, rather than merely possessing Israel's name.
Jerusalem's restoration and renewed fruitfulness would be a sign of this greater blessed age.
God keeps for himself a holy seed even when many who hold a visible place in Zion fall through unbelief.
When the Son of Man cleanses his kingdom, only those made holy will remain.
God's Providence may expose and remove sinners through judgment. But the Spirit of grace renews and converts.
He is the Spirit of judgment, enlightening the mind and convicting the conscience.
He is also the Spirit of burning, awakening holy affection and strengthening believers to pursue good with zeal.
Love for Christ and for souls, together with hatred of sin, moves believers to turn ungodliness away from Jacob.

Trials become a furnace that removes the dross from God's people. Through the Spirit's illuminating and powerful work, their sinful desires gradually lose their hold, and believers become more like the holy God.
The Lord protects his church and all who truly belong to it.
Gospel truth and appointed worship are the church's glory. Grace within a soul is that soul's glory, and God guards those who possess it.
Only the weary seek rest. Only those who recognize an approaching storm seek shelter.
Realizing that sin exposes us to divine displeasure, let us immediately take refuge in Jesus Christ and gratefully receive the protection he gives.

row.cell: The state and conduct of the Jewish nation.

div.title: God's carefully tended vineyard (verses 1–7)
div.p: Jesus Christ is God's beloved Son and our beloved Savior.
The Lord's care for Israel is pictured through the tending of a vineyard.
One day we will answer to him for all the advantages and opportunities we have received.
He planted the finest vines, gave Israel an excellent law and instituted appropriate forms of worship.
The temple was like a vineyard's tower, where God gave signs of his presence. His altar, where sacrifices were offered, represented the appointed means of grace.
God expects fruit from people who receive such privileges.
Good intentions and promising beginnings are worth something, but they are insufficient by themselves. There must be genuine fruit: thoughts, desires, words and actions guided by the Spirit.
Instead, the vineyard produced wild grapes—the products of corrupted human nature.
Where God's grace does not bear fruit, sin will.
When people who profess faith misuse their privileges and reject grace, the responsibility is their own.
They may lose their distinct standing among God's people.
A vineyard left unpruned becomes overgrown with thorns. When errors and sinful habits are never corrected, the same thing happens to a community.
God may withdraw his Spirit from people who persistently resist him, or remove the preaching of the gospel from places that have long dishonored it.
Consider the contrast between the fruit he seeks and the fruit our hearts produce.
He seeks humility, gentleness, love, patience, freedom from worldly obsession, prayer and praise.
Sin produces pride, anger, discontent, malice, contempt for God, curses and irreverent speech.
May we bear fruit patiently and finally receive everlasting life.

div.title: Warnings against greed, pleasure and moral confusion (verses 8–23)
div.p: The Lord pronounces judgment on people who devote their hearts to wealth.
Owning a house and a field and buying another is not in itself sinful.
The fault lies in never recognizing that one has enough.

p.hi: Greed is idolatry.

div.p: Many envy the prosperous person whom God calls miserable because of greed.
The Lord has many ways to empty even crowded cities. People who seek ultimate satisfaction in possessions will be disappointed.
He also warns those who live only for sensual pleasure.
Music is not wrong in itself, but becomes sinful when it diverts the heart from God.
People may continue pursuing pleasure even while divine judgments are unfolding around them.
Death lowers everyone, whether high or low.
In judging pride, God reveals both his power and his holiness.
Woe to those who deliberately pursue sinful desires, mock the Holy One of Israel and dare to challenge him.
They reverse the distinction between good and evil.
They prefer their own reasoning to God's revelation, and their personal schemes to his commands.
They treat profitable wrongdoing as prudent and duties requiring self-denial as foolish.
Drunkenness is no harmless pastime; it exposes the person to divine judgment.
Even judges may corrupt justice to protect their interests.
One sin frequently requires another sin to hide it.

div.title: The approaching instruments of judgment (verses 24–30)
div.p: Those who live in wickedness should not expect an easy life.
Sin weakens a nation's roots and destroys its blossoms—its strength and beauty.
When people reject God's word and law, they should not be surprised if he abandons them to judgment.
Under divine wrath, even mountains tremble and the powerful are afraid.
God can readily find instruments to punish people who continually provoke him.
Henry points to the Chaldeans, and later the Romans, as instruments used in the historical destruction of Judah and Jerusalem.
Those refusing to listen to God's warnings through his prophets would instead hear the threatening voices of their enemies.
They would find no refuge wherever they turned.
If God is displeased with us, no created source of comfort can finally make us secure.
Let us seek a well-founded assurance that, when every earthly support fails, God himself will remain the strength of our hearts and our portion forever.

row.cell: The vision which Isaiah beheld in the temple.
The Lord declares the blindness to come upon the Jewish nation, and the destruction which would follow.

div.title: Isaiah's vision of divine holiness (verses 1–8)
div.p: In this symbolic vision, the prophet sees the temple opened, even into its innermost sanctuary.
He stands outside while the divine presence appears upon the mercy seat, above the ark of the covenant, among the cherubim and seraphim. God's glory fills the temple.
John 12:41 explains the vision as Isaiah's sight of Christ's glory and his testimony about him.
Henry regards this as clear evidence that Jesus our Savior is God.
Through Jesus Christ, God is seated upon a throne of grace, and the way into his presence is opened.
The temple also pictures God's earthly church, filled with his glory.
The flowing hem of his robe fills the sanctuary, and all creation belongs to him. Yet he also dwells in every contrite heart.
The seraphim are holy angels. Henry explains their name as burning ones, full of love for God and zeal for his glory against sin.
They cover their faces in humility, ready to obey every command of God even without knowing all his secret purposes.
One sight of Christ in glory would put an end to human vanity, arrogance and proud ignorance.
Isaiah became overwhelmed by the awareness of his own impurity.
Without a Mediator between us and the holy God, we are undone.
Even a glimpse of divine glory exposes our supposed righteousness as filthy rags.
No human being could stand to speak before God's holiness, justice and majesty without finding mercy and grace through Christ.
The burning coal may picture the prophet's assurance that his sin was forgiven and his ministry accepted through Christ's atonement.
Only what comes through the Savior's satisfaction and intercession can cleanse and comfort the soul.
We need our sins removed to speak confidently to God in prayer or from God in preaching.
Those who recognize sin's burden and danger may seek this cleansing.
God's messengers may take courage: he has sent them to speak in his name and will sustain them in their calling.

div.title: The warning of spiritual blindness and the remnant (verses 9–13)
div.p: The Lord sent Isaiah to announce the coming ruin of his people.
Many hear the sound of God's word yet never receive its power within the heart.
God may, in righteous judgment, leave those who persistently reject truth to blindness of mind.
But no humble person genuinely seeking Christ should imagine that this punishment is meant to discourage sincere inquiry.
It falls upon those determined to retain their sins.
Let everyone ask for the enlightening Holy Spirit, so that God's mercies may become precious and the heart may avoid such dreadful hardness.
Even under judgment the Lord would preserve a holy remnant, compared with a tenth remaining.
God continues preserving his church.
Visible religious communities and professing believers may be cut back like barren branches. Yet the holy seed will put forth new growth, from which many branches of righteousness will arise.

row.cell: Ahaz threatened by Israel and Syria; and is assured their attack would be in vain.
God gives a sure sign by the promise of the long-expected Messiah.
The folly and sin of seeking relief from Assyria are reproved.

div.title: God promises that the attack will fail (verses 1–9)
div.p: Ungodly people are often punished through others who are just as wicked.
The people of Judah were terrified by the armies of Israel and Syria.
Having made God their enemy, they did not know how to find his favor again.
Isaiah was called to teach them confidence in God's protection, rather than fear of their enemies.
Ahaz regarded the attacking kings as powerful. The prophet dismissed them as the smoking ends of two burned-out torches.
The kingdoms of Syria and Israel were already nearing their end.
Worldly rulers may for a time accomplish the purposes God permits, bringing destruction to others. But when their work is complete, he can extinguish their power.
Their attack on Judah would fail because they had devised an evil plan that offended God.

p.hi: Human beings make plans; God decides their outcome.

div.p: How foolish for rulers already close to ruin to plan the destruction of their neighbors!
Isaiah therefore urged the people to believe the Lord's promise. Faith is necessary to quiet the heart during severe trouble.

div.title: The sign of the promised Messiah (verses 10–16)
div.p: People who inwardly distrust God sometimes disguise that unbelief as reverence.
They refuse to trust his word yet claim they are unwilling to test him.
Isaiah rebuked Ahaz and his court for treating divine revelation so lightly.
Distrust greatly dishonors God. But human unbelief cannot cancel his promise.
The Lord himself would give a sign.
The Messiah was to be born from this people. Judah could not be completely destroyed before that blessing was fulfilled.
The promise points to a glorious birth and gives comfort through Christ, our relationship to him and our hope in him.
He would grow as other children did, eating ordinary food in his country. Yet unlike fallen children, he would always reject evil and choose good.
His birth would be accomplished by the Holy Spirit's power, but he would not need extraordinary food from angels.
Then Isaiah speaks of the nearer, swift defeat of Judah's two enemies.

Henry offers a possible reading of the immediate sign: before Shear-jashub, the prophet's young son present with him (Isaiah 7:3), grew three or four years older, the two hostile kings would no longer rule their forces.
This is presented as Henry's interpretation, not an identification of Shear-jashub with the promised Messiah.
Because God supplied the sign even after Ahaz had refused to ask, the prophecy could raise hope far beyond the immediate political crisis.
For believers awaiting the Messiah, that hope was a lasting comfort.
How thankful we should be that the Word became flesh! May we trust him, love him and follow his example.

div.title: The cost of relying on Assyria (verses 17–25)
div.p: People unwilling to believe God's promises should expect his warnings to become frighteningly real.
No one can escape his judgments.
The Lord can sweep away a nation's supports and use whatever instruments he chooses, repaying or dismissing them as he wills.
Judah's pleasant land would be transformed. Agriculture would cease, and former fields would become desolate.
What sorrow can sin not bring upon a people?
Those who neglect the great salvation place themselves in danger of every kind of misery.
If we continually remain unfruitful despite enjoying the means of grace, we should tremble at the warning that fruit may never grow from us again.

row.cell: Comfort for those who fear God.

div.title: The coming Assyrian invasion (verses 1–8)
div.p: Isaiah was instructed to write on a large scroll or metal tablet words meaning “Hurry to the plunder; rush to the prey.”
They foretold how quickly the Assyrian army would arrive and seize enormous spoils.
Soon the wealth of Damascus and Samaria, cities that then appeared secure and powerful, would be carried away by Assyria.
The prophet appealed to the promised Messiah, who would one day appear in this land. Henry understands this appeal as resting on the Messiah's divine power to protect it in the meantime.
A gentle stream represents a mild, peaceable government. A raging flood pictures the overwhelming power of an invading conqueror and tyrant.
The invader's success is also described as a bird of prey spreading its wings across the land.
Those who reject Christ may call their rejection freedom, but they will discover it is the deepest slavery.
Yet no enemy can take a believer from Emmanuel's hand or deprive that person of the heavenly inheritance.

div.title: God as sanctuary or stumbling stone (verses 9–16)
div.p: Isaiah challenged Judah's enemies: their plans would come to nothing, and their strength would be broken.
During trouble, we must guard against fears that lead us to dishonest or sinful methods of protecting ourselves.
Reverent fear of God protects us from the tormenting fear of human beings.
If we properly understood his majesty and power, we would see that our enemies' strength remains under his control.
The Lord is a sanctuary for those who trust him.
But to those who put their fear and hope in created things, he becomes a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.
If God's truth itself offends us, it will become the cause of our ruin.
The apostle applies this warning to those persisting in unbelief toward Christ's gospel (1 Peter 2:8).
Crucified Emmanuel offended unbelieving Jews and continues to offend many who call themselves Christians.
They regard preaching of the cross as foolishness and reject his teachings and commandments.

div.title: Seek God's word instead of spiritual deception (verses 17–22)
div.p: Isaiah foresaw a time when the Lord would hide his face, yet he resolved to continue waiting for God's return in mercy.
His children's names served as divinely given reminders, calling the people to consider God's message, even though they were not miraculous signs.
Unbelieving Israelites sought guidance from diviners, employing foolish and sinful practices.
Where should we turn if we wish to know God's mind and our duty?

p.hi: To the law and the testimony.

div.p: There we discover what is good and what the Lord requires.
We must speak about divine things in words taught by the Holy Spirit and submit ourselves to their authority.
Those who consult spirits while neglecting God's word invite distress and darkness.
Leaving God means leaving the path of all true good.
A resentful heart punishes itself through its own bitterness.
People who curse God and turn away from his light will find their fears deepening, with no way of relief.
Those who deliberately close their eyes to Scripture may rightly be left in spiritual darkness.
All human troubles are small compared with the destruction awaiting people who abandon the words of Christ to pursue deception.

row.cell: The Son that should be born, and his kingdom.
The judgments to come upon Israel, and on the enemies of the kingdom of Christ.

div.title: The promised Son and his everlasting kingdom (verses 1–7)
div.p: The Syrians and Assyrians had first ravaged the regions described here.
Yet those same regions were among the first to receive Christ's preaching.
Those without the gospel walk in darkness and extreme danger.
When the gospel reaches a place—or even one person's heart—light comes.
Let us pray earnestly that this light will shine in us and make us wise for salvation.
The gospel brings joy.
But joy may be preceded by hard work, as harvest follows the farmer's labor, and by conflict, as victory and spoils follow a soldier's struggle.
Israel had been delivered from various oppressors. Those deliverances pictured the greater release of believers from Satan's yoke.
The Holy Spirit cleanses souls from sin's power and pollution, like a purifying fire.
All these blessings come through the Messiah, Emmanuel.
The prophecy says that a Child is born as though it were already accomplished, because God's promise was certain.
Before Christ became human, the church already benefited from the work he undertook.
Those waiting for Israel's consolation treasured this promise of his person and kingdom.
The Child would be born for sinners and believers throughout every age.
He is rightly called Wonderful, being both God and man.
His love astonishes angels and glorified saints.
He is Counselor: he has known God's purposes from eternity and gives wise guidance for our good. No one teaches as he does.
He is Mighty God, for only divine power could accomplish the Mediator's saving work.

p.hi: He is God, one with the Father.

div.p: He is Prince of Peace: he reconciles us with God, grants peace of heart and conscience, and will finally establish a kingdom in which people learn war no more.
He bears the responsibility for his government, and its peace and the happiness of its citizens will never end.
Henry sees the close agreement between this prophecy and New Testament teaching as showing that the Jewish prophets and Christian teachers proclaimed the same Messiah.

p.hi: No ordinary earthly king or kingdom can fulfill this description.
