div.p: Lord, grant your people the grace to know Christ through every glorious title and gracious attribute. Increase your grace in every redeemed heart.

div.title: Israel's refusal to turn from sin (verses 8–21)
div.p: People are approaching ruin when God's humbling judgments fail to humble their hearts.
His purpose in striking them is to turn them back to himself.
When lighter judgments do not bring repentance, more severe ones may follow.
Israel's leaders misled the people.
We should be wary of people who flatter us while we are doing wrong.
Wickedness had spread everywhere.
Trouble would surround the people, and they would see no way of escape.
When a nation's conduct displeases God, even former friends may turn into enemies.
The supports in which the people trusted would be taken away.
The rulers were the head, while the false prophets were likened to the tail and rushes, displaying their worthlessness.
During civil conflict, people would attack even their own relatives.
Because they did not return to the One who struck them, the judgment continued.
When God judges, his purpose will prevail.

p.hi: The proudest sinner will either bend or break.

row.cell: The Assyrian but an instrument in the hand of God for the punishment of his people.

div.title: Judgment against unjust rulers (verses 1–4)
div.p: Henry treats these opening verses as a continuation of the warning in chapter 9.
Woe to powerful rulers who devise and impose unjust laws!
Woe also to the officials who draft those decrees and record them for enforcement!
No authority or bureaucratic form can make oppression right before God.
When divine judgment comes, where will such sinners flee, and how will they escape?

div.title: Assyria as an instrument of God's Providence (verses 5–19)
div.p: See what a change sin had produced!
The Assyrian king imagined he was acting entirely by his own will.
But the tyrants of this world can become instruments of God's Providence.
The Lord intended to correct his people for hypocrisy, bring them nearer to himself and awaken genuine repentance.

p.hi: That was not Sennacherib's purpose.

div.p: He was pursuing greed and ambition.
He boasted that he had defeated many nations through his own intelligence and military strength.
He did not recognize that God had given him his position and placed the rod of power in his hand.
His victories had seemed effortless, like taking eggs from a nest while the birds remained silent.
After taking Samaria, he supposed Jerusalem would inevitably fall.
It was shameful that Jerusalem had adopted images and idolatry, allowing pagan neighbors to surpass her in those very practices.
Christians behave just as foolishly when they compete with unbelievers in worldly vanity instead of valuing the gifts that should distinguish God's people.
For an ax or saw to boast against the one using it would be absurd. Sennacherib's boasting against Jehovah was even more absurd.
When the Lord allows his people to experience suffering, he calls them to remember and confess their sins, become humble and return to duty.
The intended fruit of affliction is the removal of sin.
Once that purpose has been accomplished, God may mercifully remove the trial.
The attack on Zion would ultimately fail.
The Lord would become a consuming fire against workers of evil, destroying their strength.
The collapse of the Assyrian forces would resemble an army thrown into confusion when its standard-bearer faints.
Who can stand against the holy Lord?

div.title: The remnant delivered from Assyria (verses 20–34)
div.p: Trials can teach believers to stop making created things their final security.
Only those who return sincerely to God, rather than merely professing faith, can rest upon him with true comfort.
The Lord would justly bring destruction upon a people who provoked him, but he would also set limits to that punishment.
His people should not surrender to fear.
God's anger toward them is brief; when it passes, human anger need no longer terrify them.
The rod used for discipline would not merely be put aside. It would be thrown into the fire.
To strengthen his people's faith, Isaiah recalled God's earlier victories over their enemies.
He promised deliverance from Assyria.
Henry records that some interpreters see a further application to the Jews' release from captivity and a greater deliverance from sin and Satan's tyranny.
He also considers the phrase “because of the anointing” in relation both to faithful Israelites possessing God's grace and to the Messiah, God's Anointed One.
Verses 28–34 describe prophetically Sennacherib's advance toward Jerusalem.
There the Lord, in whom Hezekiah trusted, cut down the invader's army as a forest is cut down.
The same divine care extends to Christ's church in every age.
Because of the anointing of the great Redeemer, the yoke of every power opposing Christ must finally be broken.
Those who share in the Holy Spirit's anointing can be assured of complete and eternal deliverance.

row.cell: The peaceful character of Christ's kingdom and subjects.
The conversion of the Gentiles and Jews.

div.title: The Messiah's righteous and peaceful kingdom (verses 1–9)
div.p: The Messiah is called a Rod and a Branch, terms suggesting a small, delicate shoot that might easily be broken.
He grows from Jesse's stem, after David's royal family has been cut down and brought almost to the ground.
By the time Jesus was born, that house had sunk very low.
His humble beginning showed that his kingdom was not of this world.
The Holy Spirit rests upon him, with every gift and grace.
The fullness of deity dwells in him (Colossians 1:19; 2:9).
Henry notes that many readers recognize seven gifts of the Spirit in this description, and sees the passage as clearly teaching the Spirit's work.
The Messiah governs with perfect justice and righteousness.
He accomplishes his judgments by his word and Spirit.
Great peace belongs to his kingdom.
The gospel transforms human nature. Those who once oppressed gentle people become gentle and kind themselves.
This transformation has appeared throughout Christian history, although it awaits a far fuller manifestation in the latter days.
As the great Shepherd, Christ cares for his flock and changes the significance of suffering and death so thoroughly that these things cannot do his people ultimate harm.
God's people are freed not only from evil itself but also from the fear of it.
Who can separate them from Christ's love?
As we grow in the knowledge of the God of love, we become more like him and more loving toward those who bear his likeness.
Knowledge of the Lord will spread as widely as the sea extends.
Christians in every age have witnessed something of this blessed power, though the most glorious fulfillment remains ahead.
Meanwhile, let us live and work in ways that honor Christ and his kingdom of peace.

div.title: The Gentiles and Israel gathered to Christ (verses 10–16)
div.p: When the gospel is openly preached, Gentiles will seek Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior and find rest for their souls.
When the Lord's time arrives to deliver his people, even mountains of opposition become level ground before him.
He can quickly change dark days into glorious ones.
Henry looks forward to the Lord gathering his ancient people into the church, along with the fullness of the Gentiles, so that all may be united in holy love.
Until that time, let us follow the highway of holiness prepared for the redeemed.
Wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ unto eternal life.
Trust him to prepare the way through death, the river separating this world from eternity.

p.hi: This is a hymn of praise suited to the times of the Messiah.

div.title: A song of salvation and thanksgiving
div.p: This song would be fitting when Israel's exiles finally returned from their long captivity.
It is especially fitting when a sinner first discovers peace and joy through faith.
It also belongs to believers whose peace is renewed after God's correction for past wandering, and to all the redeemed together before God's throne in heaven.
The promise is certain and its blessings abundant.
Everything received through Jesus Christ calls us to wholehearted thanksgiving.
Through Jesus Christ, the Root of Jesse, divine anger was turned away, because he is our Peace.
Those whom God has reconciled to himself receive his comfort.
They learn to rejoice in him and in the assurance that they belong to him.
Let the believer say: I will trust God to prepare me for his salvation and keep me until its full realization.
I will entrust every concern to him, confident that he can make all things work together for good.

p.hi: Faith in God is a powerful remedy against tormenting fears.

div.p: Many Christians know God as their strength but fail to make him their song.
They remain in spiritual darkness and miss the joy that should accompany their confidence.
Those who rely upon his strength ought to praise him for it, giving him the glory and accepting the comfort.
Salvation arises from God the Father's love, reaches us through God the Son, and is applied by the renewing power of God the Spirit.
When faith sees this, the frightened sinner learns to hope in God and loses the fear that formerly enslaved the soul.
The purifying and sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit is often pictured as water springing from a fountain.
This grace comes through Christ's mediation and is conveyed to our souls through God's appointed means of worship and instruction.
Praise God that wells of salvation are open on every side, from which we may draw living water and consolation.
In the latter part of the song (verses 4–6), believers urge one another to praise the Lord and invite still more people to join them.
Disagreements about dates, seasons and other secondary matters must not divide Christian hearts.
Our deepest concern should be to belong among those to whom Christ will finally say:

p.hi: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

div.title: The appointed armies of judgment (verses 1–5)
div.p: Warnings from God's word become a heavy burden to those determined to remain wicked.
The forces gathered against Babylon are called God's consecrated or appointed ones because they are designated for this particular work and given the ability to accomplish it.
They are also called his mighty ones, for even their strength comes from him.
They would arrive from distant lands.
God can bring judgment through people who seem so far away that no one imagines they might ever become dangerous.

div.title: Babylon's defeat by the Medes and Persians (verses 6–18)
div.p: Isaiah describes Babylon's terrible overthrow by the Medes and Persians.
People who were arrogant, cruel and frightening during prosperity can become overwhelmed by terror when calamity arrives.
Every confidence and comfort would fail.
The sun and stars are described as losing their light.
Such language often appears in the prophets to picture the upheaval of governments and kingdoms.
God would confront Babylon's wrongdoing, especially pride, which brings people low.
The destruction is pictured as a general scene of horror.
Those who join themselves to Babylon should expect to share her judgments (Revelation 18:4).
People are willing to surrender all their possessions to preserve life, yet their wealth cannot ransom them from death.
The cruelty described here should make us grieve and wonder how deeply human nature has become corrupted.
Henry also addresses the suffering of infants. He connects the reality of death from life's very beginning with his doctrine of humanity's inherited guilt through the fall.
That is his theological explanation of the tragedy, not an endorsement of brutality.
The final day of the Lord will be more terrible still than the judgments described in this chapter.
The unrepentant will find no refuge.
Yet few people behave as though they believe these warnings.

div.title: Babylon's complete desolation (verses 19–22)
div.p: Babylon had been a magnificent and powerful city.
Yet Isaiah announced its total destruction, leaving it uninhabited and occupied by wild animals.
Henry sees the fulfillment of this prediction as evidence of Scripture's truth.
He also understands Babylon's ruin as a picture of the coming destruction of New Testament Babylon, and as a warning to all sinners to flee God's wrath.
For believers, it is encouragement to expect eventual victory over the enemies of their souls and of Christ's church.
Everything in the world can change and decay.
Let us therefore seek the kingdom that cannot be shaken and hold firmly to the grace through which we may serve God acceptably, with reverence and holy fear.

row.cell: The destruction of Babylon, and the death of its proud monarch.
Assurance of the destruction of Assyria.

div.title: Babylon's downfall and the humiliation of its king (verses 1–23)
div.p: God governs the whole course of Providence with the good of his people in view.
Settlement in the promised land is a gift of his mercy.
Let the church welcome those whom God himself receives.
Wherever believers live, they should recommend true faith through upright, winsome conversation and conduct.
Those who formerly opposed them may eventually be humbled and brought to obedience—a pattern that can also be seen in the gospel's progress.
The Lord himself brings about this blessed change.
His people will find rest from sorrow, burdens and fear of further suffering.
Babylon possessed vast riches. Its king used his control of wealth to dominate other nations.
He had especially oppressed the Jews, increasing the guilt that would eventually bring judgment upon him.

p.hi: Tyrants sacrifice their true interests to their passions and desires.

div.p: It is right to aspire to be like the Most Holy, because God commands us to be holy as he is holy.
But it is sinful to aspire to be like the Most High, demanding his supreme position for ourselves.
Satan used that ambition to tempt our first parents.
The proud monarch would be brought completely low.
Those who refuse to stop sinning may be stopped by God's judgment.
He would die and go down to the grave—the fate that ultimately overtakes even the greatest tyrants.
Genuine glory, meaning grace, accompanies the soul to heaven.
Earthly splendor descends with the body into the grave and comes to nothing.
Being denied an honorable burial for righteousness' sake can be borne with joy (Matthew 5:12).
But when disgrace is just punishment for sin, it points toward the final shame awaiting the unrepentant.
The fall of a tyrant can bring relief and joy to many people.
God will call to account those who destroy the peace of nations.
The picture of the king being received among the dead points, in Henry's reading, toward the world of departed spirits.
Human souls pass from this life into that world. They remain conscious there, although we cannot converse with them.
For someone who dies unholy after enjoying worldly glory and pleasure, death and judgment are dreadful indeed.
The offspring of persistent evildoers have no lasting honorable inheritance.
Babylon would become ruined and deserted.
Henry sees a further illustration of the destruction of New Testament Babylon (Revelation 18:2).
When people refuse to be cleansed through the broom of reformation, they face being swept away through the broom of destruction.

div.title: Assyria's power will be broken (verses 24–27)
div.p: Those who make themselves a burden and a yoke upon God's people should consider the judgment awaiting them.
Those who are called according to God's purpose may take comfort: everything God has determined will certainly stand.
The Lord of hosts had resolved to break Assyria's yoke.
His hand was raised to carry out that judgment, and no human power could turn it back.
Through such providential events, God demonstrates how deeply he hates sin.

div.title: The Philistines are warned (verses 28–32)
div.p: Isaiah also announced the destruction of Philistia through famine and war.
Henry says Hezekiah would become a more serious threat to them than Uzziah had been.
Their expectation of joy would end in mourning as their land suffered ruin.
The same warning applies to proud and rebellious sinners.
Yet the Lord founded Zion as a refuge for poor sinners who flee the judgment to come and trust in his mercy through Jesus Christ.
Let us tell others of the protection and comfort we have found, and urge them to seek that salvation too.

p.hi: The Divine judgments about to come upon the Moabites.

div.title: The destruction approaching Moab
div.p: Henry says this prophecy would be fulfilled within three years. Its fulfillment would confirm Isaiah's prophetic calling and support belief in the other messages he delivered.
The judgment announced against Moab unfolds in several ways.
Verse 1: The enemy would surprise the nation's principal cities. Terrible changes can come in a very short time.
Verse 2: The Moabites would seek help from their idols.
People without faith may find no genuine comforter when they suffer. Yet fear and disaster seldom lead them, by themselves, to come before the forgiving God with sincere sorrow and believing prayer.
Verse 3: Cries of grief would spread throughout the country.
It offers little relief to know that many other people share the same suffering.
Verse 4: Even Moab's soldiers would lose their courage.
God can quickly remove whatever a nation regards as its strongest protection.
Verse 5: The suffering would grieve people living nearby.
Although the Moabites were enemies of Israel, they were also fellow human beings. Their misery should still awaken compassion.
Verses 6–9: Isaiah describes widespread lamentation as Moab becomes prey to Assyria.
The country would be plundered, and famine would follow the devastation of war.
Those who dedicate themselves to gaining and storing up worldly possessions rarely consider how suddenly everything they possess may be taken away.
Let us warn even our enemies about the danger before them.
And as we warn them, pray that they may find forgiveness for their sins.

row.cell: Moab is exhorted to yield obedience.
The pride and the judgments of Moab.

div.title: Moab is called to submit and show mercy (verses 1–5)
div.p: God warns sinners how they can turn from the path of destruction. Here he gives such counsel to Moab.
The people were to send Judah the tribute they had previously agreed to pay.
Henry draws a wider lesson: turn away from sin through righteousness, and God may prolong peace.
He also applies the command to submission to Jesus Christ.
Give him your best gift—indeed, offer yourselves as a living sacrifice.
When you approach God, the supreme Ruler, come in the name of the Lamb of God.
Those refusing Christ's rule resemble a bird wandering away from its nest, exposed to the next bird of prey.
Anyone unwilling to reverence God becomes vulnerable to fear of everything else.
Moab was called to show kindness to the people of Israel.
Those who hope to receive help when they themselves suffer must show compassion to other sufferers.
The promise concerning Hezekiah's throne belongs, in an even greater sense, to the kingdom of Jesus Christ.
Serving him may not bring earthly riches, honor or public approval.
It may even expose believers to poverty and contempt.
Nevertheless, they gain peace of conscience and eternal life.

div.title: Moab's pride and judgment (verses 6–14)
div.p: Those who refuse all counsel cannot readily be helped.
Henry regards pride as especially destructive to souls.
Proud people often become easily angered, and their pride and anger lead to lies and fruitless schemes.
Moab's countryside was famous for fields and vineyards, yet invading armies would ruin them.
God can quickly turn laughter into mourning and joy into sorrow.
We should rejoice confidently in God, but receive earthly blessings with humble awareness that they may soon disappear.
The prophet felt sorrow at the destruction of such a beautiful and fruitful land.
Moab's false gods could provide no help.
But the God of Israel, the only true God, would fulfill everything he had declared.
Moab's coming judgment was close, and the people were urged to prepare.
Even the sternest warnings of God's wrath disclose a path of escape to those who take them seriously.
The only lasting escape is to submit to the Son of David and dedicate ourselves to him.
When the appointed time comes, the pride, prosperity and multitude of the wicked will all pass away.

div.title: Damascus and Israel brought low (verses 1–11)
div.p: Sin makes cities desolate.

It is strange that conquerors should glory in harming other human beings. Better for such ruined places to become grazing grounds for flocks than to shelter people openly rebelling against God and holiness.
Israel's fortresses and the northern kingdom would be brought down.
People who share in wrongdoing may rightly come to share in its consequences.
Israel's sins had made the people ripe for destruction.
Their former glory would be removed as quickly as grain disappears when a farmer harvests a field.
Nevertheless, God would preserve a small remnant.
Only a few would remain—one here and another there, as when fruit is left after harvest.
Those preserved would be brought toward holiness.
They would return to God, recognize his hand in events and give him his rightful praise.
This is the purpose of Providence under our Maker, and the work of grace under the Holy One of Israel.
The people would turn from idols, things they had invented through their own imaginations.
We have reason to regard as beneficial those trials that separate us from our sins.
God is the Rock of our salvation and our strength.
Forgetfulness of him lies at the root of every sin.
The pleasant plants and shoots imported from distant soil represent foreign and idolatrous forms of worship with their associated sinful practices.
People might cultivate those plants with great energy, but the effort would ultimately be wasted.
Let this picture teach the danger and unavoidable consequences of sin.

div.title: The Assyrian threat vanishes (verses 12–14)
div.p: The strength and rage of Assyria resembled enormous waves of the sea.
Yet once the God of Israel rebuked the invaders, they would flee like chaff before the wind.
In the evening, Jerusalem would be terrified by the presence of a powerful enemy.
By morning, the invading army would be almost entirely destroyed.
Happy are those who remember God as their salvation and depend on his power and grace.
The troubles believers endure, and the success their enemies enjoy, are both temporary.
But the lasting joy of God's people and the final defeat of those determined to destroy them will endure forever.

p.hi: God's care for his people; and the increase of the church.

div.title: God's care for his church amid uncertain events
div.p: Henry describes this chapter as one of the most difficult passages in Scripture.
The people who first received it probably understood more of its details than readers do today.
Swift messengers travel by water toward a people singled out by Providence, measured and trampled down.
God's own people may also be trampled underfoot.
Yet those who imagine they can swallow up his people discover that, although the church may be brought low, she is not abandoned or finally destroyed.
All nations should watch the movements of God's Providence and follow the directions of his will.
The Lord gives Isaiah an assurance to pass on to his people.
Zion is his resting place forever.
He watches over it and provides comfort suited to the need of each moment.
That comfort is precious precisely because it comes at the proper time.
God will judge both his enemies and the enemies of his people.
His children enjoy his care in every season, while their enemies remain exposed to his judgment in every season.
This should bring us to offer a tribute of praise.
Whatever we bring to God must be offered in the way he has appointed.
We may expect to meet him where he has chosen to make his name known.
Through these events, the nations will recognize that the Lord is God and Israel belongs to him.
They too will unite in offering spiritual sacrifices for his glory.
Happy are those who take warning from God's judgments upon others and promptly join his people.

Whatever exact land or nation Isaiah has in view, the passage teaches us not to think God has forgotten his church or ceased to govern human affairs merely because he allows evil people to prevail for a while.
He has wise reasons that we cannot presently understand.
They will become clear at the great day of his appearing, when every human work is brought into judgment and everyone receives what is due.

row.cell: Its deliverance, and the conversion of the people.

div.title: Egypt humbled through its own troubles (verses 1–17)
div.p: God would enter Egypt in judgment.
He would raise up the causes of Egypt's downfall from among its own people.
When ungodly people escape an immediate danger, they often imagine themselves safe.
But unless they repent, sin's consequences will pursue them and eventually overtake them.
The Egyptians would fall under a harsh ruler, a prediction Henry says was fulfilled soon afterward.
They were famous for learning and scientific skill.
Yet God would allow their wise men to follow corrupt plans and quarrel with one another, until the nation's own divisions made it an object of contempt and pity.
God can make sinners afraid of the very people they once looked down upon and oppressed.
He can also make evildoers terrify one another, while ordinary circumstances appear threatening on every side.

div.title: Egypt's future turning to the Lord (verses 18–25)
div.p: The prophetic words “In that day” do not always refer to the event described immediately before them.
Here Isaiah looks toward a later period.
Egyptians would learn to speak the holy language of Scripture, not merely recognizing it but using it.
Converting grace changes people's hearts, and therefore also changes their speech, because the mouth speaks from what fills the heart.
So many Jews would settle in Egypt, Henry says, that five cities would soon be filled.
A place formerly notorious for worshiping the sun would experience a remarkable spiritual reform.
Jesus Christ is the great Altar who makes the gifts offered through him acceptable.
There people would offer the gospel's spiritual sacrifices: prayer and praise.
Those wounded and humbled by God's correction should take courage.
When suffering leads them to return and call upon the Lord, he heals their souls and changes sorrowful petitions into joyful thanksgiving.
Gentile nations would be joined together within Christ's flock, under the great Shepherd.
They would also be united with the Jews.
All would be received by the same Lord and share the same blessing.
When believers meet at the same throne of grace and serve in the same work of worship, they should allow quarrels to end and be joined together through holy love.

p.hi: The invasion and conquest of Egypt and Ethiopia.

div.title: Isaiah's sign of the coming captivity
div.p: Isaiah became a sign to the people through his unusual clothing when he appeared in public.
As a prophet, he normally wore sackcloth, expressing his separation from worldly vanity.
God told him to remove it from his waist, to wear no outer garment and to walk barefoot.
This sign foretold that the king of Assyria would lead away captives from Egypt and Ethiopia in the same humiliated, stripped-down condition.
The world often judges believers foolish when their obedience to God makes them noticeably different from others.
But the Lord sustains his servants even when obedience involves particularly difficult trials.
What he asks them to endure for his sake is generally light when compared with the suffering that multitudes endure year after year through sin.
Whoever makes a created person or thing the foundation of hope, trust or pride—giving it the place belonging to God—will eventually be disappointed and ashamed.
Yet disappointment in human supports should not drive us to despair.
Instead it should drive us toward God, whose promises will not fail.
This same lesson remains important for us.
When the hour of urgent need arrives, where should we turn for help except to the Lord our Righteousness?

div.title: Babylon's capture (verses 1–10)
div.p: Babylon lay in a flat country with abundant water.
Isaiah repeatedly predicted its destruction, which Henry also sees as a picture of the downfall of the great enemy of the New Testament church foretold in Revelation.
For oppressed captives, the news of Babylon's ruin would bring relief.
For proud oppressors, it would bring distress.
Let this teach us not to rely on empty amusement and bodily pleasure, because we do not know how suddenly laughter may end in grief.
Isaiah raises the alarm as Babylon is threatened by Cyrus.
The images of a donkey and a camel appear to Henry to represent the Medes and Persians.
Babylon's idols would be unable to protect the city; instead, they would themselves be broken.
Genuine believers are like grain on God's threshing floor.
Hypocrites resemble the chaff and straw mixed among the wheat until the harvest separates them.
God's grain should expect to be threshed by suffering and persecution.
Israel endured such afflictions, yet even in them the Lord still called the people his own.
Whatever happens to the church in the past, present or future, look to God.
He has the power to do anything for his church and the grace to do everything that serves her true good.

div.title: The watchman's message to Edom (verses 11 and 12)
div.p: God's prophets and ministers are like watchmen.
In peaceful times they guard the city to see that all is well.
In times of war they look for approaching danger and warn the people.
After long spiritual sleep, it is time to wake up and work.
Our journey is long and our duties many.
The question about the night asks whether dawn and relief are approaching.
Yet many people ask God's watchmen questions only out of curiosity, demanding difficult predictions or obscure prophecies explained.
They fail to inquire about their own souls, salvation and daily duty.
The prophet's reply points to morning followed by night.
Periods of light, health, youth or prosperity may be followed by illness, old age and adversity.
Use the present morning well to prepare for the night to come.
The call is urgent: Inquire. Return. Come.
There is no time for idle delay.
Those who return to God discover how much good work remains and how little time they have to accomplish it.

div.title: The danger awaiting Arabia (verses 13–17)
div.p: The peoples of Arabia lived in tents and kept flocks and herds.
An invading army would threaten them and make them vulnerable.
None of us knows what severe distress may arrive before death.
People who now eat abundantly may later lack even necessary bread.
Neither the ability of expert archers nor the courage of strong soldiers can protect a nation from God's judgments.
What a poor kind of glory can vanish so quickly!
The Lord has spoken, and none of his words will fail.
The Strength of Israel cannot lie.
Those who possess riches and glory beyond an invader's reach are truly blessed.
Every other form of prosperity is passing away.

row.cell: The siege and taking of Jerusalem.
The wicked conduct of its inhabitants.
The displacing of Shebna, and the promotion of Eliakim, applied to the Messiah.

div.title: Jerusalem's terror and suffering (verses 1–7)
div.p: Why was Jerusalem overwhelmed with fear?
Some of the dead were not killed by swords but by famine; others may have died from terror or become helpless through discouragement.
The leaders fled but were overtaken.
God's servants who see approaching judgments and warn sinners about them feel genuine grief at the prospect.
Yet even the most dreadful horrors of a city captured by force are only a faint picture of the terrors of the final day of wrath.

div.title: Defensive preparations without faith (verses 8–14)
div.p: Judah's weakness became more obvious than ever.
The people showed both confidence in earthly strength and careless disregard for divine warning.
They strengthened fortifications and secured the city's water supply.
These were practical measures, but they acted without seeking God, honoring him or depending upon his blessing.
Every created resource becomes useful only as the Lord makes it useful.
We should thank him for each gift and use it to serve him.
The people were contemptuous of divine justice even as God corrected them.
His purpose was to humble them and call them to repentance.
Instead they pursued pleasure and acted as though judgment and eternity did not matter.
Henry sees practical unbelief in life after death as a root of the selfish security and sensuality that ruin so many people.
Such disbelief dishonors God and rejects his appointed remedy.
Whether it expresses itself through presumptuous confidence or through despair, it can lead people to willful destruction.

div.title: Shebna removed, Eliakim appointed (verses 15–25)
div.p: Isaiah's warning to Shebna exposed his pride, vanity and imagined security.
How empty is worldly greatness when death can so soon bring it to nothing!
What lasting difference does it make whether a person's body rests in an elaborate tomb or beneath ordinary grass?
Someone who uses power to drive other people about may justly find himself driven from his own position.
Eliakim would replace Shebna.
Those entrusted with authority should ask God for the grace to perform their responsibilities properly.
Eliakim's appointment also points beyond itself.
Jesus describes his own authority as Mediator through the key of David (Revelation 3:7).
He possesses complete authority over the kingdom of heaven and every affair belonging to it.
Human rulers should act as fathers to the people under their care.
It is more honorable to bring goodness to one's family through faith and service than to inherit famous names or titles.
Worldly prestige adds no true excellence to a person. It hangs upon someone like a decoration that can soon fall away.
Eliakim was compared with a nail fixed securely in a wall, on which his family could depend.
In Eastern houses, great nails or pegs were built into walls to hold household possessions.
Jesus Christ is the secure nail.
Whatever we entrust to him in faith cannot be finally lost.
He opens a door that no one can close and brings faithful believers, body and soul, into eternal glory.
But those who reject his salvation will discover that when he closes the door, no one can open it—whether they are excluded from heaven or confined under final judgment.

div.title: Tyre's commercial greatness is brought low (verses 1–14)
div.p: Tyre had become a great marketplace for the nations. Its inhabitants were especially known for festivity and entertainment, and those pleasures made them reluctant to consider the warnings God sent through his servants.
Its merchants were as wealthy and honored as princes, and they lived with all the luxury of rulers.
Yet its splendor would not keep the city from destruction. When Tyre lay waste, the merchants would flee from it and seek shelter elsewhere.

Those who move away to escape a trouble that has unsettled them may discover that a different location cannot give them inward rest. When God's judgments pursue sinners, they will overtake them wherever they go.
How could such a wealthy and powerful city fall? Its destruction was from the Almighty.
God intended its fall to reveal the emptiness and uncertainty of earthly fame, magnificence and prosperity.
The ruin of Tyre warns every city and every person to beware of pride. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled.
The Lord had the power to bring this judgment himself; he chose to use the Chaldeans as his instruments.

div.title: Tyre's recovery and the right use of wealth (verses 15–18)
div.p: Tyre's ruin would not last forever. The Lord would eventually visit the city with mercy.
Yet when Tyre returned to commercial freedom, its people would once more practice the old arts through which they tempted others.
Love of worldly wealth is spiritual idolatry. Covetousness is also a form of idolatry.
The prophecy therefore teaches those who possess wealth to employ it in God's service.

When we remain in fellowship with God while pursuing our ordinary occupations, and do everything within our ability to advance the gospel, our goods and earnings become holy to the Lord, provided our true purpose is his glory.
Christians should undertake commercial work as God's servants, treating riches as possessions entrusted to them for which they must answer as his stewards.

row.cell: God's kingdom advanced by his judgments.

div.title: Sin brings desolation (verses 1–12)
div.p: People who place all their treasure and happiness in this world will eventually discover their poverty and misery.
We should apply Scripture's teaching about the vanity and frustration of everything under the sun to our own lives.
Sin has turned the earth upside down. The world is now very different for humanity from the dwelling God originally prepared.
Even at its finest, earthly beauty resembles a flower that fades while we are still holding it.
This world brings disappointment and tears. Our lives are short and full of trouble.
The curse of sin reaches every social rank and situation. God can empty and lay waste whatever people possess.
Human sin has polluted the earth, and the Lord's righteous judgment lays it desolate.
The pleasures of sinful indulgence will end in heaviness.

God has many ways to make wine and strong drink bitter to the people who depend upon them. Bodily illness, mental anguish and the destruction of a person's estate can transform pleasure into suffering.
Let us mourn for our sin and rejoice in God. No person or event can take away joy that is rooted in him.

div.title: A small faithful remnant remains (verses 13–15)
div.p: Even after the general destruction, a few faithful people will survive.
They will be scattered like the olives left after harvest, hidden among the leaves.
The Lord knows those who belong to him, although the world does not recognize them.
When worldly people's laughter stops, the saints can still rejoice, because the covenant of grace never fails. It is both the fountain of their comfort and the foundation of their hope.
Faith enables them to rejoice even under affliction and to encourage other sufferers to do the same.
Some may glorify the Lord in the fires of severe suffering; others may do so in low, dark and muddy valleys.
In every place, however remote, and amid every trial, however hot, let us continue thinking rightly of God's goodness.
If those trials cannot turn us from trusting him, we glorify the Lord in the fires.

div.title: God's final rule over judgment (verses 16–23)
div.p: Believers may be driven to the farthest regions of the earth and still be singing rather than sighing.
Yet Isaiah mourned the miseries he foresaw pouring across the earth like a torrent, and the small number of faithful people among its inhabitants.
Sin would abound, and evil would pursue those who practiced it.
Earthly security is deeply uncertain.
Worldly people imagine they occupy the earth as though it were a palace or impregnable castle. But their habitation is more like a temporary hut set up for one night.
The creation bears a heavy burden under sin and groans beneath it.
Ultimately the present order will fall, and new heavens and a new earth will appear, in which only righteousness dwells.
People who imagine their wealth or public office makes them unreachable will discover God's judgment against pride and cruelty.
We should not presume to announce the full meaning of God's dealings before the appointed time.
No one should feel secure merely because life is prosperous. Yet no sufferer need despair merely because circumstances are miserable.
God will receive glory through every judgment.
The mystery of his Providence has not yet been fully revealed.
The defeat of the Redeemer's enemies must make way for Christ's kingdom. Then the Sun of Righteousness will shine in full glory.
Let every unrepentant sinner consider the final outcome. The ungodly will sink beneath their transgressions and not rise again, while believers enjoy everlasting happiness.

row.cell: A declaration of the gospel blessings.
The destruction of the enemies of Christ's church.

div.title: A song of praise for the Lord's protection (verses 1–5)
div.p: These words could celebrate the Jews' return from captivity. But Henry sees a greater fulfillment in praise for Christ's victories over our spiritual enemies and for the comfort he provides to all believers.
Genuine faith simply believes God's testimony and relies on the truth of his promises.
The Lord weakens proud people who consider themselves invincible, while strengthening those who are humble and look to him for support.

p.hi: God shelters his people in every kind of weather.

div.p: He protects believers from arrogant oppressors. Their insults and threats are like the noise of strangers or the fierce sun at midday: intense for a moment, but where are they when the sun goes down?
The Lord has always been and will always remain a refuge for his distressed people.
He has prepared shelter for them, and he teaches them to run to it.

div.title: The gospel feast and victory over death (verses 6–8)
div.p: The New Testament often compares God's welcoming reception of repentant sinners to a feast.
The invitation extends to all peoples, Gentiles as well as Jews.
The gospel strengthens and cheers the hearts of those who have become conscious of their sin and mourn over it.
A veil covers the nations because humanity lives in spiritual darkness.
The Lord removes that veil through the light of the gospel and the Holy Spirit's power, enabling people to recognize and welcome divine truth.
Those long dead in trespasses and sins receive spiritual life.
Christ himself, in his resurrection, triumphs over death.
Sorrow will end. Those who mourn for sin will receive comfort; those who suffer for Christ will find consolation.
Yet the promise that God will wipe away every tear will be completely fulfilled only in the joys of heaven.
Hope in that future should help us resist excessive grief now, particularly the kind of weeping that prevents us from continuing to sow and do good.
Sometimes even in this life God removes the public shame borne by his people. But at the great day all their reproach will be removed.
Let us patiently endure sorrow and disgrace, knowing their time is short.

div.title: Waiting for the Redeemer and his final victory (verses 9–12)
div.p: People who longed for the promised Redeemer received the news of his coming with joy and praise.
Glorified believers will one day enter their Lord's joy with a triumphant song.
Waiting for Christ is never in vain. His mercy arrives with abundant compensation for every apparent delay.
The hands once extended upon the cross to accomplish salvation will finally be raised in judgment against those who persistently refuse him.
Henry reads Moab here as a figure representing all opponents of God's people. Their pride will be brought down through repeated judgments.
The defeat of Moab thus pictures Christ's final victory and the overthrow of Satan's strongholds.
Therefore, beloved brothers and sisters, remain steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the Lord's work, because your work in him is not wasted.

row.cell: The Divine mercies encourage to confidence in God.
His people exhorted to wait upon Him.

div.title: God's unchanging covenant and perfect peace (verses 1–4)
div.p: The words “that day” seem to point, according to Henry, to the time when the New Testament Babylon will have been completely overthrown.
The unchanging promise and covenant of the Lord are the walls around his church.
The gates are open. Let sinners be encouraged to enter and belong to the Lord.
He keeps the person who trusts him in perfect peace: inward peace, outward peace, peace with God, peace of conscience, peace at every time and through every event.
Trust the Lord for such peace and for a lasting portion.
Everything sought from the world survives only briefly.
But those who trust God receive from him not merely comfort for the present, but strength that carries them toward everlasting happiness.
Let us acknowledge him in everything we do and depend upon him through every trial.

div.title: Waiting for God through his judgments (verses 5–11)
div.p: The righteous person's path is marked by steadiness, obedience and holy conduct.
God makes their path plain.
Their responsibility and comfort are to wait upon him and keep their desires directed toward him, even in the longest and darkest hours of distress.
We must never let suffering turn us away from God.
In a prolonged night of adversity, let our hearts desire him and pray for grace to remain faithful.
Religion without the heart has no real value, regardless of outward profession.
Even those who seek God early discover that he is already willing to receive them.
Affliction is intended to teach righteousness. Blessed are the people who learn from it.
But rebellious sinners continue resisting God because they do not consider whose commands they despise.
Those who mock his warnings will eventually feel what they now refuse to believe: falling into the hands of the living God is fearful.
They refuse to see sin's evil now, but will have to see it later.
May they abandon sin and return while the Lord is ready to show mercy.

div.title: Prayer, freedom and resurrection hope (verses 12–19)
div.p: Every creature, occupation and circumstance that brings comfort does so because God makes it helpful to us.
Even what seemed hostile may, under his Providence, become a means of good.
His people had known slavery under sin and Satan, but through divine grace they learned to hope for freedom from every former master.
Everything opposed to God and his kingdom will finally be overcome.
Suffering reveals our need of prayer.
Before distress, prayer may come a drop at a time. Under the pressure of trials, it can flow like water from a spring.
Affliction drives us into earnest, private communion with the Lord.
Henry suggests considering Christ himself as the speaker addressing his church.
Christ's resurrection is the guarantee of the deliverances foretold here.
His grace, like dew or rain reviving plants that seemed dead, can restore a church brought very low.
The promise may also refer to the bodily resurrection of the dead, particularly those united to Christ.

div.title: A place of safety during the storm (verses 20 and 21)
div.p: When danger comes, withdrawing to a safe place can be wise.
Entrust yourself to God as the One able to hide you. He will shelter his people either beneath heaven or in heaven.
Their tribulations are limited to a little while. Once ended, they will seem small compared with the happiness that follows.
God's place is the mercy seat, where he delights to dwell.
When he comes to punish, he is described as going out of his place, for he takes no pleasure in the death of sinners.
Yet no truth is more frequently taught in Scripture than his settled purpose to judge those who continue in wrongdoing.
Keep close to the Lord and separated from the world's sins.
Seek strength through secret prayer.
A day of vengeance is approaching, and believers should expect suffering before it arrives.
But that prospect need not leave them restless or terrified.

p.hi: Rest in God. Remain in him. Wait patiently for his promises.

row.cell: A promise of their recall to Divine favour.

div.title: God's fruitful and protected vineyard (verses 1–5)
div.p: Through the power of his death, and by the preaching of his gospel, Jesus Christ overcomes and will finally destroy the one who has the power of death—the devil, the ancient serpent.
The unbelieving world resembles a fruitless wilderness.
But the church is God's vineyard, tended carefully so that it will bear valuable fruit.
The Lord protects it during the night of suffering and persecution.
He also protects it during times of peace and prosperity, when temptations can be no less dangerous.
He cares not only for the vineyard's survival but also for its fruitfulness.
We need the continual watering of divine grace. If withdrawn, we wither and become unable to accomplish anything spiritually good.
God sometimes contends with his people, yet graciously invites them to reconciliation.
Where he finds only briers and thorns instead of useful vines, and those thorns stand in rebellion against him, he will tread them down and burn them.
This passage summarizes the gospel by which God's church should continually be watered.
Since sin entered the world, God has had a righteous charge against humanity; humanity has maintained an unrighteous quarrel against him.
Nevertheless, God graciously invites sinners to make peace.
Pardoning mercy is the strength of the Lord.
Cling to Christ crucified, the power of God, as a drowning person grasps a rope, branch or board within reach.
There is no other name by which we can be saved.
This is both the only way and a sure way to obtain salvation.
God is willing to be reconciled to us.

div.title: The remnant restored and the gospel trumpet (verses 6–13)
div.p: In the latter days, under the gospel, the church would become more securely established and more widely spread than the ancient Jewish church.
May our souls be constantly watered and guarded so that we produce the Spirit's fruits in goodness, righteousness and truth.
Henry observes that the Jewish people continued to exist as a numerous and distinct people, although those who persecuted them had not survived in the same way.
He regards their endurance through the centuries as an important sign supporting the Scriptures' divine origin and as a solemn warning concerning sin.
This is his stated historical and theological interpretation.
However violent the storms, God can still say, “Peace, be still.”
He permits afflictions for his people's ultimate spiritual good.
Henry says that after the Babylonian captivity the Jews showed remarkable opposition to idols and idolatry.
For all believers, discipline fulfills its purpose when it separates them from sin, its occasions and temptations.
Jerusalem flourished under divine protection; when God withdrew that protection, the city became desolate.
This also pictures the distress of a church producing wild grapes instead of good fruit.
Sinners sometimes presume that God will spare them because he is merciful and because they are his creatures. Such claims are not grounds for continuing in rebellion.
Henry understands verses 12–13 as pointing both toward the Jews' recovery after Babylon and their eventual return from later dispersion.
The passage further portrays sinners gathered to God through the preaching of the gospel, which proclaims the Lord's acceptable year.
Those hearing the gospel trumpet join the church and learn to worship God.
At the last trumpet, all the saints will be gathered together.

row.cell: The prosperity of Judah; with reproofs for sinfulness and unbelief.
Christ is pointed out as the sure Foundation for all believers.

div.title: Samaria's pride and drunkenness (verses 1–4)
div.p: Whatever people admire about themselves, however insignificant it may be, becomes like a crown to them.
But pride prepares the way for destruction.
How foolish people behave when overcome by drink!
Henry says those enslaved to drunkenness become subject to Satan. Excessive drinking is an exhausting form of bondage.
It destroys health, damages work and possessions, harms families and puts souls in danger, all to satisfy a degrading appetite.
Such behavior is particularly shameful among people who claim to worship God.
It is right for him to remove abundance when his people consistently misuse it.
What they boast about is only a fading flower or early fruit, picked and eaten as soon as it ripens.

div.title: Judah rebuked for misleading teaching (verses 5–15)
div.p: Isaiah turned toward Judah, the remaining portion of God's people.
Only those who glory in the Lord of hosts himself possess lasting happiness.
From him come the wisdom and strength required for service and spiritual conflict.
Only through Jesus Christ does the holy God graciously communicate with sinful human beings.
Teachers may be intoxicated not only by wine but also by false doctrine and imaginary ideas about the Messiah's kingdom and salvation.
Such teachers mislead themselves and many others, filling the places they influence with error.
God's people need the same lessons and principles repeated to them often, so that they understand them more clearly.
Through his word, God calls us to what truly benefits us.
Serving him is the only rest from the weary bondage of sin; lasting refreshment comes only under the easy yoke of the Lord Jesus.
The people despised these plain teachings as childish and insignificant.
Those who mock what they ought to learn may justly be judged through the very words they rejected.
A believer at peace with God can, in a figurative sense, be at peace even with death: it cannot do ultimate harm to someone belonging to Christ.
But it is absurd to imagine death can be a friend while sin makes God an enemy.
People who rely on their own righteousness or on an intended deathbed repentance are trusting lies.
To promise to stop sinning only when one has lost the physical ability to continue in it is no genuine change of heart.

div.title: Christ, the tested cornerstone (verses 16–22)
div.p: God has laid in Zion the only reliable foundation for escaping coming judgment: Jesus Christ.
This foundation was established in God's eternal purposes.
Christ is a stone: strong enough to support his entire church.
He is a tried and chosen stone, approved by God and never failing anyone who truly trusts him.
He is the cornerstone, joining the building together and bearing its weight.
He is precious to the Lord and every genuine believer.
Whoever, in any age or nation, rests the hope of an undying soul upon him will not ultimately be put to shame.
Faith in Christ quiets the soul and teaches us to wait for God's timing.
Any alternative foundation will fail.

The person who seeks justification outside Christ's righteousness, or seeks wisdom, strength and holiness without the Holy Spirit, or seeks lasting happiness outside God's favor, cannot obtain what is needed.
Self-righteousness provides a bed too short to lie on and a covering too narrow to shelter under.
The Lord will accomplish his plans and display his glory.
Those who profess to belong to his church but live like unbelieving nations should expect judgment.
Never mock the rebukes of God's word or the warnings of approaching judgment.

div.title: The Lord knows how to thresh his people (verses 23–29)
div.p: A wise farmer works carefully and treats each crop according to its nature and needs.
The Lord, who gave farmers this skill, is himself wonderful in counsel and excellent in action.
According to the situation, he warns, corrects, spares, shows mercy or brings judgment.
Afflictions are like threshing instruments in his hands.
They loosen believers' attachment to the world, remove the chaff that clings to them and prepare them for useful service.
God adjusts the trial to his people's strength.
He does not make their burden heavier or longer than is necessary.
When his purpose has been achieved, their suffering ceases.
He gathers the wheat into his storehouse, while the chaff is burned with unquenchable fire.

row.cell: Judgements on Jerusalem and on its enemies.
The senselessness and hypocrisy of the Jews.
The conversion of the Gentiles, and future blessings for the Jews.

div.title: Jerusalem humbled and its enemies defeated (verses 1–8)
div.p: The name Ariel may mean the altar of burnt offerings, according to Henry.
Jerusalem should recognize that outward religious services cannot free a nation from righteous judgment.
People who practice religion hypocritically cannot please God or make peace with him through ceremonies alone.
In former days the Lord's protection had surrounded the city, as though a mighty host of angels camped around it.
Now he would oppose Jerusalem itself.
Proud looks and speech would be brought low through humiliating events.
But Isaiah also foretold the defeat of Jerusalem's enemies.
Sennacherib's army vanished like a dream.
So the crowds that fight against God's worship through the centuries will ultimately fall.
Sinful people who lull themselves with comforting fantasies will awaken to a dreadful reality after death.

div.title: Scripture sealed to the proud, not the teachable (verses 9–16)
div.p: It is both sorrowful and astonishing to see sinners feel secure while continuing in rebellion.
Educated people dismissed the prophecies as too obscure to understand, while uneducated people excused themselves by saying they lacked learning.
But the Bible remains a sealed book to learned and unlearned alike unless they approach it with humble, teachable hearts.
We must read to learn God's truth and will.
Worship means coming near to God.
When the heart is full of reverence and love, its speech will express those affections.
Yet many offer only the labor of their lips.
They pretend to address God while their thoughts wander among countless foolish things.
They substitute their own religious inventions for the worship he has commanded.
Many participate only to follow custom or pursue their personal advantage.
There is a crucial difference between the wandering thoughts and defects that distress a genuine believer and a heart deliberately withdrawn from God.
The former needs help and repentance; the latter is the hypocrisy God condemns here.
People who hide behind religious language to serve selfish purposes deceive themselves.
Those who quarrel with God or imagine they can conceal their intentions from him effectively accuse their Creator of ignorance.
God will expose and abolish such perverse conduct.

div.title: Gentiles brought to life; Israel promised blessing (verses 17–24)
div.p: The extraordinary change promised here may concern Judah's historical circumstances, but it also looks further ahead.
Through the gospel, a great harvest of souls would be gathered from the Gentiles into Christ's church.
Then the wilderness would become a fruitful field, while the former fruitful field—the unbelieving Jewish community—would resemble a deserted forest.
People who genuinely rejoice in God even while troubled will eventually find greater cause for joy.
Meekness strengthens holy happiness.
Powerful enemies will be brought low, and mockers within the community will be judged.
We all sometimes speak carelessly or misunderstand what we hear.
But it is particularly unjust to make someone an offender for a single word.
The proud did everything possible to bring trouble upon those who corrected them.
Yet the God who redeemed Abraham from his troubles and snares will deliver Abraham's genuine children through faith.
For godly parents, one of the greatest comforts is seeing their children renewed by God's grace.
May those who have misunderstood the truth and murmured against it receive understanding and sound teaching.
The Spirit of truth can correct their errors and lead them into truth.
Let us therefore pray for people who have been misled.
True religion changes human hearts, giving a humble, devout spirit both peace and joy.

row.cell: The Jews reproved for seeking aid from Egypt.
Judgements in consequence of their contempt of God's word.
The ruin of the Assyrian army, and of all God's enemies.

div.title: Egypt is a false refuge (verses 1–7)
div.p: When the Jews faced trouble from one neighboring country, they repeatedly sought protection from another instead of looking upward to God.
Adding sin to sin can only deepen the disaster.
We escape the final consequences of wrongdoing by making Christ's righteousness our refuge and seeking the Holy Spirit's sanctifying work.
Human beings are inclined to depend on their own judgment even against God's warning.
But that trust brings shame and distress.
Judah spent great effort and wealth seeking Egyptian support.
Those sacrifices yielded no lasting protection.
See the danger of leaving God to pursue hopes grounded only in human power!

p.hi: The Creator is the Rock of Ages; the creature is a broken reed.

div.p: We should neither expect too much from humanity nor trust too little in God.
Our strength lies in remaining quiet before him, humbly depending upon his kindness and submitting peacefully to his will.

div.title: Contempt for God's word leads to ruin (verses 8–18)
div.p: The Jews were the only nation then publicly professing the Lord's name.
Yet many among them remained rebellious.
They possessed light but preferred darkness.
The prophets repeatedly restrained them through correction, keeping them from feeling comfortable in sin.
That angered the people.
Nevertheless, faithful ministers should not stop trying to awaken sinners merely because they are disliked.
God is the Holy One of Israel, and the people would discover what that meant.
They did not want to hear his commands or his hatred of sin.
They wanted to be left undisturbed.
But by despising God's word they destroyed the very foundations of their safety.
The nation would be shattered like a potter's vessel.
We should turn from our sinful paths and return to duty. That is the way of salvation.
True strength comes through quiet confidence in God and a mind resting upon him.
Instead, the people imagined themselves wiser than the Lord.
The plan they devised to rescue themselves became the very cause of their downfall.
Only a scattered few would escape as a warning to others.
Those who refuse to repent and seek happiness in God's favor and service merely hasten their ruin.
The Lord waits to be gracious to all who come to him through faith in Christ.
Happy are those who also wait upon him.

div.title: God's mercy and guidance for Zion (verses 19–26)
div.p: God's people will one day reach the heavenly Zion.
Then tears will be removed forever.
Even now, greater faithfulness in prayer would bring believers more comfort as well as more holiness.
A famine of God's word is worse than a famine of bread.
People face temptations both to the right and to the left.
Satan continually tries to draw us into side paths.
We are blessed when a faithful minister or friend, the warnings of conscience, or the Spirit's inward work corrects us when uncertain and restrains us before we go astray.
Through repentance, people come to hate the idols they once cherished.
The Lord accomplishes this daily in converting souls by his grace and teaching them to fear and love him.
Areas formerly lacking the means of grace will receive abundant instruction together with the Holy Spirit's influence.
The result should be comfort and joy for God's people.
The growing light represents increasing knowledge of divine truth.
This is the light brought by the gospel, announcing healing for the brokenhearted.

div.title: Assyria and all impenitent enemies judged (verses 27–33)
div.p: God restrains people from doing wrong.
A word is enough to direct his willing servants, while a bridle is needed to turn rebellious enemies toward their ruin.
The destruction of Sennacherib's army is also a picture of the future, everlasting judgment of those who persist in sin.
Tophet was a valley near Jerusalem.
Henry describes fires burning there to destroy offensive or dangerous things, and the hideous practice in which idolatrous Israelites made their children pass through the fire to Molech.
He treats this as an image of the certainty and severity of final punishment.
No oppressor can finally escape divine wrath.
Let sinners therefore flee to Christ and seek reconciliation with him.
Then they may be safe and blessed when the Almighty brings an end to everyone who continues in rebellion.

row.cell: The sin and folly of seeking help from Egypt.

div.title: The folly of trusting Egypt (verses 1–5)
div.p: God opposes the help that his people seek from those who practice wickedness.
Sinners can sometimes recognize how foolish their actions are when the truth is stated plainly. Yet they may still refuse to live as though they believed it.
No one can escape God's judgments; evil follows the unrepentant.
The Lord of hosts will come to defend Mount Zion.
The Lion of the tribe of Judah will fight for his church.
He will also protect Jerusalem with the tenderness of birds hovering over their young, sheltering them from harm.
God's protection joins great strength with profound compassion.
His people may trust him to preserve them.

div.title: Backsliders called to return (verses 6–9)
div.p: Israel had wandered far from God.
Yet they were still described as his children.
Let them turn back, and the Lord will heal their backsliding, however deeply sin has brought them into misery.
People often make idols of silver and gold.
Love of possessions draws hearts away from God.
Those who truly repent become ready to surrender whatever they have treated as a rival to him.
When the people abandoned their idols, the Assyrian would fall through an angel's sword.
That messenger strikes with more power than a mighty warrior, though more quietly and unexpectedly than an ordinary person.
God can make even the bravest human heart tremble.
Meanwhile, if his people keep the fire of holy love and devotion burning in their hearts and homes, they may depend upon his protection.

row.cell: An interval of trouble, yet comfort and blessings in the end.

div.title: Christ the righteous King and shelter (verses 1–8)
div.p: Jesus Christ is the righteous King promised here, and his faithful disciples share in the benefits of his reign.
The consolation and grace of his Spirit resemble rivers flowing through a dry land.
A traveler crossing a desert finds refreshing shade beneath a great overhanging rock.
Likewise, Christ's power, truth and love provide believers with their only lasting protection and refreshment as they journey toward heaven.

p.hi: Christ bore the storm himself to keep it from falling upon us.

div.p: Let frightened sinners flee to him, for he alone can shelter and renew them in every trial.
Notice how much effort wicked people put into wrongdoing.
They work hard at it, direct their hearts toward it and develop clever plans to accomplish it.
Yet our comfort is that they cannot do more harm than God permits.
Let us pray to be freed from selfishness.
A truly generous soul thinks of generous things concerning God.
Such a person asks him for wisdom and discernment, the comfort of his presence, the influence of his Spirit and, in due time, the full enjoyment of his glory.

div.title: Trouble overcome through the outpouring of the Spirit (verses 9–20)
div.p: When a people have greatly provoked the holy Lord, difficult times should not surprise them.
Many careless people refuse generosity while using their possessions for self-indulgence.
We deserve to lose earthly provisions when we use them chiefly to nourish sinful desires.
Let those who live in that way be afraid and awaken.
A genuinely blessed age arrives through the outpouring of the Spirit from above.
Only then will lasting good times come.
Henry understands the present condition of the Jewish people as continuing until a fuller outpouring of the Holy Spirit, which he still expects.
Peace and quietness grow from righteousness.
Lasting satisfaction exists only in true religion.
Real holiness is real happiness even now. In heaven, where holiness becomes perfect, happiness will also be perfect forever.
The good seed of God's word will be scattered widely.
Divine grace will water it, and patient, hardworking servants will be sent into the Lord's field.

row.cell: God's judgments against the enemies of his church.

div.title: God defeats the proud destroyer (verses 1–14)
div.p: The deceitful and proud destroyer will answer for violence and fraud.
The righteous Lord sometimes repays wicked people in the same manner in which they treated others.
Those who wait humbly upon God through faith will find him gracious.

p.hi: As each day comes, so may the strength for that day come.

div.p: If God abandoned us to ourselves for even one morning, we would be lost.
We should therefore place ourselves in his hands every morning, and undertake the day's work through his strength.
When he rises to defend his people, his enemies scatter.
True knowledge and wisdom lead to the strength of salvation, making us steadfast in God's ways.
True devotion is the only treasure that cannot be robbed or consumed.
Jerusalem faced terrible suffering.
But God's time to help his people often comes precisely when every other helper has failed.
Everyone who hears what God has accomplished should recognize that he is able to do all things.
Sinners within Zion must answer for privileges they knowingly abused, an accountability greater than that of others.
Those who reject the commands of God's word cannot claim its comforts when distress arrives.
God's wrath against unrepentant sin is pictured as unquenchable fire: the justice of the eternally living God confronting the guilt of a soul that does not cease to exist.

div.title: The security and joy of the upright (verses 15–24)
div.p: True believers remain watchful against opportunities to sin.
God's power keeps them safe; faith in that power enables them to remain at peace.
They will not lack anything truly necessary for their ultimate good.
The blessings of salvation are freely given to all who seek God in humble, believing prayer.
The upright receive bread and water, but they also see the King in his beauty—the beauty of holiness.
Remembering earlier terrors deepens the joy of deliverance.
It is good to enjoy peace in one's own home, but better still to enjoy peace in God's house.
Christ will always preserve people who serve him.
Jerusalem had no large river flowing past it.
Yet God's presence and power were sufficient to supply every need.
Through faith we receive Christ as Prince and Savior, reigning over his redeemed people.
Those who refuse his reign place their souls in peril.
Illness is removed mercifully when its spiritual result is that sin is taken away.
If guilt has been pardoned, believers have far less reason to complain about bodily suffering.
The final verse points beyond earthly blessing toward heaven, where sickness and trouble cannot enter.
The One who blots out our transgressions will also heal our souls.

row.cell: God's vengeance against the enemies of his church.

div.title: Judgment against the enemies of God's church (verses 1–8)
div.p: Isaiah describes the Lord's wars, whose purposes are righteous and whose final outcome is certain.
The warning concerns all nations.
All have benefited from God's patience; those refusing to repent must also reckon with his judgment.
The fearful description of bloodshed should impress upon our minds the seriousness of divine justice.
Henry interprets Idumea as representing the peoples set against God's church, including what he calls the kingdom of Antichrist.
The full terror of the final day awaiting people who persist in opposing Christ is beyond human comprehension.
God has appointed the time when his church will be delivered and its enemies brought down.
Until that day, we should wait patiently and not pronounce final judgments before the appointed time.
Through Jesus Christ, the Lord can show mercy to believers without compromising righteousness.
In this way he glorifies his own name.

div.title: The barrenness left by sin (verses 9–17)
div.p: Those who try to destroy God's church will never succeed in their ultimate purpose.
Instead they bring ruin upon themselves.

p.hi: What dreadful changes sin can cause!

div.p: It can turn fertile countryside into wasteland and transform a crowded city into an uninhabited wilderness.
Let us compare everything we discover in the book of the Lord with the movements of Providence around us.
Then we will seek his kingdom and righteousness more diligently.
What the Lord commands through his mouth, his Spirit will accomplish.
As the predictions of Scripture are fulfilled, the evidence of its truth continues to grow, leading toward the time when these scenes of judgment give way to better days.
Henry interprets Israel as a figure of Christ's church, and the Edomites—Israel's bitter enemies—as figures of the enemies of Christ's kingdom.
God's Jerusalem may be reduced to ruins for a period.
But the enemies who persist in opposing his church face a desolation that lasts forever.

row.cell: The flourishing state of Christ's kingdom.

div.title: The wilderness blossoms through grace (verses 1–4)
div.p: Judah prospered under Hezekiah, but the main subject of this prophecy, according to Henry, is Christ's kingdom.
Converting grace makes a soul that was once a wasteland rejoice and sing, and grow abundantly like a garden filled with flowers.
The gospel encourages the weak and fearful.
Fear weakens us; resisting fear strengthens us both for the tasks we must do and for the suffering we may have to endure.
The One who calls us to be strong has made help available through One who is mighty.
The Messiah would come to confront the powers of darkness and bring generous consolation to those who mourn in Zion.
He will come and save.
He will also come again at the end of time to judge those who oppressed his people and give the afflicted a rest that fully compensates their suffering.

div.title: The highway of holiness and eternal joy (verses 5–10)
div.p: When Christ establishes his kingdom, he works great wonders within human souls.
Through his word and Spirit, those spiritually blind begin to see.
Those who were deaf to God's calls become willing listeners.
People unable to do good receive grace to act faithfully.
Those who did not know how to speak about God or to God receive opened lips that praise him.
When the Holy Spirit came upon Gentiles hearing the gospel, the fountains of spiritual life were opened.
Much of the earth still resembles a desert, lacking the means of grace, faithful worshipers and the fruits of holiness.
But the path of godliness will be opened.
The highway of holiness is the way of God's commandments, the good and ancient way.
It is a clear road toward heaven.
Even uneducated people who know little may be kept from missing it.
It is also a safe road, for nothing can ultimately harm those traveling on it.
Jesus Christ is the way to God.
He is clearly revealed, and the duties of faithful people are plainly marked out.
Let us therefore go forward cheerfully, assured that our destination is everlasting joy and rest for the soul.
Those who enter gospel Zion by faith rejoice in Jesus Christ.
Divine consolation causes sorrow and sighing to flee.
Such hopes and expectations of eternity should overshadow both the sorrows and the fleeting delights of this present life.
Yet merely admiring Scripture's beauty is not enough.
Do we personally possess its promises through faith?
Do we love God not only as Creator but because he gave his only Son to die for us?
Are we truly walking in holiness?
These practical questions are far more useful than spending our time on curious, amusing but fruitless speculation.

p.hi: See II Kings 18:17–37, and the commentary thereon.

div.title: The Assyrian challenge to Jerusalem
div.p: For this chapter, Henry gives no new verse-by-verse exposition in his Concise Commentary.
He instead directs readers to 2 Kings 18:17–37 and the commentary already provided there.
That original cross-reference, rather than a rewritten copy of the earlier commentary, is the entire authorial content of this chapter.

p.hi: This chapter is the same as II Kings 19.

div.title: The parallel account in 2 Kings
div.p: Henry writes no additional exposition under Isaiah 37.
Instead, he explicitly refers to the parallel narrative in 2 Kings 19, where the relevant commentary has already been given.
This cross-reference is the chapter's complete authorial content in the consulted witness.

div.title: Hezekiah's illness and restoration (verses 1–8)
div.p: When we pray during sickness, God may not give us the same answer that he gave Hezekiah.

But if, through his Spirit, he strengthens our hearts, assures us that our sins are forgiven and teaches us that whether we live or die we belong to him, then our prayers have not been offered in vain.
For the earlier account, see 2 Kings 20:1–11.

div.title: Hezekiah thanks the Lord (verses 9–22)
div.p: Hezekiah recorded the condition in which he found himself before receiving mercy.
It is good to remember divine kindness, especially kindness received during sickness.
He feared he would no longer see the Lord in the land of the living.
A truly godly person does not seek life merely for its own pleasures, but so that he may serve God and enjoy communion with him.
Our present dwelling resembles a shepherd's temporary hut.
It is poor, cold and insecure; moreover, while we occupy it, we are responsible for work entrusted to us, like a shepherd tending a flock.
Our days resemble a weaver's shuttle (Job 7:6), passing quickly back and forth while each movement leaves a thread behind.
When the woven piece is complete, the Master cuts it from the loom and examines the finished work.
When a faithful person's life ends, burdens and toil end too, and rest begins.
But God determines the length of the cloth—the duration of each life.
During sickness, people often try to calculate how much time remains, but they cannot know.
Their main concern should be reaching the next world in safety.
The more deeply we experience God's kindness, the more we should love him and live for him.
It was through love for perishing sinners that Christ delivered our souls.
Forgiveness does not mean that wrongdoing becomes innocent. It means that sin is not punished as it deserves, because the Lord has provided mercy.
We may remember healing with special gratitude when we see it alongside God's pardon.
Hezekiah regarded every opportunity to glorify God as the business, delight and purpose of life.
After recovering, he resolved to increase his praise and service.
God's promises never remove the obligation to use appropriate means.
Instead, they encourage and strengthen us to employ them.
Life and health are given so that we may glorify God and do good.

p.hi: This chapter is the same as II Kings 20:12–19.

div.title: The parallel account in 2 Kings
div.p: Henry supplies no new exposition for Isaiah 39 in the Concise Commentary.
He instead directs the reader to 2 Kings 20:12–19, where the account of Hezekiah and the Babylonian visitors is discussed.
That original reference is the entire authorial text in the source witness.

row.cell: The preaching of the gospel, and glad tidings of the coming of Christ.

div.title: Comfort: the gospel and the coming of Christ (verses 1–11)
div.p: Every human life involves struggle, but the Christian life is especially a warfare.
Yet this struggle will not last forever.
When sin is pardoned, God lovingly removes the deepest cause of our trouble.
Through Christ's death and great atonement, God's mercy is displayed in a way that glorifies his justice.
The satisfaction Christ made through his death has infinite value.
A repentant sinner receives grace more than sufficient for the guilt once carried.
Isaiah's words do refer in part to the Jews' return from Babylon.
But that event is small compared with the fulfillment identified in the New Testament: John the Baptist announcing the arrival of Jesus Christ.
When eastern kings traveled through deserts, people cleared a passage for them and removed obstacles.
