So let the Lord prepare our hearts through his word and Spirit.
May proud thoughts be humbled, good desires planted, crooked dispositions straightened, harsh tempers softened and every obstacle to obedience removed.
Everything that belongs to fallen humanity, including its apparent magnificence, withers like grass and flowers.
What good will wealth, status and possessions do for a dying sinner who remains condemned?

p.hi: God's word accomplishes what human strength cannot.

div.p: The good news of Christ's coming is to be announced throughout the world.
Satan is strong and armed, but Jesus Christ is stronger and will accomplish everything he has resolved.
Christ is also the good Shepherd.
He cares tenderly for new converts, weak believers and sorrowful people.
He never demands service or permits suffering without providing grace sufficient to endure it.
May we hear his voice, follow him and prove ourselves to be his sheep.

div.title: The Lord's immeasurable power and kindness (verses 12–17)
div.p: Compared with the Creator, every creature is small.
When the Lord made the world through his Spirit, nobody advised him or told him how to act.
All the nations are to him like the remaining drop in a bucket beside the ocean, or a tiny amount of dust on a balance compared with the earth.
Yet God's love is astonishing.
Though the world is so small in comparison with him, he gave his only Son to redeem it (John 3:16).
No service rendered by the church can add anything to God's greatness.
Our souls would have been eternally lost had the Father's only Son not given himself for us.

div.title: Idols cannot be compared with God (verses 18–26)
div.p: Whatever created thing we esteem, love, fear or trust more than God becomes an idol to us, even when we do not make or worship a physical image.
Even people with little to offer may insist on having an idol of their own.
Some spend lavishly to support false gods while begrudging what is devoted to the true God's service.
Isaiah appealed to every generation and nation to recognize the Creator's greatness.
People who refuse this knowledge are often willfully ignorant.
God commands every creature and everything in creation.
The prophet appeals not only to our senses but also to our reasoning.
Consider the stars and the One who created them.
Every member of the heavenly host fulfills his will.
The Lord who governs them is also the One who has spoken his promises and pledged to keep them.

div.title: Waiting upon the Lord instead of relying on ourselves (verses 27–31)
div.p: God rebuked his people for distrusting him.
They bore the names Jacob and Israel, inherited from a man who discovered that God was faithful through every trial.
Those names reminded them that they were a covenant people.
Many needless fears and complaints disappear when we take time to examine their causes.
It is wrong to entertain unfair thoughts about the Lord; it is worse to turn those thoughts into harmful speech.
The people already knew enough of God's goodness to silence their distrust.
Where God has begun a work of grace, he will complete it.
He helps those who depend humbly upon him and act in the strength he provides.

p.hi: As each day comes, so does the strength needed for it.

div.p: By divine grace believers rise above the world's attractions.
They can run cheerfully in the way of God's commandments.
Guard against unbelief, pride and self-confidence.
If we proceed in our own power, we will faint and fall.
But when our hearts and hopes are set on heaven, God enables us to rise above difficulty and pursue the prize of our calling in Jesus Christ.

row.cell: they are encouraged not to fear.
The vanity and folly of idolatry.

div.title: God's care for his people (verses 1–9)
div.p: Could any pagan god raise up a person in righteousness, direct that person as he chose, and grant victories over nations?
The Lord did this with Abraham—or, as Henry considers more likely in this prophecy, would do so with Cyrus.
Sinners encourage one another along paths of wrongdoing. Should not those serving the living God encourage one another still more actively in his service?

God's people are descendants of Abraham, his friend. Henry calls this the highest title ever given to a human being. Through divine grace Abraham became like God in character and was admitted to fellowship with him.
Happy are the Lord's servants who have been called his friends, to walk with him in faith and holy obedience.
Such favored people need not give way to fear. The conflict may be intense, but the victory is certain.

div.title: The Lord strengthens those who must not fear (verses 10–20)
div.p: God speaks tenderly: Do not fear, for I am with you.
He is not merely near enough to be called; he is present.
Are you weak? He will strengthen you. Do you lack friends? He will help when you need help. Are you about to fall? His righteous right hand will uphold you, rewarding good and judging evil.
Some seek the ruin of God's people. But believers should not repay evil with evil. They must wait for the Lord's time.

Jacob is called a worm: weak, small, despised and readily trampled upon. God's people are worms in their humble opinion of themselves and in their enemies' proud opinion of them—but not vipers, belonging to the serpent's offspring.
God's word humbles human pride. Yet the Lord helps his people because he is their Redeemer.

He promises to turn Jacob into a new and sharp threshing instrument, prepared for useful work. Henry sees its fulfillment in the triumph of Christ's gospel and of faithful Christians over the powers of darkness.
God has prepared enough comfort to meet his people's needs and answer their prayers.
Our journey to heaven passes through the wilderness of this world. Human souls thirst for satisfaction, and grow weary of seeking in the world what the world cannot give.
Yet God promises refreshment even where no one expects it: rivers of grace and living water. Christ used living water as a figure of the Holy Spirit (John 7:38–39).
When God establishes his church in the wilderness of the Gentile world, the change will be like thornbushes turning into cedars, firs and myrtles.
These gifts are for the poor in spirit who hunger for divine light, forgiveness and holiness. God's Spirit makes barren hearts fruitful so others can recognize his work.

div.title: Idols cannot foretell or save (verses 21–29)
div.p: Often the quickest way to expose the folly of sin is to examine the reasons people give for defending it.
There is nothing in idols deserving our trust. They are worse than worthless.
Let those who offer doctrines other than salvation through Christ present their case. Can they provide a cure for the corruption of human nature?
Only Jehovah possesses irresistible power and certain knowledge of what lies ahead. He reveals his plans and fulfills them.
Henry contrasts biblical prophecy with all other predictions, which he regards as uncertain.
The return of captives from Babylon displayed God's power. But in the redemption accomplished by Christ, he revealed something far greater.
The gospel's good news—long hidden from previous ages—announces a Deliverer more glorious and powerful than the one who rescued the captive Jews.
May we belong among his obedient servants and faithful friends.

row.cell: The character and coming of Christ.

div.title: The gentle servant and his coming (verses 1–4)
div.p: This prophecy was fulfilled in Jesus Christ (Matthew 12:17).
Let us rest our souls upon him and rejoice in him. For his sake, the Father will be pleased with us.
The Holy Spirit not only came upon Christ but remained upon him without measure.
He bore patiently the contradiction and opposition of sinners.
His kingdom is spiritual. He did not arrive surrounded by earthly honors.
He treats people oppressed by doubts and fears with great tenderness.
Some are like a bruised reed. Others resemble a smoking wick newly lit, already in danger of going out.
He does not despise them or burden them with more service or suffering than they can bear.
Through many miracles and his resurrection, he fully demonstrated the truth of his holy teaching.
Through his gospel and grace he establishes principles in human minds that make people wise and just.
Distant nations will wait for and welcome his law and gospel.
If we want to make our calling and election sure and enjoy the Father's delight, we must look to Christ, listen to him, trust him and obey him.

div.title: The blessing of Christ's kingdom (verses 5–12)
div.p: Redemption restores human beings to the obedience owed to their Creator.
Christ is the light of the world.
By his grace he opens minds Satan has blinded and frees people from the bondage of sin.
The Lord has upheld his church in former times.
He now gives fresh promises, which will be fulfilled as certainly as the earlier promises were.
When Gentiles join the church, God receives glory both in them and through them.
Let us give the Creator what belongs to him, taking care never to serve created things more than the One who made them.

div.title: God's truth overcomes opposition (verses 13–17)
div.p: The Lord will reveal his power and glory.
His voice will cry out through the preaching of his word.
The gospel contains warnings as well as promises. Its warnings of judgment must be preached alongside its blessings, to awaken a sleeping world.
The Lord triumphs through the power of his Spirit.
Those who oppose and blaspheme the gospel will be silenced and brought to shame.
Obstacles to its advance will be removed.
For people blind by nature, God will show the path to life and happiness through Jesus Christ.
Where knowledge is weak, he will turn darkness into light. Where obedience is weak, he will make the path plain.
God guides the people whom he brings onto the right path, and will not abandon them.
This is prophetic language but also a promise that can encourage every believer.

div.title: The blindness and unfaithfulness of God's people (verses 18–25)
div.p: The people are called to pay attention and consider their true condition.
Many perish because they fail to notice what is clearly before them.
Their ruin comes not from a total lack of information but from carelessness.
God is pleased to make his own righteousness known.
Yet because of their sins, his people were stripped of their possessions. Henry connects this warning with the later destruction of the Jewish nation.
No one can resist or escape God's righteous anger.
Sin brings terrible harm because it provokes divine judgment.
People who refuse to be humbled by lesser judgments should expect greater ones.
How many professing Christians remain as spiritually blind as those who have never known the truth!
God delights to save sinners through Christ's righteousness, but also glorifies his justice in judging proud people who despise his mercy.
Because God once poured out judgment on a people he had specially favored, we should fear lest we, while a promise of entering his rest remains, fail to receive it.

row.cell: God's unchangeable love for his people.
The deliverance from Babylon, and the conversion of the Gentiles.

div.title: God's enduring love and protection (verses 1–7)
div.p: God's favor and good will toward his people provide abundant comfort to every believer.
Wherever there is a new creation, God himself has formed it.
All whom he has redeemed through his Son's blood he has set apart as his own.
When God is for us, what enemy should make us afraid?
What are all the lives and treasures of Egypt and Ethiopia when compared with Christ's blood?
True believers are precious in God's sight, and he delights in them.
Even when they pass through fire and water, they need not fear destruction while God remains with them.
He will uphold them and bring them through.
God will gather the faithful from every direction.
With such promises before them, they should put away anxious fear.

div.title: God's people testify against idols (verses 8–13)
div.p: The worshipers of idols are challenged to defend the objects in which they trust.
People who make idols and rely on them become like the idols themselves.
They retain human bodies and faculties, but abandon ordinary good sense.
By contrast, God's people know the power of his grace, the sweetness of his comfort, his kind Providence and the truth of his promises.
Every servant of God has a story to tell about what he has done within and for them.
Such testimony may encourage other people to recognize, believe and rejoice in his power, truth and love.

div.title: Deliverance from Babylon and the greater redemption (verses 14–21)
div.p: The prophet announces the coming rescue from Babylon.
Yet the words also point beyond that nearer deliverance.
Henry sees in them redemption through Christ, the conversion of the Gentiles and the recall of the Jews.
Everything God does to rescue sinners and bring believers to final glory is astonishing.
Yet all of it rests upon the greater wonder of love revealed in the redemption of humanity.

div.title: The Lord calls sinners to repentance (verses 22–28)
div.p: People who neglect prayer have grown weary of God.
The Master did not exhaust his servants through harsh demands; they wearied him through their repeated disobedience.
Still his mercy remains extraordinary:

p.hi: He himself blots out transgressions.

div.p: This gives sinners courage to repent, because there is forgiveness with God.
Forgiveness is a completely free act of divine mercy.
When God forgives, he no longer holds the pardoned sins against us.
He does not do so because we deserve forgiveness.
He pardons for his own mercy, according to his promise, and above all for his Son's sake.
To forgive in this way is his glory.
Can human beings justify themselves before him?
That attempt is hopeless. Our first father violated God's covenant, and all of us have followed his example.
We can expect pardon only by faith in Christ, accompanied by genuine repentance and followed by newness of life, hatred of sin and love for God.
Let us remind the Lord of the promises he has made to repentant sinners and of the satisfaction his Son has made for them.
Bring those promises before him in earnest prayer for forgiveness.
This is the sure way to be justified freely by his grace and to find peace.

row.cell: Here are promises of the influences of the Holy Spirit.
An exposure of the folly of idolatry.
Also the deliverance of God's people.

div.title: God's Spirit promised to his people (verses 1–8)
div.p: Israel is called Jeshurun, meaning “the upright one.”
Those who truly belong to Israel in the spiritual sense are people without deceit.
God acknowledges those who serve him.
He helps them through their difficulties and supports them in their service.
Water represents the Holy Spirit.
Just as water refreshes, cleanses and makes the earth fruitful, the Spirit brings spiritual renewal, purification and fruitfulness to the soul.
The gift of the Holy Spirit is the great blessing whose abundant outpouring God reserved for the latter days.
Where God gives his Spirit, he also gives every other blessing needed.
Through this gift, the church will grow greatly and spread into distant regions.
Is there any other Rock or Protector who can defend God's people?
No other being could announce in advance the things God had revealed through his prophets.
Divine predictions were ordered just as surely as God's purposes.
Who can compare with Israel's Redeemer and King?

div.title: The emptiness of handmade gods (verses 9–20)
div.p: The description of image-making exposes the foolishness of idolatry.
A person takes a piece of wood and uses part of it as fuel.
From what remains, the same person makes an image, bows before it and begs it for deliverance.
Human beings dishonor God when they attempt to represent him as a human image.
Satan blinds unbelievers' eyes, leading them into absurd reasoning about religion.
People who seek lasting happiness in worldly possessions, unbelief, superstition or any other false system are feeding on ashes.
Pride, love of sin and departure from God deceive the heart and lead it away from his truth and worship.
While our desires remain corrupt, we cling to a lie as though it were our most valuable treasure.
Are our hearts absorbed in the world's wealth and pleasures?
Those things will ultimately betray our hope.
If we depend on an outward religious profession or on our own actions to save us, we deceive ourselves as surely as idolaters do.

p.hi: Learning to suspect our own self-deception is the first step toward deliverance from it.

div.p: Anyone concerned for the soul should examine the conscience and ask:

p.hi: “Is there not a lie in my right hand?”

div.title: The Lord calls his redeemed people home (verses 21–28)

p.hi: Return to me.

div.p: People who have wandered away from God, like the ancient Jews, should hurry to return to him.
The redemption Christ accomplished for us gives us reason to expect every blessing we need from him.
Our sins resemble a thick cloud hanging between heaven and earth.
Sin separates us from God and threatens a storm of divine judgment.
When the Lord pardons sin, he wipes away and disperses that cloud.
The way to heaven is opened again.
The Sun of Righteousness scatters the cloud completely.
Comfort after pardon resembles sunshine following darkness and rain.
Israel need not despair.
Nothing is too difficult for the God who made everything and can direct every creature to accomplish his purpose.
Once people know Christ, every other kind of knowledge seems insignificant in comparison with knowing him.
God turns the schemes of Christ's enemies into foolishness and catches them in their own cleverness.
The accurate fulfillment of Scripture's prophecies confirms its truth and its divine origin.
God announced particular favors for the people who would later be exiled long before their captivity took place.
Their return would face enormous obstacles, but divine power would remove them.
God knew the person who would deliver them and revealed his name so that, when his people heard of him, they would recognize that deliverance was drawing near.
For a great person, the highest honor is to serve as an instrument of divine kindness toward God's people.
Even people who seek only their own interests fulfill God's secret purposes.
And there is a greater Shepherd than Cyrus, who carries out his Father's will until his entire work is accomplished.

row.cell: The deliverance of the Jews by Cyrus.
God calls for obedience to his almighty power.

div.title: Cyrus is appointed to deliver Israel (verses 1–4)
div.p: Cyrus is called God's anointed, because God's counsel had appointed and equipped him for an important service.
Henry recounts how, on the night Cyrus entered Babylon, the gates leading from the city to the river were left open and his army advanced through the emptied river channel.
The Lord went before Cyrus, opening the cities he besieged.
He also gave him treasures concealed in secret places.
The true God was unknown to Cyrus, yet God had known him in advance and had called him by name.
The precise fulfillment of these words should have taught Cyrus that Jehovah was the only true God and that he had prospered for Israel's sake.
Through all the changes of states and kingdoms, the Lord works for the good of his church.

div.title: The sovereign Lord cannot be challenged (verses 5–10)
div.p: There is no God besides Jehovah.
Nothing takes place outside his sovereign rule.
He creates peace, here referring to every kind of good, and he brings evil in the sense of punishment or calamity, not moral evil or sin.
God is the source of everything true, holy, good and happy.
Error, moral evil and misery came into the world through the willful apostasy of his creatures, under his permission.
Yet he restrains and overrules those evils for his righteous purposes.
This teaching comforted those longing earnestly for Israel's deliverance while waiting patiently for it.
But it chiefly points, in Henry's explanation, to the redemption of sinners through God's Son and to the Spirit's outpouring that makes the gospel fruitful.
We must not expect salvation without righteousness: the Lord has brought both together.
Oppressors must not resist God's purposes for his people.
And oppressed believers should not murmur as though God treated them unkindly.
Human beings are like earthen pots and broken pieces of pottery, made more broken still through conflict with one another.
It is as foolish for us to quarrel with God as for clay to accuse the potter.
Turn God's promises into prayers.
Ask him to cause salvation and righteousness to abound among us.
Rest assured that the Judge of all the earth will do right.

div.title: God's people will be established (verses 11–19)
div.p: Believers may ask God for what they need.
If a request is truly for their good, he will not withhold what is best.
Yet how often people call God to account, as though he owed them explanations for every part of his conduct!
Cyrus made provision for the returning Jews.
In a far greater way, God will provide for those redeemed by Jesus Christ.
The restoration would persuade many observers and bring some to faith.
Everyone who genuinely joins the Lord discovers that his service is perfect freedom.
Even when he is his people's Savior, God may sometimes seem to hide his face and permit them to experience his displeasure.
Let them wait for the Lord even then.
There is a world without end.
Our ultimate happiness or misery depends on our condition in that world.
The God we serve is the only true God.
Everything he has said is just, plain and sufficient.
He calls us to seek him, and he does not refuse prayers offered in faith or disappoint genuine faith in his promises.
He gives grace sufficient, comfort and deep satisfaction of soul.

div.title: The nations are called to God's salvation (verses 20–25)
div.p: All nations are invited to approach Jehovah, because no other being can save.
He can deliver without anyone's help.
Without him, no one can save.
When the heart submits to Jesus Christ, the body willingly bends the knee and obeys him.
People from every nation will come to Christ for blessing.
Those who hate his cause will be brought to shame.
Every believer will rejoice in Christ as Friend and Portion.
Everyone must come to him.
May we come now to the Lord our Righteousness, obeying his commandments and trusting in his salvation.

row.cell: The idols could not save themselves, but God saves his people.

div.title: Idols fall; the Lord bears his people (verses 1–4)
div.p: The surrounding pagan peoples mocked the Jews as though Bel and Nebo, their gods, were stronger than Jehovah.
But their worshipers could not save those idols.
Both the idols and the people worshiping them were carried away into captivity.
God's people therefore had no reason to fear either.
The things ungodly people expect to give them security and happiness will eventually prove unable to rescue them from death and judgment.
The true God will never fail his worshipers.
The story of every believer's life is, in a sense, a brief reflection of Israel's history.
God continually upholds our spiritual life through his grace, just as he upholds our natural life through Providence.
He will not abandon his people.
The One who began their well-being will complete it.
When age and weakness increase, they need his help as deeply as they did in childhood.
This promise to an Israel weakened and grown old as a nation also belongs to every elderly follower of Christ.
Infirmities may surround you.
People close to you may even grow weary of caring for you.
Yet God remains who he has always promised to be.
He will bear you up, carry you along your path and finally bring you home.
If we learn to love and trust him, we need not be anxious about the days or years that remain.
He will continue to care for us as creatures of his power and as people renewed by his Spirit.

div.title: False gods cannot accomplish God's purposes (verses 5–13)
div.p: The prophet exposes the folly of making an idol and then praying to it.
The excessive expenses idolaters accept put to shame the stinginess of many professed worshipers of God, who want religion to cost them nothing.
Yet serving sin always costs a great deal.
God shows how senseless and powerless idols are.
His people should act as rational human beings and avoid such practices.
Many biblical prophecies given long ago have not yet been fulfilled.
But God's fulfillment of some is a pledge that the others will also come true.
Nothing brings deeper peace of mind than confidence that God will accomplish everything he purposes.
Even people who do not know or care about his revealed will may be called upon to carry out his hidden counsel.
Heaven and earth will pass away before even the smallest part of God's word fails.
The Lord calls stubborn sinners to listen.
They are far from right standing before him, yet they are summoned to heed his word.
A sinner's salvation begins with a humble and contrite heart that trembles at God's word.
Godly sorrow leads to genuine repentance and faith in divine mercy through the obedience unto death of our divine Surety, Jesus Christ.
At the appointed time Christ came as God's righteousness and salvation for his people.
His saving work continues in the church and remains available to all who believe.

row.cell: Carelessness and confidence shall not prevent the evil.

div.title: Babylon is brought low (verses 1–6)
div.p: Babylon is pictured as a woman brought into extreme distress.
She is stripped of her former dignity and made to suffer.
Instead of sitting in splendor, she sits on the ground and grinds grain at a handmill, one of the lowest and hardest forms of labor.
God was righteous in bringing this judgment, and no one could prevent it.
The prophet celebrates the Lord of Hosts, the Redeemer and Holy One of Israel.
God sometimes permits wicked people to prevail against his people.
But those who cruelly oppress the people of God will themselves face punishment.

div.title: Pride and false confidence cannot prevent judgment (verses 7–15)
div.p: We should beware of copying Babylon's attitudes and speech.
Do not trust in tyranny and oppression.
Do not boast of your abilities, rely on yourself, or claim all your successes as proof of personal wisdom and careful planning.
Otherwise you risk sharing Babylon's judgments.
People enjoying great prosperity often imagine that hardship can never reach them.
It is also common for sinners to suppose they are safe because their wicked actions are hidden from others.
That false feeling of security will itself contribute to their destruction.
From these prophecies, learn humility and trust in God.
His word tells us what will finally become of the righteous and the wicked.
It teaches us how to escape the judgment to come, glorify God, experience peace during life, receive hope at death and enter everlasting happiness.
Let us therefore keep away from every deception that would draw us from his truth.

row.cell: The Jews reproved for their idolatry.
Solemn warnings of judgment upon those who persisted in evil.

div.title: A people proud of their name but lacking holiness (verses 1–8)
div.p: The Jews valued their descent from Jacob and used Jehovah's name as the name of their God.
They took pride in Jerusalem and the temple.
Yet their actual lives lacked holiness.
When our religion is not sincere, we are only taking the Lord's name in vain.
God had announced long beforehand what he would do, through prophecy, so that these people would have no excuse to claim credit for what occurred.
He has said and done enough to put an end to human boasting.
That makes the sin and eventual destruction of proud people even more serious.
Sooner or later, every mouth will be silenced before him.
We are all born with a disposition toward disobedience.
Where there is original sin, actual sins will follow.
Does not each person's conscience confirm the truth of Scripture on this point?
May the Lord test and refine us, and make us doers of his word.

div.title: God promises rescue for the sake of his glory (verses 9–15)
div.p: We possess nothing in ourselves that could give God a reason to show us mercy.
He spares sinners for the praise and honor of his own mercy.
God sometimes leads people into suffering in order to do them good.
He refines them, but not as completely as silver is refined.
If the Lord treated us by burning away everything worthless with absolute strictness, we would all be rejected as dross.
Instead he accepts his people though their refining is still incomplete.
Many have returned to God during the furnace of affliction.
There they became chosen vessels, and a new work of grace began within them.
God's people can take comfort that he will preserve his own honor, and for that reason will bring about their deliverance.
When he determines to deliver them, he is never at a loss for instruments.
God has established a gracious plan to save those who come to him, doing so for his own sake and the glory of his grace.

div.title: The Spirit teaches, and the Lord warns (verses 16–22)
div.p: The Holy Spirit equips people for service.
Those sent by God and by his Spirit may speak boldly.
Henry applies this passage particularly to Jesus Christ, whom the Father sent and upon whom the Spirit rested without measure.
God teaches everyone he redeems.
He teaches them how to profit from affliction and makes them sharers in his holiness.
By his grace he leads them along the path of duty.
By his Providence he leads them along the path of deliverance.
God does not delight in afflicting his people.
Had their sins not turned them away, their peace would have been continual and abundant.
Spiritual comfort belongs together with holiness of life and obedience to God's will.
Unrepentant people will suffer more deeply when they realize how happy they might have been.
The prophet assures Israel that the exiles will be rescued.
God provides for all those whom he intends to bring home.
He will not leave them without what they need for their journey.
Henry applies this provision to the grace stored up for believers in Jesus Christ.
Every good thing flows through him, just as water flowed for Israel from the rock—and that Rock was Christ.
The prophecy also points, in Henry's explanation, to spiritual redemption and to the church's deliverance from antichristian tyranny.
Yet whatever changes occur in history, the Lord's final warning to hardened sinners remains:
There is no peace for the wicked.
Guilt and divine judgment bring inward anguish and outward misery to those who continue without repentance.

row.cell: The unbelief and rejection of the Jews.

div.title: The Redeemer's mission reaches the nations (verses 1–6)
div.p: The great Author of redemption declares by what authority he undertakes his work.
The sword of his word destroys the sinful desires of his people and what is hostile to them.
His sharp arrows wound the sinner's conscience.
Yet the wounds will be healed when that sinner turns to him and asks for mercy.
Even the Redeemer, who spoke as no human being ever spoke, often seemed during his earthly ministry to labor without success.
But if Jacob will not return to God and Israel will not be gathered, Christ will still be glorious.
The promise finds part of its fulfillment in the calling of the Gentiles.
People perish in darkness, but Christ enlightens them.
Through that light he makes them holy and happy.

div.title: A covenant Savior brings pardon and liberty (verses 7–12)
div.p: The Father is the Lord, Israel's Holy One and Redeemer, who sent the Son to accomplish redemption.
Human beings, whom Christ came to save, treated him with contempt.
He willingly accepted that contempt for their salvation.
Christ is the pledge of all the blessings of the covenant.
In him, God was reconciling the world to himself.
Pardoning mercy releases people from the curse of the law.
Renewing grace releases them from the rule of sin.
Both blessings come through Christ.
He calls those living in darkness to come out and show themselves.
His people should not only see, but also be seen, bringing glory to God and receiving the comfort that comes from acknowledging him.
The path to heaven contains many difficulties.
Yet God's grace will carry believers over them and make even the mountains into a road.
These words express the gospel's free invitations, encouraging promises and outpouring of the Spirit.

div.title: God remembers his church with unfailing love (verses 13–17)
div.p: Let all creation rejoice: God will show mercy to the afflicted.
His compassion moves him toward suffering people, and his covenant secures mercy for those belonging to him.
We have no more reason to question his promises and grace than to doubt his Providence or justice.
God has a tender and lasting affection for his church.
He does not want his people to despair.
Even mothers sometimes neglect their children.
But God's compassion far exceeds even the tenderest human parent's love.
His description of his people as engraved upon his hands or sealed upon his arm means that he never forgets them.
As far as Scripture gives us evidence that we belong to his redeemed flock, we can be assured he will not forsake us.
Therefore let us diligently make our calling and election sure, and rejoice in the hope of God's glory.

div.title: Zion is gathered and enlarged (verses 18–23)
div.p: Zion is pictured as a sorrowing widow who has lost her children.
But multitudes now gather to her.
God assures her that they come to strengthen and comfort her.
Sometimes the church is deserted and small in number.
But those desolate conditions will not last forever.
God can restore what has been ruined.
He can raise up friends for returning Israelites among the Gentiles, and those friends will bring their children to join God's people.
Let everyone care tenderly for new converts and beginners in faith.
Rulers will help protect the church.
It will become clear that God is sovereign over all.
Those who wait for the fulfillment of his promises in faith, hope and patience will never finally be put to shame.

div.title: The captives are freed from a stronger enemy (verses 24–26)
div.p: Because of sin, we had become lawful captives under God's justice.
Yet we were delivered at a price of incomparable value.
God promises that even captives held by a terrible enemy will be rescued.
Henry applies this to Satan losing his prisoners, being bound and cast into the pit.
Every power seeking to enslave, persecute or corrupt the church will ultimately be destroyed.
Then the whole earth will know that our Savior and Redeemer is Jehovah, the Mighty One of Jacob.
Every effort we make to rescue fellow sinners from Satan's bondage contributes, in some measure, toward that great deliverance.

row.cell: The sufferings and exaltation of the Messiah.
Consolation to the believer, and warning to the unbeliever.

div.title: God answers his people's complaints (verses 1–3)
div.p: People who profess to belong to God sometimes complain when he treats them severely, as though he had been unjust toward them.
The Lord answers such accusations.
He did not deprive his people of their privileges without cause.
The Jews went into captivity in Babylon because idolatry violated the covenant.
Henry also connects their later rejection with the crucifixion of the Lord of glory.
God called them to turn away from their sins and avoid ruin.
Finally, his own Son came to his people, but they did not receive him.
When God calls people toward happiness and they refuse to answer, they justly experience the misery resulting from their refusal.
The passage offers evidence of God's power to answer doubts.
Even the extraordinary events surrounding Christ's suffering and death testified that he was the Son of God (Matthew 27:54).

div.title: The Messiah is taught, suffers and is vindicated (verses 4–9)
div.p: Because Jesus Christ is God and man in one person, Scripture sometimes describes him as the Lord God and sometimes as a man and servant of Jehovah.
He came to announce truths that bring comfort to broken and repentant hearts, people weary of sin and burdened by affliction.
The Holy Spirit rested upon him so that he could speak as no other person spoke.
That same divine help awakened him daily to prayer, gospel preaching, and complete reception and proclamation of the Father's will.
The Father vindicated the Son by accepting the satisfaction he made for human sin.
Christ also speaks on behalf of every believer.
Who can successfully oppose people whose Friend is Christ?
Who can condemn those whom he defends as Advocate?
The apostle Paul applies this very truth in Romans 8:33.

div.title: Light for believers; warning to the self-confident (verses 10 and 11)
div.p: A child of God fears offending the Father.
That fear often becomes most evident during periods of spiritual darkness, when the believer's other graces seem hidden.
People who truly fear God obey Christ's voice.
A sincere servant of God may go through a long season without a clear sense of eternal happiness.
What should such a person do?

p.hi: Trust the name of the Lord.

div.p: Rest upon the promises of his covenant and build hope upon them.
Trust Jesus Christ, the Lord our Righteousness, and lean upon God as our God through the Mediator.
But presumptuous sinners are warned against placing confidence in themselves.
Their supposed merit and strength appear to them like warmth and light.
Earthly comforts are mere sparks: they burn briefly and then disappear.
Yet worldly people try to warm themselves by them while enjoying the pride and pleasures of their passing light.
Those who make the world their comfort and their own righteousness their confidence will finally encounter bitterness.
A godly person's path may be dark now, but it leads to peace and everlasting light.
An ungodly person's path may appear pleasant, but it ends in lasting darkness.

row.cell: The power of God, and the weakness of man.

div.title: Remember God's grace and trust the Messiah (verses 1–3)
div.p: People blessed with new birth should remember that they were originally formed in sin.
This remembrance humbles our opinion of ourselves and deepens our appreciation of God's grace.
There is no greater comfort than becoming useful for God's glory.
The more people grow in holiness and do good, the greater their genuine happiness becomes.
Let us reflect seriously upon our guilt.
Such reflection keeps our hearts humble and our consciences awake and sensitive.
It also makes Jesus Christ more precious to us.
Remembering grace strengthens our efforts and prayers for other people's good.

div.title: God's salvation outlasts everything earthly (verses 4–8)
div.p: Christ's gospel will be proclaimed and made known.
How will we escape if we neglect it?
There is no salvation without righteousness.
Our earthly existence will pass away like smoke.
Our bodies will be laid aside like worn-out clothing.
But people whose happiness rests upon Christ's righteousness and salvation will still enjoy its comfort when time and days themselves have ended.
Clouds may hide the sun for a while, but they cannot stop its course.
Likewise, the believer will continue to enjoy the portion God has promised, while those who mock Christ remain in darkness.

div.title: The Redeemer defends and comforts his people (verses 9–16)
div.p: Those whom Christ redeemed with his blood and by his power will ultimately be delivered joyfully from every enemy.
If God intends so great a final happiness for us, will he not also give the particular rescues we need on the way?
In this changing world, joy may turn into sorrow almost instantly.
But in the world to come, sorrow will never return.
God's people prayed for a new display of his power.
He answered with the comfort of his grace.
If we feared sinning against God as we ought, we would have much less fear of human disapproval.
Happy is the person who lives in reverent fear of God.
The church of Christ remains secure through the power and Providence of the Almighty.

div.title: Jerusalem's suffering and promised release (verses 17–23)
div.p: God calls his people to attend to the things that bring everlasting peace.
Jerusalem had provoked him and was made to experience the bitter results.
People who should have comforted her became tormentors themselves.
They lacked the patience needed to keep control of their own souls, and the confidence in God's promises needed to preserve spiritual consolation.
Jerusalem was drunk, not now with the wine of Babylon's idolatry, but with the cup of affliction.
Yet God's cause may appear lost for a time without being lost forever.
He can protect it by awakening the consciences of those opposing it or by defeating their plans.
Oppressors wanted people to submit their souls to human authority—to believe and worship whatever their rulers prescribed.
But violence can obtain only outward and hypocritical conformity.

p.hi: Consciences cannot be compelled by force.

row.cell: The welcome news of Christ's kingdom.

div.title: Freedom announced through Christ's kingdom (verses 1–12)
div.p: The gospel declares freedom to those bound by fear.
Let people exhausted and weighed down by the burden of sin come to Jesus Christ for relief.
Shake off the dust of doubts and fears and loosen the chains that bind you.
Our Redeemer did not purchase salvation with silver, gold or any perishable possession.
He paid with his own precious blood.
When we consider how freely this salvation is offered and how much harm sin does even to our earthly peace, we will value Christ's redemption more highly.
Do we seek victory over every sin, remembering that God's glory requires holiness in every person who follows Christ?
The good news is that the Lord Jesus reigns.
Christ himself first announced these tidings.
His ministers now proclaim them.
As they keep themselves clean from the world's corruptions, they become welcome and beautiful messengers to those who receive their message.
Zion's watchmen could scarcely discern evidence of God's favor through the dark cloud of their afflictions.
But now the cloud is removed and they can plainly see the fulfillment of his promise.
Zion's ruined places will rejoice, and the whole world will benefit.
Henry applies this restoration to the salvation offered through Christ.

p.hi: Babylon is no place for Israelites.

div.p: Likewise, anyone enslaved to sin and Satan should make use of the liberty Christ proclaims.
The people should depart quickly and diligently, wasting no time or lingering in captivity.
But they must not depart in fearful, distrustful haste.
Those walking in obedience are under God's special protection.
Faith in that care removes the need for panicked flight.

div.title: The Messiah's suffering and exaltation (verses 13–15)
div.p: These verses begin a remarkable, detailed and faithful prophecy of the Messiah's office, character and glory.
Henry says its testimony has convinced some of the most stubborn unbelievers.
Christ is Wisdom itself.
The work of redemption reveals the wisdom of God in a mystery.
People who saw Jesus suffering might have thought that no one had ever appeared so miserable.
His sorrow seemed beyond every other sorrow.
Yet God exalted him to the highest honor.
Only Christ's gospel could reveal this saving work as God has now made it known.
Christ shed his blood for sinners once, but its saving power continues.
May those opposing him learn the wisdom of ending their opposition.
May they share in the blood of sprinkling and the baptism of the Holy Spirit, obeying Christ and praising his salvation.

row.cell: humiliation, and exaltation of Christ, are minutely described; with the blessings to mankind from his death.

div.title: The despised and rejected Messiah (verses 1–3)
div.p: Nowhere else in the Old Testament, according to Henry, is it prophesied so plainly and fully that Christ must suffer before entering his glory.
Yet even now many fail to recognize or acknowledge the divine power accompanying this word.
The authentic and supremely important announcement of salvation for sinners through God's Son is neglected.
The humble condition Christ willingly took, and the way he appeared in the world, did not match the ideas many Jews had formed of the Messiah.
They expected a figure arriving with pomp.
Instead, he grew up quietly and almost unnoticed, like a young plant.
He had none of the outward glory people would naturally expect.
His life was not merely humble in social position.
It was also filled with sorrow.
Because he was made sin for us, he endured the sentence to which our sin had exposed us.
Hearts ruled by worldly desires find nothing in Jesus that makes them seek a share in him.
And how many people still despise him through their treatment of his people or reject his teaching and authority!

div.title: Christ suffers in our place for our sins (verses 4–9)
div.p: Here Scripture describes both Christ's sufferings and their purpose.
Our Lord Jesus suffered for our sins, in our place.
All of us have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God.
Sinners love their own particular sins and cling to the evil paths they have chosen.
Our sins deserve every grief and sorrow, even the most severe judgment.
We are saved from the ruin sin deserves because our sins were laid upon Christ.
This atonement was made for our transgressions.

p.hi: It is the only way of salvation.

div.p: Our sins were the thorns on Christ's head, the nails in his hands and feet, and the spear in his side.
He was given up to death because of our offenses.
Through his suffering, Christ also purchased the Holy Spirit and God's grace for us.
By that grace, the corruption and sinful desires that afflict our souls can be put to death.
If he has taught us to value everything else as loss compared with him, we can endure our far lighter sufferings.
How can we fail to love the One who first loved us?

div.title: The willing sacrifice is exalted and justifies sinners (verses 10–12)
div.p: Come and see how deeply Christ loved us!

p.hi: We could never have placed him in our position. He placed himself there willingly.

div.p: He took away the sin of the world by taking it upon himself.
He willingly became subject to death, which is the wages of sin for us.
Consider the many graces and glories that follow his humiliation and belong to his exalted state.
Christ does not entrust the ultimate care of his family to anyone else.
God's purposes will certainly be accomplished.
Whatever is undertaken in accordance with his will will prosper.
Christ will see the result in the conversion and salvation of sinners.
Many are justified by him—those for whom he gave his life as a ransom.
We are justified by faith.
In this way God receives the greatest glory, free grace is honored, human pride is humbled and our eternal happiness is secured.
We must know and trust Christ as the One who carried our sins and rescued us from sinking beneath their weight by bearing it himself.
He has defeated the great enemies of his people: sin and Satan, death and hell, the world and the flesh.
Everything the Father intended the Redeemer to obtain will certainly belong to him.
He led captivity captive and received gifts for human beings, to give them gifts.
When we consider the Son of God's sufferings, we should remember the long record of our own transgressions.
Look upon Christ as suffering under the burden of our guilt.
Here is the firm foundation upon which a trembling sinner can rest.
We were purchased by his blood, and our lives display the glory of his grace.
For his people, Christ continually pleads and prevails, destroying the devil's works.

row.cell: The increase of the church by the conversion of the Jews and Gentiles.

div.title: The Lord enlarges his church (verses 1–5)
div.p: For a long time before Christ came, true religion appeared to have little influence across the world.
But through the preaching of the gospel, multitudes turned from idols to the living God.
This is cause for great rejoicing throughout the church.
Its boundaries are extended.
Its condition on earth remains humble and changeable, like a tent or tabernacle.
But a growing family needs a larger dwelling, and the church should expect its tent to be enlarged.
The more numerous the church becomes, however, the more carefully she must defend herself against false teaching and corruption.

p.hi: Your Maker is your Husband.

div.p: Christ is the Holy One of Israel and the Mediator of the covenant established with God's people under the Old Testament.
For ages he had been called the God of Israel.
Now he will be known as the God of the whole earth.
He cleanses his people from sin and causes every true believer to rejoice in this sacred union.
We cannot admire this mercy enough or adequately value the privilege.

div.title: Mercy greater than temporary judgment (verses 6–10)
div.p: God is slow to anger and quick to show mercy.
How sweet is the renewed comfort of his mercy when he returns to console his people!
He gathers them not because they deserve it but because he is merciful.
His compassion is great, and his kindness lasts forever.
The wrath is little when compared with the mercy.
His anger lasts a moment, while his loving-kindness is everlasting.
We should neither collapse in despair under present affliction nor give up hoping for relief.
Mountains have been shaken and moved from their places.
But none of God's promises has ever been broken by the events of history.
Mountains and hills may also represent powerful and influential human beings.
The people and created supports in which we place confidence will eventually fail.
But when friends abandon us, God remains faithful.
This promise applies both to the whole church and to individual believers.
God may correct his people for their sins, but he will not finally cast them off.
Let these assurances motivate us to make our calling and election sure.

div.title: God's people are taught, protected and justified (verses 11–17)
div.p: When God's people are afflicted and storm-tossed, let them hear his words as words of personal consolation, showing that he sees their sorrows and fears.
The church becomes glorious through the knowledge of God.
No teacher can compare with him.
The passage promises the teaching and gifts of the Holy Spirit.
Everyone whom God truly teaches learns to love other people.
Henry sees a special connection with the glorious period that will follow the church's present troubles.
More than outward splendor, holiness is the church's true beauty.
God promises his protection.
There will be neither inward terror nor outward attack able to overturn his purpose.
Soldiers may honor themselves with splendid titles.
But God calls some of them “destroyers made to destroy”, because destruction is their work.
He created them and can direct them to fulfill his own purposes.
The day is coming when he will call wicked people to account for every cruel word (Jude 15).
Security and final victory belong to every faithful servant of the Lord.
Both the righteousness by which believers are justified and the grace through which they are sanctified are gifts from God, resulting from his particular love.
Let us ask him to sanctify our souls and employ us in his service.

row.cell: An invitation to receive freely the blessings of the Saviour.
Gracious offers of pardon and peace.

div.title: Come and receive the Savior's gifts without payment (verses 1–5)

p.hi: Everyone who desires salvation's blessings is welcome to receive them.

div.p: In Christ there is enough for everyone and enough for each person.
Those satisfied with worldly things, who feel no need of Christ, experience no spiritual thirst.
They are not troubled about their souls.
But where God gives grace, he also gives a desire for grace.
Where he gives that desire, he will satisfy it.

p.hi: Come to Jesus Christ!

div.p: He is the open fountain and the rock struck to release water.
Come to the holy ordinances, to the streams that make God's city rejoice.
Come to healing water and living water (Revelation 22:17).
Jesus himself used this invitation (John 7:37).
Come and buy: make the gospel's grace your own by personally accepting it.
Come and eat: receive and enjoy the gift.
The world disappoints our expectations.
We hope to find even water there and go thirsty.
But Christ exceeds our expectations.
When we come to him, we find wine and milk.
The gifts offered cannot be assigned an earthly price.
They have already been purchased, at the full cost of Christ's own precious blood (1 Peter 1:19).
Our needs are beyond counting, and we have nothing with which to satisfy them.
If Christ and heaven belong to us, we will remain forever indebted to free grace.
Listen carefully.
Let proud hearts bow.
It is not enough to hear an invitation; accept God's offer.
All the world's wealth and pleasure cannot provide lasting consolation and satisfaction for the soul.
They do not even satisfy our bodily appetites.
Everything is vanity and frustration.
Let the disappointments of earthly life drive us to seek satisfaction in Christ alone.
Only then will our souls find rest.

p.hi: Listen, and your soul will live.

div.p: See how freely happiness is offered!
By the sure mercies of David, Henry understands the Messiah.
All the Savior's mercies are covenant mercies.
He purchased them, God promised them in him, and they are distributed through his hands.
We could not discover the way to living water by ourselves.
Christ is given as Leader and Commander, to show us what to do and to empower us to do it.
Our calling is to obey and follow him.
No one comes to the Father except through him.
He is the Holy One of Israel, faithful to his promises.
God has promised to glorify Christ by giving him the nations as his inheritance.

div.title: Seek the Lord while he may be found (verses 6–13)
div.p: God now freely offers pardon, peace and lasting happiness.
Seeking him will not be useless while his word calls us and his Spirit works upon our hearts.
But a day is coming when the opportunity will end.
That may happen during a person's earthly life.
It will certainly be over at death and judgment, when the door is closed.
Repentance requires not only a change in conduct, but also a change in the mind.
We must revise our judgments about people and things.
It is not enough to stop outward wrongdoing.
We must struggle against evil thoughts and desires.
To repent is to return to the Lord against whom we rebelled.
If we return, God will multiply pardon, just as we multiplied our offenses.
No one should trifle with that abundant mercy or use it as an excuse to keep sinning.
Human thinking differs sharply from God's thoughts concerning sin, Jesus Christ, holiness, this world and the world to come.
But nowhere does the difference appear more strikingly than in forgiveness.
We may forgive another person yet remain unable to forget the offense.
But when God forgives sin, he no longer remembers it against the sinner.
God's word is effective in Providence and grace just as surely as it governs the natural world.
His holy truth produces changes in human hearts that rain and snow, though essential for the earth, cannot produce.
It never returns to God without accomplishing the purposes for which he sent it.
If we examine the church especially, we will see how much the Lord has accomplished for it and will yet accomplish.
The Jews' return to their homeland pictured greater promised blessings.
Gospel grace transforms the person who receives it.
Rescued from coming wrath, the converted sinner experiences peace of conscience.
Christ's love moves that person to devote life to the Redeemer's service.
Someone once irreverent, quarrelsome, selfish or ruled by sensual pleasures becomes patient, humble, kind and peaceful.
The hope of helping bring about such change should move us to spread the good news of salvation.
And may the Spirit of all truth give us such a view of the fullness, freedom and greatness of God's mercy in Christ that every narrow view of sovereign grace is removed from us.

row.cell: A charge to keep the Divine precepts.
Reproof to the careless watchmen, the teachers and rulers of the Jews.

div.title: Justice, obedience and the Sabbath (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: The Lord teaches us what he expects from us.
Be honest and just in every transaction.
Observe the Sabbath carefully and keep it holy.
If we desire God's blessing upon the work of the other days of the week, we should make it a matter of conscience to honor his Sabbath.
Keep away from sin.
Blessed is the person who restrains the hands from everything that displeases God or harms the soul.
Those who, through the Holy Spirit, wait for the hope of righteousness by faith will also be found living in holy obedience.

div.title: Blessings promised to those who come to God (verses 3–8)
div.p: Unbelief often suggests discouraging fears to believers.
But God has expressly provided promises to answer those fears.

p.hi: Spiritual blessings are immeasurably better than the gift of sons and daughters.

div.p: Children require care and may become a cause of grief or shame.
But the blessings received in God's house are lasting comforts that cannot finally become bitter.
People who genuinely love the Lord will serve him faithfully.
To them, his commandments are not burdensome.
Henry identifies three blessings promised.
Help: God does not merely permit people to come; he also inclines their hearts to approach him.
Acceptance: those who come are welcomed by him.
Comfort: people who enter his house of prayer grieving may leave rejoicing.
They find relief by laying their burdens before God.
Many sorrowful hearts have become glad in the house of prayer.
The Gentiles will become one body with the Jews.
As Jesus said, there will be one flock and one Shepherd (John 10:16).
Thanks be to God: no one is separated from him except through willful sin and unbelief.
Those who come to him are accepted through the sacrifice of our great High Priest.

div.title: Careless spiritual leaders are rebuked (verses 9–12)
div.p: The prophet summons judgments that will bring desolation.
He then rebukes Israel's careless rulers and teachers.
The rebuke also applies to churches, societies and leaders in other ages.
A people are in grave danger when their shepherds sleep instead of guarding the flock and pursue worldly advantage.
Let us ask the Great Shepherd to give us pastors after his own heart.
May they feed his people with knowledge.
May believers rejoice in his holy name, and may the church continually receive people newly added to it.

row.cell: The blessed death of the righteous.
The abominable idolatries of the Jewish nation.
Promises to the humble and contrite.

div.title: The righteous enter peace at death (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: The righteous are delivered from death's sting, though not from the experience of dying itself.
The careless world fails to recognize this.
Few people mourn the loss of a righteous person as a loss to the whole community.
Even fewer regard the death of such a person as a public warning.
Yet God may remove the righteous in compassion, to spare them from seeing, sharing in or being tempted by the evils approaching.
When a righteous person dies, that person enters peace and rest.

div.title: The destructive slavery of idolatry (verses 3–12)
div.p: God summons apostates and hypocrites to stand before him.
When warned about their sins and the judgments approaching, they mocked his word.
The Jews committed idolatry before the Babylonian exile, though Henry says they did not return to the same practices afterward.
Their eagerness in serving false gods may shame our indifference in the worship of the true God.
Serving sin is degrading slavery.
People who willingly lower themselves toward hell should not be surprised at where that road leads.
Human beings are drawn toward religious practices that inflame their unholy desires.
They may consent to terrible acts if they imagine those acts will atone for previous crimes or purchase permission to indulge a favorite sin.
Henry applies this observation to pagan, Jewish and what he calls antichristian idolatry.
Anyone who replaces God with something else as the basis of hope and confidence is moving toward ruin.
Leaving the one right path leads into countless wrong paths.
The pleasures of sin quickly become tiring but never satisfy.
People who disregard God's word and Providence reveal that they have no reverent fear of him.
Sin brings no true profit.
It destroys and ruins.

div.title: Mercy for the humbled, but no peace for the wicked (verses 13–21)
div.p: Idols and their worshipers will finally come to nothing.
But those who place their confidence in God's grace will enter heaven's joy.
The Lord has no beginning, no end and no change.
His name is holy, and everyone must acknowledge him as the holy God.
He cares tenderly for people who see their condition honestly, fear his judgment and are humbled before him.
He dwells with them to revive and comfort their hearts.
Even good people may begin to think harshly of God when their suffering continues for a long time.
Therefore God will not contend forever with them.
He will not abandon the work of his own hands or allow the purchase of his Son's blood to fail.
Covetousness is a sin that particularly exposes people to divine displeasure.
See how sinful sin is!
And notice that hardship cannot reform people unless God's grace works within them.
The Lord announces perfect peace.
It is proclaimed by preaching lips and sought by praying lips.
Christ came preaching peace to Gentiles and Jews alike.
The promise also reaches later generations, who were distant in time, as well as people distant in place.
But the wicked refuse healing through God's grace and therefore cannot receive the comfort that grace brings.
Uncontrolled desires and passions make them like a troubled sea.
Fear and guilt also disturb the pleasures they seek.
God has declared—and no one can undo his word—that there is no peace for people who knowingly persist in sin.
If we have been rescued from this condition, it is only by God's grace.
The Holy Spirit gives the new heart from which grateful praise, the fruit of our lips, rises.
Salvation, with all its fruits, hopes and comforts, is God's work.
To him belongs every part of the glory.
There is no peace for the wicked.
But let the wicked abandon their ways and their unrighteous thoughts.
Let them return to the Lord, who will show mercy and abundantly pardon.

row.cell: A counterfeit and a true fast, with promises to real godliness, and,

div.title: Hypocrisy must be confronted (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: The Holy Spirit intended this warning for hypocrites in every age.
Self-love and timid Christians may urge the messenger, “Spare yourself.”
Fear of suffering and other motives may also suggest, “Spare the rich and powerful.”
But God says, “Do not hold back.”
We must obey God rather than human beings.
We all need to pray earnestly for God's help in examining ourselves.
People may advance a long way toward heaven and still fall short.
They may even go toward eternal destruction while enjoying an excellent reputation.

div.title: A true fast rejects oppression and shows mercy (verses 3–12)
div.p: Fasting is intended to humble the soul before God.
If a fast expresses no genuine sorrow for sin and does not lead us to put sin away, it is not a true fast.
The people described here had shown outward signs of sorrow at regular or specially appointed fasts.
Yet they continued indulging pride, greed and hostile passions.
Generosity and mercy are more pleasing to God than empty fasting.
Without them, fasting is vain and hypocritical.
Some people look very humble in God's house while being harsh at home and causing suffering to their own families.
No person's faith can justify that person if it does not work through love.
Still, individuals, families, neighborhoods, churches and whole nations may express genuine repentance by fasting sincerely from right motives and then turning from sin and doing good works.
We must remove the heavy yoke of sin and oppression.
Sin and sorrow can weaken the body and dry up its strength.
By contrast, duties of kindness and charity strengthen and refresh both body and mind.
People who act justly and love mercy will experience God's comfort even during earthly life.
Good works receive his blessing when they arise from love for God and neighbor and are produced in the heart by the Holy Spirit.

div.title: Honor the Sabbath as the Lord's day (verses 13 and 14)
div.p: The Sabbath is a sign between God and the people professing to belong to him.
His appointment of it shows his favor toward them.
Their faithful observance of it demonstrates obedience toward him.
Henry calls believers to turn from unnecessary travel and from pursuing their own pleasures on the holy day without the control of conscience.
They must not surrender to sensual pleasures.
On the Sabbath, they should turn from their ordinary businesses and amusements.
In both word and deed, they should mark this day as distinct from the other days of the week.
Even during Old Testament times it was called the Lord's day.
Henry says it is fitting to continue using that name, with the further significance that it is the day of the Lord Jesus Christ (Revelation 1:10).
Remembering the Sabbath to keep it holy brings spiritual comfort and benefit.
Then we may gladly say, “It is good to draw near to God.”

row.cell: Confession of sin, and lamentation for the consequences.

div.title: Sin separates us from God's help (verses 1–8)
div.p: When prayer seems unanswered and the rescue we long for does not come, the reason is not that God has grown weary of hearing prayer.
It is often that we have grown weary of praying.
See sin as it truly is: extremely sinful.
See also its consequences: extremely harmful.
Sin separates us from God and therefore deprives us of every true good while exposing us to evil.
Yet multitudes feed on false and wicked systems of belief, bringing destruction upon themselves.
Their cleverness and carefully designed schemes cannot rescue them, any more than the spider's web can protect the spider from danger.
No plan of self-made salvation can help someone who rejects the Redeemer's robe of righteousness.
Everyone who lacks the Spirit of Christ rushes toward one form of evil or another.
People who disregard divine truth and justice remain strangers to peace.

div.title: The people acknowledge their wrongdoing (verses 9–15)
div.p: If we shut our eyes against the light of God's truth, he may justly hide from us the things that would bring peace.
The sins of those who profess to belong to God are even more blameworthy than the sins of others.
A nation's wrongdoing brings public judgments when justice is not upheld by its authorities.
People may complain bitterly under calamities.
Yet no complaint can truly help them while they continue rejecting Jesus Christ and his gospel.

div.title: The Redeemer comes with the Spirit (verses 16–21)
div.p: This passage connects with the prophecies that follow.
Henry says it is generally understood as announcing the coming of the Messiah, who will be both Avenger and Deliverer of his church.
No one was able to intercede with God and turn aside his judgment.
No one stood forward to uphold justice and truth.
Therefore the Lord himself acted with his own strength and righteousness on behalf of his people.
He will make his justice against the enemies of his church clearly visible.
When the enemy threatens to sweep everything away without restraint, the Spirit of the Lord will stop him and put him to flight.
The God who delivered his people before will deliver them again.
Yet a far greater salvation was promised for the fullness of time—the redemption through the Messiah toward which all the prophets looked.
The Son of God comes as our Redeemer.
The Spirit of God comes as our Sanctifier.
Thus the Comforter remains with the church forever (John 14:16).
The word of Christ will continue in the mouths of his faithful people.
Whenever anyone claims to speak the mind of the Spirit, that claim must be tested against Scripture.
We have reason to grieve the spread of unbelief and irreverence.
But the Redeemer's cause will achieve complete victory, even on earth.
At the end, each believer will be more than a conqueror when received by the Lord into heaven's glory.

row.cell: The glories of the church of God, when the fulness of the Gentiles shall come in.
and the Jews shall be converted and gathered from their dispersions.
and the kingdoms of this world shall become the kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ.

div.title: The nations come to Christ's light (verses 1–8)
div.p: As far as we know God personally and enjoy his favor, our light has come.
If God's glory rests upon us and honors us, we should return praise to him not only with our lips but also through our lives.
Henry finds nothing in the earlier history of the Jews that fully answers the prophecy of this chapter.
He therefore understands it as looking chiefly toward events still to come, including the purity and enlargement of God's church.
The prophet describes the conversion of human souls.
They hurry toward Jesus Christ, his church, his word and appointed worship like doves flying home.
They fly there for refuge and shelter, and there they find rest.
What a wonderful sight it is to see people hastening toward Christ!

div.title: The church receives peoples from far away (verses 9–14)
div.p: God promises to be gracious.
We must begin with his promise, because every mercy flows from it.
Many people from distant countries will enter the church.
Christ always welcomes those who come to him.

p.hi: The gate of mercy remains open day and night.

div.p: Everything surrounding the church will be put to use for her welfare.
But those who refuse to submit to Christ's golden scepter, his word and Spirit, and the rules of his household, will face judgment under his iron rod.
The special advantages of different nations and kinds of people will contribute to the church's beauty.
This beauty is not merely outward greatness.
It consists chiefly in holiness, and in the gifts and comforts of the Holy Spirit that adorn and enrich gospel worship.
Blessed be God: the gates of Zion remain open to sinners returning to him.

div.title: God completes his church's glory (verses 15–22)
div.p: The final fulfillment of these promises must surpass anything the Old Testament church experienced.
Nations and kings will devote their resources to the church's good.
The rescue accomplished for her will reveal unmistakably the Lord's own work.
Everything will be transformed for the better.
No longer will the land hear threats from violent people or the cries of those who suffer violence.
Her walls will represent safety.
Her gates will proclaim praise to God.
The closing images also appear in the description of the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:23; 22:5).
Henry recognizes two possibilities for their fulfillment: a future glorious state of the church on earth, or the triumphant church in heaven.
Only a fulfillment of that magnitude matches the promise.
People who make God their only light will find him their sufficient and everlasting light.
That happiness will know neither change nor imperfection.
No earthly people are completely righteous.
But heaven contains no mixture of sin.
Those who enter it will be wholly righteous, their spirits made perfect.
The church's glory will bring honor to God.
When his work is complete, everyone will recognize its wonder.
It may now seem impossible.
But the God of unlimited power has undertaken it.
Its fulfillment may appear delayed, but the Lord will hasten it at the time appointed by his wisdom, not the time demanded by our foolishness.
Let this hope encourage us during hardship and stir us to diligence.
May we be granted a rich welcome into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

row.cell: The Messiah, his character and office.
His promises of the future blessedness of the church.
The church praises God for these mercies.

div.title: The Spirit-anointed Messiah proclaims good news (verses 1–3)
div.p: The prophets sometimes received the Holy Spirit to teach them what to say and move them to proclaim it.
But Jesus Christ possessed the Spirit always and without measure.
As a man, he was thus perfectly equipped for the work the Father had appointed him to accomplish.
People who are materially poor are often more ready to receive the gospel (James 2:5).
Yet the gospel benefits us only when we receive it with humility and meekness.
To those who are poor in spirit, Christ announced good news, as when he pronounced blessing upon the meek.

p.hi: His atoning satisfaction has been accepted.

div.p: Sin's dominion holds us under Satan's power.
But the Son is ready to make us free by his Spirit.
And if the Son makes us free, we are free indeed.
Christ came to destroy sin and Satan, and he triumphed over them through his cross.
Those who stubbornly refuse these invitations will be dealt with as enemies.
Christ was appointed to be a Comforter, and he truly is one.
He comforts all who mourn and look to him rather than to the world for relief.
His purpose is that believers should abound in the fruits of righteousness, like branches planted and tended by God.
God's mercy, Christ's atonement and the gospel of grace do not benefit people who remain proud and self-sufficient.
The Holy Spirit must humble them and show them their true character and needs.
Only then will they recognize their need of the Friend and Savior of sinners.
To people humbled before God, Christ's message is truly glad tidings.

div.title: The restored people become God's servants (verses 4–9)
div.p: These promises first address Jews returning from captivity.
But they also reach everyone whom grace rescues from spiritual bondage.
An unholy soul resembles a ruined city with broken walls or a destroyed house.
Through the power of Christ's gospel and grace, that soul is restored to become a dwelling place for God through the Spirit.
God's grace can teach us a holy detachment from worldly concerns.
Our hands may remain busy in worldly duties, while our hearts are not entangled in them but remain wholly devoted to God and his service.
Henry connects that detachment with the picture of others carrying out the plowing and vineyard work.
Everyone whom the Lord sets free, he also calls to serve.
Serving God is perfect freedom and the highest honor.
All believers have been made kings and priests to God.
They should therefore live in ways worthy of that calling.
Those who have the Lord as their portion have received an excellent inheritance and should rejoice in it.
The fullness of heavenly joy will more than compensate for everything suffered or given in service.
God loves truth and justice and therefore hates every act of injustice.
Even an offering made to God cannot justify robbery.
Indeed, theft committed under the pretense of making a religious offering is especially hateful.
May the children of godly parents demonstrate the fruit of good instruction, their parents' prayers and the Lord's blessing through the lives they lead.

div.title: The redeemed rejoice in salvation (verses 10 and 11)
div.p: Only those who are covered now by Christ's righteousness and renewed by the sanctifying Holy Spirit can finally wear the garments of salvation.
Those blessings will spread through future generations as fruit rises from the earth.
With reliable abundance and to the benefit of humanity, God will cause righteousness and praise to grow.
The good news will spread far away, until Christ's salvation is announced to the ends of the earth.
Let us pray earnestly that the Lord will cause this righteousness to grow among us.
It is the true excellence and glory of Christian faith and profession.

row.cell: God's care of his church and people.
The office of ministers in preaching the gospel.
Every hinderance shall be removed from the way of salvation.

div.title: Christ's unchanging love for his church (verses 1–5)
div.p: Here the Son of God assures his church of his enduring love and his intercession through all her trials and difficulties.
She will receive a new and pleasant name, different from any name she had before.
Before the gospel was preached widely, hardly anyone seemed sincerely concerned about the true condition of religion in the world.
But by his grace, God has produced something in his church that makes her his delight.
Let that love move us toward holiness.
If the Lord rejoices over us, we should rejoice in serving him.

div.title: Ministers and believers persevere in prayer (verses 6–9)
div.p: People who profess to belong to God must also be people of prayer.
The Lord is not irritated by earnest pleading, as human beings may be.
He himself tells us to continue crying out and give him no rest.
Jesus' parable of persistent requesting teaches the same principle (Luke 11:5–6).
When God pours out a spirit of prayer on a people, it is a hopeful sign that he is approaching them with mercy.
Notice how uncertain our earthly comforts are.
Notice also God's kindness in granting plenty, together with peace to enjoy it.
May we delight in the gatherings of God's people so that we may experience the consolation of his Spirit.

div.title: The way is prepared for salvation (verses 10–12)
div.p: God will make a way for Christ's salvation.
Every barrier will be removed.
Christ brings with him the reward of comfort and peace.
But the path before him requires humiliation and reformation.
Those he saves will be called the holy people and the redeemed of the Lord.
Holiness brings honor and beauty to a person or a place.
It makes God's people desirable and loved.
Many historical events may already have fulfilled parts of this promise and served as pledges of more glorious times still to come.
Scripture repeatedly shows the close connection between the blessing of the Jews and that of the Gentiles.
Jesus Christ will finish his work.
He never abandons anyone whom he has redeemed and sanctified.

div.title: The victorious Messiah brings judgment (verses 1–6)
div.p: In a vision, the prophet sees the Messiah returning in victory from the defeat of his enemies.
Edom serves as a picture of those enemies.
He does not travel as someone worn out by battle.
Rather, he moves in the greatness of his strength, ready to overcome every opposing power.
The Messiah declares that he has been treading the winepress of God's judgment (Revelation 14:19; 19:13).
By his own power, without human assistance, he defeats those stubbornly opposing him.
The appointed day of judgment has come as the time for rescuing his church.
When Christ first appeared on earth, he seemed weak as he poured out his own precious blood in atonement for our sins.
But at the appointed time he will appear in the full display of his strength.
The harvest is rapidly ripening, and the day determined for judgment approaches.
Let sinners seek reconciliation with their righteous Judge before he brings their strength to nothing.
Does Christ say, “I am coming soon”?
Then let our hearts respond, “Come, Lord Jesus; let the time of the redeemed arrive.”

div.title: God's mercy remembered amid Israel's rebellion (verses 7–14)
div.p: Henry understands the latter part of this chapter and all of the next as expressing, or anticipating, the prayers of Jews at their conversion.
The people remember God's great mercy and favor toward their nation.
They confess their wickedness and stubbornness, ask for pardon and grieve over the long misery they have experienced.
The Father's only Son became the Angel or Messenger of God's love.
He redeemed his people and carried them tenderly.
