Yet they complained, resisted the Holy Spirit, despised and persecuted God's prophets, and rejected and crucified the promised Messiah.
Every true comfort and hope we have comes from God's loving-kindness.
Our misery and fears arise from our sins.
Nevertheless, he is the Savior.
When sinners seek the God who in earlier times glorified himself by rescuing, feeding and guiding his purchased flock through danger, they have reason to hope.
He has also given the Holy Spirit to bless his ministers' labors.
Seeking this Savior is a hopeful sign that people are discovering the way of peace.

div.title: The church pleads with its everlasting Redeemer (verses 15–19)
div.p: The people ask the Lord to look down upon the desolate condition of the nation he once specially favored.
Would it not glorify his name to remove the veil from their hearts and restore the tribes of his inheritance?
The Babylonian captivity and the return that followed were shadows of the greater events predicted here.
God looks upon his people with tenderness and mercy.
Spiritual judgments are more frightening than any outward disaster.
We should avoid the sins that justly cause the Lord to leave people to themselves and to the deceiver.
“Our Redeemer from everlasting” is his name.
His people have always recognized him as the God to whom they could appeal.
The Lord will hear those who belong to him.
He will deliver them from oppression by those who do not bear his name.

row.cell: The church prays that God's power may be manifested.
A confession of sin, and afflictions bewailed.

div.title: The church pleads for God to reveal his power (verses 1–5)
div.p: God's people long for him to act visibly for them and among them, so that everyone will recognize his power.
This prayer also applies to Christ's second coming, when the Lord himself will descend from heaven.
They appeal to what God has done before and to the kind purposes he has announced for his people.
They need not fear that his promises will disappoint them by failing to come true, because his promises are sure.
Nor will they be disappointed by their fulfillment, because what God provides is completely sufficient.
The happiness of his people rests upon what he has planned and is preparing for them—and upon the way he is preparing them for that blessedness.
It rests on all that God has already done and everything he will yet do.
If we believe this, how could we consider anything too great to expect from his truth, power and love?
The happiness God promises is spiritual, beyond the full comprehension of unaided human understanding.
He stands ready to show grace.
Notice the fellowship between a gracious God and a soul renewed by grace.
We should conscientiously fulfill everything the Lord requires of us.
God meets those who seek to walk in his ways.
This reveals his willingness and eagerness to do them good.
He has been rightly angry with us for our sins.
But that anger is temporary for his reconciled people, whereas his favor is life, continuing and sustaining their salvation.

div.title: Confession, helplessness and appeal to the Father (verses 6–12)
div.p: In affliction, God's people confess and mourn their sins.
They admit that they have no claim upon his mercy.
Sin is the hateful thing that God opposes.
Whatever outward goodness our deeds seem to possess, if we offer them as a way of earning God's acceptance, they are only rags.
They cannot cover our guilt.
Indeed, they become like filthy rags, making our condition worse.
Even the few good works that really have excellence because they are fruits of the Holy Spirit remain imperfect and stained by the way we carry them out.
They too must be washed in the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness.
It is a dangerous sign when people stop praying.
To pray is to take hold, by faith, of God's promises of good will.
We plead those promises, cling to him and earnestly ask him not to leave us or to return to us when we feel his absence.
The people had brought their trouble on themselves through foolishness.
Sin withers sinners, like something blighted, before the wind of their own wrongdoing carries them away.
When they made themselves unclean, it was no surprise that God regarded them with displeasure.
Yet even in their foolishness, poverty and disgrace they could say:

p.hi: “You are still our Father.”

div.p: The anger they endured was the correction of a Father who could be reconciled to them.
They expected relief from him alone and entrusted their cause to him.
They did not ask, “Lord, do not rebuke us at all.”
Correction might be necessary.
Instead, their plea was, “Do not rebuke us in your displeasure.”
They described their pitiable condition.
See the ruin sin can bring upon a people!
An outward profession of holiness provides no protection against it.
The people did not tell God exactly what to say or do.
They asked him to speak for their comfort and relief.
How few sincerely call upon the Lord or stir themselves up to cling to him!
He may delay the answer to prayer.
But he will finally answer those who call upon his name and hope in his mercy.

row.cell: The calling of the Gentiles, and the rejection of the Jews.
The Lord would preserve a remnant.
The future happy and flourishing state of the church.

div.title: God calls the Gentiles and confronts unbelief (verses 1–7)
div.p: The Gentiles began seeking God and found him because he had first sought and found them.
Sometimes the Lord confronts a careless pleasure-seeker or a person openly hostile to him with the words, “Here I am!”
A sudden change follows.
Throughout the gospel age, Christ has waited to show mercy.
But the Jews, though invited, would not come.
Henry therefore says their rejection did not happen without reason.
They insisted on following whatever pleased themselves.
They grieved and resisted the Holy Spirit.
They abandoned God's temple to sacrifice in the groves.
They disregarded the difference between clean and unclean foods before the gospel removed those dietary distinctions.
Henry suggests this behavior may represent all forbidden pleasures and everything people think they will gain through sin—that hateful thing God opposes.
Jesus spoke many warnings against the pride and hypocrisy he encountered.
The charge against such conduct is clear.
We too must watch against pride and preferring ourselves to others.
Every sin, including the most secret thought of the heart, is known to God and will come under his judgment.

div.title: The Lord preserves a remnant (verses 8–10)
div.p: A cluster of grapes that seems unripe and worthless may still contain new wine.
The Jewish people have continued as a distinct people, providing witness to the fulfillment of ancient promises and prophecies.
God's chosen ones, the spiritual offspring of praying Jacob, will inherit his mountains of happiness and joy.
He will bring them safely there through the valley of tears.
Everything ultimately displays God's glory in the redemption of sinners.

div.title: The different ends of faithful and unfaithful people (verses 11–16)
div.p: Here the prophet contrasts the godly with the wicked and Jews who believed with those who continued in unbelief.
The wicked spread a table for a host of pagan deities and poured out offerings to the many false gods.
Those worshipers were willing to spend generously for their idols.
This should shame people who claim to worship the true God while begrudging his service.
See how malicious sin really is.
It means choosing to do what we know displeases God.
In every nation and age, the Lord leaves people who persist in wrongdoing and despise his gospel's call to face the consequences.
But his servants receive the bread of life and will lack nothing truly good for them.
Those abandoning God will be ashamed of their false confidence in their own righteousness and the hopes built upon it.
Worldly people congratulate themselves over possessions and prosperity.
God's servants rejoice in God himself.
He is their strength and their portion.
They honor him as the God of truth.
He promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed in him.
His people count themselves happy to belong to the God who has made them forget their troubles.

div.title: The promised new creation and peace (verses 17–25)
div.p: Through the grace and comfort believers receive from Jesus Christ, we should understand the promise of a new heaven and a new earth.
The earlier disorder, sin and misery of humanity will no longer be remembered or repeated.
The prophet describes the coming happiness of the church through many images.
A person who dies at a hundred years old will be regarded as dying young; such long life will be expected.
Henry explicitly leaves the precise fulfillment open, saying that only events will determine what these images mean.
Nevertheless, he reasons that if Christianity became universal, the decline of violence and evil could greatly extend human life.
During those blessed times, God's people will enjoy the fruits of their labor.
Children will no longer bring misery to their parents or endure misery themselves.
Sinful dispositions will be completely brought under control, and everyone will live in harmony.
The church on earth will enjoy a happiness resembling heaven.
This prophecy assures Christ's servants that a time is approaching when they will enjoy undisturbed all that they need for true happiness.
As God's fellow workers, let us attend his ordinances and obey his commands.

row.cell: God looks at the heart, and vengeance is threatened for guilt.
The increase of the church, when Jew and Gentile shall be gathered to the Redeemer.
Every enemy of the church shall be destroyed, and the final ruin of ungodly men shall be seen.

div.title: God favors the contrite heart, not empty ceremony (verses 1–4)
div.p: The Jews took great pride in their temple.
But what lasting satisfaction could the eternal God find in a house built by human hands?
He has already made heaven and earth, besides the temples constructed by people.
He looks past outward buildings to show favor to people who are poor in spirit, earnest, humble and self-denying.
Their hearts are deeply grieved by sin.
Such a heart is a living temple for God.
The sacrifice offered by a wicked person is not merely unacceptable.
It is a serious offense to God.
Henry argues that offering an animal sacrifice as though the Mosaic sacrificial law still provided atonement after Christ's completed sacrifice amounts to setting Christ's offering aside.
Likewise, treating incense as a necessary substitute for Christ's intercession dishonors his mediation, like honoring an idol.
Human beings will be deceived by the false confidences they choose for themselves.
An unbelieving heart and an unpurified conscience require no further punishment than to have their own fears become reality.
Whatever people place instead of Christ's priesthood, sacrifice and intercession will be hateful to God.

div.title: The church rejoices as the Lord gathers his people (verses 5–14)
div.p: The prophet now addresses those who tremble at God's word, giving them comfort and encouragement.
The Lord will appear to bring joy to humble believers and shame to hypocrites and persecutors.
When the Holy Spirit was poured out and the gospel was preached from Zion, great numbers were converted quickly.
God's word, especially his promises, and his appointed ordinances provide comfort to the church.
Every sinner brought to Jesus Christ increases the joy of genuine believers.
Where the gospel is received in its power, it brings a river of peace that carries us toward an ocean of boundless and everlasting happiness.
Divine consolation reaches the inward person.
The joy of the Lord becomes the believer's strength.
Both God's mercy and God's justice will be displayed and glorified forever.

div.title: Judgment on enemies and final separation (verses 15–24)
div.p: This is a prophetic announcement of the Lord's judgment upon those who oppose his church.
Henry applies it especially to what he calls antichristian opponents of the gospel in the last days.
Verses 19 and 20 describe abundant means through which sinners will be brought to faith.
These expressions are figurative, pointing to the many gracious helps God provides for bringing his chosen people home to Christ.
Everyone who comes will be welcomed.
Nothing needed for their encouragement and support will be withheld.
A gospel ministry will be established among the gathered people, with solemn worship before the Lord.
The final verse portrays the punishment of sinners in the world to come.
Then the righteous and the wicked will be separated.
Jesus himself applied this imagery to the everlasting misery of those who continue without repentance.
Let the Lord's redeemed people sing songs of victory in honor of the free grace that distinguishes them—yet do so humbly, with reverent awe.
Isaiah ends his prophecies with this striking portrayal of the opposite conditions of righteous and wicked people, a distinction that embraces the whole human race.
May God grant, for Christ's sake, that our portion be among those who fear and love his name, cling to his truth and persevere in every good work.
May we look forward to hearing Jesus Christ graciously invite his people to inherit the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

div.title: Jeremiah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Jeremiah was a priest from Anathoth, a town in the territory of Benjamin.
God called him to be a prophet when he was very young, about seventy years after Isaiah's death according to Henry's chronology.
Jeremiah continued serving faithfully for about forty years, until Judah's sins reached their full measure and national destruction followed.
The prophecies preserved in this book are not arranged in the order in which Jeremiah delivered them.
Henry notes that Benjamin Blayney attempted to arrange them more regularly, in this order:
This is a report of Blayney's proposed reading sequence, not a recommendation to rearrange the canonical biblical text or its SWORD versification.
Jeremiah's prophecies chiefly concern the idolatry and other sins of Judah, the threatened judgments, the future restoration and deliverance, and promises concerning the Messiah.
They are especially marked by plain and faithful rebukes, affectionate appeals and grave warnings.

row.cell: Jeremiah's call to the prophetic office.
A vision of an almond-tree and of a seething-pot, Divine protection is promised.

div.title: Jeremiah is called to speak God's word (verses 1–10)
div.p: Jeremiah received his call to prophetic service when he was still young.
He was appointed to speak not only to the Jews, but also to the neighboring nations.
Through the book he remains a prophet whose warnings concern the whole world.
It would be well for everyone to take those warnings seriously.
The Lord who formed us knows the particular duties and purposes for which he intends us.
But unless he makes us holy through his Spirit who creates new life, we will not be fit for his holy service on earth or his holy happiness in heaven.
We should think humbly of ourselves.
Young people should remember their inexperience and not presume to undertake tasks beyond their abilities.
Yet an awareness of our weakness and inadequacy should make us approach our work with humility, not cause us to draw back when God calls.
Those commissioned to deliver messages from God must not fear human opposition.
Through a sign, the Lord gave Jeremiah the gift needed for the task.
God's message must be delivered in God's own words.
Whatever worldly advisers or politicians believe, the true security of a kingdom is ultimately determined by God's purpose and word.

div.title: The almond tree, boiling pot and promised protection (verses 11–19)
div.p: God showed Jeremiah the approaching destruction of Judah and Jerusalem by the Chaldeans.
The almond tree, which blossoms earlier in spring than other trees, indicated how soon the judgment would come.
God also showed where the approaching destruction would originate.
Jeremiah saw a boiling pot, a picture of Judah and Jerusalem thrown into terrible turmoil.
The pot's opening, or the face of the furnace beneath it, pointed toward the north.
From that direction would come the fire and the fuel that would consume Judah.
Northern powers would unite.
The cause of these judgments was Judah's sin.
Jeremiah was to declare the whole counsel of God, not merely the parts that pleased his listeners.

p.hi: Reverence for God is the best remedy for fear of people.

div.p: It is better to have every human being against us than to have God as our enemy.
Those who know that God is with them do not need to fear anyone who opposes them.
Let us pray for the willingness to give up our private interests whenever necessary, and for steadfastness so that nothing draws us away from duty.

div.title: God reminds his people of their early devotion (verses 1–8)
div.p: People who begin well and then fail to persevere will rightly be reminded of how promising their beginnings once were.
Those who abandon a faith they once professed often oppose it more fiercely than people who never knew it.
Such people have no adequate excuse for their departure.
God's spiritual Israel should acknowledge the debt owed to him for bringing them safely through the wilderness of this world, where so many dangers threaten the soul.
How sad that people who once appeared devoted to the Lord later live in ways that make their earlier religious profession an added witness against their sins!
As we grow in knowledge, let us be careful not to lose zeal and warmth of devotion.

div.title: The fountain of life is exchanged for broken cisterns (verses 9–13)
div.p: Before the Lord punishes sinners, he pleads with them, calling them to repentance.
The charges he brings are the very matters we should confront within ourselves.
We should tremble at the anger and curse toward which people run when they reject God's favor and grace.
Grace in Jesus Christ is like water from a spring.
It refreshes, cools, cleanses and brings fruit.
It is living water because it gives life to dead sinners, revives believers who are growing weary, sustains spiritual life, and leads to eternal life.
It flows without being exhausted.
Abandoning this Fountain is the first great evil.
God's professing people do so when they neglect his word and appointed worship.
Instead they dig broken cisterns that cannot hold water.
These are the world and its possessions, along with human inventions that people trust and follow.
Let us cling wholeheartedly to the Lord alone.

p.hi: Where else could we go?

div.p: How readily we surrender the consolations of the Holy Spirit for the worthless excitements enjoyed by enthusiastic but hypocritical people!

div.title: Israel suffers the consequences of rebellion (verses 14–19)
div.p: Was Israel intended to live as a slave?
No. They were the descendants of Abraham.
Henry makes a spiritual application.
Was the human soul created to be enslaved?
No. Yet through sin it has sold its freedom and made itself captive to many sinful desires and passions.
Assyrian rulers, like lions, overpowered Israel.
People from Egypt also destroyed the nation's strength and splendor.
Israel brought those calamities upon itself by turning away from God.
The practical warning is simple:
Repent of sin, so that correction does not become destruction.
What business does a Christian have pursuing forbidden pleasures, empty sinful amusements, greed or ambition?

div.title: Judah's fruitless pursuit of sin (verses 20–28)
div.p: Despite all the advantages Judah had received, the people became like a wild vine producing poisonous fruit.
People can become as enslaved to uncontrolled desires and lusts as irrational animals are to their instincts.
God warned them not to exhaust themselves pursuing things that could bring only distress and misery.
We should never despair of the extent of God's mercy, which is sufficient to pardon our sins.
Nor should we despair of the power of his grace, which can overcome even the strongest corruption in our hearts.

div.title: Empty confidence and continued self-justification (verses 29–37)
div.p: God's judgments had failed to change the people.
Instead, they tried to justify themselves.
For people who make the world their true home and final portion, it becomes a wilderness and a dark country.
But those who dwell in God can say their inheritance has fallen in pleasant places.
The people's words reveal the presumption of sinners who have long stopped thinking seriously about the Lord.
How many days pass in our own lives without remembering him as we should!
The Lord was displeased with Judah's false confidences and would not make them succeed.
People may use all their cleverness, but they cannot find happiness through sin or discover any honest excuse for it.
They may move from one sin to another.
But no one ever hardened the heart against God, turned away from him and truly prospered.

row.cell: The children of Israel express their sorrow and repentance.

div.title: God invites the unfaithful to return (verses 1–5)
div.p: When we repent, it is good to remember the particular sins we have committed, including the places where we committed them and the people whose company encouraged them.
How gently the Lord had corrected his people!
When he receives repentant sinners, he acts as God, not merely as a human being.
Whatever you have said or done in the past, will you not turn to him from this moment forward?
Will not such grace overcome your stubbornness?
Now that pardon is announced, will you not accept its benefit?
Repentant people may expect the tender compassion of a Father welcoming a returning prodigal.
They approach him as the Guide of their youth.
Young people especially need guidance.
Those returning to God can take courage from the promise that he will not remain angry forever.
All his mercies throughout history encourage us in the same way.
What could be more desirable for a young person than to have the Lord as Father and Guide?
Parents should earnestly direct their children, day after day, to seek that blessing.

div.title: Judah's guilt is greater than Israel's (verses 6–11)
div.p: When we consider the sins committed by people who have abandoned a profession of faith, and the consequences that followed, we find abundant reason to avoid their paths.
It is dreadful to be shown more guilty than those who have already perished through their wrongdoing.
But knowing that others were even more wicked will be little comfort in everlasting judgment.

div.title: Pardon and restoration are promised (verses 12–20)
div.p: Notice how willing God is to forgive sin, and the blessings he has prepared for the age of the gospel.
These promises were proclaimed toward the north, addressing Israel's ten tribes who were captive in Assyria.
They are told how to return to God.
If we confess our sins, the Lord is faithful and just to forgive.
Henry also sees these promises reaching toward a future return of the Jews in later ages.
God graciously receives those who come back to him and, by his grace, calls them out from among others.
The ark of the covenant was not recovered after the exile.
The earlier dispensation was destined to pass away.
Henry connects this transition with the great increase of believers as Gentiles and Israelites scattered among them were brought into God's church.
The prophecy describes a happy condition for God's people.
The Lord can teach people everywhere to call him Father.
Yet no one can truly be his child without a thorough change of heart and life.
Without that renewal, we have no security against wandering away again.

div.title: Repentance acknowledges that only God can save (verses 21–25)
div.p: Sin means turning aside into crooked paths.
At the root of every sin lies forgetfulness of the Lord our God.
By sin we bring trouble upon ourselves.
But God promises to heal the backsliding of those who return.
That healing comes through his pardoning mercy, his peace that quiets the heart and his grace that renews us.
Repentant people devote themselves to God.
They reject every hope of rescue that depends on anyone else.
They trust in the Lord alone, because only he can save.
These promises point to the great salvation from sin accomplished by Jesus Christ.
Those who repent acknowledge God's justice in their troubles and condemn their own wrongdoing.
They learn to call sin shameful, even the sins in which they once found the greatest pleasure.
They come to recognize sin as death and ruin, and understand that it is responsible for their misery.
People who harden themselves in sin will receive contempt and distress.
Those who conceal their sins will not prosper.
But those who confess and forsake them find mercy.

div.title: Return to God sincerely (verses 1–2)
div.p: The first two verses of this chapter should be read together with the end of chapter 3.
Sin must be removed from the heart.
Otherwise, it has not been removed from God's sight, because the entire heart is open before him.

div.title: The hard heart must be broken up (verses 3–4)
div.p: A heart that has never been humbled resembles ground left untilled.
It is ground capable of improvement and entrusted to us for cultivation.
But it lies unused and is covered in thorns and weeds, the natural growth of a corrupt heart.
Let us beg God to create a clean heart in us and to renew a right spirit within us.
Unless a person is born again, that person cannot enter heaven's kingdom.

div.title: Judah is warned of an approaching invader (verses 5–18)
div.p: A fierce conqueror who had already defeated the surrounding nations would bring desolation upon Judah.
Jeremiah was distressed that false prophets had soothed the people into a dangerous feeling of security.
He described the enemy's approach.
Some attention had been paid in Jerusalem to outward reform.
But this was not enough.
The people's hearts needed washing, through true repentance and faith, to remove the love and pollution of sin.
When lesser troubles do not awaken sinners or bring nations to reform, a more decisive judgment will be pronounced.
The Lord's voice announces that misery is approaching.
Henry especially warns those who profess the gospel but live wickedly.
When judgment falls, the bitterness of sin's fruit and the fatal nature of its end will become undeniable.

div.title: Jeremiah grieves over Judah's coming ruin (verses 19–31)
div.p: The prophet took no pleasure in announcing messages of divine anger.
In a vision he saw the whole land thrown into confusion.
Compared with its former condition, everything had fallen into disorder.
Yet Judah's ruin would not be final.
The end of a particular earthly comfort is not necessarily the end of everything.
The Lord may correct his people with great severity, but he will not abandon them entirely.
Cosmetics, ornaments and flattering appearances will offer no protection from the coming disaster.
Neither outward privileges, religious profession nor human schemes can prevent judgment.
How miserable are people who remain like foolish children in matters concerning their souls!
Whatever else we fail to understand, may God give us wisdom in the ways of godliness.
Sin will ultimately find the sinner.
And sorrow, sooner or later, will find those who feel secure while rejecting God's warnings.

row.cell: The Jews' profession of religion was hypocritical.
The cruel proceedings of their enemies.

div.title: A profession of religion without integrity (verses 1–9)
div.p: Jerusalem could offer no one who behaved with the integrity and godliness God required. The Lord saw the people's true character through every disguise.
The poor were ignorant of God and his ways, and this ignorance led them into wickedness. Those who know nothing of God and true religion may be expected to produce the works of darkness.
But poverty itself does not make people ignorant or wicked. God has faithful people among the poor who know his way, walk in it, and do their duty.
The people Jeremiah condemned were willfully ignorant. They had chosen not to learn; their ignorance could not excuse their conduct.
The rich, meanwhile, were proud and insolent. By abusing the favors God had given them, they made their guilt worse.

div.title: God places a limit upon approaching destruction (verses 10–18)
div.p: Multitudes are ruined because they believe that God will not judge as strictly as his word declares. Satan used that same deception to bring ruin upon humanity.
Sinners are unwilling to accept any teaching as God's word if it requires them to abandon sin or disturbs their pleasure in it.
By mocking and mistreating the Lord's messengers, Judah filled up the measure of its wickedness.
God can bring suffering upon us from distant places and unexpected causes.
Yet he still had mercy reserved for his people. Therefore he placed limits on this approaching devastation.
Do not overlook God's word “nevertheless” in verse 18.
Here the Lord remembers his covenant with Israel: he displays his holiness and complete opposition to sin while still sparing the sinner (Psalm 89:30–35).

div.title: Sin explains the nation's suffering (verses 19–31)
div.p: Hearts that have never been humbled readily accuse God of treating them unjustly when suffering arrives.
But sinners may read the nature of their sin in their punishment. If we ask why the Lord permits such distress, we should examine our own wrongdoing.
The restless waves obey the boundary God has set for them. Even a sandy shore restrains the sea as effectively as a mountain, because the Lord has commanded it.
Yet human beings break through every restraint of his law and surrender themselves to wickedness.
They also disregard their own true interests.
Year after year the Lord gives the appointed weeks of harvest. People continually receive his generosity, yet rebel against the Giver.
Sin deprives us of blessings. It can make the heavens like bronze and the earth like iron.
The things of this world cannot be the best things. We must not conclude that God approves of wicked conduct simply because a wicked person enjoys prosperity.
The sentence against evil may be delayed, but it will certainly be carried out.
The question “Shall I not punish them for these things?” announces both the certainty and necessity of God's righteous judgments.
Those who follow sinful paths should remember that those paths have an end—and their final outcome will be bitter.

row.cell: All methods used to amend them had been without success.

div.title: The Chaldeans invade Judah (verses 1–8)
div.p: No human strategy can succeed in resisting God's appointed judgments.
The more we indulge the pleasures of this life, the less prepared we become to endure its troubles.
The Chaldean army would enter Judah and soon consume what lay before it.
A day of visitation is coming upon those who continue carelessly in sin, convinced that they are secure.
How foolish it is to waste our time in trivial pursuits when eternal salvation is at stake and we have spiritual enemies to resist!
The attackers hurried forward, not because they wished to carry out God's purposes, but because they wanted to fill their own treasuries.
Yet in doing what they desired, they unknowingly served his purpose.
In its natural, unrenewed state, the human heart produces evil thoughts as constantly as a fountain pours out water. The stream continues, and the spring never runs dry.
The God of mercy is reluctant to depart even from a people who repeatedly provoke him.
He earnestly calls them to repentance and reform, so that they may avert the worst consequences of their sin.

div.title: Judah refuses the ancient good way (verses 9–17)
div.p: When the Lord rises to judge, sinners of every age, social rank and sex are accountable to him.
These people had given themselves over to love of the world.
If we examine that sin by the standard of Scripture, we find it among people of every position and background.
The most dangerous enemies are sometimes those who flatter us while we sin.
May people learn to act wisely concerning their souls!
Ask for the ancient paths. The way of godliness and righteousness has always been the way God approves and blesses.
Seek the ancient paths made known in his written word.
When you find the good way, walk in it. You will be abundantly rewarded when the journey ends.
But those who refuse God's voice and will not flee to the Refuge he has appointed will learn at judgment that they have been ruined by rejecting his word.

div.title: Every warning and means of grace has been rejected (verses 18–30)
div.p: God rejected the people's outward ceremonies as worthless to atone for their sins.
Sacrifice and incense were meant to direct worshipers toward the Mediator.
When people offered them as if they could buy permission to continue sinning, their offerings provoked God.
The sins of those professing to belong to the Lord made them easy prey for their enemies. They scarcely dared show themselves.
Believers may rejoice in the hope of God's mercies, even while they see those mercies only in his promises.
Sinners should tremble at his judgments, even while they see those judgments only in his warnings.
Judah's people were deeply rebellious, and each sinner became a source of corruption to others.
Those who surrender to sin soon become tempters themselves.
They resembled ore that appears to contain valuable metal, but after refining proves to be nothing but dross.
No warning, correction or rebuke could persuade them to separate from their sins.
They would be called rejected silver—material of no use or worth.
When every means of grace leaves people unrenewed, they risk being rejected by God and left to everlasting misery.
Let us pray instead that the Lord would refine us as silver is refined.

row.cell: Confidence in the temple is vain.
The provocation by persisting in idolatry.
God justifies his dealings with them.

div.title: The temple offers no protection from unrepentant sin (verses 1–16)
div.p: Neither outward religious observances nor professions of faith nor even claims to have received revelations from God will benefit people who refuse to amend their ways and actions.
No one has a right to claim a share in free salvation while willingly continuing in known sin or deliberately neglecting a known duty.
The people imagined that the very temple they had polluted with their wrongdoing would protect them.
Those who continue sinning because grace abounds, or in the hope that grace will abound even more, effectively turn Christ into a servant of sin.
The cross of Christ, rightly understood, is the strongest remedy against that poisonous thinking.
God's Son gave himself for our transgressions. His sacrifice displays both the excellence of God's law and the dreadful evil of sin.
Never suppose that we can continue in wickedness without facing its consequences.

div.title: The people's zeal for idols condemns their indifference to God (verses 17–20)
div.p: Judah's people were proud of their enthusiasm in serving idols.
Even from that terrible example we should learn how earnestly we ought to serve the true God.
It should be an honor to be entrusted with any work for him.
We should work diligently ourselves and take care to teach our children the truths of God, just as many people diligently teach others corrupt practices.
Their idolatry expressed hostility toward God, but its consequences would fall upon themselves.
They would discover there was no escape from his judgment.
God's wrath is like an unquenchable fire.

div.title: The Lord required attentive obedience (verses 21–28)
div.p: God demonstrated that what he required from them was obedience.
His command was to listen carefully to the voice of the Lord their God.
The promise attached to that command was full of encouragement.
Let God's will be our rule, and let his favor be our happiness.
The people's disobedience displeased him.
We misunderstand the gospel as badly as those Israelites misunderstood the law if we imagine that even Christ's sacrifice reduces our obligation to obey God.

div.title: Judgment comes upon a polluted people (verses 29–34)
div.p: Jerusalem would be brought low, in token of both sorrow and slavery.
The city once set apart to the Lord would now be separated from him.
The human heart is the place where God has chosen to put his name.
But when sin holds the highest and deepest place within it, we pollute the Lord's temple.
The approaching destruction of Jerusalem was dreadful.
Many would be killed in the very place they had made a center of wrongdoing.
Evil pursues sinners even beyond death.
People unwilling to abandon empty pleasures through God's grace may have every pleasure taken away through his judgment.
How many people ruin their health and possessions without complaint while serving Satan!
May we learn to enjoy holy joys and hold every other pleasure lightly, even those that are lawful.

row.cell: The remains of the dead exposed.
The stupidity of the people, compared with the instinct of the brute creation.
The alarm of the invasion, and lamentation.

div.title: Even the dead are dishonored (verses 1–3)
div.p: No real injury can be inflicted upon a body after death.
Nevertheless, dishonoring the remains of wicked people may alarm those still alive.
It reminds us that God's justice and punishment extend beyond the grave.
Whatever happens to us in this life, let us humble ourselves before the Lord and ask him for mercy.

div.title: Judah ignores reason, conscience, Providence and Scripture (verses 4–13)
div.p: What brought this disaster upon the people?
Henry identifies four causes.

First, they refused to listen to reason. They would not exercise ordinary prudence concerning the eternal welfare of their own souls. Sin is a falling back—from the road to life toward the road to destruction.
Second, they refused to listen to conscience. They would not take the first step of genuine repentance: asking seriously what wrong they had done, convinced that they had acted wrongly.

Third, they failed to consider God's Providence and recognize his voice within it (Jeremiah 8:7). They did not use the seasons of grace he gave them. Many boast of religious knowledge, yet without the teaching of God's Spirit, even the natural instinct of birds and other creatures guides them more reliably than their supposed wisdom.

Fourth, they refused to attend to the written word of God. Many people possess ample opportunities to learn: Bibles, ministers and other means of grace. Yet they have all these resources without truly benefiting from them.
They would soon be ashamed of their own schemes.
The people posing as especially wise were the priests and false prophets.
Those leaders flattered others in their sins until the flattery led toward destruction.
They quieted fear and silenced complaints with the assurance, “Everything is well.”
Self-interested teachers promise peace when there is no peace.
Thus sinners encourage one another to continue in wrongdoing.
But when the day of judgment comes, they will find nowhere to hide.

div.title: There is healing in Christ, but the people refuse it (verses 14–22)
div.p: At last the people began to recognize God's hand raised against them.
When God himself confronts us, everything opposing us becomes frightening.
Because salvation is found only in the Lord, we should make use of the present opportunity.
Is there no medicine to heal this sick and dying nation?
Is there no skilled and faithful physician able to apply it?

p.hi: Yes. God can help and heal.

div.p: If sinners die from their wounds, they bear responsibility for rejecting the remedy.

p.hi: The blood of Jesus Christ is the balm of Gilead.

div.p: His Spirit is the Physician there, completely sufficient to heal.
The people could be healed, but would not receive the cure.
So sinners die unforgiven and unchanged, because they refuse to come to Christ for salvation.

row.cell: The people are corrected, Jerusalem is destroyed.
The captives suffer in a foreign land.
God's loving-kindness, He threatens the enemies of his people.

div.title: Jeremiah mourns the people's corruption (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jeremiah wept much. Yet he wished he could weep even more, hoping to awaken the people to a proper awareness of God's hand in their troubles.
Even withdrawing into the desert cannot remove temptation or sin.
Without communion with God through Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit's influence, the wilderness would still be a place of evil.
With these blessings, however, we can live holy lives even in crowded cities.
The people had trained their tongues to lie. They had become so untrustworthy that even a brother could not trust his brother.
In trade and negotiation, they said whatever would serve their interests, even when they knew it was false.

p.hi: God noticed every falsehood.

div.p: What good can be expected where there is no knowledge of God?
He has many ways of turning a fertile land into a barren place because of the wickedness of its inhabitants.

div.title: Death reaches every place (verses 12–22)
div.p: When the people had remained near God, Zion had heard the sounds of joy and praise.
Now their sin had changed those sounds into mourning.
People whose hearts are not humbled may grieve deeply over their suffering while refusing to grieve over the sin that caused it.
No door can be closed so tightly that death cannot enter.
It reaches even the palaces of rulers and great people, no matter how beautifully built, strongly defended or carefully guarded.
And those outside their homes are no safer.
Death takes children in the open spaces and young men from the streets.
Listen to the Lord's word and mourn with godly sorrow.
That kind of sorrow alone brings true comfort.
Through it, even the heaviest suffering can become an instrument of precious mercy.

div.title: True boasting is knowing the Lord (verses 23–26)
div.p: We live in a world filled with sin and sorrow, and earthly life will soon end in death and judgment.
How foolish it is to boast of our knowledge, health, strength or wealth when these things do not free us from sin's dominion and God's judgment!
Indeed, we will have to account for the way we used those advantages, and they may increase our guilt.
The true Israel consists of people who worship God in the Spirit, rejoice in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh.
Let us prize the distinction given by God, which endures forever.
And let us seek it diligently.

div.title: The Lord alone is God (verses 1–16)
div.p: The prophet displays the glory of Israel's God and exposes the foolishness of worshiping idols.
Charms and other attempts to gain supernatural help or discover what will happen in the future copy the wicked customs of pagan nations.
Let us stand in reverence before the Lord.
We must not provoke him by giving another being the glory that belongs to him alone.
Yet he is ready to forgive and save everyone who repents and believes in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ.
Faith learns these blessed truths from God's word.
Knowledge claimed apart from that source, when used as an alternative authority concerning God and salvation, leads to empty and worthless doctrines.

div.title: The coming destruction and the prophet's prayer (verses 17–25)
div.p: The Jews who still lived in their own land felt secure.
But sooner or later sinners will discover that everything God has said is true, including the warnings they dismissed as mere threats.
Submission to God sustains a believer through whatever sorrow he appoints.
But what can make the burden of his judgment bearable for someone who meets it with stubborn despair?
People cannot expect to prosper if they fail to take God with them through faith and prayer in every part of life.
The news of the approaching enemy was terrifying.
Yet human plans, however deeply considered and skillfully arranged, can be shattered in a moment.
Events often turn out exactly contrary to what we intended or expected.
If the Lord has guided our feet into the paths of peace and righteousness, we should ask him to enable us to continue walking in those paths.
Do not pray, “Lord, never correct me.”
Pray instead, “Lord, do not correct me in anger.”
We may bear the pain of God's correcting rod, but we cannot bear the weight of his wrath.
Those who restrain themselves from prayer reveal that they do not know God as they should.
People who know him seek him and seek his favor.
Even severe correction can become a cause for deep gratitude when it convinces sinners of truths that bring healing.
They will then humble themselves before the Lord.

row.cell: The people would be destroyed who sought the prophet's life.

div.title: God requires obedience to his covenant (verses 1–10)
div.p: God has never promised to bless rational creatures while they deliberately continue in disobedience.
Pardon and acceptance are freely promised to everyone who believes.
But no one can be saved while refusing God's command to repent, believe in Christ, separate from sin and the world, deny self and walk in newness of life.
People readily listen when speakers describe doctrines, promises and privileges.
Yet when the subject turns to duty, they often refuse to hear.

div.title: Idolatry cannot protect a nation from judgment (verses 11–17)
div.p: Evil pursues sinners and entangles them in traps from which they cannot free themselves.
In their distress, their many gods and altars provided no help.
People whose own prayers will not be accepted cannot presume to benefit from someone else's prayers.
A mere profession of religion does no good.
When trouble came, the people had relied on that profession, but God rejected it.
His altar could give them no comfort.
Remembering God's earlier favors toward them would not console them amid judgment.
Nor could those favors be used as a reason why he must rescue them now.
Every sin committed against the Lord is also a sin against ourselves.
Sooner or later its consequences will prove that true.

div.title: Jeremiah is threatened by people from his own town (verses 18–23)
div.p: Jeremiah's book reveals much about his personal suffering.
He lived in deeply troubled times.
Men from his own town secretly planned his death.
They hoped to shorten his life.
But Jeremiah outlived most of his enemies.
They also wanted to destroy his reputation.
Yet his memory has survived until today, and it will continue to be honored as long as time endures.
God knows every secret plan of those who oppose his servants and his people.
When he chooses, he can disclose those plans.
God's justice is a source of terror to wicked people but a comfort to those who trust him.
When others wrong us, we have a God to whom we can entrust our cause.
We should commit the matter to him.
And we must watch our own attitudes, lest evil overcome us.
Through patient prayer for our enemies and kindness toward them, we can overcome evil with good.

row.cell: Jeremiah complains of the prosperity of the wicked.
The heavy judgments to come upon the nation.
Divine mercy to them, and even to the nations around.

div.title: Why do the wicked prosper? (verses 1–6)
div.p: When God's ways are darkest to us, we must continue to think rightly of his character.
He has never acted unjustly toward any creature.
When we cannot understand a particular event affecting ourselves or others, we must return to the general truths we know.

p.hi: The Lord is righteous.

div.p: God knows the condition of every heart.
He sees the deceit of the hypocrite and the sincerity of the upright.
Judgment will eventually pull wicked people out of their prosperous pasture like sheep led to slaughter.
The land became barren because of the sins of those living in it.
The Lord also corrected Jeremiah himself.
The opposition he had encountered at Anathoth was small compared with what awaited him from Judah's rulers.
Our grief over evil in the world is often mixed with irritability about the trouble that evil causes us.
We live in favored times and face comparatively small difficulties.
How would we behave if called to endure what faithful believers in former generations suffered?

div.title: The Lord gives his beloved people over to judgment (verses 7–13)
div.p: God's people had been beloved by him, precious in his sight.
Yet their conduct led him to hand them over to their enemies.
Many professing churches become like speckled birds.
Their lives mix true religious profession with the world's fashions, pursuits and corruptions.
God's people may be a spectacle to others.
But in this case they had made themselves one through their own foolishness, leaving themselves vulnerable to the creatures called to prey upon them.
The whole land would become desolate.
Until judgment actually fell, almost no one would give God's warning serious attention.
When he raises his hand and people refuse to see, they may be made to feel.
Neither silver nor gold helps in the day of divine anger.
Attempts to escape suffering without repentance and deeds appropriate to it will end in confusion.

div.title: Even neighboring nations may receive mercy (verses 14–17)
div.p: The Lord would defend the cause of his people against their wicked neighbors.
But afterward he would show mercy even to those nations, if they learned the true faith.
Henry sees this as possibly looking ahead to the day when the fullness of the Gentiles comes in.
Anyone who wants a share in God's people's inheritance and hopes to reach the same final happiness must learn their ways and walk in them.

row.cell: The glory of the Jews should be marred.
All ranks should suffer misery, An earnest exhortation to repentance.
An awful message to Jerusalem and its king.

div.title: The ruined linen belt (verses 1–11)
div.p: The prophets often taught through visible signs, and here God explains the sign himself (Jeremiah 13:9–11).
Israel had been like the belt that clung closely to its owner.
God had caused the people to cling to him through the law he gave them, the prophets he sent and the blessings he bestowed.
But through idolatry and sin, they had buried themselves in foreign soil and become entangled with other nations.
They were now so corrupted that, like the ruined belt, they were no longer useful.
If we are proud of learning, power or outward privileges, God is just in allowing them to wither.
Our minds need to awaken to guilt and danger.
Yet no warning will truly change us without the Holy Spirit's influence.

div.title: The jars of judgment and a call to repent (verses 12–17)
div.p: Just as jars are made to hold wine, so the people's sins had made them vessels prepared for divine wrath.
They would be filled with judgments until those judgments led them to destroy one another.
Jeremiah begged them to give glory to God by confessing sin, humbling themselves in repentance and returning to his service.
If they refused, they would be carried into foreign lands, still enveloped in the darkness of idolatry and wickedness.
Anyone with a compassionate heart is moved by suffering, whether witnessed or only anticipated.
But a godly heart should grieve especially over the afflictions of the Lord's flock.

div.title: No one can cleanse a sinful nature without God (verses 18–27)
div.p: The message was addressed to King Jehoiakim and his queen.
Their suffering would be great.
Why had it come upon them?
Because they had persisted stubbornly in sin.
People cannot change the natural color of their skin by their own efforts.
Henry uses that biblical image to express how morally impossible it is for unrenewed sinners to reform themselves by their own strength.
Sin is the soul's corruption and disfigurement.
We were formed in it and cannot free ourselves through our own power.
But Almighty grace can accomplish what no human being can.
Neither inherited corruption nor long-established habits of sin can prevent God's Spirit, who creates new life, from transforming a person.
The Lord asks Jerusalem whether she is determined to refuse cleansing.
If someone enslaved by sin feels that changing deeply rooted desires is as impossible as changing human nature, that person should not despair.
What is impossible for human beings is possible with God.
Let us seek help from the One mighty to save.

row.cell: A drought upon the land of Judah.
A confession of sin in the name of the people.
The Divine purpose to punish is declared.

div.title: Drought and prayerful confession (verses 1–9)
div.p: The people wept, but theirs was more a cry over distress and sin than the cry of genuine prayer.
Let us be thankful for water before its absence teaches us how precious it is.
Farmers depend completely on God's Providence: unless he waters their furrows, they cannot plow and sow with confidence.
Even wild animals suffered pitiably under the drought.
The people were slow to pray, but Jeremiah prayed for them and humbly confessed their sin.
Our sins both accuse us and testify against us.
The strongest arguments in our prayers are those drawn from the glory of God's own name.
We should dread his departure more than the loss of any created comfort.
God had given Israel his word on which to hope.
In prayer, his glory should concern us more than our immediate relief.
If we return to the Lord, he will save us to the glory of his grace.

div.title: False prophets and their hearers face judgment (verses 10–16)
div.p: The Lord called the Jews “this people” rather than “my people.” They had abandoned his service; he would judge them according to their sins.
God forbade Jeremiah to intercede for them.
The false prophets were most guilty, and the Lord pronounced judgment upon them.
But the people themselves wanted to hear their false assurances, so they too would face judgment.
False teachers lead people to expect peace and salvation without repentance, faith, conversion or holiness of life.
Anyone who willingly believes a lie cannot offer deception as an excuse.
People who reject the warning will experience the very judgment they were told not to fear.

div.title: The prophet pleads for the covenant and mercy (verses 17–22)
div.p: Jeremiah confessed his own sins and the people's sins, appealing to the Lord's covenant.
No Gentile idol could help them.
Even the heavens could not give rain by themselves without their Creator.
God will always preserve people who plead before his mercy seat.
He will heal every genuinely repentant sinner.
Even when God does not grant the national relief for which we pray, he will certainly bless with salvation everyone who confesses sin and seeks his mercy.

row.cell: The destruction of the wicked described.
The prophet laments such messages, and is reproved.
He supplicates pardon, and is promised protection.

div.title: Even great intercessors could not avert judgment (verses 1–9)
div.p: Even if Moses and Samuel stood before God to plead for the people, they would not prevail.
Henry emphasizes that this is a hypothetical example, not a statement that the prophets actually stand praying in heaven.
He argues on that basis against the belief that saints in heaven pray for those on earth.
The Jews would suffer different kinds of misery under the Lord's righteous judgment.
Survivors would be driven into captivity like chaff scattered from grain.
The city once filled with people would become desolate.
Bad examples and the misuse of authority can have deadly consequences even after people die or repent of their crimes.
We should fear causing another person to fall into sin.

div.title: The prophet is despised, but God's plan stands (verses 10–14)
div.p: Jeremiah received reproach when people should have blessed him and thanked God for giving them his ministry.
Whatever difficulties God's people face, they may find sufficient strength in knowing their latter end will be good.
The Lord then confronted the nation.
Could all its strength resist his decree or stop the army of the Chaldeans?
The enemy would treat Jeremiah kindly while those with large estates would suffer severely.
Every part of the country had contributed to national guilt, and each must take its share of shame.

div.title: The Lord calls Jeremiah away from distrust (verses 15–21)
div.p: It is comforting to have a God whose knowledge embraces everything.
Jeremiah appealed to him for protection against his enemies, persecutors and slanderers.
When a minister is despised, a clear conscience can still provide encouragement.
Yet Jeremiah complained that he had gained little pleasure from his service.
Even good people can lose much of religion's joy when they indulge a fretful and restless natural disposition.
God called the prophet to abandon distrust and return to his task.
If he remained faithful, the Lord would deliver him from his enemies.
Those who stay close to God and serve him sincerely will be rescued from trouble or carried safely through it.
Many events appear frightening though they can do no final harm to a true believer in Christ.

row.cell: The justice of God in these judgments.
Future restoration of the Jews, and the conversion of the Gentiles.

div.title: Jeremiah lives in expectation of the nation's ruin (verses 1–9)
div.p: The prophet was to behave as a person expecting the destruction of his country very soon.
Because distressing days lay ahead, God told him to refrain from marriage, customary mourning for the dead and celebration.
Those wanting others to believe God's word must show through personal self-denial that they believe it themselves.
All peace—inward and outward, within the family and among the public—comes from the Lord's kindness and mercy.
When he removes peace, distress follows.
In certain extraordinary circumstances it may be right to abstain from acts that are normally our duty.
We should never cling tightly to the pleasures and concerns of this passing life.

div.title: The judgment is just (verses 10–13)
div.p: The people's response seems to have been a complaint against God.
Rather than humbling themselves and admitting sin, they justified themselves, as though the Lord had treated them unjustly.
But God answered plainly.
They were more stubborn than their ancestors.
Each one walked according to the plans of his or her own heart.
Since they refused to listen, they would be taken to an unfamiliar country.
If they had enjoyed God's favor, even the land of captivity could have been pleasant.

div.title: Restoration will foreshadow salvation through Christ (verses 14–21)
div.p: The rescue from Babylon would be remembered instead of the original exodus from Egypt.
It would also picture spiritual redemption and what Henry describes as a later deliverance of the church from antichristian oppression.
No sin can be hidden from God or overlooked by him.
He can send instruments of judgment like fishermen who use deception or hunters who pursue with force.
But Jeremiah, rejoicing in the promised mercy, addressed the Lord as his strength and refuge.
The return from captivity would be a picture of the far greater salvation accomplished by the Messiah.
The nations had often seen God's power in his anger.
They would also recognize him as the strength of his people and their refuge in times of trouble.

row.cell: The fatal consequences of the idolatry of the Jews.
The happiness of the man that trusts in God; the end of the opposite character.
The malice of the prophet's enemies.

div.title: Sin written on the heart (verses 1–4)
div.p: People often scarcely notice the sins they commit.
Yet every sin is recorded before God, and all are so engraved upon the human heart that conscience will eventually recall them.
What is engraved in the heart becomes visible in a person's conduct.
Our actions reveal the desires and purposes within us.
How much reason we have to humble ourselves before the Lord when we consider our sinfulness in his sight!
Let us depend upon his mercy and grace.
Ask him to search and test our hearts, keep us from being deceived by them and create in us, through his Spirit, a new, clean and holy nature.

div.title: The desert shrub and the fruitful tree (verses 5–11)
div.p: Someone who trusts in human beings is like a lonely shrub in a desert—the poor and useless product of barren land.
People who depend on their own righteousness and strength, imagining they can do without Christ, have made human flesh their support.
They cannot prosper in spiritual grace or comfort.
But those who make God their hope flourish like an evergreen tree.
They remain settled in peace and contentment, with no need for panic in a year of drought.
God supplies every comfort they truly need, even when created comforts are absent.
They do not stop bearing the fruit of holiness and good works.
The heart and conscience of fallen humanity are more deceitful than anything else.
They call evil good and good evil.
They pronounce peace upon people who have no true peace.
This is how desperate its corruption is.
Conscience should correct the errors of our other faculties.
But when conscience itself becomes the leader in self-deception, our situation is especially serious.
We cannot fully know our hearts or how they will behave in a sudden temptation.

p.hi: Who can understand their own errors?

div.p: Still less can we fully know or safely depend on other people's hearts.
Anyone accepting God's testimony about this will learn to watch the heart and will recognize many useful lessons for conduct.
Much about our own motives and those of others will remain unknown to us.
But nothing within us is hidden from God.
People may be deceived.
He cannot be deceived.
Those who acquire wealth dishonestly will not truly enjoy it.
At death the worldly person must leave possessions behind.
The wealth cannot follow into eternity, but its guilt can.
Someone may spend a whole life acquiring wealth, brood over it anxiously and never receive satisfaction.
Sinful gain may disappear altogether.
Let us become wise in time: earn honestly and give generously, so that we may be prepared for eternity.

div.title: The Lord is a fountain of comfort (verses 12–18)
div.p: Jeremiah acknowledged God's goodness in establishing true worship.
The Lord is an overflowing fountain of comfort, forever fresh and clear like springwater.
The sinful world's pleasures resemble muddy puddles.
The prophet asked for the Lord's healing and saving mercy.
He appealed to God as the One who knew how faithfully he had fulfilled his prophetic calling.
He humbly asked the Lord to acknowledge and defend him in the service to which he had called him.
Whatever wounds or diseases afflict our hearts and consciences, let us seek healing from God.
His hands can bind up troubled consciences and heal broken hearts.
He can cure the deepest corruption of our nature, giving us reason to praise his name.

div.title: Keep the Sabbath holy (verses 19–27)
div.p: Jeremiah had to set before both rulers and ordinary people the command to keep the Sabbath day holy.
They were to obey the fourth commandment.
God promised renewed prosperity if they obeyed.
The Sabbath is appointed for rest, not ordinary labor, except when necessity requires work.
We should watch carefully against treating the day as common.
Even our souls should not be weighed down with worldly business and anxieties on the Sabbath.
Henry compares religious life to a river: the stream runs deep or shallow according to whether the banks of Sabbath observance are maintained or neglected.
The care with which a people observe this ordinance, or the indifference they show toward it, reveals much about their spiritual condition.
Everyone should work through personal example and attention to family life to prevent its neglect.
National good matters, but even more important is the salvation of souls.

row.cell: God's power over his creatures is represented by the potter.
The Jews exhorted to repentance, and judgments foretold.

div.title: The potter, the clay and God's righteous rule (verses 1–10)
div.p: As Jeremiah watched the potter at work, God impressed two great truths upon his mind.
First, the Lord possesses the authority and power to shape and dispose of kingdoms and nations as he chooses.
He may deal with us according to his wisdom.
For clay to argue with the potter would be absurd—and so is our disputing against God's right to rule.
Second, God always acts according to settled principles of goodness and justice.
When judgment is approaching, we may be sure that sin has brought it upon us.
But sincere conversion and turning away from sin can prevent the threatened judgment—whether for individuals, families or nations.

div.title: Sinful liberty is the worst slavery (verses 11–17)
div.p: Sinners call unrestrained living freedom.
Yet slavery to sinful desires is the most dreadful form of slavery.
Judah had abandoned God for idols.
A thirsty person who reaches a cool and refreshing stream would not ordinarily abandon that reliable water for an uncertain supply elsewhere.
But Israel abandoned the ancient paths established by God's law.
Instead of walking along the safe highway, the people chose a path where they were bound to stumble.
Such is the way of idolatry and wrongdoing.
It left them miserable and their land desolate.
Earthly troubles can be endured if God continues to favor us through them.
But if he is displeased and refuses his help, we are undone.
Multitudes turn from the Lord and his Christ and leave the ancient paths to follow religious ways invented by themselves.
What will they do on the day of judgment?

div.title: Jeremiah's enemies plot against him (verses 18–23)
div.p: When Jeremiah called the people to repent, they plotted against him instead of obeying.
Sinners treat the great Intercessor in a similar way.
They speak against Christ and in that sense crucify him afresh, even while his blood pleads on their behalf in heaven.
But the prophet had performed the duty God gave him toward the people.
That consciousness of duty would be a source of rejoicing in a time of trouble.

p.hi: By the type of breaking an earthen vessel, Jeremiah is to predict the destruction of Judah.

div.title: The coming ruin of Jerusalem (verses 1–9)
div.p: Jeremiah had to announce the destruction approaching Judah and Jerusalem.
Rulers and ordinary people alike needed to hear this message.
Jerusalem's holiness had once made it the joy of the whole earth.
But sin had made the city a place of shame and disgrace before the whole earth.
There is only one way to escape God's justice:

p.hi: Flee to his mercy.

div.title: The shattered earthen vessel (verses 10–15)
div.p: Once a potter's earthen vessel has hardened and been broken into pieces, no one can fit it together again as before.
So Judah and Jerusalem would be shattered by the Chaldeans, just as Jeremiah broke the vessel.
No human hand could repair the destruction.
Yet if the people returned to the Lord, he could heal them.
The people had filled Topheth with people slaughtered in sacrifices to idols.
Therefore the Lord would fill the city with those killed as a judgment upon their sin.
Whatever human beings imagine, God will prove as terrible toward unrepentant wrongdoing as Scripture has said.
Unbelief cannot make either his promises or his warnings ineffective.
Sinners are responsible for their own stubbornness.
If they refuse to hear God's word, it is because they have deliberately closed their ears.
We must pray that God's grace will rescue us from hardness of heart and contempt for his word and commandments.

row.cell: The doom of Pashur, who ill-treated the prophet.
He regrets his ever having been born.

div.title: Pashhur becomes an object of terror (verses 1–6)
div.p: Pashhur struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks.
The prophet remained silent until God gave him a message.
To confirm that message, Pashhur received the name “Terror on every side.”
It describes a person not simply suffering but despairing, not merely surrounded by danger but terrified on every side.
Wicked people may experience dreadful fear even where no genuine danger appears.
God can make even the boldest sinner a terror to himself.
People who refuse to hear God's prophets expose their faults may later be forced to hear those same accusations from their own consciences.
How miserable is someone whose conscience has made that person a constant terror!
Friends may abandon such a person.
God may leave a sinner alive in deep misery as a visible reminder of his justice.

div.title: The Lord strengthens Jeremiah to keep serving (verses 7–13)
div.p: Jeremiah complained about the insults and injuries he endured.
But Henry notes a possible reading of verse 7:

p.hi: “You persuaded me, and I was persuaded; you were stronger than I and overcame me by the influence of your Spirit.”

div.p: When we know that we are following the path of duty God has given us, we act weakly and foolishly if discouragement makes us wish we had never begun the work.
Jeremiah discovered that divine grace was powerful enough to keep him serving despite the temptation to abandon his calling.
Whatever wrongs others do to us, we must entrust judgment to the God who says, “I will repay.”
The prophet became deeply conscious of God's presence, his protection and the promises upon which he relied.
He therefore urged himself and others to glorify the Lord.
When God's people lay their concerns openly before him, he enables them to see his deliverance.

div.title: Jeremiah laments the day of his birth (verses 14–18)
div.p: When grace wins a victory over temptation, it is right to feel ashamed of our foolishness and to marvel at God's kindness.
We should also be warned to guard our minds more carefully when another trial comes.
See how powerful a temptation Jeremiah faced—and how God's help enabled him to overcome it!
In his bitterness, Jeremiah became angry that his first breath had not been his last.
These lamentations were recorded not to teach us to repeat the same wishes, but to give us needed warnings.
People who think they stand securely must take care lest they fall.
We should pray daily:

p.hi: “Lead us not into temptation.”

div.p: How frail, inconsistent and sinful we are!
How foolish and unnatural our wishes become when discontent rules our hearts!
Consider Jesus Christ, who endured the opposition of sinners against himself, so that we will not become weary or fainthearted during our much smaller trials.

row.cell: The only way of deliverance is to be surrendering to the Babylonians.
The wickedness of the king and his household.

div.title: Surrender is the only path to survival (verses 1–10)
div.p: After the siege began, King Zedekiah sent messengers to ask Jeremiah how the conflict would end.
During danger and distress, people often seek the advice and prayers of those they normally despise and oppose.
Yet often they want only to escape the punishment of their sin, without giving up the sin itself.
Those who profess religion but persist in disobedience must not suppose their outward privileges will protect them.
The Lord may grant success even to open enemies when they are sent in judgment against his disobedient people.
The king and his officials would not surrender, but the prophet urged the people to surrender in order to preserve their lives.
No sinner on earth who truly wants a refuge has been left without one.
But the road of life is humbling.
It requires self-denial and may expose the traveler to real difficulties.

div.title: The household of David is urged to practice justice (verses 11–14)
div.p: The sin of the king and his family was especially serious because of their connection with David.
They were called to do justice immediately, before the Lord's anger burned beyond restraint.

p.hi: If God is for us, who can stand against us?

div.p: But if God is against us, who can possibly help us?

row.cell: Justice is recommended, and destruction threatened in case of disobedience.
The captivity of Jehoiakim, and the end of Jeconiah.
The doom of the royal family.

div.title: Royal authority must be exercised justly (verses 1–9)
div.p: The king of Judah sat on David's throne, and David had been a man after God's heart.
The king should have followed David's example so that he could share the benefit of the promises made to that family.
The surest way to preserve a government is for its rulers to perform the duties of government.
But sin destroys the households of princes as readily as those of ordinary people.
Who can resist destroyers whom God has appointed?
God destroys neither people, cities nor nations without the cause of sin.
Often even in this life he makes clear the wrongs for which he sends punishment.
At the final judgment, those reasons will be completely evident.

div.title: The sons of Josiah reject their father's example (verses 10–19)
div.p: The passage announces a sentence of death over two kings, wicked sons of a deeply godly father.
Josiah was spared the sight of the approaching calamity.
He was taken from this life to behold the good of the world to come.
Therefore the people had greater reason to weep for Shallum, who would live and die as a miserable captive, than for their father.
The death of a faithful believer may be cause for hope, while the continued life of an unrepentant person may rightly call forth pity.
The prophecy also announces the fate of Jehoiakim.
It is lawful for rulers and great people to build, improve and furnish their houses.
But those who make their homes grander must guard against vanity and pride.
Jehoiakim built through injustice.
His money had been acquired wrongfully, and he refused to pay his workers their wages.
God sees the wrong powerful people do to servants and laborers, and will repay in justice those who have refused to pay others what justice demands.
Even the most powerful person must regard the poorest person as a neighbor owed fairness.
Jehoiakim also shed innocent blood.
Greed, the root of every kind of evil, lay beneath his wickedness.
Children who dismiss the old ways of their parents often miss the true excellence beneath those customs.
Jehoiakim knew his father had found obedience to be a path of comfort, yet refused to follow him.
He would die without mourning, having become hated for oppression and cruelty.

div.title: The royal family's confidence collapses (verses 20–30)
div.p: Judah's condition had three distinct stages.
First, the people were arrogant during peace and security.
Then they became fearful when trouble was announced.
Finally, they were utterly crushed under the weight of disaster.
Many people feel no real shame over sin until it has brought them into the most desperate circumstances.
The king would end his days in captivity.
Those imagining themselves to be like signet rings upon God's right hand should not presume they can never be removed.
The king and his family would be transported to Babylon.
We know where we were born, but we do not know where we will die.
God knows both.
Our responsibility is to make sure that we die in Christ.
Then it will be well with us wherever death comes, even far from home.
The king who had once been admired would become despised.
People in whom God takes no pleasure may eventually become a disappointment to everyone else too.
If someone has no children, God has permitted that condition; a person who spends the available years without doing good cannot expect to prosper.
How little we should depend on royal splendor or flourishing families!
But those who hear Christ's voice and follow him possess eternal life.
They will never perish, and no enemy can tear them from his almighty hands.

row.cell: The restoration of the Jews to their own land.
The wickedness of the priests and prophets of Judah, The people exhorted not to listen to false promises.
Also the scoffers at true prophecy.

div.title: Christ, the righteous Branch and faithful Shepherd (verses 1–8)
div.p: Woe to people appointed to feed God's flock who refuse to care about the sheep's welfare!
Yet the neglected flock receives a promise of comfort.
Even if only a remnant remains, God will find his scattered sheep and bring them home.
Jesus Christ is the Branch from David's family.
He is righteous himself, and through him all his people become righteous.
He breaks Satan's illegitimate power.
The spiritual descendants of believing Abraham and praying Jacob will be rescued from the guilt and dominion of sin.
When Christ rules within a human soul, that soul lives in safety.
His name is “The LORD Our Righteousness.”
He is our righteousness in a way no created being could ever be.
His obedience unto death is the righteousness that justifies believers and gives them the right to heavenly happiness.
Our sanctification, which becomes the source of our own obedience, comes from our union with Christ and the Holy Spirit he supplies.
Every genuine believer can call upon Christ by this precious name.
We have nothing to plead except that Christ died and rose again, and that we have received him as our Lord.
The righteousness he achieved to satisfy God's law and justice is freely given to us.
Through the Holy Spirit, we are clothed in that righteousness, enabled to take hold of it and assured of our share in it.
“The LORD Our Righteousness” is a wonderfully comforting name for someone convicted of sin, conscious of guilt and aware of the need for a righteousness not their own.
This salvation surpasses every former rescue God gave his church.
May we be gathered to Christ and found in him.

div.title: False prophets make people confident in sin (verses 9–22)
div.p: The false prophets of Samaria misled Israel into idolatry.
But the Lord judged the prophets of Jerusalem to have practiced even worse wickedness, making others bold in sin.
These teachers would suffer bitter judgment.
They first persuaded themselves that wrongdoing was harmless and acted on that belief.
Then they persuaded others to accept it.
People determined to persist in evil may be given over to strong delusions.
What divine revelation had these teachers actually received?
What had they understood of God's word?
Eventually they would look back on their folly and unbelief with remorse.
True prophets' instruction and conduct lead people toward repentance, faith and righteousness.
False prophets encourage people to rest in religious forms and opinions while remaining undisturbed in sin.
Let us be careful not to follow unrighteousness.

div.title: False dreams are not God's word (verses 23–32)
div.p: No one can hide from the God who sees everything.
Why do false prophets fail to see the judgment their words are bringing upon themselves?
Consider the vast difference between their utterances and the prophecies of God's true messengers.
Their dreams must not be described as divine revelations.
Promises of peace invented by those teachers compare to God's promises as chaff compares to wheat.
The heart of a person who has not been humbled resembles a rock.
If the word of God does not melt it like fire, the word may break it like a hammer.
Who could remain safe or peaceful with almighty God against them?
His word is not a smooth, soothing or deceitful message intended to lull sinners to sleep.
Its faithfulness to truth distinguishes it from false doctrine.

div.title: Mocking prophecy cannot cancel judgment (verses 33–40)
div.p: How miserable are people forsaken and forgotten by God!
Mocking the Lord's judgments does not make them fail.
God had once taken Israel as a people close to himself.
Now they would be cast out of his presence.
It is a sign of extreme irreverence to treat God's own words as a joke.
Every idle and profane word increases the guilt sinners must answer for at judgment.
If they remain unrepentant, everlasting disgrace awaits them.

p.hi: Good and bad figs represent the Jews in captivity, and those who remain in their own land.

div.title: Two baskets of figs
