div.p: Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs set before the temple as first-fruit offerings.
The figs in one basket were very good.
Those in the other were very bad.
What creature is more degraded than someone who persists in wickedness?
And who is more valuable than a truly godly person?
This vision was intended to encourage those already in exile, assuring them that they would have a happy return.
It also warned and humbled the proud people who remained in Jerusalem, telling them that they would experience miserable captivity.
The good figs represent the faithful captives.
We cannot determine God's love or hatred simply from the outward circumstances before us.
Sometimes early suffering proves to be for the best.
When a child receives correction promptly, the correction may have a better effect.
The exile itself was intended for the people's good.
God's good purposes never fail.
Affliction convinced them of sin, humbled them under his hand, loosened their attachment to the world, taught them to pray and led them away from sin—especially from idolatry.
God promised to acknowledge these people as his own even in captivity.
The Lord recognizes everyone who truly belongs to him, whatever their outward condition.
He promised to protect them during trouble and to bring them to a glorious deliverance at the proper time.
When suffering is sanctified to us, we can trust that it will end for our good.
The people would return to God with their whole hearts.
Then they could once again acknowledge him as their God, pray to him and hope for his blessings.
The bad figs represented Zedekiah and his party who remained in the land.
They would be removed for their harm and become despised among nations.
God possesses many kinds of judgment.
People who escape one may still meet another, until they are brought to repentance.
The prophecy certainly found fulfillment in Jeremiah's time.
But Henry adds that the Spirit of prophecy may also have been looking ahead to the later scattering of unbelieving Jews among the nations.
Those who desire blessing from God should ask him to give them a heart that truly knows him.

row.cell: The Jews rebuked for not obeying calls to repentance.
Their captivity during seventy years is expressly foretold.
Desolations upon the nations shown by the emblem of a cup of wrath.

div.title: The people reject repeated calls to repent (verses 1–7)
div.p: God calls sinners everywhere to abandon their evil ways, return to his worship and service, trust in Christ and share in his salvation.
The Lord takes account of how long we have possessed the means of grace.
The longer we enjoy those opportunities without making good use of them, the heavier our responsibility becomes.
The prophets' practice of rising early to call the people reveals God's earnest desire that sinners turn from their ways and live.
A nation cannot truly be rescued while its inhabitants refuse personal reform.
Every person must turn from their own evil way.
Yet the people would not listen.
They refused the only right way to turn away God's anger.

div.title: Seventy years of captivity and the judgment of Babylon (verses 8–14)
div.p: God announced exactly how long the Jewish exile would last: seventy years.
That definite period confirmed the prophecy and also comforted believers, encouraging them to pray and trust.
Babylon's ruin was also foretold.
When the instrument God used to correct his people had completed its work, the rod itself would be thrown into the fire.
When the appointed time came to favor Zion, Babylon would be judged for its own sins, just as other nations had been judged.
Every warning in Scripture will be fulfilled.

div.title: The nations drink the cup of judgment (verses 15–29)
div.p: Scripture often represents life's blessings and calamities as cups.
The cup in this chapter pictures the coming destruction of many nations.
Nebuchadnezzar had just begun his reign and campaigns and would be the instrument.
But the destroying sword would ultimately act under God's authority.
The disorder the sword would bring upon these kingdoms is compared to the effects of excessive drinking.
This comparison should increase our hatred of drunkenness.
It deprives people of reason, can make them behave like mad people, and steals the precious gift of health.
Drunkenness is also a sin that punishes itself.
The image should also teach us to fear war.
War can quickly fill an entire country with confusion.
The nations would refuse to accept Jeremiah's warning.
But he was to tell them that the Lord of Hosts had spoken.
Resistance to almighty power would be useless.
If God's judgment begins with people who have professed faith and then turned away, unrepentant wicked people cannot expect to escape.

div.title: God's controversy with all nations (verses 30–38)
div.p: The Lord has righteous grounds of complaint against every nation and every human being.
He will judge all the wicked.
Who could avoid trembling when he speaks in displeasure?
The appointed time had arrived—the time fixed in God's own counsel for bringing desolation upon the nations.
Even the gentle and delicate would share the common distress.
People who had lived peaceably and done nothing to provoke war would still suffer its effects.
But blessed be God: there is a peaceful dwelling above for everyone who belongs to the Lord's peace.
He will preserve his church and every believer through all changes, for nothing can separate them from his love.

row.cell: The destruction of the temple and city foretold.
He is defended by the elders.

div.title: God's messenger must speak without fear (verses 1–6)
div.p: People sent to speak on God's behalf must not shape their message to please human beings or merely to protect themselves from harm.
Notice how patiently God waits for an opportunity to show mercy.
If the people continued refusing obedience, Jerusalem and its temple would be ruined.
What else could they expect?
People unwilling to submit to God's commands make themselves subject to his judgment.

div.title: Jeremiah is accused and threatened (verses 7–15)
div.p: The priests and prophets accused Jeremiah of deserving death and gave false testimony against him.
The leaders of Israel came to investigate.
Jeremiah explained that the Lord had sent him to deliver this warning.
Ministers who remain faithful to the word they have received from God need not be ruled by fear.
It is deeply unjust to blame a minister simply for preaching judgment and condemnation, when the purpose is to lead hearers toward heaven and salvation.
Jeremiah warned the people that killing or injuring him would bring still more guilt upon them.
Anyone who harms, kills or hates a faithful person who corrects wrongdoing hastens and increases their own judgment.

div.title: The elders defend the prophet (verses 16–24)
div.p: God's word gives sufficient reason to warn secure sinners that continuing in sin may lead to the removal of the Spirit's gracious work and the privileges of God's kingdom.
Consider the contrasting examples.
Hezekiah protected Micah and prospered.
Jehoiakim killed Urijah. Did he prosper?
Evil people's behavior and the consequences of their actions should deter us from following them.
Urijah faithfully proclaimed the message given to him.
But Henry judges that he acted wrongly by abandoning his appointed work.
The Lord permitted Urijah to die, while Jeremiah was protected amid danger.
Those who rely most simply upon the Lord are safest in the truest sense, regardless of outward circumstances.
Knowing that all human hearts are in God's hands encourages believers to trust him while fulfilling their duties.
He will honor and reward those who treat kindly people persecuted for his sake.

row.cell: The neighbouring nations to be subdued.
The vessels of the temple to be carried to Babylon, but afterwards to be restored.

div.title: The nations are told to accept Babylon's rule (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jeremiah had to prepare a symbolic sign announcing that the surrounding countries would become subjects of the king of Babylon.
God asserted his authority to distribute kingdoms according to his will.
Every earthly possession is a gift the Lord has chosen to permit.
We should therefore be content with our portion.
The things of this world cannot be the highest good.
God sometimes grants the largest share of worldly power or wealth to people who are wicked.
Earthly authority does not prove saving grace.
People refusing to serve the God who made them may be justly compelled to serve enemies seeking their destruction.
Jeremiah urged them to preserve their lives by submitting rather than resisting.
A meek spirit can accept even the hardest turns of Providence and make the best of a painful situation.
Many people avoid devastating judgments by submitting to humbling circumstances.
It is better to carry a lighter cross God has placed in our way than draw a heavier one upon ourselves.
The poor in spirit, meek and humble find comfort and escape many miseries that people of a proud and defiant temperament bring upon themselves.
Obeying God's will is always in our true interest.

div.title: Zedekiah must submit to the king of Babylon (verses 12–18)
div.p: Jeremiah appealed to King Zedekiah to surrender to Babylon.
Consider the comparison.
It was wise for Judah to accept the heavy and oppressive yoke of a cruel earthly ruler if that submission would preserve their lives.
How much wiser is it to accept the pleasant and gentle yoke of our Lord and Master Jesus Christ, securing the eternal welfare of our souls?
Sinners should fear the judgment awaiting those who refuse to let Christ reign over them.
Why should anyone suffer the second death, far worse than being killed by sword or famine, when submission to the Savior brings life?
Those who encourage sinners to continue in wrongdoing will perish with them.

div.title: Sacred vessels are taken away but will return (verses 19–22)
div.p: Jeremiah announced that the bronze furnishings of the temple would be carried away after the golden ones.
Everything would be transported to Babylon.
Yet the prophecy ended in a promise of mercy.
The time would come when the vessels would be brought back.
The church's prosperity may not return during our own lifetime.
But we must not despair.
God's appointed time will come.

row.cell: The false prophet warned of his approaching death.

div.title: Hananiah promises peace without repentance (verses 1–9)
div.p: Hananiah delivered a false prophecy.
His speech offered not one word urging Judah to repent or return to God.
He promised earthly blessings in God's name, but said nothing about the spiritual blessings God had always connected with his promises.
Jeremiah had often prayed for the nation, even while announcing judgment against it.
He appealed to what would actually happen as the test exposing Hananiah's falsehood.
A prophet who promises only peace and prosperity, without warning that deliberate sin cuts people off from God's favor, will prove to be a false prophet.
Anyone who refuses to proclaim the alarming as well as the encouraging parts of God's word—and fails to call people to repentance, faith and holiness—follows the pattern of the false prophets.
Christ's gospel encourages people to perform deeds worthy of repentance.
It never gives anyone permission to continue in sin.

div.title: The false prophet receives a sentence of death (verses 10–17)
div.p: Hananiah was sentenced to die.
Jeremiah told him this boldly only after receiving God's direction, not before the Lord had entrusted him with the message.
People who assure sinners that they will enjoy peace while they harden themselves against God's word bear terrible responsibility.
The Lord's servant must be gentle toward everyone.
Such a servant should willingly surrender even legitimate personal rights and leave it to God to defend the cause.
Every effort by wicked people to overturn God's purposes will only increase their own misery.

row.cell: Two letters to the captives in Babylon; In the first, they are recommended to be patient and composed.
In the second, judgments are denounced against the false prophets who deceived them.

div.title: Live faithfully while waiting in Babylon (verses 1–7)
div.p: God's written word is just as truly inspired as his spoken word.
A zealous servant of the Lord will use every means available to help people who are far away as well as nearby.
Writing is especially useful for that purpose.
The invention of printing made it still easier for many people to receive the knowledge of God's word.
The letter showed that God had not abandoned the exiles, even though their disobedience had brought his correction upon them.
If they continued to fear the Lord, they could still live comfortably in Babylon.
In every condition of life, wisdom and duty require us not to abandon the comfort we do possess simply because we lack everything we wish to possess.
The exiles were instructed to seek the welfare of the country where they were held captive.
As long as Babylon's king protected them, they should live quiet, peaceful, godly and honest lives under his authority.
They must wait patiently for God to bring deliverance at his appointed time.

div.title: God's good purposes are fulfilled in his time (verses 8–19)
div.p: Be careful when choosing which prophets to listen to.
Do not mistake people who share your preferences for prophets sent by God, or your own imaginings and dreams for divine revelations.
False prophets flatter people who enjoy being flattered.
Their hearers speak kindly to them so that the prophets will tell their hearers what they want to hear.
God promised the exiles would return after seventy years.
Henry notes that this period must be counted from the first deportation, not the final one.
The return would fulfill God's good word to them.
God's purposes are firm.
Human beings may not even know what they truly want, but the Lord is never uncertain.
At times we fear that all his plans for us are against us.
Yet for those who belong to him, even what appears evil will ultimately serve their good.
He gives them not the outcomes imagined by their fears, nor the wishes entertained by their fantasies, but the future promised to their faith—which is best for them.
When God pours out a special spirit of prayer, that is a hopeful sign that he is approaching a people in mercy.
His promises are intended to encourage prayer.
He has never told sincere seekers to seek him in vain.
But those who remained in Jerusalem would be destroyed despite the assurances given by false prophets.
The reason repeatedly stated also explains the final ruin of impenitent sinners:
God called them, but they refused to hear his word.

div.title: False prophets are judged for their lies (verses 20–32)
div.p: Jeremiah announced judgment upon false prophets who had deceived the Jews in Babylon.
Lying is wrong.
Lying to God's people in order to give them false confidence is worse.
But pretending that one's own lies are spoken by the God of truth is worst of all.
These teachers flattered others in their sins because they could not condemn those sins without condemning themselves.
Even hidden wrongdoing is known to God.
A day will come when he brings every concealed work of darkness into the light.
Shemaiah urged the priests to persecute Jeremiah.
How deeply hardened people become when they imagine their possession of power gives them the right to do harm!
The exiles were already in terrible bondage because of their contempt toward God's messengers.
Yet under that discipline, some continued sinning even more.
Suffering alone does not cure sin. The Lord's grace must work with correction if it is to renew a heart.
Those who reject the blessing of God's word, as Shemaiah did, deserve to lose its benefit.
Many charges raised against active Christians in every age amount to little more than this:

p.hi: They urge people to attend to their true interests and duties, and to wait for God's promises in his appointed way.

row.cell: Troubles which shall be before the restoration of Israel.
The blessings under Christ, and the wrath on the wicked.

div.title: God commands Jeremiah to record promises of restoration (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jeremiah was to write the very words God spoke to him.
They were words taught by the Holy Spirit.
Promises committed to writing at God's command are truly his word.
He had to record the suffering the people were experiencing and the further trouble still ahead.
Yet their calamities would ultimately have a happy end.
The church may suffer for a long time, but its afflictions will not last forever.
The Jews would be restored.
Henry sees in this prophecy not only deliverance from Babylon, but also Israel and Judah's future happy condition when converted to Christ, the Son of David and their King.
He also understands it as referring to hardships among the nations before Christ's coming.
All people must honor the Son as they honor the Father and approach the Father's worship and service through him.
Our gracious Savior pardons the sins of believers and breaks the yoke of sin and Satan.
Thus they can serve God without fear, in righteousness and true holiness throughout the remainder of life, as redeemed subjects of Christ the King.

div.title: The Lord heals what sinners cannot heal (verses 12–17)
div.p: When God is against a people, who can genuinely help them?
No one can give them the rescue they need.
Incurable suffering grows out of stubborn, incurable sinful desires.
The exiles deserved correction and lacked the power to deliver themselves.
Yet God intended to appear on their behalf and to punish their oppressors.
He would continue to do so.
Every effort to heal ourselves spiritually remains fruitless if we neglect our heavenly Advocate, Jesus Christ, and the sanctifying Holy Spirit.
The way God graciously treats each genuine convert and every returning backslider is, in spiritual effect, like the way he restores his people.

div.title: God's renewed covenant and the Messiah's mediation (verses 18–24)
div.p: The prophecy continues announcing God's favor after the people's troubles have ended.
The proper work of Christ as Mediator is to draw near to God on our behalf.
He acts as the High Priest whom we profess.
His own undertaking, in obedience to his Father's will and compassion for fallen humanity, engaged him in this work.
In doing all this, Jesus Christ is truly wonderful.
God would renew his covenant relationship with the people in keeping with his covenant with their ancestors.
“I will be your God” summarizes his gracious goodwill toward his people.
But his wrath against hardened wickedness is terrifying, like a whirlwind.
His purposes of judgment and his purposes of love will both be fulfilled.
The Lord comforts everyone who returns to him.
But whoever approaches him must do so with reverence, devotion and faith, engaging the heart sincerely.

p.hi: How will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?

row.cell: Promises of guidance and happiness; Rachel lamenting.
Peace and prosperity in gospel time.

div.title: The Lord draws his people with everlasting love (verses 1–9)
div.p: God assured his people he would restore them to covenant fellowship with himself.
When we reach an unusually low condition and difficulties seem overwhelming, it helps to remember that the church has suffered greatly before.
Yet when we experience present displeasure, we find it hard to take comfort in past signs of God's favor.
For those who, through grace, share in the Lord's love, there is great happiness in knowing that it is everlasting love.
It has existed from eternity in God's purposes and continues forever in its effects.
Those whom he loves with this love he draws to himself through the work of the Holy Spirit within their souls.
When we praise the Lord for what he has already done, let us also ask him to grant what his church still needs and expects.
When God calls us, we should not claim that we cannot come.
The One who calls also helps and strengthens us.
His goodness leads people to repentance.
His redeemed people will weep over sin with deeper bitterness and tenderness after deliverance than they did when they were suffering under captivity.
If we receive God as our Father and join the church of the firstborn, we will lack nothing truly good for us.
Henry sees these promises as looking to a future gathering of Israel from every part of the world.
He also sees in their language a figurative description of sinners converted to Christ and led along a clear and safe path.

div.title: The scattered are gathered, and sorrow gives way to joy (verses 10–17)
div.p: The God who scattered Israel knows where every one of his people may be found.
His providential gifts give us abundant reason for gratitude.
But the soul is not a fruitful garden unless watered by the dew of his Spirit and grace.
The prophecy then makes a precious promise which, Henry says, will not find its full accomplishment apart from the heavenly Zion.
Those who know God's loving-kindness and are satisfied with it need no other blessing to make them truly happy.
Rachel is pictured as rising from her grave and refusing comfort because she believes her descendants have been destroyed.
The killing of Bethlehem's children by Herod (Matthew 2:16–18) fulfilled this prophecy to some degree, but Henry explicitly says it could not be its entire meaning.
If we have a secure hope of eternal inheritance, both for ourselves and those we love, we can endure temporal suffering—and God can make those troubles serve our good.

div.title: Ephraim repents and asks God to turn him (verses 18–20)
div.p: Ephraim, representing Israel's ten tribes, mourns sin.
He is angry with himself over wrongdoing, foolishness and stubborn rebellion.
He recognizes he cannot, by his own power, remain close to God—much less restore himself when he has wandered away.
Therefore he prays:

p.hi: “Turn me, and I will be turned.”

div.p: His own will is brought into submission to God's.
When the Holy Spirit's teaching accompanied God's providential correction, the change was accomplished.
This is a comfort amid our suffering: the Lord has not forgotten us.
He has mercy reserved for everyone who seeks him sincerely—rich mercy, certain mercy and mercy fitted to their need.

div.title: The Savior prepares the road to freedom (verses 21–26)
div.p: The way from slavery to sin into the liberty of God's children is a highway.
It is both clear and safe.
Yet no one is likely to walk along it without deliberately setting the heart toward it.
The people receive encouragement from the promise of something new, unheard of and extraordinary—a creative work of almighty power.
Henry identifies it with the human nature of Jesus Christ, formed and prepared by the Holy Spirit's power.
He sees this as encouragement to the Jews to return to their land.
They were also promised a happy settlement there.
God has joined godliness with honesty.
No one may separate them or imagine that one can compensate for the absence of the other.
In the Lord's love and favor, the weary soul finds rest and the sorrowful find joy.
What could be more satisfying to see than Jerusalem's welfare and peace upon Israel?

div.title: The new covenant writes God's law upon the heart (verses 27–34)
div.p: God's people would become numerous and enjoy his blessing.
This passage is quoted in Hebrews 8:8–9 as the substance of the covenant of grace made with believers in Jesus Christ.
The promise is not that God will simply give people a different law.
Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfill it.
Rather, the same law that had been written on stone tablets will be written upon human hearts by the Holy Spirit.
Through grace the Lord will make his people willing to obey him.
Everyone will have the opportunity to know the Lord and receive the means of that knowledge.
When the gospel is proclaimed, the Holy Spirit will be poured out.
No person is finally destroyed except because of that person's own sins.
No one willing to receive Christ's salvation will be rejected.

div.title: God's covenant secures the future of his people (verses 35–40)
div.p: The sun, moon and other heavenly bodies will continue moving according to the order established by their Creator until time ends.
The roaring sea also remains under his authority.
Just as certainly, the Jews will continue to exist as a distinct people.
Henry says that scarcely any words could declare Israel's restoration more forcefully.
The rebuilding, enlargement and establishment of Jerusalem would be a pledge of the greater blessings God intended for the gospel church.
The future restoration of Israel, and every true believer's personal happiness, rest upon God's promise, covenant and oath.
His love surpasses knowledge.
Anyone who takes hold of that love receives every present mercy as a foretaste and pledge of salvation.

row.cell: God declares that he will give up his people, but promises to restore them.

div.title: Jeremiah buys land during the siege (verses 1–15)
div.p: Jeremiah was imprisoned because of his prophecies, yet he purchased a field.
That purchase was a sign.
Although Jerusalem was under siege and the land seemed about to be ruined, a time would return when people again bought and possessed houses, fields and vineyards.
Those who preach God's promises should demonstrate that they themselves believe what they teach.
Even our ordinary financial dealings and everyday business should be handled in faith, with attention to God's Providence and his promises.

div.title: Jeremiah prays to the sovereign and just God (verses 16–25)
div.p: The prophet worshiped the Lord for his infinite perfection.
Whenever we struggle to understand a particular way Providence is working, we should return to the truths that are most certain.
God is the source of all existence, power and life.
Nothing presents a difficulty too great for him to overcome.
He is a God of unlimited mercy.
He is also a God of uncompromising justice.
He directs everything according to what is best.
Jeremiah acknowledged God's righteousness in bringing judgment upon his people.
Whatever our situation, whether a personal trial or a public calamity, the Lord sees it and knows how to remedy it.
We should never quarrel with God's right to act.
But we may rightly ask to understand what his actions mean.

div.title: God's judgment and restoration both display his purposes (verses 26–44)
div.p: The Lord's answer revealed both his purposes of judgment against that generation and his purposes of mercy toward generations still to come.
Nothing but sin was responsible for the people's ruin.
Yet God promised the restoration of Judah and Jerusalem.
The people had finally fallen into despair.
The Lord answered by announcing mercy reserved for their future.
His promises are equally sure for everyone who truly believes.
He will acknowledge them as his people and show himself to be their God.
He will give them a heart that fears him.
All true Christians will possess a disposition to love one another.
They may differ in their views about lesser questions.

But they will be united in the great truths of God: the evil of sin; the low condition of fallen human beings; salvation through Jesus Christ; true holiness; the world's emptiness; and the importance of eternal things.
Those whom God loves, he loves to the end.
We have no reason to distrust his faithfulness or constancy.
We have every reason to be cautious about our own hearts.
He would settle the people again in Canaan.
Jeremiah's purchase was a pledge that many future purchases would follow the exile.
But those restored fields only faintly picture the inheritance reserved in the heavenly Canaan for people who fear God and persevere with him.
Let us therefore endure our trials, confident that he will accomplish all the good he has promised.

row.cell: The Messiah promised; happiness of his times.

div.title: God promises restoration and peace (verses 1–13)
div.p: Those who expect comfort from God must call upon him.
His promises are not given to replace prayer, but to awaken and encourage it.
These promises lead us to the gospel of Christ. In the gospel, God reveals truth to guide us and peace to give our hearts rest.
His sanctifying grace cleanses sinners from the corruption of sin, and his forgiving mercy frees them from its guilt.
When people are thus justified, washed and sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Holy Spirit, they are enabled to walk before God in peace and purity.
Many observers then recognize the difference between God's people and the surrounding world, and they come to fear his righteous judgment.
The Lord promises that people who have endured sorrow for a long time will again be filled with joy.
Where he gives righteousness and peace, he also supplies what is necessary for earthly needs. All the things we possess become genuine comforts as they are sanctified through his word and prayer.

div.title: The promised Messiah and his eternal kingdom (verses 14–26)
div.p: To complete the promised blessings, God gives the promise of the Messiah.
Christ gives his church righteousness. God has made him our righteousness, and in him believers become the righteousness of God.

p.hi: Christ is our Lord God, our righteousness, our sanctification and our redemption.

div.p: His kingdom will never end.
In this world, however, prosperity and adversity alternate like light and darkness, day and night.
God will also establish the covenant concerning the priesthood.
All true believers form a holy and royal priesthood. They offer spiritual sacrifices pleasing to God, beginning with themselves as living sacrifices.
The covenant promises will find their complete fulfillment in the Israel of the gospel.
According to Galatians 6:16, those who walk according to the gospel's rule belong to the Israel of God, upon whom are peace and mercy.
Yet we must not despise the families who were God's chosen people in ancient times, even though for a season they appear to have been set aside.

row.cell: The Jews reproved for compelling their poor brethren to return to unlawful bondage.

div.title: Zedekiah is warned of his captivity (verses 1–7)
div.p: Zedekiah learned that Jerusalem would fall and that he would die in captivity.
Nevertheless, his death would be natural, not an execution.
It is better to live and die repentant in a prison than to live and die unrepentant in a palace.

div.title: The people force their freed servants back into bondage (verses 8–22)
div.p: Under Israel's law, an Israelite was not to remain in this kind of service beyond the appointed period of seven years.
The people and their ancestors had violated that obligation.
They finally released their servants, but when it seemed possible that the siege might be lifted, they forced the people they had freed back into servitude.
People who try to deceive God with pretended repentance and incomplete reform end up deceiving themselves most of all.
Imagining that they are free to sin merely gives them the freedom to expose themselves to the most severe judgments.
When we disappoint God's rightful expectations that we will do our duty, he may justly disappoint our expectation of receiving mercy.
A reform motivated only by terror seldom lasts.
Solemn promises made to God and then deliberately broken profane his appointed ordinances.
Those most eager to bind themselves with an appeal to God's name may also be the quickest to violate their own promises.
Let us examine our hearts so that our repentance is genuine, and let God's law govern how we act.

row.cell: The Jews' disobedience to the Lord.

div.title: The Rechabites obey their ancestor (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jonadab was known for wisdom and godliness. He had lived almost three hundred years earlier; his life is also mentioned in 2 Kings 10:15.
Jonadab had instructed his descendants not to drink wine.
He also directed them to live in tents or movable dwellings, which would teach them not to regard any earthly place as their permanent home.
Remaining humble and content was the safest way for them to continue living in the land as strangers.
Humility and contentment are always wise and are often the best protection people can have.
Jonadab wanted his descendants to avoid unlawful pleasures. He therefore taught them to deny themselves even certain pleasures that were lawful in themselves.
Since we are strangers and pilgrims in the world, we should abstain from sinful bodily desires.
Those with little to lose will fear times of loss less. People who do not cling tightly to possessions will find it easier to surrender them if they are taken away.
Those best prepared to endure hardship practice self-denial and regard worldly vanities as unimportant.
The descendants of Jonadab faithfully followed the rules he had given them.
They made exceptions only where ordinary precautions were necessary for their safety during a time of widespread danger.

div.title: Their obedience exposes Judah's disobedience (verses 12–19)
div.p: The Rechabites' faithfulness was tested as a sign.
Their obedience highlighted the much greater disobedience of the Jews toward God.
The Rechabites had obeyed a man who was only a human being like themselves.
Jonadab had never done for his descendants what God had done for his people.
The Lord promised blessing to the Rechabites.

Scripture does not report how that promise was fulfilled. Henry expressed confidence that it was fulfilled and noted reports by travelers that a distinct Rechabite people could still be found in his own era. That report is a historical claim of the commentator, not an independently established identification.
Let us heed the godly advice of faithful predecessors. It is good to follow their wise counsel.

row.cell: Baruch is to write the prophecies of Jeremiah.
The princes advise them to hide themselves.
The king having heard a part, burns the roll.

div.title: Baruch writes Jeremiah's prophecies (verses 1–8)

p.hi: God himself directed that the Scriptures should be written down.

div.p: His wisdom appointed writing as an appropriate means of warning the people.
If the warning failed to change them, Judah would have still less excuse for refusing to listen.
The Lord announces judgment against sinners so that they may hear, fear and turn away from their evil ways.
Whenever anyone responds to his warnings in this way, trusting in his promised mercy, the Lord is ready to forgive their sins.
Those who refuse are left without excuse.
The seriousness of God's anger against our sin ought to stir us both to prayer and to earnest efforts to obey him.

div.title: The officials hear the scroll (verses 9–19)
div.p: Outward displays of reverence and devotion may be found among people who keep up the forms of religion but remain strangers—even enemies—to its living power.
The officials listened patiently as the whole scroll was read.
They became deeply afraid.

Yet even people convinced that a message is true and important, and inclined to help those who preach it, may still hesitate because of concerns about their safety, their personal interests or their prospects for advancement.
Such reservations can keep them from acting according to what their consciences know.
They may even try to dismiss the disturbing truth rather than obey it.

div.title: The king burns the scroll (verses 20–32)
div.p: Those who despise God's word may soon show that they hate it.
Like the king who burned the scroll, they would like to see the word itself destroyed.
This reveals the deep hostility of the sinful human mind toward God, and should make us marvel at his patience.
The officials had shown some concern about the warning.
Yet when they saw how lightly the king treated it, their own concern weakened.

p.hi: Do not treat God's word as something trivial.

div.title: The Chaldean army will return (verses 1–10)
div.p: Many people see the deadly consequences of someone else's sins, yet carelessly step into that person's place and follow the same destructive course.
When we are in trouble, we should seek the prayers of ministers and Christian friends.
But it is common for people to want others to pray for them while refusing to accept their advice.
A temporary pause in judgment may even make sinners more stubborn.
If God does not help us, no creature can truly save us.
Whatever instruments he has determined to use will fulfill his purpose, even if they appear unlikely to succeed.

div.title: Jeremiah is falsely accused and imprisoned (verses 11–21)
div.p: At times the wise course for godly people is to withdraw, enter their rooms and shut their doors (Isaiah 26:20).
Jeremiah was arrested as if he were deserting to the enemy, and he was thrown into prison.
It is nothing new for those who most faithfully serve the church to be falsely accused of secretly helping its worst enemies.
When such charges are made, we may deny them and entrust our case to the God who judges righteously.
The Lord gave Jeremiah grace to remain faithful.
He would not purchase a human ruler's mercy by betraying either God or his rightful duty toward the king.
He told the king the entire truth.
When speaking God's message, Jeremiah was bold.
When presenting his own request, he was humble and respectful.

p.hi: A lion in God's cause should be a lamb in his own.

div.p: God gave Jeremiah favor in the king's eyes.
The Lord can even turn a prison cell into pasture for his people and raise up friends to provide for them.
He can feed them even during famine.

row.cell: Jeremiah is cast into a dungeon, from whence he is delivered by an Ethiopian.
He advises the king to surrender to the Chaldeans.

div.title: Jeremiah is imprisoned and rescued (verses 1–13)
div.p: Jeremiah continued to preach God's word plainly, just as the officials continued in their malice.
Wicked people commonly regard faithful ministers as enemies because those ministers show them how much harm they are doing to themselves by refusing repentance.
Jeremiah was thrown into a dungeon.
Many faithful witnesses for God have died quietly and unnoticed in prisons.
But Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian, spoke courageously and truthfully to the king: the men who had dealt with Jeremiah had acted wickedly.
Notice how God can raise up friends to help his people in the deepest distress.
The king ordered Jeremiah's release, and Ebed-melech saw that the prophet was pulled out of the dungeon.
His particular tenderness toward Jeremiah deserves attention.
This should encourage us to stand openly for God.
In these opposing characters, we recognize an enduring difference: God's children become like their Father, while Satan's children imitate their master.

div.title: Jeremiah advises Zedekiah to surrender (verses 14–28)
div.p: Jeremiah was reluctant to repeat warnings that appeared only to endanger his own life and increase the king's guilt.
Yet he pressed Zedekiah with the truth and challenged the fear that held him back from obedience to God.

p.hi: The less people fear God, the more they tend to fear other people.

div.p: They often lack the courage to act according to their own judgments and consciences, even when they know what is right.

div.title: Jerusalem is captured (verses 1–10)
div.p: Jerusalem was so strongly fortified that its inhabitants believed no enemy could ever enter it.
But the people's sins provoked God to withdraw his protection.
Without him, the city was just as vulnerable as any other.
Zedekiah's eyes were put out.
A man who had shut his eyes to the clear light of God's word was now condemned to literal darkness.
Those who refuse to believe what God says will eventually be convinced when his words are fulfilled.
Notice the astonishing changes of Providence.
Earthly possessions and circumstances are never secure.
The Lord's judgments are just.
But whether he makes people rich or poor, neither condition will do them real good while they cling to their sins.

div.title: Jeremiah receives kind treatment (verses 11–14)
div.p: God's faithful servants are the people best prepared for whatever may happen.
Even while wicked people suffer, those who belong to God may experience rescue and comfort.
They sometimes receive more kindness from people who make no profession of religion than from people who outwardly claim to be godly.
The Lord can raise up friends for his people, do them good and fulfill every one of his promises.

div.title: Ebed-melech receives a promise of safety (verses 15–18)
div.p: God sent a message to assure Ebed-melech that his great kindness toward Jeremiah would be rewarded.
The reason for the promise was explicit: “Because you have trusted in me,” says the Lord.
God regards not only the outward service people perform, but the faith and motives from which they act.
Those who trust him while doing their duty, as Ebed-melech did, will discover that their hope does not fail even amid the greatest danger.

row.cell: Jeremiah is directed to go to Gedaliah.

div.title: Jeremiah is free to join Gedaliah (verses 1–6)
div.p: The commander of the guard seemed almost proud to have served as the instrument through which God fulfilled what Jeremiah had been sent to announce.
Many people readily recognize God's justice and truth in what happens to others, yet remain blind and careless about their own sins.
Sooner or later, everyone must see that sin is the cause of human misery.
Jeremiah was allowed to choose where to go.
He was advised to join Gedaliah, the governor appointed over the land under Babylon's king.
Henry expresses uncertainty about whether Jeremiah made the best decision in accepting this advice.
Yet people who sincerely seek sinners' salvation and the good of the church may look for signs of better days where others see very little hope.
They often prefer an opportunity to do useful work to a safer position where they cannot serve others.

div.title: A plot against Gedaliah (verses 7–16)
div.p: Jeremiah had never promised that the Jews would enjoy good times immediately following the captivity.
Yet the circumstances briefly seemed to offer hope.
How quickly that prospect was destroyed!
When God begins a judgment, he will accomplish what he intends.
So long as pride, ambition and revenge rule people's hearts, they will continually devise new schemes and stir up trouble, usually bringing ruin upon themselves.
Who would have expected another rebellion so soon after Jerusalem's destruction?
Human nature does not become good simply because it has endured great suffering.

p.hi: Only God's grace can bring real change.

div.p: Even if those imprisoned for final judgment were allowed to return to earth, their hearts would still be wicked unless their nature was renewed.
Lord, give us new hearts and the new mind that comes with new birth.
You have said that without this new birth we cannot enter your heavenly kingdom.

row.cell: Johanan recovers the captives, and purposes to retire to Egypt.

div.title: Ishmael murders Gedaliah (verses 1–10)
div.p: People who hate God's worshipers sometimes pretend to be godly in order to harm them more easily.
Death often arrives where it is least expected.
We should therefore continually examine whether our hearts and lives are in the condition we would wish to be found in when summoned before our Judge.
Sometimes a person's riches can obtain a temporary escape from deadly danger.
Yet those who imagine they can bribe death itself, saying, “Do not kill us; we have treasure hidden in the fields,” are terribly mistaken.
This sorrowful history warns us never to suppose that we are completely safe in this world.

p.hi: We cannot be certain of uninterrupted peace until we reach heaven.

div.title: Johanan rescues the captives but plans to flee (verses 11–18)
div.p: The success of wickedness is short-lived.
No one can truly prosper by hardening the heart against God.
Those who make excuses for sinful choices by pretending to fear a danger may then justly lose comfort because of real dangers.
A wise and peaceful ruler may be removed, only for a rash and ambitious person to rise in that ruler's place.
Such changes deeply affect the welfare of many people.
Only those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways can enjoy lasting steadiness and true happiness.

row.cell: Johanan desires Jeremiah to ask counsel of God.
They are assured of safety in Judea, but of destruction in Egypt.

div.title: Johanan asks Jeremiah to seek God's counsel (verses 1–6)
div.p: The commanders sought Jeremiah's help when it suited their purposes.
Whenever we face difficult or uncertain choices, we should look to God for direction.
We may pray in faith for the Spirit's wisdom within our hearts and guidance through God's Providence.
But we do not genuinely desire to know God's will unless we have already resolved to obey what he reveals.
Many promise to do whatever the Lord commands while inwardly hoping that his answer will flatter their pride and leave their favorite sins untouched.
Something will eventually expose the true condition of their hearts.

div.title: God's answer commands them to remain in Judah (verses 7–22)
div.p: If we wish to know God's will in doubtful circumstances, we must wait as well as pray.
He is ready to show mercy again to those he has corrected.
He rejects no one who trusts his promises.
His word gives enough encouragement to calm even the unreasonable fears that keep his people from their duties.
Whatever loss or hardship obedience may appear to bring, God's promises provide for it.
He will protect and deliver those who trust and serve him.
It is folly to leave the place where our duty lies merely because we meet trouble there, especially when doing so means abandoning the land God had set apart.
The very dangers we hope to avoid through sin are often brought upon us by the sin itself.
This applies to ordinary life as well.
Someone may hope to escape human suffering by moving elsewhere. Yet the troubles common to humanity will follow wherever that person goes.
Those who make solemn promises to God while deliberately hiding their intentions deserve serious rebuke.

p.hi: Their conduct reveals more than their words.

div.p: We do not always know what is truly good for us.
What we most eagerly desire and cling to may prove harmful—or even fatal.

row.cell: The leaders carry the people to Egypt.
Jeremiah foretells the conquest of Egypt.

div.title: The leaders take the people into Egypt (verses 1–7)
div.p: Pride produces conflict, both with God and with other people.
The leaders preferred their own wisdom to God's revealed will.
People often deny that Scripture is God's word because they have already decided not to submit to its commands.
When someone is determined to continue in sin, that person may even assign evil motives to the best actions.
These Jews abandoned their own land and took themselves outside the protection God had promised there.
How foolish people can be: in attempting to improve their circumstances through disobedience, they bring disaster upon themselves.

div.title: Jeremiah foretells Egypt's conquest (verses 8–13)
div.p: God can find his people wherever they are.
The Spirit of prophecy was not confined to Israel's territory.
Jeremiah announced that Nebuchadnezzar would conquer Egypt and take many Egyptians captive.
God sometimes uses one wicked person or nation to judge another.
He will also punish those who mislead people professing to belong to him or tempt them to rebel against his commands.

row.cell: The Jews in Egypt persist in idolatry.
Jeremiah then denounces destruction upon them.

div.title: The Jews in Egypt persist in idolatry (verses 1–14)
div.p: God reminded the Jews that Judah's earlier sins had brought about the country's destruction.
We ought to warn others earnestly about the danger of sin:

p.hi: Do not do it!

div.p: If you love God, do not sin, because it provokes him.
If you love your own soul, do not sin, because it destroys you.
Let conscience speak to us in this way whenever we are tempted.
The Jews whom God had sent into the land of the Chaldeans were, through his grace, being drawn away from idolatry.
But those who had deliberately gone into Egypt against his command became even more attached to idols.
When we enter situations of temptation without reason or divine calling, it is just for God to leave us to the consequences of our own choices.
If we walk against him, he will walk against us.
The greatest and most dreadful misery people experience arises from neglecting the salvation offered to them.

div.title: The people refuse to reform (verses 15–19)
div.p: These bold sinners did not even attempt to excuse themselves.
They openly declared that they intended to continue doing what God forbade.
People who knowingly disobey God often become steadily worse; sin deceives and hardens their hearts.
Their words reveal the true attitude of a rebellious heart.
Even afflictions that ought to have separated them from idolatry were interpreted by them as reasons to keep practicing it.
It is terrible when people who ought to encourage one another toward God and heaven instead encourage one another in sin and thereby prepare one another for judgment.
Combining idolatry with the worship of God and rejecting the mediation of Christ provoke God and bring ruin upon people.

Henry extends this warning against idolatry to the worship of images and what he regards as religious honors wrongly paid to saints, angels and the queen of heaven. This is his own theological application of the passage, preserved as such rather than presented as a new statement of the biblical narrative.
He urges readers to remember what happened because of the Jews' idolatrous practices.

div.title: Jeremiah announces judgment (verses 20–30)
div.p: When evil comes upon us, we should consider how we have sinned against the Lord.
We should stand in awe of him and turn from sin.
Since these people were determined to remain in idolatry, God would continue judging them.
Even the little true religion still present among them would disappear.
The earthly comforts and sources of security in which we place our greatest confidence may fail just as quickly as those in which we place little trust.
They are what God makes them, not what we imagine them to be.
A well-founded hope of sharing God's mercy is always joined with repentance and obedience.

p.hi: An encouragement sent to Baruch.

div.title: God's correction and encouragement for Baruch
div.p: Baruch had written Jeremiah's prophecies and read them aloud, as described in Jeremiah 36.
The king threatened him because of that service.
People who are just beginning to serve the Lord are often discouraged by difficulties that are small compared with what may come later.
These complaints and fears arise from the corruption remaining in their hearts.
Baruch had expected too much from earthly life, making the suffering he faced far harder to endure.
The world's hostility would not trouble us so much if we had not foolishly hoped for its approval and eagerly sought its favor.
How foolish to seek great things for ourselves here, where everything is small and nothing is secure!
The Lord understands the real reasons for our anxiety and discouragement better than we understand them ourselves.
Let us ask him to examine our hearts and restrain every disordered desire within them.

row.cell: Their overthrow after the siege of Tyre.
A promise of comfort to the Jews.

div.title: The Egyptians are defeated (verses 1–12)
div.p: The whole word of God speaks against those who refuse to obey the gospel of Christ.
But it speaks for everyone who turns to him, including those from the nations outside Israel.
The prophecy begins with Egypt.
Let the Egyptians strengthen themselves with every skill, ally and resource they possess: their efforts will be useless.
The wounds God inflicts upon his enemies cannot be healed by ordinary medicines.
In this ever-changing world, strength and prosperity soon pass from one person or nation to another.

div.title: Egypt is judged, while Israel receives comfort (verses 13–28)
div.p: Those who seized what belonged to other people would now find their own land invaded.
Egypt resembled a beautiful heifer not accustomed to bearing the yoke of subjection.
But destruction would come from the north: the Chaldeans were coming.
At the same time, God announced comfort and peace to the Israel of God.
Those promises encouraged his people while judgments were falling upon surrounding nations.
He would remain with them and correct them in measure.
He would not subject them to everlasting destruction away from his presence.

p.hi: The calamities of the Philistines.

div.title: The Philistines face judgment
div.p: The Philistines had long been enemies of Israel.
The Chaldean army would now sweep over their territory like a great flood.
When God determines to bring a people down, no one can prevent it.
When he intends to destroy the wicked, he can remove every source of assistance they rely upon.
The devastation caused by war is so dreadful that peace should be highly valued.
Yet we must submit to the Lord's appointments, because he orders everything with perfect wisdom and justice.

row.cell: Prophecies against Moab for pride and security.
For carnal confidence and contempt of God.

div.title: Moab's proud security ends in ruin (verses 1–13)
div.p: The Chaldeans would destroy Moab.
We should be thankful that our calling is to seek the salvation of people's lives and souls, not to shed their blood.
But that privilege makes us all the more accountable if we perform such a good work deceitfully or carelessly.
Moab's cities would become ruins, and its countryside would be laid waste.
There would be great sorrow and confusion.
Even if sinners could be given wings, they still could not fly beyond the reach of God's righteous judgment.
Many people persist in wrongdoing without repenting, yet continue to enjoy outward prosperity for a long time.
The Moabites had remained corrupt and unchanged, secure and devoted to bodily pleasure.
They had not experienced disruptions to their prosperity, and therefore their hearts and lives remained unchanged (Psalm 55:19).

div.title: Moab is warned, yet restoration is promised (verses 14–47)
div.p: The prophecy continues describing Moab's destruction.
These warnings were intended to awaken national repentance and reform that might prevent the disaster, or at least personal repentance and reform to prepare individuals for it.

As we read this long list of threats and the terrifying figures used to express them, it is more profitable to reflect on the power of God's anger and the justice of his judgments than to become preoccupied with explaining every image.
The destruction, however, would not be permanent.
The chapter ends by promising that Moab's captivity would be reversed in the latter days.
God would not contend even with the Moabites forever.
Henry reports that Jewish interpreters connected this promise with the days of the Messiah.
In that larger application, people from the nations who are held in bondage to sin and Satan are brought back by divine grace and become truly free.

div.title: The Ammonites face judgment (verses 1–6)
div.p: Among human beings, power often wins against what is right.
But the Almighty governs even powerful people and judges fairly.
Like the Ammonites, those who suppose everything they can seize must rightfully belong to them will discover their error.
The Lord calls people to account for every dishonest act, especially offenses committed against those who have no resources or defenders.

div.title: Judgment comes upon Edom (verses 7–22)
div.p: The Edomites were longstanding enemies of God's Israel.
Their day of judgment had now drawn near.
The warning concerned them, but it was also given for the sake of God's people, whose suffering the Edomites had made worse.
Divine judgment moves from nation to nation.
The earth is full of upheaval, and no one can escape the agents God appoints to execute his just purposes.
Even amid human violence, we should recognize the Lord's righteousness.

div.title: Syria and Damascus are humbled (verses 23–27)
div.p: How easily God can take away the courage of nations celebrated for their bravery!
Damascus became weak.
It had been a joyful city with many of the pleasures people desire.
But those who place their happiness in earthly and bodily enjoyment deceive themselves.

div.title: Kedar is scattered (verses 28–33)
div.p: Nebuchadnezzar would devastate the people of Kedar, who lived in the deserts of Arabia.
A ruler who had captured many strong cities would not spare those who lived in tents.
He acted to satisfy his own greed and ambition.
Yet God directed the events to correct an ungrateful people and warn a careless world that danger can arrive when it feels most secure.
The inhabitants would flee far away, withdrawing into the depths of the desert and becoming scattered.
But privacy and obscurity do not always bring safety.

div.title: Elam is judged, but not abandoned forever (verses 34–39)
div.p: Henry identifies the Elamites with the Persians; that is his historical identification in this commentary.
They had acted against God's Israel and would be called to account.
Evil pursues those who practice sin.
God would show them that he reigns.
Nevertheless, Elam's destruction would not last forever.
Henry understands the promise of restoration as finding its full realization in the days of the Messiah.
When believers read God's warnings against the enemies of his church, they can take courage that the result of the spiritual conflict is not uncertain.

p.hi: The One who is for us is greater than all who oppose us.

div.p: He will subdue the enemies of our souls.

div.title: Babylon's downfall and God's people's return (verses 1–7)
div.p: The Babylonian king had treated Jeremiah with kindness.
Yet the prophet was still obliged to announce the destruction of that king's empire.
When those friendly toward us are enemies of God, we must not proclaim a false peace to them.
Babylon's destruction is described as thorough and final.
But within these warnings comes comfort for the Jews.
They would return first to their God, and then to their country.
The promise of their conversion and reform prepares the way for the other blessings promised to them.
Their tears would no longer be merely the grief of worldly losses, as when they went into captivity, but godly sorrow over sin.
They would seek the Lord as their God and abandon idols.
Then they would think of returning to their homeland.
This illustrates the return of lost souls to God.
Genuine converts sincerely desire to reach the right end and continually take care to remain on the right path.
The condition of the people before their restoration was truly sorrowful.
Even when professing Christians commit sins, those sins never justify others' pleasure in persecuting or destroying them.
div.note: Verified editorial cross-reference: Jer.50.1-Jer.50.3; Jer.50.8-Jer.50.16; Jer.50.21-Jer.50.32; Jer.50.35-Jer.50.46.
Verified editorial cross-reference: Jer.50.4-Jer.50.7; Jer.50.17-Jer.50.20; Jer.50.33; Jer.50.34.

div.title: Babylon is devastated and Israel regathered (verses 8–20)
div.p: Babylon's devastation is described through many images.
The Lord's anger against sin is its underlying cause.
The nation would be laid waste because it had rebelled against God.
Sin makes people targets for the arrows of divine judgment.
The mercy promised to the Israel of God would not merely come after Babylon's destruction: its deliverance would arise through that destruction.
The scattered sheep would be gathered from the wilderness and returned to good pasture.
Everyone who returns to God and to duty discovers true satisfaction of soul.
Deliverance from suffering becomes real comfort when it comes as a fruit of forgiven sin.

div.title: God's forces bring Babylon low (verses 21–32)
div.p: Forces would be gathered and given the power to destroy Babylon.
By carrying out the task God appointed, they would bring to pass what he had announced.
Pride causes God to oppose a person and quickly brings ruin nearer.
Babylon's own arrogance would be its downfall.
She had proudly opposed the Holy One of Israel.
Who can preserve in power those whom God has determined to bring down?

div.title: The weak have a mighty Redeemer (verses 33–46)
div.p: Israel could take comfort in knowing that although God's people were weak, their Redeemer was strong.
This applies to believers who struggle under the power of sin and corruption and feel the weight of their weakness and many shortcomings.
Their Redeemer is able to guard what they entrust to him.
Sin will not have dominion over them.
He will give them the rest that remains for God's people.
Babylon's wrongdoing and punishment are also described.
Her central sins included idolatry and persecution.
The Lord does not save his people so they can remain in their sins, and he will certainly not approve the wickedness of their declared enemies.
Judgment for Babylon's sins would leave the country desolate.
When we read about prosperous Babylon's destruction and afflicted Israel's rescue, we learn to choose suffering with God's people rather than brief enjoyment of the pleasures of sin.

row.cell: Babylon's doom; God's controversy with her; encouragements from thence to the Israel of God.

div.title: Babylon's coming destruction (verses 1–58)
div.p: The details of this prophecy are interwoven and repeated.
Babylon possessed enormous treasures, but neither its waters nor its wealth could keep it safe.
Judgment would arrive when the Babylonians least expected it.
Wherever we are—even in the deepest trouble or far from home—we should remember the Lord our God.
At moments of greatest fear or greatest hope, remembering him is especially necessary.
Henry connects the grief caused by Babylon's downfall with the lament over “New Testament Babylon” in Revelation 18:9,19.
He understands the ruin of systems supporting idolatry, unbelief and superstition as clearing the way for a revival of true godliness.
In his prophetic application, a great power characterized by anti-Christian tyranny, idolatry, superstition and persecution of true Christians is as certainly doomed to judgment as ancient Babylon.
This is Henry's interpretation of the later biblical imagery, not a new identification of a particular modern group.
Many people would then mourn their sins and seek the Lord.
The lost sheep of Israel's house would return to the Good Shepherd's fold and no longer wander away.
The exact fulfillment of ancient prophecies strengthens our faith in all God's promises and the prophecies of Scripture.

div.title: The written prophecy is sent to Babylon (verses 59–64)
div.p: Seraiah was entrusted with taking the prophecy to Babylon and reading it to his fellow Jews in captivity.
Through faith they could look beyond the power oppressing them, foresee its end and be encouraged.
The world offers impressive sights and flattering promises, but Scripture announces that its proud splendor will not last.
The scroll was to be thrown into the Euphrates.
Henry connects that sign to the downfall of New Testament Babylon in Revelation 18:21.
Those who finally sink under God's wrath and curse sink forever.
Babylon and every power that opposes Christ will ultimately fall and not rise again.
Let us hope in God's word and wait quietly for his salvation.
Then we will witness the judgment of wickedness without sharing in its condemnation.

div.title: Zedekiah's final defeat (verses 1–11)
div.p: Of all the consequences of sin, we should pray most urgently against being cast away from God's presence (Psalm 51:11).
No one is finally removed from his favor without first turning away through sin.
Zedekiah fled, but his escape failed.
There is no escape from divine judgment.
Judgment catches up with the sinner wherever that person runs.

div.title: Jerusalem and its temple are destroyed (verses 12–23)
div.p: The Chaldean army devastated Jerusalem.
The chapter pays particular attention to the removal of the temple's sacred articles.
Remembering their beauty and value helps us understand how serious the people's sin was, since that sin brought about such devastation.

div.title: Judah's leaders are carried away (verses 24–30)
div.p: The leaders of the Jews had led the people astray.
Now those leaders themselves became especially visible examples of the Lord's righteous judgment.
The narrative also records two earlier deportations.
This people repeatedly became a remarkable example of both divine judgment and divine mercy.

div.title: Jehoiachin is raised from prison (verses 31–34)
div.p: For the fuller historical account of Jehoiachin's release and promotion, see 2 Kings 25:27–30.
Those living under oppression may take encouragement that waiting quietly for the Lord's salvation is not in vain.
Our times are in God's hand.
So are the hearts of everyone with whom we have dealings.
May we grow increasingly able to rest upon the Rock of Ages.
May we look forward in holy faith to the hour when God restores Zion and overthrows every enemy of his church.

div.title: Lamentations — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Henry considers Jeremiah to be the clear author of the Lamentations traditionally associated with his name.
He dates the book after the Chaldeans destroyed Jerusalem.

May it teach us to recognize sin as the cause of our calamities, and amid trials to practice submission, repentance, faith and prayer, trusting in the promised deliverance that comes through God's mercy.

row.cell: The miserable state of Jerusalem, the just consequences of its sins.
Jerusalem represented as a captive female, lamenting, and seeking the mercy of God.

div.title: Jerusalem's desolation follows her sins (verses 1–11)
div.p: At times the prophet speaks in his own person.
At other times Jerusalem is personified as a distressed woman, or the words are spoken by some of the Jews.
The lament portrays the Jewish nation's misery.
Because of the greatness of her sins, Jerusalem had become a captive and a slave.
She found no rest from suffering.
If we permit sin, our greatest enemy, to govern us, we should not be astonished when other enemies are also allowed to rule over us.
The people experienced the extremes of famine and distress.
In these terrible circumstances Jerusalem acknowledged her sins and asked the Lord to consider her suffering.
This is the only way to find rest under such burdens.
God's just anger against human transgression has filled the world with sorrow, lamentation, sickness and death.

div.title: Jerusalem mourns and seeks mercy (verses 12–22)
div.p: Jerusalem is pictured sitting in grief upon the ground.
She asks everyone passing by to consider whether her example should concern them.
Her outward suffering was great, but the guilt she felt made her inward suffering even harder to bear.
True sorrow over sin must reach the depths of the soul.
This scene shows sin's dreadful character and calls us to flee from coming judgment.
Yet however much we may learn from Jerusalem's suffering, we can learn far more from the suffering of Christ.
Does he not address every one of us from the cross?

p.hi: “Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by?”

div.p: May all our sorrows lead us to Christ's cross, teach us to attend to his example and enable us to follow him willingly and joyfully.

p.hi: Lamentation for the misery of Jerusalem.

div.title: God withdraws protection from Jerusalem (verses 1–9)
div.p: The passage gives a sorrowful picture of God's church, Jacob and Israel.
It particularly directs attention to the Lord's hand in the people's suffering.
Yet God does not become an enemy of his people simply because he is angry with them and corrects them.
When he withdraws protection, city gates and iron bars can provide no security.
It is right for God to humble people through judgment when they have degraded themselves through sin.
Those who fail to value or observe his Sabbaths and appointed worship may justly lose the comfort and benefit of them.
What use do people make of Bibles if they refuse to learn from them?
Those who misuse God's prophets may rightly lose them.
It can be painful to direct suffering people's attention to their own wrongdoing and God's judgment.
Nevertheless, that recognition may be necessary because their sins are the source of their miseries.

div.title: The terrible suffering and a call to prayer (verses 10–22)
div.p: There were many reasons for mourning.
Countless people died through famine.
Even children were killed by their mothers and eaten, in fulfillment of the dreadful warning of Deuteronomy 28:53.
Many more died by the sword.
False prophets deceived the people.
Their neighbors mocked them.

p.hi: Mocking another person's suffering is a serious sin and adds to that suffering.

div.p: Their enemies celebrated their defeat.
Yet those hostile to God's church often mistake its severe setbacks for its final destruction.
They will discover their error.
The suffering people are called to lament, and to seek comfort for their grief.

p.hi: Prayer is a remedy for every wound, even the deepest and most painful.

div.p: In prayer we bring our circumstances to the Lord and entrust them to him.

p.hi: May his will be done.

div.p: Let us fear God, walk humbly before him and take care that we do not fall.

p.hi: The faithful lament their calamities, and hope in God's mercies.

div.title: The prophet's grief and temptation (verses 1–20)
div.p: The prophet describes the darkest and most discouraging part of his experience before explaining where he found help and relief.
During his trial, the Lord seemed terrifying to him.
His affliction felt like misery itself, because sin makes suffering's cup bitter.
The struggle between unbelief and faith may become very severe.
Yet even the weakest believer is mistaken when imagining that strength and hope from the Lord have entirely disappeared.

div.title: The Lord's mercies are new every morning (verses 21–36)
div.p: Having described his distress and temptations, the prophet now shows how he rose above them.
However bad our condition is, God's mercy is the reason it is not worse.
We should notice not only what works against us, but also the gifts and promises that support us.

p.hi: God's compassion never fails.

div.p: Every morning provides fresh evidence of it.
Earthly possessions and inheritances perish, but the Lord himself is a portion forever.
It is our duty, and also our comfort, to hope and wait quietly for his salvation.
Afflictions may accomplish much good.
Many have found that bearing the yoke in youth makes them serious, humble and less attached to the world, when otherwise they might have been proud and unruly.
When suffering produces patience, patience can deepen experience, and that experience strengthens a hope that does not put us to shame.
Remembering both sin's evil and our own sinfulness shows us that we are not consumed only because of the Lord's mercies.
Perhaps we cannot yet say with steady confidence, “The Lord is my portion.”
But can we not at least pray, “I desire him as my portion and salvation; I hope in his word”?
Happy are those who learn to receive their affliction as being under God's sovereign hand.

div.title: Examine your own ways and return to God (verses 37–41)
div.p: As long as life remains, hope remains.
Rather than only complaining that things are bad, we should encourage ourselves that they may become better.
Our sins deserve far more suffering than we actually receive.
We should bring our complaint to God, not complain against God.
During disaster we are quick to examine other people's ways and blame them.
But our duty is to search and test our own ways, and turn away from sin toward God.
Our hearts must accompany our prayers.
If inward conviction does not correspond to outward words, we mock God and deceive ourselves.

div.title: The prophet weeps and waits for God (verses 42–54)
div.p: The more the prophet contemplated the devastation, the more deeply he grieved.
Yet one word of comfort remained.
While the people continued weeping, they also continued waiting.
They looked to the Lord alone for relief and rescue.

div.title: Faith finds courage in God's answer (verses 55–66)
div.p: Faith finally emerges victorious.
The prophet ends with a measure of comfort.

p.hi: Prayer is the breath of a person made new by God.

div.p: In asking for mercy, the renewed soul draws in grace like air.
In praise, that soul breathes it back.
Prayer reveals spiritual life and helps sustain it.
God calmed the people's fears and quieted their hearts.
He said, “Do not fear.”
That was the language of his grace, borne witness by his Spirit to their spirits.
And what are our sufferings compared with the sufferings of the Redeemer?
The Lord will deliver his people from their troubles and renew his church after persecution.
He will save believers with everlasting salvation, while his enemies face eternal judgment.

p.hi: The deplorable state of the nation is contrasted with its ancient prosperity.

div.title: Jerusalem's former beauty is lost (verses 1–12)
div.p: What a change has taken place!
Sin dims the beauty of even the noblest abilities and the most excellent gifts.
But the gold that Christ bestows and has tested in the fire can never be taken away.
Its outward appearance may lose its shine, but its true value never changes.
Once more we hear of the horrors of Jerusalem's siege and destruction.
As we consider what sin brought upon God's people in earlier times, we should think seriously about what the same causes might bring upon the church today.
Lord, though we have rebelled against you, turn to us and turn our hearts back to you.
Help us to fear your name.
Bless us with grace that awakens, converts, renews and strengthens.

div.title: The sins of leaders hasten the nation's ruin (verses 13–20)
div.p: Nothing brings a people toward ruin more quickly than the sins of their priests and prophets.
Even the king could not escape, for God's justice pursued him.
Yet our anointed King alone is the life of our souls.
We may dwell safely under Christ's shadow and rejoice in him even among enemies.
He is the true God and eternal life.

div.title: Zion's suffering will end; Edom faces judgment (verses 21 and 22)
div.p: The prophecy announces that Zion's troubles will reach an end.
It does not mean that she will suffer the complete punishment she deserved, but that she will experience everything God has determined to inflict.
Edom's celebration will also end.
The troubles of God's church and each believer will soon be completed.
The judgment of their enemies is drawing near.
The Lord will expose their sins, and they will lie down in lasting sorrow.
In Henry's interpretation, Edom here represents all the church's enemies.
The prophet has shown how widespread Israel's corruption was.
That reality demonstrates God's justice in the judgments he sent.
It also reveals how urgently the whole human race needs the grace of God in Jesus Christ.

p.hi: The Jewish nation supplicating the Divine favour.

div.title: The people confess their sufferings and sins (verses 1–16)
div.p: Is anyone suffering?
Let that person pray, bringing the complaint directly to God.
That is what God's people do here.
They lament not merely dangers they imagine, but hardships they are already enduring.
When we experience suffering connected with the sins of our ancestors, we may hope in the Lord's returning mercy if we remain repentant and patient.
The people confess: “Woe to us, for we have sinned!”
Our sorrow is ultimately tied to our own sin and folly.
Although our sins and God's righteous displeasure cause suffering, we may hope for his forgiving mercy, sanctifying grace and kind Providence.
Yet the guilt accumulated through a lifetime of sin will finally be judged unless a person receives an interest in the Savior who bore our sins in his own body on the tree.

div.title: The people pray for renewed favor (verses 17–22)
div.p: The devastation of the temple concerned God's people even more deeply than all their other troubles.
But despite every change on earth, God remains the same.
He is forever wise and holy, just and good.
With him there is no variation or shadow of change.
The people pray earnestly for mercy and grace:

p.hi: “Turn us to you, O Lord.”

div.p: God never abandons people before they abandon him.
If his grace brings them back to himself in obedience, he will show them favor and mercy.
If he renews our hearts, he will also renew our days through his kindness.
Troubles may weaken our hearts and dim our eyes, but the throne of mercy of our reconciled God remains open.
In every trial, let us place our entire trust in his mercy, confess our sins and pour out our hearts before him.
Guard against resentment and despair.
All who trust, fear, love and serve the Lord will find that all is well in the end.
God's judgments still occur in the earth, as in Jeremiah's time.
Let us therefore remember Zion in our prayers and seek her welfare above every earthly joy.
Spare your people, Lord, and do not allow your heritage to become a reproach under the power of other nations.

div.title: Ezekiel — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Ezekiel was a priest who was taken captive to Chaldea with Jehoiachin.
Henry believes all Ezekiel's prophecies were delivered there, at a place north of Babylon.
Their chief purpose was to comfort the prophet's fellow exiles.
Ezekiel was called to warn of terrible disasters coming upon Judah, especially judgment against false prophets, as well as against neighboring nations.
He also announced the future restoration of Israel and Judah from their places of dispersion and their blessed condition in later days under the Messiah.
Much teaching about Christ appears in this book, particularly toward its end.

row.cell: Ezekiel's vision of God, and of the angelic host.
A revelation of the Son of man upon his heavenly throne.

div.title: Ezekiel sees the living creatures (verses 1–14)
div.p: It is a mercy when God's word reaches us in the midst of affliction, and our duty to listen to it diligently.
God's voice came through the Holy Spirit, in abundant light and power.
The visions seem intended to fill Ezekiel's mind with great and exalted thoughts of God.
They would awaken fear in sinners while comforting those who feared God and humbled themselves.
The first part, in verses 4–14, pictures God attended by a vast company of angels—his messengers and servants, who do his will.
The scene inspires solemn awe of his holiness and displeasure against sin, yet also hope for blessings.
The fire is surrounded by glory.
Although we cannot discover everything about God by searching, we can see the brightness surrounding his glory.
The living creatures came from the fire, reminding us that angels receive their being and strength from God.
Their appearances combine outstanding qualities.
A human being has understanding, and the angels understand far more.
A lion represents strength and boldness.
An ox represents diligence, patience and tireless work.
An eagle represents speed, sharp vision and soaring height.
The angels surpass human beings in all these qualities.
They have wings, showing the speed with which they carry out God's commands.
They stand upright, firm and steady.
But they have hands as well as wings.
Some people rush from place to place but never accomplish useful work. They have wings without hands.
God's servants, however, are ready both to go and to act.
They move straight ahead, not turning aside to waste time on trivial matters.
Their work needs no correction because they follow the Spirit's direction.
Their fiery appearance suggests seraphim, or burning ones, representing their ardent love for God and zeal in serving him.
