Even visions we cannot fully understand can teach useful lessons.
We should attend especially to whatever concerns our peace and duty, leaving secret matters to the Lord.

div.title: The wheels picture God's Providence (verses 15–25)
div.p: The wheels represent the changing events of Providence.
A wheel turns: first one spoke is above, then another. Yet the rotation remains steady and orderly.
We need not despair during adversity: the wheel may turn in God's time.
Nor should prosperous people become proud, because their circumstances may quickly change.
The wheels stand beside the living creatures because angels serve in God's providential government.
The spirit of the living creatures is in the wheels.
The same divine wisdom, power and holiness that govern the angels direct events in the earthly world.
The wheel presents four faces, picturing Providence extending in every direction.
Wherever you look, there is a face of Providence turned toward you.
A wheel within a wheel expresses how complex and difficult to understand God's dealings can be.
Yet everything is wisely ordered.
The wheels move constantly and follow the Spirit without turning aside.
If we likewise followed the Spirit's direction, we would not repeatedly have to undo through repentance what we had done wrongly.
Their immense rims cause awe.
Thinking about the height and depth of God's counsel should humble us.
Their rims are full of eyes.
Every movement of Providence is directed by infinite wisdom.
The Lord's eyes see both good and evil everywhere.
There is no blind chance or fortune governing the world.
Above the creatures is a glorious yet fearsome firmament like crystal.
What seems to us a dark cloud is clear to God; he sees through it and knows all who live on earth.
When the angels have awakened a careless world, they lower their wings so that God's voice may be heard clearly.
The events of Providence should open our ears to God's revealed word.
The sounds of earth should lead us to listen to the voice from heaven.
How can we escape if we reject the One who speaks there?

div.title: The throne and the likeness of the Son of Man (verses 26–28)
div.p: Henry understands the figure on the throne as representing the eternal Son, the second Person of the Trinity, who would later assume human nature.
He first notices the throne.
It is a throne of glory, grace, triumph, government and judgment.
It is good news for humanity that the throne above the firmament is occupied by One who appears in the likeness of a human being.
A rainbow surrounds the throne.
This familiar sign of the covenant represents God's mercy and covenant love toward his people.
The fire of divine anger was about to break out against Jerusalem, yet limits would be set to the judgment.
God would remember his covenant.
Everything Ezekiel saw prepared him to hear what God would say.
When the prophet fell on his face, he heard the voice of One speaking.
God delights to teach the humble.
Therefore, let sinners humble themselves before him.
And let believers contemplate his glory so that the Spirit of the Lord may gradually transform them into his likeness.

row.cell: The prophet is directed what he is to do.
And encouraged to be resolute, faithful, and devoted.

div.title: Ezekiel is called to speak God's word (verses 1–5)
div.p: Ezekiel had received astonishing revelations.
To keep him from pride, God reminded him that he was still a son of man, a weak and mortal human being.
Yet the title could also be honorable, since Christ often called himself the Son of Man.
Ezekiel's prostrate posture showed reverence.
Standing upright would show greater readiness and fitness for his work.
God speaks to those who are prepared to do what he commands.
But Ezekiel lacked strength in himself.
The Spirit entered him and gave him the ability to stand.
God graciously works in us what he requires from us.
The Holy Spirit raises us to our feet by making our wills inclined toward duty.
When the Lord commands a sinner to awaken and attend to the soul's needs, the Spirit of life and grace accompanies that call.
Ezekiel was sent with God's message to the Israelites.
Many would despise it.
Yet the events would prove that a prophet had indeed been sent to them.
God's glory and the honor of his word will be upheld, whether the message becomes an aroma from life to life or from death to death.

div.title: Ezekiel must preach without fear (verses 6–10)
div.p: Anyone who wants to serve God effectively must not be ruled by fear of people.
The wicked are compared with briers and thorns, near to condemnation and burning.
The prophet must be faithful to the souls of those to whom he is sent.
Everyone who speaks God's message to others must first obey God's voice.
Discovering sin and hearing warnings of God's judgment should move us to grief and lamentation.
Those who understand God's word see that it contains terrible warnings for unrepentant sinners.
They also see that its precious gospel promises belong to repentant and believing servants of the Lord.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections

row.cell: The preparation of the prophet for his work.
His office, as that of a watchman.
The restraining and restoring his speech.

div.title: The prophet receives God's words (verses 1–11)
div.p: Ezekiel was to take God's truths into himself as food for his soul.
By feeding on them through faith, he would gain strength.
People changed by God's grace can receive with joy the same truths that bring terror to the wicked.
Ezekiel was to announce everything God had told him, and nothing beyond it.
How can anyone speak God's mind better than by using his words?
If people refused to listen, Ezekiel must not turn away in offense.
The people of Nineveh responded to Jonah's preaching, while Israel remained stubborn and unchanged.
We must leave such different outcomes under God's sovereignty and confess that his judgments are deep.
Those who refused the prophet's word also refused to learn from God's corrective judgments.
The Lord would strengthen Ezekiel.
He must continue earnestly preaching regardless of the immediate outcome.

div.title: Ezekiel is appointed a watchman (verses 12–21)
div.p: The prophet's mission caused holy angels to rejoice.
These events taught him that God had enough power to sustain him in his work.
Ezekiel was overwhelmed by grief over his people's sins and suffering, and by the majesty of the vision.
Solitude, reflection and fellowship with God can be precious.
Yet the Lord's servant must be prepared to serve the people of his generation.
God appointed Ezekiel to be a watchman for Israel.
If a watchman faithfully warns the wicked, he is not responsible for their refusal and ruin.
Although the passage concerns Israel's national covenant, Henry also applies its warning to the ultimate destiny of all people under every period of God's dealings.
Those who appear righteous need warnings as well as comfort.
Many become proud or careless, fall away and die in their sins.
Listeners to the gospel should welcome rebuke and warning, not only encouragement.

div.title: God regulates the prophet's speech (verses 22–27)
div.p: We owe every blessing of fellowship between God and humanity to Christ's mediation.
A genuine believer can say, “I am never less alone than when I am alone with God.”
When the Lord opened Ezekiel's mouth, the prophet was to speak boldly.
He must place life and death, blessing and curse, before the people, leaving them responsible for their response.

row.cell: The famine the inhabitants would suffer.

div.title: Ezekiel acts out Jerusalem's siege (verses 1–8)
div.p: The prophet was commanded to represent the siege of Jerusalem through signs.
He lay on his left side for a number of days, understood by Henry as possibly corresponding to the years since idolatry had become established.
The prophet's portrayal of the city's coming destruction served one purpose:

p.hi: To show that sin was the cause provoking the ruin of a once-flourishing Jerusalem.

div.title: Ezekiel's restricted food pictures famine (verses 9–17)
div.p: The bread that sustained Ezekiel was to be made from coarse grains and legumes mixed together.
Such food was seldom used except during extreme scarcity.
Even that was to be eaten only in a small amount.
The sign represented the desperate shortage the Jews would suffer during the siege and captivity.
When Ezekiel objected, he did not say he had been raised delicately and had never endured hardship.
Instead, he appealed to his conscientious obedience to the law: he had never eaten food forbidden to him.
It will comfort us when hardship comes if our consciences testify that we have carefully avoided even the appearance of evil.
Consider the terrible ruin caused by sin and acknowledge that God's judgment is righteous.
The people had used abundance for luxury and excess.
Their punishment through famine corresponded to that misuse.
When people refuse to serve the Lord joyfully while they have everything they need, they may end up serving enemies while lacking even the necessities of life.

row.cell: A type of hair, showing the judgments about to come upon the Jews.

div.title: The prophet's divided hair symbolizes the judgments (verses 1–4)
div.p: Ezekiel was commanded to shave his head and beard.
This signified God's complete rejection and abandonment of the people as they persisted in rebellion.
One portion of the hair would be burned inside the city, representing multitudes who would die from famine and disease.
Another would be cut apart, representing those killed by the sword.
A third would be scattered by the wind, representing people carried captive by the conqueror and others fleeing for safety to neighboring countries.
A small part of the scattered hair would be bound in the folds of his clothing to show how carefully a small remnant would be preserved.
Only a few people would be saved.
But sinners cannot escape God's anger merely by choosing a different hiding place.
The fire and sword of divine judgment will reach those who persist without repentance.

div.title: God announces the judgment upon Jerusalem (verses 5–17)
div.p: The sentence against Jerusalem is terrifying, and the language used makes it even more dreadful.
Who could stand before God when his anger is revealed?
Those who live and die without repentance face lasting judgment and will not be spared forever.
Neither people nor churches that change the Lord's commands should assume they will escape the judgment Jerusalem received.
Let us seek to honor the teaching of God our Savior in all we do.
Sooner or later, God's word will prove true.

row.cell: The calamities are to be lamented.

div.title: Idolatry brings God's judgments (verses 1–7)
div.p: War lays waste to people, places and even things that are regarded as most sacred.
God can destroy idolatry through the hands of idolaters themselves.
He is right to turn into a desolation anything we have made an idol.
Superstitions upon which people rely for safety often become the cause of their destruction.
Henry looks forward to a day when idols and idolatry will be removed from the professedly Christian church as thoroughly as they were eventually removed from among the Jews.

div.title: A small remnant will be preserved (verses 8–10)
div.p: A remnant of Israel would survive.
In time these people would remember the Lord, their obligations to him and their earlier rebellion.
Those who sincerely repent recognize sin as the hateful thing God abhors.
They become deeply ashamed of themselves because of the sins they committed.
Their repentance brings glory to God.
Whatever awakens us to remember him and to recognize the wrong we have done against him should be received as a blessing.

div.title: Lamentation and compassion for sinners (verses 11–14)
div.p: Our duty is not only to grieve over our own sin and suffering.
We should also have compassion for the misery that other people bring upon themselves through wickedness.

p.hi: Sin devastates.

div.p: Therefore stand in awe of God and turn away from it.

If we appreciate the worth of human souls and the danger facing those who do not believe, we will consider the salvation of even one sinner who flees to Jesus an ample reward for all the contempt or opposition we may encounter in serving him.

row.cell: The distress of the few who should escape.

div.title: The end of the land's prosperity (verses 1–15)
div.p: The abruptness and repetition of this prophecy show how deeply the prophet was moved by the disaster he foresaw.
The final destruction of unrepentant sinners will be just as inescapable.
Oh, may the wicked person's wrongdoing come to an end before it brings the person to an end!
For someone who refuses repentance, trouble does nothing but harm: it hardens the heart and stirs sinful desires.
Yet God can, through his grace, make the very same suffering a means of much good for another person.
The day of genuine trouble was near—not merely rumors or distant echoes.
Whatever visible effects God's judgment produces, our sin is the root beneath them.
The judgments would spread everywhere.
God would be glorified in all of them.
Now is the time of the Lord's patience and mercy.
But the time when sinners face judgment is approaching.

div.title: The surviving people suffer (verses 16–22)
div.p: Sooner or later sin brings sorrow.
Those who will not repent may justly be left to waste away under the sins they refuse to abandon.
For many people, wealth is a snare leading to ruin.
Gaining the whole world can mean losing the soul.
Riches do not help in the day of God's anger.
The world's possessions cannot meet the soul's deepest needs or bring lasting satisfaction in distress.
Even God's temple would be no protection for people who rejected his ways.
Those unwilling to be ruled by the power of godliness are unworthy to keep the honor of its outward form.

div.title: God's judgment brings captivity (verses 23–27)
div.p: People who break free of the obligations of God's law will find themselves bound by the chains of his judgment.
Because they encouraged one another in sin, the Lord would cause them to lose courage.
When God judges people according to what they deserve, distress reaches everyone.
May he enable us to seek the good portion that can never be taken away.

row.cell: The idolatries committed by the Jewish rulers.
The superstitions to which the Jews were then devoted, the Egyptian.

div.title: The idolatry within the temple (verses 1–6)
div.p: In a vision, the glorious figure Ezekiel saw seemed to take hold of him and carry him in the Spirit to Jerusalem.
There he saw a place prepared for a degrading idol within the inner court of the temple.
The entire scene was presented to the prophet as a vision.
If God gave any of us a clear view of his glory and majesty alongside the many abominations practiced in a city, we would see the justice of even his severest judgments against that city.

div.title: The elders' secret worship (verses 7–12)
div.p: A hidden room was opened to Ezekiel.
The walls were covered with pictures of creatures, and elders of Israel worshiped before them.
High position in the world does not preserve people from sinful desires or idolatry if they are abandoned to the deceit of their own hearts.
Some who quickly tire of God's service are willing to spend great time, labor and money on superstition.
Hypocrites try to conceal themselves behind a wall of outward profession.
Yet some opening remains through which careful observers may discover what they are really doing.
Much wickedness is practiced in secret.
These people imagined God could not see them.
Those who try to make the Lord responsible for their sins are especially ready for judgment.

div.title: Tammuz, sun worship and the depth of corruption (verses 13–18)
div.p: The annual mourning for Tammuz was associated, in Henry's account, with shameful practices.
He supposes that those worshiping the sun were priests.
The Lord called Ezekiel to recognize the gravity of these sins.
The reference to putting a branch to the nose is, in Henry's explanation, a custom performed in honor of an idol.
The more closely we examine human nature and our own hearts, the more wrongdoing we discover.
The more earnestly a believer searches the heart, the more humbly that person should stand before God and the more highly value the fountain opened for cleansing from sin.
Let us seek to wash there.

p.hi: A vision denoting the destruction of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the departure of the symbol of the Divine presence.

div.title: The faithful remnant is marked (verses 1–4)
div.p: It is a great comfort for believers that, even among destroyers and destruction, there is a Mediator.
He is the great High Priest, with access to heaven, and believers on earth have an interest in him.
God's glory appeared to move from above the ark toward the threshold.
This signified that the Lord was about to leave his mercy seat and announce judgment against the people.
Those marked for preservation were known by their sorrow over Jerusalem's sins.
They sighed and cried to God in prayer because of the abominations taking place in the city.
Those whom God keeps pure amid widespread wickedness he can keep safe amid widespread distress.

div.title: The judgment begins at the sanctuary (verses 5–11)
div.p: The slaughter was to begin in the sanctuary.
This showed that God is especially displeased by sins committed by people nearest to him and most privileged by his gifts.
The person appointed to protect the faithful reported that his task was completed.
This points, in Henry's application, to Christ's perfect faithfulness to his Father's trust.
The Son was appointed to give eternal life to the people entrusted to him.
He declares that he has lost none whom the Father gave him.
If we are rescued while others perish, all the credit belongs to God's mercy.
We too have deserved his wrath.
We should continue interceding for others.
But wherever the Lord shows judgment rather than mercy, he acts with no injustice: he gives people what their ways deserve.

row.cell: A vision of the burning of the city.
The Divine glory departing from the temple.

div.title: Fire from among the cherubim (verses 1–7)
div.p: The fire taken from between the wheels, beneath the cherubim, recalls Ezekiel 1:13.
Henry understands it as a sign of God's anger about to fall upon Jerusalem.
The vision shows that divine judgment is not arbitrary.
The fire of God's wrath, which brings judgment upon a nation, is just and holy.
It also points toward the great day when the earth and all its works will be consumed.

div.title: The glory of the Lord departs (verses 8–22)
div.p: Ezekiel saw how divine Providence governs events in the world.
When God withdraws from a people who have provoked his displeasure, angels above and events on earth serve to accomplish his purpose.
The Spirit of life, the Spirit of God, directs every creature in heaven and on earth so that each contributes to the divine plan.
God's departure from a rebellious people takes place by degrees.
Even when the Lord is ready to leave, he would return if the people repented and prayed.
May this warn sinners to seek the Lord while he may be found and call upon him while he is near.
And may it cause us all to walk humbly and carefully with our God.

row.cell: Divine judgments against the wicked at Jerusalem.
Divine favour towards those in captivity.
The Divine presence forsakes the city.

div.title: Judgment on Jerusalem's confident rulers (verses 1–13)
div.p: When Satan cannot persuade people that God's judgment is uncertain, he tries to make them believe it is far away.
The rulers of Jerusalem imagined themselves safe inside their city.
They compared its walls to a cooking pot and themselves to the meat protected inside.
They expected the walls to withstand the siege as confidently as a pot withstands the heat beneath it.
But people who flatter themselves toward destruction must be warned that they will have no peace while continuing in sin.
Those who would remain in the city were not the secure living inhabitants but the people buried there.
Those who feel most secure may be the least safe.
God may single out a particular sinner's judgment to warn others.
Yet Henry does not claim certainty about exactly when Pelatiah died—whether during the vision's events or near their future fulfillment.
Like Ezekiel, we should be deeply moved by the sudden death of others and continue pleading for God's mercy toward those who remain.

div.title: God promises to give his people new hearts (verses 14–21)
div.p: The godly Israelites in Babylon were scorned by those still living in Jerusalem.
But God gave the exiles gracious promises.
He would give them one heart: a heart firmly devoted to him rather than divided and wavering.
Those who are made holy receive a new spirit—a renewed character and new inclinations.
They act from new principles, follow new rules and seek new goals.
A new name or a new appearance is not enough without a new spirit.
Anyone who is in Christ is a new creation.
A sinful heart is like stone: it does not feel what it should.
People may live amid death and suffering without being concerned or humbled.
The Lord promises to make their hearts tender and responsive.
This is God's own work, a gift he promised.
The change from death to life is wonderful and blessed.
People whose inward principles are renewed will also show changed conduct.
The two belong together.
When sinners recognize how much they need these blessings, let them turn God's promises into prayers offered in Christ's name.
He will fulfill what he has promised.

div.title: God's glory withdraws from Jerusalem (verses 22–25)
div.p: The vision shows God's presence leaving the city and temple.
It rises from the Mount of Olives, which Henry takes as a picture of Christ's ascension to heaven from that same mountain.
The Lord will never finally abandon his people.
Yet a particular part of the visible church may lose the experience of his presence because of its sins.
Woe to those from whom he withdraws his presence, glory and protection.

row.cell: An emblem of the consternation of the Jews.
Answers to the objections of scoffers.

div.title: Ezekiel pictures the coming exile (verses 1–16)
div.p: Ezekiel prepared belongings for departure and broke through the wall of his house at evening, as someone trying to escape an enemy might do.
These actions pictured Zedekiah's behavior and fate.
When God delivers us from trouble, we must give him glory and help others learn from what happened, including by acknowledging our sins.
People brought through suffering to recognize the Lord may themselves become a means through which others come to know him.

div.title: The prophet eats and drinks in fear (verses 17–20)
div.p: Ezekiel was to eat and drink with fear, anxiety and trembling.
This pictured what the inhabitants of Jerusalem would experience during the siege.
Ministers announcing judgment upon sinners should speak as people who know the terror of the Lord.
Although afflictions may be deeply painful to our bodies and emotions, they can become blessed if they increase our knowledge of God.

div.title: Scoffers cannot postpone God's word (verses 21–28)
div.p: The Jews took God's patience—which should have led them to repent—as a reason to become more stubborn in sin.
Calling something a common saying does not excuse using it to speak wrongly.
Only a short step separates us from eternity and judgment.
We should therefore prepare for the life to come.
No one can avert the day of judgment by dismissing its warnings or imagining it is far off.
The only safe response is to seek peace with the Lord.

div.title: False prophets speak their own inventions (verses 1–9)
div.p: When God appoints someone to a task, he also gives wisdom for it.
The false prophets did not speak what they had received from God.
By contrast, the ministers of Christ must proclaim what God has revealed.
These false prophets did not pray or maintain fellowship with heaven.
They devised words designed to please people rather than to do them good.
They did not resist sin or call people to repentance.
Instead, they flattered people into empty expectations.
Such teachers widen the breach between sinners and God.
They persuade people they are entitled to eternal life while God's wrath still rests upon them.

div.title: Whitewashed walls cannot stand (verses 10–16)
div.p: One false prophet built the wall by announcing that Jerusalem would succeed and escape danger.
That promise made him popular.
Other prophets made the prediction appear still more convincing by coating the wall with smooth plaster.
But God's righteous judgment would come like a storm and destroy the poorly constructed wall when the Chaldeans devastated the land.
Hopes of peace and happiness that God's word does not authorize are deceptive.
They resemble a wall with a beautiful finish but no sound foundation.

div.title: False prophetesses mislead the people (verses 17–23)
div.p: It is a terrible thing to prefer pleasant lies to painful truths.
The false prophetesses tried to persuade the people that they were safe.
Henry understands their acts as imagery of giving people ease and encouraging pride through elaborate decorations.
Their schemes would fail, and God would free his people from their influence.
Christians must remain close to God's word and seek the Holy Spirit's teaching in everything.
Let us trust his promises in such a way that we also obey his commandments.

row.cell: God's purpose to punish the guilty Jews, but a few should be saved.

div.title: Idols in the heart make outward worship empty (verses 1–11)
div.p: No outward religious ceremony or reform can be acceptable to God while an idol rules the heart.
Yet many people prefer their own inventions and supposed righteousness to God's appointed way of salvation.
Sinful desires and corrupt habits become idols people set up within themselves.
God may let them continue down that path.
Sin makes a person hateful in the sight of the pure and holy God.
It also becomes hateful to the sinner when conscience finally awakens.
Let us seek to be cleansed from both the guilt and the pollution of sin in the fountain God has opened.

div.title: Judgment and the limits of others' righteousness (verses 12–23)

p.hi: National sins bring national judgments.

div.p: A sinner who escapes one judgment may still encounter another.
When people who publicly profess God's name rebel against him, they have reason to expect his judgment.
Noah's faith, obedience and prayer helped save his household, but did not save the whole world.
Job's offerings and prayers for his friends were accepted.
Daniel's intercession helped preserve his companions and the wise men of Babylon.
Yet a people who have reached the full measure of wickedness cannot expect to escape God's announced judgment simply because righteous people live among them.
Even the holiest believers are accepted personally only through Christ's suffering and righteousness.
Nevertheless, even amid the most widespread devastation, God preserves some people as living examples of his mercy.
We may trust that we will ultimately recognize the wisdom and justice of all his dealings, both with ourselves and with humanity.
Let this confidence quiet our rebellious murmuring and objections.

p.hi: Jerusalem like an unfruitful vine.

div.title: Jerusalem as an unfruitful vine
div.p: A vine is valuable when it produces fruit.
If it bears none, its wood is nearly useless and is fit only to be thrown into the fire.
In the same way, human beings are capable of producing precious fruit by living for God.
This is the true purpose for which we exist.
If people refuse that purpose completely, their lives produce none of the fruit they were made to bear and end in ruin.
How blind are those who live in total neglect of God and genuine religion!
The picture applies especially to Jerusalem.
Let us beware of an outward profession of faith that bears no fruit.
Instead, let us come to Christ, remain in him, and seek to have his words remain in us.

p.hi: A parable showing the first low estate of the Jewish nation, its prosperity, idolatries, and punishment.

div.title: Jerusalem's history pictured as an unfaithful woman (verses 1–58)
div.p: This chapter recounts God's dealings with the Jewish nation and the way the people responded to him.
It also describes the punishment that came through the surrounding nations—even through those in whom the Jews had trusted most.
The account is told as an extended parable.
An abandoned infant is rescued from death, brought up and cared for, joined in marriage and generously provided for.
Later, despite such kindness, she commits the most shameful acts of unfaithfulness and is punished for them.
Yet in the end she is received into favor and becomes ashamed of the conduct she had committed.
We must understand these expressions with regard to the customs, language and circumstances of their own time, rather than judging their tone entirely by modern expectations.
Many phrases that now seem shocking would have sounded different to their original hearers.
The purpose of the imagery was to inspire abhorrence of idolatry.
Henry believes this kind of parable was especially well suited to that end.

div.title: God remembers mercy and covenant (verses 59–63)
div.p: After a full warning of coming judgment, the Lord remembers mercy.
Mercy remains reserved for his people.
These closing verses contain a precious promise.
Part of it was fulfilled when repentant, reformed Jews returned from Babylon.
But Henry understands it to reach a fuller fulfillment in the gospel age.
God's gracious mercy should melt our hearts and awaken genuine sorrow over sin.
He will never leave a sinner to perish who humbles himself for sin and trusts in divine mercy and grace through Jesus Christ.
He will preserve that person by his power, through faith unto salvation.

row.cell: A parable relative to the Jewish nation.
to which an explanation is added.
A direct promise of the Messiah.

div.title: The parable of the great eagles (verses 1–10)
div.p: Powerful conquerors are aptly compared with birds or beasts of prey.
Yet their destructive passions are directed and overruled to accomplish God's purposes.
Those who depart from the Lord and then seek security by changing from one earthly support to another merely change the form of their sin.
They will not truly prosper.

div.title: The parable is explained and Zedekiah rebuked (verses 11–21)
div.p: The prophecy now explains the parable through the history of the Jewish nation.
Zedekiah had been ungrateful to his benefactor, which was itself a sin against God.
In every solemn oath, the one who swears calls God as a witness to the truthfulness of the promise.
We owe truth to everyone, not only to members of our own religion.
When people who profess true religion betray those who practice false religion, their profession makes their wrongdoing more serious, not less.
God will punish their treachery even more severely.
He will not leave unpunished those who misuse his name.
No one who dies still bearing unrepented guilt will escape God's righteous judgment.

div.title: God promises the Messiah (verses 22–24)
div.p: Human unbelief cannot make God's promise fail.
The tree imagery used earlier as a threat now becomes part of a promise.
Henry understands this promise as referring especially to Jesus Christ, the Son of David, God's Messiah.
Satan's kingdom has long exercised great power, but it will be broken.
Christ's kingdom, once despised and disregarded, will be firmly established.
Blessed be God: our Redeemer will be known to the farthest ends of the earth.
Under his shadow we may find refuge from the coming wrath and from every spiritual enemy and danger.
Believers bear fruit in him.

row.cell: God has no respect of persons.

div.title: Everyone is responsible before God (verses 1–20)

p.hi: “The soul that sins shall die.”

div.p: With respect to eternal life, people are treated according to their true standing: either under the old covenant of works or under the new covenant of grace, as their conduct shows.
People may suffer outwardly because of sins committed by others.
But we also have sins of our own, and God governs every circumstance for the eternal good of believers.
Every soul belongs to the great Creator.
He deals with all in justice or mercy.
No one is condemned eternally merely for another person's sin while remaining personally innocent of guilt.
All of us have sinned.
If God judged us only by his holy law, we would be lost.
Yet he invites us to come to Jesus Christ.
Consider the children of different parents.
A person whose faith is demonstrated by good works may have a wicked child whose character is entirely unlike that parent's.
The child cannot expect to escape judgment through the parent's godliness.
Likewise, a wicked person's child who walks righteously before God will not be destroyed for the sins of the parent.
That righteous child may still suffer in this life, but will share in salvation.

p.hi: This chapter is not explaining how anyone earns justification.

div.p: It describes the Lord's righteous dealings with the wicked and the righteous.

div.title: God receives the person who turns from sin (verses 21–29)
div.p: A wicked person who turns from evil ways may be saved.
The person who truly repents truly believes.
Former sins are no longer held against that person.
The righteousness shown afterward is the fruit of faith and the result of conversion, not the purchase price of salvation.
The passage does not settle the separate question of whether a genuinely righteous believer can finally apostatize.
Many people who were thought righteous for a time later turn away from God.
But verses 26–27 display the fullness of his forgiving mercy.
When sin is forgiven, it is blotted out and remembered no more.
The believer lives in righteousness, not because that righteousness pays for former sins.
Holy living itself is a blessing purchased through the Mediator.
What encouragement this offers sinners returning to God!
Verse 28 describes both the beginning of repentance and how it continues.
Genuine believers remain watchful and prayerful and continue to the end, and thus are saved.
Whenever we dispute with God, he is right and we are wrong.

div.title: The Lord calls his people to repentance (verses 30–32)
div.p: The Lord will judge each Israelite according to that person's ways.
On this basis he calls them to repent and receive a new heart and new spirit.
God commands his people to take seriously the responsibilities within their reach and to pray for the inward change that only he can give.
He has appointed means of grace and ordinances and given both directions and promises.
Those who desire a new heart should therefore seek it from him.

row.cell: A parable lamenting the ruin of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim.
Another describing the desolation of the people.

div.title: Judah's kings are pictured as young lions (verses 1–9)
div.p: Ezekiel compares the kingdom of Judah to a lioness, and its kings to her young lions.
These rulers were cruel and oppressive toward their own people.
We should acknowledge God's righteousness when those who terrified and enslaved others are in turn terrified and enslaved.
When people who profess faith form close relationships with the ungodly, their children often grow up following the standards and fashions of a wicked world.
Receiving greater authority exposes the ambition and self-interest hidden in human hearts.
Those who devote their lives to harmful acts often bring them to an end through violence.

div.title: Jerusalem is pictured as a ruined vine (verses 10–14)
div.p: Jerusalem had once been like a fruitful, thriving vine.
Now the vine had been ruined, though its roots were not completely pulled up.
Through wickedness, the people had made themselves like dry tinder waiting for the sparks of God's judgment.
Even their own branches became fuel for their destruction.
Yet blessed be God!
One Branch belonging to the royal line pictured here not only became a strong rod fit for a ruler's scepter.
He is the true and living Vine himself.
All God's chosen people, through every generation, may rejoice in him.

row.cell: The elders of Israel are reminded of the idolatry in Egypt.
God promises to pardon and restore them.

div.title: The elders are reminded of Israel's sins in Egypt (verses 1–9)
div.p: People have become terribly hardened when they ask God to let them continue sinning, even while already suffering for sin.
See Ezekiel 20:32.
God is rightly angry with people who remain determined to persist in their wrongdoing.
Ezekiel was to remind the nation of its ancestors' evil deeds so that they would recognize the justice of God's earlier judgments.

div.title: The people rebelled in the wilderness (verses 10–26)
div.p: Israel's wilderness history is recalled in both the Old Testament and the New Testament as a warning.
God had done wonderful things for his people.
He gave them his law and renewed the ancient observance of the Sabbath.
Sabbaths are privileges and signs of belonging to him.
When we honor their purpose, we discover that God himself makes us holy and truly happy in this life, preparing us for the perfect holiness and happiness of heaven.
But the Israelites rebelled and were left to suffer the judgments their sins had brought.
Sometimes God permits sin to become its own punishment.
Yet God is never the author of sin.
People may be made thoroughly miserable simply by being handed over to their own evil desires and passions.

div.title: Israel's rebellion continued in Canaan (verses 27–32)
div.p: After the people settled in Canaan, they continued rebelling.
The elders listening to Ezekiel seemed to be considering merging with the surrounding nations and their worship.
An outward profession of faith accomplishes nothing if it remains only a profession.
Sinful compromise brings no real advantage.
The worldly schemes of hypocrites will ultimately be useless to them.

div.title: God promises to restore and renew a remnant (verses 33–44)
div.p: Wicked Israelites who followed other nations in sin would not share those nations' prosperity.
Instead, God would separate them for judgment.
No one can escape the Lord's rule.
Those who refuse to submit to the power of his grace will face the power of his wrath.
But God will not lose a single one of his jewels amid the confusion of the world.
He will bring the Jews back to Israel's land and give them genuine repentance.
Their hearts will be overcome by his kindness.
The more we know of God's holiness, the more clearly we recognize how hateful sin is.
People who remain unmoved despite God's gracious means, and who insist on living without Christ like the surrounding world, are moving toward destruction.

div.title: Judgment is announced against fruitless Jerusalem (verses 45–49)
div.p: Judah and Jerusalem had been full of people, like a forest filled with trees.
Yet they produced no good fruit.
God's word speaks against those who refuse to bear the fruits of righteousness.
When he determines to bring a nation low, who can rescue it?
Even the clearest truths sounded like parables to the people.
Those who refuse to respond to God's word commonly blame the message rather than admit their unwillingness to obey.

row.cell: The ruin of Judah under the emblem of a sharp sword.
The approach of the king of Babylon described.

div.title: The sword of judgment approaches Judah (verses 1–17)
div.p: This passage explains the parable at the end of the previous chapter.
The Lord announced that Jerusalem and the whole land would be cut down.
Everyone would learn that the judgment came from his decree against a wicked and rebellious people.
Those who proclaim God's dreadful judgment on sinners should make it clear that they do not delight in the day of suffering.

p.hi: Christ's example teaches us to weep over the people whose destruction we must announce.

div.p: Whatever instruments the Lord chooses to execute judgment, he gives them the strength required for their appointed task.
The sword flashes with terror before those against whom it is drawn.
To some it is a sword; to the Lord's people it is a rod of discipline.
God is serious about this sentence, and the prophet must show the same seriousness in proclaiming it.

div.title: Nebuchadnezzar is directed toward Jerusalem (verses 18–27)
div.p: Through the Spirit of prophecy, Ezekiel foresaw Nebuchadnezzar marching from Babylon.
The king would decide his direction by divination.
Yet the Lord's wise purposes governed the outcome.
God would overthrow Judah's government until the arrival of the One whose right it is to rule.
Henry sees this as pointing beyond the immediate events to the continuing upheavals of the Jewish nation and the changes of earthly states and kingdoms.
These would prepare the way for the Messiah's kingdom throughout the earth.
The Lord secretly directs events toward his wise designs.
Even amid the most terrifying warnings of judgment, we hear a word of mercy, pointing toward the One through whom mercy comes to sinful people.

div.title: Ammon's false confidence ends in destruction (verses 28–32)
div.p: The Ammonites' diviners falsely promised victory.
The nation would ultimately lose its power and disappear from memory.
Let us be thankful that God has appointed us to serve as instruments of mercy.
We should use our understanding and abilities to do good, and keep away from those whose only skill is causing destruction.

row.cell: As the corruption is general, so shall be the punishment.

div.title: Jerusalem is accused of many sins (verses 1–16)
div.p: The prophet was told to judge the city of bloodshed.
Jerusalem deserved that name because of its crimes.
The charges were exceedingly serious: murder, idolatry, dishonoring parents, oppression, extortion, profaning the Sabbath and holy things, sexual immorality and adultery.
At the root of these wrongs lay forgetfulness of God.
Sinners provoke him because they refuse to remember him.
Jerusalem had filled the measure of her sins.
People who surrender themselves to the rule of their sinful desires may justly be handed over to their consequences.
Those determined to be their own masters cannot expect more happiness than they can supply for themselves.
It will be a miserable portion.

div.title: Israel is like worthless dross (verses 17–22)
div.p: Among surrounding nations, Israel had once been as gold and silver compared with inferior metals.
But now the people resembled the worthless residue separated from silver in the furnace.
In God's sight, persistent sinners—especially people who profess faith but turn back to sin—are without the usefulness they were meant to have.
When the Lord brings his own people into a furnace of affliction, he watches over them like a refiner guarding his precious gold.
He keeps them there no longer than necessary.
The worthless residue is separated and the good metal made pure.
If we experience severe pain or long illness and find even these temporary trials almost unbearable, we should be warned to flee the far greater wrath to come.
Unless the Holy Spirit uses our suffering to cleanse our hearts and conduct, much worse misery may await us.

div.title: Every level of society is corrupt (verses 23–31)
div.p: People of every rank and occupation contributed to the nation's guilt.
Those who possessed authority abused it.
Even buyers and sellers found ways to oppress one another.
It is a fearful sign when judgment is beginning and the spirit of prayer has weakened.
Let everyone who fears God unite to uphold his truth and righteousness, while wicked people from every profession and class unite to oppose them.

p.hi: A history of the apostacy of God's people from him, and the aggravation thereof.

div.title: Aholah and Aholibah picture Israel and Judah
div.p: The parable gives Samaria and the northern kingdom of Israel the name Aholah, meaning “her own tabernacle.”
Their places of worship came from their own inventions rather than God's command.
Jerusalem and Judah are called Aholibah, meaning “my tabernacle is in her.”
Their temple was the place God himself had chosen for his name to dwell.
The imagery and language of this passage belong to the times and circumstances in which they were used.
These humbling descriptions of fallen human nature should keep us in a spirit of repentance and sorrow over sin.
They should remove pride from our hearts and turn us away from self-righteousness.
They should also lead us to seek God's grace continually, praying that his Holy Spirit would enable us to put sinful conduct to death and live in holiness and godliness.

row.cell: The extent of the sufferings of the Jews.

div.title: Jerusalem is pictured as a pot on the fire (verses 1–14)
div.p: The pot heated over the fire represented Jerusalem being besieged by the Chaldeans.
People of every position and class were inside the city walls and were about to become their enemies' prey.
They should have removed their sins as scum is skimmed from boiling food.
Instead, they became more corrupt, and their suffering grew worse.
Jerusalem would be leveled to the ground.
The appointed hour of judgment may appear to approach slowly, but it will certainly arrive.
How sorrowful to consider how many people gain nothing from God's appointed worship or the events of his Providence!

div.title: Ezekiel's bereavement is a sign (verses 15–27)
div.p: Mourning those who die is normally a duty.
But religion and sound judgment must restrain our grief.
We should not grieve as people without hope.
Believers need not imitate the words or gestures of those who do not know God.
The people asked Ezekiel what his strange actions meant.
The Lord was about to remove from them everything they held most precious.
Just as Ezekiel did not publicly mourn his own loss in the customary manner, the people's coming sorrow would exceed ordinary expressions of lament.
Blessed be God: we need not sink under suffering forever.
Even if every earthly comfort fails and all sorrows arrive together, a broken heart and a mourner's sincere prayer remain acceptable to him.

row.cell: Against the Moabites, Edomites, and Philistines.

div.title: The Ammonites are judged for rejoicing in Judah's ruin (verses 1–7)
div.p: It is wicked to rejoice when anyone suffers, especially when the sufferers belong to God's people.
God will certainly call such cruelty to account.
Even while he permits Israel to be held captive in Babylon, he will show that he remains the God of Israel.
It is better to know the Lord while poor than to be wealthy and ignorant of him.

div.title: Moab, Edom and Philistia face judgment (verses 8–17)
div.p: The same outward event may happen to both righteous and wicked people, yet its meaning and final consequence may be entirely different.
Those who boast in any protection apart from God's power, Providence and promises will eventually be ashamed of their confidence.
People who refuse to leave vengeance in God's hands may expect his judgment to fall upon them.
The Lord's judgments are fair.
Sometimes he avenges an injury through the people who suffered it, and the justice of his action remains visible.
Those who nurture old hatreds, waiting for a chance to act upon them, are storing up wrath for the day of wrath.

p.hi: A prophecy against Tyre.

div.title: Tyre's selfish prosperity will be destroyed (verses 1–14)
div.p: It is an easily overlooked but serious sin to be secretly pleased when others decline or die because we expect to benefit, or when their downfall allows us to become more prosperous.
Such pleasure comes from selfishness and greed and from regarding the world as our source of happiness. Love for God expressly forbids that attitude.
God often brings to nothing the projects of those who hope to advance themselves through other people's ruin.
Many of the principles most commonly accepted in the world of trade directly oppose God's law.
The Lord will confront merchants whose love of money and selfishness have hardened their hearts, as they had hardened the hearts of the people of Tyre.
People have little reason to boast about goods that provoke others' envy and greed and constantly pass from one owner to another.
In acquiring, protecting and spending such wealth, people may offend God, whose anger can turn a joyful city into a heap of ruins.

div.title: The fall of Tyre warns prosperous people (verses 15–21)
div.p: Consider how important and impressive Tyre once was—and how low it would be brought.
The downfall of others should awaken us from careless confidence.
Every clear fulfillment of a biblical prophecy is like a miracle that strengthens our faith.
Everything merely earthly is vanity and frustration.
Even those whose prosperity seems most secure will soon disappear from sight and be forgotten.

div.title: Tyre's trade and riches (verses 1–25)
div.p: People who live comfortably are still to be pitied if they are unprepared for trouble.
No one should consider themselves truly beautiful or adorned except to the extent that they have been made holy.
The description of Tyre's trade reminds us that God sees what people do while conducting ordinary business.
He watches us not only when we are at church, praying and listening, but also at markets and fairs, while buying and selling.
We should preserve a conscience free of wrongdoing in all our dealings.
As the common Father of humanity, God gives different countries different resources.
One nation produces an abundance of something another lacks, and their goods can serve the needs, comfort and even enjoyment of human life.
Trade is a blessing when conducted in reverence for God.
Besides essentials, many goods become valuable chiefly through custom. Yet God permits us to enjoy them.
But when riches increase, we easily set our hearts on them and forget the Lord who gives us the ability to gain wealth.

div.title: Tyre's downfall warns those who trust worldly power (verses 26–36)
div.p: Even the strongest and most impressive kingdoms eventually fall.
Those who make created things their ultimate confidence will fall along with what they trust.
Happy are those whose help is the God of Jacob, and whose hope rests in the Lord, who lives forever.
People engaged in trade should conduct their business according to God's word.
Those who possess wealth must remember that they are stewards of God's property and should use it to do good to everyone.
Let us seek first God's kingdom and his righteousness.

row.cell: The sentence against the prince or king of Tyre.

div.title: The king of Tyre is humbled for pride (verses 1–19)
div.p: Henry identifies the prince or king of Tyre as Ethbaal, or Ithobal.
Lifted up by excessive pride, this ruler claimed honors belonging to God.
Pride is especially characteristic of fallen human nature.
No wisdom except that which God gives can bring lasting happiness, whether in this life or the life to come.
The proud ruler imagined that he could protect his people through his own power and regarded himself as equal to the inhabitants of heaven.
Yet even if we could live in the garden of Eden or enter heaven itself, we would find no true happiness without a humble, holy and spiritual heart.
Spiritual pride in particular comes from the devil.
Those who cherish it must expect destruction.

div.title: Sidon is judged and Israel promised restoration (verses 20–26)
div.p: The people of Sidon lived near Israel.
They could have learned to glorify the Lord.
Instead, they led Israelites into the worship of their own idols.
War and disease can be instruments of divine judgment.
But God will also reveal his glory by restoring his people to security and well-being.
He will heal them of their sins and relieve their suffering.
This promise will find its complete fulfillment in the heavenly Canaan, where all the saints are gathered, everything offensive is removed, and every grief and fear ends forever.
Blessed are God's church and all who truly belong to it, even while they are poor, afflicted or despised.
The Lord will reveal his truth, power and mercy through the salvation and happiness of his redeemed people.

row.cell: Also a promise of mercy to Israel.

div.title: Egypt's boasting and its ruin (verses 1–16)
div.p: Worldly people boast about their possessions while forgetting that everything they have came from God and ought to be used for him.
What reason do we have to boast?
Self is the great idol that people everywhere worship in disregard of God and his authority.
The Lord can drive people away from the very circumstances in which they feel most secure and comfortable.
Those who cling to such a person or source of security may perish along with it.
That is how pride, presumption and false confidence end.
God opposes those who harm his people, and even more those who lead them into sin.
Egypt would become a kingdom again, but a very lowly kingdom, with little wealth or political power.
Henry says its later history shows the fulfillment of the prophecy.
It is not only in justice, but also in wisdom and goodness toward us, that the Lord sometimes breaks the created supports on which we lean, so they will no longer be our confidence.

div.title: God recompenses Babylon and preserves mercy for Israel (verses 17–21)
div.p: Those who besieged Tyre gained little plunder.
But when God uses ambitious or greedy people for his purposes, he may reward them according to the desires of their own hearts; everyone receives an appropriate recompense.
Mercy would soon be shown to the house of Israel.
The history of nations helps explain ancient prophecies, and events fulfill God's word.
Even in the deepest trouble, the Lord can be sowing the seeds of future well-being.
Happy are those who seek his favor, grace and likeness.
They delight in serving him and do not covet an earthly reward.
The blessings they seek will remain theirs forever.

div.title: Egypt will be devastated (verses 1–19)
div.p: This prophecy gives a full account of Egypt's coming destruction.
Those who join themselves to God's enemies will share in their punishment.
The king of Babylon and his army would become instruments of that destruction.
God often makes one wicked person a means of judgment against another.
No place in Egypt would escape the fury of the Chaldeans.
The Lord makes himself known through the judgments he executes.
Yet all these are only present effects of divine displeasure.
They are not worthy of comparison with the wrath to come, from which Jesus delivers his people.

div.title: Egypt is weakened further (verses 20–26)
div.p: Egypt would become weaker and weaker.
If lesser judgments do not humble sinners and lead them to reform, God may send greater ones.
He justly breaks power that has been abused to oppress or cheat others.
Babylon would grow stronger.
It is useless to try to bind up the arm God has decided to break, or to strengthen people he has determined to bring down.
Those who disregard the revelations of God's truth and mercy will come to know his power and justice through the punishment of their sins.

row.cell: Its fall, and the like for Egypt.

div.title: Assyria's glory is pictured as a cedar (verses 1–9)
div.p: When we see others fall into sin and ruin, we should be warned against pride and false confidence.
The prophet presents an example of a ruler whose greatness resembled that of the king of Egypt.
Assyria is compared with a magnificent cedar tree.
Those who rise above others often become objects of envy.
But the blessings of the heavenly paradise are never spoiled in this way.
The greatest security any created thing can offer is like the shadow of a tree: narrow and fragile protection.
Let us therefore seek our safety with God, where we truly can rest.
We must recognize his hand in the rise of powerful people, rather than envy them.
Though worldly prosperity may appear firmly established, its security is only an appearance.

div.title: Assyria's fall warns Egypt (verses 10–18)
div.p: The king of Egypt resembled Assyria's king in greatness.
He also resembled him in pride, and would resemble him in ruin.
His own sin caused his downfall.
We lose no earthly comfort that we have not already forfeited many times through sin.
When powerful rulers fall, they often draw many others into destruction with them, just as many powerful rulers have fallen before them.
Their downfall should warn us to remain humble.
Look how low Pharaoh would be brought!
What would remain of his splendor and pride?
It is better to be a lowly tree of righteousness, bearing fruit for God's glory and other people's good.
The wicked may flourish like a tall cedar or a spreading bay tree, but soon they disappear and their place can no longer be found.
Let us observe the upright person: the end of that person is peace.

row.cell: It is like that of other nations.

div.title: The fall of Egypt is lamented (verses 1–16)
div.p: It is fitting for us to weep and tremble on behalf of people who will not weep or tremble for themselves.
In God's judgment, great oppressors are no better than beasts of prey.
People who admire the world's splendor will be astonished when that splendor collapses.
Those who already know how empty earthly things are will be less surprised.
When other people are destroyed by their sins, we too have reason to fear, since we also are guilty.
The instruments of Egypt's destruction were powerful, and the examples of devastation frightening.
Egypt's waters would flow like oil.
Henry understands this as a sign that deep sadness and heaviness would cover the nation.
God can quickly empty people who possess a great abundance of worldly goods.
The more things we depend on for happiness, the more occasions we create for grief when they disappear.
Even the strongest human beings are weak and helpless before God.
The destruction of Egypt pictured the destruction of Christ's enemies.

div.title: Egypt joins other nations in the grave (verses 17–32)
div.p: Many nations had been devastated and carried down to the grave before Egypt.
In the prophetic picture, they wait to receive Egypt with contempt.
Yet Judah and Jerusalem, although devastated around the same time by the same power, are not included in this list.
The difference lay in God's merciful purpose in correcting his own people and the salvation he had reserved for them.
For Judah, the suffering was not the same final descent into the pit.
Pharaoh would see the other nations and find a kind of consolation.
But the comfort wicked people imagine enjoying after death is only fantasy, not real comfort.
This picture of ruined kingdoms shows how sorrowful the present world is and how strong the rule of death appears in it.
Human beings already die quickly enough, yet they devise ingenious ways to destroy one another.
The passage also makes us look toward the next world.
Although it chiefly concerns the destruction of nations, Henry understands it to contain an unmistakable allusion to the eternal ruin of those who remain unrepentant.
How terribly Satan deceives people!
Why do they commit such evil and shed so much blood in pursuit of wealth, fame, power or pleasure?
Their anxious striving is empty.
The day will come when everyone in the grave hears the voice of Christ and comes out.
Those who have done good will rise to life; those who have done evil will rise to condemnation.

row.cell: He is to vindicate the Divine government.
Judgments on the mockers of the prophets.

div.title: Ezekiel must warn people in danger (verses 1–9)
div.p: The prophet is a watchman for the house of Israel.
His work is to warn sinners about their misery and danger and call them to abandon wickedness and live.
If people perish because he neglects that duty, he brings guilt upon himself.
Consider the responsibility borne by those who excuse sin, flatter sinners and encourage them to suppose they will enjoy peace while persisting in evil.
Human beings often show far greater wisdom about temporary dangers than about spiritual dangers.
They appoint guards for houses and sentries to warn of approaching enemies.
Yet when their everlasting happiness or misery is at stake, they resent ministers who faithfully obey the Master's command to warn them.
They would rather perish while listening to pleasant assurances.

div.title: God offers mercy to those who repent (verses 10–20)
div.p: God answered those who despaired of receiving mercy with a solemn declaration of his readiness to forgive.
The destruction of Jerusalem and its government had been determined.
But that did not determine the eternal destiny of every individual.
God promises life to the righteous.
Yet people who have made an outward profession of faith may ruin themselves through proud confidence in their own righteousness.
Depending on themselves, they fall into sin.
By contrast, people who have lived wicked lives may repent, abandon their evil conduct and be saved.
God's grace has brought about many astonishing and blessed changes like this.
When a person makes a settled break with sin, the separation between that person and God also ends.

div.title: Judah fails to learn from its ruin (verses 21–29)
div.p: People are deeply resistant to instruction when they do not recognize their dependence upon God even after every created comfort has failed them.
Many claim the special promises given to true believers while their conduct proves them to be God's enemies.
They call their unfounded expectation strong faith.
But God's own testimony declares that they have earned the warnings of judgment rather than the promised blessings.

div.title: Hearers do not necessarily obey God's word (verses 30–33)
div.p: People often come to faithful preaching for unworthy or selfish reasons.
Some attend merely to find something to criticize.
Far more come because of curiosity or habit.
Nevertheless, God can change their hearts.
Whether people listen or refuse, the outcome will eventually show that God's servant was among them.
Those who fail to appreciate God's mercies by making good use of them may justly discover their value only when those mercies are taken away.

row.cell: The people are to be restored to their own land.

div.title: Israel's shepherds neglect the flock (verses 1–6)
div.p: The people became like sheep without a shepherd.
Their enemies preyed upon them, and their land was left desolate.
No official position or high social rank places anyone beyond the correction of God's word.
Those who neglect the duties of their office and misuse the trust others have placed in them deserve rebuke.

div.title: The Lord gathers and cares for his flock (verses 7–16)
div.p: God announced that he intended mercy toward his scattered sheep.
The promise first concerned the restoration of the Jews to their own land.
It also pictured the Good Shepherd's tender care for his people's souls.
He finds them in the darkness of ignorance and leads them into his fold.
He comes to their aid in persecution and temptation.
He guides them along righteous paths and gives them rest in his love and faithfulness.
Proud, self-sufficient people oppose the true gospel and those who trust it; we must guard against their influence.
The Shepherd provides rest for troubled believers but terror for presumptuous sinners.

div.title: Christ's kingdom brings pasture and blessing (verses 17–31)
div.p: The whole nation appeared to be the Lord's flock.
But the people differed greatly in their character, and he knew how to distinguish them.
Good pasture and deep water picture the pure word of God and the practice of justice.
Henry understands verses 23–31 as a prophecy of Christ and of the most glorious periods of his church on earth.
Under Christ, the Good Shepherd, the church becomes a blessing to those around it.
Though Christ was excellent in himself, he appeared like a tender plant growing from dry ground.
As the Tree of Life, bearing every fruit of salvation, he gives spiritual nourishment to his people.
We should constantly pray for showers of blessing wherever Christ's truth is preached and for everyone who professes the gospel to be filled with the fruits of righteousness.

p.hi: A prophecy against Edom.

div.title: Edom's hatred will bring desolation (verses 1–9)
div.p: Anyone who has God against them also has God's word against them.
Those who cultivate unrelenting hatred toward God and his people display the attitude of the sinful human mind.
If they continue in it, they can expect only lasting desolation.

div.title: Edom's boastful words are known to God (verses 10–15)
div.p: When we see the vanity of this world revealed through other people's disappointments, losses and hardships, we should become less attached to possessions, not more eager to seize them.
God knows every word we speak, even the most idle.
The boldest and most defiant expression is not beyond his rebuke.
Through the defeat of his church's enemies, the Lord intends his own glory.
We may be certain that he will accomplish his purpose.
Henry looks forward to the fullness of Jews and Gentiles entering Christ's church, when opposition characterized by anti-Christian hostility will finally be removed.

row.cell: The land shall be delivered from heathen oppressors.
The people are reminded of former sins, and promised deliverance.

div.title: The land will be delivered from its oppressors (verses 1–15)
div.p: Those who treat God's people with contempt and reproach will find that the same disgrace returns upon themselves.
God promises to show favor to his Israel. We need not complain if, as human beings grow more unkind, God shows us still greater kindness.
His people will return to their own borders.
This return was also a picture of the heavenly Canaan, which belongs to all God's children and into which they will be gathered together.
When God graciously returns to a people and they return to him in obedience, their grievances will be put right.
Henry expects the complete fulfillment of this prophecy in a future event.

div.title: Former sins and promised deliverance (verses 16–24)
div.p: The restoration of Israel pictures our redemption through Christ. It shows that the ultimate purpose of salvation is God's glory.
A people's sin defiles their land. It makes the land offensive to God and unpleasant for those who live there.
God's holy name is his great name. His holiness is his greatness; nothing else makes a human being truly great.

div.title: A clean heart and the blessings of the gospel (verses 25–38)
div.p: Water pictures the cleansing of souls polluted by sin. Yet water itself can remove only outward bodily uncleanness.
Henry understands water generally as the sacramental sign of the Holy Spirit's sanctifying work. That work is always connected with the atoning blood of Christ.
When Christ's blood is applied by faith to the conscience, cleansing it from evil works, the Holy Spirit also works in the powers of the soul to remove sin's pollution.
Everyone who belongs to the new covenant receives a new heart and a new spirit and is enabled to walk in newness of life.
God promises to give a heart of flesh: a gentle, tender heart responsive to his holy will.
Renewing grace changes a soul as profoundly as if a lifeless stone became living flesh.
God places his Spirit within his people as their Teacher, Guide and Sanctifier.
His promise to give the grace we need for obedience should encourage us to keep seeking and practicing our duty.
These promises may be pleaded in prayer by all true believers in every age, and God will fulfill them.

row.cell: God restores dried bones to life.
The whole house of Israel is represented as enjoying the blessings of Christ's kingdom.

div.title: God raises dry bones to life (verses 1–14)
div.p: No created power can restore dead human bones to life. God alone can make them live.
In the vision, skin and flesh covered the bones. Then the wind was commanded to blow upon the bodies, and they came to life.
The wind pictured God's Spirit and his power to give life.
This vision encouraged the discouraged Jews. It foretold both their restoration after the captivity and their recovery from the long dispersion that continued in Henry's day.
It also clearly pointed toward the resurrection of the dead.
The same vision represents God's powerful grace in converting even the most hopeless sinners.

Let us turn to the Lord who will one day open our graves and bring us out to judgment. May he deliver us from sin now, place his Spirit within us and keep us through faith by his power until salvation.

div.title: Judah and Israel united under Christ (verses 15–28)
div.p: The symbolic action showed that the Lord would unite Judah and Israel.
Christ is the true David, the King of Israel.
Those whom Christ makes willing through his power he also leads to obey his judgments and keep his commandments.
Henry says future events will explain this prophecy further.
Few things have hindered the spread of the gospel more than divisions among believers.
Let us therefore maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Let us seek divine grace to avoid detestable things.
And let us pray that all nations become obedient and happy subjects of the Son of David, so that the Lord will be our God and we will be his people forever.

row.cell: The army and malice of Gog.

div.title: Gog and the hostile army (verses 1–13)
div.p: These events belong to the latter days.
Henry says it is supposed that these enemies will unite to invade Judea and that God will defeat them.
God not only knows who is presently hostile to his church; he also knows who will become its enemies.
Through his word, he warns them that he is against them.
Even if the wicked join together, they will not escape his judgment.

div.title: God's judgment and protection (verses 14–23)
div.p: The enemy would launch a formidable attack upon Israel.
When Israel dwells safely under God's protection, the attackers will discover how useless their attempts to destroy it are.
God's word contains promises of security that his people may treasure in advance of dangers and troubles facing the church in the latter days.
In judging sinners, God makes his greatness and holiness known.
We should therefore pray daily:

p.hi: Father, glorify your own name.

div.title: Gog's army is destroyed (verses 1–10)
div.p: The Lord will make even the most careless and hardened sinners acknowledge his holy name, either through his righteous judgment or through the abundance of his mercy and grace.
Weapons formed against Zion will not succeed.
Henry regards this prophecy as certain, although its fulfillment belongs to the latter days.
From its language, he concludes that Gog's army appears to be destroyed by a miracle.

div.title: The scale of the destruction and the work of cleansing (verses 11–22)
div.p: God will destroy a vast number of enemies to defend his people Israel.
Times of extraordinary deliverance should also be times of reform.
Everyone should do everything possible to remove what disgraces the land.
Sin is an enemy against which every person should struggle.
Those entrusted with public work, especially the work of cleansing and reforming a country, should be persistent and finish what they begin.
Whenever good work is needed, everyone should help it forward.
Receiving extraordinary favor from God should move us to cleanse ourselves from all evil.
This requires determined effort, including a careful search into the hidden corners of sin.
God's judgments against sin and sinners are a sacrifice to his justice and a feast to the faith and hope of his people.
Sin's consequences can pursue people even after their death.
After all the wealth and honor ambitious, greedy people pursue, a burial place may be all that remains to them on earth, while those who die guilty face misery in the world to come.

div.title: Israel receives God's favor again (verses 23–29)
div.p: Henry looks forward to God's showing mercy to the whole house of Israel through their conversion to Christianity.
After Israel bears the shame of having been rejected because of sin, the nations will learn to know, worship and serve the Lord.
Israel too will know him as revealed in and through Christ.
Henry expressly says past events do not fully answer this prediction.
The outpouring of God's Spirit is a pledge that his favor will continue.
He will no longer hide his face from those upon whom he pours out his Spirit.
When we pray that God never cast us from his presence, let us pray just as earnestly that he never take his Holy Spirit from us.

p.hi: The Vision of the Temple.

div.title: The temple vision and its meaning
div.p: This chapter begins a vision that continues through Ezekiel 48, at the end of the book.
Henry rightly regards it as one of the most difficult passages in Scripture.
When we cannot resolve a difficult passage, we should thank God that our salvation does not depend upon understanding every detail of it.
Everything necessary for salvation has been made sufficiently clear.
We should patiently wait for God to reveal what we cannot yet understand.
This chapter describes the two outer courts of the temple.
Henry says it is unclear whether the figure Ezekiel sees is the Son of God or a created angel.
What is certain is that Christ is both our Altar and our Sacrifice.
We should look to him in faith whenever we approach God.
Christ is salvation in the midst of the earth (Psalm 74:12), and people may look to him from every direction.

p.hi: No separate authorial heading; one short, continuous commentary.

div.title: From the courts into the temple
div.p: After Ezekiel had examined the courts, he was brought inside the temple.
When we pay careful attention to the clearer parts of religion, follow their instructions and benefit from them, we will be led into a deeper understanding of the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven.

p.hi: No separate authorial heading; one continuous commentary.

div.title: The priests' rooms and private devotion
div.p: This chapter describes the rooms for the priests, their purpose, and the dimensions of the holy mountain on which the temple stood.
There were many rooms.
Jesus said that in his Father's house are many dwelling places.
Even in God's house on earth there are many: multitudes have found a home in his sanctuary through faith, and yet there is still room.
These rooms were private, but they stood near the temple.
Similarly, our private acts of worship and prayer should prepare us for public worship and help us benefit more fully from it as circumstances permit.

p.hi: No separate authorial heading; one continuous commentary.

div.title: The glory of God and the sacrifice of Christ
div.p: After Ezekiel had surveyed God's temple, he saw the glory of God.
When the Holy Spirit shows us Christ crucified and the gifts God freely gives us through him, we become ashamed of our sins.
That humility prepares us to understand more deeply the mysteries of redeeming love.
All of Scripture should be opened and applied so that people recognize their sins and repent.
We are not now to offer sacrifices to atone for sin.
Through one offering, Christ has perfected forever those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14).
Nevertheless, we still need the sprinkling of his blood whenever we approach God the Father.
Even our best acts of worship and service are acceptable to him only through the blood that cleanses us from every sin.

p.hi: No separate authorial heading; one continuous commentary.

div.title: Christ enters by his own righteousness
div.p: This chapter contains instructions concerning the true priests.
Henry understands the prince to mean Christ.
The words of Ezekiel 44:2 remind us that no one else can enter heaven, the true sanctuary, in the way Christ did.
He entered by virtue of his own excellence, personal holiness, righteousness and strength.
He is the brightness of Jehovah's glory and entered by his own holiness.
But that way of entering is closed to everyone else.
We must all come as sinners, by faith in Christ's blood and through the power of his grace.

p.hi: No separate authorial heading; one continuous commentary.

div.title: Justice, worship and Christ our Passover
div.p: In the period foretold here, God's worship and its ministers will be provided for.
Rulers will govern justly, recognizing that their authority is held under Christ.
The people will enjoy peace, ease and godliness.
Henry says these promises seem to be expressed in images drawn from the customs of Ezekiel's own time.
Christ is our Passover sacrifice, offered for us.
We celebrate the remembrance of that sacrifice in the Lord's Supper, our Passover feast.
There we rejoice in deliverance from the Egyptian bondage of sin and preservation from the destroying sword of God's justice.
Indeed, the whole Christian life is—and must remain—a feast of unleavened bread, lived in sincerity and truth.

p.hi: No separate authorial heading; one continuous commentary.

div.title: Worship and Christian freedom
div.p: This chapter describes the appointed worship of the prince and the people and the gifts the prince may give to his sons and servants.
Our Lord has commanded us to perform many duties.
But he has also left many matters to our choice.
Those who delight in his commandments may do more than the minimum for his glory, without binding their own consciences unnecessarily or imposing unsuitable rules on others.
Yet this freedom must never become an excuse to neglect daily worship.
Nor may we fail to apply the sacrifice of the Lamb of God to our own souls for pardon, peace and salvation.

p.hi: No separate authorial heading; one continuous commentary.

div.title: Living waters, the gospel and the Spirit
div.p: The waters in Ezekiel's vision signify the gospel of Christ.
It went out from Jerusalem into neighboring countries and spread still farther.
They also picture the gifts and powers of the Holy Spirit that accompanied the gospel and enabled it to spread and bear blessed fruit.
Christ is the Temple and the Door.
The living waters flow from him, from his pierced side.
The waters grow deeper as they flow.
Notice both the gospel's progress in the world and grace's growth in the believer's heart.
Pay attention to the Holy Spirit's work under divine guidance.
When we examine God's truth, some matters are clear and easy to understand, like water reaching the ankles.
Others call for deeper investigation, like water reaching the knees or the waist.
Still others lie beyond our understanding, where we can only worship God for the depths of his wisdom, as Paul did (Romans 11).
It is wise to begin with what is most easily understood before going on to difficult and obscure subjects.
Where the gospel is preached, the promises of Scripture and the privileges of believers are made abundant in their souls by the life-giving Spirit.
They nourish and delight the heart, and never wither, fade or run dry.
Even the leaves serve as medicine.
The warnings and rebukes of God's word may be less pleasant than its consolations, but they help heal spiritual disease.
Everyone who believes in Christ and is united to him through his sanctifying Spirit shares in the privileges belonging to Israel.
There is room in the church and in heaven for all who seek the blessings of the new covenant, whose Mediator is Christ.

p.hi: No separate authorial heading; one continuous commentary.

div.title: The land and the city where the Lord dwells
div.p: This chapter describes the portion of land belonging to each tribe.
In gospel times, all things are made new.
Much of the prophecy is expressed through symbols and numbers.
God has used this manner of speech to communicate mysteries whose meaning will not become fully clear until the proper time.
