Yet access to Christ's church—both in its present struggle and its final triumph—is freely open through faith from every side.
Christ has opened the kingdom of heaven to all who believe.
Whoever desires may come and freely receive the water of life and the fruit of the tree of life.
The Lord is there, within his church, near to his people whenever they call upon him.
This is also true of every genuine Christian.
Wherever a soul has a living principle of divine grace, it can truly be said: The Lord is there.
May we be found among the citizens of that holy city.
May we live in a way worthy of that citizenship and enjoy the Lord's presence in life, in death and forever.

div.title: Daniel — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Daniel came from a noble family, perhaps even Judah's royal family.
According to the historical chronology given in Henry's introduction, Daniel was taken captive to Babylon in the fourth year of Jehoiachin, in 606 BC, while still young.
He was educated in the learning of the Chaldeans and held high office under both the Babylonian and Persian empires.
He suffered persecution for his faith but was miraculously delivered.
Henry estimates that Daniel was about ninety-four years old at the time of his last visions.
The book is partly historical, describing events affecting Daniel and the Jewish people in Babylon.
It is, however, chiefly prophetic.
Its visions and prophecies concern the four great world empires, the coming and death of the Messiah, the restoration of the Jews and the conversion of the Gentiles.
Some prophetic passages are very difficult to explain.
Nevertheless, throughout the book we find encouragement to faith and hope, examples to follow and teaching that directs our thoughts to Jesus Christ on the cross and upon his glorious throne.

row.cell: The captivity of Daniel and his companions.
Their refusal to eat the king's meat.

div.title: Daniel and his companions are taken to Babylon (verses 1–7)
div.p: In the first year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, captured Jerusalem and carried away the people and possessions he chose.
Henry notes that most interpreters date the seventy years of captivity from this first deportation.
It is in a ruler's interest to employ wise people.
A wise ruler will identify and educate people with such abilities. Nebuchadnezzar therefore ordered the chosen young men to receive instruction.
The Hebrew names of these youths each contained a reference to God.
Their pagan captors gave them new names associated with idolatry, intending to make them forget the God of their ancestors, who had guided them since their youth.
It is painful to consider how frequently public education corrupts people's principles and moral conduct.

div.title: The young men refuse the king's food (verses 8–16)
div.p: Whatever influence or favor we gain with others must be recognized as God's gift.
Daniel remained steadfast in his religion.
Whatever name others gave him, he retained the spirit of an Israelite.
The young men were concerned that eating the king's food might involve sin.
When God's people live in Babylon, they must take particular care not to share in its sins.
Young people deserve praise when they refuse to chase sensual pleasures.
Anyone hoping to grow in wisdom and godliness should learn early to practice self-control.
Daniel was determined not to defile himself by sin.
We should fear sin far more than any outward suffering.
It is easier to keep temptation at a distance than to resist it once it is near.
When other people favor us, we can make no better use of that favor than to ask their help in keeping us from sin.
People often fail to believe that avoiding excess and eating moderately can benefit bodily health until they try.
Conscientious self-restraint will bring more comfort even in the present life than sinful indulgence.

div.title: The young men grow in wisdom (verses 17–21)
div.p: Daniel and his companions remained true to their religion.
God rewarded them with outstanding knowledge and learning.
Godly young people should try to become more capable in useful work than their peers.
Their aim should not be human applause but the honor of the gospel and preparation to serve others effectively.
A country benefits—and its ruler receives honor—when those in authority can identify the people best suited for particular responsibilities and promote them accordingly.
Young people should seriously consider this chapter.
Everyone should remember that God honors those who honor him, while people who despise him will be treated lightly.

row.cell: He obtains admission to the king.
Honours to Daniel and his friends.

div.title: Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by his dream (verses 1–13)
div.p: The greatest rulers are often especially troubled by worries and anxieties.
These may keep them awake at night, while ordinary laborers sleep deeply and peacefully.
We seldom know the uneasiness experienced by people who live amid great splendor and what others imagine to be pleasure.
The king demanded that his learned men reveal the dream itself.
If they failed, he would have them executed as deceivers.
People are often more eager to know future events than to discover the way of salvation or the path of duty.
Yet knowledge of the future often increases anxiety and distress.
The king condemned people who had deceived him by claiming to possess extraordinary powers, but now demanded that they do something beyond what they had professed to be able to do.

div.title: Daniel and his companions pray for an answer (verses 14–23)
div.p: Daniel humbly prayed that God would reveal the king's dream and its meaning.
Friends who pray for us are valuable friends.
Even the greatest and best people should welcome the prayers of others.
We ought to show that we appreciate such friends and their prayers.
Daniel and his companions prayed specifically.
Whatever we request, we can expect to receive it only as a gift of God's mercy.
He invites us to bring our needs, burdens and dangers before him.
They appealed to God because of the grave danger they faced.
The mercy they sought was granted.
The earnest prayers of righteous people accomplish much.
Daniel thanked God for revealing what would save his and his companions' lives.
How much more grateful should we be that God reveals the salvation of our souls, even to people who are not counted among the world's wise and educated!

div.title: Daniel speaks before the king (verses 24–30)
div.p: Daniel corrected the king's opinion of magicians and diviners.
The inability of created beings should direct us toward the all-sufficient Creator.
God can do for us and disclose to us what no one on earth can, especially the work of redemption and the secret purposes of his love within it.
Daniel confirmed that the dream was important because it concerned the kingdoms and changing affairs of this world.
Those whom God has greatly honored should put away every thought of their own wisdom or merit, so that the Lord alone receives praise for the good they possess and accomplish.

div.title: The image and the kingdoms (verses 31–45)
div.p: The image represented successive earthly empires that would dominate nations and affect the affairs of the Jewish church.
Henry interprets its parts as follows.
First, the head of gold: the Chaldean Empire, then in power.
Second, the chest and arms of silver: the empire of the Medes and Persians.
Third, the belly and thighs of bronze: the Greek Empire, founded by Alexander.
Fourth, the legs and feet of iron: the Roman Empire.
Henry further understands the ten toes as ten kingdoms into which Rome would divide.
Some would be weak like clay, others strong like iron.
Attempts to reunite them into a stronger empire would prove unsuccessful.
These are Henry's interpretations of the vision, not independently established details supplied in its symbols.
The stone cut without human hands represents the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Christ's kingdom would rise amid earthly kingdoms and overthrow Satan's kingdom within them.
He is the stone the builders rejected, precisely because human hands had not shaped him.
He has nevertheless become the chief cornerstone.
Christ's government and peace will increase without end.
The Lord will reign not only until time ends, but after time itself is no more.
Henry believes the events fulfilled so far correspond closely to the vision, while future ages will see the stone break the whole image and fill the earth.

div.title: Daniel and his companions are honored (verses 46–49)
div.p: Our duty is to direct everyone's attention toward the Lord, the Author and Giver of all good gifts.
Some people recognize God's power and majesty without choosing to serve him themselves.
But everyone should seek God's glory and the greatest good of humankind.

row.cell: Shadrach and his companions refuse to worship it.
They are cast into a furnace, but are miraculously preserved.

div.title: Nebuchadnezzar's golden image (verses 1–7)
div.p: Henry supposes that the image's height—about thirty yards—probably included a pedestal.
He also considers it likely that the image was covered with gold plates, not cast from a solid mass of gold.
Pride and religious intolerance lead rulers to require everyone to follow their religion, whether it is true or false.
When worldly advantage attracts and harsh punishment frightens, few people resist.
Those who are careless, devoted to bodily pleasures or without faith find it especially easy to follow the crowd.
Almost any evil can be made attractive through music and celebration, or enforced through the threat of fire.
False worship has often been established and maintained through such methods.

div.title: The three men refuse to worship (verses 8–18)
div.p: True devotion tends to make a person calm, gentle and peaceful.
Superstition and devotion to false gods, by contrast, can inflame passion.
The king's demand was simple: bow down or burn.
Proud people still challenge God's authority, asking why they should fear him.
Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego did not hesitate about their duty.
They did not allow concern for life or death to override it.
When an invitation or threat plainly asks us to commit sin, we must not bargain with the temptation.
We should reject it at once, as Christ said, “Get behind me, Satan.”
The men gave a direct answer rather than inventing an evasive one.
Those who put obedience first can entrust the consequences to God.
The Lord can control and overrule all the powers arrayed against his people.

p.hi: Lord, if you will, you can deliver us.

div.p: If God is for us, we need not fear human opposition.
He may deliver us from death or through death.
We must obey God rather than people, suffer rather than sin, and never do wrong in the hope of producing something good.
God's preserving them from sinful compromise was as remarkable a miracle in the sphere of grace as his preserving them from the furnace was in the natural world.
Fear of people, love of the world and especially lack of faith cause surrender to temptation.
Strong confidence in the truth helps us avoid denying Christ or being ashamed of him.
Our answers should be gentle but firm.

div.title: God preserves them in the furnace (verses 19–27)
div.p: Nebuchadnezzar could heat the furnace as much as he wished.
Its fire could torment those cast into it only for a short time.
Henry contrasts that earthly fire with the unending torment of final judgment, referring to Revelation 14:10–11.
The event fulfilled the promise of Isaiah 43:2: those passing through the fire would not be consumed.
The three men left it to the God who preserved them within the fire to bring them out.
They walked in the midst of the flames, sustained and encouraged by the presence of the Son of God, as Henry identifies their companion.
Those who suffer for Christ likewise have his presence amid suffering, whether in a fiery furnace or in the valley of the shadow of death.
Nebuchadnezzar acknowledged them as servants of the Most High God, who could save them from his power.
God himself is the consuming fire (Hebrews 12:29).
If we could see into the eternal world, we would see persecuted believers safe from their enemies while the impenitent persecutors faced God's judgment.

div.title: Nebuchadnezzar praises God (verses 28–30)
div.p: This miracle helped the Jewish captives remain faithful to their religion and reject idolatry.
It deeply impressed Nebuchadnezzar with God's power.
But at this time it produced no lasting transformation of his conduct.
The God who preserved these faithful Jews in the furnace can also sustain us through temptation and keep us from falling into sin.

row.cell: Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges the power of Jehovah.

div.title: Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges God's power (verses 1–18)
div.p: The beginning and end of this chapter encourage us to hope that Nebuchadnezzar became an example of the power of divine grace and the riches of mercy.
After recovering from his madness, he told people far away and left a written account for later generations of how God had justly humbled and graciously restored him.
When a sinner comes to his senses, he wishes to benefit others by telling them about God's wonderful mercy.
Before explaining the judgment brought upon him for pride, Nebuchadnezzar described the warning he had received in a dream.
The meaning was explained to him.
The person represented would lose his honor and the use of his reason for seven years.
This is surely among the most severe temporal judgments.
Whatever outward affliction God allows us to suffer, we should bear it patiently and be thankful if he preserves our reason and a peaceful conscience.
Even the dreadful loss of reason would be preferable to being allowed to multiply sins or disgrace God's name without restraint.
God as the righteous Judge had determined the matter, and heaven's angels approved it.
This does not mean that God requires the angels' counsel or agreement. The language expresses the solemnity of the sentence.
Henry also connects the demand with the word of the holy ones—God's afflicted people, whose cries the Lord hears.
Let us seek blessings that can never be taken away, and especially avoid pride and forgetting God.

div.title: Daniel explains the dream (verses 19–27)
div.p: Daniel was astonished and frightened by the severity of the announced judgment against such a powerful king.
He gave his counsel with tenderness and respect.
Genuine repentance requires not only ceasing to do evil but also learning to do good.
Such repentance might not prevent every judgment.
Yet it might delay the trouble or shorten its duration.
Everyone who repents and turns to God will escape everlasting misery.

div.title: The king is humbled and restored (verses 28–37)
div.p: Pride and self-importance are particular temptations for powerful people.
They readily claim for themselves the glory that belongs only to God.
While the king's boast was still in his mouth, God's powerful word came.
Nebuchadnezzar lost his understanding and memory, and the powers of his rational mind failed.
We should beware of conduct that provokes God to remove our reason.
God opposes the proud.
The king wanted to be greater than a human being.
God justly brought him into a condition lower than a human being.
The Most High God lives forever.
His kingdom, like himself, is eternal and universal. No one can resist his power.
People can truly hope for divine honor only when they honor God, confess their sins and acknowledge his sovereign rule.
God not only restores what was lost through the sin of the first Adam, but adds glory through the righteousness and grace of the second Adam, Christ.
Afflictions last no longer than the period needed to accomplish the purpose for which God sent them.
Henry concludes that Nebuchadnezzar truly repented and became an accepted believer.
He also reports the view that Nebuchadnezzar lived no more than about a year after this restoration.
Thus the Lord knows how to humble those who walk in pride and give grace and comfort to the humble, brokenhearted sinner who calls upon him.

row.cell: Belshazzar's impious feast; the hand-writing on the wall.
Daniel is sent for to interpret it.
Daniel warns the king of his destruction.

div.title: Belshazzar's feast and the writing on the wall (verses 1–9)
div.p: Belshazzar openly defied God's judgments.
Henry reports that most historians understood Cyrus to have been besieging Babylon at the time.
Complacency and indulgence are sad signs of approaching ruin.
Merriment that dishonors sacred things is profoundly sinful.
Some songs sung at modern banquets are hardly better than the songs pagans offered to their gods.
See how God suddenly filled Belshazzar and his officials with terror.
God's written word is enough to frighten even the most proud and defiant sinner.
What we perceive of God—like the portion of the hand writing in the book of creation and the book of Scripture—should fill us with reverence for what we cannot see.
If this was his finger, what would we see if he revealed his arm, or his whole majesty?
The king's guilty conscience warned him not to expect good news from heaven.
God can make the strongest sinner tremble in an instant.
He need only allow that sinner's own thoughts to overwhelm the mind.
No bodily pain equals the inward agony that can suddenly seize a sinner in the midst of pleasure, luxury and celebration.
For some, that terror leads them to Christ for pardon and peace.
Many others fear punishment without being humbled by their sins, seeking relief through false comforts instead.
The ignorance and uncertainty displayed by people who claim wisdom, particularly concerning Holy Scripture, can only increase sinners' despair.

div.title: Daniel is called to interpret the writing (verses 10–17)
div.p: Daniel had been forgotten at court and was living quietly.
Henry estimates that he was then ninety years old.
Many consult God's servants about strange questions or obscure matters but never ask about salvation or the path of duty.
Daniel treated the offered reward as insignificant.
He spoke to Belshazzar as to someone already condemned.
If faith enabled us to see how rapidly this world is passing away, we would treat its honors and gifts as of little value.
Yet we should still perform our duties in the world and do all the useful service we can.

div.title: Daniel announces Belshazzar's judgment (verses 18–31)
div.p: Belshazzar had learned nothing from the judgments against Nebuchadnezzar.
He had instead deliberately dishonored God.
Sinners are content to worship gods that neither see, hear nor know.
But they will stand before the God to whom everything is exposed.
Daniel read the sentence written on the wall.
Henry applies its pattern as a warning to every unrepentant sinner.
At death, one's days are numbered and completed.
After death comes judgment: the sinner is weighed and found wanting.
After judgment comes eternal punishment.
While these events were taking place in the palace, Henry reports the opinion that Cyrus's army entered the city, after which Belshazzar was killed and submission followed.

Every unrepentant sinner will ultimately see God's warning fulfilled, whether that person relies upon self-righteous obedience like a Pharisee or maintains an outwardly impressive but hypocritical profession of the gospel.

row.cell: He is cast into the lion's den.

div.title: Daniel's enemies seek a charge against him (verses 1–5)
div.p: Daniel was now very old, yet still capable of important public work and steadfast in his faith.
This honored God.

Religious believers should conduct their responsibilities so faithfully that even their most watchful enemies find no grounds for accusation, except matters of worship where they follow their consciences.

div.title: Daniel continues praying (verses 6–10)
div.p: To forbid prayer for thirty days was to deprive God, for that period, of the honor due him from human beings.
It also deprived people of the comfort they receive from God.
When we are in need or danger, are we not naturally moved to pray?
We cannot live a day without God's care.
How can we expect to live thirty days without speaking to him?
Yet many people who face no law forbidding prayer go more than thirty days without offering one serious, heartfelt request to God.
Their number may far exceed those who pray regularly with humility and thanksgiving.
Persecuting laws are usually justified by false claims.
Nevertheless, Christians should avoid bitter complaints and abusive speech.
It is good to have regular hours for prayer.
Daniel prayed openly and did not conceal his devotion.
Despite his heavy workload, he did not treat public responsibilities as an excuse to neglect daily worship.
How much less excuse do people with fewer responsibilities have for ignoring their souls!
During trials, we must take care that what we call prudence is not really cowardice in God's cause.
People who surrender the life of the soul—even to preserve physical life—act foolishly.
Daniel did not shorten his time of worship by praying without thanksgiving.
He fulfilled the whole duty, prayer and praise.
Prayer rests on the sufficiency of God as almighty Creator and Redeemer, and on our needs as sinful creatures.
We should look to Christ, turning toward him in prayer even while living in the foreign land of earthly exile.

div.title: Daniel is thrown into the lions' den (verses 11–17)
div.p: It is common for acts performed faithfully from conscience toward God to be falsely portrayed as stubborn contempt for civil government.
Through thoughtlessness, we sometimes do things we later wish—like Darius—we had never done.
Daniel, a venerable and upright man, was treated like a criminal and thrown to the lions solely because he worshiped his God.
The stone placed over the den was, Henry says, surely arranged under God's Providence so that the miracle would be undeniable.
The king probably sealed it with his own signet to prevent Daniel's enemies from killing him, according to Henry's supposition.
Let us entrust our lives and souls to God while doing what is right.
We cannot entirely trust even people we serve faithfully.
But believers can always rely on God's favor and consolation.

div.title: Daniel is preserved (verses 18–24)
div.p: The best way to sleep peacefully is to keep a good conscience.
We know what Darius did not know for certain: the living God's servants have a Master who is fully able to protect them.
Consider God's power over the fiercest animals.
He can also restrain the roaring lion that constantly seeks to devour.
Daniel was preserved completely because he trusted in his God.
Those who courageously trust God while fulfilling duty will find him present to help.
The righteous is delivered from trouble, while the wicked person falls into it.
The wicked person's brief triumph ends in ruin.

div.title: Darius issues a decree (verses 25–28)
div.p: If we live in reverence for God and follow his commands, we may expect his peace.
The kingdom, power and glory belong to the Lord forever.
Yet some people proclaim God's wonderful works to others while remaining strangers to his saving grace themselves.
Let us therefore be doers of the word as well as believers, lest in the end we discover that we have deceived ourselves.

row.cell: Daniel's vision of the four beasts.

div.title: The vision of four beasts (verses 1–8)
div.p: This vision represents the same future events as Nebuchadnezzar's dream.
The great sea disturbed by winds represents the earth and its people, shaken by ambitious rulers and conquerors.
The four beasts correspond to the four empires represented by the four parts of Nebuchadnezzar's image.
Mighty conquerors are instruments through which God brings judgment upon a sinful world.
The fierce beasts portray their hateful character.
Nevertheless, each empire's authority has a limit.
God makes even human wrath serve his praise, and he restrains the anger that remains.

div.title: The Son of Man receives his kingdom (verses 9–14)
div.p: These verses comfort and strengthen God's people in view of persecutions they would experience.
Many New Testament descriptions of the coming judgment clearly refer back to this vision, particularly Revelation 20:11–12.
The Messiah is called the Son of Man.
He came in the likeness of sinful flesh and lived as a human being, yet he is also the Son of God.
Henry understands this passage as foretelling Christ's glorious coming, when he will destroy every power opposing him and make his kingdom universal upon earth.
Before the final solemn revelation of God's glory and judgment to all creation, each person's destiny will be determined at death.
Before the end, the Father will publicly give his incarnate Son, our Mediator and Judge, the nations as his willing subjects.

div.title: Daniel receives an interpretation (verses 15–28)
div.p: We should desire to understand fully and accurately what God has revealed.
Those who seek that understanding should pray earnestly and faithfully.
The angel explained the vision to Daniel.
Daniel especially wanted to know about the little horn that made war against the saints and overcame them.
Henry interprets that horn as predicting the persecution of true Christians by papal Rome.
He also interprets John's later visions as referring first to Rome and as drawing upon Daniel's prophecy.
These are Henry's historical-prophetic identifications, not details the biblical symbols themselves explicitly name.
Daniel was given the happy prospect of God's kingdom prevailing among human beings.
Henry connects this to the second coming of Christ, when God's people will triumph through the complete overthrow of Satan's kingdom.
The saints of the Most High will possess the kingdom forever.
Yet we must never conclude from that promise that earthly political dominion rests upon possession of grace.
The promised gospel kingdom is a kingdom of light, holiness, love and grace.
Its present privileges and comforts are the first taste of the kingdom of glory.
Its complete fulfillment is the eternal happiness of the saints in a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
The gathering of God's entire family will be among the blessings of Christ's return.

row.cell: Daniel's vision of the ram and the he-goat.

div.title: The ram, goat and little horn (verses 1–14)
div.p: God showed Daniel the future destruction of kingdoms that were as powerful in their time as Babylon.
If we could see the political changes that will occur after our deaths, we would be less disturbed by the changes we witness during life.
Henry identifies the ram with two horns as the empire of the Medes and Persians, the second empire.
The goat that overcame it represents Alexander the Great.
Alexander died at about thirty-three years old, while still in full strength.
His death exposed the emptiness of worldly splendor and power.
Neither can make a person truly happy.
People may dispute the causes of a prosperous conqueror's death, but the great First Cause had no more work for him to accomplish and therefore brought his life to an end.
Henry takes the four great horns arising after the first as Alexander's four principal generals.
A little horn grew into a great persecutor of God's church and people.
Henry suggests this points to what he calls the “Mohammedan delusion”, meaning Islam, which he believed had spread and at one time almost destroyed the Christian faith.
This is his polemical historical identification, not an identification explicitly stated in the vision.
God is just when he removes sacred privileges from people who despise and profane them.
He may teach people the value of worship through its absence when they refused to value it while they possessed it.
Daniel was told that the period of suffering had a fixed limit, but was not told when it would begin.
To understand God's mind, we must turn to Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
They are hidden for us, not withheld from us.
Henry acknowledges considerable difficulty in determining the precise time and expects the end of that suffering not to be distant.
God will cleanse his church at the time that brings him glory.
Christ died to cleanse his church, and he will present her blameless to himself.

div.title: The vision is explained (verses 15–27)
div.p: Henry understands the figure appearing as a man before Daniel to be the eternal Son of God.
He commanded the angel Gabriel to explain the vision.
Daniel's distress and astonishment at the suffering shown to him strengthen Henry's interpretation that a long period of calamity lay ahead for his people and the church.
When the vision ended, Daniel was instructed to keep it private for the time being.
He did so and returned to his ordinary duties.
As long as we live in this world, we have work to do.
Even those whom God has most honored should not believe themselves above everyday responsibilities.
The joy of fellowship with God must not draw us away from the duties of our callings.
Instead, we should remain with God while carrying them out.
Those entrusted with public responsibilities must fulfill them honestly.
Amid doubts and discouragement, genuine believers can look forward to a good outcome.
Let us learn to settle our minds and attend faithfully to the work appointed to each of us in the church and in the world.

row.cell: Daniel considers the time of the captivity.
His confession of sin, and prayer.
The revelation concerning the coming of the Messiah.

div.title: Daniel studies Jeremiah's prophecy (verses 1–3)
div.p: From the prophetic books, especially Jeremiah, Daniel learned that Jerusalem's desolation would last seventy years, a period now approaching its end.
God's promises are intended to encourage prayer, not to make prayer unnecessary.
The closer we see their fulfillment drawing, the more earnestly we should plead them before God.

div.title: Daniel confesses sin and prays (verses 4–19)
div.p: Our prayers should include confession: of the sins we have committed, of our faith in God and dependence upon him, of sorrow for sin and of our resolve to turn from it.
Such words must express our genuine convictions, not merely follow a form.
Daniel prayed humbly, earnestly and reverently.
He gave God glory as One to be feared and also trusted.
We should consider both God's greatness and goodness, his majesty and mercy.
Daniel confessed his people's sin as the cause of the suffering they had experienced for many years.
Everyone who seeks mercy must confess sin.
Daniel humbled himself and acknowledged the righteousness of God's judgment.
True repentance agrees that God is just.
Afflictions are sent to make people turn away from wrongdoing and learn God's truth.
Daniel also appealed in faith to God's mercy.
The Lord has always been ready to forgive.
Remembering that righteousness belongs to God humbles us; remembering that mercies belong to him encourages us.
His mercy is abundant, providing not merely a single pardon but repeated forgiveness.
Daniel pointed to the disgrace his people had suffered and the ruins of God's sanctuary.
Sin disgraces any people, especially people who profess God's name.
Faithful believers grieve over the desolation of his worship.
Daniel asked for the restoration of the Jewish captives:
Lord, hear and act! Not merely hear and answer in words, but act on our behalf, accomplishing what no one else can. Do not delay.
His prayer included several reasons for asking God to intervene, especially for the sake of the Lord Christ, through whom God shows mercy to sinners when they repent.
In our own prayers we should plead Christ's righteousness alone, not our merit.
Daniel's earnest, humble faith should guide the way we pray.

div.title: The prophecy of the Messiah's coming (verses 20–27)
div.p: God sent Daniel an answer immediately.
It was a particularly memorable answer.
We are not now entitled to expect answers through angels as Daniel received them.
Nevertheless, when we pray earnestly for what God has promised, we can receive the promise itself as an answer by faith, because the One who promised is faithful.
Daniel was shown a redemption greater and more glorious than the return from Babylon: the work God would accomplish through Christ for his church.
Anyone wishing to know Christ and his grace must devote serious attention to prayer.
The evening sacrifice pictured the great offering Christ would make at the evening of the world, in Henry's typological reading.
Through that sacrifice Daniel's prayer was accepted, and he received this revelation of redeeming love.
Henry calls verses 24–27 one of the most remarkable prophecies of Christ, his coming and his salvation.
He interprets the seventy weeks as seventy sets of seven years, or 490 years.
Around the end of that period, Christ would offer a sacrifice providing complete atonement for sin and bringing in everlasting righteousness, the ground of full justification for every believer.
Henry argues polemically that Jewish expectation of a different Messiah after the period he believes fixed by this prophecy reflects obstinate unbelief.
He also understands the crucifixion of Jesus as bringing Israel's guilt to a climax, followed by national calamities.
These are Henry's theological and chronological readings, not a license to condemn Jewish people collectively or to treat his timetable as an editorial correction to Scripture.
Every blessing given to sinners comes through Christ's one atoning sacrifice.
He, the righteous, suffered for the unrighteous to bring us to God.
This sacrifice opens the way to the throne of grace and the entrance to heaven.
The prophecy confirms the covenant with many and brings prophecy's purpose to its fulfillment.
As we rejoice in salvation, let us remember what it cost the Redeemer.
How can anyone escape who neglects such a great salvation?

row.cell: Daniel's vision near the river Hiddekel.
He is to expect a discovery of future events.

div.title: Daniel sees a glorious figure by the Hiddekel (verses 1–9)
div.p: This chapter begins Daniel's final vision, which continues to the end of the book.
A long period would pass before all its events were fulfilled, and Henry says that much remained unfulfilled in his own day.
Henry identifies the glorious figure appearing to Daniel as Christ.
That appearance should lead us to think of him with great honor and reverence.
We should marvel that he humbled himself for our salvation.
Daniel lost all strength before the vision.
Even the greatest and most godly human beings cannot bear an unrestricted revelation of divine glory.
No one can see it and live.
But glorified believers will see Christ as he is and will be able to endure and enjoy that sight.
Even when Christ seems terrifying to people convicted of sin, his word contains enough comfort to calm their hearts.

div.title: The messenger explains future events (verses 10–21)
div.p: Whenever we draw near to God in fellowship, we should remember the immeasurable distance between sinful creatures and the holy Lord.
We are dust and ashes. How can we speak before the Lord of glory?
Nothing more effectively revives discouraged believers than the assurance that God loves them.
From the first day we turn toward him in duty, he is ready to meet us in mercy.
He is eager to hear prayer.
After describing coming events, the angel was to return and oppose measures by Persian kings that would harm the Jewish people.
Angels serve God as his messengers and helpers (Hebrews 1:14).
The rulers of Persia would do much evil against the Jews with God's permission.
Yet they would have done far greater harm if God had not prevented it.
The messenger would explain God's purposes more fully, though the prophecies give only their outline.
We should study what is written in the Scriptures of truth, because they concern our eternal peace.
Satan, his angels and evil advisers may incite rulers to harm the church.
We may rejoice that Christ our Prince and his powerful angels act against our enemies.
But we should not expect this hostile world to provide us with many supporters.
Nevertheless, all God's purposes will stand.
Let each of us pray:

p.hi: Lord Jesus, be our righteousness now, and you will be our everlasting confidence—in life, in death, at the day of judgment and forever.
The vision of the Scriptures of truth.

div.title: Persian and Greek rulers, and their conflicts (verses 1–30)
div.p: The angel showed Daniel the succession of the Persian and Greek empires.
The kings of Egypt and Syria were also described.
Judea lay between their territories and suffered because of their conflicts.
Henry notes that verses 5–30 are generally understood as describing events under those governments.
He also says that from verse 21 onward, the prophecy is generally understood as referring to Antiochus Epiphanes, a cruel and violent persecutor of the Jews.
Consider how quickly worldly splendor, wealth and the power used to obtain them decay and disappear.
In his Providence, God raises one ruler and removes another as he chooses.
This world is filled with wars and conflicts arising from human desires.
God foresees perfectly every change of government, revolution and event.
Not one word he has spoken will fail.
His purposes and declarations will certainly come to pass.
While the rulers of this world fight one another like potsherds of the earth, they sometimes win and sometimes lose, deceive others and are themselves deceived.
But those who know God will trust him.
He will enable them to stand firm, carry their cross and endure their conflict.

div.title: Later conflicts and the final hope (verses 31–45)
div.p: Henry calls this remaining part of the prophecy very difficult.
He notes that commentators disagree considerably about its meaning.
He suggests that the account may pass from Antiochus to antichrist.
He sees possible references to the Roman Empire, the fourth monarchy, in its pagan, early Christian and papal forms.
These remain Henry's tentative historical-prophetic identifications, not explicitly named entities in the prophecy.
The end of God's anger toward his people approaches, as does the end of his patience toward his enemies.

To escape the ruin awaiting unbelief, idolatry, superstition, cruelty and open ungodliness, let us make God's word our standard for truth and conduct, the foundation of hope and the light along our path.
It will guide us through this dark world toward the glorious inheritance above.

row.cell: The conclusion of the vision of the Scriptures of truth.
The times of the continuance of these events.

div.title: The resurrection and final deliverance (verses 1–4)
div.p: The name Michael means “Who is like God?”
Henry understands this name and the title “the great Prince” as pointing toward the divine Savior, Christ.
Christ stood in place of his people as their sacrifice.
He bore the curse that they deserved to remove it from them.
He now stands for them as their Intercessor at the throne of grace.
After the destruction of antichrist, Henry expects the Lord Jesus to appear upon earth at the last day and bring about the complete redemption of his people.
When God delivers his people from persecution, the change is like life from the dead.
As the gospel spreads, people who seem asleep in dust are awakened to spiritual life.
Henry speaks of this awakening among Jews and Gentiles.
At the end, the multitude sleeping in the dust will literally awaken.
Some will rise to life, others to shame.
Future glory is reserved for all God's saints, those who are wise concerning their souls and eternity.

Those who help turn many people toward righteousness—bringing sinners back from error and helping save their souls from death (James 5:20)—will share the joy and glory of those they helped reach heaven.
That joy will increase their own happiness.

div.title: The remaining prophetic times and Daniel's hope (verses 5–13)
div.p: One angel asked how long these extraordinary events would last.
The reply was “a time, times, and half a time,” the period also mentioned in Daniel 7:25 and Revelation.
Henry interprets this as 1,260 prophetic days, or years, beginning when the power of God's people was scattered.
He suggests that what he calls “the imposture of Mohammed”, referring polemically to Islam, and papal domination began at roughly the same period and represented a twofold attack upon the church.
These are Henry's polemical chronology and historical identification, not a firm date supplied by the biblical passage.
Despite the long conflict, everything will end well.
Every power opposing God's purpose will be overthrown.
Holiness and love will triumph and be honored forever.
This prophecy encompasses many different events over successive ages, reaching even to the general resurrection.
Daniel was encouraged by the prospect of his own happiness at death, at judgment and through eternity.
It is good for all of us to consider our departure from this world.
We must leave it, but not until God calls us and has completed the work he assigned to us here.
It is as though God then says: Go your way. Your work is finished. Others may take your place.
The comfort Daniel received belongs to every faithful believer.
Whatever their circumstances during life, they will receive a good portion at the end.
This should be everyone's chief concern.
With such hope we can be content with our present circumstances and welcome God's will.
Believers can know happiness already: they rest in God by faith now, and a fuller rest is reserved for them in heaven.

div.title: Hosea — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Henry considers it probable that Hosea came from the kingdom of Israel.
Hosea lived and prophesied over a long period.
His prophecies sought to expose, rebuke and convince the Jewish people in general—and the Israelites in particular—of their many sins, especially idolatry.
He also drew attention to the corruption of the kingdom.
Yet Hosea invited the people to repent, promising mercy and announcing future gospel blessings.
Henry understands these promises to concern the restoration of Israel and Judah and their eventual conversion to Christianity.

row.cell: Under a figure, is represented the shameful idolatry of the ten tribes.
The calling of the Gentiles, and the uniting Israel and Judah under the Messiah.

div.title: The unfaithfulness of Israel represented (verses 1–7)
div.p: Israel was prosperous when Hosea boldly exposed its sins and predicted its destruction.
We should not flatter sinners merely because they enjoy worldly success.
That success will not continue if they persist in their wrongdoing.
The prophet had to show Israel how hateful its idolatry was.
Giving a created thing the glory belonging only to God is an offense against him.
It is like a wife giving herself to a stranger instead of remaining faithful to her husband.
The Lord surely had wise reasons for the command he gave Hosea.
The prophet's experience would provide a moving image of God's undeserved goodness and tireless patience, compared with Israel's rebellion and ingratitude.
We would become tired and bitter after enduring far less unfaithfulness from other people than the unfaithfulness with which we grieve God's Spirit.
We should be ready to bear whatever cross the Lord assigns us.
The names of Hosea's children announced the people's impending ruin.
The name of the first child, Jezreel, meaning “dispersion” according to Henry, foretold the fall of the royal family.
The second, Lo-ruhamah, meant “not loved” or “not shown mercy”, announcing that the nation would be abandoned.
God had shown Israel great mercy, but the people had abused his gifts.
Sin turns away God's mercy, even from people who profess to belong to him.
If pardoning mercy is withdrawn, no other mercy can be relied upon.
Nevertheless, although some are broken off through unbelief, God will preserve a church in the world until the end.
Our salvation comes through his mercy, not through any merit of ours.
When he undertakes to save, no one can prevent him.

div.title: God's people will be gathered (verses 8–11)
div.p: A third child was called Lo-ammi, meaning “not my people”.
The name announced Israel's temporary rejection.
God disowned the relationship the nation had claimed.
We love God because he loved us first.
But when we are cast out of covenant fellowship, our own folly is to blame.
Even in wrath, God remembers mercy.
The rejection would be neither total nor final.
The same hand that wounded the people would reach out to heal them.
Precious promises are made here concerning the Israel of God.
Henry notes that some interpreters expect their fullest realization only through a future general conversion of the Jewish people.
The apostles Paul (Romans 9:25–26) and Peter (1 Peter 2:10) also apply this promise to the gospel and to Jews and Gentiles being brought together.
To believe in Christ is to receive him as our Head, willingly submitting to his guidance and rule.
Let us pray for the glorious day when one Lord will reign over all the earth.

div.title: Israel is charged with unfaithfulness (verses 1–5)
div.p: This chapter continues the picture of Israel as an unfaithful wife, with Hosea's children representing the people.
We should recognize and love as brothers and sisters everyone whom the Lord appears to place among his children, encouraging them in the mercy they have received.
Yet every Christian must also oppose wrongdoing through example and conduct, even among people to whom we belong and whom we should respect.
Unrepentant sinners will eventually lose the privileges they misuse and spend upon their sinful desires.

div.title: God's discipline interrupts sinful pursuits (verses 6–13)
div.p: God warned what he would do to this unfaithful, idolatrous people.
They refused to turn back, so the promised consequences came upon them.
Their history is recorded to warn us.
If people overcome smaller obstacles in pursuing sin, God may raise up greater obstacles.
Those most determined to follow sinful paths often encounter the most frustration.
When a path is blocked by thorns, we may have reason to suspect that the path itself is wrong.
Obstacles placed in the way of sin can be great blessings.
They are God's hedges, protecting us by making wrongdoing difficult.
We should thank him for grace that restrains us and for the providential events that keep us from evil—even pain, illness or calamity, if they prevent further sin.
When created things disappoint our longing for happiness, those disappointments should lead us back to the Creator.
People who forget that their comforts come from God may discover that he removes those comforts in mercy, bringing them to recognize their folly and danger.
Sin and merriment cannot remain together indefinitely.
If people refuse to take sin away from their pleasures, God will take pleasure away from their sins.
If they destroy the honor of God's word and worship, it is just for him to destroy their vines and fig trees, taking away what makes them happy.
Removing the sacred feasts and Sabbaths may not disturb them—they already care little for such things.
But when God removes their sensual pleasures, sorrow will replace sinful celebration.

div.title: God's promises of reconciliation (verses 14–23)
div.p: After judgment, the Lord promised to deal gently with Israel.
Christ's promise of rest invites us to take his yoke upon us.
Conversion may be encouraged by comfort and kindness, not only by the conviction of sin.
Yet often God brings us to the end of confidence in earthly joy and in our own strength.
When every other door closes, we finally knock at the gate of mercy.
Israel would then love God more sincerely.
Instead of calling him Baali, “my lord and master,” emphasizing authority, the people would call him Ishi, a name expressing affection.
Henry sees possible fulfillments in the return from Babylon, Jewish conversion to Christ during the apostolic age, and a future general conversion of the Jewish nation.
Believers can expect greater tenderness and care from their holy God than a beloved wife receives from even the kindest husband.
When the people put away idols and loved the Lord, no creature would finally harm them.
These promises can be understood of spiritual Israel, of every genuine believer receiving Christ's righteousness, and of future Jewish conversion.
There is also a call to live in a way that does not disgrace the God who says “You are my people.”
A household behaving shamefully dishonors its head.
If God calls us his children, let us respond, “You are our God.”
Discouraged sinner, do not answer God's love with unbelief.
When he says, “You are my people,” answer in faith, “Lord, you are our God.”

p.hi: The prophet enters into a new contract, representing the gracious manner in which God will again restore Israel under a new covenant.

div.title: God's gracious covenant represented (verses 1–3)
div.p: People often dislike true religion because they prefer objects and forms of worship that allow them to indulge their sinful desires instead of putting those desires to death.
How remarkable that a holy God should show goodwill toward people whose sinful minds are hostile to him!
Hosea's actions picture God's gracious dealings with humanity after it departed from him.
They illustrate the covenant of grace he is willing to make with his people:

p.hi: They will belong to him as his people, and he will be their God.

div.p: They must acknowledge the consequences of their wrongdoing and must not return to folly.
One sign that affliction is producing good in us is that we are kept from yielding to the temptations that come with suffering.

div.title: Israel's waiting and eventual restoration (verses 4–5)
div.p: Here the meaning of the prophetic picture is applied directly to Israel.
The people would remain for a long time like a widow, deprived of joys and honors.
In the end, however, they would be received again.
Those who seek the Lord so as to find him must come to Christ and willingly become his people.
We should fear not only the Lord's greatness, but also his goodness.
We should reverence not only his majesty, but also his mercy.
Henry notes that even Jewish writers apply this passage to the promised Messiah.
He understands it as predicting a future conversion of Jewish people to Christ, for which, in his reading, they have been preserved as a distinct people.
Fear of God may first arise from knowing his holiness and just judgment.
But experiencing mercy and grace through Jesus Christ leads the heart to reverence a loving and glorious Friend and Father and to fear offending him.

row.cell: God's judgments against the sins of the people.
Idolatry is reproved, and Judah is admonished.

div.title: The sins of the people (verses 1–5)
div.p: Hosea condemned immorality as well as idolatry.
Truth, mercy and knowledge of God had disappeared from the land.
Violence and murder filled it, as Henry also recalls in 2 Kings 21:16.
Disaster was approaching and would leave the country desolate.
Our sins—whether committed as individuals, families, neighbors or nations—give the Lord cause to bring charges against us.
We should therefore submit to him and humble ourselves, lest his judgments continue toward destruction.

div.title: Priests and people reject God's knowledge (verses 6–11)
div.p: Both priests and people had rejected the knowledge of God.
God would therefore justly reject them.
They forgot his law.
They neither desired nor tried to keep it in mind or teach it to their descendants.
Therefore God would forget them and their children.
When we use for dishonor the gifts that ought to bring honor to God, those very gifts may become our shame.
The sacrifices should have warned people how seriously God regards sin: atonement was needed.
Instead, the priests encouraged sin by treating its remedy as cheap and easy.
It is wicked to be pleased with other people's wrongdoing because we expect to profit from it.
Gains acquired unlawfully cannot be enjoyed with a peaceful conscience.
Priests and people strengthened one another in wickedness, so they would share the consequences.
Those who share in sin should expect to share its ruin.
A secret sinful desire allowed to remain in the heart can gradually destroy its spiritual strength.
That explains why many professing believers become dull, lifeless and sluggish in serving God.
Some hidden desire has taken hold of their hearts.

div.title: Idolatry and God's warning to Judah (verses 12–19)
div.p: The people consulted idols instead of God's word.
That led to disorder and sin.
In doing so, they prepared punishments for themselves and helped wrongdoing spread through the nation.
Judah must not imitate Israel's idolatry.
Israel had surrendered itself to false worship and now faced the dreadful command “Leave them alone.”
When people cast off the gentle yoke of Christ, they may continue sinning until God abandons them to their chosen path.
They then receive no further warnings and feel no conviction.
Satan takes hold of them, and they move toward destruction.
Being left undisturbed in sin is a severe divine judgment.
Those who face no disturbance over their sin may ultimately be destroyed because of it.
May God keep us from that dreadful state.
His judgment, like a powerful storm, will soon carry hardened sinners toward ruin.

div.title: The Lord exposes Israel's hidden sins (verses 1–7)
div.p: God's searching eyes saw Israel's secret attachment to sin, the people's love for their wrong practices and the power those practices exercised over them.
Pride makes people stubborn in every other sin.
Judah was following the same path and would therefore fall with Israel.
People who deal falsely with the Lord are only deceiving themselves.
Those who seek God merely by bringing flocks and herds, while withholding their hearts and souls, cannot expect to find him.
Those who do not seek the Lord while he may be found will not succeed later.
It is therefore vital to seek him now, in the accepted time and day of salvation.

div.title: Judgment approaches, but repentance remains possible (verses 8–15)
div.p: The destruction announced to unrepentant sinners is not merely a warning intended to frighten them.
It is a sentence that will not be recalled if they refuse to repent.
That we receive timely warning is itself a mercy, allowing us to flee from coming judgment.
Following human commands that contradict God's commands prepares a people for ruin.
Sometimes God's judgments consume sinful people like a moth, dry rot or woodworm.
The damage proceeds quietly.
People may imagine themselves secure and prosperous, only to discover later that everything has been gradually decaying.
God often allows this process to unfold slowly to give them time to repent.
A nation, like an individual, can waste away by degrees.
Lesser judgments are sent to warn sinners and prevent greater calamities if they will listen.
When Israel and Judah were threatened, they sought protection from Assyria.
This only made their injury worse.
Affliction would eventually drive them to seek God himself.
There is hope when people begin to grieve more deeply over their sins than over their suffering.
Under conviction and correction, we should seek to know the Lord.
Those led by severe trials to seek him genuinely will find him an immediate helper and a secure refuge.
With him there is abundant redemption for everyone who calls upon him.
True, lasting peace is found only where God is.

row.cell: Israel's instability and breach of the covenant.

div.title: Return to the Lord (verses 1–3)
div.p: People who joined together to abandon God and draw one another into sin should join together to return to him.
That will bring glory to God and good to themselves.
During suffering, we are strengthened and encouraged to repent by maintaining right thoughts about God's goodness and purposes.
Deliverance from distress can be like life restored from death.
God promises to revive his people, and the assurance of his mercy should draw them back.
Henry also sees a further reference here to the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
He marvels that a prophecy concerning the church's deliverance would point toward salvation through Christ.
In his reading, the resurrection confirms that Jesus is the promised One and that believers need no other Savior.
The promised blessing is eternal life through knowing God.
God's returning favor is as certain as morning following a dark night.
He comes like the early and late rain, refreshing the ground and making it fruitful.
The grace of God in Christ is both rains: it begins and sustains the work of spiritual fruitfulness.
Just as the Redeemer rose from the grave, he will revive the hearts and hopes of everyone who trusts him.
Even a small ray of hope from God's word promises increasing light, comfort, cleansing and fruitful grace.

div.title: Israel's passing repentance (verses 4–11)
div.p: Under suffering, Israel and Judah sometimes appeared willing to repent.
But their apparent goodness vanished like a morning cloud or early dew.
They soon returned to their former corruption.
That is why the Lord sent such serious warnings through his prophets.
God's word will be the death either of sin or of the sinner.
The Lord desires mercy rather than sacrifice and knowledge of himself that produces holy reverence and love.
This exposes the folly of people who trust external religious ceremonies to compensate for lack of love toward God and other people.
As Adam broke God's covenant in paradise, so Israel broke its national covenant despite the many blessings it had received.
Judah too had become ready for judgment.
May the Lord establish his reverence and kingdom within our hearts, never abandon us to ourselves and not permit temptation to overcome us.

div.title: Israel's many sins (verses 1–7)
div.p: Israel's wickedness arose from a practical refusal to believe that God governs and sees human affairs.
The people acted as though he neither saw their sins nor cared about them.
Their wrongdoing surrounded them.
Their hearts were inflamed by sinful desires like a blazing oven.
Even when the nation was in trouble, they never thought to seek God's help.
The visible acts of sin in a person's life are only a small part of the evil within the heart.
When a sinful desire is deliberately cherished inwardly, it eventually breaks out into actual wrongdoing.
Those who tempt others into drunkenness cannot be true friends.
They often intend the other person's ruin.
Thus people become instruments of judgment against one another.
Those who continue living without prayer even during danger and distress are not merely heated with sin; they have become hardened in it.

div.title: Israel's instability and hypocrisy (verses 8–16)
div.p: Israel resembled a cake not turned over: burned on one side and still raw on the other, useless throughout.
The nation mixed the worship of Jehovah with idolatry.
Signs of approaching destruction had appeared, like gray hair announcing age, yet Israel did not notice them.
The pride that moves people to break God's law also encourages self-flattery.
God's mercy and grace are the only safe refuge, but stubborn sinners seldom think of fleeing there.
They may cry out in fear with words resembling prayer, but their hearts do not truly turn to God.
Even requests for earthly blessings may aim only to provide more fuel for sinful pleasures.
Changing from one religious group, opinion, outward form or particular vice to another still leaves people far from Christ and genuine holiness.
This is what we are like by nature, and what we will become if left to ourselves.
Let us therefore pray:

p.hi: Create a clean heart in us, O God, and renew a right spirit within us.

row.cell: Destruction threatened for the impiety of Israel.
Further threatenings for the same sins.

div.title: Israel's empty claim to know God (verses 1–4)
div.p: When Israel faced disaster, the people would claim to know God and ask for his protection.
But such words would be disregarded.
What good is it to say “My God, I know you” if we cannot also say “My God, I love you, serve you and cling to you alone”?

div.title: Idolatry produces a barren harvest (verses 5–10)
div.p: By worshiping idols, the people promised themselves abundance, peace and military success.
Those expectations would come to nothing.
They sowed seed that produced no stalk or blade.
Even if a shoot appeared, it would produce no grain.
The works of darkness are barren, and their final outcome is death.
The hopes of sinners will deceive them, while the gains they seek become traps.
In times of danger—and especially at the final judgment—every merely human or worldly strategy will fail.
The people chose to go their own way.
Like a solitary wild donkey, they became easier prey for a lion.
Human beings most resemble an untamed donkey when they seek from created things the help and fulfillment that come only from God.
Sinners may experience some sorrow.
But if it is not godly sorrow leading to repentance, it will end in lasting grief.

div.title: Corrupt worship cannot make up for disobedience (verses 11–14)
div.p: To corrupt the worship of God is a serious sin, regardless of how reasonable the excuses may appear.
The Lord had caused his law to be written down for Israel.
Yet the people neither wanted to know it nor intended to obey.
They built temples as though they remembered their Creator, but had actually forgotten him because they no longer feared him.
No one has hardened the heart against God and ultimately prospered.
As long as people despise the truths, commands and appointed worship of Scripture, elaborate and costly ceremonies of their own invention only increase their guilt.
Only worship performed according to God's word and through Jesus Christ is acceptable to him.

row.cell: The distress to come upon Israel.
The approach of the day of trouble.

div.title: Israel's misplaced joy will end (verses 1–6)
div.p: Israel offered gifts to its idols.
People who are stingy about true worship may spend lavishly on their own sinful desires.
Anyone who values the harvest floor's reward more highly than God's favor and eternal life is, in that sense, an idolater.
The people rejoiced over their harvest while having no desire to grieve over sin.
When we make the world and its possessions our idol and our portion, God is just in exposing our folly and correcting us.
Those who refuse God's laws and his love cannot expect to enjoy the Lord's land as though nothing were wrong.
When we possess the means of grace, we should ask how we would live if those gifts were removed.
The joy of fellowship with God remains secure amid earthly change.
But pleasant homes and properties bought or protected with money may be destroyed.
No famine is more dreadful than a famine of the soul.

div.title: The appointed watchmen become traps (verses 7–10)
div.p: There had been a time when Israel's spiritual watchmen walked with God.
Now they acted like a birdcatcher's snare, trapping people and bringing them toward ruin.
The people's corruption resembled that of Gibeah (Judges 19).
Their crimes would bring comparable judgment.
At first, God had found Israel delightful, like grapes discovered by a traveler in the wilderness, or the first ripe figs of the season.
These pictures show how much pleasure God had taken in his people.
Nevertheless, they abandoned him and followed idols.

div.title: Judgment reaches Israel's comforts and descendants (verses 11–17)
div.p: God departs from a person or people when he withdraws his goodness and mercy.
When the Lord has withdrawn, what can created things accomplish?
Outward comforts may remain for a time, but the true blessing is gone when God is gone.
Children as well as parents would suffer.
God's wrath dries the roots and withers the fruit of worldly comforts.
Henry points to the continued scattering of the Jewish people in his own era as a warning not to neglect or abuse gospel privileges.
Yet not every painful blow means that God is drying up the root.
Sometimes he strikes a plant so that its sap goes deeper into the root, producing greater humility, patience, faith and self-denial.
God is just when he judges people who despise the mercy he offers.

div.title: Israel is a vine without good fruit (verses 1–8)
div.p: A vine's value lies in the fruit it produces.
Israel, however, had brought none of its fruit to maturity.
The people's hearts were divided.
God is the rightful sovereign of the human heart: he requires the whole heart, not merely a share.
If our hearts were directed wholly toward God, devotion would flow strongly enough to overcome whatever lay in its path.
Israel's claims to be in covenant with God were false.
Even its administration of justice had become as poisonous as hemlock.
How sad that the visible church may still be a nearly empty vine!
Earthly prosperity is no more substantial than bubbles or foam on water, quickly broken and gone.
Sinners will one day seek shelter in vain from the very Judge they now despise when he is offered to them as Savior.

div.title: Seek the Lord and sow righteousness (verses 9–15)
div.p: God does not delight in sinners' death and destruction.
For that reason, his correction can be an act of mercy.
Sinful habits remained deeply rooted in Israel.
Enemies would gather against the people.
It is just for those who live carelessly in comfort and indulgence to learn what suffering means.
They should cleanse their hearts of sinful loves and desires and become brokenhearted and contrite.
They should abound in devotion toward God and in justice and generosity toward one another.
This is what it means to sow to the Spirit.
Seeking the Lord is a duty for every day, though there are special occasions that call us to seek him with renewed urgency.
Christ will come as the Lord our righteousness, granting his righteousness abundantly.
Those who sow righteousness reap according to mercy.
Such a harvest is a reward of grace, not a debt God owes us.
Even the profits obtained through sin bring sinners no real satisfaction.
Both sinful comforts and confidence in wicked practices will eventually disappoint.
Come, seek the Lord: hope placed in him will not deceive you.
Consider the cruelty and devastation of war.
Whatever evil is done, sin lies behind it.
How much misery human wrongdoing brings even in this life!

row.cell: God's regard for Israel; their ingratitude.
The Divine mercy yet in store.

div.title: God's parental love and Israel's rebellion (verses 1–7)
div.p: God loved the Israelites while they were weak, helpless, foolish and stubborn like little children.
He carried and fed them as a nurse cares for an infant, enduring their difficult behavior.
Everyone who has grown up should often remember God's kindness during childhood.
The Lord cared for us and worked patiently with us, not only like a father or teacher, but like a mother or nurse.
In the wilderness, he showed Israel the way forward and held them by the arms.
Through the ceremonial law given to Moses, he instructed them in his commandments.
He guided them to keep them from wandering and supported them to keep them from falling.
In the same way God's spiritual Israel depends upon his sustaining power.
It is God who draws souls to himself.
No one can come to him unless he draws that person.
He bound the people with cords of love, described by a word Henry understands as stronger than the earlier cords.
He relieved the heavy burdens they had endured.
Yet Israel responded with terrible ingratitude.
God's counsel would have saved them, but their own plans brought ruin.
They repeatedly turned away.
They could not be relied upon to remain faithful.
They turned from God, the highest good, and eagerly embraced temptation.
Their hearts had become set on doing evil.
True happiness belongs only to people whom God teaches by his Spirit, sustains by his power, and leads in his ways.
Through grace he removes the desire and dominion of sin, creates a longing for the gospel's blessed feast, and enables people to feed upon it and live forever.

div.title: God's mercy remains available (verses 8–12)
div.p: God is slow to anger and unwilling to abandon completely the people called by his name.
When a sacrifice was needed for sin and a Savior for sinners, he did not spare his own Son, so that he might spare us.
Such mercy is offered during the day of God's patience.
People who persist in sin until they exhaust that opportunity will face the great day of his wrath.
Human compassion is small compared with God's tender mercy.
His ways of welcoming returning sinners are as far above ours as heaven is above earth.
God knows how to forgive miserable sinners.
He is faithful and just to forgive because Christ has purchased pardon, and God himself has promised it.
Our trembling at Christ's word should draw us toward him, not drive us away.
The children who tremble should run to their Father.
Everyone responding to the gospel invitation will receive a place and a name in the gospel church.
Israel's religious service had become hypocritical.
In Judah, however, the people still showed regard for God's law and followed their faithful ancestors.
Let us remain faithful.
God honors those who honor him, while those who despise him will be lightly regarded.

row.cell: Judah and Israel reminded of the Divine favours.

div.title: Remember Jacob and return to the Lord (verses 1–6)
div.p: Ephraim nourished false hopes of receiving human help while living in hostility toward God.
The Jews imagined they could secure Egypt's support by offering gifts from the produce of their land.
Judah, too, was called to account.
God sees the sins of his own people and will judge them.
Israel was reminded both of what Jacob did and of what God did for Jacob.
When Jacob's faith in God's promise overcame his fears, he prevailed through God's strength in prayer.
God is Jehovah, the same yesterday, today and forever.
What was once a revelation to an individual is now a lasting memorial of God for all generations.
Those who have departed from God should return to him through repentance and faith, acknowledging him as their God.
Those already converted should walk faithfully with him in holy conduct.
Let us wrestle in prayer for the blessings he has promised, determined to continue seeking him rather than give up.
Let us seek him in the ordinances of his worship.

div.title: Israel's dishonest prosperity (verses 7–14)
div.p: Ephraim became a merchant.
Henry notes that the word can also mean a Canaanite.
The people traded on Canaanite principles, pursuing profit through greed, fraud and deceit.
They became wealthy and imagined that their prosperity proved God's favor.
But shameful sins bring shameful judgments.
They should remember not only Jacob's power with God, but also the years he served Laban.
When God has given us the privilege of his word, disregarding it makes our sin and folly all the more serious.
It is better to labor under the hardest conditions in honest poverty than to gain riches through sin.
We should compare our conduct with that of faithful believers who faced similar circumstances in the past.
Those who despise God's message will perish.
May we all receive his word with humble and obedient faith.

row.cell: The abuse of God's favour leads to punishment.

div.title: Ephraim turns from God to idols (verses 1–8)
div.p: As long as Ephraim reverenced and worshiped God, the tribe held an honored place.
But when Ephraim abandoned God for idols, it fell from that position.
The people who sacrificed to idols were told to kiss the calves, expressing worship, affection and submission.
But the Lord will not give his glory to another.
Those who worship images will therefore be brought to shame.
No lasting and genuine comfort is found anywhere except in God.
The Lord not only cared for Israel during the wilderness years; he also brought the people into Canaan, a fertile and pleasant land.
Yet worldly success, when it feeds pride, makes people forget God.
Therefore the Lord would confront them in judgment like the fiercest beasts of their forests.
Abusing divine goodness leads to more severe judgment.

div.title: Destruction through sin and mercy through redemption (verses 9–16)
div.p: Israel had destroyed itself through rebellion.
It could not rescue itself.
Its only help came from the Lord.
The same truth applies to spiritual redemption from the lost condition into which all human beings have fallen through deliberate sins.
God sometimes gives sinners the very things they wrongfully demand, but in displeasure.
For faithful believers, whether God gives or takes away, he acts in love.
For the unrepentant, both receiving and losing earthly things can become expressions of wrath and bring no true comfort.
Without repentance and faith in the gospel, sinners will soon face severe distress.
Israel's predicted national ruin also contained the promise that God would intervene mercifully and powerfully to preserve a remnant.
Yet that deliverance only foreshadowed the redemption of the true Israel through Christ's death, burial and resurrection.
Christ will destroy death and the grave.
The Lord will not abandon his promise or change his purpose.
In the meantime, Israel would be devastated for its sins.
Without good works bearing fruit through the Holy Spirit, other kinds of prosperity are as empty as uncertain worldly wealth.
God's judgment would dry up the branches and wither the shoots.
Those who rebel against him would face suffering worse than even the cruelty of warfare.
May the Lord save us from such misery and from sin, its cause.

row.cell: Blessings promised, showing the rich comforts of the gospel.

div.title: Return to the Lord with words of repentance (verses 1–3)
div.p: Israel was urged to turn from sins and idols and return to Jehovah.
The people were to come through faith in God's mercy and grace through the promised Redeemer and through careful attention to worship and service.
Take away our wrongdoing, they prayed.
Remove it as a heavy burden under which we are sinking, or as a stumbling block over which we repeatedly fall.
Take all of it away through a free and complete pardon, because we cannot remove it ourselves.
Receive our prayer graciously.
The people did not prescribe exactly which earthly benefit they desired.
They entrusted the outcome to God.
What they needed was not the good the world could show, but the good God could give.
They had to consider their sins, their needs and the remedy.
Instead of bringing sacrifices as the substance of repentance, they were to bring words that expressed their hearts' true desires.
This clearly portrays a sinner's conversion to God through Jesus Christ.
When approaching God in prayer and faith, we should first ask him to teach us what to pray for.
We must earnestly plead that he remove all our sins.

div.title: God promises healing, love and fruitfulness (verses 4–8)
div.p: Israel was invited to seek God's favor and would not seek it in vain.
He would turn away his anger.
When God loves, he loves freely.
His love does not arise from people's merit but from his own gracious pleasure.
God will be for his people everything they need.
The gifts of his Spirit are like hidden manna or dew.
Grace freely given will not be wasted.
His people will grow upward, becoming beautiful like a lily (Matthew 6:28–29).
They will also grow downward, becoming deeply rooted like the cedars of Lebanon.
Much of genuine spiritual growth occurs in the hidden roots, where it is unseen.
They will also spread like a vine, with branches reaching outward.
When believers abound in good works, their branches extend and help others.
They will be pleasing both to God and to other people.
Holiness is the soul's beauty.
The church resembles a vine and an olive tree that bear useful fruit.
God's promises belong to people who remain under the care of his appointed ordinances, not those who flee briefly into their shade merely to escape a passing hardship.
When a person comes to God, others dwelling under that person's influence benefit too.
The fruits of holiness will become visible in life.
Thus believers grow in the experience and fruitfulness of the gospel.
Ephraim will say, “What have I to do with idols anymore?”
God himself puts that resolve into the person's heart.
God's promises are a stronger foundation for putting sin to death than our promises to him.
Divine grace changes the heart so deeply that former idols become as hateful as they once were beloved.
Even suffering can be sanctified for that purpose.
Ephraim suffered because of idolatry, and the intended fruit was the removal of sin (Isaiah 27:9).
True repentance means a firm determination to have nothing more to do with sin.
The Lord receives repentant people mercifully, as the father welcomed his returning prodigal son.
God becomes their delight and defense.
They can rest happily in his shade.
The Lord himself supplies the root from which all good fruit grows.
From him come the grace and strength needed for duty.

div.title: The righteous walk in God's ways (verse 9)
div.p: Who benefits from the prophet's teaching?
Those who earnestly try to understand and know these truths.
God's providential ways are right: he does everything well.
Christ is a foundation stone to some.
To others, he becomes a stumbling stone and rock of offense.
Something appointed to bring life can, when abused through unbelief, lead instead to death.
The same sun softens wax and hardens clay.
Those who turn away even while walking among God's ordinances are in great danger.
They stumble over the Rock of Ages and draw poison from the Balm of Gilead.
Let sinners in Zion take warning.
May we learn to walk in the Lord's right ways as faithful servants, and may none of us stumble at his word through disobedience and unbelief.

div.title: Joel — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The prophet Joel warned of destruction coming upon Judah through locusts and other insects.
He called the people to repentance, fasting and prayer.
He also spoke of the blessings of the gospel and the final glorious state of the church.

row.cell: All sorts of people are called to lament it.
They are to look to God.

div.title: The devastating plague of locusts (verses 1–7)
div.p: Even the oldest people could not remember a disaster like the one about to strike Judah.
Swarms of insects would consume the crops and fruit of the land.
Henry says the language can also describe destruction by a foreign invading army.
He sees a possible reference to the devastation caused by the Chaldeans.
God is the Lord of hosts.
Every created thing obeys his command.
When he chooses, he can humble a proud and rebellious people through the smallest and most despised creatures.
God is just to remove comforts that people misuse through luxury and excess.
The more we place our happiness in bodily pleasure, the more painful it is when outward blessings are taken away.
Every extra earthly comfort we treat as necessary for happiness increases our vulnerability to loss.

div.title: Everyone is called to mourn (verses 8–13)
div.p: Those who labor only for food that perishes will eventually find that their efforts bring disappointment.
People whose joy depends upon bodily pleasures lose that joy as soon as the pleasures are interrupted or removed.
Spiritual joy, however, can flourish precisely when outward comforts fail.
Notice how uncertain and temporary created comforts are.
We need to live in constant dependence upon God and his providential care.
Notice too the destruction produced by sin.
When poverty causes true worship and godliness to weaken and deprives people of spiritual instruction, the judgment is especially severe.
