Yet God's judgments can also be merciful awakenings, stirring his people from sleep and drawing their hearts back to Christ and his salvation.

div.title: The people must turn to God (verses 14–20)
div.p: The sorrow of the people was to become repentance and humility before God.
Alongside signs of grief and shame, they were to confess and mourn their sins.
A day was to be set apart for this purpose.
People would leave ordinary work to give more attention to God's worship and abstain from food and drink as they fasted.
Everyone had contributed to the nation's guilt, and everyone shared in its calamity.
Therefore everyone was called to join in repentance.
When joy disappears from God's house, sincere religion declines and love grows cold, it is time to cry out to the Lord.
The prophet described the severity of the disaster.
Even animals suffered because of human wrongdoing.
Those who cry to God only because they want food and drink, without concern for their sin, behave little better than animals.
Yet even an animal's cries for food shame the hardness of people who never cry to God for anything.
Whatever becomes of nations or churches that persist in wickedness, believers will still find comfort in being accepted by God, when the unrepentant face his judgment.

row.cell: Exhortations to fasting and prayer; blessings promised.
A promise of the Holy Spirit, and of future mercies.

div.title: The coming judgment and call to repentance (verses 1–14)
div.p: The priests were commanded to sound the alarm about God's approaching judgments.
God's ministers must warn people about the terrible consequences of sin and reveal his judgment against human ungodliness and unrighteousness.
The vivid description portrays the devastation caused by locusts.
Henry says it may also describe the destruction wrought by Chaldean invaders.
If sinful nations need warnings about earthly disasters, how much more urgently must sinners seek rescue from the wrath to come!
Our chief concern in this life should be belonging to our Lord Jesus Christ.
We should loosen our attachment to things that will soon be taken from everyone who treats them as idols.
Repentance includes outward signs of sorrow and shame—fasting, weeping and mourning.
But tears over hardship should become tears over the sin that caused it.
Tearing our clothes is worthless if our hearts remain unbroken.
True repentance requires humbling ourselves, mourning our wrongdoing and turning away from it.
Henry says we may be confident that God will forgive genuine repentance.
But he distinguishes this from the removal of every outward affliction: that is not promised, though the possibility of relief encourages us to turn back.

div.title: A public fast and the promise of mercy (verses 15–27)
div.p: The priests and rulers were called to proclaim a solemn fast.
The sinner's plea is simple: “Spare us, good Lord.”
God is ready to help his people.
He waits to show grace.
The people asked for mercy, and he answered their prayer.
His promises are genuine answers to prayers offered in faith.
With God, speaking and acting are not separate matters.
Henry notes that some interpreters understand these promises figuratively.
On that reading, they point toward the grace of the gospel and are fulfilled through the abundant comforts kept for believers in the covenant of grace.

div.title: The Holy Spirit is promised (verses 28–32)
div.p: The promise began to be fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was poured out.
It continued through converting grace and miraculous gifts, given to both Jews and Gentiles.
God's judgments upon a sinful world precede the final judgment of the world.
To call on the Lord truly involves knowing him, having faith in him, desiring him and depending upon him.
It must also be accompanied by conscientious obedience, which demonstrates that this faith is sincere.
Those who will be delivered on the great and final day are the people effectively called from sin to God, from self to Christ, and from earthly things to heavenly things.

row.cell: God's judgments in the latter days.
The blessings the church shall enjoy.

div.title: Judgment upon the nations (verses 1–8)
div.p: Henry understands this passage as foretelling the restoration of the Jews and the final victory of true religion over its enemies.
It recalls the contempt with which Jewish people have often been treated and the low value placed upon their lives.
No one has hardened the heart against God or his church and enjoyed lasting prosperity.

div.title: The day of judgment (verses 9–17)
div.p: The prophecy challenges all who oppose God's people.
There will be no escape from divine judgment.
In that day, unrepentant sinners will be cut off from every source of comfort and joy.
Henry notes that many prophets predict the final victory of God's church over those who oppose it.
The same day will be terrible for the wicked but joyful for the righteous.
Those who belong to Christ have reason to rejoice in their Strength and Redeemer.
The acceptable year of the Lord, so full of mercy for some, will be a day of extraordinary judgment for others.
Everyone who remains apart from Christ should awaken and flee from the wrath to come.

div.title: The church's future blessings (verses 18–21)
div.p: God will pour out his blessings abundantly, and the gospel will spread swiftly to the farthest regions of the earth.
The prophet speaks through meaningful symbols.
A day is coming when everything wrong will finally be made right.
The source of these abundant blessings is God's own house, from which the streams flow.
Christ is that Fountain.
His suffering, merit and grace cleanse, refresh and make people spiritually fruitful.
The grace of the gospel flowing from Christ will reach the Gentile world, even the most distant lands.
It will produce the fruits of righteousness among them.
All the good we enjoy now—and all we hope to enjoy forever—flows from the Lord's house above, his heavenly temple.

div.title: Amos — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Amos was a herdsman and also worked in agriculture.
The same Holy Spirit guided Isaiah and Daniel in royal courts and Amos among the flocks, giving each person the ability and eloquence necessary for the assigned task.
Amos warned the twelve tribes that the nations around them would be destroyed. Since the Israelites themselves had become devoted to wickedness and idolatry, he rebuked the people severely.
Yet he also spoke of the church's restoration through the Messiah, extending into the latter days.

p.hi: Judgments against the Syrians, Philistines, Tyrians, Edomites, and Ammonites.

div.title: God's warning to the surrounding nations
div.p: God chose a shepherd and herdsman to rebuke and warn his people.
People to whom God gives abilities for service must not be despised because of their background or occupation.
The prophet announced judgment against the surrounding nations that had oppressed God's people.
The expression concerning three transgressions and four does not specify an exact number. It means many sins: these nations had filled up the measure of their wrongdoing and were ripe for judgment.
God deals with these nations in ways that resemble one another, but each judgment also contains something particular.
In every age people have shown bitter hostility toward the Lord's people.
How dreadful are God's judgments when he calls his enemies to account!

row.cell: The ingratitude and ruin of Israel.

div.title: The sins of Moab and Judah (verses 1–8)
div.p: Evil desires in the heart become visible in many forms, but God examines motives as well as conduct.
People who treat others cruelly may expect to receive cruelty in return.
The surrounding nations were condemned for wrongs against human beings. Judah's sin was dishonoring God.
The people despised the Lord's law, and he justly abandoned them to deception.
The idolatry they inherited from their ancestors did not excuse their wrongdoing.
Some of the worst abominations and most grievous oppression have been committed by people claiming to worship the Lord.
Such conduct encourages others to become unbelieving and to turn toward idolatry.

div.title: Israel forgets God's gifts and opposes his servants (verses 9–16)
div.p: We need frequent reminders of God's former mercies.
Those mercies make our later sins more blameworthy.
Israel had received help for the soul—means of grace that taught the people how to use earthly blessings well.
Those spiritual gifts were more valuable than the earthly blessings themselves.
Faithful ministers are a tremendous blessing, and God is the One who raises them up.
Sinners' own consciences can testify that God did not leave them without opportunities to learn from his grace.
Yet the people did everything possible to draw faithful believers away from him.
Satan and his agents seek to corrupt young people, especially through the promise of amusement, bodily pleasure and drinking companions.
Many promising young professing Christians have been ruined by drunkenness.
The Lord describes these sins, especially those of people professing his name, as a burden to him.
His patience may be exhausted, but his power never is.
People who reject God's word and add stubbornness to their sins will not escape judgment through wealth or strength.
We should humble ourselves before God for ingratitude and unfaithfulness.

div.title: Israel's privileges do not exempt it from judgment (verses 1–8)
div.p: The special blessings God has given us cannot protect us from judgment if we use them as permission to sin.
People cannot expect fellowship with God without first seeking peace with him.
Where there is no friendship, there can be no fellowship.
God and humanity cannot walk together unless they are agreed.
We cannot walk with him unless we seek his glory.
External privileges provide no guarantee without particular, sanctifying grace.
The warnings contained in God's word and Providence are certain.
When he sends affliction, he will not remove it until it has fulfilled its purpose.
The evil of sin comes from ourselves; we are responsible for committing it.
But the evil of trouble is under God's government, whatever human or natural agents he uses.
Henry is explicit that here “evil” means calamity, not moral evil or sin.
That should lead us to bear shared suffering patiently and ask what God intends to teach through it.
A warning given to an indifferent world increases its responsibility before the coming judgment.
How astonishing that unbelieving people can disregard both God's terrors and his mercies!

div.title: The ruin of unjust power (verses 9–15)
div.p: Power used as an instrument of injustice will rightly be brought low.
Property and wealth obtained and kept dishonestly will not remain secure for long.
Some enjoy comfortable lives, but a day of reckoning will come.
Everything in which they took pride or placed their confidence will fail them.
God will examine the wrongdoing done within their own homes: the robbery they stored up and the luxury they enjoyed.
Splendid and pleasant houses provide no defense against divine judgment.
Instead, their loss may make suffering feel even more severe.
Yet God will preserve a remnant chosen by grace, as sheep rescued from the jaws of destruction by the great and good Shepherd.

div.title: Israel is reproved for exploitation and false worship (verses 1–5)
div.p: Wealth obtained through extortion is frequently spent on bodily pleasures and fulfilling sinful desires.
What has been acquired through oppression cannot bring lasting satisfaction.
How miserable are people who seek security in religious practices that Scripture does not authorize!
They show themselves ready to believe a lie.
We should carefully examine whether our faith, hope and worship have the support of God's word.

div.title: Stubbornness despite repeated warnings (verses 6–13)
div.p: People whose hearts are governed by bodily desires wander from one created thing to another seeking satisfaction.
They labor for what never fulfills them.
Yet after repeated disappointments they still refuse to listen to the One who can meet their deepest needs.
The preaching of the gospel is like rain.
Where this rain is missing, everything withers.
People often search diligently for the food their bodies need.
How much better if they showed the same care for their souls and, where the gospel is absent, went to hear it wherever it could be found.
Israel had persisted in disobedience and idolatry.
The Lord was therefore coming against the people as an adversary.
Soon each of us must meet God in judgment.
If he examines us strictly according to our own works, we cannot stand before him.
To prepare to meet him with peace and confidence, we must meet him now through Jesus Christ, the Father's eternal Son, who came to save lost sinners.
Seek him while he may be found.

row.cell: Israel is called to seek the Lord.

div.title: Seek the Lord and live (verses 1–6)
div.p: We must not listen only to words of comfort and peace.
We must also hear and take seriously the words of God that convict and awaken us.
Whether we listen or refuse, the word he has spoken will take effect.
The Lord still offers mercy to human beings.
But many expect salvation through forms of worship they have invented, even though those practices only strengthen their condemnation.
If people refuse to come to Jesus Christ and seek mercy in him, the fire of God's judgment will break out against them.
They may turn the world itself into an idol, only to discover it provides no protection.

div.title: Repentance, justice and divine mercy (verses 7–17)
div.p: The same almighty power can easily turn the suffering of repentant sinners into prosperity and joy, or turn the wealth of defiant sinners into complete darkness.
People living in evil times often refuse plain, honest correction.
Good and wise people may conclude that speaking openly will be useless.
Those who choose to seek and love what is good can nevertheless help save a country from destruction.
We should plead God's spiritual promises, asking him to create a clean heart and renew a right spirit in us.
He remains ready to show grace to people who genuinely seek him.
Their devotion will then affect every other responsibility.
Israel, however, had already experienced judgments that passed by the people as warnings.
Now the judgments would pass through them in full force.

div.title: The terrible day of the Lord (verses 18–27)
div.p: Woe to people who eagerly desire the day of the Lord's judgment or wish for war and national upheaval because they imagine they will profit from the destruction.
The promised devastation would be so great that nobody would gain from it.
For unrepentant sinners, the day of the Lord is dark and dreadful.
When God makes a day dark, the whole world cannot make it light.
Those whom one judgment fails to reform will be pursued by another.
Escaping one danger will only place them before another.
An outward appearance of godliness with no inward reality is a double evil.
Israel repeated its ancestors' sins.
True worship requires that the Lord alone be served.
People professing religion often progress very little because they have little or no fellowship with God during their religious duties.
Sin had already brought their hearts into captivity to Satan and idolatry.
God would therefore send them into physical captivity among idol worshipers.

row.cell: The danger of luxury and false security.

div.title: The danger of luxury and false security (verses 1–7)
div.p: People often believe that those who indulge their bodies and seek physical comfort are living well.
But Amos shows the danger hidden in such ease.
Here are the pride, complacency and sensuality for which God would call the people to account.
Careless sinners are in danger everywhere.
But those who feel completely safe in Zion, become indifferent to God's warnings and abuse their sacred privileges, are in the greatest danger.
Many imagine they belong to God while continuing in sin and conforming themselves to the world.
The downfall of other people should warn us not to be self-confident.
Those entirely absorbed by personal pleasures are often indifferent to the suffering of others.
This greatly offends God.
People who build their happiness upon sensual enjoyment will be deprived of the very pleasures they love.
Those who try to push the day of judgment far away will find it approaching them sooner than they expect.

div.title: Judgment upon pride and hardened hearts (verses 8–14)
div.p: How terrible is the condition of those whose destruction God himself has declared!
He has power to fulfill his purpose, and no creature can overturn it.
Some people's hearts are so hardened that even illness and death within their own families do not move them to speak of God or worship him.
A field that refuses to be cultivated will be abandoned like a barren rock.
When we corrupt God's worship with sin, we should not be surprised if his providential dealings become bitter to us.
Let all people beware of hardening their hearts.

p.hi: God will bring down those who walk in pride.

row.cell: Visions of judgments to come upon Israel.

div.title: The visions of judgment upon Israel (verses 1–9)
div.p: God shows great patience, but he will not endure a people's stubborn rebellion forever.
Remembering the mercies we once received should make us humble when later blessings disappoint us, just as the produce of an earlier harvest should teach gratitude when the next harvest fails.
The Lord has many ways to humble a sinful nation.
Whatever trouble we experience, our most urgent prayer should be for forgiveness of sin.
Sin can quickly reduce a great nation to helplessness.
What would become of Israel if the hand that should lift the people instead opposed them?
See the power of prayer!
See what a blessing people who pray can be to an entire country.
God is ready and swift to show mercy; he waits to be gracious.
Israel was like a strong wall God himself had built to protect his sanctuary.
But the Lord stood upon that wall with a plumb line.
It had become a wall that leaned and bulged, failing the test of straightness.
God would measure Israel and expose its sin.
There comes a time when people who have often been spared will be spared no longer.
Yet even then God still called Israel his people.
The prophet's repeated prayers and their earlier successful answers should lead us to seek the Savior.

div.title: Amaziah threatens Amos (verses 10–17)
div.p: Those who accuse their brothers and sisters in faith often portray them as enemies of the king and nation, traitors and disturbers of public peace, even when they are actually among the best friends of both.
People who use religious office for wealth and promotion tend to suppose everyone else is motivated by the same interests.
But servants who have received a commission from God, like Amos, should not fear human opposition.
Had God not strengthened Amos, he could not have set his face like flint.
The Lord frequently chooses the weak and foolish things of this world to shame the strong and wise.
Yet even earnest prayers and devoted service cannot always persuade proud sinners to accept faithful warnings and rebukes.
Everyone who despises or opposes God's word risks ruin unless they repent.

row.cell: The near approach of the ruin of Israel.
A famine of the word of God.

div.title: Israel is ripe for judgment (verses 1–3)
div.p: Amos saw a basket of summer fruit, picked and ready to eat.
This showed that Israel was ripe for destruction, because the period of God's patience was nearing its end.
Summer fruit cannot be kept fresh through winter.
It must be used quickly.
Yet the people would not acknowledge either God's righteousness or their own wrongdoing when the announced judgments came.
Sinners keep postponing repentance because they mistake God's delay for a promise that he will never judge them.

div.title: Oppressors despise worship and exploit the poor (verses 4–10)
div.p: The wealthy and powerful were especially guilty of oppression and idolatry.
They resented Sabbaths and new-moon festivals, when ordinary business stopped.
Many people calling themselves Christians behave similarly.
For people whose hearts are wholly worldly, a Sabbath becomes either a day to profane or a tiresome obligation.
Yet how could we use the day better than in fellowship with God?
Even while attending religious duties, these people were mentally busy with trade and markets.
They thought worship wasted valuable business time.
People who would rather sell grain than worship God show little regard for him.
And those who lose reverence for God often soon lose ordinary honesty toward other people.
They cheated their customers.
They exploited neighbors' ignorance and desperate need, especially in trading the food needed by working poor people.
How many forms of greed and fraud make commerce hateful to the Lord!
People whose wealth comes from the misery of the poor will eventually be ruined by their own riches.
To despise the poor is to dishonor their Maker, who created rich and poor alike.
God remembers such injustice.
He will call those who commit it to account.
Desolation will arrive when they least expect it.
All earthly pleasures, possessions and even life itself are uncertain.
In the midst of life, we are near death.
How bitter will be the grief following sinful and sensual pleasures!

div.title: A famine of God's word (verses 11–14)
div.p: The worst sign of divine displeasure is a famine of hearing the word of God.
Such a famine is especially terrible during distress, when people most need God's word.
Some will think little of its absence.
Others will feel the loss deeply and travel great distances simply to hear a faithful sermon.
They will suffer the loss of mercies other people carelessly threw away.
When God judges a church that has turned from him, its members' plans to invent a path of salvation will accomplish nothing.
Even the most attractive and energetic young people will perish spiritually without the water of life that only Jesus Christ gives.
Let us value the privileges we have, seek to benefit from them and fear losing them through sin.

row.cell: The restoration of the Jews and the gospel blessing.

div.title: Israel's ruin and a remnant preserved (verses 1–10)
div.p: The prophet saw the Lord standing upon the idolatrous altar at Bethel.
No matter where sinners try to escape God's justice, his judgment will overtake them.
Those whom God brings to heaven through grace can never be thrown down.
But those who try to climb there through proud confidence in themselves will be brought low and covered with shame.
What makes escape impossible and judgment certain is that the Lord sets his eyes upon the wicked for harm rather than for good.
He would scatter the Israelites and bring suffering upon them, as grain is shaken in a sieve.
Yet some would be saved.
Henry considers the remarkable preservation of the Jews as a distinct people to be foretold here.
People who claim to belong to God while making themselves like the world should expect to be treated as the world is treated.
Their outward religious profession will not protect them from judgment.

div.title: God's church restored through Christ (verses 11–15)
div.p: Christ died to gather God's scattered children together.
Here they are described as people called by the Lord's name.
God himself speaks the promise.
He is able to fulfill it, has decided to do so, and has committed the power of his grace to accomplishing it.
Henry suggests that verses 13–15 may refer partly to the earliest Christian period.
Yet he expects a fuller and more glorious fulfillment when the fullness of both Jews and Gentiles enters the church.
We should continue praying earnestly for the promised peace, purity and beauty of God's church.
The Lord wonderfully preserves his chosen people amid even the most terrible disorders and suffering.
When everything looks hopeless, he revives his church and fills it with every spiritual blessing in Jesus Christ.
Glorious will be the age when not one of God's good promises remains unfulfilled.

div.title: Obadiah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The first part of this prophecy announces the destruction of Edom, concentrating on the injuries that the Edomites had inflicted upon the Jewish people.
The second part predicts the restoration of the Jews and the church's later glory.

row.cell: Destruction to come upon Edom. Their offences against Jacob.
The restoration of the Jews, and their flourishing state in the latter times.

div.title: Edom's pride and cruelty bring judgment (verses 1–16)
div.p: The prophecy is directed against Edom.
Henry regards its destruction as a figure of the fate of those who oppose the gospel church, just as Esau's rejection pointed beyond itself.
The prophet foretells that Edom will be plundered and brought low.
Every enemy of God's church will eventually be disappointed in whatever provides their sense of security.
God can humble those who make themselves great, and he will do so.
False security prepares people for ruin and makes that ruin more severe when it arrives.
Earthly treasures cannot be hidden so safely that thieves will never discover them.
It is wiser to lay up treasure in heaven.
Those who place their confidence in human strength may find that strength turned against them.
God, who keeps his covenant, will never deceive his people.
But people we trust and join ourselves to may cause great injury and humiliation.
God rightly deprives people of wisdom to escape danger when they refuse to use their wisdom to avoid sin.
Every act of violence and injustice is sinful.
But such acts are especially grievous when directed against God's people.
Edom's cruel conduct toward Judah and Jerusalem was remembered.
When examining ourselves, we should ask what we ought to have done and compare what we actually did with the rule of Scripture.
Sin seen in the light of God's command appears exceedingly sinful.
Those who remain idle spectators of a neighbor's suffering when they could have helped bear serious responsibility.
People imagining they will grow wealthy through the ruin of God's people are actually impoverishing themselves.
They deceive themselves when they claim as their own everything they can seize during another person's disaster.
Judgment may begin at God's own house, but it will not end there.
Let suffering believers and arrogant oppressors remember that the righteous person's trials will end, while the wicked person's final misery will not.

div.title: The restoration of Israel and the church's future (verses 17–21)
div.p: The Lord promised deliverance and holiness in Jerusalem.
The house of Jacob would recover its possessions.
Much of this prediction was fulfilled when the Jews returned to their own land.
Henry also believes it points toward the salvation and holiness of the gospel, its spread and the conversion of the Gentiles.
He expects it to encompass Israel's future restoration, the defeat of antichrist and the church's flourishing, themes he also sees in other prophets.
Only when Christ comes will the kingdom be the Lord's in its fullest sense.
Those who lift themselves against the Lord will finally be brought down.
But those who wait for him and trust him need never be overcome by fear.
Blessed be the divine Savior and Judge upon Mount Zion!
His word brings life to many, while judging and condemning people who persist stubbornly in unbelief.

div.title: Jonah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Jonah came from Galilee (2 Kings 14:25).
His miraculous rescue from the fish made him a type of our blessed Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus himself referred to the event, thereby affirming that the narrative is true.
For the almighty Creator and Sustainer of life, everything described in the book was possible.
The example of the people of Nineveh shows the abundance of God's patience and forbearance toward sinners.
The book also presents a sharp contrast between God's mercy and goodness and his servant's disobedience, impatience and irritability.
Those who know their own hearts best will understand its lessons most deeply.

row.cell: Jonah, sent to Nineveh, flees to Tarshish.
He is stayed by a tempest.
He is cast into the sea, and miraculously preserved.

div.title: Jonah flees from his calling (verses 1–3)
div.p: How sad it is to think of the great amount of sin committed in the world's large cities!
The wickedness of Nineveh was an open and defiant insult to God.
Jonah was commanded to go there immediately and warn the people publicly.
But he refused.
Few of us can honestly claim we would have eagerly accepted such a dangerous mission without hesitation.
Jonah found what looked like a providential opportunity to escape.
But a person can be outside the path of duty and still receive a favorable wind.

p.hi: The easiest route is not always the right one.

div.p: See how even the best human beings can act when God leaves them to themselves.
When we hear God's commands, we also need the Holy Spirit to bring our thoughts into submission to his will.

div.title: The storm awakens the sailors (verses 4–7)
div.p: God sent a terrible storm in pursuit of Jonah.
Sin brings storms into souls, households, churches and whole nations.
It disturbs and destroys peace.
The sailors cried out to their gods and also did everything they could to save the ship.
If only people showed as much wisdom about their souls!
They would gladly part with the wealth, pleasure and honor they cannot keep without destroying faith, conscience and ultimately salvation.
Meanwhile, Jonah slept deeply.
Sin makes people numb and careless.
We must beware of hearts hardened by its deceitfulness.
What are sinners thinking when they sleep on despite the warnings of Scripture and conscience?
We should awaken one another and encourage everyone to call on God for deliverance.
The sailors concluded that the disaster had some moral cause.
Whatever affliction we experience, we should ask the Lord what we need to learn from it.
The lot fell upon Jonah.
God has many ways of uncovering sins and sinners that everyone imagined were safely hidden.

div.title: Jonah confesses before the sailors (verses 8–12)
div.p: Jonah explained his faith.
Henry hopes he did so with sorrow and shame, confessing his guilt and honoring God's justice.
He taught the sailors about Jehovah, the Maker of sea and land.
They challenged him:
If he feared the Creator of land and sea, why had he imagined he could flee from God's presence?
When people who profess religion act wrongly, even those who do not profess it may justly rebuke them.
When sin has stirred a storm, we must address the sin that caused it.
Jonah spoke like a truly repentant person who does not want other people to suffer because of personal folly.
He accepted the sentence and acknowledged God's justice.
A guilty conscience will find no genuine peace until it abandons the sin that has troubled it.
Simply surrendering money or possessions cannot cleanse the conscience.
In the image of this account, Jonah himself must be thrown overboard.

div.title: Jonah is thrown into the sea and preserved (verses 13–17)
div.p: The sailors tried rowing against the wind of God's displeasure and the current of his purpose.
But it was useless to seek safety without dealing with the cause of the judgment.
Even an ordinary human conscience naturally fears becoming guilty of another person's death.
When God leads us through his Providence, we ought to be satisfied with his wise purposes, even when they are difficult for us to accept.
The storm stopped when Jonah was cast into the sea.
God does not discipline forever.
His correction lasts until his purpose is fulfilled and his people submit to him.
The pagan sailors may rise in judgment against many people called Christians who offer neither prayer in distress nor thanksgiving after deliverance.
The Lord commands every creature.
He can make any of them an instrument of mercy toward his people.
How wonderful his power in preserving a drowning man, and how great his pity in preserving one who had fled from and offended him!
It was because of the Lord's mercy that Jonah was not destroyed.
He remained alive in the fish for three days and three nights.
This was impossible by ordinary natural means, but everything is possible for the God who rules nature.
Jonah's preservation made him a type of Christ, as Jesus expressly taught in Matthew 12:40.

row.cell: He is delivered from the fish.

div.title: Jonah prays in the fish (verses 1–9)
div.p: Consider when Jonah prayed.
He was in distress, experiencing God's displeasure because of his disobedience.
We should pray whenever we suffer.
He had been preserved alive by a miracle and now turned to God.
Knowing that God still regards us with kindness, despite our wrongdoing, gives us courage to pray when fear of judgment has kept us silent.
Consider where he prayed: inside the great fish.
No place is unsuitable for prayer.
People may separate us from one another, but they cannot separate us from fellowship with God.
Consider whom he addressed: the Lord his God.
That encourages even people who have wandered away from their faith to return.
Consider the nature of his prayer.
The words recorded here seem to recount Jonah's experience and later reflections, rather than reproduce the exact words he said at every moment inside the fish.
He remembered how earnestly he had cried out, and how readily God had heard and answered him.
If we are to benefit from suffering, we must recognize God's hand in it.
Jonah had fled wickedly from the Lord's presence.
God could justly have withdrawn his Holy Spirit from him and never returned to him.
Only those from whom God withdraws his favor completely are truly miserable.
Jonah was perplexed but not without hope.
When he sought and trusted God in trouble, he experienced mercy.
He urged others to remain close to the Lord.
People who abandon their duty also abandon the comforts associated with fulfilling it.
As far as believers copy people who worship false things, they turn away from their own mercy and live beneath the privileges God has given them.
But Jonah's experience encourages believers in every age to trust the Lord as the God of salvation.

div.title: Jonah is released (verse 10)
div.p: Jonah's deliverance demonstrates God's power over every created thing.
It also displays his mercy toward a repentant sinner who prayed in trouble.
And it serves as a type of Christ's resurrection.
Through every change in circumstances, let us fix our faith upon our Redeemer who suffered and died, but has now risen and ascended.
Confess our sins.
Regard Christ's resurrection as a pledge of our own.
Receive every earthly and spiritual deliverance with thanks as a foretaste of eternal redemption.

row.cell: Jonah sent again to Nineveh, preaches there.
Nineveh is spared upon the repentance of the inhabitants.

div.title: Jonah returns to his calling (verses 1–4)
div.p: God employed Jonah again.
The Lord's willingness to use us in his work is evidence of peace restored between us and him.
Jonah was no longer rebellious.
He did not avoid hearing the command or refuse to carry it out.
This is what genuine repentance looks like: a changed mind and conduct, a return to assigned work and duty.
Suffering can benefit us by bringing us back to the service we abandoned.
But that change displays divine grace, because suffering by itself is more likely to drive sinners away from God than to draw them to him.
The Lord's servants must go where he sends them, come when he calls, and do what he commands.
Jonah faithfully and boldly delivered his message.
Henry says it is uncertain whether Jonah added more explanation about God's anger or simply repeated the announcement.
Its central meaning is clear.
Forty days is a long delay for a righteous God to allow before judgment, but it is little time for sinful people to repent and reform.
The announcement should make us think seriously about preparation for death.
We cannot be as confident that we will live forty days as Nineveh was that it would endure for forty days.
We would be frightened if told with certainty we had less than a month to live, yet often remain indifferent though we cannot guarantee another day.

div.title: The Ninevites repent and are spared (verses 5–10)
div.p: The repentance and reform of Nineveh were a marvel of God's grace.
The people condemned later generations that heard the gospel and did not repent (Matthew 12:41).
Even limited knowledge about God can convince people that humility, confession, prayer and turning from sin are necessary in seeking mercy.
The people followed their king's example.
The repentance became national, as was necessary when the announced judgment concerned the whole nation.
Even the cries of animals deprived of food should remind their owners to cry to God.
When praying, we must cry earnestly, with fixed attention, strong faith and sincere affection.
Every part of the heart should be involved.
It is not enough to fast because of sin.
We must fast from sin.
If we cherish evil inwardly, our prayers cannot be sincere (Psalm 66:18).
A day's appointed fast does not complete the work of repentance when the day is over.
The Ninevites hoped that God would turn from his anger.
They had less certainty of finding mercy than Christians now possess through the death and merits of Jesus Christ, the foundation of pardon for those who repent.
They dared not presume upon grace, but they did not despair.
The hope of mercy is a powerful encouragement to sincere reform.
Let us humbly cast ourselves upon God's free grace.
He sees who actually turn from evil and who continue in it.
That is why he spared Nineveh.
The account records no sacrifices offered to provide atonement.
But God did not despise broken and contrite hearts.

row.cell: Jonah repines at God's mercy to Nineveh, and is reproved.
He is taught by the withering of a gourd, that he did wrong.

div.title: Jonah resents God's mercy (verses 1–4)
div.p: God's people usually celebrate and praise his mercy toward sinners.
But Jonah made that mercy the reason for accusing God.
He spoke as though showing compassion were a defect in God's nature, when it is actually one of his greatest glories.
We all owe our rescue from judgment to his pardoning, sparing mercy.
Jonah wished for death.
Henry calls that wish foolish, passionate and deeply corrupted.
Pride and lack of charity remained within the prophet.
He had neither expected nor desired Nineveh's salvation, but had only wanted to announce and witness its destruction.
He had not been humbled enough concerning his own sins.
Nor had he entrusted his personal honor and safety to the Lord.
In this frame of mind he failed to see the great good accomplished through his service and the glory of God's mercy.
We should frequently examine ourselves.
Is this the right thing to say or do?
Can I justify the way I am acting?
Is it right to become angry so quickly, so often or for so long?
Is it right to insult other people during anger?
Is it right to resent God's mercy toward repentant sinners?
That was Jonah's sin.
How could we resent something that glorifies God and advances his kingdom?
The conversion of sinners brings joy in heaven.
It should bring joy to us, not grief.

div.title: God teaches Jonah through the plant (verses 5–11)
div.p: Jonah went outside Nineveh but stayed near the city, apparently still wishing to see it destroyed.
People who habitually complain often create troubles for themselves so that they will always have something to resent.
Notice God's tenderness toward his people even when they are foolish and stubborn.
A small gift received at exactly the needed moment can become an enormous blessing.

p.hi: A gourd in the right place may help us more than a cedar tree.

div.p: Even the smallest creatures can become great troubles or great comforts, depending on God's purpose.
People ruled by intense passions may be thrown down by a tiny disappointment or lifted up by a tiny pleasure.
Created comforts are perishable.
A small worm at the root can destroy a large and useful plant.
So our earthly comforts may disappear even when we cannot discover the immediate cause.
Sometimes the gift remains with us, but the joy it brought is gone.
The creature remains, but the comfort has disappeared.
God sent a wind that made Jonah feel the plant's absence.
Those who love to complain will find no shortage of things to complain about.
When Providence removes loved ones, possessions and pleasures, we must not resent God.
The strongest reason to silence our complaining is this:

p.hi: When our gourd is gone, our God has not gone.

div.p: Jonah treated sin and death lightly while angry.
But one soul is worth more than the whole world, and certainly more than many plants and earthly comforts.
We should care more about our own and others' immortal souls than about the wealth and enjoyment of the world.
God's readiness to show mercy gives us every reason to hope.
Those who grumble may want God's grace reserved only for themselves and people like them.
But one Lord governs all people and is rich in mercy toward everyone who calls upon him.
When we are astonished at God's patience toward this stubborn prophet, let us examine our own hearts.
Remember our own ingratitude and obstinacy, and marvel at how patiently God deals with us.

div.title: Micah — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: God raised up Micah to support Isaiah and confirm his prophecies.
Micah called the people to repentance through warnings of coming judgment and promises of mercy.
Micah chapter 5 contains an especially remarkable summary of prophecies concerning the Messiah.

row.cell: The wrath of God against Israel.
Also against Jerusalem and other cities, Their precautions vain.

div.title: God's wrath against Israel (verses 1–7)
div.p: The whole earth and everything within it is summoned to hear the prophet.
God's holy temple cannot protect people who profess to worship him while living hypocritically.
Neither the great and powerful, pictured by mountains, nor ordinary people, pictured by valleys, can protect themselves or their land from divine judgment.
God does not overlook sin among those who claim to belong to him.
Indeed, their sins especially offend him because they bring disgrace upon his name.
When we suffer the consequences of wrongdoing, it is wise to examine what particular sin has caused us to suffer.
People and places held in the greatest honor can be especially exposed to spiritual diseases.
The sins of leaders and rulers will be punished severely.
The judgment will correspond to the sin.
What the people sacrificed to their idols will never make them prosperous or truly help them.

p.hi: Wealth gained through one sinful desire is often consumed by another.

div.title: Jerusalem and the other cities cannot escape (verses 8–16)
div.p: Micah grieved over Israel's desperate condition.
But the people should not announce it in Gath, giving enjoyment to those who delight in God's people's sins or suffering.
The prophet spoke of lying in the dust as a mourner.
Let every house in Jerusalem become a house of Aphrah, meaning “house of dust” in Henry's explanation.
When God humbles us to the dust, it is right for us to humble ourselves beneath his mighty hand.
Many towns would share this grief.
Their names contained meanings that pointed to the calamities approaching them.
The intention was to awaken a holy fear of God's wrath.
All refuges other than Jesus Christ become false shelters for people who place their ultimate trust in them.
Every earthly inheritance passes to later heirs, except the heavenly inheritance.
Every human glory will eventually become shame, except the honor that comes from God alone.
Sinners may now ignore the suffering of their neighbors.
But the time for their own judgment will also come.

row.cell: The sins and desolations of Israel.

div.title: The people plan evil and exploit their neighbors (verses 1–5)
div.p: Woe to people who plan evil during the night and rise early to carry it out!
It is bad to hurt others through a sudden thought.
It is worse to act with deliberation and careful planning.
How important it is to use hours of solitude wisely!
When greed rules the heart, compassion disappears.
Once the heart is captured in that way, the hands soon practice violence and fraud.
People who are arrogant and complacent in prosperity are often the first to despair when adversity arrives.
Woe to those from whom God turns away!
Some of the most severe judgments are those that remove us from the fellowship of God's people or deprive us of the benefits of worship.

div.title: God's word rejected; the world cannot give rest (verses 6–11)
div.p: The people told God's prophets not to preach.
God would let their own wish become their punishment.
Why should a physician continue visiting a patient who refuses to be healed?
Those who silence faithful ministers and obstruct access to the means of grace are enemies not only of God but also of their country.
If people feel no reverence for God's word, what can restrain their conduct?
Sinners should not expect lasting peace in a land they have polluted with wickedness.
They would be forced to leave it, and it would become the instrument of their ruin.
This also teaches us about our present world.
Sin has corrupted it.
We should avoid sharing in its corruption.
This world was designed as a place to pass through, not our final possession.
It is our inn, not our home.
We have no lasting city here.
Let us rise and seek the enduring city above.
People determined to be deceived will find teachers willing to deceive them.
Ministers who promote self-indulgence through their teaching and example will appeal to such listeners.

div.title: The Lord opens a way for his people (verses 12–13)
div.p: These verses may refer to the captivity of Israel and Judah and their eventual return.
Henry also sees a prophecy of Jewish conversion to Christ.
The Lord would bring his people out of captivity and multiply them.
Jesus Christ would open their way to God by taking on human nature and, through the Holy Spirit, breaking Satan's chains within their hearts.
He leads his people, and they follow.
In his strength they overcome the spiritual enemies that would block their way to heaven.

row.cell: The cruelty of the princes, and the falsehood of the prophets.

div.title: Cruel rulers and dishonest prophets (verses 1–8)
div.p: People cannot expect to live wickedly and yet enjoy lasting prosperity.
They may experience the same kind of harm they have done to others.
How rarely do uncomfortable but wholesome truths reach the ears of those with high rank and public authority!
People who mislead others are preparing humiliation for themselves.
Micah possessed a burning love for God and for people's souls.
He cared deeply about God's glory, their salvation and the destruction caused by sin.
The difficulties he encountered did not drive him away from his calling.
His strength came not from himself, but because he was filled with the Spirit of the Lord.
People who act honestly can also act boldly.
Those who come to hear God's word should be willing to have their sins pointed out.
They should receive correction graciously and with gratitude.

div.title: The false confidence of leaders (verses 9–12)
div.p: Zion's walls are no reason to honor people who built them by shed blood and injustice.
Human sin does not accomplish God's righteousness.
Even acts that are outwardly useful become hateful to God and to people when they are done for dishonest profit.
Faith rests upon the Lord as the soul's foundation.
Presumption merely leans upon God as a support when it is convenient, attempting to make him serve private interests.
Claiming that the Lord dwells among us does not protect us from judgment when his presence has not restrained our evil conduct.
Micah announced that Zion would be plowed like a field because of its leaders' sin.
Henry says the prophecy was fulfilled at the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans and remained evident in his own day.
The historical interpretation belongs to Henry.
When sacred places are polluted with sin, God may rightly bring them to ruin.

row.cell: The peace of the kingdom of Christ.
The judgments to come upon Jerusalem, but the final triumph of Israel.

div.title: Peace in Christ's kingdom (verses 1–8)
div.p: The nations have not yet submitted to the Prince of Peace so fully that swords have become plowshares and warfare has ceased.
Yet these promises concerning the gospel church are precious.
They will increasingly be fulfilled because the One who promised is faithful.
In the latter days, during the reign of the Messiah, a glorious church will be established.
Christ himself will build it upon a rock.
The Gentiles once worshiped false gods.
But the people described here will hold firmly to the Lord, love him wholeheartedly and delight in obeying his will.
Those who limp in their spiritual walk are people who do not follow God's word faithfully.
The return of the captives from Babylon was a pledge of future healing, cleansing and prosperity for the church.
Christ's reign will continue until it reaches the everlasting kingdom of heaven.
We should encourage one another to attend God's appointed worship, learn his ways and obey them.
God's law must be written upon our hearts by his Spirit.
That transformation gives evidence of our share in the Redeemer's righteousness.

div.title: Jerusalem's distress and final triumph (verses 9–13)
div.p: Many nations would gather against Zion, intending to celebrate her defeat.
But they would not know that the Lord had brought them together like bundles of grain prepared for threshing.
Zion would receive strength to overcome them.
Henry says nothing in Jewish history up to his time fully corresponded to this prophecy.
He expected its fulfillment in a future event.
Whenever God assigns his people work to overcome opposition, he also provides the strength and ability they need.
Believers facing suffering should cry out in the prayer of faith, not in hopelessness.

row.cell: The birth of Christ and conversion of the Gentiles.

div.title: Christ's birth in Bethlehem and his kingdom (verses 1–6)
div.p: After announcing how greatly David's royal family would be brought low, Micah gave a promise about the Messiah and his kingdom to strengthen God's people's faith.
The prophecy reveals Christ's eternal existence as God and his work as Mediator.
His birth would take place in Bethlehem.
The Jews understood that location as the Messiah's birthplace (Matthew 2:5).
Christ's government brings happiness to his people.
They may enjoy security and rest under his care.
The promised protection from the Assyrians also represents the protection Christ gives the gospel church and individual believers against the powers of darkness.
Christ is our Peace as Priest, because he atones for sin and reconciles us to God.
Christ is our Peace as King, because he conquers our enemies.
Therefore our souls may rest confidently in him.
Christ will also provide human instruments of protection and deliverance.
Those who attempt to destroy God's church frequently bring destruction upon themselves.
Henry sees these promises as possibly encompassing the past successes of gospel preaching, the future spread of the gospel and the downfall of powers opposing Christ.
He calls this perhaps the most important single prophecy in the Old Testament, because it reveals the Messiah's personal character and the way he would be made known to the world.
It distinguishes his birth as a human being from his eternal divine existence.
Henry also understands it to predict Israel's temporary rejection and final restoration, and universal peace in the latter days.
Meanwhile, let us trust our Shepherd's care and power.
If he allows enemies to attack, he will provide the assistance we need.

div.title: The remnant of Israel and its victories (verses 7–15)
div.p: The remnant of Israel converted to Christ during the early Christian period was scattered among many nations like drops of dew.
These believers became instruments by which many additional people were brought into spiritual worship.
For people who rejected or opposed salvation, however, they became like lions.
Their message condemned those who persisted in unbelief.
God promised not only the reform of the Jews but also the purification of the Christian church.
Likewise, in our own spiritual struggles, we can expect victory when we depend simply upon the Lord our salvation, worship him and serve him diligently.

div.title: God calls Israel to account (verses 1–5)
div.p: God called the people to explain why they were tired of his worship and inclined toward idolatry.
Sin creates the dispute between God and humanity.
The Lord reasons with us to teach us how to examine our own conduct honestly.
He called Israel to remember the many favors shown both to them and to their ancestors.
They should compare those gifts with their own ungrateful and shameful behavior.

div.title: What does God require? (verses 6–8)
div.p: Henry says these verses seem to reflect the substance of Balak's consultation with Balaam about how to obtain Israel's God's favor.
A deep awareness of guilt and judgment makes people ask urgently how to find pardon and peace.
That concern may be an early sign of hope.
But we must learn that acceptance with God rests upon the atoning work of Jesus Christ.
We must also leave the sins through which we offend him.
What could satisfy God's justice?
In whose name can we come, since we have no righteousness of our own to plead?
In what righteousness can we appear before him?
The sacrifices the people proposed were impressive and expensive.
Their eagerness showed some understanding of guilt, but they did not know the right means of pardon.
People deeply convinced of their sin and danger would surrender everything they owned if that would purchase forgiveness.
But their proposals could not succeed.
The animal sacrifices received their meaning from their reference to Christ.
It was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to remove sin.
Every plan for peace with God outside the gospel fails.
No gift offered by sinners can satisfy divine justice or compensate for dishonoring God through sin.
Nor can offerings ever replace holiness of heart and a reformed life.
People may surrender almost anything except their sins.
Yet no offering makes them acceptable to God if they refuse to abandon their sins.
God commands moral duties because they are good for human beings.
Keeping his commandments brings reward in the keeping itself, as well as afterward.
God has made his requirements clear and understandable.
What he requires is not a payment for pardon, but love for him, expressed through doing justice, loving mercy and walking humbly with him.
Nothing in that is unreasonable.
If we are to walk happily with God, every thought must be brought into obedience to him.
We must do this as repentant sinners depending on the Redeemer and his atonement.
Blessed be God, who is ready to give grace to the humble person who waits for him.

div.title: Israel's injustice cannot be excused (verses 9–16)
div.p: God had made the duty to do justice clear.
The same passage now showed plainly how Israel had acted unjustly.
Hear the Lord's warning before the rod of judgment arrives.
And when correction does come, listen to its guidance.
God's voice should be heard in his acts of discipline.
People who are dishonest in business cannot be considered pure simply because they make a show of religious devotion.
What comes through fraud and oppression cannot be kept or enjoyed with genuine peace.
The possessions we cling to most tightly are often lost first.
Sin is a root of bitterness, easy to plant but difficult to remove.
It was once an honor for Israel to be called God's people.
But when they abandoned him, the name became a reproach rather than an honor.

row.cell: Reliance on God, and triumph over enemies.

div.title: Wickedness spreads even through families (verses 1–7)
div.p: The prophet grieved that he was living among people rapidly approaching judgment.
Many righteous people would suffer alongside them.
Even families and close relatives no longer brought comfort.
Neglect and contempt for family responsibilities are sad signs of widespread corruption.
People who refuse proper respect and service to their parents are unlikely to live well.
Micah found safety and consolation only in looking to the Lord and waiting for God his Savior.
During suffering, we should continually look to our divine Redeemer for faith and strength.
He will enable us to trust him and be good examples to those around us.

div.title: Trusting God while waiting for deliverance (verses 8–13)
div.p: People who have truly repented of sin find strong reasons to be patient under affliction.
When we complain to God about the wickedness of our age, we should also confess the sins of our own hearts.
We must rely on him to bring rescue at the proper time.
We should not only look to him but also look expectantly for him.
Even during our worst distress, we need not despair of salvation when we trust the Lord as the God of our salvation.
Enemies may celebrate our ruin, but eventually their pride will be silenced.
Zion's walls may lie broken for a long time, but a day will come when they are rebuilt.
Israel will return from distant places, without turning back because of discouragement.
When enemies seem to prevail, we should not become hopeless.
Though cast down, we are not destroyed.
We can combine hope in God's mercy with submission to his correction.
No obstacle can prevent the blessings the Lord has decided to give his church.

div.title: God's shepherding and complete forgiveness (verses 14–20)
div.p: When God is preparing to deliver his people, he moves their friends to pray for them.
Henry understands the prophet's prayer as applying spiritually to Christ, the great Shepherd of his sheep.
Christ leads and cares for his people while they travel through this world, where they are present but do not belong.
God's promise in answer to prayer is that he will act for them with power reminiscent of the miracles of earlier ages.
Sin brought the people into bondage.
God's forgiveness releases them from it.
Everyone who experiences pardoning mercy has reason to be amazed.
When the Lord removes the guilt of sin, so that it can no longer condemn us, he also breaks the ruling power of sin, so that it cannot continue to dominate us.
Our own strength is insufficient to defeat remaining sinful desires.
But God's grace is enough to subdue them.
If sin no longer rules us, it will not ruin us.
When God forgives, he ensures that the sin is no longer remembered against the sinner.
He throws the sins into the depths of the sea, not merely into shallow water near shore where they might reappear.
They will never rise again.
He casts all their sins into that depth, because when he pardons, he pardons completely.
The Lord will finish the work he began for us and do everything our condition needs according to his promises.
Henry connects these promises with Christ, the success of the gospel through the end of time, the future restoration of Israel and the final spread of true religion throughout the nations.
God will fulfill every part of his truth and mercy.
Nothing he promised will fail.
The One who made the promises is faithful and will accomplish them.
The security of his covenant gives strong consolation to everyone who flees to Christ for refuge and holds onto the hope set before them.

row.cell: The justice and power of the Lord.

div.title: God's justice, power and goodness (verses 1–8)
div.p: About a hundred years before Nahum, the people of Nineveh had repented when Jonah preached to them.
Their city was spared, but afterward they became even more wicked than before.
Nineveh did not truly know the God with whom it was contending.
Nahum therefore announced what kind of God he is.
Everyone should receive these words with faith.
They are terrifying to wicked people but comforting to believers.
Let sinners read them and tremble; let faithful people read them and rejoice.
The Lord's anger against sin is set beside his goodness toward his people.
They may be little known or respected in the world, but the Lord knows those who belong to him.
The Bible's portrait of Jehovah does not fit the notions of proud people who imagine they can decide what God must be like.
The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is slow to anger and ready to forgive.
Yet he will not declare the unrepentant wicked innocent.
Trouble and anguish await everyone who continues doing evil.
Who pays proper attention to the power of his anger?

div.title: Assyria's destruction and the good news of peace (verses 9–15)
div.p: The powers of evil devise many plans against the Lord and his kingdom on earth.
All such plots will finally fail.
Some sinners are brought to judgment quickly.
One way or another, God will put an end to all his enemies.
People may feel calm and secure, without the least fear of disaster.
Yet they can be cut down like grass or grain when the destroying messenger passes through.
Through the downfall of Assyria, the Lord intended to bring great deliverance to his own people.
Those who disgrace themselves through conspicuous wrongdoing may be brought to public disgrace through judgment.
The news of deliverance would be welcomed with great joy.
Scripture also applies these words to the great redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ and to the lasting good news of the gospel (Romans 10:15).
Christ's ministers are messengers announcing the peace made available through him.
How welcome this message is to those who recognize the misery and danger brought upon them by sin!
Promises made to God during times of trouble should be fulfilled afterward.
Let us be thankful for his appointed ordinances and gladly take part in them.
And let us look forward with cheerful hope to a world where the wicked cannot enter and where sin and temptation will no longer be known.

row.cell: The true cause, their sinning against God, and his appearing against them.

div.title: Nineveh's destruction is foretold (verses 1–10)
div.p: Nineveh would not be able to turn away the judgment approaching it.

p.hi: Neither human advice nor military strength can prevail against the Lord.

div.p: God looks upon proud and powerful cities and brings them low.
Nahum described in detail the terrifying appearance of the attacking army and the fear it would produce.
The Assyrian empire is pictured as a queen about to be led away captive to Babylon.
When a guilty conscience is awakened in a day of trouble, the mind may be filled with terror.
What help can stored wealth and public glory offer in such a moment, or when the day of divine wrath arrives?
Yet how many people sacrifice their souls to obtain those very things!

div.title: Assyria's cruelty brings judgment (verses 11–13)
div.p: The Assyrian kings had long terrorized their neighbors through their cruelty.
Now the Lord would break their power.
Some people excuse robbery and deceit by saying they have families to provide for.
But possessions gained through such wrongdoing will not bring lasting good to them or their households.
Those who fear the Lord and earn their living honestly may depend upon his care for themselves and those who belong to them.
God may justly remove children or the comfort parents expected to receive from them when the parents have used sinful methods to enrich the family.
People who have insulted God with their speech may find that their voices are no longer heard.
Therefore, rather than trusting in dishonest gain or worldly power, let us approach God's throne of mercy.
Through our Lord Jesus Christ we may have peace with God and know that he is for us.
Then we can trust that all things will work together for our everlasting good.

row.cell: The sins and judgments of Nineveh.

div.title: Nineveh's sins and judgment (verses 1–7)
div.p: When proud sinners are brought down, others should learn not to become proud themselves.
The destruction of this great city warns individual people who accumulate wealth through deception and oppression.
By mistreating others, they create enemies for themselves.
If the Lord decides to punish them in this life, they may find no one willing to pity them.
Everyone who seeks personal prosperity, safety and peace should act not only honestly and honorably, but also with kindness toward all.

div.title: Nineveh's complete downfall (verses 8–19)
div.p: Even the strongest fortresses cannot protect people from God's judgments.
When he determines that they must fall, they will be unable to defend themselves.
The Chaldeans and Medes would consume the land like swarms of destructive insects.
Henry also understands the multitude of hired soldiers to be among the forces that would consume Assyria itself.
He suggests that the term translated “merchants” in this passage may refer to those troops.
Those who have done evil to their neighbors will eventually experience the consequences.
Nineveh, along with many other cities, kingdoms and empires, has been ruined.
Their histories ought to warn us.
Are we any better?
Only the presence of true believers among a people provides a stronger defense than favorable geography or military strength.
When the Lord sets himself against a nation, everything it trusts in will either fail or become a disadvantage.
But he continues to show goodness to Israel.

p.hi: The Lord himself is an unconquerable stronghold for every believer in trouble.

div.p: No enemy can storm or capture that refuge.
He knows those who trust in him.

row.cell: The wickedness of the land. The fearful vengeance to be executed.
These judgments to be inflicted by a nation more wicked than themselves.

div.title: Widespread wrongdoing and the coming Chaldeans (verses 1–11)
div.p: The Lord's servants are deeply distressed when they see irreverence and violence prevail, especially among people who profess to know the truth.
People had become willing to injure their neighbors without hesitation.
We should long for the world in which holiness and love reign forever and violence will never again be seen.
God has wise reasons both for showing patience toward wicked people and for allowing his faithful servants to express their concern.
The day will come when the cry raised by wrongdoing will testify against those who committed it, while the prayers of people who suffered wrong will be heard on their behalf.
God's people were to watch what was happening among the surrounding nations, especially the rise of the Chaldeans.
They were to understand that their own land would be punished through that nation.
Yet many people assume their prosperity must continue indefinitely.
Others expect disaster to happen only after their own lifetime.
The Chaldeans were a bitter, swift, violent and merciless people.
Their forces would overwhelm those who opposed them.
But they would also commit a serious sin common among the proud: claiming all the glory of success for themselves.
The conclusion of the prophecy nevertheless contained a glimpse of comfort for God's people.

div.title: God's holiness even when a worse nation prospers (verses 12–17)
div.p: Whatever happens around us, the Lord remains our God and our Holy One.
We have offended him, but we must not therefore entertain unjust or harsh thoughts about him or his service.
It is deeply comforting that human beings may intend evil while the Lord intends good.
His counsel will stand.
Even if wicked people prosper for a time, God remains perfectly holy and does not approve of their evil.
He cannot commit injustice, nor can he look on wickedness with approval.
We must hold to this principle even when temporary events seem difficult to reconcile with it.
Habakkuk complained that people were abusing God's patience.
Because punishment did not follow their crimes immediately, their hearts grew bolder in doing wrong.
The conquerors caught some victims one by one, like fish taken on a hook; they gathered others in nets and drag-nets, capturing whole groups together.
They admired their skill and strategy.
We are all inclined to take credit for our success and good fortune.
When people worship the clever methods that made them successful, they are sacrificing to their own nets—making idols of themselves.
God will bring their impressive robberies to an end.
Death and judgment will stop those who prey upon others; in turn, they themselves will face judgment.
Whatever advantages we possess, let us give all glory to God.

div.title: Waiting for the Lord in faith (verses 1–4)
div.p: When we are troubled and uncertain about the ways of God's Providence, we must guard against the temptation to become impatient.
After presenting our complaints and requests to him, we should watch for the answer he gives through his word, Spirit and providential dealings.
What is the Lord saying to our situation?
God will not disappoint the faith of those who wait to hear his reply.
Every person is concerned with the truths contained in God's word.
The promised blessing may seem delayed for a long time, but it will come at last.
The result will more than repay the patient waiting of his people.
A humble and repentant sinner seeks an interest in this salvation.
Such a person rests upon God's promise and upon Christ, through whom that promise is fulfilled.
They not only live by faith, but also walk and work by faith, persevering until the end and receiving glory.
Those who distrust or despise God's complete sufficiency do not live uprightly before him.
The righteous shall live by faith in these precious promises even while they await their fulfillment.
Those who are justified by faith will truly live and enjoy God's blessing now and forever.

div.title: Warnings against the greed and oppression of Chaldea (verses 5–14)
div.p: The prophet announced judgment against proud, violent powers that oppress God's people.
Human beings become ensnared through the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life.
The power that had carried Israel into captivity was itself captive to these sinful desires.
We should regard only what was honestly acquired as properly ours.
Riches are like thick clay.
Gold and silver are no more than differently colored earth.
Traveling through deep mud slows a person down and makes the journey dirty.
So people who surround themselves with riches may find their progress burdened and polluted.
How foolish it is to carry such a heavy load of anxiety, guilt from acquiring and spending it, and accountability before God!
People can become so weighed down by wealth that it drags them toward destruction.
What was taken violently from others may be taken violently from the thief in turn.
Greed brings disturbance to a household.
A person greedy for gain brings trouble upon the family.
Worse, fraud and injustice call down divine judgment upon the household's affairs.
Honest gain may support a family with God's blessing.
Dishonest gain instead tends toward poverty, ruin and spiritual danger.
Those who injure their neighbors do still greater injury to their own souls.
The possessions they have accumulated will testify against them, however carefully their frauds were planned.
Few people endure a worse slavery than those devoted entirely to worldly pursuits.
They are disappointed when they fail to obtain wealth and disappointed again when they possess it.
They finally discover that the result was not merely emptiness but distress of spirit.
By humiliating the world's pretended glory, God displays his own true glory.
The whole earth will be filled with its knowledge as the waters cover the sea.

div.title: Drunkenness, exploitation and idolatry judged (verses 15–20)
div.p: The Lord pronounced severe judgment against drunkenness everywhere, from a royal palace to the smallest tavern.
Giving a thirsty or exhausted person a drink can be a work of mercy.
But deliberately making another person drunk in order to expose them, discover private matters, trap them into a bad bargain or use them for some other evil purpose is serious wickedness.
To enjoy this sin is to contribute to the destruction of both body and soul.
Punishment will correspond to the offense.
The prophet also showed the foolishness of worshiping idols.
The Lord dwells in his holy heavenly temple.
He allows us to approach him in the way he has appointed.
May we welcome his salvation and worship him through Jesus Christ and the work of the Holy Spirit.

row.cell: The prophet beseeches God for his people.
He calls to mind former deliverances.
His firm trust in the Divine mercy.

div.title: Habakkuk prays for God's mercy (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Here the word prayer appears to describe an act of devoted worship.
The prophet asks the Lord to renew his work among the people in the midst of years of trouble.
This prayer can be applied whenever the church, or individual believers, suffer afflictions and trials.
We must flee to God's mercy as our refuge.
It is the only ground on which we may plead for his help.
We must not say, “Remember what we deserve.”
We should say, “Lord, remember your own mercy.”

div.title: Remembering God's earlier deliverances (verses 3–15)
div.p: When God's people experience trouble and feel near despair, they should recall what he did in earlier generations.
They can bring those acts before him in prayer.
The resemblance between the captivity in Babylon and the earlier slavery in Egypt encourages hope that the Lord can deliver again.
God revealed himself in glory.
The powers of nature trembled and their usual course was altered.
All this served the salvation of his people.
Even events that appear least likely to help will be made to serve their deliverance.
These past victories were also pictures of the world's redemption through Jesus Christ.
The prophet spoke of salvation with God's anointed.
Joshua, who led Israel in battle, was a figure of the Savior who bears the corresponding name—Jesus, our true Joshua.
Henry understands the ancient acts of salvation as accomplished by God with reference to Christ, the Anointed One.
All the earlier wonders performed for Israel were surpassed by what happened when the Son of God suffered on the cross for his people's sins.
How glorious his resurrection and ascension were!
How much more glorious his return will be, when he puts an end to everything that opposes him and brings suffering to his people!

div.title: Joy in the Lord despite every outward loss (verses 16–19)
div.p: When trouble approaches, we need to prepare.
A sound hope through grace is accompanied by a holy fear.
Habakkuk recalled what God had done in former times.
As he considered those deliverances, his confidence returned and his heart filled with holy joy.
He decided to delight and triumph in the Lord.
Even if he lost everything else, he would not lose his God.
If the vines and fig trees fail, all the pleasures of a merely worldly heart disappear.
But people who enjoyed God when everything was plentiful can continue to find everything they need in him after possessions vanish.
They can sit among the ruins of their earthly comforts and still praise the Lord as the God of their salvation.
They rejoice in the salvation of their souls, even through the deepest distress.
Joy in the Lord is especially appropriate when losses and troubles surround us.
Even when food is lacking, showing that human beings do not live by bread alone, the Spirit can supply grace and consolation.
God's gifts make us strong for spiritual work and warfare.
With hearts enlarged by grace, we can run in the way of his commandments and rise above our troubles.
The prophet began his prayer in fear and trembling and ended in joy and triumph.
Faith in Christ prepares believers for every circumstance.
When we can speak of Jesus as our Savior, his name becomes medicine for every wound and refreshment in every care.
It is like fragrant perfume filling the soul.
Hoping for the crown of heaven, let us hold earthly possessions lightly and bear suffering with cheerful patience.
In a little while, the One who is coming will come, and we will be where he is.

div.title: Judgment against divided worship (verses 1–6)
div.p: Complete destruction was approaching, brought by the Almighty.
The prophets consistently warned that there is no peace for the wicked.
Their language pictured the devastation of the land in vivid images, as though it would be left without inhabitants.
Those facing judgment included people openly practicing idolatry.
They also included people who claimed to worship Jehovah while worshiping idols, swearing by the Lord and by Malcham.
God will not accept hearts and worship divided between himself and false gods.

p.hi: What fellowship can there be between light and darkness?

div.p: If Satan receives half of our allegiance, he will demand all of it.
If the Lord receives only half, he will accept none of it.
Neglecting God is itself an expression of irreverence and contempt.
May we not belong to those who turn away and perish, but to those who believe and receive the salvation of their souls.

div.title: Pride, oppression and indifference judged (verses 7–13)
div.p: The day appointed by the Lord was near.
The punishment of presumptuous sinners would be like a sacrifice offered to divine justice.
The royal household of Judah would have to answer for pride and vanity.
Others would answer for leaping over the threshold to invade their neighbors' rights and seize their belongings.
Traders and rich merchants would also be called to account.
The Lord would confront the comfortable and indifferent.
They believed themselves secure and said in their hearts that the Lord would neither do good nor do harm.
In effect they denied that God rewards righteousness or punishes evil.
But the day of his judgment would show that people perish for breaking his law and because they lack, through faith, any share in the Redeemer's atoning sacrifice.

div.title: The terrifying day of the Lord (verses 14–18)
div.p: The warning of approaching destruction was enough to make even sinners in Zion tremble.
The day of the Lord would reveal his anger through the punishment of evil.
It was near—a day of wrath, trouble and distress for sinners.
We must not allow God's patience to lull us into false security.
What does a person gain by obtaining the whole world if that person loses their soul?
And what can anyone give in exchange for the soul?
Let us flee from the wrath to come and choose the good portion that can never be taken away.
Then we will be ready for whatever happens.
Nothing will separate us from God's love in Christ Jesus our Lord.

div.title: Seek the Lord before judgment (verses 1–3)
div.p: The prophet called his nation to repentance as the only means of preventing national destruction.
One description of this people could mean a nation without desire: people who did not desire God, his favor or his grace and were unwilling to repent or reform.
It could also mean a nation without anything desirable: people who had nothing in themselves to recommend them to God.
He might justly have told them to leave his presence.
Instead he called them to gather before him and seek his face.
We know what his decree brings upon people who persist in sin.
Therefore everyone has urgent reason to repent while the opportunity to receive grace remains.
Seek peace with God now, before the Holy Spirit ceases striving with you, before the day of grace or of earthly life is over, and before your everlasting condition has been determined.
Let the poor, despised and afflicted seek the Lord.
