Let them seek to understand and obey his commands more faithfully and grow more humble over their sins.
The greatest hope of deliverance from national judgments lies in prayer.

div.title: Judgment on neighboring nations (verses 4–15)
div.p: People are in a truly dreadful position when the word of the Lord announces judgment against them.
Not one of his words will fail.
God will restore his people to what rightfully belongs to them, even after they have been deprived of it for a long time.
In every age, people devoted to God have commonly faced mockery and abuse.
Yet God will be worshiped not only by Israel and the strangers who join it, but also by people from the nations.
Even distant peoples will be called to account for the wrongs they have done to his people.
When those who were arrogant and cruel in their prosperity suffer, others may offer them neither sympathy nor lament.
The destruction of once-flourishing nations will nonetheless prepare the way for the overthrow of Satan's kingdom.
Let us use the advantages God has given us well.
Let us expect him to fulfill every promise.
And let us pray that our Father's name will be honored and made holy throughout the earth.

row.cell: Promises of future favour and prosperity.

div.title: Further reproof for sin (verses 1–7)
div.p: The holy God hates sin most severely when it is committed by those who live nearest to him and enjoy the greatest spiritual privileges.
A people living in sin already occupies a miserable position and will face misery if they do not repent.
Judah possessed signs of God's presence and many opportunities to know his will.
These privileges gave its people the strongest reasons to obey him.
Yet they continued in disobedience.
How sad it is that human beings often put more energy into wrongdoing than believers put into doing good!

div.title: Mercy, purification and the humble remnant (verses 8–13)
div.p: Henry understands this prophecy as looking toward the proclamation of the gospel, even when judgment would fall upon the Jewish nation.
The gospel's purifying teaching—the pure language of the Lord's grace—would teach people to speak and live with humility, repentance and faith.
Clean and godly everyday conversation is itself a good thing.
Henry also sees here a promise of the church's purity and happiness in later days.
The Lord will remove boasting.
He will leave people nothing in which to glory except Jesus Christ, whom God has made their wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.
Humility about sin and gratitude toward the Redeemer will make real believers upright and sincere, even when other people profess religion without living accordingly.

div.title: Future joy and restoration (verses 14–20)
div.p: After promises that sin will be removed come promises that suffering will be removed.
When the cause of trouble is taken away, the resulting distress can finally cease.

p.hi: What makes God's people holy will make them happy.

div.p: The promises given to a purified people find their complete accomplishment in the gospel.
Henry understands these verses principally as referring to the future conversion and restoration of Israel and the glorious days to follow.
He expects the church to experience great peace, comfort and blessing in those times.
He will save.
Jesus fulfills the meaning of his name, for he saves his people from their sins.
Before those promised days, believers may experience great sorrow and suffer disgrace.
But the Lord will rescue even the weakest believer and honor genuine Christians where they were once despised.
In Henry's interpretation, the same act of mercy would gather scattered Israel and lead its people back to their land.
Then God's Israel would receive enduring honor.

p.hi: Only the fulfillment of events will fully explain the language of the prophecy.

div.p: The righteous have many troubles, but they can rejoice in God's love.
How deeply we should honor and rejoice in the Lord when we hear such gracious words!
If we are now unable to take part in his appointed worship, we rightly feel the loss.
But one day we will be gathered into his heavenly temple.
The believer's happiness and glory will be complete, unchanging and eternal when earthly sorrows have ended.

row.cell: Haggai reproves the Jews for neglecting the temple.
He promises God's assistance to them.

div.title: The people put off rebuilding God's house (verses 1–11)
div.p: Consider the sin of the Jews after they returned from captivity in Babylon.
People working for God may be driven away from their task by difficulty or opposition.
But when that happens, they should return to the work.
The Jews did not say they would never build the temple.
They said, “Not yet.”
In the same way, people rarely say they will never repent, reform their conduct or seek God.
They merely say, “Not yet.”
Thus the great purpose for which they were brought into this world remains unfinished.
We often misunderstand the difficulties that arise while doing our duty.
We treat them as excuses to stop, when God intended them to test our courage and faith.
The people neglected God's house because they wanted more time and money for their private affairs.
God made the consequences correspond to their sin.
They tried to avoid poverty by failing to rebuild the temple, but through that neglect he brought poverty upon them.
Many worthwhile tasks have been planned and then abandoned because people thought the time was not right.
Believers lose opportunities to do good.
Sinners delay attending to their souls until the opportunity is gone.
If we work only for perishable food and possessions, we risk losing the fruits of our labor.
But work performed in the Lord for what lasts to eternal life will not be wasted.
If we want to enjoy earthly blessings for as long as they are good for us, we must have God as our Friend (see also Luke 12:33).

When our earthly affairs are frustrated or disappoint us, we should ask whether we have neglected our duties toward God and our souls while caring more about our own interests than Christ's interests.
Some say they cannot afford to contribute to religious or charitable work while spending ten times as much on unnecessary comforts and improvements for themselves.
They misunderstand their own best interests.
They are careful to decorate their houses while God's temple within their hearts lies in ruins.
Everyone therefore needs to examine the heart honestly, considering their spiritual condition.
We will be held accountable for our sins.
Our duty is to do what God commands.
Yet people often inspect everyone else's conduct closely while remaining careless about their own.
Having neglected a duty in the past is no reason to keep neglecting it.
If the Lord takes pleasure in a work well done, we should take pleasure in doing it.
Let everyone who has postponed returning to God return wholeheartedly while there is time.

div.title: God promises his presence as they resume building (verses 12–15)
div.p: The people returned to God by obeying his command.
When we listen to God's messengers, we should honor the One who sent them.
The word of the Lord succeeds when, by his grace, he stirs people's hearts to obey it.
God's power makes us willing to do his will.
When he has work to accomplish, he will find people fit for it or prepare them himself.
Each person contributed according to ability, acting out of regard for the Lord as their God.
Those who have wasted time should work to redeem it.
The longer we have delayed through folly, the more urgently we ought to begin.
God met their renewed obedience with mercy.
Those who work for him may take courage from the promise that he is with them.
If God is for us, who can be against us?
Let this promise stir us to diligence.

row.cell: Greater glory promised to the second temple than to the first.

div.title: The second temple will have greater glory (verses 1–9)
div.p: Those who serve the Lord sincerely will find encouragement to continue.
The builders could not construct a temple as splendid as Solomon's.
God is pleased when we do our best in his service.
But our proud hearts are often dissatisfied unless we can do as much as others whose abilities and opportunities are far greater than ours.
The Lord nevertheless encouraged the people to continue.
God was with them, and his Spirit and special presence remained among them.
Though he corrects his people for their wrongdoing, his faithfulness does not fail.
The Messiah, the One who was to come, would eventually be among them.
Great changes would take place among the Jewish people, but first there would be upheaval among the nations.
Henry understands the promised “Desire of all nations” as the Messiah.
He is desirable to every nation because in him all the peoples of the earth may receive the greatest blessings.
Believers had long expected and desired him.
The temple under construction would be filled with a glory surpassing the first temple's magnificence.
It would be glory of an entirely different nature.
If we possess silver and gold, we should use them to serve and honor God, because everything belongs to him.
If we possess neither, we should honor him with what we do have, knowing he will receive our service.
Henry sees the greater glory of the second temple in the personal presence of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, in human nature.
No merely material splendor could equal that.
For Henry, Jesus is the promised Christ; believers should look for no other.
He also understands the prophecy as a challenge to those Jews who rejected him, and anticipates that they will one day recognize his worth.
The later temple still witnessed much suffering.
But the promised peace finds its fulfillment in the spiritual peace Christ purchased through his blood for everyone who believes.
The changing kingdoms of the world will prepare the way for people of all nations to recognize the value of Christ.

div.title: The people's uncleanness obstructs their worship (verses 10–19)
div.p: Some people harmed this good work by attempting it with unholy hearts and hands.
They could not expect to benefit from what they were doing while holding fast to sin.
The two examples taken from the law make an important distinction.

p.hi: Holiness is not easily transferred to someone else, but moral uncleanness readily spreads.

div.p: Their sinful hearts and conduct contaminated their work and offerings in God's sight.
The same warning applies to us.
Even when performing a good duty, we should watch against our own corruption, lest it defile our service.
Once we begin to take God's commands seriously and obey them conscientiously, we may expect his gracious care.
Those who are wise will learn to recognize the Lord's steadfast kindness.
He can turn what the wicked call blessings into curses and make the prosperity of careless people bitter.
But he can also sweeten the cup of suffering for those who serve him diligently.

div.title: Zerubbabel and Christ's kingdom (verses 20–23)
div.p: The Lord promised to preserve Zerubbabel and the people of Judah in the midst of their enemies.
Henry also understands the passage as announcing the establishment and continuation of Christ's kingdom.
Those united to Christ are marked by the Holy Spirit and bear his image, distinguishing them from others.
Henry sees the prophecy reaching forward to the time when the kingdom of Christ would overthrow and take the place of the empires opposed to his cause.
The promise has special reference to Christ because Jesus descended from Zerubbabel.
He alone builds the spiritual temple of the gospel.
Jesus is the signet on God's right hand, the One to whom all authority has been given and from whom rightful authority is derived.
In him, all God's promises are Yes and Amen.
Whatever changes occur in the world, the Lord can turn them toward the eventual comfort, honor and happiness of his servants.

row.cell: A vision of the ministry of angels.
The security of the Jews and the destruction of their enemies.

div.title: Turn to the Lord before it is too late (verses 1–6)
div.p: God's almighty power and sovereign rule should move sinners to repent and return to him.
How desirable it is to have the Lord of hosts as our Friend, and how dreadful to have him as our enemy!
Consider what happened to earlier generations and the warnings God sent them through his prophets.
The only way to escape approaching ruin is to abandon our evil ways.
Where are our fathers, and where are the prophets who preached to them?
They once walked through the same streets, lived in the same houses, worked in the same shops and worshiped in the same places as we do.
Now they have all passed away.
But dying did not end their existence.
They have entered the unchanging world of eternity, toward which we are rapidly traveling.
Those who lived and died in sin are under judgment; those who lived and died in Christ are in heaven.
If we live and die as they did, we will soon join them in one condition or the other.
The disregard of earlier generations for their own souls gives us no reason to ruin ours.
Their prophets also died.
Jesus Christ alone is the Prophet who lives forever; the ministries of all other prophets have an appointed end.
What a serious thing it is that dying ministers speak to dying hearers about souls that never die!
Both stand on eternity's threshold.
The preachers died, and those who heard them died.

p.hi: But God's word did not die.

div.p: Not one part of it fell to the ground, because God is righteous and faithful.

div.title: The vision of the horsemen and the angels (verses 7–17)
div.p: Zechariah saw a dark grove of myrtle trees, sheltered by hills.
It pictured the low and distressed condition of the Jewish church.
Among those trees was a warrior on a red horse.
Henry understands this figure as Christ present among his suffering people, ready to come to their help.
Behind him stood angels, ready to carry out his purposes—some through judgment, others through mercy, and others through events containing both.
To understand the mysteries of God's kingdom, we should turn not to angels but to Christ himself.
Angels also have things to learn.
The Savior gladly teaches those who humbly wish to understand the things of God.
The nations around Judah were at peace, while the returned Jews still experienced insecurity.
This contrast prompted the intercession in the vision.
But mercy must be sought through Christ, whose prayer for his church prevails.
The Lord answered the Angel of the Covenant with good and comforting promises.
All the gospel's gracious promises come to us from Jesus Christ, who receives them from his Father in response to the intercession of his blood.
Ministers are to declare those promises throughout the world.
It is not unusual for God's enemies to enjoy worldly rest while his people undergo discipline, temptation, fear, oppression and persecution.
The prophecy offered hope for the revival of the Jews after their captivity.
Henry also regards those events as shadows of the future restoration of the church after the oppression of “New Testament Babylon” has ended.
That later application is Henry's interpretive expectation, not a newly established historical fulfillment.

div.title: The four horns and the workmen (verses 18–21)
div.p: The church's enemies aimed to erase Israel's name.
The four horns symbolized power, strength and violent hostility.
At first the prophet saw them as so formidable that the safety of every faithful person and the success of every good work seemed doubtful.
Then the Lord showed him four workmen empowered to break the horns.
Our physical eyes see the dangers that surround God's church.
Whichever way we look, we see the power of those who oppose it.
But only the eyes of faith see that the church is safe under God's protection.
When the Lord has work to accomplish, he will raise up people to do it.
He will also provide others to defend the workers and protect the work.
How much reason we have to praise the holy and eternal Spirit, who cares for the present and eternal welfare of believers and, through God's word, teaches the church the wonders of salvation!

row.cell: The Jews called to return to their own land.

div.title: The Lord surrounds his growing city (verses 1–5)
div.p: The man with the measuring line is, in Henry's reading, the Son of David, Jesus Christ.
He is the Master Builder of his church.
God knows the extent of his church and will ensure that every guest invited to the wedding supper has a place.
Jerusalem's enlargement is a gracious promise.
City walls normally protect the inhabitants but also limit the room available to them.
This Jerusalem would be as spacious as a city without walls, yet as secure as a city with the strongest walls.
There is room for multitudes no person can number.
No one who trusts in Christ will be refused.
The Lord never shuts out of heaven a genuine member of his church on earth.
God himself will be a wall of fire around his people.
No enemy can break through, undermine or attack such a wall without facing danger.

Henry sees this vision finding its fuller accomplishment in the gospel church, enlarged by the admission of the Gentiles and protected by the Son of God, especially during the glorious days still to come.

div.title: The people are called to leave Babylon (verses 6–9)
div.p: If the Lord builds Jerusalem for his people, they should inhabit it for his glory.
The privileges and promises of life among God's people should persuade us to join them whatever the cost.
When Zion is being enlarged to receive all God's Israel, remaining in Babylon is foolish.
We must not remain willingly captive to sin, even when worldly circumstances are comfortable.

p.hi: Escape for your life; do not look back.

div.p: Jesus Christ has announced freedom for captives and has accomplished that deliverance himself.
Everyone should resolve that sin will no longer rule over them.
Those who wish to belong to God's children should separate from this corrupt world (Acts 2:40).
Christ's care for his church displays God's tender love.
Whoever touches the church touches the apple of God's eye—its most sensitive and precious part.
The slightest attack is a serious offense to him.

p.hi: Christ has been sent as the Protector of his church.

div.title: God promises to dwell among his people (verses 10–13)
div.p: Henry understands the promise as announcing Christ's coming in human nature.
Many nations would turn away from idols.
God would acknowledge as his own everyone who sincerely joined himself to the Lord.
The passage announces glorious days for Christ's kingdom.
God is about to do something extraordinary and unexpected.
He will take up the cause of a people who seemed long neglected.
Meanwhile we are to submit quietly to his holy will and wait patiently for the outcome.
We may be certain that God will complete all the work he has begun.
In due time he will come to judge, finish saving his people and punish the inhabitants of the world for their sins.

div.title: Joshua is cleansed and restored (verses 1–5)
div.p: Zechariah saw Joshua the high priest standing before the Lord, accused by Satan.
Both guilt and corruption make it difficult for sinners to approach a holy God.
Because of the sins we have committed, we are liable to his justice.
Because sin still lives and works within us, we are offensive to his holiness.
Even God's people face these dangers.
Their remedy is Jesus Christ, whom God has made both righteousness and sanctification for them.
Joshua stood accused but was justified.
When we seek to worship God or serve him publicly, we should expect Satan's malice and cleverness to oppose us.
But Satan is rebuked by the One who has conquered him.
Those belonging to Christ will find him ready to defend them when the accusation is fiercest.
A converted soul is a burning brand pulled from the fire through a miracle of free grace.
Christ will not leave such a person to Satan.
Joshua appeared polluted, but he was cleansed.
He represented God's people, who remain unclean until they are washed and sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of God.
Israel had now turned away from idolatry, yet much was still wrong.
Enemies within their spiritual lives were even more dangerous than hostile neighboring nations.

p.hi: Christ detested the filth on Joshua's garments but did not reject Joshua.

div.p: He acts this way toward people chosen to serve him as priests.

p.hi: Pardoning mercy removes the guilt of sin. Renewing grace breaks sin's power.

div.p: Christ washes sinners in his own blood and makes them kings and priests to God.
Those he appoints as spiritual priests stand before God clothed in the spotless robe of Christ's righteousness and adorned with the graces of his Spirit.
The righteousness of the saints is both imputed and implanted.
It is pictured by the clean white linen worn by the Lamb's bride (Revelation 19:8).
Joshua was restored to his former honor and responsibilities.
The crown of the priesthood was placed on him again.
When God intends to revive true religion, he moves prophets and people to pray for that renewal.

div.title: The Branch of righteousness and forgiveness in one day (verses 6–10)
div.p: God equips those he calls to his service, finding them fit or making them so.
He removes believers' sins through sanctifying grace and enables them to walk in newness of life.
Just as promises to David often become promises about the Messiah, promises to Joshua point to Christ, whose priesthood Joshua's foreshadowed.
Whatever trials or duties we face, our dependence must rest upon Christ, the Branch of righteousness.
Christ is God's Servant, carrying out his Father's work, obeying his will and living for his glory.
He is the Branch from whom all our spiritual fruit comes.
His Father's eye rested upon him, especially in his suffering.

Henry observes that Christ was hidden in the grave like a foundation stone buried from sight, but adds an important qualification: the prophecy more directly describes the attention given to this precious Cornerstone.
Believers before the Savior's coming looked toward him through types and promises.
Believers after his coming look to him with faith, hope and love.
Christ appears for his chosen people like the high priest carrying Israel's names on the stones of his breastplate.
God has given the redeemed to Christ to bring them by grace to glory.
Through Christ both sin's guilt and its dominion are removed.
The decisive work was accomplished in one day—the day he suffered and died.
Once sin is taken away, nothing can ultimately destroy those sheltered by the Savior.
They can rest joyfully under his protection.
And when gospel grace works powerfully in hearts, it makes people eager to invite others to share that blessing.

row.cell: A vision of a candlestick, with two olive trees.
An explanation respecting the olive trees.

div.title: The lampstand and the two olive trees (verses 1–7)
div.p: The prophet's spirit wanted to listen, but his body was weak.
We should ask God to awaken us whenever he speaks and then rouse ourselves to pay attention.
The church is like a golden lampstand set in this dark world to give light through God's revelation.
Two olive trees stood beside it, supplying a continuous stream of oil.
The Lord brings his gracious purposes for his church to completion without depending upon human skill or labor.
Sometimes he employs human instruments, but he does not need them.
The oil pictured the abundance of grace by which he brings light and holiness to the church's ministers and members.
No human power can produce that grace or stop it from being given.
The temple's construction would therefore reach a happy conclusion.
All the difficulties were pictured as a great mountain.
Through faith, they would be brought down and made level.
Christ is our Zerubbabel.
He has encountered mountains of obstacles, but nothing is too difficult for him.
What began through God's grace can safely be entrusted to that same grace.
He will not abandon the work of his own hands.

div.title: Do not despise small beginnings (verses 8–10)
div.p: The precise fulfillment of Scripture's prophecies testifies to their divine origin.
God often chooses people who appear weak or unlikely to accomplish great things.
Therefore do not despise the dawning light.
It will grow brighter until the day reaches its fullness.
Those who feared the temple could never be completed would rejoice when they saw Zerubbabel with the plumb line, directing and supervising its completion.
The all-wise and almighty Providence that rules the earth cares particularly for the church.
Everyone carrying responsibility for the work must look to the Lord, remain aware of his Providence, depend upon his guidance and submit to the way he orders events.
Fix your faith upon Christ.
See him carrying out his work according to his glorious plan and each day bringing his spiritual building closer to completion.

div.title: The oil supplied through the Lord's anointed (verses 11–14)
div.p: Zechariah wanted to understand the two olive trees.
Henry identifies them with Zerubbabel and Joshua, the prince and the priest.
Both had received gifts and grace from the Holy Spirit.
They lived at the same time and served together in God's work.
They foreshadowed Christ's offices of King and Priest.
Those two offices are united in the one person of Jesus Christ, God and man, from whose fullness all grace is received and shared.
The two leaders helped build God's temple.
Christ builds God's church spiritually.
He is not only the Messiah, the Anointed One.
He is also the Good Olive Tree of his church, supplying its needs from his inexhaustible fullness.
The Holy Spirit is the anointing believers receive.
Through the Spirit, all the golden oil of grace flows from Christ to believers and keeps their lamps burning.
Let us seek, through the Savior's intercession and generosity, the supplies of grace that have always been sufficient for his saints in every trial and task.
Let us wait on him through his appointed ordinances, praying to be sanctified completely—in body, soul and spirit.

row.cell: The vision of a flying roll.
The vision of a woman and an ephah.

div.title: The flying scroll (verses 1–4)
div.p: The Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments are scrolls, in which God has written the great truths of his law and gospel.
They are flying scrolls: the Lord sends his word swiftly (Psalm 147:15).
This vision reveals his righteous anger against sin.
If only we could see, by faith, the curse of God's law hanging over the guilty world like a dark storm cloud, shutting out the warmth of divine favor and ready to break in thunder and lightning!
Then how welcome we would find the news of the Savior who redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us!
Sin destroys homes and families, particularly when people hurt others or give false testimony.
Nothing can shut out God's judgment—not locks, bars or walls.
Some of its consequences ruin a person's earthly possessions; others reach the soul and lead to everlasting punishment.
We have all transgressed God's law.
We therefore have no escape from its judgment except to flee for refuge to the hope announced in the gospel.

div.title: The woman inside the ephah (verses 5–11)
div.p: Zechariah saw an ephah, a container shaped like a measure used for grain.
Henry takes this as a picture of the Jewish nation filling up the measure of its iniquity.
When that measure was full, God would allow its enemies to take it captive as punishment.
The woman seated inside represents, in Henry's interpretation, the Jewish church and nation in a later corrupt period.
The heavy lead cover expresses the guilt weighing upon a sinner, carrying the unrepentant toward judgment.
Henry further understands the vision as foretelling the condemnation and dispersion of the Jews after the crucifixion of Christ and the rejection of his gospel.
The container carried into a distant land would picture their removal from their country and prolonged life elsewhere, as in the earlier captivity to Babylon.
Henry considers this later period of suffering much longer than the Babylonian exile, and interprets the picture in terms of Israel's blindness and unbelief.
These are Henry's historical and theological identifications, not independent findings or a silent revision of Scripture.
The universal application is to beware of storing up wrath for judgment.
Every crime added to the record fills the measure further.

row.cell: Joshua, the high priest, crowned as a type of Christ.

div.title: The chariots and divine Providence (verses 1–8)
div.p: The vision may represent the ways Providence governs the affairs of the world.
In all that happens, whether to the public or to private individuals, we should see events coming from between the two mountains of bronze, representing the Lord's immovable purposes and decrees.
It is as foolish to quarrel with these events as it is our duty to submit to God.
His providential purposes move with the speed and strength of chariots, but are always directed by his infinite wisdom and sovereign will.
The red horses picture war and bloodshed; the black depict its consequences—famine, disease and desolation.
The white horses indicate the return of comfort, peace and prosperity.
The mixed colors stand for events that bring prosperity to some and adversity to others, or a mixture of both.
Angels go out as messengers of God's purposes and ministers of his justice and mercy.
God also works through secret movements in human hearts by which Providence brings its plans to completion.
These are pictured by the four spirits of heaven, sent by the God of the spirits of all flesh.
All events spring from God's unchanging counsel, founded on perfect wisdom, justice, truth and goodness.
Henry considers it likely that certain historical events near the time of this vision correspond to it, but does not identify that correspondence as certain.

div.title: Joshua's crown points toward Christ (verses 9–15)
div.p: Some Jews returning from Babylon brought contributions to God's house.
Those who cannot advance good work by being physically present should contribute what they can from their resources.
If some people supply their hands, others may fill them.
Crowns were placed on Joshua the high priest.
The sign drew attention to the promise that God would raise up, in the fullness of time, a great High Priest, whom Joshua foreshadowed.
Christ is not only the Foundation of the spiritual temple but also its Founder, who builds it by his Spirit and grace.
Glory is a burden, but not too heavy for the One who upholds everything.
The cross was his glory, and he carried it.
He also bears the exceeding weight of his crown.
The counsel of peace unites Christ's priestly and royal offices.
The gospel church's peace and the believer's welfare are achieved not through two separate persons, but through two offices united in Jesus Christ.

p.hi: As Priest, he purchases peace. As King, he maintains and defends it.

div.p: The crowns were to remain in the temple as enduring witnesses to the promise of the Messiah.
We must not separate what God has joined in his purpose of peace.
We cannot approach God through Christ our Priest while refusing to submit to him as our King.
We have no sound reason to think ourselves at peace with God if we make no effort to obey his commandments.

row.cell: Sin the cause of their captivity.

div.title: The people inquire about their fasts (verses 1–7)
div.p: When we sincerely want to learn God's will in a difficult matter, we must consult his word and his ministers and seek his direction through earnest prayer.
In doubtful situations, it is wise to seek counsel from people whose special task is to search and explain the Scriptures.
The Jews wondered whether they needed to continue their fasting days now that the city and temple appeared likely to be completed.
God first answered by rebuking their hypocrisy.
These fasts were not pleasing to him unless undertaken with a better attitude and purpose.
The outward form of worship remained, but its life, soul and power were missing.
Every holy exercise should be done for God, with his word as our rule and his glory as our purpose.
We should seek to please him and receive his favor.
Instead, themselves and their own interests had occupied the center of their religious acts.
Weeping during appointed fasts was not enough.
They should have studied the earlier prophets and learned why God had confronted their ancestors.
Whether we live in prosperity or adversity, we must leave sin behind and fulfill our duties toward God.

div.title: Sin brought the captivity (verses 8–14)
div.p: The judgments God sent upon ancient Israel were recorded as warnings to Christians.
The Lord called his people not merely to keep fasts and offer sacrifices but to act justly and love mercy, bringing peace and well-being to their neighbors.
God's law governs and restrains the heart, not only the outward act.
Yet the people filled their minds with prejudices against his word.
They refused instruction and hardened themselves.
Few things are harder than the heart of a presumptuous sinner.
Consider the terrible consequences this brought upon their fathers.
Great sins committed against the Lord of hosts meet his great anger, whose power none can resist.
When sin is cherished in the heart, it will ruin our prayers.
Yet the Lord always hears a brokenhearted, repentant sinner's cry.
Those who die impenitent and unbelieving will find neither remedy nor refuge from the misery they refused to take seriously during life.

row.cell: The people encouraged by promises of God's favour, and exhorted to holiness.
The Jews in the latter days.

div.title: Jerusalem restored as a city of truth (verses 1–8)
div.p: Zion's worst enemies were her own sins.
God would remove those sins; afterward, no other enemy could finally harm her.
Those professing religion must honor that profession through honesty and godliness.
A city of truth and a mountain of holiness will become a place of peace and flourishing.
The vision of elderly people and children filling the streets together beautifully describes outward peace accompanied by abundance, moderation and contentment.
Scattered Israelites would be gathered from every direction.
God would not forsake them in the way of mercy, according to his promise.
They would not forsake him in duty, according to theirs.
Henry considers the promises partly fulfilled among the Jews between the return from captivity and Christ's coming.
He sees a fuller accomplishment in the gospel church, while saying the prophecy's complete meaning concerns either future periods of the Christian church or the future restoration of the Jews.
These are alternative possibilities in Henry's interpretation, not one verified sequence.
What seems impossible to humanity is possible with God, whose thoughts and ways are far above ours.
When true godliness is weak, we struggle to imagine so profound a spiritual transformation.
Yet the almighty recreating Spirit could accomplish it in even less time than God used to create the world.
Let everyone working for the gospel take courage and serve in genuine holiness.
Their work will not be wasted.

div.title: Promises strengthen people who obey (verses 9–17)
div.p: Those who put their hands to the plow of duty receive strength from God's promises of mercy.
Those who turn away from their fathers' sins may find that a curse has become a blessing.
Believers should show that they trust God's promises through their actions, then patiently await fulfillment.
When God is displeased, commerce may decline and people may turn against their neighbors.
When he returns in mercy, happiness and prosperity can return.
People who believe in Christ must take seriously the commands to stop lying, speak truth and peace to neighbors, hate what God hates and love what pleases him.

div.title: Fasts become joy; the nations seek God (verses 18–23)
div.p: When God comes toward us in mercy, we should meet him with thankfulness and joy.
Be faithful and honest in all your dealings.
Enjoy doing what is right, even if dishonesty would bring greater financial gain.
As far as it lies in your power, live peaceably with everyone.
Let God's truth govern your mind and his peace govern your heart.
In this way the conduct of God's earlier servants attracted the notice of people in other nations and softened their prejudices.
The prophecy announced great growth for the church.
The Jews had often adopted the idols of surrounding nations.
How astonishing that they should instead teach genuine religion even to their conquerors and to the principal nations of the world!
Yet this was foretold and, in Henry's judgment, already wonderfully fulfilled in part.
He expected future events to explain it still more fully.

div.title: God defends his church (verses 1–8)
div.p: The prophet foretold judgments against several surrounding nations.
Henry relates these warnings to wars involving the Macedonians and Alexander's successors.
Amid those conflicts, God promised to protect his own people.
His church lay among enemies like a lily surrounded by thorns.
The Lord's power and goodness are visible in his special preservation of that church.
He stations himself around it like an encamped defender.
Proud armies may pass by, leave and return, but his eyes are always upon his people.
Their opponents cannot finally prevail.
The time will come when no oppressor will pass through his people's land again.

div.title: The Messiah comes as a peaceful king (verses 9–11)
div.p: Zechariah rejoiced at the prospect of the Messiah's coming.
Henry notes that ancient Jewish interpreters also understood the passage as messianic.
Jesus openly took the role of Israel's King when he entered Jerusalem amid the people's hosannas.
But his kingdom is spiritual, not a kingdom advanced by physical force or worldly weapons.
His gospel would be proclaimed throughout the world and received among the nations.
A state of sin is a state of captivity.
It resembles a pit or dungeon without water or comfort.
By nature we are prisoners in that pit.
Through the precious blood of Christ, countless people once enslaved by Satan have been freed from the place where they would otherwise have perished without hope.
As we admire Christ's grace, let us seek to display his holiness and truth in our own hearts and actions.
div.title: Prisoners of hope are called to Christ (verses 12–17)
div.p: Henry sees the promised deliverance of the Jews as a picture of redemption through Christ and of gospel blessings enjoyed by believers.
Sinners are prisoners, yet they may be prisoners of hope.
Their condition is sad, but not beyond remedy.
There is still hope for them through God's promise.
Christ is a Stronghold and strong Tower.
Believers are safe in him from God's wrath, the curse of the law and attacks by their spiritual enemies.
We must flee to him with living faith and trust him through every trial.
The passage also refers, in Henry's interpretation, to the apostles and early preachers of the gospel.
God was manifestly with them.
His words, proclaimed through their mouths, pierced their listeners' hearts and consciences.
The Lord protected them amid persecution and filled them with his Spirit.
The Good Shepherd saved them as his flock and honored them like precious jewels in his crown.
The blessings, gifts and comforts of the Spirit poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2) and afterward are pictured here.
God's people have faced severe spiritual conflicts and will face more.
But the Lord will give them victory.
The more we serve him and experience his goodness, the more we appreciate the beauty of our Redeemer.
Whatever he gives us, let us use it gladly in his service.
After enjoying his blessings, let us exclaim, “How great is his goodness!”

row.cell: Blessings to be sought from the Lord.

div.title: Seek blessings from God, not idols (verses 1–5)
div.p: Spiritual blessings were promised through figures drawn from the abundance of earthly harvests.
Rain arriving at the right time is a great mercy.
We may ask God for it when needed and expect him to hear.
Likewise, our prayers should seek every kind of mercy at the appropriate time.
The Lord makes clouds and sends showers.
Henry sees this as a possible invitation to seek the influences of the Holy Spirit through faith and prayer, through which the blessings of God's promises are received and enjoyed.
Turning to idols for help, as earlier generations had done, was foolish.
The Lord would visit the remnant of his flock in mercy and renew their courage and strength for conflict.
Everything created is to us what God makes it.
Anyone who supports a nation like a cornerstone, or unites people who differ like nails joining beams, must ultimately be given by the Lord.
Anyone called to overcome enemies will receive strength and success from him.
Henry also applies the picture to Christ, to whom we should look for leaders and servants who unite, sustain and defend his people.
The Lord will never say that we have sought him in vain.

div.title: God gathers and strengthens his people (verses 6–12)
div.p: These precious promises concern the Jews and, in Henry's reading, also the later days of the church.
The preaching of the gospel is God's call for souls to come to Jesus Christ.
Those Christ redeemed by his blood, God gathers by his grace.
Difficulties will be overcome as decisively as the obstacles defeated during Israel's deliverance from Egypt.
God himself will be their strength and their song.
When we resist spiritual enemies and overcome them through his help, we have reason to rejoice.
If he strengthens us, then we should apply ourselves diligently to all the duties of Christian life.
We must be active in God's service and do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.

row.cell: Destruction to come upon the Jews.
The Lord's dealing with the Jews.
The emblem and curse of a foolish shepherd.

div.title: The shepherds and their people are warned (verses 1–3)
div.p: Henry understands these figurative words as predicting the destruction of Jerusalem and of the Jewish church and nation, later plainly foretold by Jesus as the time approached.
If even mighty cedars fall, how can lesser fir trees imagine they will stand?
When wise and godly people fall into sin, or influential and wealthy people fall into trouble, their downfall warns those with fewer advantages.
A nation is in a sad condition when people who ought to be its shepherds behave instead like young lions.
The pride of the Jordan was the thick vegetation along its banks.
When floods covered the banks, lions emerged roaring.
In Henry's application, Jerusalem's destruction should therefore warn other churches.

div.title: The Good Shepherd and the two staffs (verses 4–14)
div.p: Henry explains these words as announcing Christ's coming in judgment to a Jewish nation and religious community that had become deeply corrupt.
People whose minds are darkened may do wrong while justifying themselves.
But God does not pronounce innocent those who approve their own wrongdoing.
How can we ask God to bless dishonest methods of gaining wealth, or thank him for the profits of such conduct?
The community had experienced serious religious decline but failed to recognize it.
The Good Shepherd would care for his flock, giving special attention to the poor.
The prophet appears to have used two staffs.
The first, Beauty, represented the Jewish nation's privileges within its national covenant.
The second, Bands, represented the unity that had held the flock together.
Yet many preferred false teachers.
Worldly-mindedness and friendship with sin place people in hostility to God.
The prophet requested his wages and was paid thirty pieces of silver.
By divine direction, he threw them to the potter, rejecting the sum as a contemptible price.
Henry interprets this as foreshadowing Judas's bargain to betray Christ and the later use of the money.
Nothing ruins a people more surely than the collapse of their mutual bonds of fellowship.
As sin increases, love grows cold, and disagreements turn into public conflict.
People who have provoked God against themselves should not be surprised if they begin to fight one another.
Deliberate contempt for Christ brings ruin.
If professing Christians properly valued him, they would not quarrel so fiercely over trivial matters.

div.title: The foolish shepherd abandons the flock (verses 15–17)
div.p: Having shown what happens when the Good Shepherd's care is rejected, the vision shows the further misery of people abused by foolish shepherds.
Henry relates the portrait to the scribes and Pharisees as Jesus described them.
Such leaders do nothing to uphold the weak or encourage those who are discouraged.
They look only for personal comfort while treating the flock cruelly.
An idol shepherd may dress and appear like a true shepherd, receive submission and enjoy generous support.
Yet through neglect or wicked example, the shepherd lets the sheep perish.
Henry says this pattern fits leaders in many churches and nations, while interpreting the prophecy as having a particularly severe application to some Jewish teachers.
Those who deceive others toward destruction will themselves receive severe condemnation.

row.cell: Punishment of the enemies of Judah.
Repentance and sorrow of the Jews.

div.title: God protects his people (verses 1–8)
div.p: God's prophecy announces a heavy burden for the enemies of his church, but comfort and blessing for Israel.
The Lord will confuse their plans and weaken their courage.

p.hi: Henry admits the precise meaning is unclear.

div.p: Yet God often begins by calling the poor and despised, and even the weakest may become like David, courageous and excellent in all that is good.
May the labor and example of Christians be like fire among dry wood or a torch in a sheaf, spreading divine love and true religion on every side.

div.title: The Spirit leads people to mourn over Christ (verses 9–14)
div.p: The prophet describes a day when God defends and delivers Jerusalem.
When Christ first came, he wounded the serpent's head and broke the dark powers opposing his kingdom.
At his second coming, he will complete their defeat and bring down all hostile powers.
Death itself will be swallowed up in victory.
The Holy Spirit is gracious and merciful, the source of holiness and every spiritual grace.
He is also the Spirit of supplication, showing people their ignorance, need, guilt, misery and danger, and teaching them to pray.
Henry interprets this prophecy as anticipating a time when the Jews would recognize Jesus as the crucified Messiah.
They would look toward him with faith and mourn for him, in public and privately, with each person grieving personally.
There is a holy sorrow over sin that flows from the Spirit's work.
Such sorrow strengthens faith in Christ and prepares people to rejoice in God.
It is evidence of genuine grace and prayer.
That pattern applies to everyone who mourns over sin with godly sorrow.
Looking to Christ crucified moves the heart to repent of the sin for which he suffered.

row.cell: The Fountain for the remission of sins, The conviction of the false prophets.
The death of Christ, and the saving of a remnant of the people.

div.title: The fountain opened for sin (verses 1–6)
div.p: A fountain would be opened to the rulers and people of the Jews for cleansing from sin.
Henry identifies it as Christ's atoning blood united with his sanctifying grace.
He understands the fountain as having been closed to unbelieving Israel but expects it to be opened to the people when the Spirit of grace humbles and softens their hearts.

p.hi: The opened fountain is the pierced side of Christ.

div.p: We are all unclean because of sin.
Yet a fountain is open to wash us, and its streams of mercy continually flow.
Christ's blood, and the pardoning mercy of God made known through the new covenant, will never be exhausted.
This fountain is available to every believer.
Those who believe in Christ are his spiritual offspring, part of the family of David and members of the heavenly Jerusalem.
Through his grace, Christ removes the dominion of sin, even the sins to which the heart clings most strongly.
People cleansed through this fountain are both justified and sanctified.
They turn away from love of the world and from the desires of sinful flesh, the two great idols, to cling to God alone.
Henry sees a complete reformation following his anticipated conversion of Israel to Christ.
False prophets would recognize their guilt and folly and return to proper work.
When we realize we have strayed from duty, genuine repentance brings us back to that duty.
We should accept correction from friends who have helped expose our errors, even if that correction wounds our pride (Proverbs 27:6).
Above all, remember the wounds of our Savior.
He has often been wounded by professing friends and even genuine disciples when their conduct contradicts his word.

div.title: The Shepherd is struck and a remnant is saved (verses 7–9)
div.p: Henry understands this passage as a prophecy of the suffering and death of Christ.
God the Father commanded the sword of his justice to rise against his Son when the Son willingly offered his soul for sin.
Because Christ is truly God, the Father calls him “my Fellow.”

p.hi: The Son and the Father are one.

div.p: He is the Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.
As a sacrifice, he had to be slain; without bloodshed there is no remission of sins.
He had no sin of his own for which to answer.
The prophecy may encompass all his suffering, especially his agony in the garden and upon the cross, where he endured deep anguish until divine justice was satisfied.
When the Shepherd was struck, the sheep were scattered.
Jesus himself connected these words to the disciples' flight on the night of his betrayal.
Henry sees further application in the destruction of corrupt and hypocritical elements within the professing church.
He also identifies Roman judgment upon many Jews following the rejection and crucifixion of Jesus and opposition to the gospel.
That is Henry's historical and theological interpretation, not a newly established fact about Jewish people.
Yet a remnant was to be saved.
God would refine his people like gold.
He would be their God, and the ultimate result of their trials would be praise, honor and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ.

row.cell: Encouraging prospects, and the destruction of her enemies.
The holiness of the latter days.

div.title: Jerusalem's suffering and the coming of Christ (verses 1–7)
div.p: During his earthly life Jesus often stood on the Mount of Olives.
He ascended to heaven from that place, and afterward distress and desolation overtook the Jewish nation.
Henry presents this as one figurative interpretation of the vision.
But he also reports that many understand the prophecy to concern events still unfulfilled, including troubles beyond what we can now fully imagine.
He does not settle this dispute by declaring one reading certain.
Every believer can nevertheless look forward to Christ's coming in power with joy, since the Lord is their God.
For a long time, the church may be weakened and deformed by sin.
Truth and error, happiness and sorrow, may be mixed together.
The same mixture affects each believer: grace and remaining corruption coexist.
But when circumstances are darkest and hope seems most remote, God can bring light.
Deliverance may come just when his people have stopped expecting it.

div.title: Living waters and divine judgments (verses 8–15)
div.p: Some understand the living waters flowing from Jerusalem as an image of the gospel spreading from that city.
Neither the gospel and its appointed means of grace nor the grace the Holy Spirit works through them can be exhausted.
Persecution's heat, temptation's storms and other painful experiences cannot stop their lasting benefit.
The passage appears also to announce severe judgments against those who oppose the settlement of the Jews in their own land.

p.hi: Henry insists that events alone can establish how far this language should be interpreted literally.

div.p: Human rage and violence are only faint images of the hostility found among those lost in their sins.
Even animals can suffer because human beings sin and bring ruin on the world around them.
Through such judgments, God reveals his displeasure against wickedness.

div.title: The holiness of ordinary life in the latter days (verses 16–21)
div.p: Henry considers it impossible for all the nations literally to travel to Jerusalem every year to celebrate one festival.
He therefore says this language must be understood figuratively.
The Feast of Tabernacles represents gospel worship.
Every day of a Christian's life is to be lived as a holy celebration.
The Lord's Day, in particular, should receive special devotion.
Those who neglect God's appointed means of grace cannot expect to receive the benefits of fellowship with him.
This neglect becomes its own punishment: by refusing the duty, they lose the privilege.
The passage promises a time of unusual peace and purity for the church.
Ordinary work and holy worship will be governed by the same principles of faith, love and obedience.
Holiness will spread more widely because the Holy Spirit will be poured out more abundantly than before.
Even common things will become holy through their use.
Every action and enjoyment of a believer should be directed toward God's glory.
Our whole life should become one continuous sacrifice of devotion, untouched by selfish motives.
How far the church now is from such purity!
But Henry anticipates days when God will reform and enlarge it.
Still, perfect holiness and perfect happiness are found in heaven alone.

row.cell: They are careless in God's institutions.

div.title: Israel fails to recognize God's love (verses 1–5)
div.p: All our advantages, both the good circumstances we experience and the spiritual privileges we enjoy, arise from God's free love.
He is the One who makes our lives differ from other people's lives.
The suffering sinners experience or fear is the rightful consequence of wrongdoing.
But every true hope and comfort we receive is a gift of the Lord's undeserved mercy.
God chose his people so that they would be holy.
If we love him, it is because he first loved us.
Yet we are all tempted to disregard the value of his mercies while trying to excuse our own sins.

div.title: The priests dishonor God's worship (verses 6–14)
div.p: Each of us can apply to ourselves the faults exposed in the priests.
Since God is both our Father and Master, we owe him reverence and honor.
But these priests mocked the warnings given to them.
When sinners attempt to silence the convictions of their own consciences, they bring ruin upon themselves.
Those who neglect God's appointed ordinances, attend them carelessly and leave them unchanged are in effect saying, “The Lord's table is contemptible.”
The priests dishonored his name through their offerings.
They did not understand that their sacrifices pointed toward the spotless Lamb of God.
They resented their cost, treating everything that brought no worldly profit as waste.
This also warns us about our worship.
When we worship without understanding, we bring a blind offering.
When we act carelessly and without heartfelt devotion, we offer something sick.
When we rely only on outward bodily actions instead of engaging our hearts, we bring something lame.
When we allow distracted and vain thoughts to dominate worship, we offer something torn.
These are not small offenses.
They dishonor God and harm our own souls.
For an action to be acceptable to God, merely doing something outwardly good is insufficient.
It must come from a right motive, be performed in the right way and be directed toward the right purpose.
The countless mercies we continually receive make our laziness and stinginess in serving him more blameworthy.
God promised a time when spiritual worship would flourish.
The incense offered to his name pictures prayer and praise, and the pure offering is worship arising from sincerity.
That became possible when true worshipers began to worship the Father in Spirit and truth.
We may trust God's mercy to forgive our earlier sins, but not to give us permission to keep committing them.

p.hi: A willing heart is acceptable, even when its service remains imperfect.

div.p: But a deceitful person who gives the best to Satan and sinful desires while keeping the worst for God remains under judgment.
People still dishonor God's table and worship today, even if their outward religious practices differ from those of the ancient priests.

row.cell: The priests reproved for neglecting their covenant.
The people reproved for their evil practices.

div.title: The priests have violated their covenant (verses 1–9)
div.p: What Scripture says about the covenant of the priesthood also teaches us about the covenant of grace made with everyone who believes, for Christians are spiritual priests.
It is a covenant of life and peace, promising true happiness both now and in the world to come.
Being chosen as God's messengers is an honor.
A priest's lips must preserve knowledge for the people, not withhold it from them.
All are concerned to understand God's will.
We should read Scripture ourselves, but we should also welcome instruction and counsel from God's faithful messengers regarding our souls.
Ministers should devote their best effort to turning sinners back to God.
Even among those who are called God's people, many still need to turn away from wrongdoing.
Those ministers most likely to help others repent are the ones who teach sound doctrine and live holy lives in accordance with Scripture.
Many priests abandoned that way and led the people into error instead.
Those who walk with God in peace and righteousness and lead others away from sin honor him.
He will honor them, while people who despise him will be treated lightly.

div.title: Faithlessness toward God and marriage (verses 10–17)
div.p: Corrupt conduct grows out of corrupt beliefs and desires.
A person who acts falsely toward God will not act faithfully toward other people.
Some men in Judah despised the marriage covenant established by God.
They dismissed the wives from their own nation, probably so they could marry foreign women instead.
They made their wives' lives bitter while pretending before others to care for them.
But remember: she is your wife, the person most closely bound to you in this world.
A wife must be regarded not as a servant but as her husband's companion.
Marriage is bound by a solemn oath before God, and that oath must not be treated lightly.
Husband and wife should live together until death in holy love and peace.
God made one Eve for one Adam, although he had power to create more.
Why did he establish the union of one man and one woman?
Henry explains that it was for the raising of children devoted to God.
Parents must therefore live reverently before the Lord so that their children may also learn to serve him.
God declared his hatred of putting away a spouse.
Anyone wishing to avoid sin must guard the inner spirit and desires, where sin begins.
Cruelty and faithlessness in family life usually grow out of selfishness, which values personal cravings more than another person's welfare and happiness.
It is tiresome and offensive to God when people insist on justifying their wicked conduct.
Those who imagine God approves of sin are both insulting him and deceiving themselves.
Some skeptics asked, “Where is the God of judgment?”
But the day of the Lord will come.

row.cell: The Jews reproved for their corruptions.
God's care of his people; The distinction between the righteous and the wicked.

div.title: The messenger prepares the way for Christ (verses 1–6)
div.p: These opening words answer those who mocked God's promise of judgment.
The prophet announces John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ, who would prepare the way through a call to repentance.
For a long time, believers had expected the Messiah, the One who was to come.
Now his arrival was near.
He is the Messenger of the Covenant.
Those who sincerely seek Jesus will find delight in him, sometimes when they least expect it.
Through his word and the convictions brought by the Holy Spirit, Christ prepares the sinner's heart to become his temple.
He enters as the Messenger of peace and consolation.
Hypocrites and people content with empty religious forms cannot endure his teaching or stand before his judgment.
Christ came to distinguish the precious from the worthless.
He sits like a refiner, purifying his church through the gospel and renewing souls through the Spirit who works with it.
He removes the dross of inward corruption that makes human capacities useless in God's service.
A believer need not be afraid of the fiery trials of suffering and temptation through which the Savior refines his gold.
Christ will not allow the refining fire to be hotter or to last longer than is truly needed for his servant's good.
Its outcome for believers differs completely from the punishment of the wicked.
Through his intercession, Christ makes his people acceptable to God.
Without reverence for God, no spiritual good can be expected.
Wrongdoing pursues sinners.
God never changes.
Although his judgment may be delayed, it will come; he is still as opposed to sin as ever.
Yet his unchangeableness is also our comfort.

p.hi: We have not been consumed because his compassion has not failed.

div.title: Return to the Lord and honor him (verses 7–12)
div.p: The people of that generation had turned from God and neglected his appointed ways.
He graciously called them back, yet they asked, “How shall we return?”
The Lord notices how our hearts respond when his word summons us.
It is a serious perversity to use suffering as an excuse to sin, when God may have sent that suffering to separate us from sin.
The prophet called the people urgently to reform.
God must receive first place in our service.
The welfare of our souls should matter more than the comfort of our bodies.
Trust him to provide what is needful.
He has blessings ready for us, but weak faith and narrow desires often leave us without room to receive them.
Those who honor him with their possessions will discover that doing so brings no ultimate loss.

div.title: The Lord remembers those who fear him (verses 13–18)
div.p: Some people openly revealed wickedness through their arrogant words.
Christ's yoke is easy, but people who willfully persist in sin test God's patience.
We should judge such ways in light of the final judgment, when the outcome of arrogant wrongdoing will become clear.
Meanwhile, those who feared the Lord spoke kindly to one another, preserving and encouraging mutual love while sin multiplied around them.
They talked together as people who fear God and think upon his name.
Evil companionship corrupts character.
Good conversations strengthen faith and integrity.
A book of remembrance was written before the Lord.
God will not permit his children to perish alongside those who refuse faith.
They are vessels of mercy and honor, while unrepentant people face judgment.
Believers are God's precious jewels.
He preserves them when the world is burned like worthless material.
Those who now acknowledge him as their God will be acknowledged as his own.
We must serve him as loving children, not as idle children who expect everything while doing nothing.
Even his children continually need sparing mercy.
All people finally belong among those who serve God or those who refuse.
We often misjudge both categories.
But at Christ's judgment seat, every person's true character will be known.
We must examine where our own lot will lie while refusing to pronounce premature judgment upon others.
Then everyone will recognize that the truly wise and happy people were those who trusted and served the Lord.

row.cell: The judgements on the wicked, and the happiness of the righteous.
Regard to be had to the law; John the Baptist promised as the forerunner of Messiah.

div.title: The Sun of Righteousness brings light and healing (verses 1–3)
div.p: The prophecy points to both the first and the second coming of Christ.
God has appointed the time for each.
People who persist in wickedness and disregard the Lord's anger will finally experience it.
The warning certainly applies to the day of final judgment, when Christ will be revealed in flaming fire to judge the proud and everyone who continues doing evil.
Yet Christ's coming brings joyful light to those who faithfully serve him.
The Sun of Righteousness is Jesus Christ.
Through him believers are justified and sanctified, and so come into the light.
His gracious work makes sinners holy, joyful and fruitful.
The promise also depicts the gifts and comforts of the Holy Spirit, whom Christ gives to his own as light and comfort in their hearts.
He is their Sun and Shield.
The same day that burns like an oven for unrepentant sinners will be bright as morning to the righteous.
They await it more eagerly than watchmen await the dawn.
Christ came as the Sun not only to illuminate a dark world but also to heal a sick one.
Believers grow in spiritual knowledge and strength.
Their growth is like well-fed calves in a stall, not like delicate flowers that quickly wither.
Every triumph of the saints depends upon God's victory, not their own independent strength.
Another day is coming, more dreadful for everyone who persists in wickedness than anything before it.
How great the believer's happiness will be on leaving the sorrow of this world to rejoice in the Lord forever!

div.title: Remember God's law and prepare for the coming Messiah (verses 4–6)
div.p: This is the solemn conclusion not only of Malachi's prophecy but of the Old Testament.
Our consciences call us to remember God's law.
Even when no new prophets speak to us, we have the Scriptures, through which we can continue in fellowship with God.
Other people may boast about their supposedly enlightened reasoning.
But we should remain close to the holy word through which the Sun of Righteousness shines into our hearts.
The people were to wait with faith for the gospel of Christ and watch for its beginning.
John the Baptist would call for repentance and reform as Elijah had done.
Turning hearts toward God and obedience is the best preparation for the great and terrible day of the Lord.
John's message would reach people's hearts and produce a real inward change.
In this way he would prepare the way for the kingdom of heaven.
Through their sin, the Jews had exposed themselves to the law's curse.
God was ready to bring judgment, yet would once again call them to repentance and return through John's preaching.
Believers should patiently await their final release and look joyfully toward Christ's second coming, when their salvation will be completed.
Those who resist God's correcting rod must expect his judgment.
Nobody can escape the curse of God's law or enjoy the happiness of his redeemed people without turning from sin and worldliness to Christ and holiness.

p.hi: May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with us all. Amen.

div.title: The genealogy of Jesus Christ (verses 1–17)
div.p: This genealogy of our Savior has a clear and necessary purpose.
It is not a pointless list of ancestors or a display of family greatness such as worldly leaders sometimes produce.
It establishes that Jesus belonged to the nation and family from which the Messiah was promised.
God promised Abraham that a blessing would come through his descendants (Genesis 12:3; 22:18).
He promised David that the kingdom would be established through his descendants.
The promises concerning Abraham's offspring and David's throne must therefore be fulfilled in one who belongs to both their families.
Henry points to 2 Samuel 7:12, Psalm 89:3 and Psalm 132:11.
Unless Jesus truly descended from David and Abraham, he could not be the promised Messiah.
Matthew establishes that descent through recognized records.
The Son of God willingly took on our human nature.
He came near to us in our fallen, miserable condition.
Yet he remained entirely free from sin.
When we read the names in his genealogy, we should remember how low the Lord of glory was willing to stoop in order to save humanity.

div.title: An angel reassures Joseph (verses 18–25)
div.p: Consider the humble circumstances in which the Son of God entered this world.
They teach us to value godliness and holiness above worldly glory and status.
The mystery of Christ becoming human should be adored rather than treated as an object of idle speculation.
He took our nature while remaining pure from the original sin that has affected Adam's descendants.
Joseph was troubled and considered what to do.
God guides thoughtful people who seriously consider their duty, not those who never reflect.
Often his instruction comes when his servants do not know what to do next.
Divine consolation is especially precious when the soul is burdened by uncertainty.
The angel announced that Mary would give birth to the Savior of the world.
Joseph was to name the child Jesus, meaning Savior, a name corresponding to Joshua.
The name describes his work.

p.hi: He saves his people from their sins.

div.p: He removes sin's guilt through the merit of his death and breaks sin's power through the Spirit of his grace.
In saving them from sin, he saves them from divine wrath, the curse and every ultimate misery, both now and hereafter.
Christ came not to make people comfortable in their sins, but to rescue them from their sins.
He redeems them to belong to himself, the One set apart from sinners.
Joseph promptly and cheerfully obeyed the angel, without arguing or delaying.
In every step of life, especially during major decisions, we should seek God's direction by applying the general principles of his written word.
That is the safe and comforting course.

row.cell: The wise men's search after Christ.
Herod causes the infants of Bethlehem to be massacred.
Death of Herod, Jesus brought to Nazareth.

div.title: The wise men seek the newborn King (verses 1–8)
div.p: People who live far away from the usual means of grace may sometimes pursue Christ more diligently and come to know more of his salvation than those living nearby.
But no secret arts or merely human learning can bring anyone to a true knowledge of Christ.
We must learn of him through God's written word, which shines like a lamp in a dark place, and through the Holy Spirit's instruction.
When the morning star has risen in someone's heart, bringing genuine knowledge of Christ, that person desires to worship him.
Herod was old.
He had never been especially affectionate toward his own family and was unlikely to live long enough to see a newborn child grow into a political rival.
Nevertheless, he was terrified at the announcement of a new king.
He did not understand that the Messiah's kingdom was spiritual.
We must beware of lifeless faith.
A person may be convinced of many religious truths and still hate them because they challenge ambition or sinful desires.
Such a belief only increases resistance to God and his cause.
A sinner may be foolish enough to imagine that resistance will succeed.

div.title: The wise men find and worship Jesus (verses 9–12)
div.p: The wise men rejoiced when they saw the star again.
Their joy resembles that of people who have passed through a long season of temptation, spiritual darkness and fear and then receive the Spirit of adoption.
That Spirit witnesses with their spirits that they are children of God.
They may have been surprised when they found a cottage instead of a palace, and a poor mother instead of royal attendants.
But they did not turn away.
They had found the King they sought and gladly gave him their gifts.
Sincere seekers of Christ will not be disappointed because they find him and his followers in obscure places rather than among wealth and power.
Perhaps someone wants to worship Christ but thinks, “I am poor and foolish, and I have nothing to offer him.”
You still have your heart, though it is unworthy, hard and unclean.

p.hi: Give it to Christ as it is.

div.p: Be willing for him to use and change it as he pleases.
He will receive it, make it better, shape it in his likeness and give you himself forever.
The wise men offered gold, frankincense and myrrh.
Providence had sent these gifts as timely help for Joseph and Mary, who were poor.
Our heavenly Father knows what his children need.
He can appoint one person to provide for another and bring support even from the ends of the earth.

div.title: Joseph takes the family to Egypt (verses 13–15)
div.p: Egypt had once been the place of Israel's slavery and had been particularly cruel to Israelite infants.
Now God made it a refuge for the holy child Jesus.
The Lord can use even the worst places for the best purposes.
This journey tested the faith of Joseph and Mary.
Their faith was tested and proved firm.
Whenever we or our young children experience danger and hardship, let us remember the difficulties Christ himself faced as an infant.

div.title: Herod kills the children of Bethlehem (verses 16–18)
div.p: Herod ordered the murder of the young boys in Bethlehem and its surrounding villages.
Uncontrolled anger, backed by illegitimate power, can lead to almost unimaginable cruelty.
Henry writes that God was not unjust in permitting these events, because fallen human beings' lives are subject to divine judgment from the beginning.
He relates the deaths and diseases of young children to original sin.
These are Henry's theological explanations of divine permission; they do not excuse Herod's murder.
Henry calls the children's deaths their martyrdom.
How early persecution against Christ and his kingdom began!
Herod may have believed he had frustrated the Old Testament prophecies and defeated the wise men's search.
But whatever cunning and cruelty human beings devise, the Lord's purpose will stand.

div.title: Jesus returns and lives in Nazareth (verses 19–23)
div.p: Egypt could serve as a temporary place of refuge, but not as the family's permanent home.
Christ was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, so he was to return to them.
If we regarded this present world as our Egypt, a place of temporary exile and bondage, and heaven as our Canaan, our true home and rest, we would depart just as readily when the Lord calls us.
Joseph brought the family to Galilee.
They settled in Nazareth, a town people regarded with contempt.
The name Nazarene was later used as an accusation against Christ.
Wherever Providence assigns us to live, we should be prepared to share the disgrace Christ experienced.
Yet we may gladly bear his name, knowing that if we suffer with him, we will also be glorified with him.

row.cell: John the Baptist, His preaching, manner of life, and baptism.
John reproves the Pharisees and Sadducees.

div.title: John the Baptist preaches repentance (verses 1–6)
div.p: After Malachi, no prophet appeared until John the Baptist.
He began his public ministry in the wilderness of Judea, an area not densely populated or extensively settled, rather than an entirely uninhabited desert.
No place is so remote that divine grace cannot reach it.
John preached repentance.
The word means a comprehensive change of mind: a new understanding, disposition, set of affections and direction for the soul.
Consider your ways.
You have thought wrongly; think again, and think rightly.
True repentance changes how we think about God and Christ, about sin and holiness, and about this life and eternity.
A change of mind produces a changed way of living.
Gospel repentance springs from seeing Christ, recognizing his love and hoping for pardon through him.
We are invited to repent because God promises forgiveness to those who do.
Turn toward him through obedience, and through Christ he receives you in mercy.
Repentance and humility are still necessary if a person is to welcome the Lord.
To prepare a soul for Christ, much spiritual work is needed.
We must recognize sin and be convinced that our own righteousness cannot save us.
The ways of Satan and sin are crooked.
The path prepared for Christ must be made straight (Hebrews 12:13).

The secondary witness also includes a reference to Zechariah 13:1 at this point; the exact original-native placement and relevance of that reference require verification, rather than silent correction.

div.title: John warns the Pharisees and Sadducees (verses 7–12)
div.p: A sermon comes alive when its truths are applied directly to the consciences of the listeners.
John did this.
The Pharisees chiefly relied upon outward forms of religion, neglecting the weightier requirements of the moral law and the spiritual meaning of ceremonies.
Some were outright hypocrites who used a pretense of holiness as a covering for wrongdoing.
The Sadducees took the opposite extreme: they denied spirits and a future state, showing contempt for the truths others professed.
There is a coming wrath, and everyone needs to flee from it.
God does not delight in human ruin.
He warns through the written word, ministers and conscience.
People who say they regret their sins but continue deliberately committing them do not possess genuine repentance.
True penitents are humble, grateful for small mercies, patient under great suffering, watchful against every appearance of sin, faithful in their duties and charitable toward others.
We must not trust in external religious privileges.
The human heart can invent many excuses to evade the convincing and commanding power of God's word.
Many people rest on church membership and outward honors but never enter heaven.
The warning is meant to awaken the careless.
Only the regenerating Spirit of Christ can make a corrupt heart produce good fruit.
Every tree without fruit appropriate to repentance will eventually be cut down and cast into judgment, regardless of its outward gifts, reputation or impressive appearance.
If a tree does not produce fruit, it is fit only for fuel.
John's preaching also announced the purpose of the Messiah's arrival.

p.hi: No outward ordinance, no matter who administers it or by what method, can replace the baptism of the Holy Spirit and fire.

div.p: Only the Spirit's cleansing power can make a heart pure and produce the holy affections that accompany salvation.
Christ alone baptizes with the Holy Spirit.
He did so through the remarkable gifts bestowed upon the apostles (Acts 2:4).
He also grants the Spirit's graces and comforts to those who ask him (Luke 11:13; John 7:38–39; Acts 11:16).
The secondary witness prints a reference to Isaiah 21:10 near this statement; its original source context should be checked separately, without altering the pinned module.
Believers are like wheat—substantial, useful and precious.
Hypocrites are like chaff—empty and easily blown about.
They are presently mixed within the same outward religious community.
But the final judgment will separate them completely.
In heaven, believers will be gathered safely, free from corrupt neighbors and from the remaining corruption within their own hearts.
There will be no chaff among them.
Hell is the unquenchable fire that awaits impenitent unbelief and hypocrisy.
Life and death, good and evil, are set before us.
How we stand before God now determines which side of the final separation we will enter.

div.title: Jesus is baptized by John (verses 13–17)
div.p: The humility and kindness of Christ are so extraordinary that even mature believers may initially struggle to understand them.
Even people who know his will may raise objections to his way of acting.
