Those who have received much of God's Spirit should recognize their continued need to seek more grace from Christ.
Jesus did not deny that John needed the baptism Christ could give.
Yet Jesus insisted that John should now baptize him, because the Savior had entered a state of humiliation.
It was appropriate for him to fulfill all righteousness.
He acknowledged every divine institution and willingly obeyed God's righteous commands.
Through Christ, heaven is opened to sinful humanity.
The Holy Spirit descended upon him, showing that he received the Spirit's holy influences without measure.
The Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control.
At Jesus' baptism, the three Persons of the Holy Trinity were made known.
The Father affirmed the Son as Mediator.
The Son solemnly entered upon the work of redemption.
The Holy Spirit descended upon him, through whose mediation the Spirit would be given to his people.
Our spiritual sacrifices are acceptable through Christ, because he is the altar that sanctifies every gift (1 Peter 2:5).
Apart from Christ, God is a consuming fire.

p.hi: In Christ, God is a reconciled Father.

div.p: This is the gospel's message, which we must receive cheerfully through faith.

row.cell: The opening of Christ's ministry in Galilee.

div.title: Jesus is tempted by the devil (verses 1–11)
div.p: Immediately after Jesus was declared to be the Son of God and the Savior of the world, he was tempted.
Great spiritual privileges and special evidence of God's favor do not exempt anyone from temptation.
But when the Holy Spirit assures us that we are God's adopted children, that assurance answers the evil spirit's accusations.
Christ was directed into the struggle.
If we carelessly presume upon our own strength and invite temptation, we provoke God to leave us to ourselves.
Other human beings experience temptation through their own sinful desires (James 1:14).
But Jesus had no corrupt nature, and therefore his temptation came from the devil, not from inward sinful desire.
Satan is subtle, malicious and daring, but he can be resisted.
Christ's experience comforts us: being tempted is not itself sin when the temptation is refused.
In that case it is suffering, not guilt.
Satan's aim in every temptation was to lead Christ into sin against God.
First, he tempted Jesus to distrust his Father's goodness and care.
Satan often attacks when outward circumstances are difficult.
People in distress must be especially watchful.
Jesus answered the devil by appealing to what Scripture says.
This is our example.
No need, however pressing, gives us permission to use sinful means of providing for ourselves.
The Lord can and will provide through the means he appoints.
Second, Satan tempted Jesus to presume upon his Father's protection in a dangerous act.
Both despair and presumption are extremely dangerous, especially in spiritual matters.
Satan has no objection to attacking us in holy places.
Indeed, places of religious honor and worldly advancement can create particular opportunities for pride.
Those who rise high can become especially exposed to the enemy's assaults.
Satan knew enough Scripture to quote it.
A person's head may be full of biblical facts and the mouth full of religious expressions, while the heart remains hostile to God.
Satan omitted part of the promise he quoted.
Stepping outside our duty forfeits any claim that the promise authorizes our recklessness.
The secondary CCEL source places a reference to Deuteronomy 8:3 near this point, which must be collated with the published native text rather than silently relocated.
God's promises remain firm, but they do not authorize us to continue in sin so that grace may increase.
Third, Satan offered Jesus the world's kingdoms and their glory in exchange for idolatrous worship.
Worldly splendor is one of the most attractive traps for careless people.
Jesus rejected the evil offer at once: “Go away, Satan!”
Some temptations are so obviously wicked that we must not deliberate over them, but reject them immediately.
When the devil is resisted, he flees.
A heart that pauses to negotiate is almost defeated.
What can anyone gain by possessing the whole world while losing their soul?
After the temptation, Christ received help and comfort.
This encouraged him in his mission and encourages us to trust him.
He knows from experience what it is to suffer temptation and receive timely help.
Therefore he not only sympathizes with tempted believers but comes to their aid when they need it.

div.title: Christ begins preaching in Galilee (verses 12–17)
div.p: God acts justly in withdrawing the gospel and opportunities for grace from people who despise them and push them away.
Christ will not remain where he is unwelcome.
People without him live in darkness.
They may even sit contentedly in it, choosing ignorance rather than light.
When the gospel enters a place or a human heart, it is like the arrival of daylight.
Light reveals what is hidden and shows the way forward; so does the gospel.

p.hi: Repentance belongs to gospel preaching.

div.p: Not only the strict John the Baptist but also the gracious Jesus himself proclaimed repentance.
The need for it has not changed.
Henry says the kingdom of heaven was not considered to have arrived in its full form until the Holy Spirit was poured out after Christ's ascension.

div.title: Jesus calls fishermen to follow him (verses 18–22)
div.p: When Jesus began preaching, he also began gathering disciples.
They would first hear his teaching and later preach it.
They would witness his miracles and afterward testify to them.
He went not to Herod's court or to the chief priests and elders in Jerusalem, but to fishermen beside the Sea of Galilee.
The power that called Peter and Andrew could also have converted Annas and Caiaphas, because nothing is impossible with God.
But Christ chose those considered foolish by the world to put worldly wisdom to shame.
Diligence in honest work pleases Christ and does not hinder holiness.
Idleness exposes people more readily to Satan's temptations than to God's call.
It is encouraging to see young people caring for their parents and fulfilling their duties.
When Christ comes, it is good to be found working faithfully.
We should ask ourselves two questions.

p.hi: Do I belong to Christ? Am I fulfilling the calling God has given me?

div.p: These men had followed Jesus earlier as ordinary disciples (John 1:37).
Now they were called to leave their occupations and follow him more fully.
Everyone who follows Christ must be willing to give up anything when he commands it.
This encounter shows the power of Jesus' gracious calling.
He speaks, and the work is done.

div.title: Jesus teaches and heals many (verses 23–25)
div.p: Wherever Jesus went, he confirmed his divine mission through miracles.
The healings pictured the healing power of his teaching and the Holy Spirit's work through it.
We do not now ordinarily see Christ heal bodies miraculously in that way.
But when medicine brings recovery, the Lord deserves our thanks just as fully.
Jesus healed every kind of sickness and disease.
No condition was too severe or difficult for him to cure with a word.
Henry points particularly to three forms of suffering.
Paralysis was extreme bodily weakness.
Lunacy, as Henry's historical term, described severe disorder of the mind.
Demonic possession was an affliction involving both bodily and mental misery.
Christ healed all three.
By restoring bodily health, he showed that his greatest mission was to cure the diseases of the soul.
Sin is the soul's sickness, suffering and torment.
Jesus came to take away sin and heal the soul.

row.cell: Christ came to confirm the law.

div.title: Jesus teaches his disciples (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: No one can find true happiness in this life or in the next without seeking it from Christ, according to the teaching of his word.
He showed his listeners which evils they should hate and which good things they should eagerly seek and practice.

div.title: The eight blessings (verses 3–12)
div.p: Our Savior described eight kinds of blessed people.
Together, they show the principal graces that should characterize Christians.

p.hi: First, the poor in spirit are blessed.

div.p: Such people respond humbly to humble circumstances.
They are lowly in their own estimation.
They recognize their spiritual need, grieve over their guilt and eagerly desire a Redeemer.
The kingdom of grace belongs to them now, and the kingdom of glory awaits them.

p.hi: Second, those who mourn are blessed.

div.p: This is godly sorrow that produces sincere repentance, watchfulness, humility and continual dependence on God's mercy through Jesus Christ.
It also leads people to seek the Holy Spirit's continuing work of cleansing away sin.
Heaven is the Lord's mountain of joy, but our path toward it passes through a valley of tears.
God himself will comfort those who mourn in this way.

p.hi: Third, the meek are blessed.

div.p: Meek people quietly submit to God, bear insults without retaliation and respond gently or remain silent when appropriate.
Through patience they maintain possession of their own souls, even when they can scarcely hold on to anything else.
Meekness often promotes comfort, safety and even outward well-being in this life.

p.hi: Fourth, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed.

div.p: Here righteousness represents all spiritual blessings.
These blessings were purchased through Christ's righteousness and are assured by God's faithfulness.
We should desire them as earnestly as hungry and thirsty people desire food and water.
Not every desire for grace is itself a work of grace.
But this kind of spiritual longing is created by God, who will not abandon the work of his hands.

p.hi: Fifth, the merciful are blessed.

div.p: We must not merely endure our own suffering patiently.
We should do everything possible to relieve other people's misery.
We must care for their souls as well as their circumstances, pitying those trapped in sin and seeking to rescue them like burning brands pulled from the fire.

p.hi: Sixth, the pure in heart are blessed, for they will see God.

div.p: Holiness and happiness are united in this blessing.
Our hearts must be purified through faith and reserved for the Lord.
Let us pray, “Create a clean heart in me, O God.”
Only the pure are able to see God and rejoice in his holiness.
Heaven would not be happiness to an impure heart.
As God cannot approve sin, those determined to remain in sin cannot delight in his purity.

p.hi: Seventh, the peacemakers are blessed.

div.p: They love peace, seek it and work to remain quiet and respectful.
They protect peace from being broken and seek to restore it when it has been lost.
If those who make peace are blessed, woe to those who break it.

p.hi: Eighth, those who are persecuted for righteousness are blessed.

div.p: This blessing is especially characteristic of Christianity and receives more explanation than the others.
There is nothing about suffering that earns merit before God.
Yet God will ensure that those who lose anything for his sake—even life itself—will not finally lose by serving him.
How different Christ's teaching is from the world's!
The world admires the proud, fashionable, rich, powerful and victorious.
May the Lord show us mercy, acknowledge us as his children and bring us into his kingdom.
With that hope, we can face humble or painful circumstances with joy.

div.title: Salt and light (verses 13–16)
div.p: Humanity, lying in ignorance and evil, resembled a vast heap ready to decay.
Christ sent his disciples to act as salt, preserving and seasoning the world through their teaching and way of life.
If they fail in that calling, they become like salt that has lost its flavor.
A person may profess Christ while remaining without grace.
No other message or means can make that person useful apart from true saving change.
Our light must shine through good works visible to other people.
What passes privately between God and our souls should remain private.
But conduct that is naturally public should match our Christian profession and be worthy of respect.
Our goal must always be God's glory, not our own reputation.

div.title: Christ fulfills and confirms God's law (verses 17–20)
div.p: No one should imagine that Christ allows his people to take God's holy law lightly.
No sinner participates in Christ's justifying righteousness without repentance.
The mercy announced by the gospel makes a believer more deeply aware of sin, not less.
God's law becomes the Christian's guide for duty, in which the believer delights.
Anyone who deliberately permits disobedience while claiming to follow Christ—or teaches others to do so—cannot be a genuine disciple, regardless of public status.
Everyone entering God's kingdom needs Christ's righteousness imputed through faith alone.
But a renewed heart also produces a comprehensive change in attitudes and actions.

div.title: Anger and reconciliation: the sixth commandment (verses 21–26)
div.p: Some Jewish teachers had reduced the command against murder to a prohibition of the outward act of killing.
They had neglected its spiritual meaning.
Christ revealed the command's true scope, by which we will be judged and should therefore live.

p.hi: Reckless anger is murder in the heart.

div.p: Our brother or neighbor includes every human being, however lowly their station, because all people were made of one blood.
“Raca” expresses contempt flowing from pride.
“You fool”, used spitefully, expresses hatred.
Malicious slander and condemnation are like slow, secret poison.
Christ warns that what people dismiss as trivial will be brought before God's judgment.
We must protect Christian love and seek peace with everyone.
If we have injured another person, we should confess wrongdoing, humble ourselves and make or offer appropriate amends, whether the harm was done by speech or conduct.
We should do so promptly.
Unreconciled hostility hinders our fitness to participate in holy worship.
Preparing for worship provides a fitting opportunity for self-examination.
This also teaches our need to be reconciled to God through Christ.
While we live, we are still on our way to his judgment seat.
After death it will be too late.
Because life is uncertain and the matter is so serious, we must seek peace with God without delay.

div.title: Purity and fidelity: the seventh commandment (verses 27–32)
div.p: Victory over corrupt inward desires may require painful struggle.
Yet it must be pursued.
Every spiritual resource has been given to save us from sin, not to keep us comfortable in it.
Every sense and ability should be guarded against occasions of wrongdoing.
Those who lead others toward temptation, including through deliberately provocative appearance or other behavior, bear responsibility for their influence.
People accept painful medical treatments to preserve bodily life.
What should they be willing to endure to protect the eternal welfare of their souls?
God's commands are expressions of tender mercy.
His Spirit supplies the grace and consolation needed to obey them.

div.title: Truthfulness and oaths: the third commandment (verses 33–37)
div.p: Henry does not understand Christ to forbid every solemn oath.
Oaths taken in court or on other proper occasions may be lawful when made reverently and truthfully.
But oaths used needlessly in ordinary conversation are sinful.
So are verbal formulas intended to escape the responsibility of swearing truthfully while still pretending to invoke God.
The more dishonest people become, the less an oath restrains them.
The more truthful people become, the less they need oaths to be believed.
Christ does not prescribe exact words to use in every affirmation or denial.
He requires consistent truthfulness, making unnecessary oaths needless.

div.title: Refusing retaliation (verses 38–42)
div.p: We should be willing to endure injuries that can rightly be borne for the sake of peace, entrusting our affairs to the Lord.
Christians should avoid needless quarrels and fighting.
Someone may object that human nature cannot endure an insult without answering it.
But flesh and blood cannot inherit God's kingdom.
Those governed by right principles will enjoy more peace and comfort than those ruled by offended pride.

div.title: Love even your enemies (verses 43–48)
div.p: Some Jewish teachers interpreted “neighbor” as referring only to people of their own nation, religion or group, whom they already regarded as friends.
Jesus commands genuine kindness toward everyone.
We should especially care for other people's souls.
We must pray for our enemies.
Many people return kindness for kindness.
Christ calls his disciples to return good for evil.
That reveals a nobler principle than the ordinary conduct of the world.
Others greet and embrace only people from their own party or opinion.
We must not limit our respect so narrowly.
Christians ought to desire and pursue maturity and completeness in grace and holiness, following the example of the heavenly Father (1 Peter 1:15–16).
More is rightly expected from Christ's followers than from others.
Let us ask God to enable us to show, through our lives, that we truly are his children.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): 1 Corinthians 1:16.
Verified editorial cross-reference: 1Pet.1.16.

div.title: Giving without hypocrisy (verses 1–4)
div.p: Our Lord warned his followers against hypocrisy and outward display in religious duties. What we do must arise from an inward principle and aim at God's approval, not people's praise.
Giving to the needy is good and necessary. The fact that hypocrites misuse it to promote themselves does not lessen its value.
Vanity is subtle. We can begin seeking admiration before we even notice the temptation.
Jesus said that those who give in order to be seen already have their reward: people see them. That is all they wanted, and it is a miserable reward compared with God's promise.
The less we dwell upon our good deeds, the more fully God notices them.
He rewards not as an employer paying a worker no more than the wages earned, but as a Father generously blessing his child.

div.title: Praying without hypocrisy (verses 5–8)
div.p: Jesus assumed his disciples would pray. Finding a living Christian who never prays would be as unnatural as finding a living person who never breathes.

p.hi: Prayerlessness betrays gracelessness.

div.p: The scribes and Pharisees fell into two errors: seeking human admiration and using empty repetitions.
If our prayers, in which we approach God about matters of eternal importance, are made for the sake of people's praise, it is just that praise should be our only reward.
God hears even a brief, silent longing directed toward him.
His answer is a gift of grace, not a debt; there is no human merit in asking for help.
When he does not grant exactly what his people request, it is because he knows the gift is not needed or would not be good for them.
The length and wording of a prayer do not manipulate him. Some of the strongest intercessions come through groanings too deep for words.
Let us learn daily from Christ how to pray, with the right disposition of heart.

div.title: Jesus teaches us how to pray (verses 9–15)
div.p: The Lord's Prayer teaches both the subjects and the order of Christian prayer.
We are not restricted to reciting this prayer alone, or required to recite it every time. Yet using it is good, provided we understand what we say and do not repeat it without purpose.
It contains much in few words.
Its six petitions are arranged meaningfully: the first three focus especially on God's honor, and the final three concern our temporal and spiritual needs.
We seek God's kingdom and righteousness first. Only after praying for his name, kingdom and will do we ask for the support and comforts required in earthly life.
Every word teaches something.
Bread teaches moderation. We ask for what we need, rather than every luxury we might desire.

Our bread teaches honesty and diligence. We do not ask for another person's bread, or bread gained through deception (Proverbs 20:17), or through idleness (Proverbs 31:27). We seek what is honestly earned.
Daily bread teaches continual dependence upon God's Providence.
We ask him to give it, not to sell or lend it. Even the greatest people depend upon his mercy for everyday food.
We say give us, not merely give me. We must care for the poor and pray with and for our families.
We ask for it today. Just as our bodies need daily food, our souls should daily renew their desire for God. We need prayer as surely as bread.
The prayer also teaches us to hate and fear sin while hoping for mercy. We must distrust our own strength, depend on God's protecting grace, prepare to resist the tempter and avoid tempting others.
Jesus promises that those who forgive others will receive their heavenly Father's forgiveness. We must show mercy if we hope to receive it.
Christ came not only to reconcile sinners to God, but also to reconcile them to one another.

div.title: Fasting without display (verses 16–18)
div.p: Religious fasting is a duty of Christ's disciples. Yet it is principally a means of preparing the heart for other duties, not a performance with value merely in itself.
Fasting expresses the humbling of the soul (Psalm 35:13). That inward reality must be our chief concern.
Do not seek public recognition for its outward appearance.
God sees what is done in secret and will reward it openly.

div.title: Treasures, spiritual sight and masters (verses 19–24)
div.p: Worldliness is a common and deadly sign of hypocrisy.
Few things allow Satan to hold the heart more firmly while a person still maintains an outward religious profession.
Every soul looks for something to treasure above all else—something in which it places its happiness, confidence and delight.
Christ directs us toward the invisible, eternal treasures of heaven.
Through Jesus Christ we should make every effort to be sure of our interest in eternal life. Nothing earthly can compare with its incorruptible inheritance, secure beyond the changes of time.
A worldly person begins with a false principle about what matters most; therefore, the thoughts and decisions built upon that principle also go wrong.
The teaching about the eye and light also applies to false religion. A person may call something light that is actually deep darkness.
We should therefore test the principles guiding our lives by God's word, praying earnestly for the Spirit's instruction.
A person may perform occasional tasks for two employers but cannot devote the heart entirely to two masters.

p.hi: God requires the whole heart. He does not share it with the world.

div.p: When their demands conflict, one master must be chosen.
Whoever clings to the world as the supreme good will despise God. Whoever loves God must renounce the world's friendship.

div.title: Trusting God's fatherly care (verses 25–34)
div.p: Our Lord repeatedly warned his disciples against anxious, distracting and distrustful concern about everyday needs.
The poor may fall into this temptation just as easily as the wealthy fall into love of riches.
There is also a proper and necessary care for earthly duties. Jesus did not abolish that responsibility; he warned against carrying it into unbelieving anxiety.
Entrust the length of your life to God. Our times are in his hands, and his hands are good.
Entrust life's pleasures and hardships to him as well. He knows whether to make our circumstances sweet or bitter.
God has promised food and clothing; we may therefore look to him for them without being anxious over next year, old age or what we shall leave behind.
We should neither boast about tomorrow nor torment ourselves over tomorrow.
The One who gave us life and our bodies is surely able to supply the lesser necessities that sustain them.
If we attend to our souls and to eternity, we may trust him for food and clothing.
We must learn to accept the condition Providence has assigned us, just as we accept our physical stature. Worry cannot change his plans.

p.hi: Concern for our souls is the best remedy for consuming concern about worldly things.

div.p: Seek first God's kingdom. Do not imagine that pursuing true religion will cause us to starve; God knows how to supply his people even in this present life.
Through daily prayer we receive strength for daily troubles and resistance to their temptations.
Happy are those who trust themselves entirely to God's wise care. May the Spirit expose our lack of trust and remove the worldliness remaining in our hearts.

row.cell: To be doers of the word, not hearers only.

div.title: Judging others without hypocrisy (verses 1–6)
div.p: We must examine ourselves and our own conduct. But we must not make our personal opinions a law for everyone else.
Do not judge rashly or condemn a brother or sister without grounds.
Do not insist on believing the worst about people.
Jesus corrected those who quarrel over the small faults of others while tolerating much greater sins in themselves.
Some faults are like specks and others like beams; some resemble a gnat, others a camel.
This does not mean any sin is harmless. Even a tiny splinter in an eye or a gnat in a throat causes pain and danger and must be removed.
Charity may teach us to describe our brother's fault as a small splinter; true repentance and godly grief should make us regard our own sin as a large beam.
It is astonishing that people can live in a sinful and miserable condition without noticing it, just as it would be astonishing to overlook a beam lodged in one's eye.
The god of this world blinds human minds.
The first rule for anyone seeking to correct another person is therefore to reform oneself first.

div.title: Asking, seeking and knocking (verses 7–11)
div.p: Prayer is the appointed means of obtaining what we need.
Pray often, seriously and earnestly.
Ask like a beggar asking for help or a traveler asking for directions.
Seek like someone searching for a lost treasure or a merchant searching for precious pearls.
Knock like someone who longs to enter a house. Sin has shut and barred the door against us; through prayer we knock.
God grants what is requested according to his promises when he knows it is fitting for us. What more could we rightly desire?
The invitation extends to everyone who prays in faith: Jews and Gentiles, young and old, rich and poor, people of high or low standing, masters and servants, educated and uneducated.
All are equally welcome at the throne of grace.
Parents, though sometimes unwisely indulgent, generally wish to give good gifts to their children.
Our heavenly Father is perfectly wise. He knows what we need and what is truly good for us.
He would never command us to pray only to refuse to hear us—or to give us what would harm us.

div.title: Treating others well and choosing the narrow way (verses 12–14)
div.p: Christ came to teach us not merely what to know and believe, but what to do.
His instruction governs relationships with God and with everyone else—not only people who share our convictions or belong to our own party.
We should put ourselves in our neighbor's position and treat that person as we recognize it would be reasonable and right for us to be treated.
Jesus then described two ways, the right and the wrong, leading to eternal life and destruction.
There is no third destination in the life to come and no middle path in the present one.
The gate of sin is wide and already open. People can enter it without denying their sinful appetites or passions.
The road beyond it is broad and contains many different kinds of wrongdoing; it is crowded.
Yet why should anyone willingly go to destruction with a crowd rather than accept eternal life without that crowd?
The way to life is narrow.
Passing through the narrow gate does not mean our journey is finished. Self must be denied, the body disciplined and corrupt desires put to death.
Daily temptations must be resisted and duties performed. We must remain watchful through many troubles.
Still, this way is inviting because it leads both to the present joy of God's favor and to eternal blessedness.
That hope makes the hardships bearable.
People in every age have tried to explain away Christ's clear teaching.
True disciples are often regarded as unusual or unfashionable, while those who follow the majority continue on the broad road.
Be firm in your faith.
When we hear of the narrow gate and the few who find it, should we not ask whether we ourselves have entered and how faithfully we are continuing?

div.title: Recognizing false prophets (verses 15–20)
div.p: Few things prevent people from entering the narrow gate more effectively than flattering, flesh-pleasing teaching that contradicts the truth.
Such teachers are known by the tendency and effects of their doctrine.
Some aspect of their character and conduct will conflict with Christ's teaching.
A religious opinion that leads people into sin does not come from God.

div.title: Hearing and obeying Christ's words (verses 21–29)
div.p: Calling Christ our Master with our lips is not enough.
We must believe in him, repent of sin, live a holy life and love one another.
Our sanctification is God's will.
Do not trust in outward religious privileges or activities as though they guarantee acceptance. Many deceive themselves in that way and perish.
Everyone who names Christ must turn away from sin.
Others hear the word but never obey it. Their minds accumulate religious ideas without producing faithful action.
Jesus compared these listeners to two builders.
His words may require difficult acts of obedience, but we must do them.

p.hi: Christ alone is the foundation. Everything else is sand.

div.p: Some build their hope on wealth and prosperity, others on an outward profession of religion. Neither foundation can support our hopes for heaven.
A storm is coming that will test everyone's work.
At death, what hope can hypocrites retain?
The house built on sand falls at the very moment its owner most needs shelter—and when it is too late to build again.
May the Lord make us wise builders for eternity. Then nothing will separate us from the love of Jesus Christ.
The crowds were astonished at the wisdom and authority of his teaching.
His sermon remains fresh no matter how often it is read. Every word testifies to its divine Author.

Let us study the blessings and Christian graces he described with sustained attention—even spending weeks reflecting on particular ones—instead of settling for vague wishes to possess them all while actively cultivating none.

row.cell: He heals two possessed with devils.

div.title: The crowds follow Jesus (verse 1)
div.p: This verse concludes the preceding account of Jesus' sermon. Those to whom Christ has revealed himself want to know still more of him.

div.title: Jesus cleanses a man with leprosy (verses 2–4)
div.p: The man approached Jesus and worshiped him as someone possessing divine power.
His healing teaches us both whom to approach for help and how to come.
We may not know what God intends for our bodily illnesses, but we can always be confident of his wisdom and mercy.
No guilt is so great that Christ's blood cannot atone for it; no sinful corruption is so strong that his grace cannot overcome it.
To be cleansed, we must appeal to his pity. We cannot claim his mercy as a debt, but must ask for it humbly as a gift.
Those who seek Christ by faith for mercy and grace can trust his willingness to grant the spiritual help they truly need.
Afflictions are blessed when they lead us to Christ and move us to seek salvation from him.
Those whom he has cleansed from the spiritual leprosy of sin should be willing to tell faithful ministers of their condition, so that those ministers can advise, comfort and pray for them.

div.title: Jesus heals a centurion's servant (verses 5–13)
div.p: The centurion was a Roman soldier and a Gentile, yet he was a godly man. No occupation or position excuses unbelief or sin.
He was concerned for his servant. We should likewise care about the spiritual sickness of our children and those under our responsibility, bringing their needs to Christ through prayer and faith.
The centurion showed deep humility. Christ's grace makes humble people still more humble.
He also showed extraordinary faith. The less we trust our own worthiness, the more fully we can trust Christ.
He acknowledged Christ's divine authority over people and nature, just as an officer commands those under him.
We should become obedient servants of God, going and coming according to his word and Providence.
The Son of Man often finds little faith, and therefore little fruit, among people who profess to belong to his kingdom.
An outward profession may earn the title children of the kingdom. But if we rest on that title without living faith, we will be cast out.
The servant received physical healing; the centurion received Christ's approval for his faith.
Believe and receive according to Christ's promise.
Healing of the soul is both an effect and an evidence of our share in Christ's atoning blood.

div.title: Jesus heals Peter's mother-in-law (verses 14–17)
div.p: Peter was married and yet was an apostle.
Jesus' kindness to his wife's family shows his approval of marriage.
Henry explicitly argues here against the Roman church's prohibition on ministers marrying, pointing to Peter himself.
Peter's mother-in-law lived with his family, illustrating the duty of kindness toward relatives.
In spiritual healing, Scripture speaks the word and the Spirit supplies the touch, moving the heart and hands.
Ordinarily people recovering from a fever remain weak for a time.
Jesus' healing was above natural causes: the woman immediately regained enough strength to serve others.
News of his miracles spread, and many sick people came.
He healed everyone brought to him, however poor the patient or serious the disease.
Our bodies are exposed to many illnesses and troubles. The gospel's announcement that Christ bore our sicknesses and carried our sorrows gives deeper comfort than all the writings of philosophers.
Let us not resent the labor, cost or inconvenience involved in helping others.

div.title: The cost of following Jesus (verses 18–22)
div.p: The scribe was too quick to promise.
His offer to follow Christ looked determined, but many religious resolutions arise from sudden emotion without careful consideration and produce no lasting obedience.
One might have expected Jesus to welcome him enthusiastically, since a scribe could apparently bring more public influence than a group of fishermen.
But Christ knew his heart.
The man's proposal appears to have been driven by worldly ambition or love of gain.
Jesus warned him that the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head; anyone following him should expect no greater worldly comfort.
Henry judges it probable that the scribe went away.
Another man was too slow to act. He wanted to bury his father first and afterward serve Jesus.
Honoring and burying a father is a good duty, but it was not the duty Christ had assigned this man at that moment.
When Christ calls, even affection for the closest relatives and duties ordinarily proper must yield to the higher duty he now commands.
An unwilling heart always finds an excuse.
Christ called this man directly: Follow me. Henry expects that Christ's effective call gave him strength to obey and that he did follow.
The contrast is between the scribe's self-confident “I will follow you” and Christ's effective “Follow me.”
We are brought to Jesus through the power of his call, not by our own resolve (Romans 9:16).

div.title: Jesus calms the storm (verses 23–27)
div.p: Those who travel by sea and face danger there can take comfort in trusting and praying to a Savior who experienced the sea and its storms.
Everyone journeying with Christ through this world must expect storms.
Jesus shared our human nature in everything except sin. He grew tired and slept.
His sleep also tested the disciples' faith.
When they became frightened, they came to their Master.
A troubled soul may experience passions and temptations rising like waves, while God seems silent and distant.
It may cry, Lord Jesus, do not remain silent or I am lost!
True faith can still be weak. Christ's followers sometimes torment themselves with fears about present trouble and imagined future disasters.
A violent storm of doubt and fear may give way to a wonderful calm through the Spirit of adoption.
The disciples had never seen a storm become completely quiet in an instant.
The One who did this can do anything.
We may therefore trust him in every outward or inward storm (Isaiah 26:4).

div.title: Jesus casts out demons (verses 28–34)
div.p: The demons have no share in Christ as Savior and cannot expect his saving benefits.
How great is God's mysterious love for fallen humanity when fallen angels are not offered the same saving help (Hebrews 2:16)!
The demons had to acknowledge Jesus' greatness, though they had no part in him.
They rejected his authority, but they could not escape him as Judge.
Every human being must also face him.
Satan and his servants can act only as far as Christ permits.
They cannot enter even a herd of pigs without his permission, and they must leave when he commands.
God sometimes allows their destructive activity for wise and holy purposes.
The devil drives people toward sins they have already resolved to avoid and know will bring shame and grief.
It is miserable to be held captive by him.
Many people prefer their pigs to the Savior.
They do not want Christ or his word within their hearts because his teaching would overthrow the animal-like desires they insist on feeding.
Those who repeatedly tell the Lord to depart from them must fear hearing the final sentence commanding them to depart from him.

row.cell: Jesus returns to Capernaum, and heals a paralytic.
Christ raises the daughter of Jairus, He heals the issue of blood.
Christ casts out a dumb spirit.

div.title: Jesus forgives and heals a paralysed man (verses 1–8)
div.p: The friends who brought the paralysed man to Jesus showed strong, humble and active faith.
They believed he both could and would heal him. Faith that earnestly seeks Christ does not allow obstacles to prevent it.
Their humility brought the patient to Jesus rather than trying to claim an entitlement to healing.
Sin may be pardoned while illness remains. Equally, illness may disappear while sin remains unforgiven.
But when recovery from sickness accompanies the comfort of peace with God, healing becomes a special mercy indeed.
This is no excuse to continue in sin.
We may come to Christ with our sins as an illness and misery from which we want deliverance.
It is a terrible deception to approach him while treasuring those sins and intending to keep them.
The great purpose of his saving work is to separate our hearts from sin.
Jesus knows perfectly what people say within themselves. Evil thoughts are themselves sinful and offensive to him.
He demonstrated that his mission was to save his people from their sins.
Instead of continuing the argument with the scribes, he commanded the man to rise.
The man not only no longer needed to be carried on his bed; he was strong enough to carry the bed himself.
Every power and ability God gives for doing good should lead us to glorify him.

div.title: Matthew is called (verse 9)
div.p: Matthew was at work in his occupation when Christ called him, as other disciples had been.
Satan often approaches idle people with temptation. Christ frequently calls people while they are working.
By nature we resist the Lord. We therefore need him to call us by his powerful word and draw us to himself.
If he speaks by the word of his Spirit to our hearts, the world's attraction cannot hold us and Satan cannot block the path.
We rise and follow.
This saving change has Christ as its author and his word as the means.
Neither Matthew's office nor its income could detain him once Christ called.
The disciples who had been fishermen later returned to fishing on occasion. Matthew, however, was never again found pursuing his former sinful gains.

div.title: Matthew welcomes his former associates (verses 10–13)
div.p: After being called, Matthew invited former companions to hear Jesus.
He knew from personal experience what Christ's grace could accomplish and did not despair of their conversion.
People truly brought to Christ naturally long for others to be brought to him as well.
Those who imagine that their souls are perfectly healthy have no desire to receive help from the spiritual Physician.
The Pharisees despised Christ because they regarded themselves as whole.
Tax collectors and other sinners recognized their need for instruction and change.
It is easy—and sadly common—to put the worst interpretation on even good words and actions.
Those who resent other people receiving God's grace give reason to question whether they themselves possess it.
Jesus' fellowship with sinners was an act of mercy, because helping bring souls to conversion is a supreme work of mercy.
The gospel summons us to repentance, a change of both mind and conduct.
If human beings had not sinned, there would have been no need for Christ to come among them.
Have we recognized our own sickness and begun following the directions of our great Physician?

div.title: John's disciples ask about fasting (verses 14–17)
div.p: John the Baptist was then in prison.
His circumstances, strict way of life and special message led the disciples particularly devoted to him to fast frequently.
Jesus reminded them of John's own testimony concerning him (John 3:29).
Though Jesus and his disciples lived sparingly, fasting during the joy of the Bridegroom's personal presence would not be appropriate.
When Christ is present with his people, all is well.
As the presence of the sun creates day and its absence brings night, so his presence brings joy.
Jesus then used familiar illustrations of good judgment and timing.
A patch of rough, unprepared cloth sewn onto a soft, worn garment can pull away and make its tear worse.
New wine placed in weak, decaying leather containers can ferment and burst them.
But fresh wine kept in strong new skins preserves both.
These comparisons teach that we must use great care and wisdom with new believers.
Do not unnecessarily give them a gloomy, discouraging picture of Christ's service.
Teach and urge duties in ways they are ready and able to bear.

div.title: A woman's bleeding stops and Jairus's daughter lives (verses 18–26)
div.p: When someone we love dies, our loss should drive us toward Christ, who is our life.
Even the most powerful rulers are honored—not diminished—when they bow before Jesus.
Whoever seeks mercy from him must honor him.
Christ worked miracles in different ways, perhaps because he knew perfectly the varying dispositions of those who came to him.
On the way to the ruler's house, he received an appeal from a suffering woman and healed her.
If by living faith we reach out even to the hem of Christ's garment, our deepest spiritual evils will be healed.
There is no other true cure.
Nor should we fear that Christ knows the burdens and shame we hesitate to tell even our closest earthly friends.
When Jesus reached the house, he told the mourners to make room.
Sometimes worldly sorrow fills the heart so completely that people shut out Christ's comfort.
The girl was genuinely dead, though not beyond Christ's power.
The death of the righteous can particularly be regarded as sleep, awaiting their awakening.
We may not immediately understand Christ's words or actions, but they should never be despised on that account.
He sent away the mockers. Those who laugh at what they do not understand are not fitting witnesses of his works.
Spiritually dead people likewise do not rise to new life unless Christ takes them by the hand in the day of his power.

If raising one recently deceased child increased Jesus' fame, what will his glory be when everyone in the graves hears his voice and comes out—some to the resurrection of life and others to the resurrection of judgment?

div.title: Two blind men receive sight (verses 27–31)
div.p: The Jews expected the Messiah. These two blind men knew and declared publicly that Jesus was the promised Son of David.
People who lose bodily sight through Providence may nevertheless receive the full illumination of their spiritual understanding through grace.
Whatever burdens or needs we carry, the mercy of Jesus Christ is sufficient.
The men followed and cried out to him.
Christ delayed the answer to test their faith, teaching us to pray persistently without losing heart.
The central question was not merely whether they wanted sight but whether they believed.
Natural need can produce urgent cries, but only grace creates saving faith.
Jesus touched their eyes. He opens the eyes of spiritually blind people through his word accompanied by the power of grace.
He made the healing depend upon their faith.
Those who approach Jesus are treated not according to imagined expectations or outward profession, but according to faith.
Jesus sometimes instructed healed people not to spread news of the miracle.
Henry connects this to his unwillingness to encourage the popular misconception that the Messiah would simply be an earthly political ruler, provoking unrest or rebellion.

div.title: Jesus casts out a spirit that prevented speech (verses 32–34)
div.p: Henry contrasts the demon that made a person unable to speak with blaspheming opponents and says the former is the less terrible case.
Christ's cures reach the root of a problem: by breaking Satan's power, he removes its effects and opens the lips.
Pride can make people refuse even the clearest evidence.
They will accept false and absurd claims rather than Scripture because their hearts are hostile to a holy God.

div.title: Jesus sees a great harvest in need of workers (verses 35–38)
div.p: Jesus visited not only large, prosperous cities but also poor and obscure villages.
He preached and healed in those places.
The souls of the least significant people in society are as precious to Christ as those of the most prominent.
They should be equally precious to us.
Although the land had priests, Levites and scribes, Henry regarded many as worthless shepherds (Zechariah 11:17).
Jesus therefore had compassion on the people, scattered like sheep without a shepherd and perishing through lack of spiritual knowledge.
Many people remain in that condition today.
We should pity them and do everything we can to help.
The crowds eager for spiritual teaching constituted a plentiful harvest, yet truly active and faithful workers were few.
Christ is the Lord of the harvest.
We should pray that he will raise up and send many laborers who work to bring souls to him.
When God stirs people to pray earnestly for a needed mercy, this can be a sign that he intends to grant it.
Those commissioned in answer to prayer have particular reason to hope that their work will bear fruit.

row.cell: The apostles instructed and sent forth.

div.title: Jesus appoints the twelve apostles (verses 1–4)
div.p: The word apostle means messenger. These men were Christ's messengers, sent to proclaim his kingdom.
Jesus gave them authority to heal every kind of sickness.
In the grace of the gospel there is a remedy for every spiritual wound and disease.
There is no spiritual illness for which Christ lacks the power to give healing.
The names of the apostles were recorded, and that was an honor.
Yet their greater reason to rejoice was that their names were written in heaven, while the names of powerful earthly rulers eventually pass into obscurity.

div.title: The apostles receive their first mission (verses 5–15)
div.p: The apostles were initially directed to Israel.
Henry says that the gospel was not to be carried to the Gentiles until the Jews had first been offered it and refused it.
This restriction applied only to their first mission, not permanently.
Wherever they went, they were to announce: The kingdom of heaven is near.
Each word of that message matters.
They preached so that faith might be established.
They announced a kingdom to encourage hope.
They announced the kingdom of heaven to inspire love for heavenly things and a willingness to give up earthly attachments.
They said it was near, urging immediate preparation.
Jesus gave miraculous powers to confirm the truth of their teaching.
Henry judges that such signs are not now necessary, since God's kingdom has come.
Their meaning was that Christ's gospel heals spiritually sick souls and raises those dead in sin.
When proclaiming the freely given grace of God, those serving Christ should be especially careful to avoid even the appearance of working merely for pay.
The apostles received directions about entering unfamiliar towns and homes.
Christ's servant arrives as an ambassador of peace.
The message is intended even for the worst sinners, but the messenger should seek out people of upright character for hospitality and assistance.
We must pray earnestly for everyone and treat everyone courteously.
Those who reject the message must still hear the whole counsel of God, including the danger of refusing his gracious invitation.
People who hear the gospel should reflect seriously on their responsibility.
Otherwise, greater privileges may only increase the seriousness of their condemnation.

div.title: Jesus prepares his messengers for persecution (verses 16–42)
div.p: Jesus warned his disciples that persecution would come.
They should avoid conduct that provides unnecessary advantages to their enemies: political entanglements, worldly interference, the appearance of wrongdoing or self-interest, and deceitful methods.
He foretold their suffering not simply to prepare them but also so that the fulfillment of his warning would strengthen their faith.
Christ told them what difficulties would come and who might cause them.
He did not conceal the cost of serving him.
We too should count that cost.
Persecutors may behave worse than wild animals because they attack people of their own kind.
Even strong family relationships can be torn apart by hostility to Jesus.
Suffering caused by close relatives or friends is especially painful.
All who seek to live godly lives in Christ must expect opposition and many troubles along the way to God's kingdom.
But Christ coupled his warnings with counsel and comfort.
Be wise as serpents. His servants must be careful when enemies try to destroy them.
Be harmless as doves. This means not merely refusing to injure anyone but also refusing to cherish ill will.
Prudence is necessary, but not anxious and tormenting worry. Cast those cares upon God.
Christians should be more concerned about doing what is right than about speaking impressively.
When danger becomes severe, followers of Christ may move out of danger, but they must never move out of their duty.
They must not use sinful or unlawful methods to escape; a way opened by disobedience is not a door opened by God.
Fear of people is a trap. It disorders peace of mind and entangles us in sin.
We should resist it and pray against it.
Trouble, distress and persecution cannot sever God's love for his people or their love for him.
We must fear the One who can judge both soul and body, rather than be ruled by fear of human beings.
The gospel must be announced publicly because everyone has a deep interest in its truth.
The whole counsel of God must be declared (Acts 20:27).
Christ supplied reasons for courage.
The persecution his disciples would suffer would become testimony against those opposing his gospel.
When God calls them to speak for him, they may depend on his help in knowing what to say.
Knowing that trials have an appointed end helps believers endure them.
They can persevere to the end because the Lord will continue sustaining them.
He provides strength suited to the day's need.
Those who work for Christ can be encouraged that his work will certainly be accomplished.
God's Providence extends to all his creatures, even the smallest sparrows.
His people are worth more than many sparrows.
Even the hairs on their heads are numbered. The Lord knows and cares for each person who belongs to him.
We must not merely believe in Christ in private.
When called to do so, we must confess him openly, even under persecution.
Henry qualifies the warning about denial: it concerns a denial persisted in.
The promised reward of confession likewise belongs to confession that truly and consistently arises from faith and love.
Religion is worth more than everything else.
Everyone who really knows its value will be willing to surrender competing interests for it.
Christ leads his people through suffering into glory.
Those least attached to earthly life are best prepared for the life to come.
Even a small kindness shown to one of Christ's disciples is accepted when it is all a person has the opportunity and ability to offer.
But such kindness does not earn a claim against God.
We can merit nothing from his hand.
Any reward is a free gift of grace.
Let us confess Christ courageously and demonstrate love for him in everything.

row.cell: Christ's testimony to John the Baptist.
The gospel revealed to the simple. The heavy-laden invited.

div.title: Jesus continues preaching (verse 1)
div.p: Our divine Redeemer never grew tired of his work of love.
We should likewise refuse to grow weary of doing good, knowing that in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.

div.title: Jesus answers John the Baptist's disciples (verses 2–6)
div.p: There are two possible explanations for John's message.

Some believe he sent his disciples because he himself desired reassurance. Genuine faith can still be mixed with unbelief, and temptation may temporarily lead even good people to question important truths.
Yet Henry hopes John's faith did not fail in this matter and that he wanted only to have it strengthened and confirmed.
Others believe John sent them for the disciples' own benefit, so that Jesus would assure them directly.
Christ pointed them toward what they had heard and seen.
His merciful works, particularly toward poor people, identified him as the One bringing the tender mercies of God into the world.
When what people hear and see is compared carefully with Scripture, it points toward the way of salvation.
Prejudice is difficult to overcome, but allowing it to rule is dangerous.
Faith that continues despite prejudice and opposition will ultimately bring greater praise, honor and glory.

div.title: Jesus honors John the Baptist (verses 7–15)
div.p: Jesus praised John not simply to honor him but to help the listeners.
Everyone who hears God's word will have to give an account of what they did with it.
The end of a sermon is not the end of our responsibility; in an important sense, it is when the real work begins.
John practiced serious self-denial and was detached from luxury, outward pomp and sensual pleasure.
Our conduct and appearance should be consistent with our calling and situation.
John was great and good, but not perfect.
In that sense he fell short of believers already glorified in heaven.
Even the least of them knows, loves and praises God more fully than the greatest saint in this world.
But Henry judges that “the kingdom of heaven” in this passage refers more especially to the kingdom of grace, the gospel age in its power and purity.
We should be thankful for living amid the advantages of its light and love.
John's ministry stirred many people, who became his disciples.
People previously thought unlikely to have any interest in God's kingdom now strove earnestly to enter it, seeming almost like unexpected intruders.
This illustrates the urgency and zeal required of us all.
Self must be denied. Our hearts, habits of mind and fundamental dispositions must change.
Those who truly desire God's great salvation will receive it on the terms he sets, refusing to let go until they obtain his blessing.
Divine things concern everyone.
God requires that people use the abilities he gives them properly.
Many remain ignorant because they refuse to learn.

div.title: Jesus exposes a stubborn generation (verses 16–24)
div.p: Jesus reproved the self-important scribes and Pharisees.
Their behavior resembled children who refuse to join their companions' games and complain no matter how others try to please them.
Worldly people often produce petty criticisms of everyone, however good and holy the person may be.
Their objections reveal malice more than wisdom.
John's austere life displeased them, and Jesus' fellowship with people displeased them too.
Christ, completely holy and separate from sin, was accused of joining in sinners' wrongdoing.
Even spotless innocence cannot always protect a person from slander.
Jesus knew that many Jewish hearers had become more hardened against his miracles and teaching than people in Tyre and Sidon would have been.
Their judgment would therefore be more serious.
God possesses almighty power but never punishes anyone beyond what is deserved, nor withholds truth from people who genuinely long to know it.

div.title: Jesus invites the weary to find rest (verses 25–30)
div.p: Children should be grateful.
When we approach God as Father, we must also remember that he is Lord of heaven and earth.
We should come with reverence before the sovereign Ruler of all and with confidence that he can protect us from evil and give us what is good.
Jesus made the extraordinary declaration that the Father had entrusted all power, authority and judgment into his hands.
Every revelation of the Father's will and love since Adam sinned has come to us through Christ.
The Savior invites everyone who labors and is heavily burdened to come to him.
In different senses, all human beings are burdened.
Some wear themselves out pursuing wealth, position and honor.
Others exhaust themselves chasing pleasure.
People enslaved to Satan and their own desires endure the harshest bondage.
Others labor uselessly trying to establish their own righteousness before God.
Convinced sinners feel guilt and dread. Tempted and suffering believers also carry real burdens.
Christ invites them all to come to him for rest for their souls.
He himself issues this invitation.
We come when, aware of guilt and misery, believing his love and power to help, we seek him earnestly through prayer.
It is both our duty and our highest interest to come.
The gospel's summons is generous: Whoever desires may come.
All who come this way receive rest as Christ's free gift, finding peace and comfort in the heart.
But we must take his yoke and willingly submit to his authority.
We must learn from him both how to obey and how to receive comfort.
He accepts willing service even when the service is imperfect.
His commands are holy, just and good.
They do require self-denial and can bring difficulty, yet his grace provides inward joy and peace even in this life.
His yoke is, as Henry puts it, lined with love.
The help Christ supplies is so powerful, his encouragements so suitable and his consolations so strong that obedience becomes pleasant.

p.hi: The path of duty is the path of rest.

div.p: We may confidently stake our souls on the truths he teaches.
Why then would weary sinners seek rest elsewhere?
Let us come to Christ daily for deliverance from wrath and guilt, from sin and Satan, and from our worries, fears and sorrows.
Forced, unwilling obedience is a heavy burden rather than a light yoke.
It is useless to approach Jesus with our lips while keeping our hearts far from him.
Come to him and receive rest for your souls.

row.cell: Jesus defends his disciples for plucking corn on the sabbath day.
Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the sabbath.
Evil words proceed from an evil heart.
The scribes and Pharisees reproved for seeking a sign.
The disciples of Christ are his nearest relations.

div.title: The disciples gather grain on the Sabbath (verses 1–8)
div.p: When the disciples plucked grain, they acted within God's law (Deuteronomy 23:25). They had little food and were content with that modest provision.
The Pharisees did not object because the grain belonged to another person; they objected because it was the Sabbath.
Christ came to free his followers from the Pharisees' unscriptural human rules, not merely their moral corruption, and he defended what the disciples did.
The strongest person's desires must not be indulged at the expense of the weakest person's genuine needs.
Work that is necessary is lawful on the Sabbath. The day's rest should promote, not prevent, worship.

Reasonable food and care for health are proper. But forcing servants to stay home and turning a household into a scene of haste and disorder in order to prepare an indulgent feast for visitors is a very different matter.
Henry explicitly reproves such conduct, even among people who profess faith.
The Sabbath was instituted for human good (Deuteronomy 5:14). No law should be interpreted in a way that defeats its own purpose.
Christ is Lord of the Sabbath. Both the day and the appropriate work of that day belong to him.

div.title: Jesus heals a withered hand (verses 9–13)
div.p: Works of mercy are lawful and fitting on the Lord's day.
There are useful acts beyond formal worship: visiting the sick, feeding the poor, helping those needing urgent assistance and teaching young people to care for their souls.
Such things must come from love and generosity, with humility and self-denial, and are acceptable to God (Genesis 4:7, as cited in this secondary witness).
As with other miracles, this healing also has a spiritual meaning.
By nature our hands are spiritually withered; we cannot produce good works through our own power.
Christ alone gives life to the dead soul.
He works within us both the desire and the ability to obey.
His command comes with the promise of grace through his word.

div.title: The Pharisees plot against Jesus (verses 14–21)
div.p: The Pharisees looked for a charge that would allow them to put Jesus to death.
Knowing their plan and that his appointed time had not yet come, Christ withdrew.
His character and conduct fulfilled the prophet's description with extraordinary exactness.
We may confidently entrust ourselves to so kind and faithful a Friend.
He does not break the bruised reed but strengthens it.
He does not extinguish the weakly smoking wick but encourages its flame.
Let us abandon quarrelsome and angry argument and receive one another as Christ has received us.
Encouraged by his gentleness, let us pray that his Spirit will rest upon us and help us follow his example.

div.title: Jesus delivers a man oppressed by a demon (verses 22–30)
div.p: A soul held captive by Satan is spiritually blind to God's truth and unable to speak properly in prayer.
Through unbelief the devil closes the eyes; through temptation he keeps the lips from praying.
The more people admired Christ's miracle, the more urgently the Pharisees tried to discredit him.
But if Satan were helping Jesus to expel demons, his own kingdom would be fighting itself and could not stand.
And if the Pharisees claimed Jesus acted through the devil's prince, they had no valid reason to say their own followers' exorcisms used a different power.
There are two great opposed interests in the world.
Where the Holy Spirit casts out evil through conversion, leading sinners to faith and obedience, God's kingdom has come.
Anyone who refuses to welcome or assist this gracious change opposes Christ.

div.title: Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (verses 31 and 32)
div.p: Jesus first gives a gracious assurance that all kinds of sin may be pardoned on gospel terms.
He also teaches his followers to be willing to forgive insulting words directed against themselves.
Humble, conscientious believers sometimes fear that they have committed the unforgivable sin.
Yet people who have approached that sin most closely seldom feel troubled about it.

p.hi: People who sincerely repent and believe the gospel have not committed the unpardonable sin.

div.p: Repentance and faith are special gifts of God. He would not give them to someone whom he had absolutely determined never to pardon.
Even the fear of having committed this sin can be a hopeful sign that the fearful person has not committed it.
A trembling, contrite sinner has this witness within.

div.title: Words reveal what fills the heart (verses 33–37)
div.p: Our speech reveals our character, just as an accent may reveal the country we come from.

p.hi: The heart is the spring; our words are the streams.

div.p: If the source is polluted, its waters will also be polluted.
Only the grace of God, like salt used to heal a spring, can renew the heart, guide the tongue and cleanse corrupt conversation.
A wicked person's heart holds a store of evil desires.
From this store come words and deeds that dishonor God and injure neighbors.
We should continually watch ourselves, ensuring that our speech suits the character of a Christian.

div.title: The demand for a sign and the danger of empty reform (verses 38–45)
div.p: Christ welcomes holy desires and faithful prayers.
But those who ask with wrong motives may ask and receive nothing.
God gave signs to people such as Abraham and Gideon who wanted their faith strengthened, while refusing signs demanded as an excuse for unbelief.
The great proof that Christ is Messiah is his resurrection from the dead by his own power, the sign of Jonah.
As Jonah was preserved for three days and nights in the great fish and then emerged alive, so Jesus would be in the grave and then rise.
The repentant Ninevites would shame those who refused repentance.
The queen of Sheba would shame those who refused to believe Christ, even though she had less light and greater difficulties.
Jesus' warning about the returning evil spirit pictures the condition of the Jewish church and nation.
It also applies to everyone who experiences some outward moral reform without genuine conversion.
An unclean spirit may leave a person's life temporarily.
If Christ does not dwell in the heart to keep it out, it finds a place cleaned by outward reform but still ready to obey sinful suggestions.
The person may become a stronger enemy of truth than before.
Every heart is a dwelling place of evil unless through faith in Christ it becomes a temple of the Holy Spirit.

div.title: Jesus identifies his true family (verses 46–50)
div.p: Christ taught clearly, familiarly and in ways his listeners could understand.
His mother and brothers were outside asking to speak with him, when it would have been better for them to be inside listening to his teaching.
Those closest to opportunities for grace often neglect them most, assuming they will always have another chance.
Yet tomorrow is not ours to command.
Friends and relatives may unintentionally interrupt our work or distract us with earthly concerns when our souls need attention.
Jesus was fully devoted to the work his Father gave him. Lesser duties did not lead him to neglect the greater.
This does not authorize disrespect toward parents or unkindness to relatives under the pretext of religion.
It means that lesser obligations must yield when a higher duty is presently required.
Let us cling to Christ and regard every genuine Christian, whatever that person's worldly station, as the brother, sister or mother of the Lord of glory.
Love, respect and serve them for his sake and after his example.

row.cell: The parables of the mustard-seed and the leaven.
The parables of the hidden treasure, the pearl of great price, the net cast into the sea, and the householder.
Jesus is again rejected at Nazareth.

div.title: The parable of the sower (verses 1–23)
div.p: Jesus preached from a boat to avoid the crowd pressing too closely and to allow his voice to be heard.
This teaches us to use faithfully the practical arrangements Providence provides for worship, without seeking outward splendor.
Parables make divine truth clear to those willing to learn while leaving it obscure to those determined to remain ignorant.
The seed is God's word. Christ sows it, either personally or through his ministers.
Preaching to a crowd is like scattering grain: we cannot know where the seed will take root.
Four kinds of soil describe four responses of the heart.
The path represents careless hearers. Satan is both the great murderer of souls and the thief of sermons, stealing the word from those who neglect to keep it.
Rocky soil represents hypocrites who quickly display enthusiasm, sometimes exceeding the outward enthusiasm of genuine Christians.
They enjoy messages about free salvation, Christian privileges and heaven.
Yet without a changed heart, lasting conviction of sin, awareness of their need for a Savior or love for holiness, they claim assurance without foundation.
When persecution comes, or a tempting sinful advantage appears, they abandon or conceal their profession and seek an easier form of religion.
Thorny soil represents worldly cares.
Thorns came through sin and are part of the curse. They may serve a practical purpose, yet they entangle, hurt and eventually burn (Hebrews 6:8).
Worldly anxiety prevents us from benefiting from God's word.
The deceitfulness of riches harms us precisely when we trust wealth as a source of safety and happiness. It chokes the seed.
Good soil is marked by fruitfulness, which distinguishes genuine believers from hypocrites.
Christ does not say the good ground has no stone or thorn at all, only that nothing is allowed to destroy its fruit.
True believers differ in fruitfulness.
We should seek to bear the greatest possible harvest.
Hearing God's word is one of the best uses of our hearing. Let us examine ourselves: What kind of hearer am I?

div.title: The weeds among the wheat (verses 24–30 and 36–43)
div.p: The weeds picture the condition of Christ's church in this life and at the final judgment.
The parable describes Christ's care, the devil's hostility, good and bad mixed together now, and their final separation.
Sin grows readily in fallen humanity, just as weeds grow without tending.
Good seed requires care, watering and protection.
When the servants complained about weeds in a good field, their master had not caused the problem.
Whatever is wrong in Christ's church certainly does not originate with Christ.
Openly wicked people and those persistently opposing the gospel should not be treated as faithful church members.
Yet no human judgment can separate genuine believers from hypocrites perfectly.
Even opponents should be instructed with meekness, not destroyed as though we were authorized to carry out final judgment ourselves.
The great day will reveal clearly what is hard to discern in this world.
God's coming judgment should restrain us from wrongdoing.
At death believers will recognize their own heavenly glory; on judgment day they will shine before the whole world.
Their light is borrowed from the Fountain of light.
Then their sanctification will be perfected and their justification publicly made known.
May we be found among them.

div.title: The mustard seed and leaven (verses 31–35)
div.p: The gospel began in apparent smallness but would expand greatly.
So it is with God's grace in an individual heart. If grace is genuine, it grows even when its first beginnings are almost imperceptible.
Over time it becomes strong and useful.
The gospel also works like leaven, gradually but certainly transforming the heart.
Its work is often quiet and unseen (Mark 4:26–29) yet powerful and unstoppable.
The apostles introduced a small amount of gospel leaven into the great mass of humanity.
The Lord's Spirit empowered its growth.
When gospel grace enters a soul, it changes all its faculties and alters even the ways the bodily members are used (Romans 6:13).
These parables teach us to expect spiritual progress rather than instant completion.
Are we growing in grace and in holy habits?

div.title: The treasure, pearl, net and householder (verses 44–52)
div.p: Jesus gave four parables here.
First, treasure hidden in a field. People who look only at Scripture's surface may undervalue it.
Those who search Scripture and find Christ and eternal life (John 5:39) recognize a treasure worth surrendering everything else for.
Salvation cannot be purchased, yet many things may need to be relinquished for its sake.
Second, the precious pearl. Everyone is occupied pursuing something: wealth, recognition, learning or pleasure.
Most settle for counterfeit pearls.
Jesus Christ is the Pearl of great price. Having him is sufficient for genuine happiness now and forever.
Gold can be purchased too dearly; Christ never can. When sinners recognize the grace of the Savior, other gains lose their ultimate importance.
Third, the net cast into the sea. The world resembles a great sea, humanity its fish, and gospel preaching the net.
The Lord who rules the sea uses the gospel to gather people for his glory.
At the end, genuine believers and hypocrites will be separated. Those cast away will be miserable.
Fourth, the householder. A faithful gospel minister is a skilled teacher who draws out useful truth, like a host offering food from last year's store and this year's harvest.
Long-held experience and new understanding both serve the church.
We must remain students at Christ's feet, relearning old truths and discovering new lessons every day.

div.title: Jesus is rejected at Nazareth (verses 53–58)
div.p: Christ renewed his offer to people who had previously rejected him.
They dismissed him as the carpenter's son.
He was commonly believed to be so, and there is no shame in being the child of an honest tradesman.
His neighbors ought to have respected him more because he came from among them.
Instead familiarity became a reason for contempt.
Jesus performed few miracles there because of their unbelief.
Unbelief hinders people from receiving Christ's blessings.
Let us remain faithful to the Savior who has made peace for us with God.

div.title: John the Baptist is killed (verses 1–12)
div.p: Herod could not silence the accusations of his conscience.
The fear and shame troubling him were warnings of a future judgment.
But being frightened by conviction is not the same as being converted.
People who profess to favor the gospel while continuing in wickedness must not be encouraged in their self-deception.
Faithful ministers should tell them the truth, as John did.
The world may condemn such rebuke as harshness, fanaticism or a lack of courtesy.
False professors of religion and timid believers may agree.
Yet the most powerful enemies can go no further than the Lord permits.
Herod feared that John's execution would trigger a popular rebellion. It did not.
He did not fear that it would stir up his own conscience. It did.
People sometimes fear human punishment for deeds they scarcely fear divine condemnation for committing.
Occasions of excessive amusement and pleasure often provide opportunities for wicked schemes against the godly.
Herod gave a lavish reward for an empty dance while giving imprisonment and death to the prophet who sought his soul's salvation.
Henry judges that beneath Herod's hesitation lay real malice.
Otherwise, he could have found a way to avoid fulfilling his rash and wicked promise.
When faithful under-shepherds are killed, the flock need not be lost as long as its people may go to the Great Shepherd.
It is better to be drawn to Christ through suffering and loss than never to come to him at all.

div.title: Jesus feeds five thousand (verses 13–21)
div.p: When Christ and his word seem to withdraw, we should follow him, seeking spiritual instruction and God's grace before worldly advantage.
The presence of Christ and his gospel can make even a wilderness not merely bearable but desirable.
Jesus multiplied a small quantity of bread through his creative power until the great crowd was satisfied.
If we truly care about people's souls, we should have compassion on their bodies too.
We should seek God's blessing at meals.
We should avoid waste, since frugality makes generosity possible.
This miracle also represents Jesus, the Bread of Life who came from heaven to sustain perishing souls.
To worldly observers the provisions of the gospel can seem inadequate.
But everyone who receives Christ by faith with thanksgiving finds him fully sufficient.

div.title: Jesus walks on water and rescues Peter (verses 22–33)
div.p: A person who cannot be alone with God and with personal thoughts is not living as a true follower of Christ should.
At special times, especially when prayer becomes a joy and our hearts are open before God, extended private prayer is valuable.
Christ's disciples may encounter storms while faithfully doing their duty.
Through these troubles Jesus displays his grace more fully for them.
He can deliver his people by any means he chooses.
Sometimes even the apparent approach of help frightens believers because they misunderstand Christ's actions.
Those who have Christ near them and know they belong to him need not fear even death itself.
Peter walked upon the waves not for entertainment or personal glory but to reach Jesus.
Christ sustained him in this pursuit.
Exceptional support may be expected in carrying out spiritual duties, not in performing needless demonstrations of courage.
We cannot approach Christ unless his power upholds us.
Jesus told Peter to come partly to show his Lord's power, partly to reveal Peter's own weakness.
God sometimes allows his servants to make choices that expose their need and make divine grace clearer.
When we turn our eyes away from Christ toward our difficulties, we begin to sink.
When we call to him, he reaches out to save us.
Those who would be saved must come to Christ and cry to him.
Often only the realization that we are sinking makes us understand our need.
Jesus rebuked Peter for doubting.
Greater faith would free us from many needless fears.
Weak faith and persistent doubt displease Christ, for he is present to help his disciples even in the fiercest storm.
Only the world's Creator could multiply the loaves.
Only its Governor could walk upon the sea.
The disciples recognized what the miracles revealed and worshiped him.
Whoever comes to God must believe; whoever truly believes comes to him (Hebrews 11:6).

div.title: Jesus heals the sick at Gennesaret (verses 34–36)
div.p: Wherever Jesus went, he did good.
The people brought every kind of sick person to him and asked humbly for help.
The experiences of others may encourage and guide us in seeking Christ.
Everyone who touched him was fully healed.

p.hi: When Christ heals, the healing is complete.

div.p: If more people understood both who he is and how sick their souls are, they would eagerly seek his healing power.
The cure was not produced by the fingers touching the garment.
It was associated with their faith—or, more precisely, it came from Christ himself, whom faith reached for.

row.cell: He warns against things which really defile.
He heals the daughter of a Syrophenician woman.
Jesus heals the sick, and miraculously feeds four thousand.

div.title: Jesus exposes human traditions (verses 1–9)
div.p: Adding rules to God's law reflects badly upon his wisdom, as though he had left out something necessary that human beings could provide.
Such additions ultimately draw people into disobedience.
We should be deeply thankful for the written word of God.
Never imagine that Scripture's religion can be improved by additions in either doctrine or practice.
Jesus described the Pharisees' traditions as human inventions.
He showed how they violated the fifth commandment, which requires honoring parents.
