When parents needed assistance, some claimed they had dedicated all their available resources to the temple, even though they had not actually given the resources away.
On that pretext they refused their parents help.
The tradition thus made God's command ineffective.
Jesus summed up the fate of hypocritical worship: they worship God in vain.
Such worship neither pleases God nor benefits the worshiper.
They trust in what is empty and receive emptiness in return.

div.title: The heart is the source of defilement (verses 10–20)
div.p: Jesus taught that what truly defiles is not food entering the mouth.
It is the sinful speech and conduct coming out of a corrupt heart.
Only the regenerating graces of the Holy Spirit remain forever in the soul.
Likewise, the church should admit nothing as its spiritual rule or foundation except what comes from above.
We need not be troubled simply because a clear and timely declaration of divine truth offends people.
The disciples asked Jesus to explain more fully.
An honestly willing heart seeks instruction when its understanding struggles with a word of Christ.
It is the heart that is deceitful and desperately wicked (Jeremiah 17:9).
No sinful word or deed appears outwardly before it has first arisen inwardly.
Sinful actions are fruit from this corrupt source.
When Christ teaches us, he exposes the deceit and wickedness within.
He humbles us and leads us to seek cleansing in the Fountain opened for sin and uncleanness.

div.title: The Syrophoenician mother's faith (verses 21–28)
div.p: Christ's saving influence reached even remote parts of the country, anticipating the day when the ends of the earth would see his salvation.
A mother's distress for her daughter drove her to Jesus.
Even when suffering is what first brings us to Christ, he does not reject us on that account.
She did not prescribe a particular form of relief.
Her whole request was mercy.
She claimed no merit and trusted entirely in his kindness.
Parents should pray earnestly for their children, especially concerning the salvation of their souls.
A son or daughter enslaved by pride, impurity, malice or some other sin is in a state even more dreadful than bodily demonic oppression.
Such children should be brought to Christ through faith and prayer, for he alone can heal them.
God's dealings with his people may at times appear dark and perplexing.
This event teaches that Christ may have love in his heart while his face appears to frown.
We may trust him even when he seems ready to destroy our hopes.
He sometimes humbles most deeply those whom he intends to honor most greatly.
A proud heart would have rebelled at the apparent rejection.
But this woman transformed it into a new reason to ask for mercy.
She pictures the sinner who knows the desperate need of the soul.
Even the smallest crumb from the Bread of Life is precious to one who believes.
Faith especially honors Christ; he therefore especially honors faith.
He spoke, and her daughter was healed.
Those who seek the Lord and receive no immediate answer should learn to turn their very unworthiness and discouragement into reasons for pleading for mercy rather than abandoning prayer.

div.title: Jesus heals many and feeds four thousand (verses 29–39)
div.p: Whatever troubles us, our best course is to lay it at Christ's feet, submit the matter to him and accept his decision.
Those seeking spiritual healing must be willing to be governed as he pleases.
Consider the harm sin has brought into the world and the many kinds of disease to which human bodies are exposed.
Some illnesses were beyond anyone's understanding or ability to heal, yet all were subject to Christ's command.
His spiritual cures are equally wonderful.
He makes spiritually blind people see through faith.
He opens speechless mouths in prayer.
He enables those spiritually lame or disabled to walk in holy obedience.
Jesus again demonstrated his power by providing enough food for a great crowd.
Everyone ate and was satisfied.

p.hi: Those whom Christ feeds, he fills.

div.p: There is more than sufficient bread with him, and more than enough grace for both those already seeking it and those who might yet come.
After feeding the people, he sent them home.
Though he had miraculously fed them twice, they were not to expect miracles instead of ordinary provision every day.
They needed to return to their callings and their own tables.
Lord, increase our faith and forgive our unbelief.
Teach us to depend upon your fullness and generosity in all that concerns this life and the life to come.

row.cell: The Pharisees and Sadducees ask a sign.
Jesus cautions against the doctrine of the Pharisees.
Peter's testimony that Jesus was the Christ.
Christ foretells his sufferings, and rebukes Peter.

div.title: The religious opponents demand a sign (verses 1–4)
div.p: The Pharisees and Sadducees differed in their beliefs and way of life.
Yet they united in opposing Jesus.
They wanted a miracle of their own choosing.
They disregarded the signs Christ had already given through his mercy toward the sick and suffering.
Instead they demanded some impressive display that would satisfy proud curiosity.
It is great hypocrisy to dismiss signs God himself has appointed while insisting that he give signs we have invented.

div.title: Jesus warns against corrupt teaching (verses 5–12)
div.p: Christ used a picture drawn from ordinary life to teach a spiritual truth.
The disciples misunderstood his words as a warning about literal bread.
Jesus was displeased that they imagined he was as anxious about food as they were and that they understood so little of his usual manner of teaching.
At last they recognized what he meant.
Christ teaches through the Spirit of wisdom working in the heart, enabling us to understand the revelation contained in the word.

div.title: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ (verses 13–20)
div.p: Speaking for himself and the other disciples, Peter declared that Jesus is the promised Messiah, the Son of the living God.
They believed he was more than a mere human being.
Jesus called Peter blessed because God had taught him what many of his unbelieving countrymen did not know.
Christ had given him the name Peter, recalling stability or firmness in confessing the truth.
Henry observes that the Greek word translated rock is not identical to the name Peter, though the two are related in meaning.
Henry explicitly rejects the interpretation that Peter's person is the foundation rock of the church.
Rather, Christ himself is the Rock, the tested foundation.
Peter's confession is the rock in respect of doctrine.
If Jesus is not truly the Christ, those claiming to belong to him are deceived and cannot be his church.
Jesus then declared the authority Peter would exercise.
Since Peter spoke for his fellow apostles, the authority also concerned them.
The apostles could misjudge people's inward characters and could sin in their personal conduct.

But they were kept from error in faithfully announcing the way of salvation and acceptance, the rule of Christian obedience, the believer's character and experience, and the final judgment of unbelievers and hypocrites.
In those matters their declarations were right and confirmed in heaven.
Henry strongly rejects any human claim to possess independent power to forgive sins or refuse forgiveness.

p.hi: God alone forgives sin.

div.p: In common Jewish speech, binding and loosing could mean forbidding and allowing, or declaring what conduct is lawful or unlawful.

div.title: Jesus predicts suffering and corrects Peter (verses 21–23)
div.p: Christ revealed his purposes to the disciples gradually.
Only after they confessed him clearly as the Son of God did he begin teaching them directly about his approaching sufferings.
This corrected their mistaken expectation of a kingdom characterized by worldly splendor and political power.
Those who follow Christ should not expect great worldly honors.
Peter wanted Jesus to fear suffering as Peter feared it.
We are wrong to measure Christ's love and endurance by our own limitations.
Jesus responded to Peter with unusually strong indignation.
Anyone who draws us away from something good or persuades us to fear doing too much for God speaks in the language of Satan.
Every temptation to sin must be resisted firmly, not entertained through negotiation.
Those who refuse suffering for Christ's sake are valuing human interests above God's interests.

div.title: The cross and the worth of the soul (verses 24–28)
div.p: A genuine disciple follows Christ in duty now and into glory hereafter.
Such a person walks in his path, is led by his Spirit and follows where Jesus goes.
Deny yourself. This is a difficult lesson, but our Lord both taught and practiced it in redeeming us.
Take up your cross. The cross represents the troubles God permits us to bear.
We often think another person's burden would be easier than our own.
But the task and trial appointed for us is the one we are called to bear faithfully.
We must not create suffering through our own recklessness or foolishness and then congratulate ourselves for carrying a cross.
Instead, when real suffering stands in the way of duty, we must accept it and follow Jesus.
Whoever wants the honor of being called a disciple must also perform a disciple's work and duties.
We readily understand that worldly possessions have little value compared with bodily life.
How much more do they fade in value compared with the eternal soul!
Thousands surrender their souls for trivial gains, momentary indulgence, or even simple laziness and neglect.
Whatever motivates someone to abandon Christ is, in effect, the price for which Satan buys that soul.
Yet one human soul is worth more than the entire world.
Jesus knows its worth because he redeemed souls.
He also knows the worth of the world because he created it.
A dying sinner cannot buy even one more hour in which to seek pardon.
Let us value our souls rightly and turn to Christ, their only Savior.

row.cell: Jesus casts out a dumb and deaf spirit.
He works a miracle to pay the tribute money.

div.title: Jesus is transfigured before his disciples (verses 1–13)
div.p: The disciples were permitted to see something of Christ's glory as the Father's only Son.
This would strengthen their faith when they later witnessed his crucifixion.
It also gave them a glimpse of the glory prepared for believers when Christ changes them and makes them like himself.
The apostles were overwhelmed by the sight.
Peter wanted to remain on the mountain rather than descend to face the suffering he had been so reluctant to hear about.
But he did not understand what he was asking.
We are mistaken when we expect heaven's enjoyment here on earth.
Whatever temporary dwelling places or comforts we propose to build in this world, we should seek Christ's direction.
The great sacrifice by which sinful human beings could be saved had not yet been offered.
Peter and the other disciples also had important work still to do.
A bright cloud overshadowed them as Peter spoke, representing God's presence and glory.
Ever since humanity sinned and heard God's voice in Eden, extraordinary displays of God's presence have caused sinful people to tremble.
The disciples fell to the ground.
Jesus comforted them, and when they looked up again they saw their familiar Lord.
Our way to glory includes many different experiences, both extraordinary and ordinary.
When we return to daily life after sacred worship or an unusually encouraging experience, we must take Christ with us.
Then we may find comfort knowing that he remains with us.

div.title: Jesus delivers a suffering child (verses 14–21)
div.p: Children's suffering should move us to present their needs to God in earnest and believing prayer.
Jesus healed the child.
Although the surrounding people were unbelieving and perverse and gave Christ reason for displeasure, the child was not neglected.
When every other form of help fails, we may still come to Christ and trust his power and goodness.
This healing also illustrates Jesus' saving work as Redeemer.
Parents should bring to him children whose souls are held captive through Satan's influence.
He is both able and willing to heal them.
Bring them not merely through personal prayer but also through Christ's word, the appointed means by which Satan's spiritual strongholds are broken down.
It is good to distrust our own power.
But it displeases Christ when we distrust power he has promised or supplied.
The child's condition presented unusual difficulty.
Satan's strength should not discourage our faith but should move us toward deeper prayer for stronger faith.
If we are astonished by bodily demonic oppression beginning in childhood, should we not also consider the spiritual bondage of fallen humanity ever since Adam's sin?

div.title: Jesus predicts his death and resurrection again (verses 22 and 23)
div.p: Christ knew perfectly everything he would suffer.
Yet he willingly undertook our redemption.
How great was his love!
His earthly life combined outward humiliation with divine glory.
His humiliation led finally to exaltation.
Let us learn to endure the cross, regard wealth and earthly status as insignificant beside Christ, and remain content with his will.

div.title: Jesus supplies the temple tax (verses 24–27)
div.p: Peter was confident that his Master would do what was right.
Jesus spoke before Peter could explain the situation, showing that no thought was hidden from him.
We must never neglect duty simply because obeying might offend someone.
But there are times when we should give up a legitimate personal advantage to avoid causing unnecessary offense.
Only the One who knows all things could know that the required coin was in the fish.
Only almighty power could bring the fish to Peter's hook.
We should remember Christ's power and his poverty together.
If Providence appoints poverty for us, as it did for our Lord, we may trust his power.
God will supply our true needs according to his glorious riches in Jesus Christ.
Peter received help while obeying, in the course of his ordinary occupation.
We too may expect divine help along the way of faithful work.
If an unexpected need arises for which we have no provision, let us seek Christ first rather than immediately depend on other people.

row.cell: Conduct towards brethren, The parable of the unmerciful servant.

div.title: Becoming humble like children (verses 1–6)
div.p: Jesus spoke often about his coming sufferings and only briefly about his glory.
Yet the disciples focused on glory and neglected the warnings about suffering.
Many people enjoy discussing religious privileges and honors but avoid thinking about duty and trouble.
Jesus placed a young child before them.
He solemnly taught that unless they were converted and became like children, they could not enter his kingdom.
Very young children do not normally seek authority or concern themselves with social distinctions.
They are generally free of deliberate malice, ready to be taught and willing to depend upon their parents.
Children soon begin displaying less admirable qualities, often encouraged by what others teach them.
Nevertheless, these traits of early childhood provide a fitting picture of true Christian lowliness.
We need our minds to be renewed every day so that we become simple, humble and willing to occupy the lowest place.
Let us examine ourselves carefully and frequently.

div.title: Avoiding sin and caring for the little ones (verses 7–14)
div.p: Given Satan's cunning and malice and humanity's sinful weakness, occasions of temptation and offense will arise.
God permits them for wise and holy purposes, including revealing who is sincere.
Jesus has warned us about seducers, tempters, persecutors and harmful examples.
We should remain alert.
As far as we lawfully can, we must give up anything we cannot keep without becoming entangled in sin.
Outward occasions of sin should be avoided.
Living according to sinful desires leads to death.
But putting the body's sinful practices to death through the Spirit leads to life.
Christ came to save souls.
He will judge severely those who obstruct the spiritual progress of people moving toward heaven.
Should we then refuse to care for people whom the Son of God came to seek and save?
An affectionate father cares for all his children but has a particular tenderness toward the smallest.
So should our care extend to the vulnerable and spiritually immature.

div.title: Correcting a brother or sister (verses 15–20)
div.p: When one professing Christian wrongs another, the injured person should not immediately spread the complaint among other people, especially when it rests on gossip.
Instead, go privately to the person responsible.
Describe the matter kindly and explain the offense.
With a genuine Christian, this would often bring reconciliation without further dispute.
The principles of Jesus' teaching can be followed in many different circumstances, yet Christians neglect them far too often.
How few try the very method Christ explicitly gave his disciples!
Throughout such dealings, pray for guidance.
Treasure God's promises.
When believers gather in Christ's name, whatever their number or location, they should recognize his presence among them.

div.title: Forgiving from the heart (verses 21–35)
div.p: Our entire life depends upon God's mercy and forgiveness, yet we are often reluctant to forgive people who offend us.
Jesus' parable reveals how greatly sin offends the Lord and how unreasonable his servants can be.
It has three principal movements.

p.hi: First, the master's extraordinary mercy.

div.p: The servant's debt pictures our sins, which we could never repay.
Being sold into slavery represents the judgment sin deserves.
A person under strong conviction of sin may foolishly imagine that enough personal effort could satisfy God's justice.
But we cannot make payment for our own guilt.

p.hi: Second, the servant's unreasonable cruelty toward his fellow servant.

div.p: Although his master had shown him enormous mercy, he treated another person with harshness.
This does not mean wrongdoing against a neighbor is insignificant.
Such wrongdoing also offends God.
Yet we must not exaggerate offenses committed against ourselves or dwell upon revenge.
Bring complaints about wicked actions and human suffering to God and leave them with him.

p.hi: Third, the master condemns the servant's cruelty.

div.p: The greatness of human sin displays the extraordinary riches of divine forgiveness.
A true understanding of being forgiven should incline us to forgive others.

p.hi: Henry explicitly rejects the idea that God genuinely pardons someone and afterward restores that forgiven person's guilt in order to condemn them.

div.p: The servant's final judgment instead warns against the false confidence of people who claim their sins are forgiven while their subsequent conduct shows they have not received the gospel's sanctifying grace.
Real forgiveness of others must come from the heart.
Even that is not all: we should actively seek the welfare of those who have harmed us.
People who persist in merciless behavior despite bearing the name Christian will rightly face condemnation.
The humbled sinner looks entirely to free, overflowing mercy obtained through Christ's death as our ransom.
Let us ask God for renewing grace so that we forgive others as we hope to be forgiven.

div.title: Jesus enters Judea and heals the crowds (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Large crowds followed Jesus.
Whenever Christ moves on, the best response is to follow him.
They discovered that he was just as willing and able to help them there as he had been in Galilee.
Wherever the Sun of Righteousness rises, he brings healing.

div.title: Jesus responds to questions about marriage and divorce (verses 3–12)
div.p: The Pharisees hoped to draw Jesus into saying something that could be portrayed as contrary to Moses' law.
Marriage disputes are numerous and can be confusing.
They become difficult not because God's law is defective but because human beings bring sinful desire and foolishness into them.
People often decide what they want to do before they even seek advice.
Jesus referred his listeners to the creation account and the first marriage.
He thereby showed that departing from God's original design is wrong.
In deciding about marriage or singleness, we should seek the condition that best serves our souls and helps prepare and preserve us for God's kingdom.
True acceptance of the gospel produces kindness within families and faithfulness in friendships.
It teaches people to carry one another's burdens and patiently bear one another's weaknesses.
It directs them to consider the peace and happiness of relatives and friends above their own convenience.
People who do not fear God still need lawful civil restraints so that society can live in peace.
Marriage should be undertaken with great seriousness and earnest prayer.

div.title: Jesus welcomes children (verses 13–15)
div.p: It is good for us to come to Christ, and also to bring our children to him.
Young children need his blessing and are capable of receiving good from him and sharing in his intercession.
We can only ask that blessing.
Christ alone can command and bestow it.
How fortunate that Jesus possesses even greater kindness and tenderness than his finest disciples!
Let us follow his example and never discourage anyone sincerely seeking him, even when that person is weak.
Those given to Christ as part of his redeemed people will never be cast away by him.
He is displeased when others try to exclude people whom he receives.
All Christians should bring their children to the Savior, asking for spiritual blessings for them.

div.title: The rich young man asks about eternal life (verses 16–22)
div.p: Jesus knew that love of riches was the particular sin most likely to rule the young man.
His possessions may have been acquired honestly.
Yet he could not willingly give them up when Christ called him to do so.
That exposed the weakness of his professed sincerity.
Christ's promises make his commands possible to bear and his yoke pleasant.
The promise to the young man tested his faith as much as the command tested his charity and willingness to leave the world.
Those following Christ must attend to his appointed ordinances, imitate his example and submit willingly to his direction.
This must be done from love for him and dependence upon him.
Simply selling everything and giving to poor people would not itself be enough.
What matters is following Jesus.
The gospel is the only remedy for lost sinners.
Many people abstain from openly scandalous behavior while neglecting their duty toward God.
Thousands of wrong thoughts, words and deeds remain recorded against them.
Many leave Christ because they love this present world.
They may experience conviction, sincere-sounding desires and deep sorrow, yet still turn away.
We must examine ourselves because the Lord will examine us.

div.title: Riches and the reward of discipleship (verses 23–30)
div.p: Few wealthy people are free from trusting their wealth.
Few poor people escape every temptation to envy.
Human striving for earthly gain can resemble building a high wall that shuts oneself and one's children out of heaven.
People of limited means can be thankful for not facing all the temptations of great power and prosperity.
Their circumstances may be harder here, but if they enter the better world more readily, they have no reason to complain.
Jesus taught that wealth makes the Christian path especially difficult.
The gate is narrow for everyone, but in particular for the rich.
More is expected from those with greater opportunities.
They face many temptations to sin and find a prosperous world very attractive.
They must answer to God for the use of their advantages.
A person whose heart belongs completely to wealth cannot enter heaven while remaining enslaved to it.
Jesus described something impossible by merely human power.
Only the almighty grace of God can overcome this obstacle.
Who, then, can be saved?
Poverty has its own dangers. Pride and sinful desires also threaten people without riches.

p.hi: No one can save himself through created power.

div.p: The beginning, growth and completion of salvation depend entirely upon God's almighty grace.
Rich people are saved from their worldliness, not while remaining worldly.
Peter said, “We have left everything.”
What they left amounted outwardly to a few boats and fishing nets.
We tend to exaggerate our sacrifices and services for Christ.
Yet Jesus did not rebuke them.
Their possessions were few, but they were all they had, precious to them as greater wealth would be to someone else.
He graciously accepted their willingness to leave everything and follow.
Jesus promised the apostles a special dignity in the coming renewal, when the Son of Man sits upon his throne of glory.
They would share in judgment concerning people judged by the doctrine they faithfully declared.
This displays their office's honor and authority.
Everyone who gives up possessions or earthly comforts for Christ and the gospel will also receive a final reward.
May God give us faith to rely on his promise, making us willing for every service or sacrifice.
Jesus' final warning corrects another mistake.
The heavenly inheritance is not distributed like earthly inheritances, according to outward position or expectation.
It follows God's pleasure.
Do not trust outward profession or an appearance of future greatness.
Others who seem unlikely now may yet become distinguished in faith and holiness.

row.cell: The parable of the labourers in the vineyard.
The ambition of James and John.
Jesus gives sight to two blind men near Jericho.

div.title: Workers in the vineyard (verses 1–16)
div.p: The parable's first purpose appears to be showing how the Gentiles would be called after the Jews and receive equal privileges in God's kingdom.
It also teaches broader lessons.

p.hi: First, God owes no one a debt.

div.p: Second, some people who begin late and seem unpromising may, by God's blessing, grow into great knowledge, holiness and usefulness.
Third, the final reward of the saints is not measured by how long ago they were converted.
The parable describes the visible church and explains different ways in which the last become first and the first last.
Until God calls us to his work, we remain idle all day.
A sinful life is actually hard service to Satan, yet it is idleness with respect to God.
The marketplace represents the world, from which the gospel summons us.
Come away from the marketplace and serve God.
His work does not allow carelessness.
A person may drift into destruction through idleness, but the path to heaven requires diligence.

The Roman denarius, the coin paid for the day's work, is explained by Henry using a value in the currency of his own time (seven and a half old English pence), as sufficient wages then for a day's support; that historical comparison is not a modern wage conversion.
This reward does not mean obedience creates a debt God must pay.
After all our service, we are still unprofitable servants.
Nevertheless, God sets an actual reward before his people.
The eleventh-hour call is no excuse to postpone repentance until old age.
The late workers had not earlier received an offer of work.
Similarly, the Gentiles were called when the gospel first reached them.
Those who have already heard repeated gospel invitations and refused them will not be able to claim later that no one called them.
Do not be discouraged, but do not delay.
Now is the accepted time.
Proud Pharisees and merely nominal Christians often complain when God's grace is generous to others.
We tend to imagine that God has favored others too much and us too little, or that we have worked far harder than others.
But God's kindness to another person is no injustice to us.
Worldly people choose their payment in this present life.
Believers must remember that they seek heaven as their inheritance.
Why then should they expect ultimate satisfaction from earthly goods?
God punishes no one beyond what is deserved and never neglects faithful service.
By showing extraordinary grace to some, he wrongs no one.
Envy is an evil eye: resenting someone else's happiness and desiring harm for them.
It pains the envious person, displeases God and hurts neighbors.
It brings neither real pleasure, profit nor honor.
Let us abandon claims of merit and seek salvation as a free gift.
Rather than begrudging divine mercy, rejoice when God shows it to others.

div.title: Jesus predicts his suffering and resurrection (verses 17–19)
div.p: Jesus now spoke even more specifically about his approaching suffering.
As before, he also promised his resurrection and glory, encouraging and comforting the disciples.
Seeing by faith the Savior who was once crucified and is now glorified humbles proud and self-justifying hearts.
When we recognize that the Son of God needed to be humbled and suffer for the salvation of sinners, we understand more clearly the freedom and abundance of grace.

div.title: Jesus answers the ambition of James and John (verses 20–28)
div.p: The sons of Zebedee misused Christ's promise of future comfort as an opportunity for personal ambition.
Some people take even spiritual encouragement and turn it toward selfish purposes.
Pride easily besets us.
Seeking to surpass others in rank and splendor is sinful ambition.
Jesus corrected their request by speaking of the suffering his followers would endure.
Their cup could be bitter and cause trembling, yet it was not the cup of God's wrath against the wicked.
It was a cup held by their Father (John 18:11).
Suffering may be severe but it is temporary—a cup that will eventually be emptied.
Henry likens suffering for Christ to baptism, which signifies joining the Lord in covenant and fellowship.
He describes baptism as an outward and visible sign of inward and spiritual grace, and sees sufferings in Christ's service as signs of that grace too (Ezekiel 20:37; Isaiah 48:10; Philippians 1:29).
James and John did not yet understand the full meaning of Christ's cup or baptism.
Often those who speak most confidently know least about the cross.
Ambition causes profound damage among brothers and sisters.
Wherever the disciples quarreled, the desire for greatness lay beneath it.
The one who serves most diligently, suffers most patiently, seeks the good of fellow believers and labors for the salvation of souls resembles Christ most closely.
Such a servant will receive the greatest honor from Christ in eternity.
Jesus described his own death using the language of Old Testament sacrifices.
His sacrifice for human sin is the true and substantial offering, of which the legal sacrifices were only faint and incomplete pictures.
He gave his life as a ransom for many: a sacrifice sufficient for all, effective in many.
A trembling believer may therefore ask, “Why not for me?”

div.title: Jesus restores sight to two blind men (verses 29–34)
div.p: People sharing the same illness or trial do well to pray together, encouraging one another.
Christ has mercy enough for everyone who asks him.
The blind men prayed earnestly. They cried as people who genuinely desired help.
Cold, indifferent desires are unlikely to obtain what is needed.
They prayed humbly, placing themselves in the hands of the merciful Mediator.
They prayed with faith, acknowledging Jesus as Lord.
Henry attributes this confession to the Holy Spirit.
They also persevered, refusing to fall silent when others discouraged them.
Jesus received and encouraged them.
We usually recognize bodily suffering quickly and can explain it readily.
If only we recognized spiritual sickness and blindness with the same urgency!
Many spiritually blind people insist they can see.
Jesus gave the men sight, and then they followed him.
No one follows Christ blindly in the spiritual sense. First he opens the eyes through his grace; then the heart is drawn to him.
These miracles summon us to come to Jesus.
May our daily prayer be to grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

row.cell: He drives out those who profaned the temple.
The parable of the two sons.
The parable of the wicked husbandmen.

div.title: Jesus enters Jerusalem (verses 1–11)
div.p: The prophet Zechariah foretold Christ's coming as king (Zechariah 9:9).
When Jesus displayed royal glory, he did so through humility and gentleness, bringing salvation through mercy rather than earthly splendor.
The poverty and meekness of Zion's King show how unsuitable greed, ambition and pride are in those who belong to his kingdom.
The disciples obtained the donkey, but Jesus did not use it without its owner's agreement.
The equipment for his ride was whatever could be provided.
We should not consider even the clothing we wear too valuable to be offered for Christ's service.
The religious rulers who later joined the crowd mocking Jesus on the cross had not joined the crowd honoring him at his entrance.
Those who truly accept Christ as king must be ready to lay everything at his feet.
Hosanna means Save now, we pray!
How little lasting value the applause of a crowd may have!
The same people can shout Hosanna one day and Crucify him another.
Many outwardly welcome the gospel without becoming steadfast disciples.
The whole city was stirred by Jesus' arrival.
Some who awaited Israel's consolation may have rejoiced.
Others, including Pharisees, were moved by envy.
Christ's kingdom produces very different responses in human hearts.

div.title: Jesus cleanses the temple (verses 12–17)
div.p: Parts of the temple courts had become a market for animals and materials used for sacrifices, and a place for money-changing.
Christ expelled those responsible, as he had done earlier in his ministry (John 2:13–17).
His works witnessed to his true identity even more powerfully than the cries of Hosanna.
His healings in the temple fulfilled the promise that the glory of the later house would exceed that of the earlier one.
If Jesus examined the visible church today, how many hidden wrongs would he discover and cleanse?
How many things are performed under the appearance of religion that belong more properly to a den of thieves than to a house of prayer?

div.title: Jesus curses the fruitless fig tree (verses 18–22)
div.p: The barren fig tree represents hypocrites in general.
Christ seeks the reality and power of faith where he sees outward profession.
Many appear spiritually flourishing but bear leaves without fruit.
Empty profession frequently withers even in this life under Christ's judgment.
The fig tree lost its leaves because it had produced no fruit.
Henry also applies this warning to the Jewish nation of Jesus' day, interpreting its rejection of Christ, growing hardness and eventual national ruin through the fig tree.
The Lord is just in his judgments.
Let us fear becoming people who look spiritually alive while remaining fruitless.

div.title: Jesus answers those challenging his authority (verses 23–27)
div.p: Jesus now appeared publicly as Messiah.
The chief priests and scribes were especially angry because he exposed abuses they had allowed or encouraged.
He questioned them about John's ministry and baptism.
Many people fear being exposed as liars more than they fear actually lying.
They therefore say things contrary to their true thoughts or intentions, or pretend to remember and forget what suits their purpose.
Jesus declined to answer opponents determined to use any reply against him.
It is often best to avoid pointless disputes with malicious opponents.

div.title: The two sons (verses 28–32)
div.p: Parables of rebuke invite offenders to judge their own conduct by their own answers.

The two sons illustrate the contrast between people who gave an outward appearance of obedience but rejected John's mission, and people who initially resisted yet afterward acknowledged its authority and responded.
All humanity resembles children whom the Lord has raised and who have rebelled against him.
Some appear more polite and respectable in their disobedience than others.
Often an openly defiant sinner is brought to repentance and becomes God's servant, while a religious formalist becomes harder in pride and hostility.

div.title: The wicked tenants of the vineyard (verses 33–46)
div.p: The parable exposes the sin and ruin of the Jewish leaders and nation in the narrative.
Its warning also applies to everyone who possesses the outward church's privileges.
People who mistreat God's servants reveal how they would treat Christ himself.
Those faithful to his cause should not expect an entirely favorable reception from a wicked world or from merely nominal Christians.
We should ask whether, as congregations, families and individuals, we yield the fruit that ought to follow the spiritual advantages God has given us.
The owner of the vineyard will come and judge wicked tenants.
The religious leaders were builders who rejected the stone God had chosen.
They rejected Christ's teaching and laws and treated him as worthless.
Henry applies the rejected stone's acceptance to Gentiles who embraced the Savior.
Christ knows who will produce gospel fruit through the means of grace.
Unbelief destroys sinners.
But God can restrain human anger and turn even its outbreaks toward his praise.
May Christ grow increasingly precious to us as the secure Foundation and Cornerstone of the church.
May we willingly follow him even when despised and hated for his sake.

row.cell: The parable of the marriage feast.
The Pharisees question Jesus as to the tribute.
The question of the Sadducees as to the resurrection.

div.title: The king's wedding feast (verses 1–14)
div.p: Jesus pictured God's provision for perishing souls as a royal feast celebrating the marriage of a king's son.
Our merciful God provides not merely basic food but an abundant banquet for rebellious creatures.
In the salvation given through Jesus Christ there is everything needed for present comfort and eternal happiness.
The first guests invited were the Jews.
The prophets, John the Baptist and Christ himself announced the coming kingdom.
After Jesus rose from the dead, the apostles and other gospel ministers were sent to proclaim that it had arrived and to invite people to receive salvation.
The reason sinners refuse Christ is not a lack of ability for which they are innocent, but their unwillingness to come.
Treating the Savior and his great salvation lightly is a deadly sin.
Many perish not through open hatred but through carelessness about their souls.
Farmers and merchants should attend diligently to their work.
But people occupied with worldly business and profit must keep the world in their hands without letting it rule their hearts.
The parable includes a warning of the destruction coming upon the Jewish nation and its religious institutions in Henry's reading.
Persecution of the gospel's faithful messengers completes the guilt of a people.
The unexpected invitation to Gentiles was like travelers suddenly being invited to a royal banquet.
The gospel gathers souls to Christ from across the world (John 10:16; 11:52).
The guest without a wedding garment represents hypocrisy.
Everyone should prepare to be examined by the King.
The garment belongs only to those who put on the Lord Jesus, have a Christ-shaped heart, live through faith in him and regard him as everything.
Christ's imputed righteousness and the Spirit's sanctification are both necessary.
No person possesses this garment by nature or can produce it through personal strength.
A day is coming when false professors will be judged for presumptuously claiming Christian privileges without genuine faith.
Such people use even the light of the gospel to descend into darkness.
Many are called, but fewer possess the garment of Christ's righteousness and the Spirit's holiness.
Let us examine whether we are in the faith and seek the King's approval.

div.title: Paying taxes to Caesar (verses 15–22)
div.p: The Pharisees sent disciples to join with the Herodians, who favored submission to the Roman emperor.
Though the groups held opposed political views, they cooperated against Jesus.
Their words about Christ's integrity as a teacher were true, even though their motives were false.
He is indeed a faithful Teacher and bold corrector.
Jesus perceived their hypocrisy.
No disguise can hide a person's heart from him.
He did not take the role of civil judge in their dispute, since his kingdom is not of this world.
He taught peaceful submission to lawful governing authority.
The Christian faith is not an enemy of civil government.
Jesus astonished his opponents, who admired his wisdom without following its teaching and recognized his power without submitting to it.

div.title: Jesus answers the Sadducees about resurrection (verses 23–33)
div.p: The Sadducees opposed Jesus' teaching no less than the Pharisees and Herodians.
Christ explained resurrection and the future state more fully than these truths had previously been revealed.
We cannot simply infer the condition of the life to come from the patterns of this present world.
When truth is displayed clearly, it has great power.
Jesus then demonstrated resurrection teaching from Moses' writings.
God declared himself the God of patriarchs who had already died.
Their continuing relation to him showed that they still existed and could enjoy his favor.
The Old Testament therefore taught resurrection as well as the New Testament, although it would be revealed more fully after Christ himself rose as the firstfruits of those who sleep.
Errors arise from ignorance of Scripture and God's power.
Death brings an end to our earthly connections, joys, griefs and expectations.
How miserable are those who hope for nothing better beyond it!

div.title: The greatest commandments (verses 34–40)
div.p: An expert in the law questioned Jesus to test his judgment rather than merely his factual knowledge.
Love for God is the first and greatest commandment and summarizes the commands concerning our duty toward him.
Such love must be sincere, not merely spoken.
All the love we can offer is too small for his worth; therefore all our mind, affections and abilities should be directed toward him.
Love for our neighbor as ourselves is the second great commandment.
There is a corrupt form of self-love that causes serious sin and must be resisted and put to death.
But there is also a proper concern for the well-being of our bodies and souls.
That rightful concern becomes the measure of our duty to others.
We should sincerely seek our neighbors' welfare as we seek our own and often deny ourselves for their good.
Let these two commandments shape our hearts like a mold.

div.title: How can David's son be David's Lord? (verses 41–46)
div.p: After silencing his opponents, Jesus asked about the identity of the promised Messiah.
How could the Messiah be David's descendant and yet David's Lord?
He quoted Psalm 110:1.
If Christ were only a human being born centuries after David died, why would David call his descendant Lord?
The Pharisees could not answer.
Henry maintains that the answer requires acknowledging that the Messiah is the Son of God, truly David's Lord along with the Father.
He took on human nature and thus became God manifested in flesh, the Son of Man and the Son of David.
Above all other questions we should seriously ask, What do I think of Christ?
Is he glorious to our eyes and precious to our hearts?
May he become our joy, confidence and everything.
May we grow daily in his likeness and service.

row.cell: Jesus reproves the scribes and Pharisees.

div.title: Jesus rebukes religious pride (verses 1–12)
div.p: The scribes and Pharisees taught Moses' law and required obedience to it.
But Jesus charged them with religious hypocrisy.
We can judge only what we see outwardly; God examines the heart.
The Pharisees broadened their phylacteries—small cases or scrolls containing four passages from the law, worn upon the forehead and left arm.
Henry identifies the passages as Exodus 13:2–10; 13:11–16; Deuteronomy 6:4–9; 11:13–21.
Making the cases larger was intended to suggest greater devotion than that of other people.
God had instructed Israel to wear fringes on their clothing as reminders of being his distinct people (Numbers 15:38).
The Pharisees enlarged those fringes to appear more religious.
Pride was the sin they cherished most, and Jesus regularly opposed it.
It is right for learners to respect faithful teachers of God's word.
It is wrong for teachers to demand honors and become proud when they receive them.
Christ's genuine disciples are uncomfortable with being placed above everyone else.
Such pride contradicts Christianity's spirit.
Yet when we look around the visible church, can we say this humble attitude is universal?
Henry warns that something of this anti-Christian pride appears in every religious community and in our own hearts.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): Deuteronomy 9:13–21.
Verified editorial cross-reference: Deut.11.13-Deut.11.21.
Verified editorial cross-reference: Exod.13.2-Exod.13.10; Exod.13.11-Exod.13.16; Deut.6.4-Deut.6.9; Deut.11.13-Deut.11.21.

div.title: Jesus exposes the Pharisees' sins (verses 13–33)
div.p: The scribes and Pharisees opposed Christ's gospel and thereby hindered the salvation of souls.
Refusing Christ ourselves is terrible.
Preventing others from coming to him is still worse.
An outward display of devotion can conceal enormous wickedness.
Pretended piety will be judged as doubled guilt.
The Pharisees diligently sought converts to their own party, pursuing personal honor and advantage rather than God's glory or the good of souls.
They repeatedly made religious duties give way to their worldly profit.
They were exacting about smaller aspects of the law while neglecting its weightier duties.
Jesus did not condemn their care to avoid even small sins.
If swallowing a gnat is wrong, it is right to strain it out.
He condemned their inconsistency in meticulously avoiding the gnat while swallowing a camel, committing far greater wrongs.
Though they appeared devout, they lacked true sobriety and righteousness.
Our true condition is what we are inside.
Outward incentives may make a person's public conduct respectable while the inward life remains corrupt.
But when the heart and spirit are renewed, a renewed life follows.
We must therefore begin our reform with ourselves.
The Pharisees' righteousness resembled the decorations of a grave, or clothing placed upon a lifeless body.
It was only display.
Sinners deceive themselves by following the sins popular in their own generation while imagining they would have courageously opposed the sins of earlier generations.
We may claim that, if we had lived when Jesus was on earth, we would never have rejected him.
Yet Christ, through his Spirit, word and ministers, may still receive contempt from us today.
God is just when he allows persistently rebellious people to follow their own chosen desires and experience their consequences.
Jesus reveals the real character of those who oppose him.

div.title: Jesus mourns over Jerusalem (verses 34–39)
div.p: Jesus announced the misery Jerusalem's inhabitants would bring upon themselves.
He did not dwell here upon his own approaching sufferings.
The picture of a hen gathering her chicks beneath her wings illustrates Christ's tender love and faithful care for all who trust in him.
He calls sinners into that shelter, protects them and nourishes them toward eternal life.
Henry understands Jesus' words as foretelling both the dispersion and unbelief of Jewish people and their future conversion to Christ.
That is the commentator's prophetic interpretation and must not be represented as an unqualified factual claim about all Jews.
Jerusalem's guilt and its subsequent suffering were serious.
Yet merely nominal Christian churches should also fear judgment when their members refuse genuine faith.
Even now, the Savior remains willing to receive all who come to him.
It is the proud and unbelieving unwillingness of sinners, not lack of mercy in Christ, that keeps them from eternal happiness.

row.cell: Christ foretells the destruction of the temple.
The troubles before the destruction of Jerusalem.
Christ foretells other signs and miseries, to the end of the world.

div.title: Jesus foretells the temple's destruction (verses 1–3)
div.p: Jesus predicted the complete destruction of the temple.
Remembering that even the greatest earthly beauty and splendor will decay helps us avoid valuing them too highly.
The most beautiful human body will become food for worms.
The most magnificent building will eventually become ruins.
Jesus asked whether the disciples saw all these things.
We should look at worldly things in such a way that we see through them to their inevitable end.
On the Mount of Olives he began explaining events concerning Jerusalem's destruction and, beyond that, matters reaching toward the end of the world.

div.title: Warnings before Jerusalem's destruction (verses 4–28)
div.p: The disciples asked when these things would happen and what signs would precede them.
Jesus did not give a straightforward answer to the timing question.
He responded extensively to the request for signs.
Henry reads the prophecy as first concerning near events: Jerusalem's destruction, the ending of the old Jewish religious order and state, the calling of Gentiles and the gospel kingdom's spread.
The prediction also looks ahead toward the general judgment, more specifically as its conclusion approaches.
Christ's teaching was intended more to make disciples watchful than to satisfy curiosity.
It prepared them to respond wisely instead of providing an exhaustive schedule of events.
That is the kind of understanding of the times God's people should desire.
Jesus warned against false teachers, wars and upheaval among nations.
Henry regards the wars that followed rejection of Christ as a warning about refusing the gospel's offer of peace.
Those who will not hear messengers of peace may instead hear the noise of war.
Nevertheless, a heart fixed upon God can remain peaceful during public disorder.
It is contrary to Christ's desire that his disciples live continually overwhelmed by fear.
If earthly judgment is terrible, eternal judgment for those who persistently reject the Savior is far worse.
The greatest earthly troubles are only a beginning of sorrows by comparison.
Jesus also promised that some would endure faithfully to the end.
The gospel would be preached throughout the world, accomplishing its appointed purpose before the end.
Christ foretold dangers that would accompany Jerusalem's fall.
The warning would guide and comfort his disciples.
If God opens a way of escape, they should use it.
Refusing ordinary measures of safety would be testing God, not trusting him.
During public distress, prayer is especially appropriate, though it is always in season.
We may submit to whatever God sends while still praying that suffering may be prevented or lessened.
It is particularly difficult when emergencies prevent believers from enjoying worship and Sabbath rest.
Jesus promised that, for the sake of the elect, the days of calamity would be shortened.
God may use enemies to accomplish his purposes but still limit their destructive intentions.
The gospel's spread is compared to lightning: powerful and visible rather than a hidden, local secret.
Henry also understands the eagle imagery in relation to Roman armies and their eagle standards, seeing judgment against a corrupt nation.
He further says these warnings apply to Christ's final judgment (2 Thessalonians 2:1).
We should therefore make our calling and election sure and refuse to be deceived by false claims.

div.title: Jesus foretells his second coming (verses 29–41)
div.p: The prophets sometimes described future events as near in order to emphasize their certainty and importance.
Jesus announced his own return and the extraordinary change that will make all things new.
At his first coming he was rejected and opposed.
At his second he will be seen in glory.
Sooner or later every sinner will mourn.
Repentant sinners mourn now over their sins as they look to Christ and eventually reap joy.
Those refusing repentance will see the One they pierced and mourn in despair.
God's elect are scattered through many nations and places.
On the day they are gathered, not one will be missing, nor will distance prevent any from entering heaven.
Henry interprets Jesus' words about “this generation” (verse 34) as affirming that the Jewish people would continue to exist as a distinct people through history until the final judgment.
That interpretation is recorded as Henry's eschatological reading, not as an established conclusion about the verse's meaning.
People plan confidently for generations of earthly success without preparing for the certain and overwhelming event of Christ's return.
That day will overthrow every human plan opposed to God.
It will be unexpected, as the Flood was to people in Noah's time.
These warnings apply first to temporal judgments—particularly Jerusalem's imminent judgment—and second to the final judgment.
Before the Flood people continued their daily activities in careless confidence.
They did not understand, nor did they believe, until judgment came.
If we recognized how soon earthly possessions and comforts will disappear, we would cling to them far less.
Delaying thought of judgment does not delay judgment itself.
The coming of Christ will be sudden.
Men and women will be engaged in ordinary work.
Then everything else will be forgotten, and the question will become urgent: Am I prepared to meet the Lord?
The final judgment's significance for the whole world resembles the significance of death for each individual.

div.title: Jesus commands watchfulness (verses 42–51)
div.p: Watching for Christ's coming means maintaining the attitude and conduct we would willingly let our Master find us practicing.
We know our lives on earth are short.
We do not know that we will live a long time, much less when the final judgment will arrive.
His coming will be joyful for those prepared and dreadful for those unprepared.
Someone may claim to be Christ's servant while remaining unbelieving, greedy, ambitious or devoted to pleasure.
Such a person cannot expect acceptance merely from an outward profession.
Those who choose the world as their ultimate portion here face final loss in the world to come.
May our Lord find us ready.
May he declare us blessed and present us to the Father washed in Christ's blood, purified by his Spirit and prepared for the inheritance of the saints in light.

row.cell: The parable of the ten virgins.

div.title: The wise and foolish bridesmaids (verses 1–13)
div.p: The parable draws on Jewish marriage customs to teach about the great day of Christ's coming.
Christians profess to attend to him, honor him and wait for his arrival.
The wise virgins represent genuine believers and the foolish ones represent hypocrites.
The most important kind of wisdom or folly concerns the condition of our souls.
Many people carry a lamp of outward religious profession without possessing sound spiritual knowledge or lasting conviction.
They lack the inward dispositions that God's renewing Spirit creates.
Good works should shine visibly before others.
But they will not shine for long without a settled, living principle of faith in Christ and love for God and neighbors.
All ten fell asleep.
The delay pictures the interval between a person's real or apparent conversion and Christ's coming, whether through that person's death or through the final judgment.
Christ may arrive later than our expectations, but never later than the appointed time.
Even the wise virgins kept their lamps alight while failing to remain awake.
Genuine Christians may grow careless.
One degree of neglect can lead to another; those who become drowsy are in danger of falling asleep.
Fear the first signs of spiritual decline.
A sudden call came to meet the bridegroom.
Even those best prepared for death should be diligent in actually preparing for it (2 Peter 3:14).
The day will expose the truth of everyone's condition.
The foolish virgins discovered they lacked oil.
Those who settle for outward religion without true grace will discover their lack sooner or later.
A religious profession may seem sufficient during ordinary life but fail in the shadow of death.
Some want to die the death of the righteous without having lived a righteous life.
No believer can transfer saving grace to another person.
Even those possessing the most grace have none to spare; the strongest still need more from Christ.
A soul that has neglected salvation may be overwhelmed with fear on a deathbed.
The person then tries to obtain the grace that should already have been received and exercised.
Death and judgment may arrive before that person turns sincerely to Christ.
Only those prepared for heaven while living will enter it afterward.
Sudden death need not rob genuinely prepared believers of their happiness.
But the door will eventually be closed.
Hypocritical confidence may survive many warnings yet fail when admission is finally denied.
An unexpected summons may startle a true Christian, whose faith can then shine brighter.
It exposes the empty light of the mere professor.

p.hi: Watch over your soul and live in reverent dependence upon the Lord every day.

div.title: The servants and the talents (verses 14–30)
div.p: Christ does not employ servants merely to remain idle.
Everything they receive belongs to him.
Strictly speaking, nothing is theirs independently except their sin.
The gifts Christ gives are meant to be used in his service.
The Spirit's gifts are given for the benefit of others.
A day of accountability is coming.
We must answer for what we have gained spiritually ourselves and how we have served others through our opportunities and advantages.
This does not mean that improving natural abilities earns divine grace.
Rather, it is a Christian's privilege and freedom to serve the Redeemer, advance his glory and benefit his people.
Christ's love moves believers to stop living for themselves and begin living for the One who died and rose for them.
People who believe God cannot be pleased and service to him is pointless rarely accomplish anything useful for his kingdom.
They complain that God demands more than they are able to perform and condemns them for what they cannot help.
Whatever their excuses, such people reveal dislike of the Lord's character and work.
The lazy servant lost what he had been entrusted with.
This may apply to temporal gifts, but even more clearly to opportunities and means of grace.
Those who fail to recognize God's visitation can lose opportunities that would have led them to peace.
The sentence of outer darkness expresses the misery of final judgment.
Here Jesus moves beyond the story's illustration to the actual judgment it signifies.
Let us neither envy unrepentant sinners nor covet their perishing possessions.

div.title: The final judgment of the nations (verses 31–46)
div.p: Jesus described the judgment that will separate people into eternal happiness or misery.
Christ will return in his own glory as Mediator, as well as the Father's glory.
In this world righteous and wicked people share towns, churches and families.
The failures of some believers and the hypocrisy of some unbelievers often make them difficult to distinguish.
Death comes to both.
But on the great day the Shepherd will separate his own people from those who do not belong to him.
All worldly distinctions will disappear, but the distinction between holy and unholy, righteous and wicked, will remain forever.
God's people will inherit a kingdom.
Even the most glorious earthly kingdom offers only a faint comparison with their heavenly happiness.
The kingdom has been prepared.
The Father provided it in wisdom and power.
The Son purchased it.
The Spirit prepares believers to enjoy it, transforming them for the holiness of their inheritance.
It was prepared from the foundation of the world.
The saints were chosen for this happiness, and the happiness prepared for them, from eternity.
They inherit the kingdom.
An inheritance is not wages earned through personal labor.
God makes people heirs of heaven.
Jesus does not teach that charitable acts purchase eternal life.
Rather, works performed for his sake, through him, identify believers whose lives have been renewed by his Spirit.
They are effects and evidence of grace.
Those condemned had repeatedly been invited to come to Christ for life and rest, but refused.
They are justly told to depart from the One they would not approach.
Their excuses cannot reverse the judgment.
Final punishment is everlasting and cannot be changed afterward.
Life and death, blessing and curse are placed before us.
Our chosen path matters because it leads toward our final condition.

div.title: The leaders plot against Jesus (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jesus had often announced his suffering as an event still in the future.
Now he spoke of it as immediately approaching.
At the same time, the religious council plotted to put him to death secretly.
But God overruled their intentions.
Jesus, the true Passover Lamb, was to be sacrificed at that very season.
His death and resurrection were to become public events, not a secret execution hidden from the world.

div.title: Jesus is anointed at Bethany (verses 6–13)
div.p: Pouring costly perfume upon Christ's head expressed the highest honor.
Where the heart genuinely loves him, nothing seems too precious to offer him.
The more his servants and their acts of devotion are criticized, the more clearly he may reveal his acceptance of them.
Mary's loving act was so remarkable that it would be remembered wherever the gospel was preached.
Jesus' promise concerning the continuing memorial of her faith and love has been fulfilled.

div.title: Judas agrees to betray Jesus (verses 14–16)
div.p: Only twelve men were called apostles, yet one was inwardly like a devil.
We must therefore not expect any earthly religious community to be completely free from hypocrisy.
The greater a person's religious reputation, the more damage that person can cause when the heart is not right before God.
Judas knew Jesus' doctrine and life intimately.
Despite betraying him, he could not accuse Jesus of any real wrongdoing, even though such an accusation might have helped excuse his treachery.
What did Judas lack?
He had shared Christ's hospitality and lived alongside his Master.
Not lack of money but love of money lay at the root of his sin.
After arranging the betrayal, he still had time to repent and withdraw.
But lesser dishonest acts can gradually harden the conscience until worse crimes are committed without hesitation.

div.title: Jesus celebrates the Passover (verses 17–25)
div.p: Jesus directed the disciples to the place where the Passover should be prepared.
He knows the often-hidden people who are willing to welcome and support his cause.
He graciously visits those ready to receive him.
The disciples obeyed his instructions.
Those who desire Christ's presence in the gospel's Passover must also submit to his commands.
Christians should remain alert to their own weakness, especially in times of testing.
We cannot know how strongly we may be tempted or how far God may allow us to experience our own weakness.
We should therefore avoid pride and cultivate reverent self-examination.
Before the Lord's Supper it is particularly fitting to search our hearts and pray earnestly.
Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us.
We should therefore celebrate the feast with renewed repentance, faith in his blood and dedication to his service.

div.title: Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper (verses 26–30)
div.p: The Lord's Supper is the Christian counterpart to the Passover.
It commemorates a deliverance far greater than Israel's rescue from Egypt.
Take and eat means receiving Christ as he is offered, welcoming his atoning work and submitting to his grace and rule.
Even an excellent meal provides no nourishment if merely admired; it must be eaten.
So the teaching and benefits of Christ must be received personally by faith.
Henry explicitly interprets “This is my body” spiritually: the bread signifies and represents Christ's body.
We share in the sun's warmth not by placing the sun itself in our hands but by receiving its rays.
Likewise, we share in Christ by receiving his grace and the benefits of his broken body.
The wine signifies and represents his blood.
Jesus gave thanks, teaching us to acknowledge God throughout the ordinance.
He gave the cup to the disciples with the command to drink from it, all of them.
The forgiveness of sin is the great benefit conveyed to true believers in the Lord's Supper, forming the foundation for every other blessing.
Jesus then anticipated the future joy of renewed fellowship in his Father's kingdom.
Henry understands drinking anew with them as picturing the happiness and glory believers will share with Christ forever.
That consolation will always be new.
When we look upon the outward signs of Christ's body broken and his blood shed for the forgiveness of sins, let us remember the terrible cost.
The supper cost Jesus as much as if he had literally given his flesh to be eaten and his blood to be drunk.

div.title: Jesus warns of the disciples' failure (verses 31–35)
div.p: Peter's excessive confidence was the beginning of his fall.
We all tend to think too highly of our own firmness.
Those who feel most secure are often least watchful and therefore fall most quickly and terribly.
Satan actively exploits such carelessness.
God sometimes allows self-confident people to discover their weakness so that they may become humble.

div.title: Jesus suffers in Gethsemane (verses 36–46)
div.p: Humanity rebelled against God's will in a garden of pleasure.
Christ, who came to atone for humanity's sin, submitted to God's will in a garden of suffering.
Jesus took into the place of his agony the disciples who had witnessed his glory at the Transfiguration.
Those who have seen his glory through faith are best prepared to suffer with him.
Scripture describes his overwhelming anguish, sorrow, astonishment and terror.
He began suffering this particular depth of sorrow and continued until he cried, “It is finished.”
He asked whether the cup could pass from him, yet declared perfect willingness to submit to everything necessary for our redemption.
Following his example, believers must accept even the bitterest cup their Father assigns.
Nature may shrink back, but faith should submit.
Our deeper concern should be that suffering sanctifies us and that our hearts remain satisfied in God, rather than simply that every trial be removed.
It is well for us that salvation rests with the One who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
Everyone is tempted.
We should especially fear entering into temptation and being overcome by it.
Watch and pray, depending on the Lord to uphold us.
Jesus knew clearly what suffering awaited him.
Until this point he had usually spoken of it calmly.
As our Surety, he undertook responsibility for our sins.
He was made sin for us and suffered the righteous One for the unrighteous.
Henry emphasizes that Scripture attributes Christ's deepest suffering to God's own judgment upon sin.
Jesus understood perfectly the terrible evil of sin, the vast guilt he was bearing and the holiness of divine justice.
No human mind can fully conceive the suffering resulting from that knowledge.
Henry further suggests, as a possibility, that Satan tormented Jesus through terrifying temptations and suggestions.
Such thoughts would have been especially dreadful to his perfect holiness.
If the burden of imputed guilt caused such sorrow in the One who upholds all things by his power, how dreadful is the fate of those who must answer for unforgiven sin themselves!
How can anyone neglect so great a salvation?

div.title: Jesus is arrested and abandoned (verses 47–56)
div.p: Few enemies are more odious than those who claim discipleship and betray Christ with a kiss.
God does not need our services, and certainly not our sins, to fulfill his purposes.
Christ's submission to arrest and death was voluntary.
Though crucified in apparent weakness, he chose to submit.
If he had not been willing to suffer, his enemies could not have conquered him.
The disciples had abandoned everything to follow Jesus.
Now they abandoned him out of fear, though they had no better refuge to seek.
How foolish to flee from the Fountain of Life for fear of death!

div.title: Jesus stands before Caiaphas (verses 57–68)
div.p: Jesus was taken into Jerusalem.
Peter's decision to follow at a distance foreshadowed his denial.
It is dangerous to wish to be a disciple without being willing to be known as one.
Rather than obsess over the outcome of an ordeal, we should prepare to do our duty whatever the result.

p.hi: The outcome belongs to God; duty belongs to us.

div.p: False witnesses arose, fulfilling Scripture.
Christ was accused so that his people might avoid final condemnation.
If we are slandered, we should not expect better treatment than our Master received.
When Jesus was made sin for us, he remained silent, leaving his blood to speak on behalf of the guilty.
During his ministry he had not always stated his messianic identity in so direct a form, although his teaching and miracles testified to it.
Now he openly confessed that he was the Christ, the Son of God.
Remaining silent could have appeared to be an attempt to avoid suffering.
He spoke to provide an example for believers who must confess him despite danger.
Mockery and humiliation fell upon him, as described in Isaiah 50.
Let us confess his name and endure reproach, trusting that he will confess us before the Father's throne.

div.title: Peter denies Jesus and repents (verses 69–75)
div.p: Scripture records Peter's terrible failure faithfully and without concealment.
Dangerous company often leads to sin, especially when people expose themselves needlessly to temptation.
Hiding our connection with Christ when we are called to acknowledge him amounts to denying him.
Peter's denial was serious, but he fell through sudden fear, unlike Judas, who had deliberately planned betrayal.
The crowing rooster awakened Peter's conscience.
Our conscience should similarly remind us of sins we have overlooked or forgotten.
God permitted this failure to correct Peter's excessive confidence and make him more modest, humble, compassionate and useful to others.
The record has taught believers ever since.
People who mock it or use Peter's fall as an excuse to sin do so at their own peril.
We cannot know how we would behave under severe testing if God left us to our own power.

p.hi: Those who think they stand should take care lest they fall.

div.p: Distrust your own heart and trust the Lord.
Peter wept bitterly.
True grief over sin should be deep.
But it also produces change: after his repentance Peter did not deny Jesus again.
Instead he repeatedly confessed Christ despite danger.
Genuine repentance is shown by a new practice of the very duty previously neglected.
This is evidence not merely of bitter tears but of sincere sorrow.

row.cell: Christ delivered to Pilate, The despair of Judas.

div.title: Judas despairs after betraying an innocent man (verses 1–10)
div.p: People committing wicked acts rarely recognize all their consequences at the time.
But they must eventually answer for them.
Judas confessed openly to the chief priests that he had sinned by betraying an innocent person.
His words were a powerful testimony to Christ's character.
Yet the rulers remained hardened.
Judas threw down the payment and hanged himself, overcome by fear of divine judgment and despair.
Henry considers it very likely Judas died before Jesus was crucified.
The rulers who had hired Judas had themselves eagerly sought Christ's innocent blood, yet behaved as though his sin were no concern of theirs.
How readily people mock serious wrongdoing!
And how easily we reduce our sense of guilt by concentrating on another person's sin rather than our own.
But God's judgment follows truth.
Some interpreters understand the purchase of the burial field with Judas' returned money as a picture of the benefits Christ's blood would bring to strangers and Gentile sinners.
Henry mentions this as an interpretation, not an established fact about the land's original purpose.
The event is connected with prophecy (Zechariah 11:12).
Judas went a long way toward repentance, but not toward saving repentance.
He confessed sin, yet not to God.
He did not return to the heavenly Father pleading for mercy.
We should not mistake distress, confession and inward conviction for actual conversion while pride, hostility and rebellion still rule the heart.

div.title: Jesus stands before Pilate (verses 11–25)
div.p: Pilate bore no personal malice toward Jesus and hoped that he might be acquitted.
His wife's message was another warning against condemning him.
God provides many restraints against sin through Providence, friends and conscience.
It is a mercy to hear the warning “Do not do the evil thing that God hates” before we act.
Under the religious leaders' influence the crowd demanded Barabbas.
They preferred a criminal to Christ.
People who prefer this world as their ruler and ultimate portion rather than God similarly choose what will ruin them.
Pilate saw the danger of resisting the crowd, but his hesitation also showed the power of conscience even in flawed rulers.
God arranged the events to make clear that Jesus suffered not for wrongdoing of his own, but for the sins of his people.
Pilate could not free himself from guilt merely by washing his hands.
As governor, he was responsible for protecting an innocent person.
Henry interprets the crowd's self-imprecation as connected with later national suffering.
That is his historical-theological claim about the narrative, not an assignment of guilt to Jews collectively in the present.
No ordinary person can bear the guilt of another.
Only Christ, without any sin of his own, could answer for others' sins.
All of us are involved in the moral lesson.
Whenever sinners reject Christ so they may keep beloved sins, they effectively choose Barabbas instead of Jesus.
Those sins rob God of his honor and destroy souls.
Christ's blood, which the crowd rejected, is made through mercy a source of blessing and refuge to all who trust him.
Let us flee to it.

div.title: Barabbas is released and Jesus is mocked (verses 26–30)
div.p: The death by crucifixion described here was a terrible and degrading Roman punishment.
The victim was fastened to a cross that was then raised upright, leaving the person's weight hanging under severe pain.
Henry draws attention to this as the fulfillment of the figure of the bronze serpent lifted on a pole.
Jesus endured the humiliation and agony so that believers might receive eternal life, joy and glory.

div.title: Jesus is led to the cross (verses 31–34)
div.p: Christ was taken to his death like a lamb brought to slaughter and a sacrifice brought to the altar.
Even the apparent mercies of the wicked can conceal cruelty.
The soldiers compelled Simon to carry the cross.
May the Lord make us willing to carry the cross appointed for us, taking it up daily with joy as we follow Jesus.
Has anyone experienced sorrow like the Savior's sorrow?
When we consider the manner of his death, let us understand the extraordinary love with which he loved us.
As though crucifixion itself were not painful enough, the soldiers added fresh bitterness and humiliation to it.

div.title: Jesus is crucified and ridiculed (verses 35–44)
div.p: A notice placed over a criminal's head was meant to announce the crime and increase the shame of punishment.
The inscription over Jesus was intended as an insult.
Yet God turned the accusation into an acknowledgment of Christ's honor.
Two criminals were crucified beside him.
He was numbered with transgressors at his death, so that redeemed people might be numbered among the saints at their death.
His enemies mocked him.
People hostile to Christ often try to convince others of accusations against religion that they themselves know are false.
The religious leaders ridiculed his title King of Israel.
Many would accept a king who came down from the cross, offering a kingdom without the troubles through which believers must enter it.
But without the cross there is no Christ and no crown.
Those who expect to reign with Christ must be willing to suffer with him.
Jesus undertook to satisfy God's justice and submitted to the death of the worst criminals.
Details of his suffering fulfilled predictions in the Prophets and Psalms.

div.title: Jesus dies (verses 45–50)
div.p: For three hours darkness covered the scene.
Henry understands that time as the most intense agony in which Jesus confronted the powers of darkness and experienced the Father's displeasure against human sin, bearing his soul as an offering.
There had never been such hours since humanity was created.
They were central to the redemption and salvation of sinners.
Jesus cried out using the words of Psalm 22:1.
He thereby teaches us to let Scripture guide our prayers, including in the deepest suffering.
Believers may have tasted drops of bitterness, but they can hardly comprehend the suffering Christ bore.
From it they learn something of his love and of sin's terrible evil.
They see their debt to the One who rescues them from coming judgment.
His enemies mocked the cry and misunderstood it.
Many insults against God's people and word arise from similarly gross misunderstandings.
Just before death Jesus cried with full strength.
His life was not finally seized from him against his will.
He gave it freely into the Father's hands.
He offered himself through the eternal Spirit as both Priest and Sacrifice.
Then he truly died.
His soul was separated from his body; his body was really dead.
His death was necessary because he had undertaken to become an offering for sin.
He completed that sacrifice by voluntarily surrendering his life.

div.title: The veil tears and witnesses respond (verses 51–56)
div.p: The temple veil tearing signified that Christ's death opened the way to God.
Through him we may approach the throne of mercy now and later the throne of glory.
When we consider the crucifixion, our hearts should be torn in repentance, rather than merely our clothes.
A heart unmoved by the clearly proclaimed death of Jesus is harder than rock.
Graves opened and bodies of holy people who had died arose.
Scripture does not tell us exactly whom they visited, how they appeared or what later became of them.
We must not claim knowledge beyond what is written.
Extraordinary displays of divine Providence can awaken sinners and produce fear of God.
The centurion and soldiers were deeply affected.
The testimony about Jesus encourages us.
If we live for God without needlessly offending others, we may entrust our good names to him.
Let faith contemplate the crucified Christ and respond to his great love.
His faithful friends could only watch from a distance, unable to save him.
No event has displayed the evil of sin so powerfully as the beloved Son suffering on the cross, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God.
Let us willingly give ourselves to his service.

div.title: Jesus is buried (verses 57–61)
div.p: Jesus' burial had no grand ceremony.
He had no house of his own in life and no grave of his own in death.
Having no personal sin, he nonetheless possessed no burial place.
His enemies intended that he be buried with criminals.
