But God overruled their intentions, and Christ was laid in a rich man's tomb, fulfilling Isaiah 53:9.
Funerals can awaken fear of death.
Yet Christ's burial has transformed what the grave means for believers.
Remembering that change should give them hope.
We should also imitate his burial spiritually by continually putting our own sins to death.

div.title: The tomb is sealed and guarded (verses 62–66)
div.p: On the Sabbath, when the chief priests and Pharisees ought to have been occupied with worship, they instead sought Pilate's help to secure Jesus' tomb.
Their actions were permitted to provide clearer evidence of Christ's resurrection.
Pilate allowed them to guard the burial place as carefully as they wished.
They sealed the stone and stationed guards.
They believed they had made the tomb secure.
Yet guarding it against the weak and frightened disciples was needless.
Trying to guard it against God's power was hopeless.
Their apparent wisdom became folly.
God catches the wise in their own schemes.
The furious plans of Christ's opponents ultimately serve his glory.

div.title: Jesus rises from the dead (verses 1–8)
div.p: Christ rose on the third day, just as he had repeatedly predicted.
On the first day of creation's week God commanded light to shine out of darkness.
On the first day of this new week, the Light of the World shone out of the darkness of the grave.
Henry observes that the New Testament repeatedly mentions this day as the day on which Christians gathered solemnly to honor Christ.
Jesus could have rolled away the stone through his own power.
But he chose to have an angel do it.
His resurrection brought joy to his friends and fear and confusion to his enemies.
The angel comforted the women.
Those who persist in sin should fear God's judgment.
But followers of Christ may hear, “Do not be afraid.”
The resurrection is their comfort.
Our fellowship with the risen Savior is spiritual, enjoyed through faith in his word.
When we begin to treat this world as our permanent home, remembering only how pleasant it is to live here, we should recall that Jesus is no longer in the grave—he has risen.
Therefore lift your hearts toward heavenly things.
He rose as he said.
Never treat as strange what Christ's word has prepared us to expect, whether present suffering or future glory.
Faithfully contemplating the place where our Lord lay can strengthen us.
But the angel told the women to go quickly.
It was good to visit the tomb, yet God had other work for them.
When duty calls, useful service to others must take priority over the pleasure of private spiritual enjoyment.
They were to tell the disciples so those sorrowing followers could be comforted.
Christ knows where his disciples live and graciously visits them, even when they are far from an abundance of outward opportunities for worship.
Fear and joy together made the women hurry.
Christians should willingly share their experiences of fellowship with the Lord, telling one another what God has done for their souls.

div.title: The risen Jesus appears to the women (verses 9 and 10)
div.p: God's gracious encouragement often meets us while we are doing our duty.
Those who use the help they have received for the benefit of others often receive still more.
The women did not expect to encounter Jesus personally, but he was near them.
He remains near believers today through his word.
His greeting revealed his continuing love for humanity, even after entering his exalted state.
Christ desires his people to be joyful and cheerful.
His resurrection supplies more than enough reason for joy.

p.hi: Do not be afraid.

div.p: The risen Lord has defeated death to free his people from their fears.
The disciples had shamefully abandoned him during his suffering.
Yet he still called them his brothers.
This reveals his willingness to forgive and teaches us to forgive.
Despite his majesty and purity and our weakness and unworthiness, he graciously calls believers brothers and sisters.

div.title: The guards receive money to lie (verses 11–15)
div.p: Love of money can lead people into dreadful wrongdoing.
The soldiers accepted a large payment to promote a story they knew was false.
How strange that some spend generously to support falsehood while others begrudge small gifts for spreading truth!
Let us not allow a worthy cause to fail through neglect when wicked causes receive lavish support.
The religious leaders promised to protect the soldiers from Pilate's punishment.
But they could not protect them from God's judgment, which confronts those who deliberately love and tell lies.
A person promising that someone can sin deliberately without danger promises more than can be delivered.
Their story contradicted itself.
If the guards had all been sleeping, how could they know what happened?
If any were awake, why did they not awaken the others?
If they had actually fallen asleep on duty, why would they freely confess it?
And had the story been true, would the authorities not have prosecuted the apostles for the supposed theft?
Henry regards these contradictions as strong evidence of the account's falsehood.
This was not merely a failure to understand evidence.
It showed deliberate wrongdoing of the heart.
God allowed the deceivers to expose the weakness of their own plan.
Christ's resurrection is the great testimony to his identity as Son of God.
The soldiers had unusually strong evidence of the truth, yet accepted bribes to discourage belief.
Even the clearest external evidence does not convert a human heart without the Holy Spirit's work.

div.title: The risen Jesus commissions his disciples (verses 16–20)
div.p: Matthew omits some appearances of the risen Jesus found in Luke and John and moves toward the solemn commission.
Jesus had appointed this meeting before his death and appeared after rising.
Those who see Christ through the eyes of faith worship him.
Yet even sincere faith may be weak and wavering.
Jesus supplied convincing evidence of his resurrection so that faith could overcome doubt.
He commissioned the apostles and their successors in gospel ministry to go among all nations.
The salvation they proclaimed is a common salvation.
Whoever desires may come to Jesus and receive its benefits.
All people are welcome.
Christianity is the faith of a sinner who seeks deliverance from deserved judgment and sin.
The sinner approaches the mercy of the Father through the atonement of the incarnate Son and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit.
The believer gives himself to worshiping and serving Father, Son and Holy Spirit—three Persons, one God—in all the ordinances and commands Christ appointed.
Baptism is an outward sign of the Spirit's inward washing and sanctifying work, which seals and evidences a believer's justification.
We must therefore examine whether we possess the spiritual reality that baptism signifies: death to sin and new birth into righteousness, through which children of wrath become God's children.
Jesus promised his followers his constant presence.
He is with his churches and ministers all the days, every day.
There is no hour when they are abandoned by their Lord.
Without his presence, even for a moment, their work would fail.
The Savior may at times seem hidden, but he is never far away.
Let us join the final Amen.
Lord Jesus, remain with us and all your people.
Let your face shine upon us so that your way may be known throughout the earth and your saving power among all nations.

div.title: Mark — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Mark was the nephew of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10) and the son of Mary of Jerusalem, whose house was a gathering place for the apostles and early Christians (Acts 12:12).
Because Peter called Mark his son (1 Peter 5:13), it is thought that Mark was converted through Peter's ministry.
Mark was thus closely associated with the disciples of Jesus, even if he had not personally been one of them.
He wrote in Rome.

Some suppose Peter dictated the Gospel to him. Henry considers it more generally attested, however, that Peter preached in Rome and that Mark, his companion, understood his preaching accurately and was asked to write down its details.
Peter's own humility is evident in the passages that mention him.
Mark's careful account includes many events Peter personally witnessed, and the details suggest the testimony of an eyewitness.
The Gospel emphasizes Christ's miracles more than his teaching discourses.
Though it repeats many events found in Matthew, reading them again is valuable: each evangelist records the events from the perspective that most affected him.

row.cell: The office of John the Baptist.
The baptism and temptation of Christ.
He casts out an unclean spirit.

div.title: John prepares the Lord's way (verses 1–8)
div.p: Both Isaiah and Malachi spoke of the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ through the ministry of John the Baptist.
Their prophecies show that Christ comes among us with both a treasury of grace and a scepter of government.
Human corruption puts up great resistance to his progress.
When the Father sent his Son into the world, he prepared a way before him. When he sends Christ into a human heart, he likewise prepares the way.
John considered himself unworthy of the humblest service to Jesus.
The greatest saints have always been the most humble. They recognize their need of Christ's atoning blood and sanctifying Spirit more deeply than others.
The gospel promises people who repent and receive forgiveness that they will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, purified through his grace and refreshed through his consolations.
Often we gain little profit or comfort from God's ordinances, word and sacraments because we lack the divine light within us.
And we lack that light because we have not asked for it, though our heavenly Father promises to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

div.title: Jesus is baptized and tempted (verses 9–13)
div.p: Christ's baptism was his first public appearance after living unnoticed for many years.
How much genuine worth can remain unknown in this world!
Yet what is hidden will, at the appropriate time, be revealed.
Jesus took upon himself the likeness of sinful human flesh and consecrated himself for our sake so that we might become holy and be baptized with him (John 17:19).
The Father honored his submission to baptism. The Holy Spirit descended upon him like a dove.
Heaven may be said to open to us whenever the Spirit descends and works within us.
The good work God carries out in our hearts is evidence of his favorable purposes toward us.
Mark mentions that Jesus was in the wilderness among wild animals.
Even there his Father preserved him, encouraging confidence that the Father would continue providing whatever was necessary.
Special acts of protection give assurance of further help when it is needed.
The serpent tempted the first Adam in a garden and the second Adam in a wilderness, with very different outcomes.
He has continued tempting Adam's children in every place and condition.
Company has temptations; so does solitude.
No location, occupation or lawful activity is free from them—not even fasting and prayer.
Indeed, some of the fiercest assaults occur during sacred duties, yet through God's grace those duties also provide the sweetest victories.
The ministry of good angels comforts us against the malicious plans of evil angels.
But an even greater consolation is God the Holy Spirit living in our hearts.

div.title: Jesus preaches and calls disciples (verses 14–22)
div.p: Jesus began preaching in Galilee after John was imprisoned.
When God sets aside one servant, he raises up others to continue his work.
Jesus joined repentance and faith in his message.
Through repentance we acknowledge the Creator whom we have offended.
Through faith we honor the Redeemer who came to save us from sin.
Christ joined these two things; we must not separate them.
He called fishermen, people of modest worldly status who were diligent in their work and treated one another kindly.
Industry and unity are good, and Jesus delights to bless them.
Christ's followers must be willing to leave everything for his sake.
His grace makes them willing.
This does not mean everyone must literally withdraw from society.
Rather, we must hold worldly possessions and relationships loosely, giving up anything inconsistent with duty to Jesus or harmful to our souls.
Jesus faithfully observed the Sabbath by doing the spiritual and charitable work for which Sabbath rest was appointed.
His doctrine continually astonished people. The more carefully we hear it, the more reason we have to admire it.

div.title: Jesus casts out an unclean spirit (verses 23–28)
div.p: The devil is described as unclean because he has lost the purity of his original state, acts in direct opposition to God's Holy Spirit and makes human hearts impure through his suggestions.
Some people quietly attend gatherings where teachers offer only formal religion.
But when Christ comes through faithful ministers, holy doctrine and the convicting Spirit, they resist the truth and want no part in Jesus.
The unclean spirit in this story recognized Jesus as the Holy One of God.
It feared his holiness and expected destruction from him, rather than salvation.
People who tell God to depart from them speak the language of the same hostility.
The natural mind is opposed to God, particularly his holiness.
When Christ delivers souls from Satan's power, the change may produce turmoil.
The enemy tries to disturb people whom he can no longer destroy.
The witnesses wondered at the power of Jesus' teaching.
Equally astonishing changes occur when people become genuinely converted.

If we did not treat conversion with indifference, the transformation of a notoriously wicked person into a sober, righteous and godly life through preaching the crucified Savior would still astonish us.

div.title: Jesus heals many people (verses 29–39)
div.p: Wherever Jesus went, he did good.
He healed people so that they could serve him and others who belonged to him.
People prevented from attending public worship by illness or another genuine obstacle may still look for his gracious presence.
He can soothe their sorrow and reduce their pain.
The sick came in large numbers.
When we see others receiving help from Christ, it should encourage us to seek him ourselves.
Jesus withdrew to a solitary place.
He had no danger of pride or distraction, yet still sought time apart for prayer.
People who do the greatest amount of useful public work must also sometimes be alone with God.

div.title: Jesus cleanses a person with leprosy (verses 40–45)
div.p: The leper came to Christ with deep humility and full submission to his will.
“Lord, if you are willing” was not a question about Christ's compassion or power.
It was an expression of readiness to accept his decision.
We should pray with the same humility and trust.
Christ willingly shows mercy to people who willingly entrust their requests to his will.
He did not want this healing to become a means of attracting human praise for himself.
However, we have no such reason today to hesitate to proclaim Christ's praises.

row.cell: Christ heals one sick of the palsy.
Levi's call, and the entertainment given to Jesus.
Why Christ's disciples did not fast.
He justifies his disciples for plucking corn on the sabbath.

div.title: Jesus forgives and heals a paralysed man (verses 1–12)
div.p: The man's need to be carried revealed how much suffering human life contains.
The friends who carried him showed real compassion for someone in distress.
Genuine and strong faith may be expressed in different ways, but Jesus receives and approves it.
Sin is the origin of all human suffering and sickness.
To remove the effects decisively, the cause must be dealt with.

p.hi: Forgiving sin reaches the root of every disease.

div.p: Jesus demonstrated his authority to pardon sin through his power to heal the paralysed man.
Physical cures picture the even greater miracle of spiritual healing.
Sin is the soul's disease; when forgiven, it is healed.
When we understand Christ's power to transform sinful souls, we may truly say we have never seen anything like it.
Most people think they are spiritually healthy.
Believing they have no need of a physician, they disregard Christ and the gospel.
But people who have been convicted and humbled, and know there is no hope apart from the Savior, reveal faith by coming to him without delay.

div.title: Levi is called and welcomes Jesus (verses 13–17)
div.p: Levi, also known as Matthew, was a tax collector serving Rome.
Henry judges that this position was especially discreditable for a Jew of the time, and remarks that honest and fair-dealing publicans were rare.
The occupation reminded Jewish people of their subjection to Rome, leading them to despise its officials.
Yet Jesus called this man to follow him.
Through Christ, God has mercy to pardon the greatest sins and grace to change even those regarded as the greatest sinners.
There is nothing new about good and wise actions being misrepresented and condemned.
Jesus freely ate with tax collectors and people considered sinful, even when Pharisees took offense.
He had come because the world was not righteous.
Without sin, there would have been no occasion for him either to preach repentance or to purchase forgiveness.
We must not form intimate friendships with ungodly people because we love their empty and corrupt conversation.
But we should love their souls and seek their salvation.
Our great Physician has healing power within himself and could not catch the spiritual disease of those he helped.
We, however, can be harmed by bad company.
Therefore, while seeking to help others, we must guard against being led into sin.

div.title: The question of fasting (verses 18–22)
div.p: Strictly religious people often criticize others merely for failing to conform to all their personal opinions.
Jesus himself was slandered in this way.
We should be willing to endure unjust criticism while carefully avoiding conduct that truly deserves blame.
We must also fulfill every duty at its proper time and in the proper way.

div.title: The disciples gather grain on the Sabbath (verses 23–28)
div.p: The Sabbath is a holy institution given by God.
It is a privilege and benefit, not forced labor or a burden.
God never intended it to injure human beings.
We must not interpret his command in ways that undermine its own gracious purpose.
The Sabbath was established for humanity living in communities, bearing needs and troubles, and preparing for an everlasting condition of happiness or misery.
Human beings were not created in order to serve the Sabbath, as though keeping it added something to God's own happiness.
They were not commanded to observe it outwardly at the cost of actual harm to themselves.
Every rule connected with its observance must be understood according to mercy.

div.title: Jesus heals a withered hand (verses 1–5)
div.p: The man's condition was pitiful: a withered hand prevented him from earning his living.
Those unable to help themselves are particularly fitting recipients of practical charity. We should help them.
Stubborn unbelievers may have nothing truthful to say against Christ's teaching, yet refuse to surrender to it.
People notice outward misconduct, but Jesus sees the root of bitterness in the heart, including hardness and blindness.
He was grieved by that inward evil.
Those who refuse repentance should fear the judgment of the One who sees their hearts.
The Sabbath is particularly suitable for acts of mercy. A house of prayer is a suitable place for healing, but the power belongs to Christ, not to either the day or the location.
The gospel's call resembles Jesus' command to stretch out the withered hand.
If people refuse to respond, they remain responsible for refusing the gracious summons.
But if they are healed, all glory belongs to Christ's power and grace.

div.title: The crowds come to Jesus (verses 6–12)
div.p: Human sickness and suffering ultimately arise from God's just displeasure against sin.
Through Christ's atoning blood, the removal of such troubles—or their transformation into spiritual blessings—has been purchased for believers.
But we should fear the diseases of the soul even more than those of the body.
Christ can heal those spiritual troubles with a single word.
May ever more people press toward him for cleansing and deliverance from their spiritual enemies.

div.title: Jesus appoints his apostles (verses 13–21)
div.p: Christ calls the people he wills, because grace belongs to him to give.
He summoned the apostles to separate themselves from the crowd, and they came.
He gave them power to heal diseases and cast out demons.
May the Lord continue to send people who have been with him and learned from him to proclaim his gospel as servants of his gracious work.
People whose hearts are fully engaged in God's service can easily endure inconvenience to themselves.
They would rather miss a meal than miss an opportunity to do good.
Those who serve God zealously should expect difficulties caused both by the hatred of enemies and by the mistaken affection of friends.
They must be alert to both.

div.title: The scribes accuse Jesus of serving Satan (verses 22–30)
div.p: Jesus' doctrine plainly weakened the devil's kingdom.
His expulsion of demons from suffering people demonstrated the same power.
It would make no sense for Satan to support a mission directed against his own dominion.
Christ gave a serious warning about the scribes' blasphemous accusation.
The gospel offers forgiveness through Christ's saving work to even the greatest sinners.
But by this particular sin these opponents would oppose the gifts of the Holy Spirit to be poured out after Christ's ascension.
Such is the hostility of fallen hearts that they may accuse God's servants of doing Satan's work precisely when sinners are being converted and begin living holy lives.

div.title: Jesus identifies his true family (verses 31–35)
div.p: All genuine Christians have a remarkable comfort.
They are dearer to Christ as his disciples than even merely human ties to a mother, brother or sister could make people, even if those relatives were themselves holy.
The privilege remains available today.
We cannot enjoy Christ's physical presence as his first disciples did, but his spiritual presence is not withheld from us.

div.title: The sower and the soils (verses 1–20)
div.p: This parable contains teaching so important that everyone capable of hearing should pay attention.
If we do not understand the plain truths of the gospel, how will we understand its deeper teachings?
Considering the unhappy condition of people without gospel privileges should make Christ's disciples value those privileges more highly.
In the church's great field, God's word is announced widely.
But relatively few hearers receive it in a way that produces lasting fruit.
Many feel moved or enthusiastic for a time yet receive no enduring benefit.
The reason the word leaves so little permanent impression is that their hearts have not been prepared to receive it.
The devil is especially active among careless hearers, like birds eating seed left exposed on a path.
Many continue in a barren religious profession until they perish.
Shallow religious feelings cannot endure.
Many neglect the work of the heart, without which religion has no true substance.
Others are hindered by an abundance of worldly concerns and possessions.
But people who own little can also be ruined by giving themselves over to bodily indulgence.
God rightly expects fruit from everyone privileged to hear his gospel.
This includes a renewed disposition, Christian graces exercised each day and duties faithfully performed.
Ask the Lord, through his new-creating grace, to make our hearts good soil.
May his word produce good words and works through Jesus Christ, bringing glory to God the Father.

div.title: The lamp and the growing seed (verses 21–34)
div.p: Jesus taught these parables to call his disciples' full attention to his word.
Through learning from him, they would become able to teach others.
A lamp is lit to illuminate a room, not to be hidden beneath a container.
Likewise, disciples receive light in order to help others.
The growing seed pictures how God's kingdom advances.
When Christ's word occupies its rightful place in a soul, the change becomes visible through good conduct.
Growth is gradual: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.
Once genuine spiritual life has begun, it advances.
The first work of grace may seem like a very small beginning.
Even while it is still growing it produces significant blessings.
How much greater will its glory be when that work is perfected in heaven!

div.title: Jesus calms the storm (verses 35–41)
div.p: Jesus slept during the storm to test his disciples' faith and move them to pray.
Their faith was weak, but their prayers were urgent.
When our sinful hearts resemble a restless sea and our passions become unruly, let us hear Christ's command: “Be silent! Be still!”
When we experience outward conflict and inward fear, and our spirits are overwhelmed, one word from him can bring an immediate, great calm.
Jesus asked why they were so frightened.
Some fear may be understandable, but not fear so great that people imagine Jesus does not care whether his followers perish.
Such thoughts expose weakness in faith.
Even the best believers remain imperfect in this world.
Fear and faith alternate while we are here.
But soon fear will be overcome and faith will give way to sight.

div.title: Jesus releases a man held by demons (verses 1–20)
div.p: Some people deliberately persist in sin and resemble the man in this account.
God's commands act like chains restraining sinners from evil, yet people break those restraints when determined to continue wicked conduct.
This reveals Satan's destructive power in them.
A Roman legion could number six thousand soldiers or more.
The use of the name Legion in this account indicates a dreadful number of fallen spirits opposed to both God and humanity.
We are no match for our spiritual enemies through our own strength.
But through the Lord and his mighty power, even numerous enemies need not overcome us.
When Christ delivers a person enslaved by grievous sin, that person willingly sits at the Savior's feet to hear his word.
Christ changes miserable captives of Satan into saints and servants of God.
The local people disliked Jesus when they discovered their pigs had been lost.
God's patience and mercy can still be seen when a loss of property spares human life and warns sinners to seek the salvation of their souls.
The healed man eagerly told others what Christ had done for him.
Many marveled, but few followed.
It is possible to admire Christ's works while never seriously longing for Christ himself.

div.title: A woman is healed (verses 21–34)
div.p: A place that rejects the gospel may lose it to another place where the good news will be better received.
A synagogue ruler came urgently to Jesus about his twelve-year-old daughter, who was dying.
Another healing occurred during the journey.
We should do good on the road as well as at home, as Deuteronomy 6:7 teaches concerning instruction.
People often turn to Christ only after every other source of help fails.
All other helpers eventually prove powerless when asked to bring real peace to a troubled soul.
Some try distractions and worldly company.
Others immerse themselves in business or give way to excessive pleasures.
Some attempt to establish their own righteousness.
Others torment themselves through vain superstitions.
None of these methods can give the soul rest.
But the person whom Christ heals from sin experiences a real inward change for the better.
Jesus knows secret faith, just as he knows secret sins.
The woman told him everything truthfully.
Christ wants his people to be comforted and possesses the power to give peace to distressed hearts.
The more simply we depend on him and expect his gracious help, the more we recognize that he has become our salvation.
Those spiritually healed through faith have reason to go in peace.

div.title: Jairus's daughter is raised from the dead (verses 35–43)
div.p: When Jairus heard that his daughter had died, he may have wondered whether he should still ask Jesus to come.
That uncertainty is Henry's supposition rather than a stated thought of Jairus.
But do we need less of God's grace, the Spirit's comfort and the prayers of ministers and friends when death enters a household than when a family member is ill?
Faith is our best remedy against grief and fear at such a time.
Believe the resurrection and do not be overcome by fear.
Christ raised the child with a word of power.
His command pictures the gospel's call to people naturally dead in trespasses and sins.
Christ's word gives spiritual life.
All who saw the miracle or heard about it wondered at his power.
We cannot now assume that deceased children and relatives will be restored to earthly life.
But we may still find genuine consolation under our trials.

row.cell: Christ despised in his own country.
John the Baptist put to death.
The apostles return, Five thousand fed by a miracle.
Christ walks on the sea, He heals those that touch him.

div.title: Jesus is rejected in his hometown (verses 1–6)
div.p: Jesus' neighbors tried to turn others against him by calling him the carpenter.
Henry judges it probable that Jesus had worked in that trade alongside his earthly father.
By doing so, Christ honored craftspeople and all who earn their living through honest manual labor.
His followers should be content with knowing that they do good, even when they receive no praise.
How much the inhabitants of Nazareth lost through stubborn prejudice against Jesus!
May divine grace deliver us from unbelief that turns Christ into a source of judgment rather than life.
Following his example, let us teach the gospel's way of salvation even to people in poor cottages and humble rural communities.

div.title: Jesus sends the apostles to preach (verses 7–13)
div.p: The apostles knew their weakness and expected no worldly advantage.
Yet they obeyed their Master and went forward depending on his strength.
They did not entertain people with interesting but useless curiosities.
They told listeners to repent of sin and turn to God.
Christ's servants may hope that their preaching will bring many people from spiritual darkness to God and that souls will be healed through the power of the Holy Spirit.

div.title: Herod orders John's execution (verses 14–29)
div.p: Herod feared John while he was alive.
He feared him even more after his death.
He had obeyed many of John's instructions, but obedience to many commandments is not enough.
We must regard all God's commands as binding.
Herod respected John's preaching until it challenged his relationship with Herodias.
Many people welcome sound preaching so long as it does not disturb their favorite sin.
It is better for sinners to persecute faithful ministers now than to curse those ministers eternally for having concealed the truth.
God's ways are beyond our complete understanding.
Yet he will never be unable to reward his servants for what they lose or suffer for his sake.
Death could not finally surprise John, a faithful and holy man.
His enemies' apparent triumph was short-lived.

div.title: The disciples return; five thousand are fed (verses 30–44)
div.p: Ministers should do or teach nothing they would be ashamed to report to their Master.
Jesus noticed both the fears of some disciples and the exhausting efforts of others.
He provided rest for the tired and refuge for those who were afraid.
The crowds came to receive the spiritual food of his word.
After teaching them, he ensured that they had bodily food as well.
If Christ and his apostles accepted simple and modest living, we should be willing to do so.
This miracle demonstrates that Jesus came not only to restore spiritual life but also to preserve and nourish it.
There is sufficient provision in him for everyone who comes.
Only people filled with self-importance leave Christ empty-handed.
Although Jesus could supply limitless bread, he taught the disciples not to waste God's gifts.
Many people lack even ordinary food.
We ourselves may one day need what we carelessly throw away today.

div.title: Jesus walks on water and heals those who come (verses 45–56)
div.p: The church often resembles a ship at sea, tossed by storms and lacking comfort.
Christ may be for us, even while the wind and waves are against us.
The consolation for believers is that their Master is on heaven's mountain, interceding for them.
No obstacle can prevent his coming to help his people at the appointed time.
He quieted the disciples' fears by revealing his identity.
Our fears often vanish when mistaken ideas are corrected, particularly mistaken ideas about Christ.
If the disciples have Jesus among them, everything is well.
We fail to understand Christ's present works because we forget what he has already done.
If Christian ministers could now cure every bodily disease, crowds would rush to them.
How sad that so many people are more concerned about the health of their bodies than the salvation of their souls!

row.cell: The woman of Canaan's daughter cured.
Christ restores a man to hearing and speech.

div.title: God's commands and human traditions (verses 1–13)
div.p: One great purpose of Jesus' coming was to set aside the ceremonial law.
To prepare for that change, he exposed the human ceremonies added to God's law.
The clean hands and pure heart Christ gives his disciples are very different from the outward, superstitious practices of Pharisees in every age.
Jesus reproved religious leaders for rejecting God's command in the name of their customs.
Children whose parents are poor must help them as far as they are able.
If it was a capital offense under the law to curse parents, how much more terrible is leaving them to starve!
Yet the Pharisees developed a religious excuse allowing people to escape this duty while appearing devout.

div.title: What truly makes a person unclean (verses 14–23)
div.p: It is our evil thoughts, sinful desires, words and actions that defile us.
A polluted spring sends out polluted streams.
So a corrupt heart produces corrupt reasoning, appetites, passions, speech and conduct.
Understanding the law spiritually and recognizing the evil of sin should move us to seek the Holy Spirit's grace.
Only he can restrain and overcome the corrupt thoughts and affections working within us.

div.title: Jesus heals the Canaanite woman's daughter (verses 24–30)
div.p: Christ never turned away someone who sincerely fell at his feet seeking mercy.
Even a trembling and poor sinner may approach him.
This woman was not only personally faithful but also a caring mother.
Her love for her daughter led her to Jesus.
Christ's reply about children being fed first indicated that mercy for the Gentiles was approaching, not that it would be forever refused.
The woman did not speak lightly of God's mercy.
Instead, she recognized how abundant the miracles among Israel had been and asked for one cure as a crumb beside that abundance.
The Savior left proud Pharisees resisting him but showed compassion to a humble sinner who looked to him for the children's bread.
He continues seeking and saving the lost.

div.title: Jesus restores hearing and speech (verses 31–37)
div.p: People brought a man unable to hear or speak to Jesus and asked him to consider his suffering and use his healing power.
Christ used more visible actions than usual when healing this man.
They served as signs of his power and encouraged the man's faith and that of his friends.
The people who came to Jesus had different needs and received help in different ways.
Yet everyone who truly approached him for mercy received what was needed.
The same is true in the central concerns of the soul.

row.cell: Four thousand fed by a miracle.
Christ cautions against the Pharisees and Herodians.

div.title: Jesus feeds four thousand (verses 1–10)
div.p: Jesus welcomed even the humblest people who came to him for life and grace.
He knows our human weakness and takes our needs seriously.
Christ repeated the miracle of multiplying food to show that his generosity is always ready.
His favors continue to be renewed as our needs arise.
Those who live upon Christ by faith and receive his gifts with thanksgiving need not fear that his provision will fail.

div.title: Jesus warns against hardened unbelief (verses 11–21)
div.p: Obstinate unbelief always finds an excuse, however unreasonable.
Jesus refused to satisfy the demand for a new sign.
People determined never to be convinced cannot be convinced by multiplying evidence.
How much reason have we to grieve for people whose hostility to the gospel harms both themselves and others!
When we forget God's former works and distrust him, we should correct ourselves as seriously as Jesus corrected his disciples.
How often we misunderstand his words, neglect his warnings and fail to trust his Providence!

div.title: Jesus opens a blind man's eyes gradually (verses 22–26)
div.p: A blind man's friends brought him to Jesus, revealing their own faith and concern.
People spiritually blind may not yet pray for themselves.
Their family and friends should pray for them, asking Christ to touch and heal them.
This particular cure was gradual, unlike most of Jesus' miracles.
Henry sees in that pattern an image of how spiritually blind people often receive grace.
At first their understanding is confused.
But like early daylight growing toward the full light of day, their knowledge becomes clearer and clearer.
Those who despise Christ's gracious gifts risk losing the benefits they neglect.
They may discover their value only after those privileges have been withdrawn.

div.title: Peter confesses Christ and is corrected (verses 27–33)
div.p: The gospel records these things so that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.
His miracles show that he was not overcome but the Conqueror.
Once the disciples had acknowledged his identity, they were ready to hear more about his approaching sufferings.
Jesus began teaching them directly.
Christ sees what is wrong in our speech and actions even when we cannot see it ourselves.
He knows what spirit moves us more clearly than we do.
Human wisdom is foolish when it tries to set limits on God's purposes.
Peter still misunderstood the nature of Christ's kingdom.

div.title: Every disciple must follow Jesus (verses 34–38)
div.p: Large crowds repeatedly came to Christ for help.
Everyone who wants him to heal the soul must hear his teaching about self-denial.
We must not make the body's ease our supreme good.
Eternal happiness with Christ more than compensates for losing even earthly life for his sake.
But winning the whole world through sin can never compensate for the destruction of a soul.
A day is coming when Christ's cause will be revealed as glorious, though some now despise it.
Let us learn to regard all earthly things as we will regard them on the day of his appearing.

row.cell: Pain to be preferred to sin.

div.title: The transfiguration (verses 1–13)
div.p: Jesus predicted that his kingdom would soon be displayed in power.
The transfiguration gave his disciples a glimpse of that kingdom.
It is good to be removed from the distractions of the world and alone with Christ.
How much better will it be to enjoy Christ's glory in heaven with all the saints!
But even joyful experiences can create a temptation: when we are comfortable, we may stop thinking about the needs and difficulties of other people.
The Father publicly acknowledged Jesus as his beloved Son.
God accepts him and is willing to accept us through him.
We should therefore acknowledge Jesus as our beloved Savior, accept him and give ourselves to his government.
Christ does not abandon the soul merely because its experiences of joy and comfort have faded.
Jesus then explained the prophecy about Elijah, especially fitting in light of the poor treatment John the Baptist had received.

div.title: Jesus delivers a child from an evil spirit (verses 14–29)
div.p: The child's father complained that the disciples had been unable to cure him.
Jesus instead directed attention toward the lack of faith involved.
Much is promised to those who believe.
A hard heart can be softened, spiritual diseases can be healed, and people conscious of their weakness can persevere to the end.
Those who grieve over unbelief should seek Christ's grace to overcome it.
His grace is sufficient.
Everyone Christ heals is healed effectively.
Satan does not leave willingly those whom he has enslaved for a long time.
When he can no longer deceive or destroy someone, he may still attempt to fill the soul with fear and turmoil.
The disciples must not assume every task in Christ's service will be equally easy.
Some difficult work requires more than ordinary effort.

div.title: Jesus corrects the apostles' pride and intolerance (verses 30–40)
div.p: Jesus' suffering was approaching.
It would be terrible for even demons to treat him in such a way.
It is all the more astonishing that human beings should abuse the Son of Man who came to redeem them.
But Christ never spoke of his death without also speaking of his resurrection, which would remove his disgrace and should have lessened the disciples' sorrow.
Many people remain ignorant because they are ashamed to ask questions.
Jesus explained his love and grace clearly, but the disciples still struggled to understand.
We will have to answer for our speech and discussions, especially arguments about which of us deserves the greatest honor.
People most humble and self-denying resemble Christ most closely and will receive his warmest approval.
Jesus illustrated this with a child: welcoming such a child in Christ's name is welcoming Christ himself.
The disciples wanted to silence a person who was successfully helping sinners through the name of Jesus but was not working with their own group.
People today can make the same mistake.
Jesus corrected them.
Anyone truly bringing sinners to repentance, faith in Christ and holy conduct is demonstrating that the Lord is at work.
We should not reject genuine gospel service merely because the minister belongs to another circle of disciples.

div.title: Sin is worse than suffering (verses 41–50)
div.p: Jesus repeatedly spoke of the wicked person's worm that never dies and fire that is never extinguished.
Henry understands the never-dying worm as the remorse of conscience and painful self-awareness that persist in judgment.
Enduring severe hardship, suffering and self-denial during this short life is immeasurably better than enjoying every worldly pleasure for a time and suffering eternally afterward.
Like offerings presented in sacrifice, we must be seasoned with salt.
Our sinful desires and inclinations must be subdued and put to death by the Holy Spirit.
People who possess the salt of grace should show that a living principle of grace truly governs their hearts.
It will drive out corrupt tendencies that offend God or trouble their consciences.

row.cell: Christ's discourse with the rich young man.

div.title: Jesus speaks about divorce (verses 1–12)
div.p: Wherever Jesus went, people gathered to hear his teaching.
Preaching was his constant practice.
Jesus explained that Moses permitted divorce because of human hardness of heart.
That is hardly a reason to use the permission casually.
God himself joined man and woman together and fitted them to be companions, comforts and helpers to one another.
The bond God established should not be dissolved lightly.
Anyone eager to send away a spouse should consider what it would be like if God dealt with that person in the same way.

div.title: Jesus receives children (verses 13–16)
div.p: Parents and caregivers brought small children to Jesus so that he would touch and bless them.
The text gives no indication they were ill or needed bodily healing.
They may not even have been old enough to understand formal instruction.
Yet those responsible for them believed Christ's blessing would benefit their souls, so they brought them.
Jesus commanded that the children be allowed to come and that no one hinder them.
As soon as children can understand the Savior's words, they should be taught to come to him.
Adults must likewise receive God's kingdom as children receive care and instruction from parents, caregivers and teachers.

div.title: Jesus and the wealthy young man (verses 17–22)
div.p: The young ruler was earnest and wanted to know what he should do now to obtain eternal happiness.
Most people ask only for this life's pleasures and advantages (Psalm 4:6).
He sought good conduct here so he could obtain the highest good in the coming life.
Jesus helped his understanding and directed his conduct.
But the encounter ended in sorrow.
The man wanted to know what more he needed to do for eternal life.
Jesus tested whether he truly valued that life enough to bear a present cross for a future crown.
The young man wanted to follow Christ without giving up the wealth he loved.
He left in grief because he could not hold on to both ultimate treasures.
No one can serve both God and wealth (Matthew 6:24).

div.title: Wealth as an obstacle (verses 23–31)
div.p: Jesus explained the great danger facing those who possess abundant worldly goods.
People determined to acquire more wealth rarely appreciate Christ and his grace properly.
He also taught about the great salvation belonging to those with few possessions who nevertheless give up what they have for him.
One of a godly person's hardest trials is surrendering attachment even to dear friends and relatives when love for Jesus requires it.
Even people who gain immeasurably through Christ must still expect to suffer for him until reaching heaven.
Let those with little learn contentment.
Let those with much watch against love of wealth.
We should ask for grace to surrender everything if Christ requires it and to use faithfully everything we are permitted to keep.

div.title: Jesus foretells suffering and teaches humble service (verses 32–45)
div.p: Christ's persistent determination to finish the saving work assigned to him astonished his disciples and should continue to astonish us.
Worldly honor is attractive, and even Jesus' own disciples were repeatedly dazzled by it.
We need wisdom and grace to know how to suffer with him.
We may trust him to determine how much heavenly glory he will give us.
Jesus explained that worldly rulers commonly abuse their authority.
If he granted every request we make, our motives would soon reveal desire for fame, rank and power, along with unwillingness to drink from his cup or share his baptism of suffering.
Sometimes receiving exactly what we ask would ruin us.
But Christ loves his people and gives them only what is good for them.

div.title: Bartimaeus receives sight (verses 46–52)
div.p: Bartimaeus had heard about Christ's miracles.
When he learned that Jesus was nearby, he hoped to regain his sight.
Those seeking Christ's healing should recognize him as the promised Messiah.
His gracious invitation encourages us to believe that those who come to him will receive the help they truly need.
We must put aside the garment of self-sufficiency.
Like someone casting off a long garment that might hinder running, we should lay aside every weight and the sin that clings most closely to us (Hebrews 12:1).
Bartimaeus asked that his eyes might be opened.
The ability to work and earn one's bread is a real gift.
People given healthy bodies and senses should not make themselves practically disabled through foolishness or idleness.
Jesus restored his sight.
His words pointed to Bartimaeus's faith in the Son of David, in Christ's pity and power—not merely to repeated words or cries.
Jesus himself moved that faith into action.
When gospel preaching or Christian Scripture comes within reach, Christ is passing by.
That is our opportunity to come to him.
But spiritual healing is not the end of our duty.
When Christ opens our eyes, we should continue following him, learning from his teaching and honoring him in our lives.
People with spiritual sight recognize such beauty in Christ that they desire to follow eagerly.

row.cell: The barren fig-tree cursed, The temple cleansed.
The priests and elders questioned concerning John the Baptist.

div.title: Jesus enters Jerusalem (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jesus' remarkable entrance into the city showed that he did not fear the strength or malice of his enemies.
The disciples were frightened, so this would encourage them.
Christ was not overwhelmed by the suffering he knew awaited him.
Yet everything about the entry displayed his humility.
We should avoid seeking personal grandeur and willingly associate with people of modest circumstances.
How inappropriate for Christians to demand splendor when Christ deliberately rejected it!
The crowd welcomed him as the One who was to come, long promised and expected.
He came in the Lord's name.
Let us give him our best affections.
He is the blessed Savior who brings blessing, and the Father who sent him deserves our praise.
Glory to God in the highest heavens, blessed forever!

div.title: The fruitless fig tree and the temple (verses 12–18)
div.p: Jesus examined the fig tree seeking fruit.
The ordinary time for figs had not yet fully come, though it was approaching.
He found none.
The tree was made a warning not to other trees but to the people of that generation.
Henry sees it as a figure of judgment on the Jewish religious community of Jesus' day, in which Christ sought fruit but found none.
That is his historical interpretation rather than an assertion about every Jewish person.
Jesus then entered the temple and corrected the abuses taking place in its courts.
It showed that when the Redeemer came to Zion he would turn ungodliness away from Jacob.
The chief priests and scribes responded by looking for a way to kill Jesus rather than seeking reconciliation with him.
They must have feared that they were, in effect, fighting against God.

div.title: Prayer, faith and forgiveness (verses 19–26)
div.p: The disciples were astonished that the fig tree had withered so quickly.
Henry applies it again to people who reject Christ and to his historical reading of the Jewish church's condition.
We should never be satisfied with religion that does not produce good works.
Jesus taught his disciples to pray with faith.
Genuine Christian faith works great spiritual miracles.
It justifies us and thereby removes mountains of guilt, never to rise again in judgment against us.
It purifies the heart and removes mountains of sinful corruption, clearing the way for God's grace to transform our lives.
One principal reason to approach the throne of grace is to seek forgiveness of our sins.
That concern should occupy us every day.

div.title: Jesus challenges the religious authorities (verses 27–33)
div.p: Jesus showed the close relationship between his own teaching and baptism and John the Baptist's mission.
Both pointed toward establishing the gospel kingdom.
The elders who questioned Jesus were not sincerely seeking truth.
They wanted to win an argument.
He therefore did not owe them the explanation they pretended to desire.
Even without his direct reply, his works clearly demonstrated divine authority.
No human being could have performed those miracles unless God was with him.

row.cell: The parable of the vineyard and husbandmen.
The great command of the law.
Christ the Son and yet the Lord of David.

div.title: The vineyard and its wicked tenants (verses 1–12)
div.p: Through the parable, Jesus taught that God would set aside the Jewish church of his day as an outward institution that had rejected him.
The treatment faithful ministers have received in many ages is shameful.
Some have been persecuted by people who enjoyed religious privileges but failed to produce the corresponding fruit.
At last God sent his beloved Son.
We might expect people to honor someone whom the master himself loved.
Instead the tenants hated the Son precisely because he was the heir.
Christ's exaltation was the Lord's doing.
It is also God who raises up Christ in our hearts and establishes his rule there.
When he does so, it is wonderful to us.
Scripture, faithful preachers and above all Christ's incarnation summon us to honor God through our lives.
Sinners should beware of a proud, worldly attitude.
Those who mock or despise Christ's faithful ministers show the kind of reception they would have given Christ himself if they had met him during his earthly ministry.

div.title: The question about taxes (verses 13–17)
div.p: Christ's opponents pretended to seek guidance about duty, but their real purpose was to obtain an answer they could use to accuse him.
One of the most dangerous traps for Jesus' followers is becoming absorbed in worldly political quarrels.
Jesus escaped by directing them to recognize the civil obligations their nation had already accepted.
Everyone marveled at the wisdom of his answer.
Many praise the beauty or cleverness of a sermon without obeying its teaching.

div.title: Jesus teaches the resurrection (verses 18–27)
div.p: A correct understanding of Scripture—the fountain and foundation of revealed religion—is our best protection against error.
The Sadducees mocked the doctrine of resurrection.
Jesus corrected them by explaining the difference between earthly marriage and life in heaven.
Although marriage was established in the first earthly paradise, it will not continue in the heavenly one in the same way.
We create absurd ideas when we try to explain the world of spirits entirely through the arrangements of our present bodily life.
It would make no sense for the living God to remain the eternal portion and happiness of someone who had ceased to exist forever.
Thus Abraham's soul continues to exist and act, though for a time it is separated from his body.
Those who deny resurrection are seriously mistaken.
Let us pass through this dying world with a joyful expectation of eternal happiness and a glorious resurrection.

div.title: The greatest commandment (verses 28–34)
div.p: Jesus willingly teaches those who genuinely wish to understand God's will.
He explained that the greatest commandment, which contains all others in principle, is to love God with the whole heart.
When such love governs the soul, it creates a willingness to fulfill every other duty and to do what pleases him.
The old sacrificial offerings only pictured atonement for disobedience to God's moral law.
They were not themselves effective apart from repentance and faith in the promised Savior, producing moral obedience.
Since we have failed to love God and our neighbors in this way and have often done the opposite, we are condemned sinners in need of repentance and mercy.
Christ approved the scribe's understanding and encouraged him.
The man was well placed to go further.
Knowledge of God's law awakens conviction, leads toward repentance and the awareness of needing mercy, and enables us to understand justification through Christ.

div.title: David's Son and David's Lord (verses 35–40)
div.p: When we understand Scripture's teaching about Christ's person and offices, we are led to confess him as our Lord and God and obey him as the exalted Redeemer.
If ordinary people receive these truths gladly while the educated and powerful oppose them, the first have reason for joy and the second for pity.
Sin concealed beneath a display of piety is doubled wickedness and will meet an especially serious judgment.

div.title: Jesus praises the poor widow (verses 41–44)
div.p: Jesus still watches what his people give.
He knows both the amount and the motives.
He sees whether our gifts come from love for him or from a wish to be admired.
Many people would criticize the poor widow's offering.
Few would willingly imitate her.
Yet Christ commended her, so we know her action was good and wise.
At the final judgment, modest efforts of poor people to honor their Savior will receive his approval, while magnificent works of unbelievers done from wrong motives will be exposed as worthless.

row.cell: The destruction of the temple foretold.

div.title: Jesus foretells the temple's destruction (verses 1–4)
div.p: Christ places little value on impressive outward splendor where purity of heart is absent.
He looked with compassion upon ruined souls and wept over them.
We do not read that he mourned in the same way for the destruction of even a magnificent building.
Let this teach us the importance of having a lasting home in heaven, prepared for us through the Holy Spirit's work.
We should seek that preparation earnestly through every appointed means of grace.

div.title: Jesus warns against deception and persecution (verses 5–13)
div.p: Jesus answered the disciples not chiefly to satisfy curiosity but to direct their consciences and conduct.
When many people are deceived, believers should become more attentive to guarding themselves.
Christ's disciples may enjoy holy peace of mind even when everything around them is confused, provided they do not turn from their duty.
Suffering for Christ should never be allowed to draw them away from him.
Being hated by everyone is a serious trial.
Yet the work God assigned them would continue and prosper.
The servants may be crushed, but the gospel cannot be crushed.
The promised salvation is more than temporary rescue from danger.
It includes everlasting blessedness.

div.title: The approaching destruction of Jerusalem (verses 14–23)
div.p: Henry understands these warnings as pointing toward Jerusalem's destruction.
He says that rebellion against Rome and persecution of Christians accelerated the disaster, which came less than forty years after Jesus spoke.
The resulting devastation was extraordinary.
Promises that believers will receive strength to persevere fit perfectly alongside warnings not to fall away.
The more seriously we think about these events, the more reason we have to seek refuge in Christ without delay.
For the salvation of our souls, we should be prepared to relinquish every earthly attachment.

div.title: The future appearance of Christ (verses 24–27)
div.p: The disciples had confused the destruction of Jerusalem with the end of the world.
Jesus corrected that misunderstanding.
Henry distinguishes Jerusalem's tribulation from Christ's later coming and the last judgment.
Jesus foretold the final dissolution of the present arrangement of the world.
He also described his visible appearance in the clouds and the gathering of all the elect to him.

div.title: Remain watchful (verses 28–37)
div.p: This is the practical application of Jesus' prophetic teaching.
With regard to Jerusalem's destruction, Henry says the disciples should expect it soon.
With regard to the end of the world, they should not try to calculate the time.
No human being knows its day or hour.
Henry says that Christ, in his divinity, could not be ignorant of anything, while divine wisdom was communicated to his human soul according to God's pleasure.
That is his theological explanation of this passage, not a wording added to the biblical text.
The duty in either case is the same: watch and pray.
When Jesus ascended to heaven, he left meaningful work for every servant.
We should continually expect his return and remain at our assigned tasks.
The warning applies both to our individual death and to the general judgment.
We do not know whether our Master will summon us during youth, middle age or old age.
As soon as we are born, we begin moving toward death.
Our chief concern should be that Christ never finds us careless, idle, absorbed in pleasure or neglectful of duty.
His command to all is “Watch!”, so that we may be found in peace, without spot and blameless.

row.cell: The passover, Jesus declares that Judas would betray him.

div.title: Christ is anointed at Bethany (verses 1–11)
div.p: Christ poured out his soul to death for us. Can we regard anything as too precious to give him?
Do we offer him the precious ointment of our finest affections? We should love him with all our hearts, even when others misunderstand or criticize genuine devotion.

Charity toward poor people, though required, does not excuse neglecting particular acts of devotion to Jesus. Christ praised the woman's action and made it known to believers in every generation. Those who honor Christ will be honored by him.

Covetousness ruled Judas. The love of money that he had cherished became the occasion for his betrayal of his Master. The devil adapted his temptation to Judas's ruling desire and overcame him through it.
Sinful people often construct elaborate schemes to achieve their purposes. Yet the very circumstances they regard as helping them succeed will become curses to them in the end.

div.title: The Passover and the announcement of betrayal (verses 12–21)
div.p: The events surrounding this Passover were not the result of merely human foresight. The Lord knew them before they happened, as he knows everything concerning us.
If we receive him, he will dwell in our hearts.
The Son of Man went toward suffering and death as Scripture had foretold, like a lamb led to slaughter. Nevertheless, the betrayer remained guilty and faced a dreadful judgment.
God's permission of human sin does not compel anyone to sin. Nor does God's ability to bring glory out of wicked actions excuse those who freely commit them or reduce their punishment.

div.title: Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper (verses 22–31)
div.p: The Lord's Supper is nourishment for the soul. Therefore, only a small quantity of bread and wine is needed for the bodily sign.
Our Master instituted it by his own example and practice. It is to continue until his second coming.
He established it with blessing and thanksgiving, as a remembrance of his death.

The blood of Christ is repeatedly described as the price of our redemption. What comfort for repentant sinners that this blood is shed for many! If it is for many, why should I not seek its benefits myself?

The Supper signifies the communication of the blessings purchased by Christ's death. We should apply the truth of Christ crucified to ourselves, so that it becomes food and drink for the soul, strengthening and refreshing spiritual life.
It also gives an earnest and a foretaste of the happiness of heaven. Enjoying spiritual blessings should weaken our attachment to pleasures of the senses.
Whoever has tasted spiritual delights is led to desire eternal ones.
Although the great Shepherd endured every suffering without a single false step, his followers were scattered by a much smaller measure of suffering.
We are quick to think highly of our own courage and trust our own hearts. Peter should not have answered his Master with such self-confidence, but with fear and trembling.
Lord, give me grace so that I do not deny you.

div.title: Christ's agony in Gethsemane (verses 32–42)
div.p: Christ's suffering began with what was most painful: the suffering of his soul.
He became deeply amazed and distressed. Mark's words here express his anguish even more forcefully than Matthew's account.
The terrors of God stood before him, and he allowed himself to contemplate them. No sorrow had ever been like his.
He was now made a curse for us. The curses of the law were laid upon him as our Surety. He tasted death in all its bitterness.
His fear was the natural human fear of pain and death, from which human nature recoils.
Can we think lightly of sin when we see what our sins—even though they were only reckoned to him—brought upon Jesus? How can sin weigh so little upon us when it weighed so heavily upon him?
As we look upon the One we pierced, we should mourn over our sin rather than treat it as a small matter.
As man, Christ prayed that, if possible, the suffering might pass from him. As Mediator, he submitted himself completely to the Father's will: not what I will, but what you will.
The disciples' weakness returned and overcame them. Our bodies can weigh heavily upon our souls.

Yet when trouble approaches, we should prepare for it. Even believers can look upon the Redeemer's suffering drowsily: instead of being ready to die with him, they are sometimes unwilling to watch with him for one hour.

div.title: Jesus is betrayed and arrested (verses 43–52)
div.p: The religious rulers sought to destroy Jesus because he did not appear as an earthly prince. Instead, he preached repentance, reform and holy living and directed people's thoughts, desires and hopes toward the world to come.
Peter wounded one of those who came to arrest Jesus.

p.hi: It is easier to fight for Christ than to die for him.

div.p: Yet there is an important distinction between disciples who fail through weakness and hypocrites. Hypocrites may rashly call Jesus their Master and profess great affection, while delivering him into the hands of his enemies.
By their betrayal, they hurry toward their own destruction.

div.title: Jesus stands before the high priest (verses 53–65)
div.p: Jesus was condemned before the great Jewish council.
Peter followed, but the fire beside the high priest and the company of the high priest's servants were dangerous places for him. He had entered a temptation.
The council sought false witnesses diligently. Yet even by stretching their law as far as possible, their testimony was insufficient to establish a capital charge.
Jesus was asked whether he was the Son of the Blessed, meaning the Son of God.
He pointed to his second coming as proof of his identity.
The insults and violence directed against him reveal both humanity's hostility toward God and God's freely given, unspeakable love toward humanity.

div.title: Peter denies Jesus (verses 66–72)
div.p: Peter's denial began when he kept his distance from Christ.
Those ashamed of godliness are already on the path toward denying him.

People who fear spending time among Christ's followers because they might be drawn into suffering with them take a worse risk by spending time with his enemies: there they may be drawn into sin against him.
When crowds admired Jesus, Peter readily acknowledged him. Now, when Jesus was deserted and despised, Peter refused any association with him.
Yet Peter repented very quickly.
Let anyone who thinks he stands be careful not to fall.
And let anyone who has fallen remember Peter, consider their own sins, and return to the Lord with tears and earnest prayer, seeking forgiveness and renewal through the Holy Spirit.

div.title: Christ stands before Pilate (verses 1–14)
div.p: They bound Jesus.
We should often remember our Lord's bonds, remembering the One who was bound for us, and reckon ourselves bound with him.
By handing over their King, the religious leaders effectively handed over the kingdom of God. By their own action, it would be taken from them and entrusted to another nation.
Jesus answered Pilate directly but did not answer the witnesses. Their accusations were known to be false, and even Pilate was convinced of their falsehood.
Pilate hoped to appeal from the priests to the people, expecting the crowd to rescue Jesus from the religious leaders' demands.
But the priests stirred up the people still more. They cried for Jesus to be crucified.
We should judge people and events by their real character and by God's word, not by popular rumors.
No person ever received such disgraceful treatment as Jesus, the only perfectly wise, holy and excellent man ever to walk the earth.
Contemplating his mistreatment should give us a strong sense of humanity's wickedness and hostility to God and teach us to hate the sinful motives displayed by his persecutors.

div.title: Jesus is led out to be crucified (verses 15–21)
div.p: Jesus encountered death in one of its most terrifying forms: the death reserved for the worst criminals.
The cross brought shame.
Because sin had dishonored God, Christ made satisfaction by accepting the greatest disgrace human nature could bear.
Crucifixion was also regarded as a cursed death under the law (Deuteronomy 21:23).
Roman soldiers mocked Jesus as a king, just as the high priest's servants had mocked him as prophet and Savior.
Can a Christian be proud of splendid purple or scarlet clothing when such garments were used to mock Christ?
He wore the crown of thorns that we deserved, so that we might wear the crown of glory that he earned.
Sin made us liable to everlasting shame and contempt. To deliver us, Jesus freely submitted to shame and contempt.
He was led out among evildoers, though he himself had committed no sin.
The suffering of the meek and holy Redeemer continually teaches believers, who should never become weary of considering it.
After seeing what Jesus endured, how can I, a guilty sinner, indulge angry complaints, reproaches or threats when I experience harm or hardship?

div.title: Jesus is crucified (verses 22–32)
div.p: The place of Jesus' crucifixion was called the place of a skull, the customary place of execution. He was counted among transgressors in every respect.
When we look at Christ crucified, remember what was written above him: he is a King.
We must therefore submit ourselves to him as his true subjects.
Two thieves were crucified beside him, with Jesus in the middle, to deepen his humiliation.
Yet Scripture had foretold that he would be counted among transgressors because he was made sin for us.
Passersby insulted him.
They demanded that he come down from the cross before they would believe. But when he gave an even more convincing sign by rising from the grave, they still did not believe.
Anyone who truly understands the salvation purchased by the Son of God's suffering and death will seek it earnestly.
The first hope of pardon and eternal life produces thanksgiving, and the sins that brought the Lord of glory to the cross produce godly sorrow.

div.title: Christ dies (verses 33–41)
div.p: Thick darkness covered the land from noon until three in the afternoon.
The people were trying to extinguish the Sun of Righteousness.
The darkness signified the deep cloud over Christ's human soul when he offered himself for sin.
Jesus did not complain here that his disciples had forsaken him, but that his Father had forsaken him.
Especially in this suffering he was made sin for us.
Paul could rejoice even when describing his life as a sacrifice poured out in the service of the saints (Philippians 2:17).
But being offered as a sacrifice for sinners' sins was something incomparably greater.
At the instant Jesus died, the temple veil tore from top to bottom.
For unbelieving Jews, Henry takes this as an alarming sign of judgment upon their temple order and nation.
For believers, it declares the opening of a new and living way into God's holiest presence through Jesus' blood.
The centurion seems to have been deeply moved by the confidence with which Jesus had spoken to God as Father and entrusted his spirit to him.

Rightly understanding the crucified Christ reconciles believers to the thought of dying. They long to see, love and praise the Savior who was pierced and wounded to rescue them from the coming judgment.

div.title: Jesus is buried (verses 42–47)
div.p: We now stand beside the burial of our Lord.
May we, by grace, be united to him in the likeness of his burial.
Joseph of Arimathea was waiting for God's kingdom.
Those who hope to share that kingdom's blessings must be ready to acknowledge Christ's cause even when it seems utterly defeated.
God raised up Joseph to serve him at this moment.
Providence also ensured that Pilate investigated carefully whether Jesus had actually died. This removed any plausible claim that Jesus had merely survived the crucifixion.
Pilate gave Joseph permission to take the body down and bury it.
Some women watched where Jesus was laid because they intended to return after the Sabbath and anoint his body; there had been no time beforehand.
The exact location of the tomb mattered especially because Jesus would rise again.
He will not abandon those who trust and call upon him.
Death has lost its sting for the believer. It will soon end their sorrows, as it brought an end to the Savior's earthly sufferings.

row.cell: Christ's resurrection made known the women.
Christ appears to Mary Magdalene and other disciples.

div.title: The women learn that Jesus has risen (verses 1–8)
div.p: Nicodemus had brought many spices for Jesus' burial, yet the faithful women wanted to bring their own. Another person's demonstration of love for Christ should never prevent us from showing our own love.
Those whose devotion moves them to seek Jesus diligently often find that seemingly insurmountable obstacles are removed.
When we accept trouble and expense out of love for Christ, he accepts the devotion even if our plans do not succeed.
The sight of the angel ought to have encouraged the women, but instead they were frightened. We often turn what should comfort us into a cause for fear through our own misunderstanding.
Jesus was crucified, but now he is glorified. He is risen; he is no longer in the tomb, but alive again.
They would see him again. For now, they could look at the place where he had lain.
Those mourning for Jesus will receive encouragement at the proper time.
The angel named Peter particularly. This news would be precious to someone deeply grieved by his own sin.
Seeing Christ is a welcome comfort for a true penitent; and a truly repentant person is welcome before Christ.
The women went quickly to tell the disciples. Yet troubling fear may hinder us from serving Christ and other people as we would if our faith and joy were stronger.

div.title: Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene and other disciples (verses 9–13)
div.p: There can be no better news for grieving disciples than the announcement that Christ has risen.
We should seek to comfort sorrowing believers by telling them what we have learned of Jesus.
In God's wise Providence, proofs of the resurrection were given gradually and received cautiously. This made the apostles' later confident testimony more convincing.
Yet how slowly we accept the comfort offered by God's word!
While Jesus consoles his people, he may also need to rebuke their hardness of heart, both for doubting his promises and for failing to obey his commands.

div.title: Jesus commissions the apostles (verses 14–18)
div.p: The evidence confirming the gospel is abundant. People who reject it may be rightly rebuked for unbelief.
Jesus confirmed the calling of the eleven apostles and instructed them to take the gospel into all the world, preaching it to every creature.
Only those who are truly Christians are saved through Christ.
Simon Magus professed faith and received baptism, yet was later described as remaining bound in wickedness (Acts 8:13–25).
The faith that saves receives Christ in all his offices and characters, trusting him for every purpose of salvation.
It produces corresponding effects in the heart and life. Mere intellectual assent is dead faith and cannot save.
The commission reaches every creature throughout the world.
The gospel's message includes not only truths, invitations, encouragements and commands, but also solemn warnings.
The apostles received powers to perform miracles that confirmed the teaching they preached and assisted its spread among nations that had not heard it.

div.title: Christ ascends into heaven (verses 19 and 20)
div.p: After speaking to the apostles, Jesus ascended into heaven.
His sitting signifies both rest and royal authority.
He has finished his work and taken possession of his kingdom.
To sit at God's right hand declares his sovereign dignity and universal power.
Everything God does for us, gives us or accepts from us is through his Son, who is now glorified with the glory he possessed before the world existed.
The apostles went out preaching everywhere, near and far.
Their message was heavenly and spiritual, opposed to the world's ordinary desires, and met with great resistance.
They possessed none of the usual worldly supports for such a mission. Nevertheless, within a few years the gospel was announced across the known world.

Ministers today, Henry says, do not need to perform miracles to prove their message. Scripture's divine origin has already been confirmed, leaving people responsible for accepting or rejecting its testimony.

The changes the gospel continually produces when faithfully preached and genuinely believed—transforming human character and conduct—remain a constant and, in Henry's language, miraculous proof that the gospel is God's power for salvation to believers.

div.title: Luke — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Luke is generally believed to have been a physician and a companion of the apostle Paul.

Henry considers Luke's style and familiarity with Jewish rites and customs evidence that he was Jewish. At the same time, he considers Luke's Greek name and knowledge of the Greek language evidence of a Gentile background.
These apparently conflicting observations are retained as the commentator's own statements, rather than harmonized by an undocumented editorial decision.
Luke first appears in Acts 16:10–11, where he joined Paul at Troas. Henry says that he accompanied Paul to Jerusalem and was also with him during his travels and imprisonment in Rome.
The Gospel appears intended to replace the numerous deficient and unreliable accounts then circulating.
Its purpose is to provide an authentic and inspired account of Jesus' life, miracles and teaching, based on the testimony of people who heard and saw those events themselves.

row.cell: The birth of John the Baptist.

div.title: Luke's preface (verses 1–4)
div.p: Luke did not intend to write about questions on which Christians may safely disagree or remain uncertain.
He wrote about the things that are, and ought to be, firmly believed.
The teaching of Christ is what the wisest and best people have confidently entrusted their souls to, with deep satisfaction.
The great events on which our hope depends were recorded from the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning and ministers of the word.
Their understanding was brought to completeness through divine inspiration.

div.title: Zechariah and Elizabeth (verses 5–25)
div.p: The parents of John the Baptist were sinners, like everyone else, and were justified and saved in the same way as other believers.
Yet they were distinguished by their genuine godliness and integrity.
They had no children, and Elizabeth's advanced age meant they could no longer expect a child by ordinary means.
While Zechariah burned incense in the temple, the people were gathered outside in prayer.
All prayer offered to God can be accepted and answered only through Christ's intercession in the heavenly temple.
We must pray ourselves, earnestly and from the heart, if we hope to share in that intercession.
Even our best prayers receive an answer of peace only through the mediation of Christ, who always lives to intercede.
Zechariah had often prayed for a child.
Those prayers were not forgotten: prayers offered in faith are kept before God, and he may answer requests made in youth when we have reached old age.
Gifts received through prayer bring a special kind of happiness.
The promised son would be a means of turning many people to God and preparing them to receive Christ's gospel.
He would go before the Savior with courage, zeal, holiness and detachment from earthly pleasures and ambitions.
The disobedient would be turned toward the wisdom of righteous ancestors—or, more fully, toward the wisdom of the Righteous One who was coming.
Zechariah heard the angel's promise but spoke in unbelief.
