God rightly made him unable to speak because he had objected to the divine word.
Yet even that correction was kind: it prevented further expressions of unbelief and strengthened his faith.
When discipline helps us trust God's word more fully, we have no reason to complain.
Even sincere believers may dishonor the Lord through unbelief. Their mouths are sometimes closed in confusion when they should be open in grateful praise.
We should recognize the Lord's merciful attention when he looks upon us with compassion and acts for our good.

div.title: Gabriel announces Jesus' birth to Mary (verses 26–38)
div.p: Here we learn about the mother of our Lord.
We should not pray to Mary, but we should praise God for the favor he showed her.
Christ's birth was necessarily miraculous.
The angel greeted Mary as someone specially chosen and favored by the Most High, receiving an honor that generations of Jewish mothers had long hoped for.
The greeting troubled her, but the angel assured her that God had shown her favor.
She would bear a son named Jesus, the Son of the Most High, sharing in divine nature and perfection.
How precious the name Jesus—Savior—is to sinners who know their need!
We often fail to run to him because we do not recognize either our own poverty and peril or his immeasurable riches.
A person truly convinced of sin's guilt and the judgment it deserves would continually ask: Is the Savior mine?
Such a person would willingly overcome anything that hindered coming to him.
Mary's response expressed humble wonder and faith, not a demand for a sign.
Great indeed is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy 3:16, the cited source wording).
Christ's human nature was brought into being in a way appropriate for its union with the divine nature.
Like Mary, we should bring our desires into agreement with God's word.
In every difficulty, remember that nothing is impossible with God.
When we hear his promises, we should turn them into prayers:

p.hi: I am the Lord's willing servant; let it happen to me according to your word.

div.title: Mary visits Elizabeth (verses 39–56)
div.p: People in whom God has begun the work of grace benefit from sharing their experience with one another.
When Mary arrived, Elizabeth recognized the presence of the one who would become mother of the great Redeemer.
Filled with the Holy Spirit, she declared Mary and the child she carried greatly blessed because God had honored and loved them.
Mary, strengthened by Elizabeth's words and herself moved by the Holy Spirit, responded with joy, wonder and gratitude.
Mary knew she was a sinner who needed a Savior.
She could rejoice in God only through the salvation provided in the promised Messiah.
Those who recognize their need of Christ and hunger for righteousness and life in him receive the best gifts.
He fills them with spiritual blessings until they are satisfied.
The poor in spirit will find their longing fulfilled, while those who imagine they need nothing will depart empty.

div.title: John the Baptist is born (verses 57–66)
div.p: John's birth brought joy throughout the family.
His name, Johanan, was associated by Henry with “gracious”, because John would introduce the gospel of Christ, in which God's grace shines so clearly.
Zechariah's speech returned.
Unbelief had closed his mouth; believing opened it again.

p.hi: He believed, and therefore he spoke.

div.p: When God opens our lips, we ought to praise him.
It would be better to lack speech than to possess it and never use it to glorify God.
The Lord's hand was with John.
God can work in the lives of infants in ways we cannot fully explain.
We should notice what he does and wait to see what follows.

div.title: Zechariah's prophetic song (verses 67–80)
div.p: Zechariah prophesied about the Messiah's kingdom and salvation.
The gospel brings light.
In John's ministry, the dawn began to break, growing brighter until the fullness of daylight.
The gospel reveals what was hidden: the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ.
It revives those sitting in death's shadow, like condemned prisoners in a dark dungeon.
It guides our feet onto the way of peace, the path that will at last bring us to peace (Romans 3:17).
John showed strong faith, vigorous and holy affections, and freedom from excessive fear or love of the world.
Through those years he grew ready for useful work, though he lived privately until he appeared publicly as the Messiah's forerunner.
Let us pursue peace with everyone, while also seeking peace with God and with our consciences.
If God calls us to remain unknown to the world, we can still grow diligently in the grace of Jesus Christ.

row.cell: It is made known to the shepherds.
Christ with the learned men in the temple.

div.title: Christ is born (verses 1–7)
div.p: The fullness of time had come.
God sent his Son, born of a woman and born under the law.
The circumstances of Jesus' birth were extraordinarily humble.
He was born where travelers lodged, as a temporary guest in the world. His brief earthly stay teaches us to regard ourselves as sojourners here too.
Through sin, humanity had become like an abandoned newborn—helpless and without hope. Christ entered a condition resembling ours.
He knew how reluctant people are to live in humble homes, wear ordinary clothing or eat simple meals.
He knew how parents desire to decorate and indulge their children, how readily poor people envy the rich, and how often rich people look down upon the poor.
Yet when we look in faith at the Son of God made human and lying in a manger, our vanity, ambition and envy are challenged.
We can hardly contemplate that scene properly and still make earthly greatness the object of our desires for ourselves or our children.

div.title: Angels announce the birth to shepherds (verses 8–20)
div.p: Angels announced the Savior's birth, but they were sent to humble, devout and hardworking shepherds.
These shepherds were carrying out their ordinary occupation, watching their sheep.
Faithful work does not put us beyond the reach of God's gracious visits. We may remain close to him while carrying out an honest calling.
The glory of this work belongs to God: Glory to God in the highest.
All God's works display his glory, but the redemption of the world displays his glory in the highest way.
God's goodwill toward humanity, made known through the coming of the Messiah, brought peace into this world.
Here peace means all the good that flows to us because Christ took our nature upon himself.
An innumerable company of angels confirmed this welcome message.
The shepherds hurried to the place.
Having found what they were told to expect, they spread the good news about the child who was the Savior, Christ the Lord.
Mary carefully kept and considered everything that happened.
These events strengthened her devotion.
We, too, would avoid many errors in judgment and behavior if we pondered more deeply what God has revealed about his Son.
The announcement remains good news for us: a Savior, Christ the Lord, has been born.

div.title: Jesus is circumcised and presented in the temple (verses 21–24)
div.p: Our Lord Jesus was not born in sin.
Unlike sinners, he did not need the death of a corrupt nature or renewal toward holiness that circumcision symbolized.
For him, the ordinance anticipated his coming perfect obedience to the whole law, through suffering and temptation, even to death on our behalf.
After forty days, Mary went to the temple to offer the sacrifices appointed for purification.
Joseph also presented the holy child Jesus.
As a firstborn son, he was to be dedicated to the Lord and redeemed according to the law.
Let us similarly present our children to the Lord who gave them to us, asking him to rescue them from sin and death and make them holy to himself.

div.title: Simeon prophesies about Jesus (verses 25–35)
div.p: The same Spirit who sustained Simeon's hope now brought that hope to joyful fulfillment.
Those who desire to see Christ should seek him where he makes himself known.
Simeon confessed that the child he held was the Savior himself—the salvation God had appointed.
He was ready to leave the world.
How small this world appears to someone who holds Christ and beholds salvation!
Simeon's words show the comfort of a godly person's death.
Such a person departs at peace with God, at peace in conscience, and at peace with the thought of death.
Those who have welcomed Christ can welcome death.
Joseph and Mary marveled at what was said about Jesus.
Simeon's prophecy also gave them reason to rejoice with reverent trembling.
Jesus, his truth and his people continue to be spoken against.
His teaching becomes a test that reveals human character.
Some people's hidden good desires are exposed when they embrace him.
Other people's hidden corruption is revealed through their opposition to him.
Human beings will be judged according to their heart's response to Christ.
Jesus would be a suffering Savior, and his mother would suffer too because of her close relationship and love for him.

div.title: Anna speaks about Jesus (verses 36–40)
div.p: There was much wrong in the religious community of that period, but God had not left himself without witnesses.
Anna lived at the temple or attended it constantly.
She was devoted to prayer and served God in everything.
People to whom Jesus has been revealed have good reason to thank the Lord and tell others about him, as she did.
The examples of Simeon and Anna should encourage older believers.
Their gray hair is a crown of honor when they continue in the way of righteousness.
Before our lips are silenced by death, let us use them to praise our Redeemer.
It was fitting for Christ to be made like his brothers and sisters in every respect.
He passed through infancy and childhood as other children do, yet without sin and with clear signs of his divine nature.
By the Spirit of God all his powers functioned perfectly.
Other children have foolishness bound up in their hearts, as their actions and words reveal. Jesus, by contrast, was full of wisdom.
Everything he said and did was appropriate and wise, far beyond his years.
While other children reveal the corruption of fallen nature, he displayed only the grace of God.

div.title: Jesus speaks with teachers in the temple (verses 41–52)
div.p: Children honor Christ when they attend public worship.
Jesus' earthly parents remained for all seven days of the festival.
It is good to stay to the end of worship rather than hurry away from holy duties.
Those who have lost the comfort of fellowship with Christ and the assurance of belonging to him should ask where, when and how they lost these blessings and retrace their steps.
They should seek him where he has promised to make himself known.
Mary and Joseph found Jesus in the temple, where teachers of the law instructed their students.
He listened, asked questions and answered questions with remarkable wisdom.
Young people should seek the truth of God, attend the teaching of the gospel and ask their elders and teachers thoughtful questions that will deepen their understanding.
Those who seek Jesus sorrowfully can find him again with greater joy.
Jesus explained that he must be in his Father's house, attending to his Father's business.
All God's children should likewise make the Father's work their first concern, letting other matters yield to it when necessary.
Yet although Jesus was the Son of God, he submitted to his earthly parents.
How can ordinary people justify disobedience to their parents when the divine Son obeyed his?
We may fail to understand human speech because it is unclear. But we must not dismiss God's words as though they were unreliable.
What first seems difficult may later become plain.

Even the greatest and wisest can learn from this extraordinary Child that true greatness includes knowing our proper position, fulfilling our calling and refusing pleasures that conflict with our duties.

row.cell: John the Baptist testifies concerning Christ.

div.title: John the Baptist's ministry (verses 1–14)
div.p: The purpose of John's ministry was to turn people away from their sins and toward the Savior.
He did not preach loyalty to a sect or party, but a profession of repentance.
Baptism with water was the outward sign.

John taught that repentance was necessary for the forgiveness of sins. Washing with water represented the inward cleansing and renewal of heart that accompanies or results from genuine repentance, as well as a public profession of it.
John fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah 40:3.
Preparing the way for the gospel in someone's heart means bringing down proud thoughts, submitting them to Christ and removing what obstructs the coming of his grace.
John gave warnings and practical instructions.
Fallen humanity has become a brood of vipers, corrupt and hostile even toward one another.
The only escape from coming judgment is repentance, shown by a changed way of life.
Neither religious profession nor membership in the visible people of God is of any value without holiness of heart and conduct.
Such privilege only makes judgment more serious if we do not produce fruit worthy of repentance.
John addressed different kinds of people according to their circumstances and occupations.
Anyone claiming repentance must show it through a reformed life appropriate to their responsibilities.
The gospel calls us to mercy rather than empty sacrifice, doing every possible good and treating everyone justly.
The same principle that makes a person refuse dishonest gain also leads that person to restore what was gained by wrongdoing.
John gave soldiers particular instructions suited to the temptations of their work.
His answers both explained immediate duties and tested the sincerity of those asking.
No one can genuinely receive salvation through Christ without repentance, and the marks of that repentance can be seen in such actions.

div.title: John bears witness to Christ (verses 15–20)
div.p: John denied being the Messiah, but strengthened people's expectation of the long-promised Savior.
John could exhort them to repent and declare God's forgiveness upon repentance.
He could not produce repentance in their hearts or grant remission himself.
What an example of speaking highly of Christ and humbly of ourselves!
John baptized only with water as a sign of the need for cleansing.

p.hi: Christ baptizes with the Holy Spirit.

div.p: Jesus gives the Spirit to cleanse the heart, not only as water removes outward dirt but as fire purifies metal, burning away its impurities and making it fit for a new form.
John preached affectionately, pleading with his hearers.
He preached practically, awakening them to their duties and showing them what to do.
He spoke in language ordinary people could understand.
He preached evangelically, always directing his hearers toward Christ for both righteousness and strength.
He preached abundantly, withholding nothing from the counsel of God.
Yet his public ministry was abruptly stopped while he was still useful.
John rebuked Herod's many sins, and Herod imprisoned him.
People who mistreat faithful servants of God increase their own guilt.

div.title: Jesus is baptized (verses 21 and 22)
div.p: Jesus did not confess sin as the other people did, because he had no sin to confess.
Yet he prayed, as they did, remaining in fellowship with his Father.
Henry observes that the three heavenly testimonies to Jesus' identity were given while he was praying or soon afterward (Luke 9:35; John 12:28).
The Holy Spirit descended upon him in a visible form like a dove.
A voice came from heaven, from God the Father, bearing witness to God the Son.
His baptism thus displayed the truth of the Holy Trinity—three persons in the one Godhead.

div.title: The genealogy of Jesus (verses 23–38)
div.p: Matthew's genealogy shows Jesus as Abraham's descendant, through whom every family on earth would be blessed, and as heir to David's royal throne.
Luke's genealogy traces the line back to Adam, showing Jesus as the promised offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent's head.
Henry describes Heli as Mary's father rather than Joseph's, presenting this as an explanation of the apparent differences between the two Gospel genealogies.
Other learned interpreters have proposed explanations of those differences.
But our salvation does not depend on our ability to solve every genealogical difficulty. Such difficulties do not overthrow the divine authority of the Gospels.
Adam is called the son of God in the sense that he was God's offspring by creation.
Christ is both Son of Adam and Son of God, qualified to be the Mediator between God and the descendants of Adam and to bring those descendants into God's family through himself.
All flesh descended from the first Adam is like grass that dries and fades.
Those who receive the Spirit of life from the second Adam possess the eternal blessedness announced in the gospel.

row.cell: Christ in the synagogue of Nazareth.
He casts out an unclean spirit and heals the sick.

div.title: The temptation of Jesus (verses 1–13)
div.p: Being alone in the wilderness gave the tempter an apparent advantage over Jesus.
No friend was present to pray for or advise him in the hour of testing.
Jesus knew his own strength, so he could allow that situation. We know our own weakness and must not deliberately put ourselves in temptation's way.
Made like his brothers and sisters, Jesus lived in dependence upon God's providence and promise.
God's word is our sword, and faith in it is our shield.
God has countless ways to provide for his people. We can therefore trust him while remaining in the path of duty.
Satan's promises are deceptive.
If he has influence over worldly power and honor, he uses them as bait to entice people toward destruction.
Any opportunity to gain wealth or status through sin is a price offered for the soul; reject it.
Our true riches, honor and happiness are found through worshiping and serving God.
Christ would not worship Satan. When the Father delivers the kingdoms of the world to Jesus, he will not allow the worship of the devil to continue in them.
Satan also tempted Jesus to bring about his own death by throwing himself down on the strength of an unauthorized claim to divine protection.
This would have been presumption, not faith.
Do not abandon Scripture because Satan or other people misuse it.
Study it more diligently and use it to defend yourself against every kind of attack.
Let the word dwell richly within us; it is our life.
Christ overcame the devil not only for himself but for us.
He allowed the tempter to use every approach, yet Satan found nothing sinful within Jesus for the temptation to take hold of.
Resist the devil, and he will flee.
He withdrew only for a season.
Henry contrasts this earlier temptation, aimed at drawing Jesus into sin, with Satan's later persecution, aimed at bringing him to suffering.
The serpent would bruise Christ's heel yet have his own head crushed (Genesis 3:15).
We are never entirely beyond Satan's reach while we remain in this fallen world.

div.title: Jesus teaches in Nazareth (verses 14–30)
div.p: Jesus taught in the synagogues, places where people gathered to read, explain and apply Scripture, and to pray and praise God.
The Holy Spirit's gifts and graces rested upon him without measure.
Christ releases sinners from the guilt of sin and, through his Spirit and grace, from sin's corrupting power.
Through the word of his gospel he brings light to people in darkness.
Through the power of grace he opens the eyes of the spiritually blind.
He proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord.
Let sinners respond to the Savior's invitation while freedom is being announced.
Jesus' name was Wonderful.
Nothing shows this more clearly than the astonishing grace in his words and the transforming power accompanying them.
How remarkable that he spoke such gracious words to people so lacking in grace!
Prejudice often supplies an excuse for rejecting the humbling message of the cross.
People whose hearts are offended by God's word may blame the preacher's manner rather than admit opposition to the truth itself.
The teaching of God's sovereignty and right to act as he wills angers proud people.
They refuse to seek God's favor on his terms and resent those who receive the mercy they neglect.
Many still reject Jesus though they hear his words.
May we instead honor him as the Son of God and Savior of humanity, showing our faith through obedience rather than dishonoring him through sin.

div.title: Jesus drives out evil spirits and heals people (verses 31–44)
div.p: Jesus' teaching deeply affected his hearers.
Its power reached human consciences.
His miracles showed him as the conqueror of Satan and the healer of disease.
When Christ grants someone a renewed life through recovery from sickness, that life should be devoted more fully to his glory and service.
Our work should include spreading the good news about Christ, praying for those suffering in body or mind, and using our influence to bring sinners to him for healing.
He expelled evil spirits from many who were possessed.
We were not placed in the world simply to serve ourselves.
We are here to glorify God and do good to our generation.
People came looking for Jesus.
Even a desert is no longer desolate when Christ is with us.
He continues to accompany believers through his word and Spirit.

His blessings will be made known to more nations, until people throughout the earth who once served Satan recognize Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, and find redemption through his blood—the forgiveness of sins.

row.cell: The miraculous draught of fishes, Peter, James, and John called.
Levi called, Christ's answer to the Pharisees.

div.title: The miraculous catch and the calling of fishermen (verses 1–11)
div.p: After Jesus had finished preaching, he instructed Peter to return to the work of his ordinary occupation.
Time spent in public worship or religious instruction during working days need not make us less diligent in our employment.
Indeed, it can improve our conduct and frame of mind in ordinary work.
How cheerfully can we fulfill our daily responsibilities when we have first spent time with God and sought to have our work sanctified through his word and prayer!
Peter and his companions had caught nothing. Yet Jesus told them to lower the nets again.
We should not abandon our lawful occupations simply because success does not come as quickly or fully as we hoped.
It is good to act according to Christ's word, whatever recent experience may suggest.
The extraordinary catch was a miracle.
Peter acknowledged himself to be a sinner.
All of us must confess that Jesus would be justified in leaving us because of our guilt.
Yet we should also beg him not to leave, because what hope could sinners have if their Savior departed?
Rather, ask him to dwell within our hearts by faith and make them clean and new.
These fishermen left everything to follow Jesus when their fishing had become profitable.
It is especially commendable to leave riches for Christ when they are increasing and tempting us to set our hearts on them.

div.title: Jesus cleanses a man full of leprosy (verses 12–16)
div.p: The man was described as full of leprosy.
His disease pictured the corruption of our fallen nature through sin.
From head to foot we have no soundness apart from divine healing.
His words combined great confidence in Christ's power with profound humility.
A sinner who knows personal unworthiness may ask: I know Christ can make me clean, but will he receive someone like me? Will he apply his blood to cleanse my sin?
Henry encourages such a person to come to Jesus confidently, yet humbly submitting the matter to his mercy.
When we have received deliverance from the guilt and power of sin, we should tell others of Christ and help them come to him to hear his word and receive healing.

div.title: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man (verses 17–26)
div.p: Many attend gatherings where the gospel is preached but do not truly listen.
They sit near God's word without receiving it as a message addressed to them.
The friends bringing the paralyzed man teach us the importance of pressing forward earnestly toward Christ.
Such persistence shows faith, pleases Jesus and leads us to him.
Lord, grant us faith in your willingness and power to heal our souls.
Make us desire forgiveness of sins more than health, earthly prosperity or even life itself.
Enable us to trust your authority to forgive.
Then we will gladly rise and go wherever you command.

div.title: Jesus calls Levi and answers the Pharisees (verses 27–39)
div.p: How wonderful is the grace of Christ!
He called a tax collector to become his disciple and follower.
His call worked powerfully and effectively.
He came to call sinners to repentance, assuring them that forgiveness is available.
He endured with patience the hostility and contradictions directed against himself and his disciples.
He also arranged his disciples' duties according to their present strength and level of growth.
The Lord prepares his people gradually for the trials appointed to them.
We should imitate that patience when helping someone weak in faith or undergoing temptation, rather than placing burdens on them that they are not yet ready to bear.

row.cell: The disciples pluck corn on the sabbath.
Works of mercy suitable to the sabbath day.

div.title: The disciples gather grain on the Sabbath (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jesus defended his disciples because they had gathered ears of grain to satisfy a genuine need for food on the Sabbath.
Yet we must not turn that freedom for necessary work into an excuse for committing sin.
Christ calls us to remember that the day belongs to him and should be spent in his honor and service.

div.title: Jesus heals on the Sabbath (verses 6–11)
div.p: Christ was neither ashamed nor afraid to display the purpose of his grace.
He healed the man even though he knew that his enemies would use the act as an accusation against him.
We should not allow opposition to draw us away from duty or discourage us from doing good.
The wickedness of the human heart can be astonishing.

div.title: Jesus chooses the twelve apostles (verses 12–19)
div.p: We often think thirty minutes a long time to spend in meditation and private prayer.
Yet Jesus spent whole nights in prayer.
When serving God, our concern should be not to waste time, but to allow one good duty to lead into the next.
The twelve apostles are named here.
Few people have been granted greater privileges.
Yet one of them was possessed by the devil and became a betrayer.
People who live far from faithful gospel preaching should be willing to travel for it rather than go without.
It is worthwhile to travel a considerable distance to hear Christ's word and even to interrupt other business for that purpose.
The people also came to be healed, and Jesus healed them.
Christ has more than enough grace and healing power for all, and enough for each individual.
People usually regard physical disease as a worse evil than spiritual corruption.
Scripture teaches us to take a different view.

div.title: Jesus announces blessings and woes (verses 20–26)
div.p: Much of this teaching also appears in Matthew 5–7.
Henry notes that some interpreters think Jesus preached these words at a different time and place.
Everyone who takes the commands of the gospel to heart and lives according to them may also take its promises as their own and live by them.
Jesus announced woes against prosperous sinners who are actually miserable, however much the world envies them.
Those whom Christ blesses are truly blessed.
Those against whom he pronounces judgment are in dreadful danger.
The difference between the eternal outcomes of believer and unbeliever is immeasurably greater than any difference between prosperity and suffering here on earth.
The righteous may suffer greatly now, while unrepentant sinners flourish.
Their final rewards will reveal an entirely different judgment.

div.title: Jesus teaches mercy toward enemies (verses 27–36)
div.p: These commands are difficult for fallen human nature.
Yet when we are deeply rooted in faith in Christ's love, his commands become easier to accept.
Anyone who comes to Jesus to be washed in his blood and understands his great mercy may sincerely ask:

p.hi: Lord, what do you want me to do?

div.p: Let us seek to be merciful as our heavenly Father is merciful to us.

div.title: Jesus teaches justice and sincerity (verses 37–49)
div.p: Christ used these teachings often because they could readily be applied to daily life.
We should be very cautious when condemning other people, because we ourselves need mercy and understanding.
Those who are generous and forgiving also experience the benefit of that spirit.
The final and complete reward for our actions lies in the world to come.
Nevertheless, even in this life divine Providence gives encouragement to those who practice kindness.
People who follow crowds into wrongdoing take the broad road toward destruction.

p.hi: A tree is known by its fruit.

div.p: May Christ's word be planted deeply in our hearts so that our words and actions bear good fruit.
Ordinary speech usually reveals what occupies the heart.
Only those who think, speak and act according to Christ's words are preparing wisely for the trials of life and eternity.
They build their hope on Jesus Christ, the Rock of Ages.
No other saving foundation can be laid.
At death and at judgment such people are secure, because through faith they are kept by Christ's power for salvation and will never perish.

row.cell: John the Baptist's inquiry concerning Jesus.
Christ anointed in the house of the Pharisee, The parable of the two debtors.

div.title: Jesus heals the centurion's servant (verses 1–10)
div.p: Servants ought to conduct themselves in ways that earn the affection and trust of those they serve.
Masters, in turn, have a particular duty to care for their servants during sickness.
We should still bring the illness of our families to Christ through faithful and earnest prayer.
Building places where God's people can gather for worship is a good work, showing love for both God and his people.
Jesus was pleased with the centurion's faith.
He always fulfills the expectations of faith that honors his power and his love.
The servant's healing was both immediate and complete.

div.title: Jesus raises the widow's son (verses 11–18)
div.p: Jesus saw the widow following her son's body toward the grave and had compassion on her.
Consider his power over death itself.
His gospel call to everyone, and especially to young people, is to rise from the dead and receive his light and life.
When Christ restored the young man, the change became visible: he sat up.
If he has given us his grace, our conduct should reveal it.
The young man also began to speak.
Similarly, when Jesus grants spiritual life, he opens our lips in prayer and praise.
When divine power accompanying the gospel raises people spiritually dead in sin, we ought to glorify God and recognize his gracious visit to his people.
May we belong to this compassionate Savior and look with joy toward the day his voice will summon everyone from the grave.
May we share in the resurrection of life, not the resurrection of condemnation.

div.title: John the Baptist asks about Jesus (verses 19–35)
div.p: Jesus' miracles displayed his power in the natural world.
But he added the evidence of his work in the kingdom of grace: the gospel was preached to the poor.
The ministry of John had already shown that Christ's kingdom was spiritual.
John prepared the way by calling people to repentance and a reformed heart and life.
Those who were moved neither by John's ministry nor by Jesus' own teaching were rightly condemned.
They mocked the different ways God graciously addressed them.
Many people ruin themselves by refusing to take the matters of their souls seriously.
Let us show ourselves to be children of wisdom, attending to God's word and reverencing the truths and good news that unbelieving people and Pharisees ridicule.

div.title: The repentant woman and the two debtors (verses 36–50)
div.p: Only a broken heart can understand how precious Christ is and how glorious the gospel's mercy is.
Repentant sinners feel they can never express enough sorrow over their sins or enough gratitude for his kindness.
The self-satisfied are often offended that the gospel welcomes such people.
The Pharisee Simon noticed the woman's past reputation, but failed to rejoice over the evidence of her repentance.
No one can escape the coming judgment without freely granted forgiveness.
Jesus purchased that forgiveness with his blood and gives it to everyone who believes in him.
Through the parable of two debtors, Jesus led Simon to admit that someone forgiven a larger debt has reason for greater love.
Sin is a debt, and everyone is indebted to Almighty God.
Some are guilty of greater offenses than others.
But whether our debt is large or small, it is more than we can repay.
God is ready to forgive.
His Son purchased pardon for believers; the gospel promises it; and his Spirit assures repentant sinners of it and gives comfort.
Let us reject Simon's pride.
Relying on Christ alone, we should love and obey him more deeply and recommend him more earnestly to others.
The more we show genuine sorrow for sin and love for Jesus, the clearer the evidence that we have received forgiveness.
Grace transforms both the sinner's standing before God through the complete forgiveness of sins and the sinner's heart and conduct through faith in Christ.

row.cell: Christ stilleth the tempest and casteth out devils.
The daughter of Jairus restored to life.

div.title: Jesus' ministry and the women who supported it (verses 1–3)
div.p: Jesus' regular work was preaching and teaching the gospel.
The message of God's kingdom was the good news he had come to bring.
Some women accompanied him and supported his work with their own resources.
That Jesus had need of their practical kindness reveals the humble, poor condition he willingly accepted.
That he received their help shows his deep humility.
Though rich, he became poor for our sake.

div.title: The sower, the lamp and Jesus' true family (verses 4–21)
div.p: The parable of the sower contains important warnings and instructions about hearing God's word.
How blessed we are—and how completely indebted to free grace—if teaching that entertains others without transforming them becomes clear truth to us, teaching and directing our conduct.
We must notice what hinders us from benefiting from what we hear.
Do not listen carelessly or superficially.
Do not allow prejudice to block the word.
After hearing, guard your heart so that you do not lose what you have gained.
God continues or withdraws the gifts entrusted to us according to how we use them for his glory and others' good.
It is not enough merely to avoid suppressing the truth through unrighteousness.
We should also hold out the word of life, shining for people around us.
Faithful listeners demonstrate their faith by doing what Christ says.
Jesus recognizes those who hear and obey him as members of his own family.

div.title: Jesus calms the storm and drives out demons (verses 22–40)
div.p: Those who embark upon a journey at Christ's own command should nevertheless be ready for storms and even serious danger.
When guilt and fear of judgment overwhelm the soul, only Jesus can give relief.
We must turn to him and cry, Master, I am lost unless you help me!
When he brings us safely through danger, we should be ashamed of our distrustful fears and give him all the glory for our rescue.
The account of the possessed man teaches us about evil spirits.
Henry says that such spirits do not now act in precisely the same way as in that episode, but we must always be alert to their malice.
They are numerous and hostile toward humanity and its good.
Christ leads those under his rule through loving guidance.
The devil drives those under his rule with violent cruelty.
What comfort for believers that every power of darkness remains under the authority of the Lord Jesus!
It is an act of mercy when someone under Satan's influence is rescued rather than destroyed.
Christ will not force his company upon those who despise him.
People who reject him risk never receiving another opportunity, even while others would gladly welcome him.

div.title: The woman is healed and Jairus's daughter restored (verses 41–56)
div.p: While doing our duty and helping people, we need not complain simply because crowds and hurried circumstances surround us.
Yet when there is no useful purpose in such activity, wisdom often calls us to avoid it.
Some suffering people are helped, healed and saved by Jesus without attracting attention in a crowd.
The woman approached trembling, but she possessed saving faith.
Fear and trembling can coexist with true faith.
Jesus encouraged Jairus: Do not fear; only believe, and your daughter will be restored.
The loss of an only child is a terrible grief.
Trusting God through that loss and through fear that it might continue forever is exceedingly difficult.
Perfect faith overcomes fear; as fear increases, faith is often weakened.
Christ's gracious power accompanies his commands and makes them effective.
After raising the child, he told those present to give her food.
People newly raised from spiritual death likewise need spiritual nourishment, so they may grow as newborn children do.

row.cell: Peter's testimony to Christ, Self-denial enjoined.
Christ checks the ambition of his disciples.
Every thing to be given up for Christ.

div.title: Jesus sends the twelve apostles (verses 1–9)
div.p: Jesus sent out his twelve disciples, who had by then learned enough from him to begin instructing others.
They were not to seek people's respect through an impressive outward appearance.
They should go as they were, without anxiety over worldly provisions.
The Lord Jesus is the source of all power and authority, and every creature is ultimately subject to him.
If he accompanies his ministers' preaching with power to release sinners from Satan's bondage, he will also provide for their needs.
When truth and love come together in this way yet God's message is rejected, those who despise it have no excuse. Their rejection becomes testimony against them.
Herod's guilty conscience made him think John might have risen from death.
He wanted to see Jesus. Why did he not simply go to him?
Henry suggests it was probably pride or a desire to avoid another person who would rebuke his sins.
Because Herod delayed, his heart grew harder.
When he finally saw Jesus, he treated him with the same prejudice as others (Luke 23:11).

div.title: Jesus feeds the crowd (verses 10–17)
div.p: People followed Jesus, even when it was inconvenient.
He nevertheless gave them what they truly needed.
He taught them about God's kingdom and healed the sick.
Then with five loaves and two fish he fed five thousand men.
The Lord will not let people who fear and faithfully serve him lack any good thing.
When we receive the comforts of ordinary life, we should acknowledge that they come from God.
We are not worthy of them.
We owe both these gifts and the pleasure we find in them to Christ's mediation, through which the curse has been removed.
Christ's blessing can make a little accomplish much.
He fills every hungry soul and satisfies it from the goodness of his house.
There were leftovers.

p.hi: Our Father's house contains bread enough, and more than enough.

div.p: Christ's resources are not narrow or limited.

div.title: Peter confesses Jesus; the disciples must deny themselves (verses 18–27)
div.p: What comfort that Jesus is God's Anointed One!
This means he was both appointed to be the Messiah and fully equipped for his mission.
Jesus explained his approaching suffering and death.
His disciples were not to seek to prevent his suffering. They were to prepare for their own suffering as his followers.
We frequently meet crosses on the road of duty.
We must not deliberately bring suffering upon ourselves.
But when a cross is placed upon us in the course of obedience, we must take it up and follow Christ.
Our true welfare depends on the condition of our souls.
A body cannot be happy in eternity if its soul is miserable.
Yet the soul may be truly blessed even when the body endures serious pain and oppression here.
We must never be ashamed of Christ or his gospel.

div.title: The transfiguration (verses 28–36)
div.p: Christ's transfiguration gave the disciples a glimpse of the glory in which he would return to judge the world.
It encouraged them to suffer for him.
Prayer is a transforming duty. It can make a person's face shine.
Even when glorified on the mountain, Jesus was willing to speak about his coming suffering and death.
During our greatest moments of earthly joy, remember that we have no permanent city here.
How greatly we need to pray for enlivening grace!
The disciples were drowsy, but later awoke fully enough to witness what happened and report it.
People who propose building earthly tents for glorified saints in heaven have misunderstood the event.

div.title: Jesus delivers a child from an evil spirit (verses 37–42)
div.p: The child's condition was distressing.
He was oppressed by an evil spirit.
Henry regards such afflictions as more dreadful than sickness arising only from natural causes.
Satan brings terrible harm wherever he gains influence.
How blessed are those who can come to Christ!
He can do what even his disciples cannot.
With one word, Jesus healed the child.
When our own children recover from illness, it is comforting to receive them as restored by Christ's hand.

div.title: Jesus corrects the disciples' ambition (verses 43–50)
div.p: Jesus plainly predicted his suffering, but the disciples resisted understanding him because it did not fit their expectations.
He used a young child as an example of simplicity and humility.
What greater honor could someone receive in this world than to be welcomed as a messenger of God and Christ, with the Father and Son receiving that welcome as directed to themselves?
The twelve disciples had an unusually strong reason to expect other believers to identify with their group.
Yet Jesus warned them not to forbid people who were acting in his name merely because they did not follow with the Twelve.
People may be faithful followers of Christ and accepted by him even when they are not part of our own fellowship.

div.title: Jesus rejects the disciples' mistaken zeal (verses 51–56)
div.p: The disciples failed to understand the Samaritan villagers' conduct.

Their refusal to receive Jesus and his followers reflected national prejudice and sectarian hostility, rather than the kind of opposition to God's worship involved in the judgment of Ahaziah and Elijah.
The Samaritans had not assaulted or harmed them.
The cases were therefore very different.
The disciples also failed to understand that the gospel's distinctive miracles were to be works of mercy.
Most importantly, they failed to recognize what was actually moving their own hearts: pride and worldly ambition.
It is easy to boast about our zeal for the Lord while in reality pursuing our own interests, injuring others and accomplishing harm rather than good.
Jesus exposed and corrected those motives.

div.title: Following Jesus without delay (verses 57–62)
div.p: One person eagerly offered to follow Jesus, but seems not to have considered the cost.
To follow Christ we must let go of dreams of worldly greatness.
We cannot sincerely combine Christian discipleship with making earthly advantage our governing aim.
Another seemed willing to follow, but asked for a short delay.
Jesus himself had called this person.
True religion teaches kindness, family responsibility and honoring our parents.
Yet family duties must not be made excuses for neglecting obedience to God.
A third wanted time to speak with friends and arrange affairs at home.
His earthly concerns occupied more of his heart than they should.
He was placing himself within reach of a temptation that could divert him from following Jesus.
No one can attend effectively to one task while continually distracted by another.
Those who begin God's work must determine to continue.

p.hi: Looking back leads to drawing back, and drawing back leads to destruction.

div.p: Only those who persevere to the end will be saved.

row.cell: Jesus at the house of Martha and Mary.

div.title: Jesus sends out the seventy (verses 1–16)
div.p: Jesus sent seventy disciples, two by two.
This allowed them to encourage and strengthen one another.
The gospel ministry calls people to receive Christ as both Prince and Savior.
He will come with the power of his Spirit to every place where he sends his faithful messengers.
Those who receive God's grace in vain face a dreadful judgment.
To despise, belittle or mock Christ's faithful ministers is ultimately to despise God and Christ, whose message they carry.

div.title: The joy of Jesus and his disciples (verses 17–24)
div.p: Every victory over Satan comes through power received from Jesus.
He must receive all the praise.
Beware of spiritual pride, which has destroyed many.
Jesus rejoiced in the prospect of many people being saved.
The Gospel particularly records this moment of joy.
There were relatively few such moments for him, because he was a Man of Sorrows.
Yet in the hour he learned of the disciples' success and saw Satan's power being defeated, he rejoiced.
God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.
The more simply we depend upon the Son of God for teaching, help and blessing, the more we will know both Father and Son.
We will enjoy the sight of our Savior's glory and the hearing of his words and become more useful in advancing his cause.

div.title: Jesus tells the parable of the good Samaritan (verses 25–37)
div.p: We must never speak carelessly about eternal life and the way to receive it.
Such careless speech dishonors God.
No one can love God and neighbor with pure spiritual love without God's converting grace.
The proud human heart resists this truth.
Jesus described a Jewish traveler robbed, wounded and left nearly dead.
He was neglected by people who should have been his friends.
He received help instead from a Samaritan, someone belonging to a nation Jews deeply despised.
How sorrowful to see selfishness in people of every social rank!
How many excuses do we make to avoid trouble or expense in helping someone else?
The genuine Christian has the law of love written on the heart.
The Spirit of Christ lives within, renewing Christ's image in the soul.
This parable explains loving our neighbors as ourselves without regard to nation, faction or other divisions.
It also illustrates the kindness of God our Savior toward sinful and miserable people.
We resemble the wounded traveler.
Satan, our enemy, has robbed and harmed us through sin.
The blessed Jesus looked on us with compassion.
He loved us and gave his life for us while we were his enemies and rebels.
Having shown us mercy, he commands us to go and do likewise.
Each of us, according to our opportunities and abilities, must help people who are in distress and need.

div.title: Jesus visits Martha and Mary (verses 38–42)
div.p: A good sermon is not made worse simply because it is preached in a private home.
Visits among friends should be arranged so they contribute to the good of people's souls.
To sit at Jesus' feet means readiness to receive his word and submit to its direction.
Martha was preparing food and hospitality for Jesus and those with him.
Her care expressed genuine respect for her Lord and proper concern for her household.
Yet her conduct also deserved correction.
She wanted much serving: plenty of food, variety and careful attention to every detail.
Earthly responsibilities become a trap when they keep us from serving God or receiving spiritual good.
Even when hosting fellow believers, we can waste needless time and money on elaborate arrangements.

p.hi: Martha was wrong on this occasion, but she remained a genuine believer.

div.p: Henry does not claim that her ordinary life neglected the one essential thing.
God's favor is necessary for happiness; Christ's salvation is necessary for safety.
When these are our first concerns, we can attend to other matters properly.
Mary chose the good portion by submitting herself to Christ's instruction.
The things of this world will eventually be taken from us, or we will be taken from them.
But nothing can separate us from Christ's love and the share we possess in it.
Neither human beings nor demons can take it away; God and Christ will not take it away.
Let us therefore give the one essential thing our deepest attention.

row.cell: Christ encourages being earnest in prayer.
Christ casts out a devil, The blasphemy of the Pharisees.

div.title: Jesus teaches his disciples to pray (verses 1–4)
div.p: “Lord, teach us to pray” is a good and necessary request.
Only Jesus can truly teach us how to pray, through his word and Spirit.
Lord, teach me what prayer means, awaken in me the desire to pray and show me what I should ask and say.
Jesus gave the disciples a prayer very similar to the one he had taught in the Sermon on the Mount.
Matthew and Luke use slightly different wording, but Henry considers those differences unimportant to the prayer's meaning.
When praying for others and ourselves, we should approach our heavenly Father, trusting his goodness and power.

div.title: Jesus encourages perseverance in prayer (verses 5–13)
div.p: Jesus encourages us to pray earnestly and continually.
We should ask for what we truly need, as someone asks a kind neighbor for bread.
If God does not immediately answer our requests, we should not give up. He will act in his appointed time.
Especially, ask for the Holy Spirit.
We need his help to pray well, but also because all spiritual blessings are included in that one great gift.
Through the Spirit we come to know God and ourselves, repent, believe in Christ and love him. We find comfort in this life and are prepared for the happiness of the next.
Our Father is more willing to give spiritual blessings to those who ask than a loving human parent is to give food to a hungry child.
Faithful prayer quiets and steadies the heart in God.

div.title: Jesus defeats the devil's power and warns against empty reform (verses 14–26)
div.p: Casting out demons showed Jesus destroying the power of evil spirits.
Henry compares an unconverted heart to a palace where Satan exercises authority.
There can be a counterfeit peace in such a heart: a sinner feels perfectly safe, has no doubt about spiritual standing and has no fear of coming judgment.
True conversion changes everything.
It is Christ's victory over the devil's rule in a soul, restoring freedom and bringing the mind and body into service to Christ.
But a hypocrite may have a house that looks swept and decorated without being cleansed.
A sinner may confess unwillingly like Pharaoh, show false sorrow like Ahab, or carry out only a partial reform like Herod.
Such changes sweep up loose dirt while leaving a favorite sin untouched.
Outward virtues, abilities and religious appearances are decorations, not true grace.
A heart never given to Christ and never inhabited by the Holy Spirit remains unrenewed.
We should never be satisfied with an outward religion that someone may possess while still falling short of heaven.
Without Christ, the evil spirits return readily and resume their power.
May we seek real deliverance from this dreadful condition.

div.title: Those who obey God's word are blessed (verses 27 and 28)
div.p: The scribes and Pharisees insulted Jesus' teaching, but a woman marveled at the wisdom and power of his words.
Jesus directed her attention to a greater blessing.
Hearing God's word is a privilege.
But only those who hear, remember and follow it as their rule of life are truly blessed by the Lord.

div.title: Jesus warns those who demand signs (verses 29–36)
div.p: Jesus promised the sign of Jonah, which Matthew explains in relation to Christ's resurrection.
Even if Jesus himself preached constantly and worked miracles every day in a congregation, the hearers would not profit unless divine grace humbled their hearts.
Do not demand more signs or teaching than God has chosen to give.
Rather, pray for opened hearts and understanding so that the light already received will benefit us.
Beware especially that your supposed light is not really darkness.
Wrong governing principles will corrupt both judgment and conduct.

div.title: Jesus rebukes the Pharisees (verses 37–54)
div.p: We must examine our hearts and seek to have them cleansed and renewed.
While fulfilling the great demands of the law and gospel, we must not overlook smaller duties God has commanded.
When others watch our words, seeking an excuse to trap us, Lord, give us prudence and patience.
Defeat their malicious purposes, and grant us meekness enough to bear insults for Christ with joy, resting under the grace of the Holy Spirit.

row.cell: Christ reproves the interpreters of the law.
A caution against covetousness, The parable of the rich man.
A warning to be reconciled to God.

div.title: Jesus warns against denial and hypocrisy (verses 1–12)
div.p: Faith in God's universal providence should support us in danger and help us continue trusting him as we perform our duty.
God notices even sparrows and their smallest concerns. He therefore watches over the least interests of his disciples.
Those who acknowledge Jesus now will be acknowledged by him before God's angels at the final judgment.
Those who deny him to protect their life or gain worldly power will ultimately suffer a far greater loss: Christ will not acknowledge them.
But a trembling believer who has fallen and genuinely repents need not doubt the possibility of forgiveness.
That differs entirely from the hardened, determined hostility toward the Holy Spirit which, as Henry explains, is not forgiven because it is not repented of.

div.title: Greed and the rich fool (verses 13–21)
div.p: Christ's kingdom is spiritual, not an earthly empire.
Henry says Christianity does not seek political rule as its reward. It requires everyone to act justly, but does not promise worldly power or wealth as the advantage of receiving grace.
The benefits promised to Christ's disciples are of a higher kind.
We constantly need warning against greed.
Wealth cannot provide true happiness, comfort or satisfaction to a soul.
The rich fool was a clever manager of worldly affairs but neglected God's providence, life's uncertainty, the value of his soul and eternity.
Even professing believers sometimes hold up such worldly-minded people as models to imitate.
Our thoughts are not hidden from God.
When the man's land produced abundantly, instead of thanking the Lord and rejoicing that he could do more good, he was troubled: What shall I do now?
The poorest beggar could scarcely have spoken with greater anxiety.
Possessing more often creates more cares.
The man intended to use his abundance only for bodily pleasure, not to help others.
God would require his soul from him and call him to account.
What folly to pursue benefits for the body and for a few years while neglecting the soul and eternity!

div.title: Jesus calls his little flock away from anxiety (verses 22–40)
div.p: Jesus repeatedly warned against anxious, tormenting care for earthly things (Matthew 6:25–34).
Cast your cares on God, for this is the way to find peace.
Just as worry cannot change our height, it cannot give us sovereign control over our circumstances.
We should accept our situation under God's care instead of endlessly chasing worldly comforts.
Even necessary material things become harmful when pursued in panic and excessive worry.
Do not imagine every future disaster and invent needless cares in trying to prevent it.
If we value holiness, we will not be ruled by a desire for luxury.
Examine whether we belong to Christ's little flock.
He is our Master, and we are both working servants and waiting servants.
Remain ready to meet him, as household servants waiting late into the night for their master's return.
Henry connects this with Jesus' ascension, his summons to each believer through death, and his future return to judge the world.
Because the hour is unknown, remain prepared like someone guarding a house when a thief may arrive.

div.title: Watchfulness despite division (verses 41–53)
div.p: Everyone must apply Jesus' warnings personally.
Each person knows many wrong things they should avoid and many right duties they neglect. Ignorance therefore leaves no one without responsibility.
The gospel's spread would cause division and suffering.
That does not mean Christianity itself is violent or hostile; it is pure, peaceful and loving.
Conflict arises because its truth contradicts people's pride and sinful desires.
Before the gospel could be proclaimed widely, Jesus had a baptism of suffering and death to undergo—very different from baptism with water or the Spirit.
We should eagerly make the truth known even if it causes disagreement or opposition within families.
Through that witness people are converted and God receives glory.

div.title: Seek reconciliation while there is time (verses 54–59)
div.p: People should show the same practical wisdom about their souls that they show in ordinary affairs.
Hasten to make peace with God before it is too late.
When conscience tells us that our sin has set us against the Lord, come to him as God reconciling the world to himself through Christ.
While we are alive, we are still on the way, and this is the time to receive his mercy.

row.cell: Christ exhorts to repentance from the case of the Galileans and others.
The parables of the mustard seed, and leaven.
Exhortation to enter at the strait gate.
Christ's reproof to Herod, and to the people of Jerusalem.

div.title: Repent instead of judging victims (verses 1–5)
div.p: People told Jesus how some Galileans had been killed.
Henry observes that this tragedy is recorded here briefly but is not described by the historians known to him.
Jesus also mentioned people killed when a tower collapsed.
Buildings constructed for protection can become the occasion of a person's death.
He warned his listeners not to conclude that unusually great suffering proves unusually great sin.
No place or occupation can protect someone from sudden death.
Rather than condemning those who suffer, let the death of others awaken us to our own need to repent.
Jesus calls us to repentance because God's kingdom is near, and warns that unless we repent, we too will perish.

div.title: The barren fig tree (verses 6–9)
div.p: The parable reinforces this warning: a fruitless tree is eventually cut down.
Henry understands it first as applying to the Jewish people and nation.
But it also warns everyone who enjoys the privileges of God's visible church and the opportunities offered through his grace.
The Lord has endured our barrenness patiently.
We may hope for further patience, but cannot presume that judgment will be postponed forever.

div.title: The woman healed on the Sabbath (verses 10–17)
div.p: Jesus regularly attended public worship on the Sabbath.
Bodily weakness, unless extremely serious, should not ordinarily prevent us from taking part in worship.
The woman came to hear teaching and receive spiritual good, and Jesus then relieved her physical suffering.
Her healing pictures crooked souls made straight by God's grace, which then glorify God.
Jesus saw that the synagogue leader's apparent concern for Sabbath observance masked hostility toward Jesus and his gospel.
He did not really want the woman healed on any day.
But the Savior's word and power can free those who are in bondage.
Henry observes that spiritual deliverance is often experienced on the Lord's day.
Work that helps someone receive God's blessings fits the purpose of the day.

div.title: The mustard seed and leaven (verses 18–22)
div.p: As in Matthew 13, these parables show the advance of the gospel.
The Messiah's kingdom is the kingdom of God.
May grace grow in our hearts!
May our faith and love increase so clearly that they give convincing evidence of genuine spiritual life.
May God bless those who live near faithful believers through their example.
May grace spread from heart to heart until something once small grows into a multitude.

div.title: Enter through the narrow gate (verses 23–30)
div.p: Our Savior came to direct consciences, not satisfy curiosity.
Instead of How many will be saved?, ask Will I be among them?
Instead of debating another person's end, ask What must I do, and what will become of me?
Each of us must personally strive to enter through the narrow gate.
Those who are saved undergo a change of the whole person.
The warning is urgent.
But no one should despair about themselves or others.
Some who are first will be last, and some last will be first.
In heaven we may meet people we never thought would be there and miss others whom we confidently expected.

div.title: Jesus speaks of Herod and Jerusalem (verses 31–35)
div.p: Jesus accurately called Herod a fox.
Even great rulers must answer to God, and Christ had authority to expose this proud ruler's character.
Henry explicitly says this is not an example for us to imitate in insulting rulers.
Jesus knew he would die soon.
When his appointed task was completed, he would be perfected in the sense of having finished the work he came to do.
We should regard our remaining time as short and fulfill today's duty today.
Jesus is particularly grieved by the wickedness of people and places that profess a special relationship with God.
The final judgment will convince unbelievers.
Let us therefore welcome and profit from those who come in the Lord's name to invite us to share Christ's saving grace.

row.cell: Christ heals a man on the sabbath.
The necessity of consideration and self-denial.

div.title: Jesus heals on the Sabbath (verses 1–6)
div.p: The Pharisee who hosted Jesus seems to have intended harm by inviting him, as others had done.
Yet Jesus did not refuse to heal the sick man simply because opponents would object to his actions on the Sabbath.
We must carefully distinguish the demands of piety and charity, the work of genuine necessity and habits of selfish indulgence.
True wisdom from above teaches us to continue patiently in doing good.

div.title: Jesus teaches humility and generosity (verses 7–14)
div.p: Jesus notices our behavior even in ordinary daily activities.
He watches us not only during worship but also around our tables.
Human pride often brings a person low, while humility prepares the way for lasting honor.
Christ teaches us that practical charity is better than a show of importance.
He did not mean that proud people who give generously without faith can demand a reward from God.
Rather, he calls us to help poor and afflicted people from love for him.

div.title: The great banquet (verses 15–24)
div.p: This parable displays the free grace and mercy of God through Christ's gospel.
To people who recognize their spiritual poverty and misery, the gospel provides food and a feast for the soul.
The invited guests all found some excuse for staying away.
Henry applies the initial rejection to the Jewish nation's neglect of Christ's gracious invitation.
It also exposes the reluctance present in the human heart to accept the gospel.
People who reject the offer are ungrateful, treating the God of heaven with contempt and provoking his righteous anger.
When the invitation was refused, the apostles were sent to the Gentiles, and the church was filled with people from the nations.
God has not prepared the gospel's rich provision in vain.
If some refuse it, others will thankfully accept.
The poor and socially insignificant are as welcome to Christ as the wealthy and powerful.
Indeed, the gospel often prospers especially among those suffering poverty, disability or other worldly disadvantages.
At last Christ's house will be full, when the number of his elect people is complete.

div.title: Count the cost of following Jesus (verses 25–35)
div.p: Not every disciple of Christ will be crucified, but every disciple must bear a cross while performing the duties of faith.
Jesus commands us to expect this and carefully consider it.
The illustration of building a tower teaches us to count the expense of our discipleship.
The illustration of a king considering battle teaches us to weigh its dangers.
The cost includes putting sin to death, even the sinful desires we love most.
Even the boldest sinner cannot withstand God when he judges.
Who can measure the power of his anger?
Our true interest is to seek peace with him.
We need not send to discover his terms of peace; he has already offered them, and they are wholly for our good.
Every believer's faith will be tested in some form.
May we be genuine disciples, not careless in our profession or frightened away by the cross.
Then we will be good salt in the earth, spreading something of Christ's goodness to those around us.

row.cell: Parables of the lost sheep, and the piece of silver.
The prodigal son, his wickedness and distress.

div.title: The lost sheep and lost coin (verses 1–10)
div.p: The lost sheep illustrates the great work of human redemption.
The sinner has wandered away from God and is exposed to certain destruction unless brought home.
Yet the sinner does not naturally want to return.
Christ earnestly seeks and brings lost people back.
In the second parable, the missing coin was just one piece of comparatively small value.
Yet its owner searched carefully until she found it.
These pictures show the different ways God works to bring lost souls back to himself and the Savior's joy when they return.
Let us make sure our own repentance is real and leads to salvation.

div.title: The younger son's sin and misery (verses 11–16)
div.p: The parable of the prodigal son teaches what repentance is and how ready the Lord is to welcome and bless those who return.
It displays the riches of gospel grace and has helped countless sinners find encouragement to repent.
It is already wrong, and the beginning of still worse evil, when people regard God's gifts as debts owed to them.
Sinners are foolish to content themselves with receiving their good things only during this life.
Our first parents tried to become independent of God, destroying themselves and their descendants.
The same desire for independence lies beneath persistent sin.
We can recognize aspects of ourselves in the prodigal son.
A sinful condition means distance from God.
It means squandering thoughts, mental powers, time and opportunities.
It is a condition of spiritual poverty, lacking necessary food and clothing for the soul or provision for the world to come.
It is a condition of degrading bondage: serving sinful desires is like being reduced to feeding pigs.
It brings continual dissatisfaction.
Earthly wealth and bodily pleasures cannot even permanently satisfy our bodies, much less the soul.
The world and flesh cannot supply what a soul needs; they offer what poisons it instead of nourishing it.
A sinful condition is spiritual death, because the sinner lacks the life of God.
It is also a lost condition.
Unless God's mercy intervenes, those separated from him will perish eternally.
The prodigal son's misery is only a faint picture of the ruin brought by human sin.
Yet how few recognize their true condition!

div.title: The younger son's repentance and welcome (verses 17–24)
div.p: The prodigal's recovery began when he came to himself.
This is a turning point in conversion.
The Lord opens the sinner's eyes and convinces the heart of sin.
The person now sees everything—including self and God—in a different light.
The sinner recognizes that even the humblest servant of God is happier than a person still in rebellion.
It is helpful to think of God as a Father and our Father when returning to him.
The prodigal did not merely decide to return; he rose and continued until he reached home.
In the same way, the penitent sinner resolutely leaves slavery to Satan and sinful desires and returns to God through prayer, overcoming fear and discouragement.
The Lord meets such a person with unexpected signs of forgiving love.
The humble sinner is clothed in the Redeemer's righteousness.
Through the Spirit of adoption, peace of conscience and the grace of the gospel, the believer receives strength to walk in holiness.
The Savior welcomes such people with divine consolation, and grace forms within them the desire and strength both to will and to do what is right.

div.title: The elder brother resents mercy (verses 25–32)
div.p: The elder brother illustrates the spirit of the Pharisees, though Henry says the warning goes beyond them.
It also exposes the proud response that may arise when people see God's mercy extended to others.
Henry compares this resentment with the attitude of many Jews toward Gentiles who had turned to Christ.
People in every age can object to the gospel and its messengers in the same way.
How terrible to hate or despise people for whom Christ shed his precious blood, whom the Father loves and in whom the Holy Spirit dwells!
Such an attitude springs from pride, excessive confidence in one's own righteousness and ignorance of one's heart.
The mercy and grace of God shine not only when he receives a repenting prodigal.
They also appear in his gentle patience toward irritable and resentful saints.
Those children of God who remain near their Father's house enjoy an incomparable blessing: they are with him and will continue with him.
Happy are those who receive Christ's invitation with gratitude.

row.cell: The parable of the unjust steward.
Christ reproves the hypocrisy of the covetous Pharisees.

div.title: The dishonest manager (verses 1–12)
div.p: Everything we possess belongs to God.
We have only been entrusted with its use, according to his instructions and for his honor.
The manager in Jesus' parable wasted his master's goods.
We can all be charged with failing to use what God has entrusted to us as well as we should.
We will eventually be called to give an account and leave our stewardship behind.
This reminds us that death will end the opportunities we now possess.
The dishonest manager reduced the debts owed by his master's tenants to secure friends for himself.
The master praised the manager's foresight, not his dishonesty.
The parable never commends fraud or justifies cheating an employer.
It shows that people devoted to worldly goals often act with greater calculation, energy and perseverance than people who seek spiritual goals.
Worldly people choose an unworthy ultimate object, but they can teach us by the determination with which they pursue it.
How much more diligently should the children of light pursue eternal good!
True riches are spiritual blessings.
If someone squanders on self-indulgence or hoards worldly wealth entrusted by God, what evidence is there that the person is an heir of God through Christ?
Earthly riches are insecure and deceptive.
Those who are rich in faith, rich toward God and rich in Christ and his promises are truly wealthy.
Let us store treasure in heaven and look there for our lasting inheritance.

div.title: God cannot be served alongside wealth (verses 13–18)
div.p: Jesus added a solemn warning: no one can serve God and the world as rival masters.
Their interests pull in opposite directions.
The greedy Pharisees mocked his teaching.
But their defense of the law distorted its real meaning, as Jesus illustrated by speaking about divorce.
Many people cling fiercely to outward religious forms while loving wealth and opposing the power of genuine godliness.
Such people even try to stir others against the truth.

div.title: The rich man and Lazarus (verses 19–31)
div.p: Jesus contrasted the condition of a righteous and an unrighteous person in this life and the next.
Scripture does not say the rich man gained his wealth by fraud or oppression.
Its warning is more serious: someone can enjoy great wealth, luxury and pleasure and still perish under divine judgment.
The rich man's sin was using everything for himself, without concern for Lazarus.
Lazarus was godly though deeply poor and afflicted.
Even some of God's dearest servants experience enormous hardship in this world.
We are not told that the rich man actively hurt him.
But he did nothing to care for him.
Death revealed the immense difference between them.
The rich man lifted his eyes in torment.
Henry says it is unlikely that actual conversations occur between glorified saints and condemned sinners.
The dialogue instead illustrates the hopeless misery, futile desires and unrelieved suffering of those finally condemned.
Those who now despise God's people may one day long for their kindness.
But there will be no relief from final judgment.
Sinners are warned now to remember their spiritual condition, though many deliberately avoid thinking about it.
Unrepentant people may enjoy their best things only during earthly life, while believers may endure their greatest troubles only here.
The blessings of heaven will never leave the redeemed; the consequences of final condemnation will never end.
In the present life there is still no impassable gulf between sin and grace.
By God's mercy a person can repent and turn to him.
But death in sin fixes the sinner's condition.
The rich man had five brothers and wished to prevent them from joining him.
He had helped encourage their sinful path; their arrival would only increase his misery.
How many people would wish after death to undo the things they wrote, said or did!
Henry explicitly warns against using the rich man's plea to Abraham as evidence that Christians should pray to departed saints.
It is the desperate request of a condemned person, and the request was refused.
A visitor from the dead could not deliver a better message than Scripture already gives.
The corruption that rejects God's written word would also reject supernatural warnings.
Let us consult the law and the testimony (Isaiah 8:19–20), the reliable prophetic word (2 Peter 1:19).
No warning or argument produces true repentance without God's regenerating grace renewing the heart.

div.title: Original chapter outline — explicit verse-label corrections

row.cell: To avoid offences, To pray for increase of faith, Humility taught.

div.title: Avoid causing offense; forgive and serve humbly (verses 1–10)
div.p: The fact that offenses will occur does not lessen the responsibility or punishment of anyone who causes them.
Faith in God's forgiving mercy helps us overcome even great difficulties in forgiving our brothers and sisters.
Nothing is impossible for God, and remarkable things are possible to those who truly trust him.
Jesus taught the disciples that they needed deep humility.
The Lord owns and rules his creatures in a way no human master owns another person.
God cannot become indebted to us for our service.
Even our obedience does not earn a claim upon him, and our duties do not deserve a reward as though he owed us one.

div.title: Jesus cleanses ten people with leprosy (verses 11–19)
div.p: Awareness of our spiritual leprosy should humble us as we approach Christ.
It is enough to appeal to his compassion, because his mercies never fail.
We may hope to find divine mercy when we are walking in the path of obedience.
Only one of the ten healed people returned to thank Jesus.
Like him, we should bring deep humility into thanksgiving as well as prayer.
Jesus particularly noticed the grateful man: he was a Samaritan.
The other nine received physical healing.
Henry distinguishes the Samaritan as the one who also received a spiritual blessing.

div.title: The coming of God's kingdom and judgment (verses 20–37)
div.p: The kingdom of God was already among the Jewish people—or, more precisely, within some of them.
It is a spiritual kingdom established in the heart through the power of divine grace.
Jesus reminded people of earlier times when sinners continued their usual routines despite warnings of coming judgment.
Those who are careless and absorbed in pleasure will be terribly surprised when judgment overtakes them.
Henry applies this both to the Roman destruction of the Jewish nation and to Christ's future return to judge the world.
The same pattern appears in every generation: sinners live securely in wrongdoing, forgetting the end toward which they are moving.
Wherever people marked for final ruin may be, divine judgment will find them.
Let us therefore be ready for the revelation of the Son of Man.

row.cell: The parable of the importunate widow.
The ruler hindered by his riches.
A blind man restored to sight.

div.title: The widow who persisted in seeking justice (verses 1–8)
div.p: All God's people are people of prayer.
Jesus taught us to persevere, especially in asking for spiritual blessings.
The widow persisted even before an unjust judge.
She might have feared that repeated requests would only increase his hostility.
Our situation is different: our earnest prayers please our gracious God.
Yet even to the end of the world, believers will need this warning because faith can grow weak.

div.title: The Pharisee and the tax collector (verses 9–14)
div.p: Jesus told this parable to challenge those who trusted their own righteousness and despised other people.
God sees the motives and attitudes with which we approach him during worship.
The Pharisee trusted in his own supposed righteousness.
He may genuinely have avoided many public and scandalous sins.
Those were commendable things in themselves.
Many people live in ways far worse than this Pharisee, yet he was not accepted by God.
Why?
He entered the temple to pray, but his mind was filled with himself and his own good actions.
He did not consider God's grace something worth asking for.
Beware of proud religious behavior and contempt for others.
The tax collector's prayer expressed humility, repentance and a longing for God.
It was short but reached the point:

p.hi: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”

div.p: How thankful we should be that this answered prayer has been preserved for us!
The man returned home justified.
Everyone who comes to God in the same humble faith through Jesus Christ can find that mercy.
The tax collector acknowledged his sin both by fallen nature and by actual practice.
He had nothing to rely on but God's mercy alone.
God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.
Justification comes from God through Christ, so those who condemn their own sin rather than proclaim their own righteousness receive it.

div.title: Children are brought to Jesus (verses 15–17)
div.p: No child is too small or too young to be brought to Christ.
Jesus knows how to show kindness even to those who are not yet able to serve him.
He desires that children be brought to him.
Henry speaks of the divine promise given to believers and their descendants, encouraging families to welcome children into the Savior's presence.
We must all receive God's kingdom as children receive a gift.
It cannot be bought.
We must acknowledge it as a gift from our heavenly Father.

div.title: Riches hinder a ruler from following Jesus (verses 18–30)
div.p: People may have many admirable qualities yet perish because they lack one essential thing.
The ruler could not accept the terms Jesus set because they required surrendering his wealth.
Many people reluctantly leave Christ even when they would rather hold on to him.
Their conscience and sinful desires struggle, but their desires eventually prevail.
They wish they could serve both God and money.
When forced to choose, however, they surrender God rather than worldly gain.
