Their supposed obedience proves to be only an outward appearance.
Some form of love for the world lies underneath.
Peter spoke too proudly about what the disciples had left and suffered for Jesus.
Instead of boasting about our sacrifices, we should be ashamed that serving the Savior ever caused us reluctance or regret.

div.title: Jesus foretells his death (verses 31–34)
div.p: The Spirit of Christ in the Old Testament prophets had foretold both the Messiah's sufferings and the glory afterward (1 Peter 1:11).
The disciples' assumptions were so strong that they refused to understand Jesus' prediction literally.
They eagerly received prophecies about the Messiah's glory while overlooking those concerning his suffering.
We too misunderstand Scripture when we read only the parts that sound pleasant to us.
Our own pride, self-love and worldly desires can close our understanding to the true meaning of Christ's suffering, crucifixion and resurrection.

div.title: Jesus restores a blind man's sight (verses 35–43)
div.p: The blind man sat begging beside the road.
He was both blind and poor, a fitting picture of the human condition Christ came to heal.
The prayer of faith, guided by Christ's promises and resting on them, is never wasted.
Those who receive grace should acknowledge it thankfully and give God glory.
People whose eyes Jesus opens will follow him.
We should praise God not only for kindness shown to ourselves but also for mercies granted to other people.
To understand spiritual things rightly, let us come to Christ as this man did, earnestly asking him to open our eyes to the excellence of his teaching and the value of his salvation.

row.cell: The parable of the nobleman and his servants.

div.title: Zacchaeus is converted (verses 1–10)
div.p: Anyone who sincerely wishes to see Christ should imitate Zacchaeus, overcoming obstacles and making the necessary effort to reach him.
Jesus invited himself to Zacchaeus's home.
Wherever Christ comes, he opens the heart and makes it willing to receive him.
A person who sincerely wants to know Christ will be known by Christ.
Those whom Jesus calls must humble themselves and come down.
We may welcome him with joy because he brings every true good gift.
Zacchaeus publicly showed that he had genuinely been converted.
He did not expect to be justified by his good works.
Rather, by his actions he showed, through God's grace, the sincerity of his faith and repentance.
Now that Zacchaeus had turned from sin to God, he was truly blessed.
He had been saved from both sin's guilt and its power and shared in all the benefits of salvation.
Christ had entered his home, and where he comes he brings salvation.
Jesus came into this lost world to seek and save the lost, when no other salvation was available.
He seeks even those who had not begun to seek or ask for him.

div.title: The nobleman and his servants (verses 11–27)
div.p: This parable resembles the parable of the talents in Matthew 25.
When Christ calls people, he equips them with gifts needed for their responsibilities.
Anyone entrusted with power or resources must use them in service.
The Spirit's gifts are given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7).
Everyone who has received a gift must use it in serving others (1 Peter 4:10).
Christ calls his servants to account for the opportunities entrusted to them.
The parable also warns of the punishment awaiting those openly hostile to him and those who profess loyalty without genuine service.
Henry notes a distinction between the two parables:
The single mina given to each servant suggests the one gospel offered equally to all who hear it.
The different numbers of talents suggest the varied abilities and advantages through which people may make use of that same gospel.

div.title: Jesus enters Jerusalem (verses 28–40)
div.p: Christ rules all creatures and can use them as he pleases.
He knows every human heart and holds it within his sovereign power.
Jesus' triumphal entry and his disciples' joyful praise angered the proud Pharisees, who opposed him and his kingdom.
He refuses to be discouraged by the contempt of proud people but welcomes the praises of the humble.
The Pharisees wished to silence those praising him.
Yet they could not prevent God's purpose.
The Lord who can raise up children of Abraham from stones and turn stone-like hearts toward himself can bring praise even from the mouths of children.
How will people feel when the same Lord returns in glory to judge the world?

div.title: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem (verses 41–48)
div.p: Jesus looked ahead to the suffering his enemies would bring upon themselves and wept over Jerusalem, where his own precious blood would soon be shed.
His tears teach us that reflecting God's character means showing compassion and goodwill toward sinners.
No one can hold Christian truth rightly while becoming hardhearted toward people who need mercy.
Yet Jesus' compassion did not mean divine judgment was unreal.
He wept over Jerusalem, and terrible judgment later fell upon it.
The Lord does not delight in a sinner's death.
But he will fulfill his warnings against those who continue rejecting his salvation.
The Son of God did not weep for himself or over something trivial.
He knew the value of souls and the heavy weight of human guilt.
May he cleanse our hearts from every corruption through his Spirit.
May people everywhere listen carefully to the message of truth and salvation.

row.cell: The priests and scribes question Christ's authority.
The parable of the vineyard and husbandmen.

div.title: Jesus' authority is challenged (verses 1–8)
div.p: Some people claim to be investigating the evidence for revelation and the truth of the gospel, when they are really looking for excuses to continue in unbelief.
Jesus responded to the priests and scribes with a simple question about John's baptism.
Ordinary people could have answered it.
They knew John's ministry came from heaven and aimed at spiritual rather than worldly ends.
When people bury the knowledge already given to them, it is right that they should be denied further understanding.
The religious leaders refused to acknowledge what they knew.
Jesus therefore rightly declined to explain his own authority to people who would not accept the divine origin of John's mission.

div.title: The tenants of the vineyard (verses 9–19)
div.p: Jesus addressed the parable to people determined to reject his authority despite abundant evidence for it.
How many still resemble those who killed the prophets and ultimately crucified Christ!
Their hostility to God springs from a desire to live according to sinful passions without being restrained.
Everyone privileged to possess God's word should use that blessing faithfully.
The judgment will be terrible for those who reject the Son.
It will also come upon those who claim to honor him but fail to produce the fruits of obedience in due season.
The hearers recognized that the punishment in the parable was just.
Yet they could not bear to hear its application to themselves.
Sinners often persevere in a destructive path even while fearing its final consequences.

div.title: Paying taxes and giving God what belongs to him (verses 20–26)
div.p: People plotting against Christ and his gospel cannot hide their motives from him.
Jesus refused to be trapped into the false choice his questioners presented.
He exposed their dishonest intention without giving them a statement that would allow them to turn either the governor or the people against him.
Wisdom from heaven can guide those who sincerely teach God's way around traps laid by malicious people.
It also clarifies our duties toward God, civil rulers and other human beings.
By faithfully fulfilling those duties, we prevent opponents from making justified accusations against us.

div.title: Jesus answers the Sadducees about resurrection (verses 27–38)
div.p: People seeking to undermine God's truth often create artificial difficulties and then treat them as decisive objections.
We mislead ourselves and misrepresent Christ's teaching when we imagine the unseen future world must operate exactly like the visible present world.
There is a world we see now, and a world still unseen.
Consider both carefully and give your greatest attention to the one that matters most.
Believers will share in the blessed resurrection of the dead.
We cannot fully imagine or describe their future happiness (1 Corinthians 2:9).
Those who enter their Lord's joy are entirely occupied with him.
Where holiness is perfect, the restraints needed against sin here are no longer necessary.
God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
He was fully sufficient for them (Genesis 17:1) and their exceeding great reward (Genesis 15:1).
Yet their earthly lives did not receive everything embraced in those promises.
There must therefore be another life in which God fulfills the full extent of his covenant commitment to them.

div.title: Jesus silences the scribes (verses 39–47)
div.p: Some scribes praised Jesus' answer about resurrection.
Yet his question about the Messiah silenced them.

p.hi: Christ as God is David's Lord; Christ as man is David's descendant.

div.p: Jesus warned that scribes who exploited poor widows would face severe judgment.
They also misused religious practices, especially prayer, to conceal worldly and wicked schemes.
Hypocritical devotion adds another sin to wrongdoing.
Let us ask God to keep us from pride, ambition, greed and every other evil.
May he teach us to seek the honor that comes from him alone.

div.title: Jesus commends the poor widow (verses 1–4)
div.p: What we rightly give to care for poor people or to support the worship of God is, in a real sense, given to God.
Jesus receives with pleasure what his servants sincerely desire and are able to offer for his service and the good of his people.
Even the poorest of God's servants has two small coins of another kind: a body and a soul.
May Christ persuade us and enable us to present both to him!
What happiness to know that he receives them.

div.title: Jesus foretells Jerusalem's distress and his return (verses 5–28)
div.p: The disciples were curious about the date of the coming catastrophe.
Jesus answered clearly enough to teach them what they needed to do.
Knowledge is valuable insofar as it helps us act faithfully.
Although divine judgments during the gospel age often affect people's spiritual condition, God still sometimes uses outward and temporal judgments.
Jesus warned his followers that they would endure serious suffering because of his name.
He encouraged them to remain steadfast in their duty despite opposition.
God would stand beside them, acknowledge them and help them.
After the Holy Spirit was poured out, the promise was strikingly fulfilled as Jesus gave his disciples wisdom and words through the Spirit.
We may suffer losses for Christ, but in the end we will never be losers because of Christ.
In every age, and especially in times of great danger, we should carefully guard our souls.
Through Christian patience we retain our inward composure and resist the harmful emotions that trouble the heart.
Henry compares this prophecy to Old Testament prophecies in which a great future event is described together with nearer events that foreshadow it.
He understands Jesus to describe about thirty-eight years leading to Jerusalem's destruction and the dispersal of the Jewish nation.
This historical judgment is also a figure and warning concerning Christ's second coming.
Henry regards the continuing historical existence of the dispersed Jewish people as a witness to the reliability of Christ's predictions.
He also urges prayer for the day when neither Jerusalem nor God's spiritual people will remain under oppression and when both Jews and Gentiles will turn to the Lord.
In Henry's interpretation, the first historical judgment delivered Christians oppressed by hostile authorities, bringing the churches a period of rest.
When Jesus comes to judge the world, he will deliver all his people from suffering.
The destruction of Jerusalem is thus a solemn demonstration that God does not ignore sin.
His warnings to unrepentant sinners will be fulfilled, as his prophetic word was fulfilled in that judgment.

div.title: Watch and pray (verses 29–38)
div.p: Jesus taught his disciples to notice signs that helped them recognize the approach of Jerusalem's catastrophe.
Yet Henry says Abraham's descendants would not disappear altogether and would remain until the time of Christ's revelation.
Jesus warned against complacency and indulgence.
Take care of yourselves so that temptation and inward corruption do not overcome you.
No one is safe while careless about the soul.
The day of death or judgment must not find us unprepared.
It would be terrible if, when summoned to meet Jesus, we were least concerned with the very matter that should have occupied our hearts.
Those absorbed only in earthly life and lacking any fellowship with heaven will be overtaken in this way.
Seek to be ready to stand before Christ.
If you have never sought him, come to him now.
If you have not humbled yourself over your sins, begin.
If you have begun, continue in humility and faith.
Watch and pray always.
Watch against sin.
Remain watchful in every duty and use every opportunity to do good.
Those who live a life of prayer here will enjoy a life of praise in the world to come.
May we begin, use and finish every day by attending to Christ's word, obeying his commands and following his example.
Then whenever he comes, we will be found ready.

row.cell: Christ confesses himself to be the Son of God.

div.title: Judas plans his betrayal (verses 1–6)
div.p: Jesus knew every person and had wise and holy purposes in choosing Judas as a disciple.
Luke tells us how a man who knew Christ so well could betray him: Satan entered Judas.
It is difficult to say whether God's kingdom suffers more harm through open enemies or through people who claim friendship while secretly betraying it.
Without the treachery of false friends, its public enemies often could not accomplish as much damage.

div.title: Jesus observes the Passover (verses 7–18)
div.p: Jesus obeyed the ordinances of God's law, including Passover.
This teaches us to respect the ordinances he established for the gospel, especially the Lord's Supper.
Those who act on Christ's word need not fear that his instructions will fail them.
The disciples made the preparations exactly as he directed.
Jesus welcomed his final Passover.
He eagerly desired it, even knowing that suffering would soon follow, because it served his Father's glory and humanity's redemption.
With it he took leave of the old Passover ceremonies.
By fulfilling them, he brought the ceremonial law to its appointed conclusion.
The earlier Passover had pointed forward as a type.
Now the substance had come through Christ.

div.title: Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper (verses 19 and 20)
div.p: The Lord's Supper is a sign and memorial of Christ, who has already come and rescued us through his death.
It sets his sacrifice before us.
Breaking the bread reminds us that Jesus' body was given for us.
Nothing is more nourishing or satisfying to the soul than knowing that Christ has made atonement for sin and that we may share its benefits.
We keep the Supper in remembrance of what Jesus did for us when he died, and as a testimony that we are joined to him through an everlasting covenant.
The cup of wine represents his blood, shed to make atonement.

div.title: Jesus warns the disciples (verses 21–38)
div.p: How inappropriate that followers of Jesus should compete over worldly greatness, when their Master became a servant and humbled himself even to death on the cross!
On the way to eternal happiness, believers should expect Satan to sift and test them.
If he cannot destroy them, he will try to disgrace or distress them.
Few things warn more clearly of a coming fall than self-confidence, ignoring warnings and treating danger with contempt.
Unless we continually watch and pray, we may commit by evening the very sins we were determined to resist in the morning.
If left to ourselves, we would fall.
Believers remain secure through God's power and Christ's intercession.
Jesus also warned of a coming change in circumstances.
The disciples could no longer expect the same welcome or help from others.
They were to take provisions for their work.
Their enemies would become more hostile.
At first, the apostles understood his words about swords as instructions to bring literal weapons.
Henry says Jesus actually spoke of the weapons of spiritual warfare, especially the sword of the Spirit.

div.title: Christ prays in agony (verses 39–46)
div.p: The Gospel accounts reveal the fearful nature of Jesus' inward struggle.
Our gentle, humble Lord fully knew the suffering that lay ahead.
Henry notes three details given in Luke's account.
First, an angel came from heaven to strengthen Jesus.
Being strengthened by a ministering spirit belonged to his willing humiliation.
Second, as his agony increased, he prayed more earnestly.
Prayer is appropriate at all times, but especially in terrible distress.
Third, his sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground.
This showed the weight of the suffering borne by his soul.
We should pray for strength to resist sin even to the shedding of our own blood, should faithfulness ever demand it.
Whenever we imagine the pleasures of a favorite sin, remember its terrible consequences as displayed in Gethsemane.
May the Savior's agony teach us to hate and abandon sin.
He prayed, struggled and shed his blood to ransom sinners from its power and judgment.

div.title: Jesus is betrayed and seized (verses 47–53)
div.p: Nothing is more offensive or painful than betrayal by someone professing to follow and love Jesus.
People sometimes use the outward form of religion to resist its inward power.
Jesus demonstrated his own teaching by doing good to an enemy, as he would later pray for those who abused him.
Our fallen nature tends toward rash extremes.
In difficult situations, ask God for guidance before acting.
Christ accepted that his final victory would come only after his suffering was finished.
We must also be willing to wait.
The hour and power of darkness would be brief, like the temporary triumph of every wicked purpose.

div.title: Peter denies Jesus (verses 54–62)
div.p: Peter denied knowing Christ or belonging to his disciples because he feared harm.
One lie creates a strong temptation to continue lying.
Once begun, it can spread like water breaking through a bank.
The Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Henry identifies six meanings in that look.
It was convicting, reminding Peter whom he had denied.
It was rebuking, confronting his wrongdoing.
It was challenging, recalling his earlier confident promise to remain loyal.
It was compassionate, recognizing how lost Peter would be without Christ's help.
It was directing, calling Peter to examine himself.
And it was effective through grace, bringing Christ's word back to Peter's heart and enabling him to repent.
God's grace works through the word brought to remembrance, pressing it upon the conscience.
Jesus looked at the religious leaders too, but they were not transformed as Peter was.
Peter's restoration did not come from a look alone, but from divine grace accompanying it.

div.title: Jesus acknowledges that he is the Son of God (verses 63–71)
div.p: Those who condemned Jesus for blasphemy were themselves guilty of blaspheming God.
Jesus pointed toward his future coming as full proof of his identity, since they refused the evidence already available.
He acknowledged that he was the Son of God, even knowing that the confession would lead to further suffering.
They used his truthful words as the basis for his condemnation.
Their own spiritual blindness drove them forward.
Let us consider with wonder the One who endured such hostility from sinners.

row.cell: Christ speaks of the destruction of Jerusalem.

div.title: Jesus stands before Pilate (verses 1–5)
div.p: Pilate clearly understood the difference between Jesus' followers and an armed uprising.
Yet when Pilate said he found Jesus innocent, the accusers were not moved to consider whether they were becoming guilty of innocent blood.
They became even angrier.
God nevertheless brought his holy purposes to completion through the actions of people pursuing their own sinful plans.
The different parties' efforts to accuse Jesus combined instead to establish his innocence.
He was therefore shown to be the fitting atoning sacrifice for our sins.

div.title: Herod questions Jesus (verses 6–12)
div.p: Herod had heard much about Jesus' works in Galilee and longed to see him out of curiosity.
Jesus never refused the humblest beggar who sought a miracle to relieve genuine need.
But he did not grant a miracle merely to satisfy this proud ruler's curiosity.
Herod could previously have seen Christ's works in Galilee, but had chosen not to.
When he later wished to see a sign, he did not receive one.
Herod sent Jesus back to Pilate.
Wicked people sometimes become friends through their common participation in wrongdoing.
They may agree on little except hostility toward God and contempt for Christ.

div.title: Barabbas is released and Jesus condemned (verses 13–25)
div.p: Fear of people's opinions can tempt someone to act unjustly against conscience rather than risk trouble.
Pilate acknowledged Jesus' innocence and wanted to release him.
Yet to please the crowd, he proposed punishing an innocent person as though guilty.
If no fault had been found in Jesus, why should he be punished?
Pilate eventually surrendered.
He lacked courage to stand against public pressure and delivered Jesus to be crucified.

div.title: Jesus speaks to the women of Jerusalem (verses 26–31)
div.p: Our blessed Jesus, the Lamb of God, was led toward the sacrifice like a lamb brought to slaughter.
Many insulted him, but some pitied him.
His death, however, was a victory over his enemies, our deliverance and the purchase of eternal life.
Therefore, rather than merely weep over him, we should mourn over our own sins and those of our children, which brought such suffering upon him.
We should also fear what we bring upon ourselves by rejecting his grace.
If God allowed such suffering to fall upon his own Son when he was made a sacrifice for sin, what will happen to unrepentant sinners who make themselves like a dry, fruitless tree?
Even the holiest believers are like dry trees compared with the perfectly holy Christ.
If he suffered so severely, they should not assume they will suffer nothing.
How dreadful, then, is the final judgment of hardened sinners!
The Savior's suffering solemnly reveals God's justice against sin.

div.title: Jesus is crucified; the repentant criminal (verses 32–43)
div.p: Once Jesus was fastened to the cross, he prayed for those who crucified him.
The chief benefit he died to purchase for sinners is forgiveness; that is what he requested for them.
Two criminals were crucified beside him.
Their different responses picture the varied effects of Christ's cross when the gospel is preached.
One remained hardened until death.
Suffering alone cannot change a sinful heart.
The other was softened at the end of life, rescued by divine mercy from the very edge of destruction.
This must not encourage anyone to postpone repentance.
Genuine repentance is never too late, but late repentance is often not genuine.
No one can be certain of having the opportunity or capacity to repent on a deathbed.
This man's experience was exceptional.
He rebuked the other criminal's insults.
He acknowledged that he deserved his sentence.
He recognized that Jesus had suffered unjustly.
He confessed faith while Jesus was still suffering deep disgrace, before the signs that would later move the centurion.
He believed in life to come and sought happiness there—not merely rescue from the cross.
He prayed humbly, asking only “Lord, remember me.”
He left to Jesus the way that promise should be fulfilled.
Although his remaining time was brief, he showed all the fruits of repentance his circumstances allowed.
Jesus was as gracious upon the cross as upon his throne.
Amid dreadful suffering he had compassion on this repentant sinner.
Christ died to open heaven to repentant believers.
This one striking example teaches that we should despair of no sinner.
Yet it stands beside the warning of the second criminal, who died in unbelief while the crucified Savior was so near.
Usually, people die in the spiritual condition in which they have lived.

div.title: The death of Jesus (verses 44–49)
div.p: Extraordinary signs accompanied Christ's death and testified to its importance.
Jesus' final words showed that he freely offered his life.
Let us honor God through true repentance and conversion.
Let us oppose the sinful attitudes of those who crucified Christ, live soberly and righteously, and use our abilities in the service of the Savior who died and rose for us.

div.title: Jesus is buried (verses 50–56)
div.p: Some people make little outward display of religion but, like Joseph of Arimathea, are more willing to perform genuine service when needed than those who make a great show of religious devotion.
Jesus was buried quickly because the Sabbath was approaching.
The mourners' sorrow was real, but weeping must not prevent the sowing of duty.
Even while grieving Jesus' death, they needed to prepare for the holy Sabbath.
Henry urges believers to arrange ordinary business so that it does not obstruct the responsibilities of sacred rest.
He applies the principle to the Lord's day, on which the heart should be prepared for worship whatever the burdens of the preceding week.

row.cell: He appears to two disciples on the way to Emmaus.
And makes himself known to them.
Christ appears to the other disciples.

div.title: Jesus' resurrection is announced (verses 1–12)
div.p: The women showed deep love and respect for Jesus even after his burial.
They were surprised to discover the stone rolled away and the grave empty.
Believers often turn something that should bring comfort and encouragement into a source of needless fear.
The women expected to find their Master's body in burial cloths; instead, they saw angels in brilliant clothing.
The angels assured them that Jesus had risen from the dead by his own power.
They did not bring an entirely new gospel.
They reminded the women of Jesus' own words and taught them to apply what they had already heard.
Why were disciples who believed Jesus was God's Son and had heard repeated predictions of his death and resurrection so slow to believe it?
They had also watched him raise other people from the dead.
Our religious errors often come through ignorance or forgetfulness of Christ's words.
Peter now ran toward Jesus' tomb—the same Peter who had recently run from Jesus.
He remained astonished.
Many difficulties that confuse us would become clear and useful if we understood Christ's teaching correctly.

div.title: Jesus joins two travelers on the way to Emmaus (verses 13–27)
div.p: Jesus appeared to the two disciples on the day of his resurrection.
It is fitting for his followers to discuss his death and resurrection.
Such conversation can deepen knowledge, refresh memory and awaken holy affections.
Where even two believers are helpfully discussing Christ, he may come among them as a third companion.
Those who sincerely seek him will find him, and he grants understanding to those who make use of the means of instruction already available.
The disciples were prevented from recognizing Jesus at first, enabling them to speak more freely with him.
His followers can remain sorrowful even when they have great reason for joy, because weak faith keeps them from receiving comfort.
Though Jesus had entered his glorified state, he still noticed the sorrows of his disciples.
Everyone should know about his suffering and death.
Those who know Christ crucified ought to seek opportunities to make him known.
Jesus rebuked the disciples because they had failed to believe the Old Testament Scriptures.
If we better understood what God has already revealed, we would escape many avoidable confusions.
He showed that suffering was the appointed road to his glory.
But the disciples could not reconcile themselves to the cross.
Beginning with Moses, Jesus explained everything written concerning himself.
Throughout the Old Testament are prophecies, promises, prayers and types pointing toward Christ.
A golden thread of gospel grace runs through the whole fabric of Scripture.
Christ is the best interpreter of God's word.
Even after rising from death, he did not teach novel doctrines unrelated to Scripture.
He showed how the Scriptures had been fulfilled and urged his people to study them earnestly.

div.title: Jesus is recognized at the breaking of bread (verses 28–35)
div.p: If we wish Christ to remain with us, we should earnestly ask for his presence.
Those who have enjoyed fellowship with him naturally long for more.
Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to the disciples.
He probably acted with his familiar affection and authority, perhaps even using the same words he had used before.
We learn from him to ask God's blessing on our ordinary meals.
Christ makes himself known spiritually to his people.
He opens the Scriptures.
He meets believers at his table in the Lord's Supper, where he is known in the breaking of bread.
Yet full understanding comes through the opening of the mind's eyes.
Here we see only brief glimpses of Jesus; in heaven we will see him continually.
The disciples had felt the power of his exposition even before recognizing their teacher.
Scripture passages that speak of Christ warm the hearts of genuine disciples.
Teaching that awakens love for Jesus who died for us is especially fruitful.
Those to whom he reveals himself should tell others what he has done for their souls.
Sharing and comparing the experiences of grace can greatly benefit Christians.

div.title: Jesus appears to the gathered disciples (verses 36–49)
div.p: Jesus appeared suddenly and miraculously.
He offered the disciples his peace, even though they had recently abandoned him.
He promised all the spiritual blessings included in that peace.
Many of our troubled thoughts arise from mistaken views of Christ.
He knows every thought that disturbs our hearts.
He challenged the disciples' unreasonable unbelief.
Everything that happened had been foretold by the prophets and was necessary for sinners' salvation.
The world must now hear the need for repentance and the promise of forgiveness, sought through faith in Jesus' name.
Christ works upon people's minds through his Spirit.
Even good people need the Lord to open their understanding.
To think rightly about Jesus, we need not invent new explanations beyond God's revelation: we need to understand the Scriptures.

div.title: Jesus ascends into heaven (verses 50–53)
div.p: Jesus ascended near Bethany and the Mount of Olives, where his agony had begun.
The road to heaven passes through a world of sorrow and trial.
The disciples had not watched him physically rise from the grave.
They knew he had risen because they had seen him alive afterward.
But they saw his ascent into heaven, the necessary evidence that he had truly ascended.
He raised his hands and blessed them.
He did not leave in anger but in love, leaving a blessing behind.
As with his resurrection, Jesus ascended by his own power.
The disciples worshiped him.
The fresh display of Christ's glory led to renewed confession and praise.
They returned to Jerusalem with great joy.
His glory brings happiness to believers even while they remain in this world.
As we wait for God's promises, we should meet them with thanksgiving and praise.
Nothing better prepares the heart to receive the Holy Spirit.
Praise silences fear, softens sorrow and sustains hope.
We can come boldly before the Father's throne because it is also the throne of our Mediator, Jesus Christ.
Let us rely on his promises and plead them in prayer.
Let us honor his appointed worship, thank God for mercy, set our affections on heavenly things and long for the Redeemer's return to complete our blessedness.

p.hi: Amen. Even so, Lord Jesus, come quickly.

div.title: John — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)
div.p: The apostle and evangelist John seems to have been the youngest of the twelve disciples. Jesus gave him special affection and confidence; he is therefore called the disciple Jesus loved.
John was deeply attached to his Master and, according to Henry, ministered successfully in Jerusalem and outlived the city's destruction, in agreement with Jesus' words in John 21:22.

Traditional history, as Henry recounts it, says that John later lived mainly in Ephesus, after the death of Jesus' mother. Toward the end of Domitian's reign, he was exiled to Patmos, where he wrote the book of Revelation. Under Nerva, he was released and returned to Ephesus.

Henry says it was thought that John wrote his Gospel and letters there, around AD 97, and died not long afterward. These are the commentator's historical claims and dating suggestions, not independently established facts.
The Gospel's purpose is to teach Christians the true divine nature, office and character of Jesus Christ, who came to teach and redeem humanity.
John therefore selected events displaying Christ's divine power and authority and teachings that most clearly revealed his divine nature and the atoning power of his death for the world's sins.

John only briefly described, or omitted, many events already reported in the other Gospels. In doing so, Henry says, he confirmed the truth of those accounts and made room for additional teaching and events of great importance.

row.cell: John the Baptist's testimony to Christ.
Other testimonies of John concerning Christ.
Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus.

div.title: Christ is the eternal and divine Word (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jesus is called the Word because, just as our speech makes our thoughts known to other people, the Son of God came to reveal his Father's mind to the world.
John plainly affirms that Christ is God.
He existed in the beginning and was with God.
Everything that has been created was made by him—not merely through him as though he were an instrument subordinate to the true Creator.
Without him nothing came into existence, from the greatest angel to the smallest worm.
This shows his complete fitness for the work of our redemption and salvation.
Both the light of reason and the life of every living creature come from Christ and continue to depend on him.
The eternal Word shines as the true Light, yet the darkness does not understand or receive him.
Let us pray continually for eyes opened to this Light, that we may walk in it and become wise for salvation through faith in Jesus Christ.

div.title: The Word enters the world as a human being (verses 6–14)
div.p: John the Baptist came as a witness to Jesus.
It shows how dark the human mind has become that even when the Light appeared, someone had to call people's attention to it.
Christ is the true Light in the fullest sense.
Every person brought into saving light receives it through his Spirit and grace.
Those who remain unenlightened by him perish in spiritual darkness.
When Jesus took on our human nature and lived among us, the Son of the Most High entered this lower world.
He was in the world but not of it.
He came to save a lost world that he himself had created.
Yet the world did not recognize its Maker.
When he returns as Judge, the world will be forced to recognize him.
Many claim to belong to Christ while refusing to receive him, because they will not part with their sins or allow him to rule them.

p.hi: All God's children have been born again.

div.p: The new birth comes through God's word as the means (1 Peter 1:23) and God's Spirit as the Author.
Christ was always present in the world through his divine nature.
But in the fullness of time he came in a new way: God manifested in the flesh.
His divine glory shone through the veil of humanity.
Ordinarily, the people who know someone best discover their weaknesses.
It was the opposite with Jesus: those closest to him saw the most of his glory.
Though he outwardly took the form of a servant, his character was full of grace and truth.
His holy teaching and miracles revealed the glory of the Son of God.
He was fully pleasing to his Father and therefore fitted to plead for sinners; he also perfectly knew the truth he had come to reveal.

div.title: John bears witness to Christ's fullness (verses 15–18)
div.p: Christ entered public ministry after John, but in every deeper sense he existed before John.
Jesus was alive before appearing on earth as a man.
In him dwells all fullness.
Through faith, fallen sinners receive from him everything that makes them wise, strong, holy, useful and happy.
All the blessings we receive through Christ can be described with one word: grace.
Grace includes both God's goodwill toward us and God's good work within us.
God's law is holy, just and good, and we must use it rightly.
But it cannot provide pardon, righteousness or power to obey.
It teaches us how to live in a way that honors God's saving truth, but it cannot replace the gospel.
Every mercy coming to sinners comes through Jesus Christ.
No one can come to the Father except through him.
No one can truly know God except as the Father is revealed in his only-begotten and beloved Son.

div.title: John explains his own role (verses 19–28)
div.p: John refused to accept the title Messiah.
He came in the spirit and power of Elijah, but he was not Elijah himself.
He was also not the prophet they expected Moses to have promised: someone who, according to their mistaken hopes, would free them from Roman rule.
Instead, John described his mission in a way that urged people to listen and prepare.
He baptized with water as a profession of repentance and as an outward sign of the spiritual blessings the coming Messiah would give.
The Messiah was already among them, though they did not recognize him.
John said he was unworthy to perform even the lowest service for Jesus.

div.title: John calls Jesus the Lamb of God (verses 29–36)
div.p: When John saw Jesus, he pointed him out as the Lamb of God.
The Passover lamb—with its shed and sprinkled blood, its roasted flesh and the meal in which it was eaten—pictured the salvation of sinners through faith in Christ.
Likewise, the lambs offered morning and evening pointed toward Christ, who was sacrificed to redeem us to God by his blood.
John preached repentance.
Yet he taught his listeners to seek forgiveness of sins only through Jesus and his death.
It accords with God's glory to pardon everyone who depends upon Christ's atoning sacrifice.
Jesus takes away the sin of the world and has purchased pardon for those who repent and believe the gospel.
That should encourage us personally: if he takes away the world's sin, why not my sin?
He bore our sin for us, and so takes it from us.
God could have removed sin simply by destroying sinners, as he did in the old world.
Instead, he found a way to remove the guilt of sin while sparing the sinner, by making his Son sin for us—that is, a sin offering.
Seeing Jesus take away sin should teach us to hate it and resolve to abandon it.
We must not cling to what the Lamb of God came to remove.
John also testified to the sign at Jesus' baptism, when God bore witness to his Son.
He declared Jesus to be the Son of God and the promised Messiah.
John used every opportunity to lead people toward Christ.

div.title: Andrew and another disciple follow Jesus (verses 37–42)
div.p: What most strongly moves an awakened soul to follow Jesus is recognizing that he alone takes away sin.
Whatever fellowship takes place between Christ and our souls, he begins the conversation.
He asked the disciples, “What are you seeking?”
We should ask ourselves the same question when we begin following him.
What do we truly desire?
Are we seeking God's favor and eternal life?
Jesus invited them to come without delay.
Now is the accepted time (2 Corinthians 6:2).
It is good to be where Christ is, whatever that place may be.
We should care for the spiritual welfare of our relatives and seek to bring them to him.
Those who come to Jesus should come with a settled resolution to remain faithful and steadfast, like a firm stone.
Only his grace makes such perseverance possible.

div.title: Philip and Nathanael follow Jesus (verses 43–51)
div.p: True Christianity is following Jesus, devoting ourselves to him and walking in his footsteps.
Nathanael initially objected because of Jesus' home town.
Those who want to benefit from God's word must beware of prejudices against places and groups of people.
We should examine things for ourselves.
Often we discover good where we expected none.
Many people remain away from the path of faith because of unreasonable assumptions.
The best response to such prejudice is often simply “Come and see.”
Nathanael was an Israelite without deceit.
He was sincere rather than hypocritical, upright and godly.
Jesus knows what we really are.
Do we desire him to know us as genuine Christians?
Even true believers have weaknesses, imperfections and sins, but deliberate hypocrisy does not characterize the believer's heart.
Jesus knew what had happened when Nathanael was under the fig tree.
Henry says he was probably praying earnestly for the hope and consolation of Israel, unseen by human eyes.
This was evidence that Jesus knew the secrets of his heart.
Through Christ we enjoy fellowship with, and receive benefit from, the holy angels.
He unites and reconciles the things of heaven and earth.

row.cell: Christ casts the buyers and sellers out of the temple.

div.title: Jesus changes water into wine at Cana (verses 1–11)
div.p: It is a great blessing when Christ is present at a wedding.
Anyone desiring his presence and blessing upon marriage should invite him through prayer.
He will hear.
In this life we can find ourselves lacking necessities even when we expected abundance.
At this wedding, the wine ran out.
Anyone entering ordinary worldly responsibilities should be prepared for trouble and disappointment.
When we approach Christ with a need, we should humbly explain our situation and leave him free to do what he considers best.
His reply to his mother was not disrespectful.
He addressed her with the same word in a loving way from the cross.
Nevertheless, his response stands as a warning against the misplaced worship of Mary that Henry sees in later centuries.
Our prayers may be answered when we have no idea how to proceed.
A delay in mercy is not a refusal of prayer.
Those who expect Jesus to bless them should be ready to obey his instructions.
The path of duty is the path of mercy.
We should not object to the methods he chooses.
Moses' first miracle turned water into blood (Exodus 7:20).
Christ's first miracle turned water into wine.
Henry sees here a picture of the difference between the Mosaic law and Christ's gospel.
Jesus makes the ordinary comforts of creation truly beneficial to believers.
Every work of Christ is intended for practical use.
Has he changed your water into wine by granting you knowledge and grace?
Use those blessings.
The wine was excellent.
Christ's work is good even when people fail to recognize its Author.
Henry notes that miracles produced what was best of its kind.
Jesus' action permits the proper use of wine, but it does not cancel his warning against excessive eating and drunkenness (Luke 21:34).
We may enjoy appropriate celebrations with friends, but should conduct them as though we could welcome the Redeemer to join us.
Frivolity, luxury and excess dishonor him.

div.title: Jesus cleanses the temple (verses 12–22)
div.p: The first public action John records Jesus performing after Cana was driving traders out of the temple.
The priests and leaders had allowed people motivated by greed to turn its courts into a marketplace.
People still make God's house a place of commerce when their minds are occupied with worldly business during worship or when they perform religious duties for financial profit.
After cleansing the temple, Jesus gave a sign of his authority.
He foretold that his enemies would put him to death: “Destroy this temple.”
He would allow them to destroy his body.
He also foretold that he himself would raise it again in three days.
Jesus took his life up again by his own power.
His hearers misunderstood figurative language as though it were merely literal.
The disciples understood his words after the resurrection.
Observing how Scripture's promises and prophecies are fulfilled helps us understand the divine word.

div.title: Jesus knows what is in every person (verses 23–25)
div.p: Jesus knows every human being's nature, desires, character, motives and plans.
He knows us far more thoroughly than we know one another—or even know ourselves.
He understands the hidden schemes of his enemies and the real character of those who profess friendship with him falsely.
He also knows who truly belongs to him, recognizing both the uprightness and the weaknesses of sincere believers.
We can observe what someone does.
Christ sees what is in that person's heart.
Beware of an empty profession of Christianity or a faith that is merely outward and dead.
People may deceive others and even themselves, but they cannot deceive the God who searches hearts.

row.cell: The baptism of John of Christ John's testimony.

div.title: Jesus teaches Nicodemus about the new birth (verses 1–21)
div.p: Nicodemus was afraid, or ashamed, to be seen with Christ.
He therefore came to Jesus at night.
When faith is unpopular, there are many people who, like Nicodemus, hesitate to identify themselves openly with Jesus.
Yet Jesus welcomed him and taught us to encourage even weak beginnings of faith.
Nicodemus later acknowledged Christ publicly.
He was a ruler, but he did not come to discuss public affairs.
He came to talk about the condition and salvation of his own soul.
Jesus spoke immediately about the necessity and character of regeneration, the new birth, leading him to the true source of holiness.
Birth marks the beginning of life.
To be born again is to begin a genuinely new life after having lived wrongly or without proper purpose.
We need a new nature, new principles, new affections and new goals.
At our first birth we were corrupted by sin.
We must therefore become new creatures.
No stronger expression could have been chosen to describe so great a change in a person's state and character.
Something is done within us and for us that we cannot accomplish by our own efforts.
A new life begins that will endure forever.
Without it, we cannot expect to enjoy the benefits of Christ, either now or in the future.
Nicodemus misunderstood Jesus as though regenerating an immortal soul meant physically reshaping the body.
Yet he admitted his lack of understanding, demonstrating a desire to learn.
Jesus made clear that the Author of this new birth is the Holy Spirit.
Neither human intelligence nor human power can produce it.
Our corrupt nature makes the change essential.
In view of God's holiness, our own depravity and the eternal happiness promised to believers, we should not be surprised that it is so necessary.
Jesus compared the Spirit's work with water.
Henry says it is also probable Jesus was referring to baptism.
But this does not mean everyone baptized is saved, or that only baptized people can be saved.
What is indispensable is the new birth performed by the Spirit, of which baptism is a sign.
The same Greek word can refer to wind and Spirit.
God governs the wind's movement; the Spirit likewise gives his influence where, when, to whom and in whatever measure he chooses.
We may not see the origin of that work, but we can recognize its effects when a soul grieves over sin and longs for Christ.
Nicodemus still struggled to understand.
Spiritual truths seem foolish to the natural human mind.
Some people conclude that what they cannot believe cannot be proved.
Jesus' teaching about heavenly things invited Nicodemus to seek deeper understanding.
Jesus is fully able to disclose God's will, for he came down from heaven and yet is in heaven.
Here is the mystery of his two natures in one person.
He is the Son of Man, yet remains divine.
We learn these things through revelation from above, received by faith.
Jesus also taught that salvation comes through looking to him, like the Israelites bitten by poisonous serpents who survived through looking at the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:6–9).
Sin is deadly.
Whatever attraction it may seem to possess, in the end it bites like a serpent.
The remedy is set before us in the gospel.
The One we have offended has become our peace.
We receive healing by believing in Christ.
Those who despise their disease or refuse the remedy through Jesus are responsible for their own ruin.

p.hi: Look to Christ crucified and live.

div.p: Unless God's grace enables us to do this, we remain wounded by Satan and under the sentence of death.
Jesus came to save us through forgiveness, delivering us from condemnation under the law.
Here is genuinely good news.
God's love is revealed in giving his Son for the world.
How astonishing that the great God should love such an undeserving world!
Our duty is to believe in Jesus Christ, whom the Father gave as Prophet, Priest and King.
We must submit to him to be taught, governed and saved.
His promise is that whoever believes in him will not perish but have everlasting life.
Through Christ God reconciles sinners to himself.
There is no other Savior.
Those who believe in Jesus are not condemned, however great their past sins.
They are not dealt with according to their guilt.
Unbelief, by contrast, rejects God's most precious gift and the only remedy for sin.
Those who reject the Son remain condemned already, under the law's charge for their sins and without the gospel's pardon.
Such unbelief springs from the heart's hostility toward God and some form of love for sin.
People performing the deeds of darkness often refuse Christ's light because it would expose their wrongdoing.
Christ is hated because sin is loved.
The renewed heart does the opposite.
It welcomes the light, wants to know God's will and obeys even when obedience conflicts with worldly advantage.
The Holy Spirit fills the heart with God's love, making that love the governing principle of life.
While a sinner is burdened by unforgiven guilt, there can be little more than fear of divine judgment.
But when the sinner sees the righteous ground of forgiveness through Christ and trusts it personally, that fear gives way to sincere love and communion with God.
Works are good when God's will is their rule, God's glory is their goal, and God's strength enables them.
Regeneration is therefore the most important concern of life.
What benefit would abundant food, fine clothes, pleasure, success or long years give us if we died without being born again and finally heard the Judge say he never knew us?

div.title: John gladly gives way to Christ (verses 22–36)
div.p: John the Baptist was content with his own assigned place and task.
Jesus had come to perform a greater work.
John knew Christ would increase in honor and influence while fewer people followed John.
The Messiah's government and peace would have no end.
John also knew the fundamental difference between them.
Christ came from heaven as the Son of God.
John was a sinful and mortal man who could speak only about the more ordinary matters of religion.
Jesus' words were the words of God.
The Holy Spirit was given to him without measure, unlike prophets who received particular gifts for appointed tasks.
Eternal life is obtained only through faith in the Son of God.
Those refusing to believe in him cannot share in salvation.
God's wrath remains upon them forever, as Henry explicitly warns.

row.cell: His discourse with the Samaritan woman.
The effects of Christ's conversation with the woman of Samaria.

div.title: Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee (verses 1–3)
div.p: Jesus focused chiefly on preaching the gospel, a more excellent task than administering baptism (1 Corinthians 1:17).
He honored his disciples by giving them responsibility for baptizing.
We learn that the benefit of a sacrament does not depend upon the particular human hand administering it.

div.title: Jesus speaks with the Samaritan woman (verses 4–26)
div.p: The Jews and Samaritans despised one another.
Jesus traveled through Samaria on his way from Judea to Galilee.
We should avoid unnecessary exposure to temptations. When duty requires us to pass through danger, we should not linger there.
Jesus grew tired on his journey.
This shows he was truly human.
He had accepted the burdens of fallen human life in order to become a curse for us, though he himself was without sin.
He was poor and traveled on foot.
When tired, he sat beside a well without a comfortable couch to rest upon.
Should we complain when our circumstances resemble the poverty and fatigue the Son of God willingly accepted?
Jesus asked a woman for water.
She was surprised because he did not share the hatred of his countrymen toward Samaritans.
Moderation and kindness across party divisions can astonish people.
Jesus used the opportunity to teach her about divine things.
He exposed her ignorance, her sin and her need of a Savior, bringing her to conversion.
The living water means the Holy Spirit.
The coming Messiah had been promised through this image in the Old Testament.
The Spirit's grace and comfort satisfy a thirsty soul that understands its deepest needs.
The woman took Jesus' figurative words literally.
Water from Jacob's well could provide satisfaction only briefly.
Every earthly comfort eventually leaves us thirsty again.
But whoever receives God's Spirit and the gospel's consolations will receive enough to satisfy the soul completely.
The worldly heart remains occupied with worldly aims.
The woman initially wanted this water merely to avoid the trouble of visiting the well.
Sinful thinking is ingenious in escaping conviction.
Jesus then brought the truth directly home to her conscience by exposing her present way of life.
She recognized his prophetic authority.
The ability of Jesus' word to search the heart and reveal hidden sin demonstrates his divine authority.
Our arguments about religious locations would be less heated if we remembered how temporary such questions are.
The object of worship remains God as Father, but controversies about a particular worship location would no longer determine where God accepts worshipers.
Reason suggests arranging suitable and orderly places to meet.
Yet no place possesses greater acceptance before God simply by its location.
Jesus acknowledged that the Jewish people had the true worship and scriptural knowledge of God: salvation is from the Jews.
Other nations received God's saving message through them.
But the system of worship established under the old covenant was itself approaching fulfillment and conclusion.
God would be known as Father by believers from every nation.
True worship is the soul communing with God under the Holy Spirit's influence.
The prayers, requests and thanksgiving of an upright heart, moved by spiritual love, are worship that honors and pleases him.
The woman preferred to postpone the question until the Messiah arrived.
Jesus answered plainly: “I who speak to you am he.”
He revealed himself exceptionally clearly to a woman who was both a Samaritan and a social outsider.
No past sins prevent anyone from being received by Christ when they humble themselves and believe in him as the Savior of the world.

div.title: The woman's testimony reaches Samaria (verses 27–42)
div.p: The disciples were surprised to see Jesus talking with a Samaritan woman.
Yet they recognized that he must have a good reason for doing so.
When his words or providence confuse us, we can rest assured that what he does is wise and good.
Two things especially impressed the woman.
First, Jesus knew the thoughts, words and actions of human beings.
Second, his word had confronted her secret sins with power.
She told other people about the very details she might have been expected to keep hidden.
A knowledge of Christ gained through true conviction of sin is most likely to be sound and saving.
The townspeople came to hear Jesus.
He used the occasion to describe doing his Father's will as food, a task performed with joy as well as diligence.
He compared his work to harvesting.
The coming harvest is planned and awaited.
Once it arrives, everyone must work while the opportunity remains, because harvest time is brief and cannot be recovered after it passes.
God sometimes employs the weakest and most unexpected people in accomplishing great work.
Through one poor woman, Jesus spread saving knowledge throughout a town.
The townspeople's faith grew in three ways.
Its content grew: they believed Jesus to be the Savior of the whole world, not only of the Jews.
Its certainty grew: they became convinced he truly was the Christ.
Its foundation grew: they now believed because they had heard him themselves, not only because of the woman's report.

div.title: Jesus heals an official's son (verses 43–54)
div.p: The boy's father held an honorable position, but wealth and status did not protect his child from sickness.
Even the greatest people must approach God as beggars in need.
The father persisted in seeking help.
At first his faith was weak: he doubted whether Jesus could heal from a distance.
We find it difficult to believe that time and place cannot limit Christ's knowledge, love or power.
Jesus gave him a reassuring answer.
When he speaks life to a soul, his word itself gives life.
The man returned home, showing real confidence in what Jesus had said.
He did not rush home that night in panic; his mind rested in the promise.
His servants met him with news of the child's healing.
Good news comes to those who hope in God's word.
Comparing Jesus' deeds with his promises strengthens faith.
The miracle brought not only health to the child but saving faith to the household.
A personal experience of Christ's word can establish his authority firmly within a soul.
His whole family believed, and Jesus became precious to them.
The knowledge of Christ continues to spread through families, bringing spiritual health and salvation.

row.cell: The cure at the pool of Bethesda.

div.title: Jesus heals a man at Bethesda (verses 1–9)
div.p: By nature, we are all helpless in spiritual matters—blind, lame and weakened by sin.
Yet God has made full provision for our healing, if we receive it.
Henry describes an angel entering the pool and stirring its water, so that the first person to step in would be healed of whatever disease afflicted them.
He draws a lesson from the lost opportunity: do not allow an occasion for mercy to pass by, because it may never return.
The man had been unable to use his limbs for thirty-eight years.
How can we complain about one uncomfortable night when many others, better than ourselves, have scarcely known a single day of health?
Jesus chose this particular sufferer out of the whole group.
Those enduring long affliction should take comfort in knowing that God has not lost count of the years.
The man spoke of others' failure to help him, yet did not become bitter or abusive.
We should practice both thankfulness and patience.
Christ healed the man although he had neither asked Jesus for help nor expected him to come.
Jesus commanded, “Rise and walk.”
A command from God to repent and live does not mean fallen sinners can make themselves spiritually alive without divine grace.
No more did Jesus' command imply that the paralyzed man possessed the physical strength to rise without miraculous help.
The power belonged to Christ, and he must receive the glory.
What a joyful surprise when the man suddenly found himself strong and able to walk!
Likewise, spiritual healing is shown through a changed life.
If Christ has cured our souls, let us go where he sends us, take up whatever he lays upon us and walk obediently before him.

div.title: The authorities object to the healing (verses 10–16)
div.p: Someone delivered from punishment for sin may be tempted to return to sin once fear has faded, unless God's grace removes sin at its source.
The miseries from which believers have been rescued should warn us against returning to the deeds that caused them.
Every providential mercy carries the message “Go and sin no more.”
Jesus knew the warning was needed.
During illness people often make many resolutions.
Shortly after recovery, they keep only some.
After more time passes, they may forget them altogether.
Jesus spoke of the wrath to come.
Even serious pain lasting months or years is incomparable with the everlasting consequences of unrepentant sin.

div.title: Jesus declares his equality with the Father (verses 17–23)
div.p: The divine power displayed in the healing proved Jesus' identity as the Son of God.
He declared that he works together with and like his Father, doing whatever is right.
His opponents understood that he claimed a relationship to God beyond that of an ordinary human being.
They became more hostile, accusing him not only of breaking their Sabbath rules but also of blasphemy by making himself equal with God.
The Father entrusted judgment, now and at the last day, to his Son.
The purpose is that everyone should honor the Son just as they honor the Father.
Anyone who refuses that honor to Christ does not truly honor the Father who sent him, whatever else they may claim.

div.title: Jesus teaches about life and judgment (verses 24–47)
New spiritual life and the resurrection (verses 24–29)
div.p: Jesus declared his authority as the Messiah.
The time had arrived when those spiritually dead could hear the Son of God's voice and receive new life.
He also foretold a future day when those physically dead in their graves would hear his voice and rise.
The Judge of all humanity must possess perfect knowledge and unlimited power.
Let us believe his testimony so that our faith and hope rest upon God, and we may not come under condemnation.
May Christ's voice reach people dead in sin, producing works consistent with repentance and preparing them for the solemn judgment.

div.title: Jesus acts with the Father and is witnessed by his works (verses 30–38)
div.p: Jesus spoke again of the complete agreement between Father and Son, declaring himself the Son of God.
He had a witness greater than John's: the works his Father gave him to accomplish.
Those works confirmed everything he said.
Yet God's word had no abiding place in the hearts of those who refused to believe the One sent according to the ancient promises.
The Father's testimony, made effective through the Holy Spirit's power, still brings sinners to conversion and announces Jesus as the beloved Son in whom God is pleased.
When hearts are filled with pride, ambition and love of the world, there is no room for God's word to dwell within them.

div.title: Study Scripture to find Christ (verses 39–44)
div.p: The Jews believed eternal life was revealed in their Scriptures.
Some assumed that merely possessing and studying the written word meant they already had life.
Jesus challenged them to search the Scriptures more carefully.
Henry observes that Jesus' statement can be understood either as describing their practice—“You search the Scriptures”—or as commanding them—“Search the Scriptures.”
Both readings teach an important duty.
We should not only read or hear Scripture but study it diligently and carefully.
We must search for eternal life as our great goal, and for Christ as the new and living way to that life.
It is possible to be deeply learned in Scripture's wording yet unfamiliar with its spiritual power.
A person may approach biblical study seeking personal recognition instead of God's honor.
Jesus rebuked his hearers for refusing himself and his teaching, revealing their lack of genuine love for God.
Many profess great religion while showing by their neglect of Christ that they do not possess the love of God.
It is living love for the Lord within the heart that he receives.
His opponents undervalued Christ because they overvalued themselves.
How can people truly believe if they make human praise and approval an idol?

div.title: Moses' writings also point toward Jesus (verses 45–47)
div.p: Many people trust a system of doctrine, or a party associated with respected names, without understanding those doctrines or those teachers' real purposes.
The Jews in this way misunderstood Moses.
Let us read Scripture with prayer, desiring eternal life.
Notice how Christ is its great subject, and turn daily to him for the life he gives.

div.title: Jesus feeds the five thousand (verses 1–14)
div.p: John describes the miracle of feeding the crowd because it is closely connected with Jesus' teaching that follows.
Notice what the miracle produced among the people.
Even many ordinary Jews expected a Messiah who would come as a great prophet.
The Pharisees despised these people for not knowing the law.
Yet the ordinary people in some respects knew more of the One who is the law's true goal than their religious leaders did.
Still, a person can acknowledge Jesus as the promised prophet and refuse to listen to him.

div.title: Jesus walks on the sea (verses 15–21)
div.p: The disciples were following the path of duty, and Jesus was praying for them.
Nevertheless, they faced danger.
Having a share in Christ does not remove every trial or trouble of this world.
Clouds and darkness can surround children of light.
When the disciples saw Jesus walking on the water, the very approach of their deliverance frightened them.
People often mistake the coming of comfort for another threat.
Few things confront a sinner's conscience more powerfully than the Savior declaring, “I am Jesus whom you are persecuting.”
Few words comfort a believer more than his assurance, “I am Jesus whom you love.”
If we have received Jesus Christ as Lord, we may be confident that, however dark the night and strong the wind, we will soon reach the shore.

div.title: Jesus calls the crowd to seek lasting food (verses 22–27)
div.p: The people wanted to know how Jesus had arrived.
Instead of answering their curiosity, he confronted their motives for following him.
We should seek salvation with the greatest earnestness, using all the means God has appointed.
Yet salvation must be received as a gift from the Son of Man, not something we earn.
God the Father has set his seal upon Jesus, proving his divine authority.
The Son of Man is also the Son of God in power.

div.title: Jesus teaches about the bread of life (verses 28–65)
Believe in the true bread from heaven (verses 28–35)
div.p: Continually exercising faith in Christ is the most important—and often the most difficult—part of the obedience required of sinners seeking salvation.
When his grace enables us to live by faith in the Son of God, holy dispositions and acceptable service follow.
The Father once gave Israel food from heaven to sustain physical life.
Now he gives the true Bread to save souls.

p.hi: Coming to Jesus and believing in him mean the same thing.

div.p: Christ nourishes and sustains spiritual life as ordinary bread nourishes the body.
But unlike ordinary bread, which nourishes only because a body is already alive, Jesus is himself living Bread.
He gives and sustains life by his own power.
The teaching of Christ crucified remains just as strengthening and comforting to a believer now as it always was.
Jesus is the Bread that came down from heaven.
This declares the divine nature of his person, his authority and the heavenly origin of every saving benefit received through him.
May we ask sincerely, Lord, always give us this Bread.

div.title: The Father draws people to the Son (verses 36–46)
div.p: When the Holy Spirit reveals to people their guilt, danger and remedy, they become willing—even eager—to come to Jesus and surrender everything that hinders receiving his salvation.
It is the Father's will that not one of those he gave to the Son should be rejected or lost by him.
No one comes until divine grace has subdued and partly changed the heart.
Consequently, no one who truly comes to Jesus will ever be turned away.
The gospel does not find fallen sinners naturally eager to accept its humbling, holy way of salvation.
God draws people through his word and the Holy Spirit.
The hearer's duty is to hear and learn, receiving the offered grace and consenting to God's promise.
Only the beloved Son has seen the Father.
Jesus taught that his listeners needed his inward influence on their minds, as well as his spoken word and the ministers he sent.

div.title: The living Bread is greater than manna (verses 47–51)
div.p: Manna gave Israel a blessing limited to this earthly life.
The living Bread is far greater: those who feed on him receive eternal life.
This Bread refers to Christ's human nature, which he took so he might offer himself to the Father as a sacrifice for the world's sins.
Through this offering he purchased everything necessary for life and godliness for sinners of every nation who repent and believe in him.

div.title: Feed upon Christ through faith (verses 52–59)
div.p: The flesh and blood of the Son of Man refer to the Redeemer in human nature, especially Christ crucified and the redemption secured by his sacrifice.
That redemption includes forgiveness, acceptance with God, access to the throne of grace, the covenant promises and eternal life.
These blessings are called his flesh and blood because they were purchased through his broken body and shed blood, and because they nourish souls as food and drink nourish bodies.

p.hi: Eating Christ's flesh and drinking his blood mean believing in him.

div.p: We receive Christ and his benefits by faith.
The person who recognizes personal spiritual need finds in the Redeemer—God manifested in flesh—everything needed to quiet the conscience and increase holiness.
Meditating on the cross awakens repentance, love and gratitude.
We live spiritually through Christ as our bodies live through food.
We also live through him as limbs receive life from the head and branches receive life from the root.

p.hi: Because he lives, we shall live also.

div.title: Spiritual life comes through the Spirit (verses 60–65)
div.p: Christ's human nature had not previously existed in heaven.
Yet because he is God and man in one Person, it was right to say that he came down from heaven.
The Messiah's kingdom was not an earthly kingdom.
His listeners should understand by faith his teaching about living spiritually through him and receiving his fullness.
Just as a body without a soul has no living power, religious forms without God's life-giving Spirit are dead and useless.
Only the One who provided salvation can teach us to understand it and draw us to receive it by faith.
We should gladly apply to Jesus, thankful that everyone willing to come to him is assured of a welcome.

div.title: Many disciples turn away (verses 66–71)
div.p: When we entertain suspicious and harsh thoughts about Jesus' words and works, we enter into temptation.
Unless the Lord mercifully prevents it, such distrust can lead to turning back.
A corrupt heart finds an occasion for offense even in teachings that should bring the deepest comfort.
Jesus had promised eternal life to his true followers.
Some listeners focused upon his difficult sayings and left him.
The faithful disciples held to his clear promise of eternal life and remained with him.
Christ's teaching is the word of eternal life.
We must live and die by it.
To abandon Jesus is to abandon our own mercy and salvation.
His disciples believed that he was the Messiah promised to Israel, the Son of the living God.
Whenever tempted to withdraw from Christ, return to these first principles and stand firm.
Remember his searching question:

p.hi: Will you also go away?

div.p: Where else could we go?
Only Jesus grants salvation through the forgiveness of sins, true assurance, peace and joy.
He alone gives solid happiness now and opens the way toward eternal happiness.

row.cell: Christ goes to the feast of tabernacles.

div.title: Jesus goes to the Feast of Tabernacles (verses 1–13)
div.p: Jesus' brothers or relatives were disappointed when they realized following him offered no clear prospect of worldly advancement.
People without true faith sometimes offer advice to those serving God, but they generally recommend whatever promises immediate personal advantage.
The people held conflicting opinions about Jesus' teaching and miracles.
Those who thought him a deceiver spoke openly and boldly.
Many who regarded him favorably were unwilling to admit their views publicly because they feared criticism or persecution.
Something similar occurs throughout church history.
Opponents of the gospel loudly condemn its ministers while some who respect those ministers remain silent to avoid reproach.

div.title: Jesus teaches publicly at the feast (verses 14–39)
Jesus' doctrine comes from the Father (verses 14–24)
div.p: Every faithful minister can humbly adopt Jesus' declaration in an appropriate sense: the message preached is not something invented by the minister.
True doctrine comes from God's word, taught by the Spirit.
Amid the world's disputes, anyone willing to do God's will can discover whether teaching comes from the Lord or from merely human ideas.
Those determined to hate the truth risk being abandoned to deadly errors.
Jesus showed that healing someone on the Sabbath was as consistent with the day's purpose as performing an outward religious ordinance.
He called his critics to judge according to the spiritual meaning of God's law, not outward appearances.
When considering another person, we should look beyond social status and external impressions to real character and the Holy Spirit's gifts and graces.

div.title: Jesus declares his divine origin (verses 25–30)
div.p: Jesus told his hearers plainly that their assumptions about his origin were mistaken.
He had been sent by God, who remains faithful to every promise.
Jesus also declared that, despite their religious claims, they did not truly know God.
His claim to know the Father in a unique way provoked hostility.
They attempted to arrest him, yet were unable to carry out their plan.

p.hi: God can restrain human hands without changing human hearts.

div.title: Some believe but fear to speak (verses 31–36)
div.p: Jesus' teaching persuaded many people that he really was the promised Messiah.
Yet they lacked courage to acknowledge their conviction.
Christ's faithful people are in the world but not of it.
They may feel oppressed or tired by hostility here.
It is a comfort that their stay in this world is brief.
The days of earthly life and the opportunities for grace do not last forever.
People who now despise the Savior's help may desperately wish for it when suffering and judgment overtake them.
Many debated Jesus' sayings without understanding them.
Their fulfillment would ultimately show what he meant.

div.title: Jesus offers living water through the Spirit (verses 37–39)
div.p: On the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, Jewish worshipers traditionally drew water and poured it out before the Lord.
Henry says Jesus was possibly alluding to this ceremony.
Anyone longing for lasting happiness must come to Christ and submit to his guidance.
Spiritual thirst means a deep desire for blessings the world cannot provide.
The water Jesus offers signifies the sanctifying and comforting work of the Holy Spirit.
His consolation flows abundantly and continually, like a great river.
It is powerful enough to overcome doubts and fears.
Christ possesses inexhaustible fullness: grace upon grace.
The Spirit dwelling and working within believers becomes like a spring of living water, sending streams into the surrounding world.
The water refreshes and cleanses.
Henry says believers should not expect the apostles' extraordinary miraculous gifts, but may and should ask for the Spirit's ordinary and even more valuable sanctifying influence.
These blessings have flowed from the glorified Redeemer throughout the generations and into distant countries.
May we eagerly make them known to others.

div.title: The crowds and leaders disagree about Jesus (verses 40–53)
div.p: Jesus' enemies' malice often resisted reason itself.
Sometimes the reason their violent plans failed was difficult to explain through ordinary human causes.
No one has ever spoken with the wisdom, power, grace, clarity and gentleness of Jesus.
Yet some who are briefly restrained by his words and speak well of him lose those convictions and return to sin.
People too often let worldly fashion and social pressure decide matters of eternal importance.
They may effectively choose condemnation rather than endure public disapproval.
God's wisdom frequently chooses people the world despises, while human folly rejects those God has chosen.
The Lord sometimes raises up weak and fearful disciples and uses them to frustrate the designs of his enemies.

div.title: The Pharisees accuse a woman of adultery (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jesus did not find fault with the law.
Neither did he excuse the woman's wrongdoing.
Nor did he approve the Pharisees' false display of zeal for righteousness.
People who condemn others while committing the same sins condemn themselves.
Anyone called to correct wrongdoing should take special care to examine personal conduct and remain pure.
Jesus remained focused on the great work for which he came: bringing sinners to repentance, not destroying them but saving them.
He intended to lead the woman toward repentance through mercy.
He also intended to lead her accusers toward repentance by exposing their own sins.
They were seeking a way to trap him.
He sought to convict and convert them.
He did not take over the role of a civil judge.
Some offenses rightly deserve severe legal penalties, but we must not abandon our own duties to assume offices God has not assigned to us.
Jesus sent her away with a solemn warning:

p.hi: “Go, and sin no more.”

div.p: Those who help save someone's physical life should also desire to help save the person's soul.
Truly happy are those whom Christ does not condemn.
The forgiveness of former sins ought to lead us to abandon future ones.

div.title: Jesus is the light of the world (verses 12–16)
div.p: God is light, and Christ is the image of the invisible God.
One sun lights the whole world.
Likewise, one Christ gives the saving light the world needs, and no other is necessary.
Without sunlight, the world would be a dark prison.
Without Jesus, the world would be spiritually dark.
Those who follow him will not walk in darkness.
He provides the truths needed to guard us against destructive errors and the guidance needed to keep us from sins that lead to condemnation.

div.title: Jesus reveals the Father (verses 17–20)
div.p: The better we know Christ, the better we know the Father.
Those who refuse to learn from Jesus inevitably form empty and misleading opinions about God.
A person who does not know Christ's glory and grace does not truly know the Father who sent him.
The time of our departure from earth is in God's hands.
Our enemies cannot make it come earlier, and our friends cannot delay it longer than he has appointed.
Every true believer can take comfort in saying:

p.hi: “My times are in your hand.”

div.p: They are safer there than in my own.

div.title: Jesus warns against dying in unbelief (verses 21–29)
div.p: Those who live in unbelief and die in that condition are eternally lost.
Jesus' opponents belonged to this fallen world.
