But he was of a heavenly and divine nature.
His teaching, kingdom and blessings therefore contradicted their interests.
Yet everyone who accepts the grace of the gospel is delivered from the curse of the law.
Only Christ's gracious teaching supplies an argument powerful enough to turn a sinner to God.
Only the Holy Spirit supplies power to accomplish that inward change.
Some people recognize Jesus as a prophet or excellent teacher, perhaps even as greater than an ordinary creature.
But they refuse to confess him as God over all, blessed forever.
That is not sufficient honor for one who is the light and life of humanity and one with the Father.
People will finally recognize his true character either through conversion or in condemnation.
Every claim Jesus made—even his claim to the highest honor—was consistent with his Father's will.

div.title: Christ frees sinners from spiritual slavery (verses 30–36)
div.p: Many listeners were convinced by Jesus' teaching and professed to believe.
Jesus urged them to remain in his word, trust his promises and obey his instructions despite temptation.
Only then would they be shown to be his disciples indeed.
Through his word and Spirit they would discover where to find their hope and strength.
Christ spoke about spiritual freedom.
But worldly-minded people recognize only troubles affecting the body and their earthly affairs.
Tell them about legal liberty, damaged property or losses to land, and they understand immediately.
Tell them about sin's slavery, bondage to Satan, danger to their souls and freedom through Christ, and the ideas sound foreign.
Jesus taught that anyone who habitually practices sin is a slave to sin.
Through the gospel Christ offers genuine liberation, and he possesses the power to accomplish it.
Those whom the Son frees are truly free.
It is tragic that people argue passionately for other forms of liberty while remaining enslaved to sinful desires.

div.title: Abraham's children should resemble Abraham (verses 37–40)
div.p: Jesus challenged his hearers' proud confidence in their ancestry.
Being descendants of Abraham cannot benefit people whose character opposes Abraham's faith.
When God's word has no place in the heart, there is room for every kind of wickedness.
A sick person who refuses the physician's treatment and food is beyond help as long as that refusal continues.
God's truth both heals and nourishes those who receive it.
Human philosophical learning alone does not have that saving power.
Those who claim Abraham's privileges should do Abraham's works.
They should live as pilgrims in the world, maintain God's worship in their households and walk before the Lord.

div.title: The devil's lies oppose God's saving truth (verses 41–47)
div.p: Satan leads people into self-destruction and harms others through their passions.
He also destroys souls through falsehood.
He is the great promoter of lies.
Every temptation claims that evil is good or good is evil, and promises freedom through sinful behavior.
People who imitate Satan's falsehoods become his servants and share his condemnation unless they repent.
The devil's characteristic desires are especially spiritual evils: pride, envy, anger, malice, hostility to goodness, deceptive reasoning and tempting others toward wrongdoing.
Here truth means God's revealed will concerning human salvation through Jesus Christ.
That is the truth Jesus preached and his opponents resisted.

div.title: Believers will not see eternal death (verses 48–53)
div.p: Jesus gave no importance to human applause.
People who are no longer enslaved by the desire for praise can endure contempt more easily.
God will honor those who do not spend their lives seeking their own honor.
Jesus taught the everlasting happiness of those who believe.
A believer is someone who keeps the words of the Lord Jesus.
Such a person will never experience death as eternal destruction.
Believers still encounter bodily death.
Yet they are going to a place where death will exist no more (Exodus 14:13, the source's associated citation).

div.title: Jesus is the eternal “I AM” (verses 54–59)
div.p: Christ and his people depend upon God for true honor.
Human beings may know how to argue about God without truly knowing him.
Scripture associates those who do not know God with those who do not obey Christ's gospel (2 Thessalonians 1:8).
Anyone who knows Christ rightly longs to know him better.
People who have seen the dawn of the Sun of Righteousness desire his full rising.
Jesus said, “Before Abraham was, I AM.”
Abraham was a creature; Jesus is the Creator.
The name I AM is God's name (Exodus 3:14), revealing his self-existence.
Jesus is the First and the Last, unchanging through all ages (Revelation 1:8).
He existed not only before Abraham, but before every world (Proverbs 8:23; John 1:1).
As Mediator he was appointed Messiah before Abraham.
He was the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world (Revelation 13:8).
Jesus was made Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification and Redemption to Adam, Abel and all who lived and died in faith before Abraham.
His opponents prepared to stone him as a blasphemer.
He withdrew safely through his miraculous power.
Let us boldly confess what we know and believe about God.
If we share Abraham's faith, we may rejoice in the future day when Christ will appear in glory, defeat his enemies and complete the salvation of all who trust him.

row.cell: Christ give sight to one born blind.
The account given by the blind man.
The Pharisees question the man that had been blind.
Christ's words to the man that had been blind.

div.title: Jesus heals a man blind from birth (verses 1–7)
div.p: Christ restored sight to many who had lost it through illness or injury. Here he healed someone blind from birth, demonstrating power to help in the most hopeless condition.
This pictures grace giving spiritual sight to sinners who are naturally blind. The man could not see Jesus, but Jesus saw him. If we know anything of Christ, it is because he first knew us.
Unusual afflictions must not always be interpreted as special punishment for particular sins. They may instead be occasions for God to reveal his glory through his works.
Our lifetime is a working day. Let us not waste its opportunities, for we shall have time to rest when the day ends. Death's approach should make us diligent in both doing and receiving good.
Do the good you can promptly. Whoever waits until no possible objection can be raised may accomplish nothing (Ecclesiastes 11:4).

Jesus used a means that might seem more likely to blind a seeing man than to heal a blind one. Human reason cannot judge all God's methods. He often uses instruments the world despises. Those seeking healing from Christ must follow his instructions.

The man went to the pool blind and returned seeing. So God's appointed ordinances can send people away strengthened instead of weak, assured instead of doubtful, joyful instead of grieving, and enlightened instead of blind.

div.title: The healed man tells his story (verses 8–12)
div.p: People transformed by grace remain recognizably the same individuals but become remarkably different in character. Their lives testify to the Redeemer's power and recommend his salvation to others.
We can see the change produced in a soul without seeing the hand that produced it. The Spirit works like the wind: we hear its effects but cannot trace its origin or destination.

div.title: The Pharisees question the man (verses 13–17)
div.p: Jesus performed miracles on the Sabbath in a manner that offended the religious authorities. He refused to give way to interpretations that elevated human ceremonies above the substance of religion.
Works of necessity and mercy are proper on the Sabbath. Rest serves the day's sacred work rather than preventing it.
How many spiritually blind eyes have been opened through gospel preaching on the Lord's day!
Uncharitable judgments often arise because people add their own inventions to God's commands.

Christ was perfect in holiness and wisdom. His enemies found no better accusation than their repeatedly refuted charge of Sabbath-breaking. May our conduct likewise silence foolish and ignorant criticism.

div.title: The man's parents are questioned (verses 18–23)
div.p: The Pharisees hoped to discredit the miracle. They expected a Messiah, but refused to accept Jesus because his teaching contradicted their traditions and he did not display the outward pomp they desired.
Fear of people brings a snare (Proverbs 29:25). It may lead us to deny Christ, abandon his ways or violate our conscience.
Poor or uneducated people with sincere hearts can draw sound conclusions from the gospel's evidence. People driven by contrary desires can keep studying and never reach the truth.

div.title: The man is expelled (verses 24–34)
div.p: Christ's mercy is most precious to those who know how deeply they needed it. Strong and lasting love for him grows through personal experience of his grace.
We may not know precisely when, how or by what steps the Spirit changed us. Yet we may still find comfort in saying, “I was blind, but now I see.”
I once lived for earthly and sensual pleasures, but God's grace has changed me (Ephesians 5:8).
People who have experienced Jesus' saving power marvel at the determined unbelief of those surrounded by evidence of his goodness.
The man made a strong argument: Jesus was not the sinner his accusers claimed but must have come from God.
Let us examine ourselves. What are we doing for God, for our own souls and for others?

div.title: Jesus receives the man (verses 35–38)
div.p: Christ acknowledges those who acknowledge him, especially when they suffer for his truth and the witness of a good conscience.
He graciously revealed himself to the man. The gift of sight had become an even greater mercy because the man could now see the Son of God.
Only God may receive worship. By worshiping Jesus, the man acknowledged his divine nature. All true believers will worship him.

div.title: Christ rebukes the Pharisees (verses 39–41)
div.p: Jesus came to open the eyes of the spiritually blind, while those proud of their supposed wisdom remained shut up in ignorance.
People relying on worldly wisdom regarded the preaching of the cross as foolishness.
Nothing hardens the heart more than supposing that the applause of others guarantees God's approval.
Christ silenced the Pharisees, but their sin remained: they rejected the gospel of grace, so its guilt remained unpardoned and its power remained unbroken.

row.cell: The parable of the good shepherd.
His discourse at the feast of dedication.
The Jews attempt to stone Jesus.

div.title: The sheep and their shepherd (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jesus used an illustration from the way shepherds cared for sheep in the East.
As creatures dependent on their Creator, people are the sheep of God's pasture.
The church is like a sheepfold in the world, exposed to false teachers and persecutors.
The great Shepherd knows everyone who belongs to him. He protects them through his providence, directs them through his Spirit and word, and leads them as shepherds who walk ahead of their flocks.
Ministers must care for the sheep in their spiritual needs. The Spirit of Christ will open the appropriate door before them.
Christ's sheep learn to recognize their Shepherd and are cautious toward strangers who would draw them away from faith in Jesus into speculative notions about him.

div.title: Jesus, the door (verses 6–9)
div.p: Many people fail to understand Jesus' teaching because they are unwilling to understand it.
One part of Scripture helps explain another, and the Holy Spirit makes the Lord Jesus known.
Christ is the Door. What protection could be greater for God's people than having the Lord Jesus between the church and its enemies?
He opens the way of access and fellowship. His instructions for entering the fold are clear: we come through faith in Jesus Christ as the one Mediator between God and humanity.
Precious promises belong to those who enter that way.
As a good shepherd cares for a flock, Christ cares for his church and each believer. In return, he calls his people to depend on him and remain in his pasture.

div.title: Jesus, the good Shepherd who lays down his life (verses 10–18)
div.p: Christ is a good Shepherd. Some other shepherds were not thieves, yet through negligence they caused considerable harm to their flocks.
Wrong principles often produce wrong conduct.
Jesus knows those he has chosen and is certain of them. His people know the One they have trusted and are confident in him.
Here is the grace of Christ: no one could demand his life from him. He freely laid it down for our redemption.
He willingly came to be our Savior. Because our need required a sacrifice, he offered himself.
He is both the priest who offers and the offering itself.
His voluntary death was a death in the place of sinners, securing freedom from sin's deserved punishment and obtaining forgiveness.
Jesus did not merely die to defend a doctrine. He died for his sheep.

div.title: Different reactions to Jesus (verses 19–21)
div.p: Satan ruins many people by making them ashamed of God's word and appointed worship.
People would not usually let someone ridicule them into giving up the food needed to remain alive. Yet they allow ridicule to deprive them of spiritual nourishment, which is even more necessary.
If serving Christ earnestly, especially bringing his sheep into the fold, earns us insulting names, let us not be discouraged.
Our Master endured such insults before us.

div.title: Jesus at the Feast of Dedication (verses 22–30)
div.p: Everyone who has a concern to bring to Christ may find him in the temple.
Jesus seeks to lead us to believe, but often we create our own doubts.
His opponents understood the claim he was making, though they could not turn his words into a charge they could sustain.
Christ described the character and blessed condition of his sheep.
They hear and believe his word, follow him as disciples and are promised that none of them will perish.
The Son and the Father are one.
Therefore Jesus can defend his people against every enemy, which shows he claimed divine power and perfection equal to the Father's.

div.title: The attempt to stone Jesus (verses 31–38)
div.p: Christ's works of mercy and power proclaim that he is God over all, blessed forever.
They invite people to believe that the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father.
The One whom the Father sends, he sets apart as holy. The holy God will not choose people for his service without fitting them for it through holiness.
The Father's presence in the Son accounts for Jesus' miracles of divine power.
The Son's presence in the Father means Jesus knew the whole mind of the Father.
We cannot fully understand this mystery through searching, but we can know and believe what Jesus has declared.

div.title: Jesus withdraws from Jerusalem (verses 39–42)
div.p: No weapon formed against Jesus can accomplish what God forbids.
He escaped not because he was afraid to suffer, but because his appointed hour had not yet come.
The One who could deliver himself can also deliver godly people out of temptation and provide a way of escape.
Persecutors may drive Christ and his gospel out of their own town or country. They cannot drive him or his gospel out of the world.
When we know Christ by faith, we discover that everything Scripture says about him is true.

div.title: Lazarus becomes ill (verses 1–6)
div.p: Those whom Christ loves may still become ill. Bodily afflictions can correct corruption and test the graces of believers.
Jesus did not come to protect his people from every sickness or trouble. He came to save them from sin and the wrath to come.
Nevertheless, we ought to bring sick or afflicted relatives and friends to him in prayer.
God's darkest dealings serve his glory, even when they involve sickness, loss or disappointment. When God is glorified, we may rest in his wisdom.
Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus. A family enjoying affection and peace is blessed; the happiest of all are families whose members love Jesus and are loved by him.
Even in small households, how sadly often that is not true of everyone.
God's purposes remain gracious even when help appears delayed. Deliverance for an individual, household, church or nation comes at the right time.

div.title: Jesus prepares to return to Judea (verses 7–10)
div.p: Christ never brings his people into danger without going with them.
We sometimes imagine we are defending God's cause when we are mainly defending our reputation, comfort, property or safety. We must examine our motives.
God preserves our earthly day until the work appointed to us has been finished and our testimony completed.
Someone walking in the way of duty, guided by God's word and providence, may enjoy peace and confidence.
Jesus always walked in the light of his Father's will.
Those who follow their own desires, worldly customs and merely fleshly calculations rather than God's honor stumble into temptation.
Divine light guides moral action as daylight guides our physical steps.

div.title: Jesus speaks about Lazarus's death (verses 11–16)
div.p: The promised resurrection to eternal life can make the believer's death seem like putting aside one's clothes and going to sleep.
For the Christian, death is rest after a day's labor. In one respect it is better than ordinary sleep, because it ends all earthly cares and work.
The disciples hoped Jesus would not need to return to danger.
We often wish someone else could perform the good work we have been called to do when the duty exposes us to risk.
But Lazarus's resurrection would strengthen existing believers and bring many others to faith.
Let us go to Christ. Death cannot separate us from his love or remove us beyond the reach of his call.
Like Thomas, we should encourage one another in difficult times. Our Savior's willingness to die should make us willing to die when God calls us.

div.title: Jesus reaches the grieving family (verses 17–32)
div.p: A household may fear God and enjoy his blessing and still become a house of mourning. Grace does not prevent every sorrow from visiting our homes.
When God approaches us in mercy, we should go out to meet him through faith, hope and prayer, as Martha did.
Mary remained seated in the house. Her reflective disposition had previously drawn her to Jesus' feet to hear his teaching, but in this sorrow the same inclination contributed to sadness.
We should make wise use of our natural dispositions while guarding against their particular temptations.
When we do not know precisely what to request, leave the matter in God's hands.
Jesus declared himself the Resurrection and the Life. He is resurrection's source, substance, firstfruits and cause.
The redeemed soul lives happily after death. After the resurrection, both body and soul are delivered from evil forever.
Having heard Christ's word about eternity, each of us should ask: Do I really believe this?
If we believed eternal realities as we ought, today's suffering and comfort would not dominate our feelings so completely.
Christ calls us through his word and ordinances. Those who sat at his feet to be taught in peaceful days may fall at those same feet confidently for mercy during trouble.

div.title: Jesus raises Lazarus (verses 33–46)
div.p: Jesus' distress, compassionate questions and tears revealed the tenderness of his heart.
He truly shared the grief of his friends. The Savior was a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.
His tears give us an example of genuine compassion. But he did not praise sentimental people who weep over stories yet remain hard toward real suffering.
Instead of seeking only noisy amusements, let us make time to comfort the afflicted.
We have a High Priest who feels our weaknesses.
Before a soul receives spiritual life, prejudices and barriers often need to be removed, just as the stone was taken from Lazarus's tomb to make room for Christ's word.
If we trust Christ's promise and power, we will see God's glory.
Jesus taught us to address God as Father with both reverence and bold confidence. His public prayer showed the crowd that the Father had sent him as his beloved Son.
Jesus could have raised Lazarus silently by his own will and the Spirit's unseen life-giving power. Instead, he called aloud.
That call pictured both the gospel bringing spiritually dead sinners out of their graves and the final trumpet summoning the dead to judgment.
The grave of sin and the world is no fitting place for those Christ has made alive. They must come out.
Lazarus returned not merely to life but to health.
A sinner cannot give life to the soul, yet must use God's appointed means of grace. A believer cannot sanctify the self apart from God, yet must put aside every hindrance.
We cannot convert our relatives and friends, but we can instruct, warn and invite them.

div.title: The leaders plot against Jesus (verses 47–53)
div.p: This plot shows the desperate hostility toward God that can exist in the human heart.
Speaking prophetic words does not prove that a person has saving grace within.
The disaster people seek to escape through sin may be the very disaster their sin brings upon them.
So it is with people who oppose Christ's kingdom to protect their own interests.
Converting sinners means gathering them to Christ as their Ruler and Refuge.
He died to accomplish this, purchasing his people for himself and securing the gift of the Holy Spirit for them.
His love in dying for believers ought to unite them closely to one another.

div.title: Jesus withdraws before the Passover (verses 54–57)
div.p: Before celebrating the gospel Passover we should renew repentance and prepare seriously to meet God.
Among the Jews, some particularly devout worshipers went to Jerusalem early for purification before the feast.
Human schemes cannot change God's purposes.
While hypocrites become absorbed in forms and arguments, and worldly people pursue their plans, Jesus continues directing all things toward his glory and his people's salvation.

row.cell: A voice from heaven bears testimony to Christ.

div.title: Mary anoints Jesus (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jesus had once corrected Martha for being distracted by too much service. She did not respond by abandoning service altogether, as people sometimes run from one extreme into another when corrected.
She continued serving, now within hearing of Christ's gracious words.
Mary expressed affection toward Jesus, who had already shown profound love to her household.
God had anointed Christ with the oil of gladness above his companions. We ought to offer him the best fragrance of our hearts' affections.
Judas concealed an ugly sin beneath a plausible concern for the poor.
We should not suppose that someone fails to serve God acceptably merely because they do not serve in our preferred way.
When the love of money rules the heart, it becomes a kind of theft within the heart.
The grace of Christ interprets godly words and deeds charitably, making the best of their imperfections and most of their goodness.
Opportunities for service must be used, especially those least likely to return.
The authorities proposed killing Lazarus, the very person Jesus had raised. Their hatred was so unreasonable that only the heart's hostility against God explains it.
The gospel's success can enrage wicked people until they behave as if they could defeat the Almighty himself.

div.title: Jesus enters Jerusalem (verses 12–19)
div.p: All four evangelists recount Jesus' triumphal entry.
His disciples did not immediately understand all that Scripture and God's providence were accomplishing.
We, too, often understand the spiritual meaning of divine events only afterward.
Understanding that Christ's kingdom is spiritual keeps us from misusing prophecies about it.

div.title: Greeks seek Jesus (verses 20–26)
div.p: Whenever we attend sacred worship, especially the gospel Passover, our deepest desire should be to see Jesus—to know him as ours, enjoy fellowship with him and receive grace from him.
The coming of Gentiles to seek him displayed the Redeemer's glory.
A grain of wheat bears no harvest unless it falls into the ground.
Christ could have remained in heavenly glory without becoming human. Even after taking human nature, he might have entered heaven by his own perfect righteousness without suffering or death.
But then no human sinner could have been saved.
Every soul saved before Christ's crucifixion, and every soul saved afterward, depends upon the death of this grain of wheat.
Let us ask whether Christ lives within us as our hope of glory. May he loosen our attachment to trivial concerns, enabling us to serve willingly and follow his holy example.

div.title: A heavenly voice testifies to Jesus (verses 27–33)
div.p: Our sins brought distress to Christ's soul when he undertook to redeem us and offer his soul for our sins.
He was willing to suffer, yet still prayed to be delivered from suffering.
Praying against trouble can coexist with patient submission to God's will.
Christ humbled himself to satisfy the honor of God offended through human sin.
The Father had already declared Jesus his beloved Son at his baptism and transfiguration. Now a voice again confirmed that God's name had been glorified and would be glorified.
By the merit of his death Christ reconciles sinners to God, breaks death's dominion and casts Satan down as a destroyer.
Through the teaching of his cross, he breaks sin's power and drives Satan out as a deceiver.
Souls once far from Christ come to love and trust him. Ascending to heaven, Jesus draws their hearts toward himself.
There is power in Christ's death to draw sinners to him.
The gospel exalts free grace and commands duty. We must embrace both sincerely rather than separate them.

div.title: Jesus urges the people to walk in the light (verses 34–36)
div.p: The listeners misunderstood Scripture because they overlooked the prophecies about the Messiah's suffering and death.
Jesus told them the light would remain among them only a little longer. They should believe it and walk in it before darkness overtook them.
Without faith, people fail to recognize the saving significance of Jesus lifted upon the cross and cannot experience its power as revealed by the Holy Spirit.
They invent countless objections to justify unbelief.

div.title: Many refuse to believe (verses 37–43)
div.p: Conversion begins as sinners see the reality of divine things.
They learn something of God's truth and turn from sin to Christ as their happiness and their portion.
God heals them: justifying and sanctifying them, forgiving sins like open wounds and mortifying corrupt desires like hidden diseases.
But worldly approval can smother even serious convictions.
A desire for human praise can make people hypocrites when religion is fashionable and earns respect.
The same desire can make them apostates when religion is despised and threatens their reputation.

div.title: Jesus gives his final public appeal (verses 44–50)
div.p: Jesus publicly taught that faith in him is also faith in the Father who sent him.
In Christ we see the Father's glory and learn to obey, love and trust the Father.
By continually looking to Jesus, the light of the world, we are increasingly freed from the darkness of ignorance, error, sin and misery.
God our Savior's command is everlasting life.
Yet the same divine word will confirm the condemnation of those who reject or neglect it.

row.cell: Christ commands the disciples to love one another.

div.title: Jesus washes his disciples' feet (verses 1–17)
div.p: The Lord Jesus has people who belong to him. He purchased them at great cost, set them apart and called them to devote themselves to him.
Those he loves, he loves to the end. Nothing can separate a true believer from Christ's love.
Because we do not know when our last hour will arrive, we must never neglect the constant preparation it requires.

We cannot fully understand how the devil enters human hearts. Yet some sins are so dreadful, with so little ordinary enticement from the world or flesh, that Henry sees Satan's direct influence in them.

Jesus washed his disciples' feet to teach us that no task should be considered beneath us if it glorifies God and helps our fellow believers. We must undertake our duties and remove whatever hinders us.
The washing pictured the cleansing of souls from sin's pollution.
The disciples did not yet know why Jesus did everything he did. Events that initially seem painful may later reveal his kindness.

p.hi: Rejecting the gospel because its gifts seem too generous to be true is unbelief, not humility.

div.p: Only those spiritually washed by Christ have a share in him. He both justifies and sanctifies everyone whom he saves.
Peter went beyond submission and asked to be washed completely. Genuine desire for holiness seeks purity in every faculty and part of the person.

Believers receive their fundamental cleansing when they receive Christ as Savior. Yet those already justified must attend to daily cleansing, confessing fresh guilt and resisting whatever might defile them.
Yesterday's pardon should equip us to withstand today's temptation.
Nor should we be surprised if a hypocrite among Christ's professed followers is exposed.
The Lord also taught mutual service. We must accept help from one another as well as give it.
How unworthy it is to lord over fellow believers when our Master himself served them! His love continues after reconciling people who had once been his enemies.

div.title: Jesus foretells the betrayal (verses 18–30)
div.p: Jesus had often spoken about his approaching suffering and death, but the betrayal by Judas caused him particular grief.
The sins of those professing Christ's name grieve him. We should not restrict this warning to Judas.

Think of the unbeliever who studies Scripture only to undermine its authority, the hypocrite who professes Scripture while refusing to obey it, and the apostate who abandons Christ for a worthless advantage.
Human beings eat the bread supplied by divine Providence and then raise their heel against their generous Provider.
Judas departed as though tired of Jesus and his apostles.
Those who practice evil love darkness rather than light.

div.title: Jesus commands the disciples to love one another (verses 31–38)
The glory of the cross and the new command (verses 31–35)
div.p: Jesus had displayed glory through many miracles, yet spoke of his coming suffering as bringing greater glory than any miracle of his humbled ministry.
Through the cross, satisfaction was made for the wrong done to God's honor by human sin.
The disciples could not yet follow him to heavenly happiness. Believers will follow later, but must now wait and fulfill his work.
Jesus gave them a new commandment: they were to love one another for his sake and by his example, seeking each other's good and advancing the gospel together, like one body animated by one spirit.
Strangely, this command remains new to many professing believers. People attend to almost any other teaching of Christ before this one.
If Christians fail to love one another, they give others reason to doubt the sincerity of their discipleship.

div.title: Peter's confidence and Christ's warning (verses 36–38)
div.p: Peter passed over Jesus' command to love and questioned him about matters Jesus had deliberately kept hidden.
We often want to learn the secret things that belong to God rather than the revealed duties that belong to us and our children.
We prefer satisfying curiosity to directing our consciences, or debating heavenly mysteries to learning how to reach heaven.
Plain and helpful truth is often abandoned while doubtful disputes become endless quarrels.
We dislike being told we cannot do something, forgetting that without Christ we can do nothing.
Jesus knows us better than we know ourselves. He has many ways to reveal the condition of those he loves and to hide pride from them.
May we preserve the unity of the Spirit through peace, love one another sincerely and walk humbly with our God.

row.cell: He still further comforts his disciples.

div.title: Jesus comforts the disciples (verses 1–11)
div.p: Jesus' command can be considered by stressing three words.
Troubled: Do not let fear and grief overwhelm you.
Heart: Keep your inward life steady through complete trust in God.
Your: Even if others are overcome by this world's troubles, you, his disciples, should not be.
More than anyone else, Christ's followers should remain quiet in spirit when everything around them is disturbed.
The remedy for a troubled heart is faith. Trusting Christ as Mediator between God and humanity brings comfort.
He describes heaven as his Father's house, with many enduring dwelling places for the many children he will bring to glory.
Jesus will finish what he began. If he has prepared a place for his people, he will also prepare his people for that place.
He is the Way, in his person as God made flesh, through his atoning sacrifice and through his advocacy before the Father.
He is the Truth, fulfilling the promises about the Savior and leading sinners to believe them.
He is the Life, giving spiritual life through his Spirit to those dead in sin.
No one comes to God as Father without being made alive by Christ the Life, instructed by Christ the Truth and brought by Christ the Way.
Through him our prayers reach the Father and God's blessings come to us.
He is the good old way leading to rest, and the Resurrection and the Life.
Everyone who sees Christ through faith sees the Father in him.
His teaching reveals God as the Father of lights; his miracles reveal God's power; his spotless life reveals divine holiness.
The Redeemer's works display both his own glory and God's glory in him.

div.title: Jesus promises the Holy Spirit (verses 12–17)
div.p: Jesus answers petitions offered in his name that truly serve our good and are suited to our condition.
Praying in Christ's name means pleading his merit and intercession, not our own worthiness, and relying upon that plea.
The Holy Spirit is a gift secured by Christ's mediation, purchased through his merit and given through his intercession.
The word used of the Spirit describes an advocate, counselor, guide and comforter.
He will remain with Christ's disciples through the end of time, strengthening and comforting them through his gifts and graces.
Jesus' words describe a Person, whose work displays divine perfection, not an impersonal force.
The Spirit is given to Christ's disciples rather than to the unbelieving world.
This gift is a mark of God's special favor.
As the source of holiness and happiness, the Holy Spirit will abide with every believer forever.

div.title: Jesus will not leave his people as orphans (verses 18–24)
div.p: Christ promised to continue caring for his followers.
He would come to them at his resurrection, come daily through his Spirit and grace, and come certainly at the end of time.
Those who see him through faith will see him forever. The world will not see him again until his return, but his disciples can have fellowship with him even during his bodily absence.
These mysteries will be fully understood in heaven.
We must not merely store Jesus' commands in our minds. We must keep them in our hearts and lives.
The clearest evidence of genuine love for Christ is obedience to his commands.
Where this love is real, obedience follows from gratitude rather than mere compulsion.
God delights to show love to his people and to dwell with them as at home.
These privileges belong to those whose faith works through love and whose love leads to obedience, as recipients of the Spirit's renewing grace.

div.title: The Spirit teaches and Christ gives peace (verses 25–27)
div.p: If we wish to understand Jesus' teaching for our good, we must pray for and depend upon the Holy Spirit.
He brings Christ's words to remembrance and makes difficulties clear that remain obscure to others.
The Spirit of grace serves as a reminder and teacher for believers. By prayer and faith we entrust to him the truths we have heard.
Peace here includes everything truly good that Christ has promised.
It includes peace of conscience arising from justification before God.
Jesus calls it his own peace, because he is our peace.
His peace differs from the false confidence of hypocrisy and empty religion: its effects are humbling and holy.

div.title: Jesus prepares his disciples for departure (verses 28–31)
div.p: Christ invited the disciples to look beyond the earthly comfort they had considered most important.
His remaining time was short, so he gave them extensive counsel.
When we become ill or approach death, we may be unable to speak at length with those we love. Therefore give necessary counsel while we are healthy.
Jesus anticipated conflict not only with human opponents but with the powers of darkness.
Satan finds sinful weaknesses in us to exploit, because we have sinned. In Jesus he found nothing sinful through which to attack him.
The best proof of our love for the Father is doing what he commands.
Let us rejoice in Jesus' victory over Satan, the prince of this world, and imitate Christ's obedient love.

div.title: Christ is the true Vine (verses 1–8)
div.p: Jesus Christ is the true Vine.
The union of his human and divine natures, and the fullness of the Spirit in him, resemble a fruitful root sustained by rich soil.
Believers are branches growing from him.
The root remains hidden, as our life is hidden with Christ. It supports the whole vine and supplies every part of it with nourishment.
All spiritual strength and provision come from him.
The branches are many, yet joined in one root they form one vine. So genuine Christians, even when separated by geography or differing in opinions, are united in Christ.
They are also weak like unsupported branches. They cannot stand apart from the One who sustains them.
The Father is the gardener. No gardener ever tended a vineyard with more wisdom or attention than God gives his church. Under his care, it cannot finally fail.
We must bear fruit.
A vine should produce grapes, and Christians should display Christian character and a life that honors God and benefits others.
Branches that bear no fruit are removed. But even fruitful branches must be pruned.
The best believers retain mistaken ideas, passions and dispositions that need correcting.
Christ carries forward their sanctification through this cleansing work; they should receive it with gratitude.
His word has power to cleanse, producing grace and removing corruption.
The more fruitful his people become, the more the Lord is glorified.
Fruitfulness requires abiding in Christ through faith, continued dependence and fellowship with him.
Believers know from experience that whenever active trust in Christ weakens, holy affections fade, sinful tendencies return and spiritual comfort declines.
People who do not remain in him may flourish outwardly for a time in religious profession but finally achieve nothing.
A withered vine branch has no useful future except the fire.
Let us draw more simply from Christ's fullness and grow in every good word and work, so our joy in him and his salvation may become complete.

div.title: Christ's love and the command to love (verses 9–17)
div.p: Those loved by God as Father need not fear the world's hatred.
The Father loved Christ, who is perfectly worthy, and Christ loved his disciples, who were unworthy.
Everyone who loves the Savior should remain in that love and use every opportunity to show it.
A hypocrite's joy lasts briefly. Those remaining in Christ's love enjoy a lasting feast.
They show love for him by keeping his commandments.
But unless the same divine power that first poured Christ's love into our hearts continued to preserve it, we could not remain in that love for long.
The love we receive from Christ must direct our love toward one another.
Although Jesus had many things to command, he concentrated here upon brotherly love.
That one command includes many other duties.

div.title: The world's hatred of Christ's disciples (verses 18–25)
div.p: Many people fail to recognize that when they reject Christ as Prophet, Priest and King, they show ignorance of the true God whom they claim to worship.
The name into which Jesus' disciples are baptized becomes the name by which they live and die.
For those facing severe suffering, it is a great consolation to suffer because of Christ's name.
The world's ignorance of God lies at the root of its hatred toward Jesus' disciples.
The more clearly people have been shown Christ's grace and truth, the greater their guilt if they refuse to love or believe in him.

div.title: The Comforter will testify (verses 26 and 27)
div.p: The blessed Holy Spirit will maintain Christ's cause in the world despite opposition.
Believers taught and encouraged by his influence will bear witness to Jesus and his salvation.

row.cell: The promise of the Holy Spirit, and his office.

div.title: Jesus foretells persecution (verses 1–6)
div.p: Jesus warned his disciples about coming trouble so they would not be caught unprepared and overwhelmed by fear.
People genuinely opposed to God's service may pretend to be zealously serving him.
Religious language does not make wicked deeds righteous. Evil remains evil even when committed in God's name.
As Christ looked to the fulfillment of Scripture during his suffering, so should his followers during theirs.
Jesus had not previously needed to speak so fully about the Spirit's coming because he was still present to teach, guide and comfort the disciples.
When we suffer, asking where the trouble came from may leave us confused; asking where God is leading it can satisfy us, because his purpose is our good.
Sorrowful Christians often dwell on the cloud's dark side and refuse to hear the voice of joy.
The disciples' excessive attachment to this present life intensified their sadness.
Nothing so obstructs joy in God as love of the world and the worldly grief it produces.

div.title: The Holy Spirit's coming and work (verses 7–15)
div.p: Christ's departure was necessary for the Comforter to come.
The Spirit's coming followed Christ's death, which his departure would accomplish.
Jesus' bodily presence was limited to one place at a time, but his Spirit is present wherever his people gather in his name, at every time and place.
The Spirit first convicts, and then comforts.
Conviction is his work, and only he can accomplish it effectively.
He convinces sinners of sin in its many aspects: its reality, guilt, folly, pollution, source in fallen human nature and final consequence in death.
He shows the whole world guilty before God.
The Spirit also convicts concerning righteousness.
Jesus of Nazareth is the righteous Christ. His righteousness is made available to believers for justification and salvation.
The Spirit shows sinners where righteousness may be found and how they can be accepted before God.
Christ's ascension demonstrates that the ransom has been accepted and the saving righteousness completed.
The Spirit convicts concerning judgment.
The ruler of this world has been judged. When Satan's power is broken, believers can be confident that no rival power can overcome Christ.
This also directs our thoughts toward the final day of judgment.
The Spirit's coming was therefore an immeasurable benefit to the disciples.
He is not merely a guide pointing to the way but a companion helping them walk in it.
Being led into truth means more than carrying correct ideas in the mind.
It means tasting the goodness and knowing the power of truth in the heart.
He will make every profitable truth known and reveal what is to come.
The Spirit's gifts and graces, the apostles' preaching and writing, their languages and miracles—all were intended to glorify Christ.
Each of us should ask whether the Spirit has begun a good work within us.
Unless we recognize our guilt and danger, we will not understand the greatness of Christ's salvation.
The more we pray for and depend on the Spirit, the more clearly we will see the Redeemer and the more deeply we will love him.

div.title: Grief will become joy (verses 16–22)
div.p: We should remember how quickly our opportunities for grace can pass and use them faithfully.
The disciples' sorrow would soon give way to joy, like a mother's pain replaced by happiness at the sight of her newborn child.
The Holy Spirit would comfort them, and neither people nor demons, suffering nor death, could permanently steal their joy.
Believers' sorrow or gladness is closely connected with their sense of Christ's presence and favor.
The ungodly are approaching sorrow that nothing can relieve.
Believers, however, inherit joy that no one can take away.
Where is the happiness now of those who murdered the Lord, compared with the lasting joy of his friends?

div.title: Jesus encourages prayer (verses 23–27)
div.p: Asking something of the Father acknowledges spiritual need, desires spiritual blessings and recognizes that only God can supply them.
Praying in Christ's name acknowledges our unworthiness and depends entirely on Christ as the Lord our Righteousness.
Until then Jesus had often taught through brief sayings or parables that his disciples did not fully understand.
After his resurrection he intended to speak more plainly about the Father and access to him through his intercession.
Jesus repeatedly commanded prayer in his name because his mediation teaches us our sinfulness and the value and power of his atoning death, by which we approach God.
We may address the Father in Christ's name or address the Son as God in human nature who reconciles sinners to himself.
These approaches belong together because the Father and the Son are one.

div.title: Jesus' departure and the disciples' confidence (verses 28–33)
div.p: Jesus came from the Father as God revealed in human nature, and he would return to the Father and be received into glory.
The disciples understood more and their faith increased.
Yet they did not yet recognize their own weakness.
The divine nature never abandoned Christ's human nature during his sufferings.
It supported him, giving his suffering strength and worth.
When God is graciously present with us, we can be content even when everyone else deserts us.
True peace is found in Christ alone.
Through him we have peace with God, and therefore peace within our hearts.
Christ has already conquered the world.
Yet believers must remain watchful, for those who think they stand can still fall.
We do not know how we would behave under severe temptation.
Watch and pray without ceasing, so that God does not leave us to ourselves.

div.title: Christ prays concerning his own glorification (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jesus prayed as a man and the Mediator of his people, yet spoke with the majesty and authority of One who is equal to the Father.
Believers could not receive eternal life unless Christ, their Surety, had glorified the Father and been glorified by him.
The sinner's way to everlasting life is found in this Mediator. When our knowledge of God is perfected in heaven, holiness and happiness will be perfectly enjoyed.
Christ and the Father are especially glorified by the holiness and happiness of the redeemed.
For the joy set before him—his people brought to salvation—Jesus endured the cross and despised its shame.
When he obtained this, the purpose of his soul's suffering was fulfilled and he was satisfied.
We learn that glorifying God is a necessary evidence that we belong to Christ, through whom eternal life is God's free gift.

div.title: Christ prays for the disciples given to him (verses 6–10)
div.p: Jesus prays for those who belong to him.
The Father has given them to Christ like sheep to a shepherd for protection, a patient to a physician for healing and children to a teacher for instruction.
Jesus will faithfully return the charge entrusted to him.
Our confidence in Christ rests on this: everything he is, has, says and does, and everything he will yet accomplish, comes from God.
In this prayer he particularly intercedes for his believing people, rather than the world considered as a whole.
But no person who desires to come to God, recognizing their own unworthiness, should be discouraged by that distinction.
Jesus is willing and able to save completely everyone who comes to God through him.
Earnest conviction of sin and desire for his salvation are hopeful signs that grace is already working—evidence of God's choice through the Spirit's sanctification and faith in the truth.
Christ's disciples belong to the Father. He will care for his own.
The ground of Jesus' request is “All mine are yours, and yours are mine.” This expresses the Father and Son's unity.
The Son claims no one as his own who is not also devoted to his Father's service.

div.title: Christ prays for his disciples and all believers (verses 11–26)
Protection from the evil of this world (verses 11–16)
div.p: Jesus does not ask that his followers become wealthy and powerful.
He asks that they be protected from sin, strengthened for duty and brought safely to heaven.

p.hi: The soul's prosperity is the best prosperity.

div.p: Christ appeals to the holy Father to preserve the disciples by his power and for his glory, keeping them united in love and work according to the Father and Son's union.
Nor does he ask that they be taken out of the world to escape human hostility.
They have work to accomplish for God's glory and other people's good.
Instead, he asks that they be kept from the evil one, from corruption through the world, from remaining sin within themselves and from Satan's cunning and power.
They must pass through this world like travelers through hostile territory, as Jesus himself did.
They were not left on earth to pursue the same ends as those around them, but to glorify God and serve their generation.
The Spirit present in genuine Christians is opposed to the spirit of this world.

div.title: Sanctification through truth (verses 17–19)
div.p: Jesus prays not only that his people be kept from evil but that they be made holy.
Even disciples must seek sanctifying grace.
The instrument is God's truth: his word is truth.
To be sanctified is to be set apart for God and his service.
Christ asks the Father to accept their work and accompany them in fulfilling it.
Jesus devoted himself entirely to the task the Father gave him, especially offering himself without blemish to God through the eternal Spirit.
The holiness of genuine believers comes through Christ's death, which purchased the gift of the Holy Spirit.
He gave himself for his church to sanctify it.
If our understanding of divine truth never produces holiness, either our understanding is mistaken or we have received truths as mere ideas rather than living and active faith.

div.title: Unity among all who will believe (verses 20–23)
div.p: Jesus prays especially that believers be one body under one Head, animated by one Spirit, through their union with Christ and with the Father in him.
The more Christians quarrel about lesser matters, the more doubt they cast upon Christianity.
Let us seek the unity of the Spirit in peace, praying that believers grow increasingly united in understanding and judgment.
Such unity will testify to the truth and excellence of the gospel and deepen our fellowship with God and other believers.

div.title: The redeemed behold Christ's glory (verses 24–26)
div.p: As One with the Father, Jesus asks that everyone given to him, including people who would believe later, be brought to heaven.
There the whole redeemed company will behold his glory as their beloved Friend and Brother and find happiness in him.
Jesus has made known and will continue making known God's name and character through his teaching and his Spirit.
The result is that the Father's love for the Son may abide with those joined to Christ.
United to him by one Spirit, they will be filled with all God's fullness and enjoy blessedness far beyond what we can now imagine.

div.title: Jesus is arrested in the garden (verses 1–12)
div.p: Sin first entered the human story in the garden of Eden. There the curse was pronounced and a Redeemer promised.
Now in another garden, that promised descendant entered conflict with the ancient serpent.
Jesus would also be buried in a garden.
Whenever we walk in a garden, we may remember the sufferings Christ endured in one.
Jesus knew everything about to happen. Yet he stepped forward to ask the crowd whom they sought.
When people wanted to force him to wear an earthly crown, he withdrew (John 6:15). When they came to force him to a cross, he freely presented himself.
He had come into this world to suffer, and would enter the next to reign.
Jesus demonstrated his power when the arresting party fell backward. He could have struck them dead but refused.
The soldiers' willingness to allow the disciples to escape quietly after the attempted resistance must also be attributed to divine power.
Jesus gives an example of meekness in suffering and complete submission to God's will.
Our earthly trials are like a cup. They are given to us by a Father, whose authority is right, whose affection is kind and whose purposes cannot wrong us.
If Jesus accepted his appointed cup, how can we distrust the love of our Father when he appoints much lighter burdens to us?
We were bound by the bonds of our sins and the yoke of our transgressions.
To free us from that bondage, Christ became a sin offering and willingly allowed himself to be bound.
We owe our freedom to his bonds. Thus the Son makes his people free.

div.title: Jesus before Annas and Caiaphas; Peter's denials (verses 13–27)
div.p: Peter denied his Master. The other Gospels supply further details about this event.
Beginning to sin is like opening a floodgate: a small beginning can quickly become destructive.
Lying is particularly fruitful in evil. A lie often requires another to support it, and then another.
When God clearly calls us into danger, we may trust him to help us honor him.
But when we enter danger without a clear call of duty, we have reason to fear being left to dishonor ourselves.
Jesus' accusers did not even address the miracles through which he had helped so many people and confirmed his teaching.
They rejected his truth while deliberately refusing to look at its evidence.
Jesus appealed to the people who had heard him openly. His doctrine can safely be submitted to those who truly know it and judge fairly.
Even when wronged, we must not react with passionate resentment.
Jesus reasoned calmly with the person who struck him. We may follow that example.

div.title: The accusation and predicted manner of death (verses 28–32)
div.p: The authorities knew it was unjust to execute a man who had done such good, yet they wanted to avoid the public disgrace of their actions.
Many people fear the scandal of wrongdoing more than the wrongdoing itself.
Jesus had predicted being delivered to the Gentiles and put to death.
He had also said he would be lifted up.
If condemned under the Jewish legal process, he would have been stoned; Roman crucifixion fulfilled his prediction.
Our own manner and time of death are likewise known to God, though concealed from us.
That knowledge should release us from anxiety: Lord, let what you have appointed happen when and how you have appointed it.

div.title: The King whose kingdom is not worldly (verses 33–40)
div.p: Pilate asked whether Jesus was the King of the Jews—the long-expected Messiah.
Jesus answered with a question, not to evade Pilate, but to make him consider what he was doing.
Jesus had never claimed earthly political authority, and no charge of treasonous conduct could be established against him.
He explained his kingdom.
Its nature is spiritual: it is established in human hearts and consciences, with spiritual wealth, power and glory.
Its supports and weapons are spiritual. It does not need violence or use force to advance. It opposes not earthly kingdoms but sin and Satan's reign.
Its purpose is spiritual.
As the Truth, Christ is also King: he conquers through truth's compelling evidence and rules through truth's rightful authority.
Those who belong to the truth are his subjects.
Pilate asked, “What is truth?”
When we read Scripture and listen to preaching, we should ask that question sincerely and pray to be led into all truth.
Many ask it without the patience to keep seeking or humility to receive the answer.
Pilate's statement that Jesus was innocent confirms that Christ was condemned as a criminal despite deserving none of the accusations.
It also reveals the purpose of his death: to become the sacrifice for our sins.
Pilate tried to satisfy every side, guided more by worldly calculation than by justice.
Sin is a robber, yet people foolishly choose it over Christ, who alone can truly enrich them.
Let us answer false accusations as Jesus did, and never turn away from him as though crucifying him again.

div.title: Jesus is condemned and crucified (verses 1–18)
div.p: Pilate could hardly have imagined how future generations of great and godly people would reverently remember Christ's sufferings.
Jesus willingly endured public ridicule.
Let everyone who believes look upon Jesus in his suffering. Behold him with faith and love, and continually fix your attention on him.
If hatred made Jesus' enemies more determined to oppose him, should not love make us more diligent in serving him and his kingdom?
Pilate appears to have suspected that Jesus might be a person far above the ordinary human condition.
Even natural conscience can make a person afraid of fighting against God.
Christ suffered for the sins of Jews and Gentiles. In God's wise purpose, Jewish leaders planned his death and Gentile authorities carried it out.
If Jesus had not been rejected by human beings, we would have remained rejected before God.
The Son of Man was handed over to unreasonable and wicked people.
He was led away on our behalf so that we might escape.
He was fastened to the cross like a sacrifice bound upon the altar.
Scripture was fulfilled. He did not die among temple sacrifices but among criminals executed by public authority.
Let us contemplate his suffering with faith.
Was there ever sorrow like his sorrow?
Look upon him bleeding and dying, and let love for him lead you to live for him.

div.title: Christ's final hours on the cross (verses 19–30)
div.p: John records remarkable circumstances of Jesus' death in fuller detail than elsewhere.
Pilate refused to alter the inscription on the cross at the priests' request. Henry attributes this to God's hidden influence, preserving a statement of Christ's kingship and authority.
The Roman soldiers' conduct fulfilled several Old Testament prophecies. Everything God has written must be fulfilled.
Dying, Jesus provided tenderly for his mother.
When God takes one earthly source of comfort from us, he may raise up another from an unexpected place.
Christ teaches everyone to honor parents during their life and at their death, meeting their needs and promoting their comfort as far as possible.
Above all, consider his final announcement: “It is finished.”
The Father's purposes concerning Christ's suffering had been fulfilled.
All Old Testament types and prophecies pointing to the suffering Messiah had reached their fulfillment.
The ceremonial law had reached its end, because the reality it foreshadowed had now arrived.
Transgression was dealt with through the bringing in of everlasting righteousness.
The sufferings of his body and soul were complete.

p.hi: The work of human redemption and salvation was accomplished.

div.p: His life was not taken from him against his will; he freely gave it up.

div.title: The soldier pierces Jesus' side (verses 31–37)
div.p: The soldiers confirmed that Jesus had died.
He died more quickly than crucified prisoners ordinarily did, a sign that he had laid down his life voluntarily.
The spear opened the source of bodily life; no ordinary human body could have survived such a wound.
Its solemn attestation suggests that the detail had particular meaning.
Blood and water flowed from his side.
Henry understands them as signs of the two great blessings believers receive through Christ:
Blood for justification, bringing atonement and forgiveness.
Water for sanctification, bringing cleansing and holiness.
Both flow from the pierced side of the Redeemer. The crucified Christ provides merit for our justification and the Spirit's grace for our sanctification.
This comforts fearful believers: Jesus provides both the pardon they need and the holiness they lack.
The refusal to break Jesus' legs fulfilled Scripture (Psalm 34:20), prefigured in the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46).
May we always look toward the Savior whom our sins have pierced, sometimes even against the warnings and mercies we had already received.
He gave both blood and water so that in his name we might be justified and sanctified.

div.title: Jesus is buried (verses 38–42)
div.p: Joseph of Arimathea had been a secret disciple.
Those who follow Christ should confess him openly. Yet someone timid in a smaller trial may show courage in a greater one.
When God has work to do, he can raise up people suited to it.
Nicodemus, another secret friend though not a constant public follower, helped prepare Jesus' body for burial.
Grace that begins like a bruised reed can grow as strong as a cedar.
These wealthy men showed that the dishonor of the cross had not reduced their love for Christ or their respect for his teaching.
We should fulfill today's duties when the opportunity arises, trusting God to carry out his promises in his own time.
Jesus was assigned a grave among the wicked as someone executed for a crime, but was with the rich in his death, fulfilling Isaiah 53:9.
Those seemingly incompatible circumstances could hardly have been predicted from ordinary human knowledge.
He was placed in a new tomb, removing any excuse to confuse the identity of the One who would rise.
Nor should believers be particular about the location of their own burial: Jesus was buried in the tomb conveniently at hand.
The Sun of Righteousness had set for a little while, soon to rise with greater glory and never set again.

row.cell: The sepulchre found to be empty.

div.title: The tomb is found empty (verses 1–10)
div.p: If Christ had given his life as a ransom but never taken it up again, there would be no clear evidence that God had accepted his sacrifice as satisfaction for sin.
Mary was distressed to find his body missing.
Believers who are weak in faith often complain about circumstances that are actually grounds for hope and joy.
It is fitting for disciples who enjoy special privileges to be especially active in fulfilling their duties, enduring effort and risk in good work.
We should do our best without envying those who do better or despising people who are slower yet do everything they can.
The disciple whom Jesus especially loved reached the tomb first. Christ's love motivates devoted service more effectively than anything else.
Peter followed behind. He had denied Jesus, and a guilty conscience can slow our service to God.
The disciples had not yet understood Scripture's teaching that Christ must rise from the dead.

div.title: Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene (verses 11–18)
div.p: Those who seek Christ with affection—even through tears—have reason to hope they will find him.
Sometimes believers complain about clouds and darkness even when God uses them to humble their hearts, put sin to death and make Christ more precious.
Even an angel's presence and smile cannot satisfy a soul without Jesus and the Father's favor in him.
Only those who have experienced spiritual desertion fully know the pain of losing the felt assurance of Christ's love and hope of heaven.
But Christ often exceeds the expectations of those seeking him.
Mary's longing to find Jesus was unmistakable.
He made himself known by speaking to her. Christ commonly reveals himself personally to his people through his word applied to the soul.
Those who love Jesus delight in acknowledging him as their Master.
He warned Mary not to expect the same form of his bodily presence as before.
Through union with Christ, his Father is our Father, and his God is our God.
Christ shares our human nature, while believers are made partakers of the divine nature through grace.
His ascension to heaven, where he intercedes for us, brings great consolation.
Earth is not our final home or resting place; since Jesus ascends, our desires should seek the things above.
Those who know Christ's word should help others benefit from it.

div.title: Jesus appears to the gathered disciples (verses 19–25)
div.p: This happened on the first day of the week, a day the New Testament repeatedly mentions and which Henry understands as established as the Christian Sabbath in remembrance of the resurrection.
The disciples had locked the doors for fear of persecution.
Jesus nevertheless stood among them, arriving miraculously and silently.
When believers must gather privately, locked doors cannot keep Christ's presence away.
When he assures them of his love through the Spirit, he gives comfort in his promise that because he lives, they will live also.
Seeing more of Christ always brings greater joy to disciples.
Jesus breathed upon them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.”
Their spiritual life and fitness for ministry depend entirely on him.
When Christ's word is received by faith in the heart, its true effect comes through the Spirit's life-giving breath; without it there is neither light nor life.
Jesus commissioned the apostles to declare the way sins are forgiven.
Henry explicitly rejects the view that the apostles possessed an independent power to forgive or condemn as judges.
They were authorized to declare the marks of those God accepts or rejects at the final judgment.
Through their teaching we can discern genuine believers from false professors.
When we meet in Christ's name, especially on his appointed day, he will meet with us and speak peace.
Disciples should strengthen one another by telling absent friends what they heard and experienced.
Thomas required conviction on his own terms. In doing so he limited the Holy One of Israel.
He might justly have been left to his unbelief after so much evidence.
Sometimes disciples prolong their own sorrows through neglect or refusal to believe.

div.title: Thomas sees and believes (verses 26–29)
div.p: God appointed that one day in seven should be kept holy from the beginning.
Henry understands Christ's repeated appearances at the disciples' assemblies on the first day of the week as confirming that day for worship under the Messiah.
The church has continued observing it through the generations.
Jesus knows every unbelieving word and thought.
Yet he graciously accommodated Thomas's weakness instead of leaving him in unbelief.
We likewise should bear with the weak (Romans 15:1–2).
The warning remains: unbelief deprives people of grace, hope, joy and fellowship with Christ.
Thomas was ashamed of his former unbelief and responded with affectionate confession: “My Lord and my God.”
He laid hold of Christ wholeheartedly.
Jesus graciously receives genuine believers even when their faith is slow or weak.
All who hear or read the gospel are called to receive the testimony God has given concerning his Son (1 John 5:11).

div.title: Why these signs were written (verses 30 and 31)
div.p: Jesus performed many other signs, but these were written down so that readers might believe he is the promised Messiah, Savior of sinners and Son of God.
Through that faith they may receive eternal life by his mercy, truth and power.
May we believe Jesus is the Christ and, by believing, have life through his name.

div.title: Jesus appears beside the sea (verses 1–14)
div.p: Christ usually reveals himself to his people through his appointed ordinances.
But he may also visit them by his Spirit while they are engaged in ordinary work.
Disciples benefit from being together in common conversation and everyday labor.
The time for their new public work had not yet arrived. Meanwhile they could earn their own support and avoid becoming a burden to others.
Christ often reveals himself when his followers are most at a loss.
He knows their material needs, promising not only sufficient grace but also what is necessary for daily provision.
God's Providence extends to the smallest details. Happy are those who acknowledge him in everything.
Humble, diligent and patient workers may encounter failure after failure, yet their efforts are not wasted. Sometimes they live to see a happy change after many struggles.
Obeying Christ's instructions is never a loss. It is like casting the net on the right side of the boat.
Jesus demonstrates his care by providing what no one else could supply, often in unexpected ways.
He would see to it that those who had abandoned everything to follow him lacked no truly good thing.
Later mercies should also remind us of earlier ones, so that we do not forget the bread already received from his hand.
The disciple whom Jesus especially loved was the first to recognize him: “It is the Lord!”
John had remained near Jesus during the sufferings and now recognized him first.
Peter, known for zeal, was the first to reach Jesus.
God gives different gifts and different ways of honoring Christ. Yet all faithful servants can be acceptable to him.
The others stayed in the boat, pulled the net and brought the catch to shore.
They should not be called worldly: their diligent work served Christ just as truly.
Jesus had a meal prepared for the disciples.
We need not speculate about precisely where it came from; the important lesson is his loving care.
Although the fish were numerous and large, none was lost and the net remained intact.
The net of the gospel has gathered multitudes, yet it remains strong enough to bring more souls to God.

div.title: Jesus restores Peter and commands him to shepherd (verses 15–19)
div.p: Jesus addressed Peter by his former name, as if his denials had deprived him of the name Peter.
When Peter replied, he appealed to Jesus' knowledge of his love, but did not claim to love him more than the other disciples.
If our conduct has made our sincerity doubtful, we should not be surprised when others question it.
Remembering former sins—even forgiven sins—renews the sorrow of a genuinely repentant person.
Yet Peter, conscious of his sincere love, appealed solemnly to Christ, who knows every secret of the heart.
Our failures ought to make us more humble and watchful.
The sincerity of our love for God must be tested.
We should repeatedly ask the Lord, who searches hearts, to examine whether our love is genuine.
No one is qualified to feed Christ's lambs and sheep who does not love the Good Shepherd more than worldly advantage or any earthly object.
Whatever manner of death God appoints, a godly person's concern should be to glorify him in dying, just as in living.
Our final purpose is to belong to the Lord and die at his command.

div.title: Jesus speaks about John's future (verses 20–24)
div.p: Pain, suffering and death can frighten even an experienced believer.
But the hope of glorifying God, leaving a sinful world and being present with Christ can make us willing to follow him through death into glory.
Jesus calls each disciple to attend to personal duty, not become preoccupied with the hidden future of oneself or others.
Many things we worry about are really not our business.
Let us work quietly and fulfill our own calling instead of meddling in other people's affairs.
Some curious questions concern God's hidden plans or the unseen world. We need not pretend to answer them.
If we concentrate on following Jesus, we will have little desire or time to intrude into what does not belong to us.
This passage also shows how unreliable unwritten traditions can be.
Let Scripture explain Scripture, for it is its own light and, to a large extent, its own evidence.
Christ's exact words easily corrected the mistaken rumor about John.
The language of Scripture is the safest expression of biblical truth—the words taught by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:13).
Believers who disagree about technical theological language and its uses may still unite in Scripture's own words and love one another.

div.title: The Gospel's final sentence (verse 25)
div.p: Only a small part of everything Jesus did has been recorded.
We should thank God for what he has given in Scripture: so much truth in comparatively little space.
Enough has been written to guide our faith and govern our conduct.
More was not needed for that purpose.
Even as it is, much of the Bible is neglected, forgotten or made the subject of fruitless disputes.
In heaven we may look forward to discovering more completely all that Christ did and said, and the full story of his providence and grace in our own lives.
May that blessed knowledge be ours.
These things are written so that we may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (John 20:31).

div.title: Acts — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The book of Acts connects the Gospels with the Epistles.
It records important events involving the apostles Peter and Paul and the Christian church from the Savior's ascension until Paul's arrival in Rome, a period of about thirty years.
Luke wrote the book. He witnessed many of the events he describes and accompanied Paul to Rome.
But Acts is not a complete history of the Christian church during those years, or even a complete biography of Paul.
Henry identifies two major purposes in its narrative.

First, it records how the Holy Spirit's gifts were communicated at Pentecost and how the apostles' miracles confirmed the truth of Christianity. The gifts showed that Jesus' promises had really been fulfilled.
Second, it demonstrates the right of Gentiles to be received into the church of Christ.
Much of Acts consists of public addresses and sermons delivered by different people.
Their words and manner fit the speakers and the circumstances in which they were spoken.
Henry judges that most of the speeches preserve the substance rather than necessarily every word originally spoken.
All, however, direct attention to Jesus as the Christ, the anointed Messiah.

row.cell: Matthias chosen in the place of Judas.

div.title: The risen Christ prepares the apostles (verses 1–5)
div.p: The Lord Jesus explained to the disciples the work they would undertake.
He commanded them to remain in Jerusalem until the promised Holy Spirit had been poured out.
This would be baptism with the Holy Spirit, granting miraculous power while also enlightening and sanctifying their souls.
Because Jesus himself spoke the promise, we may depend confidently upon it.
All God's promises find their Yes and Amen in Christ.

div.title: Jesus ascends to heaven (verses 6–11)
div.p: The disciples eagerly asked about matters their Master had never encouraged them to investigate.
Jesus knew that his ascension and the Spirit's teaching would soon correct their misunderstandings.
He therefore rebuked their curiosity rather than giving the political timetable they sought.
This warns the church in every age against desiring knowledge God has not authorized us to seek.
Christ had already told them their duties before his death and again after his resurrection.
That revealed knowledge was sufficient for faithful service.
It is enough that Jesus promises believers strength suited to the trials and tasks before them.
Through the Spirit they can bear witness to him on earth in the ways he gives, while Christ governs their concerns in heaven with perfect wisdom, truth and love.
When we stand idly watching or wasting time, thinking of his return should awaken us to work.
When we are trembling with fear, the same promise should comfort and encourage us.
May we await his return steadfastly and joyfully, diligently seeking to be found blameless.

div.title: The disciples pray together (verses 12–14)
div.p: God knows how to provide safe gathering places for his people.
The disciples devoted themselves to prayer.
Everyone belonging to God should be a praying person.
The disciples lived amid danger and uncertainty.
Prayer is the proper response to affliction, because it brings fears and cares before God.
An enormous task lay ahead of them. Before beginning, they earnestly sought God's presence.
They waited for the Spirit's coming by praying continually.
People are best prepared to receive spiritual blessings when their hearts are inclined to prayer.
Jesus' promise that the Spirit would soon come did not make prayer unnecessary. It strengthened and encouraged their praying.
Even a small congregation can grow rapidly when its members are united in love, exemplary in conduct, earnest in prayer and wisely zealous for Christ's cause.

div.title: Matthias is chosen to replace Judas (verses 15–26)
div.p: The apostles' central calling was to bear witness to the resurrection of Jesus, the great proof that he is the Messiah and the foundation of our hope.
Apostolic office was not given to create worldly prestige or dominion, but to preach Christ and the power of his resurrection.
The believers appealed to God, who knows every heart better than any human being knows it—including its owner.
God should choose his own servants.
When he shows us his choice through Providence or through gifts supplied by the Spirit, we should gladly accept his will.
Let us recognize his hand in all that occurs, especially when a responsibility or trust is entrusted to us.

row.cell: The descent of the Holy Spirit at the day of Pentecost.
The apostles speak in divers languages.
The piety and affection of the disciples.

div.title: The Holy Spirit is poured out at Pentecost (verses 1–4)
div.p: While Jesus was with them, the disciples had repeatedly argued about which would be greatest.
Now those quarrels had ended, and they had lately prayed together more earnestly.
If we desire the Spirit's blessing, let us be of one accord.
Believers may disagree in opinion and personal interests, but should agree to love one another.
Where brothers and sisters live in unity, the Lord commands his blessing.
A mighty rushing wind announced the Spirit's arrival.
It pictured the Spirit's powerful work in human minds and through them in the world.
His convicting work prepares the way for his comfort.
The strong gusts of that holy wind prepare hearts for its gentle breezes.
Something resembling flames of fire rested on each disciple, fulfilling John the Baptist's announcement that Christ would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.
The Spirit works like fire: softening hard hearts, burning away impurity and kindling reverent, loving devotion.
Believers then offer spiritual sacrifices, as sacrifices once burned upon the altar.
The disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit more fully than before.
They received greater sanctifying grace, became less attached to this world and more acquainted with the world to come.
They enjoyed stronger comfort, more assurance of Christ's love and more hope of heaven; grief and fear were overwhelmed.
They also received miraculous gifts for advancing the gospel.
They spoke, not by recalling prepared thoughts, but as the Spirit supplied their words.

div.title: The apostles speak in different languages (verses 5–13)
div.p: The division of languages begun at Babel had long hindered the spread of knowledge and religion.
The apostles could not have advanced the gospel throughout many nations without a gift that enabled them to speak those languages.
This gift also confirmed that their authority came from God.

div.title: Peter explains the promise of the Spirit (verses 14–21)
