div.p: Peter's sermon showed how completely he had recovered from his earlier fall and how fully he had been restored to God's favor.
The man who had denied Christ now confessed him boldly.
Peter explained that the miraculous pouring out of the Spirit should move his hearers to embrace faith in Jesus and join his church.
The event fulfilled Scripture and followed Christ's resurrection and ascension, confirming both.
Although filled with the Spirit and able to speak miraculously, Peter did not set aside the Scriptures.
Disciples of Christ never outgrow their Bibles.
The Holy Spirit was not given to abolish Scripture, but to help believers understand, receive and obey it.
No one will escape final condemnation except those who call upon the Lord through his Son Jesus Christ, Savior of sinners and Judge of humanity.

div.title: Peter proclaims the crucified and risen Jesus (verses 22–36)
div.p: Peter used the Holy Spirit's gift to preach Jesus himself.
He recalled Christ's suffering and death, which his listeners had witnessed only a few weeks before.
Christ's death must be considered in two distinct ways.
As God's purpose, it revealed extraordinary grace and wisdom: divine justice would be satisfied, God and sinners reconciled and Christ glorified according to an eternal counsel that could not fail.
As the people's act, it was terrible wickedness and folly.
Jesus' resurrection removed the disgrace attached to his execution.
Peter explained it at length.
Jesus was God's Holy One, set apart for the work of redemption.
His death and suffering would open the way to everlasting blessedness for himself and all who belong to him.
The event took place as Scripture foretold, and the apostles were eyewitnesses.
The resurrection was also confirmed by the Spirit whom Jesus poured out, giving visible miraculous gifts and divine power to his disciples.
Through Christ the way of life is revealed, and believers may hope to enjoy God's presence and favor forever.
All these blessings arise from faith that Jesus is Lord and the anointed Savior.

div.title: Three thousand people respond to the gospel (verses 37–41)
div.p: From the beginning, God accompanied the gospel message with divine power, bringing thousands to the obedience of faith.
Neither Peter's words nor the miracle the crowd had seen could have brought about this conversion apart from the Holy Spirit.
When the eyes of sinners are opened, they feel conviction of sin and sorrow of heart.
Peter called them to repent and publicly confess Jesus as Messiah through baptism in his name.
They were promised forgiveness and participation in the Spirit's gifts and graces.
True repentance also involves separating from wickedness rather than continuing to identify with it.
Repentant believers show sincerity by breaking with sinful ways.
By God's grace, three thousand people accepted the gospel invitation.
All genuine believers receive the Spirit's indispensable adopting, converting, guiding and sanctifying grace.
This must be distinguished from the apostles' special miraculous gifts.
Repentance and forgiveness are still proclaimed in Christ's name even to the worst sinners.
The Holy Spirit still confirms God's promise in believers' hearts.
The promise remains for us, our children and those far away.

div.title: The first believers share their lives (verses 42–47)
div.p: These verses describe the church's earliest days.
It was young and, like the innocence of infancy, marked by unusual sincerity.
The believers faithfully continued in God's appointed means of worship and lived in prayer and devotion.
When Christianity rules the heart, believers seek fellowship with God through the ordinances in which he promises to meet his people.
What they had experienced lifted their hearts above worldly possessions.
The Spirit filled them with such love that they treated one another's needs almost as their own.
Thus they had things in common not by abolishing private property, but by overcoming selfishness and practicing generosity.
God knew these believers would soon face persecution and displacement from their possessions in Judea.
Every day the Lord inclined more people to receive the gospel.
They were not merely outward professors but people truly received by God through regenerating grace.
Those whom God has appointed for everlasting salvation will be brought to Christ, until knowledge of his glory fills the earth.

row.cell: A lame man healed by Peter and John.

div.title: Peter heals a man who could not walk (verses 1–11)
div.p: The apostles and first Christians continued to attend the temple's times of prayer.
Peter and John seem to have received divine direction to perform this miracle upon a man more than forty years old, who had been unable to walk since birth.
In the name of Jesus of Nazareth, Peter commanded him to stand and walk.
If we want to help spiritually helpless people, we likewise must act in Christ's name and through his power.
We call sinners to rise and walk in holiness through faith in him.
What a delightful thought: every faculty of our fallen nature that has become powerless through sin can be healed by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.
What holy joy will we experience when God's Spirit strengthens us to enter the courts of his house!

div.title: The source of the miracle (verses 12–18)
div.p: Notice the difference between Jesus and the apostles when performing miracles.
Jesus spoke with almighty authority and did not refuse the honor due to his divine miracles.
The apostles, by contrast, referred every miracle to Christ and rejected honor for themselves except as unworthy instruments of his power.
This reveals Jesus' unity and equality with the Father, while the apostles remained weak and sinful human beings wholly dependent upon him.
Useful servants must therefore be deeply humble.

p.hi: Not to us, Lord, but to your name belongs the glory.

div.p: Every crown must be placed at Christ's feet.
Peter showed the crowd the seriousness of its guilt in rejecting Jesus, but did not intend to drive sinners into anger or despair.
Those who reject Christ act in ignorance, but that does not excuse their wrongdoing.

div.title: Repentance and times of refreshing (verses 19–21)
div.p: Everyone seeking forgiveness and the comfort of Christ's pardoning love must be urgently called to repentance.
Blessed are those who have experienced the refreshing assurance that forgiven sins bring.
The Holy Spirit did not reveal the precise dates and periods of every future event.
Such matters remain obscure and are not necessary for faithfulness.
When sinners recognize their wrongdoing, they call upon God for pardon.
To those who repent, turn to Christ and believe, times of refreshing come from the Lord's presence.
During our earthly period of testing, the glorified Savior remains physically out of sight; we are called to live by faith.

div.title: Moses' prophecy and the blessing of turning from sin (verses 22–26)
div.p: Peter cited the words of Moses, the prophet whom the Jewish hearers most honored and in whose name some were tempted to reject Christianity.
Moses' warning exposed the terrible consequences of refusing to hear Christ.
Jesus came to bring a blessing.
He also sent his Spirit as the great blessing of redemption.
Christ blesses us by turning us away from our wrongdoing and saving us from our sins.
By nature, people cling to sin. Divine grace changes that affection so we not only leave sin behind but come to hate it.
No one should imagine happiness is possible by continuing in wrongdoing when God teaches that the blessing consists in being turned away from evil.
It is not enough to seek rescue merely from the punishment sin deserves.
Anyone who truly understands the gospel also desires to be rescued from sin itself.
And no one should expect such a change apart from faith in and reception of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.

row.cell: The apostles boldly testify to Christ.
Peter and John refuse to be silenced.
The believers unite in prayer and praise.
The holy charity of the Christians.

div.title: Peter and John are imprisoned (verses 1–4)
div.p: The apostles proclaimed the resurrection from the dead through Jesus Christ.
That resurrection opens the whole happiness of the future life, and it can be obtained through Christ alone.
Those who are saddened by the glory of Jesus' kingdom are in a miserable position, for his kingdom's glory will last forever.
Harmless and useful servants of Christ have often suffered persecution for faithful service and loving work, while wicked people escaped consequences.
Even today people may face reproach for reading Scripture, praying with others or discussing faith.
But if we obey Christ's commands, he will sustain us.

div.title: The apostles testify boldly before the rulers (verses 5–14)
div.p: Filled with the Holy Spirit, Peter declared that the miracle had taken place by the name and power of Jesus of Nazareth.
Jesus is the Messiah whom these leaders crucified.
The healing confirmed the apostles' testimony that Christ had risen and was indeed the promised Savior.
The rulers had to face a choice: they must be saved by the Jesus they had crucified or perish in their sins.
The name of Jesus is offered to every nation and generation as the only means of salvation from divine judgment.
When greed, pride or corrupt desires rule the heart, people close their minds to light and treat those devoted to Christ crucified as ignorant.
Christ's disciples should live in such a way that those who meet them recognize they have been with Jesus.
His presence makes them holy, heavenly-minded, spiritual and joyful, lifting their affections above this world.

div.title: Peter and John refuse to remain silent (verses 15–22)
div.p: The authorities wanted to prevent Christ's teaching from spreading.
But they could not prove the message false or dangerous.
They were unwilling to admit that their real objection was the way it exposed their hypocrisy, injustice and oppressive conduct.
People who properly value Christ's promises do not give undue weight to the world's threats.
Peter and John cared deeply for people in danger of eternal ruin and knew that only Jesus could save them.
They therefore continued faithfully warning others and explaining the way of salvation.
No one can enjoy inward peace or walk uprightly while directing conduct by changing social opinions rather than the stable standard of truth.
Beware of trying to serve both God and the world.
Such divided allegiance eventually makes people unfaithful to both.

div.title: The believers pray for courage (verses 23–31)
div.p: Christ's servants benefit greatly from fellowship with others who share their faith.
The believers prayed to the God who created everything and governs every event. The Scriptures would be fulfilled.
Jesus had been anointed as Savior and was therefore appointed to become the sacrifice making atonement for sin.
Nevertheless, divine Providence's ability to bring good from wickedness does not make human sin less evil.
In a time of threatening persecution, the believers did not pray mainly that all difficulty would disappear.
Instead they asked for steadfastness and courage to continue their work.
They did not say, “Lord, allow us to abandon the task now that it is dangerous.”
They asked for grace to carry out their duty without fear of people.
Anyone who seeks God's help for faithful service may trust him for strength to continue.
God answered with a visible sign.
The place shook so that their faith would remain unshaken.
The believers received a greater filling of the Holy Spirit than before, enabling them not only to feel encouraged but to speak God's word boldly.
When the Lord strengthens us through his Spirit, we know we need not be ashamed (Isaiah reference in the source is abbreviated as “Isa 17,” to be checked against the original-native edition).

div.title: The believers care for one another (verses 32–37)
div.p: The disciples' love fulfilled Christ's last commandment and his prayer for their unity.
When God's Spirit is poured out upon believers, the same love grows.
The apostles preached Christ's resurrection, a historical event which, properly explained, summarizes believers' privileges, duties and consolation.
The converts' words and deeds showed clear evidence of divine grace.
They were no longer attached to the world.
They did not confiscate other people's property.
Rather, they held their own possessions lightly, treating them as available to serve their brothers and sisters.
They had surrendered earthly security in their affections for Christ and expected persecution might soon strip them of their goods.
That is why they were of one heart and soul and why no one among them lacked what was needed.
The proceeds of gifts were entrusted to the apostles.

Public charity should be distributed carefully to people with genuine need, particularly those unable to support themselves or reduced to poverty because they did what was right or remained faithful under persecution.
Barnabas was a notable example of this generosity.
Preparing for gospel service, he disentangled himself from some of this life's business.
When love and generosity are practiced appropriately for the circumstances, they make the church's testimony especially persuasive.

row.cell: The death of Ananias and Sapphira.
The power which accompanied the preaching of the gospel.
The apostles imprisoned, but set free by an angel.
The apostles testify to Christ before the council.
The advice of Gamaliel, The council let the apostles go.

div.title: Ananias and Sapphira are judged (verses 1–11)
div.p: Ananias and Sapphira wanted to be regarded as exceptionally devoted Christians, although their hearts were not genuinely devoted to Christ.
Hypocrites sometimes make a real material sacrifice in one area because they hope to gain a greater advantage elsewhere.
The couple loved worldly wealth and distrusted God's Providence, imagining they could serve both God and money.
They thought they could deceive the apostles.
Through Peter, the Holy Spirit recognized the unbelief ruling Ananias's heart.
Satan may have suggested the deception, but he could not have filled Ananias's heart with this wickedness without Ananias's consent.
The lie was an attempt to deceive the Spirit of truth who spoke and acted through the apostles.
Their sin was not keeping part of the proceeds from selling their land.
They were free to keep the entire price if they wished.
The crime was trying to gain an undeserved reputation for self-sacrifice by telling a terrible lie, motivated by vanity and greed.
Anyone imagining they can deceive God will only fatally deceive their own soul.
How sad when married people, who should encourage each other toward goodness, reinforce each other in evil!
The sudden judgment also served as a warning of mercy to many others.
It urged serious self-examination, prayer and fear of hypocrisy, greed and pride. It restrained false profession from spreading unchecked through the church.
God hates falsehood.
We must avoid not merely direct lies but also gaining advantage through deliberately ambiguous words and double meanings.

div.title: The apostles' message and healing spread (verses 12–16)
div.p: God's judgment on hypocrites encouraged sincere believers to hold more firmly to one another and to the gospel ministry.
Whatever strengthens the church's purity and good reputation also promotes its growth.
Yet only the power that worked miracles through the apostles can rescue sinners from sin and Satan and bring them into God's people.
Christ works through all his faithful servants. Anyone who comes to him for healing will find him ready to help.

div.title: An angel releases the apostles from prison (verses 17–25)
div.p: No prison can be so secure or dark that God cannot visit his people there and, if he chooses, bring them out.
Recovery from illness and release from suffering are not granted merely so we can enjoy earthly comforts.
They are opportunities to honor God through renewed service.
Gospel preachers should not hide in private places while they still have opportunities to proclaim Christ before large gatherings.
They must speak to the poor as well as to the powerful.
The souls of ordinary and overlooked people are as precious to Christ as the souls of rulers.
The message concerns everyone; therefore speak to everyone.
Speak as people prepared to stand by it in life and death.
Proclaim all the words of the heavenly life, compared with which ordinary earthly life hardly deserves the name.
These are the words the Spirit supplies, the gospel words through which sinners are saved.
People who become angry at gospel success are miserable indeed.
Even seeing God's power oppose their plans may not stop them.

div.title: The apostles testify before the council (verses 26–33)
div.p: Some people dare to commit wicked actions but cannot endure having those actions described to them afterward.
We cannot receive Christ's healing and redemption without agreeing to be ruled by him.
Faith receives the Savior in all his offices.
Jesus came not to save us while leaving us in our sins, but to save us from our sins.
If Christ had been exalted merely to give political rule and power to Israel, the chief priests would gladly have welcomed him.
But they did not value or recognize their need of repentance and forgiveness, the blessings Christ came to give.
Wherever true repentance occurs, forgiveness is certainly granted.
No one is freed from sin's guilt and deserved punishment without also being freed from its rule and power, turning from sin and against it.
Christ gives repentance through his Spirit working with the word.
He awakens conscience, produces sorrow for sin and works a real change in heart and conduct.
The Spirit's gifts show that God commands obedience to the exalted Christ.
Those who refuse his reign face judgment.

div.title: Gamaliel counsels restraint; the apostles rejoice (verses 34–42)
div.p: The Lord still holds every human heart in his hand.
Sometimes he uses even the good judgment of people without faith to restrain persecutors.
Ordinary wisdom calls us to caution, and history shows that religious frauds usually fail before long.
Suffering disgrace for Christ is a true honor, because it makes us more like him and offers opportunities to serve his cause.
The apostles rejoiced that they had been counted worthy of that disgrace.
If we suffer because we do right, and God's grace enables us to endure it well, we too have reason to rejoice.
The apostles did not preach themselves but Jesus Christ.
That was what most offended the priests.
Ministers must always preach Christ crucified and Christ glorified, treating other subjects only as they relate to him.
Whatever our station in life, we should seek to make Christ known and glorify his name.

div.title: Servants are appointed for the church (verses 1–7)
div.p: Until this point the disciples had been described as united in one mind.
But as their number increased, complaints and murmuring began to arise.
The apostles were already fully occupied by God's word. Their teaching, prayer and responsibility for it demanded their attention and energy.
Those chosen to administer the distribution of material support had to possess the appropriate qualifications.
They needed the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit to handle that trust faithfully.
They were to be truthful, trustworthy and opposed to greed.
Everyone appointed to serve the church should be commended to God's grace through the prayers of the congregation.
The church blessed these servants in the Lord's name.
God's word and grace receive special glory when they transform people who seemed least likely to respond.

div.title: Stephen is falsely accused (verses 8–15)
div.p: Stephen's opponents could not answer his reasoning, so they prosecuted him as a criminal and arranged false witnesses.
It is an extraordinary protection of Providence that even more godly people have not been murdered through perjury and abuse of legal procedures.
Many who hate Christ's followers have shown no scruples about false oaths and injustice.
Wisdom and holiness can make someone's face shine, yet they do not prevent mistreatment.
What can be said of human beings who claim to be rational but attempt to support religion through lies and murder?
History contains countless examples of this contradiction.
The deepest cause lies less in the intellect than in the fallen heart, deceitful and deeply wicked.
Nevertheless, someone serving the Lord with a clear conscience, cheerful hope and the consolation of God can remain calm and even joyful in the face of danger and death.

row.cell: Stephen reproves the Jews for the death of Christ.

div.title: Stephen defends himself from Israel's history (verses 1–50)
Abraham, Joseph and the promises of God (verses 1–16)
div.p: Stephen had been accused of blaspheming God and abandoning Israel's religion.
He therefore showed that he was a true descendant of Abraham and valued the history and promises of God's people.
The promise to Abraham advanced slowly toward fulfillment.
That slow development revealed its spiritual meaning, looking beyond earthly Canaan toward the heavenly country.
God was with Joseph in his troubles.
Through his Spirit he gave Joseph personal comfort and favor in the eyes of those around him.
Stephen reminded the hearers of Israel's humble beginnings, correcting their pride in the nation's later greatness.
He recalled the patriarchs' envy of Joseph.
The same hostility toward God's appointed deliverer could now be seen in the rejection of Christ and his servants.
The patriarchs' desire for burial in Canaan showed faith looking toward an everlasting home.
When long-established religious customs have been distorted, it is wise to return to their original meaning.
To learn the nature and fruits of justifying faith, study Abraham, the father of believers.
His call reveals the power and freedom of divine grace and what conversion truly means.
Outward religious forms and distinctions count for little compared with separation from sinful ways and wholehearted dedication to God.

div.title: The childhood and early work of Moses (verses 17–29)
div.p: Do not despair when God's promises appear slow to unfold.
Times of suffering often become times when the church grows.
God may be preparing deliverance precisely when his people face their darkest hour.
Moses was exceedingly beautiful before God.
The beauty most precious in God's sight is holiness.
He was preserved wonderfully in infancy because God intended to employ him in an important work.
If God guarded the infant Moses, how much more surely will he protect the purposes of his beloved Son Jesus against those opposing him!
Stephen's enemies insisted upon the honor of Moses and his law to discredit Jesus.
But if they had not deliberately resisted the truth, they could have seen that Jesus delivers from a slavery worse than Egypt's bondage.
Human beings may prolong their own troubles, yet God will care for his servants and carry out his merciful plans.

div.title: Moses meets God and leads Israel (verses 30–41)
div.p: No one should imagine God can act only in a particular location.
He can lead his people into a wilderness and speak comfort to them there.
The bush burned without being consumed.
It pictured Israel enduring Egypt's furnace of affliction without destruction.
Henry also regards it as a possible type of Christ's incarnation, in which divine and human natures are united.
The deaths of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did not end God's covenant relationship with them.
Jesus himself used that continuing covenant to prove the future life (Matthew 22:31).
Abraham died, yet God remains his God; therefore Abraham lives.
The gospel has brought life and immortality into clear light.
Moses, as Israel's deliverer, was an important type of Christ.
God hears the sighs of his persecuted people and acts from compassion.
Israel's rescue from Egypt pictured Jesus descending from heaven for our salvation.
The very Jesus whom Stephen's audience rejected was appointed by God as Prince and Savior, just as the Israelites once rejected Moses.
Calling Moses an instrument does not dishonor him.
Jesus infinitely surpasses him.
Indeed, Stephen honored Moses by declaring his prophecy of Christ fulfilled.
God, who had given Israel ceremonies through Moses, had the authority to change those ceremonies through his Son.
Yet Israel had wanted to return to slavery rather than obey Moses.
Likewise many refuse Christ because they love this present evil world and their own works.

div.title: Idolatry and God's true dwelling place (verses 42–50)
div.p: Stephen reminded the people of their ancestors' idolatry.
God permitted them to pursue false worship as judgment for having first abandoned him.
It did not dishonor God when the tabernacle gave way to the temple.
Nor did it dishonor him when the earthly temple gave way to spiritual worship; eventually the spiritual order will lead to everlasting worship in heaven.
The whole universe belongs to God.
He is present everywhere and fills creation with his glory.
He therefore does not need a building to contain him or reveal that he is divine.
Heaven is his throne and earth his footstool.
None of our services enriches the One who created everything.
After the human nature of Christ, the dwelling place most precious to God is a broken and spiritually renewed human heart.

div.title: Stephen confronts his accusers (verses 51–53)
div.p: Stephen seems to have been preparing to explain that temple service must give way to worship in spirit and truth.
He recognized that his listeners would not receive the argument.
With wisdom, courage and power from the Holy Spirit, he rebuked their hostility.
When clear reasoning only hardens opponents of the gospel, they must still be warned about their guilt and danger.
Their stubbornness resembled the resistance of their ancestors.
Fallen human hearts contain a fleshly principle that resists the Holy Spirit.
But Henry also teaches that among God's chosen people this resistance is overcome by grace at the appointed time.
The gospel now came through the Holy Spirit, not merely through angels.
Yet Stephen's opponents refused both God's law and his gospel.
Their guilty consciences were disturbed, but instead of repentance and prayer, they sought relief by killing the person who exposed their sin.

div.title: Stephen is killed while praying (verses 54–60)
div.p: Nothing gives greater comfort to a dying believer or encouragement to a suffering believer than seeing Jesus at God's right hand.
Through faith we too can look toward him there.
Stephen prayed two brief prayers as he died.
Jesus is truly God, the One to whom we may pray and in whom we may place our confidence in life and death.
Those who have trusted him during life may find comfort in him at death.
Stephen also prayed for his persecutors.
Their wrongdoing was dreadful, but if they would honestly acknowledge and repent of it, God would not finally hold it against them.
Stephen's death came suddenly and violently.
Yet Scripture says he fell asleep.
He prepared himself for death with the calmness of someone going to bed.
He will awaken on the morning of the resurrection, entering the Lord's presence, where joy is complete and pleasures endure forever.

row.cell: Philip's success at Samaria. Simon the sorcerer baptized.

div.title: Saul persecutes the church (verses 1–4)
div.p: Persecution must not make us abandon God's work, though it may send us to serve him in another place.
Wherever mature believers are driven, they carry knowledge of the gospel and can tell others of Christ's worth.
When a sincere desire to do good governs the heart, opponents cannot close every possible opportunity for useful service.

div.title: Philip preaches in Samaria; Simon professes faith (verses 5–13)
div.p: Wherever the gospel advances, evil spirits are driven out—especially the unclean influences that entice people toward fleshly desires and war against their souls.
The illnesses healed in Samaria were among the hardest to cure by natural means. They vividly pictured sin's deep disease.
Pride, ambition and the desire for greatness have brought immense damage upon the world and the church.
People had treated Simon the magician as though he were God's great power.
See how easily people lacking discernment misunderstand spiritual things!
But divine grace was powerful enough to turn them toward Christ, who is Truth itself.
They attended carefully to Philip's preaching, recognized it as coming from God rather than human invention and submitted to it.
Nevertheless, people whose hearts remain devoted to greed can assemble with genuine believers and participate in religious practices for some time.
Some are impressed by signs proving divine truth without ever experiencing the truth's sanctifying power.
The gospel can affect the mind outwardly while producing no inward holiness.
Not everyone who professes belief has experienced saving conversion.

div.title: Peter exposes Simon's hypocrisy (verses 14–25)
div.p: The converts in Samaria had not yet received the Spirit in the form of the extraordinary miraculous gifts first bestowed at Pentecost.
We should pray that everyone whose spiritual welfare concerns us receives the renewing grace of the Holy Spirit, the gift containing every spiritual blessing.
No person can bestow the Spirit merely by laying hands on another.
Yet we must diligently teach the people for whom we pray.
Simon wanted the honor and power of an apostle, not the heart or character of a Christian.
He wanted glory for himself rather than good for others.
Peter exposed his error.
Simon treated worldly money as though it could purchase forgiveness, the Holy Spirit and eternal life.
Such an attitude is incompatible with saving grace.
God knows the heart exactly as it is.
A proud and greedy heart cannot be right before him.
A person may remain under sin's control while displaying an outward appearance of religion.
When offered money as an inducement to wrongdoing, remember how quickly wealth perishes and reject it.
Christianity must not become a business for earning worldly advantage.
Even thoughts and desires may be terribly sinful.
False beliefs, corrupt affections and evil schemes need repentance.
Yet forgiveness is promised when repentance is genuine.
Henry is careful: the doubt concerning Simon is whether his repentance was sincere, not whether God would forgive if he truly repented.
Lord, give us a faith unlike Simon's—one that transforms the heart instead of merely admiring miracles.
Keep us from using religion to satisfy pride or ambition, and especially from the subtle spiritual pride that seeks admiration even for appearing humble.
Teach us to seek honor from God alone.

div.title: Philip explains Scripture to the Ethiopian official (verses 26–40)
div.p: God directed Philip to a desert road.
He sometimes opens opportunities for ministry where they seem least likely to appear.
When traveling, we should consider how we might do good to the people we meet.
We need not be excessively distant toward strangers.
Even when we know nothing else about them, we know they have souls.
People with demanding responsibilities should redeem the time for worship and Scripture study, using brief available moments wisely.
When reading Scripture, pause to ask whom and what its authors were describing.
Above all, direct your attention toward the Redeemer.
The Ethiopian understood through the Spirit's teaching how Scripture was fulfilled in Christ.
He came to understand the Messiah's kingdom and salvation and desired to belong among Jesus' disciples.
Anyone sincerely searching Scripture for truth will benefit.
Henry understands the Ethiopian's confession as expressing simple reliance upon Christ for salvation and wholehearted devotion to him.
Let us seek this same faith through diligent Scripture study and the Spirit's instruction, until it governs our hearts.
After his baptism, Philip was taken away by the Spirit.
This helped confirm the official's faith.
Once sinners know Jesus and his gospel, they can continue rejoicing on their way, carrying out their ordinary responsibilities with new motives and in a new spirit.
But water baptism in the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit is not enough without the inward baptism and renewing work of the Holy Spirit.
Lord, grant that renewing grace to every one of us, that we may go on our way rejoicing.

row.cell: Saul is persecuted at Damascus, and goes to Jerusalem.

div.title: Saul encounters the risen Jesus (verses 1–9)
div.p: Saul was so deeply mistaken that he believed attacking Christ's name was service to God.
Persecution had become as natural to him as breathing.
Yet we should never despair that regenerating grace can convert even the greatest sinner, or that the Lord's mercy can forgive even terrible sin.
It is a clear sign of divine favor when God's grace within us or Providence around us prevents us from carrying out sinful plans.
Saul saw the Righteous One (see Acts 22:14; 26:13).
How near the unseen world is to us!
God only needs to lift the veil, and realities appear beside which even the most impressive earthly things seem insignificant.
Saul surrendered without conditions, asking what Jesus wanted him to do.
Christ's self-revelation humbles sinners and brings down their proud opinion of themselves.
For three days, Saul ate nothing. God allowed this period of spiritual anguish to continue.
His sins stood before his conscience, and he felt unable to understand his spiritual condition.
When people truly recognize their guilt, they cast themselves entirely upon the Savior's mercy and ask how he would have them live.
God directs the humbled sinner.
He often leads people toward the joy and peace of faith through serious conviction and sorrow over sin.
Yet those who sow in tears will reap in joy.

div.title: Ananias visits Saul; Saul preaches Jesus (verses 10–22)
div.p: A good work had begun in Saul when he knelt before the Lord, asking what he must do.
Jesus never abandons someone brought sincerely to that place.
Behold the proud Pharisee, merciless oppressor and daring blasphemer praying!
The same wonder can take place today in the life of an unbeliever or notorious sinner.
Such prayer is different from outward recitation.
Before conversion, Saul had said prayers; now he really prayed.
Regenerating grace creates a praying heart.
Just as a living person must breathe, a spiritually living Christian must pray.
Even experienced disciples may hesitate before God's commands.
Ananias had trouble believing Saul was truly changed.
Yet God delights in surpassing our narrow expectations, transforming people we considered fit only for judgment into objects of his mercy.
The Spirit's teaching removes the scales of ignorance and pride.
A converted sinner becomes a new creation, wanting to commend Jesus Christ, the anointed Son of God, even to former associates.

div.title: Saul faces persecution and joins the disciples (verses 23–31)
div.p: Anyone beginning to walk with God should expect trials.
Yet the Lord knows how to rescue his servants and make a way through temptation.
Saul's conversion is a strong evidence of Christianity's truth.
But the event itself could not convert a hostile human heart.
Only God's power to make a person new can produce true faith.
Believers can be too suspicious of people they previously distrusted.
Caution is reasonable in a deceptive world, but we must also practice charity (1 Corinthians 13:5).
God brings genuine believers into fellowship with his people and may let them testify before those who once saw their hatred of the gospel.
Christ directed Saul to leave Jerusalem and be sent to the Gentiles (Acts 22:21).
The Lord's witnesses cannot be killed before their appointed testimony is complete.
Persecution subsided for a time.
Believers walked uprightly, enjoyed the Holy Spirit's comfort and grew as others joined them.
They lived through the Spirit's consolation not only in hardship but also in rest and prosperity.
Those who walk carefully are most able to walk joyfully.

div.title: Peter heals Aeneas (verses 32–35)
div.p: All genuine Christians are saints, or God's holy people.
That name belongs not only to famous figures such as Peter and Paul but to every sincere believer in Christ.
Jesus chose patients whose conditions were hopeless by ordinary means to show how helpless fallen humanity is.
When we were without strength, Christ sent his word to heal us.
Peter claimed no personal power.
He directed Aeneas to look to Jesus for the healing.
The truth that Christ alone gives the power for holiness does not excuse us from acting.
Although Jesus makes us well, we must rise and use the strength he gives.

div.title: Dorcas is raised to life (verses 36–43)
div.p: Some people speak beautifully about charity while doing very little.
Tabitha, also called Dorcas, was known for good works rather than impressive talk.
Even Christians without money to give can practice charity through their hands and their feet—working, visiting and helping others.
The best praise is the testimony of a person's own deeds.
It is ungrateful to receive kindness and then fail to recognize it.
While depending entirely on Christ's fullness for our own salvation, we should also long to be full of good works, bringing glory to him and benefit to his people.
People like Dorcas make the gospel attractive through their practical conduct.
Henry contrasts her useful service with people who devote their lives to outward appearance, dress and vanity.
God's power accompanied Peter's word, and Dorcas returned to life.
When God awakens dead souls to spiritual life, an early sign is that the eyes of their understanding open.
This miracle shows that the Lord can restore what we have lost and govern all events for the good of those who trust him and the honor of his name.

row.cell: Cornelius directed to send for Peter.
The gifts of the Holy Spirit poured out.

div.title: Cornelius is told to summon Peter (verses 1–8)
div.p: Until this point, those admitted to the Christian church through baptism had been Jews, Samaritans or converts who had accepted circumcision and Moses' ceremonial law.
Now Gentiles would receive every privilege of God's people without first becoming Jews.
Genuine religion is sometimes found where we least expect it.
Where reverence for God rules a heart, it produces both acts of charity and acts of devotion.
Neither excuses neglect of the other.
Henry considers it certain that Cornelius truly trusted God's word as far as he understood it, although he did not yet have clear knowledge of Jesus Christ.
This early faith, Henry explains, was already the Holy Spirit's work through Christ's mediation, even before Cornelius consciously knew the Mediator.
The same is true when anyone formerly dead in sin receives spiritual life.
Through Christ, Cornelius's prayers and charitable gifts were accepted. Apart from that mediation they could not merit God's favor.
When heaven directed Cornelius to send for Peter, he obeyed without arguing or delaying.
We should waste no time in matters concerning our souls.

div.title: Peter's vision (verses 9–18)
div.p: Peter's prejudices against Gentiles would have prevented him from entering Cornelius's home if God had not prepared him.
For a Jew, hearing that formerly unclean animals must now be treated as clean amounted to learning that the old ceremonial restrictions of Moses' law had ended.
Peter soon discovered how this vision applied to his mission.
God knows in advance what work he will give us and prepares us for it.
Often we understand what he has taught only when we encounter the occasion to use it.

div.title: Peter goes to Cornelius (verses 19–33)
div.p: Once a call to service becomes clear, we should not be paralyzed by needless doubts arising from prejudice or inherited opinions.
Cornelius had invited his relatives and friends to hear Peter.
We should not want to enjoy every spiritual blessing alone.
It is an act of friendship and kindness to invite family and friends to worship and learn with us.
Cornelius explained the divine message that had prompted him to summon Peter.
Our aims are right when we attend gospel preaching because God has appointed this means of grace.
What a privilege for a minister to speak to people who have truly gathered in God's presence to hear everything he has commanded!
That was the readiness of Cornelius's household.

div.title: Peter preaches Jesus to the Gentiles (verses 34–43)
div.p: No one is accepted by God except through the covenant of mercy and the atoning work of Jesus Christ.
But wherever genuine religion is found, God accepts it without regard to names, nations or religious factions.
Reverence for God and works of righteousness are the practical substance of true religion.
Yet these works are effects of special grace and signs of acceptance, not the cause of a person's acceptance before God.
What is still lacking in true knowledge or maturity will be supplied in due time by the Lord who began the work.
Cornelius and his hearers already knew the broad gospel message proclaimed in Israel, beginning with John's baptism of repentance.
That message was the good news of peace with God through Jesus Christ.
They needed to understand that Jesus, through whom God and sinners are reconciled, is Lord of all.
He is Lord not only as God over all, blessed forever, but also in his work as Mediator.
Every authority in heaven and on earth belongs to him, and all judgment has been entrusted to him.
God accompanies those he has anointed by his Spirit.
Peter told them about Jesus' resurrection and its proofs.
Christian faith responds to testimony.
It rests upon the foundation supplied by the apostles and prophets, through the witness they gave.
Everyone will answer to Jesus as Judge and must therefore seek his favor.
Those who trust him receive justification through his righteousness.
The forgiveness of sins is the foundation of every other saving blessing, removing the guilt that prevents sinners from receiving them.
If sins are pardoned, all will finally be well.

div.title: The Holy Spirit comes before water baptism (verses 44–48)
div.p: On other occasions, the Spirit had visibly come upon people after baptism, strengthening their faith.
Here he came upon the Gentiles before water baptism.
God thereby showed that he is not bound to outward signs or ceremonies.
These people were neither circumcised nor yet baptized when they received the Spirit.
It is the Spirit who gives life; human flesh cannot do so.
The new believers magnified God and spoke about Christ and the benefits of redemption.
Whatever gifts we receive, we must use them to honor God.
Jewish Christians were astonished to see the Holy Spirit given to Gentiles.
Our mistaken ideas about God's work often make his ways appear harder to understand than they really are.
Because the Gentiles had unmistakably received the baptism and gifts of the Spirit, Peter concluded they must not be refused the outward ordinance of water baptism.
The reasoning was sound: how can we deny the sign to those who have already received the reality signified?
Those who have begun knowing Jesus should continually desire to know him more.
Even people filled with the Holy Spirit need to keep learning God's truth every day.

row.cell: The success of the gospel at Antioch.
The disciples named Christians, Relief sent to Judea.

div.title: Peter explains the welcome of Gentiles (verses 1–18)
div.p: The weakness of fallen human nature appears even in godly people when they are displeased to hear that others have received God's word, merely because the Lord did not work according to their own religious expectations.
We too often assume that certain people cannot be helped, even though they may prove eager to learn when given an opportunity.
It seriously harms the church to exclude people from fellowship and God's appointed means of grace because they are not like us in every respect.
Peter carefully explained what had happened.
We should make allowance for the weaknesses of fellow believers.
Rather than becoming offended or responding angrily, explain our motives and show what we have done and why.
Preaching through which God grants the Holy Spirit plainly has divine approval.
Those deeply devoted to their own religious regulations should take care not to oppose God.
People who love the Lord will glorify him when they learn that he has granted repentance leading to life to fellow sinners.
Repentance itself is God's gift.
His mercy does not merely accept repentance when offered. His mighty grace produces it within us.
He removes a heart of stone and gives a tender heart of flesh.
A broken and contrite spirit is the sacrifice God receives.

div.title: The gospel spreads in Antioch (verses 19–24)
div.p: The first witnesses who brought the gospel to Antioch had been scattered from Jerusalem through persecution.
What was intended to damage the church became the means of blessing it.
Human hostility was overruled to bring praise to God.
What should Christ's ministers preach but Christ crucified and glorified?
Their preaching was accompanied by divine power.
Ministers could only speak to the outward ears of listeners; the Lord himself reached hearts and consciences.
People believed the gospel's truth and turned from a careless, worldly way of life toward holiness and spiritual-mindedness.
They turned from empty ceremonies to worship in spirit and truth.
Above all, they turned to the Lord Jesus, who became everything to them.
This is the work of conversion that must take place in every one of us.
True faith produces this turning to the Lord.
When Jesus is preached simply and according to Scripture, he grants success.
Sincere believers like Barnabas, filled with faith and the Spirit, rejoice in grace working in others.
Barnabas possessed both the grace of faith and the fruits of faith working through love.

div.title: Believers are called Christians and send relief (verses 25–30)
div.p: Until then Jesus' followers had commonly been called disciples, meaning learners.
They now began to be called Christians.
The name properly describes someone who, after serious consideration, follows Christ, believes his promises and makes obedience to his teaching and example the principal concern of life.
Many people bear the title Christian although it does not truly describe them.
The name without the reality increases guilt rather than granting benefit.
But genuine faith carries the promises of this life and the life to come.
Lord, help Christians set aside needless labels and divisions and love one another as Christ's followers should.
Genuine believers care for brothers and sisters experiencing hardship.
Such compassion bears fruit to God's praise.
If everyone in the world lived as a true Christian, how joyfully would people help one another!
The earth would resemble one great family whose members sought to be kind and dutiful toward one another.

row.cell: The martyrdom of James, and the imprisonment of Peter.
He is delivered from prison by an angel.

div.title: James is killed and Peter imprisoned (verses 1–5)
div.p: James was a son of Zebedee.
Jesus had told him that he would drink his Master's cup and share his baptism of suffering (Matthew 20:23).
That prediction was now fulfilled.
Those who suffer with Christ will reign with him.
Herod imprisoned Peter.
Persecution, like other kinds of sin, is a downhill path.
Once people begin following it, stopping becomes increasingly difficult.
Anyone whose main purpose is pleasing people makes an easy target for Satan.
James finished the work appointed to him.
Peter, however, still had tasks to perform and was therefore safe despite appearing destined for an early death.
In a generation that prays coldly or scarcely prays at all, we may struggle to imagine the seriousness and intensity of the church's prayers for Peter.
If persecution became as severe as it was under Herod, faithful Christians would learn again what prayer from the depths of the soul means.

div.title: An angel delivers Peter (verses 6–11)
div.p: A clear conscience, living hope and the Holy Spirit's comfort can make people calm even when they expect death.
Such peace may come to people who once were terrified by the thought of dying.
God often intervenes when trouble has reached its most desperate point.
Peter could trust that the Lord would bring his trial to the conclusion most suited to God's glory.
People delivered from spiritual imprisonment should follow their Deliverer just as the Israelites followed God out of Egypt.
They may not know the road ahead, but they know whom they are following.
When God chooses to save his people, obstacles cannot prevent him.
Even iron gates open before his power.
Peter's rescue pictures the redemption accomplished by Jesus.
Christ does more than announce release to captives.
He brings them out of prison.
Only afterward did Peter fully realize what God had done.
Similarly, believers may have genuine renewing grace before they possess a clear assurance that God has changed them.
The Comforter will eventually enable them to recognize that blessed transformation.

div.title: Peter returns to the praying believers (verses 12–19)
div.p: God's promise to finish what he begins still leaves room for human prudence.
The disciples continued praying earnestly.
We ought to pray persistently and not lose heart.
As long as we are waiting for a needed mercy, keep asking God for it.
Yet sometimes we find it hardest to believe the very answer we desire most deeply.
Christ commands self-denial and willingness to suffer.
But these commandments do not cancel our duty to protect our own safety through lawful means.
During public danger, believers may trust God as a hiding place that persecutors cannot discover.
Those who carry out persecution are themselves exposed to danger under God's judgment.
Their rage often falls indiscriminately upon innocent people nearby.

div.title: Herod is judged (verses 20–25)
div.p: Many pagan rulers claimed divine honors.
Herod's guilt was even greater because he knew the word and worship of the living God and yet accepted such honors without rebuking the blasphemy.
His pride and vanity prepared him for judgment.
God guards his own glory.
Those who refuse to glorify him may encounter his justice.
Our physical bodies are frail and already contain the beginnings of their own decay.
God need only speak, and human life can quickly end.
We may learn from the people of Tyre and Sidon, who sought peace with Herod because they depended upon him for provisions.
We have offended the Lord by sin, yet depend upon him for life, breath and everything else.
We should therefore humble ourselves and seek reconciliation through the appointed Mediator, who stands ready to help us, before judgment overtakes us.

row.cell: The mission of Paul and Barnabas.
He preaches to the Gentiles, and is persecuted by the Jews.

div.title: Paul and Barnabas are sent on mission (verses 1–3)
div.p: What a remarkable gathering of believers!
The different names reveal how God chooses servants from varied places and walks of life.
Zeal for his glory can lead people to abandon attractive relationships and worldly prospects to advance his cause.
The Spirit of Christ makes his ministers both willing and able to serve, and draws them away from distractions that would prevent their work.
Christ's ministers are appointed to labor, not to seek status.
Their task is to carry out Christ's work under the Spirit's guidance for the Father's glory.
The congregation prayed for Barnabas and Saul to receive blessing and the Holy Spirit's power for their mission.
Whatever procedures are followed or means employed, the Holy Spirit alone calls and equips gospel ministers for their calling.

div.title: Paul confronts Elymas (verses 4–13)
div.p: Satan particularly tries to keep powerful and influential people from genuine faith because their example affects many others.
Here Saul is first called Paul and afterward continues under that name.
Henry explains the two names as reflecting Saul's Jewish heritage and Paul's Roman citizenship.
Under the Holy Spirit's direct influence, Paul exposed Elymas's true character without acting from uncontrolled anger.
A combination of deliberate deceit and harm to others is a fitting description of one acting as the devil's child.
Those who oppose Jesus' teaching are enemies of genuine righteousness.
Christ's way alone leads to heaven and lasting happiness.
Some people not only leave that way themselves, but deliberately persuade others to reject it.
Such people can become hardened in sin.
The Roman governor was astonished both by the gospel's effect upon his conscience and by the divine power confirming it.
The more deeply we know Christ's teaching, the more reason we have to marvel.
Someone who begins work for God but looks back is not fit for the kingdom.
Likewise, people unwilling to face opposition or endure hardship are not prepared for gospel ministry.

div.title: Israel's history and the promised Savior (verses 14–31)
div.p: When we meet to worship God, we should not only pray and praise; we must also read and hear his word.
Public reading is important, but reading alone is not enough.
Scripture should be explained and the people exhorted from it, so they can apply it to themselves.
Paul's sermon touched on the truths most likely to lead Jewish listeners to receive Jesus as their promised Messiah.
Even a brief view of God's dealings with Israel reveals divine mercy and patience amid human ingratitude and stubbornness.
Paul moved from David to the Son of David, presenting Jesus as the promised descendant.
Jesus accomplishes what the judges of ancient Israel could not: he saves sinners from their worst enemies—their sins.
When the apostles preached Christ as Savior, they never hid the cross.
They preached Christ crucified.
Our complete separation from sin is pictured by burial with Christ.
But Jesus also rose again and did not undergo corruption.
That resurrection was essential to the message.

div.title: The resurrection and the sure mercies of David (verses 32–37)
div.p: Christ's resurrection was the great evidence that he is the Son of God.
Death could not hold him, for he possesses life in himself.
He freely laid it down with the intention and power to take it up again.
The sure mercies promised to David concern everlasting life.
Jesus' resurrection guarantees that life; even now the blessings of redemption are a pledge of what is coming.
David served his own generation well.
We were not born only for ourselves.
We should seek to benefit the people placed around us.
But Jesus' service reaches every generation.
May we trust the One declared God's Son by his resurrection, walk with God by faith, serve our own generation according to his will and finally fall asleep with the joy of a blessed resurrection.

div.title: Forgiveness and justification through Christ (verses 38–41)
div.p: Everyone hearing the gospel must recognize two truths.
First, through the One who died and rose again, forgiveness of sins is proclaimed.
However numerous or serious our sins, they can be forgiven without dishonoring God's justice.
Second, only people who believe in Christ receive complete justification from guilt they could never be justified from through Moses' law.
The great need of a convicted sinner is to be acquitted from all guilt and accepted as righteous before God.
If even one charge remains, the sinner is ruined.
Christ brings complete justification because he has made complete atonement.
He justifies us not only as our Judge but as the Lord our Righteousness.
What the law could not accomplish because of human weakness, the gospel accomplishes.
This blessing lays the foundation for every other saving gift.
The warnings against unbelief are given so sinners will take heed.
People are ruined by treating religion with contempt.
Those who refuse to wonder at God's grace and be saved will finally wonder at his judgment and perish.

div.title: Paul turns toward the Gentiles (verses 42–52)
div.p: Some Jewish hearers resisted the apostles' teaching.
When they could not answer its truth, they blasphemed Christ and the gospel.
Contradiction can harden into blasphemy.
When Christ's opponents are bold, his advocates should become more courageous.
While some treated themselves as unworthy of eternal life, others—people who might have seemed less likely—eagerly wanted to hear more.
The Old Testament had foretold the Gentiles' inclusion.
What light, power and treasure the gospel brings!
Its truths, commands and promises are excellent.
Those whom the Father drew and in whom the Holy Spirit made the gospel call effective came to Christ (Romans 8:30).
Henry describes those who were disposed toward eternal life—concerned for their eternal condition and intent on gaining that life—as believers in Christ, in whom God has stored everlasting life.
He immediately attributes the disposition and faith to God's grace working within them.
Godliness among people of honorable standing is a good thing.
But outward devotion becomes grievous when used as a pretext for hating Christ.
The more we cherish the comforts of true faith, the better prepared we will be to bear hardships for its sake.

row.cell: A cripple healed at Lystra, The people would have sacrificed to Paul and Barnabas.
Paul stoned at Lystra, The churches visited again.

div.title: Paul and Barnabas preach in Iconium (verses 1–7)
div.p: The apostles spoke plainly and persuasively, with evidence of the Holy Spirit's presence and with such warmth and concern for people's souls that their listeners could recognize God's hand in their work.
Yet their success was not the achievement of their manner of preaching. It belonged to the Spirit of God, who worked through that preaching.
Perseverance in doing good despite danger and hardship is a blessed sign of grace.
Wherever the Lord's servants are driven, they should look for ways to proclaim the truth.
As Paul and Barnabas continued in Christ's name and strength, the Lord confirmed the word of his grace.
He has assured us that his word is true. We may confidently entrust our souls to it.
Jews and Gentiles were divided from one another, yet their hostility to Christians united them.
If the church's enemies combine to destroy it, should not its friends unite to protect and strengthen it?
God provides shelter for his people amid storms. He is their refuge and will continue to be their hiding place.
During persecution, believers may rightly leave one location without abandoning their Master's work.

div.title: A man is healed at Lystra; the crowd offers worship (verses 8–18)
div.p: All things are possible to those who believe.
Faith is God's precious gift. Through it, we are freed from the spiritual helplessness into which we were born and from the sinful habits later formed.
We become able to stand upright and walk joyfully in the Lord's ways.
When Jesus, the Son of God, appeared in human likeness and performed many miracles, people did not respond by offering sacrifices to him.
Instead, they made him the victim of their pride and hatred.
Yet after Paul and Barnabas performed one miracle, the crowd wanted to worship them as gods!
The same influence of the ruler of this world that closes sinful minds against truth makes errors and false beliefs seem easy to accept.
Notice that the apostles did not tear their clothes when people talked about stoning them.
They did so when people talked about worshiping them.

p.hi: God's honor mattered more to them than their own safety.

div.p: God's truth does not need the service of human falsehood.
His servants might easily gain improper honors by quietly tolerating other people's mistakes and sins.
But they should fear and reject that kind of respect more than criticism or disgrace.
When the apostles spoke to Jews, who already rejected idols, they principally proclaimed God's grace through Christ.
When they addressed Gentiles, they also needed to correct mistaken ideas about natural religion and false worship.
Compare their words with the view that worship offered to a god under any name, or in any manner, is equally acceptable to the Almighty.
Even the strongest reasoning, warmest appeals and clearest miracles barely restrain people from dreadful errors and practices.
Without God's special grace, none of these can turn sinners' hearts toward him and holiness.

div.title: Paul is stoned and the churches strengthened (verses 19–28)
div.p: See how relentlessly some opponents pursued the gospel.
In a public riot they stoned Paul.
The sinful human heart is difficult to restrain from evil in one direction, yet easily persuaded toward evil in another.
If Paul had allowed himself to be called Mercury, the people would have worshiped him.
When he insisted on being a faithful servant of Christ, they stoned him and threw him outside the town.
People who readily accept powerful delusions can stubbornly refuse to love the truth.

p.hi: Converts need to be strengthened in faith; plants need to take root.

div.p: A minister's work is not only awakening sinners, but also establishing believers.
Only the grace of God can establish disciples' souls securely.
We should expect considerable suffering, yet take courage: it does not mean we will be destroyed or lost.
The One to whose power and grace the new believers and churches were commended was clearly the Lord Jesus, in whom they had believed.
Committing them to him was itself an act of worship.
Whatever little good we do, all praise belongs to God.
He works within us both to desire and to do his will, and he works alongside our efforts to make them fruitful.
Everyone who loves Jesus should rejoice when he opens the door of faith to people who had once been strangers to his salvation.
Like the apostles, let us remain in fellowship with those who know and love the Lord.

row.cell: The dispute raised by Judaizing teachers.

div.title: Teachers dispute Christian liberty (verses 1–6)
div.p: Some visitors from Judea taught the Gentile believers in Antioch that they could not be saved unless they obeyed the whole ceremonial law of Moses.
In this way they sought to destroy Christian liberty.
We are strangely inclined to suppose that everyone who acts differently from us must be wrong.
This teaching burdened the Gentile believers and discouraged them.
Wise and good people try to avoid quarrels and controversies whenever they can.

p.hi: But when false teachers oppose central gospel truths or introduce harmful teaching, we must be willing to confront them.

div.title: The Jerusalem council discerns God's work (verses 7–21)
div.p: Peter's words about God purifying hearts by faith show that justification by faith and sanctification through the Holy Spirit cannot be separated.
Both are gifts from God.
We should thank God for the privilege of hearing the gospel and ask for faith that the great Searcher of hearts will approve, confirmed by the Holy Spirit's seal.
In that way our hearts and consciences are purified from sin's guilt, and we are freed from burdens people try to impose upon Christ's disciples.
Paul and Barnabas described concrete evidence that God himself accepted the gospel preached to Gentiles who had not submitted to Moses' ceremonial law.
To demand that law afterward would be to reverse what God had accomplished.
James therefore argued that Gentile converts should not be burdened with Jewish religious rites.
They should avoid food sacrificed to idols as evidence of their rejection of idolatry.
They should also avoid sexual immorality, which Gentile culture did not condemn seriously enough and which formed part of some pagan religious practices.
James further advised abstaining from things strangled and from blood.
This had been forbidden under the Mosaic law.
Now it was important to respect the association of blood with the sacrifices still being offered and avoid needlessly grieving Jewish Christians or prejudicing Jews who had not yet believed.
But the historical reason for that temporary restriction has long ceased, Henry says, so believers remain free in this matter as in similar matters.
Converts should be warned against even the appearance of former sins and practices likely to tempt them.
Christian liberty should be exercised with moderation and good judgment.

div.title: The council's letter reassures the Gentiles (verses 22–35)
div.p: The apostles and church leaders could declare that the Holy Spirit guided their decision.
It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them not to impose more requirements than those already described—requirements important either in themselves or because of the particular circumstances.
Gentile converts were comforted that they were not compelled to keep the outward ceremonial regulations that could neither cleanse nor quiet the conscience.
The teachers who had disturbed them were corrected.
Church peace was restored and an approaching division was averted.
The people therefore had reason to thank God.
Many ministers served in Antioch.
When others labor faithfully in teaching God's word, that does not excuse us from work.
Their zeal and usefulness should stir us up instead of making us idle.

div.title: Paul and Barnabas separate (verses 36–41)
div.p: Even excellent ministers can quarrel.
This private disagreement between Paul and Barnabas nevertheless ended in a way that did not prevent further gospel service.
Barnabas wanted his nephew John Mark to accompany them.
We should be alert to partiality when promoting our own relatives.
Paul judged Mark unfit for the service and honor of the mission because he had earlier departed from them without their knowledge or consent (see Acts 13:13).
Neither would yield, so they separated.
The best believers are still human and subject to the same sinful passions as others.
Perhaps each side was partly at fault, as so often happens in disputes.
Only Christ's example is perfect.
It should not surprise us that wise and good people disagree.
While we remain imperfect, we will not reach complete unity of mind.
That awaits heaven.
Yet pride and anger remaining even in sincere believers cause enormous harm in the church and the wider world.
Many at Antioch, unfamiliar with the extent of Paul and Barnabas's former devotion, would hear of their quarrel and departure.
Our own conduct can likewise damage the cause we genuinely wish to serve.
Pray constantly that unholy tempers will not lead us to harm Christ's work.
In epistles written after this event, Paul spoke with honor and affection about both Barnabas and Mark.
Loving Savior, may everyone professing your name be reconciled through love received from you—a love not easily provoked and ready to forgive and bury offenses.

row.cell: Paul takes Timothy to be his assistant.
Paul proceeds to Macedonia, The conversion of Lydia.
An evil spirit cast out, Paul and Silas scourged and imprisoned.
The conversion of the jailer at Philippi.

div.title: Paul chooses Timothy for the mission (verses 1–5)
div.p: The church has good reason to expect useful service from young ministers who begin with Timothy's spirit.
But when people refuse to yield or accommodate others in anything, they appear to lack even the first elements of a Christian spirit.
There is little reason to expect such people to teach the gospel's doctrines and commandments successfully.
The council's decree had the purpose of setting aside the burdensome ceremonial law and outward regulations.
It established a spiritual way of serving God, suited to the nature of both God and humanity.
Through this, believers were strengthened in faith, and the church grew daily.

div.title: Paul reaches Macedonia and Lydia believes (verses 6–15)
div.p: Ministers' movements and their opportunities to bring others the means of grace are directed in a special way by divine Providence.
We must follow that direction.
If God prevents us from carrying out what we planned, we ought to submit and trust that his decision is best.
People need spiritual help greatly.
They should therefore seek it, invite those able to instruct them and respond promptly when God calls.
God's worshipers should assemble solemnly on the Sabbath whenever possible.
If a synagogue is unavailable, be thankful for a smaller, more private place to gather.
Do not abandon fellowship when an opportunity exists.
Lydia was among Paul's hearers.
She had an honorable occupation, which Luke mentions to her credit.
Although responsible for a business, she found time to attend to her soul.
We cannot excuse neglecting religion by saying we have a trade to run.
We have both work in the world and a God to serve and souls to care for.
Christianity does not necessarily take us away from ordinary business; it teaches us how to conduct it.
Pride, prejudice and sin keep divine truth outside the understanding and affections until grace opens a way into them.
The Lord alone opens a heart to receive and believe his word.
We must trust Jesus Christ. No one comes to God as Father except through the Son as Mediator.

div.title: Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned (verses 16–24)
div.p: Satan is the father of lies.
Yet he sometimes speaks important truths when doing so can advance his purposes.
False and ungodly people who claim to proclaim the gospel can do great harm by causing careless observers to confuse them with Christ's genuine servants.
People doing good by leading sinners out of wrongdoing may nevertheless be slandered as troublemakers.
They teach others to fear God, trust Jesus, abandon sin and live holy lives, but are accused of introducing dangerous customs.

div.title: The Philippian jailer turns to Christ (verses 25–34)
div.p: God's consolations for servants suffering in his cause are neither few nor insignificant.
How much happier sincere Christians can be than the enemies who enjoy outward prosperity!
Even in deep darkness, we may cry to God.
There is no place and no hour when sincere prayer is inappropriate.
No suffering, however intense, should completely prevent us from praising him.
Christianity shows its divine origin in part by obliging us to respect and protect our own lives.
Paul shouted so that the jailer could hear and heed him: “Do yourself no harm!”
The warnings of Scripture against sin and all approaches to it have the same merciful purpose.
Do not ruin yourself.
Do not bring harm upon your own life through sin, for nothing can ultimately harm you as sin can.
Even regarding bodily health, Scripture warns us against practices that injure us.
Conversion changes how people speak about and to faithful believers and ministers.
The jailer's question became intensely serious.
His own salvation—formerly farthest from his thoughts—became his deepest concern.
He was anxious about his precious soul.
People convinced of sin and genuinely concerned about salvation will surrender themselves to Christ.
Here is the gospel, the covenant of grace, in a few words:

p.hi: “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.”

div.p: The Lord so blessed that word that the jailer was immediately softened and humbled.
He now treated Paul and Silas with kindness and compassion.
Professing faith in Christ, he was baptized together with his household.
The Spirit worked such strong faith in them that their doubts gave way.
Paul and Silas knew through the Spirit that God had worked within them.
Once sinners are converted, they begin to love and honor people they once despised or hated, seeking to relieve the very suffering they once wanted to increase.
As faith's fruits become visible, terror gives way to trust and joy in God.

div.title: Paul and Silas are honorably released (verses 35–40)
div.p: Paul was willing to endure suffering for Christ.
He did not seek revenge or personal satisfaction.
Yet he refused to depart as though he had deserved the unlawful punishment imposed upon him.
He therefore required a public and honorable release.
He was not insisting on a small point of wounded pride.
It was a matter of justice, important not merely for himself but for the cause he represented.
When an appropriate apology is offered, Christians should not continue expressing personal anger or demand excessive compensation for wounded feelings.
The Lord makes his faithful people more than conquerors through every conflict.
Instead of being destroyed by sufferings, they can become comforters of fellow believers.

row.cell: The noble conduct of the Bereans.
The scornful conduct of the Athenians.

div.title: Paul preaches in Thessalonica (verses 1–9)
div.p: The purpose of Paul's preaching and reasoning was to prove that Jesus is the Christ.
Christ had to suffer for us, because otherwise he could not purchase our redemption.
He also had to rise again, because otherwise he could not apply that redemption to us.
We proclaim that Jesus is the Messiah.
Therefore, we may hope for salvation through him, and we must submit to his rule.
Some unbelieving Jews were angry because the apostles preached salvation to Gentiles.
How strange that people begrudge others privileges that they themselves refuse to accept!
Neither rulers nor ordinary citizens should fear the spread of genuine Christian faith, although turbulent people sometimes use religion as a cover for evil schemes.
We should distance ourselves from those who misuse religion for wrongdoing.
Then we can show our desire to act uprightly in society while still claiming the right to worship God according to conscience.

div.title: The Bereans search the Scriptures (verses 10–15)
div.p: The Jews at Berea gave serious attention to the message.
They did not merely hear Paul preach on the Sabbath.
They examined Scripture every day, comparing its teaching with what the apostles reported.
Christ's doctrine has nothing to fear from honest inquiry.
Those defending it ask only that people examine fully and fairly whether the message is true.
Genuinely noble people take Scripture as their rule and constantly consult it.
May all who hear the gospel resemble the Bereans, receiving the word eagerly but checking daily in Scripture whether the teaching is true.

div.title: Paul encounters Athenian philosophers (verses 16–21)
div.p: Athens was famous for intellectual learning, philosophy and the fine arts.
Yet some people highly regarded for intelligence and knowledge are remarkably childish, superstitious, credulous and irreverent in spiritual matters.
Athens had become full of idols.
Anyone zealous for Christ should be ready to speak on his behalf in whatever company opportunities arise.
Most educated Athenians paid little attention to Paul.
Others, including representatives of philosophical schools whose principles especially opposed Christianity, commented on his teaching.
Paul continually proclaimed two central subjects: Christ and the life to come.
Christ is the Way; heaven is the destination.
The Athenians found these teachings unfamiliar after centuries of their own intellectual traditions.
They wanted to hear more, but not because they judged the message good.
They were attracted to it because it seemed strange and new.
They brought Paul to a place where such matters were examined.
People who constantly pursue conversation about something new often become meddlesome.
They spend their precious time talking without accomplishing good.
Our time deserves wiser use, because how we employ it has consequences reaching into eternity.

div.title: Paul proclaims the Creator and coming judgment (verses 22–31)
div.p: This sermon was addressed to Gentile idolaters who did not know the true God.
Its starting point therefore differed from Paul's preaching to Jews.
When speaking to Jews, Paul appealed to prophecy and miracles to lead them to recognize and trust the Redeemer.
When speaking to Gentile idolaters, he began with God's ordinary works of creation and providence, leading them to recognize and worship their Creator.
Paul had seen an altar inscribed “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.”
Henry notes that other writers recorded this feature of Athenian religion.
Even after multiplying idols, the Athenians thought there might be another god they did not know.
How many people called Christians likewise practice religious ceremonies earnestly while not truly knowing the God they claim to worship!
Paul proclaimed glorious truths about the Lord he served and urged his hearers to serve.
God had been patient with idolatry for a long time.
But the period of such ignorance was ending: through his messengers, God now commanded all people everywhere to repent.
Different philosophical schools would find Paul's teaching challenging because it exposed the emptiness or error of their cherished beliefs.

div.title: Some Athenians mock, others believe (verses 32–34)
div.p: Athenians treated Paul more politely in outward manner than people in some other towns.
Yet their contempt for his message and indifference toward it were no less serious.
The subject deserving the greatest attention often receives the least.
Those who mock must answer for their mockery.
God's word, however, never accomplishes nothing.
Some people will respond, join themselves to the Lord and continue listening to his faithful servants.
The certainty of future judgment, with Christ as our Judge, should move everyone to abandon sin and come to him.
Whatever starting point a gospel message uses, it must lead ultimately to Christ and his authority, because salvation and resurrection come from him and through him.

row.cell: Paul at Corinth, with Aquila and Priscilla.
He continues to preach at Corinth.
Apollos teaches at Ephesus and in Achaia.

div.title: Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla (verses 1–6)
div.p: Paul had the right to receive support from the churches he established and the people he taught.
Yet he continued working at his trade.
No one should despise honest work that provides daily bread.
Jewish families commonly trained their children in a trade even when they also provided education or property.
Paul took care to avoid needless prejudice, even when the prejudice was unreasonable.
Love for Christ is the best bond among believers.
Fellowship with other Christians makes labor, contempt and even persecution easier to bear.
Many Jews continued contradicting and blaspheming the gospel.
Not only did they refuse faith themselves, they tried to stop other people from believing.
Paul therefore left them.
But he did not abandon his ministry.
Even if Israel did not gather, Christ and his gospel would still be glorified.
The Jewish hearers had received the first opportunity to hear him and could not claim he had refused them the message.
When some oppose the gospel, we should turn to others willing to hear.
Our grief over the unbelief of many should not prevent us from thanking God for those who are converted.

div.title: Paul continues serving in Corinth (verses 7–11)
div.p: The Lord knows who belong to him, including those who will later become his through his work within them.
We should not despair about any city or people.
Even in wicked Corinth, Christ had many people.
He will gather his chosen flock from the places where its members are scattered.
Encouraged by this promise, Paul continued teaching in Corinth, and the church grew strong and numerous.

div.title: Paul appears before Gallio (verses 12–17)
div.p: Paul intended to show that his preaching did not encourage people to worship God unlawfully.
But Gallio would not accept the Jews' complaint about an issue outside his civil authority.
That was right: he should leave Jewish religious disputes to the Jews and refuse to let them use such arguments as an excuse to persecute others.
