But Gallio was wrong to speak contemptuously about God's law and faith, which he could and should have learned about.
Whether Jesus is the Messiah, whether the gospel comes from God and how God must be worshiped are not trivial disagreements about names and words.
They are matters of tremendous importance.
Gallio acted as though ignorance of Scripture were something to boast about and God's law beneath his notice.
If he merely refused to be disturbed by wicked people's insults, that was commendable.
But if he was indifferent when innocent people were mistreated, his indifference had gone too far.
People who learn of God's servants' suffering but feel no sympathy, offer no prayer and take no interest in helping resemble Gallio in his worst attitude.

div.title: Paul travels and encourages believers (verses 18–23)
div.p: While Paul saw that his work was fruitful, he continued working.
Our times belong in God's hands.
We make plans, but he decides their outcome.
Every promise concerning our plans should therefore be made in submission to God's will.
We must seek not merely permission from Providence but the Lord's own direction about our movements.
For a faithful minister, spending time with other believers is valuable refreshment.
Disciples remain weak and imperfect.
Ministers should help strengthen them by directing them to Christ, their Strength.
In whatever position God has given us, let us earnestly pursue Christ's cause.
We should plan as wisely as we can, yet depend on the Lord to accomplish those plans if he judges them good.

div.title: Apollos teaches and learns more fully (verses 24–28)
div.p: Apollos understood and taught as much of Christ's gospel as John the Baptist's ministry had revealed, but no further.
Henry thinks Apollos probably knew Jesus had died and risen, but had not yet been instructed clearly about the meaning of those events.
Apollos did not have the apostles' miraculous gifts.
Nevertheless, he used the gifts he actually possessed.
The Spirit grants gifts according to his measure for the good of others.
Apollos was an energetic and affectionate preacher, fervent in spirit.
He cared deeply for God's glory and the salvation of precious souls.
He was a man devoted to God, equipped for the work God had given him.
Aquila and Priscilla encouraged Apollos by attending his ministry.
They did not despise him for what he lacked or lower his reputation in the eyes of others.
They understood the disadvantages under which he had learned.
Through long companionship with Paul, they had learned more about the gospel, and they shared that knowledge with him.
Younger students can benefit greatly from speaking with mature Christians.
Even people who believe through grace continue needing instruction.
While we remain in this world, some unbelief persists and our faith is still imperfect.
The Jews whom Apollos addressed already honored Moses.
If they accepted that Jesus is the Messiah, Moses' own law directed them to listen to him.
Ministers' work is to preach Christ.
They must not merely assert the truth, but explain and defend it with gentleness as well as power.

row.cell: Paul instructs the disciples of John at Ephesus.
The Jewish exorcists disgraced. Some Ephesians burn their evil books.

div.title: Paul instructs disciples of John at Ephesus (verses 1–7)
div.p: In Ephesus Paul found religious people who looked toward Jesus as the promised Messiah.
They had not yet been taught to expect the Holy Spirit's extraordinary miraculous powers or to understand that the gospel was, in a particular way, the ministry of the Spirit.
But they were ready to welcome the teaching.
Paul explained that John the Baptist never intended people whom he baptized to stop with John.
He directed them to believe in the One coming after him, Jesus Christ.
They gladly received this fuller knowledge and were baptized in Jesus' name.
The Holy Spirit then came upon them in a remarkable and overwhelming way.
They spoke in different languages and prophesied, as the apostles and the first Gentile converts had done.
We do not now expect the same extraordinary miraculous powers.
Nevertheless, every person professing to be Christ's disciple should ask whether they have received the Holy Spirit's seal in his sanctifying work, as evidence of genuine faith.
Many people seem scarcely to have heard of the Holy Spirit.
Others dismiss every account of his grace and comfort as mere illusion.

Such people may rightly be asked what their baptism means to them, because they evidently do not understand the inward spiritual reality pictured by the outward sign in which they place so much confidence.

div.title: Paul teaches publicly; miracles confirm the message (verses 8–12)
div.p: When persistent argument and persuasion only make people more hardened in unbelief and blasphemy, we must withdraw from their fellowship and, when appropriate, lead others away from it.
God confirmed the preaching of his early servants through miracles.
Hearers unwilling to accept their spoken testimony could recognize the power of God through the works he performed.

div.title: False exorcists are exposed; evil books destroyed (verses 13–20)
div.p: People, especially among the Jews, sometimes claimed or tried to drive out evil spirits.
If we resist the devil through faith in Christ, he will flee from us.
But if we imagine Jesus' name or his miracles operate like a magical formula, Satan will prevail against us.
True sorrow for sin includes honest confession to God in prayer, and confession to people we have wronged whenever the circumstances require it.
If God's word gained greater influence among us, many owners of corrupt, irreligious and immoral books would themselves destroy them.
Will these Ephesians not stand as witnesses against people who claim Christ's name while trading in such writings for profit or allowing themselves to possess them for pleasure?
If we are serious about salvation, we must give up every pursuit and enjoyment that weakens the gospel's hold upon our minds and hearts.

div.title: A riot erupts over the worship of Artemis (verses 21–31)
div.p: Travelers to Ephesus frequently bought little silver shrines or models of the famous temple to take home after visiting.
The craftsmen profited from other people's superstition and used it to advance their own financial interests.
People cling fiercely to what produces their wealth.
Many turn against Christ's gospel because it calls them to abandon profitable but sinful occupations.
Some will defend ideas obviously absurd and false, such as gods made by human hands, so long as their worldly interests depend on those ideas.
The city became full of confusion—a common and natural effect of zeal for false religion.
The desire to defend Christ's honor, together with love for fellow believers, can lead courageous servants to risk danger.
God sometimes raises up friends of Christianity among people who do not share true faith but have witnessed the honest and consistent conduct of its followers.

div.title: The riot is quieted (verses 32–41)
div.p: Some Jews attempted to distinguish themselves from Christ's servants during the uproar.
Those who now are ashamed of being associated with him will face consequences on the day of final judgment.
At last a public official used his authority to calm the crowd.
Here is a valuable rule for both private and public affairs: do not act rashly.
Take time to consider.
Keep your emotions under control.
Do not do in haste what you will later regret.
Ordinary legal procedures should restrain popular riots; in a well-governed society they generally do.
Many people fear human courts far more than God's judgment.
How valuable it would be to calm our own unruly passions by remembering that soon we must answer before the Judge of heaven and earth!
God's overruling Providence keeps a measure of public peace through his otherwise mysterious rule over human minds.
Without it, people would destroy one another.
It is difficult to look around without seeing people behave like Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen.
Arguing with those enraged by party loyalties and disappointed greed may be as dangerous as confronting wild animals.
They imagine every objection answered as soon as they show that the practice being questioned makes them wealthy.
Whatever group, party or religious label embraces this attitude, it is worldly and should be rejected by all who value truth and godliness.
Do not lose heart.
The Lord on high is mightier than the roar of many waters.
He can also quiet the rage of a crowd.

row.cell: Paul's discourse to the elders of Ephesus.

div.title: Paul travels and serves (verses 1–6)
div.p: Disorder or opposition may force a Christian to leave a particular place or change a planned course.
But wherever believers go, their work for God and delight in serving him should remain the same.
Paul considered it worthwhile to spend five days traveling to Troas, though he would stay there only seven.
He knew, as we should, how to redeem the time spent traveling and turn it toward useful purposes.

div.title: Eutychus is restored to life (verses 7–12)
div.p: The disciples read Scripture, reflected, prayed and sang in private, maintaining their fellowship with God.
But they also came together for public worship and maintained fellowship with one another.
They gathered on the first day of the week, the Lord's day.
Henry understands that day as one that all disciples should keep holy.
In the breaking of bread, believers remember both Christ's body broken for us as a sacrifice for our sins and the benefits of that body given to us as spiritual nourishment and a feast for our souls.
In the earliest church, the Lord's Supper was ordinarily received every Lord's day in remembrance of Christ's death.
Paul preached during this assembly.
Preaching God's word should accompany the sacraments.
His listeners were willing to hear, and seeing that, Paul spoke until midnight.
Sleeping while listening to Scripture can reveal a low esteem of God's word.
We should guard against needless sleepiness and seek hearts attentive enough to the message that sleep is driven away.
Yet we must distinguish physical weakness, which deserves tenderness, from contempt, which deserves firm correction.
Eutychus's fall interrupted Paul's message.
But the miracle of restoring him to life confirmed that same message.
Because the congregation did not know when they would see Paul again, they made full use of his presence.
They considered a night's lost sleep well spent.
How rarely do we give up hours of rest for worship!
How frequently do people lose them through amusement or sinful revelry!
Spiritual life does not grow easily within fallen human hearts, whereas worldly habits grow readily.

div.title: Paul continues toward Jerusalem (verses 13–16)
div.p: Paul was eager to reach Jerusalem, yet continued seeking ways to do good while traveling.
Every godly person should act similarly.
In God's work, our own preferences and the wishes of our friends sometimes must give way.
We should not spend more time with loved ones when duty calls us elsewhere.

div.title: Paul speaks to the elders at Ephesus (verses 17–27)
div.p: The elders knew Paul was not motivated by scheming or selfish ambition.
Anyone serving God acceptably and helping other people must act with humility.
Paul's preaching was plain: he explained his message so others could understand.
It was powerful: the gospel testified for those receiving it and against those rejecting it.
It was useful: he sought to inform their understanding and reform their hearts and conduct.
It was hardworking: he labored diligently.
It was faithful: he did not withhold necessary rebuke or the message of the cross.
It was Christian and evangelical: he did not concentrate on speculative ideas, doubtful matters, politics or questions of civil government.
He proclaimed repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.
These two, with their genuine fruits and effects, provide the essential summary of salvation.
Without them no sinner escapes judgment; with them no one misses everlasting life.
The elders should not imagine Paul left Asia because he feared persecution.
He fully expected hardship, yet continued because he was confident God directed him.
We should thank God that we do not know everything awaiting us in the next year, week or even day.
It is enough for God's child to know that strength will be provided for each day's need.
We do not know what tomorrow brings, and ought not wish to know.
The powerful work of the Holy Spirit binds a believer to duty.
Even when persecution and trouble are expected, Christ's love compels the Christian to continue.
None of these dangers turned Paul from his work or deprived him of his true comfort.
Our life's business is to prepare for a joyful death.
Believing he would never see the elders again, Paul appealed to the integrity of his teaching.
He had proclaimed the whole counsel of God.
As he had preached a pure gospel, he had preached it completely, regardless of whether people would accept or reject it.

div.title: Paul warns, prays and says farewell (verses 28–38)
div.p: If the Holy Spirit has made ministers overseers and shepherds, they must remain faithful to their trust.
They should recognize the care their Master has for his flock.
This church belongs to the One who purchased it with his own blood.
The blood belonged to Jesus as a man.
Yet his divine and human natures are so closely united that Scripture calls this the blood of God, because it is the blood of the One who is God.
This gives Christ's sacrifice its infinite worth, sufficient to redeem believers from every evil and purchase every good.
Paul cared affectionately for the elders' souls and their future welfare.
He commended them to God and the word of his grace.
That word is not only the foundation of hope and source of joy, but also the rule for holy conduct.
Even the most mature believers can grow further.
God's word helps them.
Those who are not sanctified could not be welcome guests with the holy God, nor would heaven truly be heaven to them.
But heaven is certain for those born again, in whom God's likeness has been renewed, as certain as his power and truth.
Paul's own example showed freedom from excessive attachment to worldly gain.
That example would help the elders pass through earthly life with more comfort.
He quoted a saying of the Lord Jesus: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
Henry regards this as something Jesus often told his disciples.
Worldly-minded people think differently.
They fear giving unless they can receive something in return.
To them profit through taking seems the happiest thing possible.
But Christ teaches that giving is greater and more blessed.
Giving makes us more like God, who gives to everyone and needs nothing from anyone, and like Jesus, who went about doing good.
May the mind of Christ be in us.
When friends must part, prayer is a fitting farewell.
Those who counsel and pray for one another may experience many tears and painful separations.
But they will meet again before God's throne, never to part again.
Christ's presence would accompany Paul on his journey, and that same presence would remain with the elders he left behind.

row.cell: Paul at Cesarea. The prophecy of Agabus, Paul at Jerusalem.
He is persuaded to join in ceremonial observances.
Being in danger from the Jews, he is rescued by the Romans.

div.title: Paul's journey toward Jerusalem (verses 1–7)
div.p: When our affairs go well, we ought to recognize God's Providence.
Whenever Paul arrived somewhere, he searched for disciples and found them.
His friends foresaw his troubles. Because they loved him and cared about the church, they mistakenly thought God's honor would be better served if he remained free.
Their earnest efforts to dissuade him made his godly determination even clearer.
Paul teaches us by both instruction and example to pray continually.
The disciples' last farewell was made sweeter by prayer.

div.title: Agabus predicts trouble; Paul reaches Jerusalem (verses 8–18)
div.p: Paul received clear warning of the suffering ahead, so it would neither surprise nor terrify him.
Scripture gives us the same warning: through many troubles we must enter God's kingdom.
His friends' weeping began to weaken his resolution. Yet Christ had told his followers to take up their cross.
Paul was distressed that they so insistently pressed him toward something he could not do without wronging his conscience.
When trouble approaches, we should not merely say, “The Lord's will must be done; there is nothing we can do.”
Rather we should say, “Let the Lord's will be done.” His will expresses divine wisdom, and he orders all things according to it.
Once trouble comes, God's accomplished will should quiet our grief.
When trouble approaches, God's promised will should quiet our fears.
Our response ought to be Amen; let it happen.
It is an honor to become an old disciple of Christ, kept by God's grace in the path of duty, steady in faith, growing in experience into old age.
We should welcome fellowship with such believers, because their years can teach us wisdom.
Many believers in Jerusalem received Paul gladly.
We may imagine that we too would have welcomed him, but unless we welcome his doctrine, we would not truly welcome the apostle.

div.title: Paul joins ceremonial observances (verses 19–26)
div.p: Paul credited God with all his success, and the Jerusalem believers gave God praise.
God had honored him greatly, yet the other apostles did not envy his fruitful service; they glorified the Lord.
James and the elders asked Paul to accommodate Jewish Christians through some compliance with ceremonial law.
They thought this was prudent.
But Henry judges that clinging to ceremonial shadows after their substance, Christ, had come was a serious weakness.

The religion Paul preached did not destroy the law but fulfilled it. He proclaimed Christ as the law's goal for righteousness, along with repentance and faith, in which the law retains its proper use.
Even disciples of Christ sometimes gave too little regard to Paul, despite his remarkable character and work, simply because his attachment to Jewish ceremonies differed from theirs.
This illustrates the danger of religious prejudice.
The apostles were not beyond criticism in every action.
Henry adds that it would be difficult to defend Paul from the charge of yielding too much in this matter.
Trying to win the approval of unyielding zealots and party-minded people is usually futile.
Paul's concession did not succeed: the very action intended to calm opposition inflamed it.
But God overruled both the elders' advice and Paul's compliance for a wiser purpose.
Nothing would satisfy people determined to destroy Christianity.

p.hi: Sincere integrity is safer than compliance against one's better judgment.

div.p: This also warns us never to pressure people to act contrary to their conscientious convictions merely to please us.

div.title: The Romans rescue Paul from his accusers (verses 27–40)
div.p: Paul was attacked in the temple, where he ought to have been safe.
His opponents falsely accused him of teaching and acting against Mosaic ordinances.
People who intend well and act lawfully often find themselves accused of actions they never contemplated.
Sometimes an attempt to oblige others becomes the very thing used against us.
God may protect his servants through people who have no affection for Christianity but who feel compassion for suffering people or value public peace.
Many are misled by false ideas about good people and faithful ministers.

Yet the Lord intervenes at the right time to protect his servants from wicked and unreasonable people, giving them opportunities to speak for themselves, plead the Redeemer's cause and spread his glorious gospel.

row.cell: Paul directed to preach to the Gentiles.
The rage of the Jews Paul pleads that he is a Roman citizen.

div.title: Paul describes his conversion (verses 1–11)
div.p: Paul addressed the enraged crowd with the customary courtesy and goodwill.
He described his earlier life carefully and made clear that his conversion was entirely the work of God.
Condemned sinners are struck blind by the power of darkness, and that blindness continues, as it did among those who rejected the gospel.
But sinners brought under conviction are temporarily blinded not by darkness but by light, as Paul was.
For a time they are bewildered and uncertain so that afterward they may receive spiritual understanding.
A straightforward account of how the Lord brought us from opposing the gospel to professing and promoting it, told in the right spirit, can move hearers more deeply than elaborate speeches.
Such an account does not itself prove every Christian truth, but the transformation in Paul's life provided striking confirmation of God's power.

div.title: Paul is sent to the Gentiles (verses 12–21)
div.p: Paul went on to describe how his change of life was confirmed.
When the Lord chooses a sinner to know his will, he humbles and enlightens that person and leads them to Christ and his blessed gospel.
Jesus is called the Righteous One, for he is Jesus Christ the righteous.
Everyone called to understand God's will must look to Christ, through whom God has revealed his goodwill toward us.
The great gospel privilege signified and sealed by baptism is the forgiveness of sins.

When Paul was commanded to be baptized and wash away his sins, he was called to receive the comfort of pardon through Jesus Christ, take hold of Christ's righteousness and seek power to put his sinful desires to death.
Do not stop at the outward sign. Make sure you possess the cleansing from sin that it signifies.
The gospel duty to which baptism commits us is to seek forgiveness in Christ's name and in dependence upon him and his righteousness.
God appoints his workers both their time and their place.
They ought to follow his direction even when it contradicts their preferences.
Providence plans more wisely for us than we plan for ourselves.
When Christ sends someone, his Spirit accompanies that servant and enables them to see fruit from their labors.
Yet no one is reconciled to the gospel except through God's special grace.

div.title: Paul appeals to his Roman citizenship (verses 22–30)
div.p: The crowd listened to Paul's account of his conversion until he mentioned his mission to the Gentiles.
Their national prejudices were so strong that they refused to hear more.
Their violent behavior astonished the Roman commander, who assumed that Paul must have committed a terrible crime.
Paul invoked his rights as a Roman citizen, exempting him from coercive examinations and punishments intended to force a confession.
His manner showed remarkable peace and confidence.
The commander was surprised that a Jew living in modest circumstances possessed such a valuable privilege; the commander had paid a great deal for his own citizenship.
Paul replied that he had been born with it.
Let us place far greater value on the freedom into which God's children are born, a liberty no amount of money can purchase for someone who remains unregenerate.
Paul's appeal immediately stopped the unlawful treatment.
Many people avoid sinful actions because they fear human authorities, although they would not be restrained by reverence for God.
Paul simply asked, “Is it lawful?”
He knew God could sustain him through any suffering genuinely required for Christ's sake.
But if the threatened suffering was unlawful and could properly be avoided, his faith directed him to avoid it.

p.hi: He never turned away from the cross his divine Master placed along his path; neither did he leave that path in search of an unnecessary cross.

row.cell: Paul's defence before the council of the Jews.
Paul's defence. He receives a Divine assurance that he shall go to Rome.
The Jews conspire to kill Paul, Lysias sends him to Cesarea.

div.title: Paul defends himself before the council (verses 1–5)
div.p: Here we see what an honest person is like.
Such a person sets God continually before them and lives as in his sight.
Their conscience governs their words and deeds. According to the best of their knowledge, they avoid evil and cling to what is good.
They act conscientiously in every part of life.
People who live this way before God can, like Paul, have confidence both toward God and toward others.
Paul's answer to the high priest included a deserved rebuke and a warning of judgment.
Nevertheless, Henry judges that Paul seems to have spoken with too much anger after being struck.
Even people occupying high office may be told about their failures and may rightly face public complaint.
But these objections must be expressed appropriately, because God's law still requires respect for those in authority.

div.title: The council divides; Christ reassures Paul (verses 6–11)
div.p: The Pharisees held the traditional Jewish belief in resurrection.
The Sadducees rejected Scripture and divine revelation in this matter. They denied a future state, and therefore had neither hope of everlasting joy nor fear of everlasting suffering.
Paul could truthfully say that he was being tried because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead.
It was legitimate for him to state his position on this disputed question and thereby move Pharisees to protect him from unlawful violence.
How easily God can defend his cause!
The Jewish leaders appeared united in opposition to Christianity, but their motives differed.
The wicked have no secure friendship with one another.
God can turn their apparent agreement into open disagreement in an instant.
The Roman commander rescued Paul from violent people, but could not tell him what the future held.
God's own consolation was much more valuable.
Whoever opposes us, we need not fear if the Lord stands beside us.
Christ desires his faithful servants to remain joyful and courageous.
Paul may have thought that he would never reach Rome.
But God assured him that he would testify there too, because Paul's desire to go to Rome arose from a wish to honor Christ and do good.

div.title: A conspiracy is exposed; Paul is sent to Caesarea (verses 12–24)
div.p: False religious beliefs, when adopted by people governed by sinful passions, can provoke astonishing cruelty.
Yet God easily defeats the most carefully designed schemes of wickedness.
Paul understood that divine Providence ordinarily works through reasonable and prudent means.
Had he neglected the means available to protect himself, he could not have rightly expected God to preserve him by extraordinary intervention.
A person unwilling to use available abilities and opportunities has neither reason nor revelation guaranteeing God's assistance.
By trusting the Lord, we may expect him to preserve us from every evil work and bring us safely into his heavenly kingdom.
Heavenly Father, through your Holy Spirit and for Christ's sake, grant us this precious faith.

div.title: Lysias writes to Felix (verses 25–35)
div.p: God has instruments for every task he intends to accomplish.
The natural abilities and moral virtues of unbelieving people have often been used to protect his persecuted servants.
Even people who care little about Christian doctrine may recognize the difference between the honest conduct of upright believers and the zeal of false religious professors.
All human hearts are in God's hand.
Blessed are those who trust him and commit their way to him.

row.cell: The speech of Tertullus against Paul.
Felix trembles at the reasoning of Paul.

div.title: Tertullus accuses Paul (verses 1–9)
div.p: Here we see a danger faced by powerful people: their accomplishments are praised beyond measure while their sins are never honestly exposed.
Such flattery hardens people and encourages them to continue doing evil, as happened with Felix.
God's prophets were accused of disturbing the land, and the Lord Jesus himself was accused of misleading the nation.
The same accusations were now brought against Paul.
Selfish passions often drive people to persecute others.
Skills of speech and public persuasion can be used to mislead people and turn them against the truth.
How different Paul and Felix will appear on the day of judgment from the descriptions Tertullus offered!
Christians should neither seek the praise of irreligious people nor be troubled by their insults.
Worldly flatterers can make the most wicked people appear almost divine, while treating the best people on earth as dangerous rebels.

div.title: Paul answers Felix (verses 10–21)
div.p: Paul gave a truthful explanation of his conduct.
It cleared him of criminal charges and exposed the real reason for the violence directed against him.
We must never abandon a good path simply because others give it a bad name.
When we worship God, it is a comfort to worship the God of our fathers, receiving no other rule for faith and conduct than the Scriptures.
Scripture also teaches that there will be a resurrection followed by final judgment.
The prophets and their teaching were to be tested by their fruit.
Paul labored to maintain a conscience without offense toward both God and human beings.
He diligently avoided sin and pursued godliness in every situation.
What if other people accuse us of loving God too much?
Do we shrink from that accusation?
Many people would rather be accused of almost any weakness—even serious wrongdoing—than of earnest love for Jesus Christ and devotion to his service.
Can such people really expect Christ to acknowledge them when he comes in glory before God's angels?

What would please the Savior more than seeing a faithful servant on earth gladly admit, if it is considered an offense, that he loves the Lord who died for him with all his heart, soul, mind and strength?
Such a believer will not silently watch God's word despised or hear his name profaned.
He will rather risk the world's ridicule and hatred than incur the disapproval of the gracious Lord whose love is better than life.

div.title: Felix trembles but postpones repentance (verses 22–27)
div.p: Paul reasoned with Felix about righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come.
These were exactly the subjects the oppressive governor and the woman living with him needed to hear.
They needed repentance, forgiveness and the grace of the gospel.
Righteousness concerns our conduct in life, particularly toward other people.
Self-control concerns the ordering and government of our inner life before God.
Someone who neglects both has neither the true form nor the power of godliness and faces God's righteous anger at judgment.
The prospect of future judgment can make even the boldest person tremble.

p.hi: Felix trembled—but nothing more followed.

div.p: Many hear God's word and become frightened without being changed.
They fear sin's consequences yet continue loving and practicing it.
Delay is dangerous whenever eternal salvation is at stake.
Felix deferred the conversation until a more convenient moment.
Scripture does not report that such a moment ever came.
Now is the accepted time; today is the day of salvation.
Felix eagerly ended the interview, but what business could be more urgent than reforming his life or saving his soul?
Many sinners start up like someone awakened by a sudden loud noise, then fall almost immediately back into sleep.
We must not be deceived by occasional outward displays of religious interest, whether in ourselves or others.
Above all, we must not treat God's word lightly.
Do we imagine that hearts naturally become softer with age, or that the world's influence inevitably weakens?
We are in danger now, and tomorrow may be too late.

row.cell: Paul before Festus, he appeals to Caesar.
Festus confers with Agrippa respecting Paul.

div.title: Paul appeals to Caesar (verses 1–12)
div.p: See how restless malicious people are.
Persecutors treat the opportunity to satisfy their hatred as a special favor.
But preaching Christ as the fulfillment and goal of the law was no offense against that law.
In times of persecution, God's people need wisdom and prudence as well as patience.
Innocent people may rightly insist on their innocence.
Paul was prepared to submit to lawful proceedings and let the legal process take its course.
If he truly deserved death, he would accept the penalty.
But if the accusations were false, no one could justly deliver him to his enemies.
For the moment Paul was neither released nor condemned.
This shows how gradually Providence sometimes unfolds.
We often discover that both our hopes and our fears were premature, as God keeps us waiting on him.

div.title: Festus consults Agrippa about Paul (verses 13–27)
div.p: Agrippa governed Galilee.
Festus acknowledged an important Roman legal principle: a person accused of wrongdoing must have the opportunity to confront the accusers and answer the charges (verse 16).
How many hasty and unjust judgments does that principle condemn!
Even a non-Christian governor, guided only by natural understanding, could follow the law and established custom in this matter.
Yet many professing Christians neglect truth, justice and charity when judging brothers and sisters.
Worldly people and political officials may regard questions of divine worship, salvation and the gospel as doubtful or unimportant.
Notice how lightly Festus spoke of Christ and the controversy between Jewish leaders and Christians.
But the day is approaching when Festus and everyone else will recognize that the affairs of the entire Roman Empire were insignificant compared with the truth of Christ's resurrection.
Those who had the means to learn God's truth yet despised them will understand their folly and sin.
A distinguished company gathered to hear Paul.
They intended only to satisfy their curiosity about a prisoner, but they were about to hear the gospel.
People still sometimes come to hear God's word with great pomp, motivated by curiosity rather than a desire for truth.

Although ministers today do not ordinarily stand in the dock defending their lives, some hearers still sit in judgment upon them, looking for any statement they can use as a charge rather than listening to learn God's will for their salvation.
Yet all the grandeur of the assembly was eclipsed by the real glory of the poor prisoner.
What were their splendid clothes and rank beside Paul's wisdom, grace, holiness, courage and steadfast endurance for Christ?
It is a great mercy when God makes our innocence and upright conduct plain, leaving opponents without any proven charge.
Sometimes he causes even our enemies to do us justice.

row.cell: His conversion and preaching to the Gentiles.
Festus and Agrippa convinced of Paul's innocence.

div.title: Paul defends himself before Agrippa (verses 1–11)
div.p: Christianity teaches us to explain the reason for our hope, while also giving proper honor to those entitled to it—without flattery or fear of human beings.
Agrippa knew the Old Testament well and was therefore better equipped to judge the dispute about whether Jesus was the Messiah.
Surely ministers preaching faith in Christ may expect to receive a patient hearing.
Paul affirmed that he retained everything good in the religious training he had received.
He had lived morally and avoided the public wickedness and cunning greed of some Pharisees.
He had also held sound religious beliefs and revered God's ancient promise to the fathers, making that promise the foundation of his hope.
Paul understood that none of this former morality could justify him before God.
Yet he mentioned it because it disproved his enemies' charges and could bring honor to Christ.
Though he counted these things as loss in order to gain Christ, they were relevant to his defense.
His Christian faith did not continue his youthful zeal for the ceremonial law.
The sacrifices and offerings had been fulfilled and superseded by the great Sacrifice they foreshadowed.
He no longer treated the ceremonial washings as binding, because Christ's priesthood had fulfilled the Levitical priesthood.
But the great principles of true religion remained those for which he had always cared.
Christ and heaven are two central doctrines of the gospel.
God has given eternal life, and that life is in his Son.
These were the matters promised to the fathers.
Israel's continual religious duties testified to faith in that promise.
The prospect of eternal life should move us to steadfast devotion.
The Sadducees opposed Paul for teaching resurrection; other Jewish leaders joined them because he proclaimed Jesus as risen and as Israel's promised Redeemer.
Many divine promises seem impossible only because people forget the infinite power and perfection of the God who promised them.
Paul acknowledged that during his days as a Pharisee, he had been a bitter enemy of Christianity.
Everything in his background seemed opposed to conversion.
Even people who were outwardly strict before conversion may later find much to repent of, including actions they previously regarded as religious duties.

div.title: Paul recounts his conversion and mission (verses 12–23)
div.p: Paul became a Christian through God's power, when Christ revealed himself both to him and within him, even while Paul was actively pursuing sin.
He became a minister through Christ's authority, because the same Lord who appeared in heavenly glory commanded him to preach to Gentiles.
The world lies in darkness and must receive light.
People ignorant of the way to eternal peace must be taught it.
But the world also lies in sin and needs sanctification and reform.
It is not enough to open people's eyes; their hearts must be renewed.
They must be brought not only from darkness to light, but also from Satan's power to God.
Everyone genuinely turned from sin to God receives more than pardon: a rich eternal inheritance.
Forgiveness opens the way to that inheritance.
Nobody can be happy without holiness. Those who will be saints in heaven must begin to be saints while on earth.
We are made holy and saved through faith in Jesus Christ.
By faith we rely on him as the Lord our Righteousness and surrender ourselves to him as the Lord who rules us.
Through this faith we receive forgiveness, the gift of the Holy Spirit and eternal life.
Christ's cross offended the Jewish leaders.
They were enraged that Paul proclaimed the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies, including that Christ would be the first or principal one raised from the dead.
The prophets also foretold that the Messiah would bring Gentiles to know God.
What reasonable objection could anyone have to this?
A genuine convert can explain the reasons for Christian hope and the change in personal life.
Yet people who preach repentance and conversion have often suffered persecution for doing so.

div.title: Festus and Agrippa hear Paul's appeal (verses 24–32)
div.p: We should speak truthfully and soberly in every situation, without being unsettled by unjust criticism.

Faithful gospel workers are often dismissed as dreamers or mad people because they believe wonderful events and insist that others, regardless of social status, need the same faith and diligence for salvation.
The apostles, prophets and even the Son of God faced such accusations.
Those made wise for salvation by divine grace need not be shaken by them.
Agrippa saw much evidence in favor of Christianity.
For a time his reasoning and judgment were persuaded, but his heart was not changed.
His attitude and conduct remained far from the humility and spiritual character of the gospel.
Many people become almost persuaded to take faith seriously.
They recognize the excellence of God's ways and feel strong convictions about their duties, yet they fail to act on them.
Paul urged everyone to become truly Christian.
Christ's grace is sufficient for all, and faith in him is absolutely necessary for salvation.
The gospel offers deliverance from spiritual bondage to Gentiles and the lost world.
Yet people are often unwilling to admit they need a transforming work of grace in their own hearts.
Beware of hesitation that becomes fatal.
Being almost a Christian is very different from possessing the faith and life of a true believer.

row.cell: Paul and his companions endangered by a tempest.
He receives a Divine assurance of safety.

div.title: Paul sails toward Rome (verses 1–11)
div.p: God's counsel had determined that Paul should reach Rome before Festus decided to send him there.
The Lord had work for Paul to do in that city.
The account records the route they followed and the places where they landed.
God encourages those who suffer for him to trust his care, because he can move unexpected people to befriend them.
Sailors must make the best use of whatever wind they receive.
So must we all while traveling across the ocean of this world.
Even when circumstances are against us, we should keep making progress as well as we can.
Some people avoid losing ground in adversity but do not make progress during favorable conditions.
Others, including genuine Christians, spend so much effort merely maintaining their spiritual condition that they hardly advance.
A harbor that looks pleasant is not necessarily safe.
Many people show respect to faithful ministers while refusing their advice.
Eventually events expose the emptiness of such confidence and the foolishness of that conduct.

div.title: The ship is overtaken by a storm (verses 12–20)
div.p: People who set out on life's voyage with favorable conditions cannot know what storms are waiting ahead.
Therefore we should never assume that earthly security has been permanently achieved.
We are not completely safe until we enter heaven.
For many days the sailors saw neither sun nor stars.
Believers sometimes experience an equivalent spiritual darkness, walking without any felt light or comfort.
Look how easily worldly wealth changes from something greatly desired into a heavy burden.
In a crisis it may become too heavy to carry safely—even heavy enough to sink the person holding onto it.
Worldly people readily surrender wealth to preserve their lives, yet are reluctant to use it for godliness, charity or suffering for Christ.
Anyone would choose to lose possessions rather than life.
Yet many choose to wreck faith and a good conscience rather than part with property.
The sailors tried every available method to save themselves, without success.
When sinners finally abandon confidence in their own ability to save themselves, they may be ready to receive God's word and trust his mercy through Jesus Christ.

div.title: Paul receives assurance of deliverance (verses 21–29)
div.p: Paul had warned the sailors, but they refused to listen.
Nevertheless, he offered them renewed comfort when they faced danger.
Those who admit their folly and turn from it can still receive help.
People often bring trouble upon themselves by refusing to be content and trying to improve their circumstances against wise advice.
Notice Paul's solemn profession that he belonged to God.
No storm can prevent the Lord's favor from reaching his people; he is always available to help.
Faithful servants can be encouraged during difficulties: as long as God has more work for them, he will preserve their lives.
Had Paul needlessly placed himself in dangerous company, he might have shared the consequences without such a promise.
But because God had called him into these circumstances, the others were preserved for Paul's sake.
God told him the people on board had been given to him.
Nothing gives a good person greater satisfaction than knowing they can be a blessing to others.
Paul comforted his companions with the comfort he had received from God.
Since God always keeps his promises, people who trust those promises should remain joyful.
With God, speaking and acting are not separate things.
Likewise, for believers, faith and enjoying the certainty of God's promise should belong together.
Hope is the soul's sure and steadfast anchor, reaching within the veil.
People in spiritual darkness should cling to Christ and not set out upon another dangerous voyage.
Remain with him and wait until the day dawns.

div.title: Paul encourages everyone to persevere (verses 30–38)
div.p: God had appointed the final outcome: the passengers would be saved.
He also appointed the means of their rescue, including the experienced sailors.
Our duty is to use the means available to us; the outcome belongs to God.
We do not trust God but test him when we claim his protection while refusing reasonable steps within our power.
How selfish people often are! Some are prepared to preserve themselves even by exposing others to destruction.
How blessed the people on this ship were to have Paul among them.
He was in fellowship with heaven and brought courage and encouragement to those around him.
Worldly sorrow leads to death, while joy in God brings life and peace even in danger.
The promises of God comfort us only as we believe and depend on him to fulfill them.
We must wait for promised salvation through the means he appoints.
If God has chosen us for salvation, he has also appointed that we receive it through repentance, faith, prayer and persevering obedience.
It is deadly presumption to expect his saving promise to be fulfilled while refusing those appointed means.
People are encouraged to trust Christ as their Savior when those inviting them clearly demonstrate that they trust him themselves.

div.title: The passengers are shipwrecked (verses 39–44)
div.p: The ship had survived the storm in open water, where it had room to move.
Yet when it became stuck, it broke apart.
The same can happen to the heart that fastens its affections upon worldly possessions.
When Satan's temptations break against that heart, it may perish.
But while the heart remains above the world, it can endure the storms of daily cares and troubles.
The sailors could already see the shore, yet they still suffered shipwreck at the harbor.
This teaches us never to grow careless merely because safety appears near.
However severe the difficulties along the path to God's promised salvation, the promise will certainly be fulfilled.
In due time all believers will arrive safely in heaven.
Lord Jesus, you have assured your people that none who belong to you will perish.
You will bring them all safely to the heavenly shore.
What a joyful arrival that will be!
You will present them to your Father and grant your Holy Spirit full and eternal possession of them.

row.cell: Paul preaches to the Jews, and abides at Rome a prisoner.

div.title: Paul receives kindness on Malta (verses 1–10)
div.p: God can turn strangers into friends, especially during suffering.
People whose manners are regarded as unsophisticated may show more kindness than those thought to be highly civilized.
The islanders' compassion condemns many inhabitants of supposedly civilized nations who profess Christianity but fail to help people in distress.
When the viper attached itself to Paul, the islanders assumed he was a murderer whom divine justice was punishing.
They understood that God rules the world and that events do not happen through mere chance, not even the smallest events.
They also understood that wicked deeds deserve punishment and good actions deserve reward, and that murder is particularly terrible.
But they made two mistakes.
First, they assumed God punishes every wicked person during this life.
In fact, some receive judgment now as evidence of his Providence, while others remain unpunished for a time as a warning of judgment to come.
Second, they assumed everyone who suffers an extraordinary calamity must be extraordinarily wicked.
Revelation corrects this error. Godly people often experience great afflictions that test and strengthen their faith and patience.
Paul escaped the bite unharmed.
Likewise, by Christ's grace, believers may shake off Satan's temptations with holy determination.
When other people insult and accuse us, we may cast away their unjust reproaches as Paul cast the snake into the fire, provided our consciences testify to our integrity.
Such attacks can do no lasting harm unless they draw us away from our duty.
God made Paul remarkable among the islanders, preparing the way for them to receive the gospel.
Wherever the Lord leads his people, he can raise up friends and make them a blessing to others who are suffering.

div.title: Paul reaches Rome (verses 11–16)
div.p: Ordinary travel details are seldom worth remembering.
But fellowship among believers and kindness shown by friends deserve to be recorded.
The Christians in Rome were not ashamed of Paul because he was a prisoner.
They were even more careful to show him affection and respect, greatly comforting him.
When friends treat us kindly, we should recognize God moving their hearts and give him thanks.
When we meet people who honor Christ in unfamiliar places, we have reason to praise God.
How many powerful conquerors have entered Rome in magnificent triumph, crowned with honor, yet brought harm to the world!
Paul entered chained as a poor prisoner, but he was a greater blessing to humanity than any of them.
This should correct our admiration for worldly status.
God can give prisoners favor in the eyes of their captors.
When he does not immediately release his people from captivity, he may still make their bondage easier or give them peace while enduring it.
For this, they can be thankful.

div.title: Paul meets the Jewish leaders (verses 17–22)
div.p: Paul was honored by the fact that those examining him had found no criminal wrongdoing.
He had appealed to Caesar to clear his name, not to accuse his nation.
True Christianity concerns what matters to all human beings, rather than narrow opinions or private interests.
It seeks no earthly reward as its ultimate goal; its benefits are spiritual and eternal.
Yet Christ's holy religion has always been spoken against.
In towns and villages where Jesus is proclaimed as the only Savior and people are called to a changed life, those who follow him are still dismissed as a sect, party or dangerous group.
Such reproaches will continue as long as people live in opposition to God.

div.title: Paul preaches Christ while imprisoned (verses 23–31)
div.p: Paul tried to persuade Jewish hearers concerning Jesus.
Some were affected by God's word; others became harder.
Some received light, while others closed their eyes.
The gospel has always produced these different responses.
Paul warned them that the Holy Spirit had described such resistance beforehand.
Those who hear the gospel but pay no attention should tremble.
Who will heal them if they refuse God's remedy?
The listeners went away debating among themselves.
But people can argue extensively without reasoning rightly.
They may find fault with one another while refusing the truth.
Discussion alone cannot convince sinners unless God's grace opens their understanding.
Although we grieve for those rejecting salvation, we should rejoice that God sends his salvation to others who will receive it.
If we are among them, we should thank him for the grace that made us different.
Paul remained resolved to know and preach Jesus Christ and him crucified.
When Christians are distracted from their chief purpose, let them ask: What does this have to do with Jesus? Does it bring us nearer to him and help us walk in him?
Paul preached Christ, not himself, without being ashamed of the gospel.
He had only limited opportunities for service while imprisoned, but he did not complain.
The door opened to him was narrow, yet no one was permitted to close it.
God made that opportunity fruitful for many, so that believers appeared even in Nero's household (Philippians 4:22).
Paul's chains themselves promoted the gospel (Philippians 1:13).
Believers in Rome and Christians throughout the world have reason to thank God that Paul spent a mature period of his Christian life in captivity.
Henry considers it probable that, while imprisoned and perhaps chained to a soldier, Paul wrote Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians and Hebrews.
This is Henry's historical interpretation, not a verified assertion about the disputed authorship of Hebrews.
These writings display great Christian love and spiritual experience.
Today's believers may possess less of Paul's sense of triumph and heavenly joy.
Yet everyone who follows the same Savior has the same certainty of final safety and peace.
May we live increasingly in the Savior's love and seek his glory in every deed.
Through his strength, may we overcome our enemies now.
And through his undeserved grace and mercy, may we share the company of those who sit with him on his throne, as he overcame and sat at the Father's right hand forever.

div.title: Romans — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The apostle Paul's purpose in writing to the Romans appears to have been to answer the objections of unbelieving Jews while teaching those who believed, to strengthen Christians and bring idolatrous Gentiles to faith.
He also wanted to show that a Gentile convert had the same standing in God's favor as a Jewish believer.
These purposes are brought together as Paul answers the unbelieving Jew and defends the believing Gentile.
The letter explains plainly how a sinner may be accepted by God and justified in his sight: solely through grace, by faith in the righteousness of Christ, without distinction of nation or people.
It also answers the objections of Jewish Christians who tried to combine the law and the gospel as joint conditions for acceptance before God and exclude Gentiles from the Messiah's saving blessings.
The letter concludes by urging holiness through practical instruction.

row.cell: Prays for the saints at Rome, and expresses his desire to see them.
The gospel way of justification by faith, for Jews and Gentiles.
The sins of the Gentiles set forth.

div.title: Paul's commission (verses 1–7)
div.p: The gospel Paul proclaimed fulfilled the promises previously given through the prophets.
It concerns Jesus Christ, the Son of God and promised Savior, descended from David in his human nature and declared to be the Son of God through divine power by his resurrection from the dead.
Professing Christianity does not consist simply in understanding religious ideas or agreeing that certain propositions are true.
Still less does it consist in obstinate disputes.
It consists in the obedience of faith.
Only those effectively called by Jesus Christ are brought to this obedience.
Christians have a privilege: they are loved by God and belong to the people he loves.
They also have a duty: they are called to holiness, to be saints.
Paul greeted them by asking God to give them grace to sanctify their souls and peace to comfort their hearts.
Both come from God's free mercy, as the Father reconciled to believers through the Lord Jesus Christ.

div.title: Paul's prayers and desire to visit Rome (verses 8–15)
div.p: We show love toward fellow believers not only by praying for them, but also by giving thanks to God for them.
When considering our plans and desires, we should remember to say, “If the Lord wills” (James 4:15).
A journey becomes successful or otherwise according to God's will.
We should gladly share the gifts and opportunities entrusted to us.
We should find joy in making others joyful, particularly in fellowship with people united with us in Christian faith.
If Christ has redeemed us through his blood and converted us by his grace, we belong entirely to him.
For his sake, we owe everyone whatever good we are able to do.
This service is not optional generosity beyond duty; it is our duty.

div.title: The gospel reveals justification through faith (verses 16 and 17)
div.p: These verses introduce the theme of the whole letter.
Paul charges all humanity with sin.
He announces the only way to escape condemnation: faith in God's mercy through Jesus Christ.
He then builds on that salvation the need for purity of heart, grateful obedience and continuing growth in Christian grace, which living faith in Christ alone can produce.
God is holy and just; we are guilty sinners.
To stand before him, we need a righteousness that meets his justice.
Such a righteousness has been brought by the Messiah and revealed in the gospel.
Here is a gracious way to be accepted despite our guilt: the righteousness of Christ, who is God, arising from a satisfaction of infinite value.
Faith is essential not only at the beginning, but throughout the Christian life.
Paul does not say that faith first brings us into a justified state and afterward our works keep us there.
It is from faith to faith throughout: faith presses forward and overcomes unbelief.

div.title: All people need the gospel because of sin (verses 18–25)
div.p: Paul begins showing that every person needs the gospel's salvation.
No one can obtain God's favor or escape his wrath by personal works.
No human being has perfectly fulfilled every duty toward God and neighbor.
Nor has anyone always lived according to the moral understanding already given.
Sin includes ungodliness, offenses against duties owed to God, and unrighteousness, offenses against duties owed to others.
Its cause includes holding back or suppressing the truth through wrongdoing.
Every person sometimes does what they know is wrong and neglects what they know is right.
Therefore, no one can claim perfect innocence through ignorance.
The Creator's invisible power and deity are displayed through his creation so clearly that idolaters are left without excuse.
Yet rational creatures exchanged worship of the glorious Creator for worship of animals, creeping creatures and lifeless images.
They wandered from God so far that true religion would have disappeared without the gospel's revelation.
Whatever claims are made for the sufficiency of unaided human reason to discover God's truth, understand moral duty and direct life properly, the historical facts contradict them.
Human beings have dishonored God with absurd idolatries and superstitions, and degraded themselves through shameful desires and acts.

div.title: Human beings abandon God's truth (verses 26–32)
div.p: Human depravity demonstrates Jesus' words: light came into the world, but people loved darkness more than light because their deeds were evil.
Divine truth did not please them.
Human beings can reason themselves out of believing what they dislike, even against strong evidence.
But no bondage is worse than being given over to one's own sinful desires.
Because the Gentiles rejected the knowledge of God, they committed deeds opposed to reason and to their own welfare.
Human nature remains fallen, whether a person is from a pagan background or claims the Christian name.
Paul's charges apply, in greater or lesser measure, to people in every age until they submit to Christ through faith and are renewed by divine power.
Everyone has reason to grieve over inward corruption and secret resistance to God's will.
Therefore, this chapter calls us all to examine ourselves, recognize our guilt deeply and understand the necessity of rescue from condemnation.

row.cell: The Jews could not be justified by the law of Moses, any more than the Gentiles by the law of nature.
The sins of the Jews confuted all their vain confidence in their outward privileges.

div.title: Judgment is based upon our true conduct (verses 1–16)
div.p: The Jews thought they were a holy people who deserved their privileges, even while they were unthankful, rebellious and unrighteous.
But everyone who behaves this way, of every nationality, generation and social position, must remember that God judges according to a person's true character.
The matter is so plain that we may appeal to the sinner's own conscience.
Every deliberate sin expresses contempt for God's goodness.
Although disobedience appears in many different forms, it grows from the same underlying root.
True repentance requires hatred of former sinfulness.
It comes from a change in the inner person, leading us to choose good and refuse evil.
Repentance also involves recognizing our own inward misery.
This great transformation is conversion, and every human being needs it.
Sinners' ruin comes from a heart that remains hard and unrepentant.
Such people are described as storing up wrath for themselves.
In Paul's account of righteous conduct, notice how demanding God's law is.
It requires pure motives, rejecting actions performed for merely selfish ambitions or earthly ends.
His account of unrighteousness shows contention against God as a principle of evil.
The fallen human will stands in enmity toward him.
Even Gentiles without the written law possess an inward moral awareness through the light of nature.
Conscience bears witness.
Sooner or later it will testify, approving or condemning people according to their response to what they knew.
Nothing should bring greater fear to sinners or greater comfort to saints than the fact that Jesus Christ will be the Judge.
At his judgment, hidden acts of devotion will receive their reward, and secret sins will be exposed and punished.

div.title: Mere profession cannot excuse Jewish sin (verses 17–24)
div.p: Paul now addressed Jewish people who professed to know God but continued in sinful behavior.
There is a right way to glory in God: humbly, thankfully and through faith.
This attitude lies at the heart of true religion.
But there is also proud boasting in God and in possessing outward religious privileges.
This lies at the heart of hypocrisy.
Spiritual pride is the most dangerous kind of pride.
A grave evil committed by people who profess the faith is that their conduct brings dishonor upon God and religion.
Some look down on neighbors who possess only a lifeless outward form of godliness.
Yet these critics may themselves trust in a lifeless form of religious knowledge.
Others boast of the gospel while living such unholy lives that they cause God's name to be blasphemed.

div.title: True belonging to God requires inward renewal (verses 25–29)
div.p: No outward form, ordinance or religious theory benefits a person without regenerating grace.
Such grace leads a sinner to seek God's righteousness through faith.
A Christian who is merely one outwardly is no more a genuine Christian than an Israelite who was only outwardly a Jew was spiritually faithful.
Neither is true baptism merely something outward in the flesh.
The real Christian is someone who inwardly believes and shows obedient faith.
The true baptism of the heart is the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
This brings a spiritual frame of mind and a willingness to follow God's truth in holy living.
Let us pray that we may become real Christians inwardly, in heart and spirit rather than only in outward letter.
May we be baptized not merely with water but with the Holy Spirit.
And may our praise come from God, not from human beings.

row.cell: Both Jews and Gentiles cannot be justified by their own deeds.
It is owing to the free grace of God, through faith in the righteousness of Christ, yet the law is not done away.

div.title: Paul answers objections (verses 1–8)
div.p: The Mosaic law could not save people while they remained in their sins or rescue them from sin by its own power.
Yet Israel's privileges gave the Jewish people many means through which salvation could be learned and received.
Their appointed worship, education in knowledge of the true God and the blessings given to Abraham's descendants were all means of grace.
Undoubtedly God used them to convert many people.
Most importantly, the Scriptures had been entrusted to Israel.
Possessing God's word and his appointed worship is a people's chief blessing.
God's saving promises belong to those who believe.
Therefore, the unbelief of some—or even many—who outwardly profess faith cannot make his faithfulness fail.
He will fulfill his promises toward his people and carry out his judgments upon unbelief.
The fact that God will judge the world should silence every accusation that he is unjust.
The unbelief and wickedness of some Jews demonstrate humanity's need for God's righteousness through faith, and also God's justice in punishing sin.
The notion that we should do evil so that good may result is more common in sinners' hearts than openly on their lips.
Few people admit such a principle plainly.
But true believers know that duty belongs to us, while outcomes belong to God.
We must not commit one sin or tell even one lie because we hope—or even feel certain—that God may use it to bring glory to himself.
Anyone who thinks and acts that way deserves condemnation.

div.title: All humanity is under sin (verses 9–18)
div.p: Everyone is under sin in two respects.
We are under its guilt, like people carrying an unbearable burden.
We are also under its power, enslaved to practice evil.
Old Testament passages describe the fallen, corrupt condition of all people until grace restrains or changes them.
Despite the advantages some people enjoy, the same descriptions apply to many who call themselves Christians.
Their beliefs and actions show that they do not fear God.
Where there is no fear of God, we cannot expect true goodness.

div.title: Jews and Gentiles cannot be justified by law (verses 19 and 20)
div.p: It is useless to seek justification through obeying the law.
Everyone must admit guilt.
“Guilty before God” is a dreadful verdict.
No one can be justified by a law that condemns them for breaking it.
The corruption of our fallen nature makes justification through our own actions forever impossible.

div.title: God provides righteousness through Christ (verses 21–26)
div.p: Must sinful humanity remain forever under divine judgment?
Is the wound incurable?

p.hi: No. Blessed be God, another way has been opened.

div.p: It is the righteousness of God—righteousness that he has appointed, provided and accepted.
It is received through faith in Jesus Christ, the anointed Savior.
Justifying faith receives Christ in all three of his anointed offices: Prophet, Priest and King.
It trusts him, accepts him and clings to him.
Jewish and Gentile believers are equally welcome to God through Christ.
There is no difference.
Christ's righteousness is given to all who believe.
It is not merely offered from a distance but placed upon them like a crown or robe.
This comes through entirely free grace and mercy.
Nothing in us deserves such gifts.
It comes freely to us, but Christ purchased it and paid the price.
Faith therefore looks particularly to Christ's blood, through which he made atonement.
In this salvation God declares his righteousness.
His hatred of sin is evident because nothing less than Christ's blood could satisfy for it.
And God's justice does not require that a debt be paid a second time once the Surety has paid it and God has accepted that payment as full satisfaction.

div.title: Faith excludes boasting without abolishing God's law (verses 27–31)
div.p: God has arranged justification and salvation so that human boasting is excluded from beginning to end.
If our own works saved us, people would have reason to boast.
Justification by faith excludes such boasting completely.
But believers are not left lawless.
Genuine faith is active and produces obedience.
Faith justifies, however, not by being a meritorious act or a good work, but by uniting the sinner to Jesus Christ.
Through that relationship the believer receives pardon and justification for the Savior's sake.
A person refusing that union remains under condemnation.
The law still serves a purpose.
It convicts us concerning past sins and directs us concerning future obedience.
We cannot be saved by law as a covenant that promises life on condition of perfect obedience.
Yet we acknowledge and obey its rightful demands as a rule of life in the Mediator's hand.

row.cell: The doctrine of justification by faith is shown by the case of Abraham.
He received the promise through the righteousness of faith.
And we are justified in the same way of believing.

div.title: Abraham shows justification by faith (verses 1–12)
div.p: To answer Jewish objections, Paul first appealed to Abraham, the ancestor in whom the Jews took greatest pride.
Abraham had many remarkable qualities.
Yet he had nothing to boast about before God.
Like everyone else, he was saved by grace through faith.

Without even considering the years before Abraham's call or the times his obedience and faith failed, Scripture plainly states: “He believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).
If a person could perform everything demanded by the law, the reward would be owed as a debt.
That was clearly not Abraham's situation, because righteousness was counted to him through faith.
When Scripture says faith is counted as righteousness, it does not mean that faith justifies us as a small or large piece of our personal righteousness.
Rather, faith is the appointed means of uniting us to the One called “The Lord our Righteousness.”
Only forgiven people are truly blessed.
Abraham was justified years before he was circumcised, as Scripture makes clear.
Consequently, circumcision was not necessary for his justification.
Circumcision was a sign of humanity's original corruption and an outward seal.
It confirmed God's promises to Abraham and his descendants, as well as their duty to belong to the Lord.
It also assured Abraham that he already shared in the righteousness received by faith.
Thus Abraham became the spiritual father of all believers who follow his example of obedient faith.
For Christians, the Holy Spirit's seal in sanctification, making us new creations, provides inward evidence of righteousness through faith.

div.title: Abraham believed the promise (verses 13–22)
div.p: The promise to Abraham was given long before the law of Moses.
It pointed to Christ and to the promise in Genesis 12:3: through Abraham, every family of the earth would be blessed.
The law produces wrath by exposing sinners to God's judgment for transgression.
Because God intended to grant people a true claim to the promised blessings, he established that they would be received through faith, so that the gift would be entirely by grace.
It would then be secure for all people who share Abraham's faith, Jews and Gentiles alike throughout every age.
Calling Gentiles who were not previously God's people, and justifying sinners, was an act of divine power calling what did not exist as though it existed.
Abraham's faith reveals what trusting God means.
He believed God's testimony and expected God to fulfill his promise, hoping even when the circumstances seemed hopeless.
Weak faith continually focuses on difficulties that stand in the way of a promise.
Abraham did not treat God's word as a proposition whose truth depended upon endless debate.
Unbelief lies beneath our wavering when we doubt divine promises.
Strong faith overcomes fear and thereby honors God.
God honors faith, and faith gives God particular glory.
But faith is only the instrument by which we receive Christ's righteousness and redemption.
The instrument receiving a gift cannot be identical with the gift itself.
Abraham's faith did not justify him through its own merit or value.
It justified because it brought him into participation in Christ.

div.title: Believers are justified on the same basis (verses 23–25)
div.p: The account of Abraham's justification was recorded for later generations, especially people who would hear the gospel.
Like him, we are not justified because our works are meritorious.
We are justified through faith in Jesus Christ and his righteousness.
This truth is the great foundation of Christian comfort.
Christ earned our justification and salvation through his suffering and death.
Yet the accomplished power and perfection of his work for us are inseparable from his resurrection.
Through death he paid the debt.
Through resurrection he received the acquittal (Isaiah 53:8).
When he was declared discharged, we who belong to him were also released from the guilt and penalty of our sins.
The final verse of this chapter is therefore a brief summary of the whole gospel.

row.cell: The happy effects of justification through faith in the righteousness of Christ.
That we are reconciled by his blood.
The fall of Adam brought all mankind into sin and death.
The grace of God, through the righteousness of Christ, has more power to bring salvation, than Adam's sin had to bring misery,

div.title: The blessings flowing from justification (verses 1–5)
div.p: A profound change occurs in a sinner's position before God when that person becomes a true believer, whatever their past may have been.
Justified by faith, they have peace with God.
A holy and righteous God cannot be at peace with sinners while they remain under sin's guilt.
Justification removes that guilt and establishes peace through our Lord Jesus Christ, the great Peacemaker and Mediator between God and humanity.
The happy condition of believers is a state of grace.
We have been brought into this grace, showing that we were not born in this condition.
Nor could we enter it by our own abilities.
We are brought into it as pardoned offenders.
And we stand in grace: a posture indicating firmness and perseverance.
We remain secure, sustained by divine power.
The hope of sharing God's coming glory gives believers reason to rejoice even now.
Suffering produces perseverance not by its own power, but through God's grace working in and through it.
People who endure patiently often receive great comfort from God, increasing alongside their sufferings.
Trials also teach them necessary lessons about themselves.
Christian hope will not disappoint because it is sealed by the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of love.
The Spirit graciously pours God's love into believers' hearts.
A true knowledge of God's love enables us to remain unashamed of both our hope and our suffering for Christ.

div.title: Christ's blood brings reconciliation (verses 6–11)
div.p: Christ died for sinners who were not merely useless or weak.
They were guilty and hateful through sin, deserving a judgment that would have displayed God's perfect justice.
Christ died not to save us in our sins, but to save us from them.
He died for us while we were still sinners.
The sinful mind is not merely at odds with God but is hostility itself toward him (Romans 8:7; Colossians 1:21).
God intended not only to rescue sinners from punishment but also to transform them.
While people remain in sinful rebellion, Henry describes mutual loathing between them and God (Zechariah 11:8).
That Christ should die for such people is an incomparable mystery of love, worthy of eternal worship and wonder.
We may imagine one person risking death for a righteous person, although Paul treats this as no more than a possibility.
But what purpose would that sacrifice serve?
It would release the intended beneficiary from the suffering or penalty.
Christ's death does not exempt believers from ordinary bodily death, which they still experience.
Therefore the evil he died to remove is more terrible than death itself: sin and the righteous wrath due to sin.
By grace believers are brought to repent and trust Christ, and are justified by the price of his shed blood and by faith in that atonement.
How much more will the living, risen Lord preserve them from final surrender to sin and Satan and from permanent departure from him!
The risen Christ will complete the saving purpose of his dying love.
Those trusting him not only rejoice in hope of heaven and even amid suffering, but also rejoice in God himself as their unchanging Friend and all-sufficient portion, through Christ alone.

div.title: Adam's sin brought death to humanity (verses 12–14)
div.p: Paul now compares the evils resulting from the fall of Adam, humanity's first father, with the blessings purchased by Christ.
The purpose is to show that Christ's benefits do more than merely remove Adam's evils.
When Adam sinned, his nature became guilty and corrupt, and that fallen condition passed to his descendants.
In Adam, all have sinned.
Death entered through sin, because death is sin's wages.
The consequence included physical, spiritual and eternal death.
Had Adam not sinned, death would not have come upon him.
But death's sentence was passed upon him as upon a criminal, and spread through all humanity like a disease no one escapes.
The fact that sin prevailed in the world before the Mosaic law demonstrates humanity's solidarity with Adam's transgression.
Death ruled not only over adults who personally chose sin but also over infants.
Henry interprets this as evidence that Adam's descendants share the condemnation flowing from his first sin.
Adam was a type of the One to come, who would serve as Surety of a new covenant for those united to him.

div.title: Christ's righteousness brings a greater blessing (verses 15–19)
div.p: Through one man's offense, the whole human race became exposed to condemnation.
But God's free grace, mercy, righteousness and salvation come through Jesus Christ, who was truly human and yet the Lord from heaven.
Through Christ, the multitude of believers enters a safer and more exalted condition than the state lost in Adam.
The free gift does not simply place them back in a new probationary trial.
Instead, it establishes them in a justified condition, as Adam would have enjoyed had he remained faithful.
Despite the differences, the comparison is striking.
Through one person's offense, sin and death prevailed to bring condemnation.
Through one person's righteousness, grace prevails to justify all who are united to Christ through faith.
God's gracious gift abounds through Christ to many.
Yet great numbers prefer to remain under sin and death rather than seek the blessings of grace's reign.
Christ will never cast out anyone willing to come to him.

div.title: Grace exceeds the increase of sin (verses 20 and 21)
div.p: Through Christ and his righteousness, we receive greater privileges than those lost in Adam.
The moral law revealed the sinfulness of many thoughts, attitudes, words and actions.
In this sense transgressions multiplied.
The law did not create more sin; rather, it revealed the sin already there.
Just as bringing brighter light into a room exposes dust and filth previously hidden, God's law exposes our corruption.
The entrance of the law made Adam's offense and its consequences in our hearts appear more clearly.
The law's warnings make the comfort of the gospel sweeter.
Through Paul, the Holy Spirit teaches a deeply consoling truth suited to sinners everywhere.
Whatever one person's advantages compared with another's, every human being has sinned, stands condemned by the law and needs forgiveness.
A righteousness capable of justifying cannot be made from a mixture of sin and holiness.
No one has a claim to eternal reward without pure and spotless righteousness.
Let us therefore seek the righteousness of Christ.

row.cell: Believers must die to sin, and live to God.
This is urged by their Christian baptism and union with Christ.
They are made alive to God.
And are freed from the dominion of sin.
The end of sin is death, and of holiness everlasting life.

div.title: Believers are dead to sin (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Paul strongly insists upon the necessity of holiness.
He does not weaken or explain away the gospel's free grace.
Instead, he demonstrates that justification and holiness are inseparably joined.
We should reject with abhorrence any suggestion that believers ought to continue sinning so that grace may increase.
Genuine believers have died to sin; therefore they ought not continue living under its rule.
The same person cannot be dead to sin and at the same time alive to it as a chosen way of life.
Someone who wishes to be dead to sin but assumes that continual indulgence is permitted is deceiving themselves.
