div.title: Baptism signifies death and resurrection with Christ (verses 3–10)
div.p: Baptism teaches the need to die to sin, to be buried as it were to ungodly and unholy pursuits, and to rise to new life with God.
Unholy professing Christians may have received the outward sign of death to sin and a new birth into righteousness.
Yet they have never genuinely passed from Satan's family to God's family.
The fallen nature called the old man—inherited from humanity's first father Adam—is crucified with Christ in every true believer, through grace flowing from the cross.
That sinful nature is weakened and dying.
Nevertheless, it continues to struggle for life and even for victory.
But the whole body of sin, everything opposed to God's holy law, must finally be removed.
Believers are no longer to be enslaved by sin.
Instead, they live to God and find happiness in serving him.

div.title: Alive to God, resist sin's remaining impulses (verses 11–15)
div.p: Paul provides some of the strongest reasons for avoiding sin and pursuing holiness.
Believers are freed from sin's reign, alive to God and expecting everlasting life.
It is therefore right for them to be deeply concerned about growing in holiness.
Sinful desires are not entirely uprooted during this earthly life.
Christians must resist their impulses, striving earnestly through divine grace so those desires do not gain victory while they live in mortal bodies.
Remember that this struggle will one day end.
That knowledge should encourage believers who are often deeply troubled by the impulses of sin.
Offer every ability and every part of the body to God as instruments or weapons ready for the work and warfare of righteousness.
God's covenant of grace provides strength.

p.hi: Sin shall not rule over you.

div.p: God's promises are more powerful in putting sin to death than the promises we make to God.
Sin may struggle in genuine believers and cause them deep distress, but it will not reign over them.
It may trouble them without governing them.
Does such an encouraging promise permit someone to practice sin deliberately?
Certainly not.
Such an idea contradicts God's perfection and the very purpose of his gospel.
What stronger reason can we have to resist sin than Christ's love?
How could we sin against such goodness?

div.title: Sin and obedience are two different kinds of service (verses 16–20)
div.p: Everyone serves the master whose commands they obey.
That master may be the sinful desires of the heart, which lead to death.
Or it may be the new spiritual obedience planted by regeneration, which leads to righteousness.
Paul rejoiced that the believers had obeyed the gospel from their hearts.
They had been placed into its teaching like metal into a mold.
Just as melted metal becomes a new vessel when cast into a different form, believers become new creations.
Service to Christ brings genuine freedom of mind and spirit, completely unlike slavery to sin.
Christians recognize their rightful Lord as their Father and themselves as his adopted children and heirs.
Sin's dominion consists in willing slavery.
It does not consist merely in being attacked by a hated power that the believer resists.
Those now serving God once served sin.

div.title: Sin's wages and God's gift (verses 21–23)
div.p: The apparent pleasure and advantage of sin do not deserve the name fruit.
Sinners plow iniquity, sow emptiness and reap what they have planted.
Shame entered the world through sin, and shame continues to follow it.
Sin ends in death.
Its path may seem pleasant at first, but the end is bitter.
Believers are freed from that condemnation.
Where genuine and growing grace produces fruit leading to holiness, the outcome is everlasting life.
This is a blessed end.
The path may climb uphill through a narrow, thorny road, yet life awaits at its end.
Eternal life is God's gift through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Christ purchased it, prepared it, prepares us for it and preserves us until we receive it.
He is everything in our salvation.

row.cell: Believers are united to Christ, that they may bring forth fruit unto God.
The use and excellence of the law.
The spiritual conflicts between corruption and grace in a believer.

div.title: Believers are released from law as covenant and joined to Christ (verses 1–6)
div.p: As long as people remain under the law as a covenant by which they seek justification through personal obedience, they remain enslaved to sin in one form or another.
Only the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus can free sinners from the law of sin and death.
Believers are delivered from the law's condemning power for their past sins.
They are also delivered from the way the law, through their fallen nature, provokes indwelling sin.
This is not freedom from God's law as a rule for living.
It is freedom from the law as a covenant of works.
In profession and privilege Christians live under a covenant of grace, the gospel of Christ, not under the Mosaic law as a covenant of works.
Paul compares this change to marriage to a new husband.
Believers are joined to Christ.
Death ends the binding relationship to the former husband, just as death frees an enslaved worker from the former master's yoke.
Through living and effective faith, believers have died to law as covenant and become united to Jesus Christ.
They now live in dependence upon him and in obedience to him.
Good works come from union with Christ, as a vine bears fruit because it remains joined to its roots.
No fruit acceptable to God is produced before union with Christ.
The law and the best efforts of people still in fallen flesh cannot restore love for God, overcome sinful desires or create inward sincerity.
Those blessings come through the Holy Spirit's special sanctifying work.
Without the renewing, recreating grace of the new covenant, we can achieve no more than outward conformity to the letter of a rule.

div.title: God's holy law exposes the sin in us (verses 7–13)
div.p: To understand sin as we must for repentance, peace and pardon, we need to examine our hearts and lives against God's law.
Paul did not recognize the sinfulness of his thoughts, motives and conduct until the law revealed it.
That perfect standard exposed faults far more numerous than he had imagined.
But the law provided no mercy or grace to rescue him from his guilt.
Anyone who understands fallen human nature recognizes a tendency to want forbidden things merely because they are forbidden.
We readily notice this in children while ignoring it in ourselves.

The more humble and spiritually mature a Christian becomes, the more clearly that believer recognizes Paul's description of spiritual struggle—from the first conviction of sin to later growth in grace.
Paul once lived as a Pharisee, apparently respectable but ignorant of the law's spiritual depth and of his own inward corruption.
When the Holy Spirit brought God's command to his conscience, Paul understood its demands.
His sinful nature then rose in resistance.
He recognized sin's evil, his own helplessness to keep God's law and his condition as a condemned criminal.
The commandment was not the cause of sin.
Rather, fallen corruption used the commandment as an opportunity to stir up sinful impulses.
The law remains holy, just and good.
It does not tolerate sin, but exposes and condemns it even within our hearts.
Corrupt nature can twist even the best things.
The same heat softens wax and hardens clay.
Good food or medicine can become harmful if used wrongly, though its proper purpose is to nourish or heal.
Similarly, the law exposes deadly corruption, but sin is the poison that kills.
The ruin comes from sin, not from the law itself.

div.title: Remaining sin troubles the mature believer (verses 14–17)
div.p: Measured against God's holy rule, Paul recognized that he fell far short of perfection.
He described himself as carnal, like a person sold unwillingly to a cruel master he hates but cannot escape without help.
The genuine Christian is unwillingly troubled by remaining sin and cannot remove its last chains until a gracious and powerful Friend delivers them.
This remaining corruption painfully hinders service to God like that rendered by angels and perfected believers.
Henry interprets Paul's strong language as reflecting his great progress in holiness, profound self-abasement and hatred of sin.
If we cannot understand the depth of this struggle, perhaps we have far less holiness and insight into God's law and our own hearts.
Many believers have recognized their own condition in Paul's words.
Paul describes the daily conflict with remaining original corruption.
At times he fell into thoughts, words or actions that his renewed judgment and affections rejected.
When he distinguished his spiritual, renewed self from the flesh in which sin remained, he did not suggest people are no longer accountable for their sinful deeds.
He emphasized their evil: sin opposes both right reason and renewed conscience.
Sin dwelling in someone does not prove that it rules them.
A person may live in a country or city without governing it.

div.title: The believer delights in holiness while resisting the flesh (verses 18–22)
div.p: The purer and holier a person's heart becomes, the more sensitive that person is to the sin remaining within.
Believers increasingly recognize the beauty of holiness and the excellence of God's law.
Their desire to obey grows through grace.
Yet they do not completely accomplish the good they desire.
Remaining sin rises within them, so they sometimes act wrongly despite their settled intention to obey.
This troubled Paul deeply.

Just as the flesh fights the Spirit and prevents the believer from doing all the good desired, so the Spirit also resists the flesh and prevents the believer from doing everything sinful desire suggests.
How different this is from those who willingly satisfy sinful impulses, ignore conscience and proceed deliberately toward ruin!
True believers, under grace, sincerely delight in God's law and the holiness it demands according to the inward person renewed in true holiness.

div.title: Christ alone delivers from the continuing struggle (verses 23–25)
div.p: Paul is not describing a person who willingly follows the flesh.
He describes someone deeply concerned not to follow it.
Some abuse these verses to excuse their sin, as they abuse other Scriptures.
Yet serious Christians should thank God for the comfort he gives through this passage.
Abuse by sinners is no reason to reject Scripture or a well-grounded interpretation of it.
Only someone engaged in this struggle can deeply understand Paul's cry: “What a wretched man I am!”
Paul could not deliver himself.
This made him thank God all the more earnestly for the salvation revealed through Jesus Christ, who would finally free him from this enemy.
According to his renewed mind, will, affections and purposes, Paul served God's law.
Yet within his flesh the remaining corrupt nature continued fighting against his mind.
He did not serve sin by approving or freely living in it.
He remained unable to remove all its influence, even at his best, and therefore had to seek help from beyond himself.
Paul thanked God for Christ as his deliverer, atonement and righteousness, not for some holiness produced within himself as the ground of justification.
He did not trust in personal righteousness.
He wanted to obey God's law in every respect, but sin prevented perfect obedience.
For sinners who remain imperfect, the only final rescue is God's free grace in Jesus Christ.
God could, by divine power and the Holy Spirit, remove all remaining sin from Christians even during this life if he had so chosen.
But in his wisdom he allows this struggle to continue.
It reminds believers of the miserable condition from which grace rescued them.
It prevents self-confidence.
And it keeps all their consolation and hope fixed upon the rich, free grace of God in Christ.

row.cell: The freedom of believers from condemnation.
Their privileges as being the children of God.
Their assistance from the Spirit in prayer.
Their interest in the love of God.

div.title: No condemnation for those united to Christ (verses 1–9)
div.p: The Lord may discipline believers, but they will never be condemned with the world.
Through union with Jesus Christ by faith, they are safe from that condemnation.
The essential question is what governs their conduct: flesh or Spirit, old or new nature, corruption or grace?
For which do they make provision, and which directs their plans?
The unrenewed will cannot fully obey any commandment.
God's law requires inward obedience as well as outward conduct.
God showed his hatred of sin through the suffering of his Son in human flesh.
Through that sacrifice, believers may be pardoned and justified.
Christ satisfied God's justice and opened the way of salvation.
By the Holy Spirit, the law of love is written on believers' hearts.
They do not perfectly fulfill the law's righteousness by their own strength.
Nevertheless, God's grace produces within them something answering the law's true purpose.
Spiritual people give attention to God's favor, the good of the soul and eternal concerns.
Which subjects do we enjoy thinking about?
What governs our decisions and plans?
Are we wiser about the world, or about our own souls?
Someone living only for pleasure is spiritually dead (1 Timothy 5:6).
A sanctified soul possesses true life, and that life brings peace.
The unregenerate mind is not merely hostile toward God at times; it is hostility itself.
Divine grace can turn a previously worldly person toward obedience.
But the carnal mind itself must be broken and cast out; it cannot become obedient while remaining carnal.
We can examine our state by asking whether the Spirit of God and Christ lives in us.
Having Christ's Spirit means being given a mind that in some measure resembles the mind of Jesus, expressed through conduct consistent with his commands and example.

div.title: The Spirit assures and leads God's adopted children (verses 10–17)
div.p: If the Spirit dwells in us, Christ himself dwells in our hearts through faith.
Grace within the soul becomes a new nature.
The soul is made alive toward God and begins a holy happiness that will last forever.
Christ's imputed righteousness guarantees its preservation from death.
Therefore, we must walk according to the Spirit rather than the flesh.
Anyone habitually living for corrupt desires will die in sin, whatever religious profession they make.
No pleasure the present world offers deserves comparison with the glory promised to believers.
By the Spirit, let us increasingly put the flesh to death.
Regeneration gives a new divine life to the soul, even if its earliest expression is weak.
God's children receive the Spirit who teaches them to behave as children, not as slaves.
Henry contrasts this with the Old Testament believers' relative bondage under the shadows and uncertainty of that dispensation, before the Spirit of adoption was poured out abundantly.
He also refers to the sense of bondage and fear experienced by many saints at the beginning of conversion.
Some people falsely reassure themselves that God is at peace with them.
But the Spirit bears witness to truly sanctified people by bringing divine peace to the conscience.
Even when following Christ appears costly now, no one will finally lose by belonging to him.

div.title: Present suffering and future glory (verses 18–25)
div.p: The troubles of God's people belong to this passing life.
Compared with eternal glory, they are light and momentary.
How differently Scripture and the world judge present sufferings!
All creation seems to wait eagerly for God's children to be revealed in glory.
Through humanity's fall, creation has suffered disorder, weakness and corruption.
Creatures now often harm one another, and humans misuse them as instruments of sin.
Yet creation remains under hope.
God will finally free it from bondage caused by human wickedness.
Human misery caused by ourselves and one another shows that the world will not remain forever as it is.
Believers have received the firstfruits of the Spirit, strengthening their longing, hope and expectation.
Sin is the guilty source of the suffering introduced into God's creation.
It brought misery upon earth and the judgment of hell.
No tear, groan or pain in human body or soul exists apart from the effects of sin.
Beyond human suffering, consider sin's dishonor to God's glory, which so many people disregard.
Believers are already brought into safety through Christ.
Yet their present comfort rests chiefly in hope of what is coming, rather than full enjoyment now.
Nothing in the passing world can provide the satisfaction promised by that hope.
We need patience on a long and difficult road.
The One who is coming will come, even if his arrival seems delayed.

div.title: The Spirit helps believers to pray (verses 26 and 27)
div.p: Christians have many weaknesses.
If left to themselves, they would be overwhelmed.
But the Holy Spirit supports them.
As the Spirit who enlightens, he teaches them what to pray for.
As the Spirit who sanctifies, he awakens and sustains the graces needed for prayer.
As the Spirit who comforts, he calms fears and carries them through discouragement.
The Holy Spirit is the source of every genuine desire directed toward God, including desires too deep to express in words.
The Spirit who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit and the renewed desires of believers, and intercedes for them.
Their enemy cannot overcome this gracious help.

div.title: God's unbreakable purpose works for believers' good (verses 28–31)
div.p: What is genuinely good for God's people is whatever does their souls good.
Every providential circumstance serves the spiritual good of those who love the Lord.
It loosens their attachment to sin, brings them closer to God, frees them from love of the world and prepares them for heaven.
When believers depart from their proper character, God uses correction to bring them back.
Paul describes the causes and order of salvation as a golden chain that cannot be broken.

p.hi: First, those whom God foreknew he predestined to become like his Son.

div.p: Those he appointed for final happiness and glory he also appointed to the necessary path of grace and holiness.
The whole human race deserved judgment.
Yet for reasons not fully known to us, God determined to recover some people through regeneration and the power of his grace.
He planned that they should be conformed to Christ's likeness.
In this life, that transformation begins as they are renewed and follow his example.

p.hi: Second, those he predestined he also called.

div.p: This is an effective call from self and earth toward God, Christ and heaven as our final end, and from sin and emptiness toward grace and holiness as the path.
It is the gospel's call.
When God's love begins to rule hearts once hostile to him, that demonstrates his calling according to his purpose.

p.hi: Third, those he called he justified.

div.p: None receive this justification apart from God's effective call.
Those who continue resisting the gospel remain under guilt and judgment.

p.hi: Fourth, those he justified he also glorified.

div.p: Effective calling breaks sin's reigning power; justification removes sin's guilt.
Nothing can finally separate that soul from the glory God intends.
This strengthens faith and hope because God's way and work are perfect.
Paul responds with amazement at the immeasurable dimensions of Christ's love.
With most other subjects, familiarity can weaken our sense of wonder.
But deeper knowledge of the gospel's mysteries produces even greater amazement.
While God stands for us and we abide in his love, we may confidently resist the powers of darkness.

div.title: Final victory through Christ's inseparable love (verses 32–39)
div.p: No gift in heaven or earth displays God's free love so greatly as giving his coequal Son to make atonement on the cross for human sin.
Every other saving blessing follows from our union with Christ and participation in him.
God will provide everything that can serve the believer's genuine good.
The One who prepared a crown and a kingdom will provide what is needed on the way to them.
People may claim they are innocent even while charges remain against them.
But when God justifies, the verdict ends the matter.
Christ paid the debt through his death.
More than that, he rose again, proving divine justice had accepted his sacrifice.
We have a Friend at God's right hand, possessing all authority and continually interceding for us.
Believer, does your soul cry, If only I belonged to him, and he belonged to me; if only I could please him and live for him?
Do not endlessly trouble yourself with unproductive doubts.
Recognize your sin, then trust the One who justifies the ungodly.
You were condemned, but Christ died and rose again.
Flee to him.
Having shown love by giving his Son, will God suddenly abandon that love?
Troubles neither cause nor demonstrate any reduction in it.
Believers may lose many things, but what truly matters remains.
No one can take Christ from the believer or take the believer from Christ.
By contrast, worldly possessions cannot promise such permanence.
Homes, loved ones and estates will all eventually be left behind.
Death dissolves every worldly attachment.
Those without Christ will be left with what they would gladly lose but cannot: the guilt of unforgiven sin.
Yet people united to Christ cling to him even as everything else is taken away.
Death breaks the union of body and soul, but it brings the believer's soul into closer communion and everlasting joy with the beloved Lord Jesus.

row.cell: The apostle's concern that his countrymen were strangers to the gospel.
The promises are made good to the spiritual seed of Abraham.
Answers to objections against God's sovereign conduct, in exercising mercy and justice.
This sovereignty is in God's dealing both with Jews and Gentiles.
The falling short of the Jews is owing to their seeking justification, not by faith, but by the works of the law.

div.title: Paul's grief for his people (verses 1–5)
div.p: As Paul prepared to speak about the rejection of unbelieving Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, he expressed extraordinary love for his own people.
He called Christ to witness and appealed to a conscience enlightened and guided by the Holy Spirit.

Henry interprets Paul's willingness to be accursed as a readiness to endure disgrace, crucifixion and even a period of extreme horror and distress if that could save his nation from the destruction approaching through unbelief.
Indifference toward the eternal condition of other human beings contradicts both the law's command to love and the gospel's mercy.
The Israelites had long professed worship of Jehovah.
They possessed the law and its national covenant.
Their temple worship pictured salvation through the Messiah and provided means of fellowship with God.
The promises about Christ and his salvation were entrusted to them.
Christ rules over all as Mediator, and he is also God blessed forever.

div.title: God's promise reaches Abraham's spiritual descendants (verses 6–13)
div.p: The rejection of unbelieving Jews under the gospel did not break God's promises to the patriarchs.
His promises and warnings will be fulfilled.
Grace is not inherited through family bloodlines.
Outward membership and advantages in the visible church do not always bring salvation.
Some descendants of Abraham were chosen and others were not.
God acted according to the counsel of his own will.
God knew both Esau and Jacob as sinful from birth, naturally children of wrath like others.
If left to themselves, both would have continued in sin.
But for wise and holy reasons not revealed to us, God intended to change Jacob's heart while leaving Esau to his own perversity.
Henry draws from this history a lesson about God's dealings with fallen humanity.
Scripture distinguishes people who outwardly profess faith from those who genuinely believe.
Many enjoy religious privileges without becoming God's children.
Nevertheless, everyone is encouraged to use diligently the means of grace God has provided.

div.title: God's sovereign mercy is just (verses 14–24)
div.p: Everything God does is just.
The difference between those made holy and others comes from God's grace alone.
His grace comes before and effectively changes those he saves.
It is distinguishing grace, freely given by a Benefactor who owes it to no one.
No sinner deserves it.
Therefore, those who are saved should thank God alone, while those who perish have only themselves to blame (Hosea 13:9).
God is bound only by what he has freely promised in his covenant, his revealed will.
He has promised to receive rather than reject anyone who comes to Christ.
But the grace that first draws a sinner to come is a special gift granted according to his will.
“Why does he still find fault?” is not an objection the creature is entitled to press against the Creator.
The truth as revealed in Jesus humbles human pride and exalts the sovereign Lord.
We are too weak and ignorant to pronounce judgment on God's hidden purposes.
As a potter decides what to make from clay, God possesses sovereign authority over his creation.
He does no injustice, however difficult his purposes may appear to us.
He will demonstrate his hatred of sin.
But he also prepares vessels of mercy.
Sanctification prepares the soul for glory, and this is God's work.
Sinners prepare themselves for judgment through their sins; God prepares saints for heaven.
Everyone he intends to receive in glory is made fit for heaven through grace in this life.
Who are these vessels of mercy?
Those whom God has called, from Jews and Gentiles alike.
No injustice exists in God's patience toward guilty sinners, even when he delays their final judgment.
The guilt belongs to hardened sinners themselves.
Though such truths exceed our ability to understand fully, those who love the Lord should adore his pardoning mercy and recreating grace, and diligently make their calling and election sure.

div.title: Jewish and Gentile believers share God's mercy (verses 25–29)
div.p: The Old Testament foretold both the rejection of unbelieving Jews and the inclusion of Gentiles.
Seeing Scripture fulfilled confirms the truth of God's actions.
That anyone should be saved is a wonder of divine power and mercy.
Even the remnant preserved would have perished like the rest if God had treated them according to their sins.
Henry warns that even among the many people who profess Christianity, it is to be feared only a remnant may finally be saved.

div.title: Faith, not legal works, brings righteousness (verses 30–33)
div.p: The Gentiles had not understood their guilt and misery or urgently sought a remedy.
Nevertheless, many received righteousness by faith.
They did not need to become Jewish proselytes or submit to the ceremonial law.
They embraced Christ, believed in him and accepted the gospel.
Many Jews spoke of justification and holiness and desired to be counted God's special people.
But they sought it in the wrong way.
Instead of humbling themselves and receiving Christ through faith, they tried to obtain righteousness by obeying the requirements and ceremonies of the Mosaic law.
The unbelieving Jews were offered righteousness, life and salvation on the gospel's terms.
But they did not want or accept those terms.
Have we personally sought to know how to be justified before God, receiving that blessing through faith in Christ, the Lord our Righteousness?
Those who do will not be ashamed at the final judgment.
Then false refuges will disappear under God's righteous judgment, and no hiding place will remain except the refuge God has provided in his Son.

row.cell: The apostle's earnest desire for the salvation of the Jews.
The difference between the righteousness of the law, and the righteousness of faith.
The Gentiles stand on a level with the Jews, in justification and salvation.
The Jews might know this from Old Testament prophecies.

div.title: Paul's desire for Israel's salvation (verses 1–4)
div.p: Many Jews built their hope on a false foundation, refusing Christ's free salvation through faith.
People in every age make the same mistake in different forms.
The law's exacting demands were meant to reveal our need of salvation by grace through faith.
Its ceremonies pictured Christ fulfilling its righteousness and bearing its curse.
Even under the Mosaic law, everyone truly justified before God received that blessing through faith in the perfect righteousness of the promised Redeemer.
The law is not destroyed, nor are God's intentions disappointed.
Through Christ's death, satisfaction has been made for our breaking of the law, and its purpose has been accomplished.
Christ fulfilled the whole law.
Therefore, whoever believes in him is counted righteous before God as though they themselves had fulfilled it.
People who understood either God's justice as Governor or his righteousness as Savior would not continue imagining they could justify themselves.

div.title: The righteousness of faith is available through Christ (verses 5–11)
div.p: Sinners who recognize their guilt do not need to trouble themselves about where this righteousness can be found.
When we speak of seeing, receiving or feeding upon Christ, we mean Christ as he is offered and promised in God's word, not someone we must physically retrieve from heaven or from the depths.
Justification through faith in Jesus Christ is a plain teaching.
God brings it before people's minds and hearts, so unbelief has no excuse.

If a person confesses faith in Jesus as Lord and Savior of lost sinners and sincerely believes in the heart that God raised him from the dead, that resurrection reveals the Father's acceptance of his atonement.
Such a person is saved through Christ's righteousness imputed by faith.
Yet no faith truly justifies unless it also has power to sanctify the heart and direct its affections through love for Christ.
We must give our whole selves to God—the soul by believing in the heart and the body by confessing with the mouth.
Those who trust Jesus will never regret that confidence.
Such faith will never leave a sinner ashamed before God, and believers should acknowledge it openly before others.

div.title: The same salvation is offered to Jews and Gentiles (verses 12–17)
div.p: There is not one God generous to Jews and another less generous to Gentiles.
The Lord is one Father who gives the same promise to all who call on Jesus' name.
Jesus is the Son of God, God manifested in human flesh.
Genuine believers call upon him humbly and sincerely.
But how can anyone call upon the divine Savior without first hearing about him?
What is the Christian life if not a life of prayer?
Prayer acknowledges our dependence upon Christ and expresses our desire to entrust ourselves to him and expect every blessing from him.
The gospel therefore had to be preached to the Gentiles.
Someone had to tell them what to believe.
How welcome this good news should be to those hearing it!
The gospel is given not merely to be known and believed, but also obeyed.
It is not simply a system of opinions; it is a guide for living.
Faith begins, grows and becomes strong through hearing.
But faith grows through hearing the word as God's own word, not merely as human information.

div.title: The prophets already foretold Gentile inclusion (verses 18–21)
div.p: Could the Jews have known that God would call Gentiles?
Yes. Moses and Isaiah had already announced it.
Isaiah clearly presented God's grace as taking the initiative in receiving Gentiles.
Was this not true of us?
Did God not love us first and reveal himself when we were not seeking him?
His patience toward people who continually provoke him is astonishing.
The time of divine patience is called a day.
Like daylight, it gives people light and opportunities to work.
But, like a day, it is limited and followed by night.
God's long patience makes persistent disobedience more blameworthy.
We can wonder that God's mercy is not overcome by human wickedness.
We can also wonder that human wickedness continues resisting God's mercy.
And we can rejoice that through the spreading gospel, millions have heard the message of divine grace.

row.cell: The rejection of the Jews is not universal.
God overruled their unbelief for making the Gentiles partakers of gospel privileges.
The Gentiles cautioned against pride and unbelief, The Jews shall be called as a nation, and brought into God's visible covenant again.
A solemn adoring of the wisdom, goodness, and justice of God.

div.title: God preserves a believing Jewish remnant (verses 1–10)
div.p: God preserved a chosen remnant of Jewish believers, who received righteousness and life through faith in Jesus Christ.
They were kept according to the election of grace.
If their election was by grace, it could not have been based on works, either already performed or foreseen in advance.
Every genuinely good disposition in a fallen creature is the effect of God's grace, and therefore cannot be its cause.
Salvation from first to last must be either grace or a debt owed for merit.
These principles are so opposed that they cannot be mixed.
God glorifies his mercy by changing the hearts and desires of people who were once rebellious.
How deeply should believers praise him!
The nation as a whole was like someone in deep sleep.
They failed to recognize danger or their need for the Savior and did not realize how close they stood to everlasting ruin.
David, moved by the Spirit, foretold Christ's sufferings at the hands of his own people and announced dreadful judgments upon those responsible (Psalm 69).
Henry explains David's prayers against enemies as prophetic warnings of divine judgment, not merely expressions of personal anger.
God's judgments endure, and worldly-mindedness can make our spiritual eyes dark.

div.title: Gentiles are grafted into God's people (verses 11–21)
div.p: The gospel is a community's greatest treasure.
The unbelieving Jews' rejection of Christ became the occasion for many Gentiles to be reconciled to God.
Henry expects the future reception of Jews into the church to resemble a great resurrection from spiritual death into righteous life.
Abraham was like the root of God's people.
Jewish descendants remained branches of the olive tree until the nation rejected the Messiah.
Their inherited place in Abraham's covenant community was, figuratively, cut off.
Gentiles were grafted into the tree, becoming members of God's church and receiving Abraham's spiritual privileges.
Every human being is naturally like a wild branch.
Conversion resembles grafting such a branch into a fruitful olive tree.
Henry notes that a wild branch was sometimes grafted into a declining fruitful tree and helped it regain vitality.
Gentiles were received by free grace.
They should therefore avoid self-confidence, pride and ambition.
If they have only dead faith or an empty profession, they can turn away from God and lose their outward religious privileges.
If we stand, it is through faith, not personal worth.
Knowing our own guilt and helplessness should make us humble, watchful and alert against self-deception and temptation.
Not only is justification first received through faith.
Believers also remain justified to the end by faith alone, yet by a faith never alone, for it works through love toward God and other people.

div.title: Gentiles warned; future mercy promised to Israel (verses 22–32)
div.p: Among all forms of judgment, spiritual judgment is the most severe.
Paul speaks especially of it here.
The future return of Jewish people to the blessings of God's covenant is not nearly as astonishing as the earlier inclusion of Gentiles among Abraham's children.
The fact that Gentiles now possess these blessings does not prevent Jewish people from being welcomed back.
By rejecting the gospel and resenting its proclamation to Gentiles, many Jews had become enemies of God.
Yet God's gracious promises to their faithful ancestors remained important.
When God's appointed time arrives, this enmity will end and his faithfulness to those earlier promises will be displayed.
True grace never seeks to restrict God's mercy to a favored group.
People who have received mercy should seek to extend it to others.
Henry makes an important qualification: the Jews' future restoration will not mean bringing back the Old Testament priesthood, temple worship or ceremonial system.
Those have come to their appointed end.
Rather, they will be brought to faith in Jesus Christ and become one flock with Gentile believers under Christ the great Shepherd.
Israel's captivities, dispersion and exclusion from visible covenant privileges picture the discipline believers may receive for wrongdoing.
God's continuing concern and promised future kindness toward this people demonstrate his patience, love and mercy.

div.title: Paul worships God's incomprehensible wisdom (verses 33–36)
div.p: Paul understood the mysteries of God's kingdom as deeply as almost anyone who has lived.
Yet he confessed that he could not reach the bottom of God's wisdom.
He sat humbly on the edge of that immeasurable depth and worshiped.
Those who know the most in this imperfect life often recognize their limitations most clearly.
God's wisdom is not only deep but rich, overflowing with everything truly precious.
His counsel has depth and height, breadth and length (Ephesians 3:18), beyond human knowledge.
The distance between the infinite Creator and his creatures prevents us from fully comprehending his ways.
What human being is fit to teach God how to govern the world?
Paul adores God's sovereign wisdom.
Everything in heaven and earth, especially everything concerning our peace and salvation, comes from God in creation, exists through him in Providence and is intended for his glory.
God is the source of all.
Through Christ we return to God as our final end.
If all things are from and through him, all should be to him and for him.
Whatever we begin, let God's glory be our final purpose.
Above all, when speaking about his hidden counsels, let us respond in worship rather than self-confident argument.
The saints in heaven do not dispute; they praise.

row.cell: Believers are to dedicate themselves to God.
To be humble, and faithfully to use their spiritual gifts, in their respective stations.
And to peaceable conduct towards all men, with forbearance and benevolence.

div.title: Offer yourselves to God (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Having completed the part of the letter in which he explained Christian doctrine, Paul now urges believers to live out its consequences.
He appeals to them by the mercies of God to present their bodies as living sacrifices.
How powerful a reason this is!
Every day we receive fresh evidence of the Lord's mercy.
In response, let us offer him everything we are, everything we possess and everything we can do.
Even then, how small is our return compared with the riches we have received!
Such worship is acceptable and reasonable.
It is service that we can understand and explain.
Conversion and sanctification involve the renewing of the mind.
They do not change the substance of the human soul but transform its qualities and direction.
Growing in holiness means dying increasingly to sin and living increasingly for righteousness.
This renewing work continues until it is perfected in glory.
Its great enemy is conformity to the world.
Do not plan your happiness as though it depended upon earthly things that will soon vanish.
Do not adopt the customs of those ruled by bodily desires and love of passing things.
The Holy Spirit's work begins by illuminating the understanding.
He then renews the will, affections and conduct until the whole person increasingly resembles God in knowledge, righteousness and true holiness.
To be godly is to give ourselves to God.

div.title: Humility and useful gifts within Christ's body (verses 3–8)
div.p: Pride comes naturally to fallen humanity, and we must guard against it.
All believers form one body in Christ, who is its Head and the center of their unity.
Different members are fitted and called to different forms of service.
Our aim must be to do all the good we can for one another and for the common benefit.
Considering the abilities entrusted to us and how far we fall short of using them properly should humble us.
But we must avoid the opposite mistake.
Under the pretense of humility and self-denial, we must not become lazy or inactive in serving others.
We should not say, “I am nothing, so I will sit still and do nothing.”
Rather: “I am nothing in myself; therefore, through Christ's grace, I will use every ability I have.”
Whatever our gifts and circumstances, let us serve humbly, diligently, cheerfully and sincerely.
Seek not personal credit or gain, but the good of others for this life and the life to come.

div.title: Sincere love and faithful service (verses 9–16)
div.p: Christian love must be genuine, free from hypocrisy and empty compliments.
Depending on God's grace, we should hate evil and hold firmly to everything good, kind and useful.
It is not enough merely to perform good actions occasionally.
We must cling to goodness.
Love summarizes all our duties toward one another.
Paul calls for the tender affection of parents toward children—natural, sincere, neither forced nor merely ceremonial.
Love for God and others, together with zeal for the gospel, makes wise Christians diligent even in ordinary business, improving their skills to serve well.
We must serve God spiritually, under the Holy Spirit's influence.
We honor him by trusting him, especially when we rejoice in hope.
God is served not only by work.
When he calls us to endure suffering, patiently waiting without rebellion is also true worship.
Those rejoicing in hope are better prepared to be patient in suffering.
We must persevere in prayer without growing cold or weary.
Kindness must extend beyond friends and fellow believers.
We should harbor no hatred toward enemies.
Love expressed only in kind words is false if a brother or sister needs material help and we can provide it but refuse.
Welcome people doing good work; show hospitality to strangers as opportunities arise.
Bless and do not curse.
Do not bless someone during prayer and curse the same person afterward.
Let goodwill be consistent.
Genuine Christian love shares other people's joys and sorrows.
Seek agreement in spiritual truth wherever possible.
Where believers cannot agree about every detail, they should still agree in affection.
Do not be impressed by worldly pomp, rank or public reputation.
Accept the place assigned by God's Providence.
Nothing is beneath us except sin.
We cannot sincerely serve humbler people while remaining full of our own importance.
That pride must be put to death.

div.title: Peace, forgiveness and overcoming evil (verses 17–21)
div.p: Since human beings became enemies of God, they have readily become enemies of one another.
Christians living in a world often unfriendly to Christ should expect opposition.
Never repay evil with evil.
Such retaliation belongs to people acting only on instinct, without regard for God or eternity.
Instead, carefully consider how to act honorably and commendably toward everyone, giving no needless reason to despise the Christian faith.
Seek peace when it is possible without offending God or wounding conscience.
Do not take personal revenge.
This instruction is difficult for fallen nature, so Paul also says to leave room for anger to pass.
When someone is intensely angry, allow time for their feelings to settle rather than escalating the confrontation.
Our duty is clear.
If persistent kindness does not soften an enemy, we still must not seek vengeance.
Judgment belongs to God.
In conflict, those who retaliate are defeated by evil, while those who forgive become conquerors.
Learn to defeat evil designs either by changing the other person's intention or by preserving your own peace.
Someone who rules their own spirit is stronger than a mighty warrior.
God's children should recognize what a sweet gift it is to feel and act this way through his Spirit.

row.cell: The duty of subjection to governors.

div.title: Submit to lawful civil authority (verses 1–7)
div.p: The gospel's grace teaches peaceful submission where pride and fallen thinking see only reasons to grumble.
Whatever the character of the people who govern us, their rightful authority must be respected and obeyed.
In the ordinary course of public affairs, rulers are a terror not to peaceful and honest people but to evildoers.
Because sin corrupts human beings, some are restrained from crime only by fear of punishment.
If you benefit from government, do what you can to preserve public order rather than disturb it.
Private people should behave quietly and peacefully in the place God has assigned them (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
Christians must not engage in fraud or dishonest tricks.
Smuggling, trafficking in contraband, withholding lawful duties or deliberately evading taxes violates God's express command.
Such wrongdoing also harms honest neighbors, who may be left carrying a greater burden.
Anyone who participates in or assists these schemes shares responsibility for them.
It is painful to find professing Christians defending dishonest practices of this kind.
The godly should be known as peaceable and honest members of their communities, regardless of how others behave.

div.title: Fulfill your duties through love (verses 8–10)
div.p: Avoid unnecessary expenditure.
Do not enter debts you lack the ability to repay.
Avoid reckless speculation, rash promises or other decisions that may prevent you from giving everyone what is owed.
Do not remain in anyone's debt.
Give others what rightly belongs to them.
Never spend on yourself what you owe to someone else.
Many understand how troublesome debt is, but think too little about its moral seriousness.
Love toward other people includes all the duties of the second table of the law.
The last five of the Ten Commandments are summed up in the command, “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
We should love others with the same sincerity, even when not necessarily with exactly the same degree or intensity as self-love.
Loving someone means sincerely seeking that person's welfare.
From this flows the golden rule: treat others as you would wish them to treat you.
Love is a living, active principle of obedience to the law.
We should avoid every degree of harm to other people's bodies, relationships, possessions and reputations.
And beyond avoiding harm, we should seek to be useful in every situation.

div.title: Wake from spiritual sleep and put on Christ (verses 11–14)
div.p: Paul teaches four things for the Christian's daily direction.
First, when to awaken: now.
Wake from careless spiritual security, laziness, negligence, spiritual death and spiritual dullness.
We live in a busy and dangerous time.
Our final salvation is nearer than when we first believed.
We are closer to the end of the journey, so we should watch our path and increase our diligence.
Second, how to prepare: the night is nearly gone and day is approaching.
Take off the works of darkness, like clothing worn through the night.
Put on the armor of light.
A Christian should regard themselves as undressed if unarmed.
The Holy Spirit's graces form our armor against Satan's temptation and the assaults of this evil world.
Above all, put on Christ.
Take his righteousness for justification.
Receive his Spirit and grace for sanctification.
Receive him as Lord to govern and Jesus to save; in both, he is the Christ anointed by the Father.
Third, how to walk: now that we are awake and ready, we must not sit still.
Live in a way that pleases the God who always sees us.
Walk honorably as in daylight, avoiding the deeds of darkness.
Excessive drinking and wild behavior often accompany sexual immorality, quarrels and envy (Proverbs 23:29–35).
Fourth, what to provide for: first, provide for your soul.
But bodily needs also matter.
Two kinds of bodily concern are forbidden: anxious, burdensome preoccupation and indulgence of disordered desires.
Natural needs should be met, but sinful appetites restrained.
Asking God for food we truly need is right; Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread.
But demanding food merely to gratify craving provokes God (Psalm 78:18).

row.cell: The Jewish converts cautioned against judging, and Gentile believers against despising one the other.
And the Gentiles exhorted to take heed of giving offence in their use of indifferent things.

div.title: Do not despise believers with different convictions (verses 1–6)
div.p: Differences of opinion existed even among Christ's first followers and their disciples.
Paul did not try to erase every such difference.
Forcing people to agree with a doctrine or follow outward observances without personal conviction would be hypocritical and useless.
Trying to produce absolute uniformity of opinion among Christians would be unproductive.
Therefore, do not let fellowship be spoiled by endless arguments over words.
When tempted to despise a brother or sister, ask: Has God received this person? If so, how dare I reject them?
A Christian exercising liberty should not ridicule a cautious believer as ignorant or superstitious.
A scrupulous believer should not condemn someone who uses liberty, because God accepts the believer without treating food distinctions as grounds for acceptance.
We take God's place when we claim to judge the hidden motives and intentions of other people.
The question of observing certain days is similar.
Those understanding that Christ fulfilled the old ceremonial observances no longer considered Jewish festivals binding.
But merely being personally satisfied about a practice is not enough.
Our confidence must be grounded in God's word.
Do not act against a doubtful conscience.
We readily treat our own convictions as the standard everyone else should follow, even when the matter is genuinely disputable.
Christians should not condemn each other over lesser matters.
Thankfulness to God, the Giver of our blessings, makes ordinary enjoyments good and sweet.

div.title: We all belong to the Lord who judges us (verses 7–13)
div.p: Though some believers are strong and others weak, all must agree on this: we do not live for ourselves.
Anyone bearing Christ's name who deliberately makes personal pleasure the highest goal contradicts genuine Christianity.
Our life's purpose is to please God, not ourselves.
True Christianity makes Christ central in everything.
Believers may differ in knowledge, spiritual strength and conduct over lesser matters, yet they all belong to the same Lord and seek to serve him.
Christ rules the living and will raise the dead.
Do not despise or condemn one another, because all will soon give an account before him.
Thinking seriously about final judgment would quiet much rash criticism.
Let each person examine their own heart and life.
Those careful to judge and humble themselves are less likely to despise their neighbors.
We must avoid saying or doing anything likely to make others stumble or fall.
Henry distinguishes a lesser offense causing grief from a more serious action drawing someone into actual guilt.

div.title: Freedom must be governed by love (verses 14–18)
div.p: Christ deals gently with people who possess genuine grace even when that grace is weak.
Remember why Christ died for our brothers and sisters.
Leading someone into sin threatens that person's soul.
Christ denied himself so far as to die for them.
Should we not deny ourselves some lawful enjoyment to protect them?
We cannot stop every careless tongue from criticizing us.
But we should avoid giving needless grounds for such criticism.
Sometimes we should forgo what is otherwise lawful because using our liberty selfishly would damage our testimony or another person's conscience.
Good actions can be spoken against when we perform them without charity.
Protect the honor of the faith we profess.
Righteousness, peace and joy are central blessings of God's kingdom.
Toward God, our concern is to stand justified through Christ's death and sanctified through the Spirit's grace.
Toward our neighbors, our concern is peace, love and charity toward everyone.
Within ourselves, the blessing is joy in the Holy Spirit, a joy arising from knowing God as our reconciled Father and heaven as our promised home.
Only devotion to Christ makes our service acceptable to God.
People most pleased with God tend to please him most.
They enjoy and promote peace and spiritual joy, and wise and good people recognize the value of their conduct.
Other people's disapproval should not rule us.

div.title: Pursue peace without violating conscience (verses 19–23)
div.p: Many people speak loudly about wanting peace yet fail to practice the things that create it.
Gentleness, humility, self-denial and love make for peace.
We cannot strengthen one another spiritually while fighting and arguing.
Some ruin God's work in themselves through excess in food and drink, yielding to bodily desires.
Others injure fellow believers by deliberately provoking their consciences.
An act may be lawful in itself and yet wrong because of the circumstances, especially when it leads another person toward sin or distress.
This applies to every morally indifferent practice that injures a fellow Christian's grace, comfort or good resolve.
When Paul asks, “Do you have faith?” he refers here to knowledge and certainty about Christian liberty.
Enjoy your freedom thankfully, but do not use it in a way that troubles others.
Nor should you act while your own conscience remains in doubt.
How excellent are the blessings of Christ's kingdom!
It does not consist in outward ceremonies but in righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
Serving God is better than any other service.
We are not called to live and die for ourselves but for Christ, to whom we belong.

row.cell: Directions how to behave towards the weak.
All to receive one another as brethren.
The writing and preaching of the apostle.

div.title: The strong should care for the weak (verses 1–7)
div.p: Christian liberty was given not for our own pleasure, but for God's glory and other people's good.
We should please our neighbors for the benefit of their souls.
This does not mean indulging their sinful wishes or participating in wrongdoing to gain their favor.
If we try to please people in that way, we cease acting as servants of Christ.
Christ's whole life was marked by self-denial, not self-indulgence.
The most mature Christian is the one who most resembles him.
Nothing was more foreign to Christ's spotless holiness than being made sin and a curse for our sake, the righteous suffering for the unrighteous and bearing the reproaches directed against God.
He bore sin's guilt and its curse.
We are called to bear only some of the trouble that results from sin.
He bore the presumptuous crimes of wicked people; we are asked only to bear the failings of weaker believers.
How can we refuse to be humble and self-denying toward one another when we are members of one body?
The Scriptures were written for our benefit as much as for their original readers.
Those who know God's word deeply and can use it wisely are truly learned.
Comfort arising from God's word is the surest and sweetest support of Christian hope.
The Holy Spirit, our Comforter, is the pledge of the inheritance to come.
Unity of mind must be formed according to Christ's command and example.
It is God's precious gift, and we should ask him earnestly for it.
Christ shows himself gentle and humble to draw disciples toward him.
His servants, especially those strong in faith dealing with weaker believers, should imitate that spirit.
God's glory must be the final purpose of our deeds.
Few things promote it more than love and kindness among those who confess Christ.
People united in Christ have every reason to agree in affection.

div.title: Jews and Gentiles should welcome one another (verses 8–13)
div.p: Christ fulfilled the promises made to the Jewish people.
Therefore Gentile believers have no justification for despising them.
Gentiles brought into God's church become fellow participants in patience, suffering and praise.
The Scriptures call all nations to praise the Lord.
This shows that God intends them to come to know him.
People will not sincerely seek Christ until they trust him.
The entire plan of redemption is designed to reconcile us both to the gracious God and to one another.
This produces lasting hope of eternal life through the Holy Spirit's sanctifying and comforting power.
Our own strength cannot accomplish these things.
Where hope is genuine and abundant, therefore, the Spirit deserves all the glory.
The apostle prays for all joy and peace—every kind of true spiritual joy and peace sufficient to overcome fear and doubt through the Spirit's power.

div.title: Paul's ministry serves God's sanctifying work (verses 14–21)
div.p: Paul was convinced the Roman Christians possessed knowledge, goodness and loving dispositions.
He wrote nevertheless to remind them of duties and dangers, because God had appointed him a minister of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles.
Paul proclaimed the gospel.
Yet the thing that made his Gentile converts acceptable as offerings to God was their sanctification.
That was the Holy Spirit's work, not something Paul could produce by himself.
Nothing unholy can please the holy God.
Conversion belongs to the Lord.
Paul therefore took satisfaction in God's work, not in merely human achievements.
Even a great preacher cannot make a single soul obedient unless God's Spirit accompanies the ministry.
Paul particularly sought the good of people still living in spiritual darkness.
Whatever genuine good we accomplish, Christ works through us to do it.

div.title: Paul's intended journeys and the gift for Jerusalem (verses 22–29)
div.p: Paul placed Christ's work above his personal wishes.
He would not abandon the urgent work of founding churches simply to make a desired visit to Rome.
We should always do what is most necessary first.
Do not feel insulted when friends put duties pleasing to God ahead of visits or compliments that would please us.
Every Christian should support good work, especially the conversion of souls.
Fellowship among Christians is like a foretaste of heaven on earth, anticipating their final gathering to Christ.
Yet even its richest joy is incomplete compared with fellowship with Christ himself, which alone fully satisfies the soul.
Paul was traveling to Jerusalem carrying material assistance for believers there.
God loves cheerful giving.
Every exchange between Christians should express the union they share in Jesus Christ.
Because Gentiles received the gospel through Jewish believers, they owed their Jewish brothers and sisters material help in their bodily needs.
Paul spoke cautiously about what he expected from human companions, but confidently about what he expected from God.
We should expect little of fallible people and much of the faithful God.
How delightful it is when God's gospel comes with the fullness of its blessings through the Spirit's power!

div.title: Paul asks for prayer (verses 30–33)
div.p: Learn to value the earnest, effective prayers of righteous people.
We should avoid conduct that would forfeit the loving prayers of those devoted to God.
If we have known the Holy Spirit's love, we ought not neglect this service of praying for one another.
Those who want to prevail in prayer must strive earnestly in it.
Those asking others to pray for them should not neglect their own prayer.
Though Christ knows our needs perfectly, he wants us to bring them to him.
We must pray that God will restrain enemies' hostility and preserve and strengthen our friends' goodwill.
Every joy we receive depends on his will.
Let us pray earnestly with and for one another, asking that through Christ and the Holy Spirit's love, great blessings will rest upon Christians and upon the work of their ministers.

row.cell: The apostle recommends Phebe to the church at Rome, and greets several friends there.
Cautions the church against such as made divisions.
The epistle concludes with ascribing glory to God.

div.title: Paul commends Phoebe and greets the believers (verses 1–16)
div.p: Paul recommended Phoebe to the Roman Christians.
Christians ought to help one another in practical affairs, especially when people are strangers in a new place.
We do not know how much help we ourselves may need in the future.
Paul asked the believers to assist a woman who had already helped many people.
Those who water others will themselves receive refreshment.
Although Paul carried the daily concern of many churches, he still remembered individual people.
He sent personal greetings, describing their character and showing affection for them.
He also greeted believers he could not name individually, so no one should feel forgotten.
He regarded all of them as brothers, sisters and saints.
At the end he sent the united greetings of Christ's churches.

div.title: Beware teachers who create division through deception (verses 17–20)
div.p: How earnest and affectionate Paul's warnings are!
Teaching that contradicts the sound doctrine of Scripture opens the door to offenses and divisions.
If truth is abandoned, unity and peace cannot survive for long.
Many call Jesus their Lord and Master while failing to serve him.
Instead they pursue worldly, bodily and selfish interests.
False teachers corrupt people's understanding by first gaining power over their affections.
They distort judgment by exploiting trust.
Therefore we must guard our hearts diligently.
Deceivers commonly target people who have become sensitive or uncertain through conviction.
A receptive disposition is valuable under wise guidance, but can also leave someone open to deception.
Be wise enough not to be deceived, yet simple and sincere enough never to become a deceiver.
Paul looks for God's promise of victory over Satan.
This victory includes the defeat of Satan's plans to corrupt, disturb and destroy souls and to keep them from peace with God and final enjoyment of heaven.
When Satan appears to be winning and everything seems lost, the God of peace will intervene for his people.
Persevere a little longer in faith and patience.
If Christ's grace remains with us, who can prevail against us?

div.title: Greetings from Paul's companions (verses 21–24)
div.p: Paul added warm greetings from those with him who were known to Roman believers.
Seeing relatives become holy and useful is a wonderful comfort.
Not many powerful or noble people are called, but some are.
Believers may lawfully serve in civil office.
Henry hopes that public offices in Christian communities, as well as offices in the church, will be entrusted to prudent and steadfast Christians.

div.title: Glory to God through Jesus Christ (verses 25–27)
div.p: What truly establishes souls is the plain preaching of Jesus Christ.
Our redemption and salvation through him form a great mystery of godliness.
Yet thanks be to God, enough of that mystery has been made clear to lead us into heaven if we do not deliberately neglect salvation.
Life and immortality have been revealed through the gospel.
The Sun of Righteousness has risen upon the world.
The writings of the prophets not only became clearer through Christ.
They also make known God's saving mystery to all nations.
Christ is the Savior offered to every nation.
The gospel is revealed not merely to be discussed or argued about, but to be obeyed.
The obedience of faith is obedience to the word of faith, brought about through the grace of faith.
Every act of praise that fallen human beings offer to God and that he accepts must come through Jesus Christ.
Only through Christ are our persons and works acceptable to the Father.
We must speak of his righteousness alone.
As Christ mediates our prayers, so he mediates our praise now and forever.
We are called to obedient faith.
Every degree of true wisdom comes from the only wise God.
Therefore, through both words and deeds, let us bring glory to him through Jesus Christ, praying that the Lord's grace will be with us forever.

div.title: 1 Corinthians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The church at Corinth included some Jews but more Gentiles.
Paul had to confront Jewish religious superstition on one hand and Gentile believers' sinful conduct on the other.
The church's peace was disturbed by false teachers who undermined the apostle's influence.
This produced two opposing groups.
One insisted strongly upon Jewish ceremonies.
The other tolerated excesses opposed to the gospel, encouraged by the luxury and sins widespread in Corinth.
Paul wrote this letter for two purposes.
First, he intended to correct the disorderly conduct and abuses that had been reported to him.
Second, he wanted to give satisfactory answers to questions upon which Corinthian believers had requested his judgment.
It is remarkable how Paul combined Christian gentleness with firmness, moving from general truths directly toward correction of the church's errors and sins.
He explained God's truth and will about different matters with powerful arguments and an energetic style.

row.cell: Exhortation to brotherly love, and reproof for divisions.
The doctrine of a crucified Saviour, as advancing the glory of God,
and humbling the creature before him.

div.title: Paul's greeting and thanksgiving (verses 1–9)
div.p: Through baptism, people who profess Christianity are dedicated to Christ and obligated to holiness.
But the true church of God consists of those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, and who call upon Christ as God manifested in human flesh for every blessing of salvation.
They acknowledge and obey him as their Lord and the Lord of all.
This is what marks genuine members of his church.
Christians are distinguished from those who disregard God by the fact that they cannot live without prayer.
They are distinguished from Jews and pagans in that they call upon the name of Jesus Christ.
Notice how frequently Paul names our Lord Jesus Christ in these verses.
He was not afraid to speak of Christ often or give him too much honor.
To everyone calling on Christ, Paul offered his familiar greeting of grace and peace.
He desired that God's mercy would pardon them, his grace would sanctify them and his peace would comfort them, all through Jesus Christ.
Sinners have no peace with God and receive no true peace from him apart from Christ.
Paul thanked God for their conversion and for the grace Christ had given them.
They had been enriched with spiritual gifts, including speech and knowledge.
When God gives both, he provides great opportunities to be useful.
These gifts were works of the Holy Spirit, through which God confirmed the apostles' witness.
Those waiting for Jesus' return will be preserved by him to the end and declared blameless at his appearing through rich and freely given grace.
What a glorious hope—to be kept by Christ's power against inward corruption and Satan's temptations!

div.title: Paul calls the church away from division (verses 10–16)
div.p: In the central truths of religion, believers should agree in understanding.
Where opinions still differ, they should remain united in affection.
Agreement in major matters should outweigh disputes about lesser ones.
There will be perfect unity in heaven.
The closer believers approach that unity here, the closer they come to Christian maturity.
Paul and Apollos were both faithful servants of Christ, helping believers in faith and joy.
But contentious people organized themselves into rival factions.
Even the best institutions can be corrupted: the gospel itself may be misused as a weapon for quarrelling.
Satan has always treated division among Christians as one of his chief methods of opposing the gospel.
Paul allowed other ministers to perform most baptisms while he focused on preaching, which he regarded as the more useful task entrusted to him.

div.title: Christ crucified reveals divine wisdom (verses 17–25)
div.p: Paul had received extensive Jewish learning.
Yet the plain preaching of Jesus crucified proved more powerful than the combined rhetoric and philosophy of the pagan world.
This is the heart of the gospel.
Christ crucified is the foundation of our hope and the source of our joy.
Through his death we live.
Preaching that lost sinners are saved through the suffering and death of God's Son seems foolish to those moving toward destruction.
People controlled by sensuality, greed, pride or ambition recognize that the gospel threatens the pursuits they love.
But those who receive the gospel and are enlightened by the Holy Spirit discover more divine wisdom and power in the crucified Christ than in any other work of God.
God allowed much of the world to follow the guidance of its proudly asserted human wisdom.
History shows that this wisdom could not discover or preserve a right knowledge of God the Creator.
God chose to save believers through what the worldly call the foolishness of preaching.
This does not mean preaching that deserves to be called foolish.
Rather, the message of Christ appears foolish to people proud of worldly wisdom.
Plain proclamation of Christ continues to distinguish those responding to God's saving grace from those refusing it.
The world despises salvation by faith in a crucified Savior, who is God in human nature and purchased the church with his own blood.
Yet God has used that message through every generation to save multitudes who believe, freeing them from ignorance, deception and wickedness.
Even the weakest instruments God employs are more effective than humanity's greatest natural strength.
There is no foolishness or weakness in God.
What people call foolish or weak defeats their most admired wisdom and power.

div.title: God chooses the lowly to humble human pride (verses 26–31)
div.p: God did not chiefly choose the world's philosophers, eloquent speakers, political leaders or wealthy and influential figures to proclaim his gospel.
He knows which people and methods most serve his glory.
Not many noble people are called, but some have been called in every age.
They too need forgiveness, and some have gladly confessed Christ despite their status.
A humble believer who possesses little wealth or formal education may understand the gospel better than a scholar who studies Scripture merely as human writing instead of the word of God.
Even children have sometimes understood divine truths well enough to answer unbelievers.
The reason is that God himself taught them.
The purpose is that no human being should boast before him.
Our relationship to Christ does not arise from our own wisdom or effort.
Through God's sovereign choice and regenerating grace we are brought into Jesus Christ by faith.
Christ becomes for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.
He gives us everything we need or could rightly desire.
As Wisdom, through his word and Spirit, Christ teaches us from the fullness of his knowledge and makes us wise for salvation and service.
As Righteousness, he is the atoning sacrifice for guilty sinners deserving judgment.
As Sanctification, he remedies our fallen corruption.
And as Redemption, he will finally free the soul from all sin and the body from the grave.
All this fulfills the word of Jeremiah 9:23–24, that every person should boast only in the Lord's favor, sufficient grace and precious salvation.

row.cell: The plain manner in which the apostle preached Christ crucified.
The wisdom contained in this doctrine.
It cannot be duly known but by the Holy Spirit.

div.title: Paul's plain preaching of Christ crucified (verses 1–5)
div.p: Jesus Christ—his person, offices and sufferings—is the heart of the gospel.
He should be the main subject of every gospel minister's preaching.
This does not mean leaving out other parts of God's revealed truth and will.
Paul proclaimed the whole counsel of God.
Few people understand the fear and trembling experienced by faithful ministers who recognize their own weakness.
They know how inadequate their abilities are and feel their responsibility deeply.
When ministers simply proclaim Christ crucified, any genuine saving success must come from God's power accompanying his word.
Through that power, sinners believe and receive salvation.

div.title: God's deep wisdom revealed in Christ (verses 6–9)
div.p: Those who receive the gospel as divine truth and examine it under the Holy Spirit's light see more than the outward historical facts about Jesus' crucifixion.
They recognize God's deep and wonderful plan of wisdom.
This is the mystery now revealed to the saints (Colossians 1:26).
It had been hidden from the pagan world and only dimly pictured by Old Testament types and distant prophecies.
Now the Spirit of God has disclosed it.
Jesus is the Lord of glory, a title too exalted for any merely created being.
Many people would not oppose God's saving work if they truly understood his wisdom in redemption.
God has prepared blessings for those who love and wait for him that bodily senses cannot discover and human teaching cannot fully convey.
We cannot yet imagine their greatness.
We must receive these promises as they are revealed to us in Scripture.

div.title: The Holy Spirit enables spiritual understanding (verses 10–16)
div.p: God reveals true wisdom through his Holy Spirit.
This helps demonstrate the divine authority of Scripture (2 Peter 1:21).
It also bears witness to the deity of the Holy Spirit.
He knows and searches all things, even the depths of God.
No one can know God's inner purposes except his Spirit, who is one with the Father and the Son and reveals divine mysteries to the church.
Henry sees here testimony to the Holy Spirit's true deity and distinct personhood.
The apostles were not governed by worldly principles.
They received revelation of these truths through God's Spirit, together with the Spirit's saving impact upon them.
They communicated them in plain language taught by the Holy Spirit, instead of relying upon artificial rhetoric or manipulative human eloquence.
The natural person, even when regarded by the world as wise, does not receive the things of God's Spirit.
Pride in worldly reasoning can oppose spiritual truth as strongly as the crudest sensuality.
A mind sanctified by God recognizes the beauty of holiness.
This does not destroy its ability to reason about ordinary natural affairs.
But the unregenerate person does not understand the principles, pleasures and activity of divine life.
Only the spiritual person receives from God the knowledge of his saving will.
How little people understand of God's mind through merely natural powers!
The apostles received the Spirit's help to disclose it.
The mind of Christ, and God's mind as revealed in Christ, are made known in the Holy Scriptures.
Christians are privileged to receive that revelation through the Spirit, experience his sanctifying work within and bear good fruit in life.

row.cell: The Corinthians reproved for their contentions.
The true servants of Christ can do nothing without him.
He is the only foundation, and every one should take heed what he builds thereon.
The churches of Christ ought to be kept pure, and to be humble.
And they should not glory in men, because ministers and all things else are theirs through Christ.

div.title: Quarreling reveals spiritual immaturity (verses 1–4)
div.p: Simple gospel truths about human sin, God's mercy, repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ benefit many believers more than difficult mysteries.
A person may know a great deal about Christian doctrine yet remain a beginner in living faith and spiritual experience.
Arguments and quarrels over religion reveal remaining worldliness and immaturity.
True religion makes people peaceable rather than contentious.
Sadly, many professing Christians continue behaving too much like the surrounding world.
Some believers—and even ministers—show carnality through boastful rivalry, eagerness to dispute and willingness to despise or insult others.

div.title: Ministers are servants; only God produces growth (verses 5–9)
div.p: The ministers over whom the Corinthians fought were only instruments God had chosen to use.
We must never put ministers in God's place.
The person planting and the person watering belong to one work.
Both serve the same Lord, receive the same revelation and pursue the same purpose.
Their different gifts come from the same Holy Spirit and should be used in sincere cooperation.
Those who work diligently and faithfully will receive God's reward.
They cooperate in God's work to advance his glory and the salvation of souls.
The Lord knows their labor and will ensure it has not been wasted.
They are workers in God's field and God's building, both of which remain under his careful supervision.

div.title: Christ is the only foundation (verses 10–15)
div.p: Paul was a wise builder, but God's grace made him one.
Spiritual pride is especially shameful because it turns the Lord's greatest gifts into fuel for our vanity and self-idolatry.
Every Christian worker must be careful.
A person can build poorly upon a good foundation.
Only things consistent with the foundation should be placed upon it.
We must not combine a merely worldly life with divine faith or join sinful practices to a claim of Christianity.
Jesus Christ is the firm, unchanging Rock of Ages.
He can bear every burden God places upon him and every burden the sinner brings to him.
There is salvation in no one else.
Remove Christ's atonement, and the foundation of Christian hope disappears.
Among those who profess to build on Christ, Henry describes two kinds of workers.
Some proclaim the truth as it is in Jesus and build only what agrees with that truth.
Others build things that cannot survive the coming test, though they profess the same good foundation.
We may misjudge ourselves or others.
But a day is coming when every work will be seen in its true light, without disguise.
Those whose work spreads true and pure religion will receive a reward, far greater than they deserve.
Other workers' corrupt teachings, human inventions and unauthorized religious practices will be exposed and rejected.
The fire that tests these works is figurative, not literal fire.
No ordinary flame can consume a doctrine or a religious ceremony.
The test applies to everyone's work, including Paul and Apollos.
Let us consider the effects of our undertakings, compare them with Scripture and judge ourselves, so that God need not condemn our work.

div.title: God's church must remain holy (verses 16 and 17)
div.p: Elsewhere in the letter we learn that some Corinthian false teachers promoted unholy ideas.
Such instruction threatened to corrupt and destroy God's building, which should be preserved pure.
People spreading doctrines that encourage an unholy church bring judgment upon themselves.
Christ dwells by his Spirit within genuine believers.
Christians profess to be holy and should therefore seek purity in heart and conduct.
Anyone who believes themselves to be a temple of the Holy Spirit while remaining indifferent to personal holiness and the church's peace and purity is deceived.

div.title: Do not boast in human wisdom or ministers (verses 18–23)
div.p: Having an exaggerated opinion of our own wisdom is self-flattery, and self-flattery leads quickly to self-deception.
The wisdom admired by the world is foolishness before God.
He can easily confound its supposed experts.
Even the thoughts of the most intelligent humans contain weakness, error and emptiness.
This should humble us and make us eager to learn from God.
