Do not let claims of human expertise turn you from the plain truth revealed by Christ.
Human beings often resist the very purposes for which God blesses them.
Consider the spiritual wealth of true believers: “All things are yours.”
Ministers and appointed means of grace serve their good.
Even the world belongs to them in the sense that infinite divine wisdom gives them as much of it as is good for them, together with God's blessing.
Life belongs to believers as time to prepare for eternity.
Death belongs to them as a messenger bringing them from sin and sorrow to their Father's house.
Present things sustain them during the journey.
Future things will delight them forever at its end.
If we belong to Christ, all truly good things are secure for us.
Believers are subjects of his kingdom.
He is our Lord, and we ought to accept his authority gladly.
God in Christ reconciling sinful people to himself and pouring out grace upon them is the heart of the gospel.

row.cell: The true character of gospel ministers.
He claims their regard as their spiritual father in Christ, and shows his concern for them.

div.title: Ministers are servants entrusted with Christ's work (verses 1–6)
div.p: The apostles were servants of Christ, and should never be treated as if they were their Master. Yet they should not be undervalued, because the Lord had entrusted them with something of extraordinary importance. Their calling was honorable precisely because of this responsibility.
Paul rightly cared about his reputation. But someone whose chief ambition is to please other people cannot remain a faithful servant of Christ.
It is a comfort that human beings will not be our final judges.
Nor can we make ourselves safe simply by giving ourselves a favorable verdict. Our judgment of our faithfulness is no more dependable than our own works are sufficient to justify us before God.
A day is approaching when everything now concealed will be brought into the light. People's hidden sins and the secrets of their hearts will be disclosed.
Then every believer wrongly slandered will be vindicated, and every faithful servant will be approved and rewarded.
For now, God's word is our best standard for judging people and their conduct.
Pride frequently lies beneath quarrels. The same self-importance that leads us to admire ourselves too highly can also make us give excessive honor to the teachers we prefer.
We will not become inflated in favor of one leader against another if we remember that all ministers are instruments appointed by God and equipped with gifts from him.

div.title: The apostles' sufferings expose worldly boasting (verses 7–13)
div.p: We have no grounds for pride.
Everything genuinely good in who we are, what we possess and what we do comes from God's rich, freely given grace.
It would be absurd for a sinner rescued from destruction by sovereign mercy to boast about gifts received from that mercy.
Paul described the apostles' circumstances by an image drawn from the cruel spectacles of the Roman games (verse 9).
Men were compelled to fight one another for the crowd's entertainment. Even a victor who survived one fight was kept for another, until eventually he too would be killed.
Believers should remember that many eyes are upon them when they struggle with trouble or temptation. Such knowledge should encourage faithfulness and patience.
Paul wrote, “We are weak, but you are strong.”
Christians do not all experience the same trials. Some endure much greater hardships than others.
The apostles suffered in body and reputation. They were treated like the most contemptible people on earth, the dirt swept away and the refuse discarded.
Yet love for Christ and devotion to his work carried them through their suffering.
Everyone determined to be faithful to Jesus must be prepared for poverty and contempt, if these come.
Christ's disciples are called to follow his example and obey his commands even when the world despises or mistreats them.
It is far better to be rejected as Paul was than to possess the world's approval while abandoning Christ.
Those regarded by the world as worthless may be precious to God. He will receive them and grant them a place with him.

div.title: Correction should be loving and spiritually effective (verses 14–21)
div.p: When correcting wrongdoing, distinguish between the person and the sin.
A loving and affectionate warning is more likely to lead to genuine reform than a harsh rebuke.
Although Paul could speak with a father's authority, he preferred to appeal to the Corinthians in love.
Ministers should provide an example, and believers should imitate them only insofar as they imitate Christ in faith and conduct.
Christians may misunderstand matters or differ in their opinions. Yet Christ and the truth he has revealed remain the same yesterday, today and forever.
Where the gospel is truly effective, it comes not only in words but also in the power of the Holy Spirit.
The Spirit gives life to sinners who were spiritually dead.
He releases people from slavery to sin and Satan, renews them inwardly and outwardly, and comforts, strengthens and establishes the saints.
Persuasive human speech cannot accomplish these things. They require God's power.
It is a blessed disposition when love and gentleness govern our conduct while we still exercise the rightful authority entrusted to us.

row.cell: The apostle blames the Corinthians for connivance at an incestuous person;
and directs their behaviour towards those guilty of scandalous crimes.

div.title: The church must not tolerate scandalous sin (verses 1–8)
div.p: Paul exposed a shameful abuse that the Corinthian church had overlooked.
It seems that party loyalty and a mistaken view of Christian liberty had protected the offender from correction.
It is grievous when professing Christians commit crimes that even unbelievers would be ashamed to commit.
Spiritual pride and false teaching encourage these scandals and allow them to spread.
How terrible sin's effects can be!
Satan rules wherever Christ does not rule. Anyone who remains outside Christ's kingdom remains under Satan's power.
The example of an influential person can do exceptional harm, spreading widely through the community.
Corrupt principles and sinful practices, if left uncorrected, can harm the whole church.
Believers need new hearts and new lives.
Both their everyday conduct and their religious worship must be holy.
The sacrifice of Christ our Passover does not make personal or communal holiness unnecessary.
On the contrary, his sacrifice supplies the strongest reasons and motives for pursuing it.
Without holiness, we can neither live by genuine faith in Christ nor benefit comfortably and fruitfully from the ordinances he has appointed.

div.title: Avoid close fellowship with those who dishonor Christ's name (verses 9–13)
div.p: Christians should avoid close and familiar fellowship with those who openly disgrace the Christian name while claiming to belong to him.
People persisting in such conduct should, as far as possible, be left to the companionship of others who follow the same sins.
It is a sorrowful fact that some people called Christians are more dangerous companions than those who openly remain outside the faith.
The church must not let outward profession conceal openly scandalous behavior.

row.cell: Cautions against going to law in heathen courts.
Sins which, if lived and died in, shut out from the kingdom of God.
Our bodies, which are the members of Christ, and temples of the Holy Ghost, must not be defiled.

div.title: Settle disputes as brothers and sisters (verses 1–8)
div.p: Christians ought not to quarrel with one another, because they are brothers and sisters in Christ.
If they gave this relationship proper weight, many lawsuits, arguments and disputes would never begin.
Where serious injury to ourselves or our families is involved, we may use lawful means to obtain justice.
Paul's instruction should not be turned into an absolute ban on seeking legal redress.
Nevertheless, believers should have a forgiving disposition.
Whenever possible, they should refer disputes to trustworthy people among their fellow believers instead of bringing every disagreement into court.
Many disagreements are small enough to be settled readily if we first conquer our own passions.
Learn to bear with each other and yield where appropriate.
Even people of limited learning and experience may be able to settle quarrels if the parties are prepared to listen.
It is shameful when minor disputes among Christians become so bitter that no one among them can help reconcile them.
Peace within one's own mind and tranquillity among neighbors are worth more than winning a case.
When lawsuits occur between believers, something has already gone wrong in their relationships.

div.title: Grace changes people who once practiced serious sins (verses 9–11)
div.p: Paul warned the Corinthians against numerous grave sins, including sins in which some of them had formerly lived.
This warning carried particular force because the Corinthians had become proud of their supposed knowledge and wisdom.
All unrighteousness is sin.
Any sin deliberately practiced and left unrepented—any sin allowed to reign—shuts a person out of God's kingdom.
Do not deceive yourselves.
People naturally flatter themselves with the idea that they can live in sin, die belonging to Christ and enjoy heaven.
But no one can sow to the flesh and reap eternal life.
Paul reminded the Corinthian Christians of the tremendous change the gospel and God's grace had produced in them.
Christ's blood and the washing of regeneration can remove all sin's guilt.
Our justification comes from the suffering and merit of Jesus Christ.
Our sanctification comes from the Holy Spirit's work.
These two graces are inseparably joined: everyone made righteous before God is also made holy by God's grace.

div.title: Believers' bodies belong to Christ (verses 12–20)
div.p: Some Corinthians appear to have argued that everything was lawful for them.
Paul opposed this dangerous idea.
Christ has truly set believers free, and they should remain firm in that liberty.
But no Christian should willingly become a slave to any bodily appetite.
Our bodies belong to the Lord.
They are meant to serve as instruments of righteousness leading to holiness, not instruments of sin.
Jesus Christ's resurrection brought honor to his body.
The future resurrection will also bring glory to believers' bodies.
The hope of that resurrection should encourage Christians to refuse sexual immorality and other practices that dishonor the body.
The believer's soul is united to Christ through faith.
Therefore the whole person becomes a member of his spiritual body.
Some sins may be resisted through direct struggle, but sexual immorality must be fled.
Its destructive consequences have ruined many lives.
Its harm affects not only the body but often the mind.
Christ redeemed our bodies from deserved condemnation and hopeless slavery through his atoning sacrifice.
We must keep them clean as vessels suitable for our Master's use.
United to Christ as one spirit and purchased at a price of immeasurable value, we belong wholly to him.
May we spend the rest of our lives, until the final day and hour, glorifying God with our bodies and our spirits, which are his.

row.cell: The apostle answers several questions about marriage.
Married Christians should not seek to part from their unbelieving consorts.
Persons, in any fixed station, should usually abide in that.
It was most desirable, on account of the then perilous days, for people to sit loose to this world.
Great prudence be used in marriage; it should be only in the Lord.

div.title: Marriage and remaining unmarried (verses 1–9)
div.p: Paul answered questions the Corinthians had raised about marriage.
He considered it good for some Christians to remain unmarried under the particular circumstances of that time.
Yet marriage and its blessings have been established by God's wisdom.
No one may break his law. Within its perfect requirements, however, God grants freedom to serve him in ways suited to people's different abilities and circumstances.

p.hi: Other people are often poor judges of these circumstances.

div.p: Each Christian should consider personal responsibilities and seek God's counsel before deciding.

div.title: Marriage to an unbelieving spouse (verses 10–16)
div.p: A husband and wife should not separate except on grounds Christ permits.
Divorce was common among Jews and Gentiles in Paul's time, sometimes for the smallest reasons.
But marriage is God's institution, appointed as a lasting commitment.
We are to pursue peace with all people, insofar as it depends upon us (Romans 12:18).
How much more should we seek the comfort and peace of those closest to us, even if a spouse does not share Christian faith!
Married people should make it a serious aim to promote each other's happiness.
Why should someone professing Christ abandon a husband or wife when that relationship offers a particularly important opportunity to show genuine love?
Stay and work earnestly for the conversion of your spouse, where remaining in the marriage is the duty God has given.
In every calling and relationship, God has called believers to peace.
Do everything possible to maintain harmony, as far as truth and holiness permit.

div.title: Serve Christ faithfully in your present condition (verses 17–24)
div.p: Christianity reaches people in every social position and circumstance.
Someone can honor the gospel through faithful conduct in any lawful occupation or place.
Christians should be content with the position assigned to them and behave in a way that reflects their faith.
Our happiness depends on what we are in relation to Christ, not what we are in the world's eyes.
Faith must not be used as an excuse to abandon natural or civil responsibilities.
Normally believers should carry out their existing duties quietly and contentedly, trusting divine Providence.

div.title: Live with eternal priorities in troubled times (verses 25–35)
div.p: Considering the troubles facing believers at that time, remaining unmarried could be preferable.
Paul did not thereby condemn marriage.
How contrary to his instruction are those who forbid marriage to large groups of people or bind them with vows of celibacy regardless of whether this calling suits them!
Paul encouraged Christians to hold the things of this world loosely.
In personal relationships, do not set your heart entirely on their comforts.
In suffering, do not let worldly grief dominate, because joy in God remains possible even amid sorrow.
In earthly pleasures, remember that they are not your final rest.
In business, even when trade prospers and wealth increases, hold possessions as though they were not your ultimate property or hope.
In every worldly concern, keep the world from ruling your heart, so you will not misuse its gifts when they are placed in your hands.
All earthly things are temporary appearances.
Nothing here lasts.
Prudent attention to practical responsibilities is a duty.
But anxious and overwhelming preoccupation with them is wrong.
The best calling for a person is the one that most benefits that person's soul and best guards against worldly traps and distractions.
Examine the advantages and dangers of your circumstances. Use the former wisely and avoid the latter as much as possible.
Whatever legitimate responsibilities occupy you, always preserve time for the Lord's concerns.

div.title: Wise decisions about marriage and widowhood (verses 36–40)
div.p: Henry explains that Paul is understood by some to be discussing the responsibility of parents when arranging marriages for their children.
On this reading, children should seek and normally follow parental guidance in choosing a spouse.
But parents must also consult their children's wishes.
Parents do not have unlimited power to dictate such a lifelong decision without good reasons or regard for their children.
Paul concludes with advice to widows.
Remarriage is not unlawful, provided it is undertaken in the Lord.
In choosing close relationships and considering a change in circumstances, we should be governed by reverence for God, his commands and dependence upon his Providence.
A change of life should follow careful thought and a reasonable expectation that it will help rather than harm spiritual concerns.

row.cell: The danger of having a high conceit of knowledge.
The mischief of offending weak brethren.

div.title: Knowledge without love produces pride (verses 1–6)
div.p: Nothing proves ignorance more commonly than a conceited opinion of one's own knowledge.
A person may know many facts yet know nothing in the way that truly matters.
Those who become proud of what they understand are often the least likely to use it well.
Satan harms some people through pride in intellectual powers, just as he tempts others through bodily pleasures.
Knowledge that makes people arrogant, self-confident and dismissive of others is just as dangerous as self-righteous pride, even when the information itself is accurate.
Without holy love and godly affections, all our knowledge is worthless.
The pagans worshiped many beings they called gods or lords, some considered greater and others lesser.
But none was God in truth.
Christians know the one God who created everything and rules over everything.
Paul speaks of one God, the Father, as the Godhead who alone is the rightful object of all religious worship.
He also speaks of one Lord, Jesus Christ: Emmanuel, God manifested in flesh, one with the Father and united with us.
Christ is the appointed Mediator and Lord of all.
Through him we come to the Father, and through him the Father gives us every spiritual blessing by the Holy Spirit's power and work.
We must refuse religious worship not only to idols, but also to creatures wrongly treated as divine, including saints and angels.
Above all, examine yourselves: do you truly approach God through faith in Christ?

div.title: Do not harm weaker believers through careless liberty (verses 7–13)
div.p: Eating a particular kind of food or abstaining from it does not make a person acceptable before God.
Yet Paul warns against creating a stumbling block for a weaker believer.
Someone with a sensitive conscience might imitate a person who knows an idol is nothing.
But instead of eating the food simply as ordinary food, the weaker believer might eat it as an offering to the idol, becoming guilty of idolatry.
The distinction matters.
A person possessing Christ's Spirit will love people whom Christ loved enough to die for them.
Injuries done to Christians are done to Christ himself.
The most serious injury is entangling them in sin and wounding their consciences.
Christians must be especially careful not to put others in a position where they may stumble, even through an act harmless in itself.
If we must guard other people's souls in this way, how much more carefully should we protect our own!
Avoid moving unnecessarily close to evil or even its appearance.
Many people excuse such risks in public life by arguments that sound plausible.
But no one can sin against a brother or sister without offending Christ and endangering their own soul.

row.cell: The apostle shows his authority, and asserts his right to be maintained.
He waved this part of his Christian liberty, for the good of others.
He did all this, with care and diligence, in view of an unfading crown.

div.title: Paul has a right to material support (verses 1–14)
div.p: It is nothing new for ministers to receive unkind treatment in return for good intentions, diligent work and fruitful service.
Paul answered his critics and made himself an example of self-denial for other people's good.
He possessed the right to marry, like other apostles.
He could also claim adequate support for a wife, and for children if he had any, from the congregations he served.
He was not required to earn all this through his own manual labor.
Those who care for our souls should receive provision for their bodily needs.
Yet Paul deliberately surrendered this right rather than allow demanding his support to hinder the gospel's work.
The duty of supporting gospel ministers nevertheless remains with the people they serve.
A minister may waive a right, as Paul did.
But congregations who deny or withhold the support due to ministers violate Christ's command.

div.title: Paul gives up liberty to win people for Christ (verses 15–23)
div.p: It is a minister's honor to deny personal advantage in order to serve Christ and lead people to salvation.
When a minister voluntarily gives up lawful support for the gospel's sake, that person goes beyond the minimum required by the office.
By preaching without payment, Paul showed his zeal and love.
This gave him encouragement and hope in his own soul.
He understood that the ceremonial law had become a yoke removed by Christ.
Yet he was willing to comply with its observances where this could help Jewish hearers overcome prejudice, listen to the gospel and be brought to Christ.
He never broke Christ's commandments merely to please people.
But wherever lawful, he adapted his conduct to those he served, seeking to win at least some.
Doing good was the great work of his life.
He refused to let insistence upon personal privileges obstruct that goal.
We must guard against extremes and trust Christ alone, rather than our own flexible conduct, for salvation.
And we must never tolerate error or misconduct that injures others or brings disgrace upon the gospel.

div.title: Run the race for an unfading crown (verses 24–27)
div.p: Paul drew upon the races and athletic contests held at the Isthmian games, familiar to the Corinthians.
In the Christian race, everyone may run in such a way as to obtain the prize.
This is powerful encouragement to persevere with all our strength.
The contestants followed strict diets, trained their bodies, became accustomed to hardship and practiced their skills.
Similarly, those concerned for their eternal welfare must fight against sinful bodily desires.
The body must not be allowed to govern the soul.
Paul urged believers to beware of indulging appetite or giving in to temptation.
He himself recognized the danger of yielding to the desires of the flesh.
If even an apostle needed holy fear and watchfulness to remain faithful, how much more do we need them!
Let us learn humility and caution and remain alert to the dangers facing us while we live in mortal bodies.

row.cell: The great privileges, and yet terrible overthrow of the Israelites in the wilderness.
Cautions against all idolatrous, and other sinful practices.
The partaking in idolatry cannot exist with having communion with Christ.
All we do to be to the glory of God, and without offence to the consciences of others.

div.title: Israel's privileges did not guarantee salvation (verses 1–5)
div.p: Paul reminded the Corinthians of the ancient Israelites to warn them against fellowship with idolaters and false confidence while continuing in sin.
Through a miracle Israel passed through the Red Sea, while the Egyptians pursuing them drowned.
That passage was a type of baptism.
The manna with which God fed the people pictured Christ crucified, the Bread from heaven. Everyone who receives him truly will live forever.
Christ is the Rock on which the Christian church is built.
From him streams of spiritual refreshment flow to believers, picturing the Holy Spirit's gracious work through Christ.
Yet Israel's privileges did not prevent judgment upon unbelief and sin.
Neither possession of religious privileges nor a profession of truth can secure heavenly happiness for someone whose heart remains unconverted.

div.title: Learn from Israel's sins and God's faithful protection (verses 6–14)
div.p: Sinful appetites grow stronger when they are indulged.
Therefore, restrain them as soon as they arise.
If we want to avoid Israel's judgments, we should fear falling into its sins.
Those who deliberately tempt Christ may be left under the power of the ancient serpent, their enemy.
Complaining against God's providential dealings and his commands greatly offends him.
Nothing written in Scripture is useless.
We are obligated to learn from its warnings.
Others have fallen; we may fall too.
A Christian's protection against sin includes distrusting personal strength and self-confidence.
God has not promised to preserve us from falling while we neglect watchfulness.
But Paul's warning is joined to great encouragement.
Others have carried burdens and faced temptations like ours.
Through divine grace, we can also endure and overcome.
God is both wise and faithful.
He knows what we can bear and will not permit temptation to overwhelm his people beyond what he enables them to endure.
He will provide a way of escape.
That may mean removing the trial or preventing it from destroying us spiritually.
We have every reason to flee sin and remain faithful.
When we hold firmly to him, temptation cannot finally defeat us.
Whether the world smiles upon us or treats us harshly, it remains a danger.
Through Christ, believers are strengthened to resist both its threats and its enticements.
Reverence for the Lord, planted within the heart, is a great means of protection.

div.title: Idolatrous worship cannot be combined with Christ's table (verses 15–22)
div.p: Participating in the Lord's Supper is a public profession of faith in Christ crucified and grateful worship of him for his saving work.
Through this ordinance, believers express their unity in Christ.
Like grains gathered together in one loaf, or members forming one body, Christians share fellowship with Christ and with each other.
Paul confirms this meaning by referring to the Old Testament sacrifices.
Those eating from the sacrifices participated in the worship associated with the altar.
Similarly, eating food as part of an idol's sacrifice meant taking part in worship of that idol and having fellowship with what stood behind the idolatry.
A person cannot share communion with Christ and demons at the same time.
It would contradict Christianity itself.
Christians should also beware of places and occasions that encourage them to offer themselves to sinful bodily pleasures, the desires of their eyes or the pride of life.
Such conduct provokes God.

div.title: Use liberty for God's glory and others' good (verses 23–33)
div.p: Some food previously offered to idols could lawfully be eaten.
For example, meat given to a pagan priest might later be sold in a public market as ordinary food.
But believers must ask more than “Is this permitted?”
They must also ask “Is this beneficial and does it build up others?”
Christianity does not forbid ordinary kindness or justify rude conduct toward people who differ from us in their religious beliefs or practices.
The freedom to eat common food must, however, be distinguished from participating in a religious feast involving idol worship.
Christian liberty must never be exercised so carelessly that it harms others or brings unnecessary disgrace on us.
Whatever we eat, drink or do, we should do everything for God's glory, seeking to honor him.
This is religion's great purpose and a guide to conduct even where Scripture does not supply a detailed rule.
A holy, peaceable and generous spirit can overcome the hostility of even determined opponents.

row.cell: The apostle, after an exhortation to follow him,
Also contentions, divisions, and disorderly celebrations of the Lord's supper.
He reminds them of the nature and design of its institution.
And directs how to attend upon it in a due manner.

div.title: Imitate Paul only as he imitates Christ (verse 1)
div.p: Henry believes this opening verse properly belongs with the previous chapter's conclusion.
Paul preached teachings the Corinthians ought to believe, but also lived in a way they ought to follow.
Nevertheless, Christ is our perfect example.
We should imitate the actions of human beings described in Scripture only insofar as those actions resemble Christ's.

div.title: Order and appropriate dress in worship (verses 2–16)
div.p: Paul now begins considering abuses in public Christian gatherings, a subject continued in chapter 14.
Corinthian believers had received many spiritual gifts but had fallen into serious mistakes in using them.
As Christ did the Father's will and sought God's glory, Christians must openly acknowledge their submission to Christ and seek his honor.
Even our clothing and outward conduct should avoid bringing dishonor upon him.
Henry teaches that the woman was created to assist and comfort the man, and therefore should not conduct herself in public worship as if claiming independence from the order God appointed.
He interprets “power” on the woman's head as a veil, worn because of the angels who are present as witnesses of worship.
Their presence should restrain believers from misconduct in the assembly.
Yet Henry immediately adds that man and woman were created for one another.
They ought to bring mutual comfort and blessing, not live as a slave and a tyrant.
God's ordering of leadership and submission, both in Providence and in grace, aims at mutual assistance and benefit.
In the churches of that time, women commonly attended and participated in public worship wearing veils, and Henry considers it right that they did so.
Christianity generally permits a nation's social customs when they do not contradict truth and holiness.
It does not endorse deliberate eccentricity merely for the sake of appearing different.

div.title: Divisions and selfishness at the Lord's table (verses 17–22)
div.p: Paul rebuked abuses of the Lord's Supper.
When ordinances do not help people grow spiritually, they may instead harden them.
Corinthian gatherings were marked by divisions and disputes.
People can worship in separate congregations while still loving one another.
They can also remain together in the same congregation while behaving without love.
Henry judges that this lack of charity is the more serious kind of schism.
An unworthy and careless way of receiving the Supper adds guilt.
Some wealthy Corinthians treated poorer Christians shamefully during the meal or accompanying love feast.
They consumed the food they had brought before poorer members could share it.
Some remained hungry while others had more than enough.
What ought to have strengthened fellowship became a cause of division.
Avoid any conduct that dishonors the sacred meal.
We may not commonly turn it into an occasion of gluttony now.
But do we sometimes turn it into a support for self-righteous pride or a cover for hypocrisy?
Do not rest in outward forms of worship.
Examine the heart.

div.title: Christ's institution and proper reception of the Supper (verses 23–34)
div.p: Paul knew the Lord's Supper through revelation from Christ.
Its visible signs are bread and wine.
The food eaten is still called bread even when Christ calls it his body.
Henry understands this as clear evidence that the bread is not literally transformed into flesh.
Matthew records Christ commanding the disciples all to drink from the cup (Matthew 26:27).
Henry takes this wording as opposing the withholding of the cup from any believer.
These outward signs represent Christ's body broken and blood shed, along with every blessing flowing from his death and atoning sacrifice.
Christ took bread and cup, gave thanks, broke the bread and distributed both bread and cup.
Believers are to take, eat and drink, doing so in remembrance of him.
Yet the visible actions are not the whole or even the principal part of the ordinance.
The believer must receive Christ as Lord and Life, surrender to him and draw nourishment from him through faith.
The Supper remembers Christ dying for us and Christ now interceding at God's right hand on the basis of his sacrifice.
It also celebrates God's grace in our redemption.
We declare that Christ's death is our life, the source of hope and spiritual comfort.
We proclaim his death and plead it as the accepted sacrifice and ransom.
This ordinance was not appointed for only a few years.
It continues as part of the church's life.
Paul then warns against receiving it with a corrupt attitude, maintaining fellowship with sin and death while claiming to renew covenant fellowship with God.
Such hypocrisy is seriously guilty and may lead to divine judgment.
But the warning must not discourage genuine believers who fear their own weakness from attending the Supper.
The Holy Spirit did not cause this passage to be written to frighten sincere Christians away from their duty.
Satan has often misused it for precisely that purpose.
Paul was speaking to believers and warning them about temporal judgments through which God disciplined his offending servants.
In judgment, God remembers mercy.
He often corrects those he loves.
It is better to endure suffering now than to remain miserable forever.
Therefore self-examination is necessary for a right approach to the Lord's table.
If we examine ourselves thoroughly, condemn what is sinful and correct our ways, we may avoid divine discipline.
Paul concludes by warning them not to repeat the disordered practices that brought dishonor upon the Supper.
May our worship never become an occasion for provoking the Lord's judgment.

row.cell: The variety of use of spiritual gifts are shown.
In the human body every member has its place and use.
This is applied to the church of Christ.
And there is something more excellent than spiritual gifts.

div.title: Spiritual gifts serve the church, not personal pride (verses 1–11)
div.p: The extraordinary gifts of the Holy Spirit were powers given during Christianity's first generations, helping convince unbelievers and spread the gospel.
Spiritual gifts and saving grace are very different.
Both are freely given by God.
But grace is given for the salvation of the person receiving it.
Gifts are given for the good and salvation of others.
Someone may therefore possess remarkable gifts without possessing saving grace.
The Corinthians exercised many extraordinary gifts in public gatherings, sometimes making a public display of them while lacking true godliness and Christian love.
Before conversion they had been pagans, not governed by Christ's Spirit.
No one can truly confess Christ as Lord with believing dependence upon him unless the Holy Spirit produces that faith.
Nor could anyone truly believe in their heart, or confirm Christ's message through a miracle, without the Spirit's power.
There are different gifts and offices, but all come from one God, one Lord and one Spirit: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the source of spiritual blessings.
No gift exists merely for the recipient's benefit.
Serving others with a gift makes its use truly fruitful.
Paul's examples include understanding the truths of Christianity clearly, expressing doctrine accurately, knowing mysteries and giving wise guidance.
They also include healing, miracles, a special ability to explain Scripture, and speaking or interpreting languages.
All knowledge of God's truth and all ability to share it must result in glory to God alone.
Indeed, greater gifts create greater temptations to pride.
Those possessing them need more grace to remain humble and spiritually minded, and may undergo more difficult experiences through which God humbles them.
No one has reason to boast about gifts received or despise others who lack them.

div.title: Every member contributes to Christ's one body (verses 12–26)
div.p: Christ and his church form one body, with Christ as Head and believers as members.
Baptism is a divinely appointed outward ordinance identifying people with this body.
It signifies new birth and is associated with the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5).
But only the Spirit's renewing work, not outward baptism by itself, makes a person a living member of Christ.
Likewise, believers receive strength through fellowship with Christ at the Supper not simply by drinking wine, but by receiving the one Spirit.
Every member of the body has a particular form, position and purpose.
Even a member regarded as insignificant belongs to the body.
Differences among members are necessary.
Christians likewise have different abilities and responsibilities.
We should fulfill the duties of our own positions without resentment, rivalry or complaining.
All the members need one another.
Every member of Christ's body can and ought to be useful to fellow members.
The entire body should be united by the strongest bonds of love.
All its members should seek the good of the whole.
Every Christian depends upon others and ought to give as well as receive help.
How much more the spirit of unity should govern the church!

div.title: God appoints different offices and gifts (verses 27–31)
div.p: Hatred, jealousy, pride, contempt and quarrels are unnatural among Christians.
They resemble members of the same body fighting or ignoring one another.
Paul condemns the pride and contentiousness with which the Corinthians compared spiritual gifts.
The Holy Spirit appoints different offices and distributes distinct abilities.

Henry describes leading ministers, teachers able to interpret Scripture, others laboring in word and doctrine, workers able to heal sickness, those helping people in weakness, people managing the church's charitable funds and practical administration, and those able to speak different languages.
Notice that speaking languages comes last in this list.
How empty it is to possess this gift merely to entertain people or exalt oneself!
God does not give every gift to every believer.
If he did, the church would cease to have differentiated members, as though a natural body were made entirely of eyes or ears.
The Spirit distributes gifts according to his own will.
Christians must be content when given a less visible responsibility, without despising those with greater abilities.
Likewise, those given more prominent gifts must never despise those with less.
How blessed the church would be if every member faithfully performed the duty assigned!
Instead of seeking the highest status or most impressive gifts, leave the appointment of God's instruments to him.
Final approval will not belong to those who sought the most prominent positions, but to those who faithfully used the trust given them and worked diligently for their Master.

row.cell: The necessity and advantage of the grace of love.
Its excellency represented by its properties and effects;
and by its abiding, and its superiority.

div.title: Without love, even great gifts accomplish nothing spiritually (verses 1–3)
div.p: The more excellent way mentioned at the end of the previous chapter is love in its fullest meaning, genuine love toward both God and other people.
It is not merely what people commonly call charity—giving money or material goods.
Without this love, even the most impressive spiritual gifts are worthless for the person possessing them and count for nothing in God's sight.
A clear mind and profound learning are of no value spiritually without a loving and generous heart.
Someone may give away money freely and even extravagantly while lacking genuine concern for others.
Doing good to another person brings us no spiritual benefit if we act without love for God and goodwill toward people.
Even giving up all our possessions brings no blessing if our hearts remain withheld from God.
Nor will the most painful suffering earn God's approval in that condition.
How deceived are people who expect acceptance and reward for works that are limited, imperfect, and often corrupted by selfishness!

div.title: Christian love is recognizable in its character and actions (verses 4–7)
div.p: Paul described the effects of love so that we can examine whether this grace is present in our hearts.
If it is absent, we should not be satisfied until God grants it.
Christian love is evidence of regeneration, a test of our profession of faith in Jesus Christ.
The beautiful description also shows the Corinthian believers how far their actual behavior differed from it.
Love is the enemy of selfishness.
It does not put personal praise, reputation, profit or enjoyment above the good of others.
But this does not mean love destroys every proper concern for our own well-being.
A loving person need not ignore personal needs and legitimate interests.
Rather, love never pursues its own benefit at someone else's expense or by neglecting another person's welfare.
It willingly gives priority to others' needs when required.
How gentle and attractive Christian love is!

How beautiful Christianity would appear to the world if everyone professing it were governed by this divine principle, giving proper attention to the command upon which Christ himself placed such emphasis.
Let us ask ourselves: Does this love live in my heart?
Has it shaped my conduct toward everyone?
Am I willing to abandon selfish ambitions?
We need watchfulness, diligence and prayer.

div.title: Love will remain when other gifts pass away (verses 8–13)
div.p: Love is more excellent than the impressive gifts the Corinthians admired because it endures.
Love lasts throughout eternity.
Our present knowledge resembles childhood, while the life to come resembles maturity.
How confused and limited a child's understanding appears compared with that of an adult!
When we reach heaven, we will look back upon our best earthly abilities and most valued spiritual gifts with similar recognition of their limitations.
Everything we understand now is dark and incomplete compared with future knowledge.
We see as though through a mirror's reflection or a riddle.
In heaven, however, our knowledge will be freed from confusion and error.
Only heaven's light will remove the clouds that now hide God's face from us.
Love surpasses not only extraordinary spiritual gifts, but even the other central graces—faith and hope.
Faith receives God's revelation and rests upon the divine Redeemer.
Hope looks toward future happiness and waits for it.
But in heaven faith becomes sight and hope becomes enjoyment.
We no longer need to believe that something unseen is true once we see it, or hope for what we already enjoy.
Love, however, becomes perfect.
In heaven we will love God perfectly and love one another perfectly.
What a blessed state, surpassing every earthly comfort!
God is love (1 John 4:8, 16).
Where believers see him face to face as he is, love reaches its greatest height and its full perfection.

row.cell: Prophecy preferred to the gift of tongues.
The unprofitableness of speaking in unknown languages.
Exhortations to worship that can be understood.
Disorders from vain display of gifts;
and from women speaking in the church.

div.title: Explaining Scripture is more useful than uninterpreted languages (verses 1–5)
div.p: Henry understands prophesying in this passage as explaining Scripture.
Paul compared it with speaking in other languages.
Uninterpreted tongues attracted more attention and more readily gratified spiritual pride.
But they did less to accomplish Christian love's purpose, because they did less to benefit hearers' souls.
No one can be spiritually built up by words they do not understand.
Even the finest teaching accomplishes no good among hearers who cannot speak or understand the language being used.
The value of every ability or possession depends upon how useful it is.
Even sincere religious feeling must be guided by understanding, or it may dishonor the very truths people claim to promote.

div.title: Worship without intelligible speech cannot edify (verses 6–14)
div.p: Even an apostle could not build up the church if his words were incomprehensible to his hearers.
Speech that communicates no meaning to its audience is like speaking into the air.
The speaker and hearers become foreigners to one another.
The purpose of speech has not been fulfilled.
Christian gatherings should conduct every act of worship in a way that allows everyone to join in and receive spiritual benefit.
Plain, readily understood language is most appropriate for public worship and religious teaching.
A true follower of Christ should care far more about helping others than about earning a reputation for brilliant scholarship or eloquent speaking.

div.title: Speak and pray so that hearers understand (verses 15–25)
div.p: People cannot sincerely agree with prayers whose meaning they cannot understand.
A faithful gospel minister is far more concerned to benefit other people's souls than to earn public admiration.
That concern shows the minister is Christ's servant.
Children enjoy novelty and unusual displays.
Believers should not imitate that weakness.
We should be like children without malice or deceit, yet mature in our understanding of God's righteousness and ignorant only of the techniques of wrongdoing.
Henry regards it as a fearful judgment when people are led by teachers who force them to worship in an unfamiliar language.
No benefit can come from instruction that is not understood.
If unbelieving visitors enter a church and hear unintelligible preaching or prayer, they may conclude Christianity is absurd.
But when Scripture is clearly explained and the great truths and duties of the gospel are proclaimed, even an unbeliever or someone without formal education may be converted.
God's word may awaken conscience, expose secret sins and move that person to acknowledge their guilt and confess that God truly is present among his people.
Scripture, when clearly and faithfully taught, has extraordinary power to touch the heart.

div.title: Orderly worship should build up the whole congregation (verses 26–33)
div.p: Public worship should always be governed by one purpose: “Let everything be done for building up.”
If someone speaks in a language unknown to the congregation, another person must be able to interpret it.
Then two miraculous gifts can work together to build up the church and confirm the hearers' faith.
Those explaining Scripture should also speak in an orderly sequence.
Two or three may address a meeting, but not simultaneously.
Someone genuinely inspired by the Spirit of God will show decency and order in delivering what God has revealed.
God never teaches us to neglect our duties or behave in ways unworthy of our age and responsibilities.

div.title: Conduct in worship and apostolic instruction (verses 34–40)
div.p: Paul urged believing women to seek answers about religious matters from their husbands at home.
Henry draws the lesson that Christian families should gather for spiritual conversation and growth in knowledge.
The Spirit of Christ cannot contradict himself.
Claims of spiritual revelation that contradict the apostle's instruction cannot come from that same Spirit.
Churches preserve peace, truth and order when they seek what benefits the congregation, are patient with what does not harm its welfare, and maintain good conduct, decency and order.

row.cell: The apostle proves the resurrection of Christ from the dead.
Those answered who deny the resurrection of the body.
The resurrection of believers to eternal life.
The mystery of the change that will be made on those living at Christ's second coming.
The believer's triumph over death and the grave, An exhortation to diligence.

div.title: Christ's resurrection is the gospel's foundation (verses 1–11)
div.p: The resurrection points toward life beyond the grave.
Henry argues that the philosophers' teachings offer nothing comparable to the doctrine Paul proclaims.
Christ's death and resurrection are the foundation of Christianity.
If they are removed, every hope of eternal life collapses.
Believers stand firm through trial by holding closely to this gospel.
A person who abandons the gospel's faith has believed in vain.
Christ's resurrection was foretold in the Old Testament Scriptures.
Many witnesses saw him after he rose.
Paul had received exceptional privileges, but he kept a humble opinion of himself.
God can convert sinners into saints by grace and use the memory of their past sins to make them humble, diligent and faithful.
Paul attributed everything good within him to the grace of God.
True Christians can recognize what God has done for them, in them and through them, yet also see how far they remain from their duty.
They therefore regard themselves humbly before the Lord.
All the apostles agreed upon the central testimony: Jesus Christ was crucified and rose from the dead.
This is the heart of Christian faith.
In this truth they lived and died.

div.title: Denying resurrection makes Christian hope empty (verses 12–19)
div.p: Paul had established that Christ rose.
He now answered those denying the future resurrection of the body.
If Christ had not risen, there could have been no effective justification or salvation.
Faith in someone still held by death would be empty.
The resurrection of Jesus is the proof of our future bodily resurrection.
Even believers who died trusting Christ would have perished in their sins if he had never risen.
If resurrection and future reward were impossible, every Christian hope would be confined to this life alone.
Then believers, especially under the persecution experienced in the apostles' day, would be more miserable than other people.
But this is not their actual condition.
Christ's people possess solid comfort and hope even amid severe trials and persecution.

div.title: Christ's victory guarantees resurrection to those united to him (verses 20–34)
div.p: Everyone joined to Christ through faith has a secure promise of resurrection through his rising from the dead.
Through the first Adam's sin, the human race became mortal and inherited fallen nature.
Through Christ's resurrection, everyone brought into the spiritual life of his people by the Holy Spirit will rise and live forever.
There is an order in the resurrection.
Christ himself is the firstfruits.
At his coming, his redeemed people will rise.
Henry says the wicked will also rise later, and then this present order of things will come to its end.
If we wish to triumph on that day, we must now submit to Christ's rule, receive his salvation and live for his glory.
The completion of Christ's saving work will bring all glory to God, and his people will serve and enjoy him forever.
Paul mentions people “baptized for the dead.”
The meaning is not certain.
Henry suggests as one possibility that baptism here figuratively means suffering, persecution or martyrdom, as in Matthew 20:22–23.
He asks what would become of people who suffered terrible injuries or lost their lives for faith in resurrection if the dead never rose.
Whatever Paul meant, the Corinthian readers evidently understood his argument.
Without resurrection and eternal life, the suffering required by Christian faith would have no promised reward.
But we are not animals who simply live and die without a future.
Failure to believe in resurrection and the life to come reveals ignorance of God.
Recognizing God's existence and Providence, and seeing the many injustices of this life—where good people often suffer most—should lead us to expect a future state in which matters will be put right.
Avoid close fellowship with people who encourage ungodliness.
Warn children and young people especially to avoid corrupting companionship.
Awaken to righteousness and stop sinning.

div.title: God can raise bodies transformed for heaven (verses 35–50)
div.p: Two questions arise.
First, how can dead people rise? By what power and means?
Second, what kind of bodies will they possess? Will they have exactly the same shape, size, organs and qualities?
Henry distinguishes the first as an objection from those opposing resurrection and the second as a question from curious but doubtful minds.
God's almighty power answers the first.
Each year we see a partial analogy in grain sown into the ground and springing into life.
It is foolish to deny that God's power can raise the dead while we see him continually bringing life from what appears dead.
As to the second question, grain changes greatly when it grows, and resurrected bodies will also be transformed.
We do not fully understand how life arises from a seed.
God's ordinary works of creation and Providence should humble us as well as lead us to admire him.
Different kinds of plants and earthly bodies vary.
So do the heavenly bodies and their glories.
Likewise, the raised bodies will be fitted for the heavenly state and may display varied glory.
Burial resembles placing seed in the ground so that it may spring up later.
Though a dead body is repellent now, believers will rise with bodies made fit for everlasting union with spirits perfected in holiness.
To God all things are possible.
He gives spiritual life through the Holy Spirit now, and will later give new life and transformation to the body by the same Spirit.
The dead in Christ will not simply rise; they will rise gloriously transformed.
Their new bodies will be appropriate for the world in which they will live forever.
Our bodies in their present weakness and need cannot possess or enjoy heaven in that form.
Therefore, do not sow to sinful flesh and reap corruption.
The body follows the soul's spiritual condition.
Someone neglecting the life of the soul wastes the highest gift of this present life.

div.title: The living will be changed; death's defeat calls for steadfastness (verses 51–58)
div.p: Not every believer will die before Christ returns.
But all believers will be changed.
The gospel reveals many truths that earlier generations did not clearly know.
In the place to which the risen Lord brings his saints, death will no longer exist.
We therefore seek full assurance of faith and hope.
Even during pain or when death approaches, we may think calmly about the grave, confident that our bodies will sleep there, while our souls will be with the Redeemer.
Sin gives death its harmful power.
Sin is death's sting.
But Christ removed that sting through his own death.
He made atonement and obtained forgiveness.
The law gives sin its condemning strength.
No human being can satisfy all the law's demands, bear its curse fully or undo personal transgressions through self-righteousness.
This brings terror to people who remain unbelieving and unrepentant.
Death may seize a believer, but it cannot keep that believer in its power.
How many reasons for thanksgiving and joy flow from Christ's death, resurrection, sufferings and victories!
Paul therefore concludes by urging believers to be steadfast, established in the gospel they received and unshaken in their hope of being raised incorruptible and immortal.
They must abound in the Lord's work, continually serving him and obeying his commands.
May Christ grant us faith and strengthen it, so that we may not only be safe, but also joyful and triumphant.

row.cell: A collection for the poor at Jerusalem.
Exhortation to watchfulness in faith and love.

div.title: The collection for believers in Jerusalem (verses 1–9)
div.p: Good examples from other Christians and congregations ought to encourage us toward generous action.
It is wise to set aside resources for good purposes.
Those rich in the present world should be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:17–18).
Diligence alone will not make anyone prosperous without God's blessing (Proverbs 10:4, 22).
What better encouragement toward charity for God's people than remembering that everything we possess is God's gift?
Acts of mercy are genuine fruit of love for God and are appropriate ways of serving him on the Lord's Day.
Ministers carry out their proper work when they encourage and assist efforts of charity.
A Christian minister should remain concerned for the people among whom he has worked faithfully and fruitfully for a long time.
Every plan should be made with submission to God's Providence (James 4:15).
Opposition and enemies do not necessarily discourage faithful, successful ministers.
Such difficulty may instead increase their zeal and courage.
They are often more troubled by the hardness of their hearers' hearts and the backsliding of professing Christians than by attacks from outsiders.

div.title: Timothy and Apollos should receive honorable treatment (verses 10–12)
div.p: Timothy was doing the Lord's work.
Therefore, to needlessly trouble him was to grieve the Holy Spirit, and to despise him was to dishonor the One who sent him.
Those engaged in Christ's work deserve kindness, respect and consideration.
Faithful ministers should not compete through jealousy.
They should protect one another's reputation and usefulness and show sincere concern for one another's welfare.

div.title: Watchfulness, firmness and active love (verses 13–18)
div.p: A Christian is always exposed to spiritual danger.
Therefore, believers must remain watchful, established in the gospel's faith and unwilling to abandon it.
Faith in Christ alone enables them to stand firm when temptation comes.
But Christian courage must always be accompanied by love governing the heart and visible in conduct.
There is a great difference between steadfastness in Christ and agitated, uncontrolled excitement.
Paul commended some people who served Christ and cared for the church.
Those who serve believers, protect the churches' honor and help remove unjust reproaches deserve grateful respect and love.
The Corinthians should willingly recognize everyone who worked with Paul and assisted him in his service.

div.title: Greetings and final appeal to love Christ (verses 19–24)
div.p: Christianity does not abolish courtesy.
True religion encourages kind, considerate and helpful behavior toward everyone.
People who use their faith as an excuse for bitter, unfriendly conduct misrepresent Christianity.
Christian greetings should not be empty compliments.
They express real goodwill and ask God's grace and blessing upon others.
Every Christian household should resemble a small Christian church.
Where two or three gather in Christ's name and he is present among them, there is a church.
Paul ends with a solemn warning.
Many people constantly pronounce Christ's name without genuinely loving him in their hearts.
No one sincerely loves Christ while refusing his commands or despising his law.
Some people are Christian in name only.
They do not love Jesus Christ the Lord sincerely and therefore do not belong to God's people or enjoy his favor.
Whoever does not love the Lord Jesus Christ remains without the remedy of salvation.
Let us never be satisfied with religious profession alone.
Ask whether we possess love for Christ, desire for his salvation, gratitude for his mercy and obedience to his commands.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ contains every good gift needed for this life and eternity.
Wishing that grace upon a friend is wishing the greatest possible good.
We cannot desire anything better, and we should not desire anything less for our brothers and sisters in Christ.
True Christianity makes us seek the blessings of both worlds for those we love.
Paul had spoken plainly and rebuked the Corinthians' faults with necessary severity.
But he departed in love, affirming his affection for them in Christ.
May our love be with everyone who belongs to Christ Jesus.
Examine yourselves.
Do all things seem worthless when compared with Christ and his righteousness?
Do you knowingly indulge some sin or neglect a duty you know God requires?
Such serious and honest questions help reveal the spiritual condition of our souls.

div.title: 2 Corinthians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Paul's second letter to the Corinthians was written probably about a year after the first.
Its contents are closely connected with that earlier letter.
Paul considered how his earlier message had been received. The response gave him reason to thank God, who enabled him to fulfill his responsibility toward the believers.
Many Corinthians showed signs of repentance and improved their conduct.
Others, however, continued following false teachers.
Paul delayed visiting the church because he did not want to discipline them severely before giving them an opportunity to change.
Some then accused him of unreliability and inconsistency.
They also attacked him as proud, self-glorifying and harsh, speaking about him contemptuously.
Nevertheless, this letter shows the same deep affection for the Corinthian believers that appeared in the first, the same concern for the gospel's honor and the same courage in correcting their sins.
The first six chapters are mainly practical.
The remaining chapters address the Corinthian church's particular circumstances more directly, while still providing instruction useful to Christians everywhere.

row.cell: The apostle blesses God for comfort in, and deliverance out of troubles.
He professes his own and his fellow-labourers' integrity.
Gives reasons for his not coming to them.

div.title: God comforts us and enables us to comfort others (verses 1–11)
div.p: We are encouraged to come confidently to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find the help we need.
The Lord can give peace to a troubled conscience and calm the most violent passions of the soul. He gives these blessings as the Father of his redeemed family.
Our Savior himself tells us not to let our hearts be troubled.
Every true comfort comes from God, and our sweetest comforts are found in him.
He speaks peace to the soul through the free forgiveness of sins. He also comforts us through the life-giving work of the Holy Spirit and the abundant mercy of his grace.
He heals broken hearts, binds up painful wounds and gives hope and joy even amid the heaviest sorrows.
God does not comfort us merely to make us happier. He also intends his gifts to make us useful to other people. He provides enough comfort to sustain those who sincerely trust and serve him.
Even when suffering brings us to the point of despairing of life itself, we may trust the God who is able to bring people back from death.
That trust does not disappoint.
Remembering deliverance in the past strengthens our faith and hope for the future. Earlier mercies place us under an obligation to trust the Lord again.
We also owe one another more than prayers for relief. We should join in praise and thanksgiving when prayers are answered, giving thanks to God for benefits received.
In this way both our trials and the mercies that follow them may become blessings to ourselves and to others.

div.title: Paul appeals to the integrity of his conduct (verses 12–14)
div.p: Paul knew that, considered as a sinner, he had no ground for boasting except Jesus Christ.
But as a believer, he could rightly rejoice that his conduct agreed with the faith he professed.
Conscience bears witness not merely to an isolated action but to the settled direction and pattern of a person's life.
We should therefore examine our conduct as a whole, rather than judging ourselves by one good or bad act taken alone.
A life is properly ordered when it proceeds from a principle of grace within the heart.
With such a conscience, we can entrust our reputation to the Lord.
Nevertheless, there are times when we should take suitable steps to clear our name, especially when the honor of the gospel or our ability to serve others depends upon it.

div.title: Why Paul changed his travel plans (verses 15–24)
div.p: Paul answered the accusation that his failure to visit Corinth showed him to be fickle or unreliable.
Faithful Christians should guard their reputation for sincerity and steadiness.
They should make decisions carefully and not change them without substantial reasons.
God's own promises never become less certain because human plans change.
They are given through Jesus Christ and are confirmed by the extraordinary works God accomplished in his Son's life, resurrection and ascension.
The Holy Spirit establishes believers firmly in gospel faith.
His life-giving work is a pledge of everlasting life, while his consolations anticipate everlasting joy.
Paul delayed his visit because he hoped to spare the Corinthians the painful rebuke he might otherwise have needed to administer before seeing the effect of his first letter.
Our spiritual strength comes through faith, and so must our joy and comfort.
Faith is accompanied by holy dispositions and the fruits of grace.
These fruits help protect us against self-deception in a matter so important.

row.cell: Reasons for the apostle not coming to Corinth.
Directions about restoring the repentant offender.
An account of his labours and success in spreading the gospel of Christ.

div.title: Paul explains his reluctance to bring sorrow (verses 1–4)
div.p: Paul wanted his next visit to Corinth to be a joyful meeting rather than an occasion for painful confrontation.
He wrote his earlier letter trusting that the Corinthians would respond in ways that were good for them and comforting to him.
He hoped they would gladly remove the causes of distress between them.
We should never take pleasure in causing another person pain, even when our responsibilities require us to give a warning or correction that hurts.
Necessary discipline should be undertaken reluctantly, from love and for the other person's good.

div.title: Forgive and restore the repentant offender (verses 5–11)
div.p: Paul called the Corinthians to restore to fellowship the person who had done wrong.
That person had recognized the offense and had been deeply distressed by the correction already received.
Even grief over sin must not be allowed to make people unable to perform their remaining duties or drive them into hopeless despair.
Satan can take advantage of excessive severity by persuading a penitent person to think harshly of God and of religion, until that person loses hope altogether.
The enemy can also use the church's refusal to forgive as a weapon against Christ's congregations and ministers.
When Christians appear unforgiving, their public witness suffers, divisions arise and the gospel's ministry is hindered.
Therefore correction requires wisdom.
Church leaders must avoid two opposite errors: tolerating wrongdoing as though it were harmless, and treating repentant sinners with excessive harshness.
Satan has many schemes and knows how to use even our mistakes to cause harm.

div.title: The gospel triumphs through Christ (verses 12–17)
div.p: Every victory enjoyed by a Christian comes through Jesus Christ, who deserves all the honor and praise.
When the gospel spreads and bears fruit, believers have good reason to rejoice.
In ancient victory processions, sweet-smelling perfumes were spread around the participants.
Similarly, the name and salvation of Jesus are like fragrant ointment poured out wherever his gospel is proclaimed.
But people respond differently to this fragrance.
For some, the gospel becomes an aroma of death leading to death. They reject it and are ruined by that refusal.
For others it becomes an aroma of life leading to life. It awakens people who were spiritually dead in sins, continues strengthening their spiritual life and finally brings them to everlasting life.
Paul felt the dreadful seriousness of this task.
We should share that concern.
The ministry is far greater than our personal abilities. We have no sufficient strength in ourselves; our sufficiency comes from God.
Everything we do in religion must be done sincerely and consciously before God.
What is done for show or through dishonest motives does not come from him and cannot be acceptable to him.
May we watch our motives and seek the inward witness of conscience, instructed by the Holy Spirit, so that we speak in Christ and of Christ with genuine sincerity.

row.cell: The preference of the gospel to the law given by Moses.
The preaching of the apostle was suitable to the excellency and evidence of the gospel, through the power of the Holy Ghost.

div.title: The gospel brings greater glory than the ministry of the law (verses 1–11)
div.p: Humble, spiritually minded people dislike even the appearance of praising themselves or seeking human applause.
Faithful ministers find their greatest joy and the best testimony to their work in the changed hearts and lives of the people they serve.
The Corinthians themselves were evidence of Christ's work through Paul's ministry.
Christ's law was written upon their hearts, and his love had been poured into them.
This message was not engraved on stone tablets, as the law given through Moses had been.
It was written on living, softened human hearts (Ezekiel 36:26).
Henry draws an important distinction: the hearts are fleshy, meaning soft and receptive, not fleshly, meaning governed by sinful appetites.
The Holy Spirit's creative and renewing power softened those hearts so that they could receive Christ's law.
All the glory belongs to God.
Our entire dependence is upon him, so all the praise must be his as well.
The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
The written law exposes sin and announces its curse and death.
But merely possessing the outward words or forms of the gospel also leaves a person unchanged when the Holy Spirit does not give life through them.
The old covenant ministry revealed human guilt and God's just anger.
The gospel reveals grace and Emmanuel, God with us.
It shows the righteousness God provides through faith and explains the mercy and forgiveness available through Jesus Christ, leading to eternal life.
The glory of this gospel far exceeds that of the Mosaic dispensation, as a brighter light outshines a lesser one.
But even the New Testament becomes merely a dead letter when treated only as a religious system or external form, without dependence on the Spirit's power to awaken and transform the soul.

div.title: The veil is removed and believers are transformed (verses 12–18)
div.p: Ministers of the gospel should speak plainly and clearly.
Believers living under the old covenant saw only partial and passing glimpses of the Savior's glory.
Unbelievers often stopped at the visible ceremonies and did not look beyond them.
But the gospel openly calls us to believe, love and obey.
The message of Christ crucified has been stated as clearly as human language can express it.
Under the law, a veil lay upon people's hearts.
That veil is removed by the biblical teaching concerning Christ when God converts a person to himself.
The ignorance that once obscured the heart is lifted.
Those who believe and enjoy the gospel receive wonderful freedom: they can now delight in walking according to God's commandments.
They see the glory of the Lord without the former veil.
Christians should cherish these privileges and make full use of them.
But we must not be satisfied with knowing doctrines without experiencing the transforming work of the Spirit.
His work makes us increasingly like the character and purpose of Christ's glorious gospel and unites us more closely to our Lord and Savior.
Through Scripture we behold Christ as in a mirror.
Just as reflected light causes a face to shine, looking upon the Lord by faith changes believers so that his glory begins to shine in their lives.

row.cell: The apostles laboured with much diligence, sincerity, and faithfulness.
Their sufferings for the gospel were great, yet with rich supports.
Prospects of eternal glory keep believers from fainting under troubles.

div.title: Faithful ministry and treasure in fragile vessels (verses 1–7)
div.p: Even the best people would lose heart if they did not receive God's mercy.
But the mercy that has helped us through earlier difficulties and sustained us until now can be trusted to sustain us to the end.
The apostles did not hide dishonorable purposes beneath a convincing appearance of goodness. They did not make the gospel ministry a tool for personal advantage.
People who live sincerely and uprightly will generally retain the respect of wise and good observers.
Through the gospel, Christ reveals his glory to human minds.
But the devil's purpose is to keep people in ignorance. Since he cannot prevent the gospel's light from entering the world, he strives to keep individuals away from it or set their hearts against it.
Henry traces rejection of the gospel to the deliberate blindness and wickedness of the human heart.
The apostles did not preach to exalt themselves or make themselves the center of the message.
They proclaimed Jesus Christ as Savior and Deliverer, the One who saves completely everyone who comes to God through him.
Ministers are servants for people's spiritual good, but that does not mean becoming servants of their passing moods or sinful desires.
Seeing sunlight fill the sky is wonderful. But the light of the gospel shining into a human heart is even more wonderful and beneficial.
Light marked the beginning of the original creation. Likewise, the Holy Spirit's first work in a person's new creation is to shine spiritual light into the soul.
Yet this treasure of gospel truth and grace has been placed in earthen vessels.
Christian ministers share the weaknesses, temptations and emotions of other people.
God could have commissioned angels to announce the gospel, or chosen the most highly admired people in the world.
Instead, he chose comparatively weak and unimpressive instruments.
This made the Lord's power more evident, both in sustaining his ministers and in transforming the people who received their message.

div.title: Severe suffering sustained by grace (verses 8–12)
div.p: The apostles experienced extraordinary suffering, yet they also received extraordinary support.
Friends may abandon believers, and enemies may persecute them.
But God will not leave or forsake his people.
There may be inner fears as well as outward conflicts. Nevertheless, God's servants are not destroyed.
Paul described their sufferings as reflecting the sufferings of Jesus Christ.
Through them, the power of Christ's resurrection and the grace flowing from the living Savior could also become visible.
Compared with the apostles' hardships, many other Christians at that time enjoyed relatively comfortable circumstances.
The contrast should make those of us living in ease thankful rather than indifferent to the sufferings of faithful servants.

div.title: Eternal glory outweighs present trouble (verses 13–18)
div.p: Faith is an effective remedy against faintheartedness in affliction.
The apostles knew that Christ had been raised and that his resurrection guaranteed their own.
This hope gives courage in suffering and lifts believers above the fear of death.
Their trials also served the church's good and God's glory.
A minister can serve the church not only through preaching and conduct but even through suffering endured faithfully.
The hope of everlasting life was the apostles' comfort and support.
What physical sight might judge to be heavy, long and unbearable, faith recognized as light and momentary when measured against what lay ahead.
All temporal affliction becomes light in comparison with the immeasurable weight of eternal glory.
If Paul could describe his many severe and prolonged trials as light and brief in this sense, how should we view our comparatively small difficulties?
Faith teaches us to judge both present suffering and eternal hope correctly.
Some things are visible; others are unseen.
The unseen realities of God's promised future are eternal, whereas the visible things of this world are temporary.
Let us stop making earthly advantages our highest ambition or present suffering our greatest fear.
Instead, let us diligently seek assurance of the everlasting happiness God promises his people.

row.cell: The apostle's hope and desire of heavenly glory.
This excited to diligence. The reasons of his being affected with zeal for the Corinthians.
The necessity of regeneration, and of reconciliation with God through Christ.

div.title: Our future home and the presence of Christ (verses 1–8)
div.p: Faith assures the believer that life does not end at the grave.
Through God's grace, we also possess a solid hope of heaven as our home, place of rest and shelter.
Our Father's house has many dwelling places. God himself is its Architect and Builder.
Heaven's joy is what God has prepared for those who love him.
Our present bodies are like temporary tents or poor houses of clay, decaying and slowly collapsing on foundations of dust.
The body can feel like a heavy burden, especially when sickness and suffering come.
But believers groan most deeply because of the body of sin—the corrupt desires that still remain within them and continually trouble their souls.
Death will remove our earthly bodies and comforts, and it will end the outward troubles of this life.
But believers will be clothed with praise, righteousness and glory.
The Holy Spirit's present graces and comforts are pledges of the everlasting life and consolation ahead.
God is already with us through his Spirit and his appointed means of grace. Yet this is not the same as being with him in the full way we hope to enjoy in heaven.
Now we live by faith; there we shall live by sight.
Until then, it is both our duty and our good to continue walking by faith.
These verses clearly teach the happiness enjoyed by the souls of believers when they are absent from their bodies and present where Jesus reveals his glory.
We are bound both to our present bodies and to our Lord.
Each has a claim upon our affections.
But how much more powerfully does Christ call the souls he has loved, chosen and received from the Father to be united closely with himself!
Compared with being separated from the Lord, why should death itself be our greatest fear?

div.title: Future judgment and Christ's love inspire service (verses 9–15)
div.p: The hope of heaven should stir us toward greater effort and obedience, never toward laziness or sinful complacency.
Remember the coming judgment—the solemn terror of the Lord.

Knowing how dreadful the Lord's vengeance will be against those who persist in evil, Paul and his companions used every proper argument and appeal to persuade people to believe in Jesus and live as his disciples.
Their zeal served God's honor and the welfare of the church.
Christ's love will produce similar devotion in us when we consider it carefully.
All humanity was lost, dead in sins, enslaved to evil and unable to rescue itself.
Without Christ's death, we would have remained in that miserable condition forever.
Therefore the goal of our living and acting must not be ourselves but Christ.
A Christian's life belongs to him.
Sadly, many show that their professed faith and love are hollow by continuing to live entirely for themselves and this world.

div.title: A new creation reconciled to God through Christ (verses 16–21)
div.p: A renewed person lives by new principles, follows new rules, seeks new ends and keeps new company.
The believer becomes a new creation.
The heart is not merely repaired or adjusted; God gives an entirely new heart.
We are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.
We remain the same human beings, yet our character and conduct are transformed.
Regeneration means much more than an external improvement in behavior.
Someone who once saw no beauty in Christ and felt no desire for him now loves the Savior above everything.
Before regeneration, the heart is hostile to God, and God is justly offended by sin.
Yet reconciliation is possible.
Through Jesus Christ, the God whom we have offended has reconciled us to himself.
By divine inspiration the Scriptures were written as the message of reconciliation, announcing that peace has been made through the cross and explaining how we can receive its blessings.
God gains nothing from our hostility or our reconciliation; he loses nothing if we remain enemies.
Nevertheless, he graciously appeals to sinners to lay aside their hostility and accept his salvation.
Christ knew no sin.
Yet he was made sin for us—not made a sinner, but made a sin offering, a sacrifice for sin.
