The purpose was that we might become the righteousness of God in him, freely justified by divine grace through the redemption accomplished in Jesus Christ.
How could we ever consider any sacrifice, labor or suffering too great for the One who gave his beloved Son as an offering for our sins so that we might be declared righteous in him?

row.cell: The apostle, with others, proved themselves faithful ministers of Christ, by their unblamable life and behaviour.
By affection for them, And by earnest concern, that they might have no fellowship with unbelievers and idolaters.

div.title: Faithful servants during the day of salvation (verses 1–10)
div.p: The gospel is a word of grace sounding in our ears.
The present time is the day of salvation: the gospel is offered, the means of grace are provided, and God's saving invitation can be received now.
Tomorrow is not ours. We do not know what will happen to us or even where we will be.
We have a day of grace today. Let us not neglect it.
Ministers should remember that they are God's servants and behave in every circumstance as people entrusted with his work.
Paul did this through patience under suffering, sincere motives and a manner of life appropriate to his calling.
Believers also need God's grace when people speak well of them or speak against them.
They need grace to receive approval without becoming proud, and to bear criticism with patience.
Christians have nothing to boast of in themselves, yet in Christ they possess everything.
Such contrasts form the fabric of the Christian life.
Our path to heaven passes through changing circumstances and conflicting opinions.
In all of them, we should strive to be approved by God.
When the gospel is preached faithfully and fully received, it can improve even the poor person's earthly condition.
Money once wasted recklessly is saved. Time once spent in harmful pursuits is put to constructive work.
In comparison with former sinful living, such people become richer even in this world, while also receiving the far greater riches of the world to come.

div.title: Love and separation from sinful partnerships (verses 11–18)
div.p: Paul's affection for the Corinthians led him to warn them against binding themselves in fellowship with people who reject God.
Here unbelievers means those who do not have genuine saving faith.
Faithful pastors will warn the people they love not to become unequally yoked.
The harmful consequences of ignoring Scripture's warnings concerning marriage can be very serious.
A marriage that was meant to provide a suitable helper can instead become a trap.
Henry makes an important qualification: people already bound in such a marriage without having deliberately chosen to disregard God's command may look to him for consolation under that cross.
But believers who willingly enter those unions despite Scripture's warnings should expect considerable distress.
The warning also extends to ordinary social relationships.

Henry counsels believers not to choose wicked people as their closest companions, while explicitly recognizing that it is impossible to avoid every encounter, conversation or shared situation with them.
The point is to resist being drawn into others' sinful practices.
Come away from those who devote themselves to wrongdoing.
Reject the futile pleasures, pursuits and moral corruption of this present world.
If it is considered a wonderful privilege to be the son or daughter of an earthly ruler, how much greater is the dignity and happiness of being a son or daughter of Almighty God!

row.cell: An exhortation to holiness, and the whole church entreated to bear affection to the apostle.
He rejoiced in their sorrowing to repentance.
And in the comfort they and Titus had together.

div.title: Pursuing holiness and receiving faithful ministers (verses 1–4)
div.p: God's promises give us strong reasons to pursue holiness.
We must cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles the body and the spirit.
If we hope in God as our Father, we should desire to become holy as he is holy and to resemble our heavenly Father.
Only his grace, working by the Holy Spirit, can truly cleanse us.
Nevertheless, growth in holiness should be the constant object of our prayers and efforts.
It is dangerous when people regard gospel ministers as contemptible, because contempt for the messenger may lead to contempt for the gospel.
Ministers must not flatter anyone, but they should show gentleness toward everyone.

They may ask for esteem and goodwill when they can honestly say that they have corrupted no one through false teaching or flattering words, defrauded no one, and never pursued their own advantage at another person's expense.
Paul's great affection for the Corinthians moved him to speak freely to them.
That affection also led him to speak proudly of their progress wherever he went.

div.title: Godly sorrow leads to genuine repentance (verses 5–11)
div.p: Paul and his companions faced conflict outside and fears within.
They met opposition from both Jews and Gentiles, while also carrying deep anxiety for people who had embraced the Christian faith.
But God comforts those who are downcast.
We should look beyond the human means through which comfort arrives and recognize God as the source of every true consolation and blessing.
There is a profound difference between godly sorrow and the sorrow of this world.
Sorrow that agrees with God's will, seeks his glory and is produced by the Holy Spirit makes the heart humble, contrite and submissive.
It moves the believer to put sin to death and walk in newness of life.
This repentance belongs with saving faith in Jesus Christ and participation in the blessings of his atoning sacrifice.
Worldly regret can mourn consequences without turning from sin.
But genuine repentance bears visible fruit.
When the heart changes, the life and actions change.
The Corinthians' repentance produced indignation against sin, against their own past conduct, and against the tempter and his agents.
It produced watchfulness and a careful fear of falling into sin again.
It brought a strong desire to be reconciled to God.
It stirred zeal for duty and opposition to wrongdoing.
It also prompted practical attempts to correct the harm their sins had caused.
Deep humility before God, hatred of all sin, faith in Christ, a new heart and a new life together characterize the repentance that leads to salvation.
May the Lord grant this repentance to each of us.

div.title: Mutual encouragement through Titus and the Corinthians (verses 12–16)
div.p: Paul's confidence in the Corinthians had not been disappointed.
He had shared that confidence with Titus, and the good news now allowed him to look toward their future with joy.
This passage teaches the mutual responsibilities of pastors and congregations.
Believers should ease the difficulties of pastoral service by showing respect and willing obedience.
Pastors, in turn, should care faithfully for their people and encourage them by expressing satisfaction, joy, affection and tenderness when they respond well.

row.cell: The apostle reminds them of charitable contributions for the poor saints.
Enforces this by their gifts, and by the love and grace of Christ.
By the willingness they had shown to this good work.

div.title: God's grace produces generous service (verses 1–6)
div.p: We must recognize the grace of God as the source of every genuinely good quality in us and every good deed we accomplish.
It is a great gift from God to be made useful to others and eager to participate in good work.
Paul praised the generosity of the Macedonian believers.
They did not have to be pressured to contribute. They actually pleaded with Paul to accept their gift.
Whatever we spend in God's service, we are merely returning to him something that already belongs to him.
But our contributions will not be accepted by God or truly benefit us unless we first give ourselves to the Lord.
Acknowledging divine grace as the source of good works both honors their true Giver and teaches us where to find the strength to perform them.
Spiritual joy expands the heart and moves it to loving service.
How different this is from people who refuse to join any good undertaking unless others press them repeatedly!

div.title: Christ's generosity is our greatest example (verses 7–9)
div.p: Faith is the root of a life that pleases God (Hebrews 11:6).
Those who abound in faith should also grow in other graces and good works, especially those motivated by love.
People who talk the most are not always the most active in doing good.
But the Corinthians had already shown diligence in understanding and speaking about the faith, as well as in putting it into practice.
Paul urged them to add another grace to these virtues: generous care for poor believers.
The greatest reasons for fulfilling our Christian duties come from the grace and love of Jesus Christ.
Christ was rich because he was God, equal with the Father in power and glory.
Yet he not only became human for our sake; he also became poor.
He humbled himself to the point of offering his life upon the cross as a sacrifice to ransom our souls.
From what glory to what poverty our blessed Lord descended for us!
And through his poverty, what riches he has opened to us!
Our greatest happiness is to belong entirely to him and be available for his service.

div.title: Finish the generous work you began (verses 10–15)
div.p: Good intentions resemble buds and blossoms: they are pleasant and give promise of fruit.
But if they produce no actual good deeds, their promise comes to nothing.
A good beginning is valuable, yet its benefit is lost without perseverance.
When people sincerely intend to do good and act according to the resources and abilities they possess, God does not reject them for what they cannot do.
But this does not excuse anyone who imagines that good intentions or merely claiming willingness is enough for salvation or for performing duty.
God's providence distributes earthly possessions unequally.
Some have much; others have little.
Those with abundance are therefore able to help people who lack necessities.
God intends that by supplying one another's needs, there should be a kind of equality.
Henry expressly rejects a forced leveling that would destroy private ownership; such a system, he argues, would remove the opportunity for voluntary generosity.
Everyone should feel responsible to help those in need.
Paul illustrates the point through the gathering and distribution of manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16:18).
In the end, even the wealthiest person needs only the ordinary necessities of life—food and clothing—while many who possess little still receive those necessities.

div.title: Titus and trustworthy companions administer the collection (verses 16–24)
div.p: Paul recommended the brothers entrusted with receiving and carrying the gift so that the Corinthians would know whom they could trust.
Christians have a duty to act prudently and remove unnecessary grounds for suspicion.
It is essential to behave honestly before God.
But we should also take appropriate care to appear honest before other people, so that our integrity is visible and our usefulness is not hindered.
A clear public reputation and a pure conscience are both valuable for effective service.
The men commended by Paul glorified Christ through their work.
They were honored by him as faithful servants entrusted with his service.
When others place confidence in us, we should regard that confidence as a further reason to act well.

row.cell: The reason for sending Titus to collect their alms.
The Corinthians to be liberal and cheerful, The apostle thanks God for his unspeakable gift.

div.title: Titus is sent to help complete the collection (verses 1–5)
div.p: When we want others to do good, we should treat them with care, gentleness and good judgment, allowing appropriate time for the work.
Christians should consider what brings honor to their public profession of faith.
They should seek to make the doctrine of God their Savior attractive in everything they do.
Supporting needy believers is such an obvious duty that one might think Christians would need no reminder.
Yet self-love competes so powerfully against the love of Christ that we often need to be reminded and encouraged to fulfill even familiar obligations.

div.title: Give thoughtfully, freely and cheerfully (verses 6–15)
div.p: A mind ruled by earthly interests may regard charitable gifts as money thrown away.
But when gifts arise from proper motives, they are like seed sown in a field, with the promise of a valuable harvest.
That does not mean we should give thoughtlessly.
Works of mercy, like all other good works, should be carried out with careful thought and a real purpose.
We should consider both our own circumstances and the needs of the people we hope to help.
Whether the gift is large or small, it should be given freely, without resentment and with joy.
Some people give generously and yet find their resources increased.
Others hold back more than they ought and become poorer.
With stronger faith and greater love, we would spend less wastefully on ourselves and sow more generously in hope of a good result.
Can someone ultimately lose by doing what pleases God?
God can make every kind of grace abound toward us and within us.
He can grant an increase of spiritual and temporal blessings, provide enough for our needs and enable us to live contentedly with what we possess.
His provision is not intended only for personal comfort.
He also gives us resources with which to meet other people's needs, treating them as seed that should be sown.
Acts of charity show whether our professed submission to the gospel is real.
They honor the Christian faith and bring praise and glory to God.
Let us follow Christ's example, continuing to do good without growing weary and recognizing that it is more blessed to give than to receive.
Above all, thank God for his indescribable gift.
His grace inclines some believers to give and moves others to receive with gratitude.
And his greatest gift is Jesus Christ, the priceless expression of his love.
Through Christ, every other blessing necessary for life and godliness comes freely to us, beyond anything we can adequately measure or express.
May his glorious name be praised forever!

row.cell: The apostle states his authority with meekness and humility.
Seeks the glory of God, and to be approved of him.

div.title: Ministry uses persuasion, not coercion (verses 1–6)
div.p: Some people thought poorly of Paul and spoke about him with contempt.
Yet he recognized his own weaknesses and spoke humbly of himself.
We, too, should remember our limitations and remain humble even when others criticize or insult us.
The work of Christian ministry is spiritual warfare, directed against spiritual enemies and toward spiritual purposes.
Physical force is not the way of the gospel.
Its methods are earnest persuasion, the power of truth and the gentleness of wisdom.
A person's conscience answers to God alone.
People must be persuaded to follow the Lord and obey their duty, not forced into religious obedience.
Nevertheless, the Christian's spiritual weapons are powerful.
The evidence supporting the truth is compelling.
Sin and Satan resist the gospel fiercely within human hearts.
Yet see what victories God's word achieves!
Even means that appear weak to human eyes become powerful when the Lord works through them.
The preaching of Christ's cross by faithful, praying people has repeatedly overthrown idolatry, ungodliness and wickedness.

div.title: Do not judge ministry by outward appearance (verses 7–11)
div.p: Paul's outward appearance seemed unimpressive to some who despised him.
But this was a false standard of judgment.
We must not assume that lacking impressive worldly qualities proves someone is neither a genuine Christian nor a capable and faithful minister.
Remember that the Savior himself was humble.
External prestige is not the measure of spiritual authority or service.

div.title: Seek God's approval, not self-congratulation (verses 12–18)
div.p: Comparing ourselves with people who surpass us can help keep us humble.
Paul adopted a better standard than the self-praise of his opponents.
He would speak only about the responsibility and field of service God had actually assigned him, not boast beyond his appointed measure.
Few things lead to so much error as judging people and opinions through our own prejudices.
How often people assess their religious character according to the expectations and values of the world around them!
But God's word provides a different standard.
Among all forms of flattery, self-flattery is the most dangerous.
Instead of praising ourselves, we should strive to be approved by God.
Our boasting belongs in the Lord who saves us.
We should value other things only as evidence of his love or as opportunities to advance his glory.
Rather than seeking the applause of people, let us desire the honor that comes from God alone.

row.cell: The apostle gives the reasons for speaking in his own commendation.
Shows that he had freely preached the gospel.
Explains what he was going to add in defence of his own character.
He gives an account of his labours, cares, sufferings, dangers, and deliverances.

div.title: Paul warns against another gospel (verses 1–4)
div.p: Paul wanted to protect the Corinthians from the corrupting influence of false apostles.
There is one Jesus, one Spirit and one gospel to be proclaimed and received.
Why should hostile schemers turn the Corinthians against the apostle who had first taught them the faith?
They should not listen to people who, without just reason, tried to draw them away from those God had used to bring them to conversion.

div.title: Paul served without using ministry for personal gain (verses 5–15)
div.p: It is far better to speak plainly while living openly and consistently with the gospel than to be admired by thousands and lifted up in pride.
A person admired as an impressive speaker may still disgrace the gospel through sinful attitudes and an unholy life.
Paul deliberately avoided giving his opponents any basis for accusing him of self-interested motives in preaching.
He would not let the false teachers in Corinth gain that advantage over him.
Hypocrisy is a real danger, particularly because Satan exerts considerable influence over people who continue living in disobedience.
But we must beware of an opposite temptation too.
Satan can advance his purposes by setting good works against Christ's atonement, as though salvation could be earned rather than received by faith and grace.
False workers will eventually be exposed, and their efforts will end in ruin.
Henry argues that Satan's servants can sometimes present the law alone or the gospel alone in misleading ways.
The test of a sound system is whether it teaches the law as rightly understood and upheld through faith in Christ's righteousness and atoning work, together with participation in his Spirit.

div.title: Paul explains why he must defend his integrity (verses 16–21)
div.p: Christians ought to humble themselves in obedience to the Lord's command and example.
Nevertheless, wisdom is needed to decide when it is appropriate to speak of things we have lawfully done.
That includes acknowledging what God has done for us, within us and through us.
Paul's defense was not merely boasting.
He referred to real behavior that exposed the character of the false apostles.
How astonishing that such people could bring their followers into bondage, take advantage of them and even insult them—and still retain their allegiance!

div.title: Paul's hardships as a minister of Christ (verses 22–33)
div.p: Paul recounted his work and suffering not from pride or love of applause, but to honor God, who had strengthened him for such service.
His experiences also revealed the difference between his ministry and the claims of opponents who tried to destroy his reputation and usefulness.
Consider the long record of dangers, deprivation, trouble and suffering!
And notice his patience, perseverance, diligence, cheerfulness and usefulness amid it all.
How little reason do we have to love this world's luxury and splendor when this blessed apostle experienced so much hardship while serving Christ.
Our hardest work and greatest sacrifices often seem small compared with Paul's.
Even our troubles may be scarcely noticeable beside his.
His example should lead us to examine whether we truly follow Christ.
Here we may learn patience, courage and steadfast trust in God.
Let us think less highly of ourselves.
Above all, let us speak strictly and consistently truthfully before God's presence, attributing everything to his glory as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, blessed forever.

row.cell: Which were improved to his spiritual advantage.
The signs of an apostle were in him, His purpose of making them a visit; but he expresses his fear lest he should have to be severe with some.

div.title: Paul's heavenly revelations (verses 1–6)
div.p: There is no serious doubt that Paul was speaking about himself.
He did not know exactly how his experience had occurred.
Perhaps heavenly realities were shown to him while his body remained in a trance, as had sometimes happened to earlier prophets.
Perhaps his soul was temporarily separated from his body and taken into heaven.
Or perhaps both his body and soul were caught up together.
Paul himself did not know, and Henry does not pretend to resolve the matter.
We are neither capable of understanding nor meant to know every detail of heaven's glorious life at present.
Paul did not try to publish a description of everything he heard.
Instead, he proclaimed the teaching of Jesus Christ.
That teaching is the foundation upon which the church rests and upon which our faith and hope must be built.
The vision should enlarge our expectations of future glory, but it should also make us content with the ordinary means God has provided for learning his truth and will.

div.title: The thorn in the flesh and sufficient grace (verses 7–10)
div.p: Paul explained how God kept him humble after receiving extraordinary visions and revelations.
The Lord allowed a thorn in the flesh so that Paul would not become proud.
Scripture does not tell us what this thorn was.
Henry leaves open whether it was a severe outward trouble or a powerful temptation.
God can turn even the reproaches of enemies to good by using them to expose and restrain our pride.
When God loves us, he will not leave us to become proud beyond measure.
Spiritual burdens may be used to cure spiritual pride.
Paul called the thorn a messenger of Satan.
Satan meant it for evil, but God overruled it for good.
Prayer is a remedy for every wound and a source of help in every illness or trial.
When we face thorns in the flesh, we should devote ourselves to prayer.
If an answer is not given at the first or second request, we should continue praying.
Troubles teach us to pray. Troubles that remain can teach us perseverance in prayer.
God accepts the prayers of faith, but he does not always grant what we ask.
Sometimes he grants a request in judgment; at other times he refuses a request in love.
If he does not remove our trouble or temptation but gives us sufficient grace, we have no reason to complain.
Grace includes God's gracious favor toward us.
It is enough to illuminate and strengthen our souls, sustain our life and comfort us amid suffering.
God's strength is made perfect in human weakness.
Our weakness becomes the occasion for his grace to appear even more clearly.
When we know we are weak in ourselves, we are moved to Christ for strength and enjoy the supply he gives.

div.title: Paul defends his concern for the Corinthians (verses 11–21)
div.p: We should defend the good reputation of faithful people when that reputation is unfairly attacked.
We owe particular gratitude to those whom God has used to bring spiritual blessings into our lives.
Paul's words demonstrate the character and intentions of a faithful gospel minister.
His chief aim was to do good.
He expressed concern that on his next visit he might find professing believers living in sins that required painful correction.
Even the failings of those under their care can deeply humble faithful ministers.
God may use those disappointments to humble ministers who would otherwise be tempted by pride.
The Corinthians' behavior showed how far the false teachers had drawn their followers away from godliness.
How grievous that such sins can be found among people professing the gospel!
Yet this happened even during the apostles' own lives and has happened far too often since.

row.cell: And ends the epistle with a salutation and blessing.

div.title: A warning and an examination of genuine faith (verses 1–6)
div.p: The Lord patiently bears with sinners because he is gracious.
But his patience does not mean that he will never judge.
Those who remain obstinate and refuse to repent will eventually meet the judgment they have resisted.
At the crucifixion, Jesus appeared weak and helpless to the world.
But his resurrection and living power revealed that he was truly divine.
Similarly, the apostles often appeared insignificant and contemptible in human eyes.
Yet God used them as instruments through which his power became evident.
Paul called the Corinthians to examine themselves.
They should test their attitudes, conduct and spiritual experience as gold is tested with a touchstone.
If they could see genuine evidence that Christ had accepted them, they ought also to recognize the authenticity of Paul's apostolic service.
We should examine whether Jesus Christ lives in us.
His presence is known through the Holy Spirit's work, the graces he produces and the establishing of Christ's kingdom in our hearts.
Let us question our own souls sincerely.
We are either genuine Christians or deceiving ourselves.
Unless Christ dwells within us through his Spirit and the power of his love, our claimed faith is dead and we remain unapproved by the One who will judge us.

div.title: Pray for holiness rather than merely escape from suffering (verses 7–10)
div.p: The greatest good we can pray for, both for ourselves and for those we love, is that we should not sin.
We have far more reason to pray to be preserved from doing evil than merely to be spared from suffering evil.
Paul wanted the Corinthians not only to turn away from wrongdoing, but also to grow in grace and holiness.
When we warn other people, we should also pray earnestly that they may stop doing wrong and learn to do what is good.
We should gladly see others become strong in Christ's grace, even if their growth reveals our own weakness.
And we should ask God to enable us to use every ability and opportunity he has entrusted to us.

div.title: Final encouragement and blessing (verses 11–14)
div.p: Paul ended his letter with several valuable exhortations.
God is the Author of peace and Lover of harmony.
He loves his people and is willing to live at peace with them.
We should therefore seek to live in such a way that separation from believing friends is only temporary.
We long to meet again in the world where parting will be unknown.

Paul's blessing asks that believers receive every benefit made available through the free grace and favor of Jesus Christ, purposed by the Father's free love, and applied and given by the Holy Spirit.
What a fitting conclusion to a letter containing both stern warnings and tender pastoral care!

row.cell: The apostle Paul asserts his apostolic character against such as lessened it.
He reproves the Galatians for revolting from the gospel of Christ under the influence of evil teachers.
He proves the Divine authority of his doctrine and mission; and declares what he was before his conversion and calling.
And how he proceeded after it.

div.title: Christ appointed Paul; grace and peace come from God (verses 1–5)
div.p: Paul was appointed an apostle directly by Jesus Christ, and therefore also by God the Father, who shares the Son's divine nature and appointed him to be Mediator.
Grace includes both God's loving favor toward us and the good work he performs within us.
Peace includes the inward comfort and outward wellbeing that are truly necessary for us.
Both blessings flow from the Father as their source through Jesus Christ.
Notice the order: grace first, then peace. Genuine peace cannot exist without grace.
Christ gave himself for our sins to make atonement for us. God's justice required that sacrifice, and Jesus accepted it willingly.
Consider the infinite cost paid for our sins!
Sin is so destructive that nothing less than the gift of the Son of God could put it away.
We ought to understand how dreadful sin is.
Pay special attention to the words “for our sins.”
Our sinful nature would prefer to make itself worthy through its works before coming to Christ.
It wants the healthy person, not the person who needs a physician, to be the Savior's patient.
But Christ died not only to rescue us from God's wrath and the curse of his law.
He also came to free us from the corrupt practices and habits to which we are naturally enslaved.
Those who have not been delivered from this present evil world through the Holy Spirit's sanctifying work have no basis for assuming that Christ's blood has saved them from its condemnation.

div.title: Paul warns against another gospel (verses 6–9)
div.p: Anyone seeking a different route to heaven from the gospel of Christ is tragically deceived.
Paul rebuked the Galatians because they were abandoning justification through Christ alone.
Yet he corrected them with tenderness, recognizing that false teachers had deliberately led them astray.
When we reprove others, we must be faithful to truth while seeking to restore them gently.
Some teachers wanted to put works of the law in the place of Christ's righteousness.
By doing so, they corrupted Christianity itself.
Paul solemnly declared a curse upon anyone who tried to establish such a false foundation.
Other so-called gospels may flatter human self-righteousness or make room for worldly desires.
Either way, they are Satan's inventions rather than Christ's gospel of grace.
We must hold two truths together.
Rejecting God's moral law as a rule for Christian living dishonors Christ and destroys true religion.
But trusting our supposedly good works to justify us before God is equally fatal for anyone who persists in that false hope.
Be zealous for good deeds, but never put them where Christ's righteousness alone belongs.
And do not teach ideas that could lure others into such a dangerous deception.

div.title: Paul's message came by revelation from God (verses 10–14)
div.p: Paul's aim in preaching was to bring people into obedience to God, not to human authorities.
He would never change Christ's teaching to gain people's favor or avoid their hostility.
In matters of eternal truth, we must not fear human disapproval or seek approval through merely clever speech.
Paul received the gospel through revelation from heaven.
Unlike many Christians, he had not been led toward Christ merely by upbringing or education.

div.title: Christ's grace transformed Paul's life (verses 15–24)
div.p: God wonderfully brought Paul to the knowledge of and faith in Jesus Christ.
Everyone who is genuinely converted is called through divine grace.
Conversion is the work of God's power, acting within the heart.
It benefits us little for Christ merely to be shown to us outwardly unless he is also revealed within us.
Once Paul received this call, he prepared to obey immediately.
He did not pause to protect his wealth, public reputation, comfort or even his life.
The churches rejoiced when they heard about his conversion.
What cause for thanksgiving whenever God's people learn that a former opponent has been brought to faith!

Even believers who have never met such a person should glorify God for his power and mercy in salvation and for all the service that new believer has already rendered or may yet render to Christ's cause.

row.cell: The apostle declares his being owned as an apostle of the Gentiles.
He had publicly opposed Peter for judaizing.
And from thence he enters upon the doctrine of justification by faith in Christ, without the works of the law.

div.title: The other apostles recognize Paul's calling (verses 1–10)
div.p: Paul faithfully explained the gospel he preached among the Gentiles and intended to continue preaching.
It was Christianity free from any requirement to become Jewish.
He understood that many people disliked this message, but he was not ashamed to acknowledge it.
He wanted to ensure that neither his earlier work nor his future ministry would be damaged by confusion or opposition.
Although we must trust God for the fruit of our work, we should still take reasonable precautions to prevent misunderstandings.
Some practices may be lawful in themselves.
But if accepting them in particular circumstances would betray gospel truth, we must refuse.
Nothing should be done that undermines the gospel.
Paul met the other apostles but received no addition to his knowledge or authority from them.
Recognizing the grace God had given him, they welcomed Paul and Barnabas as fellow workers.
They acknowledged Paul's equal apostolic calling, agreeing that Paul and Barnabas should go principally to the Gentiles while the others continued working among the Jews.
This division of labor agreed with Christ's purpose.
The gospel belongs to God, not to us. Ministers are entrusted with preserving and declaring it, never owning or altering it.
Paul also showed sincere charity toward Jewish believers, even though some of them were unwilling to show equal generosity toward Gentile converts.
Differences of opinion did not make him unwilling to help them.
Christians should extend such goodwill to all genuine disciples of Jesus.

div.title: Paul publicly corrects Peter's public inconsistency (verses 11–14)
div.p: Despite Peter's important calling and reputation, Paul rebuked him when his behavior harmed the truth of the gospel and the church's peace.
Peter and those who followed him acted inconsistently with the principle they professed.
Through Christ's death, the dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles had been removed, and believers were no longer bound to follow Moses' ceremonial law as a condition of acceptance.
Because Peter's error was public, Paul reproved him publicly.
Henry carefully distinguishes two actions.
Paul could wisely tolerate and temporarily observe Jewish ceremonies when they were not themselves sinful.
Peter, however, withdrew from Gentile believers in a way that encouraged people to think those ceremonies were necessary for salvation.
That was a failure of courage and a betrayal of gospel freedom.

div.title: We are justified through Christ, not the law (verses 15–19)
div.p: Having shown that he was not inferior to Peter or any other apostle, Paul turned to the gospel's foundational doctrine.
Why had they believed in Christ?
Was it not to be justified by faith in him?
Then how foolish to return to the law and expect justification by moral efforts, sacrifices or ceremonial observances!
Although the immediate controversy involved ceremonial law, the argument against dependence on moral works for justification is just as strong.
Seeking justification through Jesus does not make Christ a servant of sin.
Paul understood from the law itself that the law could not justify sinners by their works.
Its sacrifices and cleansings were no longer required because Christ had fulfilled them by offering himself for us.
As far as justification by the law was concerned, Paul was as dead to it as a dead person is to the threats of old enemies.
Yet this did not mean he could live lawlessly or carelessly.
Instead, he was freed to live for God, devoted to him through the motives and grace of the gospel.
The claim that justification by faith alone encourages sin is an old but entirely unjust accusation.
Using grace as permission for sin would make Christ the promoter of sin, a thought that should horrify every Christian heart.

div.title: Crucified with Christ, living by faith (verses 20 and 21)
div.p: Paul described the Christian's hidden spiritual life through his own experience.
The old person is crucified (Romans 6:6), yet the renewed person lives.
Sin is put to death while grace grows.
Believers enjoy the comforts and triumphs of grace, but none of that grace originates in themselves.
They live in complete dependence upon Jesus Christ.
Though still physically alive, they no longer live according to the sinful nature.
Genuine faith fixes upon Christ's personal sacrifice:

p.hi: He loved me and gave himself for me.

div.p: Paul had been moving farther and farther from God.
The corruption of his desires and understanding was so great that no lesser price could have redeemed him.
Consider what Christ paid!
Some claim to believe the Christian doctrines but have only the outward form of godliness without its power.
True faith in Christ crucified means more than accepting the historical fact that he died.
It includes being crucified with him, leaving the old way of life behind.
Grace can never be combined with human merit as its basis.
It would cease to be grace if it were not entirely free.
The more fully we depend on Christ for everything, the more willingly we obey his commandments.
He lives and rules within the believer.
We live by faith in the Son of God—a faith that works through love, produces obedience and transforms us toward his holy likeness.
Such a believer neither misuses God's grace nor treats it as worthless.

row.cell: The Galatians reproved for departing from the great doctrine of justification alone, through faith in Christ.
This doctrine established from the example of Abraham.
From the tenor of the law and the severity of its curse.
From the covenant of promises, which the law could not disannul.
The law was a school master to lead them to Christ.
Under the gospel state true believers are all one in Christ.

div.title: Christ crucified and the Spirit received by faith (verses 1–5)
div.p: The Galatians' departure from the gospel was especially unreasonable because Christ crucified had already been clearly preached among them.
They had also participated in the Lord's Supper, where his suffering and its meaning had been set before them.
Had they received the Holy Spirit by keeping the Mosaic law or by any meritorious works of their own?
No.
They received him by hearing and believing the message of justification through faith in Christ alone.
God's favor and approval had been demonstrated through that message.
How foolish to reject the ministry and doctrine through which God had already blessed them!
Sadly, people often turn from Christ crucified, the very heart of Christianity, toward empty distinctions, moral instruction without the Savior or unsupported religious speculations.
Satan works through different people and methods to blind minds so they will not trust the crucified Redeemer.
Where are the Spirit's fruits most clearly produced—where salvation is taught by works of law, or where it is taught by faith in Christ?
Henry answers confidently: among those who proclaim justification by faith.

div.title: Abraham was accepted by faith; Christ bore the curse (verses 6–14)
div.p: Paul used Abraham's example to prove the gospel doctrine the Galatians had abandoned.
Abraham trusted God's word and promise.
Through that faith he was regarded by God as righteous.
When Scripture is said to foresee something, the Holy Spirit who inspired it is the One who foresaw.
Abraham was blessed by believing God's promise, and others receive that blessing in the same way.
Let us study what Abraham trusted, the nature of his faith and the effects it produced.
No one escapes the law's curse through obedience, because its curse falls upon sinners and all have sinned.
A lawbreaker already stands under condemnation and cannot look to the same law as a way of earning acquittal.
The righteous are those rescued from death and wrath and brought into life under God's favor.
This happens through faith, not meritorious works.
Justification by faith was not an invention of the Christian era.
It was taught long before Christ's coming and has always been the only way sinners have been justified.
Though the law cannot free us from its own curse, faith in Christ can.
Jesus redeemed us by being made a curse for us.
Henry explains that Christ was made sin as a sin offering, not himself made sinful, and was placed for a time under divine punishment—not separated from God.
His suffering warns sinners to flee God's righteous wrath more strongly than the law's threats alone.
If the Father did not spare his Son when he bore our sins, how can the unrepentant expect to escape judgment?
Yet from the cross Christ freely invites sinners to take refuge in him.

div.title: God's covenant promise was not cancelled by the law (verses 15–18)
div.p: The covenant God made with Abraham was not cancelled when the law came through Moses.
God's promise was given to Abraham and his Seed.
It continues through Christ, who lives forever, and through those who belong to him by faith.
This helps us understand the difference between the law's promises and the gospel's promises.
The law addresses each individual person under its requirements.
The gospel's promises are made first to Christ, and then through him to those who are joined to Christ by faith.
We must distinguish promise and law, not only as abstract teachings but also in how they shape our desires and our lives.
If the promise is made dependent upon legal merit, it is turned back into law.
Keep Christ continually before your eyes as the sure defense of faith against any attempt to rely upon human righteousness.

div.title: The law reveals sin and points toward the promise (verses 19–22)
div.p: If God's promise already provided salvation, why was the law added?
Even Israel, the people chosen for special privileges, remained sinful.
The law did not introduce a second route to justification.
Instead, it revealed the seriousness of sin and showed sinners their need for God's promise.
It pointed toward Jesus Christ, through whom alone sins could be forgiven and people made righteous.
The promise came directly from God.
The law was given through the ministry of angels and through a mediator, Moses.
It could not therefore have been intended to cancel the earlier promise.
A mediator acts between parties, not merely for one against the other.
The law's great purpose was that, recognizing their guilt and inability to achieve righteousness by lawkeeping, sinners might believe in Christ and receive the promised blessing through faith.
God's holy, just and good law, which remains the standard of moral duty, cannot be an enemy of Christ's gospel.
When correctly understood, it supports the gospel's purpose.

div.title: The law leads sinners to Christ as a teacher leads a child (verses 23–25)
div.p: The ceremonial law could not itself give saving knowledge and life.
Its practices, especially sacrifices, pointed forward to Christ so that sinners might be justified through faith.
In this sense the law was like a servant charged with taking a child to school.
It led people to Christ, the Teacher who reveals the true way of justification and salvation.
The gospel gives believers a much clearer knowledge of divine grace and mercy than the older order did.
Many people remain like prisoners in a dark dungeon, content in their sins and blinded by Satan through worldly pleasures and interests.
When the sinner awakens, the true danger becomes clear.
God's grace and mercy now appear as the only hope.
The Holy Spirit often uses the law's warnings to awaken a conscience and reveal the need for Christ.
The sinner is moved to rely upon Christ's suffering and merits for justification by faith.
Then the law, under the Spirit's instruction, becomes a loved rule of duty and a standard for daily self-examination.
Used in this way, it leads the believer to depend more completely, not less completely, upon the Savior.

div.title: Through faith, believers become God's children in Christ (verses 26–29)
div.p: Genuine Christians enjoy privileges far greater than those experienced under the old covenant.
They are no longer treated like distant servants but received as children of God.
Having accepted Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior and relying upon him for justification and salvation, they receive the status of sons and daughters.
But no outward form or profession, by itself, secures these privileges.
Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not truly belong to him.
In baptism, believers put on Christ and openly profess themselves his disciples.
Baptism points toward being joined with Christ's death and resurrection, so that believers die to sin and live in newness and holiness.
But putting on Christ according to the gospel is not merely outward imitation.
It requires new birth and complete inward change.
The God who makes believers heirs will provide for them.
Therefore let us carry out the duties entrusted to us and commit every other care into his hands.
Our greatest concern should be heaven.
This world's things are small by comparison.
The heavenly city of God is the inheritance of his children.
Above all, seek to be assured of that inheritance.

row.cell: The folly of returning to legal observances for justification.
The happy change made in the Gentile believers.
The apostle reasons against following false teachers.
He expresses his earnest concern for them.
And then explains the difference between what is to be expected from the law, and from the gospel.

div.title: From bondage to the adoption of God's children (verses 1–7)
div.p: Paul spoke plainly against those trying to combine the Mosaic law with the gospel in a way that brought believers back into bondage.
The old covenant contained many demanding ceremonies and restrictions.
Like a child placed under tutors and guardians, God's people lived under a form of instruction that did not yet reveal fully what those observances meant.
The gospel brings Christians into a happier and freer condition.
These verses display the wonder of God's love.
The Father sent his Son into the world for our redemption.
The Son humbled himself and suffered for us.
The Holy Spirit graciously comes to dwell in believers' hearts.
We were by nature children of disobedience and exposed to divine wrath.
Through grace we become children whom God loves, and the Spirit begins shaping us into the family likeness.
In human families only the eldest son commonly received the special inheritance.
But every one of God's children shares the inheritance of an eldest son.
May our attitudes and actions demonstrate our adoption!
May the Holy Spirit bear witness with our spirits that we are God's children and heirs.

div.title: Do not return to the slavery of false worship (verses 8–11)
div.p: The Gentile Christians had turned from idols to the living God and had received adoption through Christ.
This change came entirely through God's free and generous grace.
How serious, then, to abandon the freedom he had given!
All genuine knowledge of God begins with him.
We know him because he first knew us.
Although Christianity forbids worshiping idols, many still practice idolatry in their hearts.
Whatever a person loves and values most becomes that person's god.
Some make wealth their god; others enthrone pleasure or sinful desire.
Some worship an imaginary god who possesses only mercy and no justice.
They assume God will pardon them even as they refuse repentance and continue in sin.
Even people who once professed faith confidently can be drawn away from the simplicity and purity of the gospel.
The more mercy God has shown us in giving us gospel knowledge and freedom, the greater our foolishness if we surrender those blessings.
Members of the visible church should therefore examine themselves carefully rather than resting in a few outward signs of religious life.
Paul feared that his labor might have accomplished little, yet he continued laboring.
Perseverance in duty despite uncertain results is wisdom and reverence toward God.
Each person should follow this rule in the place and calling assigned to them.

div.title: Paul appeals to the Galatians as their friend (verses 12–18)
div.p: Paul wanted the Galatians to agree with him about the Mosaic law, but also to remain united with him in love.
Whenever we correct someone, we should make clear that the correction comes from concern for God's honor and that person's genuine welfare.
Paul reminded them of the physical difficulty he had experienced when he first preached among them.
At that time they had welcomed him gladly as God's messenger.
But human admiration and respect are sadly unstable.
We should labor above all to be approved by God.
The Galatians once regarded themselves as happy to receive Christ's gospel.
Why should they now act as though it had been a mistake?
Christians must not stop telling the truth merely because some people might feel offended by it.
The false teachers pretended affection for the Galatians, but their motives were self-serving rather than sincere.
Paul gave an excellent rule: be zealous in a good cause at all times.
Zeal should not appear briefly and then vanish. It should remain steady.
How blessed the church would be if believers held to that kind of faithful eagerness!

div.title: Paul's concern until Christ is formed in them (verses 19 and 20)
div.p: The Galatians had begun to regard Paul almost as an enemy.
Yet he assured them of his genuine friendship and parental affection.
He was deeply troubled about their spiritual condition and wanted to learn whether they would recover from their present deception.
The strongest evidence that a sinner has received justification is that Christ is being formed within that person through the renewing work of the Holy Spirit.
But this inward transformation cannot be expected while someone continues seeking acceptance with God through the law instead of Christ.

div.title: Hagar and Sarah picture two covenant arrangements (verses 21–27)
div.p: Paul illustrated the difference between relying upon Christ and relying upon the law through Isaac and Ishmael.
The historical account of Sarah and Hagar has its ordinary literal meaning, but Paul explained that the Holy Spirit also intended it to point toward a deeper spiritual truth.
The two women form suitable pictures of two different covenant arrangements.
Sarah represents the heavenly Jerusalem, God's true church, living in freedom and becoming the spiritual mother of believers.
Those born of the Holy Spirit and united to Christ through genuine faith belong to Abraham's promised spiritual descendants.

div.title: Freedom in Christ, not a new bondage (verses 28–31)
div.p: Paul applied this interpretation to his readers.
Believers are children of the free woman, not the slave woman.

Since their privileges under the gospel are so great, it would be absurd for Gentile Christians to return to a legal arrangement that could not rescue even unbelieving Jews from spiritual bondage or condemnation.
Henry makes an important qualification.
We would not have identified this allegorical meaning in Sarah and Hagar if the apostle had not revealed it, but because the Holy Spirit disclosed it through Paul, its divine intention is certain.
The allegory explains the teaching rather than serving as an independent proof of it.
It illustrates the covenant of works and covenant of grace, and the attitudes of legalistic and gospel-minded religion.
Good works attempted in a person's own strength belong to the legalistic spirit.
Works arising from faith in Christ reflect the gospel.
The first spirit produces bondage to sin and death.
The second produces freedom—not freedom to sin, but freedom to fulfill duty.
The first spirit leads to persecution, while the second is marked by love.
People who treat God's servants with a violent, harsh or controlling spirit should examine themselves.
Even a genuine believer may temporarily fall back into an approach based upon personal merit or self-strength, especially through unbelief or neglect of God's promises.
Such a person may also treat other believers harshly instead of lovingly.
Yet this is not the believer's settled way of life.
A genuine believer will find no rest until returning to dependence on Christ.
Let us ground our hope upon Scripture and demonstrate through cheerful obedience that our hearts and treasure truly belong in heaven.

row.cell: An earnest exhortation to stand fast in the liberty of the gospel.
To take heed of indulging a sinful temper.
And to walk in the Spirit, and not to fulfil the lusts of the flesh: the works of both are described.

div.title: Stand firm in the freedom Christ gives (verses 1–6)
div.p: Christ will not be the Savior of anyone who refuses to trust and receive him as the only Savior.
We must heed Paul's warning to remain firm in the doctrine and freedom of the gospel.
The Holy Spirit teaches true believers to await everlasting life and righteousness as God's gift through faith in Christ, not as payment for their own good works.
A Jewish Christian might continue observing certain traditional ceremonies or make use of the freedom not to observe them.
A Gentile believer might likewise disregard those customs or participate in them.
The decisive issue was not trusting those practices as the basis of acceptance with God.
No outward privilege or religious label can make a person acceptable without genuine faith in Jesus Christ.
True faith is active: it works through love for God and for fellow believers.
May we be among those who, through the Spirit, await the hope of righteousness by faith.
The danger does not lie in the indifferent character of some outward ceremonies.
It lies in attaching saving value to them in place of faith in Christ.
Without faith expressing itself in love, everything else is worthless by comparison.

div.title: Keep running the Christian race without accepting false teaching (verses 7–12)
div.p: Christian life is like a race.
We must run faithfully and continue until the prize is obtained.
Simply claiming the name Christian is not enough.
Our manner of life should agree with that profession.
Many begin well but become distracted, slow down or leave the path.
Those who notice their faith weakening should ask seriously: What is hindering me?
The false teaching troubling the Galatians added works of the law to faith in Christ as necessary for justification.
Paul showed that such persuasion did not come from God but from Satan.
Churches must beware of encouraging those who follow destructive error and especially those who spread it.
When correcting wrongdoing, we should distinguish teachers who mislead from people who have been misled.
Some Jewish opponents resented the gospel's claim that Christ alone saves sinners.
If Paul had agreed that Mosaic observances must be added to faith for salvation, he and other believers might have avoided much persecution.
But even the first traces of this corrupting leaven had to be resisted.
People who persist in disturbing Christ's church with such teaching will face God's judgment.

div.title: Gospel freedom is for loving service, not sin (verses 13–15)
div.p: The gospel teaches godliness (1 Timothy 6:3).
It never provides permission to indulge sin.
On the contrary, Christ's freedom gives us the strongest reasons to resist and put sin to death.
The whole moral law is summarized in the command to love your neighbor as yourself.
Believers should help and encourage one another.
If they instead attack one another because of different opinions, the resulting conflict opens the way for spiritual harm.
The God of love may withdraw the felt comfort of his grace; the Spirit of love is resisted, and the evil spirit who seeks destruction gains an advantage.
How much better if Christians spent less energy biting and devouring one another and more energy opposing sin within themselves and their communities!

div.title: Walk by the Spirit and cultivate his fruit (verses 16–26)
div.p: When believers seek to live under the guidance and power of the Holy Spirit, sinful desires may still arise and struggle against them.
But those desires need not rule over them.
The Christian life involves a real conflict between remaining corruption and renewing grace.
Genuine believers long for the Spirit's grace to gain a complete and speedy victory.
Those who yield themselves to the Holy Spirit are no longer under the law as a covenant requiring merit or exposed to its curse.
Their hatred of sin and desire for holiness show the reality of the salvation they have received.
The works of the flesh are numerous and plainly sinful.
People who persist in them will not inherit heaven.
How terrible that many who profess Christianity nevertheless continue those practices while claiming to expect salvation!
The fruit of the Spirit describes the qualities produced by a renewed heart.

As Paul's list of sinful practices particularly includes actions that injure people and relationships, his list of spiritual fruits especially emphasizes attitudes and actions that make Christians kind and beneficial toward one another.
The Spirit's fruit both benefits the believer and makes Christian fellowship more joyful.
These traits give evidence of the Spirit's guidance.
The contrast teaches us which practices we must resist and which virtues we must cultivate.
Genuine Christians take that duty seriously.
Sin must no longer reign in their mortal bodies (Romans 6:12).
They seek to put it to death, not merely excuse it.
Christ will not acknowledge as his faithful people those who voluntarily surrender themselves as slaves to sin.
And it is not enough merely to stop doing wrong: we must learn to do good.
Our conduct follows the power that governs our hearts (Romans 8:5).
Let us labor to put the body's sinful deeds to death and to live in spiritual newness.
Do not seek vain praise, provoke one another or become envious.
Instead, cultivate more abundantly the good fruits which through Jesus Christ bring praise and glory to God.

row.cell: Exhortations to meekness, gentleness, and humility.
To kindness towards all men, especially believers.
The Galatians guarded against the judaizing teachers.

div.title: Carry one another's burdens (verses 1–5)
div.p: Christians should carry one another's burdens.
Doing this fulfills the law of Christ, which calls us to mutual patience, compassion and practical support.
We travel through life together and should help fellow travelers under heavy loads.
It is easy to assume that we are wiser and better than others and therefore entitled to lecture them.
But that attitude is self-deception.
Someone who claims a superiority that does not exist will eventually discover the bitter consequences.
Such pride wins no genuine respect from God or other people.
Paul calls every believer to examine their own work.
The better we know our hearts and conduct, the less likely we are to despise others—and the more willing we become to help them through weakness and suffering.
Sins that seem small when committed become a heavy burden when their account must be given before God.
No one can pay another person's ransom through personal ability.
Sin is a spiritual weight upon the soul.
When someone feels no weight of guilt at all, that is reason for especially serious self-examination.
Many people are spiritually dead and therefore have no awareness of sin's burden.
When we recognize its weight, we should seek release through the Savior and learn to avoid every sin.

div.title: Sow to the Spirit and do good without growing weary (verses 6–11)
div.p: Some people neglect religious duties while continuing to display an outward profession.
They may deceive other people, but they cannot deceive God.
He knows both conduct and motive, and he will not be mocked.
This present life is sowing time.
In the world to come, we shall reap the result of what is sown now.
There are two kinds of sowing: to the flesh and to the Spirit.
Those who live under the rule of sinful desires should expect misery and ruin, not eternal happiness.
But those who, under the Holy Spirit's guidance, live by faith in Christ and cultivate the graces of Christian living will reap everlasting life from the Spirit.
We often become tired of doing our duty, particularly doing good for others.
We must guard against that discouragement.
The promised reward is given to those who persevere in good work.
Every person should seek opportunities for useful service within their own responsibilities and means.
Do good while you are alive, making it a central purpose of your life.
When new opportunities arise, act on them as far as your abilities allow.

div.title: Boast only in Christ's cross and become a new creation (verses 12–15)
div.p: Proud and worldly-minded people often want just enough religion to preserve an impressive public appearance.
Paul's greatest source of joy and honor, however, was the cross of Jesus Christ.
By the cross he meant Christ's suffering and death, the saving work of the crucified Redeemer.
Through Christ's cross, the world is crucified to the believer and the believer to the world.
The more we contemplate what the Savior endured from this world, the less attractive its praise and pleasures become.
Henry illustrates this with the dreadful appearance of someone dying by crucifixion.
The person beholding such suffering is not charmed by the victim's former physical beauty.
Nor would a dying person hanging upon a cross be captivated by the earthly scenes still visible in the final moments.
Likewise, to those who truly believe in Jesus Christ, worldly attractions lose their power in comparison with him.
There is a new creation.
Old attitudes and desires give way to a new understanding and way of living through the regenerating work of the Holy Spirit.
Believers enter a new world.
Created in Christ for good works, they receive a life increasingly marked by holiness.
This change affects the mind and heart, leading us to trust Jesus and live for God.
Where such genuine inward and practical faith is missing, outward religious labels and professions accomplish nothing.

div.title: Peace and mercy in the grace of Christ (verses 16–18)
div.p: The greatest distinction between people is not status or religious ceremony, but a new creation formed in Christ's likeness through faith.
God promises peace and mercy to those who walk according to this rule.
Peace includes reconciliation with God, an untroubled conscience and the earthly comforts genuinely needed for our good.
Mercy means a share in the free love and favor of God in Christ, the fountain from which every other blessing flows.
God's written word must guide us, in both doctrine and conduct.
May his grace always be with our spirits, sanctifying, enlivening and comforting us.
May we remain ready to defend the honor of the truth that gives us life.
Paul carried the marks of Jesus in his own body—scars received from persecutors because he remained faithful to Christ and the gospel.
He addressed the Galatians as brothers and sisters, displaying humility and tender love.
He ended by praying that they would receive Christ's gracious favor, both in its actual benefits and in the assurance that it was theirs.
We need no greater blessing for happiness than the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Paul prayed not that Moses' law or righteousness earned by works would remain with them, but that Christ's grace would live in their hearts and spirits, giving life, comfort and strength.
His final Amen expressed both his earnest wish that this blessing might be theirs and his confidence that it would be granted.

div.title: Ephesians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Paul wrote this letter while a prisoner in Rome.
Its purpose appears to have been to strengthen the Ephesians in their faith in Christ.
He wanted them to recognize the greatness of God's love and the dignity and excellence of Jesus Christ, so they would not be shaken by the apparent disgrace of his cross.
Paul taught that they had been saved by grace.
Although they had once lived in a wretched condition, they now enjoyed the same privileges as Jewish believers.
He encouraged them to persevere in their Christian calling and live in a way that agreed with their profession.
That involved faithfully performing both the common duties of Christian living and the particular duties arising from family and social relationships.

row.cell: A salutation, and an account of saving blessings, as prepared in God's eternal election, as purchased by Christ's blood.
And as conveyed in effectual calling: this is applied to the believing Jews, and to the believing Gentiles.
The apostle thanks God for their faith and love, and prays for the continuance of their knowledge and hope, with respect to the heavenly inheritance, and to God's powerful working in them.

div.title: Grace, peace and a faithful profession (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: Every Christian ought to be a saint, someone set apart for God.
Those who do not truly belong to him here will not become saints in heavenly glory.
Genuine saints are faithful believers in Jesus Christ who live consistently with their profession of belonging to him.
Grace means God's undeserved love and favor together with the spiritual blessings that flow from it.
Peace includes the inward and outward blessings that are genuinely good for us.
Grace comes first; peace follows. There is no true peace without grace.
Neither grace nor peace comes from any source apart from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Even the most mature believers need fresh supplies of the Holy Spirit's grace and should long for further growth.

div.title: Chosen in Christ for adoption and holiness (verses 3–8)
div.p: Spiritual and heavenly blessings are the greatest blessings of all.
Possessing them, we cannot finally be miserable; lacking them, we cannot finally be happy.
These gifts flow from God's gracious decision in Christ before the foundation of the world.
He chose believers to become holy, separated from sin, dedicated to God and sanctified by the Holy Spirit.
Everyone chosen for happiness as the final goal is also chosen for holiness as the appointed path.
In love, God predestined believers to be adopted as his children through faith in Jesus Christ, publicly receiving the privileges of that relationship.
The reconciled, adopted, forgiven sinner therefore gives all the praise to the gracious Father.
His love planned redemption, did not spare his own Son, and brought believers to hear, trust and embrace his salvation.
What rich grace to provide his own Son as our Surety and freely hand him over for us!
This salvation does not encourage wrongdoing.
Instead, it reveals how hateful sin is and how seriously it deserves divine judgment.
The believer's conduct as well as speech should proclaim the glory of God's mercy.

div.title: The mystery of redemption and the Spirit's seal (verses 9–14)
div.p: God made known to believers the mystery of his sovereign purpose and the way he would redeem and save them.
These truths would have remained hidden forever if the Lord had not revealed them through his written word, the preached gospel and the Spirit of truth.
In his own person, Jesus Christ brought together God and humanity, who had been separated by sin, and satisfied the wrong that caused their separation.
By his Spirit he produces faith and love, uniting us to God and to one another.
Christ distributes his blessings according to his gracious will.
Through his divine teaching, some are brought to see the glory of truths that others continue to reject or even mock.
What a gracious promise that the Holy Spirit will be given to those who ask for him!
The Spirit's sanctifying and comforting work seals believers as God's children and heirs of heaven.
His present blessings are the first fruits of everlasting happiness.
We were created and redeemed for this purpose.
Everything God has done for us aims ultimately at the praise of his glory.

div.title: Paul prays for greater understanding and hope (verses 15–23)
div.p: God has stored up every spiritual blessing for us in his Son, Jesus Christ.
He calls us to seek and receive those blessings through prayer.
Even the strongest Christians still need others to pray for them.
When we hear encouraging news about Christian friends, we should respond by praying for their continued growth.
Genuine believers still need much heavenly wisdom.
Even the best of us resist God's rule at times, though submitting to him is the only path to true rest.
How often do we trade our inward peace for a brief pleasure!
If we spent less time arguing and more time praying with and for one another, we would see more clearly the hope of our calling and the riches of God's glorious inheritance.
We should long to experience the mighty power of divine grace beginning and continuing the work of faith within us.
It is extraordinarily difficult for a soul to trust Christ completely and place every hope of everlasting life upon his righteousness alone.
Nothing less than God's almighty power can produce such faith.
Christ supplies the needs of those who trust him and gives his blessings abundantly.
Being united to Christ himself, we share the fullness of grace and glory found in him.
How foolish to seek righteousness apart from him!
If we understood what we have been called to receive, we would eagerly seek Christ.
As we recognize our weakness and the strength of our spiritual enemies, we see more clearly the greatness of the power that converts the believer and guarantees the completion of salvation.
This knowledge should move us, through love, to live for our Redeemer's glory.

row.cell: The riches of God's grace towards men, shown from their deplorable state by nature, and the happy change Divine grace makes in them.
The Ephesians called to reflect on their state of heathenism.
And the privileges and blessings of the gospel.

div.title: Saved by grace from spiritual death (verses 1–10)
div.p: Sin is death to the soul.
Someone dead in trespasses and sins has no appetite for genuine spiritual happiness.
Seeing a dead body fills us with dread. The undying human spirit has departed, leaving behind the ruined remains of its earthly life.
But if we understood the matter correctly, we would be far more deeply disturbed by a soul spiritually dead in sin.
Living in sin means adopting the patterns of this world.
Wicked people become slaves of Satan, who works through proud and sinful desires and rules in hearts that resist God.
Scripture teaches that people are naturally children of disobedience and exposed to wrath, whether their sins take the form of bodily indulgence or the equally serious pride of the spirit.
What reason we all have to seek the grace that can turn children of wrath into God's children and heirs of glory!
The source of God's mercies is his great love and rich compassion.
Every genuinely converted sinner is a sinner saved from both sin and wrath.
Saving grace is God's free, undeserved favor.
He saves us not by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.
Grace also gives the soul new life.
A regenerated person now lives in holiness, having been born of God.
Through God's pardoning and justifying grace, that person is freed from sin's guilt.
While sinners roll in the dust, believers sanctified by Christ's grace are raised spiritually to sit in heavenly places, no longer ruled by this world's values.
God's past acts of conversion and salvation encourage future generations to hope in his mercy and grace.
Our faith, conversion and eternal salvation are not works we have accomplished.
No one can boast.
Everything is the gift of God, accomplished as he gives life through his power.
God also prepared us for good works.
He gives us knowledge of his will, while the Holy Spirit transforms us so that we increasingly glorify him through holy conduct and perseverance.
This teaching cannot honestly be used to justify wrongdoing.
Anyone claiming that salvation by grace encourages sin has misunderstood or rejected Scripture's teaching.

div.title: Remember what it meant to be far from Christ (verses 11–13)
div.p: Christ and his covenant are the foundation of all Christian hope.
Paul described the Gentiles' former condition in terrible terms.
But who could rescue themselves from that condition?
How sad that the same description may apply even to some people who have been baptized in Christ's name while still lacking genuine faith.
Consider the horror of being permanently separated from God's people, cut off from the body of Christ, excluded from the covenant of promise and left with no hope and no Savior.
A person in that condition has no fellowship with God as a loving Father and must face his righteous judgment.
What genuine believer can think about that danger without trembling?
Salvation is far from those who persist in wickedness.
Yet God comes close to help his own people through Christ's suffering and death.

div.title: Christ makes peace and opens access to the Father (verses 14–18)
div.p: Jesus Christ made peace through the sacrifice of himself.
In every sense Christ himself is our peace.
He is the author, center and substance of our reconciliation with God.
He also unites believing Gentiles and Jews into one church.
Through Christ's person, sacrifice and mediation, sinners are allowed to approach God as Father and are welcomed into his presence.
Their worship and service are received under the Holy Spirit's instruction, because they are united to the Father and the Son.
Christ purchased the right of access to God.
The Spirit gives us the desire to come, the strength to come and grace to serve acceptably.

div.title: One household and one holy temple (verses 19–22)
div.p: Paul described the church through several pictures.
It is a city: everyone truly converted receives the rights of citizenship.
It is a family household: believers become members of God's own family—his servants and children.
It is a building founded upon the teaching of Jesus Christ, proclaimed through Old Testament prophets and New Testament apostles.
God now dwells within every believer.
Through the power and presence of the Holy Spirit, God's people become his holy temple.

row.cell: The apostle sets forth his office, and his qualifications for it, and his call to it.
Also the noble purposes answered by it.

div.title: Paul's calling to make the gospel mystery known (verses 1–7)
div.p: Paul was imprisoned because he had faithfully preached God's truth.
Yet he was a prisoner of Jesus Christ, protected and cared for by the very Lord for whose sake he suffered.
The gospel's promises and joyful announcement all come from God's rich grace.
Through that message, the Holy Spirit ordinarily produces grace in human souls.
The mystery Paul described was God's once-hidden purpose of salvation through Jesus Christ.
Earlier generations had not received such a clear and full account of it as was given to the New Testament apostles and prophets.
A central part of the revelation entrusted to Paul was that Gentiles would be called to salvation through faith in Christ.
The gifts of divine grace are accompanied by God's effective power.
The Lord not only appointed Paul to his apostolic office.
He also equipped him to carry out its responsibilities.

div.title: The unsearchable riches of Christ are announced (verses 8–12)
div.p: When God gives people an honorable calling, he often makes them humble in their own eyes.
And where he gives the grace of humility, he gives the other graces needed for duty.
Notice how magnificently Paul describes the unsearchable riches of Jesus Christ!
Many have not received these riches.
Yet what a privilege even to hear them proclaimed and freely offered!
Those who refuse such a gift have no reason to blame its Giver.
Both the first creation—when God brought the world into existence from nothing—and the new creation, when sinners are transformed by converting grace, come from God through Jesus Christ.
Christ's spiritual riches remain as vast and certain as ever.
Angels marvel at God's wisdom in redeeming his church.
Yet self-satisfied and worldly people often dismiss that same wisdom as foolishness.

div.title: Paul prays for strength and a deeper knowledge of Christ's love (verses 13–19)
div.p: Paul seemed more troubled by the possibility that the Ephesians would become discouraged because of his suffering than by the suffering he had to endure himself.
He therefore asked for spiritual blessings, the greatest gifts of all.
He prayed for strength through God's Spirit in the inner person.
This includes strength of soul and faith so that believers can serve God and perform their duties.
When Christ's law is written upon the heart and his love is poured into it, Christ lives there.
Where his Spirit dwells, Christ himself dwells.
We should desire that good affections become deeply rooted and stable within us.
How wonderful to enjoy a settled awareness of God's love for us in Christ!
Consider the dimensions Paul uses to describe that love.
Its breadth reaches people of every nation and social rank.
Its length continues from eternity past to eternity future.
Its depth reaches people sunk in the deepest sin and misery.
Its height raises them into heavenly happiness and glory.
Those who receive grace upon grace from Christ's fullness can be described as being filled with God's fullness.
Should that not satisfy the human heart?
Why do we try to complete our happiness by filling ourselves with a thousand worthless distractions?

div.title: End prayer with praise (verses 20 and 21)
div.p: Prayer should naturally lead to thanksgiving and praise.
Because of what Christ has already accomplished in our souls, we may ask and expect even more from his grace.
The conversion of sinners and the comfort of believers will bring glory to Christ forever.

row.cell: Exhortations to mutual forbearance and union.
To a due use of spiritual gifts and graces.
And to take heed of the sins practised among the heathen.

div.title: Walk together in humility and unity (verses 1–6)
div.p: Few duties are urged more strongly in Scripture than living in a manner worthy of the calling to Christ's kingdom and glory.
Humility opposes pride.
Gentleness makes us reluctant to provoke others and slow to become offended or angry.
We discover so many faults in ourselves—faults we sometimes find hard even to forgive ourselves—that we should not be surprised to find weaknesses in others that are difficult to overlook.
All believers hope in one Christ and look forward to one heaven.
They should therefore be of one heart.
They share one faith in its object, Author, nature and power, receiving the same great truths of religion.
They have been admitted into the church through one baptism with water, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, as a sign of regeneration.
God the Father dwells in believers as within his holy temple, through his Spirit and special grace.

div.title: Christ gives different gifts for the body's growth (verses 7–16)
div.p: Every true believer receives some measure of grace for the mutual good of God's people.
Christ distributes his gifts in the way that seems best to him.
He received gifts and graces to give them to his church, especially the gift of the Holy Spirit.
The knowledge required is more than merely understanding Christian ideas or acknowledging intellectually that Christ is the Son of God.
It produces trust and obedience.
There is fullness in Christ, and every believer receives a measure from that fullness according to God's wise decision.
Yet we will not reach complete maturity until heaven.
