God's children continue growing throughout this life, and their growth brings glory to Christ.
The more someone uses their particular responsibilities and gifts for the spiritual benefit of other people, the stronger the evidence that genuine Christian love has taken root in the heart.

div.title: Put off the old life and put on the new (verses 17–24)
div.p: Speaking by Christ's authority, Paul urged the Ephesians not to live like unbelieving Gentiles who followed empty ideas and sinful desires.
People everywhere still live under the influence of confused, worthless thoughts.
We therefore need to distinguish genuine Christian life from a merely Christian name.
Without saving knowledge, people remain in darkness and often prefer the darkness to the light.
They resist holiness.
Yet holiness is what God commands and approves, and it reflects something of his purity, righteousness, truth and goodness.
The gospel's truth becomes especially beautiful when seen in Jesus himself.
Our sinful nature is described as an old person, made up of many related desires and habits that reinforce one another.
Corrupt desires are deceptive.
They promise happiness but actually deepen misery and lead toward destruction unless they are resisted and put to death.
We must take them off like a dirty, worn-out garment.
But it is not enough to abandon corrupt principles.
We must receive new and gracious principles in their place.
The new person is a renewed nature, created through God's mighty power and governed by regenerating grace.
That grace enables a new life of genuine righteousness and holiness.

div.title: Speak truth, control anger and work honestly (verses 25–28)
div.p: Paul gave practical examples of conduct that should adorn a Christian profession.
Reject falsehood.
Do not flatter or deceive people.
God's children should hate lying and refuse to practice it.
We must also guard against uncontrolled anger.
Sometimes wrong behavior must be confronted.
Yet even when displeasure is justified, we must express correction without sinning.
We give the devil an opportunity when early sinful impulses no longer grieve us, when we consent to them or when we repeat evil actions.
Resist sin and avoid even circumstances that invite wrongdoing.
Idleness creates temptation, including temptation to steal.
People should work diligently not only to provide for themselves but also to have something with which to help those in need.
What should we think of professing Christians who become rich through fraud, exploitation and deceit?
Charitable gifts cannot be acceptable when obtained through dishonesty or robbery.
God rejects the attempt to make an offering out of stolen goods.

div.title: Use words that build up and forgive as God forgave (verses 29–32)
div.p: Corrupt speech comes from corruption in the speaker and harms the thoughts and conduct of listeners.
Christians should avoid such talk.
Instead, through their conversations they should encourage people to think seriously and should strengthen, warn and comfort fellow believers.
We are called to be kind to one another.
True kindness grows out of love within the heart and expresses itself through humble, courteous conduct.
Notice how God's forgiveness becomes the reason for our forgiveness.
We had no rightful cause to sin against him, yet he forgave us.
We therefore ought to forgive other people as he has forgiven us.
Lies, corrupt speech and conversation that arouses sinful desires grieve God's Holy Spirit.
So do bitterness, rage, uncontrolled anger, shouting, slander and malice.
Do not provoke the holy and blessed Spirit to withdraw his gracious influences and felt presence.
Our bodies will be redeemed from the grave at the resurrection.
Wherever the Holy Spirit lives as the Sanctifier, his presence is the pledge of the joy and glory of that future redemption.
How lost we would be if God withdrew his Holy Spirit from us!

row.cell: Directions to a contrary behaviour, and to relative duties.
The duties of wives and husbands are enforced by the spiritual relation between Christ and the church.

div.title: Imitate God's forgiving love (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: God has forgiven believers for Christ's sake.
Therefore we should imitate God, especially in his love and willingness to forgive.
This is how beloved children should resemble their heavenly Father.
God's love shines most clearly in the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
We should continually consider the greatness of that love and shape our conduct by it.

div.title: Live as children of light (verses 3–14)
div.p: Sinful sexual desires must be opposed and put away.
We should fear and detest the sins Paul lists.
The warnings address not only obvious acts of wrongdoing but also practices many people consider unimportant.
Corrupt speech is not useful.
It pollutes those who speak and harms those who listen.
Christian joy ought to be expressed through words that contribute to God's glory.
A greedy person makes money into an idol, transferring to wealth the hope, confidence and happiness that belong to God alone.
Those who surrender themselves to sinful desires or love of the world do not belong to the kingdom of grace and will not enter the kingdom of glory.
Yet even people guilty of dreadful sins can become children of obedience when they repent and believe the gospel.
God's wrath is then turned from them.
How dare we treat lightly the very sins that call down his just judgment?
Sinners resemble people walking in darkness.
They do not understand where they are going or the consequences of their actions.
But God brings about a wonderful change through grace.
Believers must walk as children of light, with knowledge and holiness.
Works of darkness are unfruitful, whatever profit they seem to offer, because they end in ruin for those who refuse repentance.
We may share in other people's sins in many ways: through praise, advice, agreement or hiding their wrongdoing.
If we participate in their sins, we should fear sharing in their judgment.
Henry also says we should rebuke wrongdoing rather than quietly approve it.
A good person may be ashamed even to speak about sins that others shamelessly commit.
It is not enough merely to recognize that a behavior seems shameful.
We must understand that it violates God's holy law.
Like the prophets and apostles, we should call those asleep and dead in sin to wake up and rise, so that Christ may give them light.

div.title: Use your time well and seek the Spirit's fullness (verses 15–21)
div.p: Another safeguard against sin is careful, thoughtful living.
Without watchfulness, a person cannot preserve purity of heart and conduct.
Time is a gift entrusted to us by God.
When used outside his purposes, it is wasted.
If we have wasted much of our past, we should become more diligent in the time that remains.
Many dying people would gladly give the whole world to recover a little time.
Yet how little we value it now, and how freely we spend it on worthless things!
People often complain about the wickedness of the age.
It would be better if their concern moved them to redeem the time.
Neglecting our souls and remaining ignorant of duty reveal profound foolishness.
Drunkenness rarely comes alone.
It leads people into further sins and provokes God's displeasure.
The person ruled by drink becomes a terrible example to family and community and rushes toward ruin.
When exhausted or sad, we should not try to lift our spirits through intoxicating drink, which can deepen the misery.
Instead, seek through earnest prayer to be filled with the Holy Spirit, and avoid grieving our gracious Comforter.
All God's people have reason to sing with joy.
Even when we are not singing aloud, we should remain continually thankful.
There is never a shortage of reasons for gratitude—even during hardship—because God's dealings have a gracious purpose for his people.
He guides believers away from sin and teaches them to submit to one another in the duties he has commanded, for his glory and their mutual good.

div.title: Marriage reflects Christ's union with the church (verses 22–33)
div.p: Henry explains the wife's duty as submitting to her husband in the Lord, honoring and obeying him from a principle of love.
He describes the husband's duty as loving his wife.
The example for that love is Christ's love for the church: genuine, pure and constant despite her shortcomings.
Christ gave himself for the church so that he might sanctify her in this life and glorify her in the world to come.
He grants believers a principle of holiness and delivers them from sin's guilt, pollution and rule through the work of the Holy Spirit.
Baptismal water is the outward sign of that inward work.
The church and its members will not be entirely without fault until the day of heavenly glory.
But only those being sanctified now will be glorified then.
Paul's reference to Adam's words has a literal meaning about marriage.
It also has an additional spiritual meaning, as marriage provides a picture of the union between Christ and his church.
Human husbands and wives will both have weaknesses and failures in the present life.
Those imperfections do not cancel their married relationship.
All the responsibilities of marriage can be summarized by unity and love.
As we worship and rejoice in Christ's gracious, self-giving love, let husbands and wives learn their corresponding duties toward one another.
Such faithfulness can prevent many evils and spare families a great deal of pain.

row.cell: The duties of children and parents.
All Christians are to put on spiritual armour against the enemies of their souls.
The apostle desires their prayers, and ends with his apostolic blessing.

div.title: Children and parents honor God within the family (verses 1–4)
div.p: Children have a duty to obey their parents.
True obedience involves inward respect as well as outward compliance.
Throughout history, people who have honored their parents have often experienced the benefits of that discipline.
Parents also have serious duties.
They must avoid impatience and unreasonable harshness.
They should act prudently, explain what is right and seek to convince their children's judgment instead of relying solely on force.
Children should be taught through appropriate, compassionate correction and instruction in the duties God commands.
These responsibilities are often neglected, even in families that profess Christianity.
Some parents' behavior turns their children against religion.
That does not excuse the children's disobedience, but it may have contributed dreadfully to it.
Only God can change a heart.
Yet he often blesses parents' faithful teaching, godly example and prayers.
Parents who care mainly that their children will become wealthy or socially accomplished, while showing little concern for their souls, should not expect God's blessing upon that priority.

div.title: Servants and masters are accountable to Christ (verses 5–9)
div.p: Paul's teaching addresses the obligations of servants and masters.
Henry notes explicitly that in the ancient setting these servants were generally enslaved people.
The apostles instructed both enslaved workers and their masters in their duties so that wrongs might be reduced, until slavery itself was rooted out through Christianity's influence.
Workers are instructed to act with respect, honesty and faithfulness.
They should not merely pretend to obey while planning to disregard their responsibilities.
Nor should they work well only when their supervisor is watching.
The Lord Jesus sees their service, and devotion to him should make them sincere and diligent in every lawful task.
Work done in love rather than resentment can become easier to perform and pleasing to Christ.
Even humble and exhausting service carried out from duty and for God's glory receives his reward.
Those exercising authority also have obligations.
Act toward those under your authority as you would wish to be treated.
Be fair and show sincere concern for their wellbeing.
Do not be tyrannical, harsh or domineering.
You have a Master in heaven, and before Jesus Christ you and the people working under you are fellow servants.
If everyone remembered their duties toward God and the account they must soon give him, relationships within households would become more just and peaceful.

div.title: Put on the whole armor of God (verses 10–18)
div.p: Our spiritual struggle requires courage and strength from God.
Those wishing to show genuine grace must seek every necessary grace and put on the whole armor of God, which he supplies.
The armor is meant to be worn throughout the battle.
We cannot lay it aside until our struggle is ended and our course completed.
Our battle is not against human enemies alone, nor only against our remaining sinful nature.
We face an enemy who possesses countless ways to deceive unstable souls.
Evil spirits assault us in the things that concern our souls, seeking to destroy God's image within us.
By grace we must resolve not to yield to Satan.
Resist him and he will flee.
But every concession to evil gives him further ground.
If we doubt the justice of our cause, the faithfulness of our Leader or the strength of our armor, we give him an advantage.
Paul drew his picture from a heavily armored soldier facing fierce attack.
There is no armor for the back—nothing for someone who retreats from Christian duty.
Truth and sincerity are the belt that holds the armor in place.
There can be no true religion without genuine sincerity.
Christ's righteousness credited to us is the breastplate protecting us against God's judgment.
Christ's righteousness implanted within us also strengthens the heart against Satan's attacks.
Resolution protects our legs.
The gospel of peace prepares our feet to stand firmly or move forward over difficult ground.
We need a clear knowledge of the gospel to find proper motives for obedience during trials.
Faith is essential in the hour of temptation.
Like a shield, faith receives Christ and the benefits of redemption, relying on the unseen realities of his promise.
Satan's fiery darts include violent temptations and harsh thoughts about God or ourselves.
Faith applies God's word and Christ's grace to extinguish them.
Salvation is our helmet.
The solid hope of victory and eternal life helps keep our thoughts from being corrupted.
For attack, the apostle names one weapon only: the sword of the Spirit, God's word.
It opposes evil desires and blasphemous thoughts rising from within.
It also answers unbelief and false teaching arriving from outside.
Even one biblical passage understood accurately and used rightly can destroy a powerful temptation or objection.
Prayer holds every piece of our armor together.
We have many responsibilities, but we must keep regular times for prayer.
Formal prayer is not always possible while performing other duties.
Nevertheless, brief prayers lifted to God throughout the day are always appropriate.
Our ordinary thoughts should be directed toward holy things.
Prayer should include public, private, secret, shared, solitary, solemn and spontaneous petitions.
It should contain confession, requests for mercy and thanksgiving.
Every prayer must depend on the Holy Spirit's gracious help and instruction.
Continue praying even when answers seem delayed.
And pray not only for yourself, but for all God's people.
Our enemies are powerful and our strength is small.
But our Redeemer is almighty.
Through his strength we can overcome.

div.title: Pray for gospel ministers and receive the blessing (verses 19–24)
div.p: The gospel was a mystery until God made it known.
Ministers of Christ are entrusted with proclaiming that revelation.
Even the most gifted and respected ministers need the prayers of ordinary believers.
We should pray especially for servants of Christ exposed to severe danger or hardship through their work.
Paul wished his readers peace, love and faith.
Peace includes reconciliation with God, a clear conscience and harmony among believers.
The Spirit gives the graces that produce faith, love and every Christian virtue.
Paul asked for these gifts to increase even in people who had already begun receiving them.
Every blessing comes from God through Jesus Christ our Lord.
Divine grace includes God's favor and every spiritual and earthly good that flows from it.
Such grace belongs to those who sincerely love the Lord Jesus Christ.

div.title: Philippians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The Philippian believers cared deeply about the apostle Paul.

Paul wrote to strengthen their faith, encourage them to live in a manner worthy of Christ's gospel, warn them against teachers who wanted to impose Jewish practices, and express gratitude for their generosity and Christian kindness.
Henry describes this as the only one of Paul's letters containing no explicit or implied rebuke.
Instead, every part displays Paul's praise and confidence in the Philippians.
He addresses them with a particular warmth and affection that any attentive reader can recognize.

row.cell: The apostle offers up thanksgivings and prayers, for the good work of grace in the Philippians.
He expresses affection, and prays for them.
Fortifies them against being cast down at his sufferings.
He stood prepared for glorifying Christ by life, or death.
Exhortations to zeal, and constancy in professing the gospel.

div.title: Thanksgiving for God's work among the Philippians (verses 1–7)
div.p: The greatest honor of even the most distinguished minister is to be a servant of Jesus Christ.
Those who are not genuinely saints here on earth will never become saints in heaven.
Apart from Christ, even the best believers remain sinners, unable to stand before a holy God.
There is no genuine peace without grace.
True inward peace grows from knowing God's favor.
And all grace and peace originate with God our Father, the fountain of every blessing.
Paul had been badly treated at Philippi and had seen relatively little immediate fruit from his efforts.
Yet he remembered the believers there with joy.
We should thank God when other Christians grow in grace, receive comfort, develop gifts or become useful servants.
We benefit through their growth, and God receives the glory.
The work of divine grace will not reach perfection until the day when Jesus Christ appears.
Yet we may be confident that God will complete every genuine work of salvation he has begun through regeneration.
That confidence must not rest upon outward appearances, but upon evidence of a new creation leading to holiness.
Believers grow especially dear to the ministers through whose service they have received spiritual help.
Those who suffer together for God's cause should likewise hold one another dear.

div.title: Paul prays for growing love and discernment (verses 8–11)
div.p: Should we not love and show compassion to the people whom Christ loves and pities?
No one possesses so much of a grace that no further growth is needed.
Paul wanted the believers to recognize differences and choose what is most excellent.
Christ's truths and commands really are excellent.
They reveal their excellence to an attentive mind.
Sincerity should govern our behavior and is an ornament to all Christian graces.
Believers should not be quick to take offense.
They should be especially careful not to offend God or one another.
What brings God the greatest honor also brings us the greatest good.
We should not leave it doubtful whether our lives bear any spiritual fruit.
A small amount of Christian love, discernment and fruitful service should never satisfy us.

div.title: Paul's imprisonment advances the gospel (verses 12–20)
div.p: Paul wrote while a prisoner in Rome.
He wanted the Philippians not to be discouraged or ashamed of his suffering for Christ.
God's wisdom and goodness had turned his imprisonment into a means of advancing the gospel.
People who would otherwise never have known Paul or heard the message now learned about him and began asking questions.
Paul was troubled not only by enemies but also by supposed friends who preached Christ out of envy and rivalry, hoping to make his imprisonment harder.
What a miserable attitude toward a faithful servant of God!
Yet Paul remained composed and joyful.
If our troubles lead to blessings for other people, we should take comfort and even rejoice.
Every experience that contributes to our salvation does so through the Spirit of Jesus Christ.
Prayer is the means God has appointed for seeking that help.
Our highest ambition should not be to win human applause or escape the cross.
We should hope to remain faithful under temptation, contempt and suffering.
Let Christ decide how we can best serve his glory.
He may use us through hard work or suffering, through diligence or patience, by our living to honor him or even by our dying in his service.

div.title: To live is Christ; to die is gain (verses 21–26)
div.p: For a person who lives only for this world, death is great loss.
That person loses earthly pleasures, possessions and hopes.
But for a genuine believer, death is gain.
It ends remaining weakness and misery, delivers the believer from the troubles of life and brings the soul into possession of the highest good: Christ himself.
Paul's difficult choice was not whether earthly existence was better than heaven.
There is no comparison between those two conditions.
His struggle was between two good things: serving Christ here or enjoying Christ's presence in heaven.
Faith and divine grace can make believers willing to die.
On earth we continue struggling against sin.
With Christ, we will be free forever from sin, temptation, grief and death.
Nevertheless, those who have the strongest reason to desire heaven should remain willing to live and serve as long as God still has work for them.
When God gives mercies we did not expect, his providential hand becomes especially evident in them.

div.title: Live as citizens worthy of the gospel (verses 27–30)
div.p: People who profess Christ's gospel should behave like those who believe its teachings, submit to its commands and rely upon its promises.
The word translated conduct or conversation originally evokes the life of citizens who seek their city's honor, peace, safety and prosperity.
The gospel contains truths so valuable that they are worth struggling to defend and practice.
Opposition is real, and we must persevere.
People may drift carelessly toward destruction.
Those seeking heaven must remain watchful and diligent.
Christians can enjoy unity of heart and affection even when they differ in judgment on many lesser matters.
Faith is God's gift for Christ's sake.
The ability and willingness to trust him come from God.
If we suffer disgrace or loss for Christ's sake, we should also regard that opportunity as a gift.
But the bodily suffering itself does not earn salvation.
Persecution is not meritorious.
Our salvation comes from God alone, and both faith and patience are his gracious gifts.

row.cell: Exhortations to a kind, humble spirit and behaviour.
Diligence in the affairs of salvation, and to be examples to the world.
The apostle's purpose of visiting Philippi.

div.title: Practice Christlike humility and kindness (verses 1–4)
div.p: Paul continued calling Christians to unity of mind and a humble attitude, following the example of Jesus.
Kindness is the law of Christ's kingdom, the lesson of his school and the identifying clothing of his family.
The Lord's compassion toward us should move us to show compassion to one another.
Seeing believers live in loving agreement brings great joy to faithful ministers.
Christ humbled himself for our sake.
How inappropriate for pride to govern those who belong to him!
We should examine our own faults strictly, identifying our weaknesses quickly.
Toward others, however, we should be ready to make generous allowances.
Caring about other people does not mean becoming busybodies who interfere in every private matter.
Neither outward peace nor inward peace can endure without humility of heart.

div.title: Jesus Christ humbled himself and was exalted (verses 5–11)
div.p: Jesus Christ's example is the standard for our attitudes and behavior.
If we would receive the blessings of his death, we should seek to resemble him in life.
Henry explicitly distinguishes Christ's two natures.
In his divine nature, Jesus is the eternal, only-begotten Son who shares God's nature (John 1:1).
Equality with God was his by right, and he could rightly receive divine worship.
In his human nature, he became like us in every respect except sin.
Of his own free will he stooped from the glory he shared with the Father before the world existed.
The passage describes two states of Christ: humiliation and exaltation.
He did not merely assume a human appearance.
He entered a lowly human condition, without worldly magnificence.
His life was marked by poverty and suffering.
His deepest humiliation was dying on a cross, the death assigned to criminals and slaves, bearing public contempt and hatred.
His exaltation involved his human nature united to his divine nature.
At Jesus' name, everyone should bow—not because of the mere sound of a word, but because of the authority of Jesus himself.
Confessing Jesus Christ as Lord glorifies God the Father.
The Father wills that the Son should receive the honor rightly given to the Father (John 5:23).
What greater reason could there be for self-denying love?
Do we love and obey the Son of God in this way?

div.title: Work diligently because God is at work within you (verses 12–18)
div.p: Christians must diligently use the appointed means that lead toward salvation, persevering until the end.
We should be careful not to fall short despite our many privileges.
Work out your salvation, because God works within you.
God's action is not an excuse for laziness.
It encourages our greatest effort because we know our work, carried out by his grace, will not be wasted.
Yet in everything we must depend upon God's grace.
His gracious work within us awakens and strengthens our effort.
His favor is the reason he does such good within our souls.
Do your duties without grumbling or endless quarrelling.
Rather than constantly complaining about the work assigned, concentrate on performing it well.
Avoid giving others good reason to stumble.
God's children should be distinguishable from the world's prevailing conduct.
The more corrupt others become, the more careful we should be to remain blameless and harmless.
The teaching and example of consistent believers can light the way for others, like a lighthouse warning sailors away from rocks and guiding them safely into a harbor.
Let us shine in that way.
The gospel is the word of life, revealing eternal life through Jesus Christ.
Paul's language of running pictures energetic, determined effort.
His language of laboring pictures steadfast, careful work.
God wills that believers should rejoice often.
People blessed with faithful ministers have good reason to rejoice with them.

div.title: Timothy and Epaphroditus serve sincerely (verses 19–30)
div.p: We are in a good spiritual condition when fulfilling duty becomes natural to us—meaning sincere, willing and free from pretense.
We commonly place our own reputation, comfort and safety above truth, holiness and duty.
Timothy did not.
Paul hoped for freedom from imprisonment not primarily to enjoy himself but to do good for others.
Epaphroditus wanted to return to Philippi to comfort the believers who had been distressed over his illness.
Henry thinks his illness seems to have resulted from his service to God.
Paul therefore urged the Philippians to hold him in even greater affection.
Mercies restored after we nearly lost them bring a special joy.
That is a reason to value recovered health, friendship or service more deeply.
And blessings received in answer to prayer should produce particularly sincere gratitude and rejoicing.

row.cell: The apostle cautions the Philippians against judaizing false teachers, and renounces his own former privileges.
Expresses earnest desire to be found in Christ; also his pressing on toward perfection; and recommends his own example to other believers.

div.title: Christ's righteousness matters more than every human privilege (verses 1–11)
div.p: Sincere Christians rejoice in Jesus Christ.

The prophet referred to false prophets as silent dogs (Isaiah 56:10). Paul seems to have that language in mind when he warned against dangerous teachers. Like fierce dogs, they barked at and attacked those who faithfully professed Christ's gospel.
They insisted upon human works in opposition to faith in Jesus, but Paul called them evil workers. They were the concision, cutting apart and dividing Christ's church.

Every religious exercise is empty unless the heart is truly engaged. We worship God through the Holy Spirit's strength and grace, taking our joy in Christ rather than in merely outward practices or experiences.
We cannot guard too seriously against doctrines that oppose or misuse the gospel of free salvation.
If Paul had wanted to boast about human advantages or rely upon his own religious record, he had more reason than almost anyone to do so.
But everything he had counted as gain during his life as a Pharisee he now counted as loss because of Christ.
Paul was asking the Philippians to do nothing he had not already done, and to trust their souls to no foundation other than the One on whom he had staked his own eternal hope.
He regarded worldly possessions, religious distinctions and claims of personal merit as worthless compared with knowing Christ personally through faith in his salvation.
This was not merely an easy claim made while he still enjoyed life's comforts. Paul had actually lost everything for the privilege of belonging to Christ.
He went further. Whatever tried to rival Christ in his heart, or pretended to provide merit before God, he counted as the foulest refuse, something thrown away.
True knowledge of Christ changes a person's judgments, desires, conduct and character so deeply that the person seems to have been made anew.
It is far better to lack worldly wealth than to be without Christ and his word.
Paul therefore resolved to hold fast to Christ and heaven.
Guilty sinners need a righteousness in which they can appear before God. Christ provides that righteousness, and it is complete and perfect.
People who trust themselves cannot receive its benefit. Faith in Christ's blood is the appointed means by which we receive this saving gift.
We become conformed to his death as we die to sin, just as Christ died for sin. Through his cross, the world becomes crucified to us and we to it.
Paul was willing to act or suffer in whatever way was necessary on his path toward the glorious resurrection of believers.
This hope sustained him through all his labor and trouble.
He did not expect to attain that resurrection through his own righteousness or merit, but through the merits and righteousness of Jesus Christ.

div.title: Keep pressing forward toward Christ and heaven (verses 12–21)
div.p: Paul's sincere dependence upon Christ did not mean he had already obtained the prize or had already become perfectly like the Savior.
He refused to be satisfied with past service or his present measure of grace.
He reached forward eagerly to become more like Jesus.
A runner must not stop before finishing the race. Likewise, Christians who hope for heaven must continue pressing toward it through holy desires, confident hope and persevering effort.
Eternal life is God's gift in Jesus Christ. We cannot enter heaven as our home except through Christ, who is the Way.
Believers seek to become increasingly like him, including in suffering and death: they die to sin and crucify sinful desires.
Genuine Christians differ greatly in the progress they have made, but all experience something of this change. Christ becomes everything to them, and their hearts turn toward the world to come.
They may also differ in judgment about lesser questions.
Those differences should not cause believers to condemn one another.
They are united in Christ and expect soon to meet in heaven. Let them therefore stand together on the great truths they share and patiently await further light on less important matters.
By contrast, the enemies of Christ's cross set their minds upon sinful bodily appetites.
Sin is shameful, and is even more disgraceful when a sinner takes pride in it.
The life of those absorbed in worldly desires may seem pleasant for a time, but it ends in death and judgment. People who choose that path will share that end.
A Christian's life belongs in heaven, where Christ the Head is and where the believer's lasting home awaits.
Our citizenship and deepest affections should therefore be directed there.
Christ has also reserved glory for the bodies of his people.
At the resurrection, their bodies will not simply live again. They will be raised into a glorious condition, transformed by Christ's almighty power.
Let us be prepared for the return of our Judge.
Ask him daily to renew our souls in holiness, rescue us from spiritual enemies and make both our bodies and souls instruments of righteousness in his service.

row.cell: The apostle exhorts the Philippians to stand fast in the Lord.
Gives directions to some, and to all in general.
Expresses contentment in every condition of life.
He concludes with prayer to God the Father, and his usual blessing.

div.title: Stand firm in the Lord (verse 1)
div.p: Our confident hope of eternal life should make us steadfast and constant in following Christ.
Believers have different gifts and enjoy different measures of grace. Yet all have been renewed by the same Holy Spirit, so we are brothers and sisters in Christ.
To stand firm in the Lord is to stand by his strength and grace, not our own.

div.title: Agree, rejoice and bring every concern to God (verses 2–9)
div.p: Believers should seek unity of mind and be ready to help one another.
Paul had experienced the benefit of his friends' assistance and knew how much other gospel workers would value similar help.
Let us seek sound assurance that our names are written in the book of life.
Rejoicing in the Lord is deeply important to Christian living. Believers need to be called to it again and again, because that joy outweighs every reason for sorrow.
Let opponents observe our moderation concerning outward circumstances and the calmness with which we bear losses and suffering.
The day of judgment is coming. For believers it will bring complete redemption; for the ungodly, destruction.
Not every kind of concern is wrong.
There is diligent care, which is our duty and includes wise planning and an appropriate awareness of responsibilities.
But there is also anxious, distrustful care, which is sinful, foolish and destructive to inward peace.
The appointed remedy for oppressive anxiety is constant prayer.
We should not pray only at fixed times, but turn to the Lord in everything.
Combine thanksgiving with requests. Do not merely ask for what you lack; recognize the mercies you have already received.
God knows our desires and needs better than we do. He requires prayer so that we acknowledge our dependence upon him and learn to value his gifts.
The peace of God is the comforting knowledge of reconciliation with him, a share in his favor and hope of heavenly happiness.
No words can fully express its value.
Through Jesus Christ this peace protects hearts and minds. It keeps believers from sinning under troubles or being overwhelmed by them, granting calmness and inward contentment.
Christians should seek and preserve a good reputation for virtuous conduct before God and upright people.
We should remain faithful to every kind of virtue whether or not other people praise us.
Paul's teaching and conduct agreed. He offered his own life as an example.
The way to enjoy the God of peace is to remain close to our duty.
Every privilege and the whole of our salvation come from God's free mercy, yet the enjoyment of those blessings is associated with sincere, holy conduct.
Even that obedience is God's own work within us. All praise belongs to him—not to human beings, words or deeds.

div.title: Learn contentment in poverty and prosperity (verses 10–19)
div.p: Helping a faithful minister who is suffering is a good work.
Genuine Christian sympathy does not stop at feeling sorry for people. It moves us to do what we can to help them.
Paul had often known imprisonment, poverty, hardship and physical need.
Yet through every circumstance he learned to be content—to bring his desires into agreement with the situation God appointed and to use it as well as possible.
Discontent can arise even when circumstances are favorable.
Pride, unbelief, restless desire for what we lack and sudden dissatisfaction with what we possess all contribute to it.
When brought low, we should pray for patient submission and confidence in God.
When raised to prosperity, pray for humility and a heavenly mind.
A steady, contented spirit in every circumstance is a special gift of grace.
In poverty, believers should not abandon their comfort in God, distrust his Providence or pursue unlawful means of meeting needs.
In prosperity, they must not become proud, careless or worldly.
In fact, prosperity is a harder spiritual lesson than poverty, because plenty brings greater temptations than scarcity.
Paul was not writing to pressure the Philippians for another gift.
He wanted to encourage the charitable love they had already shown, assuring them that it would receive God's reward.
Through Christ we receive grace to do what is good, and through Christ we expect the reward.
Everything we possess comes through him. Therefore we should use everything for him and his glory.

div.title: Praise the Father and receive Christ's grace (verses 20–23)
div.p: Paul closed his letter with praise to God.
Even when weakness and fear trouble us, we should look to the Lord not as an enemy but as our Father, ready to pity and help us.
Glory therefore belongs to him as Father.
God's favorable acceptance of reconciled souls, together with every gracious quality produced within them, is purchased through Christ's merit and applied through his intercession.
For this reason those blessings are rightly called the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

div.title: Colossians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: This letter was sent because difficulties had arisen among the Colossians, probably through the influence of false teachers. Those difficulties led them to seek Paul's guidance.
The letter's purpose is to show that all hope of human redemption rests on Jesus Christ, in whom alone are complete fullness, perfection and sufficiency.

Paul warned the Colossians against both teachers who wanted to impose Jewish observances and notions arising from worldly wisdom, human inventions and traditions. All of these could undermine complete dependence upon Christ.
The first two chapters teach the beliefs Christians must hold. The last two chapters teach the conduct those beliefs require: the doctrine of faith and the duties of Christian life for salvation.

row.cell: The apostle Paul salutes the Colossians, and blesses God for their faith, love, and hope.
Prays for their fruitfulness in spiritual knowledge.
Gives a glorious view of Christ.
And sets out his own character, as the apostle of the Gentiles.

div.title: Faith, hope and love grow from the gospel (verses 1–8)
div.p: All genuine Christians are brothers and sisters in Christ.
Faithfulness should mark every Christian role and relationship.
Faith, hope and love are the three great graces of the Christian life, and we have reason to bring each of them before God in prayer and thanksgiving.
When we place our hope firmly in the reward God has prepared in the life to come, we become more willing to use earthly resources for the good of others.
The heavenly inheritance is safely stored for believers; no enemy can take it away.
The gospel is God's true word, and we can safely entrust our souls to its promises.
Those who hear the gospel should also bear its fruit.
They ought to obey it, allowing it to shape their convictions, principles and conduct.
Worldly affection often arises from advantage or similarity in habits. Carnal affection seeks pleasure.
Both forms of affection are easily mixed with selfishness and other corrupt motives.
But Christian love is born of the Holy Spirit and is marked by holiness.

div.title: Paul's prayer for knowledge, strength and endurance (verses 9–14)
div.p: Paul prayed continually that the believers would be filled with knowledge of God's will and spiritual wisdom.
Good words are not enough without good works.
The God who gives his people strength possesses glorious power, and the blessed Holy Spirit is the source of this work within them.
God's promises are abundant. We need not restrict our prayers or hopes for spiritual strength as though he lacked resources to provide it.
God's grace in the believer's heart is his power, a power full of glory.
A special purpose of this strength is to sustain us during suffering.
There remains work to be done even when we are afflicted.
Amid trials, believers can give thanks to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose special grace prepares them to share in the inheritance of the saints.
Those once enslaved by Satan become willing subjects of Jesus Christ.
Everyone destined for heaven must be prepared for heaven while still here.
Those who receive the inheritance of God's children must also receive the training and character of his children.
Through faith in Christ, they enjoy redemption, purchased through his atoning blood, and thus receive forgiveness of sins and every spiritual blessing.
What mercy to be delivered from Satan's kingdom and brought into the kingdom of Christ!
All present suffering will eventually end, and every believer will be among those who come through great tribulation into glory.

div.title: Christ creates, sustains and reconciles all things (verses 15–23)
div.p: In his human nature, Christ makes the invisible God visible.
Whoever has seen Christ has seen the Father.
We should contemplate these mysteries with humble faith, recognizing God's glory in Jesus Christ.
Scripture describes the Son as born or begotten before any creature existed, representing his eternity in language we can understand.
All things were created through him and for him.
His power brought them into existence.
They exist according to his will and for his praise and glory.
He also sustains everything by his powerful word.
As Mediator, Christ is the Head of the church, which is his body.
All its grace, strength and life come from him.
All fullness dwells in Christ: fullness of merit and righteousness, strength and grace sufficient for all who believe.
God displayed his justice by requiring complete satisfaction for sin.
Christ's death was the fitting means through which sinners could be redeemed and reconciled to their Maker.
Though God hates sin, he was pleased to reconcile fallen human beings to himself through Jesus Christ.
We were formerly enemies in our minds, displaying hostility through wicked actions.
Yet through Christ's sacrifice and death in our human nature, we can be reconciled.
We should neither explain away these mysteries nor imagine that our limited minds can comprehend them completely.
Rather, we should behold the beauty of this plan of salvation and rejoice in the hope it gives.
If God has shown such extraordinary love toward us, how should we respond?
Be constant in prayer and diligent in holy service.
Do not continue living for yourself.
Christ died for us not so that we would persist in sin, but so that we would die to sin and live for him.

div.title: Paul serves Christ's church through suffering (verses 24–29)
div.p: The sufferings of Christ the Head and of his church as the members of his body are spoken of together.
Yet their purposes are not the same.
Christ suffered to redeem his church. His people suffer for other reasons.
The afflictions we endure are a small share compared with the bitter cup he drank for us.
A Christian can be said to complete what remains of Christ's sufferings when that person takes up the cross, follows his example and patiently bears the trials God assigns.
Let us thank God for revealing mysteries hidden through many generations and for making known the riches of his glory among us.
Since Christ is preached among us, we should ask seriously: Does he truly live and reign within us?
Only Christ's indwelling provides a firm ground for the hope of his glory.
We must remain faithful even to death, enduring every trial, so that we may receive the crown of life and reach the final purpose of our faith—the salvation of our souls.

row.cell: The apostle expresses his love to, and joy in believers.
He cautions against the errors of heathen philosophy; also against Jewish traditions, and rites which had been fulfilled in Christ.
Against worshipping angels; and against legal ordinances.

div.title: Christ contains the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (verses 1–7)
div.p: Our souls prosper when we acquire clear knowledge of the truth as it is in Jesus.
That truth should be believed in the heart and confessed openly when circumstances call for it.
Knowledge and genuine faith make a soul rich.
The stronger our faith and the warmer our love, the greater comfort we receive.
The treasures of wisdom are hidden in Christ not to keep them from us, but to preserve them for us.
They remain hidden from proud unbelievers, yet are displayed in Christ's person and saving work.
Beware of persuasive but misleading words.
Evil ideas and practices often appear attractive through clever disguises.
People who try to draw us into wickedness aim to rob us of what is precious.
Every professing Christian claims to have received Jesus Christ as Lord, agreeing to belong to him.
But we cannot grow in Christ until we are first rooted in him and founded upon him.
Having been established in faith, we should continue increasing in it and developing its fruits.
Thanksgiving must accompany this growth.
God justly withholds some blessings when people receive his gifts without grateful hearts.

div.title: Complete in Christ, not in religious shadows (verses 8–17)
div.p: There is a form of philosophy that rightly exercises our minds.
By studying God's works in creation, it leads us toward knowledge of him and confirms faith.
But there is another kind of philosophy that is empty and deceptive, entertaining human imagination while undermining belief.
It involves speculative questions beyond our knowledge or of no real importance.
Following the world's patterns draws us away from Christ.
All the ceremonies of the old covenant were shadows.
Their true substance is found in Jesus Christ.
His complete sacrifice for sin and his revelation of God's will supply everything those outward observances could not provide.
To be complete in Christ means to possess everything necessary for salvation.
We are in him not merely when we look toward a distant Savior, but when the Holy Spirit creates faith in our hearts and joins us to Christ our Head.

Inward circumcision of the heart, putting sinful desires to death, dying and being buried to sin and the world, and rising to newness of life are realities portrayed in baptism and brought about through Spirit-given faith.
These show that God forgives sins and frees believers from the law's curse.
We were spiritually dead in sins, but Christ makes us alive.
His death is the death of our sins; his resurrection brings life to our souls.
Christ removed the ordinances that burdened Jewish believers and formed a dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles.
When the substance came, the shadows disappeared.
Every mortal human being is guilty under the written law's sentence of death.
How dreadful, then, the condition of those who scorn the Son of God's blood, through which alone that condemning record can be wiped away!
Do not be troubled by narrow, legalistic judgments concerning food, drink and Jewish festivals.
Setting aside time for God's worship and service is a moral obligation that does not change.
But the obligation is not inseparably tied to the seventh day of the week.
Christians keep the first day, the Lord's Day, in remembrance of his resurrection.
All Jewish ceremonies were shadows pointing toward the gospel's blessings.

div.title: Christ alone is our Mediator and Head (verses 18–23)
div.p: Appealing to angels for help can appear humble, as though people admitted they were too unworthy to speak directly to God.
But this is not permissible worship.
It gives a created being the honor belonging to Christ alone.
Such apparent humility is actually pride.
Worshiping angels means failing to honor Christ, the only Mediator between God and humanity.
To seek other spiritual intercessors is to insult the Lord, the Head of the church.
Those who release their hold on Christ grasp at things that cannot help them.
Christ's body, the church, is a growing body.
Genuine believers cannot live according to the world's fashions.
Wisdom means remaining close to the gospel's appointed means, entirely submitted to Jesus Christ, the church's only Head.
Self-imposed hardship and fasting can look like exceptional spirituality or willingness to suffer.
But practices invented by human preference do not honor God merely because they are difficult.
They actually gratify self-will, self-admiration, self-righteousness and contempt for others.
Their appearance of wisdom is extremely shallow, and they do not provide true spiritual benefit or overcome sinful desires.
Let us regard as morally indifferent whatever the Lord has left to individual freedom.
Grant other believers the same liberty.
Remember how quickly earthly things pass away, and use them to glorify God.

row.cell: The Colossians exhorted to be heavenly-minded;
to live in mutual love, forbearance, and forgiveness;
and to practise the duties of wives and husbands, children, parents, and servants.

div.title: Seek what is above, where Christ reigns (verses 1–4)
div.p: Because Christians are free from the ceremonial requirements of the Mosaic law, they should pursue gospel obedience all the more carefully.
Heaven and earth pull our affections in different directions.
We cannot make both the chief purpose of our lives.
Love for the one weakens attachment to the other.
Regenerated people are dead to sin because its dominion has been broken through grace.
Its remaining power is gradually reduced as God's Spirit works in the soul.
At last, when believers are perfected in heavenly glory, sin's power will disappear completely.
To be dead in this sense means that the Holy Spirit enables us to put sinful desires to death, value earthly things less and long for heavenly blessings more.
We have not yet seen Jesus Christ with our own eyes.
But our comfort is that our life is secure with him.
The Holy Spirit brings the living water of Christ's grace into believers' souls through faith.
Christ lives within them by his Spirit, and they live for him in everything they do.
When Christ returns, all the redeemed will be gathered together.
Those whose lives are now hidden with him will appear with him in glory.
Since we look forward to such happiness, why should we set our deepest affections upon a world that passes away?

div.title: Put to death sinful desires and worldly greed (verses 5–11)
div.p: We must oppose the sinful habits and impulses that draw us toward the world's values.
Treat them like weeds or destructive pests that spread and ruin everything around them.
They must be put to death, restrained and continually resisted.
Make no provision for satisfying sinful desires.
Avoid situations that tempt us, including sensual indulgence, attachment to worldly pleasures and greed.
Greed is idolatry because it gives earthly things the love and devotion that belong to God.
Sin must be put to death because if we do not destroy it, it will destroy us.
The gospel transforms not only bodily desires but also the higher faculties of the mind and soul.
It strengthens the proper rule of reason and conscience over appetite and passion.
Country of origin, social position and the circumstances of life do not establish different standards of holiness.
Everyone is called to be holy.
For the Christian, Christ is all—the only Lord and Savior, the foundation of every hope and the source of all true happiness.

div.title: Clothe yourselves with compassion, forgiveness and gratitude (verses 12–17)
div.p: Christian duty includes more than avoiding harm.
We must do all the good we can for other people.
Those chosen and loved by God ought to be humble and compassionate toward everyone.
While sin remains in our hearts, disagreement and conflict may still occur.
But believers must forgive one another, imitating the forgiveness through which we ourselves have been saved.
Let God's peace rule in our hearts.
It is his own work among his people.
Thanksgiving to God helps make our character agreeable and useful to others.
The gospel is the word of Christ.
Many people possess that word but allow it to live within them only weakly. It has little authority over their lives.
Our souls flourish when we are filled with Scripture and the grace of Christ.
When we sing psalms, our hearts should feel the truths we sing, rather than merely pronounce words.
Whatever our occupation, perform everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, relying upon him with faith.
Those who do all things in his name will never lack reasons for gratitude to God the Father.

div.title: Serve Christ faithfully in every household relationship (verses 18–25)
div.p: The New Testament letters that most fully proclaim God's grace and the glory of Christ are also among those that explain our ordinary Christian responsibilities most carefully.
We must never separate gospel privileges from gospel duties.
Henry describes wives' duty as submission to their own husbands, not to cruel rulers or harsh tyrants.
Their husbands are bound to treat them with tender, faithful love.
Children who obey their parents are most likely to prosper.
Parents must likewise be gentle and compassionate, while children fulfill their duty of obedience.
Servants should obey their masters in everything consistent with their duty to God, their heavenly Master.
Their work must be just, honest and diligent, not driven by selfish calculation or outward pretense.
Believers who fear God remain faithful even when no human supervisor watches, because they know God sees their conduct.
They should work energetically rather than lazily, and cheerfully rather than resenting the position in which Providence has placed them.
Their encouragement is that through lawful and faithful service they serve Christ himself, who will reward them gloriously.
But those who do wrong will be held accountable for the wrong.
This applies equally to masters who treat servants unjustly.
The righteous Judge will judge both parties fairly.
Master and servant stand on the same level before his tribunal.
How much happier would the world be if genuine Christianity influenced every rank, relationship and condition of life!
But people who profess the gospel while neglecting duties and giving just grounds for complaint to those around them deceive themselves and bring disgrace upon Christ's message.

row.cell: Masters to do their duty towards servants.
Persons of all ranks to persevere in prayer, and Christian prudence.
The apostle refers to others for an account of his affairs.
Sends greetings; and concludes with a blessing.

div.title: Masters must treat servants justly (verse 1)
div.p: Paul continued addressing the obligations of masters toward their servants.
They must provide not only basic justice, but strict fairness and kindness.
Masters should treat those under their authority in the same manner they hope God will treat them.

div.title: Persevere in prayer and speak with gracious wisdom (verses 2–6)
div.p: No Christian duty can be performed rightly unless we continue in earnest prayer and remain alert with thanksgiving.
Believers should pray especially for their ministers.
They should also act rightly toward people who do not believe.
In every encounter with unbelievers, we ought to seek their good and commend the Christian faith by every appropriate means.
Use your time diligently.
Even when a Christian commits no obvious act of wrongdoing, simple carelessness may cause other people to develop lasting prejudice against the gospel.
Let all our conversation be wise and suited to the occasion.
The subject need not always be spiritual, but the conversation must always be conducted with Christian grace.
Even when discussing ordinary things, our manner should reflect the Lord we serve.
Grace is like salt seasoning our speech, keeping it from corruption.
It is not enough merely to answer another person's question.
We must answer truthfully, wisely and in an appropriate way.

div.title: Fellow servants share Christ's privileges (verses 7–9)
div.p: Gospel ministers serve Jesus Christ and are also fellow servants to one another.
They share one Lord, though he assigns different responsibilities and abilities to each.
Knowing that other believers care about us brings tremendous comfort when we face life's troubles.
Earthly position or circumstances make no difference to the spiritual relationship between sincere Christians.
They share the same gospel privileges and should receive the same respect and love.
See the wonderful change divine grace produces!
Previously unfaithful servants become faithful, beloved brothers, and people who once acted wrongly become trustworthy partners in doing good.

div.title: Paul commends faithful coworkers and ends with grace (verses 10–18)
div.p: Paul had once disagreed seriously with Barnabas over Mark.
But now he was not merely reconciled with Mark—he recommended him to the churches.
What an example of Christian forgiveness!
When someone has sincerely turned from a fault, we should not hold it against that person forever.
We must forget as well as forgive.
Paul drew strength and encouragement from the fellowship of saints and gospel ministers.
Some were fellow servants, others fellow prisoners, and all shared in working out their own salvation while seeking the salvation of other people.
Earnest, effective prayer has great power.
Yet some who are called to ministry fall short of their responsibilities.
Worldly praise or criticism, the influence of false teaching or selfish ambition can draw them into preaching and living in ways that fail to fulfill their calling.
But those who proclaim the same gospel Paul preached and follow his example may expect God's favor and blessing.

div.title: 1 Thessalonians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: This letter is generally regarded as the earliest of Paul's epistles.
Henry says it appears to have been written following encouraging news that the church in Thessalonica remained steadfast in faith in the gospel.
The letter is marked by affection and confidence.
Compared with some other Pauline letters, it offers more comfort and practical instruction and less extended doctrinal discussion.

row.cell: The faith, love, and patience of the Thessalonians, are evident tokens of their election which was manifested in the power with which the gospel came to them.
Its powerful and exemplary effects upon their hearts and lives.

div.title: Faith, love and hope show God's powerful work (verses 1–5)
div.p: Every good gift comes from God, and sinners have no lasting good to expect except from God through Christ.
Because God has become our Father through Jesus, we can seek from him the very best blessings.
We should pray not only for ourselves but continually remember other believers before God.
Genuine faith acts. It changes both the heart and the conduct of the person who believes.
Faith works through love for God and love for neighbors.
Well-grounded hope of eternal life produces patient endurance.
Sincerity is shown when, in everything we do, we seek above all God's approval.
How can we recognize the evidence of God's electing grace?
Not merely through religious words on our lips, but through the gospel's power within our hearts.
That power puts sinful desires to death, loosens our attachment to the world and lifts our thoughts toward heavenly things.
Unless the Holy Spirit comes with God's word, its words remain a dead letter to the hearer.
The Thessalonians received the gospel through the power of the Holy Spirit.
They became so convinced of its truth that doubts and objections could not easily unsettle them.
They were willing to give up everything for Jesus and entrust their souls and eternal destiny to the gospel's revelation.

div.title: Conversion gives visible testimony and hope in Christ's return (verses 6–10)
div.p: When careless, ignorant or immoral people turn from sinful habits and relationships to trust and obey the Lord Jesus, their changed lives become a powerful witness.
They begin living soberly, righteously and devotedly toward God.
Such a transformation speaks for itself.
Old Testament believers waited for the Messiah's first coming.
Christians now wait for his return.
He has not yet returned, but God has raised him from the dead.
This resurrection gives everyone an assurance that Christ will come to judge the world.
He came first to purchase salvation.
When he comes again, he will bring salvation to its full completion, granting final deliverance from the wrath still to come.
Let everyone flee without delay from that wrath and take refuge in Jesus Christ and his salvation.

row.cell: The apostle reminds the Thessalonians of his preaching and behaviour.
And of their receiving the gospel as the word of God.

div.title: Paul preached honestly, not for personal gain (verses 1–6)
div.p: Paul's ministry was not motivated by worldly ambition or self-interest.
Suffering for a good cause should strengthen our holy determination, not destroy it.
The gospel met powerful opposition from the beginning.
Its messengers struggled earnestly to proclaim it in the face of hostile resistance.
Paul's message was true and pure, and his manner of speaking was without deceit.
Christ's gospel aims to put sinful desires to death and bring people under the living power of faith.
Our strongest reason for sincere conduct is to remember that God sees everything we do and knows even the most distant thoughts of our hearts.
He searches our motives, and from him alone comes the reward we should seek.
Paul demonstrated sincerity by refusing flattery, greed, ambitious self-promotion and empty pursuit of praise.

div.title: Gentle care and a worthy life (verses 7–12)
div.p: Gentleness and tenderness beautifully commend Christian faith.
They most closely resemble God's gracious way of dealing with sinners through the gospel.
They are also among the best means of winning people.
We should be faithful not only in our general Christian calling, but also in the particular roles and relationships God assigns to us.
Our great gospel privilege is that God has called us to his kingdom and glory.
Our corresponding duty is to walk in a manner worthy of God.
Our chief work in life should be to honor, serve and please him.

div.title: The word of God bears fruit amid persecution (verses 13–16)
div.p: God's word should be received with affections suited to its holiness, wisdom, truth and goodness.
Human words are as fragile as the people who speak them.
They can be false, foolish and unreliable.
But God's word is holy, wise, just and faithful.
We should treat it accordingly.
That word worked powerfully within the Thessalonians, making them an example to others through faith, good works and patient endurance of persecution.
Murder and persecution are hateful to God.
No kind of religious zeal can ever excuse them.
Few actions more seriously fill up people's measure of sin than opposing the gospel or blocking others from hearing the way of salvation.
Many despise Christ's pure gospel, and its faithful proclamation has been obstructed in many ways.
But those who prevent spiritually dead sinners from hearing the message cannot claim to please God.
People who deny others access to the Bible have cruel hearts.
They oppose both God's glory and the salvation of their neighbors.

div.title: Paul's longing for reunion and Christ's coming (verses 17–20)
div.p: Our time together in this world is brief and uncertain.
In heaven, holy souls will meet again and never be separated.
Paul wanted to return to his friends.
He could not come at that moment and feared he might never be able to see them again during earthly life.
Yet Jesus Christ himself will return, and nothing can prevent that coming.
May God provide faithful ministers to those who serve him in the gospel of his Son.
May he send such servants into places still darkened by unbelief.

row.cell: The apostle sent Timothy to establish and comfort the Thessalonians.
He rejoiced at the good tidings of their faith and love.
And for their increase in grace.

div.title: Timothy strengthens believers facing persecution (verses 1–5)
div.p: The more we enjoy walking in God's ways, the more strongly we should desire to persevere in them.
Paul sent Timothy to strengthen and comfort the Thessalonian believers.

He wanted to confirm their faith in its object—Jesus Christ, the Savior of the world—and in its promised reward, which was more than sufficient to compensate for all their losses and repay their labor.
But Paul was concerned that the work he and his companions had accomplished might prove fruitless.
If Satan cannot stop ministers from teaching God's word, he will try to prevent that teaching from bearing fruit.
No faithful servant wants to work in vain.
It is God's purpose that his people should enter his kingdom through many afflictions.
The apostles did not flatter converts with promises of worldly prosperity.
They plainly taught them to expect trouble and suffering, following the example of Jesus, the Author of our faith.
Because Christians would face danger, it was important that they be warned in advance.
Knowledge of the trial to come would help protect them from the tempter's schemes.

div.title: Good news of faith and love encourages Paul (verses 6–10)
div.p: Our thanksgiving is imperfect in this world.
But one great purpose of preaching is to strengthen and advance believers' faith.
The means God uses to bring faith into existence are also the means he uses to increase and confirm it.
His appointed ordinances and especially the hearing of his word serve both purposes.
Faith comes through hearing, and it is strengthened through hearing.

div.title: Prayer for growing love and holiness (verses 11–13)
div.p: Prayer is an act of religious worship, and worship belongs to God alone.
We approach God in prayer as our Father.
Prayer is not only offered in the name of Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus is our Lord and Savior, prayer can be addressed directly to him.
Acknowledge God in all your ways, and he will guide your paths.
Mutual love is required of every Christian.
Love comes from God and fulfills both the gospel's command and the moral law.
We need the Holy Spirit's work for continued growth in grace, and prayer is the appointed means of seeking that help.
Everyone who hopes to enter heaven must pursue holiness.
Our behavior must not contradict our profession of holiness.
The Lord Jesus will certainly return in glory, bringing his holy people with him.
Then we will see both the beauty and the necessity of holiness.
No heart will remain firmly established at that final day without it.
And nobody who lacks it will avoid condemnation.

row.cell: To brotherly love, peaceable behaviour, and diligence.
Not to sorrow unduly for the death of godly relations and friends, considering the glorious resurrection of their bodies at Christ's second coming.

div.title: Pursue holiness in body, mind and will (verses 1–8)
div.p: It is not enough merely to remain in the faith of the gospel.
We must grow in the work that genuine faith produces.
Christ's commandments provide the rule for our conduct.
God's will is that believers receive renewal through the Holy Spirit, grow in holiness and faithfully perform their assigned responsibilities.
Pursuing this holiness requires careful restraint over bodily appetites and senses, as well as over the thoughts, choices and desires that can direct them toward sin.
God calls no one into his family so that the person may live an unholy life.
Rather, he teaches and enables his children to walk before him in holiness.
Some people treat moral commands lightly because they hear them from human ministers.
But these are God's commands, and despising them means despising God himself.

div.title: Love one another, live quietly and work faithfully (verses 9–12)
div.p: When we see a good quality in another person, we should acknowledge and commend it, helping that person grow still more.
Everyone genuinely taught by God learns to love fellow believers.
The Holy Spirit's teaching is greater than the teaching of human beings.
Human instruction is useless without God's inward work.
Even people already known for love and other virtues need to grow in them and persevere until the end.
It is especially desirable to cultivate a peaceful spirit and calm manner of life.
Satan works to stir up conflict, and our own hearts are too willing to become agitated.
We should therefore make it our purpose to live quietly.
People who meddle continually in other people's affairs often have little peace themselves and create great disturbances among their neighbors.
They often neglect the related command to work diligently in their own responsibilities.
Christianity does not remove us from ordinary employment and household duties.
It calls us to be faithful and diligent within them.
Laziness can cause serious poverty and hardship.
Those who work diligently at appropriate tasks often earn what they need and find honest satisfaction in their labor.

div.title: Hope in the resurrection brings comfort in bereavement (verses 13–18)
div.p: These verses comfort family and friends of believers who die.
Grieving the death of loved ones is entirely appropriate.
We may weep for our loss, even while their death is their gain.
Christian faith does not forbid natural affection, and saving grace does not erase our human feelings.
But we should resist becoming overwhelmed with grief in the manner of those who have no hope of a better life.
Death is unfamiliar, and we know little through ordinary experience about what follows it.
Yet we have reliable assurance of the resurrection and the return of Jesus Christ.
These truths relieve the fear of death and bring genuine comfort when Christian friends die.
All God's people will meet again and never be separated.
But the chief happiness of heaven is being with the Lord himself: seeing him, living with him and enjoying him forever.
We should encourage one another during seasons of sorrow rather than weakening each other's courage or increasing despair.
The resurrection and the Lord's return offer many truths with which we can give real comfort.
Yet the thought of appearing before God's judgment seat is comforting only for those who have reason to know their sins have been forgiven.
The Holy Spirit must bear witness within them, and their hearts must be renewed and purified so that they love God and sincerely seek his honor.
We cannot regard ourselves as safe unless this is true of us, or at least we earnestly desire this renewing work.

row.cell: The apostle exhorts to be always ready for the coming of Christ to judgment, which will be with suddenness and surprise.
He directs to several particular duties.
And concludes with prayer, greetings, and a blessing.

div.title: Be prepared for Christ's sudden coming (verses 1–5)
div.p: It is neither necessary nor useful to demand to know the exact date of Jesus Christ's return.
Even the apostles were not told that time.
We should learn and observe the times and opportunities for work God has given us.
But the hour at which we must give an account of our lives is unknown, and we do not need to know it.
Christ's coming will take many people by surprise, as our Lord himself taught.
For each individual, death has much the same significance that the final judgment has for humanity as a whole.
The same warnings therefore apply to both.
Christ's return will be terrifying for those who live in ungodliness.
Destruction will overtake them while they imagine themselves safe, entertain empty hopes and pursue distracting pleasures.
They will find no way to escape that day's terror and punishment.
But for the righteous it will be a happy day.
Believers are not in darkness; they are children of the light.
How many people tell themselves that everything is peaceful and safe while destruction hangs over them!
Let us awaken ourselves and one another and remain watchful against our spiritual enemies.

div.title: Stay sober and encourage one another (verses 6–11)
div.p: Most people fail to think about eternal matters.
Some are asleep, giving them no thought at all.
Others are dreaming, imagining them falsely.
Christians should be known for moderation in earthly things.
With the light of the gospel shining upon them, how could they neglect their souls or forget the world to come?
We need the spiritual armor of faith, love and hope.
Faith teaches us that God always sees us and that we must prepare for another life.
Love for him and his purposes keeps us awake and sober.
Hope of salvation moves us to avoid anything that would weaken our trust in Christ.
Our hope is secure because salvation comes through the Lord Jesus Christ, who died to atone for sins and ransom souls.
We should strengthen one another through prayer, praise and good example, helping one another learn to live for the Lord with whom we hope to live forever.

div.title: Respect ministers, help the weak and return good for evil (verses 12–15)
div.p: Gospel ministers are known by their work: serving and honoring the Lord.
Their responsibility is not only to offer advice but also to warn their flock about dangers and reprove wrongdoing.
Church members should honor and love faithful ministers because their work concerns the wellbeing of souls.
Believers should maintain peace with one another and do everything reasonable to prevent quarrels.
But loving peace never excuses tolerating sin.
Those who are frightened, discouraged or sorrowful need encouragement.
A kind word can help greatly.
We must bear with one another, practice patience and restrain anger.
This applies toward everyone.
Whatever people do to us, we are still commanded to do good to others.

div.title: Rejoice, pray, give thanks and test all teaching (verses 16–22)
div.p: We should enjoy earthly comforts as blessings that will not last forever.
But joy in God can last always.
A genuinely religious life is marked by continual joy.
We would have more reason to rejoice if we prayed more faithfully.
Prayer helps us with legitimate business and every good work.
Those who pray continually will also find continual reasons for thanksgiving.

We should thank God for blessings that spare us trouble and those that prevent greater harm; for common and extraordinary mercies; for past and present gifts; and for both earthly and spiritual benefits.
Thanksgiving should not be restricted to pleasant circumstances.
We may thank God even amid trials, corrections and painful providences, because he intends them for the good of his people even when we cannot yet understand how.
Do not extinguish the Holy Spirit's work.
The Spirit is compared to fire because he illuminates, gives life and purifies the soul.
Fire can be put out by taking away its fuel or covering it with water or earth.
Likewise, believers resist the Spirit's work when they indulge sinful desires, become absorbed in earthly things or refuse to follow the holy affections he has awakened.
Paul's reference to prophecies here concerns the preaching, explanation and application of Scripture.
Do not despise preaching merely because it is plain or repeats truths we have heard before.
Search the Scriptures.
Test everything and hold firmly to what is good.
Turn away from sin and from whatever resembles, leads toward or borders upon it.
People who are careless about tempting circumstances and early approaches to wrongdoing will soon fall into actual sin.

div.title: Pray for complete sanctification and share Scripture widely (verses 23–28)
div.p: Paul prayed that believers would become more completely sanctified.
Even the best Christians remain only partly sanctified in this life.
We should therefore pray for and strive toward complete holiness.
Without God's sustaining power we would fall away.
Ask him to finish the work he began so that we may be presented without fault before his glorious throne.
Believers should pray for one another, expressing genuine family love in this way.
Paul also directed that this letter be read to every believer.
Henry draws an explicit lesson: ordinary Christians are not merely permitted to read Scripture; they have a duty to read it.
The Bible should not be confined to a language people cannot understand.
It should be translated and made accessible, because everyone needs to know God's word.
Scripture should be read aloud in every public congregation, especially to help those with little education.
We need nothing more for true happiness than the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.
He is a fountain of grace that never stops flowing and provides everything necessary for his people.

div.title: 2 Thessalonians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Paul wrote this second letter to the Thessalonians soon after the first.
He had learned that some believers had understood his earlier letter as predicting that Christ's return and the day of judgment would occur during their own lifetime.
Some responded by neglecting their ordinary earthly responsibilities.
Paul wrote again to correct this misunderstanding, which was also interfering with the spread of the gospel.
His earlier teaching agreed with the prophets of the Old Testament.
There were still purposes in God's eternal counsel to be fulfilled before the Lord's day.
He had spoken of Christ's return as near because its certainty makes it ever relevant, not because its date had been revealed.
This teaching led Paul to foretell remarkable events in the later history of the Christian church, demonstrating the prophetic gift with which God had equipped him.

row.cell: The apostle blesses God for the growing state of the love and patience of the Thessalonians.
And encourages them to persevere under all their sufferings for Christ, considering his coming at the great day of account.

div.title: Faith, love and patience grow under affliction (verses 1–4)
div.p: Where saving grace is genuine, it will also grow.
The path of the righteous is like light growing brighter and brighter until the perfect day.
When we observe this growth, all the glory belongs to God.
As faith becomes stronger, love should also increase, because faith works through love.
The Thessalonians' patience and faith deserved to be held up as an example to other Christians.
Their sufferings were not proof that God's grace had failed.
Rather, trials permitted by Providence and persecution inflicted by people increased the exercise of their faith and patience, enabling them to remain firm through trouble.

div.title: Christ's return brings justice, rest and glory (verses 5–10)
div.p: If our religion is worth anything, it is worth everything.
People who cannot bring themselves to suffer for it either lack genuine religion or have not learned how precious it is.
Yet suffering does not earn heaven, any more than good works earn it.
