Patient endurance can prepare us to enjoy the promised joy, but it does not purchase that joy.
One of the clearest signs of a person moving toward destruction is a spirit of persecution and hostility toward God's people.
The Lord will bring judgment upon those who trouble his servants.
There remains a rest for God's people, free from sin and sorrow.
God's righteousness guarantees that good and evil will receive their final judgment.
This assurance should terrify hardened sinners and sustain believers.
Faith that looks toward judgment can begin to understand some of Providence's difficult purposes, which otherwise appear confused and inexplicable to unbelievers.
Jesus will appear from heaven in the glory and power of the heavenly world.
His light will expose and his power will consume those who are like worthless chaff.
This appearing will be dreadful for people who refuse to know God—especially those who reject his revealed gospel or profess to believe it while refusing obedience.
The truth of the gospel is given to us so that we may obey its commands.
Sinners may be spared for a long time, but their final punishment will certainly come.
They have chosen to do sin's work and will receive sin's wages.
In this life God often judges sinners through created instruments.
At the final day, destruction will come from the Almighty himself.
How dreadful to meet the full power of his anger!
But that day will be joyful for believers who receive and obey Christ's gospel.
Jesus Christ will be admired and glorified by his saints and within his saints.
His grace and power will be displayed in everything he has purchased, accomplished and bestowed upon them.
How magnificent the glory he will give his people!
Yet how much more splendid is the Giver of that glory.
God's justice in judging wicked people will be acknowledged.
But the glory of his mercy in saving believers will be an even greater cause of wonder and worship.
Even angels will marvel.
The most ordinary believer will receive happiness beyond the widest human imagination, for Christ will be glorified in all those who believe, without exception.

div.title: Pray for God to complete the work of faith (verses 11 and 12)
div.p: Faith in Christ's coming should make us pray more, both for ourselves and for other people.
Every good quality in a believer springs from God's gracious good pleasure.
That is why it is called grace.
God has many merciful purposes for his people.
Paul prayed that he would complete their work of faith through divine power, so that other acts of obedience would also grow.
God's power not only begins faith but continues and sustains it.
This is the purpose of the grace of our God and Lord Jesus Christ, revealed to and at work within believers.

row.cell: Cautions against the error that the time of Christ's coming was just at hand. There would first be a general apostasy from the faith, and a revealing of the antichristian man of sin.
His destruction, and that of those who obey him.
The security of the Thessalonians from apostacy; an exhortation to stedfastness, and prayer for them.

div.title: Do not be deceived about the Lord's return (verses 1–4)
div.p: When errors arise among Christians, we should correct them.
Faithful servants should be especially careful to remedy mistakes that have grown from misunderstanding their own words or actions.
Our cunning adversary looks for opportunities to harm us.
Satan may encourage false teaching even through the misuse of Scripture's words.
We may be unsure about the time of Christ's return, but we have every reason to be sure that he will return.
Believers in every generation of the church, and the faithful before Christ's first coming, have trusted this promise.
All God's people will be gathered to Christ to live with him in happiness forever.
But wrongly assuming the time is already at hand creates a danger.
When the predicted date passes, the disappointed person may begin to doubt the event's certainty itself.
False doctrines resemble wind that makes water churn and ripple.
Our minds can be just as unstable.
It is enough to know that Jesus will return and gather his people.
Paul gave a reason the Thessalonians should not yet expect the final day: a great falling away would take place first, bringing the revelation of the man of sin, Antichrist.
People have debated at length who or what this figure is.
The man of sin not only commits wicked acts but promotes and commands others to sin.
He is called a son of destruction because his own ruin is certain, while he becomes the instrument through which many others are destroyed in body and soul.
The imagery of God's temple points to a usurper who claims God's authority within the Christian church and demands honors belonging to God alone.

div.title: Corrupt religion and false miracles (verses 5–12)
div.p: Something was restraining the full appearance of the man of sin.
Henry supposes that this restraint was the power of the Roman Empire, which Paul did not name explicitly at the time.
Corruption in doctrine and worship, followed by the usurpation of authority, entered gradually.
Thus the mystery of lawlessness advanced step by step.
Superstition and idolatry were promoted under the appearance of devotion.
Bigotry and persecution were justified through claims of zeal for God's glory.
The mystery of lawlessness had already begun during the apostles' lives, when some professed zeal for Christ but actually opposed him.
Paul announced the destruction of this antichristian condition.
God's pure word joined with God's Spirit exposes its deceit.
In the Lord's appointed time, it will be destroyed through the brightness of Christ's coming.
False signs, visions and miracles can be used to support deceptive doctrine.
Some may be fraudulent displays or claimed miracles intended to mislead people.
Those willingly deceived did not love the truth and therefore refused to believe it.
They found pleasure in false notions.
God leaves such people to themselves, and they consequently enter deeper sin, experience spiritual judgment here and face eternal punishment afterward.
Henry concludes that many of these prophecies had already been fulfilled and confirmed Scripture's truth.
As a seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Protestant commentator, he specifically identifies the papal system and the Roman Catholic Church with this antichristian pattern.
That identification is preserved as Henry's historical interpretation, not as an independently established fact or as a replacement of the biblical text.
He also insists that the Lord has not yet completely destroyed this evil through his appearing, and that further prophecies remain to be fulfilled before the end.

div.title: The elect persevere through faith and the Spirit's holiness (verses 13–15)
div.p: When many turn away from the faith, we can rejoice that God preserves a remnant chosen by grace.
We should also desire evidence that we belong to that remnant.
The perseverance of God's children rests upon his everlasting love, present from before the world's foundation.
Yet the promised end must never be separated from the appointed means.
Faith and holiness belong together, just as holiness and eternal happiness belong together.
God's outward call comes through the gospel.
That call becomes effective through the inward work of the Holy Spirit.
Believing God's truth brings the sinner to trust Christ, love him and obey his commands.
The Holy Spirit seals the gospel upon the heart.
Henry says we have no certain evidence of any apostolic teachings delivered outside the contents of Holy Scripture.
Therefore we should hold firmly to the apostolic doctrines preserved in Scripture and reject unsupported additions and vain traditions.

div.title: Christ himself gives enduring comfort (verses 16 and 17)
div.p: We may and should pray not only to God the Father through Jesus, but also directly to the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior.
We pray in Christ's name to his Father, who has also become our Father through him.
The love of God in Jesus Christ is the fountain of everything good we now possess or hope to receive.
Believers have strong reason to receive lasting consolation, because grace gives them a secure hope.
The free grace and mercy of God—not personal worth or merit—are the foundation of that hope.
The more joy we take in God's word, deeds and ways, the more likely we are to persevere in them.
When we waver in faith, hesitate in our duties or continue in uncertainty and distrust, it is no surprise that we fail to experience the joys of Christian faith.

row.cell: The apostle expresses confidence in the Thessalonians, and prays for them.
He charges them to withdraw from disorderly walkers, particularly from the lazy and busybodies.
And concludes with a prayer for them, and a greeting.

div.title: Pray for faithful gospel work and for one another (verses 1–5)
div.p: Christians who live far apart can still meet at the throne of grace.
Even when people can offer one another no other practical help, they may give and receive genuine, valuable service through prayer.
Opponents of gospel preaching and persecutors of faithful ministers act unreasonably and wickedly.
Many do not believe the gospel. We should not be surprised when such people become restless and malicious toward those who proclaim it.
Sin itself is the greatest evil, but there are other dangers from which we need God's protection.
His gracious promises encourage us to trust him.
When God has given his promise, its fulfillment is certain.
Paul was confident about the Thessalonians, but that confidence was founded upon his confidence in God, not on human reliability.
He prayed for spiritual blessings.
We are sinful and miserable because we so often set our affections upon the wrong things.
There is no genuine love of God without faith in Jesus Christ.
If through God's special grace we possess this saving faith, we should earnestly ask for grace to obey the Lord without reservation, loving God and patiently enduring for Christ's sake.

div.title: Do honest work, correct the disorderly and never tire of doing good (verses 6–15)
div.p: Those who have received Christ's gospel must live in ways appropriate to it.
People who were able to work but refused to work should not be supported in their deliberate idleness.
Christianity does not endorse laziness.
Resources consumed by those unwilling to work are then unavailable to encourage diligent people or support the sick and afflicted.
Being faithful in our ordinary employment is also a duty of our Christian calling.
Some people wanted support while doing no work.
They also became meddlesome and self-important, interfering with other people's affairs.
They caused considerable harm.
Using religion as a disguise for idleness or any other sin is a serious corruption of Christianity.
A servant waiting properly for the return of the Master should be doing the work the Master commanded.
An idle mind is easily occupied by Satan and our own sinful desires.
The human mind is always active. If it is not doing good, it will often turn toward evil.
It is a rare and excellent combination to be energetic in one's own work and quiet about other people's affairs.
Those who refused to work peacefully were to be corrected.
Believers could withdraw familiar fellowship from them when necessary.
Yet the aim remained their good, and correction should take the form of loving admonition, not hatred.
God will be with those who continue in his ways.
Do not grow tired of doing good.
Continue faithfully until your task is finished.
The time for complete rest will come in heaven.

div.title: Pray for peace and Christ's grace (verses 16–18)
div.p: Paul prayed for the Thessalonians, and we should seek the same blessings for ourselves and our friends.
He especially desired peace with God.
He prayed that they would enjoy that peace always and in every circumstance, using all the means of grace God provides.
We can wish nothing better for those we love than God's gracious presence.
If the Lord is with us, our location and the absence of other people cannot destroy our happiness.
Through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we hope to enjoy peace with God and his presence.
His grace supplies everything necessary for true safety and happiness.
However much grace we ask God to give other people, there will always be enough for us too.

div.title: 1 Timothy — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Henry understands the purpose of this letter to be Paul instructing Timothy, whom he had left at Ephesus, in the selection of suitable church officers and the faithful administration of an orderly gospel ministry.
Paul also warned about false teachers, whose clever distinctions and endless disputes corrupted the gospel's purity and simplicity.
He urged Timothy to devote himself to this responsibility with diligence, faithfulness and zeal.
These themes occupy the first four chapters.
Chapter 5 gives directions concerning particular groups of people in the church.
The last chapter condemns quarrelling and contentious speculation, exposes the danger of loving money and calls wealthy people to good works.

row.cell: The design of the law as given by Moses.
Of his own conversion and call to the apostleship.
The obligation to maintain faith and a good conscience.

div.title: Christ our hope; teaching that builds up faith (verses 1–4)
div.p: Jesus Christ is the Christian's hope.
Every hope we possess of everlasting life rests upon him.
When Christ lives within us, he is the hope of glory.
Paul appears to have been the one God used to bring Timothy to faith.
Timothy then served beside Paul in gospel ministry, like an obedient son working with a loving father.
Teaching that provokes endless uncertainty and argument does not build up the church.
Speculative disputes often tear down Christian fellowship rather than strengthen it.
The only way to preserve and grow in godliness of heart and conduct is to exercise faith continually in God's truth and promises through Jesus Christ.

div.title: The purpose of the law is genuine love (verses 5–11)
div.p: Anything that weakens our love for God or for fellow believers undermines the purpose of God's commandments.
The gospel fulfills its purpose when sinners, through repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ, are moved to practice Christian love.
People who are declared righteous in God's appointed way do not find the moral law an enemy.
But unless we are justified through faith in Christ and genuinely turn from sin, the law's curse still stands against us.
Even according to Christ's glorious gospel, an unrepentant person remains unfit for heaven's holy happiness.

div.title: Paul's conversion displays Christ's mercy to sinners (verses 12–17)
div.p: Paul knew he would justly have perished if the Lord had counted his sins strictly and judged him for every wrongdoing.
He survived spiritually only because of the extraordinary mercy and grace shown to him when he was dead in sin.
God worked faith and love for Jesus within his heart.
The statement is true and wholly reliable: the Son of God willingly and deliberately came into the world to save sinners.
No one who considers Paul's experience can reasonably doubt Christ's love or power to save someone who truly desires to trust him.
Jesus Christ died on the cross.
He now reigns on the throne of glory and saves all who come to God through him.
Let us praise the grace of God our Savior and give glory to Father, Son and Holy Spirit—three Persons in one Godhead—for everything accomplished in us, through us and for us.

div.title: Fight the good fight with faith and conscience (verses 18–20)
div.p: Christian ministry is warfare against sin and Satan under Jesus Christ, the Captain of salvation.
The good hopes other believers place in us ought to encourage us to perform our duty.
In every responsibility, we should seek an upright conscience.
Even the severest judgments of the early church were intended to stop further wrongdoing and bring the offender to repentance.
Anyone tempted to throw away a good conscience or use the gospel as an excuse for sin should remember that this is also the way to make shipwreck of faith.

row.cell: Prayer to be made for all persons, since the grace of the gospel makes no difference of ranks or stations.
How men and women ought to behave, both in their religious and common life.

div.title: Pray for everyone through Christ the one Mediator (verses 1–7)
div.p: Disciples of Jesus should be people who pray.
Christians should pray without excluding anyone on account of nation, religious group, social rank or party.
Our Christian responsibilities can be summed up in two words:
Godliness means worshiping God rightly.
Honesty means behaving well toward all people.
These obligations belong together.
Someone who refuses to give God what is due to him cannot be truly honest.
And someone dishonest toward neighbors cannot be truly godly.
We should abundantly practice what God our Savior regards as good and acceptable.
There is one Mediator, Jesus Christ, who gave himself as a ransom for all.
This saving way has been appointed for Jews and Gentiles from every nation.
Everyone willing to come by this way may approach God's mercy seat to seek forgiveness and reconciliation.
Sin created hostility between humanity and God.
Jesus Christ, our Mediator, establishes peace.
God appointed that his ransom and its blessings would become known at the proper time.
Before Christ came, the Old Testament spoke about his suffering and the glory that would follow, still awaiting their full revelation.
Those who are saved must come to knowledge of the truth, because God has appointed truth as the way of salvation.
We cannot be ruled by truth we do not know.

div.title: Prayer, modesty and the responsibilities of men and women (verses 8–15)
div.p: Under the gospel, prayer is not limited to a particular sacred building.
Believers should pray privately, with families, at meals, while traveling and in gathered worship, whether the meeting is large or small.
They must pray in love, without anger, hatred or hostility toward anyone.
They should pray with faith, rather than skepticism or contentious dispute.
Henry calls Christian women to modesty in clothing, avoiding pride in splendid, expensive or conspicuous appearance.
He says good works are the best adornment, precious in God's sight.
Cleanliness and a modest appearance should matter more than impressive fashion.
It would be good if professing Christians were free from vanity concerning clothes.
Instead of spending so much time and money adorning themselves and their children, they should give more to the sick and distressed.
Dress that contradicts a person's Christian profession or situation is not a harmless matter.
These are divine commands, not merely customs.
Henry follows Paul's restriction on women acting as public teachers in church, understanding that role as exercising authority.
He emphasizes, however, that believing women may and should teach their children the principles of true religion at home.
Women must also learn everything necessary for salvation.
Paul refers to the order of creation and to Eve's earlier participation in transgression.
But Henry also draws a word of comfort from the promise concerning childbearing.
He understands salvation “in” or “with” childbearing as coming through the Messiah born of a woman, with a word of comfort for those who continue in sobriety.
The particular suffering associated with childbearing should also move men to exercise authority with tenderness, gentleness and loving affection.

row.cell: The qualifications and behaviour of gospel bishops.
And of deacons and their wives.
The reason of writing about these, and other church affairs.

div.title: The character required of an overseer (verses 1–7)
div.p: When a man desires the pastoral office from genuine love for Jesus Christ and concern for human souls, and is willing to deny himself and endure hardship by devoting his life to that work, he desires a good work.
Such an ambition deserves approval if the person also possesses the required qualifications.
A minister should give others as little just reason for complaint as possible.
Otherwise his behavior may bring disgrace upon the office he holds.
He ought to be sober, self-controlled and moderate in his actions and in his enjoyment of the created comforts God provides.
Scripture connects sobriety and watchfulness because each supports the other.
The families of ministers should be good examples to other families.
Beware of pride!
Pride was the sin that turned angels into devils.
A minister should have a good reputation among neighbors, with no justified scandal arising from his past conduct.
To encourage ministers who serve faithfully, Christ has made this gracious promise:
“I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).
He will equip his ministers for their duties, sustain them through difficulties, comfort them amid their work and reward their faithfulness.

div.title: The integrity required of deacons (verses 8–13)
div.p: Deacons were first appointed to distribute the church's charitable assistance and manage its affairs.
Henry notes that some among the early deacons also became pastors or evangelists.
Deacons therefore received an important public trust.
They must be serious, prudent and dependable.
We should not entrust a public responsibility to anyone until that person has demonstrated fitness for the work involved.
People closely associated with ministers also need to live in a way consistent with Christ's gospel.

div.title: The church proclaims the mystery of godliness (verses 14–16)
div.p: The church is God's household and dwelling place.
It upholds and displays Scripture and Christ's teaching, much like a pillar holding up a public proclamation.
When a church abandons its role as pillar and foundation of the truth, believers may and should leave it.
Loyalty to God's truth must come first.
The great mystery of godliness concerns Jesus Christ.
He is God who became human and appeared in human flesh.
God was pleased to reveal himself to the human race by his Son taking human nature.
Although Christ was accused of being a sinner and put to death as a criminal, he was raised by the Spirit, vindicated against every false charge.
Angels attended and served him, because he is their Lord.
The Gentiles welcomed the gospel that the Jews rejected.
Remember that God was revealed in the flesh to take away our sins, redeem us from all lawlessness and purify a people for himself eager to perform good works.
These magnificent teachings must be made visible through the Spirit's fruit in our conduct.

row.cell: Of departures from the faith that began already to appear.
Several directions, with motives for due discharge of duties.

div.title: Reject false restrictions and receive God's gifts with thanks (verses 1–5)
div.p: The Holy Spirit spoke in both the Old and New Testaments of a widespread departure from faith in Christ and the pure worship of God.
This would occur during the Christian era, described as the last days.
Some false teachers declare evil what God has permitted.
Others command as necessary duties what he has left to human freedom.
God has given us more than enough opportunity for watchfulness, self-denial and obedience through his actual commandments.
We do not need invented duties that forbid the things he has allowed.
Nevertheless, permission never justifies immoderate or improper use of God's gifts.
Nothing we receive will truly benefit us unless we seek his blessing upon it through prayer.

div.title: Godliness is more valuable than outward self-denial (verses 6–10)
div.p: External forms of restraint have only limited value.
What good is it to discipline the body while failing to put sin itself to death?
The hardest work performed merely in outward practices cannot make a person holy.
The great value of godliness rests partly upon God's promises.
Those promises include blessings in this present life, but especially in the life to come.
When we lose something for Christ's sake, we will not ultimately lose through belonging to Christ.
Christ is described as Savior of all people.
How much more will he reward those who sincerely seek him and serve him!
He will provide what is truly good for those whom he has made new creations.

div.title: Teach by doctrine and example, even when young (verses 11–16)
div.p: Young people's age will not make them contemptible if they avoid vanity, foolish behavior and corrupt habits.
Those who teach others through doctrine must also teach through their lives.
Their words should build up believers, and their conduct should be holy.
They should be examples of love for God and for faithful people, and of heavenly-mindedness.
Ministers ought to regard these responsibilities as their principal calling and work.
Through such diligence, their progress will become visible, benefiting both themselves and other people.
This is the path toward growing in knowledge and grace while helping others grow as well.
A minister's doctrine must be biblical, clear, centered on the gospel and practical.
It should be carefully stated, explained, defended and applied.
Such responsibilities leave little time for pursuing worldly pleasures, pointless social visits, frivolous conversation or purely decorative amusements.
May every believer also grow in a way that others can recognize.
May each seek to experience the gospel's power within the soul and produce its fruit in daily conduct.

row.cell: Directions as to the elder and younger men and women.
The respect to be paid to elders. Timothy is to take care in rebuking offenders, in ordaining ministers, and as to his own health.

div.title: Correct others with respect and gentleness (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: We should respect people according to their age and responsibilities.
When someone younger has acted wrongly, correction should never be given from a desire to find fault.
It should be motivated by a desire to help that person grow.
Great meekness, wisdom and care are required when correcting anyone, even when correction is clearly deserved.

div.title: Care for widows and needy family members (verses 3–8)
div.p: Honor widows who are truly without support.
Provide practical relief and assistance for their needs.
When parents become poor and their children possess the means to help, those children have a duty to support them as fully as they can.
Widowhood can bring deep loneliness and distress.
But widows should trust the Lord and continue in prayer.
Anyone who lives entirely for worldly pleasure is spiritually dead while still physically alive.
How many professing Christians live in that condition, even into old age!
Men and women who refuse to support needy relatives effectively deny the faith they profess.
If they spend on sinful indulgence what should have been used to maintain their households, their conduct is worse than that of unbelievers.
A professing Christian who embraces corrupt ideas or practices can bring greater dishonor upon the faith than someone who has never claimed to believe it.

div.title: Faithful charity and suitable church service (verses 9–16)
div.p: Anyone appointed to public church service must be free from justified accusations of wrongdoing.
Some people may be worthy recipients of charitable help without being suitable for an official ministry role.
Those wishing to receive mercy in adversity should be willing to show mercy in prosperity.
People who are eager to perform good work generally prove faithful when entrusted with responsibility.
Those who become idle rarely remain merely inactive.
They often begin interfering in the affairs of neighbors and sowing discord among fellow believers.
Christians should relieve destitute relatives whenever possible.
That allows the church to direct its shared resources toward those who are completely abandoned and have no relatives able to help them.

div.title: Honor faithful ministers and judge without favoritism (verses 17–25)
div.p: Churches must provide adequate material support for ministers.
Those who labor diligently in teaching and leading God's people deserve special honor and esteem.
That support is their rightful due, just as an employee deserves payment for work performed.
Paul solemnly instructed Timothy not to show favoritism.
We must continually guard against participating in other people's sins.
Keep yourself pure—not only by avoiding similar misconduct, but also by refusing to approve, encourage or assist wrongdoing by others.
Paul also instructed Timothy to care for his physical health.
We should neither make our bodies masters that control our lives nor treat them as slaves to be abused.
Instead, care for them so that they remain as useful as possible for serving God.
Some sins are visible to everyone long before judgment.
Others remain concealed for a time.
Yet the Lord will bring hidden acts and the true purposes of every heart into the light.
Remembering that day, let everyone fulfill their responsibilities—whether public or private, high or low—so that God's name and teaching are never disgraced through our conduct.

row.cell: The duty of Christians towards believing, as well as other masters.
The advantage of godliness with contentment.
A solemn charge to Timothy to be faithful.
The apostle repeats his warning to the rich, and closes with a blessing.

div.title: Respect lawful authority and reject teaching driven by greed (verses 1–5)
div.p: Christians should not imagine that greater religious knowledge or privilege gives them permission to despise unbelieving masters, disregard lawful duties or expose employers' faults maliciously.
Those whose masters also believe in Christ must not withhold proper respect merely because they share equal spiritual privileges.
Instead, their common faith should move them to serve with greater diligence and goodwill.
The only teaching to which we must give unconditional agreement is the sound teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ.
People who know very little are often the proudest, precisely because they do not know themselves well.
Pride leads to envy, quarrels, insults, hostile suspicions and useless disputes.
These arguments may sound clever but contain no solid spiritual truth.
They arise in minds corrupted by sinful desires, ignorant of the gospel's transforming power and motivated by worldly advantage.

div.title: Godliness joined with contentment is great gain (verses 6–10)
div.p: Those who turn Christianity into a business for their own worldly advancement will eventually be disappointed.
But those who make godliness their true calling can rely upon God's promises for this life and the life to come.
Genuine believers can know their final happiness is secure.
When they are also content with their present circumstances, they already have enough.
Even in the greatest poverty, we cannot own less than we possessed when we were born.
At death, even the richest person can finally carry away little more than a burial shroud, coffin and grave.
Nature can be satisfied with relatively little.
If our natural needs can be content with a little, grace should be content with even less.
The necessary things of life should limit the Christian's ambitions.
With food and clothing, we should seek to remain thankful.
Consider the danger of greed.
Paul does not condemn everyone who is rich.
He warns those who are determined to become rich—people who place their happiness in wealth and pursue it as their highest goal.
Such people expose themselves to the devil's temptations.
They may turn to dishonest methods to increase their possessions.
They may become so overwhelmed by business that they have no time or desire left for spiritual duties.
They may enter relationships that draw them into wrongdoing and folly.

p.hi: What sin will love of money not draw people toward?

div.p: Someone may possess a great deal of money without loving it.
But where money is loved as an idol, it drives the person toward every kind of evil.
Different sins and vices grow out of this root in different ways.
We can see examples everywhere, especially in periods of wealth, luxury and careless religious profession.

div.title: Fight the good fight and live for eternal things (verses 11–16)
div.p: No one should set the heart upon earthly possessions, but such attachment is particularly inappropriate in a servant of God.
Those who belong to the Lord should concentrate upon his purposes and commands.
Christian life involves genuine conflict with corruption, temptation and the powers of darkness.
Eternal life is the crown offered to strengthen our determination.
We are called to take hold of it.
Those who possess much wealth especially need clear instruction about its dangers and proper uses.
But a minister cannot warn them sincerely while secretly craving the very pleasures their money can purchase.
Christ's return is certain.
Its exact time is not ours to know.
The radiance of God's glory is more than mortal eyes can bear.
We can approach him only as he has made himself known to sinners in and through Jesus Christ.
Henry explains that this passage adores the divine nature without distinguishing the Persons, because its statements are true of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
God has made himself known to us through the human nature of Jesus, the Father's only-begotten Son.

div.title: Be rich in good works, not merely possessions (verses 17–21)
div.p: Being wealthy in this world is entirely different from being rich toward God.
Few things are more uncertain than earthly wealth.
Rich people should recognize that God is the One who gives wealth.
Only he can also give them the heart to enjoy it rightly.
Many people own much but obtain little true comfort from it because they cannot use it wisely or generously.
What good is a large estate except as an opportunity to do more good?
Let genuine faith in Christ show itself through loving actions and generosity.
Take hold of eternal life rather than following the self-indulgent, greedy and ungodly, who will eventually lift up their eyes in torment.
Knowledge that contradicts the truth of Christ's gospel is not genuine wisdom.
If it were true knowledge, it would recognize and welcome gospel truth.
People who elevate human speculation above faith risk abandoning the faith altogether.
Grace contains every spiritual good.
Grace is the beginning and pledge of glory.
Where God genuinely gives his grace, he will also bring the person into glory.

div.title: 2 Timothy — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The first purpose of this letter appears to have been to tell Timothy what had happened during Paul's imprisonment and to ask him to come to Rome.
Paul was uncertain whether he would live to see Timothy again, so he also provided a wide range of counsel and encouragement to help him discharge his ministry faithfully.
Because this was a personal letter to one of Paul's closest friends, written amid the distress of imprisonment with death approaching, it offers a striking glimpse of the apostle's character.
It also gives compelling evidence that Paul sincerely believed the doctrines he preached.

row.cell: Paul expresses great affection for Timothy.
Exhorts him to improve his spiritual gifts.
Tells of many who basely deserted him; but speaks with affection of Onesiphorus.

div.title: Paul thanks God for Timothy's faith (verses 1–5)
div.p: The promise of eternal life in Christ Jesus is the central message of ministers appointed according to God's will.
The blessings Paul asked for Timothy are the finest we can desire for those we love, including peace with God the Father and Jesus Christ our Lord.
All the credit for the good we do belongs to God.
True believers in every age share the same essential faith. Their faith is sincere and enduring, because it lives in them as an active principle.
The example of Lois and Eunice should encourage faithful women who teach children.
Some of the most helpful ministers Christ's church has known owe deep gratitude to God for the earliest impressions of faith made upon them by their mothers and other female relatives.

div.title: Stir up God's gift and guard the gospel (verses 6–14)
div.p: God has not given believers a spirit of cowardice or slavery to fear. He gives power, courage, resolution, love for him and a sound, peaceful mind.
When his strength supports us, we can bear affliction faithfully.
Whenever Paul spoke of Christ and redemption, he loved to dwell on them at length. Christ was all his salvation and should be all our desire.
The gospel's calling is holy and makes people holy. Salvation comes entirely by free grace, given in God's eternal purpose in Christ Jesus before the world began.
All the gifts God grants to fallen humans reach us through Christ alone.
The prospect of eternal happiness through him, the Resurrection and the Life, should move us to make our calling sure.
Those who remain faithful to the gospel need not be ashamed, though its opponents will eventually be ashamed.
Paul had entrusted his life, soul and eternal future to Jesus. Only Christ can preserve a soul through life, death and the last judgment.
A day is coming when everyone will be asked what they did with the soul entrusted to them. Did they serve sin or Christ?
The humblest genuine Christian stands upon the same foundation of hope as Paul: believing in Jesus and recognizing the saving change he has brought to the heart.
Timothy must hold firmly to the Holy Scriptures and the trustworthy pattern of gospel truth. Mere intellectual agreement is insufficient; we must love that truth.
The gospel is a precious deposit entrusted to believers. We must preserve it whole and pure, not through confidence in our own intelligence or heart but by the Holy Spirit living within us.

div.title: Remember faithful Onesiphorus (verses 15–18)
div.p: Many had shamefully deserted Paul. In contrast, Onesiphorus often encouraged and refreshed him through letters, counsel and comfort, without being ashamed of his imprisonment.
A good person seeks opportunities to do good.
Death and judgment are momentous realities. If we wish to receive mercy then, we must seek it from the Lord now.
For ourselves and our friends, the greatest request we can make is that we find mercy from God when we pass from time into eternity and stand before Christ's judgment seat.

row.cell: The apostle exhorts Timothy to persevere with diligence, like a soldier, a combatant, and a husbandman.
Encouraging him by assurances of a happy end of his faithfulness.
Warnings to shun vain babblings and dangerous errors.
Charges to flee youthful lusts, and to minister with zeal against error, but with meekness of spirit.

div.title: Serve faithfully as soldier, athlete and farmer (verses 1–7)
div.p: As trials increase, our faith, resolution and love for God and Christ should become stronger. That is not the same as relying on our own strength.
All Christians, and ministers especially, must remain loyal to Christ their Captain, determined to please him.
We must struggle against our sinful desires and corrupt habits, but we cannot expect a crown unless we compete according to the rules.
We must do good in the right way, lest our good actions themselves be spoken against. Even zeal for outward ceremonies or doubtful controversies can misdirect our energies.
The farmer must labor before receiving the harvest; the runner must run before receiving the prize. We must perform God's will patiently as we wait for what he promised.
Alongside prayer that God will give others understanding, we must encourage them to reflect carefully on what they hear and read.

div.title: Remember Jesus and endure (verses 8–13)
div.p: Suffering believers should look to Jesus, the Author and Perfecter of faith, who endured the cross and shame for the joy before him and now sits at God's right hand.
We should not be surprised when good people are treated badly.
Even when his servants are imprisoned, God's word cannot be bound.
Paul's suffering arose from his work for the gospel.
If we have died to this world's pleasures, profits and honors, we will live with Christ eternally in a better world.
Jesus is faithful both to his promises and to his warnings. The former secures believers' salvation; the latter makes unbelievers' condemnation certain.

div.title: Avoid quarrels and become a useful vessel (verses 14–21)
div.p: People eager to quarrel commonly dispute minor matters. Arguments over words can tear down God's work.
Some false teachers had not rejected the resurrection outright but distorted its meaning. Such error can overturn the temporary belief of some professing Christians.
The solid foundation has two assurances: God knows and preserves those who truly belong to him, and everyone who calls upon Christ must turn away from wrongdoing.
To enjoy the comfort of God's promises, we must seriously perform the duty that accompanies them. Christ gave himself to redeem us from every lawless deed (Titus 2:14).
The church is like a house containing vessels made from various materials, some for honorable service and others for common use.
When dishonorable vessels are removed, those God approves are prepared for his service. We must seek to be holy vessels, useful to the Master.

div.title: Correct opponents with meekness (verses 22–26)
div.p: The more earnestly we pursue what is good, the further we will move from evil.
Fellowship with faithful believers helps keep us separate from fruitless works of darkness.
The repeated warnings against religious quarrels show that true faith depends more on believing and doing what God commands than on intellectual cleverness in controversy.
A person who loves fighting and speaks fiercely is poorly equipped to teach.

p.hi: Teaching rather than persecution is Scripture's method of addressing people in error.

div.p: Only God, who reveals the truth, can grant the repentance by which a person accepts it.
There is no uncertainty about his forgiving those who actually repent. What we cannot know is whether he will grant repentance to a particular person who currently opposes him.
Sin traps people in the devil's snare and makes them his captives. They cannot escape except through repentance as God's gift, which we should ask for in persistent prayer.

row.cell: The apostle foretells the rise of dangerous enemies to the gospel.
Proposes his own example to Timothy.
And exhorts him to continue in the doctrine he had learned from the Holy Scriptures.

div.title: Dangerous times and false religious appearance (verses 1–9)
div.p: Perilous times can arise even while the gospel is being preached. Persecution from outside the church is dangerous; corruption inside it is more dangerous still.
People increasingly gratify sinful desires instead of pleasing God and fulfilling their duties.
When everyone is eager to obtain more and anxiously protect possessions, people become dangerous to one another.
Those who do not fear God will not respect others. Children disobeying parents make life unstable.
Ingratitude for God's mercies feeds irreverence. We misuse God's gifts when we make them fuel for sinful passions.
Lack of natural affection in parents, unchecked temper and contempt for what is good also create perilous times.
God deserves our highest love, yet the sinful mind opposes him and prefers almost anything—especially bodily pleasure.
The appearance of godliness is entirely different from its power. Christians must distance themselves from people shown to be religious hypocrites.
Throughout the church's history, manipulative people have used flattery and pretended spirituality to gain the trust of the gullible and uninformed.
Their followers are always embracing new ideas but never seek the truth found in Jesus.

Like the Egyptian magicians, these deceivers resist truth with corrupt minds and lack genuine faith. Yet Satan and the spirit of error can mislead nations or churches only as far and as long as God permits.

div.title: Follow Paul's teaching and endurance (verses 10–13)
div.p: The more fully we understand Christ's doctrine as the apostles taught it, the more firmly we should hold to it.
When we know only part of the persecution believers suffer, we may be tempted to abandon their cause.
People may tolerate a merely formal profession of Christianity, while openly holding fast to Christ's truth and faithfully practicing godliness arouses the world's scorn.
By God's grace, faithful people grow in holiness. But through Satan's schemes and their own corrupt desires, wicked people grow worse.
The road of sin goes downhill: those who deceive others also deceive themselves. The history of the visible church sadly demonstrates the Holy Spirit's warning through Paul.

div.title: Remain in the God-breathed Scriptures (verses 14–17)
div.p: Anyone who seeks firm knowledge of God's ways must learn the Holy Scriptures, God's own revelation.
Childhood is especially suitable for learning. The greatest education children can receive begins with Scripture.
We must not leave the Bible neglected and scarcely ever opened.
The Bible is a trustworthy guide toward eternal life.
Prophets and apostles did not invent their message; they delivered what God gave them (2 Peter 1:21).
Scripture is profitable for every part of Christian living. Everyone needs instruction, correction and rebuke; the Bible addresses every situation.

If we loved our Bibles more deeply and remained closer to their teaching, we would benefit now and at last enjoy the happiness they promise through faith in Jesus Christ, the central subject of both Testaments.
The best defense against error is a solid knowledge of God's truthful word.
The greatest kindness to children is to teach them the Bible from an early age.

row.cell: The apostle solemnly charges Timothy to be diligent, though many will not bear sound doctrine.
Enforces the charge from his own martyrdom, then at hand.
He cautions, and complains of such as had deserted him; and expresses his faith as to his own preservation to the heavenly kingdom.
Friendly greetings and his usual blessing.

div.title: Preach the word despite resistance (verses 1–5)
div.p: People may grow weary of Christ's plain gospel and prefer entertaining stories to clear, searching preaching.
They reject sermons that speak directly to their consciences and are relevant to their lives.
Those who truly care for human souls must remain watchful, accept the painful consequences of faithful ministry and use every opportunity to make the pure gospel known.

div.title: Paul's nearing death and his crown (verses 6–8)
div.p: The blood of Christian martyrs is not an atoning sacrifice. Yet their death can be an offering that acknowledges God's grace and truth.
For a good person, death is release from the prison of this world and departure to enjoy the world to come.
Paul had kept the faith and the gospel's doctrines, as both Christian and minister.
What comfort to be able to say this near the end of life!
The crown awaiting believers is a crown of righteousness purchased through Christ's righteousness. They have not yet received it, but it is securely reserved for them.

Believers may rejoice even amid poverty, pain, illness and death. But those who neglect the duties belonging to their calling weaken the evidence of their faith and may approach death troubled by uncertainty.

div.title: Come soon; bring books and necessary things (verses 9–13)
div.p: Love of the present world often causes people to abandon Christ's truth and ways.
Although Paul was guided by divine inspiration, he still wanted his books.
As long as we live, we still need to learn.
The apostles did not despise human means of meeting life's needs or of gaining further instruction.
Let us thank God for the writings of wise and faithful Christians from earlier generations, and use our reading so that our progress becomes evident to others.

div.title: Human supporters fail; the Lord does not (verses 14–18)
div.p: False brothers and sisters may be as dangerous as open enemies.
People willing to oppose someone like Paul deserve caution.
The Christians in Rome had eagerly greeted Paul when he arrived (Acts 28). But when standing with him appeared dangerous, they all deserted him.
Though God could justly hold their failure against them, Paul prayed for their forgiveness.
He was delivered from the lion's mouth, which Henry identifies as possibly Nero or one of his judges.
If the Lord stands beside us, he will strengthen us through trials and dangers. His presence more than compensates for the absence of everyone else.

div.title: Farewell and blessing (verses 19–22)
div.p: Nothing more is needed for true happiness than the Lord Jesus Christ present with our spirits. All spiritual blessings are united in him.
The finest prayer we can make for friends is that Christ will dwell with their spirits, make them holy, save them and eventually receive them to himself.
Many who believed as Paul did are already before God's throne praising their Lord. May we follow their example.

div.title: Titus — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Paul's letter gives Titus instructions concerning elders in the church and the manner in which he should teach and exhort the congregation.
Later it directs him to encourage obedience to civil authorities, insist upon good works, avoid foolish disputes and reject heretical teaching.
The instructions are clear and straightforward. Christianity was not designed to serve worldly ambition or selfish purposes: it is God's wisdom and God's power.

row.cell: The qualifications of a faithful pastor.
The evil temper and practices of false teachers.

div.title: Gospel truth leads to godliness and hope (verses 1–4)
div.p: Everyone freed from slavery to sin and Satan is a servant of God.
True gospel teaching accords with godliness and teaches us to reverence the Lord.
The gospel gives not only faith but hope, turning heart and mind away from the world and lifting them toward heaven.
God promised its message long ago. We should be thankful for the privilege of hearing it.
Since faith comes from hearing God's word, everyone appointed and called to preach must proclaim that word.

Grace is God's free favor and acceptance. Mercy brings the results of that favor, including pardon for sin and freedom from misery now and forever. Peace flows from mercy: reconciliation with God through Christ our Peace, and right relationships with ourselves and God's creatures.
Grace is the source from which these blessings flow.

div.title: Qualifications for elders and overseers (verses 5–9)
div.p: Paul's requirements for elders, also called bishops or overseers, agree with those given to Timothy.
Pastors oversee God's flock, set an example and serve as stewards of God's household. For that reason their conduct must be above reproach.
Paul explains both the qualities they must possess and the conduct they must avoid.
They must be faithful servants of Christ, capable ministers of the teaching and practice of the gospel, and examples of good works.

div.title: Confront false teachers without becoming harsh (verses 10–16)
div.p: Faithful ministers must resist false teachers promptly, so that their folly is exposed before it spreads further.
These teachers used religion to pursue selfish worldly gain. Love of money lay beneath their actions.
They should be refuted by sound teaching from Scripture.
Christians should reject conduct condemned even by ordinary human conscience: lying, envy, crafty cruelty, sensual brutality, sloth and idleness.
Yet Christian gentleness is not cowardly tolerance of sin and error; nor is it angry impatience.
The character of people and nations may differ, but the fallen human heart is deceitful in every place and age.
Even the sharpest correction must seek the offender's good and restoration to sound faith.
For those defiled by unbelief, even lawful and good things are misused and turned into sin.
Many claim to know God while denying him through their actions. Such hypocrisy is miserable: the appearance of godliness without its power.
But we should be slower to level that accusation at others than to examine whether it applies to ourselves.

row.cell: The duties which become sound doctrine.
All is enforced from the holy design of the gospel, which concerns all believers.

div.title: Sound teaching should shape every age (verses 1–8)
div.p: Older disciples of Christ should make every part of life consistent with Christian teaching.
Older men are to be sober. Growing frailty is no excuse for excess; they should seek consolation in closer fellowship with God, not self-indulgence.
Faith operates through love: loving God for himself and people for his sake.
Older people may become irritable or complain excessively and should guard against those temptations.
Scripture does not spell out a rule for every word, gesture or expression, but gives general principles governing all of life.
Young women should behave with discretion and self-control. A careless decision can expose them to dangerous temptation.
Their conduct should prevent God's word from being dishonored. Neglecting ordinary responsibilities brings reproach on Christianity.
Young men are often eager and thoughtless. They need earnest encouragement toward sound judgment and self-control.
Henry regards pride as a particularly destructive danger for young people.
A Christian should seek to silence unjust accusations through upright conduct. What an honor when even an enemy seeking fault has no genuine wrongdoing to report!

div.title: Serve faithfully in earthly responsibilities (verses 9 and 10)
div.p: Those serving earthly masters should fulfill lawful responsibilities as service rendered ultimately to Christ; he rewards faithful duty.
They should avoid provoking or disrespectful speech and receive deserved correction without argumentative excuses.
Trying to justify a wrong already committed makes it worse.
They must not steal or misuse entrusted possessions, but should handle them faithfully and contribute to the good of those they serve.
“If you have not been faithful with what belongs to someone else, who will give you what is your own?” (Luke 16:12).
A faithful life adorns Christian teaching.

div.title: God's grace trains us to holy living (verses 11–15)
div.p: The message of grace and salvation is for people of every rank and condition.
It teaches us to renounce sin and refuse an earthly, sensual life inconsistent with our heavenly calling.
We are called to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives, despite temptations, bad examples, mistreatment and the sinful desires still remaining in believers.
We must look to God in Christ as the one we hope in and worship.
The gospel also teaches us to anticipate another world's glory. Our blessed hope will be complete when Christ appears in glory.
The purpose of his death was to bring us into holiness and happiness.
Jesus Christ is the great God and our Savior—not a Savior merely as God, still less merely as a human being, but the God-man, two natures united in one person.
He loved us and gave himself for us. We should love him and give ourselves to him.
Redemption from sin and sanctification belong together. Jesus frees his people from guilt and condemnation and purifies them through the Holy Spirit, making them his own people eager for good works.
All Scripture helps us perform our duties rightly.
Ask whether we truly rely on grace that saves the lost, pardons the guilty and makes the impure holy.
The less we boast of supposed good works or trust them for acceptance, and the more we boast in Christ alone, the more eager we should become to perform genuinely good works.

row.cell: Obedience to magistrates, and becoming behaviour towards all, are enforced from what believers were before conversion, and what they are made, through Christ.
Good works to be done, and useless disputes avoided.

div.title: A gracious salvation produces civil duty and kindness (verses 1–7)
div.p: Spiritual privileges do not weaken civil obligations; they confirm them.
Good intentions and pleasing words are not enough unless accompanied by good deeds.
Christians must not be quarrelsome but should show gentleness toward everyone, not only their friends, exercising wisdom (James 3:13).
Christ's followers should not act harshly even toward the weakest, lowest or most objectionable person.
People enslaved to sin have many competing masters: pride pulls them one way, greed another. They become hateful toward one another.
It is the misery of sinners to hate; it is the duty and happiness of believers to love.
We are delivered from this condition entirely by God's mercy and freely given grace, Christ's merits and sufferings and the Holy Spirit's work.
God the Father is God our Savior, the source of the Spirit's teaching, regeneration and saving work, all given through Christ.
The beginning is God's kindness and love for humanity. His gracious love changes the heart through the Spirit.

p.hi: Good works must be found in saved people, but they do not cause salvation.

div.p: God creates in believers a new principle of grace and holiness, making them new people.
Many want heaven eventually without wanting holiness now. They want the end without the necessary beginning.
Baptism is the outward sign and seal of this inward new birth—the washing of regeneration.
We must neither disregard baptism nor place confidence merely in the outward washing.
Without the response of a good conscience, the outward act brings no saving benefit.
It is the Holy Spirit who inwardly renews us, enables us to kill sin, perform duty, walk in God's ways and produce the fruits of righteousness.
The Spirit and his gifts come through Jesus Christ our Savior, whose work brings us from grace to eternal glory.
Justification means a sinner is freely forgiven and accepted as righteous through Christ's righteousness received by faith.
God remains righteous and upholds his own law because Christ has satisfied divine justice. The sinner cannot earn such acceptance.
Eternal life is promised; the Spirit creates faith and hope that bring that promised future close to our hearts and fill us with joy.

div.title: Insist on good works and refuse empty disputes (verses 8–11)
div.p: After declaring God's saving grace, Paul presses the need for good works.
Those who trust God must seek opportunities to do good, moved by love and gratitude.
Avoid foolish controversies, clever but useless distinctions, vain speculation and the constant pursuit of novelty.
Love instead the sound doctrine that most effectively builds up the church.
Sins we now dismiss as small may feel unbearably heavy when God awakens our consciences.

div.title: Live fruitfully and ask for grace (verses 12–15)
div.p: Christianity is not an empty profession.
Believers must produce fruits of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to God's glory and praise.
It is not enough to refrain from wrongdoing. We must actively do good.
Let the members of our households engage in honest work and support themselves and their families. Every Christian should seek legitimate work and fulfill that calling in God's presence.
Paul closes with friendship and sincere prayer.
“Grace be with you all.” He desires God's favor, its fruits and its growing presence in their souls.
Grace is the greatest gift we can ask for ourselves or others. In it is contained every true good.

div.title: Philemon — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Philemon lived in Colossae. Henry describes him as a man of some wealth and standing who had come to faith through Paul's ministry.
Onesimus was enslaved to Philemon. He had fled, reached Rome and there became a Christian through Paul's preaching.
Henry understands Paul to have kept Onesimus with him long enough to see evidence of genuine conversion.
Onesimus wanted to repair the harm done through his departure, yet feared the punishment that could follow. He therefore asked Paul to write on his behalf.
Henry praises Paul's letter as particularly compelling and beautiful in its reasoning and appeals.

row.cell: The apostle's joy and praise for Philemon's steady faith in the Lord Jesus, and love to all the saints.
He recommends Onesimus as one who would make rich amends for the misconduct of which he had been guilty; and on behalf of whom the apostle promises to make up any loss Philemon had sustained.

div.title: Paul's joy in Philemon's love (verses 1–7)
div.p: Faith in Christ and love for him should unite believers more closely than outward family or social ties.
Paul remembered his friends individually in private prayer. We should also bring Christian friends before God regularly, thinking about what they need and carrying them in our hearts.
Differences of opinion or practice in nonessential matters should not destroy affection between believers faithful to the truth.
Paul wanted to know whether his friends' faith and love were real, growing and fruitful.
Philemon's good deeds comforted and encouraged him and others. They therefore desired that he would continue increasing in these fruits for God's glory.

div.title: Paul's loving appeal for Onesimus (verses 8–14)
div.p: It does not diminish our dignity to ask humbly, even when we could demand something as a matter of authority.
Paul chose to appeal through love rather than command on behalf of the man converted through his ministry, Onesimus.
The name Onesimus means “useful.” Formerly he had been unprofitable to Philemon, but conversion had made him useful.
Those living without holiness do not fulfill the highest purpose of their existence.
What a wonderful change conversion brings: turning evil into good and the formerly unprofitable into useful people!
Henry describes religious servants as a treasure to a household because they conscientiously use their time and fulfill their trusts.
Yet opportunities for useful service elsewhere should not lead anyone to ignore genuine obligations. A key sign of repentance is a desire to fulfill duties formerly neglected.
In Henry's reading of the events, Onesimus acknowledged his wrongdoing in leaving and now wished to make amends.
We often do not know what providential purposes God will accomplish through changes of place or plans originally undertaken for wrong reasons.
Without God's overruling mercy, some of our own sinful plans would have led us to ruin.

div.title: Receive a repentant brother and forgive the debt (verses 15–22)
div.p: We must never minimize the evil of sin itself. But when dealing with a repentant sinner, we should follow God's merciful example and cover the offense rather than keep holding it against the person.
People changed by grace can become blessings to those around them.
Christianity does not abolish genuine obligations toward others; it guides us in fulfilling them rightly.
Repentant people should openly acknowledge harm done to others. Henry understands Onesimus to have admitted his fault to Paul.
Fellowship between Christians does not erase distinctions of property.
Paul's proposal that another person's debt should be charged to him voluntarily illustrates one person accepting another's obligation to free that person from a deserved penalty.
Henry sees this as a figure of Christ willingly bearing the punishment of our sins, so that we may receive his righteousness.
Although Philemon was Paul's spiritual son, Paul appealed to him as a brother.
And although Onesimus was a poor enslaved man, Paul pleaded for him as earnestly as if asking a great personal favor.
Christians should bring one another joy and encouragement. People can expect trouble from the world, but should find consolation among other believers.
When comforts disappear, trust the Lord, use the available means and persevere in prayer. Prayer is powerful, but it does not earn what God grants.
Believers who never meet again on earth will soon meet before God's throne to praise his redeeming love.

Onesimus's conversion should encourage the most deeply guilty sinners to seek God. It must never become an excuse for postponing repentance: many die in their sins, and hardening the heart against present conviction is dangerous.

div.title: Paul's greetings and blessing (verses 23–25)
div.p: Believers may find especially great enjoyment of God's presence when suffering together for Christ.
Grace is the finest blessing we can wish for ourselves or others. Paul began and ended his letter with it.
All grace comes from Jesus Christ, who purchased and gives it.
If his grace is with our spirits, what more do we need for true happiness?
Let us learn now to value what people often recognize only when dying: even the smallest portion of genuine grace and faith is worth more than an earthly kingdom.

div.title: Hebrews — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: The letter presents Christ as the purpose, foundation, substance and truth of everything pictured by the Mosaic law. The legal ceremonies had no power, in themselves, to save the soul.
A central teaching is that Jesus of Nazareth is truly God.

Unconverted Jews tried to persuade Jewish Christians to leave the faith. They claimed that the law of Moses was superior to the Christian gospel and spoke against everything connected with the Savior.

The writer therefore explains the superiority of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and the blessings flowing from his suffering and death as the sacrifice for sins. Christianity is fuller and more excellent than the Mosaic ceremonial system.

Henry understands the principal aim as encouraging believing Hebrews to advance in knowledge of the gospel, become established in Christian faith and resist apostasy, against which strong warnings are given.
Although the first audience was the Hebrew Christians of that time, the letter remains vital to the whole church.

Knowledge of Jesus Christ is the heart of all Scripture. The ceremonial law is full of Christ, and the gospel is full of Christ. The lines of both Testaments meet and harmonize beautifully in him; the letter seeks to show that unity.

row.cell: The surpassing dignity of the Son of God in his Divine person, and in his creating and mediatorial work.
And in his superiority to all the holy angels.

div.title: God's final revelation through his Son (verses 1–3)
div.p: In earlier generations, God spoke to his people at various times and in various ways: sometimes directly, sometimes through dreams, visions and divine influence upon prophets' minds.
The gospel revelation is greater because God has now spoken through his Son.
When we contemplate the power, wisdom and goodness of Jesus Christ, we behold those of his Father too (John 14:7). The entire fullness of deity dwells really, not merely symbolically, in Christ.
When the world fell under the curse and judgment of sin, God's Son sustained it by almighty power and goodness as he undertook its redemption.
The glory of his divine person and mediatorial office leads us to the glory of his grace.
Because of who Jesus is, his suffering possessed sufficient worth to satisfy the honor of God offended by human sin.
We cannot thank God enough for revealing salvation to sinners with increasing clarity.
And that Christ himself purified us from our sins is a wonder of love exceeding all our power to praise or admire.

div.title: Christ is greater than every angel (verses 4–14)
div.p: Some Jews treated angels with excessive, even idolatrous reverence because the law and other divine messages had been delivered through them. Some regarded them as intermediaries and offered them forms of religious homage.
The writer therefore shows not only that Jesus created all things, including angels, but also that the risen Messiah, exalted in human nature, rules over all angels and powers.
He establishes this from comparisons with the Old Testament.
Angels are servants who carry out God's will. But Christ is God: without deity he could not have accomplished the Mediator's work or worn his crown.
As the Messiah, the Anointed One, he was equipped and confirmed for this mediatorial office.
Christ has equals only as a human being, while as Son of God he surpasses every prophet, priest and king who ever served God.
Psalm 102:25–27 speaks of his almighty work in creating the world and transforming it.
He will fold up the earth and heavens like a garment when their present use is finished and they will no longer be abused, yet he remains forever the same.
Like a sovereign who remains sovereign when ceremonial clothing is put away, Christ never loses his dignity.
Sin changed the world for the worse; Christ will transform it for the better. Let this make us watchful and eager for the world to come, rather than attached to fading things.
Though Jesus has done so much to make people his friends, some remain his enemies. Eventually they will become his footstool, whether through humble submission or final destruction.
Angels, even the most exalted, remain servants under Christ.
Believers now possess the status of heirs, not yet the full inheritance.
Angels minister to them under Christ and the Spirit: resisting evil spirits, protecting their bodies, and giving instruction or comfort.
At the last day they will gather the saints, while people who set their hopes on perishing treasure will be driven from Christ's presence into everlasting misery.

row.cell: The duty of stedfastly adhering to Christ and his gospel.
His sufferings are no objection against his pre-eminence.
The reason of his sufferings, and the fitness of them.
Christ's taking the nature of man, and not his taking the nature of angels, was necessary to his priestly office.

div.title: Do not drift away from the gospel (verses 1–4)
div.p: Because Christ is greater than the angels, we must pay careful attention to his message.
Our minds and memories resemble leaking vessels; without attention, what is poured into them escapes.
Our fallen nature, temptations, worldly concerns and pleasures all contribute to this forgetfulness.
The great sin against the gospel is neglecting its wonderful salvation—treating God's saving grace in Christ as unimportant, ignoring both its value and our desperate need of it.
Judgments under the gospel are chiefly spiritual and are therefore more terrifying, not less.
Even partial negligence may bring reproof and spiritual darkness without ultimately destroying a believer.
Christ's teaching was confirmed by those who heard him—the evangelists and apostles who witnessed his words and works—and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to God's will.
God provided reliable grounds for faith and a firm foundation for hope.
Let us therefore attend to the inspired Scriptures, which preserve the witness of those who heard the Lord, and choose the good portion that cannot be taken away.

div.title: Christ's suffering and exaltation (verses 5–9)
div.p: God has not placed either the church's present condition or its final restoration under the rule of angels.
Christ reigns and will bring every earthly kingdom under his dominion.
Why was Christ given to humanity? Because of God's grace.
His unlimited authority followed his humiliation and death. Ancient Scripture finds fulfillment in him.
God has shown wonderful kindness in creation and Providence, yet human sin has repaid those gifts shamefully.

div.title: Christ leads many children to glory (verses 10–13)
div.p: Carnal people may despise Christ's cross, but believers recognize its particular glory.
It was fitting for the Author of salvation to reach the appointed completeness of his mediatorial work through suffering, as he leads many sons and daughters to glory.
His path to the crown ran through the cross; the path of his followers must also pass through trials.
Jesus sanctifies his people. He purchased and sent the Holy Spirit, who makes believers holy as the Spirit of Christ.
Believers are set apart and equipped for sacred purposes. Christ and his people have the same heavenly Father, who is God, and through Christ believers are brought into that family relationship.
When Jesus calls them brothers and sisters, that does not make him merely their equal. His grace in calling them family reveals his dignity and their dependence.
The writer illustrates this relationship from Psalm 22:22, Psalm 18:2 and Isaiah 8:18, as cited in the source commentary.

div.title: He took our nature to save us (verses 14–18)
div.p: Fallen angels were left without a redeemer. Christ did not come to save them and therefore did not take an angelic nature.
An angel could not provide an appropriate sacrifice for human sins.
The Son took our human nature, despite fully knowing the suffering and death involved. His sacrifice was sufficient and suited to those it redeemed.
Through this atonement, his people are delivered from Satan's slavery and receive forgiveness through faith.
Those afraid of death should not try to silence their fears through bravado, despair, worldliness or human tricks.
Instead, seek pardon, peace, grace and a living hope of heaven through the One who died and rose again.
Because Christ himself suffered and experienced temptation without ever sinning, he understands and readily helps his tempted people.
Those facing temptation should not conclude that temptation itself makes them too unworthy to pray.
Henry reassures believers that no soul sincerely crying to the Lord in faith from the danger of temptation will be abandoned to perish.
When temptation first surprises us, turn immediately to him. Prompt prayer is a wise way to stop its progress.

row.cell: The superior worth and dignity of Christ above Moses is shown.
The Hebrews are warned of the sin and danger of unbelief.
And of necessity of faith in Christ, and of stedfastly following him.

div.title: Christ is greater than Moses (verses 1–6)
div.p: Consider Jesus as the Apostle of our confession, sent by God to reveal the faith we proclaim and the hope we hold.
Consider him as Christ, the anointed Messiah, both Apostle and High Priest.
Consider him as Jesus, our Savior, healer and great Physician of souls.
Reflect upon what he is in himself, what he means to us and what he will be to us for eternity.
Careful meditation on Christ teaches us more of him.
The Jews rightly valued Moses' faithfulness, but Moses was only a type of Christ.
Christ made and owns the house—his church and people—and governs it as sovereign Lord.
Moses served faithfully within the house; Jesus rules it as the eternal Son of God.
It is not enough to begin Christian life well. We must persevere in faith to the end.
Meditating on Christ's person and salvation continually supplies wisdom and fresh reasons to trust, love and obey him.

div.title: Do not harden your hearts (verses 7–13)
div.p: Periods of testing can easily become periods of provoking God.
Provoking him when he is exposing our complete dependence upon him is especially serious.
Hardness of heart gives rise to every other sin.
Other people's sins—including relatives' sins—should warn us.
The sins of people professing God's name grieve him as well as offend him.
The Lord is slow to destroy and waits patiently to show grace.
But prolonged, unrepented sin ultimately brings judgment. There is no rest under God's wrath.
All who wish to reach heaven must watch themselves.
Once we permit distrust of God, deserting him may soon follow. Those who believe they stand should beware of falling.
Tomorrow does not belong to us, so make good use of today.
Even the strongest believers need fellow Christians' encouragement.
And the weakest or least esteemed members deserve that same care from the whole church.
Sin disguises itself in many ways. It seems beautiful but is vile, promises pleasure but destroys, promises much and delivers nothing.
Allowing one sin prepares the way for another, and repeated wrongdoing strengthens the habit.
The deceitfulness of sin hardens the soul.

div.title: Share in Christ through persevering faith (verses 14–19)
div.p: The privilege of God's people is being partakers of Christ—of his Spirit, new nature, graces, righteousness and life, and of what he has done and will do.
We must continue in the same sincere faith with which we began.
Perseverance gives evidence of the genuineness of our faith.
Listening to Scripture often can be a means of salvation, yet hearing without obedience increases responsibility under divine judgment.
Both the happiness of sharing Christ's complete salvation and the warning of everlasting misery should move us to persevere.
Do not put confidence in outward membership or religious professions.
Pray to be among the true believers who enter heaven, rather than among those who fall through unbelief.
Our obedience grows as faith grows; neglect and sin flourish where unbelief gains the upper hand.

row.cell: Humble, cautious fear is urged, lest any should come short of the promised rest, through unbelief.
Arguments and motives to faith and hope in our approaches to God.

div.title: Strive to enter God's promised rest (verses 1–10)
div.p: Gospel privileges are greater than those available through Moses' law, although the gospel was preached in substance under both Testaments.
In every generation, many hear God's word without benefiting. Unbelief is the root of unfruitful hearing; faith gives life to the word received.
Partial neglect and careless, wavering profession can make people fail to reach the promised rest.
Therefore pursue a sure entrance into God's kingdom.
Just as God finished his creating work and then rested, he will bring believers to the completion of their appointed labor and give them rest.
A greater and more spiritual Sabbath remains than the seventh-day rest or the land into which Joshua led Israel.
There is rest in grace, comfort and holiness now, through Christ and his gospel, and rest in glory afterward.
Henry identifies the rest chiefly in view as the heavenly rest promised to God's people after the labor and distress of earthly life, when Christ appears.
Unbelief excludes people from both true spiritual rest here and eternal rest thereafter.
God has always revealed that the human soul finds rest in him, and that its only way into that rest is faith in his promises through his Son.

div.title: God's word searches us; our High Priest welcomes us (verses 11–16)
div.p: The goal is spiritual and eternal rest: grace here and glory afterward, in Christ on earth and with Christ in heaven.
Let us work diligently and encourage others to do the same. Labor for God makes final rest more satisfying.
The Holy Scriptures are God's word. When he brings Scripture to the heart through his Spirit, it powerfully convicts, converts and comforts.
It humbles pride, softens rebellious hearts, exposes thoughts, motives and selfish ends, and cuts away sinful habits deeply rooted in the soul.
The word shows sinners what is inside them.
Hold fast Christian doctrine in the mind, its living principles in the heart, its public confession on the lips and practical obedience in the life.
Christ fulfilled one part of his priestly service on earth, dying for us. He fulfills another part in heaven, interceding and presenting his people's offerings.
To save humans, he needed fellow-feeling born of genuine human experience. He encountered the effects of sin that can be experienced without sharing its guilt.
God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3), yet Jesus himself was entirely holy.

Because Christ was perfectly holy and pure, he was all the more unwilling in his very nature to sin and felt its evil more deeply. That makes him all the more concerned to deliver his people from sin's guilt and power.
This excellent High Priest invites us to come boldly to the throne of grace.
We need both mercy to pardon sin and grace to purify the soul.
