Besides asking for our daily needs, we should prepare through prayer for special seasons of temptation—through adversity or prosperity, and especially for the hour of death.
Approach reverently, but not as people dragged before a criminal court: we are welcomed to a mercy seat.
We enter the holiest place through Jesus' blood. He is our Advocate, who has purchased everything the soul needs.

row.cell: The office and duty of a high priest abundantly answered in Christ.
The Christian Hebrews reproved for their little progress in the knowledge of the gospel.

div.title: Jesus fulfills the high priest's calling (verses 1–10)
div.p: A high priest must share our human nature. The need for such a priest shows that humans have sinned and cannot approach the holy God on their own.
But everyone who comes to God through our great High Priest, Jesus Christ, is welcome.
He tenderly intercedes for those who have strayed from the paths of truth, duty and happiness, and can lead them back from error and suffering.
Only someone appointed by God can expect divine help and blessing in performing this sacred office.
In his earthly life Jesus truly shared human weakness short of sin. He hungered, suffered temptation and faced death.
He taught us not merely that we should pray but that we should pray earnestly and fervently. How many of our prayers are dry and unfeeling, unlike those Christ offered with tears!
He was strengthened to bear the terrible suffering appointed to him.
The only complete deliverance from death is to be carried through it. Christ rose and was exalted, and he saves fully those who come to God through him.
Jesus also taught his people to learn humble obedience in the afflictions God permits.
We need correction to learn submission. His obedience in our nature encourages our own obedience and assures us that divine help and comfort are available amid temptation.
Having been perfected for his great mediatorial work, Jesus is the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him.
Are we among those people?

div.title: Grow beyond spiritual infancy (verses 11–14)
div.p: Dull or inattentive hearers make gospel teaching difficult.
Even believers who possess some faith can be slow to understand and believe.
God rightly expects much from those who have received much.
To be inexperienced in the word of righteousness is to lack practical spiritual experience.
True Christian understanding includes a spiritual taste and delight in the goodness, sweetness and excellence of the gospel.
The joy found in experiencing God's grace and love in Christ is too great to express adequately.

row.cell: The Hebrews are urged to go forward in the doctrine of Christ, and the consequences of apostacy, or turning back, are described.
The apostle expresses satisfaction, as to the most of them.
And encourages them to persevere in faith and holiness.

div.title: Progress toward maturity and beware apostasy (verses 1–8)
div.p: Every part of God's truth and will must be explained to those professing the gospel and pressed upon their hearts and consciences.
Outward matters have their proper place, but they can consume attention that should be directed to more important things.

p.hi: A repentant sinner, confessing guilt and crying for mercy, must not take this warning as proof that forgiveness is impossible.

div.p: Nor does this text prove that a person genuinely made new in Christ can become a final apostate.
According to Henry, it is not describing people who had only an empty religious name and no experience of gospel truth, because such people have little from which to fall.
It does not refer to temporary spiritual decline, ordinary backsliding or even grave sins into which believers may fall under powerful temptation.

Instead, the sin warned against is an open and deliberate repudiation of Christ, arising from hatred toward him and his people, approving the actions of his murderers after knowing gospel truth and tasting some of its comfort.
Of such persons it says that renewal to repentance is impossible.
This is not because Christ's blood would be insufficient to pardon such a sin.
Rather, the sin itself is a settled opposition to repentance and everything leading to it.
Those frightened by misunderstanding their own condition should recognize the difference between deliberate, hostile renunciation and the grief of a repentant conscience.
Warn seriously against apostasy, but do not unnecessarily terrorize weak believers or discourage those who have fallen and now repent.
True believers do more than taste God's word: they drink it in and bear fruit, like well-watered soil.

A merely nominal Christian who remains fruitless or produces deceit and self-interest comes close to the terrible apostasy just described; Henry says everlasting misery awaits such a person. We must watch ourselves with humility and prayer.

div.title: Works of love accompany salvation (verses 9 and 10)
div.p: Certain qualities belong to genuine salvation and lead to eternal salvation.
They are better evidence than outward enlightenment or temporary religious experiences.
Acts of love done for Christ's glory and for his people are signs of saving grace.
Genuine love is active love; and works are genuinely good only when they spring from love for Christ.

div.title: The sure promise and anchor of hope (verses 11–20)
div.p: Christian hope means confidently anticipating what God has promised, desiring those blessings and valuing them.
Hope, like faith, may vary in strength.
God's promise comes from his eternal purpose, settled among Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
His counsel and oath are two unchangeable things. God cannot lie, because lying contradicts his will and nature.
His promises therefore ensure believers' salvation just as his warnings confirm judgment upon unbelief.
Believers inherit those promises.
God's comforts are strong enough for the heaviest trials.
Every sinner fleeing to divine mercy through Christ's redemption under the covenant of grace, leaving behind other confidences, finds refuge.
We are like ships at sea, threatened by storms and shipwreck.
Gospel hope is the soul's secure anchor. Its strength rests upon God's free grace, Christ's merits and intercession, and the Spirit's powerful work.
Christ himself is the object and basis of our hope.
Set your affection on things above and wait patiently for his appearance, when believers will share his glory.

row.cell: A comparison between the priesthood of Melchizedec and that of Christ.
The excellence of Christ's priesthood above the Levitical priesthood is shown.
The faith and hope of the church encouraged from this.

div.title: Melchizedek foreshadows Christ (verses 1–3)
div.p: Melchizedek met Abraham as he returned from rescuing Lot.
His name means King of Righteousness, expressing a character that made him a figure of the Messiah and his kingdom.
The name of his city means Peace. As king of peace, he prefigured Christ the Prince of Peace, who reconciles humanity to God.

Scripture does not record the beginning or end of Melchizedek's life. Through this silence, he represents the Son of God, whose existence is eternal and whose priesthood has no predecessor or successor.
Scripture everywhere honors the great King of Righteousness and Peace, our glorious High Priest and Savior.
The more carefully we study it, the more we discover that the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

div.title: A priesthood greater than Levi's (verses 4–10)
div.p: Melchizedek's greatness shows that the promised High Priest whom he represented must be greater than the Levitical priests.
Abraham's highest privilege was possessing God's promises.
Anyone who receives these promises for present and eternal life is truly rich and blessed.
Everyone who receives Jesus Christ enjoys that honor.
Let us engage in spiritual struggles trusting his word and strength, credit our victories to his grace and seek his blessing in all our ways.

div.title: Jesus, priest of an everlasting covenant (verses 11–25)
div.p: The Levitical priesthood and its law could not bring perfection; they give way to a new priesthood through which believers may be made complete.
The law itself revealed that Levitical priests were frail and mortal. They could not preserve even their own earthly lives, much less save others' souls.
But Jesus holds his office through the power of endless life within himself.
He can preserve his own life and grant spiritual and eternal life to everyone trusting his sacrifice and intercession.
The better covenant for which Jesus is Surety is contrasted here not with the covenant of works, which condemns transgressors, but with the covenant at Sinai and its legal dispensation.
The new covenant gives Christ's church clearer knowledge, fuller liberty and richer privileges.
Aaron's order required many priests and successive high priests, but Christ is the one everlasting High Priest.
He is therefore able to save completely, at every time and in every circumstance.
Since our privileges exceed those of believers under the old dispensation, we should desire deeper spirituality and holiness.

div.title: The pure and sufficient High Priest (verses 26–28)
div.p: Christ's holiness is complete.
His very nature contains no habit, principle, tendency or desire toward sin. Even the best Christians still experience sinful inclinations, but none existed in him.
He is harmless and free from every actual wrong: he committed no violence, and no deceit was found in his mouth.
He is entirely undefiled.
We may struggle even to avoid being implicated in others' sins, but Jesus is free from every such stain.
Therefore no one who comes to God in the name of his beloved Son need despair.
Jesus will deliver his people in temptation, suffering, prosperity, death and final judgment.

row.cell: The excellence of Christ's priesthood above that of Aaron is shown.
The great excellence of the new covenant above the former.

div.title: Christ is the High Priest we need (verses 1–6)
div.p: The central conclusion is that believers possess exactly the High Priest they need.
The Son took human nature, lived on earth and offered himself to God as a sacrifice for his people's sins.
We must never approach God or present any worship to him except through Christ, depending on his merits and intercession.
Only in the Beloved are we accepted.
All worship and obedience must stay close to God's word, the complete and perfect standard.
Jesus is the purpose and fulfillment of the law of righteousness.
The covenant contrasted here with Christ's superior covenant was made with Israel as a nation, with promises of temporal advantages.
The gospel promises, made certain through Christ, concern spiritual blessings and eternal life of infinitely greater worth.
Praise God for a priest suited perfectly to our helpless condition.

div.title: God writes his law on believers' hearts (verses 7–13)
div.p: Christ's priesthood surpasses Aaron's through the covenant of grace that he mediates.
The law held sinners accountable but could neither remove their guilt nor quiet the conscience terrified by sin.
Through Christ's blood full forgiveness is provided, and God will remember believers' sins no more.
God once wrote his law for his people. Now he promises to write it within them.
He gives them understanding to know and believe it, memory to retain it, hearts to love it, courage to confess it and power to obey it.
When this foundation is laid, obedience becomes wiser, more sincere, willing, determined, steady and joyful.
The Holy Spirit's abundant work through gospel ministry brings an increase of Christian understanding across every sort of person.
May God fulfill this promise in our time and bless his ministers, so that many may believe and turn to him!
True knowledge of God comes together with the pardon of sins.
That forgiveness is freely given, complete and unchangeable.
Forgiveness opens the door to every other spiritual blessing, while unforgiven sin blocks mercy and brings judgment.
Let us examine whether the Holy Spirit has taught us to know, love, fear, trust and obey Christ sincerely.
All worldly vanity, external religious advantage and empty notions of faith will soon pass away. Those who trust in them rather than Christ will be miserable forever, as Henry warns.

row.cell: The Jewish tabernacle and its utensils.
The necessity, superior dignity, and power of his priesthood and sacrifice.

div.title: The tabernacle points to Christ (verses 1–5)
div.p: The writer explains how Israel's ceremonies prefigured Christ.
The tabernacle was a movable temple. It pictured both the church's temporary condition on earth and Jesus Christ's human nature, in which the fullness of deity truly dwelt.
Its furnishings and ordinances pointed to Jesus as the Light and Bread of life, and to his divine person, holy priesthood, perfect righteousness and prevailing intercession.
From the beginning, Christ was all in all.
Read in the light of the gospel, the ceremonial objects reveal God's wisdom and strengthen faith in the One they represented.

div.title: The limitations of the old sanctuary (verses 6–10)
div.p: Christ, our High Priest, first shed his blood before entering heaven.
Likewise, no believer can enter God's gracious presence now or his glorious presence hereafter except through Jesus' blood.
Sins are deep errors of heart, understanding and conduct. Who can recognize all their own wrongs?
Their guilt cannot be washed away except through Christ's atonement.
We plead his blood here on earth while he pleads for us in heaven.
Some Israelites, instructed by God, understood something of communion with him through the promised Redeemer. But many saw no further than the external rites.
The ceremonial forms could neither remove the pollution and dominion of sin nor settle the worshiper's guilt and inward doubts.
The gospel age should therefore be an age of reformation, clearer knowledge and greater love, with ill will toward none and goodwill toward all.
Greater freedom in spiritual life and expression brings greater responsibility for holy conduct.

div.title: Christ enters heaven through his own blood (verses 11–14)
div.p: Every true spiritual blessing—past, present or future—rests upon Christ's priestly work.
Our High Priest entered heaven once for all, having obtained eternal redemption.
The Holy Spirit showed that older sacrifices could remove ceremonial uncleanness from the outward person, granting certain outward privileges.
Their power did not extend to the conscience.
Christ's blood has an infinitely greater effect because he offered himself without any sinful stain in his nature or life.
His sacrifice cleanses even deeply guilty consciences from dead and sinful works, so that we may serve the living God.
Just as contact with a corpse made an Israelite outwardly unclean, sinful works defile the soul.
The same grace that seals forgiveness recreates and renews the defiled person.
Nothing weakens gospel faith more than undermining the direct saving power of Christ's blood.
We cannot measure the depth of his sacrifice or fully comprehend its wisdom, love and grace. But faith finds life, food and refreshment in contemplating it.

div.title: The testament and the death that makes it effective (verses 15–22)
div.p: Scripture uses both covenant and testament for God's solemn dealings with humanity.
A testament is the willing disposition of an inheritance to those specified, taking effect through the testator's death.
Christ therefore died not only to purchase salvation's blessings but also to establish their distribution to his people.
Through sin, all became guilty before God and forfeited every good thing.
God nevertheless proclaimed a covenant of grace to display the greatness of his mercy.
Not even a sinner's religious duties can be clean unless guilt is removed through an adequate sacrifice, upon which the worshiper continually depends.
All truly good works owe their existence to this all-sufficient cause.
We should present our spiritual offerings as sprinkled and purified by Christ's blood.

div.title: His one sacrifice and promised return (verses 23–28)
div.p: The sacrifices of Christ are infinitely superior to those prescribed by the law.
The older sacrifices could neither secure pardon from sin nor give power to overcome it.
By one sacrifice, Jesus has destroyed the devil's works, so that believers may become righteous, holy and happy.
No wisdom, education, virtue, wealth or power can protect human beings from death.
Likewise, only Christ's atoning sacrifice can rescue sinners from condemnation on the day of judgment.
Those who despise or neglect this great salvation will not escape eternal punishment, Henry warns.
The believer knows the Redeemer lives and trusts that they will see him.
This is the patient hope of the church, expressed in the prayer: “Come, Lord Jesus.”

row.cell: The insufficiency of sacrifices for taking away sin, The necessity and power of the sacrifice of Christ for that purpose.
An argument for holy boldness in the believer's access to God through Jesus Christ, And for steadfastness in faith, and mutual love and duty.
The sufferings of believers, and encouragement to maintain their holy profession.

div.title: Repeated offerings cannot remove sin (verses 1–10)
div.p: The tabernacle and rituals of the Sinai covenant were signs and pictures of the gospel.
The sacrifices repeatedly offered by Israel's high priests could not make worshipers perfect through the pardon of sins and cleansing of conscience.
But God manifested in the flesh became the sacrifice.
Christ's voluntary death upon the cursed tree served as the ransom.
Because the sufferer possessed infinite worth, his willing suffering had an infinite saving value.
A true atoning substitute had to be capable of consenting freely to stand in sinners' place; Jesus did so.
Everything Christ accomplished comes from God's sovereign will and grace.
The righteousness he brought and the sacrifice he offered once have lasting, eternal power.
Through his blood those coming to God receive inner comfort, forgiveness and strength and motivation for obedience.

div.title: One sacrifice secures full and final pardon (verses 11–18)
div.p: The gospel covenant brings complete and final forgiveness, unlike the former order.
Under the law, offerings had to be repeated. They provided at most the forms of pardon belonging to that earthly dispensation.
But one sacrifice of Jesus Christ secures spiritual forgiveness for people from every age and nation, rescuing them from judgment beyond this life.
No human ceremony or invention can replace his sacrifice.
We must therefore trust this one Savior and seek assurance of his work through the Spirit's sanctification producing obedience.
As God's law is written on our hearts, we may know we are justified and that he will remember our sins no more.

div.title: Draw near and encourage one another (verses 19–25)
div.p: Having explained Christ's sacrifice, the writer applies it to Christian living.
Since believers have an open way into God's presence, they must make use of it.
We come through Jesus' blood and its atoning merit.
The harmony of God's absolute holiness and forgiving mercy became clear through the suffering of his incarnate Son.
Heaven's way is through the crucified Savior; his death becomes life for believers.
To stay needlessly far away would show disrespect for Christ's welcome.
The call for bodies washed in pure water recalls the law's purifications; baptism's water reminds Christians to live in holiness.
Receiving comfort and grace from our reconciled Father, we should adorn his teaching in every respect.
Think actively about how to serve one another.
Stir one another up toward love and good works; fellowship among believers is a powerful aid to perseverance.
As trials and death approach, become more diligent, not less.

div.title: The danger of deliberate apostasy (verses 26–31)
div.p: The warning concerns a complete, final rejection of the Savior.
Henry describes people who knowingly and decisively despise Christ, the only Savior; resist the Spirit, the only Sanctifier; and renounce the gospel, the only saving way.
Some hardened sinners taste terrible forebodings of judgment even during earthly life.
Dying after refusing divine mercy is more dreadful than suffering ordinary punishment.
Astonishingly, not only God's justice but his despised grace and mercy testify against such rejection.
Yet none of this means that a sinner grieved over sin must be excluded from mercy.
No one willing to accept Christ's sacrifice will be refused its benefit.

p.hi: Jesus never casts out those who come to him.

div.title: Persevere through suffering until the promised reward (verses 32–39)
div.p: Early Christians endured many kinds of suffering and difficult struggles.
Christian love is not selfish: it makes us pity, visit, help and intercede for fellow sufferers.
Earthly possessions are only shadows; heavenly happiness lasts forever and cannot be taken away by enemies.
It will richly repay every loss endured here.
For now, much of the believer's happiness remains in promise.
Even after our work seems finished, patience may require us to live on and wait until God's time for our reward.
Christ will come for believers at death, end their troubles and give the crown of life.
The struggle may be fierce, but it is brief.
God is not pleased with an outward religious profession that does not persevere.
Those sustained by grace through earlier trials can hope for grace to continue living and dying by faith, until they receive the salvation of their souls.

row.cell: The nature and power of faith described.
It is set forth by instances from Abel to Noah.
By Jacob, Joseph, Moses, the Israelites, and Rahab.
The better state of believers under the gospel.

div.title: The nature and power of faith (verses 1–3)
div.p: From the world's beginning, faith has distinguished God's servants.
The Holy Spirit plants this principle through regeneration, making us receive the truth about justification through Christ's suffering and merits.
Faith and hope concern the same promised blessings.
Faith confidently expects that God will accomplish everything promised in Christ.
It gives the soul a present foretaste and reality of things promised for the future, and convinces the mind of realities invisible to the eyes.
It also approves all that God has revealed as holy, just and good.
Such faith shaped the obedience, service and endurance of the people Scripture commends.
The Bible gives the true account of creation's origin.
We should not distort its account merely to accommodate changing human speculations.
Everything visible came into being by God's command.

div.title: Abel, Enoch and Noah (verses 4–7)
div.p: Abel presented an atoning sacrifice from the firstborn of his flock, admitting that as a sinner he deserved death and could hope for mercy only through the great future Sacrifice.
Cain's jealous hatred of an accepted worshiper prefigured the persecution and even murder of faithful believers in every age.
Though dead, Abel still speaks through his example.
Enoch was taken so that he did not experience death, anticipating Christ's receiving into heaven the believers alive at his return.
We cannot approach God unless we believe him to be as he reveals himself in Scripture and seek him wholeheartedly.
Noah's faith expressed itself in building the ark as instructed.
His trust and obedience exposed others' unbelief and rebellion.
Godly examples may either bring sinners to conversion or expose and condemn their unbelief.
People warned of judgment should flee to Christ for refuge and become heirs of righteousness by faith.

div.title: Abraham and Sarah trust God's promises (verses 8–19)
div.p: Faith often requires us to leave earthly connections, interests and comforts.
Those sharing Abraham's faith obey God's call even when they cannot know the future.
They remain in the path of duty, expecting God to fulfill his promises.
Abraham's test was to obey simply and completely.
Sarah regarded God's promise as dependable because God was both able and willing to fulfill it.
Those included in God's promises do not always receive the promised blessings quickly.
But faith can bring distant hopes near, delighting in them and living as strangers and pilgrims traveling toward heaven.
Faith even helps believers face death cheerfully.
Those genuinely called out of sin do not want to return to it.
All true believers seek their heavenly inheritance, and stronger faith deepens this longing.
Despite their sinful condition and outward poverty, God is not ashamed to be called their God.
They should not be ashamed of him or of his people, nor bring shame upon his name.
Abraham's offering of Isaac was an extraordinary test (Genesis 22:2).
We should overcome doubts and fears through trust in God's almighty power.
The best way to enjoy earthly comforts is to surrender them to God; he then returns or replaces them as he knows best.
Compare Abraham's obedience with our willingness to accept even lesser acts of self-denial, trusting God to compensate our losses and bring blessing even through suffering.

div.title: Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Israel and Rahab (verses 20–31)
div.p: Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future. Present possessions are not the highest blessings, and having them or lacking them does not prove divine love or hatred.
Jacob lived and died by faith.
Faith is vital throughout life, but especially at death, enabling believers to honor the Lord through patience, hope and joy.
Joseph's faith sustained him through temptation, persecution, and later honors and power at Pharaoh's court.
Freedom from wicked laws is a great blessing. When such laws exist, we should use every lawful means to protect ourselves.
Henry notes that Moses' parents displayed faith mixed with some unbelief, which God graciously overlooked.
Faith strengthens us against enslaving fear of human beings and reveals God's greatness and earthly power's emptiness.
The pleasures of sin are brief. They must end either in speedy repentance or ruin.
Worldly pleasures become sinful whenever enjoying them requires turning from God and his people.
Suffering is better than sin, because even the smallest sin is more evil than the greatest suffering.
Moses chose to share the reproach of God's people rather than enjoy Egypt's treasures.
Christ considers their reproach his own, giving it greater worth than an empire's wealth.
Moses made this choice as an adult capable of understanding its cost.
It is especially important to choose God's service when worldly pleasures are most accessible and appealing.
Believers may rightly seek the promised reward.
Trusting God's presence enables perseverance through any difficulty.
We are rescued from judgment not by our own works but by Christ's blood and credited righteousness.
True faith finds sin bitter even while receiving forgiveness.
Israel's deliverance and the fall of Jericho show God's power to overcome even mighty opposition through faith.
Faith desires not only a covenant with God but also fellowship with his people, willing to share their circumstances.
Rahab's actions demonstrated her faith, but they did not merit her justification, because even her act was imperfect and could not satisfy God's perfect justice.

div.title: More faithful witnesses, enduring trials and persecution (verses 32–38)
div.p: The more we study Scripture, the more we discover there is still to learn.
Many Old Testament believers possessed strong faith even though God's promises were less fully revealed to them.
How sad if in the brighter light of the gospel so few believe and faith is so weak!
Faith enables great achievements without promoting self-importance.
Gideon teaches humility amid success. Barak sought God's help in danger and gave thanks for deliverance.
Through faith, God's servants can overcome even the roaring lion seeking someone to devour.
Samson shows faith triumphing over enemies even in death. Jephthah reminds us that God graciously uses deeply undeserving people, whose faith still acknowledges him.
David endured severe tests and left the Psalms as a lasting witness of faith.
Samuel shows how valuable it is to begin trusting God young.
Faith enables service in whatever work God assigns and can overcome the opposition of kings and kingdoms.
Doing righteousness is a greater honor than performing miracles.
Faith receives promises and patiently waits for their fulfillment.
Though believers do not expect dead relatives to return to life in this world, they can endure loss through hope of a better resurrection.
The cruelty of persecutors is dreadful; so is the power of grace that enables the faithful to endure it.
The world is not worthy of those saints whom it treats as unworthy even to live.
It does not value their company, counsel, example or service, because it rejects Christ and his grace (Hebrews 11:39).

div.title: God's better provision for believers (verses 39 and 40)
div.p: The world thinks the righteous are unfit to remain alive, while God declares the world unworthy of them.
Although the world's reasons are wrong, both judgments show that believers' true rest is not in this world.
God receives them from it.
The Hebrew Christians have received even better privileges through the gospel.
Therefore obedient faith, patient hope and loving service should grow in proportion to those greater gifts.
If we do not share the genuine faith of these earlier believers, Henry warns that their example will condemn us at the last judgment.
Let us pray continually for greater faith, follow their shining examples, and finally be made perfect with them in holiness and happiness, shining like the sun in our Father's kingdom forever.

row.cell: An exhortation to be constant and persevere, The example of Christ is set forth, and the gracious design of God in all the sufferings believers endured.
Peace and holiness are recommended, with cautions against despising spiritual blessings.
The New Testament dispensation shown to be much more excellent than the Old.

div.title: Run the race by looking to Jesus (verses 1–11)
div.p: Believers are called to a race of faithful perseverance in Christ whose outcome is either everlasting glory or everlasting misery.
The sin that so easily entangles us is especially the sin to which our own habits, circumstances or age make us vulnerable.
As long as a cherished sin remains unrestrained, it hinders spiritual progress and strengthens discouragement.
When tired and fainthearted, remember the holy Jesus, who endured suffering to rescue us from eternal misery.
Fixing our thoughts upon him strengthens holy affection and restrains sinful desires.
Our trials are small compared with his agonies, what we deserve, and the hardships borne by many others.
Even believers are inclined to lose heart because of remaining sin and imperfect grace.
Although enemies may cause our troubles, God our heavenly Father can use those troubles as fatherly correction.
We should not treat affliction as meaningless, but neither should we collapse in bitterness or despair.
Our Father may let others continue in sin for a time, but he corrects his own children for their good.
Human parents sometimes discipline out of anger or selfishness; the Father of our souls never afflicts his children merely to satisfy passion.
Earthly life is a kind of spiritual childhood in which we still need teaching and correction.
When made perfect in heaven, we will understand his wisdom more fully.
God's discipline is not condemnation. Received with faith and patience, it promotes holiness.

div.title: Pursue peace and holiness; do not despise grace (verses 12–17)
div.p: Affliction can make believers' hands hang down and their knees weak.
Yet they must gather courage for the spiritual race.
Faith and patience enable us to pursue peace and holiness as diligently as a person pursues a calling.
Peace with people from different groups and parties is helpful for holy living.
But peace and holiness must remain together: there is no genuine peace in continuing sin.
An unmortified desire may seem dead and then spring up like a poisonous root, spreading trouble through the community.
The danger of apostasy appears when someone, like Esau, values momentary sensual pleasure above God's blessing and heavenly inheritance.
People who despise these blessings now will not always regard them so lightly.
A profane person may desire God's blessing while refusing the means God appointed to receive it.
But God will not detach the blessing from his appointed way or combine it with indulgence in sin.
No one who sincerely seeks his mercy and blessing will ultimately seek in vain.

div.title: Zion's covenant and reverent worship (verses 18–29)
div.p: Sinai was a physical mountain, illustrating how much of the Mosaic order concerned outward and earthly matters.
The gospel is kinder and suited to our weakness. Through Christ we may approach God with boldness.
But without a Savior, even the most outwardly righteous person must despair before Sinai's holy law.
The gospel church is Mount Zion. Believers receive clearer views of heaven and heavenly desires.
Every child of God is an heir with the privileges of the firstborn.
A person still devoted to selfish desires and earthly pride would find heaven's holy fellowship strange and uncomfortable.
Christ is the Mediator of the new covenant, bringing God and humans together, keeping them in fellowship, interceding for us, calling us back to God and finally gathering his people in heaven.
His blood establishes this covenant.
Unlike a cry for vengeance, Christ's sprinkled blood speaks mercy for sinners.
We must not refuse his gracious voice from heaven.
God's patient appeal under the gospel does not remove judgment against those who reject such kindness.
Acceptable worship requires reverence and godly fear, empowered by grace.
God is as holy and just under the gospel as under the law.
Believers' inheritance is secure and every saving blessing is given freely as they pray.
Seek grace to serve him with reverent love.

row.cell: Exhortations to various duties, and to be content with what Providence allots.
To respect the instructions of faithful pastors, with cautions against being carried away by strange doctrines.
Further exhortations to duties, that relate to God, to our neighbour, and to those set over us in the Lord.
This epistle to be seriously considered.

div.title: Love one another and be content (verses 1–6)
div.p: Jesus gave himself to redeem a people eager for good works.
Faith in him is the strongest bond of genuine friendship.
Christians are called to many duties, especially contentment.
The opposite is greed: an excessive desire for earthly possessions mixed with envy of people who have more.
Because we possess treasures in heaven, we can be content even in humble earthly circumstances.
People who cannot be content now would often be just as discontent if their position improved.
Adam lived in paradise and was discontent. Some angels were not content even in heaven.
Yet Paul learned contentment in every circumstance, including poverty and loss.
The great divine promise sums up all the others: “I will never leave you or forsake you.”
Henry notes that the original expression contains five negatives emphasizing certainty.
Believers have God's gracious presence in life, at death and forever.
Human opposition can accomplish nothing beyond God's rule; he can turn even hostility to his people's good.

div.title: Follow faithful leaders while holding fast to Christ (verses 7–15)
div.p: Remember the teaching and example of faithful ministers who completed their service honorably.
Some leaders die and others will soon die, but Jesus Christ, the church's Head and High Priest, never changes.
He is the same across both Testaments and forever—equally merciful, strong and sufficient.
He continues feeding hungry souls, strengthening the fearful and welcoming repentant sinners.
He still rejects pride and self-righteousness, despises empty religious profession and teaches all whom he saves to love righteousness and hate evil.
Our hearts are established through free grace applied by the Holy Spirit, not through deceptive innovations.
Christ is both our Altar and our Sacrifice, consecrating what we offer.
The Lord's Supper is the feast of the gospel Passover.
Clinging to Levitical sacrifices would exclude people from the Christian altar according to the old law's own structure.
Therefore we must go outside the camp to Christ—leaving the ceremonial order, sin, the world and selfish confidence.
Through his blood we are set apart to God.
Our present home cannot endure, because sin and death will not let us remain.
Seek through faith the rest and peace only Jesus provides.
Bring to God through Christ a continuous sacrifice of praise, including worship, prayer and thanksgiving.

div.title: Serve others, respect biblical leaders and pray (verses 16–21)
div.p: Help meet people's spiritual and bodily needs according to your means.
Such offerings please God, who receives them and blesses their givers through Christ.
Submit to your living ministers only so far as their teaching agrees with God's will revealed in Scripture.
No Christian is too wise or important to learn.
Believers must search the Scriptures and receive their ministers' counsel insofar as it agrees with that standard.
It benefits the congregation when its pastors can give a joyful rather than grieving account of its spiritual condition.
Faithful ministers must fulfill their responsibility; stubbornly unfaithful hearers bear responsibility for their own ruin.
Pray earnestly for ministers. The more sincerely a church prays, the more benefit it may expect from their service.
Even ministers with a good conscience need others' prayers.
God is the God of peace, reconciled to believers and the source of reconciliation between himself and sinners.
He desires peace among his churches and places spiritual peace in believers' hearts.
His covenant rests securely on the blood of his Son.
The great prayer is that Christians may become fully equipped for every good work and fitted for the fellowship and happiness of heaven.
Every good thing wrought within us is God's work, through Christ and by his Spirit.

div.title: Receive this exhortation and remain in grace (verses 22–25)
div.p: Even believers, because sin remains, sometimes reject important and comforting truth when it challenges them.
They must therefore be urged to receive rather than resent loving instruction.
Christians should have the law of love and kindness written in their hearts toward one another.
True religion teaches gentleness, courtesy and consideration, not harshness or rudeness.
May God's favor remain with you, and may his grace work continually in you, producing the fruits of holiness as the first taste of heavenly glory.

div.title: James — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: James's letter is among the New Testament's most instructive writings.

It chiefly addresses errors that had arisen among Jewish Christians. Rather than providing the extensive doctrinal explanations found in some other apostolic letters, it sets out an excellent summary of the practical duties of believers.
The leading truths of Christianity appear throughout.

Read carefully, the letter fully agrees with Paul's teaching concerning grace and justification. It strongly calls for hopeful patience, the obedience of faith and the practical exercise of love. Its warnings, rebukes and encouragements suit the different people addressed.
Its truths must be maintained, and its rules of conduct remain applicable in every age.
Christ has no dead, fruitless branches. Faith is not an idle grace: wherever true faith exists, it produces the fruit of good works.

row.cell: How to apply to God under troubles, and how to behave in prosperous and in adverse circumstances.
To look upon all evil as proceeding from ourselves, and all good from God.
The duty of watching against a rash temper, and of receiving the word of God with meekness.
The difference between vain pretences and real religion.

div.title: Trials should produce patience, prayer and humility (verses 1–11)
div.p: Christianity teaches us to rejoice during trials. God sends such experiences in love, using them to strengthen the graces already at work within us and prepare us for the crown of life.
During a trial we must let patience, not passion, direct what we say and do. When patience has completed its work, it equips us for the Christian race and spiritual warfare.

We should not pray only for an affliction to be removed. More importantly, ask for wisdom to use the trial rightly: wisdom to govern our spirits and manage our responsibilities. When we come to God acknowledging our weakness and folly, we may confidently claim his promise to give wisdom to anyone who asks.

Those whose chief concern is their spiritual and eternal welfare become wiser through suffering. Their faith and devotion remain steady instead of rising and falling with outward circumstances. Instability may not always cost a person worldly respect, but it cannot please God.

Whatever our situation, we can rejoice in God. People of low standing may rejoice because faith makes them rich heirs of God's kingdom. The wealthy may rejoice when humbling trials teach them that worldly possessions fade and that happiness comes from God, not from things destined to perish.

div.title: Evil comes from our sinful desires; good gifts come from God (verses 12–18)
div.p: Not every sufferer is blessed. The blessing belongs to those who persevere in the path of duty through trials. Their love for God will be fully rewarded in the world where love is perfected.
God's commands and providential trials reveal what rules a person's heart. Yet nothing sinful in our thoughts or actions can be attributed to God.

A refining fire may expose impurities without creating them. Likewise, divine testing reveals the corruption already present in us; God is not its author. Blaming our sinful nature, circumstances or lack of self-control upon God falsely makes him responsible for wrongdoing.
The origin of sinful temptation lies within our own hearts. Stop its earliest movements, or the evils that follow remain our responsibility.
God takes no pleasure in humanity's death and does not cause its sin.

He is unchanging. The sun appears different when clouds pass before it, although the sun itself has not changed. So the variations we experience arise from our condition, not from change in God's goodness.

Every good gift comes from him, especially new birth through divine grace. Through his renewing work, a Christian becomes so changed as to seem made anew. We should dedicate every capacity to his service, becoming firstfruits among his creatures.

div.title: Listen humbly rather than speaking in anger (verses 19–21)
div.p: When suffering, do not accuse God. Open your heart and ears to receive what he teaches.
Those wishing to control their tongues must first govern their passions. Anger is the worst contribution we can make to a dispute.
Cast away wrongdoing as a person throws off filthy clothes. This includes corrupt thoughts, desires and affections, not merely visible conduct.
Receive God's word with humility and teachability. Welcome even correction of your faults, not only enduring it patiently but receiving it with thanks.
God's word intends to make us wise for salvation. People who attend to it merely for selfish or trivial advantages dishonor the gospel and harm their own souls.

div.title: Be doers of the word rather than forgetful hearers (verses 22–25)
div.p: Even if we heard a sermon every day from an angel, hearing without obedience could never bring us to heaven.
Those who only hear deceive themselves. At the end, self-deception will prove the most dangerous deception of all.
God's word acts as a mirror. It exposes the corruption of our hearts and conduct.

The law reveals the stains of sin; the gospel shows Christ's blood as the cleansing remedy. But looking into that mirror helps nothing if we go away, forget the stains, and refuse the cleansing offered.
Study the word for direction and continue in what it teaches. Its promises bring present comfort and future reward.
Every part of revelation has a purpose: leading sinners to Christ for salvation and helping believers walk in freedom by the Spirit of adoption, obeying God's holy commands.
Notice the distinction: the blessing does not come because of the merit of our deeds, but is experienced in faithful doing. What counts is not merely talking but walking.
As believers continue in obedience, Christ becomes more precious to them and they become increasingly prepared for their inheritance in light.

div.title: Genuine religion controls speech and practices love (verses 26 and 27)
div.p: People who work harder to appear religious than to be religious have an empty profession.

An uncontrolled tongue, eagerness to expose other people's faults or attempts to belittle their wisdom and godliness betray this emptiness. A slanderous tongue cannot be reconciled with a truly humble and gracious heart.
False religion reveals itself through impurity and lack of compassion. True religion teaches us to act continually in God's presence.
A pure life belongs together with sincere love and charity. Genuine religion is measured by how these qualities shape the heart and conduct.
What matters in Jesus Christ is faith working through love—faith that purifies the heart, puts sinful desires to death and obeys God's commandments.

row.cell: All professions of faith are vain, if not producing love and justice to others.
The necessity of good works to prove the sincerity of faith, which otherwise will be of no more advantage than the faith of devils.

div.title: Faith must not lead us to favor the wealthy (verses 1–13)
div.p: Those professing faith in Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, must not favor people according to wealth, clothing or social appearance. Such judgments contradict discipleship to the lowly Jesus.
This instruction does not justify rude or disorderly behavior. Ordinary civil respect remains appropriate.
But preference must never distort church appointments, the church's handling of offenses or any other matter of religion.
Careful self-examination helps us recognize these inconsistencies.

Places of worship require money to build and maintain. Henry allows that people who contribute may in some circumstances receive suitable accommodation. Nevertheless, if Christians were more spiritually minded, poor worshipers would be treated with much greater attention.

Lowly circumstances can favor inward peace and growth in holiness. God could provide every believer with worldly wealth if it would truly be good for them. Yet he has chosen people who are rich in faith and heirs of his kingdom.
Consider how wealth and worldly power can bring vice and disgrace upon religion.
God's royal law requires us to love our neighbor as ourselves. It comes from the King of kings. Anyone acting unjustly is condemned by it.
No number of good deeds can pay for an earlier sin. Under the covenant of works, breaking even one divine command brings condemnation that no past, present or future obedience can remove.
Those who are in Christ enjoy a different standing. They can serve God without slavish fear: God's commandments are not bondage, but their own sinful desires are.

Final judgment will be without mercy for those who remain unrepentant. Yet God delights to pardon and bless people who deserve condemnation. Everyone receiving his mercy should show mercy in their conduct.

div.title: Living faith is proved through good works (verses 14–26)
div.p: It is wrong to mistake mental agreement with the gospel for the whole of Christianity.
True faith alone grants us a share in Christ's righteousness, atonement and grace, and saves the soul. But it produces holy fruit and reveals its reality in good works.
Merely agreeing that doctrines are true is very different from saving faith.
Outward profession can win the esteem of religious people or even worldly advantages. But what value is that if a person gains the world and loses the soul?
An opinion about the gospel, without obedience, is not living faith.
The believer must not simply assent to what the Bible says but consent from the heart to receive Christ. Genuine believing involves the whole person, not only the understanding.
Abraham and Rahab illustrate that justifying faith does not remain alone.
Abraham believed God, and this was credited to him as righteousness. His faith then produced obedience even when obedience tested his reason, affections and interests.
That is the meaning of justification through works in James: not empty profession or faithless observance, but faith made visible through obedience.
Rahab's actions showed how faith could change a sinner. Her deed demonstrated faith alive in the heart, not merely agreement in the mind.
The finest outward works without faith are dead because they lack the right root and purpose. But a claimed root of faith without fruit is also effectively dead.
Faith is the root; good works are the fruit. Both must be present.
The only alternatives are living as God's friend or remaining his enemy.
Faith that justifies and saves leads us to live for God and toward God, refusing what opposes him.

row.cell: Cautions against proud behaviour, and the mischief of an unruly tongue.
The excellence of heavenly wisdom, in opposition to that which is worldly.

div.title: The tongue can set a life on fire (verses 1–12)
div.p: A tongue that is not controlled is one of the greatest dangers in human life.
Human speech has repeatedly thrown private and public affairs into confusion, in every age and social condition.
Hell contributes far more to the sinful fire of human speech than people usually realize. When words serve sin, they are set ablaze by that evil source.
No one can tame the tongue without God's grace and help.
James does not suggest control is absolutely impossible, but that it is extremely difficult.
Some sins diminish with age as opportunities decrease. But uncontrolled speech can grow worse when physical strength fails and people become increasingly irritable, bitter or dissatisfied.
A person contradicts himself by praising God's perfection with one breath and condemning good people for using different words or expressions with the next.
Genuine religion will not accept this contradiction.
A sanctified heart should produce holy and useful speech. Just as one tree does not produce another kind of tree's fruit, true believers should not normally produce curses, lies, boasting and abuse.
Nevertheless, many professing Christians find it easier to control bodily appetites than to govern their words.
Let us depend on God's grace, refuse to bless and curse with the same tongue, and strive for consistency between speech and behavior.

div.title: Wisdom from above is pure, gentle and peaceable (verses 13–18)
div.p: There is a great difference between claiming wisdom and possessing it.
Those who think or speak cleverly are not wise according to Scripture unless they also live and act wisely.
True wisdom is demonstrated by humility and gentleness.
Envy, malice and rivalry produce disorder and make people ready for almost any evil work.
Such wisdom comes from earthly principles, seeks earthly goals and operates through worldly motives.
By contrast, the wisdom James describes closely resembles the Christian love Paul describes. Each provides a clear test for our professed spiritual progress.
Heavenly wisdom is not disguised, crafty or deceitful.
It is sincere, open, steady and consistent, refusing the clever manipulations the world admires.
May purity, peace, gentleness, teachability, mercy and the fruits of righteousness in our conduct show that God has given us this excellent gift.

row.cell: Here are cautions against corrupt affections, and love of this world, which is enmity to God.
Exhortations to undertake no affairs of life, without constant regard to the will and providence of God.

div.title: Resist sinful desires and submit to God (verses 1–10)
div.p: Quarrels and conflicts arise from corrupt desires within the human heart.
We need to put to death the sinful passions that struggle within us. Worldly and bodily desires are like illnesses that never permit lasting contentment.
They also hinder prayer, diverting our longings away from God.
We may misuse even a genuine mercy after receiving it, because our hearts are wrongly directed.
When people ask God for prosperity, their aims may be corrupt. A prayer arising chiefly from selfish lust rather than spiritual grace rightly receives no answer.
Worldliness is hostility toward God. An enemy can be reconciled, but a settled attitude of hostility must itself be abandoned.

A person may possess many things in this life and remain within God's love. But the one who sets the heart upon the world and would conform to it rather than lose its friendship chooses opposition to God.
The Holy Spirit does not produce envy, greed and self-centered striving. Our fallen nature does.
The Spirit teaches us to use what we have for the good of those around us.
God's grace changes the worldly spirit into another kind of disposition.
The proud resist God's truth with their understanding, God's commands with their will, and God's providence with their passions. It is no wonder, then, that God opposes the proud.
The humble receive greater grace because they recognize their need, pray for help and give thanks for what they receive.
Submit your mind to God's revealed truth, your will to his commands, and your circumstances to his providence.
The devil continues pursuing people who yield to him. But those who put on God's whole armor and resist firmly will see him retreat.
Let sinners turn to God and seek his grace. All sin must be mourned, either now through godly sorrow or hereafter in eternal misery.
The Lord will comfort a person who genuinely grieves over sin and exalt one who humbles himself before him.

div.title: Speak kindly and plan in dependence upon Providence (verses 11–17)
div.p: Let our speech be governed by kindness as well as truth and justice.
Christians are brothers and sisters. We must not elevate personal opinions into laws for everyone else.
The law of God judges us all; we have no authority to replace it with our own preferences.
Consider how quickly ambitious, calculating people leave God out of their plans!
Human life is brief and uncertain. We may calculate the exact minute of tomorrow's sunrise, but cannot control when a cloud of vapor will vanish.
Our circumstances and pleasures disappear just as quickly, yet eternal happiness or misery depends upon how we respond to God in this short span.
We may make responsible plans for ourselves, family and friends, but should always acknowledge that our times belong to God.
Providence frequently overturns even careful human schemes.
Submit every intention and action to the Lord's will. Worldly boasting about future success is foolish, harmful and often a path to disappointment.
Sins of omission are as real as sins of commission.
Not doing the good we know we should do will come into judgment just as doing known evil will.
How diligently we should avoid neglecting prayer, meditation and self-examination, as well as obvious outward sins!

row.cell: The judgments of God denounced against rich unbelievers.
Exhortation to patience and meekness under tribulations.
Cautions against rash swearing Prayer recommended in afflictive and prosperous circumstances, Christians to confess their faults to each other.
The happiness of being the means of the conversion of a sinner.

div.title: Oppression and self-indulgence face judgment (verses 1–6)
div.p: Public disasters fall especially heavily upon people who live securely in sensual pleasure, although every social class suffers in such times.
The treasures people idolize will soon perish.
Those hoarded possessions will remain only as evidence against their owners at judgment.
Never defraud or oppress other people. Avoid even the appearance of doing so.
God does not forbid reasonable and lawful enjoyment, but living for pleasure, especially sinful pleasure, provokes his anger.
Indulgence in bodily appetites makes people unfit to attend to the concerns of their souls.
Upright people may be condemned and killed by oppressors. God notices their suffering.
Above all, Henry writes in the collective language of his period that “the Jews” had condemned and crucified Jesus Christ, the righteous One.

div.title: Wait patiently for the Lord's coming (verses 7–11)
div.p: A farmer patiently waits for a crop. Should believers be less willing to wait for a crown of glory?
If our waiting is longer, the prize is far greater.
The Lord's coming is near in the sense that his promises will be fulfilled and his people's losses and sufferings repaid.
Humans measure time by their short lifespans. But thousands of years are like a few days to God.
A handful of years can seem endless to us, yet all time is a moment to him.
Consider Job. God's pity and tender mercy were not evident to everyone during his trials, but the outcome made them clear.
Believers, too, will discover that their endurance ends in blessing.
Serve God and bear difficulties in faith, assured that the end will crown everything.
Only eternal happiness in him is secure. Every other object of hope is temporary.

div.title: Pray in suffering, confess faults and seek grace (verses 12–18)
div.p: Careless and profane swearing shows contempt for God's name and authority.
It gives no real profit, pleasure or honor. It is an unnecessary expression of hostility to God, even among people who profess his name and participate in worship.
The Lord will not treat his name as meaningless.
When suffering, prayer is especially fitting. The heart is humbled, and prayer becomes the means through which faith and hope grow.
The healing of sick people is attributed not to anointing with oil but to prayer.
During illness, cold, formal prayers are inadequate. We should pray in faith.
The chief blessing to ask for ourselves and others in sickness is the forgiveness of sins.

Do not encourage people to postpone repentance by suggesting that a final confession, minister's absolution, words of exhortation or religious ceremony will remedy an entire life deliberately lived without godliness.
Confessing faults to one another helps restore peace and brotherly love.
An effective prayer comes from a righteous believer justified in Christ and walking by grace in obedient holiness.
Its earnestness is formed in the heart through the Holy Spirit, awakening holy affections, believing expectations and dependence on God's promises at his mercy seat.
Elijah's example shows prayer's power.
We must never regard the result as a person's merit, but as God's grace.
It is not enough merely to repeat a prayer. We must truly pray while praying, concentrating thought and directing sincere desires toward God.
Though answers today may not involve as many visible miracles, just as much divine grace may accompany them.

div.title: Restore sinners instead of merely changing their opinions (verses 19 and 20)
div.p: No wise or holy person should claim never to be mistaken or refuse to acknowledge an error.
Practical wrongdoing often rests on mistaken principles or beliefs.
But genuine conversion means turning a sinner away from the error of a sinful life.
It is not merely changing religious party, preferred opinion or way of thinking.
The only way to have sin truly covered is to forsake it.
When one person is converted, many sins are prevented in that person and potentially in others whom they influence.
The salvation of one soul is worth infinitely more than preserving multitudes of human lives or benefiting an entire nation.
Whatever our position, let us work without sparing effort in God's service, knowing labor done for the Lord is never wasted.
Henry marvels that for six thousand years God had continued multiplying pardons without exhausting his grace.
Divine mercy remains an ocean always full and always flowing.
May we receive this mercy through Christ's blood and the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit.

div.title: 1 Peter — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Peter's letter applies the same great doctrines found in Paul's letters to the practical life of believers.
It is especially marked by gentleness, tender affection and humble love.
Though brief, it provides a clear summary of the comfort and instruction Christians need on their journey toward heaven.
It directs their thoughts and desires toward eternal happiness, and strengthens them against sinful corruption within and temptation and suffering from outside.

row.cell: The apostle blesses God for his special benefits through Christ.
Salvation by Christ foretold in ancient prophecy.
All are exhorted to holy conversation.
Such as is suitable to their principles, privileges, and obligations.

div.title: A living hope through Christ's resurrection (verses 1–9)
div.p: This letter addresses believers scattered among nations who remain strangers in whichever country or city they inhabit.
They should credit salvation to the Father's electing love, the Son's redemption and the Holy Spirit's sanctification, giving glory to one God in three persons, into whose name they were baptized.
Worldly hope is often an uncertain expectation, resting on sand. Many people's ideas about heaven are no more than blind guesses.
But God's children possess a living hope, both in its object and in its active effects: it encourages and comforts them in trouble and gives strength to overcome obstacles.
This springs entirely from God's abundant mercy.
The heavenly inheritance is incorruptible, undefiled and unfading. It cannot run out, become polluted or lose its glory.
Every worldly possession comes with imperfection. Even a beautiful home may hide anguish; luxurious beds and full tables cannot prevent bodily illness or an uneasy heart.
Possessions are frequently acquired or used sinfully, and they soon pass away like flowers.
God gives his people grace and preserves them for glory.
The hope of this inheritance ought to show in the believer's demeanor and conduct.
God does not enjoy afflicting people, yet his wise love can appoint sharp trials to reveal and strengthen their faith.

p.hi: Gold loses material in the refining fire; faith may gain firmness and strength through testing.

div.p: Gold eventually perishes and purchases only perishable things, while proven faith yields praise, honor and glory.
Believing Christ's excellence and love awakens an affectionate response of love toward him.
God's glory and our happiness belong together. When we seek the former sincerely now, we will possess the latter fully where evil can no longer reach us.

div.title: The prophets foretold Christ's suffering and glory (verses 10–12)
div.p: Jesus Christ was the great subject of the prophets' study.
They examined the sufferings appointed for him and the glory afterward, discovering the central gospel message: he was handed over for our sins and raised for our justification.
God often answers our genuine needs rather than our exact requests.
The teaching of the prophets and of the apostles agrees because the same Holy Spirit gave their message.
The gospel's success depends on the Spirit's working and blessing. Therefore study carefully the Scriptures that explain salvation.

div.title: Be holy in every part of life (verses 13–16)
div.p: Travelers, runners, workers and soldiers gathered their flowing garments so they could act freely.
Christians should likewise prepare their minds and desires for active service.
Be sober, alert against spiritual dangers, moderate in behavior, humble in judging yourselves and restrained in your opinions as well as actions.
Complete trust in God's grace goes together with earnest effort in duty.
Holiness is both the desire and the duty of every Christian.
It belongs in every occupation, condition and relationship.
Pay special attention to temptations toward which your own nature inclines you.
God's written word is the surest guide to Christian conduct.
God makes those whom he saves holy.

div.title: Live in reverent gratitude for redemption (verses 17–25)
div.p: Holy confidence in God as Father and reverent fear of him as Judge belong together.
When believers act sinfully, the Lord may correct them as a Father.
They should neither doubt his promises nor surrender to enslaving terror of his wrath, but honor his holiness.
A person with no reverent fear becomes careless and exposed to Satan. But someone overcome by despair loses the courage to use the spiritual privileges already given.
The price of redemption is Christ's precious blood.
Not only open wickedness but also unprofitable, empty living is dangerous, even when defended as family tradition.
It is foolish to say that a practice must be right merely because our ancestors followed it.
God planned special mercy for his people long before he revealed it.
Now that Christ has come, the light of the gospel, strength of faith and effectiveness of God's appointed ordinances are more abundant than before.
Through union with Christ by faith, his present glory assures believers that they will be with him (John 14:3).
The soul must be purified before it can abandon self-centered desires.
God's word, planted in the heart by the Holy Spirit, creates spiritual life and changes thoughts, desires and conduct until they lead toward eternal life.
Human nature apart from grace resembles grass and its flower: vigorous for a moment and soon gone.
We should therefore receive and love the living, enduring word, valuing it above everything else.
Keep it in your heart as the greatest treasure available now and the certain pledge of the inheritance stored in heaven.

row.cell: A temper suitable to the Christian character as born again, is recommended.
Holy conversation among the Gentiles directed.
Subjects exhorted to pay all proper obedience to their civil governors.
Also servants to their masters, and all to be patient, according to the example of the suffering Saviour.

div.title: Desire the Word and grow upon Christ the Cornerstone (verses 1–10)
div.p: Evil speech reveals malice and deceit within the heart and keeps us from benefiting from Scripture.
New life requires appropriate nourishment.
Just as a newborn eagerly seeks milk, a Christian should eagerly desire God's word.
Our Lord Jesus Christ is merciful to miserable sinners and possesses an abundance of grace.
Yet even the finest of God's servants taste only a small part of his full comfort during earthly life.
Christ is called a Stone, teaching that he is his people's protection, security and foundation.
His nature, office and work make him infinitely precious.
All true believers are a holy priesthood, consecrated to God and useful to others through spiritual gifts and graces.
But even their best prayers and praises become acceptable only through Jesus Christ.
As the chief Cornerstone, Jesus unites the entire church into one eternal temple and bears its weight.
To be built upon him means truly to believe in him, but many people deceive themselves about what faith involves and whether they share his salvation.
Though the world should fall apart, the person truly resting on this foundation need not fear. The believer runs quickly toward Christ but never discovers any reason to flee from him.
God's people are one chosen family, different from the world in heart, principle and conduct, because they were chosen in Christ and sanctified by the Spirit.
He called them from spiritual darkness into light so that they would show his praise through true confession and holy conduct.
Being without divine mercy is miserable even if a person enjoys every worldly advantage.
Nothing moves people toward genuine repentance as tenderly as the right understanding of God's mercy and love.
Do not abuse grace while claiming to be saved by it. Those who receive mercy should live as God's people.

div.title: Abstain from sinful desires and live honorably (verses 11 and 12)
div.p: Even believers chosen by God require warnings against serious sin.
Sinful bodily desires wage war against the soul. Being given over to them is a dreadful judgment.
A day of divine visitation may bring others to repentance through God's word and grace.
Then the consistent, holy conduct of Christians will have helped bring about this change and their observers will glorify God.

div.title: Respect civil authorities without abusing Christian freedom (verses 13–17)
div.p: A Christian life must be honest.
That honesty includes fulfilling genuine duties arising from relationships and responsibilities.
Such conduct obeys God's will and silences foolish, malicious accusations.
Christian freedom must never become an excuse for wrongdoing or neglecting obligations.
In every relationship, remember that we are God's servants.

div.title: Bear unjust treatment by following the suffering Savior (verses 18–25)
div.p: In Peter's time many servants were enslaved people, frequently under pagan masters who treated them harshly.
The apostle called them to fulfill their obligations reverently toward God, even under unreasonable rulers.
One person's sinful conduct never justifies another's wrongdoing.
Nevertheless, Henry also insists masters must be gentle and kind to servants and people under their authority.
Patience when punished for an actual fault is no remarkable achievement.
But remaining upright when wrongfully mistreated, without seeking revenge, displays divine grace and will be rewarded by God.
Christ's death is not only an example of patient suffering. He carried our sins and their deserved punishment, satisfying divine justice and taking guilt away.
The intended fruit of his sufferings is that sinners die to sin and live for righteousness.
Through his death and resurrection believers receive not just an example but power and motivation to do so.
Christ was wounded and crucified as the sacrifice for sin; by his wounds the diseases of our souls are healed.
Human beings wander from the shepherd through their own sinful choices, leaving themselves exposed to countless dangers.
Conversion is the grace-given return to Christ, the Shepherd and Overseer of souls.

row.cell: The duties of wives and husbands.
And encouraged to patience under persecutions for righteousness' sake, considering that Christ suffered patiently.

div.title: Wives and husbands should honor God in their lives (verses 1–7)
div.p: A believing wife should carry out her duties toward her husband even when he does not obey God's word.
People who reject religion often watch professing Christians' lives very closely. It is therefore important that our actions match our words.
Peter does not forbid clothing or personal care. He condemns vanity, extravagance and costly self-display.
Few of us know where to set appropriate limits on food and clothing. If poverty did not restrain them, many would continually desire more than they need, spending time and money on trifles.
The apostle commends adornment that cannot perish: the Holy Spirit's graces beautifying the soul.
A Christian's chief concern should be governing the inner spirit.
A gentle and peaceful heart will win more genuine respect and affection than elaborate clothing worn with a quarrelsome temper.
Christian duties should be performed willingly, out of love and obedience to God.
Wives are to show respect not from terror or panic, but from the desire to please God and live rightly.
A husband's duty includes honoring his wife, protecting her, trusting her and supporting her rightful authority.
Husband and wife are heirs together of life's blessings and the inheritance to come. They should live peacefully, treating one another with consideration.
Prayer sweetens their life together.
It is good for a family to pray together, but husbands and wives should also pray together privately and with their children.
To pray much, live holy lives. And to live holy lives, pray much.

div.title: Show compassion, speak truth and seek peace (verses 8–13)
div.p: Christians will not always agree in every detail. Nevertheless, they should show compassion and love one another as brothers and sisters.
Anyone desiring a good life now or eternal life afterward must control the tongue, refusing malice, insults and deceit.
Turn away from evil, do all possible good and pursue peace with everyone.
God sees and cares for the upright, and no one can ultimately defeat those who follow Christ, the perfect example of doing good to others.

div.title: Explain your hope gently and endure suffering for righteousness (verses 14–22)
div.p: We honor God before others when our conduct encourages them to glorify him.
Be ready to explain the reason for Christian hope, with gentleness and reverent fear of God.
When we truly fear the Lord, other fears lose their power.
A good conscience performs its function faithfully.
It is dreadful when sin and suffering meet, because wrongdoing makes affliction more painful, lonely and destructive.
It is better to suffer for doing what is right than to suffer for wrongdoing.
Jesus gives us the supreme example.
The sinless One suffered in the place of sinners so that he could reconcile us to God and bring us to eternal glory.
He died with respect to his human nature and was raised through the Holy Spirit's power.
If even Christ passed through suffering, believers should not expect to escape all suffering themselves.
God knows precisely what opportunities and warnings people have received.
Henry explains that Christ by his Spirit preached through Noah to the people of that generation, warning them before judgment.
God's patience endured for a long time, but finally came to an end.
Henry understands the spirits of those who rejected Noah's warning as having been committed after death to the prison of hell, from which, in his interpretation, there is no redemption.
Noah's rescue in the ark through the flood pictured the rescue of true believers through the Holy Spirit's saving work.
To avoid confusion, Peter distinguishes baptism's outward washing from the spiritual reality it signifies.
Water by itself only cleanses bodily dirt.
The saving reality is the Holy Spirit's regenerating grace, producing repentance, faith and the desire to live uprightly before God.
Do not rest on outward religious acts.
Many were baptized and faithfully attended worship yet never trusted Christ, and died without receiving his salvation.
Seek instead to be cleansed by the Spirit and Christ's blood.
Christ's resurrection from the dead assures believers of purification and peace.

row.cell: The consideration of Christ's sufferings is urged for purity and holiness.
And the approaching end of the Jewish state, as a reason for sobriety, watchfulness, and prayer.
Believers encouraged to rejoice and glory in reproaches and sufferings for Christ, and to commit their souls to the care of a faithful God.

div.title: Christ's sufferings call us to holiness (verses 1–6)
div.p: The strongest arguments against sin come from Christ's sufferings.
He died to destroy sin.
He willingly endured terrible suffering yet never consented to the least sin.
Temptation succeeds against people because of the corruption already within them.
True believers no longer make sinful desires the rule of life. They seek to do God's will.
Conversion brings a wonderful change to thoughts, judgments, loves, habits and conduct.
A converted person deeply regrets how much life was previously wasted in sin.
One wrongdoing leads easily to another. Peter identifies six related sins.
Christians should avoid not only obvious wickedness but also actions that lead toward sin or even bear its appearance.
Henry understands the gospel to have been preached to people who have since died.
Although they were slandered as wrongdoers by proud, worldly people, some even killed for faith, the Holy Spirit gave them spiritual life and enabled them to live to God.
Therefore do not be disheartened when the world despises or reproaches those who belong to Christ.

div.title: Keep sober, pray and serve as the end approaches (verses 7–11)
div.p: Henry understands the destruction of the Jewish nation and its religious order, foretold by Christ, as close at hand.
The same passage naturally directs everyone to reflect upon the approach of death and judgment.
Knowing life's end is near should make us self-controlled in worldly matters and earnest in prayer and religion.
Because believers all have faults, love must be willing to overlook, excuse and forgive the failings of others.
Otherwise Satan can turn ordinary mistakes into endless conflicts.
But love does not atone for the sins of the person who shows it or earn God's forgiveness.
Christian work is both important and difficult. The goodness of our Master and the greatness of his reward require serious diligence.
In every duty, pursue God's glory above personal ambition.
Someone living only for reputation, possessions or selfish advantage rests upon goods destined to disappear.
But a person who entrusts everything to God can say the Lord is my portion. Glory through Christ alone is solid and everlasting.

div.title: Suffer as Christians, not because of wrongdoing (verses 12–19)
div.p: Patience under persecution, trust in God's promises and obedience to the Holy Spirit's word bring glory to God.
By contrast, people who insult Christians for their faith dishonor the Holy Spirit.
It may seem unnecessary to warn believers against serious crimes. But opponents falsely accused them of such conduct, and even the best Christians need warnings against great sins.
There is no comfort in troubles brought upon ourselves through wrongdoing and folly.
Jesus had warned of a time of great calamity (Matthew 24:9–10), and it was approaching.
If the trials of this life can be so dreadful, how terrible will the final judgment be for the impenitent!
Scripture says the righteous are scarcely saved.
This does not mean God's purpose or promise of salvation is uncertain.
It means believers pass through immense difficulties: temptations, suffering, conflict outside and fear within.
The hardest obstacles are often not outward troubles but remaining sinful desires and inward corruption.
The end of someone who delights in sin and mocks the righteous will be far more dreadful.
The only sure care for our souls is to entrust them to God through prayer while continuing patiently to do what is right.
He will govern everything for the believer's final good.

row.cell: Younger Christians are to submit to their elders, and to yield with humility and patience to God, and to be sober, watchful, and stedfast in faith.
Prayers for their growth and establishment.

div.title: Shepherd God's flock under Christ the Chief Shepherd (verses 1–4)
div.p: Peter exhorted rather than commanded the elders.
He did not claim the right to rule all pastors and churches.
Peter and a small number of others uniquely witnessed Christ's sufferings. But all true believers share the promised glory when Christ appears.
The scattered, poor and afflicted Christians were God's own flock.
Their redemption came through the great Shepherd and they were called to live in holy love and fellowship according to God's will.
They are also called God's heritage or clergy, meaning God's chosen and special possession, set apart for his service and favor.
Christ is the Chief Shepherd of the entire flock.
Faithful ministers will receive a crown of unfading glory, worth infinitely more than earthly influence, possessions or pleasure.
