div.title: Humble yourselves, cast your cares on God and resist the devil (verses 5–9)
div.p: Humility preserves peace and good order in churches and societies. Pride disturbs them.
When God grants humility he also supplies wisdom, faith and holiness.
Submitting to our reconciled God brings greater comfort than selfish ambition.
His help comes in his own wise time, not always according to the timetable we imagine.
He waits patiently. Can we not wait for him?
Confidence in his wisdom, power and goodness helps us endure every difficulty.
Cast upon him every concern: personal and family matters, troubles of the present and anxiety about the future, concern for ourselves, others and the whole church.
These cares become deeply harmful when they arise from unbelief, torment the mind, prevent us from doing our duty and steal the joy of serving God.
The remedy is to leave outcomes to God's wise and gracious ordering.
Trust in his good purposes calms the soul.
All lasting spiritual consolation comes from God and the Holy Spirit.
Satan continually seeks to destroy souls, laying snares to lead them toward eternal ruin.
We must be sober in outward and inward life, governing ourselves by temperance.
We must be alert, aware of spiritual danger and watching against his schemes.
Be steadfast through faith.
No one can fight securely on swampy ground. Faith places the soul upon the solid ground of God's promises.
Remember that believers throughout the world experience the same kinds of suffering. Their trials should strengthen our patience in our own.

div.title: Seek the God of all grace and stand firm in his peace (verses 10–14)
div.p: Peter prays to the God of all grace.
His four petitions describe growth:
Perfect asks that believers advance toward spiritual maturity.
Establish asks that their instability be healed.
Strengthen asks that the graces, especially the weakest, increase.
Settle asks that they rest upon a secure foundation, Christ himself.
Perseverance and growth in grace should therefore be among every Christian's first concerns.
Christian teaching proves its reality through the change it makes in the heart and the fruit it produces in life.
Genuine brotherly love is not merely polite words. It is Christ's recognizable mark upon his disciples.
Wicked people sometimes enjoy a temporary false peace, but their hope is empty.
All lasting peace is founded on Jesus Christ and flows from him.

div.title: 2 Peter — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: This letter is closely related to Peter's first letter.
Having described the blessings to which God calls Christians, the apostle urges those who have received these gifts to grow in grace and virtue.
He warns against false teachers, deceivers and people who mock the promised return of Christ.
He refutes their claims and explains why the great day of Christ's coming has been delayed.
The letter describes the solemn circumstances and consequences of that day, and calls believers to diligence, steadfast faith and holy living.

row.cell: Exhortations to add the exercise of various other graces to faith.
The apostle looks forward to his approaching decease.
And confirms the truth of the gospel, relating to Christ's appearing to judgment.

div.title: Grow in the graces of living faith (verses 1–11)
div.p: Faith unites both weak and strong believers to Jesus Christ and truly purifies their hearts. Every sincere believer is justified before God through faith.
Faith produces genuine godliness, doing things no other grace can do in the soul.
Every fullness is found in Christ. Through the Holy Spirit he gives forgiveness, peace, grace, spiritual knowledge and new principles of life.
God's promises invite believers to ask whether they really have been made new inwardly and share in the divine nature.
Turn these promises into prayers for the Spirit's transforming and cleansing work.
Add knowledge to virtue by growing in understanding of God's complete truth and will.
Add self-control to knowledge: moderation in relation to this world's goods and pleasures.
Add patience to self-control: a cheerful submission to God's will amid troubles.
Suffering can produce patience, enabling us to carry crosses and losses with quiet submission.
Add godliness to patience: holy desires and affections that mark true worshipers.
Love your Christian brothers and sisters tenderly. They have the same Father and Master, belong to the same household, travel toward the same country and inherit the same kingdom.
Work to gain assurance of your calling and election through believing and doing what is right.
Such perseverance is evidence that God's mercy and grace sustain us so that we will not finally fall away.
Those diligent in living faith will enter the everlasting kingdom triumphantly, reigning with Christ forever.
It is in carrying out good works, not in pretending that works purchase acceptance, that believers should expect to approach this promised entrance.

div.title: Peter prepares for his death (verses 12–15)
div.p: We must become firmly established in the truth so that every changing opinion will not overturn us.
Pay special attention to those aspects of Christian truth most needed in our own day and to errors currently opposed to it.
The body is the soul's tent, a temporary dwelling that can be moved and taken down.
As death approaches, Peter grows more diligent in his appointed work.
Nothing makes death more peaceful than knowing we have sincerely followed Jesus and sought his glory.
Those who fear the Lord naturally speak of his loving kindness.
The enduring written word enables God's people to pass on the knowledge of him after they are gone.

div.title: Scripture is the Spirit-inspired word of God (verses 16–21)
div.p: The gospel is not weak speculation. It comes with divine power (Romans 1:16).
The law shows humanity's miserable condition under sin, but it does not provide the saving cure.
Jesus crucified, revealed in the gospel, heals the soul.

Rational arguments alone often fail to change a person ruled by greed, anger or lust. One piece of gold outweighs every argument for the greedy person; someone furious will not listen; a single tempting smile can defeat mere reasoning.
But the gospel announces Christ's precious blood, shed to save sinners from hell and to make satisfaction for their sins.
That message has the power to make believing hearts burn and to move even opponents, like Agrippa, toward recognizing its truth (Acts 26:28).
God is pleased with Christ and accepts people in him.
Old Testament prophets foretold both the promised Messiah and the gospel's salvation, speaking and writing through God's Spirit.
Their words provide a firm foundation for faith.
When the Spirit brings Scripture's light into a dark understanding, it is like daybreak spreading toward full daylight.
Everyone should study Scripture to understand its real meaning.
True Christians recognize God's word through the sweetness, spiritual power and divine glory they experience in it.
Fulfilled prophecies concerning Christ and his church testify to Christianity's truth.
The Holy Spirit inspired the prophets' actual words, guiding their communication so that what they wrote faithfully expressed what God had revealed.
The Scriptures must therefore be received and honored as the words of the Holy Spirit, with all their clarity, simplicity and power from God.
Receive the word in faith and cherish the Bible as a book written by holy people instructed by the Holy Spirit.

row.cell: Believers are cautioned against false teachers, and the certainty of their punishment shown from examples.
An account of these seducers, as exceedingly wicked.
But as making high pretences to liberty and purity.

div.title: False teachers face certain judgment (verses 1–9)
div.p: The path of error is harmful, yet many people readily enter it.
Let us give Christ's enemies no valid reason to speak against his holy name or the salvation offered through him, the Way, Truth and Life.
False teachers deceive by using invented and manipulative words.
They lead others astray and bring judgment upon themselves.
God's dealings in earlier history illustrate his justice.
Angels were cast down from their dignity and glory because they disobeyed God.
Even creatures dwelling in heaven will suffer judgment if they sin.
Sin belongs to darkness; darkness is its deserved outcome.
God judged the ancient world in Noah's days. The number or social position of wrongdoers cannot make sin acceptable.
When wrongdoing spreads throughout a society, judgment may spread widely too.
God can turn fruitful land to desolation and flourishing cities into ashes.
No political strategy can prevent his judgment on unrepentant sin.
The God who preserves his servants through fire and water (Isaiah 43:2) can use the same elements in judgment.
When judgment falls upon the wicked, the Lord can preserve the righteous.
Living among evil people brings either grief over their sins or guilt through participating in them.
Yet God's children can remain faithful even in deeply corrupt surroundings, because Christ's grace within them is stronger than Satan's temptations or wicked examples.
God often places surprising obstacles in people's path before they commit sin, as though warning them to reconsider.
His wisdom and power ensure that his merciful purposes will be fulfilled.
Some wicked people escape visible punishment now because they are reserved for the day of judgment, when they will be punished with the devil and his angels.

div.title: The arrogance and corruption of deceptive teachers (verses 10–16)
div.p: False teachers and their followers abandon themselves to sensual desires.
They refuse to submit their thoughts to Christ's obedience, violate God's holy commands and go progressively deeper into impurity.
They also despise lawful authority God requires them to respect.
Their hearts are fixed upon temporary earthly gain, which they both desire and promise.
Those who presume upon God's grace as permission to indulge sin have special reason to tremble.
Some treat the moral demands of Scripture as though the gospel freed them from obeying God.
Christians should keep their distance from such teaching and conduct.

div.title: False promises of freedom lead to slavery (verses 17–22)
div.p: God's true word is living water that refreshes people who receive it.
False teachers resemble empty springs or clouds without rain, because they possess no saving truth.
As clouds can block the sunlight, false teaching can darken people's understanding with words lacking substance.
Because these deceivers spread darkness in this world, Henry says it is just that the mist of darkness should be their portion in the next.
While promising freedom, these teachers are themselves slaves of their sinful desires.
Their passions have conquered them completely.
Anyone entangled by sin is more easily overcome. Christians must remain close to God's word and beware people who confuse and mislead them.
Deliberate apostasy after knowledge is more serious than ignorance.
Speaking falsely against God's good way of salvation exposes a person to severe judgment.
This condition is dreadful. Yet Henry adds a critical qualification: it is not utterly without hope.
Just as a leper may be cleansed and a dead person raised, a person grieved by their departure from faith may still find mercy.

p.hi: If your backsliding grieves you, believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved.

row.cell: The design here is to remind of Christ's final coming to judgement.
He will appear unexpectedly, when the present frame of nature will be dissolved by fire.
From thence is inferred the need for holiness, and stedfastness in the faith.

div.title: Scoffers deny Christ's promised return (verses 1–4)
div.p: Christians should have their purified minds awakened to active and joyful holiness.
In the gospel age scoffers will arise who make light of sin, mock salvation through Jesus Christ and ridicule his promised return.
A central teaching of faith concerns what God has promised, not what human beings can verify through past experience.
Scoffers will keep attacking that promise until Christ returns.
They see no dramatic change and therefore refuse to fear God (Psalm 55:19).
They assume that because God has not previously done something, he cannot do it or never will.

div.title: God's patience and the coming judgment (verses 5–10)
div.p: If the scoffers remembered God's judgment in the flood, they would not ridicule the warning of another world-wide judgment.
The same word that governed the ancient world has announced that the present heavens and earth will pass through fire.
This event is certain because God is truthful and powerful.
Human beings see an immense difference between a day and a thousand years. But all past, present and future are continually before God.
A delay of a thousand years is no more to him than our postponing something for an hour.
We struggle to understand eternity and wrongly imagine God must experience time as we do.
What people call slow fulfillment is actually divine patience.
It gives God's people time to grow in knowledge, holiness, faith, patience and good works, glorifying him by what they do and endure.
Everyone will give account of actions done in the body, whether good or evil.
Therefore live humbly, examine yourselves often and take final judgment seriously—even while others behave as though accountability would never come.
Christ will come unexpectedly, when people feel secure.
Splendid palaces and everything in which worldly people seek happiness will pass through judgment.
God's fire will consume what human sin has corrupted and refine what belongs to his work.
How foolish to make earthly possessions our ultimate portion when everything visible is passing away!
Seek happiness beyond this world.

div.title: Pursue holiness while growing in the knowledge of Christ (verses 11–18)
div.p: The certainty of Christ's return calls us to complete and universal holiness, not a minimal standard.
Genuine knowledge of Christ changes a person's life.
Believers await new heavens and a new earth, freed from present corruption and sin.
Only those clothed in Christ's righteousness and sanctified through the Holy Spirit will dwell there.
God is faithful to his promises.
Those whose sins are pardoned and who are reconciled to him are secure. Seek peace with all people, together with holiness.
Do not expect to face the Lord in peace if you spend the present day idle and careless.
We have work to complete before he calls us home.
The delay in his appearing should move us to faithful service, not impatience or moral carelessness.
Proud and corrupt people distort difficult passages of Scripture to suit their own views.
But the misuse of Paul's letters is no reason to discard them or any other part of the Bible. Human sin can twist every good divine gift.
When Scripture contains difficult teachings, prepare yourselves to understand them by obeying what is already clear.
Self-denial, distrust of our own pride and submission to Christ's authority are necessary if we are to embrace all gospel truth.
Reject human opinions that conflict with God's revealed law.
Those swept away by error lose their own steadfastness.
To remain firm, keep growing in faith, virtue, knowledge and every grace.
Seek not only to know more about Jesus Christ, but to become more like him and love him more deeply.
Such knowledge leads to thanksgiving and to praise that begins now and will continue forever.

div.title: 1 John — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: This letter explains Christianity's fundamental doctrines and their practical consequences.
It appears to have been written especially to confront false, ungodly beliefs and behavior.
Above all, it refutes attempts to diminish Christ's full deity, or to deny the reality and saving power of his sufferings and death as an atoning sacrifice.
It also opposes the claim that people saved by grace no longer need to obey God's commands.
Everyone who professes to know and enjoy fellowship with God is called to walk in holiness rather than sin.
An outward profession is empty when a person's conduct does not show the evidence of holy life.
The letter therefore encourages genuine Christians to remain in fellowship with the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, persevere in true faith and grow in purity.

row.cell: The apostle prefaces his epistle to believers in general, with evident testimonies to Christ, for promoting their happiness and joy.
The necessity of a life of holiness, in order to communion with God, is shown.

div.title: The apostles testify to the incarnate Word of life (verses 1–4)
div.p: The apostle writes about the eternal and uncreated Excellence, the One who existed from the beginning equal with the Father, and eventually appeared in human nature to save sinners.
For years the apostles witnessed Christ's wisdom, holiness, miracles, love and mercy.
They saw him crucified for sinners and then raised from the dead.
They also touched him, giving them direct evidence of his bodily resurrection.
This divine person—the Word of life and Word of God—took human nature to become the Author and Giver of eternal life through the redeeming power of his blood and the renewing work of his Spirit.
The apostles proclaimed what they had seen and heard so that others could share their comfort and eternal blessings.
They enjoyed access to God the Father, experiencing his truth inwardly and displaying it through their conduct.
Fellowship with the Father and the Son begins and continues through the work of the Holy Spirit.
Christ's gifts do not resemble scarce worldly possessions, which provoke jealousy when shared.
God's joy and fellowship are sufficient for all, so any number of people may receive them without diminishing anyone else's share.
Those who truly know this fellowship naturally wish for other people to share the same blessedness.

div.title: Walking in God's light requires confession and cleansing (verses 5–10)
div.p: The message from Jesus, the eternal Word, deserves joyful reception.
God is perfect light in a world of spiritual darkness.
His doctrines and commands share the purity of his nature.
Just as God's perfect happiness cannot be separated from his holiness, our happiness grows as we become holy.
Walking in darkness means living contrary to God's revealed will.
God does not enjoy heavenly fellowship with people who choose to remain unholy.
A professed faith contradicted by a persistently sinful life is false.
Yet the eternal Son took flesh and blood, died to wash away our sins in his own blood, and gives us the sacred influences through which sin is progressively overcome.
The command to walk in holiness is an effect and evidence of knowing God through Christ, not a basis for claiming our own righteousness.
Even people walking closest to God recognize that their best days and deeds remain mixed with sin.
The atoning sacrifice God has provided demonstrates the sinfulness of humanity and the continuing need of believers for pardon.
Christians must therefore keep confessing their sins and applying by faith to Christ's blood.
Let us plead guilty before God, humbly ready to learn the worst about our own condition.
Confess sin honestly in its full seriousness, relying solely on God's mercy and faithfulness through Christ's righteousness for complete forgiveness and deliverance from sin's power and practice.

row.cell: The apostle directs to the atonement of Christ for help against sinful infirmities.
The effects of saving knowledge in producing obedience, and love to the brethren.
Christians addressed as little children, young men, and fathers.
All are cautioned against the love of this world, and against errors.
They are encouraged to stand fast in faith and holiness.

div.title: Jesus is our righteous Advocate (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: We have an Advocate before the Father, who willingly and completely pleads for everyone seeking forgiveness and salvation through him.
He is Jesus, the Savior, and Christ, the anointed Messiah.
He alone is the Righteous One: free from sin in his nature and, as our Surety, perfectly obedient to God's law.
People of every land and generation are invited to seek God through his all-sufficient atonement and this new and living way.
When properly understood and received, the gospel turns the heart against every sin and ends its deliberate practice, while also giving wonderful relief to guilty consciences.

div.title: Knowing Jesus produces obedience and brotherly love (verses 3–11)
div.p: What sort of knowledge of Christ could fail to recognize his worthiness of our obedience?
Disobedience in conduct exposes both dishonesty and the absence of genuine religion.
God's love accomplishes its purpose in those who keep his commands.
Through grace it progressively renews them, although no believer becomes absolutely perfect during this life.
If Christ's commands were kept universally, the earth would begin to resemble heaven.
The command to love one another has existed since creation, yet is new for Christians because of the new motives, rules and obligations arising from their relationship with Christ.
Those who hate other believers remain in spiritual darkness.
Christian love values another person's soul, guarding against anything harmful to that person's purity or peace.
Where spiritual darkness rules the mind, judgment and conscience become confused about the way to eternal life.
We should therefore examine ourselves seriously and pray for God to show us what we are and where we are going.

div.title: Children, young people and parents in faith (verses 12–14)
div.p: Christians at different stages of life have particular responsibilities, but some commands—including mutual love and refusing worldliness—belong to everyone.
Even the youngest genuine disciple is forgiven.
Long-standing Christians still need teaching. No one becomes too old to hear Scripture or receive helpful correction.
Young Christians may have gained spiritual strength, resisted early temptations, abandoned corrupt habits and associations and entered through the narrow gate of conversion.
Children in Christ know God as their Father.
Mature believers know the One who existed before the world's creation and therefore should be ready to let the world go.
Young people are honored when they become strong in Christ through grace.
Through God's word they overcome the wicked one.

div.title: Do not love the passing world (verses 15–17)
div.p: The things of this world may be desired, possessed and used for the purposes God intended, according to his grace and for his glory.
But believers should not value them for the sinful purposes to which people often turn them.
As love for the world increases, love for God declines.
Henry groups worldly desire into three forms.
First, the desire of the flesh: pursuing sensual gratification and bodily pleasures.
Second, the desire of the eyes: delighting in wealth and possessions through greed.
Third, the pride of life: craving prestige, luxury, honor and applause.
Worldly objects and even the desires directed toward them will pass away. But love for God will not fail.
People have tried to escape these warnings through clever distinctions about how far they may love the world and still claim to be Christians.
But the passage's meaning is plain.
Unless victory over worldliness begins inwardly, a profession of faith has no lasting root or fruit.
Because worldly temptations are so attractive to our corrupt nature, we must remain watchful and prayerful, seeking victory over the ruler of this world.

div.title: Reject lies about the Son and the Father (verses 18–23)
div.p: Henry calls anyone antichristian who rejects Christ's true person or any essential aspect of his work.
Rejecting the Son also denies the Father, and rejects God's appointed salvation.
The prophecy that deceivers would appear should make Christians vigilant.
The visible church cannot know with certainty who among its professed members truly belongs to Christ.
False teachings expose some who seemed to belong and warn others to remain humble.
True Christians are anointed by the Holy Spirit, receiving his grace, gifts and privileges.
The most dangerous lies of Satan often concern the person of Jesus Christ.
Only the Spirit's anointing can preserve believers from such deception.
We should judge kindly all who truly trust Jesus as the divine Savior, obey his word and seek fellowship with them.
At the same time, Henry urges Christians to pray with compassion for those denying Christ's deity, atonement or the Holy Spirit's renewing work, while clearly resisting those teachings.

div.title: Remain in the truth and practice righteousness (verses 24–29)
div.p: The truth of Christ dwelling within a person provides a means of separation from sin and unites that person to God's Son (John 15:3–4).
How highly we should value gospel truth!
Through it God assures believers of eternal life.
The Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, teaches everything needed to know God in Christ and to recognize his glory in the gospel.
John's affectionate words “little children” show that he seeks to persuade through love.
Gospel privileges carry matching duties.
Those anointed by Jesus should remain in him and live by the new spiritual nature he grants.
Faithful perseverance through times of testing is evidence of new birth from Christ.
Beware of knowing the truth while living unrighteously.
Those genuinely born of God bear his holy likeness and follow his righteous ways.

row.cell: The apostle admires the love of God in making believers his children.
The purifying influence of the hope of seeing Christ, and the danger of pretending to this, and living in sin.
Love to the brethren is the character of real Christians.
That love described by its actings.
The advantage of faith, love, and obedience.

div.title: The astonishing privilege of being God's children (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: The world understands very little of the happiness of Christ's genuine followers.
It scarcely imagines that humble, poor and despised believers are God's favored children and will dwell with him in heaven.
Let Christians endure earthly hardships contentedly. They live in a land of strangers, where their Lord was mistreated before them.
God's children must walk by faith and live through hope, looking forward to the return of Jesus Christ.
At his appearing, they will be recognized by their resemblance to their Head.
Seeing Christ will transform them into his likeness.

div.title: Hope in Christ requires abandoning sin (verses 3–10)
div.p: The Lord is too holy to allow anything unclean or wicked to dwell in his presence.
A hope of heaven that makes room for indulgence in sinful desires is the hope of hypocrites, not of God's children.
Those loved and adopted by God should express gratitude through humble and willing obedience.
Sin means rejecting the divine law.
Christ had no sin whatsoever.
He took the human weaknesses that expose us to suffering and temptation, but never our moral corruption or inclination toward sin.
Anyone who abides in Christ does not continue in a settled practice of sin.
Abandoning sinful behavior is a principal evidence of genuine union with Jesus and saving knowledge of him.
Be alert against self-deception.
Righteous conduct shows the work of righteousness within.
A person cannot deliberately act like the devil while genuinely living as a disciple of the Son who came to destroy the devil's works.
New birth is the Holy Spirit's inward renewal. True religion is not merely a skill acquired through training; it is a new nature.
The regenerated person cannot continue sinning in the same unrepentant manner as before.
The mind sees sin's evil. The heart develops an aversion to it. A new spiritual principle opposes sinful actions. When sin nevertheless occurs, genuine repentance follows.
Deliberate, settled sin becomes repugnant to the believer.
God's children and the devil's children reveal different characters.
Those rejecting true religion and hating God's people show their allegiance by these actions.
The person justified through faith is also taught and inclined toward righteousness by the Spirit.
Let everyone who professes Christianity examine themselves by these marks.

div.title: Love for believers shows the passage from death to life (verses 11–15)
div.p: Love Jesus Christ, recognize the greatness of his love and therefore love all believers who belong to him.
Such love is a special fruit of faith and a reliable sign of new birth.
Human nature's corruption explains why ungodly people often despise and oppose God's children.
But love for our Christian family helps us recognize that we have passed from death to life.
This is not merely loyalty to a religious party, or affection toward people who share our outward label or opinions.
It is love arising from the grace of God active in a renewed heart.
That life of grace is the beginning of everlasting glory.
People who deliberately hate other believers show that this new life is missing.

div.title: Christ's blood calls us to practical compassion (verses 16–21)
div.p: What astonishing love: God redeemed the church with his own blood.
Surely we should love the people whom he has loved so deeply.
The Holy Spirit is grieved by selfishness, and a selfish heart is left without true comfort, in darkness and terror.
How can a person claim to understand Christ's love for perishing sinners while valuing worldly goods above the suffering of a brother or sister?
Each act of selfishness weakens the evidence that a person has been converted.
Habitual and deliberate refusal to help others decisively contradicts the profession of a changed heart.
If conscience rightly condemns a known sin or neglected duty, God's judgment also condemns the wrong.
Therefore teach conscience well, listen to it and take it seriously.

div.title: Confidence before God through faith and love (verses 22–24)
div.p: Through the Spirit of adoption and faith in our great High Priest, believers may approach their reconciled Father confidently.
They may ask freely, and God grants what is good for them.
Heaven proclaimed goodwill to humanity; likewise those approaching heaven must have goodwill toward people, especially other believers.
Anyone following Christ in this way abides in him as a refuge, ark and resting place, and through him abides in the Father.
Union between Christ and believers comes through the Spirit he has given.
Faith takes hold of God's promises and leads the mind to consider them.
The Spirit changes the heart, transferring a person from Satan's power to God's.
Do you long for peace with God more than worldly profit, pleasure or status?
Nothing should hold you back from following Christ.
Our confidence rests on God's own testimony through the Spirit.

row.cell: Believers cautioned against giving heed to every one that pretends to the Spirit.

div.title: Test teaching about Jesus Christ (verses 1–6)
div.p: Christians familiar with Scripture, humbly depending on God's instruction, can distinguish teaching consistent with the apostles from teaching opposed to it.
The center of revealed religion is Jesus Christ's person and saving work.
False teachers adapt their message to worldly standards, desires and tastes so that people ruled by sin will not be offended.
They often gain rapid approval and numerous followers because the world loves what belongs to itself.
But true teaching about the Savior's person leads human beings away from the world and toward God.
This marks the Spirit of truth in contrast to the spirit of error.
Teaching that is pure and holy, consistent with the apostles and Scripture, gives good grounds for recognizing divine truth.
It is no surprise that worldly people follow teachers whose message suits their own purposes.

div.title: God's love begins with his free mercy (verses 7–13)
div.p: The Spirit of God is the Spirit of love.
Anyone unable to love God's likeness in his people has no saving knowledge of the Lord.
God's nature is kind, and he delights to give happiness.
His law requires love. Had all obeyed it, humanity would have enjoyed perfect happiness.
The gospel shows how forgiveness and salvation can be granted while upholding God's glory and justice.
Thus it reveals that God is love.
Some mysteries remain dark to our limited understanding.

God has shown his love so fully that only unbelief and refusal to repent prevent sinners from receiving eternal happiness, although strict justice would condemn us to hopeless misery because we have broken our Creator's laws.
We cannot adequately express the greatness of God's free, astonishing love for people who deserved judgment and who could neither increase nor diminish his greatness.
God could have made other worlds and other creatures by his word, yet he chose to redeem sinners through Christ.
Search the universe for love in its greatest splendor: it is found in the person and cross of Jesus Christ.
Love did not begin with our loving God.
He loved us first.
His love is not intended to remain fruitless in us.
It reaches its appropriate purpose as we become loving, just as faith finds its fulfillment in good works.
This is evidence that God dwells within us through his regenerating Spirit.
Love makes believers diligent in every good duty. It oils the wheels of their affections and moves them to help brothers and sisters willingly.
A person performing work with resentment does it badly.
The statement that God lives in us and we in him would be too magnificent for mortals to claim if God himself had not revealed it.
Those truly convinced they are his children cry “Abba, Father” and seek his will while hating sin.
Such a transformed heart bears the Holy Spirit's witness.

div.title: Love casts out servile fear and produces obedience (verses 14–21)
div.p: The Father sent the Son to be the Savior of the world.
The apostles testify to this.
Confessing Jesus as God's Son involves faith in the heart, acknowledgment with the lips and a life that remains faithful despite worldly flattery or hostility.
A final judgment will come.
Blessed are those who await the Judge with holy confidence, recognizing him as Friend and Advocate.
Love for God assures believers of his love.
It enables them to suffer for Christ, confident they will share his glory (2 Timothy 2:12).
Distinguish reverent fear of God from being terrified of him.
Love-motivated obedience is unlike forced labor under an angry master. It is the willing service of a child to a beloved father, benefiting the whole household.
Many doubts and fears show that love has not yet grown toward maturity.
God invites sinners to share his salvation. Those changed by his love should rejoice, while giving him all the glory.
The Holy Spirit's adoption and God's love in the heart provide strong evidence of conversion.
Test this through the way you treat fellow believers.
Someone claiming to love God but deliberately nurturing anger, revenge or selfishness contradicts their own confession.
But when natural hostility becomes affection and gratitude, thank God for this pledge of eternal happiness.
We cannot truly claim to love the unseen God while hating the brothers and sisters we can see.

row.cell: Brotherly love is the effect of the new birth, which makes obedience to all God's commandments pleasant.
Reference to witnesses agreeing to prove that Jesus, the Son of God, is the true Messiah.
The satisfaction the believer has about Christ, and eternal life through him.
The assurance of God's hearing and answering prayer.
The happy condition of true believers, and a charge to renounce all idolatry.

div.title: New birth brings love and victory through faith (verses 1–5)
div.p: True love for God's people is different from ordinary kindness or loyalty to a group.
It is united with love for God and obedience to his commands.
The Holy Spirit who teaches love also teaches obedience. A person who deliberately continues in sin or neglects known duties cannot claim to love God's children genuinely.
God's commandments are holy, just and good rules of liberty and happiness.
Those born of God do not regard these duties as a burden. Instead, they grieve that they cannot obey him more fully.
Self-denial remains necessary, but believers possess a spiritual principle that helps them persevere through obstacles.
They may fall under trials, yet rise again to continue the struggle.
People without faith in Christ remain bound, in one way or another, to the world's customs, opinions and interests.
Faith is the means and spiritual armor of victory.
Through faith we cling to Christ and refuse the rule of worldly sinful desires.
Faith purifies the heart from the sensual appetites by which the world gains control.
Believers possess the indwelling Spirit, stronger than the power ruling this world.
Jesus' own life teaches them to renounce the world's sinful ways.
They cannot rest content with it, but continue striving toward heaven.
Either we overcome the world through Christ's example and grace, or it will finally overcome us.

div.title: The Spirit, water and blood testify to Christ (verses 6–8)
div.p: Human beings are defiled inwardly and outwardly, especially through the power and pollution of sin in their nature.
Jesus Christ provides regeneration and the renewing work of the Holy Spirit to cleanse us.
Henry notes that some interpreters understand the two sacraments in the water and blood:
Baptism represents the Holy Spirit's washing and regeneration.
The Lord's Supper represents Christ's shed blood and receiving him by faith for forgiveness and justification.
These cleansing realities were also pictured in the old covenant's sacrifices and purification rites.
By the water, the soul is cleansed and made fit for heaven.
By the blood, the sinner receives justification, reconciliation and acceptance as righteous before God.
Christ's blood satisfies the law's curse, so that the Holy Spirit's cleansing work may be given.
Both water and blood flowed from the crucified Redeemer's side.
Jesus loved his church and gave himself to make her holy, cleansing her through the word and presenting her glorious and without stain (Ephesians 5:25–27).
The Holy Spirit confirms this saving work and cannot lie.
Henry also comments on three heavenly witnesses:
The Father testified repeatedly from heaven that Jesus is his beloved Son.
The Word declared unity with the Father and taught that seeing him reveals the Father.
The Holy Spirit descended upon Christ at baptism, spoke through the prophets and testified to his resurrection and mediatorial authority through gifts given to the apostles.
He expressly adds that whether this particular passage is quoted or not, the doctrine of the Trinity in unity remains firmly established.
He then discusses three witnesses to Christ's person and salvation:
First, the Holy Spirit, regenerating hearts that were naturally hostile to God.
Second, the water, displaying Christ's purity and cleansing power, visibly represented through the transformed lives of his people and the sign of baptism.
Third, the blood, his ransom for sinners and the fulfillment of the older sacrifices.
All three testify together to the same Savior and the same salvation.
Rejecting this testimony is not a minor disagreement: it amounts to dismissing the Spirit's witness concerning Christ.

div.title: God's testimony gives assurance of eternal life (verses 9–12)
div.p: People readily act upon human testimony in everyday affairs.
It is unreasonable to dismiss God's testimony concerning his Son while treating ordinary human witnesses as credible.
True believers know their guilt and their need for such a Savior.
They discover that Jesus Christ fits every spiritual need.
His word has humbled, healed, awakened and comforted them.
Their attitudes, desires and enjoyments have changed.
They are not the people they formerly were, though they still struggle with remaining sin, worldly temptation and evil powers.
Through faith in Christ they receive strength to continue toward a better world.
A believer thus possesses an inward witness, even though seasons of darkness may trouble assurance.
Refusing God's record about the Son effectively calls God a liar.
Those who reject Jesus as the divine Son, refuse his teaching as Prophet, deny his atonement as High Priest, or resist his rule as King, remain spiritually dead and condemned.
Neither outward morality, scholarship, religious ceremonies nor doctrinal opinions can substitute for trusting him.

div.title: Pray according to God's will and intercede for others (verses 13–17)
div.p: The testimony of Scripture calls us to believe in God's Son and receive the gospel promise of eternal life.
Believers should gratefully accept God's word and abound in his service, confident that faithful labor is not wasted.
Christ invites us to bring requests and anxieties to him, even while we struggle with sin.
But all prayer must be submitted to God's will.
Some prayers are answered quickly. Other answers come in a better way than the one we requested.
Pray for other people as well as yourselves.
We cannot rightly ask God to pardon people while they deliberately remain impenitent and reject his salvation, as though forgiveness could be granted while they remain determined to refuse it.
But we may pray that they repent, receive faith in Christ and enjoy all the saving mercies that follow.
Intercede for people who have stumbled, that they may be restored, and for those facing temptation or affliction.
We should be especially thankful that no sin genuinely repented of is a sin unto death.

div.title: Remain in Christ and keep yourselves from idols (verses 18–21)
div.p: Humanity belongs to two opposing dominions: God's kingdom and the power of the evil one.
True believers belong to God, live through his grace and are directed toward his glory.
Others remain under the power of the wicked one, whatever religious label, social standing or outward profession they bear.
The Son brings believers to the Father. Through the indwelling and active work of the Holy Spirit, they share the love and favor of both Father and Son.
Blessed are those who know that God's Son has come and possess a heart willing to trust the One who is true.
May we know this privilege, turning from all idols, false teachings and idolatrous love of earthly things.
Through faith, God's power preserves his people for eternal salvation.
To the living and true God belong glory and dominion forever. Amen.

div.title: 2 John — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: This short letter is much like a condensed form of John's first letter. It treats the same central truths in fewer words.
The apostle commends the elect lady for giving her children a virtuous and godly upbringing.
He urges her to remain in Christ's doctrine, persevere in the truth and carefully avoid false teachers.
Above all, he appeals to her to practice the great command of Christian love and charity.

row.cell: The apostle salutes the elect lady and her children.
Express his joy in their faith and love.

div.title: Grace, mercy and peace to the elect lady (verses 1–3)
div.p: Christianity turns courteous expressions into genuine love and respect.
An older disciple deserves honor, and an elderly apostle serving Christ deserves still more.
John wrote to a distinguished Christian woman and her children.
It is good when the gospel reaches people of high standing. But the woman was loved for her holiness, not her rank.
Families need encouragement and direction in their duties and affection at home.
Those who love truth and piety in themselves should also love them in others. Wherever genuine faith takes root, it remains.
John asks God to give grace, mercy and peace.
Grace is God's free favor and the source of every spiritual blessing.
Mercy is the freely given pardon Christians continue needing, even after receiving much grace.
Peace is a clear conscience and a tranquil heart grounded in reconciliation with God, along with whatever outward prosperity will truly serve their good.
All these blessings must be received in truth and love.

div.title: Rejoice when children walk in truth and love (verses 4–6)
div.p: A godly education begun early in life is a wonderful blessing.
Children may be loved also for the faithful example of their parents.
It delighted John to find children following in their parents' faithful footsteps and likely to support the gospel in their own generation.
May God bless such households and raise up more to imitate them!
How sorrowful, by contrast, when parents teach their children unbelief, godlessness and moral corruption.
Walking rightly means living according to God's word.
The command of Christian love may be called new because Christ announced and modeled it in a new way, yet it has always been a divine command.
Because this love may weaken under temptation or apostasy, John returns to it repeatedly and earnestly.

div.title: Resist false teachings about Christ (verses 7–11)
div.p: The deceiver brings error concerning Jesus Christ's person or his saving office.
Such teaching undermines the Lord's glory and kingdom.
Deceivers are no recent development; they were active even during the apostles' lives.
The more widespread they become, the more alert Christ's disciples must remain.
It is grievous for people to lose spiritual progress once made.
Persevering in Christ to the end is the way to receive the full promised reward.
Holding fast to the Son's truth unites believers to the Father as well, for Father and Son are one.
Reject both people who deny Christ's true teaching and conduct that contradicts his commands.
Anyone refusing to confess Christ as the Son of God and the source of salvation from sin and guilt should not be encouraged or given a platform to spread that error.
But John does not command rudeness toward every person who differs in secondary matters.
Show genuine kindness and a good spirit toward Christians who disagree on lesser questions while remaining firm in the essential doctrines of Jesus' person, atonement and holy salvation.

div.title: Hope for the joy of meeting face to face (verses 12 and 13)
div.p: John reserves much for an in-person meeting.
Writing can strengthen and comfort people, but seeing one another in person often does so still more.
Maintain Christian fellowship by every suitable means, seeking mutual joy.
In fellowship with the saints we enjoy many present blessings and anticipate eternal happiness together.

div.title: 3 John — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: This letter is addressed to a converted Gentile.
Its chief purpose is to commend his steadfastness in faith and his hospitality, especially toward ministers who proclaim Jesus Christ.

row.cell: The apostle commends Gaius for piety and hospitality.
Cautions him against siding with Diotrephes, who was a turbulent spirit; but recommends Demetrius as a man of excellent character.
He hopes soon to see Gaius.

div.title: Gaius shows faith through generous hospitality (verses 1–8)
div.p: Those loved by Christ should love their fellow believers for his sake.
Prosperity of the soul is the greatest blessing available on this side of heaven.
Grace and physical health make fine companions. Grace makes good use of health.
Yet a rich and gracious soul may inhabit a weak body. In that situation, grace is exercised through patient submission.
It is right to pray that people whose souls prosper might also enjoy health, providing further opportunities for service.
For many outwardly successful religious people, one could wish the reverse: that their souls might prosper as much as their health and circumstances.
Living faith works through love.
Those who receive genuine spiritual benefit should testify truthfully to the church, giving a good report of the people who helped them.
Godly people rejoice when they hear of other believers' growth in grace.
Faithful parents and ministers delight to see those they have taught living in a way that honors their profession.
Gaius overlooked minor disagreements among sincere believers and freely helped everyone who bore Christ's likeness and performed his work.
He was upright in doing so.
A faithful Christian can hear deserved praise without becoming proud, because any good found in that person leads back to the foot of Christ's cross.
We should consider not only what we are required to do, but also what good we have an opportunity to do.
Even ordinary acts of kindness can serve God's glory.
Those who have resources should support faithful preachers who freely proclaim Christ.
People unable to preach themselves can still welcome, assist and encourage those who do.

div.title: Do not imitate Diotrephes; follow what is good (verses 9–12)
div.p: Guard both heart and speech.
Diotrephes was controlled by ambition and pride.
It is wrong to neglect doing good personally. It is even worse to hinder others who want to do good.
Counsel offered in a loving spirit is more likely to be accepted.
Imitate what is good, because someone who does good from a genuine love for it shows evidence of being born of God.
People performing evil while boasting of knowing God deceive themselves.
Do not follow proud, selfish or harmful examples merely because they come from people of rank or influence.
Instead imitate God's love and the example of Jesus.

div.title: Demetrius's good reputation and the joy of personal fellowship (verses 13 and 14)
div.p: Demetrius had a good testimony.
A favorable reputation in the gospel and the churches is worth more than worldly status.
Few people are praised by everyone; sometimes universal applause is even a bad sign.
Blessed are those whose character and conduct commend them to God and to other people.
We should be willing to testify when someone lives faithfully, especially when our testimony can stand examination by people who know that person's life closely.
Speaking face to face can avoid the delay, confusion and misunderstandings that written letters sometimes create.
It is right for Christians to enjoy meeting one another.
John closes with the blessing peace—asking that genuine happiness be granted.
People who hope to dwell together in heaven should gladly greet one another on earth.
Keeping company with faithful Christians and following their example helps cultivate inner peace, peace with fellow believers and hope of everlasting fellowship in glory.

div.title: Jude — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: Jude's letter addresses everyone who believes the gospel.
It appears intended to guard Christians against false teachers who had begun entering the church and spreading dangerous beliefs.
These teachers reduced Christianity to a nominal confession and outward profession, denying that believers must live holy lives.
They encouraged sinful conduct while flattering people with the hope of eternal life.
The apostle exposes the deceivers' character and announces their judgment, then closes with warnings, encouragement and counsel for believers.

row.cell: The apostle exhorts to stedfastness in the faith.
The danger of being infected by false professors, and the dreadful punishment which shall be inflicted on them and their followers.
An awful description of these seducers and their deplorable end.
Believers cautioned against being surprised at such deceivers arising among them.
The epistle ends with an encouraging doxology, or words of praise.

div.title: Called from sin and urged to contend for faith (verses 1–4)
div.p: Christians are called out of the world, away from its sinful attitudes, and above the world, toward heavenly and eternal realities.
They are called from sin to Christ, from emptiness to seriousness, and from uncleanness to holiness, according to God's purpose and grace.
If they are made holy and eventually glorified, all credit and glory belong to God alone.
The One who begins grace's work in the soul also carries it on and perfects it.
Do not rely on yourselves or on the amount of grace you imagine you have accumulated. Trust God himself.
His mercy is the source of everything good we possess or hope to receive.
Mercy helps not only miserable people but guilty sinners.
From this mercy comes peace through assurance of pardon; from peace grows love: Christ's love for us, our love for him and brotherly love for one another.
Jude desires not small portions of these blessings, but a rich abundance in believers' souls and fellowships.
The gospel invitation excludes no one except those who stubbornly reject it. Its blessings are enjoyed by believers, weak and strong alike.
Those who have received the message of common salvation must contend earnestly, but not angrily or violently, for its truth.
Lying in support of truth is evil. Angry abuse does not help either.
The apostles contended by courageously and patiently suffering for the truth, not by making people suffer for refusing religious opinions they regarded as important.
Oppose those who enter the church secretly, like snakes, to corrupt the faith.
Especially dangerous are those who turn the abundance of God's saving grace into an excuse to sin more boldly.
Grace aims to free people from sin and bring them back to God.

div.title: Outward privilege cannot protect unrepentant sinners (verses 5–7)
div.p: Religious privileges, outward profession and apparent conversion cannot protect people who persist in unbelief and disobedience.
The Israelites who perished in the wilderness witnessed extraordinary miracles daily, yet were judged for unbelief.
The fallen angels rejected the places God assigned them; pride contributed fundamentally to their fall.
They await the great judgment.
If even glorious angels could not escape judgment, no human sinner should think social standing or religious distinction will provide safety.
Sodom's destruction warns people to flee desires that attack their souls (1 Peter 2:11).
God remains as pure, just and holy as ever.
“Stand in awe, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:4).
Only the Holy Spirit renewing the soul into God's likeness can preserve someone from destruction among God's enemies.
Even highly dignified creatures gain no exemption from judgment.
How then should sinful humans tremble, who drink wrongdoing like water (Job 15:16)!

div.title: Corrupt teachers and their certain end (verses 8–16)
div.p: These false teachers are dreamers whose corrupt teaching wounds and defiles souls.
They are restless and rebellious, forgetting that lawful authorities are established under God's providence (Romans 13:1).

On the dispute concerning Moses' body, Henry supposes that Satan wanted the location of his grave revealed so the Israelites would be tempted to worship Moses; the plan was restrained and the devil resorted to blasphemy.
This is Henry's conjecture, not an independently stated fact of the biblical account.
Even during serious disagreements we must not use slanderous or abusive accusations.
We should defend those who belong to God.
People who reject Christianity often live in contradiction to basic principles of natural religion.
They may boast of wisdom while being compared to unreasoning animals, corrupting themselves through things that ought to be obvious.
Their chief problem is not a lack of intelligence but corrupt desires and disordered wills.
It is a disgrace when professing Christians deny their religion through their lives.
God will correct these evils in his own way and time, not through human attempts to pull up wheat together with weeds.
How grievous when people seem to begin in the Spirit and end in sinful flesh.
They are described as twice dead: first dead through fallen nature and later showing further evidence of spiritual death through hypocrisy.
They resemble barren trees ready to be burned.
Raging waves frighten people at sea but can no longer harm them once they reach harbor.
False teachers face judgment in the present world and the world to come.
They flash like meteors or falling stars, then sink into the blackness of darkness forever.
Jude quotes a prophecy connected with Enoch, a passage not recorded elsewhere in Scripture.
Henry emphasizes that one clear biblical testimony suffices to establish a divine warning.
The announced coming of the Lord for judgment is a solemn reality.
Notice how often ungodly is repeated.
Many now mock not only godliness but the very words used to distinguish it from evil.
Unjust harsh speech about others will be judged too.
People who live only to satisfy sinful appetites are seldom content; their desires and complaints become their own rule.
Those most devoted to sensual pleasure often surrender most readily to uncontrolled anger.
God's servants have long announced judgment upon this way of life.
Follow other people only insofar as they follow Christ.
div.note: Unplaced links from original edition (not translated citations): Judges 1:17–23.
Section reference (editorially corrected): Jude.1.17-Jude.1.23.

div.title: Keep the faith and rescue others with discernment (verses 17–23)
div.p: People governed by sensual desires separate themselves from Christ, his church and the Holy Spirit's holiness.
This is infinitely worse than leaving a particular visible church over secondary opinions or questions of outward government or worship.
Those lacking the Holy Spirit do not belong to Christ.
Saving faith is holy: it works through love, cleanses the heart and overcomes the world.
Such fruit distinguishes it from empty belief.
Pray in the Holy Spirit: under his influence and direction, according to Scripture, with faith, earnest affection and perseverance.
The hope of eternal life strengthens our resistance against sinful enticements.
Keep watch over one another, correct one another faithfully but prudently, and set good examples.
Different people need different forms of care.
Show tenderness and compassion toward those who are weak or confused.
Warn those who are willful and persistently reckless with the seriousness appropriate to their danger.
Every attempt to restore sinners must be united with real hatred of sin and a refusal to participate in works of darkness.
Avoid whatever leads into wrongdoing or even appears evil.

div.title: God is able to keep his people and present them blameless (verses 24 and 25)
div.p: God is not only able to preserve believers from falling but also willing to do so.
He will present them without fault before his glory.
Not because they never sinned, but because without divine mercy and Christ's sufferings and merits they would rightly have been condemned.
All genuine believers were given by the Father to the Son.
He has lost none and will lose none of them.
Now remaining sin fills believers with fears, questions and grief.
But their Redeemer has committed himself to presenting them faultless.
Where sin no longer exists, sorrow will vanish too.
Where holiness is perfected, joy will be perfect.
Look often to the Lord who keeps us from falling, sustains and increases the work of grace begun in us, and will bring us blameless into his glorious presence.
Our joy then will exceed everything earth could give, and God's delight in his people will be complete.

p.hi: To the One who wisely planned and perfectly accomplishes our salvation belong glory, majesty, dominion and power, now and forever. Amen.

div.title: Revelation — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)
div.p: John's Revelation consists of two principal parts.
First, it concerns “the things that are”: the church's condition at the time.
It includes the apostle's vision of Jesus Christ, his command to write what he sees (Revelation 1:9–20), and the messages to the seven churches of Asia.
Those messages undoubtedly addressed the actual condition of each church then.
But their teachings, warnings, encouragements, praise, rebuke and promises are useful to the whole church in every age.
Second, Revelation describes “the things that will take place afterward”: prophecy concerning the church's future from the time John saw these visions.
This book is intended to promote spiritual growth.

It warns careless sinners, directs awakened people toward salvation, strengthens weak believers, comforts tempted and suffering Christians, and especially encourages martyrs faithful to Christ while enduring cruel persecution from Satan and his followers.

row.cell: The Divine origin, the design, and the importance of this book.
The apostle John salutes the seven churches of Asia.
Declares when, where, and how, the revelation was made to him.
His vision, in which he saw Christ appear.

div.title: The revelation of Jesus Christ and its blessing (verses 1–3)
div.p: This book is the revelation of Jesus Christ. Indeed, all Scripture comes through him and ultimately concerns him.
Its chief purpose is to reveal God's intentions concerning the church and the nations in relation to it, continuing to the end of the world.
These events are certain to happen, and their fulfillment would begin soon.
Although Jesus is himself God, possessing light and life in himself, as Mediator he receives instructions from the Father to reveal to humanity.
Through Christ we know what to expect from God and what God requires from us.
The book pronounces a blessing on people who read and listen to its prophecy.
But merely hearing or reading is insufficient. Keep its message in memory, thought, affection and practice.
Even when the prophetic meaning is difficult, its mysteries reveal something of God, awaken reverence and purify the soul.
No other part of Scripture speaks more fully of the gospel or gives a stronger warning against sin.

div.title: Grace and peace from the Triune God (verses 4–8)
div.p: There is no true peace without grace. Where grace comes first, real peace follows.
John's greeting is an act of adoration to the Holy Trinity.
The Father is the eternal and unchanging Lord who is, was and is to come.
The Holy Spirit is described as the seven Spirits, the one perfect Spirit of God working through a diversity of gifts and operations.
Jesus Christ is the faithful Witness, the Firstborn from the dead and the Ruler over the earth's kings.
He knows all God's purposes and will raise his people by his own power.
Every ruler's plans are subject to him and every ruler must answer to him.
Sin stains the soul with guilt and corruption. Only Jesus' blood can remove that stain.
He shed his blood to satisfy divine justice, obtaining pardon and purification for his people.
He has made believers kings and priests.
As kings they overcome the world, put sin to death, govern their own hearts, resist Satan and prevail through prayer.
As priests they enter God's presence and offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable through Christ.
For these blessings, glory and rule belong to him forever.
Jesus will judge the world.
In the day of his appearing, everyone will see how wise and happy his friends were and how miserable his enemies are.
Henry warns that Christ's coming will terrify those who wound and crucify him by apostasy and astonish the ungodly world.
Remember his return often.
He is the Beginning and the End, the Almighty, the eternal and unchanging One from whom all things come and for whom they exist.
Anyone hoping to share his everlasting glory must willingly receive and honor him now as Savior, knowing he will return as Judge.

div.title: John sees the vision on the Lord's Day (verses 9–11)
div.p: John was suffering not for wrongdoing but for bearing witness to Jesus Christ, Emmanuel and Savior.
The Spirit of glory rested upon this persecuted apostle.
He received his vision on the Lord's Day, the first day of the week, which Henry identifies as the Christian Sabbath in remembrance of Christ's resurrection.
Those who call Jesus their Lord should honor him on his day.
Henry urges dedicating the Lord's Day wholly to spiritual duties, rather than spending its hours in sensual amusements or worldly pleasures.
John was in a serious, reverent and heavenly frame of mind through the Spirit's influence.
Believers seeking fellowship with God should turn thoughts and desires away from earthly distractions.
Sometimes Christians are prevented by necessity, not by choice, from joining public worship.
Even then they may find divine comfort through private prayer, meditation and the Spirit's presence.
Neither confinement nor external hardship can separate them from Christ's gracious voice and power.
John then heard a loud voice like a trumpet calling him.

div.title: The glorious Son of Man among his churches (verses 12–20)
div.p: The churches receive light from Jesus Christ and his gospel and are called to shine before others.
The golden lampstands picture their purity and value.
Not only ministers but all church members should live so that people glorify God.
Jesus stood among the lampstands, showing that he remains with his churches, filling them with light, life and love.
His long robe may signify righteousness and priestly mediation.
The golden sash may picture the preciousness of his love for his people.
His white hair may signify majesty, holiness and eternity.
His eyes like flame may show his knowledge of hearts and coming events.
His feet like refined bronze may show the firmness and excellence of his purposes and deeds.
His voice like rushing waters may reveal the irresistible power of his word.
The seven stars represent the ministers of the churches, whom Christ sustains and guides.
The sword represents his justice and the searching power of his word (Hebrews 4:12).
His face shone brighter than mortal eyes could bear.
Overwhelmed by this glory, John fell down.
We can be content to walk by faith during earthly life.
Jesus comforted John with “Do not fear.”
He revealed himself as the First and the Last, truly God.
He was once dead—the same One the disciples saw crucified—but now lives eternally, having overcome death.
He possesses supreme authority over death and the unseen world, judging with a sentence no one can overturn.
Listen to his voice, receive his love and obey his word.
What will he withhold from those for whom he gave his life?
Commit yourselves entirely to the One who rules all things wisely.

row.cell: Epistles to the churches in Asia, with warnings and encouragements, To the church at Ephesus;

div.title: Ephesus: return to your first love (verses 1–7)
div.p: The churches differed greatly in purity of teaching and genuine godliness.
Christ's messages to them therefore continue speaking to churches and believers in every age.
Although Jesus reigns in heaven, he walks among the churches on earth, observing their strengths, weaknesses and needs.
He commended Ephesus for diligent service.
Christ remembers every hour of work his servants perform; no faithful labor is wasted.
But diligence alone is not sufficient. We also need patience in suffering and patience in waiting.
Although Christians owe gentleness to people, they must not be indifferent to sin.
The Ephesian church had not ceased loving Christ altogether. It had lost the intensity of its first love.
Christ is displeased when believers become cold and careless toward him.
Calling this decline harmless or normal excuses a sin Christ requires us to repent of.
The church should grieve over this spiritual cooling, confess it humbly and recover its former zeal, prayerfulness and watchfulness.
Indifference toward truth and error, good and evil, may be mislabeled charity, but it is not Christian charity.
The Christian life remains a struggle against sin, Satan, the world and the flesh.
Persevering believers receive the promised Tree of Life, not merely a return to Eden but perfect, everlasting joy in heaven.
During earthly life, anticipate that joy through faith, fellowship with Christ and the Spirit's comforts.
Do not expect uninterrupted peace or freedom from spiritual conflict before heaven.

div.title: Smyrna: remain faithful through suffering (verses 8–11)
div.p: Jesus is the First, because he created everything and existed before all things, with God and himself God.
He is the Last, because he will judge everyone.
The One who died and lives again is the suffering believer's Brother and Friend.
Consequently even people in severe poverty may be spiritually rich, honored amid humiliation and happy under trials.
Some wealthy people are spiritually destitute. Some outwardly poor Christians are rich in faith, good works, privileges, gifts and hope.
When people lose earthly possessions for Christ and a clear conscience, he makes up for the loss through spiritual wealth.
Jesus arms his people against approaching trials: Do not fear.
He not only commands courage but supplies strength to practice it.
The trials were permitted to test, not destroy, his faithful people.
His promised crown of life is certain and fitting: a life exhausted or surrendered for Christ is rewarded with a far greater, eternal life.
The second death is immeasurably more terrible than bodily death because it is everlasting. Henry describes its terror as dying and always dying.
Those spared that judgment through Christ can patiently bear any suffering encountered in this world.

div.title: Pergamum: reject false liberty and hold fast (verses 12–17)
div.p: God's word is a two-edged sword, able to strike at both sin and sinners.
Believers need not fear the sword of Christ's judgment if they remain obedient.
Jesus knows both the opportunities and the temptations arising from the places where his people live.
Pergamum remained faithful through difficult trials, refusing both open apostasy and accommodation merely to avoid suffering.
Christ commended its faithfulness but rebuked its failure to confront false teaching.
A distorted understanding of Christian liberty can become a bitter root from which serious sin grows.
Repentance is required not only of individuals but also of congregations and communities that sin together.
The conqueror receives Christ's hidden spiritual nourishment and consolations, unknown to the world.
The new name signifies adoption into God's family.
The Holy Spirit makes believers understand the reality of this new identity through the work he has performed in their hearts.

div.title: Thyatira: love must not tolerate corrupt teaching (verses 18–29)
div.p: Jesus notices good works born of love, faith, zeal and patience.
Yet his flaming eyes also see any wrongdoing the church permits.
He rebukes, disciplines or judges such evil.
He praised Thyatira's ministers and members for growth in goodness and wisdom.
All Christians should desire their latest works to be their best works.
But the church tolerated people who seduced others into wickedness.
By judging deceivers, Christ shows that he knows hearts, motives, plans and the hidden spirit of every person.
Those remaining undefiled receive encouragement.
It is dangerous to disregard God's mysteries; it is also dangerous to become fascinated by Satan's supposed secret depths.
The less experience believers have of his deceits, the better.
Christ cares tenderly for his faithful servants and imposes no burden that is not for their good.
He promises rich reward to those who persevere, including fitting wisdom and authority.
Christ brings the dawn of grace and glory into the soul and gives himself for its enjoyment.
After every spiritual victory, continue resisting the enemy until the end.

row.cell: Epistles to the church at Sardis;

div.title: Sardis: wake up and strengthen what remains (verses 1–6)
div.p: Jesus Christ possesses the Holy Spirit, with all the Spirit's powers, graces and operations.
He knows his churches and all their works. He exposed the hypocrisy and terrible spiritual decline of Sardis.
Outwardly, the church seemed healthy. Inwardly, much of its religion was only a form of godliness without its power: it had a reputation for life but lacked the principle of life itself.
Many members were hypocrites altogether; others retained spiritual life but had fallen into weakness and disorder.

Christ therefore called them to wakefulness, watchfulness and energetic obedience. They were to depend on the Holy Spirit's grace to revive faith and holy affections and to strengthen those who had not yet died spiritually.
Whenever we stop watching, we lose ground.
Their works were unfinished and hollow. Prayers lacked sincere holy desires, acts of giving lacked genuine love, and Sabbath observance lacked fitting devotion of heart.
Their outward forms did not match their inward condition; once the spirit of worship is missing, its forms cannot continue for long.
To seek revival in ourselves and others, we must compare what we profess with how we actually live. This should humble us, awaken us and move us to hold firmly to what remains.
Christ warns of severe consequences for ignoring his counsel, yet he does not leave the church without hope.
He remembers the faithful remnant at Sardis and promises them honor.
Those who overcome will receive white clothing: the purity of grace perfected in the purity of glory.
Christ holds the book of life, remembering all who will inherit eternal life and those who maintain genuine devotion amid evil times.
On the great day, he will acknowledge the names of his faithful people before God and all the angels.

div.title: Philadelphia: the open door and enduring faithfulness (verses 7–13)
div.p: Jesus Christ holds the key of authority and government over the church.
He opens opportunities for his congregations, opens doors for his ministers to speak, and opens hearts to receive his word.
He also shuts heaven's door to those who waste their time of grace in spiritual sleep and to those who continue in evil, however confident they may seem.
Philadelphia received praise, though also a gentle correction.
Christ accepts a little strength, but believers must never be content to remain weak. They should grow in grace, become strong in faith and bring glory to God.
Christ can display his favor so clearly that even enemies of his people must acknowledge it.
Through grace their opposition may soften, and they may desire fellowship with those they once opposed.
He promises to preserve faithful believers in their hardest trials.
Those who have kept his gospel in times of peace will find that he sustains them during temptation and persecution.
The same grace that made them fruitful in peaceful days will enable them to remain faithful in suffering.
Christ promises an enduring reward to those who overcome.
He will make them pillars in God's temple, monuments to his free and powerful grace that will never be destroyed or removed.
His new name written upon them will identify the Lord under whose leadership they fought and won their spiritual battle.

div.title: Laodicea: repent of complacency and welcome Christ (verses 14–22)
div.p: Laodicea was the last and worst of the seven churches of Asia.
Jesus calls himself the Amen: unwavering in his purposes and faithful to all his promises.
If religion matters at all, it matters supremely. Christ requires earnest devotion.
Yet many who profess the gospel are neither hot nor cold. They show little concern for essential matters while becoming angry and combative about minor disputes.
Christ warns such people of severe judgment.

Their indifference gives others a false picture of Christianity. Some conclude that the faith is unholy; others suppose it cannot bring real satisfaction, since its professed followers are so lifeless and quick to seek happiness from the world.
Self-conceit and self-deception are among the roots of this spiritual inconsistency.
What a difference between Laodicea's opinion of itself and Christ's judgment of it!
We must not deceive our own souls. Henry warns that many are in hell who once believed themselves far along the road to heaven.
Pray earnestly that God will keep us from flattering ourselves.
People grow proud as religion becomes outward and worldly.
The Laodiceans imagined themselves rich, yet were spiritually poor; they believed they could see, but were blind to their condition and danger.
They lacked the clothing of justification and sanctification. Exposed to sin and shame, they were naked, without the shelter of God in whom alone the soul finds lasting safety.
Christ nevertheless offered them the counsel they needed.
He revealed where genuine riches could be found and how to receive them.
They must relinquish sin and self-confidence, not anything truly valuable, so that they might receive the treasures he gives.
From Christ they must receive white clothing: his righteousness counted as theirs for justification, together with holiness and sanctification.
By yielding to his word and Spirit, they would receive sight to recognize their way and their final destination.
Let us examine ourselves by the standard of Scripture and ask the Holy Spirit to remove pride, prejudice and worldly desire.
Sinners should receive the rebukes of God's word and correcting providence as signs of concern for their souls.
Christ stands at the door and knocks through providential events, Scripture's warnings and teaching, and the influences of his Spirit.
Those who open to him enjoy his fellowship.
What we offer him may be a poor meal, but what he brings supplies a rich feast of fresh grace and consolation.
Christ overcame every temptation and conflict he faced.
Those who are made like him in his trials will also be made like him in glory, sharing his promised victory.
The final call to listen belongs not only to these seven congregations, but to everyone.

row.cell: A vision of God, as on his glorious throne, around which were twenty-four elders and four living creatures.
Whose songs, and those of the holy angels, the apostle heard.

div.title: The heavenly throne and its worshipers (verses 1–8)
div.p: After Christ commanded John to record the things concerning the churches, he received another vision.
He saw a throne in heaven, representing the Lord's universal authority.

The glorious One seated on it was not described through human features that could be copied into an image. Only surpassing brightness was revealed, pointing to the excellence of God's nature and his awesome justice.
A rainbow surrounded the throne, an appropriate sign of the covenant of promise established with Christ as head of the church and with all God's people in him.
Its prevailing green color suggested the renewing and refreshing character of the new covenant.
Around the throne were twenty-four seats with twenty-four elders.
Henry considers it probable, not certain, that they represent God's whole church.
Their seats signify honor, rest and satisfaction.
Their places around the throne signify nearness to God and the privilege of seeing and enjoying him.
Their white clothing symbolizes both the righteousness credited to believers and their holiness; their golden crowns signify glory shared with God.
Lightning and voices proceeded from the throne: solemn declarations to the church of God's sovereign will and purpose.
Before it burned seven lamps of fire, signifying the gifts, graces and operations of the Holy Spirit throughout Christ's churches, given according to the will of God who sits on the throne.
In the gospel church, the cleansing basin is the blood of Jesus Christ, which washes away all sin.
Everyone entering God's gracious presence on earth and his glorious presence in heaven must be cleansed by that blood.
John also saw four living creatures standing between the throne and the elders.
Henry proposes that these seem to signify genuine ministers of the gospel, serving between God and his people.
The features of the creatures represent wisdom, courage, diligence and discretion, together with holy desires that rise toward heaven.
This is Henry's proposed symbolic reading, not an identification the passage explicitly settles.

div.title: Eternal thanksgiving and worship (verses 9–11)
