div.p: All true believers attribute their redemption, conversion, present privileges and future hopes entirely to the eternal and most holy God.
This gives rise to the thankful and harmonious praises of the redeemed in heaven.
If we wish to imitate them on earth, let our praise be constant rather than intermittent, united rather than divided, thankful rather than cold and mechanical, and humble rather than self-confident.

row.cell: A book sealed with seven seals, which could be opened by none but Christ, who took the book to open it.
Upon which all honour is ascribed to him, as worthy to open it.

div.title: The sealed scroll and the Lamb (verses 1–7)
div.p: John saw a scroll of parchment in the hand of the One seated on the throne, closed with seven seals.
It represented God's purposes, soon to be revealed.
The designs and methods of divine Providence concerning the church and the world are established and fixed, yet remain hidden from created minds until God reveals them.
The seals would be opened one after another, not all at once, as the Lord unfolded his purposes until they were fully accomplished.
No creature could open or even read the scroll.
Only the Lord could do so.
People who have already seen something of God's glory long to see more, and those who know him wish to understand his will.
Yet even good people can be too eager to investigate the hidden mysteries of his government.
When answers are delayed, their eager curiosity may turn into sorrow.
John wept because he could not read God's secret decrees.
How many others should weep, rather, over their ignorance of Christ's gospel, on which eternal salvation depends!
We do not need to know in advance every event that may happen to us.
Both eager speculation about future prosperity and advance knowledge of coming calamities could make us less prepared for present duties, spiritual conflicts and the enjoyment of current blessings.
Nevertheless, through Scripture's promises and prophecies we may rightly seek to know the final outcome for believers and Christ's church.
The incarnate Son has prevailed, so we may learn everything we need to know.
Christ stands as Mediator between God and his ministers and people.
He is called the Lion, yet appears as a Lamb who has been slain.
The marks of his suffering show that he intercedes in heaven by virtue of the satisfaction he has made for sin.
The Lamb's seven horns signify perfect power to accomplish God's will, and his seven eyes signify perfect wisdom to understand that will and execute it effectively.
The Father entrusted his eternal purposes to Christ.
Christ gladly received them because he delights to reveal his Father's will.
He also gives the Holy Spirit to make God's truth and will known.

div.title: All creation honors the Redeemer (verses 8–14)
div.p: The world has good reason to rejoice that God deals with human beings in grace and mercy through the Redeemer.
He rules not merely as our Creator but as our Savior.
The harps signify praise, while the bowls of incense represent the prayers of the saints.
Prayer and praise should therefore always go together.
Christ has redeemed his people from bondage to sin, guilt and Satan.
He has not merely bought their freedom.
He has given them extraordinary honor, making them kings and priests.
As kings, they are called to govern their own spirits and overcome both the world and the evil one.
As priests, they enjoy access to God and may offer spiritual sacrifices.
The worship offered to the Lamb shows unmistakably that Jesus Christ is worthy of the same worship as the Father, from all creatures and forever.
Blessed are those who will praise him in heaven and eternally bless the Lamb who set them apart for himself by his blood.
Father, Son and Holy Spirit deserve our highest worship.
Let every creature proclaim the Lord's greatness and adore his majesty.

row.cell: The opening of the seals, The first, second, third, and fourth.

div.title: The first four seals (verses 1–8)
div.p: Christ the Lamb opened the seals in succession.
At the first seal John saw a white horse and its rider.

Henry suggests that this seems to represent a period of peace or the early progress of Christianity in its purity, when the Lord sent his apostles to teach all nations and promised to remain with them to the end of the world.
The gospel advances under God's favor, spiritually equipped against its enemies and destined for final victory.
The second seal revealed a red horse, signifying destructive judgments.
War and persecution take away one of the greatest earthly blessings—peace—and turn people who should love and help one another into enemies who kill one another.
Henry sees a correspondence with later Christian history, when some church leaders neglected love and peace, fought among themselves and resorted to the sword, becoming guilty through violence.
The third seal disclosed a black horse, the color of mourning, suffering, darkness and ignorance.
Its rider carried a yoke.
Henry applies this to efforts to bind disciples under superstitious religious requirements, as Christian practice became corrupted when it moved away from its original purity.
The excessive prices of necessities, while costly luxuries went unharmed, can also picture the scarcity of spiritual nourishment.
God invites thirsty souls to receive what sustains spiritual life (Isaiah 55:1).
Yet where ignorance and superstition dominate, true knowledge and godliness become scarce.
When people despise their spiritual food, God may withdraw ordinary bread as a judgment.

p.hi: A famine of bread is dreadful, but a famine of God's word is worse.

div.p: At the fourth seal came a pale horse, ridden by Death.
Hades, the state of eternal misery of those who die in sin in Henry's interpretation, followed him.
In times of widespread destruction, many die without preparing for eternity.
This seal pictures slaughter and devastation that destroy the supports of ordinary happiness and ravage people's spiritual lives.
Henry relates these images to the growth of the mystery of iniquity, exerting influence over both lives and consciences.
He explicitly cautions that the exact periods covered by these four seals cannot be established because the changes were gradual.
Every instrument of judgment remains subject to God's command.
Public calamities happen only when he permits them, and extend no further than his permission allows.

div.title: The fifth seal: faithful martyrs await justice (verses 9–11)
div.p: At the fifth seal, John saw the souls of martyrs beneath the altar, at the feet of Christ in heaven.
Persecutors can kill the body, but cannot kill the soul.
God has prepared a better dwelling for those who remain faithful until death.
They enter heaven not because their own death deserves that reward, but because of Christ's sacrifice.
They suffered for the word of God, the worthiest cause for which a person could give earthly life.
They trusted and confessed God's word without abandoning it.
They entrusted their cause to the Lord, to whom vengeance belongs.
He comforts his afflicted people and regards their shed blood as precious.
As their persecutors' guilt grows, so the number of Christ's faithful martyrs is brought to completion.
Then the Lord will send judgment on those who afflict his servants and grant unbroken rest and happiness to the afflicted.

div.title: The sixth seal: upheaval and the wrath of the Lamb (verses 12–17)
div.p: Opening the sixth seal brought a great earthquake.
John's images describe vast upheavals that shake the foundations of governments and churches.
Scripture's prophecies often use such bold symbols for great historical changes, while they also point toward the world's end and the day of judgment.
Every rank and condition of person will be terrified.
Wealth, strength, courage and worldly distinction will offer no defense.
People will wish to hide so completely that they might cease to exist.
Although Jesus is the Lamb, his wrath against sin is terrible.
If the Redeemer who normally intercedes and turns away judgment becomes our enemy, who remains to plead for us?
Human beings have days of opportunity and times of grace.
God also has a day when he will display righteous anger against evil.
Henry understands the scene as apparently referring to the overthrow of paganism in the Roman Empire. This is his historical interpretation of the symbol, not a certainty established by the text.
In that reading, idolaters hide in dens and caves and seek in vain to escape the approaching fall.
Whenever the signs of the times remind believers that the King of kings is coming, they should openly confess Christ and his truth before others.
However much contempt people may inflict now, bearing it briefly is better than experiencing everlasting shame.

row.cell: A pause between two great periods.
The peace, happiness, and safety of the saints, as signified by an angel's sealing 144,000.
The blessedness and glory of those that suffered martyrdom for Christ.

div.title: God's people are sealed before the coming judgments (verses 1–8)
div.p: In the Bible's figurative language, the four winds blowing together signify terrible and widespread destruction.
But the destruction is delayed.
Seals are used to identify the possessions belonging to a particular owner.
This seal represents the witness of the Holy Spirit impressed upon believers' hearts.
The Lord would not allow his people to enter their trials before they had been marked as his, so they might be prepared for the conflicts before them.
The seal is placed upon the forehead.
It can be seen by both friends and enemies, although believers themselves recognize it only as they look steadily into the mirror of God's word.
The number of those sealed, 144,000, may represent the remnant God has preserved.
Although God's church is a small flock compared with the ungodly world, it is in fact a great society, and the Lord will make it greater still.
The universal church is represented here under the figure of Israel.

div.title: A great multitude gives praise to God and the Lamb (verses 9–12)
div.p: After the first believers who came to Christ, the converted Gentile nations followed them.
Together they joyfully acknowledged that their salvation came from God and the Redeemer.
When we worship, we draw near to God, but we can do so only through Christ.
Without a Mediator, sinners could not approach the throne.
The worshipers' white robes signify justification, holiness and victory.
Their palm branches are the emblems carried by conquerors in triumph.
So every faithful servant of God will finally appear after fighting the good fight of faith and finishing the appointed course.
The redeemed will openly and fervently praise both the Father and the Son for their great salvation.
We can already see what heaven's work will be.
Let us begin it on earth, devoting our hearts increasingly to thankful praise and longing for the place where both our praise and our happiness will be perfect.

div.title: The martyrs' heavenly rest and comfort (verses 13–17)
div.p: Faithful Christians deserve respect and careful attention.
Anyone who wishes to learn should not be ashamed to ask someone able to explain a matter.
The way to heaven leads through many trials.
But even the greatest suffering cannot separate Christ's people from the love of God.
Indeed, affliction can make heaven more welcome and its glory more precious.
The redeemed do not become pure through the blood they themselves shed as martyrs.
Only the blood of the Lamb cleanses sinners from their guilt and makes their robes white before God.
Other blood stains; Christ's blood alone cleanses.
In heaven they are happy in their service.
Heaven is a state of service without suffering, and rest without idleness—a delightful rest filled with praise.
They once experienced sorrow and shed tears because of sin and suffering.
But God, with the tender care of a father, will wipe every tear away.
Remembering this should sustain Christians under their present troubles.
Every redeemed person owes eternal happiness entirely to sovereign mercy.
God's worship is their delight; his presence and favor complete their joy.
They cannot imagine any greater happiness.
May all his people come to him for needed grace and offer him all praise and glory.

row.cell: The seventh seal is opened and seven angels appear with seven trumpets, ready to proclaim the purposes of God.
Another angel casts fire on the earth, which produces terrible storms of vengeance.
The seven angels prepare to sound their trumpets.
Another angel denounces greater woes to come.

div.title: The seventh seal, silence and the prayers of the saints (verses 1–6)
div.p: When the seventh seal was opened, profound silence followed in heaven.
Henry suggests two possible meanings.
The church may have been quiet, since its cries under oppression reach heaven.
Or the silence may have expressed solemn expectation.
Seven angels received trumpets with which to announce God's purposes.
Jesus Christ, the great High Priest of the church, holds a golden censer and abundant incense.
This signifies the fullness of merit in his glorious person, through which he intercedes.
How much more eagerly we should study the fullness of Christ, learn his excellence and recognize the compassion with which he carries out his work as our Intercessor!
Prayers recommended by Christ in this way are received and heard in heaven.
Their acceptance leads to great changes on earth.
Christian worship and the Christian faith are pure and heavenly in their origin.
Yet when they enter the world and encounter sinful human passions and worldly plans, great disturbances may follow.
Henry connects these prophetic images with Jesus' words in Luke 12:49.

div.title: The first four trumpets and the announcement of coming woes (verses 7–13)
div.p: At the first trumpet, hail and fire mingled with blood appeared.
Henry suggests this may picture a storm of heresies and destructive errors falling upon the church, or a tempest of physical destruction.
At the second trumpet, a great mountain burning with fire fell into the sea and a third of the sea became blood.
Some interpreters take the mountain to represent leaders of persecution.
Others associate it with Rome's devastation by the Goths and Vandals, accompanied by much cruelty and bloodshed.
These are interpretations Henry reports, not identifications established by the text.
At the third trumpet, a star fell from heaven.
Some interpret it as a prominent ruler.
Others take it to signify a powerful individual who corrupted Christ's churches.
The gospel's doctrines are springs that nourish spiritual life, comfort and strength.
When those springs become mixed with dangerous errors, people encounter bitterness and spiritual ruin where they had hoped to find refreshment.
At the fourth trumpet, the heavenly lights—the sun, moon and stars—were darkened.
Henry applies this to guides and governors, who occupy high positions and should provide light and beneficial influence to others.
When a people receive the gospel without allowing it to transform their hearts and lives, terrible judgments may follow.
God warns people through his written word, ministers, their consciences and the signs of the times.
If people are surprised by judgment after such warnings, they bear responsibility.
God's anger can make every comfort bitter and even life itself burdensome.
Yet he sets boundaries around the worst judgments in this world.
Corruption in a church's doctrine and worship is itself a great judgment, and frequently both the cause and a warning of further calamity.
Before the remaining three trumpets sounded, a solemn warning announced that still worse troubles were approaching.
If lesser judgments fail to bring repentance, the church and world must expect greater ones.
Let sinners seek rescue from coming wrath.
Let believers prize and thank God for their privileges and patiently continue in doing good.

row.cell: The fifth trumpet is followed by a representation of another star as falling from heaven and opening the bottomless pit, out of which come swarms of locusts.
The sixth trumpet is followed by the loosing of four angels bound in the great river Euphrates.

div.title: The fifth trumpet: smoke and locusts (verses 1–12)
div.p: At the fifth trumpet, a star fell from heaven.
Henry interprets the fallen star as someone who ceased to be a servant of Christ and became a servant of the devil, releasing destructive spiritual influences against the churches.
The abyss opened and a great cloud of smoke rose from it.
The devil advances his schemes by blinding people's eyes, extinguishing light and knowledge, and spreading ignorance and error.
A swarm of locusts emerged.
Henry sees them as pictures of Satan's agents who promote superstition, idolatry, error and cruelty.
The grass and trees symbolize true believers, whether young in faith or more mature, whom the locusts are not permitted to harm.
Others would experience a hidden poison in their souls, first losing spiritual purity and later losing their peace.
The locusts had no authority over those marked with God's seal.
The Lord's powerful and discriminating grace preserves his people from total and final apostasy.
The torment would be extremely severe but limited to a comparatively short period.
Even faithful believers may share the outward sufferings experienced by their society, while being protected from the spiritual corruption of error.
Henry sees such heresies as a means of testing and revealing genuine Christians, citing 1 Corinthians 11:19.
He also says early Christian writers connected the image with an early, widespread invasion of corrupting teachers.
This is his account of the image's possible historical reference.

div.title: The sixth trumpet: destruction and stubborn impenitence (verses 13–21)
div.p: At the sixth trumpet, four angels bound at the Euphrates were released.
Henry suggests that the power of the Turks is the subject of this vision.
He understands their period of dominance as limited by God and connects their military violence with what he calls a destructive false religion.
This is Henry's historical and polemical interpretation, not an identification established by the text of Revelation or a judgment about individual people today.
The people described as opposing Christ did not repent despite these terrible events.
One enemy of the church may become an instrument of divine judgment upon another.
Henry connects this with idolatry and corruption among professing Christians, including what remained of the churches of the East.
The historical developments grieved him, but he believed a careful reading of Scripture and history could strengthen Christians' faith and hope as they contemplated Providence.
The final warning concerns people who escape one judgment without repenting.
They continue in idolatry, injustice and cruelty, until divine judgment finally overtakes them.

row.cell: The Angel of the covenant presents a little open book, which is followed with seven thunders.
At the end of the following prophecies, time should be no more.
A voice directs the apostle to eat the book;
and tells him he must prophesy further.

div.title: The glorious angel and the seven thunders (verses 1–7)
div.p: John saw another vision.
Henry suggests that the figure communicating the revelation was probably Jesus Christ himself, or at least appeared in a way intended to reveal Christ's glory.
The Lord veils the greatness of his glory because mortal eyes cannot bear it.
He also conceals some of his dealings with the world.
The rainbow over the figure's head reminds us that Christ continually remembers his covenant.
The dreadful voice was answered by seven thunders, solemn and awe-inspiring expressions of divine revelation.
We do not know what those thunders announced or why their message was withheld.
Events of great importance—possibly concerning the history of Christ's church—may not be disclosed in the public prophecies of Scripture.
Nevertheless, the Lord has pledged through his unfailing word that the righteous will finally be saved and that true religion will ultimately triumph on earth.
Although the fulfillment may not yet have come, it cannot be far away compared with eternity.
For each of us personally, the time when earthly life ends is certainly near.
Then time will be over for us.
Believers will enter a happy eternity, from which they will see and rejoice in the triumph of Christ and his cause.

div.title: John eats the little scroll and must prophesy again (verses 8–11)
div.p: Most people find it appealing to learn about events that lie ahead.
Those who love God also rejoice to receive his word.
But when John fully absorbed the contents of the prophetic scroll, their meaning became bitter.
They foretold terrible things: fierce persecutions of God's people and devastating judgments upon the world.
Knowing these sufferings in advance would bring grief, despite the initial sweetness of receiving the revelation.
Let us seek to be taught by Jesus Christ and to obey his commands.
Meditate on his word daily, allowing it to nourish your soul.
Then share that word faithfully in whatever responsibilities God has given you.
The sweetness of studying Scripture will sometimes be mixed with sorrow when we compare its truths with the condition of the world, the visible church and our own hearts.

row.cell: The state of the church is represented under the figure of a temple measured.
They are slain, after which they arise and ascend to heaven.
Under the seventh trumpet, all antichristian powers are to be destroyed and there will be a glorious state of Christ's kingdom upon earth.

div.title: God's temple and its worshipers are measured (verses 1 and 2)
div.p: The symbolic measuring of the temple seems to recall Ezekiel's vision.
Henry proposes several possible purposes: preserving the church during public danger, testing its condition, or reforming it.
God's people must be examined to see whether they pursue his glory as the purpose of worship and follow his word as the rule for everything they do.
Those remaining in the outer court picture people who worship wrongly or pretend to have sincere hearts; their hypocrisy will eventually be exposed.
God will preserve a temple and an altar—true worship—somewhere in this world until the end of time.
He carefully watches over his church.
The holy city represents the visible church.
It may be trampled and filled with idolaters, unbelievers and hypocrites, but its period of devastation is limited.
The Lord will ultimately rescue his people from their troubles.

div.title: The witnesses suffer and are restored (verses 3–13)
div.p: During periods when the church was oppressed, God maintained faithful witnesses to declare the truth of his word and worship and the goodness of his ways.
They were few, yet enough to accomplish the task.
They prophesied in sackcloth, signifying both the persecution and hardship they endured and their grief at the sins against which they testified.
God sustained them through their long and difficult service until their assigned work was complete.
Henry interprets the 1,260 years as an extended period of testimony during which Antichrist, understood as a great instrument of Satan, would eventually attack the witnesses with force.
He believed the witnesses' final suffering and restoration were probably still future in his own time.
He also acknowledged that Christians might again endure severe outward persecution, and that there was already abundant reason to mourn the state of religion.
He suggested that the depressed condition described could refer particularly to the Western church.
These are Henry's historically situated proposals about prophetic fulfillment, not dates or identifications certain from the biblical text.
People hardened against divine truth rejoice when they manage to silence, banish or kill faithful witnesses, because the witnesses' teaching and conduct trouble their consciences.
But the Spirit of life from God revives the spiritually dead.
He will restore his people and renew the church's seemingly dying witness.
Such revival terrifies its enemies.
Where there is guilt, there is fear; a persecuting spirit can be cruel but remains cowardly.
The vindication and public honor of those who suffered for God will itself be part of the judgment against their persecutors, both in this world and at the last day.
Christ's witnesses must not grow tired of serving or suffering, nor impatiently seize a reward before its time.
They must wait until their Master calls them.
The revival and exaltation of the witnesses brings a mighty upheaval to their opponents' dominion.
Henry cautions that events alone will disclose the precise meaning of those prophecies.
But the broader principle is clear: when God's work and witnesses revive, Satan's work is defeated.

div.title: The seventh trumpet and God's kingdom (verses 14–19)
div.p: Before the seventh and final trumpet, a solemn announcement demands attention.
The saints and angels in heaven recognize God's and the Savior's right to rule the entire world.
But the nations answer God's righteous anger with their own rebellion.
The Lord begins rewarding his people's faithful work and suffering.
His enemies become more hostile and thereby increase their own guilt and hasten judgment.
The opening of God's heavenly temple might picture freer fellowship between heaven and earth: more frequent prayer and praise rising to God and blessings descending.
Henry nevertheless considers it more likely that the image represents changes in the church on earth.
During what he calls Antichrist's reign, God's law was set aside in favor of human traditions and decrees, and Scripture was withheld from ordinary people.
Now God's word is brought openly before everyone.
The ark's reappearance then symbolizes God's returning presence and favor through Jesus Christ, the atoning sacrifice for sins.
Henry relates this to the Protestant Reformation and the extraordinary events surrounding it.
The God who heard prayer answered it through mighty acts of righteousness.

row.cell: A description of the church of Christ and of Satan, under the figures of a woman and of a great red dragon.
Michael and his angels fight against the devil and his angels, who are defeated.
His vain endeavours to destroy her, He renews his war against her seed.

div.title: The woman and the dragon (verses 1–6)
div.p: John saw the church pictured as a woman in heaven, the mother of believers.
She was clothed with the sun, representing the way believers are justified, sanctified and made radiant through union with Christ, the Sun of Righteousness.
The moon beneath her feet showed her greater light compared with the reflected and weaker revelation received through Moses.
Her crown of twelve stars represented gospel teaching proclaimed by the twelve apostles, a glory belonging to all genuine believers.
She labored to bring forth a holy family, desiring that sinners' conviction would lead to their conversion.
The red dragon represents Satan and his chief agents—those who govern in his interests on earth.
Henry identifies this particular historical embodiment with the pagan Roman Empire, the city of seven hills.
He interprets the ten horns as ten kingdoms and the seven crowns as seven forms of government.
Those are his historical and symbolic interpretations, not settled facts supplied by the passage itself.
The dragon's tail sweeping away a third of the stars pictures the persecution and seduction of ministers and teachers.
The enemy sought to crush Christianity.
Nevertheless, the church brought forth a faithful and vigorous people in whom Christ was formed anew.
The Son of God will govern the nations, and his people share the honor he wins for them.
God protected this blessed offspring.

div.title: The dragon's defeat and the church's weapons (verses 7–11)
div.p: The dragon's attack upon the church ultimately damaged his own cause.
Henry understands the conflict in heaven as being fought in Christ's church, the kingdom of heaven present on earth.
He identifies the opposing sides with Christ, the great Angel of the covenant, and his faithful people, and Satan with his instruments.
The church's strength rests in having Jesus Christ as Captain of its salvation.
Henry connects the dragon's defeat with pagan idolatry being driven out of the Roman Empire through Christianity's spread.
The church owes its deliverance and strength entirely to its King and Head.
The devil hates God's presence, yet is willing to appear before him in order to accuse believers.
We must take care not to provide grounds for such accusations.
When we do sin, we should confess before God, condemn our own wrongdoing and entrust our case to Jesus Christ as Advocate.
God's people overcome Satan through three means.
First, the blood of the Lamb is the only foundation of their hope.
Second, their testimony to the gospel is powerful through God to bring down spiritual strongholds.
Third, they show courage and patience in suffering, loving Christ more than their own lives and being willing to die rather than abandon his cause.
Henry sees these as the instruments through which Christianity overcame pagan idolatry.
He argues that if Christians had continued to rely upon these spiritual weapons, instead of other means, their victories would have been greater, more lasting and more glorious.
We too must trust the Lamb's blood alone, without adding anything else as a basis for salvation.

div.title: The dragon persecutes the remaining faithful (verses 12–17)
div.p: Christ's church and its friends rightly praise God for deliverance from pagan persecution, although further trials await.
The wilderness is desolate and dangerous, inhabited by serpents and scorpions and lacking ordinary comforts.
Yet it can also be a place of refuge and safety.
Even withdrawal into such a refuge did not completely protect the woman from the dragon.
Henry records two proposed interpretations of the flood that the dragon sent against her.
Some understood it as the barbarian invasions that overwhelmed the Western Roman Empire, with pagan opponents hoping that the destruction would also end Christianity.
But people acting from worldly interests nevertheless protected the church through those upheavals, so the end of the empire did not secure a victory for idolatry.
Alternatively, the flood might mean a torrent of error threatening to sweep away God's people.
Neither identification is presented as certain.
Defeated in his attempts against the church as a whole, Satan turned his anger against particular believers and communities.
Faithfulness to God and Christ in teaching, worship and conduct exposes Christians to spiritual opposition.
That conflict continues until the final enemy is destroyed.

row.cell: A wild beast rises out of the sea, to whom the dragon gives his power.
Another beast, which has two horns like a lamb, but speaks as a dragon.
It obliges all to worship its image, and receive its mark, as persons devoted to it.

div.title: The first beast and its persecuting authority (verses 1–10)
div.p: John saw a terrifying beast rising from the sea.
Henry understands it as a tyrannical, idolatrous and persecuting power emerging from great public disturbances.
He connects it with worldly empires that had oppressed God's people for centuries, beginning as far back as the Babylonian captivity.
He particularly relates the fourth beast of Daniel's prophecy to the Roman Empire, under which many believers suffered cruel persecution.
The dragon—Satan—supplied the beast's authority and supported its power.
The wounded head may, in Henry's interpretation, signify the overthrow of Roman pagan idolatry.
Its healing may symbolize what Henry polemically called “popish idolatry”, a revived form of the same spiritual evil under a different outward appearance.
This reflects Henry's historical Protestant interpretation, not a fact or identity demonstrated beyond dispute by Revelation 13.
The world admired the beast's power, strategy and success.
People gave honor and obedience to the devil's instruments, granting creatures reverence that belongs to God alone.
Yet Satan's authority and his apparent success remain strictly limited.
Christ has a chosen remnant, redeemed by his blood, recorded in his book and sealed by his Spirit.
The beast and its allies may conquer the body and take away physical life, but cannot conquer the souls of genuine believers or make them finally abandon their Savior and join his enemies.
Those whose names are written in the book of life are characterized by endurance in gospel faith and faithful worship of God during severe temptation.
Encouraging this steadfastness is, Henry says, the principal design of the whole book of Revelation.

div.title: The second beast, enforced worship and the number 666 (verses 11–18)
div.p: Those who see the first beast as a form of worldly power interpret the second as another oppressive authority—a spiritual power disguising itself as true religion and concern for people's souls.
It presents itself as derived from Christ, and initially appears gentle.
But it soon speaks like the dragon.
Its false teaching and harsh commands reveal, in Henry's understanding, that it serves Satan rather than the Lamb.
It exercises the first beast's authority for the same end: drawing people away from the worship of the true God and placing human consciences under human control.
Henry describes deceptive signs and supposed miracles as instruments used to persuade people to worship the image of the earlier persecuting power.
Harsh censures are another means.
Those refusing its worship may be deprived of ordinary civil rights, opportunities to buy or sell, and positions of profit or trust.
Receiving its mark signifies binding oneself to advance its cause with all one's influence, strength and efforts.
To make the beast's image is to establish a form of its worship and authority.
To worship that image is to submit to the defining practices of the power it represents.
The beast's number is 666.
It invites the exercise of human wisdom while displaying the far greater wisdom of God.
But Henry says explicitly that the intended person or institution remains a mystery.
The number has been applied to nearly every religious controversy.
He even considers it reasonable to doubt whether its true meaning had yet been discovered.
What the believer can understand is that every enemy of God is known and numbered.
Their power has a limit, and their appointed end will come.
All nations will finally submit to the King of righteousness and peace.

row.cell: Those faithful to Christ celebrate the praises of God.

Three angels; one proclaiming the everlasting gospel; another, the downfal of Babylon; and a third, the dreadful wrath of God on the worshippers of the beast. The blessedness of those who die in the Lord.
A vision of Christ with a sickle, and of a harvest ripe for cutting down.
The emblem of a vintage fully ripe, trodden in the wine-press of God's wrath.

div.title: The Lamb and his faithful people on Mount Zion (verses 1–5)
div.p: Mount Zion represents Christ's gospel church.
Jesus remains with her even amid all her troubles.
His presence protects the church from destruction and secures the perseverance of his people.
They appear with honor.
God's name written upon their foreheads shows that they openly and boldly confess faith in God and Jesus Christ, and then live in a way consistent with that confession.
Even in the darkest periods, some believers have been willing to suffer and die for the truth and worship of Christ's gospel.
They kept themselves from the wicked practices of those Henry identifies with Antichrist.
Their hearts were sincerely devoted to God.
They were freely forgiven in Christ, bringing glory to him and receiving glory in him.
Let our prayer, our labor and our ambition be to belong to that company.
The passage speaks about people truly justified and sanctified.
No hypocrite, however convincing an outward appearance may be, can be judged without fault before God.

div.title: The gospel proclaimed, Babylon warned and the faithful blessed (verses 6–13)
div.p: Henry suggests that this scene appears to describe the progress of the Protestant Reformation.
He sees the four proclamations or declarations in this passage as encouragement for Christians to remain faithful during testing.
This is his historical reading, not a prophetic date or identification independently established here.
The everlasting gospel is God's great means of bringing people to fear him and give him glory.
Its proclamation shakes the foundations of powers hostile to Christ and hastens their downfall.
Those who continue willingly serving the beast and promoting its cause, Henry warns, face misery of both soul and body forever.
Believers, by contrast, should be willing to endure hardship and loss while obeying God's commands and confessing their faith in Jesus.
May God grant us that patience.
Consider the blessedness of those who die in the Lord.
They die united to Christ and in the service of his cause; they belong to him when death comes.
They rest from sin, temptation, grief and persecution, where the wicked cease troubling them and the weary find repose.
Their works follow them.
Those works do not go before them as a price paid for salvation or a title by which to claim it.
They follow as evidence that these believers lived and died in Christ.
Remembering their service will bring joy, while their reward will far exceed any labor or suffering they endured.
The Holy Spirit assures them of this by his inward testimony and through the written word.

div.title: The harvest and the winepress (verses 14–20)
div.p: The warnings and earlier judgments have failed to bring universal repentance.
The wickedness of the nations reaches its full measure, so they become ripe for judgment.
The harvest can represent God's merciful gathering of righteous people into heaven when they are ready.
Grain is harvested when it has ripened.
In the same way, God's faithful people will be gathered into Christ's storehouse at the proper time.
The grape harvest and winepress, by contrast, represent judgment on Christ's enemies.
The Lord does not destroy them until their sins have ripened into complete guilt.
The winepress expresses the wrath of God in some dreadful calamity—Henry suggests probably the sword and bloodshed of the wicked.
God's patience toward sinners is an astonishing miracle.
But although his patience lasts a long time, it will not last forever.
When sin has reached its full measure, judgment is near.

row.cell: A song of praise is sung by the church.
Seven angels with the seven plagues; and to them one of the living creatures gives seven golden vials full of the wrath of God.

div.title: The redeemed sing of God's holiness and deliverance (verses 1–4)
div.p: John saw seven angels in heaven preparing to carry out the last judgments.
Henry interprets their task as bringing the destruction of Antichrist to completion.
In his reading, Babylon's wickedness had reached its full measure, and therefore the time had come for God's full judgment against it.
Yet the scene also contains extraordinary consolation.
Believers still living amid the world's distress are like people standing upon a sea of glass mixed with fire.
They can look forward to their final deliverance even before it arrives.
Every new mercy they receive gives them reason to sing a new song of praise.
The more we discover of God's wonderful works, the more we will celebrate his greatness as the Lord God Almighty, Creator and Governor of all worlds.
But his title Emmanuel, King of the saints, makes him especially dear to those he has redeemed.
Anyone who understands God's power in judgment, the value of his favor and the glory of his holiness should worship him alone with deep reverence.
His praise rises above heaven and earth.

div.title: The angels receive the bowls of judgment (verses 5–8)
div.p: In judging Antichrist and those associated with that power, God fulfills the prophecies and promises of his word.
The angels are prepared for their work.
Their clean white clothing and golden bands across their chests symbolize the purity, holiness, righteousness and excellence of God's judgments.
They are ministers of divine justice and carry out their task without wrongdoing.
They receive the bowls containing God's righteous anger.
Even the weakest creature becomes irresistible when the Lord appoints it as the means of his judgment.
The angels receive the bowls from one of the four living creatures.
Henry interprets the living creature as representing a minister of the true church and regards the action as an answer to the prayers of God's servants and people.
He expects the removal of Antichrist to shake the entire world.
Even sincere believers might face confusion and suffering while that judgment unfolds.
God's greatest deliverances for the church sometimes come through awesome and astonishing acts of Providence.
The church will not enter its fully blessed condition until its stubborn enemies have been removed and halfhearted or merely formal Christians have been purified.
When everything contrary to Scripture has been cleansed away, the church will become spiritual, pure and united, firmly established in faithful worship and service.

row.cell: The first vial is poured out on the earth, the second on the sea, the third on the rivers and fountains.
The fourth on the sun, the fifth on the seat of the beast.
The sixth on the great river Euphrates.
And the seventh on the air, when shall follow the destruction of all antichristian enemies.

div.title: The first three bowls and God's righteous judgment (verses 1–7)
div.p: We should pray that God's will may be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Here John sees a succession of terrible acts of divine Providence.
These judgments seem to recall the plagues of Egypt: similar sins are met by similar punishments.
Henry connects the seven bowls with the earlier seven trumpets, which he interprets as representing the rise of Antichrist.
In that reading, the downfall of the church's enemies resembles the manner in which their power first grew.
The earth, air, sea, rivers and cities associated with this wicked power are subjected to judgment.
The destruction expresses God's opposition to the evil in which that society had participated.
The angels witnessing and carrying out God's judgment praise his justice and truth.
They honor him for avenging his servants, whose persecutors had inflicted cruel suffering on the saints and prophets.

div.title: The fourth and fifth bowls: suffering without repentance (verses 8–11)
div.p: The human heart is so deeply corrupted that even the most severe misery does not by itself bring a sinner to repentance.
God's special grace is necessary.
Hell itself is filled with blasphemy.
People who understand human history, Scripture and their own hearts should know that suffering sometimes makes sinners more furious against God, even when they recognize his hand in their troubles.
Let sinners seek repentance through Christ and the renewing grace of the Holy Spirit now.
Otherwise, Henry warns, they will remain unhumbled and unrepentant, increasing guilt and misery through all eternity.
Darkness is the opposite of knowledge and wisdom.
It therefore pictures the confusion and folly of idolatrous followers of the beast.
Darkness also opposes pleasure and joy and thus pictures anguish and inward distress.

div.title: The sixth bowl: Euphrates, deception and watchfulness (verses 12–16)
div.p: Henry offers alternative possible interpretations of the drying of the Euphrates.
It probably symbolizes, in one reading, the destruction of Turkish power and idolatry, preparing a way for the return of the Jews.
In another reading, Babylon represents Rome under a symbolic name, because the city could not then be named openly.
In that case, the fall of Rome would also devastate the trade and resources on which its power depended.
Henry adds that perhaps an opening would follow for the Eastern nations to join Christ's church.
These are his tentative historical interpretations, not established identifications or a timetable supplied by the prophecy.
Before losing his power, the great dragon gathers his remaining forces for one desperate conflict.
God warns the church so that his people may prepare for severe trials and temptation.
Christ therefore calls his professed servants to watch, expect his sudden return, and avoid the shame of being found apostates or hypocrites.
Christians disagree about the dates and seasons of future events.
Yet on one essential point they agree: Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, will return suddenly to judge the world.
For people who live near him, that coming is a joyful hope.
They do not wish to postpone it.

div.title: The seventh bowl and Babylon's overthrow (verses 17–21)
div.p: When the seventh angel emptied his bowl, Babylon's destruction was completed.
The church triumphant in heaven saw it and rejoiced.
The church still struggling on earth saw its deliverance and could rejoice in victory.
God remembered the great and wicked city.
For a time he had seemed to overlook its idolatry and cruelty, but he had not forgotten.
Even things that had appeared most secure were carried away in the collapse.
Yet people continued to blaspheme.
The severest judgments cannot produce repentance without God's grace.
Indeed, becoming more stubborn against God in response to his righteous judgments is a sure warning of final destruction.

row.cell: One of the angels who had the vials, explains the meaning of the former vision of the antichristian beast that was to reign 1260 years, and then to be destroyed.
And interprets the mystery of the woman, and the beast that had seven heads and ten horns.

div.title: The woman on the scarlet beast (verses 1–6)
div.p: Henry identifies the woman with Rome, and more particularly interprets the symbols as pointing from pagan Rome toward what he calls papal Rome.
In his account, pagan Rome conquered and ruled mainly through military power, while allowing subject nations much of their previous religion and custom.
He accuses the later papal system of gaining and keeping power over kings and nations through political manipulation, deception, and promises of spiritual advantage.
This is Henry's historical Protestant polemical interpretation, not an identity conclusively settled by the text of Revelation or a statement about every Roman Catholic believer.
Worldly honor, riches, ceremony and pride appeal to minds governed by bodily desires and worldly ambitions.
Yet outward prosperity and splendor provide no security against God's judgment.
Henry understands the golden cup as a symbol of enticing appearances, deception and influence that lead others into idolatry and sin.
The woman is called the mother of prostitutes, picturing a power that trains others in false worship and wickedness.
She is also described as drunk with the blood of the saints and martyrs of Jesus, persecuting them without being satisfied.
Henry is horrified by the extraordinary quantities of Christian blood shed by people who called themselves Christians.
He believes such persecution gives solemn confirmation to the warnings found in biblical prophecy.
Do not be deceived by fashionable, profitable or outwardly magnificent religion.
Turn instead from the mystery of iniquity and study the great mystery of godliness.
Look to Christ's example and learn humility and thankfulness.
The more we resemble him, the less easily false religion deceives us.

div.title: The beast's heads, horns and final defeat (verses 7–14)
div.p: The beast “was, and is not, and yet is.”
In Henry's reading, the ancient form of pagan Roman idolatry and persecution had disappeared, yet another form of religious domination later revived similar patterns.
Those living within its influence would submit blindly to deception, except for the faithful remnant God had chosen.
The beast's seven heads were, in his interpretation, the seven hills of Rome and seven forms of government.
He explained the sequence as five already past, one existing when John wrote, and one still future.
In his polemical scheme, the papacy became an eighth ruling authority, restoring idolatry in a new form.
The ten horns represented ten kings whose kingdoms were yet to rise when John received the vision.
Henry associated them with kingdoms arising after the Roman Empire's breakup, temporarily supporting Rome's interests.
These are specific interpretive claims made by Henry, not a historical reconstruction independently established by the biblical text.
Whatever the details of those symbols, Christ must reign until every enemy is under his feet.
He wins because he is King of kings and Lord of lords, holding ultimate authority over every earthly and spiritual power.
His followers are called and equipped for faithful service and will remain loyal to him.

div.title: The rulers turn against the woman (verses 15–18)
div.p: God governs even the hearts and purposes of rulers.
Through his Providence they accomplish what he has foretold without intending to fulfill his plan.
The kings eventually discover their foolishness and how the woman had deceived and enslaved them.
They become instruments in her destruction.
Henry connects the great city that ruled kings in John's day with Rome.
In the final conflict, people who had united to commit wrongdoing turn upon one another with hatred and fury.
The wicked may become active agents of each other's downfall.
Believers, however, will be welcomed into the Lord's glory.
The Lord's people are his own portion.
His purposes stand firm, and he will accomplish all that pleases him, for his glory and the lasting happiness of those who serve him.

row.cell: Another angel from heaven proclaims the fall of mystical Babylon.
A voice from heaven admonishes the people of God, lest they partake of her plagues.
The church called upon to rejoice in her utter ruin.

div.title: Babylon's fall and the call to come out (verses 1–8)
div.p: The downfall of mystical Babylon has been settled within God's purposes.
John sees another angel from heaven.
Henry suggests that the figure seems to be Christ himself, coming to defeat his enemies and spread the light of his gospel among the nations.
Babylon's wickedness is great.
It has abandoned true worship for idols, drawn people of all classes into spiritual unfaithfulness, and kept them loyal through wealth and luxury.
Henry understands the image as referring especially to spiritual commerce: people gaining riches by exploiting the sins, ignorance and foolishness of others.
God solemnly warns those who hope to receive mercy that they must come out of Babylon.
Henry also urges them to support its destruction, meaning the overthrow of the evil system depicted here.
There may be people who genuinely belong to God even within Babylon.
But his people must answer his call and separate from its wrongdoing.
Those who knowingly participate in the sins of the wicked expose themselves to the same judgments.

div.title: The kings and merchants mourn (verses 9–19)
div.p: Those mourning over Babylon have shared both its sensual pleasures and its commercial gains.
The kings of the earth were flattered into idolatry.
Henry accuses Babylon of permitting them to oppress their subjects so long as they remained obedient to her power.
The merchants profited, in his interpretation, by trading in indulgences, pardons and honors.
These observations express Henry's particular historical critique of what he regarded as the Roman Antichrist, not an identity the passage establishes beyond dispute.
Babylon's allies were willing to share her sinful pleasure and wealth, but not her punishment.
Their sorrow was purely worldly.
They did not grieve over God's anger against sin, only over their own lost conveniences.
This reveals the worldly spirit Henry associates with Antichrist.
The splendor and riches of wicked people will not protect them when judgment comes; they may even make the loss harder to bear.
The passage speaks of enslaved people and human souls as commodities.
Henry connects these images with destructive spiritual commerce that brought ruin to countless souls.
He explicitly observes that such wrongdoing is not limited to the system he identifies with Rome.
Successful merchants everywhere should therefore learn to seek the unsearchable riches of Jesus Christ alongside their earthly work.
Otherwise, riches may fly away even before death, leaving the desired pleasures gone.
In any case, death will soon end all their trade.
Without reconciliation to God, worldly wealth will be exchanged for the coffin and the worm, and the fire that cannot be quenched.

div.title: Heaven rejoices at the end of oppression (verses 20–24)
div.p: The same deliverance that makes God's servants rejoice on earth also brings rejoicing to the angels in heaven.
Henry expects even the apostles—whose memory he says was honored at Rome in ways he judged idolatrous—to rejoice in the fall of Babylon.
This is part of his historically situated Protestant reading of the passage.
Babylon's destruction reveals God's justice.
Because her fall is final, the persecuting power will never again trouble the faithful.
The vision supplies a sign assuring them of this complete end.
Let us learn from the errors and sins that brought others to ruin.
Recognizing how unstable all earthly possessions and institutions are, set your affections on things above.

row.cell: The church in heaven and that on earth triumph, and praise the Lord for his righteous judgments.
A vision of Christ going forth to destroy the beast and his armies.

div.title: The church praises God and the marriage of the Lamb is announced (verses 1–10)
div.p: When we praise God for mercies already received, we also express confidence and desire for the blessings yet to come.
Heavenly angels and redeemed people join in this triumphant song.
Christ is the Bridegroom of the church he has redeemed. Their glorious union will be complete in heaven.

Henry also suggests that the beginning of the millennium—which he describes as a thousand-year reign of Christ, or an era of happiness upon earth—can be understood as the celebration of their marriage here on earth.
In that happy condition, Christ's church will be purified from errors, divisions and corruptions in its doctrine, discipline, worship and conduct.
The Lord will then openly acknowledge her as his beloved and his delight.
Her clothing is not the bright and ostentatious display of the mother of prostitutes.
Instead, she wears clean, white linen: Christ's righteousness credited to her for justification and given to her in sanctification.
The marriage feast consists of God's trustworthy gospel promises, made plain, applied and sealed to believers by the Holy Spirit through the appointed ordinances.
Henry understands this as pointing to abundant grace and comfort for Christians in the happier days still to come.
When John tried to honor the angel religiously, the angel refused and directed him to worship God alone.
Henry applies that refusal against worship directed to bread and wine, saints or angels.
He also rejects worship given to Christ by those who deny that he is truly God by nature, because religious worship belongs to God alone.
The God who speaks truth here is the One worthy of worship, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

div.title: Christ defeats the beast and its armies (verses 11–21)
div.p: Christ appears as the glorious Head of his church, riding a white horse—a sign of righteousness and holiness.
He wears many crowns because he is King of kings and Lord of lords.
His garment is portrayed as dipped in blood.
Henry connects this both with Christ's own blood, through which he purchased his mediatorial authority, and with the blood of the enemies over whom he triumphs.
He is called the Word of God.
No creature can comprehend the full glory of this name.
Yet Scripture tells us what we need to know: the Word is God revealed in human flesh.
The angels and saints who follow him share his purity and righteousness.
He now carries out the judgments foretold in the written word against those who resist him.
His royal name declares his rightful authority and warns even the greatest earthly rulers to submit to him.
Otherwise they must fall.
Every power of earth and hell may join the struggle, but none can defeat him.
These verses concern weighty events announced by God's prophets.
Those who followed wicked leaders will not be excused simply because they obeyed orders.
What a useless defense it will be on the day of judgment to say, “We merely followed our leaders and did what other people did.”
God has given us his word as the rule of life.
Neither the conduct of the majority nor the orders of powerful people can justify disobeying it.
Those who blindly follow the multitude in sin will go where that multitude goes, Henry warns: into the burning lake.

row.cell: Satan is bound for a thousand years.
The first resurrection; those are blessed that have part therein.

div.title: Satan is restrained (verses 1–3)
div.p: The vision uses a figure to show the restraint placed upon Satan himself.
Through his almighty power, Christ will prevent the devil from misleading humanity as he has previously done.
Christ always possesses both the power and the means to break Satan's influence.
He shuts the prison by his power and seals it by his authority.
The church will enjoy a time of peace and prosperity.
Yet all her trials will not be over.

div.title: The first resurrection and the reign of the saints (verses 4–6)
div.p: The saints reign during the same period in which Satan is bound.
Those who suffer with Christ will reign with him in his spiritual and heavenly kingdom, reflecting his wisdom, righteousness and holiness.
Henry identifies this with the first resurrection, a blessing reserved for those who truly serve Christ and suffer for his sake.
Only holy people can be truly blessed, and everyone made holy will ultimately share that blessing.
We know something of the first death, and it is deeply frightening.
We have never directly experienced the second death, but it is more dreadful still: the soul's eternal separation from God.
May we never know it.
Those who share in a spiritual resurrection are delivered from its power.

Henry expects that after the destruction of antichristian, idolatrous and persecuting powers, a thousand years will come in which pure Christianity—right teaching, worship and holiness—will spread throughout the earth.
Through the almighty work of the Holy Spirit, fallen human beings will be made new.
Faith and holiness will then become as widespread as unbelief and wickedness appear to be now.
Imagine how many diseases, hardships and cruelties might disappear if all people became sincere and consistent Christians.
Public and private conflicts would cease, and happiness would increase in countless ways.
People would seek to relieve others' distress instead of increasing it.
We should pray for those promised days and do everything our public or private responsibilities allow to prepare the way for them.

div.title: Satan is released and the last conflict comes (verses 7–10)
div.p: While the present world remains, Satan's power will not be altogether destroyed, even when his activity has been restrained.
As soon as he is released, he returns to deceiving the nations and stirring them to war against God's saints and servants.
Would that Christ's ministers and people were as energetic and persistent in doing good as the enemies of his kingdom are in doing evil.
But God himself will fight the final and decisive battle for his people.
The victory will be complete, and all its glory will belong to him.

div.title: The final resurrection and judgment (verses 11–15)
div.p: After the events just foretold, the end approaches swiftly.
The vision mentions nothing else before Christ appears to judge the world.
On that great day, the Lord Jesus Christ will be seen in the majesty and terror of the Judge.
All the dead must stand before him: small and great, young and old, low and high, poor and rich.
No one is too insignificant to have gifts and duties to account for.
No one is important enough to escape the accounting.
The judgment includes not only those alive at Christ's return but everyone who has died.
A book of remembrance records good and evil.
The hidden book of each sinner's conscience will also be opened.
Actions long forgotten will be recalled.
Another book is Scripture, the rule by which human lives are judged.
The opening of the book of life also shows the Lord's knowledge of his people and his recognition of their repentance, faith and good works, revealing the blessings of the new covenant.
People will be judged according to their works, because their conduct reveals the principles that governed them.
Those whom the gospel has justified and acquitted will be recognized as justified and acquitted by the Judge.
They enter everlasting life without any further fear of death, hell or wicked enemies.
All these enemies are destroyed.
The second death is the final separation of sinners from God.
Our urgent concern should be to examine whether Scripture now confirms or condemns the way we live.
Christ will one day judge humanity's secrets according to the gospel.
Who could endure that judgment without his mercy?

row.cell: A new heaven, and new earth: the new Jerusalem where God dwells, and banishes all sorrow from his people.
Its heavenly origin, glory, and secure defence.
Its perfect happiness, as enlightened with the presence of God and the Lamb, and in the free access of multitudes, made holy.

div.title: The new heaven, new earth and new Jerusalem (verses 1–8)
div.p: The new heaven and the new earth will not be separated from one another.
The glorified bodies of the saints will belong to a heavenly condition.
The former world, with all its unrest and conflict, will have passed away.

The declaration that there will be no sea fittingly represents freedom from conflicting passions, temptation, distress, uncertainty and fear—everything that divides believers or interrupts their fellowship.
The new Jerusalem is God's church in its renewed and perfected condition, the church triumphant.
Her blessedness comes entirely from God and rests completely upon him.
God's presence with his people will no longer be interrupted as it is here.
He will dwell among them continually.
Every effect of former suffering will disappear.
His children have often wept because of their sin, their troubles and the distress of the church.
But in that state there will be neither the signs nor the memory of former sorrows.
Christ makes everything new.
When we genuinely desire the Redeemer to renew our hearts and nature, we can trust him to bring our circumstances also into the fullness of happiness he promises.
The certainty of this future rests on the character of God himself.
He calls himself Alpha and Omega, the Beginning and the End, pledging that he will fulfill what he has said.
Worldly and sinful pleasures resemble poisoned, muddy water.
Even the best earthly comforts are like a small quantity of water stored in a cistern.
When we make idols of them, they become broken cisterns and yield only disappointment.
But Christ's gifts are like water flowing from an abundant spring: pure, refreshing, inexhaustible and everlasting.
The sanctifying comforts of the Holy Spirit prepare God's people for heavenly joy, like streams providing water in the wilderness.
Those described as cowardly shrink from the hardships of true religion because they do not believe.
They may refuse the cross of Christ while still rushing into severe wickedness.
The terrors of the first death are followed by something incomparably worse for the unrepentant: everlasting death.

div.title: The heavenly city's glory and security (verses 9–21)
div.p: God gives his holy angels many different tasks.
Sometimes they sound trumpets announcing divine judgments and warnings to an unthinking world.
At other times they reveal heavenly realities to those who will inherit salvation.
Those seeking a clear view of heaven should ascend, as it were, the mountain of meditation and faith.
The vision portrays the perfected, triumphant church in all her glory.
Her glory rests on her relationship with Christ.
Heaven's happiness consists in fellowship with God and becoming like him.
The image changes from bride to city, reminding us to draw the broad spiritual meaning rather than try to interpret every architectural detail literally.
The city's wall signifies complete security.
No evil or enemy can harm anyone who dwells there.
Its enormous size assures us that there is room for all God's people.
The foundation of its safety is God's promise and power, and what Christ has purchased.
The twelve kinds of precious stone may represent the varied beauties of gospel doctrine, the Spirit's graces, or the perfections of Christ himself.
Henry offers these as possible meanings, not as an identification of each individual stone.
The city has gates because everyone whom God has made holy is freely admitted.
Its gates are pearls, pointing toward Christ, the Pearl of great price, who is our way to the Father.
Its street is pure gold, clear as glass.
What people prize most highly on earth is beneath the feet of the saints in heaven.
The redeemed enjoy rest, but not sleep, inactivity or idleness.
They have joyful fellowship both with God and with one another.
Even these magnificent images are only faint representations of the happiness to come.

div.title: The Lord God and the Lamb illuminate the city (verses 22–27)
div.p: Direct and perfect fellowship with God will more than replace the religious ordinances believers now need on earth.
The absence of a separate temple reveals the unity and equal deity of the Son with the Father.
Without the sun's light, this world would be dreadful.
But in heaven God's glory gives light, and the Lamb is its lamp.
Through Christ, God becomes an everlasting source of understanding and joy to the redeemed.
There is no night and no need to close the city's gates.
All is peaceful, secure and full of divine light.
No sinful, unclean, idolatrous, false or deceitful thing can enter.
Everyone there has been made perfectly holy.
For now, even the saints struggle with remaining corruption, which interrupts worship and communion with God.
But on entering heaven's true sanctuary, they are washed through Christ's blood and presented to the Father without stain.
No hypocrite or person devoted to falsehood can enter.
Because nothing impure enters God's heavenly city, these glimpses of its glory should move us to work diligently toward holiness in the fear of God.

row.cell: A description of the heavenly state, under the figures of the water and the tree of life, and of the throne of God and the Lamb.
The truth and certain fulfilling of all the prophetic visions, The Holy Spirit, and the bride, the church, invite, and say, Come.

div.title: The water and tree of life (verses 1–5)
div.p: The streams of comfort we find on earth are often muddy and mixed with trouble.
But the water in this vision is clear and refreshing.
It gives life and preserves the lives of all who drink, flowing forever.
The river pictures the life-giving and sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit, given to sinners through Jesus Christ.
The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, applying salvation to our souls through his renewing love and power.
The trees of life draw nourishment from the pure river flowing from the throne of God.
God's presence is the health and happiness of the saints in heaven.
The tree represents Christ and all the blessings of his salvation.
The leaves that heal the nations show that God's favor and presence supply every good thing needed in that blessed world.
The devil has no power there.
He cannot draw the saints away from serving God, nor disturb them while they worship.
God and the Lamb are spoken of as one.
Service in heaven brings not only freedom but honor and a share in the kingdom.
There is no night, pain or discouragement.
Worship and enjoyment of God will never be interrupted.
No humanly invented distractions, amusements or pleasures will be needed.
How different this is from merely earthly ideas of heaven—even those that imagine only refined intellectual pleasures!

div.title: The sure prophecy and the invitation to come (verses 6–19)
div.p: Jesus Christ, speaking through his angel, solemnly confirms the truth of the book and especially the final vision.
He is the faithful and true Lord God.
Holy angels delivered God's message to his holy servants.
The visions concern things that must come to pass, and Christ will come quickly and make their truth evident.
John also received a confirmation from the integrity of the angel who had explained the vision.
When John offered him religious worship, the angel refused and reproved him.
Henry takes this as another testimony against worship directed toward saints and angels, which belongs to God alone.
The Lord calls all people to heed these declarations.
The book is left open, and its words will have an effect.
People devoted to wickedness may grow more hardened, while sincere believers will be strengthened and further sanctified.
Never suppose that lifeless or disobedient faith will save.
The First and the Last pronounces blessing on people who keep his commandments.
The book excludes from heaven the wicked, unjust and especially those who love and practice falsehood.
It cannot itself be dismissed as false without contradicting the solemn testimony it gives.
There is no secure middle state between fidelity to Christ and continuing rebellion against him.
Jesus, the One who gives prophecy, has provided the churches with this light before dawn, assuring them that the brightness of the full day is coming.
The prophecy closes with an open invitation to all humanity to receive freely the gospel's promises and blessings.
The Holy Spirit, speaking through Scripture and working within the conscience of sinners, says, “Come to Christ for salvation.”
The bride, the whole church on earth and in heaven, likewise says, “Come and share our joy.”
No one should hesitate.
Whoever is willing may come and receive the water of life without payment.
May everyone hearing or reading this invitation receive it at once.
The solemn warning at the end condemns anyone who would corrupt God's word by adding to it or taking anything away.

div.title: The final promise and blessing (verses 20 and 21)
div.p: After making these things known to his people on earth, Christ seems, in Henry's description, to take his leave and return to heaven.
But he assures them that his return is near.
While we carry out our different duties, regardless of the labor, difficulties or grief we face, we can hear our Lord's promise with joy:

p.hi: “I am coming quickly.”

div.p: He will bring an end to the toil and suffering of his faithful servants.
He comes with a reward of grace, generously recompensing every work of faith and every labor of love.
He comes to receive his persevering people into his presence, where they will live with him forever.

p.hi: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

div.p: The book ends with a blessing.
Only by Christ's grace can we continue expecting his glory with joy, be prepared for it and be preserved until we receive it.
His appearing will bring joy to those who already share his grace and favor.
May everyone add a sincere Amen.
Let us thirst more earnestly for Jesus' gracious influence in our souls and his presence with us until his grace reaches perfection in glory.
Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as in the beginning, now and forever.
Amen.
